en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the First Fifty Discourses of the Middle Collection (Majjhimanikāya)
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition To him whose heart is cooled by compassion,
and whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom;
I pay homage to the Sugata, the teacher of the world of humans and devas, who is liberated from all destinies.
I pay homage to that unsurpassed Dhamma, free from defilements, which the Buddha— having both developed and realized the state of Buddhahood— has attained.
I bow my head in homage to the Noble Saṅgha, the assembly of the eight, who are the heart-born sons of the Sugata and the destroyers of Māra’s army.
Thus, with a mind full of serene confidence, may the merit arising from this homage to the Triple Gem [be mine].
By the power of which [work], having become one whose obstacles are well-dispelled,
[I have compiled] this excellent Majjhima Āgama, marked by its middle length,
praised by those awakened after the Buddha, and a crusher of opposing doctrines.
For the purpose of explaining the meaning, the Aṭṭhakathā was first compiled by five hundred masters, and subsequently recited again in the communal chanting.
It was then brought to the island of Siṃhala by the Great Mahinda, the master.
It was established in the Sinhalese language for the benefit of the island-dwellers.
Having now removed that delightful Sinhalese language,
I shall transpose it into a faultless tongue appropriate to the method of the Canon.
Not transgressing the agreement with the elders who are lamps of the lineage of elders,
who possess most skillful discernment, and who dwell in the Mahāvihāra—
I shall clarify the meaning, setting aside the matter that has been repeatedly discussed before.
For the sake of the satisfaction of good people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma,
there is the discourse on virtue, the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), all the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna),
and the detailed exposition of the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and attainments (samāpatti), together with the methods of conduct.
All the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the compendium of wisdom (*paññā-saṅkalanā-nicchaya*), the aggregates (*khandha*),
elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), faculties (*indriya*), and the four noble truths (*ariyasacca*);
the teaching on the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) with its perfectly pure and subtle methods;
The path of the unliberated sequence consists of the cultivation of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā).
Since all of this has been thoroughly and perfectly explained by me in the *Visuddhimagga*, I shall not analyze it further here.
“The Path of Purification stands in the midst of these four Āgamas and will clarify the meaning as it was spoken therein. Since this has been done,
one should therefore take that [work] along with this one.
"Understand the meaning of the Majjhima Saṅgīti from the commentary.
Regarding this, the Majjhima Saṅgīti consists of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa, and the Uparipaṇṇāsa.
It comprises seventy-five sections (*paṇṇāsaka*). By way of chapters (*vagga*), having formed five chapters for each fifty [verses], it consists of a combination of fifteen chapters.

By way of discourses (*sutta*), there are one hundred and fifty discourses plus two additional discourses. By way of words (*pada*), there are eighty thousand and five hundred and twenty-three words. Thus said the ancients:
“Eighty thousand words, And additionally five hundred.”
"Furthermore, twenty-three [sections] are stated; thus the text is established.

In terms of syllables, there are seven hundred and forty-five thousand syllables. In terms of recitation units (*bhāṇavāra*), there are eighty recitation units and one half-recitation unit plus twenty-three additional sections.
In terms of thematic connections (*anusandhi*), it is categorized by way of the connection of questions, the connection of intention, and the connection of the subject matter as it occurs.
In brief, the connection is threefold; in detail, however, there are three thousand nine hundred connections here.
Thus the ancients have said: "Three thousand connections, and likewise nine hundred;"
"By way of connection, these have been explained for the one of middle capacity.
In this regard, among the *paññāsas* (fifties), the *Mūlapaññāsa* is the beginning; among the *vaggas* (sections), the *Mūlapariyāyavagga*; and among the *suttas*, the *Mūlapariyāyasutta*.
Even for that, the introduction beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam me sutaṃ*) is the beginning, spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council (*mahāsaṅgītikāla*).
Furthermore, this [account] was explained in detail at the beginning of the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method already explained there.
1. The Chapter on the Root Exposition (*Mūlapariyāyavagga*).
1. Commentary on the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta* Now, as for this introduction beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*), therein: *evaṃ* is an indeclinable particle (*nipātapada*).
*Me* and so forth are nouns (*nāmapada*). In the phrase "dwells at Ukkaṭṭhā," *vi-* is a prefix (*upasaggapada*) and *harati* is a verb (*ākhyātapada*).
By this method, first, the analysis of the words (*padavibhāga*) should be understood.
As for its meaning (*attha*), the word *evaṃ* has many distinct senses, such as comparison, instruction, praise, censure, acceptance, manner, indication, and determination.
For instance, it occurs in the sense of comparison in such passages as: "Much wholesome [deed] should be done by a mortal who is born thus."
In such cases as “Thus you should advance; thus you should retreat,” it is used in instruction (*upadesa*). In such cases as “So it is, Blessed One;
so it is, Sugata,” it is used in encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*).
In such cases as “Indeed, this outcaste woman praises that shaven-headed ascetic, whoever he may be,” it is used in censure (*garahaṇa*). “‘So it is, venerable sir,’ [he replied].”
In such passages as "Those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One," it refers to the acceptance of speech.

In such passages as "Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way," it refers to a manner of expression. In such passages as "Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Ānanda is;
having approached him, speak these words of mine to the ascetic Ānanda: ‘[May he be] free from illness and free from affliction... [it refers to a command].

Inquire after his lightness, strength, and well-being, saying: "The young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, asks whether the venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from affliction, and enjoying lightness, strength, and well-being. And say this as well:
"It would be well indeed if the venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya."
In such passages as "out of compassion," it is used in the sense of an illustration. "What do you think, Kālāmas: are these states wholesome or unwholesome?
"Unwholesome, venerable sir. "Are they blameworthy or blameless? "Blameworthy, venerable sir. "Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?
"Censured by the wise, venerable sir. "When fully undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering..."
“Do they lead [to welfare] or not? What is your view in this matter? “Venerable sir, when they are fully undertaken and adopted, they lead to harm and suffering;
such is our view in this matter. In such passages, it is used in the sense of emphasis. Here, however, it should be understood in the senses of mode, indication, and emphasis.
Therein, by means of the word *evaṃ* (thus) in the sense of mode, he illuminates this meaning: [the teaching] which is skillful in various methods and originates from many underlying tendencies.

Who is capable of understanding in every way the word of that Blessed One—which is perfect in both meaning and phrasing, possesses manifold miracles, is profound in its penetration of the teaching of the Dhamma and its meaning, and reaches the range of hearing for all beings according to each one’s own language—even by exerting every effort to generate a desire to hear, [one must say]: "Thus have I heard; by me also..."
"In one way, it is 'heard' (sutaṃ).

By way of indication, while liberating himself [from the charge] that "I am not self-become, nor was this realized by me," he indicates the entire discourse that is now to be spoken with the words, "Thus have I heard; it was heard thus by me. By way of emphasis, [it is said]:
"Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are bhikkhus of great learning, this is the foremost..."
“Ānanda is the foremost among those who possess wisdom, mindfulness, steadfastness, and attendants—namely, Ānanda.

Thus was he praised by the Blessed One; and likewise by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta): “The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in etymological interpretation, and skilled in what precedes and follows.
In accordance with such praise for his state of excellence, [the text describes] his own power of retention.
By revealing [the teaching], he generates in beings a desire to hear it, thinking: "Thus have I heard; and that is neither deficient nor redundant in meaning or in phrasing;
it is to be understood exactly thus and not otherwise.
The word *me* (by me) is seen in three senses. For instance, in such passages as "What is sung to the accompaniment of verses is not fit to be eaten by me," and so forth.
The meaning is "by me. In such passages as, "It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief," the meaning is "to me.
In such passages as, "Be my heirs to the Dhamma, monks," the meaning is "my.
But here, both of the two possible meanings—"heard by me" and "heard from me"—are appropriate.

The word *suta*—this term *suta*, both with and without prefixes—is divided into many meanings, such as going, renowned, moistened, accumulated, application, cognizable by the ear, and that which is known by following the door of the ear.

For instance, in phrases such as "gone forth with the army" (*senāya pasuto*), the meaning is "going. In phrases such as "of one who has heard the Dhamma and sees it" (*sutadhammassa passato*), the meaning is "of one whose Dhamma is renowned.
In phrases such as "the lustful toward the lustful" (*avassutā avassutassa*), the meaning is "moistened toward the moistened."

In such passages as “By you, merit has been accumulated, not small,” the meaning is *upacita* (accumulated). In such passages as “The wise who are intent on *jhāna*,” the meaning is *jhānānuyutta* (devoted to *jhāna*).

In such passages as “Seen, heard, and sensed,” the meaning is *sotaviññeyya* (to be cognized by the ear). In such passages as “One who retains what is heard, one who stores what is heard,” the meaning is *sotadvārānusāraviññātadhara* (one who retains what is cognized through the pursuit of the ear-door). But here, it is [to be understood] by way of the ear-door.
The meaning is either "that which has been apprehended" (*upadhārita*) or "the act of apprehending" (*upadhāraṇa*). For when the word *me* has the sense of *mayā* (by me), it is appropriate to say:
"Thus have I heard—that which was apprehended by me following the path of the ear-door. When it has the sense of *mama* (my), it is appropriate to say:
"Thus have I heard—that which is my apprehension following the path of the ear-door."

Thus, among these three terms: *evaṃ* (thus) is an indication of the function of consciousness, such as ear-consciousness and so forth; *me* (by me) is an indication of the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness;
*sutaṃ* (heard) is an indication of the apprehension that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous, by way of negating the state of not hearing.
Likewise, *evaṃ* indicates the state of occurrence of that stream of consciousness proceeding through the ear-door upon a manifold variety of objects.
“Me” is a declaration of oneself; “sutaṃ” (heard) is a declaration of the Dhamma. This is the summary here:
“In the course of consciousness proceeding toward various kinds of objects, nothing else was done by me; rather, this was done, and this Dhamma was heard.

Likewise, “evaṃ” (thus) is a declaration of that which is to be demonstrated; “me” is a declaration of the person; “sutaṃ” is a declaration of the person’s function. This is what is meant: “The discourse that I shall demonstrate, that has been heard by me in this way.”

"Thus" (*tathā*) means "in this way" (*evam*). For that continuum of consciousness in which there is the grasping of various meanings and verbal expressions through the occurrence of various modes, there is the description of those various modes.
For "thus" (*evam*) is a designation of mode; "I" (*me*) is a designation of the agent; and "heard" (*suta*) is a designation of the object.
At this point, by means of the continuum of consciousness occurring in various modes, the final determination of the grasping of the object by the agent possessing that [continuum] is accomplished.

Alternatively, *evaṃ* is a designation for the function of the person; *sutaṃ* is a designation for the function of consciousness; and *me* is a designation for the person associated with both functions.
Herein, this is the summary: by me—a person possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing—the term "heard" is applied by way of the function of consciousness.
In this context, "thus" (*evaṃ*) and "mine" (*me*) are designations of what does not exist according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), which is the true reality (*saccikaṭṭha*).
For what is there here that exists in the ultimate sense to receive such a designation as "thus" or "mine"?
"Hearing" (*suta*) is a designation of what does exist. For that which is apprehended here by the ear exists in the ultimate sense.
"Thus" (*tathā*) and "so" (*evaṃ*), being expressible by depending on this or that [object], are designations by way of dependence (*upādāpaññatti*).

"Hearing" (*suta*), being expressible in relation to what has been seen and so forth, is a designation by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*). And here, by the word "thus," he illuminates non-delusion;
for one who is deluded is not capable of various kinds of penetration. By the word "hearing," he [illuminates] the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard.
It illuminates. For one whose learning has been forgotten does not, after some time, claim, "I heard this.
Thus, through non-delusion, wisdom (*paññā*) is established; through non-forgetfulness, however, mindfulness (*sati*) is established.
In that regard, there is the capacity to grasp the phrasing through mindfulness preceded by wisdom, and the capacity to penetrate the meaning through wisdom preceded by mindfulness.

Through the application of proficiency in both of these, one achieves the status of a Dharma-treasurer, owing to the capacity to preserve the treasury of the Dhamma, which is perfected in both meaning and phrasing.
According to another method: by the word "thus" (evam), he illuminates wise attention (yoniso manasikāra); for in one who attends unwisely, there is an absence of penetration in its various modes.
By the word "heard" (*suta*), he indicates non-distraction, because one whose mind is distracted lacks the capacity for hearing.
For indeed, even when told of every kind of excellence, a person with a distracted mind says, "I have not heard it; say it again.
And herein, through wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), he establishes right self-application and prior merit-making, since for one who has not rightly applied himself, [these are impossible].

Or because of the absence of that [wholesome state] in one who has not previously performed merit. Furthermore, through non-distraction, one accomplishes the hearing of the true Dhamma and reliance upon a true person (sappurisa).
For one whose mind is distracted is unable to hear, and there is no hearing for one who does not attend upon a true person.
Another method: "In this way" (*evam*) refers to the grasping of various meanings and phrasing due to the occurrence of diverse modes within the continuum of consciousness.

It exists; thus it is said that there is a description of its various characteristics. And such a noble state does not belong to one who has not previously performed merit for the sake of a rightly wishless self;

therefore, by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), he illustrates his own perfection of the latter two wheels through this noble state, and by the word "heard" (*suta*), he illustrates the perfection of the former two wheels through the application of hearing. For indeed, in an unsuitable place...
Nor is there any hearing for one who dwells devoid of reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*).

Thus, through the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, his purity of intention (*āsaya-suddhi*) is established; through the accomplishment of the former two wheels, his purity of application (*payoga-suddhi*) is established. By that purity of intention, the excellence of realization (*adhigama-vyatti*) is established;

by purity of application, the excellence of scripture (*āgama-vyatti*) is established. Thus, for one whose application and intention are pure, and who is endowed with both scripture and realization...

Just as the dawn is the precursor to the rising of the sun, and just as wise attention is the precursor to wholesome karma, so too the introductory setting (*nidāna*) deserves to be the precursor to the Blessed One’s words; thus, establishing the setting, he said, "Thus have I heard," and so forth.

According to another method: by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which indicates various modes of penetration, [the author] demonstrates the existence of his own perfection in the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).

He illuminates. By the word "heard" (*suta*), he demonstrates the possession of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language (*dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidā*) through the illumination of the penetration of the various things to be heard.
And by speaking this statement "thus" (*evaṃ*), which illuminates appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), he demonstrates:
"These states have been examined by me with the mind and well-penetrated by view. By speaking this statement "heard," which illuminates application to hearing, [he demonstrates...]
—“Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and mastered by speech,” he declares.
By both of these [statements], while demonstrating the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing, he generates respect for listening.

For one who does not listen with respect to a teaching that is perfect in both meaning and phrasing is excluded from great benefit; therefore, having generated respect, the Dhamma should be heard with careful attention.

By this entire phrase, “Thus have I heard,” the Venerable Ānanda, by not laying claim to the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the plane of the unworthy person; by professing himself a disciple, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he withdraws the mind from what is not the true Dhamma and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma. “Entirely...”
By declaring, "This was indeed heard by me, and it is the word of that very Blessed One," he liberates himself;
he refers back to the Teacher, he anchors the word of the Victor, and he establishes the guide to the Dhamma.
Furthermore, by saying "Thus have I heard," he does not claim the state of having produced [the teaching] himself, but rather explains the prior statement.
“This was received by me in the presence of that Blessed One— the one confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, the possessor of the ten powers, the one who stands in the place of the bull,
the roarer of the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma,
the Wheel-turner of the excellent True Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“No doubt or hesitation should be made here regarding the meaning, the doctrine, the phrases, or the syllables.
Thus it destroys lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans and produces the perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
“It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching;”
"Thus have I heard"—thus speaks this disciple of Gotama.

"Ekaṃ" (one) is a designation for a numerical limit. "Samayaṃ" (at one time) is a designation for a delimited occasion. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time) is an indication of an unspecified [occasion]. In that context, the word *samaya* [is used] in the sense of:
A gathering, a moment, a time, An assembly, a cause, or a view.
It is seen in the senses of acquisition, abandoning, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as, "Perhaps we might go tomorrow, taking into account the time and the occasion," the meaning is "assembling.
In such passages as, "Monks, there is indeed only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," [the meaning is "opportunity"].
*Khana*: In such passages as “the time of heat,” “the time of feverish distress,” and so forth, it means *time*. In such passages as “The great assembly in the forest,” it means *a multitude*.
“Furthermore, Bhaddāli, this occasion was not understood by you: ‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī;
the Blessed One will know me, thinking, “The bhikkhu named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’”
In such passages as, "This occasion, Bhaddāli, was also not penetrated by you," it refers to the cause (*hetu*). In such passages as, "Now at that time,
the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta was staying at Mallikā’s Park, in the single-hall Tindukācīra grove,
which was a place for debating doctrines," it refers to a view (*diṭṭhi*).

In such passages as, “The goal that is in this very life, and the goal pertaining to the future life—the wise person who realizes these goals is called ‘wise’,” it refers to acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
In such passages as, “Through the realization of conceit rightly, he made an end of suffering,” it refers to abandoning (*pahāna*). [And in the passage], “Of suffering...”
In such passages as "the meaning of oppression, the meaning of the conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization," it refers to penetration (*paṭivedha*).

Here, however, its meaning is time (*kāla*). By this, he indicates "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*) among those periods that constitute the divisions of time, such as the year, the season, the month, the half-month, night, day, the morning, midday, evening, and the first, middle, and last watches of the night, as well as the moments (*muhutta*) and so forth.

In this regard, although among these periods such as the year and so forth, whatever discourse was spoken in whichever year, season, month, fortnight, portion of the night, or portion of the day—all that was well-known and well-determined by the Elder through his wisdom.
For it is because [he knew]: "Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month... [and so on].
When it is stated thus— “on such-and-such a fortnight, on such-and-such a part of the night,
or on such-and-such a part of the day”— it is not possible to easily memorize, recite, or cause others to recite it, and much would have to be said; therefore,
condensing that meaning into a single phrase, he said, “at one time.”

Furthermore, there are these various occasions of the Blessed One among gods and humans— such as the occasion of his descent into the womb, the occasion of his birth, the occasion of his spiritual urgency,

the occasion of his great renunciation, the occasion of his practice of austerities, the occasion of his victory over Māra, the occasion of his full enlightenment, the occasion of his dwelling in happiness in this very life, the occasion of his teaching, and the occasion of his final Nibbāna—
which are exceedingly well-known and distinguished by many different times.

Among those times, it indicates one specific time known as the "time of teaching" (*desanā-samaya*). Furthermore, among the times for the functions of wisdom and compassion, it is the time for the function of compassion;

among the times for practice for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others, it is the time for practice for the welfare of others; among the times for the two duties of those who have assembled, it is the time for discourse on the Dhamma;
and among the times for the practice of teaching, it is the time of teaching (*desanā-samaya*). Among these as well—
Referring to one among the various occasions, he said, "on one occasion. But why, in this instance,
is there not an indication using the locative case— as in the Abhidhamma passage, "at whatever time [a state] of the sense-sphere," or in other Sutta passages such as,
"Bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures"?

In the Vinaya, the phrase "At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One" is expressed using the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*), whereas here, instead of doing so, the locative case (*upayogavacana*) is employed in the expression "At one time.

This is because the meaning is possible both there [in the Abhidhamma] and here [in this text], yet in different ways. For in that case—the Abhidhamma—and in other Sutta passages, the sense is that of a locus (*adhikaraṇattha*), or the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇattha*).
And it is possible [to explain it thus]: for "occasion" (*samaya*) has both the sense of time and the sense of a collection.
By means of the state of that "occasion"—which consists of the momentary convergence of causes—for those phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) mentioned therein, their existence is characterized;
therefore, the locative case is employed there in order to indicate that meaning.

In the Vinaya, both the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible. For that occasion of the promulgation of the training rules was difficult to discern even for Sāriputta and others;

thus, by means of that occasion acting as the cause and the instrument while he was promulgating the training rules, and having regard for the reason for the promulgation of those training rules, the Blessed One dwelt here and there. Therefore, it is for the purpose of illustrating that meaning [that this is stated].
In that case, the designation was made using the instrumental case.
However, here and in other similar instances, the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) is possible.
For at whatever time the Blessed One taught this or another sutta, he dwelt at that very time continuously in the abiding of compassion; therefore—
Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating that meaning, the designation of the accusative case is employed here.
Thus it is said:
“Having regard to this or that meaning, by means of the locative and the instrumental;”
“Except for the specific occasion mentioned, it is used here in the sense of an instrument.
However, the ancients comment: “Whether it be ‘at that time,’ ‘by that time,’ or ‘on one occasion,’ this is merely a difference in expression;
in all cases, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, even when “on one occasion” is stated, [it carries that same sense].
The meaning should be understood as “at one time.

*Bhagavā* means venerable (*garu*). For in the world, they call what is venerable “the Blessed One” (*bhagavā*). And since he is venerable to all beings by virtue of being distinguished by every excellence, he is to be known as “the Blessed One. It has also been said by the ancients:
“The word ‘Bhagavā’ is the best; the word ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme.”
“Because he is endowed with such reverence, the Blessed One is called by that name.
Furthermore:
“He is fortunate, he has overcome [defilements], he is disciplined, and he is distinguished by his excellences.”
“Bhattava, the Blessed One has gone beyond becoming;

therefore he is the Blessed One.”—The detailed meaning of this term should be understood according to this verse, which is already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati-niddesa*).
Up to this point, by the expression “Thus have I heard,” the Dhamma as it was heard is shown, thereby demonstrating the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One.
He makes it manifest. By this—saying, "This dispensation has not yet passed away from its Teacher;
this is your Teacher"—he consoles the people who were distressed by the absence of the Teacher.
By the words "At one time the Blessed One," he shows that at that particular time the Blessed One was not present.

He accomplishes the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the form-body (rūpakāya). By means of this, he inspires a sense of urgency in people who are intoxicated by the pride of life, making them think: "Even the Blessed One—the teacher of such noble Dhamma, the possessor of the ten powers, whose body was as firm as a vajra-strike—has passed away; what hope for life can be conceived by anyone else?
And he generates enthusiasm for the True Dhamma (saddhamma).

By saying "Thus," he indicates the perfection of the teaching (*desanā-sampatti*). By "heard by me" (*me sutaṃ*), he indicates the perfection of the disciple (*sāvaka-sampatti*). By "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*), he indicates the perfection of the time (*kāla-sampatti*).
By "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), he indicates the perfection of the teacher (*desaka-sampatti*). Regarding the phrase "dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā": here *ukka* means a torch;

and because that city was built while torches were kept burning even at night with the thought, "May the auspicious day, the lucky moment, and the favorable constellation not pass us by," it is called Ukkaṭṭhā.
"Daṇḍadīpikāsu" means having been caught in a net and being held; it is said that [the Buddha] was staying there.

This locative case is used in the sense of proximity. "Viharati" (he dwells) is a general indication of one who possesses any particular dwelling among the postures, the divine dwellings, the brahma-dwellings, or the noble dwellings.
Here, however, [it refers to] among the distinctions of standing, walking, sitting, and lying down.

This is an illustration of the Blessed One’s association with one of the postures among the various postures. By this it should be understood that the Blessed One dwells whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
For the Blessed One, having interrupted the discomfort of one posture with another, carries on and maintains his physical existence without falling; therefore, he is said to "dwell" (*viharati*).
Regarding the phrase "Subhagavana": here, it is called *subhaga* because of its auspiciousness (*subhagattā*), meaning it possesses beautiful glory and beautiful objects of desire.
For people, taking food, drink, and other provisions, spend their days right there in that forest celebrating festivals, social gatherings, and festivities, enjoying the pleasure of wealth;
moreover, they long for ever more beautiful and desirable objects of desire within it.

“We shall obtain a son; we shall obtain a daughter”—for them, it becomes exactly so. Thus, it is *subhaga* because of its beautiful glory (*sundarasirika*) and because of its beautiful desire (*sundarakāma*).
Furthermore, it is *subhaga* because it is beloved by many people. It "wins over" (*vanati*), thus it is *vana*;
the meaning is that through its own excellence, it causes beings to feel devotion and arouses affection for itself. It "seeks" (*vanute*), thus...

Or, the meaning is that the forest, as it were, requests all living beings, saying, "Come and enjoy me," through the various scents of blossoming flowers, the warbling of intoxicated cuckoos and other birds, and the swaying branches, twigs, shoots, and foliage moved by gentle breezes. That which is both beautiful (*subhaga*) and a forest (*vana*) is a "beautiful forest" (*subhagavana*);
[the Blessed One dwelt] in that beautiful forest. Now, a forest is of two kinds: planted and self-grown. Among these—
The Veḷuvana, Jetavana, and so forth were planted; the Andhavana, Mahāvana, Añjanavana, and so forth grew of their own accord. This too should be understood as having grown of its own accord.
Regarding the phrase "at the foot of the king of sāla trees," here the *sāla* tree itself is called "the *sāla*. As it is said: "Just as, monks..."

A great *sāla* grove not far from a village or town, which was covered with its *eḷanda* fruits, and also the "between-the-twin-*sāla*-trees," refers to the eldest tree among the forest lords. As it is said:
"O King, in your own realm, in your own park-land..."
“Straight-trunked great sāl trees, blue-hued and delightful.
This refers to any tree whatsoever; as it is said: “Then, monks, that māluva seed might fall at the foot of a certain sāl tree.
But here, the tree intended is the preeminent lord of the forest. Furthermore, the word *rāja* (king) applies to that very [tree].
It establishes the state of being the eldest. As it is said: “O Brahmin, of the well-established, righteous King Nigrodha-tree.
In this context, the compound is twofold: either “the king of the *sāla* trees,” thus *sālarājā*; or “he is a *sāla* tree and, by virtue of being the eldest, he is also a king,” thus *sālarājā*.
“Root” (*mūla*) means proximity. For this word “root” (*mūla*) [is used] in such passages as: “He should pull up the roots, even down to the size of a reed-stalk. etc.
It is seen in the sense of "at the very root" in such passages as "Greed is an unwholesome root. It is used in the sense of an "unshared cause" in such passages as [the definition of roots].
It is used in the sense of "nearby" in such passages as "As long as the shadow extends until midday, and the leaves fall in the windless air, to that extent is the vicinity of the tree's root.
Here, however, it is intended in the sense of "nearby"; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "in the vicinity of the king of sāla trees."
In this regard, it might be argued: "If the Blessed One was staying at Ukkaṭṭhā, then it should not be said that he was 'at the foot of the royal sāla tree in the Subhaga Grove';

and if he was staying there, then it should not be said that he was 'at Ukkaṭṭhā,' for it is impossible to stay in both places at one and the same time. However, this should not be viewed in such a way.
But did we not say: "This locative case is used in the sense of proximity"?

Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges or the Yamunā are said to be "grazing on the Ganges" or "grazing on the Yamunā," so too here, since the Subhaga Grove at the foot of the king of sāl trees is in the vicinity of Ukkaṭṭhā, one dwelling there is said to be "in Ukkaṭṭhā."
“He dwells in Subhaga Grove at the foot of the king of *sāla* trees. The mention of Ukkaṭṭhā is for the purpose of indicating the village where he goes for alms;
the remaining words are for the purpose of indicating a dwelling place suitable for one who has gone forth.
Therein, by praising Ukkaṭṭhā, the Venerable Ānanda shows that the Blessed One provides assistance to householders.

By the praise of the Blessed One’s good fortune and so forth, there is the act of showing favor to those who have gone forth. Likewise, by the former [verse], through the acceptance of the four requisites, there is the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification;
by the latter, through the abandoning of sensual objects, there is the demonstration of the means for avoiding devotion to sensual pleasure.
Furthermore, by the former, there is the application to the teaching of the Dhamma; by the latter, the inclination toward seclusion. And by the former, there is the approach through compassion.
By the former [verse], there is the non-departure from wisdom; by the latter, the state of being unstained while performing the welfare and happiness of others.

By the former, there is a comfortable dwelling characterized by not abandoning righteous happiness; by the latter, that which is characterized by application to the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). By the former, there is the abundance of assistance rendered to human beings.
The former [verse] refers to one born in the world and raised in the world; the latter refers to being unsullied by the world. By the former, it is said:

"Bhikkhus, there is one person who, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Who is that one person? [The answer follows: "It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. By the latter, it is shown that although he has arisen in the world and grown up in the world, he remains untainted by the world.
From the statement, “The Tathāgata is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” [the first phrase] indicates the fulfillment of the purpose for which the Blessed One appeared;

by the latter [phrase], it indicates his dwelling in a place appropriate to where he appeared. For the Blessed One appeared in a grove alone—first in the Lumbinī grove and second at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)—due to his appearance both mundane and supramundane; therefore, his dwelling was likewise in a grove.
The application of the meaning here should be understood according to this method, beginning with "he shows.
In that context, "there" (*tatra*) indicates place and time; for it indicates "at that time" when he dwells, and "at the foot of that king of *sāla* trees" where he dwells.
Alternatively, it indicates the place and time appropriate for what is to be spoken, for [the teaching] does not [occur] otherwise.
The Blessed One speaks the Dhamma at an inappropriate place or time. Here, the phrase beginning with “It is not the right time, Bāhiya” serves as the proof.

The particle *kho* is a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*), a particle used for emphasis, or one signifying the initial point of time. The term *Bhagavā* is an indication of his status as the World-Honored One.

The word *bhikkhu* refers to a person suitable for listening to the discourse. Furthermore, in this context, “one who begs is a *bhikkhu*; [he is so called because of] the practice of begging... [and so forth].
The meaning of the words should be understood according to the method beginning with: "‘Ajjhupagato’ means ‘a monk,’ and so forth.
*Āmantesi* means he addressed, spoke to, or called out to; this is the sense here. However, it also occurs in the sense of making known, as it is said:
“I address you, monks; I announce to you, monks. It also occurs in the sense of summoning, as it is said: “Come, you, monk.”
"Address Sāriputta in my name.

The term "bhikkhave" (O monks) is an indication of the manner of address. And it is stated because [the monk] is established through the possession of qualities such as the habit of begging (*bhikkhana-sīlatā*).

For a monk (*bhikkhu*) is so called not only because he possesses the quality of the habit of begging, but also because he possesses the quality of the nature of begging (*bhikkhana-dhammatā*), and because he possesses the quality of performing begging well (*sādhukāritā*).

Those skilled in grammar consider this [the correct form]. And by means of that speech, which is perfected through the possession of qualities such as the habit of begging, he reveals the mode of livelihood practiced by those who are inferior or superior, thereby effecting the suppression of the states of arrogance and dejection.

Furthermore, by the address "Bhikkhus," preceded by a glance from eyes made gentle by the expansion of compassion, he brings them face-to-face with him. And by that very speech, which indicates his desire to speak...
It generates in them a desire to hear. And by that very sense of addressing them, it enjoins them to listen and attend carefully;
for the success of the Dispensation depends upon careful listening and attention.
If it is asked why he addressed only the bhikkhus when other gods and humans were present, it is because they were the eldest, the most excellent, the closest, and always in his presence.
The Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is indeed common to all assemblies. Among these assemblies, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to arise [in the dispensation].
They are the most excellent because, beginning from the state of homelessness, they followed the Teacher’s conduct and received the entire dispensation.

They are the closest because, among those seated there, they are in the immediate presence of the Teacher. They are always in close attendance because they move within the Teacher’s personal vicinity.
Furthermore, they were the vessels for his teaching of the Dhamma because they possessed the practice exactly as instructed.
Moreover, since this teaching was intended specifically for certain monks alone, he addressed them by name.
Herein, it might be asked: "For what purpose did the Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma, first address the monks, rather than [others]?"

"He teaches only the Dhamma" means for the purpose of arousing mindfulness. For monks may be sitting there thinking of something else, with distracted minds, reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to their meditation subject; if the Dhamma were taught without addressing them, they would wonder:
"What is the basis of this teaching? What is its cause? By what occasion was it taught?"
Being unable to discern it correctly, they might either grasp it wrongly or not grasp it at all.
Therefore, for the purpose of arousing mindfulness in them, the Blessed One first addresses them and afterwards teaches the Dhamma.
"Bhadante" is a term of respect, or a response to the Teacher; however, in this context, it is "bhikkhave" (O monks).
Addressing them, the Blessed One spoke to those bhikkhus. Addressing him as "Venerable Sir," they replied to the Blessed One.
Likewise, the Blessed One addressed them as "Bhikkhus. They replied "Venerable Sir.
He caused the response "Bhikkhus" to be given, and they gave the response "Venerable Sir. "Those bhikkhus" refers to those whom the Blessed One addressed. Of the Blessed One...
*Paccassosuṃ*: they responded to the Blessed One’s address; being face-to-face, they heard and accepted it—this is the meaning.
*Bhagavā etadavoca*: the Blessed One spoke this entire discourse that is now to be recited.
And up to this point, [the description] by the Venerable Ānanda of the lotus pond with its water as bright as white and blue lotuses, pure and sweet-tasting...
For the sake of easy ascent, it possessed jeweled staircases beautified by the splendor of arrangements of stainless stone slabs; its white ground was strewn with sand resembling scattered pearls.
Like a bathing place, it was surrounded by well-proportioned walls and variegated railings.
As if desiring to touch the path of the stars, the excellent palace rose up loftily, providing for easy access a staircase made of ivory, smooth and soft planks, and entwined with golden creepers.
Like a flight of stairs possessing a brilliant splendor arising from the radiance of a multitude of jewels;

like a great gate with wide, well-established doorposts illuminated by the spreading luster of gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and the like, for the purpose of entering easily into a great mansion adorned with the glory of vast sovereignty and wealth—a mansion where the sweet voices of the household folk are heard mingled with the sounds of clashing golden bracelets, anklets, and the like, as they move about and speak and laugh;
and like [the Dhamma] which indicates the profound nature of the Buddhas’ knowledge of teaching, endowed with both meaning and phrasing.
For the sake of easy comprehension of this sutta, the introduction (nidāna), adorned with the time, place, teacher, subject matter, assembly, and location, has been spoken;
the commentary on its meaning is now complete.
Commentary on the Arrangement of the Sutta.
Now, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the discourse (sutta) set forth by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with, "I shall teach you the exposition of the root of all phenomena.

Since this commentary on the discourse becomes clear when spoken after investigating the setting-forth of the discourse, we shall first investigate that setting-forth of the discourse. For there are four settings-forth of discourses.
[Discourses are] those based on one’s own inclination, those based on the inclination of others, those dependent on a question,
and those arising from a specific occasion. Among these, those discourses which the Blessed One spoke solely out of his own inclination,
without being requested by others— namely, the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, the *Vattha Sutta*, the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, and the *Mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta*— are those based on one’s own inclination.

The *Ariyavaṃsa-sutta*, the carrier of the discourses on the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), and the carrier of the discourses on the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the path factors (*maggaṅga*)—these and others like them constitute the "deposition according to one's own inclination" (*attajjhāsayo nikkhepo*). However, those such as:
"Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation have indeed matured; what if I were now to [instruct] Rāhula... [are examples of the other types].

"Having overcome [them], one should further destroy the taints"—thus these were spoken according to the inclinations of others, having taken into account their underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*), patience, intention, aspiration, and capacity for awakening.
Such are, for example, the *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta*, the *Mahārāhulovāda Sutta*, the *Dhammacakkappavattana*, and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta*. Of these...
The laying down [of the teaching] is according to the inclinations of others.

However, having approached the Blessed One, the four assemblies, the four castes, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, asuras, yakkhas, the great kings, the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm and so forth, and Mahābrahmā—these and others [heard him say]: "The factors of enlightenment, the factors of enlightenment."

"Venerable sir, they are called 'hindrances, hindrances,' venerable sir. Are these, venerable sir, the five aggregates of clinging?"—in this manner they ask questions, beginning with: "What indeed is the best wealth for a person?

When thus questioned, the Blessed One spoke those discourses such as the *Bojjhaṅga-saṃyutta* (Connected Discourses on the Factors of Enlightenment) and others, as well as other [discourses] from the *Devatā-saṃyutta*, *Māra-saṃyutta*, *Brahma-saṃyutta*, *Sakkapañha*, *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, and *Sāmaññaphala*.
The *Āḷavaka*, *Sūciloma*, *Kharaloma* Suttas, and others—their presentation is dependent upon the questions asked.
However, those which were spoken in reliance on a specific occasion that arose are as follows:
the *Dhammadāyāda*, *Cūḷasīhanāda*, *Candūpama*, *Puttamaṃsūpama*, *Dārukkhandhūpama*, *Aggikkhandhūpama*, *Pheṇapiṇḍūpama*, and *Pāricchattakūpama*.
And so forth. These are the four modes of presentation (*nikkhepa*).
Among these four, this sutta belongs to the mode of presentation arising from a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppattika-nikkhepa*).
For this was presented by the Blessed One on account of a specific occasion. On what specific occasion? On account of pride that had arisen based on the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
It is said that five hundred brahmins, masters of the three Vedas, later heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma.
Perceiving the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, they went forth in the presence of the Blessed One.
Before long, having mastered the entire word of the Buddha, they developed conceit based on their mastery of the scriptures, thinking: "Since..."

“Whatever the Blessed One speaks, we understand it immediately; for the Blessed One does not say anything without releasing the three genders, the four cases, and the seven inflections. And when he speaks thus, there is no knotty point for us.
Having become disrespectful toward the Blessed One, from that time forth they neither attended upon him nor listened to the Dhamma.
They did not go [to the Blessed One] frequently. The Blessed One, knowing their mental disposition, thought:
"These are incapable of realizing the path or the fruit without first breaking this thicket of conceit.

Taking as the occasion for instruction the conceit that had arisen in them based on their mastery of what they had heard, the Blessed One—being skilled in teaching—began the discourse known as the "Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena" (Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya) for the purpose of shattering their conceit.
In this context, "the exposition of the root of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*) means the exposition of the root of all things.
"All" (*sabbe*) refers to those without exception; for this word *sabba* denotes the absence of remainder. Whichever term it connects with, it indicates that [term] in its entirety.
For example: "All form is impermanent, all feeling is impermanent, [all things] included within the aggregates of existence..."

Regarding the phrase "in phenomena" (*dhammesu*): this word *dhamma* is seen to apply to the scriptures, the truths, concentration, wisdom, nature, individual essence, emptiness, merit, attainment, the knowable, and so forth.
For in such passages as, "Here, a bhikkhu masters the *dhamma*: the discourses (*sutta*), the mixed prose and verse (*geyya*)... and so on, the word *dhamma* refers to the scriptures.
In such passages as, "One who has seen the *dhamma*, one who has known the *dhamma*," it refers to the truths. [And in the passage] "Thus are your *dhammas*... [it refers to nature].
In such passages as "the Blessed Ones," it refers to concentration (*samādhi*).
[And as it is said: "O Lord of Monkeys, he in whom these four qualities exist—truth, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity—surpasses even what has been seen."
In such passages as "By means of wisdom," it refers to *paññā* (wisdom).

In such passages as "Subject to birth, subject to aging, and likewise subject to death," it refers to *pakati* (nature). In such passages as "Wholesome phenomena (*kusalā dhammā*)," it refers to *sabhāva* (intrinsic nature).
In such passages as "At that time, indeed, there were phenomena (*dhammā*)," it refers to *suññatā* (emptiness). [And] "The Dhamma well-practiced..."
In such passages as "it brings happiness," it refers to merit (*puñña*). In such passages as "there are two indeterminate states" (*aniyata-dhammā*), it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).
In such passages as "all phenomena (*dhammā*) in all their modes come within the range of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha," it refers to the knowable (*ñeyya*).

But here, it occurs in the sense of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Regarding that, this is the etymological derivation: they are called *dhammā* because they bear their own characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).
The word *mūla* has already been explained in detail. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇahetu*).
The word *pariyāya* occurs in the sense of a teaching, as in such passages as, "Bear this in mind as the 'Madhupiṇḍika discourse'. And:
"There is indeed, O Brahmin, a way (*pariyāya*) by which one speaking correctly of me might call me a proponent of non-action (*akiriyavāda*)."
In such passages as “the ascetic Gotama,” it refers to a cause (*kāraṇa*). In such passages as “Ānanda, whose turn is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?,” it refers to a turn or opportunity (*vāra*).
But here, it applies both to a cause and to a teaching (*desanā*).

Therefore, regarding the phrase “the discourse on the root of all phenomena” (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*), it means either the cause designated as the unique reason for all phenomena, or the teaching concerning the cause of all phenomena.

Or rather, the meaning should be understood in this way: because this sutta is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*), it should not be understood that all phenomena existing in the four planes are "all phenomena.
Rather, only those phenomena included within personality (*sakkāya*) belonging to the three planes should be understood without exception;
this is the intended sense (*adhippāya*) here.

This particle *vo* is seen in the senses of the direct object (*paccatta*), the objective case (*upayoga*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*sampadāna*), the possessor (*sāmivacana*), and as a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*).
Indeed, it is seen in the sense of the direct object in such passages as: “But are you, Anuruddhas, living together in harmony and mutual affection?
It is seen in the sense of the objective case in such passages as: “Go, monks; I dismiss you. It is seen in the sense of the instrument in such passages as: “You must not dwell in my presence.”
In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the discourse on forest-dwelling,” it is used in the dative case.

In such passages as, “Sāriputta, all that has been well-spoken by you,” it is used in the genitive case. In such passages as, “Those noble ones whose bodily actions are purified,” it serves merely to complete the meter.
However, in this instance, it should be understood as being in the dative case.
"Bhikkhus" is an address to those who have turned their attention toward him by way of response.
"I shall teach" is the formal undertaking of the teaching. This is what is meant: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the root cause of all phenomena;
by a second method, I shall teach you the teaching on causes. "Listen to that" means listen to that matter, that cause, that—
"Listen to the teaching being spoken by me; attend to it well. Herein, "sādhukaṃ" and "sādhu" have the same meaning.
Furthermore, this word *sādhu* is seen in the senses of entreaty, acceptance, encouragement, beauty, and strengthening.
For instance, in such passages as, "It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to teach me the Dhamma in brief," it occurs in the sense of entreaty.
It is seen [in the sense of] acceptance, as in: “‘Excellent, venerable sir,’ that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s speech...
and so forth. It is seen [in the sense of] encouragement, as in: “‘Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! and so forth. It is seen [in the sense of] praise, as in:
“‘Excellent is King Dhammaruci; excellent is the wise man.’”
"In 'Sādhu mittānam addubbho, pāpassa akaraṇaṃ sukhan'ti," and so forth, the word *sādhu* means "excellent.

In such instances as "Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, sādhukaṃ suṇāhi" ("Therefore, brahmin, listen well"), the word *sādhuka* itself is used in the sense of "firmly" (*daḷhīkamme*), and it is also said to mean "an injunction" (*āṇatti*).
Here too, this word should be understood in these two senses: as "firmly" and as "an injunction."
It also applies to the term *sundara*. For it is shown thus: "Listen to this firm Dhamma in the sense of being made firm, grasping it well-learned;
listen according to my command in the sense of an injunction; listen to this beautiful, auspicious Dhamma in the sense of being beautiful. Thus it is illustrated.
"Pay attention" (*manasi karotha*) means "be mindful," which is to say, "apply your minds";
the intention is that you should listen with undistracted minds and fix them upon [the teaching]. "Now, listen to this here" is a prohibition against the distraction of the faculty of hearing.
"Pay close attention" is a prohibition against the distraction of the faculty of mind, by way of enjoining the strengthening of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Here, the first [section] is for warding off the grasping of a distorted apprehension of the phrasing (*byañjana*), while the latter is for warding off the grasping of a distorted apprehension of the meaning (*attha*).
By the former, he enjoins one to listen to the Dhamma; by the latter, he enjoins one to retain and investigate the teachings already heard.
Furthermore, by the former, he demonstrates: "This Dhamma possesses the phrasing; therefore, it is to be heard. By the latter, he demonstrates: "It possesses the meaning; therefore..."
"Should be attended to in the mind": this should be understood as follows. Either the word "carefully" (*sādhuka*) is to be construed with both phrases:
because this Dhamma is profound in its nature (*dhamma*) and profound in its teaching (*desanā*), therefore listen carefully;
and because it is profound in its meaning (*attha*) and profound in its penetration (*paṭivedha*), therefore attend to it carefully in the mind. Thus is the construction to be understood.
“I shall speak” means “I shall teach. Regarding the phrase “Listen to that,” it is said:
“I shall not teach the promised teaching only in brief, but rather I shall speak it in detail as well”;
for these words express both brevity and detail. As the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:
“He teaches in brief as well, and he speaks in detail;
like the song of the sālika bird, he utters inspired eloquence.
When this was said, those bhikkhus, having become full of enthusiasm, replied to the Blessed One, the Teacher, saying, “So be it, venerable sir.”
They accepted the words; that is to say, they received them. Then the Blessed One said this to them;
he spoke the entire sutta beginning with "Here, monks," which is what was now to be said. In this context, *idha* is a particle used as a designation of place.
This term is sometimes used with reference to the world, as it is said: "Here, the Tathāgata arises in the world."
In some instances, it refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*). As it is said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic. In some instances, it refers to a location.
As it is said: “While standing right here, having become a deity, I have regained my life-span once more—know this, O venerable ones.”

In some instances, it serves merely to complete the meter. As it is said: "In this case, monks, I would have been one who has eaten and is invited. However, here it should be understood as spoken with reference to the world. "O monks":
he addresses the monks again in order to teach the doctrine exactly as it was promised.

By both [expressions], it is meant: "O monks, in this world. "In the uninstructed worldling (*puthujjana*)"—here, however, because of the absence of both scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), [he is so called].

"One who is unlearned" (*assutavā*) should be understood as follows: For one who lacks both scripture (*āgama*)—because they are devoid of study, inquiry, and discernment regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, truths, the modes of conditionality, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth—and who lacks realization (*adhigama*)—because they have not attained that which is to be attained through practice—he is to be known as "unlearned" due to this absence of both scripture and realization. And he is as follows:
A worldling (*puthujjana*) is so called because of the causes such as the generation of manifold things, or because this person is included among the multitude.
For he is a worldling by virtue of being the generator, etc., of manifold defilements and so forth. As it has been said:
They are called *puthujjana* because they generate various defilements; they are called *puthujjana* because they have not abandoned the various views of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*);
they are called *puthujjana* because they look toward the faces of various teachers; they are called *puthujjana* because they have not emerged from the various realms of existence;
they are called *puthujjana* because they perform various diverse volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*); they are called *puthujjana* because they are swept away by various diverse floods (*ogha*).
They are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various individual fevers; they are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various individual anxieties;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually attached, greedy, infatuated, muddled, obsessed, stuck, clinging, and hindered by the five strands of sensual pleasure;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually shrouded, covered, enveloped, and obstructed by the five hindrances.

"Hidden and covered up" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*). Alternatively, they are called *puthujjana* because they are included among the many (*puthu*)—those who have passed beyond the path of counting, who are turned away from the noble Dhamma, and whose conduct consists of base qualities.

Or, this person is "separate" (*puthu*), having gone into a distinct category, being dissociated from the noble ones who are endowed with virtues such as morality and learning; thus he is a *puthujjana*. Thus, by these [reasons]...
“An uninstructed worldling”: by these two phrases, it is said— Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
one is the blind worldling, and one is the virtuous worldling.

Two types of worldlings (*puthujjana*) have been mentioned; it should be understood that among them, the blind worldling is the one referred to here. Regarding the passage beginning with "one who does not see the Noble Ones" (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*):

"Noble Ones" (*ariya*) refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha. They are called "Noble Ones" because they are far removed from defilements (*ārakattā kilesehi*), because they do not proceed toward what is not the goal (*anaye na-iriyana-to*), because they proceed toward the goal (*aye iriyana-to*), and because they are worthy of being sought by the world together with its devas (*sadevakena ca lokena araṇīya-to*). Or, in this context, it may refer to the Buddhas alone.
The Noble Ones (ariya). As it is said: "In the world with its devas, bhikkhus... the Tathāgata is called 'the Noble One'.
Regarding the term "True Persons" (sappurisa), here the Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata should be understood as "True Persons.

For they are "True Persons" because they are beautiful persons (purisa) due to their possession of supramundane qualities. Or rather, all these [categories] are stated in both ways; for Buddhas too are both Noble Ones and True Persons.
And so too are Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha. As it is said:
“He who is grateful and mindful of benefits, wise, a friend of the good, and firm in devotion;”
“He performs his duties with care for one who is suffering;
such a person they call a true man.
Thus far, indeed, the disciple of the Buddha is described by means of [qualities] such as gratitude and so forth, and it is said that he possesses virtuous friends and firm devotion.

"Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas. Now, one who has the habit of not seeing those noble ones (ariya) and does not perform well in seeing them should be understood as "one who does not see the noble ones" (ariyānaṃ adassāvī).
And he is twofold: one who does not see with the eye and one who does not see with wisdom (ñāṇa);

among these, it is the one who does not see with wisdom who is intended here. For even if the noble ones are seen with the fleshly eye or the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), [they are still not truly seen].
They are indeed "not seen. This is because those eyes grasp only the mere color, and not the domain of the noble state (ariyabhāva).
Even jackals, dogs, and the like see the Noble Ones with their eyes, yet they are not seers of the Noble Ones.
Here is an illustration: it is said that there was an attendant of an elder monk whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava), who had gone forth in old age and resided at Cittala Mountain.
One day, having walked for alms together with the Elder and returning behind him while carrying the Elder’s bowl and robes,
he asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, what are those called 'Noble Ones' (Ariyas) like? The Elder said, "In this case, a certain elderly man,
though he carries the bowl and robes of the Noble Ones and follows their conduct while walking along with them, does not recognize the Noble Ones at all."
“Thus, friends, the noble ones are difficult to understand. Even when this was said, he did not understand it. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing;
only seeing through knowledge is true seeing. As it is said: “Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this putrid body? He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me.
Therefore, even one who sees with the eye [sees only the physical].

One should be understood as "one who has not seen the Noble Ones" because he does not perceive with wisdom the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as seen by the Noble Ones, because he has not attained the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones, and because he has not seen the qualities that constitute a Noble One nor the state of being a Noble One.

"Unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones" means he is unproficient in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones distinguished by the foundations of mindfulness and so forth. Regarding "undisciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones": here—
Discipline (*vinaya*) is twofold, and each of these two is fivefold here.
Because he lacks that [discipline], he is called "undisciplined" (*avinīta*).
For this discipline is twofold: the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*) and the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*). And within these two kinds of discipline, each one...

The Vinaya is fivefold. For the Vinaya of restraint is fivefold: the restraint of virtue, the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, the restraint of patience, and the restraint of energy.

The Vinaya of abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by way of its own constituent part (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*), abandoning by eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*), abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-pahāna*), and abandoning by escape (*nissaraṇa-pahāna*).

In this context, “He is endowed with, fully endowed with, this restraint of the Pātimokkha”—this is the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). “He guards the eye faculty; he attains restraint over the eye faculty”—this is the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*).
“Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “mindfulness is their dam.”
“I call it the restraint of the streams;
by means of wisdom they are closed off.
This is the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). “He is patient with cold and heat”—this is the restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*). “A sensual thought that has arisen...”
“He does not consent”—this is the restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*).

Furthermore, this entire restraint is called “restraint” (*saṃvara*) because it restrains those things that ought to be restrained and those things that ought to be disciplined, such as bodily misconduct; and it is called “discipline” (*vinaya*) because it disciplines them.
Thus, first of all, restraint-discipline (*saṃvara-vinaya*) should be understood as being divided fivefold.

Likewise, among the insight-knowledges such as the discernment of name-and-form, there is the abandoning of this or that disadvantage by means of this or that insight-knowledge, because they stand in opposition to it, just as darkness is [dispelled] by the light of a lamp.
For example: by the definition of name-and-form, personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is abandoned;
by the discernment of conditions, the views of no-cause and wrong cause are abandoned; and subsequently by that very same knowledge...
By the overcoming of doubt, the state of being perplexed is abandoned; by the comprehension of groups, the grasping of "I" and "mine";

by the determination of what is and is not the path, the perception of a path where there is no path; by the vision of arising, the view of annihilationism; by the vision of passing away, the view of eternalism;
by the vision of danger, the perception of safety in what is dangerous; by the vision of disadvantage, the perception of gratification; and by the contemplation of disenchantment...

By means of the perception of delight, there is the desire for deliverance; by means of the knowledge of the desire for deliverance, there is the absence of that desire; by means of the knowledge of equanimity, there is the absence of equanimity;

by means of conformity, there is the reversal of the state of opposition toward the stability of phenomena and toward Nibbāna; and by means of the change-of-lineage, there is the abandoning of the grasping at the sign of formations—this is called abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-pahāna*).

Furthermore, that abandoning of various defilements such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which occurs by means of concentration— distinguished as access and absorption— and which prevents the continuation of existence just as a blow from a jar [destroys] moss on the surface of water,

is called "abandoning by suppression" (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*). That which, through the cultivation of the four noble paths, results in the absolute non-arising of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination within the individual continuum of one who possesses those respective paths—
in accordance with the method stated as "for the abandoning of speculative views" and so forth— is [abandoning by eradication].

This is called abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, that state of the defilements being subsided at the moment of the fruit (*phala*) is called abandonment by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).

That Nibbāna, which has abandoned all conditioned things because it has escaped from all the conditioned, is called abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*). And all this abandonment is abandonment in the sense of relinquishing (*cāga*).
In the sense of disciplining (*vinayana*), it is the *Vinaya*; therefore, it is called "discipline as abandoning" (*pahānavinaya*).

Alternatively, because each specific discipline arises for one who has abandoned this or that [defilement], it is also called "discipline as abandoning. Thus, discipline as abandoning should be understood to be fivefold.
Thus, this discipline (*vinaya*) is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail.

Because it does not exist for this unlearned worldling (*puthujjana*), owing to his broken restraint and his failure to abandon what ought to be abandoned, he is called "undisciplined" (*avinīta*) due to its absence.
This same principle applies to one who has not seen true persons (*sappurisa*) and is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons.
Regarding the phrase "undisciplined in the Dhamma of the true person" (*sappurisadhamme avinīto*), there is no difference in meaning here. As it has been said:
"Those who are noble (*ariya*) are the same as those who are true persons (*sappurisa*); those who are true persons are the same as those who are noble.

That which is the Dhamma of the noble ones is the same as that which is the Dhamma of the true persons; that which is the Dhamma of the true persons is the same as that which is the Dhamma of the noble ones."
The Dhamma itself is their noble discipline; whatever is their noble discipline is their discipline of the true person.

Whatever is their discipline of the true person is their noble discipline. Whether one speaks of the "noble" or the "true person," whether of the "Dhamma of the noble" or the "Dhamma of the true person," whether of the "noble discipline" or the "discipline of the true person"—these are identical, one, of the same meaning, equal, of the same portion, of the same origin, and indeed the very same thing.

"But why did the Blessed One, after saying, 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the exposition of the root of all phenomena,' fail to teach that very exposition and instead define the worldling (*puthujjana*) by saying, 'Here, bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the Noble Ones'?
It was in order to reveal that meaning through a teaching of the Dhamma based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā dhammadesanā*). For the Blessed One’s [teaching] is based on the Dhamma...

There are four modes of teaching by way of the Dhamma and the person: a teaching on the Dhamma based on the Dhamma, a teaching on the person based on the Dhamma, a teaching on the person based on the person, and a teaching on the Dhamma based on the person.
In this regard, there is first a fourfold teaching by way of the Dhamma and the person, such as:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. Which three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
“Feeling. These, monks, are the three feelings. Such is to be understood as a teaching on the Dhamma based on the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*).
“The person consists of six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four foundations.
Such is a teaching on the person (*puggaladesanā*) based on the Dhamma. “There are these three persons, monks, who exist and are found in the world... [and so forth].
In the world. Which three? The blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed. And what, monks, is the person who is blind?
Such is a teaching concerning persons based on the category of persons. “And what, monks, is the fear of an unhappy destination?
Here, monks, a certain person reflects thus: ‘The result of bodily misconduct is evil in the life to come…’ [and so on].”
"He maintains himself in purity. This, monks, is called the fear of a miserable destination"—such is a teaching of the Dhamma based on the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhānā).

Now, since here the worldling (puthujjana) is one whose basis is not fully understood, and since the conceiving (maññanā) rooted in non-comprehension is the very root of all those states intended here, it is therefore by showing the worldling that [the teaching] is presented as being based on the individual.

In order to reveal that meaning through the teaching, it should be understood that the Blessed One defines the worldling (*puthujjana*) thus: "Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling is one who has not seen the Noble Ones.
The commentary on the placement of the sutta is concluded.
The Explanation of the Earth Section:

Having thus pointed out the worldling, [the author] now, demonstrating the conceiving (*maññanā*) produced by all the phenomena of the personality-aggregate (*sakkāya-dhamma*) regarding such bases as earth, says:
"Earth as earth," and so forth. Therein, there is the earth of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-pathavī*) and the earth of constituent matter (*sasambhāra-pathavī*).
Earth is fourfold: objective earth, conventional earth, characteristic earth, and constituent earth. Among these, "And what, friends, is the internal earth element?
That which is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, and solid"—in such passages as this, it is called characteristic earth.
"One might dig the earth or have it dug"—in such passages as this, it is called constituent earth. And as for the head-hairs and so forth...

There are twenty components, as well as external materials such as iron and copper. That which is called "earth" together with its constituent qualities such as color and so forth is "earth with constituents" (*sasambhāra-pathavī*).
However, that which appears in passages such as "One person perceives the earth-kasina" is "objective earth" (*ārammaṇa-pathavī*), and it is also called "sign-earth" (*nimitta-pathavī*).
One who has attained the jhāna of the earth-kasina is reborn in the world of the gods by way of his arrival [there].
It receives the name "earth deity. This should be understood as conventional earth (*sammuti-pathavī*). All of that is found here.

Among those [types of earth], whatever earth this worldling perceives as earth—perceives it as "earth," perceives it through a portion of earth—he perceives it as "earth" by grasping worldly convention and through a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*).
In this way, even while not relinquishing the portion of earth, one perceives it by way of such expressions as “a being” or “belonging to a being.
One should not ask why one perceives it in this manner;
for the worldling is like a madman—he grasps at whatever object in whatever manner. Alternatively, the reason here is precisely the noble ones’ lack of vision [of the truth] and so forth.
Or rather, it was stated by the Blessed One himself when he said to others,
"It is not fully understood by them. Having perceived that earth as earth— that is, having perceived that very earth through such a distorted perception—

subsequently, due to the statement, "Proliferation (papañca) and conceptualization (saṅkhā) have perception as their source," one is here [afflicted] by the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views which have attained strength.
By means of what are called "conceivings" (*maññanā*), one conceives, imagines, and discriminates; one grasps [things] in various ways as being other than they are.

Therefore it is said: "one conceives earth. And for one who conceives in this way, in order to show those conceivings by way of the gross method, the twentyfold internal earth is described by way of the formula beginning with, "What is this: head-hairs, body-hairs... and so forth. And this...
In the Vibhaṅga: “Therein, what is the external earth element? That which is external, hard, of a harsh nature, hardness, the state of hardness, not clung-to internally.
Namely: iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, pearl, gem, beryl, conch, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, emerald, grass...”
"Wood, gravel, pebbles, earth, stone, and mountains"—thus external earth has been described.
Taking that which is "sign-earth" from the triad of internal objects, this application of meaning is stated:
"One conceives earth" means one conceives "I am earth" through the three types of conceiving, or one conceives "earth is mine."

One conceives "another's earth," one conceives "earth belonging to another"; or else, one conceives internal earth through the conceiving of craving, through the conceiving of pride, and through the conceiving of views. How so?
For herein, one generates desire and lust for the hair and so forth; one relishes the hair, delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it. [The same applies to] body hair...
Nails, teeth, skin, or some other object of lust. Thus one conceives of the internal earth-element through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhāmaññanā*).
Or, by way of such a method as "May my hair be thus in the future," or "May my body hair be thus," one brings about delight therein.
"By means of this virtue... [or] by means of this holy life, may I... [and so forth].
Or, by way of such thoughts as, "May my hair be glossy, soft, fine, and dark," one directs the mind toward the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired.
In this way, one conceives of internal earth through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).
Likewise, based on the excellence or deficiency of one's own hair and so forth, one generates conceit (*māna*), thinking, "I am superior."
“Or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior. In this way, one conceives of internal earth through the conceiving of pride (*māna-maññanā*).
Furthermore, according to the method presented in the passage, “That which is the soul is the body,” to whom does one adhere as being the “soul”?
