This same method applies to the body hairs and so forth. In this way, one conceives of internal earth through the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*).
Alternatively, by way of opposition to this process—namely, the realization that "Friends, both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element;
this is not mine"—one adheres to the earth, distinguished by hair and so forth, thinking:
"This is mine, this am I, this is my self. In this way, one clings to the internal earth.
He conceives by means of the conceiving of views. Thus, first, he conceives the internal earth element by means of three kinds of conceiving.
And just as with the internal, so too with the external. How? For this person generates desire and lust for iron, copper, and so forth;
he relishes them, delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, thinking, "This is my iron, this is my copper," and so on.
By way of this method, one regards, protects, and guards iron and so forth as "mine"; thus, through the conceiving of craving, one conceives of external earth.

Or else, one here brings about delight [thinking], "May iron, copper, and so forth be mine in the future," or, "By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall come to possess such equipment as iron, copper, and so forth."
He sets his heart on the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired. In this way, he conceives of external earth through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).
Likewise, depending on the success or failure of his own iron, copper, and so forth, he generates conceit (*māna*), thinking, "I am superior to this," or "I am equal," or "I am inferior.
In this way, he conceives of external earth through the conceiving of conceit (*māna-maññanā*).
He conceives. Having become one who perceives a soul (*jīva*), he furthermore adheres to it as "this is the soul. This same method applies to gold and other such things.
Thus, one conceives of external earth through the conceiving of views.
Alternatively: "In this case, someone regards the earth-kasiṇa as self: 'What is the earth-kasiṇa, that am I.'"
"He who says, 'That is the earth-kasiṇa,' regards both the earth-kasiṇa and himself as non-dual"—according to this method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*, one adheres to the sign-earth as "self.

Thus one conceives of external earth through the conceiving of views. In this way, one conceives of external earth by means of the three types of conceiving. Thus, first of all, it is said: "one conceives of earth."
Herein, three kinds of conceiving (*maññanā*) are to be understood. From this point on, we shall speak in brief. Regarding the phrase "he conceives in earth":
here, "in earth" (*pathaviyā*) is a locative case. Therefore, he conceives, "I am in earth";
he conceives, "earth is my possession, earth is an impediment to me"; he conceives, "another is in earth"; [he conceives] regarding another's...
"To conceive of 'something' as an impediment to the earth" is the meaning here.
Alternatively: "How does one regard the self in relation to form? Here, someone regards feeling...
perception... volitional formations... consciousness as the self; it occurs to him: 'This indeed is my self; that..."
The method for the meaning of the passage, “But does he regard the self as being in this form, or does he regard the self as being in form?

has been stated; by that same method, having taken the phenomena such as feeling and so forth as the self, and then from among the internal and external earth elements, having imagined any earth element whatsoever as its locus, [he thinks]: “But this earth element is my self.”
When one conceives [of the self] as "I am conceiving of earth," this is his conceiving by way of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*).
Furthermore, when he generates affection for that very self and pride based upon it, conceiving by way of craving and pride (*taṇhā-māna-maññanā*) should also be understood.

However, when—by that same method—he conceives "that self of mine is indeed earth," then conceiving by way of views alone is appropriate. Yet others maintain that the other two types of conceiving also apply here.
Regarding the phrase "he conceives from earth" (*pathavito maññati*): here, *pathavito* is an ablative expression.

Therefore, it should be understood that one "conceives from earth" when, conceiving either of the arising or the emergence [of a self] from earth—whether for oneself or for another, including their equipment—as being of the aforementioned varieties, or conceiving that "the self is other than earth. This is his conceiving through views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*). In that very same...
Furthermore, for one who produces affection and conceit toward the basis conceptualized by the conceiving of views, the conceivings of craving and conceit are also to be understood.

Others say: having developed the earth-kasiṇa as limited, and then grasping another self that is immeasurable, one conceives of oneself as being outside of the earth, thinking "my self is external to the earth"; thus, one conceives from the earth.

Regarding the phrase "he conceives 'the earth is mine,'" it should be understood that here only one kind of conceiving—namely, the conceiving of craving—is found, occurring in this manner: "He appropriates the great earth through the influence of craving.
And this [craving] extends to all internal and external things according to their aforementioned classifications, such as: "My hair, my body hair, my iron, my copper."
“Should be applied to earth”:
“One delights in earth” means that one delights in earth in the manner already described—that is, one relishes it, clings to it, and so forth through craving and the rest.
Since this meaning is already established by the phrase “one conceives earth,” why [is it stated again]?

If it is asked, "Is this what was said?"—this has not been investigated by the ancients. However, this is my own opinion, or rather, it arises from the elegance of the teaching or from the perception of its danger.

For that element of the Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*), through the thorough penetration of which the Blessed One became endowed with the elegant display of teachings varied by manifold methods—that very element has been thoroughly penetrated by the Blessed One.
Therefore, having first shown the arising of defilements by way of conceiving (*maññanā*), [he now shows their cessation].
Now, he says this either to show by way of delighting [in the world] or as a skillful teaching:

"Whoever conceives of earth, conceives in earth, conceives from earth, or conceives 'earth is mine'—since he is unable to abandon the craving or the view dependent upon earth, he indeed delights in earth. Whoever...
And he delights in earth; he delights in suffering, for suffering is a danger.
This was said also by way of seeing the danger. And this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, whoever delights in the earth element, he delights in suffering.
Whoever delights in suffering, I say that he is not liberated from suffering."
Having thus spoken of conceiving and delighting with earth as the basis, he now says, "For what reason?
Because it is not fully understood by him, I say," revealing the reason why that person conceives and delights.
The meaning of this is: for what reason does that worldling conceive of that earth; for what cause does he conceive?
"If one rejoices," [the Buddha says], "I declare that for him there is no full understanding. This means: because that object is not fully understood by him, therefore [he rejoices].
For whoever fully understands the earth element, he fully understands it by means of three kinds of full understanding:
full understanding as the known (*ñātapariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and full understanding as abandonment (*pahānapariññā*).
In this context, what is full understanding as the act of knowing (*ñātapariññā*)? One fully understands the earth element thus: "This is the internal earth element;
this is the external earth element; this is its characteristic; these are its function, manifestation, and proximate cause. This is full understanding as the act of knowing.
What is full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*)? Having known it thus, one scrutinizes the earth element as impermanent, as suffering, and as a disease.
By way of forty-two aspects, this is the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*). What is the full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*)?
Having investigated in this way, one abandons desire and lust for the earth element by means of the supreme path; this is the full understanding through abandoning.

Alternatively, the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the full understanding through knowing (*ñātapariññā*); the sequence beginning with the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*) up to the end of the method of conformity (*anuloma*) is the full understanding through investigation.
Knowledge of the Noble Path is full understanding as abandonment. One who fully understands earth does so by means of these three kinds of full understanding;
yet that worldling lacks those full understandings, and therefore, because of this lack of full understanding, he conceives of earth and delights in it.
Thus the Blessed One said: "Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling... and so forth.
"One conceives earth, one conceives in earth, one conceives from earth, one conceives 'earth is mine,' one delights in earth.
For what reason? Because it has not been fully understood by him, I say.
The commentary on the section on earth is finished.

**Commentary on Water and the Like** Regarding the phrase "water as water," here too, water is fourfold by way of characteristic, constituent, object, and conventional designation. Among these: "In this context, what is the internal water element? That which is internal, belonging to oneself, water, watery, moisture... ...[continues with] ...viscidity. This refers to the characteristic. As for the constituent: "In this body, there is water, watery, moisture, viscidity, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, water, watery, moisture, viscidity, whether it be in the head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, excrement, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, water, watery, moisture, viscidity, whether it be in the head-hairs, etc., or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, water, watery, moisture, viscidity, that is the internal water element. In such passages as "The state of cohesion belonging to internal form that is clung-to (upādinna)," it refers to *lakkhaṇāpo* (characteristic water).

In such passages as "One who is learning the water-kasiṇa grasps the sign in water," it refers to *sasambhārāpo* (composite water). All the rest is exactly the same as what was stated regarding earth.
However, in the method of application (*yojanānaya*), there are twelve divisions stated by way of bile, phlegm, and so forth.

The internal water element. In this regard, what is the external water element? Whatever is external, belonging to water, having the nature of water, moisture, having the nature of moisture, the state of cohesion of matter, which is not clung to externally. That is to say:
the sap of roots, the sap of trunks, the sap of bark, the sap of leaves, the sap of flowers, the sap of fruits; milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey.
"Molasses, or waters from the earth, or waters from the sky"—thus should the external water element be understood as it is spoken of;
and also that which is the "sign-water" in the triad of internal objects.
In this section on fire (*tejo*), the detailed explanation should be understood according to the same method stated previously. However, regarding the method of application here:

“The internal fire element of fourfold division, which has been described as: ‘that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion’—this is the internal fire element.
In this context, what is the external fire element? That which is external fire, of the nature of fire, heat, of the nature of heat, warmth, of the nature of warmth.”
The external fire element should be understood as that which is not clung to externally, such as:

a wood-fire, a chaff-fire, a grass-fire, a cow-dung-fire, a husk-fire, a rubbish-fire, a forest-fire, the heat of a fire, the heat of the sun, the heat of a heap of wood, the heat of a heap of grass, the heat of a heap of grain, and the heat of a heap of goods.
Thus should the external fire element be known.
Regarding the application of this air-element as "blowing" or "moving," the internal air element is described as follows:

"Upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds residing in the belly, winds residing in the bowels, winds following along the limbs, razor-like winds, knife-like winds, lotus-stalk-like winds, inhalation, and exhalation.
In that regard, what is the external air element?
Whatever external air there is, or that which has become air, the state of rigidity of form, not clung to externally. That is to say:
eastern winds, western winds, northern winds, southern winds; winds with dust, winds without dust;
cold winds, hot winds; slight winds, violent winds; black winds, *verambha* winds, winged winds, *supaṇṇa* winds.
The external air element should be understood as that which is described as "the wind from a palm-leaf fan" and "the wind from a fan. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
And at this point, regarding that which was said:
"When one thing has been stated, those things which have the same characteristic as it..."
“All are said to be stated,” thus is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra) stated.

In this way, the Mode of Conveying Characteristics is stated in the *Netti*; by means of it, when the four primary elements (bhūta) are grasped, derivative form (upādārūpa) is also necessarily grasped, because it does not transcend the characteristic of form. And that which is both primary and derivative form—
The aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). Therefore, by saying, “The uninstructed worldling conceives earth, water, fire, and air,” it is also stated in terms of meaning that he regards form as self.
By saying, “He conceives in earth, in water, in fire, and in air,” it is also stated that he regards the self as being in form. From earth...
By saying, "He conceives [the self] as water, fire, or air," it is established that the self is other than form;

thus, it is also said that he regards the self as possessing form, or form as being in the self. In this way, these four conceivings based on the category of form should be understood as views of personal identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
Among them, one is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), and three are views of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are only two views; this too is a specific point of meaning.
The commentary on the section on water is finished.
The commentary on the section on earth, etc., begins.

3. Having thus explained conceiving (maññanā) based on formations by way of form, he now speaks the passage beginning with "he perceives beings as beings" in order to point out those beings—among whom both the formations and the beings themselves are included—in which the worldling conceives.
In this context, the word *bhūta* (being) refers to the five aggregates, non-humans, elements, existing beings, those whose taints are exhausted, trees, and so forth.
It is seen. For in such passages as, “Monks, regard this as ‘it has come to be’ (bhūta),” it is seen in reference to the five aggregates.
In the passage, “Whatever beings have gathered here,” it refers to non-human beings.

In the passage, “Monk, the four great elements are the causes,” it refers to the primary elements (dhātu). In passages such as, “An offense of expiation (pācittiya) regarding what has come to be,” it refers to that which exists. And [in the passage], “Whoever...”

In the phrase "become a devourer of beings" (*kālaghaso bhūto*), it refers to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). In the phrase "all beings in the world shall lay down their composite frame" (*sabbeva nikkhipissanti bhūtā loke samussayaṃ*), it refers to sentient beings (*satta*).
In the phrase "for the destruction of the forest of beings" (*bhūtagāmapātabyatāya*), it refers to trees and so forth.

Here, however, it applies to sentient beings, but not without distinction; for here, "beings" (*bhūta*) refers specifically to those sentient beings who dwell below the realm of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*).

In that context, "perceiving what has come to be as it has come to be," and so forth, follows the method already stated. However, in the passages beginning with "he conceives of what has come to be," all three types of conceiving (*maññanā*) should be applied.

How so? For, according to the method stated—"He sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure"—having grasped what has come to be as beautiful and happy, [he conceives].
One is lustful; one is not lustful even after seeing, nor after hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or knowing.
Thus, through the conceiving of craving regarding what has become, one conceives:
"O, may I be reborn in the company of wealthy khattiyas," and by such a method, one fixes the mind on the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
In this way, one conceives through the conceiving of craving regarding what has come to be (*bhūta*).

Furthermore, based on the success or failure of oneself and of beings, one regards oneself as superior; or, regarding any being among beings, one regards that being as inferior while regarding oneself as superior;
or one regards oneself as equal to a being, or a being as equal to oneself. As it is said: "In this case, someone..."
"By reason of birth... or by some other basis, one regards oneself as equal to others at an earlier time;
later, one regards oneself as superior, and regards others as inferior. Such conceit... this is called *mānātimāna* (conceit beyond conceit).
Thus, one conceives through the conceiving of conceit regarding what has come to be.
But regarding what has come to be, one conceives through the conceiving of views by thinking, "It is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change," or by thinking,
"All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, devoid of vigor, determined by destiny, chance, and inherent nature,
and experience pleasure and pain within the six classes of birth. Thus, one conceives regarding what has come to be by means of these three types of conceiving.
How does one conceive regarding beings? One desires for oneself rebirth among this or that class of beings, or the arising of happiness therein.
Thus, first of all, one conceives regarding beings through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).

Or, desiring rebirth among beings, one gives gifts, undertakes moral discipline, and performs the observances of the Uposatha day. In this way as well, one conceives regarding beings through the conceiving of craving.
Having grasped beings by way of a collective perception, one regards some beings as superior, while regarding others as equal or inferior.

Thus, one conceives through the conceiving of pride regarding beings. Likewise, one conceives some beings as permanent and stable, and others as impermanent and unstable; or one conceives, "I am one among these beings. Thus, regarding beings...
One conceives by means of the conceiving of views.

Regarding the phrase "one conceives from what has come to be" (*bhūtato maññati*): here, it should be understood that one conceives from what has come to be when, conceiving the arising of either oneself or another—along with their equipment—from whatever source whatsoever as something that has truly come to be; this is his conceiving of views. In that very [context]...

When one produces affection and conceit toward the basis (vatthu) that has been conceptualized by the conceiving of views, the conceivings of craving and conceit (taṇhāmānamaññanā) are also to be understood.
However, in the phrase "he conceives 'It is mine' regarding what has come to be," only the conceiving of craving is found there. And this [conceiving] occurs in such ways as:
"My sons, my daughters, my goats and sheep, my chickens and pigs, my elephants, cattle, horses, and mares."

It should be understood that [the world] proceeds for me according to this method. "He delights in the elements" is exactly as previously stated. Regarding the phrase "because they are not fully understood by him":
here it should be understood that because the designations for the elements—which are based upon formations (*saṅkhāra*)—are not fully understood, the elements themselves remain uncomprehended.
The construction, however, should be made according to the method already explained.

Having thus shown, in brief, the basis for conceiving (*maññanāvatthu*) by way of both formations (*saṅkhāra*) and beings (*satta*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "deities among deities" (*deve devatā*) in order to show it in detail through its divisions, such as specific planes (*bhūmivisesa*).
Therein, they are called "deities" (*devā*) because they shine (*dibbanti*) with the five strands of sensual pleasure or by their own psychic power (*iddhi*);
the meaning is that they play and they illuminate. They are threefold: conventional deities (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and...
"Pure deities": conventional deities (sammutideva) are kings, queens, and princes; deities by birth (upapattideva) are those from the gods of the Four Great Kings upwards;
pure deities (visuddhideva) are the Arahants whose taints are exhausted.
Here, however, deities by birth are to be understood, yet not without distinction—excluding Māra together with his retinue from the world of the Paranimmittavasavatti gods.

The remaining six [classes] belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) are intended here by the term "gods" (deva). In that regard, the entire commentary on their meaning should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on the elements (bhūta-vāra).
Regarding the term *pajāpati*, Māra should be understood as the *pajāpati* here.

However, some say that this is a designation for the Great Kings and others who are the lords (*adhipati*) of those respective gods. But since they are already included by the mention of "gods" itself, [that view is incorrect].

"Inappropriate" is rejected in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. However, it is Māra himself who is intended here by the term "Lord of Creatures" (*pajāpati*), because he exercises sovereignty over the generation known as "creatures.
Where does he dwell? In the heavenly world of the Paranimmitavasavatti gods.
For there, King Vasavatti rules his kingdom. Māra exercises his authority over his own retinue in one particular region.
They say he dwells like a son of a bandit-king in the border regions of a kingdom. And here, by the mention of Māra alone, the inclusion of Māra’s retinue should also be understood.

As for the method of construction here: having seen or heard that Pajāpati is handsome, long-lived, and full of happiness, one becomes enamored and conceives through the conceiving of craving: "O, that I might attain companionship with Pajāpati!"

Or, by way of the method beginning with "May he be reborn as a *pajāpati*," even one who directs the mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained conceives of the *pajāpati* through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).

Furthermore, having actually attained the state of a *pajāpati*, one generates the conceit, "I am the lord and sovereign over progeny," and thus conceives of the *pajāpati* through the conceiving of pride (*māna-maññanā*). [And one conceives of him thus: "The *pajāpati* is permanent and eternal."
Or, one who conceives that "it will be annihilated" or "it will perish," or that "helpless, powerless, and lacking energy, being transformed by the nature of destiny and chance,
one experiences pleasure and pain within the six classes of birth"— such a person should be understood as conceiving of a creator through the conceiving of views.
Regarding the phrase "in Pajāpati," only one type of conceiving of views (diṭṭhi-maññanā) is applicable here. Its occurrence should be understood as follows:
Here, a certain person conceives thus: "Whatever phenomena exist in Pajāpati, all those are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.
Or alternatively, he conceives: "In Pajāpati there is no evil; no evil deeds are found in him."
Regarding the phrase "from the Lord of Creatures" (*pajāpatito*), three types of conceiving (*maññanā*) are found here. How so?
Here, a certain person conceives of the arising or the emergence of either himself or another, together with their requisites, from the Lord of Creatures;
this is his conceiving by way of view (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*). Furthermore, as he generates affection and pride toward that very object conceived through that conceiving by way of view—
Craving-conceit and the conceit of "I am" should also be understood. However, in the phrase "Pajāpati is mine," only the conceit of craving is found.
This should be understood as occurring in one who clings possessively, in such a manner as: "Pajāpati is my teacher, my master," and so forth.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase *brahmaṃ brahmatoti*: here, one is called *brahmā* because he has been developed (*brūhita*) by various specific qualities.
Furthermore, the term *brahmā* is used for the Mahābrahmā, as well as for the Tathāgata, a brāhmaṇa, parents, and that which is supreme.
For instance, in such passages as “the Sahassa-brahmā, the Dvisahassa-brahmā,” it is the Mahābrahmā who is called *brahmā*. [As it is said: “Monks, ‘brahmā’ indeed...”
“...this is a designation for the Tathāgata”— herein, [the word] "Tathāgata" [is used].
"The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing,
who has gone to the end of the world and transcended all states of existence;"
“The taintless one, who has abandoned all suffering,
whom I have attended upon as my Brahmā, is called Truth.”— In this context,
the word “brahman” is used.
“‘Brahmā’ refers to parents; they are called ‘former teachers.
Here [in that context], it refers to parents. In the phrase “he turns the supreme wheel of Brahmā” (*brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti*), it refers to the supreme.
But here, the first-born Brahmā, who lives for an eon (*kappāyu*), is intended. By mentioning him alone, the Brahmapurohitas and the Brahmapārisajjas are also included.
They should be understood. Furthermore, the commentary on their meaning should be understood according to the same method stated in the section on the Pajāpati deities.

Regarding the section on the Ābhassara deities: because light radiates and spreads from their bodies, as if sparks were falling repeatedly like the flame of a torch, they are called "Radiant" (Ābhassara).
By including them, the entire plane of the second jhāna is included.
All these—namely the Parittābhas, Appamāṇābhas, and Ābhassarās—should be understood as dwelling on a single plane. Regarding the section on the Subhakiṇhas:

they are "Subhakiṇha" because they are strewn and overspread with beauty; that is, their bodily radiance and complexion are a single dense mass of beauty, as magnificent as a glowing ball of gold placed inside a golden casket.
By including them, the entire third jhāna plane is encompassed.
They are included. All these—namely, the Parittasubhas, Appamāṇasubhas, and Subhakiṇhas—should be understood as dwelling on the same level.

In the section on the Vehapphalas, they are called "Vehapphalas" because their fruit (phala) is vast (vipula). They are called Brahmas belonging to the plane of the fourth jhāna. As for the application of the method of meaning, it should be understood in these three sections exactly according to the method stated in the section on the beings (bhūta).
In the section on the Abhibhus, one who overcomes is an "Abhibhū. What does he overcome? The four formless aggregates. This refers to the state of non-percipient existence.
This is a designation. The non-percipient beings (asaññasatta-devā) exist on the very same level as the Vehapphala deities, in one and the same place;
they remain for the duration of their lifespan in whatever posture they were born in, appearing like figures in a painting.
All of them here are included by the term "Abhibhū. Some say that "Abhibhū" refers to the Sahassa Brahmā, and so forth.
According to that method, they describe the overlord-Brahmās (adhipatibrahmā) here and there.
However, it should be understood that this is incorrect because he is already included by the mention of "Brahmā" itself. Furthermore, the method of construction here is as follows:

having heard that the Overlord is "handsome and long-lived," one who generates desire and lust for him conceives of the Overlord through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhāmaññanā*), thinking: "O, may I [attain] companionship with the Overlord!"

Furthermore, by the method beginning with “May he be reborn,” one who directs the mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained conceives of the Overcomer through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).
However, when one regards oneself as inferior and the Overcomer as superior, one conceives of the Overcomer through the conceiving of pride (*māna-maññanā*).
And when one misapprehends [the Overcomer] by way of such statements as “The Overcomer is permanent and eternal,” one conceives of the Overcomer through the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*).
"It conceives" (maññati) is how it should be understood. The rest is exactly according to the method stated in the section on Pajāpati.
The commentary on the sections on the elements (bhūta), etc., is finished.
The commentary on the sections on the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), etc. [now follows].

4. Thus, while the Blessed One was showing the world of the gods in successive order, having shown the state of non-perception by means of the term "overcome" (*abhibhū*), he now—since this is a discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) and the Suddhāvāsa gods stand on the side of liberation (*vivaṭṭapakkhe*), for those gods are indeed Non-returners whose taints are exhausted;
or else, because those gods have a lifespan of several thousands of eons and exist only at the time of a Buddha’s appearance—[proceeded further].
But Buddhas do not arise even in incalculable eons; at such times, that plane is empty. For the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) are to the Buddhas what a royal campsite is to a king.
And for that very reason, they are not included among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) or the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*), because these [stations] exist at all times.
Therefore, showing the plane where they are always found:

Having passed beyond the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), he speaks of the "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) and so forth. Therein, "the base of infinite space" refers to the four wholesome, resultant, and functional aggregates belonging to that plane.
And these should be understood as pertaining only to those reborn there, taking into account that this is a discourse on the delimitation of existence (*bhava*).
This same method applies to the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) and the others. As for the application of the meaning, it is the same in all four of these sections.

The [sections on] the *abhibhū* should be understood according to the method already stated. Furthermore, the conceit of "I am" (*mānamaññanā*) here is also consistent with the method stated in the section on *Pajāpati*.

The commentary on the sections beginning with the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) is concluded. Now begins the commentary on the sections beginning with the seen and the heard (*diṭṭhasuta*).
5. Having thus shown the basis for conceiving (*maññanāvatthu*) in detail through its divisions such as the specific planes (*bhūmivisesa*), he now says "The seen is [conceived as] 'seen,'" etc.,

in order to show the various phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmakadhamma*) that constitute the entire basis for conceiving— namely, those included within personal existence (*sakkāyapariyāpanna*)—
by subsuming them under the four categories beginning with the seen.
In this context, "seen" means seen by the fleshly eye and seen by the divine eye;
it is a designation for the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). Therein, "he conceives what is seen" means he conceives the seen by means of the three types of conceiving.
How so? Seeing the sense-sphere of visible form with the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure, he generates desire and lust for it, relishes it, and rejoices in it.
For this was also said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, beings are enamored, greedy, infatuated, muddled, and obsessed with the form of a woman;
they grieve for a long time, following under the sway of the form of a woman. Thus one conceives through the conceiving of craving regarding what has been seen.
Or else, one brings about delight here [thinking]: “May my form be thus in the future,” or one brings about delight in the excellence of form.
Or, desiring it, one gives a gift—this is the detailed explanation. In this way too, one conceives of what is seen through the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).
Furthermore, based on the excellence or deficiency of one’s own or another’s physical form (*rūpa-sampatti/vipatti*), one generates conceit (*māna*).

Thinking, “I am superior to this person,” or “I am equal,” or “I am inferior”—in this way, one conceives of what is seen through the conceiving of conceit (*māna-maññanā*). [This refers to] the sense-sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*).
However, one conceives [it] as permanent, stable, and eternal; one conceives of a self and what belongs to a self;

one conceives of the auspicious and the inauspicious—in this way, one conceives of what is seen by means of the conceiving of views. Thus, one conceives of what is seen by means of these three types of conceiving.
How does one conceive in regard to what is seen? One who conceives of a self in form by way of the method of viewing [it as such] conceives in regard to what is seen.
He conceives. Or, just as [one conceives] in regard to wealth or grain, so too, when one conceives that "lust and so forth are in form," one conceives in regard to what is seen.

This is his conceiving by way of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*). Furthermore, when he generates affection and pride toward that very same basis which has been conceived through that conceiving by way of views, conceiving by way of craving and pride (*taṇhā-māna-maññanā*) should also be understood.
Thus he conceives in regard to what is seen. The rest is as in the section on earth.
This should be understood in the manner already stated.
"Heard" (suta) means heard by the physical ear and heard by the divine ear; this is a designation for the sense base of sound.

"Known" (muta) means grasped after having been sensed and having been reflected upon; the meaning is "having come into contact and approached. It is said that it is cognized when there is mutual friction between the faculties and their objects; this is a designation for the sense bases of odor, flavor, and tangibles.
"Known" means known by the mind; this is a designation for the remaining seven sense bases, or for the mental object (dhammārammaṇa).

Here, however, only that which is included within the personality-sphere (sakkāya) is obtained. The detailed exposition here should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on the seen.
The commentary on the section on the sutta of the seen, etc., is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Unity, etc. (6).

Having thus shown the entire diversity of personality (*sakkāya*) by means of the four [categories] beginning with "seen," he now says, "Unity" and "Diversity," etc., showing that very same [personality] in two ways: by way of the section on those who have attained meditative absorption (*samāpannaka*) and by way of the section on those who have not attained it (*asamāpannaka*).
For by "unity," he shows the section on those who have attained absorption; and by "diversity," he shows the section on those who have not attained it.
The meaning of these terms is as follows: "oneness" (*ekatta*) is the state of being one; "manifoldness" (*nānatta*) is the state of being diverse.

As for the construction here, one should analyze the section on those in meditative attainment according to the four aggregates, and the section on those not in attainment according to the five aggregates.

Then, having investigated accordingly—following both the method of the Teaching in such passages as "one regards form as self," and the method of the Commentary as set forth in the Earth-section and so forth—one should proceed.
[These views] are to be understood. Some, however, say that "unity" refers to the method of unity (*ekattanaya*) and "diversity" refers to the method of diversity (*nānattanaya*).
Others say it refers to the adherence to wrong views, such as: "The self is percipient of unity and is healthy after death; the self is percipient of diversity.
Since none of these are intended here, they are all inappropriate.
Having thus shown all identity (sakkāya) in two ways, he now says "all as all" and so forth, showing that very same thing by condensing it into one.
The method of construction here is as follows: "Experiencing all [as gratification], he conceives all through the conceiving of craving.
By way of such thoughts as "These beings were created by me," conceiving what was created by himself, he conceives all through the conceiving of pride.
He conceives. One who conceives according to such modes as, "Everything is caused by past karma; everything is caused by the creation of a Lord;
everything is without cause or condition; everything exists; everything does not exist," should be understood as conceiving everything through the conceiving of views.
How does he conceive regarding everything? Here, a certain person holds such a view: "My self is great."
Thus, having conceptualized the entire world of beings as the sphere of that [self], he conceives: "This self of mine is in everything.

This is his conceiving through views. Furthermore, as he generates affection for that very self and pride based upon it, his conceiving through craving and pride should also be understood. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on earth.
Having thus shown all of *sakkāya* as one, he now says "Nibbāna is Nibbāna" in order to show it as one by another method as well.

Therein, "Nibbāna" refers to: "When, sir, this self is fully endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure and enjoys them—this much, sir, is the supreme Nibbāna in the present life for this self."
The supreme Nibbāna-in-this-life (parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna), which is presented in five ways beginning with the passage "he has attained," should be understood.
In that regard, one who relishes Nibbāna conceives by means of the conceiving of craving (taṇhā-maññanā).

By generating the conceit "I have attained Nibbāna" through that Nibbāna, one conceives by means of the conceiving of conceit (māna-maññanā). While it is not actually Nibbāna, one conceives of it as Nibbāna...
It should be understood that one who grasps [the self] as permanent and so forth conceives by means of the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*).
However, having grasped a self other than Nibbāna, one who conceives, "This self of mine exists in this Nibbāna," conceives in relation to Nibbāna;
this is his conceiving of views. Furthermore, he feels affection for that very self and [clings to] that which is based upon it...
When conceit arises, craving, conceit, and the act of conceiving should also be understood. This same method applies to the conceiving of [something] as *nibbāna*.
For there too, having grasped a self other than *nibbāna*, one conceives thus: "This is *nibbāna*; this is the self; and this self of mine is other than this *nibbāna*.
Thus conceiving, one conceives [in relation] to *nibbāna*; this is his conceiving by way of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*). In that very [state]...
For one who generates affection for oneself and the conceit based upon it, craving, conceit, and the conceiving of "I" should also be understood.
Furthermore, when one conceives, "Oh, how happy I am in Nibbāna," it should be understood that one conceives, "Nibbāna is mine.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. Here, however, is the summary verse:
For an ordinary person who does not understand this personal existence (sakkāya) as it truly is,
all conceivings arise within that personal existence.
This [existence] is loathsome, fragile, suffering, and without a guide.
The fool, opposing that [teaching], grasps at conceiving.
As he contemplates self-identity as beautiful and as pleasant,
his conceiving through craving is like that of a moth in a flame.
Fixated on the perception of permanence and beholding prosperity therein,
there arises through conceit the imagining [of self], just as one might imagine [the presence of] excrement in filth.
For the unawakened one who perceives "I am" and "this is mine" within the self;
Just as with a reflection in a mirror, there arises conceiving through one’s view.
This so-called "conceiving" is indeed a subtle bond of Māra—
loose yet difficult to release— by which the worldling is bound.
Though struggling much, he does not transcend personal existence (sakkāya),
like a dog tied with a leash to a firmly erected post.
Thus, clinging to personal existence, he is subject to birth and old age.
And by diseases and other sufferings, he is constantly and violently struck.
Therefore I say to you, O fortunate ones: contemplate this personal existence (sakkāya) as unsatisfactory, as foul, as subject to dissolution, and as non-self.
"This is its inherent nature; seeing this thus, the wise one, having abandoned all conceivings, is liberated from all suffering.
The commentary on the section on unity is finished.
The first method of exposition, concerning twenty-four types of worldlings (*puthujjana*), is concluded.
7. Commentary on the second method of the section on trainees (*sekha*):
Thus, the Blessed One [described] among the bases such as earth, etc., the worldling who is the root of all phenomena pertaining to the self-identity (*sakkāya*).
Having shown the conduct [of the worldling], he now says, “And that bhikkhu who is a trainee,” etc., in order to show the conduct of the trainee regarding those very same bases.
Therein, *yo* is the word of reference; *so* is the word of demonstration. The particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion, as in such passages as “this too is an undetermined dhamma.
And by means of it, he includes the person by way of the commonality of the object.
Not by way of similarity of person (*puggalasabhāga*); for those persons below are deficient in view, whereas here they are endowed with view, so there is no similarity between them.
However, as for the object (*ārammaṇa*), it is the same for the persons below and the same for these [above]. Therefore it is said:
"He groups the person together by way of similarity of object, not by way of similarity of person. By the phrase "that which is also... [it is shown...]

However, it should be understood that by means of the entire statement, the learner (*sekkha*) who is now to be described is being shown. "O monks, O bhikkhus"—this is exactly as previously explained.
In what sense is one a "learner" (*sekkha*)? One is a learner by virtue of having attained the qualities of a learner (*sekkhadhamma*).
For this has been said: "In what way, venerable sir, is one a learner? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with right view that is still in training..."
“He possesses right concentration that is still in training... In this way, bhikkhu, one is a trainee.
Furthermore, one is a trainee because one trains. For it has been said: “One trains, bhikkhu, therefore one is called a trainee.
And what does one train in? One trains in higher virtue, one trains in higher mind, and one trains in higher wisdom.”
“Because he trains, O bhikkhu, he is therefore called a ‘trainee’ (sekha).
Even a virtuous worldling who fulfills the practice in accordance with the truth, who is perfected in virtue, guarded in the doors of the senses, moderate in eating,
devoted to the practice of wakefulness, and during the first and last watches of the night [devoted] to the states conducive to enlightenment...
He dwells devoted to the practice of meditation with the thought: "Today or tomorrow I shall attain one of the fruits of recluseship.

He too is called a *sekkha* because he trains (*sikkhati*). However, in this context, it is specifically the one who has attained penetration (*paṭivedha*) who is intended as a *sekkha*, not the worldling (*puthujjana*).
"By him the mind has not been reached" means *appattamānaso*. "Mind" (*mānasa*) refers to passion, consciousness, or even Arahantship. [As it is said: "Wandering in the sky..."
In the passage, “The snare, which wanders as the mind,” it is lust (*rāga*) that is the mind. In the passage, “Consciousness (*citta*), mind (*mano*), the mental (*mānasa*),” it is consciousness.
In the passage, “A trainee (*sekkha*) who has not attained the mind may pass away, O you who are heard by the people,” it refers to Arahantship. Here too, Arahantship alone is intended.
Therefore, what is meant is “one who has not attained Arahantship.”
*Anuttaraṃ* means supreme; the sense is that it is peerless. *Yogakkhemaṃ* means secure from the four bonds (*yoga*);

what is intended here is specifically *arahatta* (Arhatship). Regarding *patthayamāno*: there are two kinds of aspiration (*patthanā*), namely, the aspiration of craving (*taṇhā-patthanā*) and the aspiration of desire (*chanda-patthanā*).
In the passage, "For one who aspires, there are yearnings, or even trembling over what has been planned," this refers to the aspiration of craving.
“The Evil One’s stream is cut off, shattered and rendered useless;
be full of gladness, O bhikkhus, for you have attained security.
Herein, the desire for wholesome action—the aspiration—is intended in this context. It is by means of that aspiration that one [strives].
One who desires to attain and reach that security from bondage (yogakkhema) should be understood as being inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and tending toward it.
"He dwells" (viharati) means that he carries the body without letting it fall, having interrupted the suffering of one posture with another posture.
Alternatively, it is also said: "He dwells in faith, resolving that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,'" and so forth.
The meaning here should be understood according to the *Niddesa*. "He directly knows earth as earth" means he directly knows earth by way of its earth-nature;
he does not perceive it with a perception that is distorted in every respect, as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) does.
Rather, he knows it with distinguished knowledge; thus, while resolving upon this earth-nature as "earth," he [also perceives it] as "impermanent."
It is said that one directly knows it as "suffering" and also as "non-self. And having directly known it thus, it is said that one should not conceive of earth.
"Conceives" means he conceives. However, this [person] is neither one who conceives nor one who does not conceive;
rather, it should be understood that this word is used here as a particle (nipāta) in this sense. What, then, is the intended meaning here?

It is said: First, the worldling (puthujjana) is called one who "conceives" because he has not abandoned all forms of conceiving. The one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) does not conceive because he has abandoned them.
As for the trainee (sekha), however, the conceiving of views has been abandoned, while the others have become attenuated;
therefore, he cannot be said to "conceive" like the worldling, nor can he be said to "not conceive" like the one whose taints are destroyed.

"‘It is to be fully understood by him’: for that trainee (*sekkha*), because he has entered the fixed course of rightness and is destined for full enlightenment, those bases of conceiving are to be fully understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding;

yet they are not as yet un-understood like those of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), nor are they already fully understood like those of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). The rest is entirely according to the method already stated."
The discussion of the second method by way of the trainee (sekkha) is finished.
8. Explanation of the third method and subsequent methods regarding the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava):
Having thus shown the activity of the trainee with respect to the bases such as earth and so forth, [the author] now shows the activity of the one whose taints are destroyed.
“Bhikkhus, even that bhikkhu who declares himself an arahant,” and so forth. Herein, the word *api* (even/also) has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).

By this, he shows that here both types of commonality are obtained. For the trainee (*sekha*) is similar to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) by virtue of being a noble person (*ariyapuggala*);
thus, commonality of person is obtained. However, commonality of object is exactly as previously stated. “An arahant”—and so forth.
“Distant from defilements” (ārakakileso), “far removed from defilements” (dūrakileso), means that the defilements have been abandoned. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu an arahant? Evil, unwholesome states—defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—are far removed from him. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is an arahant.”
"...is one who has become. "One whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*): there are four taints—the taint of sensual desire... [and so on] ...the taint of ignorance.

These four taints have been destroyed, abandoned, cut off, and stilled in the Arahant; they are incapable of arising again, having been burnt up by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, he is called "one whose taints are destroyed. "One who has lived the holy life" (*vusitavā*):
he has lived, dwelt, and resided in the dwelling with the Teacher, in the dwelling of the Noble Path, and in the ten dwellings of the Noble Ones.

Having completed the rains residence, he is one who has finished his stay and practiced the course of conduct; thus, having lived the holy life and performed what was to be done, the seven trainees—reckoned from the "virtuous worldling" upwards—are said to be performing what is to be done by means of the four paths. For one whose taints are destroyed, all that was to be done has been done and brought to completion;
there is nothing further for him to do for the attainment of the destruction of suffering. Thus he is "one who has performed what was to be done. For it is said:
“For that bhikkhu who is rightly liberated, whose mind is at peace, there is no accumulation of what has been done, nor does anything further to be done exist.

Regarding “one who has laid down the burden”: there are three burdens—the burden of the aggregates (*khandha-bhāra*), the burden of the defilements (*kilesa-bhāra*), and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra-bhāra*). Of these, he has laid down these three...
The burden has been laid down, removed, set aside, and cast off; therefore, he is called "one who has laid down the burden.

"One who has attained his own goal" means he has reached his own goal (*sadattha*); it is said that his own goal (*sakattha*) is what is meant. Here, the letter *k* has been changed to *d*, making it *sadattha*.
And by "his own goal," one should understand *arahatta* (Arhatship). For that, in the sense of being bound to oneself and in the sense of not abandoning oneself...
And in the sense of the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*), one's own welfare is called "one's own interest" (*sakattha*).

"One whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed": the "fetters of existence" are the ten fetters—namely, the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill-will, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of adherence to rites and rituals, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, and the fetter of ignorance.
For these fetter beings to various states of existence, they bind them fast, or they fetter one state of existence to another;

therefore, they are called "fettering to existence" (*bhavasaṃyojana*). These fetters to existence have been completely exhausted and abandoned by the Arahant, burnt away by the fire of knowledge; for that reason, he is called "one whose fetters to existence are completely exhausted. He is "liberated through perfect knowledge" (*sammadaññā vimutto*).

Here, "having fully understood" (*sammadaññā*) means having understood correctly (*sammā aññāya*). What is meant? It is the meaning of aggregates as aggregates, the meaning of sense bases as sense bases, the meaning of elements as elements;

or else, it is the meaning of suffering as oppression, the meaning of origin as arising, the meaning of cessation as peace, the meaning of the path as seeing, or [the understanding] that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth.
"Having rightly understood, known, determined, weighed, and made manifest the distinction as it truly is.

"Liberated": there are two kinds of liberation—the liberation of the mind (*citta-vimutti*) and *nibbāna*. The Arahant is liberated through the liberation of the mind because his mind is freed from all defilements;
he is also liberated in *nibbāna* because he is intent upon *nibbāna*. Therefore, it is said: "By right knowledge..."
"…is liberated. "It has been fully understood by him": for that Arahant, that basis for conceiving has been fully understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*).
Therefore, it is said that he does not conceive that basis, or he does not conceive that conceiving; the rest is exactly as previously explained.

In the section on Nibbāna, however, three sections beginning with "through the destruction of lust" (*khayā rāgassa*) have been stated. These should also be expanded upon in the sections on earth (*pathavī*) and so forth.
And this section on full understanding (*pariññāvāra*) should also be expanded upon in the section on Nibbāna.

When expanding it, one should join [the phrase] with all the words beginning with "it is fully understood by him," and then again join it with "due to the destruction of lust, he is free from lust. This same method applies to the others.
However, as for the teaching, since what is stated in one place is effectively stated in all places, it has been abbreviated.

Regarding the phrase "by the destruction of lust, he is one who has become free from lust": here, because an outsider is free from lust for sense-pleasures but not by the destruction of lust, whereas an Arahant is [free] precisely by its destruction, it is therefore said, "by the destruction of lust, he is one who has become free from lust.
This same method applies to hatred and delusion as well. And just as when it is said, "I say that this has been fully understood by him," [it is because it has been fully understood].
The meaning is that he does not conceive that object or that conceiving; likewise here, because he is free from lust, it should be understood that he does not conceive that object or that conceiving.
And in this context, the section "it is fully understood by him" is stated for the purpose of showing the perfection of the development of the path. The others...
Rather, it should be understood as being for the purpose of demonstrating the fulfillment of the realization of the fruit (*phalasacchikiriyā*). Or, for two reasons, the Arahant does not conceive:

because the basis (*vatthu*) has been fully understood (*pariññāta*) and because the unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*) have been eradicated (*samucchinna*). Therefore, by the section on full understanding, he illustrates the full understanding of the basis regarding the basis;
by the other [sections], he illustrates the eradication of the unwholesome roots. Therein, among the latter...

This distinction should be understood regarding the three sections: for in the first three sections, having seen the danger in lust (*rāga*), one dwells contemplating suffering and is liberated by the desireless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*);
through the destruction of lust, he becomes free from lust (*vītarāga*).

Having seen the danger in hatred (*dosa*), one dwells contemplating impermanence and is liberated by the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*); through the destruction of hatred, he becomes free from hatred (*vītadosa*).
"Having seen the great danger, dwelling contemplating non-self, liberated by way of the void liberation, one becomes free from delusion through the destruction of delusion.
If it is argued that this being the case, one person would not be liberated by all three liberations, and thus the two instances [of the word "even"] should not have been stated, that is not so. Why?
Because there is no restriction. For it was stated without restriction: "And as for that bhikkhu, monks, who is an Arahant..."
However, it was not stated whether he was liberated by means of the desireless liberation or by the other; therefore, everything that applies to an Arahant must indeed be stated.

Or, without distinction, any Arahant whatsoever—despite the fact that the destruction of lust and the other defilements is the same for all—[is so called] because of the full understanding of the suffering inherent in change.

Through the destruction of lust, one is called "free from lust" because of the full understanding of the suffering of suffering; through the destruction of hatred, one is "free from hatred" because of the full understanding of the suffering of formations;
through the destruction of delusion, one is "free from delusion" because of the full understanding of the suffering of formations.

Alternatively, through the full understanding of a desirable object, one is free from lust through the destruction of lust; through the full understanding of an undesirable object, one is free from hatred through the destruction of hatred; [and through the full understanding of a neutral object...]

Because of the full understanding of delusion, one is "free from delusion" through its destruction. Alternatively, because the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling has been eradicated, one is "free from lust" through the destruction of lust; and because the underlying tendencies to aversion and delusion regarding other feelings have been eradicated, one is "free from hatred" and "free from delusion.

Therefore, in order to show this distinction, he said: "Because of being free from lust through the destruction of lust... [and so on] ...because of being free from delusion through the destruction of delusion."

The exposition of the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth methods by way of one whose taints are destroyed is concluded. Now, having thus shown the activity of one whose taints are destroyed regarding the bases such as earth and so forth, [the text proceeds] to show his own activity. The commentary on the seventh method, the Chapter on the Tathāgata. 12.
Thus, having demonstrated the functioning of one whose taints are exhausted with respect to objects such as earth and so forth, [the author now demonstrates] his own functioning.

"Monks, the Tathāgata also, while giving [this gift]... and so forth he said. Therein, "Tathāgata": the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata" for eight reasons: he is a Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) in such a way (tathā);
he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) in such a way; he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa);
he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true dhammas (tathadhamma) as they really are; he is a Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they truly are...
The Tathāgata is so called because of his speaking thus, because of his acting thus, and because of his overcoming [all things]—thus he is the Tathāgata.

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata because he has come thus? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones came having exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world, just as the Blessed One Vipassī came, just as the Blessed One Sikhī came, and just as the Blessed One Vessabhū came.
“Bhagavā, just as the Blessed One Kakusandha, just as the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and just as the Blessed One Kassapa have come.
What is meant by this? By that same resolve (*abhinīhāra*) with which these Blessed Ones came, our Blessed One has also come.

Or alternatively: just as the Blessed One Vipassī... [and so on] ...just as the Blessed One Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), [fulfilled] the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity (*sīla-nekkhamma-paññā-vīriya-khanti-sacca-adhiṭṭhāna-mettā-upekkhā-pāramī*).
Having fulfilled these ten perfections (pāramī), ten secondary perfections (upapāramī), and ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī)— thus fulfilling the thirty perfections—

and having sacrificed the five great sacrifices, namely, the sacrifice of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, children, and wife; and having fulfilled the preliminary practices, former conduct, teaching of the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of others, and so forth.
Having reached the pinnacle of the practice of wisdom, he has come; likewise, our Blessed One has also come.

And just as the Blessed Vipassī... [and so on] ...just as the Blessed Kassapa, having developed the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path, [has come].

He has come having cultivated [the path]; likewise, our Blessed One has also come, thus he is the Tathāgata. Just as in the world Vipassī and the other sages have arrived here at the state of omniscience; so too has our Blessed One. Thus he is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come from the world of phenomena (dhamma) to the world of beings (satta), and from the world of beings back to the world of phenomena, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma exactly as it is, he is the Tathāgata. Or again, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was by previous Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Or yet again, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it will be by future Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Or finally, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma exactly as it is, just as it was, and just as it will be, he is the Tathāgata. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was by past Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it will be by future Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it is now by present Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was, just as it will be, and just as it is now, he is the Tathāgata. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was by past Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it will be by future Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it is now by present Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was, just as it will be, and just as it is now, he is the Tathāgata. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was by past Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it will be by future Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it is now by present Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was, just as it will be, and just as it is now, he is the Tathāgata. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it was by past Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it will be by future Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has come to the realization of the Dhamma just as it is now by present Buddhas, he is the Tathāgata. Likewise, this Sage of the Śākyas has also come [in that way];
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, the Seer.
Thus, because he has come in such a way, he is the Tathāgata.
How is he “thus-gone” (*tathāgata*)? He is a *tathāgata* because he went in such a manner as the Blessed One Vipassī went when he was newly born...
[and so on] ...as the Blessed One Kassapa went. And how did he go? For immediately upon being born, he stood with level feet upon the earth and went seven steps toward the north.
As it is said: "Immediately upon being born, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta..."
Standing with even feet upon the earth, he proceeds seven steps toward the north while a white parasol is held over him;
he surveys all directions and utters this lion’s roar:
"I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world; this is my final birth."
“There is now no further becoming.
And his departure was true and not false, serving as a precursor to the attainment of many distinguished qualities.
For the fact that he stood with level feet immediately upon birth was a sign of his acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

The facing toward the north is the omen for the state of transcending the entire world. The taking of seven steps is the omen for the acquisition of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
The waving of the yak-tail whisks mentioned here in the verse, "Golden-handled yak-tail whisks are waved," is the omen for the crushing of all rival teachers.
The holding of the white parasol is the omen for the acquisition of the supreme, stainless white parasol of the liberation of *arahantship*.

The surveying of all directions was the omen for the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. The utterance of the bull-like voice was the omen for the irreversible turning of the supreme Wheel of Dhamma.
In the same way, this Blessed One also went forth. And that going of his was real and not false, by virtue of being the omen for those very specific attainments. Thus said the ancients:
“Just as a newborn calf, O Lord of Bulls,
touches the earth with level feet,
so did Gotama take seven steps.”
And the gods held up that white parasol.
Having gone seven steps,
Gotama surveyed the quarters all around.
"He uttered speech endowed with eight factors,
like a lion standing upon the summit of a mountain"—
thus he is called the Tathāgata.
Or alternatively, just as the Blessed One Vipassī... [and so on] ...just as the Blessed One Kassapa, so too this Blessed One,
having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation, ill will through non-ill will, sloth and torpor through the perception of light,
restlessness and remorse through non-distraction, doubt through the discernment of phenomena, and having shattered ignorance through knowledge, has gone forth.
Having dispelled discontent with gladness, having opened the door-panel of the hindrances with the first jhāna,
having stilled the smoke of applied and sustained thought with the second jhāna, having faded away from rapture with the third jhāna,

and having abandoned pleasure and pain with the fourth jhāna, [one abandons] perceptions of form, perceptions of sensory impact, and perceptions of diversity through the attainment of the base of infinite space.

Having transcended it, he has gone beyond the perception of the base of infinite space by means of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness; he has transcended the perception of the base of infinite consciousness by means of the attainment of the base of nothingness;
and he has transcended the perception of the base of nothingness by means of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

By means of the contemplation of impermanence, he has abandoned the perception of permanence; by means of the contemplation of suffering, the perception of pleasure; and by means of the contemplation of non-self...
the perception of self through the contemplation of disenchantment; delight through the contemplation of dispassion; lust through the contemplation of cessation;
grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment; the perception of solidity through the contemplation of destruction;

accumulation through the contemplation of vanishing; the perception of permanence through the contemplation of change; the sign through the contemplation of the signless; and [craving] through the contemplation of the desireless.
the adherence to aspiration, the adherence to misapprehension through the contemplation of emptiness, the adherence to grasping at a core through higher wisdom and insight into phenomena,

the adherence to delusion through knowledge and vision according to reality, the adherence to attachment through the contemplation of danger, the lack of reflective discernment through the contemplation of reflection,
the adherence to bondage through the contemplation of turning away, and the [fetters] associated with views by means of the path of stream-entry.

Having shattered the defilements, having abandoned the gross defilements by means of the path of once-returning, having eradicated the subtle defilements by means of the path of non-returning, and having utterly cut off all defilements by means of the path of arahantship—he has gone. Thus also he is a Tathāgata because he has "gone thus" (tathā-gata).
How is he a Tathāgata because he has "come to the true characteristic" (tathalakkhaṇa)? The characteristic of hardness in the earth element is "thus" (tatha).
It is not otherwise. The characteristic of the water element is trickling; the characteristic of the fire element is heat; the characteristic of the air element is distension;
the characteristic of the space element is non-resistance; the characteristic of the consciousness element is cognizing.

The characteristic of form is being affected; the characteristic of feeling is experiencing; the characteristic of perception is perceiving; the characteristic of volitional formations is forming; the characteristic of consciousness is cognizing.

Applied thought has the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object. Sustained thought has the characteristic of continuous mental engagement. Rapture has the characteristic of pervading. Pleasure has the characteristic of gratification. One-pointedness of mind has the characteristic of non-distraction.

Contact has the characteristic of touching. The faculty of faith has the characteristic of resolution. The faculty of energy has the characteristic of exertion. The faculty of mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing. The faculty of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction. The faculty of wisdom has the characteristic of discerning.

The characteristic of the power of faith is unshakability by lack of faith; of the power of energy, by laziness; of the power of mindfulness, by forgetfulness; of the power of concentration, by agitation; and of the power of wisdom, by ignorance.
The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor is establishing; of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, discerning;
of the energy enlightenment factor, exertion; of the rapture enlightenment factor, pervading; and of the tranquility enlightenment factor...

The characteristic of tranquility. The characteristic of non-distraction for the enlightenment factor of concentration. The characteristic of reflective discernment for the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
The characteristic of seeing for right view. The characteristic of directing toward for right intention. For right speech...
The characteristic of right action is grasping. The characteristic of right livelihood is purification.
The characteristic of right effort is exertion. The characteristic of right mindfulness is establishing. The characteristic of right concentration is non-distraction.
The characteristic of ignorance is unknowing. The characteristic of volitional formations is intending. The characteristic of consciousness is cognizing.

The characteristic of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) is bending toward objects; the characteristic of form (*rūpa*) is being affected; the characteristic of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) is being a base;

the characteristic of contact (*phassa*) is touching; the characteristic of feeling (*vedanā*) is being felt; the characteristic of craving (*taṇhā*) is being a cause; the characteristic of clinging (*upādāna*) is grasping;
the characteristic of becoming (*bhava*) is accumulating; the characteristic of birth (*jāti*) is arising; the characteristic of aging (*jarā*) is decaying.

Death has the characteristic of passing away; the elements have the characteristic of emptiness; the sense bases have the characteristic of being bases; the foundations of mindfulness have the characteristic of establishing;
the right efforts have the characteristic of striving; the bases of psychic power have the characteristic of succeeding; the faculties have the characteristic of predominance.

The characteristic of the powers is unshakability. The characteristic of the factors of enlightenment is leading out. The characteristic of the path is being a cause. The characteristic of the truths is suchness.
The characteristic of serenity is non-distraction. The characteristic of insight is contemplation. The characteristic of serenity and insight is having a single flavor.

The characteristic of their yoke-mate relationship is not overstepping one another. The characteristic of purification of virtue is restraint. The characteristic of purification of mind is non-distraction. The characteristic of purification of view is seeing.
The characteristic of the knowledge of exhaustion is cutting off. The characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is tranquility.
The characteristic of desire is the root. The characteristic of attention is origination. The characteristic of contact is convergence. The characteristic of feeling is meeting together.
The characteristic of concentration is preeminence. The characteristic of mindfulness is sovereignty. The characteristic of wisdom is...

That is its characteristic of being subsequent. It has the characteristic of being the essence of liberation. It has the characteristic of being the ultimate consummation of Nibbāna, which is immersed in the deathless;

it is suchness, not otherwise. Thus, because he has come by way of the course of knowledge, having reached and attained it without missing it—thus possessing the characteristic of suchness—he is the Tathāgata.
Because he has come to such a characteristic of suchness, he is the Tathāgata.
How is he the Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of things as they really are (*yāthāvato*)?
The "true nature of things" (*tathadhammā*) refers to the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, these four are true, not false, not otherwise.
Which four? 'This is suffering,' bhikkhus—this is true, this is not false, this is not otherwise," and so on in detail.
The Blessed One has fully awakened to these; therefore, because he has fully awakened to them as they truly are (*tathā*), he is called the *Tathāgata*.

For here the word *gata* has the sense of "fully awakened. Furthermore, the meaning of the arising and occurrence of aging-and-death through the condition of birth is *tatha*—it is not otherwise, it is not different...
[and so on] ...the meaning of the arising and occurrence of volitional formations through the condition of ignorance is *tatha*.

It is suchness, unerring, not otherwise. Such is the conditionality of volitional formations with respect to ignorance; such is the conditionality of consciousness with respect to volitional formations...
[and so on] ...such is the conditionality of aging-and-death with respect to birth.
All that the Blessed One has fully awakened to; therefore, because he has fully awakened to these such-like phenomena, he is called the Tathāgata.
Thus, because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of phenomena as they really are, he is called the Tathāgata.

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they truly are? The Blessed One [perceives] that form-object which comes within the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems throughout the world with its gods... [and so on] ...including its devas and humans.

It exists. One knows and sees it in all its aspects. By knowing and seeing it thus—whether by way of the desirable and undesirable, or by way of the terms applicable to what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—one [identifies]: "What is that form which is the form-base (rūpāyatana)?
It is that form derived from the four great elements which possesses visible appearance, is demonstrable, is impinging, and is blue..."
When analyzed by way of numerous names—such as "Pītaka" and so forth—through thirteen recitations and fifty-two methods, it remains exactly as it is;
there is nothing false in it. This same method applies to sounds and other objects that come into range through the ear-door and the other sense-doors.
And this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... [pe] ...among devas and humans has been seen..."
“Whatever has been heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind—that I know...

that I have directly known; that is understood by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata does not stand [clinging] to that. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of seeing things as they truly are (*tathadassitā*).
In this context, the derivation of the term *Tathāgata* should be understood in the sense of “one who sees thus.”
How is the Tathāgata one who speaks thus? From the night the Blessed One sat upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and,
having crushed the heads of the three Māras, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-sammāsambodhi),

until the night he attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) between the twin sāla trees— within this interval measuring forty-five years— [he spoke thus].
