Whatever discourse, verse, and so forth, up to the "flower-like" (vedalla) teachings were spoken by the Blessed One during the first,
middle, or last period of his enlightenment— all that is irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing, neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect,
and a subduer of the intoxication of lust, hatred, and delusion; therein there is not even as much as a hair’s tip [of fault].
When it is compared, all of it is exactly as it was—unfailing and not otherwise—just as if it were stamped with a single seal, measured by a single scale, or weighed on a single balance.
Therefore he said: "Cunda, between that night when the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and that night when [he passes away] into the Nibbāna-element without residue..."
“He attains final Nibbāna; whatever he speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between [his birth and his passing] is all exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore he is called the Tathāgata. Here, the word *gata* has the sense of “spoken.

Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of speaking what is thus (*tathāvāditā*). Furthermore, *āgada* means speaking; it means speech. Since his speech (*āgada*) is thus (*tatha*), that is, unerring, [he is a Tathāgata]. [The change from *d* to *t* occurs by rule.]
Having applied the syllable *takāra*, the word *tathāgata* should be understood as established in this sense.
How is he a *tathāgata* by virtue of acting accordingly (*tathākāritā*)? For the Blessed One’s body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body.
Therefore, he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts. And for one who is such, as...
The meaning is that the body of the Tathāgata proceeds in the same way as his speech. And just as the body, so too his speech proceeds in accordance with what has gone (tathā-gata);
thus he is the Tathāgata. Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata acts according to how he speaks, and he speaks according to how he acts.
Thus, acting according to how he speaks and speaking according to how he acts, he is therefore called the 'Tathāgata'. Thus...
He is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly.

How is he a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits, he overcomes all beings throughout immeasurable world-systems across the horizontal expanse, both by virtue, by concentration, and by wisdom.
In terms of liberation as well as the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no measure or limit for him;
he is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed, the king of kings, the god of gods, the supreme among the Sakkas, and the supreme among the Brahmas. Therefore it was said:
"Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... [and so on] ...in this world with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing."
“...he is a master. Therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like an *agada* (antidote). But what is this?

It consists of the splendor of his teaching and the accumulation of his merit. For by means of that, this powerful Physician, like snakes with a divine antidote, [overcomes] all those who hold opposing views.

He overcomes the world together with its devas; thus, because he is "tatho" (true) and "aviparīto" (unerring) in overcoming the entire world, and because he is a remedy consisting of the elegance of his teaching and the power of his merit—changing the letter *da* to *ta*—he should be understood as the "Tathāgata.
In this way, he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.
Furthermore, he is a *Tathāgata* because he has gone (*gato*) to suchness (*tathāya*); he is a *Tathāgata* because he has gone to what is real (*tathaṃ*).

"Gone" (*gato*) means understood, transcended, attained, or entered. In this context, he is a *Tathāgata* because he has gone to—that is, understood—entirety of the world through the full comprehension of its diagnosis (*tīraṇapariññā*).

He is a *Tathāgata* because he has gone beyond—that is, transcended—the origin of the world through the full comprehension of its abandonment (*pahānapariññā*). [He is a *Tathāgata*] regarding the cessation of the world...

He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to, that is, attained, suchness (*tathatā*) through direct realization. He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to, that is, entered upon, the true path leading to the cessation of the world.
Therefore, as it was said by the Blessed One: "The world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the *tathāgata*;
the *tathāgata* is detached from the world. The origin of the world, monks, has been [fully awakened to] by the *tathāgata*..."
The origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata.
The cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata.

The practice leading to the cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the practice leading to the cessation of the world has been cultivated by the Tathāgata. That which...
“Monks, whatever has been realized by the Tathāgata in this world with its devas... all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;
therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata. This is how its meaning should also be understood.

And this is merely a brief introduction to the illumination of the Tathāgata’s state of being a Tathāgata; however, only the Tathāgata himself could describe the Tathāgata’s state of being a Tathāgata in every aspect.

Regarding the two terms "Arahant" and "Sammāsambuddho": first, one should understand them as "Arahant" for these reasons: because he is far from (*āraka*) enemies (*ari*); because he has destroyed (*hata*) the spokes (*ara*) [of the wheel of craving]; because he is worthy (*araha*) of requisites and so forth; and because there is no secrecy (*raha*) in his doing of evil.

Furthermore, he is called "Sammāsambuddho" because he has awakened (*buddhattā*) to all phenomena both correctly (*sammā*) and by himself (*sāma*). This is the summary here. For a detailed explanation of these two terms, it is set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* in the commentary on the recollection of the Buddha (*Buddhānussati-vaṇṇanā*).
Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata has fully understood the limit": here, the meaning should also be understood as "that basis for conceiving has been fully understood by the Tathāgata.
"Fully understood the limit" means having reached the further shore of full understanding, having reached the culmination of full understanding; it is said to be fully understood without remainder.
For although the Buddhas and their disciples alike abandon defilements through various paths, [the distinction lies in the thoroughness].
There is no difference [in the result], but there is a difference in terms of full understanding (*pariññā*). For disciples attain *nibbāna* by comprehending only a portion of the four elements.
However, for Buddhas, there is not even an atom’s worth of conditioned phenomena that has not been seen, weighed, scrutinized, and realized through their knowledge.
The commentary on the seventh method, the section on the Tathāgatas, is concluded.
Commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter, the Tathāgata-vāra-aṭṭhama-naya:
Regarding the passage beginning with "Delight is the root of suffering," "delight" (*nandī*) refers to craving of the past. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to the five aggregates.
"Root," etc., follows. "Having understood thus" means having known that former delight of existence as "the root of this suffering."
“Becoming” (bhava) refers to kamma-becoming. “Birth” (jāti) refers to the resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandhā). Because they are born, they are called “birth.
Alternatively, this teaching is given under the heading of birth. This too should be connected with the phrase “having understood thus. For the meaning here is:
“Having known that rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) arises from kamma-becoming. “Of one who has come to be” (bhūtassa) means of a sentient being.

"Old age and death" means both old age and death. This is what is meant: "For a being who has come into existence by means of that rebirth-existence (upapattibhava), there is old age and death for the aggregates"—having understood it thus.
Up to this point, [the Blessed One] sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the invincible throne (aparājitapallaṅka) and, having comprehended [this], attained omniscience.

Demonstrating that the cause for the absence of conceptualizations (*maññanā*) lies in the penetration of that dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), he shows that very same dependent origination as having four summaries, three links, three time periods, and twenty aspects.
But how, in this much, is it all shown? For here, "delight" (*nandī*) is one summary.
From the statement "of suffering," suffering is the second; from the statement "existence [comes] from becoming," existence is the third; birth, aging, and death are the fourth.
Thus, first of all, four summaries (saṅkhepa) should be understood—the meaning is "sections" (koṭṭhāsa).
Furthermore, between craving and suffering there is one junction (sandhi); between suffering and existence there is the second; and between existence and birth...
And the third is the interval. Thus, three joints should be understood as being like the intervals between four fingers, with four sections [of bone] in between.
Therein, "delight" (*nandī*) is the past time; birth, aging, and death are the future;
and suffering and existence (*bhava*) are the present—thus the three times should be understood. Furthermore, among the five aspects in the past, craving (*taṇhā*) is indicated by the term "delight."

By that [ignorance], even though they have not yet arrived, ignorance (*avijjā*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are indeed grasped by way of their characteristic as conditions.

However, by the mention of birth, aging, and death, those aggregates for which such birth, aging, and death occur are already stated; thus, future consciousness (*viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are also implicitly grasped.
In this way, these are [summarized]: "In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance, the exertion is formations, the attachment is craving, and the approaching is..."
Grasping, volition, and becoming— these five factors are the conditions for rebirth-linking here from the previous kamma-process existence.
Rebirth-linking consciousness, descent [into the womb], mentality-materiality, the sensitivity of the sense bases, contact, and feeling—
these five factors are the conditions here in the present existence for the kamma performed in the past.

Here, due to the ripening of the sense bases (*āyatana*), there is delusion which is ignorance (*avijjā*); the exertion is volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*); the attachment is craving (*taṇhā*); the approaching is clinging (*upādāna*); and the intention is becoming (*bhava*).
These five factors here in the kamma-process existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking in the future.

In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness (*viññāṇa*); the descent [into the womb] is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the sensitivity is the sense base (*āyatana*); the touched is contact (*phassa*); and that which is felt is feeling (*vedayita*).
“Feeling—these five factors are the conditions for future rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) due to karma performed here.
Thus, the twenty modes with the characteristics thus defined should be understood here.

In this way, having understood that “delight is the root of suffering,” and that “from existence comes birth, and for one who has come to be, there is aging and death,” all of this constitutes the fourfold compendium.
It should be understood that dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) has thus been shown as having three connections, three divisions, and twenty modes.
Now, regarding the passage beginning "Therefore, bhikkhus...

I say I am fully enlightened," we shall provide a commentary on the previously unstated words and conclude with the meaning through the application of the terms. "Tasmā ti ha" means simply "therefore."
The syllables *ti* and *ka* are particles (*nipāta*). "All" (*sabbaso*) is a term meaning "without remainder.

"Of all cravings" (*sabbataṇhānaṃ*) refers to all those cravings spoken of as "delight" (*nandī*). "Destruction" (*khaya*) means by way of the supramundane path, through absolute destruction. "Dispassion" (*virāga*) and the other terms are synonyms for destruction itself.
For whatever craving is destroyed, it becomes dispassionate, ceased, abandoned, and relinquished. "Destruction" (*khaya*)...

Or rather, this is common to the function of all four paths. Therefore, it should be applied thus: through the first path, from the fading away (*virāga*); through the second, from cessation (*nirodha*); through the third, from relinquishment (*cāga*);
and through the fourth, from relinquishing-letting-go (*paṭinissagga*). Or else: by the destruction of those cravings (*taṇhā*) by which one might perceive earth as "earth";
by the fading away of those [cravings] by which one might conceive of earth; and by the relinquishment of those [cravings] by which one might conceive in relation to earth.

[The word] "cessation" (*nirodha*) should be applied here as follows: "the relinquishing of those [conceptions] by which one might conceive of earth; the renunciation of those [conceptions] by which one might conceive 'earth is mine';
the destruction of those [conceptions] by which one might conceive of earth... [and so on] ...the renunciation of those [conceptions] by which one might delight in earth.
In this way, the construction should be made, and nothing is contradictory.
*Anuttaraṃ* means unsurpassed, devoid of anything superior, and most excellent. *Sammāsambodhiṃ* means perfect self-enlightenment;
or alternatively, it means praised and beautiful enlightenment. *Bodhi* refers to the Bodhi tree, the Path, omniscient knowledge, and Nibbāna—as in the phrases:
"He was first fully enlightened at the foot of the Bodhi tree" and "Between the Bodhi [tree] and Gayā."
In the passage where it says "the tree where [he] arrived is called the Bodhi," it refers to the tree. In the passage where it says "knowledge regarding the four paths," it refers to the path.
In the passage where it says "the one of vast intelligence attains the supreme Bodhi," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).

In the passage where it says "having reached the deathless, the unconditioned Bodhi," it refers to Nibbāna. However, in this context, it refers to the Blessed One’s knowledge of the path to Arahatship.
This is what is intended. Others say it is "the knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
Is the path to Arahantship for disciples the supreme enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhi*) or not? It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities.
For in their case, the path to Arahantship bestows only the fruit of Arahantship for some, the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) for some, and [other qualities] for some.

It bestows the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), for some the four analytical insights (*catasso paṭisambhidā*), and for others the knowledge of the perfection of discipleship (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).

It also bestows the knowledge of private enlightenment (*paccekabodhiñāṇa*) upon those who are *paccekabuddhas*. However, for Buddhas, it bestows the attainment of all virtues, just as an anointing ceremony confers upon a king the state of sovereignty over the entire world.
Therefore, no one else whatsoever possesses unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhi*).
"Abhisambuddho" means he has directly known, he has penetrated; it is said that he has reached and attained it. "Iti vadāmi" means:
thus I say, I declare, I teach, I prescribe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain.
Herein, this is the construction: "The Tathāgata too, bhikkhus... [as before] ...does not conceive earth... [as before] ...does not delight in earth."
"For what reason? Because delight is the root of suffering; from becoming comes birth; for one who has come to be, there is aging and death.
Having understood this thus. In this context, "having understood" (*iti viditvā*): the particle *iti* has the sense of a cause.
By this, it is said that because this dependent origination has been understood and penetrated. Furthermore, because having understood this dependent origination in this way—
Whatever craving has been called "delight" in the case of the Tathāgata, that has been abandoned in every way;
and through the complete destruction of all those cravings... [as before] ...the Tathāgata has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, because he has awakened thus, he does not conceive of the earth, nor does he delight in the earth—I say this. Thus, because he has awakened, he neither conceives nor delights.
"I say" is what is meant.

Alternatively, because craving has been entirely exhausted by his having understood dependent origination according to the method beginning with "Delight is the root of suffering," therefore, monks, through the total destruction of all cravings... [the Tathāgata] has awakened to full enlightenment.
I say this: because he has thus fully awakened, he does not conceive of the earth... [and so on] ...he does not delight in it.
For wherever the word "because" (*yasmā*) is not explicitly stated and instead "therefore" (*tasmā*) is used, one should supply "because" (*yasmā*) in each such instance and connect the text;
this is the method of the Teaching (*sāsanayutti*). This same principle applies everywhere.
"Thus spoke the Blessed One": from this point, beginning with the conclusion of the introduction up to the words "I say he has attained full enlightenment," the Blessed One—
demonstrating his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), which is supremely profound and finds no foothold for others' wisdom—

did so by means of one section on worldlings (*puthujjana*), one section on those in training (*sekkha*), four sections on those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), and two sections on Tathāgatas.

Having adorned it with eight great sections, each of which is further embellished by twenty-four intermediate sections beginning with "earth," he spoke this body of doctrine consisting of two *bhāṇavāra*s.
Indeed, this Sutta, endowed with the splendor of teachings in various methods, was [recited] in a voice as sweet as the song of the karavika bird, pleasant to the ear.

Even as he spoke with a Brahma-voice, which was like a consecration of the nectar of immortality for the hearts of wise men, those five hundred bhikkhus did not rejoice in the Blessed One’s words; they did not approve of this speech of the Blessed One. Why?
Because of ignorance. It is said that they did not understand the meaning of this sutta, and therefore they did not rejoice.
For at that time, even though this discourse was endowed with such a variety of methods and the elegance of exposition,
it was as if a mouthful of delicious food had been placed before them, bound shut by a thick, broad strip of cloth. And has not the Blessed One,
for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, [striven] to make known to others the Dhamma he himself taught?
Having fulfilled the perfections, he attained omniscience. Why, then, did he teach in such a way that they did not understand?
This has already been stated in the very analysis of the presentation of this sutta: "He began the teaching on the Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena for the purpose of breaking pride.
Therefore, there is no need to say anything further here; thus it was taught for the purpose of breaking pride.
Having heard this sutta, those bhikkhus thought: "Indeed, even one who holds wrong views perceives this very earth;
so too does one in training, an arahant, and the Tathāgata. What is this? How is this named? They reflected: "Previously, we understood whatever was spoken by the Blessed One immediately;
but now, regarding this *Mūlapariyāya*, [we do not know] its end or its limit."
"Or rather, we neither know nor see [them]; oh, how immeasurable and incomparable are those called Buddhas!
Thinking thus, like snakes that have shed their skins, they became free from pride and came respectfully for the purpose of attending upon the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma.
Now at that time, the bhikkhus, having sat down in the Dhamma hall, raised this discussion:

“Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas! For those brahmin renunciants, who were so intoxicated by pride and conceit, have been humbled by the Blessed One through the teaching on the ‘Root Discourse’ (Mūlapariyāya).
This conversation among the bhikkhus was still unfinished when the Blessed One emerged from his fragrant chamber and, performing a miracle appropriate for that moment, appeared in the Dhamma Hall.
Having sat down upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, he said to those bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you currently seated?
They reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
"Bhikkhus, it is not only now; formerly as well, I [saw] these very ones wandering about with their heads held high by pride, and with their pride humbled..."
"…did he do so. Then, on this occasion of the arising of this matter, he brought up this past event:
"Once upon a time, monks, a certain world-renowned brahmin lived in Bārāṇasī;

he was a master of the three Vedas, including the glossaries (Nighaṇṭu) and liturgical formulas (Keṭubha), along with phonology (Sakkharappabheda) and etymology (Padaka), with history as the fifth [Veda]."
He was a master of exposition, unerring in the Lokāyata system and the marks of a Great Man; he taught the mantras to about five hundred young brahmins.
These young brahmins were wise, grasping much quickly and reflecting well upon it, and what they had learned did not perish from them.
That brahmin, moreover, did not keep anything back like a teacher’s secret fist, but taught them as one pours water from one jar into another.
Having had all those young men master every craft, he said to them, "This much is the craft that is beneficial both in this present life and in the life to come.
Those young men, conceiving the pride of thinking, "Whatever our teacher knows, we too know;
we too are now teachers," from then on lived without respect for their teacher and abandoned their duties. The teacher—

Having understood this, he thought, "I shall humble their pride. One day, when those young brahmins had come to his attendance hall, paid their respects, and sat down, he said to them, "Sirs, I wish to ask a question; are you capable of answering?
They replied impulsively, "Ask, teacher! Ask, teacher! just like those intoxicated by the pride of learning. The teacher said:
“Time devours all beings, including itself;
and he who has become a devourer of time devours the one who cooks beings.”—
“Dear ones, answer this question.”
Having reflected thus, being unable to understand it, they remained silent. The teacher said, "Enough, dear ones; go now; you may discuss it tomorrow," and dismissed them.
Ten or twenty of them, having gathered together, could not see either the beginning or the end of that question.
Returning, they reported to the teacher, "We do not understand the meaning of this question. The teacher [said] to them...
For the sake of reproving him, he spoke this verse:
“Many heads of men, hairy and large, Are fastened upon their necks; Yet here, perhaps, is one who truly has ears.”
The meaning of the verse: Many heads of men are seen;
all of them are hairy, all are large, and all are fixed upon a neck, not held in the hand like a palm fruit.
There is no difference between them in these respects. But here, the word “one with ears” (*kaṇṇavā*) is said with reference to oneself. “One with ears” means...

"He is wise. But not one of them had an ear-hole; having heard this, those young brahmins became abashed, with shoulders slumped and heads cast down, scratching the ground with their fingers, and remained silent.
Then, seeing their lack of shame, the teacher said, "Learn the question, dear ones," and he answered the question.
"Time" (*kāla*) refers to the time before the meal, the time after the meal, and so forth.
"Beings" (*bhūtāni*) is a designation for sentient beings (*satta*). For time does not devour the skin, flesh, and so on of beings;
rather, it is said to "eat" and "devour" them by exhausting their life-span, beauty, and strength, crushing their youth, and destroying their health. All [these] together with themselves.
Thus devouring, he leaves nothing out; he devours everything. Not only does he devour other beings, but together with them, he even devours himself.
For the time before the meal does not reach the time after the meal. This same principle applies to the time after the meal and so forth.
And "one who devours time" (*kālaghaso*) is a designation for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
For he is called "one who has eaten death" (*kālaghaso*) because he remains having spent his life consuming [the results of] future rebirths.

He is called "one who has cooked the cooker of beings" (*bhūtapacaniṃ pacī*); that is, he has cooked—that is, burned with the fire of knowledge and reduced to ashes—that craving which cooks beings in the states of misery (*apāya*).
There is also a reading *pajaniṃ*, meaning "that which produces" or "that which brings about rebirth."

Then those young men, seeing the meaning of the question made clear by their teacher’s answer—just as the uneven terrain of the night becomes visible by the light of a thousand lamps—thought: "From now on, we shall live in the service of our teacher for the rest of our lives;
truly great are these teachers, for we had fostered a pride in our own great learning and yet did not understand the meaning of even a four-line verse."
"I know," they said; thus, with their pride humbled, they performed the proper service for their teacher just as before and became destined for heaven.

"Monks, at that time I was their teacher, and these monks were the young brahmin students. In this way, I previously caused those who were wandering about with their heads held high by pride to have their pride humbled.

Having heard this Jātaka, those monks thought, "In the past, too, we were harmed by pride alone," and becoming even more thoroughly humbled, they became devoted to their own beneficial meditation subjects.

Then, on one occasion, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī and stayed at the Gotamaka Shrine. Perceiving that the maturity of knowledge in these five hundred bhikkhus had reached its peak, he delivered this Gotamaka Sutta:
“Bhikkhus, it is with direct knowledge that I teach the Dhamma, not without direct knowledge; with a foundation, I teach the Dhamma...
with a basis for wonder, I teach the Dhamma, not without a basis for wonder. For me, bhikkhus, when teaching the Dhamma with direct knowledge...”
"From dawn... [as before] ...it is not without wonder. Counsel should be given; instruction should be given.
And it is enough for you, monks, to be satisfied, enough to be elated, enough to be joyful: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened;
the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing rightly. This is what the Blessed One said. And with this exposition, the Blessed One—
"While this was being spoken, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook.

Upon hearing this discourse, those five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) on that very seat. Thus, the teaching reached its conclusion at this point.
The commentary on the eighth method, the section on the Tathāgata, is finished.
The commentary on the *Mūlapariyāyasutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished. 2.
The commentary on the *Sabbāsavasutta*.
14. Thus have I heard... [pe] ...at Sāvatthī: this is the *Sabbāsava-sutta*. Herein, this is the commentary on the previously unexplained words:
"Sāvatthī" is the city that served as the dwelling place of the seer Savattha;
thus do the etymologists say, just as one speaks of Kākandī, Mākandī, or Kosambī. However, the teachers of the Commentaries say: "Whatever there may be among humans for use and enjoyment..."

*Sāvatthī* is so called because "everything exists here" (*sabbam ettha atthi*). It is also *Sāvatthī* based on the statement, "When the Teacher was present, when asked 'What goods are there?', he would reply, 'Everything is there'.
Furthermore: "At all times, all requisites are provided in Sāvatthī."
Therefore, taking all these factors together, it is called Sāvatthī.
It is the delightful city of the Kosalans, beautiful to behold and enchanting,
never devoid of ten sounds, and well-supplied with food and drink.
“Sāvatthī, the supreme city of the gods, has attained growth and abundance; it is prosperous, flourishing, and delightful, like the city of Alakamandā.
In that Sāvatthī, at Jetavana—here, he is called Jeta because he conquers (*jināti*) his own adversaries. By the king...
Or, he is called Jeta because he was born when his enemies were conquered (*jita*); or, out of a desire for auspiciousness, he was given that very name, Jeta.
The grove of Jeta is Jetavana. For it was planted, grown, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner;
therefore it is called Jetavana, and [the phrase] "in that Jetavana" refers to that place.
"Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery": here, that householder was named Sudatta according to the name given by his parents.

However, because he provided alms-food (*piṇḍa*) to the destitute (*anātha*) at all times—due to the fulfillment of all his desires, the absence of the stain of stinginess, and his possession of qualities such as compassion—he became known as Anāthapiṇḍika.
Living beings especially find delight (*āramanti*) therein.
Or, it is a "pleasure grove" (*ārāma*) for those who have gone forth;

the meaning is that people come from here and there and delight, find enjoyment, and dwell without weariness because of its beauty—due to its flowers, fruits, and so on—and because it possesses the five factors of an ideal dwelling, such as being neither too far nor too near.

Alternatively, it is called a "pleasure grove" because, by means of the aforementioned excellence, even when one has gone to various places, one brings them back within oneself and finds delight therein.
For indeed, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had purchased the park from Prince Jeta at a cost of eighteen crores of gold by covering it with a layer of gold coins,
and after having had dwellings constructed for eighteen crores of gold and completed the festival of the monastery for eighteen crores of gold—
thus, through this relinquishment of fifty-four crores of gold— he [dedicated it] to the community headed by the Buddha.
It was offered to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is called "the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. In that monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika.
And here, the mention of "in Jeta’s Grove" is the praise of the former owner, while "in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika" is the praise of the latter owner.
What is the purpose of praising these two? It is so that those who desire merit may follow their example.
For in that instance, when the gate-tower palace was being built, there were eighteen crores of gold obtained from the sale of the land and trees worth many crores;
this was the gift of Jeta, while for Anāthapiṇḍika it was fifty-four crores.
Thus, by praising those two, the Venerable Ānanda shows that those desiring merit perform meritorious deeds, and thereby encourages others who desire merit to follow their example.
Why did the Blessed One speak this sutta, beginning with "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the method for the restraint of all taints"?
It was for the purpose of showing the practice leading to the destruction of the taints, starting from the purification of the defilements of those bhikkhus.
In that context, "the method for the restraint of all taints" means the cause for the restraint of all taints—that is, the cause which constitutes restraint—by means of which they are restrained.
Having been closed off, they go to destruction—which is to say, non-arising and cessation—they are abandoned and do not proceed;
this is the meaning of "cause" (*kāraṇa*). In this context, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*āsavanti*); it is said that they stream and proceed even from the eye... up to the mind.

Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow according to their nature as far as the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), or according to their scope as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). These [are the *āsava*].
The meaning is that these [defilements] occur having made this very sphere their limit. For this particle *ā* has the sense of making something one's limit (*antokaraṇa*).
They are called *āsava* (taints) in the sense of being fermented for a long time, like wine and the like; they are also called *āsava* because they are "like taints.

For in the world, wine and such things that have been fermented for a long time are called *āsava*. And if they are *āsava* in the sense of being fermented for a long time, then only these [defilements] deserve to be so called.
For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is discerned; before this, ignorance did not exist,” and so forth.
Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) and pour out the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Of these etymologies, the former ones apply where the defilements (*kilesa*) are referred to as *āsava*, while the latter applies to karma as well. And it is not only...
The defilements (kilesa) themselves are indeed the taints (āsava), but there are also various kinds of calamities.

For in the Suttas, in the passage: "Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma for the sake of restraint from the taints pertaining only to the present life," it is the defilements that constitute the root of dispute which are referred to as taints.
“Those taints by which one might be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;
by which one might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain human status—
those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.”
Herein, there are the actions pertaining to the three planes and all remaining unwholesome states.

Regarding the phrase, "for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives," here the various calamities consist of the reproach of others, remorse, execution, imprisonment, and so forth, as well as the manifold sufferings of the woeful states. As for these taints, they are to be understood according to how and where they have been presented.
In this regard, they should be understood as follows.
For in the Vinaya, these are first presented in two ways: "for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives.
In the *Saḷāyatana-vagga*, they are stated thus: "Friends, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance."
They appear in three ways. In other discourses and in the Abhidhamma, those same [three] appear together with the taint of views as fourfold.
In the *Nibbedhikapariyāya*: "Bhikkhus, there are taints leading to hell;
there are taints leading to the animal realm; there are taints leading to the sphere of hungry ghosts; there are taints leading to the human world."
“There are taints leading to the world of the devas”—thus they appear in five ways. In the *Chakkanipāta*:
“There are, bhikkhus, taints to be abandoned by restraint,” and so forth—in this manner they appear in six ways.
But in this sutta, those same [taints] appear in seven ways together with those to be abandoned by vision. This, then, is the etymology and the classification of the term *āsava*.
Regarding the term *saṃvarapada*, however: it is called *saṃvara* because it restrains (*saṃvarayati*). The meaning is that it covers over, prevents, and does not allow [the unwholesome] to proceed.
For instance, in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, I allow you to enter seclusion after having restrained the door while secluded during the day," and "I call it the restraint of the sense-faculties;
by means of wisdom they are covered over," it refers to *saṃvara* in the sense of covering over.

This self-restraint (saṃvara) is fivefold: restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara), restraint of mindfulness (satisaṃvara), restraint of knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara), restraint of patience (khantisamvara), and restraint of energy (vīriyasaṃvara).
Among these, “endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha” refers to restraint of virtue; for here it is the virtue of the Pātimokkha that is called restraint.
In such passages as “he attains restraint over the eye-faculty,” it is restraint of mindfulness; for here it is mindfulness that is the restraint.
It is said: “I declare the restraint of the streams; by means of wisdom they are closed off. This refers to the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*).

Here, it is stated that it is called “restraint” (*saṃvara*) in the sense of closing off, because “by means of wisdom they are closed off. Furthermore, according to the method beginning with, “He is patient toward cold... [and so on]...
he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire,” the restraints of patience (*khanti*) and energy (*vīriya*) are also presented right here. And of these—
The state of restraint (*saṃvara*) should be understood because it is included under this summary heading: "the method for the restraint of all taints" (*sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāya*).
Furthermore, these five kinds of restraint are indeed presented here; among them, the restraints of patience and energy have already been mentioned.

However, the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) is expressed here by the words: "He [avoids] that improper seat and that improper resort. And: "Reflecting wisely... [is the restraint of mindfulness].
"Restraint by means of the faculty of the eye" refers to restraint through mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*). "Reflecting upon everything" refers to restraint through knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*).
By taking the most prominent [factor], however, seeing, employing, and developing constitute restraint through knowledge.

They are called "modes" (*pariyāya*) because phenomena proceed by means of them; what is meant is that they go toward arising or cessation. Up to this point, it is the "mode of restraint regarding all taints" (*sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāya*).
Whatever needs to be said here has already been stated. 15.
Now, regarding the phrases "of one who knows" (*jānato*) and so forth: "one who knows" (*jānato*) means of one who knows; "one who sees" (*passato*) means of one who sees.
Both terms have the same meaning; only the phrasing differs. Even though this is so, [the term] "one who knows" refers to the person by way of the characteristic of knowledge (*ñāṇalakkhaṇa*).
He explains: for knowledge has the characteristic of knowing. "Sees" is said with reference to the power of knowledge, for knowledge has the power of seeing.
A person endowed with knowledge sees the phenomena revealed by knowledge through that knowledge, just as one with eyes sees forms with the eye.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of generating wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) that one knows how unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) does not arise.
"Seeing"—this is the essential point here. However, some teachers utter much conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), which is not appropriate to this meaning.
"The destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*) means the abandoning of the taints, the arising of the absolute destruction of the taints, the state of being destroyed, the state of non-existence;
for this alone is the meaning of the destruction of the taints in this sutta and in such passages as, "Through the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind."
In other contexts, however, even the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna are called the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya). For it is said:
“For the trainee who is still in training, following the straight path, Knowledge regarding destruction comes first; immediately after that, full knowledge follows.”

In such passages as these, the path is called the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*); in passages such as “Through the destruction of the taints one becomes a recluse,” it refers to the fruit. [And it is said:
“For one who observes the faults of others, who is constantly perceiving blame;”
"In such passages as 'His taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints,' nibbāna is called 'the destruction of the taints.
As for 'not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see'—the meaning is: 'I do not speak [of this] for one who neither knows nor sees. By this..."
Those who claim that purity comes through restraint and so forth even for one who does not know and does not see are refuted.

Alternatively, by the first two phrases the means was stated; by this [phrase], the negation of what is not the means is expressed. And here, in brief, it is shown that knowledge is a synonym for the restraint of the taints (*āsava-saṃvara*).
Now, wishing to show that which leads to the destruction of the taints for one who knows, [the Blessed One asks]: "And what, bhikkhus, for one who knows?"
He began with the tail; regarding that, there are many kinds of knowledge. For some monk, by his very nature, knows how to make a sunshade (*chatta*);
another knows how to make one of the various requisites such as robes (*cīvara*).

When such a person performs these tasks while standing at the head of the observance (*vatta*), it cannot be said that such knowledge is not the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the paths and fruits. However, he who [is devoted] to the Teaching...
Having gone forth, one knows how to perform medical treatments and the like; for one who knows in this way, the taints (āsava) simply increase.
Therefore, showing that very thing by which the destruction of the taints occurs for one who knows and sees, he said:
"proper attention (yoniso manasikāra) and improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra)."
In this context, "appropriate attention" (yoniso manasikāra) means skillful attention, path-attention;

it is the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the application, the directing, and the attention toward the impermanent and so forth, by way of the method beginning with "it is impermanent," or by way of that which is in conformity with the Truths.
This is called appropriate attention.
"Unwise attention" (*ayoniso manasikāra*) means attention that is not a skillful means, attention that is off the path.

To attend to what is impermanent as permanent, to what is suffering as happiness, to what is non-self as self, and to what is foul as beautiful—this is unwise attention, attention that is off the path.
Or else, the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the mental engagement, the directing of the mind, and the attention that is contrary to the Truths—this is called unwise attention.

"He attends to. For one who knows how to generate such wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and who sees in such a way that unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) does not arise, there is the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
Now, showing the logical justification for this very point, he said: "Monks, through unwise attention... [etc]... they are abandoned. By that—

What is meant? Since the taints arise for one who attends to things unreasonably and are abandoned by one who attends to them reasonably, it should be understood that for one who knows how to arouse reasonable attention and sees in such a way that unreasonable attention does not arise, there is the destruction of the taints. This, then, is the brief commentary on this point.
This, however, is the detailed exposition: herein, the entire subsequent sutta is bound together by these two terms, "properly" (*yoniso*) and "improperly" (*ayoniso*).
Indeed, the entire subsequent sutta is stated by way of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*).

For the round has its root in improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), and the turning away from the round has its root in proper attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). How so? For when improper attention increases...
He fulfills two factors: ignorance and craving for existence. When there is ignorance, there is the formula: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise...

[and so on] ...there is the origination of this mass of suffering. When there is craving, there is the formula: "With craving as condition, clinging arises... [and so on] ...there is the origination [of suffering].
Thus, this person, who is full of improper attention, is like a ship lost by the force of a gale.

Like a herd of cattle fallen into a whirlpool in the Ganges, or like a beast of burden yoked to a water-wheel, it repeatedly undergoes whirling and revolving among the wombs of existence, the destinations, the stations of consciousness, and the abodes of beings;
such, then, is the cycle rooted in improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*).
But when proper attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) increases—“For one endowed with proper attention, monks, this... [it leads to the cessation of the cycle].

Because of the statement, “It is to be expected for a bhikkhu that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path,” he fulfills the Eightfold Path with right view as its foremost.

And that which is right view is true knowledge (*vijjā*); with the arising of that true knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance (*avijjā*). With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)... [and so on].
"Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering"—in this way, the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) should be understood as rooted in wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).
Thus, the entire subsequent sutta is bound together by these two phrases.

And since it is so bound, because the arising [of suffering] would not be intelligible if it were stated after the prior demonstration of the abandoning of the taints (*āsava*), [the sequence is thus established].
This is logical. For what has already been abandoned does not arise again; rather, it is logical that there is the abandoning of those things that have arisen.
Therefore, even by way of the reverse order of the summary, he said: "Bhikkhus, for one who attends to things unskillfully (*ayoniso*), etc.
Therein, "attending to things unskillfully" means for one who generates the aforementioned kind of unskillful attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). Those that have not yet arisen...

Regarding the phrase "and thus the taints arise": here, it refers to one who, having previously never before obtained requisites such as robes or any other pleasant object from attendants, co-residents, or pupils, attends to it unreasonably as "beautiful" and "pleasant";
or else, it refers to one who attends unreasonably—either in this way or that—to some other object never experienced before.

The taints arise; it should be understood that they arise as something previously unarisen, for otherwise, in this beginningless saṃsāra, there would be no such thing as taints that have not arisen before.

Furthermore, even regarding a basis or an object experienced in the past, by virtue of one's natural purity, or through any one of the following—namely, recitation, interrogation, mastery of the scriptures, new work, or wise attention—previously...
Having not arisen previously, they suddenly arise later through such-and-such conditions;

these too should be understood as "arisen" in the sense that what was unarisen now arises. Furthermore, when they arise repeatedly upon those same bases and objects, they are said to "increase" once they have already arisen.
For there can be no increase of those things that have arisen for the very first time.

"And as for 'properly,' monks": herein, one whose taints do not arise either through natural purity—as was the case with the Venerable Mahākassapa and Bhaddā Kāpilānī—or by means of such causes as recitation and interrogation, yet who knows:
"My taints have not been eradicated by the Path; come now, for their eradication..."
"I shall practice. Then, by the cultivation of the path, he eradicates them all. It is said that for him, those taints (*āsava*) that have not yet arisen do not arise.

However, when taints arise suddenly due to a lapse of mindfulness while one is still acting as an agent, he becomes stirred with a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) and, striving with wise attention (*yoniso padahanto*), cuts off those taints. For him—
"Those that have arisen are said to be abandoned," as in the case of the Elder Mahātissa of Maṇḍalārāma.
It is said that he was receiving his formal instruction in that very monastery; then, while he was walking for alms in the village, a defilement arose toward an unwholesome object.
Having suppressed it through insight (vipassanā), he returned to the monastery. Even in his dreams, that [defilement]...
The object did not appear clearly to him. Thinking, "This defilement, having increased, will lead to rebirth in the states of misery," he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having taken leave of his teacher and departed from the monastery, he received the meditation subject on the foulness (*asubhakammaṭṭhāna*)—the antidote to lust—from the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita.
Entering a thicket of trees, he took up a rag-robe (*paṃsukūlacīvara*).
Having spread out [the seat] and sat down, he severed the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure by means of the path of non-returning;

then, rising and paying homage to his teacher, he reached the stage of the recitation on the following day. However, for those [defilements] that have already arisen and are currently present, there is no abandoning through the practice of the path.

16. Now, taking up this very phrase, "the arisen taints are abandoned," the King of Dhamma, who is skilled in the various modes of teaching, spoke the passage beginning with, "There are, bhikkhus, taints to be abandoned by seeing," in order to expand the teaching and reveal other causes for abandoning those taints which are being abandoned in their various aspects. Therein:
"To be abandoned by seeing" means they are to be abandoned by the act of seeing. This method applies everywhere.
Regarding the commentary on the taints (āsava) to be abandoned by seeing:
now, desiring to explain those terms in their proper sequence, [the Blessed One said]: "And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by seeing?"

Having posed the question, "What is to be abandoned?", he began the teaching by way of reference to the individual, starting with the words, "Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling," according to the method already explained in the commentary on the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*.

In that context, "he does not understand the phenomena that should be brought to mind" means he does not understand those phenomena that should be adverted to and attended to. "That which should not be brought to mind" [is as follows]:...

The opposite of this is the case. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. However, there is no fixed rule regarding these phenomena (dhammas) based on their intrinsic nature (*dhammata*) such that "these must be attended to" and "those must not be attended to";

rather, there is a distinction based on their mode (*ākāra*). In whatever mode they serve as a basis for the arising of unwholesome states when being attended to, they should not be attended to in that mode.
In whatever mode they serve as a basis for the arising of wholesome states, in that mode [they should be attended to].
[These things] should be brought to mind. Therefore, he said: "Bhikkhus, for one who brings such phenomena to mind, the unarisen taint of sensual desire...
and so forth. In this context, "for one" (*yass*) means for that uninstructed worldling (*puthujjana*). "Bringing to mind" (*manasikaroto*) means attending to or directing the attention toward them.
Regarding the phrase "the unarisen taint of sensual desire," the particle *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). Therefore, just as...
When it is said, “Bhikkhus, as far as beings exist—whether footless or two-footed... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them,” the meaning is “both the footless and the two-footed.

And just as when it is said, “for the stability of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking existence,” the meaning is “both those who have come to be and those seeking existence”;
and just as [in the phrase] “from fire or from water... [the meaning is both].
When it is said, “or from the breaking of friendship,” the meaning is: from fire, from water, and from the breaking of friendship; so too here, the meaning should be understood as:
the unarisen taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases. The same applies to the remaining [taints].

And herein, the taint of sensual desire is lust for the five strands of sense pleasure. The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) is the will and lust for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, namely, attachment to meditative absorption (*jhānanikanti*).
And [it] is accompanied by views such as eternalism and annihilationism. Thus, the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) also merges into the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*).
The taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) is non-knowing regarding the Four Noble Truths.

Therein, for one who attends to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) as gratification, the unarisen taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*) arises and the arisen increases. For one who attends to sublime states (*mahaggatadhamma*) as gratification...

The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises when it has not yet arisen, and having arisen, it increases. It should be understood that for one who attends to the phenomena in the three planes as being the basis for the four perversions (*vipallāsa*), the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) arises when it has not yet arisen, and having arisen, it increases.
The "bright side" (*sukkappakka*) should be elaborated by way of the opposite of the method already stated.

But why are only three outflows (āsava) mentioned here? Because they are the opposites of liberation. For the outflow of sensual desire (kāmāsava) is the opposite of the wishless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha), while the other two are the opposites of the signless and emptiness liberations (animitta-suññata-vimokkha).
Therefore, by showing that those who give rise to these three outflows are deprived of the three liberations, whereas those who do not give rise to them possess them, [the text] mentions these three.
It should be understood that [the outflows] have been stated thus. Or rather, it has been explained that the outflow of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is indeed stated here as well.
"By way of attention to phenomena that should not be attended to" means by reason of attention;
what is meant is: because one attends to those phenomena, therefore [they arise]. This same method applies to the second phrase as well: "Unarisen outflows arise..."
"And arisen taints increase"—this is the conclusion, stated without distinction, regarding the very taints mentioned below. 18.
At this point, as for that "uninstructed worldling" who was mentioned in the teaching based on the individual to illustrate the taints to be abandoned through vision:
because, for one who attends to things "unwisely," monks, not only those [taints] that have not yet arisen...

Thus, having shown the obsession with even the taints of sensual desire and the rest—which were described in general terms as "taints arise conditioned by improper attention"—he now shows those taints that are to be abandoned through vision by means of that same person, saying:
"He attends improperly thus: 'Did I exist in the past? and so forth. This is stated under the heading of doubt.
And herein, this teaching was commenced in order to show the taint of views as well.

Its meaning is as follows: he in whom these taints arise in the manner described is a worldling (*puthujjana*); and he who is described by the method beginning with "the uninstructed" is likewise a worldling.
Such a person attends to things in an improper way, by means that are not skillful and by a wrong path. How so?

“Did I exist in the past? … [and so on] … where will he go? What is meant by this? He attends to the matter in an improper way (*ayoniso*), whereby the sixteenfold doubt (*vicikicchā*)—stated in the manner beginning with “Did I exist?”—arises in him.
Therein, “Did I exist? Or did I not exist? arises based on the mode of eternalism (*sassata*) and the mode of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppatti*).
He doubts whether his own self existed or did not exist in the past. It should not be asked "for what reason," for the foolish worldling, like a madman, functions in whatever way he may.

Furthermore, improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) alone is the reason here. But what is the reason for such improper attention? It is that very state of being a worldling, which is absent in the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
Or [it refers to] non-seeing and so forth. But surely even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) attends to things thoroughly (*yoniso manasikaroti*).

Who says that he does not attend to them? However, being an ordinary person is not the cause in that case; rather, hearing the true Dhamma, having virtuous friends, and so forth, are the causes therein.
For fish, meat, and the like are not fragrant by their own nature; they become so through the condition of artificial preparation (*abhisaṅkhārapaccaya*).
Furthermore, there are fragrances as well.

Thinking, "What indeed was I?", one entertains doubt based on birth, gender, and rebirth: "Was I a khattiya? Or was I one among the others—brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, or humans?
Thinking, "In what manner indeed?", one entertains doubt based on physical form: "Was I tall? Or short, fair, dark, large-statured, small-statured, and so forth?"

"Another" means he doubts. Some, however, say that he doubts as to the cause, thinking "for what reason did it come to be? based on the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord (Issaranimmāna) and so forth.

"Having been what, did I become what?"—this refers to birth and so on; he doubts his own successive states, such as: "Having been a khattiya, did I become a brahmin... [and so on] ...having been a deva, did I become a human? In all these cases, "addhāna" is a designation for time.

"Shall I exist or shall I not exist?"—relying on the modes of eternalism and annihilationism, one wavers regarding the existence or non-existence of oneself in the future. The rest here is exactly as previously stated.
"Or in the present time"—this refers to taking the entire present period, beginning from the current rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) up to the limit of death (*cuti*).
"One is perplexed internally" means one is doubtful regarding one's own aggregates (*khandha*).
[The thought] "I am" arises. One doubts one's own existence, wondering, "Do I indeed exist? Is this reasonable? Whether it is reasonable or unreasonable—what need is there for such deliberation here?
Furthermore, they cite this example in this context: It is said that the son of Cūḷamātā was shaven, while the son of Mahāmātā was not shaven.
They shaved that son [of Cūḷamātā]. He stood up and wondered, "Am I the son of Cūḷamātā?"
He reflected: "The doubt 'Am I indeed? arises.
The doubt 'Am I not indeed? suspects one's own non-existence. Regarding this, there is the following story:
It is said that a certain man catching fish, thinking his own thigh—which had become cold from being in the water for a long time—was a fish, struck it. Another...
While guarding a field on the edge of a cemetery, he lay down terrified and huddled together.
Upon waking, he thought his two knees were *yakkhas* and struck them. Thus he doubted, thinking, "Am I not [a human]?
Being a khattiya, he doubted his own status as a khattiya, wondering, "What indeed am I? This same method applies to the others as well.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as being a deva while not knowing one’s state as a deva. Yet even he doubts in this manner: "Am I possessed of form, or am I formless?
If it is asked why the khattiyas and others do not know [this], it is because their rebirth in various families occurs beyond the range of direct perception (*apaccakkha*).
Furthermore, householders such as the *potthalika* and others perceive those who have gone forth as householders, and those who have gone forth likewise...
“Is my deed indeed blameworthy?”—in such a manner they perceive themselves as householders. And even kings perceive themselves as gods, just like ordinary men.
How so? It is exactly according to the method already stated: “How am I? However, in this case, they grasp onto the notion that there exists within [the body] something called a “soul” (jīva).
Based on its shape and form, one who is doubting whether "Am I long, or am I short, square, triangular, hexagonal, octagonal, or sixteen-sided? should be understood as doubting "How indeed am I?
However, there is no one who does not know the present shape of their own body.
"From where has he come, and where will he go?"—thus one doubts regarding the place from which the individual existence (attabhāva) comes and the place to which it goes.
Having thus shown doubt (vicikicchā) in its sixteenfold division, now that this teaching was commenced to show the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) under the heading of this doubt, [the text] shows it:
"For him who attends to things in such an improper manner (ayoniso manasikaroto), of the six..."

He says, "Of views," and so forth. Therein, it is meant that just as this doubt arises for that person, so too, because of the firm establishment of that very unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) accompanied by doubt, one of the six views arises for him. In all those instances, the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*).
What is meant is that a view arises in such and such a manner. Herein, the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*)—“I have a self”—grasps the existence of a self at all times.

“Truly and actually” means from the standpoint of what has come to be and from the standpoint of what is firm; it means grasping it as “this is the truth” with a sense of actuality and extreme firmness. However, the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) is: “I have no self.”

Because an existing being grasps at various forms of non-existence (vibhava) here and there. Alternatively, the former [view] is the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) because it grasps that [the self] exists in all three times;
the latter is the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi) because it grasps that only the present exists.
The latter [view] is also the annihilationist view because it grasps that [the self] does not exist in the past and future, like those who hold the view that offerings are merely ashes.
One who grasps that "there was simply nothing in the past" holds an eternalist view (*sassataditthi*) of spontaneous origination (*adhiccasamuppatti*).

Regarding the phrase "I perceive myself by means of self," having grasped the aggregates as "self" under the heading of the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*), one perceives the remaining aggregates through perception;
thus it occurs: "By means of this self, I perceive this self. Regarding "by means of self, [perceiving] non-self," it refers to the aggregate of perception alone.
Having grasped [the self] as "self" and the other four aggregates as "not-self," for one who knows them through perception, this occurs:

perceiving the aggregate of perception as "not-self" while grasping the other four as "self. For one who knows them through perception, this occurs: [perceiving the self] as "not-self" by means of what is not-self.
All these are indeed the views of eternalism and annihilationism.
Furthermore, "one who speaks" (*vada*), "one who feels" (*vedayya*), and so forth, are modes of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) specifically to the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*).
In this context, "one who speaks" (*vada*) means one who performs verbal action; that is what is meant. "One who feels" (*vedayya*) means one who knows and experiences;
that is what is meant. What does he experience? There, in various circumstances, he experiences the ripening (*vipāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
"In each and every" means in those various classes of beings, destinies, stations, abodes, and bodies, or in their respective objects. "Eternal" (*nicca*) means devoid of arising and passing away.

"Stable" (*dhruva*) means firm and substantial. "Permanent" (*sassata*) means existing at all times. "Of an unchanging nature" (*avipariṇāmadhamma*) means not subject to abandoning its own essential state;
like a *kakaṇṭaka* (a kind of bird), it does not undergo various transformations. "For all eternity" (*sassatisama*) refers to the moon, the sun, the ocean, the great earth, and the mountains.
By worldly convention they are called "eternal. "Eternal-like" means equal to the eternal.
This view arises for one who grasps that it will remain exactly as it is for as long as the eternals endure.
This is what is called a "position of views," monks, and so forth. Here, "this" is a demonstrative indication of that which is about to be discussed.
And this is called "gone to views" (*diṭṭhigata*) by way of its connection with the act of viewing, not by way of its connection with the views themselves.
Here, "view" (*diṭṭhi*) is itself "gone to views," just as excrement is "gone to dung. Alternatively, this seeing has "gone among views" because it is included within the sixty-two views;
thus it is "gone to views. Or else, that which has been reached by a view is "gone to views. For this—such as "I have a self"—is merely the reaching of a view.
"What is meant is that here there is no self, nor anything permanent. And this view is a "thicket" (*gahana*) in the sense of being difficult to extricate;
a "wilderness" (*kantāra*) in the sense of being difficult to cross over and in the sense of being dangerous, like a wilderness of famine or a wilderness of wild beasts;
and a "disorder" (*visūka*) in the sense of piercing through right view or in the sense of being contrary to it—sometimes [viewing] things as eternal...
Because it sometimes grasps at annihilation, its movement is distorted; thus it is called "fluttering" (*vipphandita*). In the sense of binding, it is a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
Therefore he said: "The thicket of views... the fetter of views. Now, showing that very same sense of binding, he said: "Bound by the fetter of views," and so forth.
This is the summary of its meaning: by means of this fetter of views...

The worldling (*puthujjana*), being fettered by these [defilements] such as birth and so forth, is not liberated. Or rather, to say more: he is not even released from the suffering of the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

20. Having thus shown the outflow of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) in its sixfold division, since the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) is already indicated by the mention of the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the others—for those overcome by ignorance (*avijjā*) [cling to them] for the sake of sensual pleasure, or for the sake of the happiness of existence (*bhava-sukha*) and the purification of existence—[it need not be mentioned separately].
Outside of this [Dhamma], recluses and brahmins cling to rules and observances; therefore, without showing that [clinging],
and because it is already included by the mention of "views," he now shows the person who abandons the taints that are to be abandoned by seeing,
and in order to show the abandonment of those taints, [he speaks] first of the worldling who attends to things in an improper manner.
Having shown their arising, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with, "But the one who has heard, monks," in order to show the abandoning of their opposite.
Its meaning should be understood according to the method explained below and by way of its opposite, up until the point where it says, "This is suffering.
And as for the opposite: it is the opposite of one who is unskilled and undisciplined in the Noble Dhamma in every respect.
This should be understood as "the learned noble disciple, skilled in the noble Dhamma, well-disciplined in the noble Dhamma.

Furthermore, from the time insight reaches its summit until the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), he should be understood as a "noble disciple" in a sense corresponding to that [intermediate] state.
21. Regarding the passage beginning with “He attends wisely thus: ‘This is suffering,’” the exposition of the meaning is as follows:
That noble disciple who takes the four truths as his subject of meditation understands that the aggregates of the three planes, excluding craving, are suffering;
craving is the origin of suffering; the non-occurrence of both is cessation; and the path is that which leads to cessation. Thus, having previously [learned] from the presence of a teacher...
Having mastered the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, at a later time, having ascended the path of insight,
he attends wisely to those aggregates belonging to the three planes as "this is suffering," and he both directs his attention and contemplates them by means of the appropriate method and way.
For here, until the attainment of the stream-entry path, insight proceeds with mental attention as its primary instrument.
He applies appropriate attention thus: "That craving which gives rise to and brings about this very suffering is the origin.
And because both suffering and its origin cease and no longer proceed upon reaching this state, he applies appropriate attention thus: "This, namely Nibbāna, is the cessation of suffering."
He attends wisely, thinking: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—the Noble Eightfold Path that brings about cessation.
He both directs his attention and practices insight by means of this method and this path.

Herein, this is the method: adherence exists in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), but it does not exist in the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*). Therefore, [he reflects]: "This exists in this..."
By means of the method beginning with "the earth element and water element in the body," etc., one discerns the four primary elements and, following that,
the derived material phenomena within one's own continuity, and thus defines them as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). As one defines that,
when the consciousness and mental factors arise taking those as their object, one defines them as these four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
Then he defines these five aggregates as suffering. Furthermore, in brief, they consist of only two portions:
name and form. This name-and-form arises with cause and condition;
he defines its causes and conditions as ignorance, the craving for existence, kamma, nutriment, and so forth. Then, of those...
Having defined the specific characteristics of the conditions and the phenomena produced by those conditions exactly as they are, he applies the characteristic of impermanence, thinking:
"These phenomena, having not been, come to be. He applies the characteristic of suffering, thinking: "They are suffering because they are oppressed by arising and passing away.
He applies the characteristic of non-self, thinking: "They are non-self because they do not exercise mastery over themselves. Having thus applied the three characteristics:
Proceeding with insight in successive order, he attains the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
At that moment, he penetrates the four truths through a single penetration and realizes them through a single clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*).

He penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding (*pariññā*), origin through the penetration of abandoning (*pahāna*), and cessation through the penetration of realization (*sacchikiriyā*).
He penetrates the path by means of penetration through development (*bhāvanā-paṭivedha*). He realizes suffering through the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*)...
[and so on] ...he realizes the path through the clear realization of development (*bhāvanā-abhisamaya*), yet not by means of mutually distinct knowledges.

For by means of a single knowledge alone, he both penetrates and realizes cessation as its object (*ārammaṇa*) and the remaining [truths] by way of their functions (*kicca*). At that time, it does not occur to him thus:

—“I fully understand suffering,” or …pe… “I develop the path. Furthermore, for one who realizes cessation by making it the object through penetration, that very knowledge performs the function of fully understanding suffering, the function of abandoning the origin, and the function of developing the path.
For him who thus attends wisely by means of this method:

Three fetters are abandoned: personality-belief with its twenty bases, doubt with its eight bases, and the misapprehension of rules and observances—which consists in the misapprehension that purification comes through rules and observances such as "purification by virtue" or "purification by conduct.
In this context, among the four taints, personality-belief and the misapprehension of rules and observances are both taints, because they are included within the taint of views.

And as for the fetters (*saṃyojana*): doubt (*vicikicchā*) is indeed a fetter, but not an outflow (*āsava*). However, it is called an outflow in the passage, “The outflows to be abandoned by vision,” because it is included therein.
As for the statement, “These are called... [to be] abandoned,” these—namely, personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the rest—are what are known as the outflows to be abandoned by vision.

He spoke thus while showing [this]. Alternatively, since this personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) has been analyzed in its own specific form as "any one of these six views that arises," he said with reference to it: "These, monks, are called...

And because that [personality-belief] is abandoned together with those things to be abandoned by simultaneous arising (*sahajāta-pahāna*), when the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is being abandoned, that which is co-arising with it...
In the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), both the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) are abandoned.

However, the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*)—which is to be abandoned simultaneously [with those two]—arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view by way of the aspiration for the supernatural powers of *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and so forth.

Likewise, the taint of ignorance associated with that [taint of existence], as well as the taint of ignorance that produces killing and other such acts in the two types of consciousness accompanied by grief (*domanassa*), [are abandoned].
Likewise, the outflow of ignorance associated with a mind of doubt is also abandoned; thus, in every respect, all three remaining outflows are abandoned.
Therefore, the use of the plural number should be understood in this sense. This is the intention of the ancients. "To be abandoned by vision":
"vision" refers to the path of stream-entry; the meaning is that they are to be abandoned by that. Why is it the path of stream-entry?
Regarding "seeing": it is because it sees Nibbāna for the first time. Is it not the case that the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhu*) sees it even earlier?
It is not that it does not see; however, having seen it, it does not perform the task that ought to be done because the fetters have not been abandoned. Therefore, it cannot be said that it "sees.
Just as, even after seeing a king somewhere, one has not truly "seen" him in the sense of accomplishing the purpose by presenting a gift.
“The village-dweller who says, ‘Even today I do not see the king,’ is the illustration here.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by seeing is finished.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by restraint follows.

22. Having thus shown the taints (*āsava*) that are to be abandoned by vision, he now says, "And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint (*saṃvara*)," in order to show those enumerated immediately following them.
In this way, the connection is to be understood in all instances. Hereafter, we shall explain merely the meaning.
But surely, there is no such thing as an influx (*āsava*) that cannot be abandoned by either vision (*dassana*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā*);

so why does he show them separately as being abandoned by restraint (*saṃvara*) and so forth? The influxes, which have been suppressed in the preliminary stage by restraint and the other means, reach total eradication through the four paths;
therefore, in the preliminary stage of those paths, [they are abandoned] by these five modes.
He spoke thus showing the abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).

Therefore, this first path of seeing (*dassanamagga*) which has been mentioned, and the three paths that will now be spoken of under the name of "development" (*bhāvanā*), should all be understood as having this as their preliminary practice (*pubbabhāgapatipadā*).

In this context, "here" (*idha*) means in this teaching. "Reflecting" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) means having reflected. Herein, this word *saṅkhā* [is used] in the senses of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*), designation (*paññatti*), and counting (*gaṇanā*).

It is seen [in various senses]. In such passages as “Having reckoned, he partakes of one [thing],” it is seen in the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). In such passages as “The conceptual proliferation of perceptions and formations (*saṅkhā*) operate,” it is seen in the sense of a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*).
In such passages as “The reckoning (*saṅkhā*), the designation (*samaññā*), of those respective phenomena,” it is seen in the sense of a description (*paññatti*).
In such passages as “It is not easy to reckon (*saṅkhātuṃ*),” it is seen in the sense of counting (*gaṇanā*). But here, it should be understood in the sense of knowledge.
"Reflecting wisely" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*) means reflecting by way of a method or a path; that is to say, having understood and having examined.
And here, "reflecting wisely" should be understood as reflecting upon the danger in non-restraint. This [reflection] is as follows:
"It would be better, monks, for the faculty of the eye to be pricked by a red-hot iron pin—burning, blazing, and glowing—"

"It is thoroughly polished, but one does not seize upon the signs or secondary characteristics among forms cognizable by the eye"—thus it should be understood according to the method of the "Discourse on the Burning.
