Regarding the phrase "he dwells restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty":

here, the eye itself is the faculty, thus it is the "eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriya*); it is "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because of restraining, that is to say, because of closing off or shutting [the senses].
This is a designation for mindfulness (*sati*). "Restraint of the eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriyasaṃvara*) means restraint regarding the eye-faculty.
It is like the expressions "a crow standing on a pit," "a tortoise in a well," or "a deer in the forest," and so forth.

In that regard, although there is neither restraint nor non-restraint within the eye-faculty itself—for it is not dependent upon the sensitive matter of the eye (*cakkhupasāda*)—[the term is used figuratively].

Or else, forgetfulness arises even when mindfulness is present. Furthermore, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye, after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) arises and ceases, performing the function of adverting;
then the eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing; then the resultant mind-element performs the function of receiving.

Then, the resultant rootless mind-consciousness element performs the function of investigation; thereafter, the functional rootless mind-consciousness element arises and ceases while accomplishing the function of determining.
Immediately following that, the impulsion (javana) occurs.

In this process as well—neither at the time of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), nor at the time of any of the stages such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth—is there either restraint or non-restraint.

Or [these may] exist [prior to that moment]. However, at the moment of impulsion (*javana*), if immorality (*dussīlya*), forgetfulness (*muṭṭhasacca*), ignorance (*aññāṇa*), impatience (*akkhanti*), or laziness (*kosajja*) arises, this constitutes non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Even though it occurs in such a way, it is called "non-restraint of the eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriye asaṃvaro*). Why?
Because when that exists, the door is unprotected, as are the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), and the other process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*).

How so? Just as when the four gates of a city are left unguarded, even though the interior houses, storehouses, inner chambers, and so forth are well-secured, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded;
for once thieves have entered through the city gate, they may do whatever they wish—exactly so it is when misconduct and other such faults arise in one's mental continuum.
When that lack of restraint exists, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the process-thoughts beginning with adverting (āvajjana).
But when virtue and the other [faculties] have arisen, the door is guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-thoughts beginning with adverting.
How is this so? Just as when the city gates are well secured, even though the houses and such within are not themselves secured, nevertheless—
In a city, all goods are well-guarded and well-protected. For when the city gates are closed, there is no entry for thieves;

in the same way, when impulsion (javana) arises regarding virtue (sīla) and so forth, the "gate" is well-guarded—namely, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), and the other process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta).
Therefore, even while arising at the moment of impulsion, [the mind] is well-guarded by the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya).
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*). Here, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*).
One who is restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty is "one restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty";

the meaning is that he is "endowed" with it. For it is said in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha": "By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is endowed... [and so on] ...he is possessed of it."
Having combined these, the meaning should be understood as "one who is restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty.
Alternatively, *saṃvuto* means "restrained," which is to say he has closed or shut it. One who is restrained by the restraint in the eye-faculty is "restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty";
that is, one who has applied the door-bolt of mindfulness, known as the restraint of the eye-faculty, at the eye-door.
"Closed" means he has shut it fast, like a door-panel at the entrance of a house; this is what is meant.

And this very meaning is more appropriate here, for in such passages as "for one who dwells with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, or for one who dwells with it restrained," this same meaning is seen.
"He dwells" means that, being thus restrained by the restraint of the faculty of the eye, he dwells in whatever mode of conduct.

Regarding the phrase "whatever [evil] of his," etc., the meaning should be understood as follows: for whatever restraint of the faculty of the eye belongs to that bhikkhu who dwells without having restrained it—that is, without having closed or shut it.
Alternatively, the syllable *ye* is a substitute for *yaṃ*, and the particle *hi* is used to fill out the meter; thus the meaning is "of whomsoever" (*ye assa*).

"Would arise" means they would be produced. "Taints, vexation, and fever" refers to the four taints as well as other defilements that cause vexation, namely the fever of the defilements and the fever of kamma-result.

For when a desirable object comes into range at the eye-door, the taint of sensual desire arises in one who relishes and delights in it by way of attachment to sense-pleasures, thinking, "I shall obtain such [an object] in another happy state of existence."
For one who relishes the aspiration for existence, the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises; for one who grasps at "a being" or "belonging to a being," the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) arises;
and the ignorance co-arising with all of these is the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). Thus, the four taints arise.
The other defilements associated with them are afflictions and fevers, or their future results. For these also [arise] only for one who has not restrained himself.
"They might arise while he is dwelling" is what is said.

"Evaṃsa te" means "they would be so for him. It is said that by this means they do not exist, and not otherwise. This same method applies to such passages as "one who reflects wisely and is restrained by the restraint of the ear-faculty," and so forth.
"These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned through restraint" refers to the four [taints] at each of the six doors.

Having thus explained this, it is said that the twenty-four taints (*āsava*) are to be abandoned through restraint (*saṃvara*). And in all these cases, it should be understood that "restraint" refers specifically to the restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*).
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by restraint is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Use (Paṭisevanāpahātabba-āsava): 23.
Regarding the passage beginning with “Reflecting wisely upon the robe,” all that needs to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the discourse on virtue (*sīla*).
“Whatever of his” means whatever one of the requisites—such as robes, almsfood, and so forth—belongs to him. “Not using” means in this way...
For one who does not use [them] wisely. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

However, here it should be understood that the arising of the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*) occurs for one who longs for robes and so forth not yet obtained, or who relishes those already obtained.

Likewise, the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises for one who relishes through the aspiration for existence, thinking, "I shall obtain such things in another fortunate existence or a happy state of rebirth. As for myself...
The arising of the taint of views should be understood as occurring in one who establishes the self-perception: "I obtain" or "I do not obtain," or "This is mine.

Furthermore, the taint of ignorance is co-nascent with all [the other taints]. Thus, the arising of the four taints and their feverish burning should be understood also from the production of the nine types of feeling.
“Monks, these are called the taints to be abandoned by using. Having thus set forth four taints for each individual condition,
making sixteen taints in total, it is said that these are to be abandoned by this reviewing and using known as “restraint through knowledge.”
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by using is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Forbearance:
"By means of wise reflection, he is patient with cold": having reflected by way of a skillful method and path, he is patient.
Cold is endured and borne by one who is cold; unlike a person lacking in heroism, he does not waver or tremble at even a slight chill, nor does he abandon his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

On the contrary, like the Elder Lomasavaṅga, even when touched by no small amount of cold, he does not waver or tremble, but attends solely to his meditation subject. It is said that the Elder [dwelt] in the Piyaṅgu Cave on Mount Cetiyapabbata.

While dwelling in the meditation hall during the interval between rains in the season of snowfall, he spent his time in the open air without ever abandoning his meditation subject, having reflected upon the hell of the world-intervals. In this way, the application of the meaning should be understood regarding heat and other such conditions as well.
For it is only that bhikkhu who endures even excessive heat who, like this Elder, is said to be "one who is patient with heat."
It should be understood as follows: It is said that during the summer season, after his meal, the Elder sat on the walkway outside.
While attending to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), sweat was pouring from his armpits. Then his pupil said to him, "Venerable sir, sit here;
this place is cool. The Elder replied, "Friend, it is out of fear of the heat that I am sitting here," and [he described] the Great Niraya Hell of Avīci.
Having reflected thus, he sat down. And here, "heat" should be understood as the heat of fire;
however, this instance was mentioned by way of the heat of the sun.
Furthermore, even one who, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), has not obtained food or drink for two or three times—his own...
Even when struck by excessive contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and sun, he does not abandon his meditation subject,
as he reflects upon rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts and remains unperturbed. Even when struck by the touch of crawling reptiles,
he does not abandon his meditation subject, as he reflects upon the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Having reflected upon his previous existence, in which he had been turned over many times into the mouths of lions, tigers, and other beasts, he does not abandon his meditation subject (kammatthāna) even when provoked, just like the Elder Padhāniya.
This is what is meant by the phrase: "He is patient with hunger... [and so on]... and the touch of reptiles.
It is said that while the Elder was listening to the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa) in the Kaṇikāra Padhāniya Hall at Khaṇḍacela Monastery, a venomous snake—[its fangs were drawn]—approached him.
A snake bit him. Although the Elder knew this, he sat with a serene mind and listened only to the Dhamma. The force of the poison became rigid.
The Elder, beginning with the circle of his full ordination, reflected upon his virtue and, thinking "I am one whose virtue is pure," gave rise to rapture (*pīti*).
With the arising of that rapture, the poison recoiled and entered the earth. There, right then and there, the Elder attained one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*).
Having attained insight and developed it, he reached the state of Arahatship.

But he who, upon hearing even harsh speech—even that which is offensive because of its very offensiveness and as unpleasant as the "final matter"—reflects only on the virtue of patience and does not waver, like the Elder Abhaya the Dīghabhāṇaka; this one—
"He should be understood as one who is patient with ill-spoken words and offensive paths of speech.

It is said that because the Elder spoke on the practice of the Great Noble Lineage (mahāariyavaṃsa) due to his contentment with requisites and delight in meditation, the entire great village would come [to hear him]. Great honor arose for the Elder, which another elder was unable to endure.
Unable to endure this, the Dīghabhāṇaka reviled him, saying, "You who claim to preach the Ariyavaṃsa are creating a clamor all night long!
Both of them, walking along the same path toward their respective monasteries, traveled for the distance of one *gāvuta*.
Throughout that entire *gāvuta*, he continued to revile him. Then, at the point where the paths to the two monasteries diverged,
Standing there, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka paid homage to him and said, "Venerable sir, this is your path.
He went on as if he had not heard. The elder also went to his monastery, washed his feet, and sat down.
His pupil asked him, "Venerable sir, why did you say nothing at all to him even though he was reviling you for an entire league? The elder—
“Patience alone, friend, is my burden; not impatience. Even if one word were to be extracted [from my speech], I do not see any separation from my meditation subject,” he said.
And here, it should be understood that the word itself is the path of speech.
Furthermore, as for the bodily feeling that has arisen, it is painful in the sense of being suffering, intense in the sense of being thick, and harsh in the sense of being rough.
They are harsh; they are bitter in the sense of being pungent; they are unpleasant due to the absence of gratification; they are disagreeable because they do not increase the mind’s delight;
and they are life-taking because they are capable of depriving one of life. One simply endures them and does not waver. Such is his nature, like the Elder Padhāniya at Cittala Pabbata.
This is how he should be understood as "one who is accustomed to enduring arisen [feelings]... [and so forth]."
It is said that while the Elder was standing after spending the night in strenuous effort, wind arose in his belly.
Unable to endure it, he twisted and turned about. Standing by the side of the walkway, the Elder Piṇḍapātika addressed him:
"Friend, one who has gone forth should be patient. He replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and became motionless.

"Sleeping. The wind split him from the navel up to the heart. The Elder, having suppressed that sensation and practicing insight (vipassanā), became a non-returner (anāgāmī) in an instant and attained final nibbāna.
"Yañhissa" means: if even one single thing among cold and so forth were to happen to him. "Anadhivāsayato" means: of one who does not endure it.
To one who does not endure [it]. The rest is exactly as previously stated. Furthermore, the arising of the taints (*āsava*) here should be understood in this way:
for one touched by cold and longing for heat, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises; so it is in all cases.

For one longing for existence (*bhava*), thinking, "In our state of attainment, in a fortunate realm of rebirth, there is neither cold nor heat," the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises. [Thinking], "It is cold for me; it is hot for me..."
Grasping is the taint of views; ignorance is the taint associated with all [the other defilements].

“These are called... pe ... to be abandoned by endurance”—thus, taking each one from among cold and so forth, there are four for each, making many taints that are to be abandoned by this endurance known as restraint through patience.
The meaning is "it is called. Furthermore, it should be understood that this patience (*khanti*) is called "endurance" (*adhivāsanā*) because it endures phenomena such as cold and so forth;
having taken them upon itself, it simply dwells with them. It does not reject them by being unable to bear them.
The commentary on the taints (*āsava*) to be abandoned through endurance is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Avoidance (25):
“One avoids a fierce elephant through wise reflection” means that one who claims, “I am a recluse,” should not stand near a fierce elephant.
For on that account there might even be death, or suffering amounting to death; thus, by this means—
Having reflected by way of the path and the condition, he avoids and retreats from a fierce elephant.
This same method applies everywhere. "Fierce" (*caṇḍa*) means wicked; it is synonymous with "wild" (*vāḷa*). "Stump" (*khāṇu*) refers to a stump of acacia wood or the like.
"Thorny place" (*kaṇṭakaṭṭhāna*) means the location of thorns; what is meant is that space where thorns are found. "Pit" (*sobbha*)—from all sides...
“With its edges cut away” means having its sides severed on one side. A “cesspool” (*candanikā*) is a place for discarding leftovers, water, feces, filth, and so forth.
A “drain” (*oḷigalla*) is a place where those very same things, along with mud and the like, flow out;
it is filled with impurities even up to the knees, and both of these places are infested by non-human beings. Therefore, they should be avoided.
Regarding "anāsane" (in an improper seat): here, an improper seat is *anāsana*; in meaning, this should be understood as a secluded or concealed seat whose specific location is not fixed.

Regarding "agocare" (in an improper resort): here too, an improper resort is *agocara*; it is fivefold, consisting of [resorts such as] prostitutes and so forth. Regarding "pāpake mitte" (evil friends):
these are despicable, immoral persons who merely resemble friends, or actual enemies. "Bhajantaṃ" means one who associates with or serves them.
"Learned fellow-celibates" (*viññū sabrahmacārī*) refers to wise ones endowed with intelligence; this is a designation for monks.
For they practice this holy life (*brahma*) together—sharing the same formal acts, the same recitations, and the same training—and therefore they are called "fellow-celibates.
"In evil matters" means in base matters. "They would believe" means they would have faith or would be convinced.
“Surely this venerable one has done it, or will do it.
Regarding the phrase *yaṃhissa*: it refers to any one among the elephant and so forth. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Furthermore, the arising of the taints (*āsava*) here should be understood in this way: for one who, being touched by suffering caused by elephants and so forth, longs for pleasure, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises.
It arises. The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) belongs to one who yearns for existence, thinking, "In this state of rebirth, in this happy destination, there is no such suffering as this.
The taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is the misconception, "An elephant tramples me," or "A horse [tramples me]. The taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) is associated with all of these.
These are called... [as before] ... "to be abandoned by avoidance. These four [taints] are presented according to each of the examples, beginning with the elephant.
It should be understood that, having categorized them into four groups, numerous *āsava*s are said to be abandonable by this avoidance known as restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*).
The commentary on the *āsava*s abandonable by avoidance is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the *āsava*s abandonable by dispelling (*vinodana*).
26. "By means of wise reflection, one does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire" means that, by way of such a method as: "This thought is unwholesome;

it is blameworthy; it has a painful result; and it leads to one's own harm," one reflects wisely upon the danger in a thought of sensual desire, [thereby abandoning] whatever has arisen, come into being, or been produced in relation to various objects.
He does not tolerate thoughts of sensual desire; having brought them to mind, he does not dwell upon them, nor does he dwell upon them within himself—this is the meaning.
What does he do when he does not tolerate them? He abandons them, he discards them.
Is it like throwing rubbish into a basket? No, rather, he dispels them, strikes them down, pierces them, and expels them.

"Is it like driving away an ox with a goad? No; rather, he brings it to an end, he makes it reach its limit. He does so in such a way that not even its end remains, not even a mere fragment. But how does he do so?
"He causes it to go to non-existence" means he causes it to go to non-existence bit by bit;
what is meant is that he acts so that it is thoroughly suppressed by the abandoning through suppression (*vikkhambhana-ppahāna*). This same method applies to ill-will and cruelty-thoughts.
And here, "thought of sensual desire" (*kāma-vitakka*) is that which is described in the *Vibhaṅga* as "the reasoning, the thought, the wrong intention associated with sensual desire.
The same method applies to the others. Regarding the phrase "as each as they arise": this means "in each instance as they have arisen," that is, at the very moment of their arising.
Having dispelled them once they have arisen, he does not remain indifferent for a second time; even if it happens a hundred times, he does not neglect them.
He dispels them as they arise, one by one. "Evil, unwholesome" means evil in the sense of being blameworthy, and unwholesome due to a lack of skill.
"States" refers to those very same thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, or indeed all nine great types of thought. Among these, three have already been mentioned.
The remaining ones are: thoughts of relatives, thoughts of the country, thoughts of immortality, and thoughts associated with compassion for others.
“Thought associated with gain, honor, and renown; thought associated with not being despised”—these are the six. “Whatever of these he may have”:
regarding these thoughts, whatever [of them] he might possess; the rest is exactly as previously stated. Herein, sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) is simply the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*).

Its specific distinction is the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*). The taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is that which is associated with it. In all thoughts, there is the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
In this way, the arising of the taints (āsava) should also be understood. These are called... [pe] ... "to be abandoned by removal.

These taints, described in the manner mentioned above by way of sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) and so forth, are [abandoned] by means of this—namely, the restraint consisting of energy accompanied by the contemplation of the danger (ādīnava) in each respective thought.
It should be understood that they are said to be "abandoned by means of removal.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by removal is finished.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by cultivation.
27. "He develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor by means of wise reflection":

having reflected by way of the method and the path upon the danger in non-development and the benefit in development, he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor; this same method applies everywhere.
And here, although these are intended as supramundane enlightenment factors arising at the time of the three higher paths, [the same principle holds].

Nevertheless, for the sake of non-confusion regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) among beginners, I shall provide an exposition of their meaning according to a method that combines both the mundane and the supramundane.
Here, however, setting aside the mundane method, only the supramundane method should be adopted.
First, regarding the seven initial terms stated in the sequence beginning with "the mindfulness factor of enlightenment" (*satisambojjhaṅga*):
The analysis [of the factors] should be understood by one who is discerning according to their meaning, their characteristics and so forth, their sequence, and their completeness or lack thereof.

Therein, first, in the case of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*), it is "mindfulness" in the sense of remembering. Furthermore, its characteristic is establishing and its characteristic is non-forgetfulness.
Or rather, for it has also been said: "Just as, great king, a royal treasurer does not neglect the King’s property, [reporting]:
'So much, great king, is the silver; so much is the gold;

so much is the property,' even so, great king, when mindfulness arises, it does not neglect the wholesome and unwholesome, the blameworthy and blameless, the inferior and superior, the dark and bright, and their counterparts."
"It does not confuse the Dhamma. These are the four foundations of mindfulness"—thus it is said in detail. Its function is non-confusion;
for this characteristic was stated by the Elder precisely in terms of its function. Alternatively, its function is non-forgetfulness.

It is manifested as being directed toward the objective field. Mindfulness itself is the enlightenment factor; thus it is the "mindfulness-enlightenment-factor" (*satisambojjhaṅga*). In that context, it is called an "enlightenment factor" (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is a limb (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*) or of one who is enlightened (*bodhisatta*).
What is meant by this? This is that harmony of factors (*dhammasāmaggī*) which, arising at the moment of the mundane and supramundane paths,

serves as the antidote to numerous calamities— namely, laxity and agitation, the foundations [of these], the accumulation [of kamma], devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism—
and which consists of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Because the noble disciple awakens through the harmony of the Dhamma, he is called "Bodhi" (the Awakened One).
"He awakens" means that he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or that he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or that he realizes Nibbāna itself;
as it is said: "Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

It is a "factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is a factor of that enlightenment (*bodhi*) which is defined as the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), just like the factors of jhāna or the factors of the path.

Furthermore, since the noble disciple is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) on account of awakening by means of this aforementioned harmony of states, it is a "factor of enlightenment" because it is a factor of that enlightenment, just like the factors of an army or the factors of a chariot. Thus said the teachers of the commentaries.

“Or, they are called ‘factors of enlightenment’ because they are the factors for a person who is awakening. Furthermore, according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: “In what sense are they ‘factors of enlightenment’ (*bojjhaṅga*)?
They are factors of enlightenment because they conduce to enlightenment; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken further;
they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken thoroughly; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken fully,” and so forth.
The meaning should be understood. A factor of enlightenment that is praised or beautiful is a "perfect enlightenment factor" (*sambodhyaṅga*).

This being so, it is precisely a perfect enlightenment factor that is the "mindfulness-enlightenment-factor" (*satisambojjhaṅga*). That is the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor. In this way, first, the analysis of one initial term should be understood by way of its meaning, its characteristic, and so forth.
In the second [jhāna] and those that follow, however, it is the investigation of the Dhamma consisting of the Four Noble Truths; thus it is *dhammavicaya*.

It has the characteristic of investigating, the function of illuminating, and the manifestation of non-delusion. Because of its heroic nature and because it must be set in motion according to the method, it is *vīriya* (energy).
It has the characteristic of exertion, the function of supporting, and the manifestation of non-sinking. It gladdens; thus it is *pīti* (rapture).
It has the characteristic of pervading, or the characteristic of satisfaction; its function is to refresh body and mind; it is manifested as their very elation.
It is called "tranquillity" (*passaddhi*) because it allays the distress of body and mind. It has the characteristic of peace; its function is to crush the distress of body and mind;

it is manifested as the state of coolness consisting in the non-distraction of body and mind. It is called "concentration" (*samādhi*) because of its concentrating [the mind]. It has the characteristic of non-distraction.
Or, it has non-distraction as its characteristic; its function is to unify consciousness and mental factors; it is manifested as the stability of consciousness.

It is called equanimity (*upekkhā*) because of its state of looking on with indifference. Its characteristic is the act of reflecting or, alternatively, the act of bearing evenly; its function is to prevent deficiency or excess, or its function is to cut off partiality;
it is manifested as a state of neutrality. The rest is exactly as described by the method already stated. Thus...
The analysis of the remaining factors according to their meaning, characteristics, and so forth, should also be understood.

Regarding the sequence: here, because of the statement, "Monks, mindfulness, indeed, I declare to be all-beneficial," the mindfulness enlightenment factor is mentioned first, as it is supportive to all the remaining enlightenment factors. Following that, "He, thus... [and so on].

The purpose of the sequential arrangement of the remaining enlightenment factors is stated in the Sutta itself in such passages as: “Dwelling mindfully, he investigates that state with wisdom,” and so forth.
In this way, the analysis of the sequence should be understood here. As for "neither deficient nor redundant":
why did the Blessed One teach exactly seven enlightenment factors, neither fewer nor more? It is because they are the opposites of lethargy and agitation.
And as being universal. For here, three factors of enlightenment are the opposites of sluggishness. As it is said:

"But on whatever occasion, bhikkhus, the mind is sluggish, that is the time for the cultivation of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the time for the cultivation of the energy factor of enlightenment, and the time for the cultivation of the rapture factor of enlightenment."
There are three opposites to restlessness. As it is said:

"But at whatever time, monks, the mind is restless, that is the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the time for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment. However, one among these is universal. As it is said:
—“And mindfulness, monks, I call the all-beneficial. The reading “all-beneficial” (*sabbatthaka*) is also found;

the meaning of both is that it is desired everywhere. Thus, because they are the opposites of lethargy and agitation and because they are all-beneficial, exactly seven factors of enlightenment have been stated, neither fewer nor more. In this way, the determination regarding their neither being deficient nor excessive should be understood here.

Thus, having first understood the explanation of the meaning of the seven initial terms stated in the manner beginning with “the enlightenment factor of mindfulness,” one should now understand the following regarding the phrases “he develops it based on seclusion,” and so forth. “He develops” means he increases;
the sense is that he repeatedly produces and brings about [the factors] within the continuum of his own mind. “Based on seclusion” means dependent upon seclusion.
“Vivitta” means seclusion (*vivittatā*). This seclusion is fivefold: seclusion as a factor, seclusion by suppression, seclusion by eradication, seclusion by subsiding, and seclusion as escape.
Its various distinctions should be understood according to the method stated in the passage, “one who is undisciplined in the noble Dhamma.
For it is this very thing that is called “discipline” (*vinaya*) there. Thus, regarding these five kinds of seclusion:

"Dependent on seclusion" means that one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor dependent on seclusion by way of its specific function, dependent on seclusion by way of its eradication, and dependent on seclusion by way of its escape;

this is how the meaning should be understood. For thus, when a yogi devoted to the development of the enlightenment factors is at the moment of insight (vipassanā), he is dependent on seclusion by way of its specific function and dependent on seclusion by way of its escape through his underlying aspiration.

At the time of the path, however, one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) based on seclusion through abandonment as its function, and based on seclusion as escape as its object. Some say it is based on fivefold seclusion;

for they extract the enlightenment factors not only at the moments of powerful insight, the path, and the fruit, but also during the jhānas that serve as the basis for insight—namely, the kasiṇa-jhānas, the ānāpāna-jhāna, the foulness (asubha) jhānas, and the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) jhānas.
They extract [this meaning], and it has not been refuted by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathās.
Therefore, according to their opinion, at the moment these jhānas arise, they are based on seclusion through suppression by way of their function alone.
And just as it was said that "at the moment of insight, it is based on seclusion as escape by way of aspiration," so too one develops it as being based on seclusion through subsiding.

It is appropriate to speak thus. This same method applies to those [factors] based on fading away (*virāga*), and so forth. For fading away and the rest are indeed identical with seclusion (*viveka*).
However, in this context, relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāga-vossagga*) and relinquishment as launching into (*pakkhandana-vossagga*).

Therein, relinquishment as giving up occurs by way of partial eradication (*tadaṅga*) at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), and by way of total eradication (*samuccheda*) at the moment of the path (*magga*).

The abandoning of defilements. "Leaping forward and relinquishment" refers to leaping forward toward Nibbāna through the state of being inclined toward it at the moment of insight (vipassanā), and by taking it as an object at the moment of the Path (magga).
Both of these are appropriate within this method of explaining the meaning that is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
For in this way, this mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) [abandons] the defilements in the manner already described.

He relinquishes and leaps into Nibbāna. By this entire expression, "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*), it means that which is tending toward the state of relinquishment, and that which has reached that state; likewise, that which is maturing and that which has matured. This is what is meant:

"For this bhikkhu devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment, just as the mindfulness factor of enlightenment [leads] to the state of relinquishment through the abandonment of defilements..."
"And it ripens into the state of leaping forward toward Nibbāna and relinquishment; and he develops it in such a way that it becomes fully ripened.
This same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
However, in this context, Nibbāna itself is "seclusion" (*viveka*) because it is secluded from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*), and because it is the state of dispassion for all [phenomena].
It is called "dispassion" (virāga) because it is free from lust, and it is called "cessation" (nirodha) because its nature is cessation. Furthermore, the path itself results in relinquishment;
therefore, one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor based on seclusion, by way of its occurrence with seclusion as its object. Likewise, it is based on dispassion and based on cessation.
And this occurs through the total cutting off of the defilements at the moment of the arising of the Noble Path, by way of their abandonment and by way of leaping forward into Nibbāna.
And "ripened" (*pariṇata*) and "fully matured" (*paripakka*) should be understood as having this very same meaning.

This method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "whatever of these": it refers to whichever among these factors of enlightenment may belong to him. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

However, in this context, regarding the arising of the taints (*āsava*), because these factors of enlightenment associated with the three higher paths have not been developed, those taints that would otherwise arise—namely, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*)—[do not arise].

The taints are threefold: the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). This principle should be understood as follows: "For one who develops [the path], these taints do not exist.

These are called... *pe* ... "to be abandoned by development. It should be understood that these three taints are said to be abandoned by this cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) associated with the threefold path.
28. Now, praising the bhikkhu who has abandoned the taints in these seven ways, [the text] states the benefit of his abandonment of the taints:
And by showing these very reasons for generating zeal in beings toward the abandoning of the taints (*āsava*), he said: "But from the time, monks... [as before]... he made an end of suffering.
In that context, *yato kho* is the particle *to* used in the genitive sense; thus it means "of which" (*yassa kho*).
However, the ancients explain it as "at which time" (*yasmiṃ kāle*). As for "those taints to be abandoned by seeing," those taints...
Those things to be abandoned by vision are abandoned by vision itself; he does not perceive them as abandoned while they are still unabandoned.
Thus is the detailed explanation for all cases.
"Restrained by the restraint of all taints" means covered by all the coverings that shut out the taints, or [restrained] by the coverings of all the taints.
"He has closed it": he has cut off craving—cut it all, severed it, and utterly eradicated it.
"He has turned back the fetters": he has overturned the tenfold fetter and rendered it stainless. "Truly" means by way of cause and reason.
"The breakthrough to conceit" refers to both the breakthrough through the vision of conceit and the breakthrough through its abandonment; for the path of arahantship, in terms of its function, is...

He sees conceit; this is his "realization through seeing. Once seen by him, however, it is abandoned at that very moment, just as the life of beings bitten by a poisonous snake is ended by the sight of the poison. This is his "realization through abandoning.
"He has made an end of suffering": thus, because conceit has been correctly seen and abandoned by means of the path of Arahantship.
These are: the "limit of the boundary" as spoken of thus, "It decays within the fastening of the body, or at the edge of the green [grass]";
the "inferior limit" as spoken of thus, "This, bhikkhus, is the lowest of livelihoods"; the "limit as a section" as spoken of thus, "Personal existence (sakkāya) is one limit";
and the "limit as a culminating point" as spoken of thus, "This indeed is the end of suffering, through the destruction of all conditions."
Thus, regarding these four extremes, he made an end—the end reckoned as the fourth limit, the final limit—of the entire suffering of saṃsāra;
he established its boundary and its enclosure. What is meant is that he left behind only the suffering remaining in his very last physical existence.
“Those bhikkhus were elated” means they were well-disposed, with contented minds, or with minds associated with rapture and joy.

“They rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words” means that they welcomed [the teaching] from head to foot, thinking: “The Blessed One’s words concerning the conclusion of suffering are well-spoken and well-uttered; ‘So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata! and thus they expressed their approval.

Whatever has not been stated here has not been stated because it was already stated previously and because it is easy to understand. Therefore, everything should be reviewed word by word according to what has been said.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by cultivation is finished.
[From] the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Sabbāsavasutta is finished.
3. The commentary on the Dhammadāyādasutta:
"Thus have I heard" is the Dhammadāyādasutta. However, because its introduction (nikkhepa) is based on a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppattika), therefore—
Having shown that, we shall now provide a word-by-word commentary on the text not previously explained. By what occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) was this [sutta] delivered?

It was regarding gain and honor (*lābhasakkāra*). It is said that great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One, as befits one who has fulfilled the accumulation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) over four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*).
Twin great clouds rained down in all directions, creating a great flood.
As if all the perfections had combined and resolved, "We shall manifest our fruition within a single existence," they produced a great flood of gain and honor.
Then, from every direction, Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and others arrived with food, drink, vehicles, garments, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands, crying out:
"Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods, the Bull among Men, the Lion among Men?"

They seek out the Blessed One. Even after bringing provisions by means of hundreds of carts, being unable to obtain an audience, they stand and follow him, cart-axle to cart-axle, for a distance of a league on all sides, just as the Brahmins of Andhakavinda and others did.
All this is according to the method already set forth in various sections of the Khandhaka and the Suttas.
This should be understood. Just as it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

And this has been said: "Now at that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus likewise..."

"He is honored... [and so on] ...with the requisites. Likewise: "Cunda, as far as any Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world today, I do not see any other single Saṅgha that has attained such a pinnacle of gain and a pinnacle of fame as this Bhikkhu Saṅgha, Cunda."
The gains and honors that arose for both the Blessed One and the community of monks became immeasurable when combined, like the waters of two great rivers.
Gradually, the monks became intent upon requisites and indulgent in requisites.
Even after the meal, when oil, honey, molasses, and other items were brought, they would strike the gong and say, "For us..."
“Give it to the teacher! Give it to the preceptor! they cried out with loud and great clamor.
This conduct of theirs became known even to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, perceiving that it was improper, gave rise to a sense of spiritual urgency and reflected:
“It is not possible to lay down a training rule [simply because] requisites are unallowable; for the sons of good family are dependent upon requisites.”
This is the way of life for a recluse. Come now, I shall teach the practice of being an heir to the Dhamma.
This will serve as a proclamation of training rules for clansmen who desire to train, and it will be like a full-length mirror set up at the city gate.
For just as when a full-length mirror is set up at the city gate, the four castes, seeing their own reflections, perceive their blemishes—
“Just as those who have abandoned [ornaments] become free from fault, even so, sons of good family who desire training and wish to adorn themselves with the ornament of application—
having reflected upon this teaching which compares all bodily [ornaments] to slaves, and having avoided the practice of being heirs to material things,
they will fulfill the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma and quickly make an end of birth, aging, and death. It was on this occasion that he spoke this discourse.
In this regard, "Bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things" means:
"Bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not to material things; be recipients of my Dhamma, and do not be recipients of my material things. In this context, the Dhamma is also twofold.
—The direct teaching (nippariyāya-dhamma) and the indirect teaching (pariyāya-dhamma). Material things (āmiṣa) are also twofold:
direct material things and indirect material things. How so? The ninefold supramundane Dhamma, consisting of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna, is the direct Dhamma;

it is the Dhamma that has been realized, not a Dhamma by way of any indirect method, cause, or pretext. But as for this [Dhamma] which is dependent upon the turning away from the round of existence...

It is wholesome, as follows: here someone, aspiring for the turning away from the round of existence, gives gifts, undertakes moral discipline, performs the observance-day rites, honors the physical shrine with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, listens to the Dhamma, teaches it, and brings about the meditative attainments;
by acting in this way, he gradually attains the deathless Nibbāna, the Dhamma in its ultimate sense.

This is the figurative (pariyāya) Dhamma. Likewise, the four requisites beginning with robes are material gifts (āmisa) in the primary sense alone; they are not a gift by any other figurative means, cause, or pretext.

However, as for this skill pertaining to the round of existence—namely, when someone here, aspiring to the round and desiring a state of prosperity, gives a gift... [and so on] ...until he produces meditative attainments (samāpatti).
Acting in this way, one gradually attains the prosperity of gods and humans; this is called "the material gift by way of method" (*pariyāyāmisa*).
In this regard, even the Dhamma that is not a method belongs exclusively to the Blessed One.
For it is because of what was taught by the Blessed One that monks attain the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna. And this has been said: "For that Blessed One, O Brahmin, [is the source] of the unarisen..."
“He is the arouser of the path not yet arisen, the producer of the path not yet produced, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path. And now his disciples dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.
And: “Indeed, friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become vision itself...”
“The Tathāgata is one who has become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become Brahmā; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, even the Dhamma as a method belongs only to the Blessed One. For it is precisely because it was spoken by the Blessed One that they know thus:
“One giving a gift while aspiring for the turning away from existence... [and so on] ...producing meditative attainments, gradually...”
“...he attains the deathless Nibbāna. Even the non-figurative material gifts belong to the Blessed One alone.
Indeed, it was precisely because they were permitted by the Blessed One that the monks obtained high-quality robes, beginning with the case of Jīvaka.
As it is said: “I allow you, monks, a householder’s robe. Whoever wishes may be a wearer of rag-robes; whoever wishes,” and so forth.
“Monks, let him accept a robe from a householder. Monks, I praise contentment with whatever one receives.
Previously, monks did not obtain choice almsfood; they subsisted solely on morsels of food collected by way of the alms-round.
While staying at Rājagaha, the Blessed One said: “Monks, I allow you: a meal for the Saṅgha, a designated meal...”
Because it was thus authorized—[namely] "invitations, meals by ticket, fortnightly meals, Uposatha meals, and meals on the first day of the lunar half-month"—exquisite food was obtained.
Likewise for lodgings. For previously, monks had only such lodgings as natural caves and the roots of trees;
however, because it was thus authorized by the Blessed One: "Monks, I allow five kinds of shelters," [luxurious lodgings were permitted].
They obtained these dwellings: monasteries, gabled houses, palaces, pavilions, and caves. Previously, they had used only urine and myrobalan as medicine;
however, because the Blessed One himself authorized them by way of such statements as, "I allow you, monks, five kinds of medicine, namely:
ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses," they obtained various medicines.
Even the "successive material goods" belong to the Blessed One alone. For they know it precisely because it was spoken by the Blessed One:

"One who aspires to a state of prosperity, having given gifts, observed virtue... [and so forth]... and having produced meditative attainments, gradually obtains successive material goods, namely divine prosperity and human prosperity.
That very thing is so, because even the "non-figurative Dhamma" (nippariyāya-dhamma) is likewise.
Whether it be the Dhamma in its figurative sense, the non-figurative material gift, or the figurative material gift, all belong to the Blessed One alone.
Therefore, demonstrating his own ownership therein, he said: "Bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things.
Be heirs to that twofold Dhamma which belongs to me; and as for this [Dhamma] which belongs to me alone—
This is the portion of material goods; do not become its heirs. Be masters only of the portion of the Dhamma, not of the portion of material goods.

For one who, having gone forth in the Conqueror’s teaching, dwells intent upon requisites, manifesting the four bases for the arising of craving, and has cast off the burden regarding the practice in accordance with the Dhamma—such a person is called an heir to material goods. Do not be like that.

Do not be such [as those]. However, one who dwells devoted to practice, making reflective consideration his guide as he makes use of the permitted requisites out of fewness of desires and so forth, and who is seen to conform to the four noble lineages—such a person is called a "heir to the Dhamma.
The meaning is: "Become like that."

Now, in order to show those who thought then—or who might think in the future—"Why does the Blessed One speak thus as if he were desirous of gain from his disciples?"—that "I speak thus because I am desirous of very sublime gain," he said: "Among you...
[etc. ...I am not an heir to material things."
This is its meaning: "I have compassion, sympathy, and a desire for the welfare of you all;
by what cause and by what means might my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, masters of the portion of the Dhamma, and not heirs to material things?
This, however, is the underlying intention: it seems the Blessed One saw that in the past, those who valued material things stumbled over material things.

Thus, for the bhikkhu Kapila, as well as for the many hundreds of wicked bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, and others mentioned in the manner beginning with "even his outer robe was ablaze," there is the filling of the states of misery (apāya);
and for those who have gone forth in his own dispensation, such as Devadatta and others, there is likewise [the same].

However, for those who revere the Dhamma, such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others, there is the attainment of qualities such as the direct knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore:
Desiring their liberation from the states of misery and the attainment of all virtues, he said:
"I have compassion for you, so that my disciples may be heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things.
One who values requisites becomes devoid of luster and brilliance, like a counterfeit coin among the four assemblies or like extinguished embers; therefore, his mind turns away [from them].
One who values the Dhamma, possessing splendor, moves as a conqueror like a lion; therefore he spoke thus:

"I have... [etc. ...I am not an heir to material things. Having thus made it known that "Bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things"—this being spoken by one desiring a more sublime gain out of compassion, and not by one seeking worldly profit—[the Buddha now speaks] regarding the failure to act upon this advice:
Showing the danger, he said: “And you, bhikkhus... [etc. ...are not heirs to the Dhamma. Herein, “you too would be heirs to that” means:
you too would be heirs to that by way of being heirs to material things (*āmisa*), and not by way of being heirs to the Dhamma.
“To be pointed out,” “to be set apart,” or “to be defined”—you would be objects of reproach for the wise.
It has been said. What was it? "The Teacher’s disciples dwell as heirs to material things, not as heirs to the Dhamma. [He thought:
"I too might be censured for that"—meaning, I too might be censured because of that state of being your heirs to material things rather than heirs to the Dhamma.
What was it? "As heirs to material things... and so forth. The Blessed One said this in order to make them exceedingly gentle.
This is the intended meaning here: "If you, monks, should wander about greedy for material things, then wise people will reproach me there, saying:
'How is it that one who is omniscient is unable to make his own disciples heirs to the Dhamma rather than heirs to material things?
It is just as when teachers and preceptors see monks who are not endowed with proper decorum.
People will reproach me, saying, "Whose are these co-residents? Whose are these pupils?
Just as parents, upon seeing sons or daughters from noble families who are immoral and of evil character, reproach them, saying, "Whose are these sons?
Whose are these daughters? even so will wise people reproach me, saying, "How can it be that one who is all-knowing..."
“[The Teacher] is not able to make his disciples heirs to the Dhamma rather than heirs to material things.
Having thus shown the disadvantage in failing to follow this advice, he spoke the words beginning with “And you [should follow] me,” etc., showing the benefit in following it.
In that context, the phrase “I too would not be pleased by that” refers to one who fulfills the duties, just as in the case of a person who completes their assigned tasks.
When young bhikkhus—endowed with the proper deportment like elders of a hundred years who are accomplished in recitation and interrogation—are seen, people ask, "Whose co-resident pupils are they?
or "Whose resident pupils are they? and upon hearing, "They are [the pupils] of so-and-so," they think, "It is fitting for that elder;
he is truly capable of exhorting and instructing. Thus, the teachers and preceptors are neither blameworthy nor censurable. In this very same way...
I too, by virtue of being your heirs to the Dhamma rather than heirs to material things,

am a witness to those disciples who have practiced the Nālaka practice, the Tuvaṭṭaka practice, the Candūpama practice, the Rathavinīta practice, the Mahāgoṇisigāla practice, and the Mahāsuññata practice, and who have become witnesses to contentment with the four requisites and delight in the cultivation of the noble lineages.

“With minds turning away from craving for conditions, they dwell like the moon released from clouds. When it is said, “Of the ascetic Gotama,” the wise would neither find fault nor censure him, thinking:

“The Blessed One is truly omniscient; he has indeed been able to cause his disciples to abandon the practice of being heirs to material things and to fulfill the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma. Thus, in this [context]...

Having understood the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) regarding the term "footstep," the remainder should be understood by way of the opposite of the method stated for the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*).
Having thus shown the benefit in practicing this instruction, he now hands over that instruction, saying: "Therefore, bhikkhus, [listen] to me...
[and so on] ...not heirs to material things."
30. Having thus delivered this exhortation, he now spoke the words beginning with "In this regard, monks," in order to praise her as one who fulfills the practice of being an heir to the Dhamma.
For even upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One, there are indeed those who proceed toward that very goal.
In this context, "in this regard" (*idha*) is a particle. "Having eaten" (*bhuttāvī*) means having eaten; it is said to mean "one who has completed the task of eating."
"Pavārita" means one who has been invited for an invitation according to need (*yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*); it is said that having eaten as much as needed, he has finished his meal and is satisfied.

For there are four kinds of invitations: the invitation for those who have completed the rains residence (*vassaṃvuṭṭha-pavāraṇā*), the invitation regarding requisites (*paccaya-pavāraṇā*), the invitation regarding what is not left over (*anatiritta-pavāraṇā*), and the invitation according to need (*yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*).
In this context, [it refers to the latter]: "Monks, I allow you, for those who have completed the rains residence..."
“Let the monks perform the *pavāraṇā* by means of three grounds”—this is the *pavāraṇā* for those who have completed the rains retreat (*vassaṃvuṭṭha-pavāraṇā*).

“Venerable sirs, I wish to invite the Saṅgha to provide me with medicine for four months,” and “except for the [formal] *pavāraṇā* and except for the permanent *pavāraṇā*”—this is the *pavāraṇā* of requisites (*paccaya-pavāraṇā*).
“One is said to have been invited when food is perceived, when a meal is perceived, and within arm’s reach.”
"He stands and offers it; a refusal is perceived; this is called 'one who has been invited' (pavārita)"—this refers to the invitation regarding what is not left over (*anatiritta-pavāraṇā*).
"He has personally satisfied and served him with choice food and delicacies"—this refers to the invitation according to need (*yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*).
This is what is intended here. Therefore it was said: "'One who has been invited' means one who has been invited by way of the invitation according to need."
"Paripuṇṇo" means fulfilled by food. "Pariyosito" means one whose meal is finished; it should be understood as an elision of the latter member of the compound (*pariyosita-bhojana*).
The meaning is: as much as ought to be eaten has been eaten, and the act of eating is concluded for me. "Suhito" means satiated;
or rather, it is said that he is happy because of the absence of the suffering of hunger. "Yāvadatthaṃ" means as much as is required.
"I have need of food; all that is in the bowl. And here, the latter three terms are the proofs for the former three: for he who has finished is one who has eaten;
he who is satisfied is one who has been invited to accept as much as he requires; and he who has had as much as he required is one whose needs are fulfilled.
Or alternatively, the former are the proofs for the latter: for it is because he has eaten that he is... [satisfied].
Because he has been invited (*pavārita*), therefore he is satisfied (*suhita*). Because he is complete (*paripuṇṇa*), therefore he has had as much as he required (*yāvadattha*).
All of this should be understood as having been stated by way of a hypothetical supposition (*parikappa*).

The word *siyā* (might) is used both in the sense of certainty and in the sense of an alternative. For example, in the statement, "The earth element might be internal, it might be external," it is used in the sense of certainty.
“*Siyā aññatarassa bhikkhuno āpatti vītikkamo*”: this refers to the act of assigning [the robe]. Here, both are permissible.
*Atireka-dhammo* means that which is in excess. Likewise for *chaḍḍanīya-dhammo*. The meaning is: it is both superfluous and fit to be discarded;
nothing else need be done with it. *Atha* means at that time. *Jighacchādubbalyapareto* means overcome by hunger and weakness.
And for eight or ten days they were overcome by weakness and afflicted [by hunger].
In that situation, some who were hungry were not weak and were able to endure the hunger; however, to show that these [others] were not like that, he stated both conditions.
"Tyāham" means "those I. "Sace ākaṅkatha" means "if you wish."
"Appaharite" means where green grass has not grown; the meaning is: in that place where there is no grass liable to be destroyed by the scattering of alms-food.

By this, both a place devoid of grass and a great thicket of tall grass are included—where even when alms-food is discarded by cartload, the grass does not perish—and such a place is considered "appropriated" (pariggahita) under the rule concerning the destruction of living plants (*bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*).
For this was said for the purpose of non-disturbance.
"In one free from living beings" means in a great body of water that is devoid of living beings that would have to die by being overwhelmed by the alms-food;
for it is only in small amounts of water that tiny creatures die when the food is thrown in and stirred up, but not in large reservoirs and the like.
For this was said for the purpose of protecting small creatures. "I will submerge" means I will cause [it] to sink.
"Therein, of one" refers to one of those two. It was said, "But it has been stated," referring to him who has heard this teaching of the Dhamma well and reviews it again and again.
This word *vutta* is also seen in the sense of "hair-removal," as in "a *kāpaṭika*..."
In such passages as "the young brahmin with a shorn head," and so forth; and even when used in the sense of "sown," as in "just as autumn seed sown in a field grows," and so forth;
and even when used in the sense of "spoken," as in "this was spoken by the Blessed One, this was spoken by the Arahant," and so forth. But here it should be understood in the sense of "spoken.
For its meaning is: "This has indeed been spoken. "One of the material requisites" means one of the four requisites consisting of material things.
"Ekam" means "one. "Yadidam" is a particle; it remains the same in all genders, cases, and numbers, and its meaning must be adapted accordingly in each instance.
Here, however, its meaning is "this which. "This which is called alms-food"—this is what is meant by "a certain kind of material gift.
"Yaṃnūnāhaṃ" means "it would be well if I. "Evaṃ" means "just as I am spending this present moment."
In this very way, he would spend, pass, and let elapse day and night.

He—desiring the state of being an heir to the Dhamma—would not eat that almsfood, which even the world with its devas ought to receive upon their heads and which is the leavings of the Sugata; rather, he would reflect upon it as being like a fire on one's head.
He would pass that day and night in that very state of weakness from hunger.
Now, as for "the second": in this version, this is the summary; if that bhikkhu, while thinking, "What if I...
[pass the time]? were to think even this much: "Indeed, medicine is needed by one who has gone forth in the forest thick with wild beasts," [he would seek it].

Just as it is difficult to seek almsfood even in a village thick with the wild beasts of the five strands of sensual pleasure, this almsfood—being both free from the disadvantage of seeking and superior to that of the Well-Gone One—is like a well-born noble prince.
Furthermore, there are five reasons why almsfood should not be consumed, namely: [regarding] the person...
Having censured it, one should not consume it, thinking, "This belongs to a person who is shameless.
Because of its impure origin, one should not consume it, thinking, "It was produced through the instigation and encouragement of a nun.
Out of compassion for the owner, one should not consume it, thinking, "The monk who is the owner of this almsfood is hungry. He, being satisfied, [gives it] to him...
It should not be consumed out of compassion for one's resident pupils and others, thinking, "The resident pupils or others dependent on them are hungry";
for they too are well-nourished and satisfied. Furthermore, it should not be consumed due to a lack of faith, thinking, "The monk who is the master of the alms-food is faithless.
It is because of these reasons that this [alms-food] is liberated. For the Blessed One is compassionate toward those who possess a sense of shame.
Thinking, "This almsfood is the foremost, its source is pure, the Blessed One is nourished and satisfied, and there is no other person who can take its place;
of those with faith in the world, the Blessed One is the foremost," and having thus reflected, he should eat that almsfood...
[and] spend his time. To this extent, even one who performs the duties of a recluse without eating is indeed one for whom it is proper to eat.
Almsfood has not been eaten [in vain]. Even one who performs the duty of a recluse after eating has eaten only what ought to be eaten.
There is no distinction regarding the almsfood itself; however, there is a distinction regarding the person. Therefore, in order to show this, he said:
"Even though he... and so forth.

In this context, *kiñcāpi* is a particle used in the sense of granting permission and expressing praise. What does it grant permission for? That monk’s blameless enjoyment [of food]. What does it praise? Performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) after having eaten. This is what is meant: even if that monk were to eat only what should be eaten and perform only what should be performed, nevertheless, at that very moment, it would be as if I had said: "I allow you, monks, the blameless enjoyment of food; I praise the performance of the duties of a recluse after having eaten. Thus, by means of this statement, he grants permission and offers praise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "I allow you, monks, the blameless enjoyment of food; I praise the performance of the duties of a recluse after having eaten. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the Blessed One spoke these words because he saw that the monks were not undertaking the duties of a recluse after eating. For it is said: "The Blessed One, seeing that the monks were not undertaking the duties of a recluse after eating, spoke thus. Why did he see them not undertaking the duties of a recluse? It is said: "The Blessed One, seeing that the monks were not undertaking the duties of a recluse due to
"The first bhikkhu" refers to that first bhikkhu who, having rejected even that alms-food, practices the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*);
he alone is more worthy of honor and more praiseworthy than the second bhikkhu— just as one who is braver among two brave men or wiser among two wise men—
and it is said that he is to be honored and praised to a greater degree than the second bhikkhu.
Now, establishing that matter by means of a reason, he said, "For what reason? and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
there might be a question from you, "Why is that bhikkhu more worthy of honor and more praiseworthy than the Blessed One?

[The answer is: "Because of that" (*taṃ hi tassa*); that is, because that refusal of almsfood was for the sake of that bhikkhu’s long-term fewness of wishes... [and so on] ...up to his arousal of energy.

It will turn out thus. How so? For if, at a later time, there should arise in him excessive desire for requisites, or evil desire, or great desire, then he will restrain him with this very thorn of the rejection of almsfood, saying:
"Hey! Having rejected even the almsfood left over by the Sugata, you have now given rise to such a desire! Thus...
Reflecting thus, this same method applies to the prevention of discontent and lack of austerity when they have arisen.
In this way, it will lead him to fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity.
Regarding "to being easy to support," the commentary here is as follows: in this case, someone might be difficult to support for himself and also for his attendants.
He is difficult to support. One person is easy to support and easy to satisfy for both himself and his attendants.
How so? For he who, having received sour things and the like, seeks out non-sour things; who discards what was received at one house while seeking at another house;
and who, having wandered through the entire village, enters the monastery with an empty bowl and lies down—this person is difficult to support for himself. He who...
Furthermore, even when given alms such as boiled rice, meat, and curries that fill his bowl, he displays a sullen countenance and a state of displeasure;
or, right in their presence, he disparages that alms-food, saying, "What have you given? and gives it instead to novices, householders, and others.
Such a person is a burden to his supporters. Seeing this, people [avoid him] from afar.

They avoid him, thinking, "This bhikkhu is difficult to support; he cannot be maintained. However, one who, having received whatever food—whether coarse or refined—eats it with a contented mind and, having gone to the monastery, performs his own duties, is easy for himself to support.
And one who, without disparaging the gift of others—be it small or great, coarse or refined—is satisfied in mind...
Having become cheerful of face, he eats right in their presence and then departs; this is one who is easy to support for his attendants.
Seeing this, people become exceedingly confident, thinking, "Our venerable sir is easy to support;
he is satisfied with even a little," and having given their promise, they support him.

In that regard, if at a later time a thought should arise in him due to his own or his attendants' being difficult to support, he should restrain it by means of this very thorn of the refusal of alms-food, reflecting thus:
"O, you who have refused even the food left over from the Sugata, how can you give rise to such a thought? Reflecting in this way, thus will it be for him.
It will lead to being easy to support. But if sloth should arise in him, he will ward it off with this very goad:

"O you who at that time rejected even the alms-food left over by the Sugata, and while overcome by hunger and weakness performed the duty of a recluse—how is it that today you are devoted to sloth? Thus reflecting, he restrains himself.
In this way, it will lead to his exertion of energy. Thus, this refusal of almsfood will lead to his fewness of desires for a long time...
[and so on] ...it will lead to his exertion of energy. In this way, these five qualities being fulfilled will fulfill the ten bases of discourse.
How so? For in this very text, three [qualities] are presented by way of fewness of wishes, contentment, and the arousal of energy;
the remaining ones are subsumed under effacement (*sallekha*). This is indeed the name for all topics of discourse, namely, effacement.
As it is said: "And whatever discourse there is, Ānanda, that is conducive to effacement, favorable to the removal of mental hindrances, and leading exclusively to disenchantment..."
"It leads to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. That is to say:
talk on fewness of desires," and so forth in detail. Thus, these five qualities, when fulfilled, will fulfill the ten bases of discourse.
The ten bases of discourse, when fulfilled, will fulfill the three trainings.
How so? For among these, the four discourses on fewness of wishes, contentment, non-association, and virtue are comprised within the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
The three discourses on seclusion, the arousal of energy, and concentration are comprised within the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*).
And the discourses on wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—

These three are comprised within the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*). Thus, when the ten bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*) are fulfilled, the three trainings (*sikkhā*) will be fulfilled.
When the three trainings are fulfilled, they will fulfill the five aggregates of the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha-dhammakkhandha*). How so?
For the fulfilled training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is itself the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*)...

The aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, the training in higher wisdom, and the aggregates of wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training—thus, when these three trainings are fulfilled, they will fulfill the five aggregates of the qualities of one beyond training.
When the five aggregates of the qualities are fulfilled, they will fulfill the deathless Nibbāna. It is just as when there is a heavy rain on a mountain peak above.
When a great rain cloud has poured down, it fills the mountain clefts and ravines. These, being filled, fill the small pools; the small pools fill the large pools;
the large pools fill the streams; the streams fill the great rivers; and the great rivers fill the great ocean, the sea.
In the same way, when these five qualities are fulfilled in that bhikkhu, they lead to the fulfillment of the ten bases of discourse.
Having done so, they will eventually fulfill the deathless Nibbāna.
Seeing this meaning—that by practicing the way of the heirs of the Dhamma, this bhikkhu obtains the supreme heirship to the Dhamma—the Blessed One said:
"For what reason? Because for that bhikkhu, monks... and so forth.

Having thus established by reason that the state of being more worthy of honor and praise belongs to that bhikkhu, the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with "Therefore, bhikkhus, listen to me," in order to direct those bhikkhus toward that same state. What is meant? This is what is said:
because one who, having consumed that alms-food, should practice the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), would be excluded from these five root virtues.
"But whoever should do it without having eaten, he becomes a sharer in these [faults]—therefore, monks, ... [as before] ... not heirs to material things.
This is what the Blessed One said; that is, the Blessed One spoke this portion of the sutta from the conclusion of the introduction down to "not heirs to material things.
Having spoken this portion of the sutta, the Sugata—by means of the beautiful practice...
The Blessed One, having indeed attained the designation "Sugata" because he has gone [to the goal], rose from his seat and entered the monastery.

Having risen from the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, he entered the monastery—his own Great Fragrant Chamber—while the assembly remained undispersed. Why? For the purpose of praising the Dhamma.
It is said that when Buddhas enter the monastery before their teaching is concluded, they do so for two reasons: for the purpose of praising a person, or... [the text continues].
Or for the purpose of praising the Dhamma. Entering for the purpose of praising a person, he thought thus:
"This summary of the exposition has been recited by me in brief, but not analyzed in detail.
The monks who receive the Dhamma will, after learning it, approach Ānanda or Kaccāna and ask them; they, having compared it with my own knowledge, will explain it."
Then those who receive the Dhamma will ask me again; to them I shall praise those individuals, saying: "Bhikkhus, Ānanda has spoken well, Kaccāna has spoken well.
Even if you were to ask me about this matter, I would explain it in exactly the same way.
Having thus praised them, they will conceive respect for them and approach those bhikkhus.
“Those monks will also enjoin them in the meaning and the Dhamma; being so enjoined by them, and fulfilling the three trainings, they will make an end of suffering.
As he was entering for the purpose of honoring the Dhamma, he thought thus, just as he had thought while still here: “When I have entered the monastery...”
While censuring that very heir to material things and praising the heir to the Dhamma, Sāriputta, sitting right here in this assembly, will teach the Dhamma.
Thus, this teaching—expounded by both of us with a single-minded intention—will be supreme and weighty, like a stone umbrella. In the sense of crossing over the four floods...
It will be like a boat placed at a landing place, and like a chariot yoked with four noble steeds in terms of proceeding along the path.

And just as when a king, having issued a command to the assembly saying, "This is the penalty for one who acts thus," rises from his seat and ascends to his palace, the general seated right there carries out that command established by the king; even so...
“Sāriputta, who is seated right here in this assembly, will deliver the teaching that I have set forth after praising it;
thus, this teaching, delivered by the wisdom of both of us, will blaze forth with even greater power, like the midday sun.
Having said this, he rose from his seat for the purpose of honoring the Dhamma and entered the monastery.
In such instances, it should be understood that the Blessed One vanished from his very seat and entered the monastery by means of the movement of his mind.
For if he had gone by means of the movement of his body, the entire assembly would have followed surrounding him;
having been dispersed once, they would have been difficult to reconvene. Therefore, the Blessed One entered solely by means of the movement of his mind.
31. When the Blessed One had thus entered [the city], the Venerable Sāriputta—desiring to praise that Dhamma in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention—said this...
(as above). Herein, "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment.
"Sāriputta" is the name of that Elder; and it is derived from his mother's side, not from his father's. For he was the son of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī.
Therefore, he is called Sāriputta. "Not long after he had departed" means not long after he had gone away.
Regarding the address "Friends, monks," when the Blessed Buddhas address their disciples, they call them "monks.
However, the disciples, thinking "May we not be equal to the Buddhas," first say "Friends" and afterwards say "monks. And by the Buddhas...
When addressed, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus gives the response "Venerable Sir," and the disciples [respond] "Friend.
Regarding the phrase "In what way, friends" (*kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso*): here, *kittāvatā* is a word denoting a limit; it means "by how much. The particle *nu* is used for inquiry.
The syllable *kho* is merely an expletive. "Of the Teacher dwelling in seclusion" refers to [the three...].
"While the Teacher dwells in seclusions—that is, in the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites—[they] do not train according to seclusion.
