This means they do not train even in one of the three types of seclusion; they become merely heirs to material things. It was with this meaning in mind that the Venerable Sāriputta questioned the bhikkhus.
This same method applies to the bright fortnight as well.
When this was said, the bhikkhus, desiring to hear that matter, spoke the words beginning with "From afar indeed...
and so forth. Therein, "from afar" means even from across a kingdom, even from across a province, or even from a distance of many yojanas; "nearby" means in close proximity.
"To know" means to understand or to realize. "Let the Venerable Sāriputta himself be inspired to speak" refers to the Venerable Sāriputta alone.
The meaning is: "Let there be a portion; let the Venerable Sāriputta, however, divide it after setting aside his own portion. For the Venerable One’s portion is this: the explanation of the meaning;
whereas our portion is the hearing of it—this is the intended sense here, which thus accords with the characteristics of the words.
Some, however, say: "'Let it occur to him' means 'let it appear. Others say: "'Let it present itself.'"
"They shall bear" means they will take up and master [the teaching]. Then, wishing to speak to them, the Elder said, "Therefore," and so forth.
In this context, "therefore" (*tena*) is a word expressing a reason; "hi" is a particle. The sense is:
"Since you desire to hear, and since you have placed the burden upon me, therefore listen. Those monks also accepted the words of the Elder.
Therefore he said: “‘So it is, friend,’ … [and so on] … they replied.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta spoke as follows, showing in three ways the same point that had been stated by the Blessed One—who was censuring those who inherit material goods—in a single way: “In this case, friends, …”
“While the Teacher dwells in seclusion... [as before] ...in this way, friends, disciples do not train in accordance with the seclusion of the Teacher who dwells in seclusion.
To this extent, the Blessed One, censuring the practice of those who inherit material gifts, said: “You too would become consumers of that.”
He said: "The meaning of what you yourself asked—'In what way... [pe] ...do they not train accordingly'—is well-expounded in detail.
And that was done without even touching upon the Blessed One’s state of being one who accepts gifts.
For it is fitting for the Blessed One alone, as he favors his disciples, to say, 'I too shall be one who accepts gifts from him,' and not for the disciples."
This same method applies to the bright fortnight as well; this, then, is the application of the sequence of connections here.
This, however, is the commentary on the meaning: "here" means in this Dispensation; "of the Teacher who is secluded" means of the Teacher who is utterly secluded by the three kinds of seclusion.
"They do not train in seclusion" means they do not train in bodily seclusion; they do not fulfill it.
This has been stated. However, if he were speaking with reference to the threefold seclusion, there would be no distinction in the question;
for this is the section on the answer. Therefore, by this phrase he shows bodily seclusion; by the words beginning with "and of those states," mental seclusion;
and by the words beginning with "those who are luxurious," seclusion from acquisitions. Thus, in brief, the meaning here should be understood.
"Of those states": he says this with reference to greed and so forth, which he will later describe in the manner beginning, "In that regard, friends, greed is evil," and so on.
"They do not abandon" means they do not relinquish; what is meant is that they do not fulfill seclusion of mind (*cittaviveka*).
"Luxurious" (*bāhulika*) means those who practice for the sake of an abundance of robes and other requisites. "Those who take the teaching laxly" means they are slack (*sāthalikā*).
Regarding the phrase "with the hindrances as their precursor": here, "hindrances" (*okkamana*) refers to the five hindrances in the sense of descending [into the mind].
Thus, it is meant that they have the five hindrances as their precursor. Regarding "in seclusion": this refers to Nibbāna, which is seclusion from the substrata of existence (*upadhiviveka*).

"Having laid down the burden" means having cast off the yoke; it means not even making an effort toward its attainment. By this much, it is said that they do not fulfill seclusion from the substrata of existence.
Having spoken thus far in an unrestricted manner, he now spoke the passage beginning with "In this regard, friends," while restricting the teaching. Why?
Because if it were stated without such restriction as "by three grounds," the disciples might become indifferent, thinking, "He seems to be speaking of someone else, not of us.
But when it is stated by specifying "the elders, the novices, or those of middle standing," they feel respect, thinking, "He is speaking of us."
They act as follows: just as when a king says, "The city streets must be cleared by the ministers," they do not clear them while wondering, "By whom should they be cleared?
yet when the drum sounds, "Each person's own house-front must be cleared," everyone clears and decorates them in an instant—this should be understood as being exactly like that.
In this context, "therein" (*tattha*) means among those disciples. "Elders" (*therā*) refers to those who have ten years of seniority. "By three grounds" (*tīhi ṭhānehi*) means by three reasons.
For this word *ṭhāna* is seen to denote sovereignty, stability, a moment, and a reason. Indeed, it is used in the sense of sovereignty in such passages as:
"But what deed did the Venerable Devānaminda perform to attain this station? And so forth. It is also used in the sense of skill [in discerning] the possible...

In such passages as “he is one who hits the mark,” it refers to stability (*ṭhiti*). In such passages as “this occurs to the Tathāgata at the right occasion (*ṭhāna*) and at the right moment (*khaṇa*),” it refers to the moment.
In such passages as “the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible,” it refers to a cause (*kāraṇa*). But here, it refers specifically to a cause.
For a cause is called a “standing-point” (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands therein, being dependent upon it for its existence.
"By this first ground, the elder bhikkhus are to be censured. Here, "to be censured" (*gārayha*) means they ought to be criticized.
Being so-called elders, they do not resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets or jungle retreats; they do not relinquish lodgings within the vicinity of a village;
they dwell increasing their delight in social company; they do not fulfill even physical seclusion during the time between the new and full moon.
"What kind [of people] were they?"—thus he shows that they are to be censured in this way, thinking, "Friends, they receive this censure. Regarding the phrase "by the second ground":
here too, friends, even though these elders are such [as they claim], they do not abandon those qualities such as greed which the Teacher has declared must be abandoned;
nor do they attain one-pointedness of mind by sitting to one side for even as long as a finger-snap.

The construction should be made as follows: "They do not obtain [these things]; they are to be censured for thinking, 'What were they like in the time of the new and middle [dispensations]?'—thus, friends, they receive this censure.
Regarding the phrase "by the third ground," here too [the meaning is]:
"Friends, these are indeed elders, yet they do not subsist by any [proper means], being devoted to the practice of adorning their putrid bodies with robes, bowls, and lodgings."
The construction should be understood as follows: "They dwell not fulfilling seclusion from the substrates (*upadhiviveka*);
what were they like during their middle and new stages?"—thus they are to be censured. "Friends, they receive this censure"—this is what is being shown.
This same method applies to the middle and new periods. However, this is the distinction: "middle" refers to those from five years up to nine years; "new" refers to...

They are said to be "less than five years old. Just as it was stated there regarding what they were like during the periods of youth and middle age, so here one should apply the explanation by stating:
what were they like at the time of being new [monks], what will they be like at the time of being elders, and what will they be like at the time of being middle-aged elders?
32. And in this case, the meaning for the bright side (*sukkapakkha*) should be understood by way of the opposite method to that stated for the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*).
Here, however, is the summary: Indeed, these elders, though being such [senior monks], resort to remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets through a succession of leagues;
even when it is the proper time to approach a village lodging, they do not go there—thus.
Even with bodies grown old, those who have initiated energy inspire confidence in the donors of requisites;
by this first point, the elders are praiseworthy and receive praise.
Having abandoned greed and the other defilements, they fulfill mental seclusion—this great elder, too, was surrounded by his co-residents and pupils.
Even when it was time to sit down after making the offering, and even while remaining in such an age, he would enter [the forest] after performing his meal duties and depart in the evening;
having entered in the evening, he would depart at dawn.

He performed the preliminary work for the *kasiṇas*, produced meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), realized the paths and fruits, and in every way fulfilled mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*)—by this second [method].
For this reason, elder bhikkhus are praised and receive commendation.

At a time when it would be appropriate for an elder to wear fine garments such as those made of linen, silk, or cotton—garments that are light and pleasant to the touch—even at such a time, this great elder wears robes made of rags from the dust-heap;
having taken up the Dispensation without laxity, free from hindrances, he enters into the attainment of fruition and dwells in seclusion from the acquisitions (upadhiviveka).
By this third point—that he dwells fulfilling [the training]—the elders become praiseworthy;
they receive praise. This same method applies to the sections on the middle and new [monks]. 33. Regarding "Therein, friends," what is the connection?
Thus, having censured the practice of those who are heirs to material things in nine ways, by means of nine...

Praising the practice of being an heir to the Dhamma, and having concluded the teaching by way of eighteen aspects, [the Blessed One] spoke this passage beginning with "In this regard, friends, there is greed...

in order to show specifically, as "these are those," those things called "dhammas to be abandoned" in the statement: "And those dhammas for which the Teacher has declared abandonment, they do not abandon. This is the connection.

Furthermore, below, the Dhamma was taught by way of a figurative exposition (*pariyāya*). But the material gift (*āmisa*) was taught both by way of a figurative exposition and by way of a non-figurative exposition (*nippariyāya*). Now, in order to explain the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*), which is the Dhamma in its non-figurative sense, this was said.

This is the connection (*anusandhi*) here. In that context, "therein" (*tattha*) is an indication of the past teaching; it means: "in the teaching stated in the manner beginning with, 'While the Teacher dwelt in seclusion, his disciples did not train in seclusion,'" and so forth. And greed is evil, and hatred...
And "evil" (*pāpa*): these two states are evil and base; he shows that they are to be abandoned.

Therein, greed (*lobha*) has the characteristic of coveting. Hatred (*dosa*) has the characteristic of malice. Among those two, greed arises upon obtaining the requisites of one who inherits material things, while hatred arises upon not obtaining them.
Through greed one longs for what has not been obtained; through hatred one becomes distressed when not obtaining it. And greed [arises] toward the object to be given...
There is hatred toward one who does not give or who gives what is unpleasant. Through greed, one fulfills the states rooted in the nine kinds of craving;
through hatred, the five kinds of stinginess.
Now, showing the means for their abandonment, he said: "And for the abandoning of greed," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: its...
"But for the abandoning of evil greed and hatred, there is a middle way"—this was said with reference to the Path.
For the Path does not approach, does not go near, these two extremes—greed being one extreme and hatred being the other;
it is liberated from these extremes, and therefore it is called the "middle way. Of these...
It is called "middle" (*majjhima*) because it is situated in the middle of existence, and "practice" (*paṭipadā*) because it is to be practiced.

Likewise, the pursuit of sensual pleasure is one extreme, the pursuit of self-mortification is another extreme, eternalism is one extreme, and annihilationism is another extreme; this should be elaborated upon in the same manner as previously stated.
Furthermore, with the phrases "the maker of vision" (*cakkhukaraṇī*) and so forth, he praises that very practice, for it leads to the seeing of the truths.

In the sense of being a guide for seeing, it is "the maker of vision" (*cakkhukaraṇī*). In the sense of making things known through knowledge of the truths, it is "the maker of knowledge" (*ñāṇakaraṇī*).

Because it pacifies greed and the other defilements, it leads to peace (*upasama*). Because it shows that the four truths are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), it leads to direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
"Enlightenment" (*sambodha*) means the Path; because it leads to that end, it leads to enlightenment (*sambodhāya saṃvattati*).
For it leads to the path itself for the sake of the path, because it performs the task that must be done by means of the path. That which is called Nibbāna is "conditionless" (appaccaya);
however, because it leads to its realization—that is, to the act of making it directly manifest—it is said to "lead to Nibbāna.
This is the essential point here; any description other than this is mere proliferation (papañca).
Now, desiring to show that middle way in its specific form, he asks, "And what is it? and answers in the manner beginning with, "This very one.

In this context, the word "this very" (*ayameva*) is a term of emphasis, intended to exclude any other path and to demonstrate that this is common to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha.
And thus it has been said: "This alone is the path; there is no other for the purification of vision."

It is "Noble" (ariya) because it is far removed from the defilements; it is also "Noble" because it leads to the abandoning of enemies, because it is taught by the Noble One, and because it leads to the attainment of the noble state.
It is "eightfold" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it is endowed with eight factors, and not because it is devoid of factors like the five-fold musical instruments and so forth.
It is called the path because it goes along killing the defilements, or because it seeks them out.

*Nibbāna* is so called because it is extinguished [of defilements] or because it is sought by those who desire *Nibbāna*. It is called the *magga* (path) because it is traveled or because it is practiced by them.
The phrase "namely" (*seyyathidaṃ*) is a particle; its meaning is "if one asks what that is," or "what are those eight factors?
For each individual factor is indeed the path itself. As it is said: "Right view is both the path and the cause. The ancients also say:
“The path of seeing is right view; the path of directing is right intention... [and so on] ...the path of non-distraction is right concentration.
Among these factors beginning with right view: right view has the characteristic of seeing rightly; right intention has the characteristic of directing rightly;
right speech has the characteristic of encompassing rightly; right action has the characteristic of originating rightly.
Right livelihood has the characteristic of complete purification. Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion.
Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing [the mind]. Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure.
Their etymological derivation should also be understood in this same manner: "right seeing" is *sammā-diṭṭhi*.
In this context, when right view arises, it abandons wrong view along with its concomitant defilements and ignorance;
it takes Nibbāna as its object and sees associated states. However, it does so through non-delusion rather than by taking them as objects;
therefore, it is called "right view."
Right intention abandons wrong intention and the defilements opposed to it, takes Nibbāna as its object, and correctly directs the associated mental states; therefore, it is called "right intention.
Right speech abandons wrong speech and the defilements opposed to it, takes Nibbāna as its object, and correctly sustains the associated mental states; therefore, it is called "right speech."
Right action abandons wrong action and the defilements opposed to it, takes Nibbāna as its object, and rightly originates associated states; therefore, it is called "right action.
Right livelihood abandons wrong livelihood and the defilements opposed to it, takes Nibbāna as its object, and rightly purifies associated states; therefore, it is called "right livelihood."
Right effort abandons wrong effort, the defilements opposed to it, and laziness; it takes Nibbāna as its object and correctly exerts the associated states. Therefore, it is called "right effort.

Right mindfulness abandons wrong mindfulness, the defilements opposed to it, and takes Nibbāna as its object; it correctly establishes the associated states. Therefore, it is called "right mindfulness."

Right concentration abandons wrong concentration and the defilements opposed to it, as well as restlessness; it takes Nibbāna as its object and rightly concentrates the associated states. Therefore, it is called "right concentration.
Now, with the words "This, friends," he concludes that very path. Its meaning is this:
that which was described by combining all four supramundane paths into one as the "Eightfold Path"—this, friends... leads to Nibbāna.
Having thus shown greed and hatred among the states to be abandoned, as well as the means for their abandonment, he now says, "In this regard, friends, anger...
and so forth, showing other states to be abandoned and the means for their abandonment. Therein, anger has the characteristic of being provoked to wrath, or the characteristic of ferocity;
its function is to cause malice; it is manifested as resentment. Its characteristic is also that of persistent attachment.
Enmity (upanāha) has the function of not relinquishing resentment; it is manifested as the state of persistent attachment to anger. And this has been said:
"Anger occurs at the earlier time, enmity at the later time," and so forth.
Slander (makkha) has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others; its function is their destruction; it is manifested as the concealment of those [faults].
Slander has the characteristic of seizing upon a point of similarity; its function is to equalize one’s own qualities with those of others;
it is manifested as attending to the measure of others’ qualities.
Envy has the characteristic of being dissatisfied with the success of others, or alternatively, the characteristic of intolerance toward it; its function is lack of delight therein.
Therefore, its manifestation is the state of being averse [to sharing]. Stinginess (macchariya) has the characteristic of concealing one’s own prosperity;
its function is the lack of delight in others sharing one’s own prosperity; its manifestation is contraction.
Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of concealing the evil one has done; its function is the hiding of that [evil]; its manifestation is the obscuring of it. One’s own...
Deceit has the characteristic of manifesting qualities that do not exist; its function is to bring those [qualities] to light;
it is manifested as making those [qualities] appear even through bodily gestures.

Arrogance has the characteristic of the mind’s inflation; its function is to live without deference; it is manifested as lack of gentleness. Hostility has the characteristic of seeking preeminence in action; its function is opposition; it is manifested as disrespect.

Conceit has the characteristic of swelling up; its function is the sense of "I"; it is manifested as a state of inflation. Excessive conceit has the characteristic of over-swelling; its function is an excessive sense of "I"; it is manifested as a state of extreme inflation.

Intoxication has the characteristic of being intoxicated; its function is the grasping of intoxication; it is manifested as madness. Negligence has the characteristic of the mind's relinquishment toward the five strands of sensual pleasure;
its function is the non-provision of relinquishment; it is manifested as the absence of mindfulness.
In this way, the characteristics and other attributes of these phenomena are to be understood. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Vibhaṅga* beginning with, "Therein, what is anger?
Furthermore, specifically in this context, one who is an heir to material goods becomes angry when he does not receive for himself and another receives, even once.
Arisen anger is merely anger; beyond that is resentment (*upanāha*). Thus, being angry and resentful, he slanders the virtues of another who possesses even a small amount of gain;
he also adopts a competitive attitude, thinking, "I am just like him. This is his slandering (*makkha*) and disparaging (*paḷāsa*);
thus, being a slanderer and a disparager, he envies [another] regarding their gains, honor, and so forth, thinking, "What has this one got that I do not?"
He becomes corrupted; this is his envy (*issā*). But if he possesses some success, he cannot endure its being shared with others;
this is his stinginess (*macchariya*). Furthermore, for the sake of gain, he conceals his own existing faults;
this is his deceit (*māyā*). He proclaims qualities that do not exist; this is his craftiness (*sāṭheyya*). Practicing in this way, if...
He obtains gain according to his desire and becomes stiff and hard-hearted because of it;
he is unable to be admonished with the words, "This should not be done thus"—this is his stubbornness (*thambha*).
But if someone says something to him, "This should not be done thus," he becomes agitated in mind and frowns, saying with force, "Who are you to me? and speaks overbearing words.
This is his agitation (*sārambha*). Then, through stubbornness (*thambha*), conceiving himself as "I alone am superior," he becomes arrogant (*mānī*).
Through agitation, thinking "Who are these [others]? while despising others, he becomes over-arrogant (*atimānī*); this is his pride (*māna*) and over-arrogance (*atimāna*).

By means of that pride and over-arrogance, he generates intoxication (*mada*) in many forms, such as the intoxication of birth and so forth. Being intoxicated, he becomes heedless regarding the objects of sense-pleasure and the like.
"This is his intoxication and negligence.

Thus, the heir to material things is not freed from these evil states and others of a similar kind. In this way, first, the states to be abandoned should be understood. As for the means of abandonment, it is exactly the same everywhere both in terms of the text and its meaning.
However, for the sake of proficiency in the cultivation of knowledge, one should understand here this classification, sequence, and method of development.
Regarding that, first as to its classification: this middle way is sometimes the noble eightfold path and sometimes the sevenfold path.
For when it arises by way of the supramundane first jhāna, it is the eightfold path; by way of the remaining jhānas, it is the sevenfold path.
However, here it is called "eightfold" according to the highest description. From this...
For there is no path-factor [in the unwholesome]. Thus, first, the distinction here should be understood.
Furthermore, right view is the best among all wholesome states, as it is said: "Wisdom, they say, is the best of wholesome things.
And in the section on the wholesome, it is the forerunner, as it is said: "And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner?"
“He understands right view as right view, and he understands wrong view as wrong view,” so it is said at length.
And as it is said: “Knowledge, monks, is the forerunner for the attainment of wholesome states.
The remaining factors are produced from that [knowledge] as their source, as it is said: “In one of right view, right intention arises... [and so on].”
“Right concentration comes to one who possesses right mindfulness. Therefore, these factors are stated in this sequence; thus the order here should be understood. As for the method of development:
some develop insight preceded by serenity, while others develop serenity preceded by insight. How so?
Here, a certain person first produces either access concentration or absorption concentration.
This is serenity (*samatha*); he then contemplates that [serenity] and its associated states through insight (*vipassanā*) as impermanent and so forth—this is insight.
Thus, first comes serenity, and afterwards insight. Therefore it is said: "He develops insight preceded by serenity.
As he develops insight preceded by serenity, the Path arises for him; he, [having developed it]...

One cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that path; as one cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that path, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are exhausted. In this way, one develops insight preceded by serenity.
However, here someone, without having even produced the aforementioned serenity, [contemplates] the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent and so forth.
He sees with insight; this is insight (*vipassanā*). With the fulfillment of that insight, because of the relinquishment of phenomena arisen therein as its object, one-pointedness of mind arises;
this is serenity (*samatha*). Thus, first comes insight and afterwards serenity.
Therefore it is said: "One develops serenity preceded by insight. For him, [there is] serenity preceded by insight...
For one who develops serenity, the path arises; he pursues that path... pe ...he cultivates it repeatedly.
As he pursues that path... pe ...the underlying tendencies are exhausted. Thus one develops serenity preceded by insight.
But for one who develops insight preceded by serenity, and also for one who develops serenity preceded by insight—
At the moment of the supramundane path, serenity and insight are indeed conjoined. In this way, the method of development (bhāvanānaya) should be understood here.
Thus ends the commentary on the Dhammadāyāda Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

4. Commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta 34. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Bhayabherava Sutta. Herein is the commentary on the words not previously explained: *atha* is a particle used in the sense of non-interruption.
*kho* is used in the sense of emphasis; it means that [the Blessed One was] residing at Sāvatthī in the monastery without interruption. Thus it is said.
...it exists. "Jāṇussoṇī" is not a name given to him by his parents; rather, it was obtained through the acquisition of a particular office.
This office of the *purohita* (chaplain) is indeed called the "Jāṇussoṇī position," and since that was granted to him by the king, he is therefore called "Jāṇussoṇī.

He is a *brāhmaṇa* because he recites (*aṇati*) the *brahma* (the Veda); the meaning is that he rehearses the *mantras*. For this alone is the [defining characteristic] of those who are *brāhmaṇas* by birth.
This is a statement of etymology. Furthermore, the Noble Ones (ariya) are called "brahmins" because they have banished evil (bāhitapāpa).
Regarding the phrase "he approached where the Blessed One was": the word *yena* is used in the instrumental case with the sense of the locative;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "he approached to that place where the Blessed One was. Or else, it means "by which [reason] the Blessed One [was honored] by gods and humans..."
"He should be approached; for that reason he approached"—thus is the meaning to be understood here.

And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached? With the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities, just as a great tree that is constantly laden with fruit is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying its sweet fruit.
“Approached” (*upasaṅkami*) means that he had gone; “having approached” (*upasaṅkamitvā*) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, it means that having gone in this manner, he went to a place even closer than before, which is reckoned as the vicinity of the Blessed One.
“He exchanged greetings with the Blessed One” means that just as the Blessed One was asking him about his health and so forth, so too did he [ask the Blessed One].
He too experienced a joy equal to that of the Blessed One; like cold water meeting warm water, they were harmonized and attained a state of unity.
And by means of that [greeting] beginning with, "I hope it is bearable for you, Master Gotama; I hope it is sustainable;
I hope that Master Gotama and the disciples of Master Gotama are free from illness, free from affliction, light-bodied, strong, and living in comfort,"...
It is "conducive to amity" (*sammodanīya*) because it generates the joy of gladness known as *pīti* and *pāmojja*, and because it is appropriate for such gladness to arise;

and it is "conducive to remembrance" (*sārāṇīya*) because, through the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, it is of a nature that deserves to be recalled and continuously maintained for a very long time.
Furthermore, it is "conducive to amity" in the sense of being pleasant when heard, and [it is conducive to remembrance] in the sense of being pleasant when recollected.
And it is memorable. Thus, having exchanged greetings that are delightful through the purity of their phrasing and memorable through the purity of their meaning—
having thus concluded, brought to a close, and finished that delightful and memorable conversation—
he sat down to one side, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come.
“*Ekamante*” (to one side) is a neuter locative designation, as in such expressions as “the moon and sun move unevenly.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he sat down in such a way that he was seated to one side.
Alternatively, this accusative case is used in the sense of a locative. “*Nisīdi*” means he sat down; for wise men [approach] one who is worthy of honor.
Having approached, they sit to one side with skill regarding seating; and this [monk] was one among them, therefore he sat to one side.
But how does one sitting "sit to one side"? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. Namely:
too far away, too near, upwind, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind. Sitting too far away...
For if he wishes to speak, he must speak in a loud voice. Sitting too close, he causes physical contact.
Sitting upwind, he is troubled by the odor of the body. Sitting on high ground, he manifests disrespect.
Sitting directly in front, if he wishes to look at him, he must gaze with eye meeting eye.
[If one sits] too far back, if one wishes to see [the Teacher], one must stretch out the neck to see him.
Therefore, he sat having avoided these six faults of sitting; thus it is said, "he sat to one side. "Yeme" means "those who are these.
"Kulaputtā" (sons of good family) are of two kinds: sons of good family by birth and sons of good family by conduct. Therein—
"At that time, there was a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the foremost family in that very Thullakoṭṭhika"— thus,
those who have come forth from high-born families are called "clansmen by birth. However, those who have come forth as "clansmen who, with faith,
have gone forth from the home life into homelessness," even if born into any ordinary family, are those endowed with virtuous conduct.
"Of good family and virtuous conduct. Here, however, they are "sons of good family" for two reasons.
"With faith" means by means of faith. "From the home" means from the household life. "To homelessness" refers to the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*).
For here there is no household life, thus it is "homelessness"; or because the work beneficial to the household—such as farming and cattle-tending—is absent here.
The meaning is as follows: A *bhikkhu* is one for whom there is no home (*agāra*); thus he is a "homeless one" (*anagāra*). The state of being a homeless one is "homelessness" (*anagāriya*).

"Those who have gone forth" (*pabbajitā*) means they have approached it; thus, what is meant is that they have approached what is designated as homelessness—that is, the state of a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*)—in every respect.
"Foremost" (*pubbaṅgama*) means one who goes before, a leader. "One who does much" (*bahukāra*) means one who is of great benefit through the performance of deeds for the welfare of others.
"Master Gotama encourages them": Master Gotama causes those sons of good family to undertake and trains them in the higher morality and so forth.
"That body of people": that multitude of persons. "Falls into conformity with his view": they follow in accordance with his seeing;
the meaning is that whatever view, whatever conviction, and whatever preference Master Gotama has, they too come to have that same view, that same conviction, and that same preference.
But why did he speak thus? It is said that previously, having seen many sons of noble families living in the midst of the household,
enjoying themselves with the five strands of sensual pleasure like sons of the gods, and being well-guarded both within and without,
he later heard the sweet-savored Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One and, out of faith, went forth from the home.
Having gone forth, he saw them content with mere food and clothing, dwelling in forest lodgings that were unprotected by anyone, yet unafraid and unsuspecting, joyful and exultant;
and having seen them, he reflected, "Upon what support has this comfortable dwelling of these sons of noble family arisen?
and he conceived faith in the Blessed One, [thinking], "The ascetic Gotama."
He obtained [it]. He came into the presence of the Blessed One to announce that confidence; therefore, he spoke thus.
Then the Blessed One, accepting those words and expressing his approval, said: "It is so, O Brahmin," and so forth.
For here, the particle *evaṃ* has the sense of acceptance and approval of the statement. "Having dedicated it to me" (*mamaṃ uddissa*)—
"Directed toward me": "With faith" means precisely with faith. He says this with reference to those who are not driven by debt, nor by fear, and so forth;

for the Blessed One is a leader only for such as these, and not for others. "Difficult to achieve" means difficult to bring about, hard to endure, and impossible for those of little power to plunge into—this is what is meant. "Wilderness and forest tracts" refers to both wildernesses and...

And forest-dwelling sites (*vanapatthāni*). In this regard, although it is stated in the Abhidhamma in an absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*) that "all this is forest once one has gone out beyond the threshold post (*indakhila*)," nevertheless,

it should be understood that only that which is described as a "dwelling site producing the forest-dweller's practice" (*āraññikaṅga-nipphādaka*), namely "the last [boundary] being five hundred bow-lengths," is intended here.
"Vanapattha" means a place beyond the vicinity of a village, a location where people do not frequent, where no plowing is done and no sowing takes place.
And this has also been said: "‘Vanapattha’ is a designation for remote lodgings; ‘vanapattha’ is a designation for lodgings in forest thickets;
‘vanapattha’ is a designation for terrifying places; ‘vanapattha’ is a designation for places that cause the hair to stand on end."
“‘Forest-dwelling’ (vanapattha) is a designation for dwellings that have boundaries; ‘forest-dwelling’ is not a designation for dwellings frequented by people.
And here, setting aside this one formulation, forest-dwellings are to be understood by the remaining formulations.
“Remote” (panta) means bounded and very far away. “Solitude is difficult to practice” refers to physical solitude.
It is difficult to perform. It is hard to find delight in; it is not easy to take pleasure in. "In solitude" means in the state of being alone. What does this show?

Even when physical seclusion has been achieved, it is difficult to make the mind find delight therein. For this world delights in pairs [of opposites]. "They carry me away," they think—meaning they carry one off as it were, devour one as it were.
"The mind" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*). "Of one who does not obtain concentration" refers to access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).
This refers to one who does not attain access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). What does it show?
It shows that for such a bhikkhu, the forests—due to the various sounds of grass, leaves, deer, and other such things, as well as terrifying [noises]—are thought to distract the mind;
thus spoke the brahmin, being astonished by the forest-dwelling of sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith.
The Discourse on the Section on Bodily Action (Kāyakammantavārakathā) 35.
Then the Blessed One, having accepted and rejoiced in each of those statements of his in the same manner as before with the words, “So it is,
Brahmin,” and so forth— since such [actions] occur only for those who lack the discernment of objects (*ārammaṇa*) regarding the sixteen bases—
Those lodgings were difficult to obtain; they were not for those intent on grasping at objects,
and since the Bodhisatta himself was of such a nature, he spoke the words beginning with "But for me too" in order to demonstrate how difficult it was for one like him to obtain such lodgings.
In this context, "even before full enlightenment" means even prior to enlightenment; that is to say, at a time subsequent to the attainment of the Noble Path.
"Of one who has not yet fully awakened" means of one who has not yet penetrated the Four Truths.

"While being still only a bodhisatta" means while being only a being capable of awakening, a being worthy of attaining perfect self-enlightenment, or simply a being intent upon enlightenment (*bodhi*).

"Ever clinging. From the moment he made his resolution at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara—due to the perfection of that resolve through the convergence of the eight factors—the Tathāgata became "clinging" (*lagga*) to enlightenment, thinking, "This must be attained by me," and he came along without ever relinquishing his exertion for its realization;
therefore, he is called a *bodhisatta*. "Of him, of mine": of that very *bodhisatta* thus [described].
"Of me who am mindful. "Whatever recluses or brahmins," means whoever have gone forth or are addressers of "friend.
"With impure bodily action" means endowed with impure bodily action such as the taking of life and so forth.
"Because of the fault of impure bodily action" means because of the fault consisting of one's own impure bodily action.
It is the cause of fault; what is meant is that it is the reason for performing impure bodily actions.
*Hava* is a particle used as an emphatic expression. *Akusala* means blameworthy and insecure. *Bhayabherava* means fear and terror;
this is a designation for both mental trepidation and a terrifying object. In that context, "fear" (*bhaya*) is unwholesome in the sense of being blameworthy, while "terror" (*bherava*)—
It should be understood in the sense of being insecure. "They call out" means they shout. How so?

For having committed acts such as the destruction of life, they think, "We have done what is improper; if those whom we have offended were to find us out, they would now pursue us and bring about our ruin and disaster.
Thus, they enter the forest and sit down in the midst of thickets or among bushes.
Upon hearing even a slight sound of grass or a leaf, they tremble and are terrified, thinking, "Now we are lost.
Having arrived there, they feel as if surrounded by others, as if bound, and as if slain.
Thus, they summon and call out that fear and terror by way of attributing it to themselves.
"But it is not that I... [as before] ...I do not frequent them. As for "ye hi vo," here *vo* is merely a particle. "The Noble Ones" (*ariyā*) refers to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha.
"With purified bodily action" means being such as they are. "I am one among them" means I belong to their number.
"I too was one among them. For the Bodhisatta, whether as a householder or as one gone forth, was indeed pure in his bodily actions.
*Bhiyyo* is a particle used in the sense of "moreover" or "exceedingly. *Palloma* means "smoothness of hair," that is, security and well-being;
this is the meaning. *Āpādiṃ* means "I attained"; that is, I attained an exceeding state of well-being, or I attained well-being in an exceeding manner.
It has been said: "For dwelling in the forest" means for the purpose of dwelling in the forest.
The discussion on the section concerning bodily action is finished.
[Now follows] the commentary on the section concerning verbal action, etc.
36. This method applies everywhere. However, this is the distinction:
first, regarding the section on verbal action, "impure verbal action" means being endowed with impure verbal actions such as false speech and so forth. How do they summon fear and terror?
By destroying another's welfare through false speech, by creating dissension among friends through malicious speech, and through harsh speech...
Having pricked the vitals of others in the midst of an assembly with useless speech and ruined the livelihoods of other beings, they think, "We have done what is improper;
if those whom we have offended were to find out, they would now pursue us and bring about our ruin and disaster.
Thus, they enter the forest and sit among the reeds or within the thickets.
Upon hearing even a slight sound of grass or a leaf, they tremble and are terrified, thinking, "Now we are lost!
Having thus become as if surrounded by others, as if bound, and as if slain, they summon that fear and dread into themselves by way of attributing it to themselves; they call it forth.
In the section on mental action (*manokammanta*), "those with impure mental action" means those endowed with impure mental action such as covetousness and the like.
How do they summon fear and terror? By giving rise to covetousness and improper greed toward the goods protected and guarded by others;
by becoming angry with others; and by causing other beings to adopt wrong views.
"We have done what is improper... [and so forth]... they call out and summon by way of attributing it to themselves.

In the section on livelihood, "those of impure livelihood" means those who possess an impure livelihood consisting of twenty-one types of wrong search, such as the practice of medicine, acting as a messenger, usury, and so forth.
How do they summon fear and terror? Having maintained their livelihood in this manner...
They hear: “It is said that the bhikkhus who purify the Dispensation, possessing the Three Piṭakas, have set out to purify the Dispensation;
they will arrive here today or tomorrow. Having entered the forest, or while traveling between villages... [and so on]... they tremble and are terrified.
For when those [monks] arrive and surround them, they feel as if they have been captured, and they become like those dressed in white robes. The rest is exactly the same.

37. From this point on, regarding the terms "covetous" (*abhijjhālu*) and so forth, although covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are already included within mental action (*manokamma*), they should nevertheless be understood as being mentioned again by way of being hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). In that context, "covetous" means one whose habit is to covet the goods and property of others.
"Intensely lustful toward sense-pleasures" (*kāmesu tibbasārāgā*) means having abundant defilement-lust for objective sense-pleasures (*vatthukāma*). How do these invite fear and terror?

Their objects of perception become unsettled; for those dwelling in the forest with unsettled objects of perception, what was seen during the day presents itself at night as a terrifying fear: "With agitated minds, they tremble even at a slight thing;
seeing a rope or a creeper, they perceive it as a snake; seeing a stump, they perceive it as a *yakkha*."
"Just as those who perceive a plain or a mountain to be an elephant might meet with ruin and disaster through snakes and other dangers," so it is here; the rest is exactly the same.

"Byāpannacittā" means having a corrupted mind due to the loss of its natural state. For a mind that follows after defilements (*kilesa*) loses its natural state and becomes putrid, like old food mixed with sauce. "Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā" means having a corrupt intention of the mind.
This means they are possessed of an unwholesome intention of mind that produces harm for others.

How do they summon fear and terror? The manner in which they summon fear and terror should be understood from this point forward according to the same method explained in the section on covetousness (*abhijjhālu*).
However, wherever there will be a distinction, we shall explain it there. "But I am not one whose mind is malevolent..."
Here, however, he shows that he is one whose mind is filled with loving-kindness (*mettā*) and whose mind is intent on welfare; for such are the Bodhisattvas.
In this way, throughout all [passages], the virtues of the Bodhisattva are to be extolled by means of the opposites of the faults mentioned.

39. "Overcome by sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitā*): they are overcome, mastered, or seized by sloth (*thina*), which is a sickness of the mind, and by torpor (*middha*), which is a sickness of the remaining body; it is said that they are full of sleep.
40. "Agitated" (uddhatā) means having a nature of restlessness (uddhacca), with a mind that is flickering.
For through restlessness, the mind flickers over a single object like a banner on a flagpole moved by the wind. "With unpeaceful minds" (avūpasantacittā) means with unextinguished minds;
here, it is appropriate to understand this as referring to remorse (kukkucca).

41. "Full of doubt, wavering" (*kaṅkhī vicikicchī*): here, this is indeed a single fifth hindrance. It is called "doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) because of its doubting of an object, thinking, "What indeed is this?";
it is called "wavering" (*vicikicchā*) because of the state of being unable to reach a decision, thinking, "This alone is it.
Monks and brahmins who possess these qualities are thus described as "full of doubt, wavering."

42. "Those who praise themselves and disparage others": this is a designation for those who exalt themselves, lift themselves up, and place themselves in a high position, while they disparage, revile, and criticize others, placing them in a low position.
How do they invite fear and terror? They do so when others say, "So-and-so and so-and-so, it seems, exalt themselves..."

“They are reviling us, treating us like slaves; seize them! Thus pursued, they flee, enter the forest, and proceed—this should be detailed with examples corresponding to bodily actions, such as [hiding] between trees or within thickets. 43.

*Chambhī* means possessed of a paralysis that causes the body to stiffen and the hair to stand on end. *Bhīrukajātikā* means those whose very nature is timid; it is said they are full of fear like village children, lacking courage and being cowardly.
44. *Lābha-sakkāra-siloka*: Here, "gain" (*lābha*) means that which is obtained; it is a designation for the four requisites.
"Honor" (*sakkāra*) means a beautiful act; for the requisites themselves—when prepared in various ways, both excellent and inferior, and beautiful and handsome—are called "honors.
It also refers to the act of others showing respect toward oneself, or worship with flowers and so forth. "Fame" (*siloka*)...
This is the praising of [one's own] qualities; "gain, honor, and fame" refers to gain, honor, and fame collectively.
"Desiring" means longing for them. The expression "arousing fear and terror" is exactly like that used for the section on covetousness.
To illustrate this point, they relate the story of Piyagāmika:

It is said that there was a certain monk named Piya-gāmika who, seeing the gains received by monks who had undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), thought, "I too shall undertake an ascetic practice and thereby produce gains.
Having thus resolved, he undertook the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground (sosānikaṅga) and lived in a cemetery.
Then one day, an ox that had been released from work, having grazed during the day, [entered] at night into a thicket of flowers in that cemetery.
He stood there chewing his cud with his head held high. Piyagāmika, having stepped out from his walking path at night, heard the sound of the bull’s jaw and thought:
"Surely this creature, greedy for gain, has lived in the charnel ground; knowing this, the King of the Devas has come to harass me.
He placed his palms together in reverence before the old bull and said: "O noble being, King of Devas, today for one night..."
“Forgive me; from tomorrow onwards, I will not do so again,” he said, and stood paying homage and entreating him throughout the entire night.
Then, when the sun had risen, seeing him, he struck him with a walking stick and drove him away, saying, “You terrified me all night long.
45. *Kusītā* means those who have fallen into indolence. *Hīnavīriyā* means those who are inferior in energy, devoid of it, or lacking in vigor.
This has been said. In this context, those who are *kusīta* (lazy) are devoid of the exertion of physical energy; those of inferior energy (*hīnavīriya*) are devoid of the exertion of mental energy.
They are unable to perform even the mere defining of the object (*ārammaṇa-vavatthāna*). For them, whose objects are not defined, everything is exactly as before.

46. *Muṭṭhassati* means one whose mindfulness is lost. *Asampajāno* means one who is devoid of wisdom (*paññā*). And in contrast to this, [the opposite is expressed as]: "I am one whose mindfulness is established."

According to the wording, this is indeed a section on mindfulness (*satibhājaniya*). However, wisdom (*paññā*) is mentioned here for the purpose of illustrating the weakness of mindfulness. For mindfulness is twofold: that associated with wisdom and that dissociated from wisdom. Among these, that associated with wisdom is strong, while that dissociated from it is weak.

Therefore, even when they possess mindfulness, because they lack clear comprehension (*asampajañña*), they are indeed of muddled mindfulness (*muṭṭhassati*), owing to the weakness [of their mindfulness].
"To show that mindfulness has no function of mindfulness," it is said, "unmindful" (*asampajānā*).
Being thus forgetful and unmindful, they are not even able to establish the mere definition of the object; everything else is exactly as before.

47. "Unconcentrated" (*asamāhitā*) means devoid of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*). "With wandering minds" (*vibbhantacittā*) means with distracted minds, due to the absence of concentration.
With restlessness having gained an opportunity, the minds of those who are devoid of concentration wander among various objects;
through restlessness, they quiver over a single object like a forest monkey among the branches of a forest.
In the manner previously described, being thus unconcentrated and with wandering minds, they are not even able to establish the definition of the object; everything else is exactly as before.
48. *Duppaññā* is a designation for those devoid of wisdom (*nippaññānaṃ*). However, there is no such thing as "corrupt wisdom" (*duṭṭhā paññā*).
*Eḷamūgā*: [the term] *eḷa-mukhā* is used; the letter *kha* has been changed to *ga*. It means "those with saliva on their faces.
For when those of poor wisdom speak, saliva drips from their mouths, and saliva is called *ela*. As it is said: "Behold the saliva-dripping snake, the double-tongued one."
Therefore, they are called "dumb and deaf" (*eḷamūga*). There is also the reading *elamukha*. Some read *elamuga*, others *elamuka*;
in all cases, the meaning is "mouth of dullness" (*elamukha*). How do they invite fear and terror?
Those of poor wisdom, being dumb and deaf, are unable to perform even the mere defining of an object. For those whose objects are not defined—
For those dwelling in the forest, what was seen during the day appears at night as a source of fear and terror.
With their minds agitated, they tremble even at a slight thing; seeing a rope or a creeper, they perceive it as a snake;
seeing a stump, they perceive it as a *yakkha*; and seeing dry land or a mountain, they perceive it as an elephant. Thus they meet with misfortune and ruin through snakes and other such dangers.
"They become as if brought near. Thus they summon and call out to that fear and terror by way of attributing it to oneself.
Regarding the phrase "I am endowed with wisdom" (*paññāsampannohamasmi*): here, "endowed with wisdom" means endowed with or possessed of wisdom;

yet this is not the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), nor the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*), but rather the wisdom of defining the object (*ārammaṇa-vavatthāna-paññā*) in these sixteen instances.
The meaning [is as follows]. The remainder is exactly according to the method stated everywhere.
The commentary on the section on verbal action, etc., is finished.
The discernment of the sixteen bases and objects is completed.
The Commentary on Fear, Terror, Lodgings, and So Forth. 49.
Regarding the phrase "Tassa mayhaṃ" (To me): what is the connection? It is said that while the Bodhisatta was scrutinizing these sixteen objects of perception, he saw no fear or terror;
for what is called fear and terror [does not exist] in such nights and in such lodgings.
"Since it is perceived, let us search for it there as well"—thus he undertook a search for fear and terror.
Now, the Blessed One, demonstrating this matter to the brahmin, said: "Tassa mayhaṃ...
and so forth. In that context, both *yā* and *tā* are terms used respectively for the mention and the description of the nights. Regarding the word *abhijñātā*, here *abhi-* [is used].

The prefix (*upasagga*) has the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). Therefore, "well-known" (*abhiññātā*) should be understood as "known by such characteristics as the fullness of the moon or the waning of the moon. In the word "distinguished" (*abhilakkhitā*), there is merely the prefix;

therefore, "distinguished" means simply "characterizable," that is, they are to be characterized for the purpose of undertaking the Uposatha, listening to the Dhamma, making offerings, showing honor, and so forth.
It is said that they are to be observed and characterized.
"The fourteenth" means one night that completes the fourteen days starting from the first day of the fortnight;
likewise for the fifteenth and the eighth. "Of the fortnight" refers to both the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight. These three [days] in each [fortnight]...
Having established [the dates] for six nights, one must therefore apply the term "fortnight" (pakkha) in all instances:
"the fourteenth day of the fortnight," "the fifteenth day of the fortnight," and "the eighth day of the fortnight. Now, why is the fifth day not included? Because it does not occur at all times.
For even when the Blessed Buddha had not yet appeared, and even after he had passed away without entering final nibbāna, the fifth day was indeed not specially marked.
But after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, the Elders who compiled the Dhamma reflected, "The hearing of the Dhamma occurs only rarely.
Thereupon, having made a formal resolution, they established the fifth day as the day for the hearing of the Dhamma; from that time forward, it became a distinguished occasion.
Thus, because it was not held at all times, it is not included here.
“Tathārūpāsu” means of such a kind. “Ārāmacetiyāni” refers to groves themselves—such as flower-groves, fruit-groves, and so forth—which are called “grove-cetiyas.
For they are called “cetiyas” in the sense of being honored; that is to say, in the sense of being worthy of worship.
“Vanacetiyāni” refers to groves themselves—such as groves for sacrificial offerings, beautiful forests, and groves of *devasāla* trees—which are called “forest-cetiyas. “Rukkhacetiyāni” refers to...
Tree-cetiyas are simply venerable trees located at the gates of villages, market towns, and so forth.
For worldly people, either imagining them to be inhabited by deities or perceiving them as divine themselves, pay homage to and worship these very trees in monasteries and forests;
therefore, all such [trees] are called cetiyas. "Terrifying" means causing fear, [such that one feels dread] even upon seeing or hearing [them].
They produce fear. "Along with horripilation" means they occur together with the bristling of the body hair, because they produce horripilation even as one enters [the forest].
"I might perhaps see it" means: "I might indeed see that very thing which causes fear and terror.
"At another time" means: at a time other than the moment when he had thought, "What if I were to... and so forth.
And therein, O Brahmin, when I dwell, I stay in such kinds of lodgings as are fit for the offerings and sacrifices of men—
places of the *yakkhas* where the ground is strewn and drenched with flowers, incense, flesh, blood, fat, marrow, heart-lungs, spirits, and liquors; places which,
like a single heap, belong to the *yakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, and *pisācas*, and at the sight of which, even by day, one’s heart, it seems, breaks.
Referring to that state, he said: "And while I am dwelling there, O Brahmin.

"A wild animal comes" means that a wild animal—whether a cow-eared deer, a rhinoceros, a dīpa-deer, a boar, or other such species—comes, striking its horns or its hooves; for here, the name "wild animal" (maga) applies to all four-footed creatures.
In some places, however, even the black jackal is so called, as it has been said:
“Your shoulders are like those of a bull, your stride like that of a lion;
O King of Nagas, homage be to you! May we receive something [from you].
“Or a peacock causes a stick to fall”: this means that a peacock shakes a dry stick from a tree and causes it to fall. By the mention of the peacock—
And here, the inclusion of "all" birds is intended; therefore, it is said that "any bird whatsoever.
Alternatively, by the word "or," it means "either a peacock or some other bird. This same method applies to the previous mention of "paths" as well.
"Or the wind stirs up a mass of leaves" means the wind shakes a heap of fallen leaves. "This, surely, is that fear and terror."
Regarding the phrase "it comes," that which comes is indeed this fear and terror. From this point onward, it should be understood that the object itself is the fear and terror.
Because it is the object of both slight and intense fear, form—which is the object of pleasure—is like pleasure itself.
[Thinking: "Why indeed do I dwell desiring nothing but fear?"—I am indeed... what?
I dwell desiring and wishing for fear with absolute certainty as the sole cause.
"Yathābhūtaṃ yathābhūtassa" means: by whatever posture (iriyāpatha) one has been, will be, is, or has become endowed with while existing.
"Me" means in my presence. "Tathābhūtaṃ tathābhūto vā" means: by that very same posture.
"Existent" means having come to be, being present, existing, or being endowed [with that state]. "Indeed, I... [as before]...

I was training myself" refers to how, it is said, while the Bodhisatta was walking, when those objects of fear and terror—such as the sounds of the wild beasts' horns and hooves—arose on that path, the Great Being neither stood, nor sat, nor lay down; rather, he continued walking, investigating [the situation].
When he investigates thoroughly, he does not see any fear or terror; it is merely the sound of the path, the horns, and the hooves.
Having understood that "this is just this, not fear or terror," he then stands, sits, or lies down.
To show this meaning, he said, "So indeed I... and so forth. This same method applies to all the intermediate sections. And from here on:
It should be understood that the postures are stated not according to their sequential order, but according to their proximity;
for when fear and terror come upon one who is walking, he does not stand, sit, or lie down, and when they come upon one who is standing, he does not walk—
thus they are stated according to their proximity.
The commentary on the dwellings that cause fear and terror is finished.
50. Commentary on the Abiding Without Delusion:

Having thus demonstrated his own absence of fear and terror even in terrifying places, he now spoke the passage beginning with “There are, brahmin,” in order to demonstrate his own abiding without delusion in those situations where meditators might become deluded.
In this context, "there are" means they exist, are found, and are perceived.

"Taking it to be night when it is indeed night" means that while it is actually night, they perceive it as day, thinking, "This is day. "Taking it to be day when it is indeed day" means that while it is actually day, they perceive it as night, thinking, "This is night. But why do they have such perceptions?

Or [he emerges] due to a lack of skill in emerging, or from the cry of a bird. How so? Here, someone who has attained the white kasiṇa performs the preliminary work by day, enters attainment by day, and arouses the intention:
"I shall emerge by day alone. Yet he is not skilled in delimiting the duration. Having passed the day, he emerges during the night. This occurs because of the pervasion of the white kasiṇa.

It becomes clear, distinct, and well-defined for him. Because he has applied attention with the thought, "I shall emerge during the day," and because of the clarity and distinctness of the pervasion of the white kasiṇa, he perceives it as day even though it is actually night.
However, in this case, someone who has attained mastery over the blue kasiṇa, having performed the preliminary work at night and entered jhāna at night, thinks, "I am emerging at night."
He arouses the mental application, yet he is not skilled in delimiting the duration. Having passed the night, he emerges during the day;
and because of his pervasion of the blue kasiṇa, it remains unclear and unmanifest for him.

Because of his having aroused the mental application, "I shall emerge at night," and because of the lack of clarity and manifestation in the pervasion of the blue kasiṇa, [he emerges] during the day itself.
He perceives it as being the same time as night. Thus, first of all, they have such a perception simply due to a lack of skill in emerging from meditation.

Furthermore, regarding the sound of birds: here, someone may be sitting within his lodging, and then during the day, birds such as crows that cry out by day, thinking it is still day because of the moonlight, cry out at night for various other reasons. He [hears] their sound...
Having heard [the sound], one perceives it as day even though it is actually night.
Furthermore, suppose someone here is sitting in a mountain cave—deep, concealed by dense forests, and where the light of the sun has vanished during a period of seven-day rains.
Then, at that time, even at the hour of noon, nocturnal birds such as owls and others cry out there in the night.
There, hidden in complete darkness, they cry out by means of the perception that it is night or for other reasons.
Hearing their sound, one perceives it as night even though it is actually day. Thus, through the cries of birds, they come to have such a perception.
"This, I say" (*idam aham*) refers to this very perception of mine. "I call it dwelling in delusion" (*sammohavihārasmiṃ vadāmi*) means it is included within the category of dwelling in delusion.
It is said: "I declare that it is included within one of the states of delusion.
Furthermore, O Brahmin... [as before] ... "I perceive," thus the Bodhisatta’s distinction between day and night is manifest;
even when the moon and sun are not visible during the seven-day intervals, he knows precisely: "This much time has passed since the morning meal."
"It has gone; this much is the time after the meal, this much is the first watch, this much is the middle watch, and this much is the last watch"—thus he spoke.
And it is no wonder that the Bodhisatta who has fulfilled the perfections knows this;
for even among the disciples who abide in partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*), the demarcation of day and night is evident.
It is said that at the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra, the Elder Godatta would take his meal when it was two finger-breadths [above the horizon] and eat it when it was one finger-breadth [above].
Even when the sun was not yet visible, he would enter his lodging at dawn and depart at that same time.
One day, the monastery attendants, thinking, "We shall watch for the time the elder departs tomorrow," prepared the meal and stood at the base of the time-pillar.

They sat down. The Elder departed at exactly two finger-breadths [of shadow] remaining. From that time on, it is said, even when the sun was no longer visible, they would strike the gong based solely on the Elder’s perception that it was time for his departure.
At the Ajagara Monastery as well, the Elder Kāḷadeva struck the watch-gong during the rainy season; this was the Elder’s established custom.
He did not himself set the watch-timer in motion, but had other bhikkhus do so.
Then, when the first watch had passed, as soon as the Elder stood up having taken the mallet, the watch-timer would fall either once or twice;
thus, having performed his ascetic duties throughout the three watches, the Elder entered the village at daybreak and took almsfood.
Having returned to the monastery at mealtime, he takes his bowl and goes to his daytime dwelling place in the monastery to practice the duties of a recluse.
When the other monks see the time-marker pillar but do not see the elder, they send someone to fetch him.
That monk either sees the elder as he is departing from his daytime dwelling place or on the path; thus it is with knowledge of a limited range.
The demarcation of days and nights is evident even for those disciples who have attained stability; how much more so, then, for Bodhisattvas?

Regarding the passage, "But whoever, O Brahmin... might speak thus," it means that if anyone were to speak while saying, "O Brahmin, he who has arisen in the world as a being subject to non-delusion...
[leading] to the welfare and happiness of gods and humans," they would be speaking correctly.

"Speaking rightly, he would not be a speaker of falsehood. The connection between the words should be understood thus: "Speaking only my own words, he would speak rightly; speaking rightly, he would not be a speaker of falsehood.
In this context, "of a nature not subject to delusion" means having a nature free from delusion.
"In the world" refers to the world of human beings. "For the welfare of many people" means for the benefit of the multitude.
"For the welfare" means for the sake of benefit; he is one who teaches the welfare pertaining to both the present life and the future life through the perfection of wisdom.
"For the happiness of many" means for the sake of the happiness of many people; he is a giver of the happiness of requisites through the perfection of generosity.

"Out of compassion for the world" means for the sake of compassion for the world; through the perfection of loving-kindness and compassion, he is a protector and guardian of the world like a mother and father.
Regarding the phrase "for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans":

it should be understood that by mentioning "gods and humans" here, he refers specifically to those sentient beings who are capable and ready to be trained, and shows his own manifestation for their attainment of Nibbāna, the Path, and the Fruits.

For when "welfare" (*atthāya*) is stated, it means "for the ultimate goal," which is Nibbāna; and when "benefit" (*hitāya*) is stated, it means "for the sake of the Path that brings about that [Nibbāna]."

This is what is meant: for there is no benefit higher than the path leading to Nibbāna. When "for the sake of happiness" is said, it means "for the sake of the happiness of the attainment of fruition," because there is no happiness higher than that. And this has been said:
"This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future."
The commentary on the dwelling in non-delusion is finished.
51. Commentary on the preliminary practice and so forth:
Thus, having shown the Brahmin his own dwelling in non-delusion, which culminates in the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha, the Blessed One—
Now, in order to show from the preliminary stage onwards the path by which he attained that state of non-delusion which has reached its ultimate limit, he said:
"But, Brahmin, when I had begun... Some, however, say: "Having heard of this state of non-delusion, this thought arose in the Brahmin: 'By what [means]...'"
‘...by this practice I have attained this state,’ perceiving his thought and showing him,
‘By this practice I have attained this supreme abiding free from delusion,’ he spoke thus.
In that context, ‘But energy was aroused by me, brahmin,’ means, brahmin, it was not by me [that this supreme...]
A dwelling free from delusion was not attained by one who is indolent, forgetful, with a restless body, or with a distracted mind;
rather, for the sake of attaining it, energy was exerted by me. While seated at the seat of enlightenment, the fourfold energy was exerted by me;
that is to say, it was applied, firmly maintained, and set in motion without slackness.
And because it was indeed initiated, this [energy] became unwearied.
"Mindfulness was established and unconfused": not only was energy present, but mindfulness too was established by way of being directed toward the object;
and because it was established, it was unconfused. "The body was calmed" means through the arising of calmness of both body and mind.

My body, too, became tranquil. In this context, because the material body becomes tranquil precisely when the mental body is tranquil, it is said "the body is tranquil" without distinguishing between the mental body and the material body.
"Unagitated" means that it is unagitated precisely because of its tranquility; what is meant is that it is free from distress. The mind was concentrated.
"Unified" means that my mind was correctly applied, well-established, and as if fixed;
and because it was concentrated, it was unified, immovable, and unwavering. To this extent, the preliminary practice leading to jhāna has been explained.
Now, beginning with the first jhāna attained by means of this practice, up to the culmination of the threefold clear knowledge (vijjāttaya)—

Showing the distinction, he said, "He indeed... and so forth. Regarding that, whatever needs to be said concerning the passage, "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... having attained the fourth jhāna, he dwelt therein," has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the discourse on the earth-kasiṇa.
For while there it is phrased as "he dwells having attained," here it is "he dwelt"; this alone is the difference.
The distinction: Having done what did the Blessed One dwell having attained these jhānas? Having developed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Which one?
The meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati).
Furthermore, these four jhānas serve as bases for one-pointedness of mind for some, while for others they serve as the foundation for insight (vipassanā).
For some, they serve as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*); for some, as the basis for cessation (*nirodha*); and for some, they have the purpose of transcending existence (*bhavokkamana*).
Among these, they serve the purpose of one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

For, having entered [these states] with the thought, "Having attained them, we shall dwell happily for the day with one-pointed minds," they perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) with the kasiṇas and thus produce the eight attainments (*samāpatti*). For trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), however...
For those who, having emerged from attainment, develop [the jhānas] thinking, "With a concentrated mind, I shall practice insight," these serve as the bases for insight (vipassanā-pādaka).
However, for those who, having produced the eight attainments, enter the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and then, having emerged from attainment,
produce [the jhānas] while aspiring for the direct knowledges described in the passage beginning, "Being one, he becomes many," [these jhānas serve as the bases for direct knowledge].
For those [who develop them for this purpose], they serve as the bases for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

However, for those who, having produced the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), remain without consciousness for seven days, and then—having attained Nibbāna as cessation in this very life—develop them with the thought, "We shall dwell in happiness," they serve as the bases for cessation (*nirodhapādaka*). Furthermore, for those who [develop] the eight attainments...
They develop it thinking, "Having produced [this state], we shall arise in the Brahma-world without falling away from jhāna," and for them, it serves the purpose of ascending to existence.
However, this fourth jhāna was developed by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree;

it should be understood as that which served as the basis for his insight (vipassanā), the basis for his direct knowledges (abhiññā), the accomplisher of all tasks, and the bestower of all mundane and supramundane qualities.
The commentary on the preliminary practice is concluded.
Commentary on the Discourse on Past Lives (Pubbenivāsakathā): 52.
Showing a portion of those qualities which he was the giver of, he said: "When his mind was thus concentrated," and so forth.
Therein, both the word-by-word commentary on the two types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and the method of development (*bhāvanā-naya*) have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
For there, it is stated: "When his mind is thus concentrated... he directs [it]"; here, however, it says: "he directed [it].
Furthermore, this section on absorption (*appanā-vāra*)—namely, "This, O Brahmin, is my..."—is not found there; this is the only difference. Therein... [the rest of the passage follows].
"He" refers to "I. "I directed [my mind]" means I brought it forth. From the word "directed," the meaning here of "he" should be understood as "I was.
And since this knowledge of recollecting past lives has come down by way of the Blessed One, therefore: "Having passed away from there..."
Regarding the phrase “reborn here,” the construction should be understood as follows. Here, “having passed away from there” refers to the reviewing of one who is turning back [from death].
Therefore, “reborn here” means immediately after this present rebirth.
“Arose in such-and-such a place” should be understood as referring to the Tusita heaven. “There too I was of such-and-such a name” refers likewise to that Tusita heaven.
I was a son of the gods named Setaketu. "Of such a clan" means I was of the same clan as those deities.
"Of such a complexion" means I was of a golden complexion. "With such food" means I had the divine ambrosia as my food. "Experiencing such pleasure and pain" means experiencing such divine pleasure;

as for pain, it was merely the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*). "With such a limit to my lifespan" means having a lifespan limited to seventy-five billion and sixty million years.
"Having passed away from there" means: I, having passed away from that Tusita heaven. "Reborn here" means: reborn here in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.
In the passage beginning with "This, O Brahmin, is my... and so forth, "my" (*me*) means by me. "Knowledge" (*vijjā*) is so called in the sense of making known.
What does it make known? One's former abodes. "Ignorance" (*avijjā*) is that which conceals those very same former abodes, in the sense of not making them known.
Delusion is what is called "darkness. That very delusion is called "darkness" in the sense of being a concealer.
Knowledge is what is called "light," in the sense of producing illumination. And here, the meaning is that "knowledge has been attained";
the remainder is words of praise. As for the construction [of the sentence] here: "Indeed, this knowledge has been attained by me; for me, whose knowledge has been attained..."
"Ignorance has been dispelled" means it has been destroyed. Why? Because true knowledge (*vijjā*) has arisen. This same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Regarding the word *yathā*:
here *yathā* is used in the sense of a comparison; *taṃ* is a particle. "Of one who is heedful" by not being separated from mindfulness;
"of one who is ardent" through the exertion of energy; "of one whose self is directed" by having no regard for body or life—that is, of one whose mind is sent forth [in concentration].
The meaning is this: "Just as for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, ignorance would be dispelled and true knowledge would arise;
darkness would be dispelled and light would arise—even so has ignorance been dispelled by me, true knowledge has arisen;
darkness has been dispelled and light has arisen. I have obtained a fruit exactly corresponding to this application of my striving."
The commentary on the Discourse on Past Lives is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye: 53.

In this discourse on the passing away and rebirth of beings, because the text is presented here according to the Blessed One’s own words, it says, “I see, I understand”; this is the distinction. The remainder is exactly as described in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Herein, "knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). "Ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the ignorance that conceals the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. Furthermore, for Great Beings who have fulfilled the perfections, there is no need for preliminary work (*parikamma-kicca*);
for they recollect their manifold past lives at the very moment they direct their minds toward them.
They see beings with the divine eye. Therefore, the method of development described there, beginning with the preliminary work, has no purpose here.
