The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the divine eye is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 54.
Regarding the third true knowledge, "When his mind is thus concentrated," it should be understood as the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā).

"For the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints" means for the purpose of the knowledge of the path of arahantship; for the path of arahantship is so called because it destroys the taints.
"It is called the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*); and this knowledge is included therein. "They directed their minds" means they brought forth the mind of insight (*vipassanā-citta*).

Regarding such statements as "This is suffering," he understood the entire Truth of Suffering—realizing its intrinsic characteristic—as it truly is, thinking: "Suffering is just this much; there is nothing beyond this."
I penetrated the knowledge [of suffering]. And I understood that the craving which produces that suffering is "this is the origin of suffering.
Furthermore, I understood that the state where both of these cease upon reaching it—the non-occurrence of those two—is Nibbāna, "this is the cessation of suffering.
And I understood that the Noble Path which brings about that [cessation] is "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," through the penetration of their intrinsic characteristics.
The meaning should be understood as: "I directly knew, I understood, and I penetrated [it] as it truly is.

Having thus shown the truths according to their specific characteristics (*sarūpato*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "These are the taints" (*ime āsavā*) in order to show them by way of the defilements (*kilesavasena*) through a figurative method (*pariyāyato*).
Regarding the phrase "to me who was knowing thus and seeing thus" (*tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato*): it means "to me who was knowing in this way and seeing in this way."
Along with insight (vipassanā), he speaks of the path that has reached its culmination. "From the taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsavā*) means from the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
By the phrase "was liberated," he shows the moment of fruition; for at the moment of the path the mind is being liberated, while at the moment of fruition it has become liberated.
By the phrase "the knowledge 'it is liberated' regarding what is liberated," he shows the knowledge of review. By the words "birth is destroyed," and so forth...
The Blessed One, reviewing that plane with that very knowledge, directly knew (abbhaññāsi) such things as "birth is exhausted.
But which birth of the Blessed One was exhausted, and how did he know it? First of all, his past birth was not exhausted, because it had already been exhausted previously;
nor was it the future birth, because there is no further effort to be made regarding the future; nor was it the present birth, because it still exists.

However, that birth—which, due to the non-cultivation of the path, would arise as a variety of one, four, or five aggregates within one, four, or five aggregates-of-existence births—has been exhausted by the fact that it has reached the state of non-arising through the cultivation of the path.
Having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the cultivation of that path, he reflects: "In the absence of defilements, even though karma exists, it will not lead to rebirth in the future."
Knowing thus, he directly knew it.
“Vusitam” means lived, fully lived; the meaning is that it has been performed, practiced, and brought to completion. “Brahmacariyam” refers to the holy life of the Path;

for together with the virtuous worldling (puthujjanakalyāṇaka), the seven types of trainees (sekkha) are said to dwell in the dwelling of the holy life, whereas one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)—
The residence has been completed. Therefore, reviewing his own life of purity (brahmacariya), the Blessed One directly knew: "The life of purity has been lived.

"What was to be done has been accomplished" means that the sixteenfold task—consisting of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing with respect to the four truths by means of the four paths—has been brought to completion.
For even those such as the virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) [only partially] accomplish that task.
They perform [their duty], having exhausted the taints and accomplished what was to be done. Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own duty, directly knew: "What was to be done has been done.
"There is nothing further of this nature" means: now there is no more of this state of being, namely, the state of these sixteen duties, because of the destruction of the defilements.
Or rather, he directly knew: "There is no further task for me regarding the cultivation of the path. Furthermore, "in this state" means:
from this present state, from this current continuity of aggregates of such a kind, there is no further continuity of aggregates for me.
These five aggregates, however, remain having been fully understood, like trees whose roots have been cut. They [will cease] with the cessation of the final consciousness.
He discerned: "They will go out like a fire without fuel.

Now, demonstrating to the brahmin his attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*), which is embraced by such reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*), he said: "This, O brahmin, is my... and so forth.
In this context, *vijjā* (true knowledge) is the knowledge of the path to Arahantship; *avijjā* (ignorance) is that which conceals the Four Noble Truths.

Ignorance (*avijjā*). The rest is exactly as previously stated. To this extent, by means of the knowledge of past lives, he demonstrated his dwelling in non-delusion to the brahmin, showing how he had encompassed all the qualities of omniscience through these three types of higher knowledge (*vijjā*): the knowledge of the past through the knowledge of past lives;
the knowledge of the present and future through the divine eye; and all mundane and supramundane qualities through the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).
The commentary on the discourse on the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) is finished. 55. Commentary on the reason for dwelling in the forest:
When this had been said, it is said that the brahmin thought: "The ascetic Gotama claims omniscience; even today—"
"And yet he does not abandon dwelling in the forest; could there perhaps be something else for him to do?
Then the Blessed One, having understood his underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), spoke the words beginning with "It may be, brahmin," by way of following that very intention.
Therein, "It may be, brahmin, that it might occur to you" means, brahmin, it could possibly happen to you in this way.
"But this, brahmin, should not be viewed in that way. This means, brahmin, you should not view my practice of dwelling in remote lodgings as being due to a lack of freedom from lust and so forth.
Having thus rejected the incorrect reason for practicing in remote lodgings, he stated "There are two things, indeed...
and so on, in order to show the correct reason. In this context, *atthavaso* simply means "the purpose" (*attha*). Therefore, there are two...
"O Brahmin, 'for the sake of a benefit' means, O Brahmin, that I am indeed seeing two benefits and two reasons;

this is what is meant. Regarding the phrase 'one's own dwelling in happiness in this very life' (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*): here, 'this life' (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to this present, visible personal existence (*attabhāva*).
'Dwelling in happiness' (*sukhavihāra*) refers to the well-being of all four postures (*iriyāpatha*); for even when one is alone in the forest..."
Even down to the basic needs of defecation and urination, all postures become comfortable; therefore, this meaning should be understood as "dwelling in happiness in the present life.
And "out of compassion for future generations": how is it that future generations are shown compassion through dwelling in the forest?
For when sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith [hear of] the Blessed One’s dwelling in the forest...

"Seeing that even the Blessed One does not abandon forest dwellings—when for him there is nothing to be fully understood, nothing to be abandoned, nothing to be developed, and nothing to be realized—how much more so should we?
Thinking thus, they will consider that they must certainly dwell there. In this way, they will quickly bring an end to suffering. Thus, the later [disciples]...
"The people are shown compassion. Demonstrating this point, he said: "And out of compassion for future generations.
The commentary on the reason for dwelling in the forest is finished. Now follows the commentary on the expression of appreciation for the teaching.
56. Having heard that, the brahmin, being pleased, spoke the words beginning with “anukampitarūpā” (of compassionate nature).
Therein, “anukampitarūpā” means one whose birth is compassionate, one whose very nature is compassionate. “Janatā” means a multitude of people. “Yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhenā” means:
just as the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would show compassion, so too is he of a compassionate nature.
Having spoken thus, and further rejoicing in that teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! In this context, the word *abhikkanta* is seen in the senses of destruction, beauty, handsome, and rejoicing.
As in: "The night has passed, venerable sir; the first watch has ended; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time. And so forth.
For it is seen in the sense of destruction: “This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons,” and so forth. It is used in the sense of beautiful in such passages as:
“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with the glory of psychic power, illuminating all directions with most excellent beauty?”—

In such cases as these, it means "beautiful. In expressions such as "Excellent, venerable sir" (*abhikkantaṃ, bhante*), it means "rejoicing. Here too, it is used in the sense of rejoicing. And because it is used in rejoicing, it should be understood that what is being said is: "Well done, well done, O Gotama! As it is said:
"A wise person employs repetition (*āmeḍita*) in fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, grief, laughter, and joy."

And it should be understood that this term is stated twice here: once by way of clarity and once by way of praise. Alternatively, *abhikkantaṃ* means *abhikantaṃ*. It means "exceedingly desired," "extremely pleasing," or "most beautiful.
In this context, he praises the teaching with one instance of the word *abhikkanta*, and his own confidence with the other.
This is the intended meaning here: "Excellent, Master Gotama, is this Dhamma-teaching of Master Gotama; excellent indeed!"
"That is, my confidence has arisen because of Master Gotama’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Or rather, he praises the Blessed One’s own words by referring to two pairs of meanings: "Master Gotama’s word is excellent" because it destroys faults and because it brings about the attainment of virtues;
likewise, because it generates faith and because it generates wisdom, and because it is meaningful and well-phrased.
It should be applied by way of such qualities as: having clear words, profound meaning, being pleasant to the ear,
touching the heart, not exalting oneself, not disparaging others, being cool with compassion, being bright with wisdom, being delightful upon first hearing,
being capable of withstanding scrutiny, being pleasant while being heard, and being beneficial when investigated.
Beyond that, he further praises the teaching itself by means of four similes. Therein, "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face-downward or having its opening turned downward.

"One would turn it upward" (*ukkujjeyya*) means one would make its opening face upward. "Covered" (*paṭicchanna*) means concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth. "One would uncover it" (*vivareyya*) means one would remove the covering.
"Of one who is lost" (*mūḷhassa*) means of one who is confused about the directions. "One would point out the path" (*maggaṃ ācikkheyya*) means [pointing it out] while taking him by the hand.

“He would say, ‘This is the path. Regarding the phrase “in darkness”: this refers, first of all, to the fourfold darkness consisting of the dark fortnight, the fourteenth day of the lunar month, midnight, and dense forest thickets or masses of clouds; such is the literal meaning of the words.
However, this is the application of the intended meaning: just as someone might set upright what had been overturned, so too [he sets upright] those who are turned away from the True Dhamma.
By raising me up from unrighteousness, just as one would uncover what has been concealed;

by revealing the Teaching that had been hidden in the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation, just as one would point out the path to one who is lost; and for one who has set out upon a bypath or a wrong path...
"By you, who has pointed out to me the path to heaven and liberation— just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness—

by holding aloft the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which veils the forms of the Jewels, the Buddha and the rest, for me who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see them;
because these have been made manifest by the venerable Gotama through these various methods, the Dhamma has been proclaimed by him in manifold ways."
The commentary on the praise of the teaching and the expression of appreciation is finished. Now, for the commentary on the manifestation of confidence:
having thus praised the teaching, one who manifests confidence by means of this teaching with a mind full of faith toward the Triple Gem acts as follows:
He said, "Esāhaṃ... and so forth. Therein, "esāhaṃ" means "this I am. "Bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" means:

"I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge"—that is, with the intention that "the venerable Gotama is my refuge and ultimate resort, the protector from suffering and the provider of welfare"—I go to, I resort to, I serve, I attend upon the venerable Gotama; or rather, I know him thus, I awaken to him thus.
For those roots whose meaning is "going," their meaning is also "understanding" (*buddhi*). Therefore, for the phrase "I go," the meaning expressed is "I know" or "I understand.
Regarding the words "the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus":

here, it is called "Dhamma" because it sustains (*dhāreti*) those who have attained the Path, realized Cessation, and are practicing according to the instructions, preventing them from falling into the states of misery.

Thus, in terms of its meaning, it consists of both the Noble Eightfold Path and Nibbāna. For this has been said in detail: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them.
And it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Dhamma of the scriptures together with the Noble Fruits. For this has been said in the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*:
“The fading of lust, unshakable, sorrowless, the Dhamma that is unconditioned and not repulsive;
this sweet, skillful, well-expounded Dhamma—approach it for the sake of refuge.
Here, “the fading of lust” refers to the Path. “Unshakable and sorrowless” refers to the Fruit. “The Dhamma that is unconditioned” refers to Nibbāna.
"Non-repulsive, sweet, proficient, and well-analyzed"—thus the aggregates of all phenomena are analyzed by means of the Three Piṭakas.

It is "congregated" (saṅgha) because it is gathered together by way of view and virtue; in its actual sense, it is the collection of the eight noble persons. For this has been said in that very *Vimānavatthu*:
"And where they say a gift yields great fruit, among the four pure pairs of persons..."
"And those eight persons who see the Dhamma—go to this Saṅgha for refuge.
Here, "the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" means the community of bhikkhus. At this point, the brahmin has declared the three goings for refuge.
The commentary on the manner of his expression of confidence is concluded.
Commentary on the Discourse on Going for Refuge:

Now, for the sake of proficiency regarding those goings for refuge, this method should be understood: the refuge, the act of going for refuge, he who goes for refuge, the classification of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, its defilement, and its analysis.

To explain: first, according to the meaning of the words (*padatthato*), it is called a *saraṇa* because it "destroys" (*hiṃsati*). The meaning is that for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, it destroys, that is, annihilates, fear, terror, suffering, and the affliction of miserable rebirths; this is a designation specifically for the Triple Gem.

Alternatively, the Buddha "destroys" (*hiṃsati*) the fear of sentient beings by causing them to proceed toward what is beneficial and turning them away from what is harmful. From the wilderness of existence...

The Dhamma is a refuge by way of delivering one across [the flood of suffering] and by way of providing consolation; the Saṅgha is a refuge by way of causing the attainment of abundant fruit even from small acts of service.
Therefore, by this method as well, the Triple Gem is a refuge.

The act of going for refuge is an arising of consciousness that proceeds with the aspect of having that [Triple Gem] as its supreme resort, with defilements dispelled through confidence and reverence for it. A sentient being endowed with that [consciousness] goes for refuge.
The meaning is that one approaches these three refuges with the aforementioned arising of consciousness, thinking: "These are my refuges; these are my ultimate resort.
Thus, first of all, this triad—refuge, the act of going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge—is to be understood.
Regarding the classification of the act of going for refuge, however, there are two kinds: supramundane and mundane. Of these, the supramundane...

For those who have seen the Truths, at the moment of the Path, through the complete eradication of the defilements of going for refuge, it succeeds in its function with respect to the entire Triple Gem, having Nibbāna as its object.
For worldlings, mundane going for refuge succeeds by means of the suppression of the defilements of going for refuge;
it has the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object, and in terms of its actual meaning, it is the acquisition of faith in the objects that are the Buddha and the rest.
Right view rooted in faith is called "rectification of view" (*diṭṭhijukamma*) among the ten bases for meritorious action.
This occurs in four ways: by surrendering oneself, by making that [the Buddha] one's supreme refuge, by entering into discipleship, and by prostration.
Among these, "surrendering oneself" means: "Starting from today, I surrender myself to the Buddha..."

“I surrender myself to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha”—this is the surrendering of oneself to the Buddha and the others. “Having them as one’s refuge” means the state of having them as one’s refuge, thinking:
“From today onward, consider me one who has the Buddha as his refuge, the Dhamma as his refuge, and the Saṅgha as his refuge.
“Entering into the status of a pupil” means: “From today onward, I am...”
"Regard me as a resident pupil of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, and of the Saṅgha"—thus is the undertaking of the status of a student.
"Prostration" means: "From today onwards, I shall perform salutation, rising from my seat, joining of palms, and respectful service toward these three objects alone—the Buddha and the rest;
regard me thus,"—thus is the supreme act of devotion toward the Buddha and the others.
For by performing even one of these four modes, the going for refuge has indeed been undertaken.
Furthermore: "I surrender myself to the Blessed One; I surrender myself to the Dhamma; I surrender myself to the Saṅgha.
I surrender my life; my self is surrendered, my life is surrendered—until the end of life."
“I go for refuge to the Buddha; the Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection”—thus too should self-surrender be understood.
“If I were to see the Teacher, I would indeed see the Blessed One; if I were to see the Well-Gone One, I would indeed see the Blessed One;
if I were to see the Perfectly Enlightened One, I would indeed see the Blessed One.”
"May I go forth"—in this way, Mahākassapa’s entry into discipleship should be understood as being like his taking of refuge.
[He said: "Thus I shall wander from village to village, from town to town, paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and to the excellent nature of the Dhamma."
In this way, one’s taking of refuge and having that as one’s ultimate resort should be understood as being like that of Āḷavaka and others.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet,
kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name.
"Brahmāyu am I, O Gotama; Brahmayu am I, O Gotama"—thus too should prostration be understood.

Furthermore, this [prostration] is fourfold by way of kinsmen, fear, teachers, and those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*). Among these, taking refuge occurs through prostration to one worthy of offerings, and not through the others.
For it is by way of the supreme (*seṭṭha*) that refuge is grasped, and it is by way of the supreme that it is broken.
Therefore, if a member of the Sākiya or Koliya clans pays homage thinking, "The Buddha is our relative," the taking of refuge is not truly accomplished.

Or if someone pays homage out of fear, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power; if he is not worshipped, he might even cause me harm," the taking of refuge is likewise not truly accomplished.
Or if [one pays homage] during the time of the Bodhisatta in the presence of the Blessed One...
Recalling something he had learned during the time of the Buddha:
"One should enjoy wealth with one part, employ two parts in work,
and set aside the fourth as a reserve for times of misfortune."

Having received such an instruction, one who pays homage thinking, "He is my teacher," has not yet formally taken the refuges. However, for one who pays homage thinking, "This one is the foremost person worthy of offerings in the world," by that very act the refuges have been taken.

For a lay follower (upāsaka) or lay follower (upāsikā) who has thus taken the refuges, the going for refuge is not broken even when they pay homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sects, thinking, "This is my kinsman," let alone one who has not gone forth. The same applies to a king.
Regarding bowing out of fear: for if one were not to bow to a teacher who is honored by the whole kingdom, he might even cause harm.
Likewise, there is no breach of the precept even if one bows to a non-Buddhist teacher of some craft or skill, thinking, "This is my teacher.
In this way, the various types of going for refuge should be understood.

And here, regarding the supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of recluseship are the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*), while the destruction of all suffering is the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*). For it has been said:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, Sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom.”
Suffering, the origin of suffering, and the transcendence of suffering;
and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering—
this indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge.
“By coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
Furthermore, its fruit of benefit should be understood by way of not falling into [the view of] permanence and so forth. For it has been said:
“It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent...”
It is impossible that he would approach anything as a self, or approach anything as pleasant; it is impossible that he would deprive his mother of life,
deprive his father of life, deprive an Arhat of life, with a malicious mind draw blood from a Tathāgata, cause a schism in the Saṅgha,
or point to another teacher— such a thing cannot exist.”
Furthermore, for mundane going for refuge, both the attainment of existence and the attainment of wealth are indeed the fruit. For it is said:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they shall not go to a plane of misery."
“Having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the divine host.
Furthermore, it is said: “Then Sakka, lord of the devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable...”
Mahāmoggallāna approached him... [as before] ...and as Sakka, lord of the devas, was standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him:
"It is indeed good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha;
it is because of going for refuge to the Buddha, lord of the devas, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, attain a happy destination."
‘They will be reborn in the heavenly world. They surpass other devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, divine beauty, happiness, fame, sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
This same method applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha as well. Furthermore, by way of the Velāma Sutta and others, [the benefits] of going for refuge—
The distinction of the fruit is to be understood. Thus should the fruit of going for refuge be understood.
In that regard, mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth regarding the three objects;
it is not of great radiance, nor does it have great extension. For the supramundane, there is no defilement. And of the mundane...
The breach of the going for refuge is twofold: blameworthy and blameless.
Therein, the blameworthy occurs through such acts as surrendering oneself to another teacher and so forth; it yields an undesirable fruit. The blameless occurs through death;

because it is without karmic ripening, it is fruitless. However, there is no breach whatsoever of the supramundane refuge. For even in another existence, a noble disciple [does not go to] another teacher...
"One does not recite [the formula]"—in this way, the defilement and the breach of going for refuge should be understood.
"May the venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower" means: may the venerable Gotama remember me thus, "This one is a lay follower"; that is, may he know it.
The commentary on the discourse on going for refuge is finished.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Method for Lay Followers (*Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā*) Furthermore, for the sake of proficiency in the method for lay followers (*upāsaka*), one should understand this supplementary material: who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower? What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is his failure? What is his success? In that regard, who is a lay follower?
Any householder who has gone for refuge to the Three is a lay follower. For it is said: "From the time, Mahānāma... [and so forth].
“A lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
To this extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower. Why is he called a *upāsaka*?
Because of his attendance (*upāsana*) upon the Triple Gem. For he attends upon the Buddha, thus he is a *upāsaka*; he attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, thus he is a *upāsaka*.

What is his virtue? It is the five abstinences. As it is said: "Insofar, Mahānāma, as a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from fermented and distilled liquors that are the basis for negligence—he is, to that extent, a virtuous lay follower."
What is right livelihood? It is the maintenance of life by means that are lawful and equitable, having abandoned the five kinds of wrong trade. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower. Which five?
Trading in weapons, trading in living beings, trading in meat, trading in intoxicants, and trading in poisons. These, bhikkhus, are the five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower."
What is failure? That which is the failure of that very virtue and livelihood is his failure.
Furthermore, that by which he becomes an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*) and is both defiled and despised—that too should be understood as his failure.
And in terms of their actual meaning, these are five states, beginning with lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). As it is said: "Bhikkhus, one endowed with five qualities..."
He is a lay follower who is a *caṇḍāla* among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and a reproach among lay followers. By what five [qualities]?
He is faithless; he is immoral; he is a superstitious omens-seeker; he believes in auspicious signs rather than in karma;
and he seeks outside this [Dhamma] for those worthy of offerings and performs meritorious deeds there.”
What is his accomplishment? It is his accomplishment in virtue (*sīla-sampadā*) and his accomplishment in livelihood (*ājīva-sampadā*).
It consists of the five qualities beginning with faith (*saddhā*), which constitute his state as a jewel. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a lay follower becomes a jewel among lay followers, a lotus among lay followers, and a white lotus among lay followers. With which five? He is faithful..."
“He is virtuous; he does not rely on superstitious omens; he believes in karma, not in omens;
he does not seek those worthy of offerings outside this [Dhamma]; and he performs meritorious deeds here first.
Regarding the phrase *ajjatagge*, here the word *agga* is seen to mean "beginning," "limit," "portion," or "best. "From this day forward, friend..."
In such passages as, "O gatekeeper, I shut the door against the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs," it is seen at the beginning.
In such passages as, "With that very fingertip one might touch that fingertip; the tip of a sugarcane, the tip of a bamboo," it is seen at the end.
In such passages as, "Whether it be sour-tipped, sweet-tipped, or bitter-tipped, monks, I allow [the use of] a portion from the monastery or a portion from the courtyard... it is seen in the middle.

In passages such as "let him divide [it]," it refers to a portion. In passages such as, "Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them," it refers to the best.

Here, however, it should be understood as referring to the beginning. Therefore, *ajjatagge* means "starting from today" (*ajjatan*); thus the meaning here should be understood. *Ajjatan* means the state of being today. Alternatively, the reading is *ajjadagge*.
The syllable *da* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*); the meaning is "having made today the beginning.
"As long as life lasts" (*pāṇupetaṃ*) means accompanied by life; that is, for as long as my life continues, for that long it is accompanied [by the precepts].

May the venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has gone for refuge through the three refuges and who has no other teacher, and who acts as one who makes things allowable (*kappiyakāraka*).

"May he know this. For even if someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, 'He is not the Buddha,' nor of the Dhamma, 'It is not the Dhamma,' nor of the Saṅgha, 'It is not the Saṅgha.
Having thus gone for refuge by surrendering himself, and having invited [the Blessed One] to accept the four requisites, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and—
Having circumambulated him three times, keeping him to his right, he departed.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Duties of a Lay Follower is finished.
From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta:
57. "Thus have I heard... the Venerable Sāriputta"—this is the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained.
As it is here, so it is in all the Suttas. Therefore, from this point on, we shall not say even this much more, but will provide only the commentary on the previously unexplained terms.

"Four" is a limitation by number. "Persons" (*puggala*) means beings, men, or individuals. By this much, one should not take it to mean the Mahāthera who was a proponent of the *puggala* (the person);
for this venerable one is the foremost among the sons of the Buddha, and he [expounded] the teaching of the Blessed Buddha...
He teaches without deviation.
This is the commentary on the discourse concerning the teaching of conventional and ultimate truth.
The teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is twofold: the teaching of convention (*sammutidesanā*) and the teaching of the ultimate (*paramatthadesanā*). Among these, [the term] *puggala*...
A being, a woman, a man, a kshatriya, a brahmin, a deva, or Māra—such is a teaching by way of conventional designation (*sammutidesanā*). Impermanent, suffering, non-self;
the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and foundations of mindfulness—such is a teaching by way of ultimate truth (*paramatthadesanā*).
In this regard, those who, having heard the teaching by way of convention, penetrate its meaning and abandon delusion, attain distinction.
To those capable of attaining [realization], he teaches the teaching of conventional designation (*sammutidesanā*).

But to those who, having heard the teaching according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), have penetrated its meaning, abandoned delusion, and are capable of attaining distinction, he teaches the teaching of the ultimate sense.
In this regard, there is this simile: just as one skilled in local dialects who provides a commentary on the meaning of the three Vedas...
The teacher explains in the Tamil language to those who understand the meaning when it is spoken in Tamil;
to those who [understand] any one of the Andhaka languages and so forth, he explains in each of those respective languages.
Thus, having approached a skillful and proficient teacher, those young students quickly master the craft. In this context, the Blessed Buddha is like the teacher.
The three Piṭakas stand as things to be expounded, like the three Vedas. Skill in conventional and ultimate truth is like proficiency in the local dialects.
Those beings to be trained, capable of penetrating the teachings on the conventional and the ultimate, are like young students from various regions and languages.
The Blessed One’s teaching by way of the conventional and the ultimate is like a teacher’s instruction in the Tamil language and so forth.
These [two truths] are to be understood. And it is said in this regard:
“The Fully Enlightened One, the best among speakers, proclaimed two truths:
The conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.”
Conventional speech is true by reason of worldly consensus;
ultimate speech is true by reason of the actual nature of phenomena.
Therefore, [this is the teaching] of the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in conventional expression.
“For one who expresses conventional usage, no false speech arises.

Furthermore, for eight reasons the Blessed One speaks of the discourse on the person: to illustrate moral shame and dread of blame; to illustrate the ownership of one’s own karma; to illustrate individual personal effort;
to illustrate the immediate (ānantariya) karmas; to illustrate the divine abodes (brahmavihāra); to illustrate past lives; [and so forth].
[This is] for the purpose of illustrating the purification of the sacrificial gift (dakkhiṇā) and for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention.
For if it were said, "The aggregates, elements, and bases feel shame and dread of wrongdoing," the great mass of people would not understand;

they would fall into confusion and become resistant, asking, "What is this that you call the aggregates, elements, and bases feeling shame and dread of wrongdoing? [On the other hand, if one says], "A woman feels shame..."
But when it is said, "The person—the Khattiya, the Brahmin, the deva, or Māra—is afraid," one knows [the truth], does not fall into delusion, and does not become an adversary.
Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).

The same principle applies even when it is said, "The aggregates have karma as their own; the elements and the sense-bases [have karma as their own]. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating that one is the owner of one's own karma (*kammassaka*).

Even when it is said, “The great monasteries such as Veḷuvana were caused to be built by aggregates, elements, and bases,” the principle is the same. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating individual human agency.
Even when it is said, “Aggregates deprive a mother of life, they commit the offense of shedding the blood of an Arhat, and they commit the schism of the Saṅgha;
so too do the elements and the bases,” the principle is the same. Therefore, the Blessed One [speaks of the person] for the purpose of illustrating the immediate (ānantariya) karmas.
He speaks in terms of a person. Even when it is said, “The aggregates feel loving-kindness; the elements and the sense bases [feel it],” the same principle applies.
Therefore, the Blessed One speaks in terms of a person for the purpose of illustrating the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Even when it is said, “The aggregates recollect past lives; the elements and the sense bases [recollect them],” the same principle applies. Therefore, the Blessed One...

He speaks of a person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating past lives. Even when it is said, "The aggregates (khandhā) receive the gift; the elements (dhātuyo) and the sense-bases (āyatanāni) [receive it]," the great multitude does not understand; they fall into confusion and become resistant, thinking, "What is this that is called 'the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases receiving [the gift]'?
[Therefore he says: "It is persons who receive [the gift]—those who are virtuous and of noble character."

But when it is spoken, one understands; one does not fall into confusion, nor does one become an adversary. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating the purification of offerings.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention; they employ worldly designations, worldly terminology, and worldly expressions.
They teach the Dhamma while remaining [within the conventional]. Therefore, even for the sake of not abandoning worldly convention, the Blessed One speaks of the "person" (puggala).
Consequently, this venerable one also, in order not to contradict the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One—who is skilled in worldly usage—spoke while standing within worldly convention, saying:
"Friends, there are these four persons. Therefore, in this context, according to the ultimate sense (paramattha)...
A person should be understood only by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*), without grasping [at it as a substantial entity].
"Existent, found" means existing and being perceived according to worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*). "In the world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).
In such passages as "one who is still with blemish," however, "blemish" (*aṅgaṇa*) is sometimes said to refer to the defilements (*kilesa*). As it is said: "In that regard..."
What are the three stains? Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, and delusion is a stain. In some instances, it refers to any kind of impurity or mire, as in the passage:
"He exerts himself for the abandoning of that very dust or stain.
In other instances, it refers to a particular type of ground, as understood from such terms as "the Bodhi-terrace" (*bodhi-aṅgaṇa*) and "the shrine-terrace" (*cetiya-aṅgaṇa*).
In this context, however, various kinds of intense defilements (*kilesa*) are intended by the term "stain" (*aṅgaṇa*). For it will be said:
"Friends, 'stain' is a designation for evil, unwholesome states that fall within the range of desire. Together with a stain is "one who has a stain" (*sāṅgaṇa*).

Being one who has a stain means being one who possesses defilements. "He does not understand as it really is: 'There is a stain within me'" means he does not comprehend his own state of defilement as it truly is.
He does not even know that there is defilement within his own mental continuum.

He does not know it according to its true nature, thinking: "These things called defilements are harsh and cruel; they should be abandoned and not grasped, being like poison, filth, or a poisoned arrow.
One who knows that it exists and knows it in this way understands: "There is a blemish within me," as it truly is.

...is said to "understand. However, one for whom the defilements have neither been eradicated by the Path nor have they arisen because they were restrained by some other means—this person is intended here as "one without blemish" (*anaṅgaṇa*).
One does not understand, as it really is, "there is no blemish within me," thinking: "My defilements do not exist because they were restrained by some other means, not by the Path."

He does not know them as "completely eradicated," nor does he know them according to their actual nature, thinking: "If they were to arise, they would cause great harm, being harsh, fierce, and like poisoned arrows.
However, one who knows "it does not exist because of this reason" and knows it in this way is said to "understand as it really is: 'There is no blemish within me. In that regard:
Among those four types of persons, or among those two who possess blemishes, "yvāyam" means "this one who"; "yāyam" is also a reading. 58.
"What, friend Sāriputta, is the cause, what is the reason?"—by both of these, he asks for the very reason.
"By which of these... means by which cause, by which reason, of these two, one is a superior person and one is an inferior person.
"It is declared; what is the cause, what is the condition?"—thus should the connection here be understood.
In that context, although it is stated as "he does not understand" and "he understands," this very pair—understanding and non-understanding—is both the cause and the condition.
However, the Elder, by virtue of his own versatile eloquence, spoke again the words beginning with "Therein, friend... in order to demonstrate that [point] more clearly.
Regarding the phrase "for him this is to be expected" (*tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ*): for that person, this is to be anticipated.

It means it is to be desired that "he will attain only this, and nothing else," which is to say it is certain to happen. This is said with reference to the lack of generating desire and so forth, as stated in the sequence beginning with "he will not generate desire."
And in that regard, "he will not generate desire" means that, being unaware [of the fault], he will not generate the desire of wishing-to-act for the sake of abandoning that blemish.
"He will not strive" means that he will not make an effort stronger than that;
"he will not arouse energy" means that he will not arouse, nor set in motion, firm-rooted energy. This is what is meant.
"Sāṅgaṇo" means one who has blemishes (*aṅgaṇa*) such as these—lust and so forth.
"Saṃkiliṭṭhacitto" means having a mind that is thoroughly defiled by those very same [blemishes], being a mind that is stained, oppressed, and tormented. "Kālaṃ karissati" means he will die.
"Seyyathāpi" means just as if. "Kaṃsapātī" means a vessel made of bronze. "Ābhatā" means brought; either from a marketplace or...
"From a smith’s family" means from a shop or from the house of smiths who work with bronze vessels. "With dust" means with adventitious dust, such as soil and the like.
"With grime" means with the rust produced right there on the iron. "Overgrown" means covered.
"They would not use it" means they would not make use of it by putting water or fresh food into it and so forth. Nor...
"They would cause it to be purified" means they would have it made thoroughly clean by means of washing, scrubbing, and so forth.
"In a dusty place" (*rajāpathe*) means on a dusty path. Or this is the very reading:

in a place where dust arrives, or in a place where rain falls, or beneath a bed, or in a granary, or within a vessel—meaning wherever it is besprinkled with dust. It would become more defiled, seized by filth.
By being placed here on the king’s highway, it becomes more defiled; that is to say, it becomes more heavily coated with grime due to its being unfit for use and its lack of cleansing.
And this is a question-and-answer statement. Therefore, its meaning should be understood thus:
"Friend, if that bronze bowl were treated in this way, after some time it would become more defiled and more heavily coated with grime than the clay bowl."
"Or whether it is a bronze bowl—it would indeed be difficult to know for certain, would it not? The Elder, acknowledging this, said: "It is so, friend.
Then the General of the Dhamma, establishing a simile, said: "In the same way," and so forth. Herein, the application of the simile should be understood as follows:
a person with blemishes is like a stained bronze bowl. Not using a thoroughly defiled bronze bowl is the beginning [of the comparison].
The acquisition of the going-forth by that person from one who is occupied with medical practice and the like is like throwing dust into the path of one who has already received it.
His subsequent performance of medical practice and the like while gradually training under his teachers and preceptors is like a defiled bronze bowl becoming even more defiled.
For one who stands here, death occurs while still possessed of blemish. Or else, there is the gradual transgression of *dukkaṭa* and *dubbhāsita*;

for one who stands here, death occurs while still possessed of blemish. Or else, there is the gradual transgression of *pācittiya*, *thullaccaya*, *saṅghādisesa*, and *pārājika*, as well as the commission of immediate (*ānantariya*) karmas such as matricide; here—
"Death with a mind possessed of blemish.
Regarding the phrase "he will die with a defiled mind," this should not be understood as meaning he will die with an unwholesome (akusala) consciousness.
For all beings die only with their natural consciousness, which is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-citta). However, this...
It should be understood that this was said with reference to the fact that one will die without having purified the continuum of the mind.
In the second instance, "they would polish it" means they would make it as pure as the surface of a mirror by means of washing, scrubbing, soft ash, rubbing, and so forth.
And "not placing it in a dusty place" means not leaving it in the kind of location previously described.
Or they might place it in a basket, a casket, or the like; or, having wrapped it, they might hang it on a peg.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. And the application of the simile here should be understood as follows:

the person capable [of purification] is like the tarnished bronze bowl. Just as starting with the use of the tarnished bronze bowl and ending with its placement in a clean spot, so it is for that person.
For one receiving the going-forth, it is the obtaining of the going-forth in the presence of virtuous bhikkhus.
Those who exhort and instruct him, seeing even the slightest negligence, administer disciplinary measures and repeatedly teach him;
as that person trains under his teachers and preceptors, he becomes purified and cleansed in time, just like a defiled bronze bowl.
In due course, there is the practice of right conduct; for one established herein, there is death without blemish.

Alternatively, having gradually become established in purified virtue, having mastered the Buddha’s word appropriate to oneself, having undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), and having taken up a meditation subject suitable to oneself, one abandons living in a monastery near a village and dwells in a remote lodging.

For one established herein, there is death without blemish (*anaṅgaṇakālakiriyā*). Alternatively, by performing the preliminary work for the *kasiṇas* in due order and thereby producing the eight attainments, there is the suppression of the defilements;

and by emerging from the jhānas that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*) and practicing insight, there is the removal of the defilements by their very roots (*tadaṅganivāraṇa*), the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to the realization of Arahantship—for one established herein, there is indeed death with absolute freedom from blemish.

On the third occasion, "the sign of beauty" (*subhanimitta*) refers to a desirable object that serves as a basis for lust. "He will attend to it" (*manasi karissati*) means he will direct his attention toward that sign when his mindfulness has failed.
"Because of his attending to the sign of beauty" (*tassa subhanimittassa manasikārā*) means because of that person’s act of attending to the sign of beauty.
"He will exalt" (*anuddhaṃsessati*) means he will harm or overcome [himself]. For lust—
It should be understood that when [the mind] arises, it cuts off the wholesome section and, remaining itself as an unwholesome javana, it subverts the wholesome consciousness.
The remainder should be grasped according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, the application of the simile here should be understood as follows: by nature, it is with few defilements, like a pure bronze bowl.

The person free from blemish (anaṅgaṇa-puggala). Just as placing [food] on a dust-heap after first refusing to eat from a perfectly pure bronze bowl, so it is for that person receiving the going-forth (pabbajjā); everything following this is exactly like the first section.

In the fourth section, regarding the phrase "he will not attend to the sign of beauty" (subhanimittaṃ na manasi karissati): because of the absence of a lack of mindfulness toward that [sign], that sign...
He will not be offended; the remainder should be understood according to the second section.
“This, friend,” and so forth, follows the same method as what was stated in the passage beginning with “Who, friend?
60. Now, desiring to make that fault manifest in its various aspects, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—
Being questioned in the manner beginning with “Is it a courtyard, a courtyard? he answered that by saying, “Of evil things indeed, friends,” and so forth.

Therein, “of the range of desire” (*icchāvacarānaṃ*) means of those that fall within the range of desire; the meaning is: of the various kinds of grounds for anger that arise and proceed by way of desire.
“That which here for someone” (*yaṃ idhekaccassa*) refers to that by which desire would thus arise for a certain person here.
"That possibility, that cause exists; it is found," so it is said. "I might have fallen into [an offense]" means "I would have become one who has fallen.
"And the monks might not know me" means "and the monks would not recognize me.
What, then, is the possibility here? It is the desire for gain. For a monk who desires gain, even if he is naturally meritorious, is honored by people.
Being thus respected, he thinks: "When the elders learn that a monk has committed an offense, they inform the middle-ranking monks;
they inform the junior monks; the juniors inform the scavengers and others in the monastery; and they inform the nuns who have come for exhortation.
In this way, the four assemblies come to know of it in succession. Thus there is an obstruction to his gains. Oh, if only I were not to commit an offense..."
"I might fall into trouble, and yet the monks would not know me.
As for the statement, "the reason by which other monks would know that monk exists indeed;
it is not non-existent," this is because the elders, having learned [of his situation], inform the middle-ranking monks.
Thus, by the method previously described, he becomes well-known among the four assemblies.
Being thus well-known and overcome by infamy, even after entering a hundred villages and gleaning at a hundred places like a fence-post, he departs with his bowl as clean as when it was washed.
Then, thinking, "The monks know that I have fallen into an offense; I have been expelled by them in this way," [he reflects].
He becomes angry and displeased; for this reason he is both angry and overcome by anger, and displeased and overcome by dejection.
Furthermore, friends, that which is anger and that which is resentment—both of these are stains, friends—and they are included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Anger and that lack of confidence which is included within the aggregate of feeling—both of these should be understood here as "blemish" (*aṅgaṇa*).
And this is stated with reference to such types of persons. However, greed is included by way of its prior stage, and delusion is indeed included by way of association.
Anurādha wishes to take a monk who is just like the previous one, lead him to a lodging on the outskirts of the monastery, lock the door, and accuse him.

Indeed, there is this possibility—that is, this reason exists—whereby he might bring that monk before the fourfold assembly and have a competent and disciplined [monk] say: "In such-and-such a place, you performed medical treatment..."

They should admonish him in the manner beginning with the words "He said," and so forth. He becomes well-known among the four assemblies. Being thus well-known, he is overcome by infamy; all of this is exactly as described previously.

"A person with a counterpart" means a person who is equal [to another]. "Equal" means one who has committed an offense. "Counterpart" means the one who admonishes. This refers to one who, being precisely one who has committed an offense—
He desires to reproach [the other], thinking: "You too have fallen into this and that offense; first rectify yours, and afterwards you may reproach me.
Furthermore, a person who is equal in birth and so forth is a "counterpart" (sappaṭipuggala).
For he is indeed equal to himself in terms of birth, family, great learning, proficiency, ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and so on.
He desires a reprimand, thinking that what is spoken by such a person will not be excessively painful. Regarding the term *appaṭipuggala*:

here, one who is unfit to be a counterpart (*paṭipuggala*) is an *appaṭipuggala*. Because he is unlike [the transgressor] in these respects—such as the nature of the offense—he is unfit to be an adversary, an opponent, or a reprover;
this is what is meant. Thus, "he is angry" means that he becomes angry in this way because of this very reproach from one who is an *appaṭipuggala*.
In the fourth instance, *aho vata* is seen in the sense of reproach, as in: “Oh, how wise we are! Oh, how learned and masters of the three Vedas we are!
It is also used in the sense of aspiration, as in: “Oh, would that they were to anoint me to the kingship while I am still young!
Here, it is used only in the sense of aspiration. *Paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā* means having asked again and again.
This bhikkhu, desiring gain, wishes to question the Blessed One about himself;
and that is by way of a question for approval (*anumatipucchā*), not by interposing the path, the fruit, or insight.

For he sees the Blessed One together with the great elders such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, and Rāhula [saying]: "What do you think, Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Rāhula? Is the eye permanent...?"
Or impermanent?”—thus questioning again and again as he teaches the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly;
while people speak in praise, saying, “Those wise elders please the Teacher’s mind,” and present him with gains and honors.
Therefore, desiring those gains and honors, one thinks thus and plants a stake that has been dug and set in the ground.
He stood as if right before the Blessed One.
Thinking, "So he is angry," the Blessed One, without even taking notice of him, questioned another elder and taught the Dhamma;
because of that, he became angry with both the Blessed One and the elder. How does he become angry with the Blessed One? [Thinking: "I..."
"From the time of my going forth, I have not known him to go outside the Gandhakuṭi courtyard;
at all times he does not leave me like a shadow, and there is not even a single teaching of the Dhamma after asking about me by name.
At that moment, having merely seen the Elder, he asks about him and teaches the Dhamma"—thus the Blessed One was provoked. How?
The elder becomes resentful: "This aged elder sits before the Blessed One like a stump;
when indeed will those who perform legal acts according to the Dhamma bring him to an unfit state and expel him?
For if this man were not in this monastery, the Blessed One would surely converse with me. In this way, the elder becomes resentful.
"Purakkhatvā purakkhatvā" means having placed [them] in front, one after another; it is synonymous with "having surrounded.

This person, too, is merely desirous of gain. For he sees learned bhikkhus entering a village with a large retinue, worshipping at a cetiya, and observes the success they enjoy as well as the lay devotees showing signs of faith toward them because of their confidence.
Therefore, he desires it thus. "Is provoked" means that he is provoked in two situations: regarding the monks and regarding the elder.
How regarding the monks? "These [monks] take whatever robe or alms-food arises for me and enjoy it, yet there is not even one who follows behind me taking my bowl and robe"—thus [he thinks].
The monks were dissatisfied. How was it for the elder? He thought: "This aged elder makes himself known in various places;
when indeed will those who perform legal acts according to the Dhamma expel him?
If he is not there, they will certainly surround me alone."
*Bhattagge* means in the dining hall. *Aggāsana* means the seat of the senior monk of the Saṅgha. *Aggodaka* means the water of honor (the water for the feet).
*Aggapiṇḍa* means the alms-food of the senior monk of the Saṅgha. Or, in all these cases, *agga* is a designation for what is excellent.
In that regard, the desire "May I alone receive it" is not excessively blameworthy. However, the thought "May no other bhikkhu receive it" is exceedingly blameworthy.
This seeker of gain is also pleasing through his manner of wearing robes and other such qualities; sometimes he goes forth, and sometimes he falls away from the order.
Because of that, not receiving afterwards the seats and other things he had previously obtained, he thought thus:
"That bhikkhu shall not receive"—that is, that bhikkhu shall not receive among the foremost seats and so forth for the elders, nor accordingly for those of middle rank or others.
He receives new things—whatever they may be—that are all of the lowest quality, such as seats and so forth. "Angry" means that he is angry in two respects:
toward laypeople and toward the elders. How toward laypeople? [Thinking: "These monks obtain [offerings] by depending on me during auspicious ceremonies and the like;
these [laypeople], 'Venerable Sir, having taken so many monks, out of compassion for us..."
When people say, "Do it," and immediately take that elderly elder—whom they have only just seen that moment—and depart, thinking, "Let it be for now;
we shall know when their need arises," the people become resentful. How do the elders become resentful?
They think, "If these people did not exist, the people would invite me alone," and thus the elders become resentful.
"Anumodeyyaṃ" means "I would offer an expression of appreciation. This man was also desirous of gain; he knew some kind of fragmentary appreciation, thinking:
"Many women come to the place of appreciation; if they recognize me, from then on they will give alms in bowls.
It was with this aspiration that he thought thus. "Ṭhānaṃ" refers to the appreciation offered by those who are well-versed in the scriptures.
"The burden"—by this it is meant that one who is well-versed in the scriptures (*bahussuta*) should give his approval. "Enraged" (*kupita*):
he too is provoked in three respects—toward people, toward the Elder, and toward the preacher of the Dhamma. How toward people? [They think]:
"Previously these people would come to me alone and request, 'May our Elder Nāga, may our Elder Sumana, give us his approval,' but today he did not say anything."
In this way, people become angry. How does it affect the elder?

“This senior of the Saṅgha does not say, ‘Go to the elders Nāgatthera and Sumanatthera, who are your own family supporters; he will give the blessing,’” thinking thus, the elder becomes angry. How does it affect the Dhamma-preacher? “As soon as the elder has finished speaking, [the listener] is like a cock that has received a blow.”

"It rains very hurriedly, as if in competition; there is no one to drive this man out, for if he were not here, I alone would be able to give the Dhamma talk"—thus does the preacher of the Dhamma become angry.
"Those who have come to the monastery" means those assembled in the vihāra. This person, too, being desirous of gain, [gives] some kind of fragmentary Dhamma talk.

He knows; he sees such places where monks, having gathered from two or three *yojanas* away, listen to all-night Dhamma discourses, and where young novices, with joyful hearts, give shouts of approval with a great roar, saying, "Excellent!
Excellent! Then, on the following day, when the monks have entered the village, the lay devotees ask them, "Who, venerable sirs..."
“Preach the Dhamma,” they said. They replied, “So-and-so and so-and-so. Hearing this, people with faith paid great honor to those preachers of the Dhamma. Desiring that for himself, he thought thus:
“The burden of teaching the Dhamma belongs to those who are learned and skilled in exposition; therefore, one who is learned should teach”—this is what is meant. “Being angry” means...
Not even obtaining the opportunity to speak a single four-line stanza, he becomes angry at his own dullness, thinking, "I am dull-witted and lacking in wisdom; how could I possibly teach?
[He goes] for the purpose of exhorting the bhikkhunīs, or for the purpose of recitation, or for the purpose of interrogation, or for the purpose of making an offering.
Having come to the monastery, [he observes] the bhikkhunīs assembled there. This one, too, is desirous of gain; it occurs to him thus:

"These bhikkhunīs have gone forth from great families. When they enter those families and sit down, people will ask, 'In whose presence do you receive exhortation, recitation, or questioning? Then they will say, 'The one named so-and-so...'"
“The noble one is learned; give him [the task], perform it for him!”—thus a desire arises in him. “The occasion”:

instruction and so forth are indeed the burden of those who are learned; therefore, it is meant that the learned one should teach. “Angry”: he too becomes angry in two instances, and regarding those nuns [he thinks]:
“Previously, these [nuns] relied upon me for the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and so forth...”
They obtained [this opportunity], and so they have now gone at that very moment into the presence of the elder Mahallaka who had just been seen.
And as for the preacher of the Dhamma, [the thought occurred to him]: "He has indeed given these women an exhortation spontaneously.
Regarding "of the lay followers" (upāsakānaṃ): it refers to the lay followers who had gone to the monastery. They were great lay followers whose business affairs had been relinquished.
Having entrusted the work of their sons and brothers to others, they wander about listening to the Dhamma; this person wishes to teach them for what reason?

Thinking: "Once these people have gained confidence, they will inform the female lay followers as well, and then, together with the female lay followers, they will bring offerings and honor to me alone.
A place [for teaching] should be assigned only to one who is learned (*bahussuta*). "An angry one" (*kupita*)—means:
This [attitude] also becomes agitated in two situations: first, regarding the lay followers, thinking, "They hear [the Dhamma] elsewhere;
they do not come to us because they think, 'We shall hear it in the presence of our own family preceptor (kulūpaka). Let it be for now; we shall find out when their need arises';
and second, regarding the Dhamma-preacher, thinking, "It is he who teaches them."

"Of the female lay followers" means those who have come to the monastery. "Female lay followers" refers to those who have assembled for the purpose of performing acts of honor such as offering seats, or on the Uposatha day, or for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
The rest is exactly according to the method explained in the section on male lay followers (*upāsaka*). "They would honor" means they would perform it with care and they would perform it beautifully.
By this, one aspires for the honoring being done toward oneself to be performed with care and to be beautiful. "They would revere" means they would treat it as weighty. By this...
He aspires to have himself placed in a position of esteem by the bhikkhus. "Māneyyuṃ" means they would love him.
"Pūjeyyuṃ" means that honoring him, respecting him, and loving him, they would worship him with the requisite requisites; thus he aspires for the worship of requisites.
"Ṭhānaṃ" refers to this method described as being "dear, respected, and venerable," as well as being learned and virtuous.
The meaning is that monks ought not to act in such a manner because of him. "Angry" means he is angry in two respects:
toward the monks, thinking, "They are honoring this [other monk]," and toward the elder, thinking, "If this one were not here, they would honor me alone.
This same method applies to the three subsequent sections.
"Of fine robes" means of robes such as those made of silk (*paṭṭa*), *dukūla*, *paṭṭuṇṇa*, or *koseyya*—robes that are expensive, delicate, and pleasant to the touch.
Here too, the wish "May I alone be the recipient" is not excessively blameworthy; however, the wish "May no other bhikkhu be a recipient" is greatly blameworthy.
"Of excellent almsfood" means of the finest almsfood filled with ghee, oil, honey, sugar, and so forth.

"Of excellent lodgings" means of the finest beds, chairs, and so on, worth many hundreds of thousands. "Of medicinal requisites for the sick" means of the best medicines such as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth.
In all these cases, the place [is frequented] by those who are learned and meritorious.
And it should be applied [as follows]. "Angry" means that he becomes angry in both places in all instances. Regarding people, [he thinks]:

"These have no sense of familiarity at all; even though I have lived with them for a long time, and though I go from house to house for the sake of rag-robes, alms-food, or for the sake of ghee, oil, and so forth, they do not give me anything refined even for a single day."
“They do not give the requisites [to others], but as soon as they see an elderly newcomer, they give him whatever he desires.
And regarding the Elder, [the monks thought]: “This man too is an elder who wanders about merely showing himself to them;
when indeed will those who perform Dhamma-deeds expel him? If he were not here, I alone would be the recipient of gains.”
"Of these, friends, this is... refers to the spheres of desire (*icchāvacara*) mentioned in the nineteen preceding instances. 61.
"They are both seen and heard": the spheres of desire are not seen with the eye, nor are they heard with the ear, because they are objects of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).
However, for a person who has not abandoned the spheres of desire, bodily action proceeds by way of those spheres of desire.
Having seen [them], they are as if already seen; having heard [of them], their verbal conduct is as if already heard. Therefore it is said: “They are both seen and heard.

They are seen at the time of direct perception (*paccakkha*), and they are heard at a time when they are out of sight (*tirokkha*), such as when one hears, “It is said that such-and-such a monk is like this.

The phrase “even though” (*kiñcāpi*) is a word expressing both favor and reproach. By it, he shows favor toward the practice of forest-dwelling (*āraññika*), while reproaching the failure to abandon the sphere of desire.

In this regard, the application is as follows: although that bhikkhu, having rejected lodgings within a village, is a forest-dweller and lives in a remote and secluded dwelling, these various spheres of desire have not yet been abandoned by him.
Although he, having rejected extra acquisitions, is an alms-food eater; and although he, having avoided the practice of greediness, is one who goes for alms in regular order.

Although he rejects robes given by householders and becomes a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*), "wearing coarse robes" (*lūkhacīvaradhara*)—here, "coarse" (*lūkha*) should be understood as coarse in three ways:
coarse in terms of the cutting tool, coarse in terms of the yarn, and coarse in terms of the dye.
Among these, that which has been cut into pieces with a knife is "coarse in terms of the cutting tool."
That which is deficient in value is called "coarse in price"; that which is sewn with thick, long thread is called "coarse in thread," and it is deficient in touch, being rough to the touch.
That which is dyed with dye is called "coarse in dye," and it is deficient in color, being discolored.
Even though that bhikkhu wears robes that are coarse in blade, coarse in thread, and coarse in dye...
"He exists, and these many spheres of his desire are seen and heard to be unabandoned;
yet, wise fellow-celibates neither honor him... nor revere him. "For what reason?"—here, *taṃ* is merely a particle;
*kissa hetū* means "for what cause"? For those [desires] of his... are indeed seen and heard.
"Evil things manifest," this is what is meant. "Because these spheres of desire have not been abandoned"—this is the intended meaning here.
Now, making that point clear by means of a simile, he said: "Just as if," and so forth. Therein, *kuṇapaṃ* is a dead body.
*Ahikuṇapaṃ* is the corpse of a snake. The others are likewise. And herein, because they are exceedingly repulsive and loathsome, it is these very things [that are being described].

It should be understood that three [types of corpses] have been mentioned. For people even consume the carcasses of other animals, such as rabbits and pigs, after preparing them with pungent condiments and the like.
But they feel revulsion toward the carcasses of these [beings] even when they are fresh;
what need is there to mention when they have become putrid through the passage of time? "Having composed" means having expanded or completed.
"Having taken a corpse and placed it in a bronze bowl" is what is meant. "By another" means by someone else. "Having covered it over" means having closed it with a lid.
"In the midst of the market" means at the entrance of the street crowded with many people, located between the shops.

"They would enter" means they would go there. "As if each were distinct" means as if they were clean and pure, or as if they were pleasant and unpleasant. Furthermore, [this refers to] the bridal goods.
It is said: "Viya. "Vadhukā" is a term for a mother; the *jañña* is the gift being carried for her.
In both cases, the repetition is used either out of respect or as a mark of praise. There is also a reading: “*Jaññañ-jaññaṃ byā*.
“Apāpuritvā” means having opened. “*Tassa saha dassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyyā*” means that upon seeing it, a sense of repulsiveness would arise toward that corpse.

At the very moment of seeing him, that person’s unpleasantness would remain. "Unpleasantness" (*amanāpatā*) is a designation for the mind and mental factors that have arisen [thinking], "This is unpleasant.
The same method applies to "repulsiveness" (*paṭikūlatā*) and "loathsomeness" (*jegucchata*). "Even for those who are hungry" means even for those who are famished.
"There would be no desire to eat" means there would be no wish to consume; how much more so for those who are already satiated?
What is meant is that the desire to eat would not arise even earlier than for those who possess the [other] requisites.
Herein, this is the application of the simile: his mark of renunciation is like a pure bronze bowl;

the non-abandoning of the sphere of craving is like the stuffing of it with a corpse; and the covering up with another bronze bowl is like [the concealment of faults] by means of the forest-dweller’s practice and so forth.
The concealment of the sphere of desire is like the public’s displeasure upon seeing a corpse after opening a bronze bowl;
similarly, by not adopting the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññika-aṅga*) and instead displaying the sphere of desire, one fails to show respect to one’s fellow celibates. 62.
On the side of the wholesome (*sukkapakkha*), however, the phrase "even though" is a word of appreciation and support; by it, one supports the state of being a forest-dweller.
He praises the abandoning of desire. "One who accepts invitations" means one who receives invitations. "With black grains removed" means having searched for and set aside the black grains.
"With many soups and many curries": here, "soup" (sūpa) refers to that which is taken up by the hand; "curry" (byañjana) refers to the additional side-dishes.
Thus, it is "with many soups" such as fish, meat, mung-bean soup, and so forth, and with various kinds of curries made from meat and other ingredients.
"Many kinds of condiments" is what is meant. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
And in the application of the simile: the preparation of the choice rice meal is like the abandoning of the sphere of desire;
the covering over with another bronze dish is like the concealing of the abandonment of the sphere of desire by such things as living in villages, which arise from the state of having few desires.
Just as the sight of excellent rice-food is pleasing to people when a bronze bowl is opened,

so too should the honoring of fellow practitioners of the holy life be understood through the demonstration of the abandonment of the sphere of desire, rather than by taking up village monasteries and the like.
"A simile occurs to me, friend Sāriputta"— that is, a simile presents itself to me, friend Sāriputta.
The intention is: "I wish to speak one simile. "Paṭibhātu taṃ" means "may it occur to you," "may it appear to you";
the intention is: "speak it. Regarding the phrase "ekam-idāhaṃ": here, *idaṃ* is merely a particle;
it is said that "at one time I [spoke]," where the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. "Rājagahe viharāmi Giribbaje": "Rājagaha" refers to...
This is the name of that city. However, because it stands like a fence (vaja) surrounded on all sides by mountains, it is called Giribbaja.
"I dwell in that city" means that I dwell depending upon it. Then, as for "atha khvāhaṃ," it means "then indeed I.
Here, *atha* is a particle used at the beginning of a new section or topic (*aññādhikāra*). *Khu* is used merely to fill out the metrical line (*padapūraṇa*).
"During the morning time" (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*) means the period of the early part of the day. The meaning is "at the morning time" (*pubbaṇhasamaye*);
or, "the time of the morning" (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*), meaning one moment in the morning—thus, the accusative case is used to express an absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*).
"Having dressed" (*nivāsetvā*) means having put on; this refers to the act of putting on and changing the lower robe (*nivāsana*) in the monastery.
It should be understood thus. Having arranged [the robe] for the purpose of entering the village, by way of wearing it as an undergarment—for he was not unwrapped prior to that.
"Taking bowl and robe" means having taken the bowl with the hand and the robe with the body. "For alms" means for the sake of alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*).
"Samīti" is his name. "Son of a cartwright" means son of a chariot-maker. "Son of Paṇḍu" means son of Paṇḍu.
An Ājīvaka is a naked ascetic. "Son of an old wagon-maker" means he is the son of an ancient family of wagon-makers.
"Standing near" means having approached and remained there. "Crooked" (vaṅka) means bent to one side. "Wry" (jimha) means like a path followed by a snake.
"Splits" (dosa) refers to pith, unevenness, knots, and so forth. "In whatever way" (yathā yathā) is a particle used in the sense of time; it means "whenever" or "at whichever time."
This has been said. "In such and such a way" (*tathā tathā*) also refers only to time; it means "at this or that time.
He reflected in accordance with his own Suttas, while the other cut exactly at the point he had thought of at that very moment.
"Satisfied in mind" (*attamano*) means having a mind of one's own, a contented mind, a mind seized by rapture and joy. "He uttered words of satisfaction" (*attamanavācaṃ nicchāresi*).
He uttered, spoke, or pronounced words that were appropriate for a state of gladness, or for a mind that is joyful;
this is what is meant. “As if knowing heart with heart” means as if knowing one mind by means of another mind.
“Lacking faith” means being devoid of faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. “Seeking a livelihood” means being oppressed by debt, fear, and so forth.
Being unable to live outside [the community], they remain here seeking a livelihood. "Not with faith" means not out of faith.

"Deceitful and fraudulent" means endowed with deceit (*māyā*) and fraud (*saṭheyya*). "Cheats" (*ketavino*) means those who have practiced deception; what is meant is that their fraud has reached its full development.
For fraud, because it displays non-existent qualities, is equated with displaying the qualities of non-existent goods and is thus called "deception" (*kerāṭiya*).

It is said: "Haughty" (*unnaḷā*) means those whose reed (*naḷa*) has risen up; what is meant is that their empty pride has arisen. "Fickle" (*capalā*) means endowed with fickleness through the adornment of bowl, robes, and so forth.

"Garrulous" (*mukharā*) means harsh-mouthed; what is meant is that they have harsh speech. "Loose-tongued" (*vikiṇṇavācā*) means having unrestrained speech, babbling useless words even during the day.
"Unrestrained in the doors of the sense faculties" (*indriyesu aguttadvārā*) means having unguarded doors of action regarding the six sense faculties.
"Immoderate in food" means those who do not know the measure in food—that is, the moderation that should be known regarding seeking, receiving, and consuming;
they are those who lack knowledge of this. "Not devoted to wakefulness" means not devoted to staying awake.

"Lacking regard for the state of a recluse" means having no expectation for the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*); the meaning is that they are devoid of practice in accordance with the Dharma. "Without intense reverence for the training" means...
