They do not have great reverence for the training rules, or they are prone to transgressing the offenses. "Luxurious" and so forth is stated in the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta*;
"lazy" and so forth is in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*. "By means of a discourse on the Dhamma" means by means of a teaching of the Dhamma.
"Faithful from the home" refers to those who were faithful by nature, and those who, having become ordained, went forth from the home into homelessness out of faith.
"‘They drink, as it were; they eat, as it were’ means they drink as if they were drinking and they eat as if they were eating.
Uttering words of gladness, they drink as if with their speech; expressing deep appreciation, they eat as if with their mind.
‘Sādhu vata’ means ‘how beautiful indeed! ‘Sabrahmacārī’ may be pronounced either short or long. If it is short, it refers to one above Sāriputta; if it is long—"
Regarding "among fellow celibates" (*sabrahmacārīnaṃ*): when it refers to Sāriputta, the meaning is that the fellow celibate Sāriputta has caused us to emerge from unwholesome states.
When it refers to "fellow celibates," the meaning is that the fellow celibates have caused [us] to emerge from unwholesome states.

"A youth" (*daharo*) means one who is young. "A young man" (*yuvā*) means one established in the state of youth. "By nature fond of adornment" (*maṇḍanakajātikoti*) means having a disposition toward ornamentation.
In this context, some who are young are not truly youthful, such as those who are excessively immature;
others, though youthful, are not of a decorative nature, such as those whose character is tranquil or who are overcome by laziness, calamities, and so forth.
Here, however, one who is both young and youthful and of a decorative nature is intended; therefore, he spoke thus. Blue lotuses and the like are mentioned because they are well-known in the world.
"Itihate" means "thus they. "Both great nāgas" (ubho mahānāgā) refers to two great nāgas; for both these chief disciples are called "great nāgas.
Herein, this is the etymological explanation: they do not go by way of desire and so forth, thus they are *nāgas*;
they do not return to the defilements abandoned by their respective paths, thus they are *nāgas*; they do not commit various kinds of evil (*āgu*), thus they are *nāgas*. This is the meaning here.
This is the summary. The detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Mahāniddesa*. Furthermore:
“He commits no offense whatsoever in the world, having released all fetters and bonds;”
“He does not cling anywhere;
liberated, such a one is called a ‘great nāga’ because of his true nature.
Thus should the meaning here be understood. “Great nāgas” (mahānāgas) are those who are more worthy of honor than other nāgas whose taints have been destroyed.
And the meaning is that they were even more praiseworthy. *Aññamaññassa* means one [person] to another. *Samanumodiṃsu* means they rejoiced together.
In this regard, by means of this simile, Mahāmoggallāna rejoiced; the General of the Dhamma rejoiced with the words, "May it occur to you, friend.
Therefore it is said: "They rejoiced together in each other’s well-spoken words."
The commentary on the discourse explaining the teaching of the conventional and the ultimate is finished.
The commentary on the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
