“Venerable sir, the surface of the great earth is endowed with excellence; its flavor is like pure, unadulterated honey”—this is what is meant by “endowed with sweetness.
Here, however, both “endowed with perfection” (*paripuṇṇa-sampanna*) and “endowed with possession” (*samaṅgi-sampanna*) are acceptable.
Therefore, the phrase “endowed with virtue” (*sampanna-sīla*) means either having virtue that is perfect or having virtue that is possessed. Thus it should be understood here.
The meaning must be understood. In what sense is it "virtue" (*sīla*)? It is virtue in the sense of "conducting" (*sīlana*). Its detailed exposition is given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Therein, by the phrase "of perfect virtue," just as a field is made complete by the removal of defects in the soil, so too [is one] by the removal of defects in virtue.

The fulfillment of virtue has thus been explained. For just as a field may be incomplete and possessed of four defects—the seed-section, the sowing-section, the water-section, and the manure-section—therein, the "seed-section" refers to where, here and there, the seeds are broken or rotten; these...
Wherever they sow, the crop does not grow there; the field becomes broken.
"Broken sowing" (vappakhaṇḍa) means that when an unskilled person sows seeds, he drops them here and there. For in this way, the crop does not grow everywhere, and the field becomes broken.
"Broken watering" (udakakhaṇḍa) means that in some places there is too much water, or in others there is none at all.
For even there, the crops do not grow; the field becomes ruined.
What is called "a salt-encrusted field" is where a farmer, while plowing the soil with a plowshare four or five times over a certain area, makes it too deep, and from that salt arises;
even there the crop does not grow, and the field becomes ruined—such is that [place].
A field does not yield great fruit or great benefit; for even if one sows much there, one obtains little.
However, through the removal of these four defects, the field becomes complete. Such a field yields great fruit and great benefit.
In the same way, [the mind] possessed of the four defects—being broken, perforated, spotted, and mottled—is likewise deficient.
Virtue remains incomplete. Such virtue is neither of great fruit nor of great benefit.
However, through the disappearance of these four defects, the field of virtue becomes complete; such virtue is then of great fruit and great benefit.
By the phrase "possessors of virtue" (*sīlasamaṅgino*), it is meant that they have become endowed with, have attained the union of, and are possessed of virtue in this sense.
"Having offered, dwell"—this is precisely what is meant. In this regard, the perfection of virtue arises from two causes:
by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue.
Both of these have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding this, the Elder Sumana, who dwelt at Dīpa Vihāra, said: "By the words 'possessed of perfected virtue' (sampannasīlā), the Blessed One has merely indicated the fourfold purification of virtue;
then, by the phrase 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,' he has shown therein the preeminent virtue in detail.
However, his pupil, the Elder Cūḷanāga, master of the Three Piṭakas, said: "In both instances, the restraint of the Pātimokkha was [intended] by the Blessed One."
It was said that the restraint of the Pātimokkha alone is virtue (*sīla*). However, not conceding that the other three [types of restraint] have the status of being called "virtue," he said:
"The restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is merely the guarding of the six doors;

purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi*) is merely the arising of requisites through what is lawful and equitable; and [the restraint regarding] requisites consists in the use of the requisites already obtained..."
The mere consuming [of food] after reflecting, "This is for this purpose," is the restraint of the Pātimokkha in its direct sense;
it alone is virtue (*sīla*). For one whose [restraint] is broken, it cannot be said—just as of a man whose head is severed—that he will protect his remaining hands and feet.
But for one whose [restraint] is intact, just as of a man whose head is unsevered, he will protect his life and the rest once again.
"Having restored them to their natural state, one is able to guard them. Therefore, having indicated the restraint of the Pātimokkha by the phrase 'perfect in virtue' (sampannasīlā),
and having stated 'perfect in the Pātimokkha' (sampannapātimokkhā) as a synonym for that very same term,
[the author] spoke the passage beginning with 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' (pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā) in order to explain it in detail."
In this context, "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"Perfect in conduct and resort" means perfect in both conduct and resort. "In even the slightest" means in those that are very minor.
"Offenses" means unwholesome states. "Seeing danger" means seeing them as fearful. "Having undertaken" means having correctly taken up. "Train in the rules of training" means...
"Train yourselves by undertaking each of those training rules. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and train yourselves by undertaking the training rules," the summary here is this:
undertake and train in whatever is to be trained in among all the divisions of training, whether physical or verbal.
However, in detail, these include all [the disciplines] such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth.
The steps have been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. 65.
Why was this section beginning with "If he should desire" commenced? It is for the purpose of showing the benefits of virtue (*sīla*).
Even if those who have recently gone forth or those who are lacking in wisdom should think thus: "The Blessed One says, 'Fulfill virtue'; but who indeed [is capable] in the fulfillment of virtue?"
"What is the benefit, what is the distinction, what is the increase? He spoke thus in order to show them these seventeen benefits.

[He did so] thinking, "Perhaps, even upon hearing of this benefit—beginning with being dear and pleasing to one's fellow celibates and ending with the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya)—they might fulfill their virtue," just like the merchant Visakaṇṭaka. The merchant named Visakaṇṭaka is called a sugar merchant.
It is said that he took molasses, treacle, sugar-candy, sugar, and other such items in a cart, went to a frontier village, and shouted, "Take poison-thorns!
Take poison-thorns! Hearing this, the villagers thought, "Poison is indeed harsh;
whoever eats it dies. A thorn also kills by piercing; both of these are harsh. Who here [would take them]?"
Thinking, "This is the benefit," they bolted the doors of their houses and sent the children away. Seeing this, the merchant thought, "These villagers are clever at bargaining;
come now, I shall have them take [the goods] by some stratagem. He said, "Take very sweet things! Take very delicious things!
You can get sugar, molasses, and rock-sugar at a low price; you can even get them for counterfeit māsakas and counterfeit kahāpaṇas!"
He proclaimed it. Hearing that, the villagers, joyful and delighted, came and took [the medicine] after paying a high price for it.

In this regard, the Blessed One’s words—“Monks, dwell possessed of perfected virtue... train yourselves by undertaking the rules of training”—are like the merchant’s proclamation, “Take poison-thorns! “Both of these are harsh; who…”
Just as the villagers thought, "There is a benefit here," so did the Blessed One say, "Dwell possessed of virtue.
Then the monks thought, "Virtue indeed is harsh, rough, and opposed to play and such; what, then, is the benefit for those possessed of virtue?
Thereupon, the merchant spoke these words: "Take [the fruit] that is exceedingly sweet," and so forth.

The statement beginning with "If he should desire" (ākaṅkheyya ce) should be understood as being for the purpose of revealing the seventeen benefits, starting with being dear and pleasing to the Blessed One and ending with the destruction of the taints (āsava).
In that context, "if he should desire" means if he should wish; "and may he be dear" means [dear] by way of eyes of affection.
"It should be contemplated" means it should serve as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the arising of affection.

"Endearing" (*manāpa*) means that which increases their mental delight, or that which is to be attained by their minds; what is meant is that it should be suffused with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Venerable" (*garu*) means one who occupies a position of respect for them, like a stone parasol. "One to be cultivated" (*bhāvanīya*) means: "Surely this venerable one, knowing..."

"He knows; seeing, he sees"—thus is he to be esteemed. "He is one who fulfills precisely the virtues" means that he should be one who fulfills precisely the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*);
it is said that he should be endowed with them in a complete and perfected manner. "Devoted to internal serenity of mind" means engaged in the serenity of his own mind;
for here, "internal" (*ajjhatta*) or "one's own" (*attan*)—
Or rather, this is one and the same thing; there is only a difference in the phrasing (*byañjana*). However, in the sense of the locative case, this word *samatha* is used in the accusative.

It is established through its connection with the prefix *anu*. "One whose jhāna is not cast out" (*anirākatajjhāno*) means one whose jhāna has not been removed externally, or one whose jhāna is not destroyed;
for this term "casting out" (*nirākaraṇa*) has the sense of removal and destruction, as seen in such expressions as "having cast out stubbornness, living in humility," and so forth.
Its application should be understood.
"Endowed with insight" means being engaged in the sevenfold contemplation;

the sevenfold contemplation consists of the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of non-self, the contemplation of disenchantment, the contemplation of dispassion, [the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment].

Contemplation of cessation and contemplation of relinquishment—these have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "One who increases [his practice] in empty huts" means one who expands [his meditation] in empty huts;

and herein, a monk who, having taken up a meditation subject by way of serenity and insight, enters an empty hut and sits there day and night, should be understood as "one who increases [his practice] in empty huts. [This applies even when sitting] in a multi-storied palace, etc.
However, even while performing [these actions], it should be understood that one does not increase [the defilements] in empty dwellings.
And up to this point, just as the teaching on the wanderings of craving (*taṇhā-vicariya*), although initially commenced by way of craving,

became a teaching on the three kinds of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) through a gradual process— because craving is the basis for conceit and views, which then lead back to conceit and views— so too is this teaching.

It should be understood that although this was first undertaken by way of the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), because virtue is the foundation for serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), the teaching on the three trainings arose after one has entered into serenity and insight.
For here, up to the point where it says, "He is one who fulfills [himself] precisely in regard to the virtues," the training in higher virtue has been stated. "Internally... [and so forth].

By the phrase "devoted to mental serenity, not neglecting jhāna," the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) is indicated; by the phrase "possessed of insight" (vipassanā), the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is indicated.
Furthermore, by the phrase "one who frequents empty huts," both trainings are stated together:
the training in higher mind through the cultivation of empty huts by way of serenity, and the training in higher wisdom by way of insight. Thus, it is said having included both trainings.
And here, by the phrases “devoted to internal mental tranquility, not neglecting jhāna,” it is one-pointedness of mind that protects virtue which is being described.
By the phrase “by means of insight,” it is the discernment of formations that protects virtue.
How does one-pointedness of mind protect virtue? For one who lacks one-pointedness of mind, when afflicted by disease—
When it arises, one is distressed; struck down by that illness and with a distracted mind, one even destroys one's virtue while attempting to alleviate the illness.
However, for one who possesses one-pointedness of mind, having suppressed that painful illness, they enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*);
at the moment of entry, suffering is cast far away and a more powerful happiness arises.
Thus, one-pointedness of mind protects virtue.
How does the discernment of formations protect virtue? For one who lacks the discernment of formations, there arises a strong sense of "mine" regarding the personal identity, thinking, "Form is mine;
consciousness is mine. Such a person, in times of famine, disease, fear, and the like— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the context of the preceding portion.*
Even when prosperity arrives, one who destroys his virtue merely nourishes his own physical frame.
However, for one who possesses discernment regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), there is no strong sense of "mine" or affection toward that physical frame;
thus, even if such times of famine, disease, fear, and so forth should arise, even if his intestines come out of his body, and even if he withers and dries up until he is broken into pieces—
Or even if he has a hundred or a thousand [wives], he does not ruin his virtue to nourish his own person. Thus, the discernment of formations protects virtue.
By the phrase "one who frequents empty huts," however, the cultivation, increase, and constant practice of both these qualities are shown.

Thus the Blessed One said this because there is nothing else that must be done by one who desires these four qualities—“to be dear to my fellow celibates, pleasing to them, respected by them, and esteemed by them”—other than simply being endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).
For it is one such as this who becomes dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by his fellow celibates. And so it has been said:
“One who is endowed with virtue and vision, established in the Dhamma, speaking truth, and performing his own duty—that person the world holds dear.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should desire: “May I be dear and pleasing to my fellow celibates, and held in high esteem...”
And having stated, "He should also cultivate [these]... thus he becomes one who fulfills the precepts alone... [and so on]...

in empty huts," the Blessed One now said, "Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should desire to be a recipient of gains," and so forth. For even by one who aspires for the acquisition of requisites and the like, this alone is to be done and nothing else; therefore, he spoke these words. And herein, the Blessed One did not prescribe the fulfillment of virtue and the rest for the sake of gain.
It should be understood that he speaks. For the Blessed One, having ceased talk for the sake of seeking food, does not utter speech employed for such purposes;
thus he exhorts his disciples. How then could he speak of fulfilling virtue and the other perfections for the sake of gain?
However, this was said with reference to the inclinations of individuals. For there might be those whose inclination would be: "If we were not to be distressed by the four requisites..."
"May we be able to fulfill virtue and so forth"—it was with reference to their underlying inclination that the Blessed One spoke thus.
Furthermore, this is the flavor and benefit of virtue, namely, these four requisites.

For indeed, wise people take out what has been stored in granaries and the like, and without giving it even to their children or using it themselves, they give it to those possessed of virtue; such is the [benefit] of virtue.
This was said for the purpose of showing the assembly of those who possess flavor (sarasānisaṃsa).

In the third instance, *yesāhaṃ* means "of whom I am. *Tesaṃ te kārā* means "those services performed by them"—that is, those services consisting of the giving of requisites (*paccaya*) performed toward me by those gods or humans. For even the gods give requisites to those endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), and not only [humans].
It was humans themselves, just as Sakka [did] for the Venerable Mahākassapa. "Great fruit" and "great benefit"—these two are identical in meaning;
there is only a difference in expression. Or, they are called "great fruit" because they yield great worldly happiness.

They are called "great benefit" because they serve as conditions for great supramundane happiness. For even a ladleful of alms-food, when given to one endowed with virtues such as moral discipline, [yields great results].

Even a leaf-hut built on ground worth only five *ratanas* and given as a gift protects one from the miserable states and the abyss for many thousands of eons, and in the end, it becomes a condition for the deathless element of *parinibbāna*.
In this regard, there are illustrative cases such as, "I gave milk-rice," and so forth; indeed, the entire *Petavatthu* and *Vimānavatthu* serve as proof. Therefore, by those who give requisites...
This shows that even one who desires the great fruitfulness of deeds performed for oneself must likewise be endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

In the fourth section: "relatives" (*ñāti*) refers to those on the side of one’s mother-in-law and father-in-law; "blood relations" (*sālohita*) refers to those connected by blood, such as paternal uncles, grandfathers, and so forth;

"departed ones" (*petā*) are those who have gone to the state of the departed; "the deceased" (*kālaṅkata*) are those who have died. "Their" (*tesaṃ taṃ*) refers to their state of having a mind of confidence toward me.
Or it is the recollection with a confident mind. For if a monk’s deceased father or mother,
having become confident in mind, recollects that monk thinking, "Our relative was an elder, virtuous, and of beautiful character," then for him,
both that confidence of mind and even that mere recollection becomes of great fruit and great benefit.
It is indeed capable of warding off miserable rebirths for many hundreds of thousands of eons and of leading one ultimately to the Deathless.

For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—to those bhikkhus, I say, bhikkhus, [this is] the vision..."
“I say it is of great benefit. I say, bhikkhus, that hearing [the Dhamma], recollecting [it], following after [them], approaching [them], and attending upon those bhikkhus is of great benefit.

Thus, he shows that even one who desires the great fruit of the mental serenity and recollection toward their kinsmen and blood relations must themselves be endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).
66. On the fifth occasion, may I be one who endures discontent and delight—that is, one who endures, overcomes, and masters both discontent and delight.
And herein, "discontent" (arati) refers to weariness with regard to higher wholesome states and secluded dwellings; "delight" (rati) refers to delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"May discontent not overcome me" means that discontent shall not master or overwhelm me.
One should not overwhelm [them]. "Arisen" means born, produced. For one endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (sīla) endures both aversion and attraction;
having crushed them, he stands firm. Therefore, this shows that even by one who desires such a self, one must indeed be endowed with virtues such as moral discipline.
In the sixth section, "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to both mental terror and the object [of that fear], while "the terrifying" (*bherava*) refers only to the object.

The remainder is exactly as explained in the fifth section. For one endowed with virtues such as morality overcomes, overwhelms, and stands firm having crushed fear and terror, just like the Elder Mahā Datta, who dwelt at Ariyakoṭiya.
It is said that as the Elder was traveling along the road, he saw a certain beautiful forest grove and thought, "I shall perform my ascetic duties right here today before departing.
Descending from the path, he spread out his outer robe at the foot of a tree, sat down cross-legged, and took his seat.
Due to the power of the Elder’s virtue, the children of the tree-deity were unable to maintain their own natural forms.
Being unable [to move him], they raised a great outcry. The deity also shook the tree, but the Elder sat there motionless.
That deity emitted smoke and then flames, yet she was not able to move the Elder; thereupon, she approached in the guise of a lay follower, paid homage, and stood before him.
When asked, "Who is this? she replied, "Venerable sir, I am the deity dwelling in this tree."
“You have caused these transformations,” [the king said]. “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. When asked, “Why? he said:
“Venerable sir, because of the power of your virtue, the children were unable to maintain their own natural forms and cried out in distress;
therefore, I did this in order to frighten you away. The Elder said: “In that case, venerable sir, why do you not dwell here? Is it not comfortable for me?”
"Previously you did not speak at all; but now, do not say anything. I am ashamed because of the words that Ariyakoṭiya Mahādatto has gone away out of fear of non-human beings.
Therefore, I shall dwell right here, but you may dwell wherever you like from this day forward.
Thus, one endowed with virtues such as moral discipline becomes a conqueror of fear and terror. Therefore, for those of such a nature—
This shows that even one who desires [the goal] must be endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).
In the seventh section, regarding the term *ābhicetasikānaṃ*: "abhiceto" refers to an excellent, purified mind, or to "higher mind" (*adhicitta*);
those things born in the "abhiceto" are *ābhicetasikāni*, or they are *ābhicetasikāni* because they are dependent upon the "abhiceto."
"Of those dwelling in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ*) means: of those dwelling in happiness in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamme*).

"Present life" (*diṭṭhadhammo*) refers to one's own directly perceived personal existence; the meaning is "of those who have become dwellers in happiness therein. This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhānas.
For when meditators have entered into them and are seated, they experience in this very personal existence the undefiled happiness of renunciation.
They find [this], therefore they are called "abidings in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
"One who obtains at will" (*nikāmalābhī*) means one who obtains according to his own desire; it is said that he is capable of entering attainment at whatever moment he so desires.
"One who obtains without difficulty" (*akicchalābhī*) means he is capable of entering attainment by simply suppressing opposing states with ease.
"An obtainer without difficulty" means one who obtains what is not difficult—that is to say, one capable of emerging at the very moment of his own choosing.
For some are indeed obtainers [of jhāna], yet they are unable to attain it at whatever moment they desire.
Some are able to attain it in that way, but they suppress the obstructive factors only with difficulty. Another...
He enters [the attainment] in such a way that he suppresses obstructive states with ease, yet he is unable to emerge at the predetermined limit exactly as if using a water-clock.
Furthermore, whoever desires this threefold perfection must also be one who fulfills his duties regarding the precepts alone.
Thus, although the opportunity for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) has arrived since the jhānas that serve as their basis have been explained, the Blessed One does not yet take them up; rather,
because the benefit of the virtues (*sīla*) is not limited solely to the jhānas that serve as the basis for the higher knowledges and to the higher knowledges themselves,
but extends further to the four formless jhānas (*āruppa-jhāna*) and the three lower noble paths (*ariya-magga*), he therefore includes all of these.
In order to show this, he said: "If one should desire... those that are peaceful," and so forth.
Therein, "peaceful" means peaceful both by way of the peace of its factors and the peace of its object.

"Liberations" (vimokkha) means because they are liberated from opposing states and because they are resolutely intent upon their objects. "Having transcended forms" means having transcended the meditative absorptions (jhāna) of the form realm.
The syntactical connection is: "those liberations which, having transcended forms, are peaceful. For otherwise, it would not be understood what one does after "having transcended forms.
They are called "formless" (ārūppa) because they are devoid of form both in terms of their object and their result.
"Having touched with the body" means having touched—that is, having reached and attained—by means of the mental body (nāmakāya). The rest is as already stated.
This is what is meant: “Even that bhikkhu who desires to dwell having touched these liberations must likewise be one who fulfills his virtue.

In the ninth section, “of the three fetters” refers to the three bonds consisting of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
For these fetter them—namely, the aggregates, destinies, and states of existence—to the aggregates, destinies, and states of existence.
Or, action [is called a fetter] because of its fruit; therefore they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*), meaning "bonds.

"By the complete destruction" means by way of total exhaustion. "Stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) means one who has entered the stream. "Stream" (*sota*) is a designation for the Path. "Stream-enterer" refers to the person who possesses that [stream].
As it was said: "This, Sāriputta, is called 'the stream, the stream. Which indeed..."
"Sāriputta, is it the stream? "Indeed it is, Bhante; it is this very Noble Eightfold Path. That is to say: right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.
"Sāriputta, one is called a 'stream-enterer,' a 'stream-enterer. But who, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?
"Bhante, whoever is endowed with this Eightfold Path, he is called a stream-enterer."
“The stream-enterer is this venerable one of such a name and such a clan. Here, however, the name of the fruit is given by means of the path;
therefore, the one established in the fruit should be understood as a “stream-enterer. Regarding the term *avinipātadhammo*: that which causes one to fall away is a “fall” (*vinipāta*);
one whose nature is not to have such a fall is “one whose nature is not to fall” (*avinipātadhammo*). This means it is said that he is not of a nature to fall into the states of misery (*apāya*).

Why? Because those states leading to the woeful states have been abandoned. He is "one whose ultimate resort is enlightenment" (*sambodhiparāyaṇa*) because his final destination and goal is enlightenment;
the meaning is that he will certainly reach the three higher paths. Why? Because he has already attained the first path.
"In the precepts alone" means that even one who desires to become such as this must fulfill the precepts alone.
Although the three fetters were already completely destroyed by the first path at the tenth stage, they are mentioned here for the purpose of praising the once-returning path.
"By the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion" means by their state of being attenuated, or by the act of making them attenuated.
In this context, attenuation should be understood through two reasons: by their infrequency of arising and by the mildness of their obsession.
Furthermore, for a once-returner (sakadāgāmī), defilements do not arise frequently as they do for the common worldling who follows the cycle of existence;
rather, they arise only occasionally and in a sparse manner, like sprouts in a field that has been sparsely sown.
And even when they do arise, they do not arise as they do for the common worldling—crushing, spreading, covering, and creating darkness.
They arise very slowly, becoming thin in form, like a layer of clouds or like the wings of flies.

Regarding this, some elders say: "Although the defilements of a once-returner arise after a long time, they arise thickly, for his sons and daughters are seen. But this is not authoritative; [for] sons and daughters...
For [the fetters] exist even by the mere touching of the limbs and members [of the body].
His attenuation of the defilements is to be understood through two causes alone: through their infrequency of arising and through the weakness of their obsession.
"Sakadāgāmī" means one whose nature is to come back once; that is, having come to this world only once—only a single time.

Having come to the human world by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For even one who, having developed the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmi-magga*) here, attains final nibbāna right here, is not included here.
Nor is one who, having developed the path here, is reborn among the devas and attains final nibbāna right there.
Nor is one who, having developed the path in the world of the devas, [attains final nibbāna] right there. Nor is one who, having developed the path in the world of the devas...

Having developed [the path] here in this very human world, he is reborn and attains parinibbāna. However, one who develops the path here, is reborn in the world of the devas, and after remaining there for the full span of his lifespan, is reborn again right here and attains parinibbāna—this latter type is to be understood as included here.
"He would make an end of suffering" means he would bring about the termination of the suffering of saṃsāra.
"I would act. "In the precepts alone" means that even one who desires to be such [an arahant] is one who fulfills the precepts alone.
In the eleventh section, "of five" is the limit of the number. "Lower-fettering" (*orambhāgiya*): "lower" (*ora*) is said to mean "below";
thus the meaning is "belonging to the lower part," with the intention being "conditions for rebirth in the sense-sphere world (*kāmāvacara-loka*). "Fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the fetters (*bandhana*), these should be understood as being the same as the fetters previously mentioned, together with the fetters of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*byāpāda*).

For one who has not abandoned these, even if they have arisen in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), they will nevertheless be reborn in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) upon the exhaustion of their lifespan; such a person is like a fish that has swallowed a hook attached to a long line.
And he should be understood as being like a caged bird. Furthermore, it should be understood that even the statements previously mentioned here are intended solely for the purpose of praise.
"Spontaneously born" (*opapātiko*) is a term used to exclude the remaining modes of birth.

"One who attains final nibbāna right there" means one who attains final nibbāna in that very Brahmā-world. "One whose nature is not to return from that world" means [not returning] from that Brahmā-world by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Furthermore, it has the nature of non-returning. Regarding the phrase "in the very precepts": even one who desires to be such [an Anāgāmin] is one who fulfills the precepts. 68.
Although the discussion of the fourth path has thus been stated regarding the path of the Non-Returner, the Blessed One did not take that up;

rather, he [taught this] because the benefit of the precepts is not only the superknowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-abhiññā*), but also the five mundane superknowledges (*lokika-pañca-abhiññā*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate those [higher knowledges] as well; because the teaching reaches its conclusion once the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) has been explained;

and because, were that the case, this discourse would be called a "discourse on mere bald higher knowledge" since these qualities have not been mentioned; and in order to demonstrate the fulfillment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*);
and because for one established on the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*), the manifestation of psychic power (*iddhivikuppanā*) succeeds with ease.
Because he has eradicated sensual lust and ill will, which are the hindrances to concentration, the non-returner (anāgāmī) is one who fulfills both virtue and concentration;
therefore, even when demonstrating mundane direct knowledges (lokīyābhiññā) in their proper place, the Teacher spoke thus, beginning with "If he should wish...
manifold," and so forth—this is the connection.

In this context, the commentary on the five mundane higher knowledges (lokīyābhiññā), which appear in the sequence beginning with “the various kinds of supernormal power,” has been set forth together with the method of cultivation in the *Visuddhimagga*.

69. Regarding the sixth higher knowledge, “through the destruction of the taints”: this means through the destruction of all defilements by means of the path of Arahatship. “Taintless” (*anāsava*) means devoid of taints.

Regarding the phrase “liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom” (*cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ*): here, by the word “mind” (*ceto*), it refers specifically to that which is associated with the fruit of Arahatship.
By the terms "concentration" (*samādhi*) and "wisdom" (*paññā*), only the wisdom associated with them is being spoken of.

In this context, concentration should be understood as "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) because it is liberated from greed, and wisdom as "liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) because it is liberated from ignorance. And this was said by the Blessed One:
"For whatever is his concentration, bhikkhus, that is his faculty of concentration; for whatever is his wisdom, bhikkhus..."
That is his faculty of wisdom. Thus, monks, through the fading away of lust comes liberation of mind; through the fading away of ignorance comes liberation by wisdom.
Furthermore, it should be understood here that liberation of mind is the fruit of serenity, while liberation by wisdom is the fruit of insight.
"In this very life" means in this very personal existence. "Having realized for oneself through direct knowledge" means by means of one's own wisdom.

"Having made it manifest" means having known it by one's own direct experience, independent of others. "Having attained, may I dwell" means that having reached and fulfilled it, I should dwell [in it].
"In the very precepts" means that even one who desires to attain liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom after thus shaking off all taints, should be one who fulfills the precepts alone.
Thus the Blessed One, having spoken on the benefits of virtue up to the stage of Arahantship, now spoke this conclusion, condensing all those benefits of virtue, saying:
“Bhikkhus, dwell with virtue perfected… [as before] …having undertaken it; this was said by me with reference to this.
This is its summary meaning: “Bhikkhus, dwell with virtue perfected… [as before] …having undertaken it.”
"Train yourselves in the rules of training"—this which was previously spoken by me, all of this applies to a bhikkhu who is perfected in virtue:
he becomes dear and pleasing to his fellow practitioners of the holy life; he is respected and esteemed; he gains the requisites;

he makes the gift of requisites bear great fruit for those who provide them; he makes the act of recollecting his former kinsmen yield great results; and he is able to endure both the unpleasant and the pleasant.
He is a conqueror of fear and dread; he is a possessor of the fine-material-sphere jhānas and the immaterial-sphere jhānas;

and because he has personally realized through direct knowledge these qualities—the three lower fruits of recluseship, the five mundane superknowledges, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—it was with reference to this that this was said.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, and the [disciples] were uplifted in mind.
Those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The commentary on the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*,
the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
7. Commentary on the Vatthasutta (The Discourse on the Cloth). 70.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Vatthasutta. In this context, "Just as if, monks, there were a cloth" is merely a statement of a simile.
And when the Blessed One makes a comparison, he sometimes first shows the simile and afterwards shows the meaning.
In some instances, it shows the meaning first and the simile afterwards; in others, it shows the meaning by surrounding it with a simile;
and in others, it shows the simile by means of the meaning. For instance:
"Bhikkhus, suppose there were two houses with doors, and a man with sight [stood there]..."
Having first shown the simile from the entire *Devadūta-sutta* while saying, "Standing in the middle,
he would see," he then spoke to show the meaning. Furthermore, by way of the passage beginning, "He goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains,
as if through space," he first showed the entire meaning of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and subsequently [presented] the simile.

He spoke while demonstrating [the meaning] by means of the simile: “Just as if, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood,” and so forth; in this very manner, he spoke while demonstrating the entire *Cūḷasāropama-sutta* by surrounding the meaning with similes. Then, he spoke by means of the passage beginning:
“But here, monks, some sons of good family master the Dhamma—the discourses... pe... just as if, monks, a man needing a water-snake.”
By this method, [the Blessed One] spoke thus, showing how even the entire *Alagaddasutta*, the *Mahāsāropamasutta*, and other such suttas present the meaning by surrounding it with a simile.
Here, however, he first shows the simile and afterwards shows the meaning. But why did the Blessed One do so?
Why does he show [the simile]? Either through the inclination of the individual (*puggalajjhāsayena*) or through the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsena*).
For those individuals who easily penetrate the meaning being explained after first seeing a simile, he shows the simile first.
This method applies everywhere. And it is because of the thorough penetration of that element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) that one attains the elegance of the teaching.
It has been well-penetrated by him. Therefore, this Lord of Dhamma, King of Dhamma, who has attained the elegance of teaching, teaches the Dhamma in whatever way he desires;
thus it should be understood that he demonstrates it either through the inclination of the individual or through the elegance of his teaching.
In this context, "cloth" refers to cloth that is naturally pure. "Soiled" means defiled by adventitious impurities such as dust and dirt;
"stained" means soiled by being taken hold of by stains such as sweat and grime.
Regarding the phrase "in various dyes," here "dye" itself is "dyed. "Should apply" means he should bring it near. "If [the cloth] is blue... and so forth.
"Or for the sake of blue, or for the sake of something blue"—this is what is meant. The same applies everywhere.
For when a dyer prepares [dye] for the sake of blue, he prepares blue pigments such as copper-blue (*kaṃsanīla*) or palāsa-blue (*palāsanīla*).
When preparing for the sake of yellow, he prepares yellow pigments resembling the *kaṇikāra* flower. When preparing for the sake of red, he prepares [pigments] resembling the *bandhujīvaka* flower.
"Red-hued" (*lohitakaraṅge*): when applying it for the purpose of madder, it has a pale red hue resembling the *kaṇavīra* flower.
Therefore it is said: "If [the cloth] is blue... [and so on]... if it is madder-colored.
"Its color would be poorly dyed" (*durattavaṇṇamevassa*): its color would indeed be badly dyed. "Its color would be impure" (*aparisuddhavaṇṇamevassa*): even though its color is blue...
It would not be pure even in its remaining colors. For such a cloth, even when placed in a blue jar, does not become deep blue;

nor, even when placed in other jars, does it take on colors such as yellow and so forth; it takes on only the color of a withered blue flower, a *kuraṇḍaka*, a *kaṇikāra*, a *bandhujīvaka*, or a *kaṇavīra* flower.
Why is that? For what reason, for what cause, does that cloth become like this? Or, in regard to that cloth...
"For what reason does the dye turn out to be of such a poor color and impure hue?
Because the very state of defilement of that cloth is the cause here, and nothing else, he said: "Because of the impurity of the cloth, monks."
"Even so indeed" is the application of the simile. "In a defiled mind" means in a mind that is defiled.
But why did the Blessed One make the comparison with a defiled cloth? It is for the purpose of showing the great fruitfulness of effort.
For just as a cloth defiled by adventitious stains, being naturally white, shines forth again when washed; [so too does the mind].
It is pure; there, effort is not fruitless, as it would be with wool from a black sheep born among white ones.
Likewise, the mind is defiled by adventitious defilements. But by nature, it is pure throughout the entire process of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum.
As it is said: "This mind, monks, is luminous, though it is defiled by adventitious defilements..."

"It is defiled by defilements. It should be understood that he used the simile of the soiled cloth to show that effort is fruitful, meaning that when it is being purified, it can be made even more radiant, and thus effort therein is not in vain.
"A bad destination is to be expected" means that with such a mind, a bad destination is to be anticipated; he will surely reach a state of misery.

"Nothing else"—this means that a miserable destination (*duggati*) should be desired [as one's goal], in the sense that it will inevitably come to pass. Furthermore, this so-called "miserable destination" is twofold:

the miserable destination of practice (*paṭipatti-duggati*) and the miserable destination of rebirth (*gati-duggati*). The miserable destination of practice is also twofold: the miserable destination of practice for householders and the miserable destination of practice for those who have gone forth from the household life.
For a householder with a defiled mind kills living beings, takes what is not given, and fulfills all ten courses of unwholesome action;

this is his miserable practice as a householder. Established therein, at the breaking up of the body, he goes to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the sphere of hungry ghosts; this is his miserable destination.
Even one who has gone forth into homelessness in this Dispensation may go on errands and missions with a defiled mind,
practice medicine, strive for the schism of the Saṅgha or the destruction of a shrine, and maintain his livelihood by giving bamboo and other such things;
he fulfills every kind of improper conduct and unsuitable resort— this is his miserable way of practicing the homeless life.
Abiding therein, with the breakup of the body, he goes to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the sphere of hungry ghosts;
he becomes what is called a "monk-ghost" (samaṇayakkha), a "monk-peta.
With his outer robe and other belongings ablaze, his body set on fire, he wanders about uttering cries of distress—this is his miserable destination.

The phrase "Just as if" (*seyyathāpi*) has begun to show the bright fortnight (*sukkapaṅkha*); its meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated regarding the dark fortnight (*kaṇhapaṅkha*).

Furthermore, in this context, "a happy destination" (*sugati*) is twofold: the happy destination of practice (*paṭipatti-sugati*) and the happy destination of rebirth (*gati-sugati*). The happy destination of practice is also twofold:

the happy destination of the practice of a householder (*agāriya-paṭipatti*) and the happy destination of the practice of one who has gone forth (*anagāriya-paṭipatti*). For a householder is one whose mind is purified...
He abstains from taking life and from taking what is not given, and he fulfills all ten courses of wholesome action;
this is his happy practice as a householder. Established therein, at the breaking up of the body, he is reborn among the great humans or among the great gods; this is his happy destination.
One who has gone forth as a homeless wanderer in this Dispensation, with a purified mind, purifies the fourfold morality of complete purity,
undertakes the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), and— having taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to himself among the thirty-eight objects—
dwells in remote lodgings, performs the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, and generates the meditative attainments (jhānasamāpatti), [attains] the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga).
He develops... [and so on] ...he develops the path of non-returning; this is his happy destination in the practice of homelessness.

Established therein, at the breaking up of the body, he is reborn either in the human world among the three great families, or among the six classes of sense-sphere deities, or in the ten Brahma-abodes, or in the five Pure Abodes, or in the four formless realms; this is his happy destination as a rebirth-destination.

71. Having stated that when the mind is thus defiled, an unhappy destination is to be expected, whereas when it is undefiled, a happy destination is to be expected, he now speaks the passage beginning with "And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind?
Covetousness and unrighteous greed... in order to show by which secondary defilements the mind becomes defiled.
In this context, covetousness (*abhijjhā*) is the desire and lust for one’s own belongings, while it is improper greed (*visamalobha*) for the belongings of others.

Alternatively, whether it concerns one’s own belongings or those of another, desire and lust for what is appropriate and fit is covetousness, whereas desire and lust for what is inappropriate and unfit is improper greed.
However, the Elder said: "Why do you make such a distinction? Whether it be appropriate or inappropriate, lust is *visama* (improper), and hatred is *dosa*."
From the statement "delusion is uneven, it is uneven," there is no greed whatsoever that is not uneven;
therefore, greed itself is *abhijjhā* in the sense of coveting, and it is *visama* in the sense of being uneven. These two have the same meaning; only the phrasing differs.
Furthermore, this uneven greed (*abhijjhā-visamalobha*), having arisen, defiles the mind and does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called "a defilement of the mind."
Just as this is so, so too is ill-will (*vyāpāda*) that arises from nine bases of resentment;

anger (*kodha*) arises from ten bases of resentment. Enmity (*upanāha*) is the repeated obsession of the mind. Slander (*makkha*) is the destruction of the good deeds of one who is either a householder or a homeless renunciant.
For instance, even a householder, being poor, might be placed in a high position by someone compassionate toward him, yet by another...
At another time, thinking, "What has she done for me?", he destroys the good work she had performed. Likewise, even one who has gone forth— from the time he was a novice monk—
having been assisted by his teacher or preceptor with the four requisites and through instruction and interrogation,
and having been trained in skill in the methods of Dhamma-talks and the treatises, at a later time [is treated thus] by kings, royal ministers, and others.

When one who is honored and respected, yet acts with a lack of affection toward teachers and preceptors, is told, "This person was supported and raised by us from our very childhood, yet now he has become devoid of affection," he replies, "What have you done for me?
and thereby destroys their good deed; such is his *makkha* (sycophancy/denigration), which destroys the merit of a good deed performed.
Having arisen, it defiles the mind and does not allow it to shine; therefore, it is called "a corruption of the mind.
And just as this [corruption] arises, so too, when it overwhelms even a person of great learning by way of such expressions as, "The destination of even such a learned person is uncertain;
what difference is there between you and me?", it becomes a grasping that seizes upon equality.

*Paḷāsa* is the disparaging of others' honors and so forth; *issā* (envy) is the inability to endure others' success. *Macchariya* (avarice) is the intolerance of one's own prosperity being shared with others.
*Māyā* is deceitful conduct. *Sāṭheyya* (crookedness) arises from a state of *kerāṭika* (hypocrisy).
For a *kerāṭika* is like a "fish of the lair" (*āyatanamaccha*). It is said that the "fish of the lair" is a fish whose tail... [is hidden].
He shows the heads of his companions in order to make them know, "I am like you.
In the same way, a person who acts like a curlew (kerāṭika) approaches whichever Suttantika or Abhidhammika he encounters and says to him: "I am your constant companion;
you are compassionate toward me; I will not let you go. Thus, these [people] think, "This one is respectful..."

‘They will think we have respect for them. This crookedness arising through such a state of scheming, once arisen, defiles the mind and does not allow it to shine forth. Therefore, it is called a "corruption of the mind.
And just as this is so, it likewise acts to make the head stiff—like a leather bag filled with air—and causes one’s conduct to be unsteady and unable to withstand the wind.
Stiffness (thambha). Exertion for further improvement (taduttarikaraṇa-sārambha). This is obtained in two ways: by way of the unwholesome (akusala) and by way of the wholesome (kusala).
Therein, in the case of a householder, it arises from making something twice as good as an ornament or the like seen made by another;
and in the case of one who is not a householder, it arises from the conceit of making something twice or even more than twice as much as another has mastered or spoken.
When it arises as unwholesome: in the case of a householder, when seeing another giving even a single *salākabhatta* (ticket-meal) and wishing to give two or three oneself;

and in the case of one who has gone forth (*anagāriya*), when another has taken only one *nikāya* (section of the scriptures), not out of pride but simply upon seeing that, wishing to overcome one's own laziness and take up two *nikāyas* oneself.
When it arises, it is wholesome; however, in this context, the unwholesome is intended.
For once arisen, this [state] defiles the mind and does not allow it to shine forth. Therefore, it is called "a defilement of the mind.
And just as this [defilement], so too pride—which occurs by way of the mind's inflation based on birth and so forth—and that which occurs by way of excessive inflation...
Excessive conceit (*atimāna*) is intoxication (*mada*), which is a mode of grasping through pride.

Negligence (*pamāda*), arising by way of the mind’s release toward the strands of sensual pleasure, once arisen, defiles the mind and does not allow it to become luminous. Therefore, it is called "a defilement of the mind.
But why does the Blessed One, when showing these defilements, show them beginning with greed (*lobha*)? Because that is their first appearance.
For among all beings, wherever they may have been reborn—even including those in the Pure Abodes—greed arises first of all by way of attachment to existence;
thereafter, depending on their respective appropriate conditions, the others arise as far as possible.
Furthermore, these sixteen are not the only defilements of the mind; rather, it should be understood that by this method, all defilements whatsoever are included.
72. Having thus far shown defilement (*saṃkilesa*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "But that, monks," in order to show purification (*vodāna*).

Therein, "having understood thus" means having known in this way. "He abandons" means he abandons by means of the noble path through the mode of abandonment as total eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
In this regard, abandonment should be understood in two ways: according to the sequence of defilements and according to the sequence of the paths. According to the sequence of defilements...
To that extent, these six defilements—covetousness, improper greed, stubbornness, hostility, conceit, arrogance, and intoxication—are abandoned by the path of Arhatship.
The four defilements—ill will, anger, resentment, and negligence—are abandoned by the path of Non-returning.
The six defilements—slander, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, and fraud—are abandoned by the path of Stream-entry.

According to the sequence of the paths, however, by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), these six are abandoned: hypocrisy (*makkha*), spite (*palāsa*), envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), deceitfulness (*māyā*), and craftiness (*sāṭheyya*).

By the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*), these four are abandoned: ill-will (*byāpāda*), anger (*kodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), and negligence (*pamāda*). By the path of arahantship (*arahatta-magga*), these six are abandoned:
covetousness and improper greed (*abhijjhā-visamalobha*), obduracy (*thambha*), contentiousness (*sārambha*), conceit (*māna*), arrogance (*atimāna*), and vanity (*mada*).

In this context, however, it should be understood that whether these defilements are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry or by the remaining paths, the statement beginning with "he abandons covetousness and improper greed, the corruption of the mind," is spoken specifically with reference to their abandonment by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).
This is the traditional lineage of interpretation regarding the origin [of these defilements] here; and they belong specifically to the fourth path above.

It is appropriate because it has been demonstrated; for by means of the third path, there is the abandoning of the remaining unwholesome greed (*visama-lobha*) and so forth that were not yet abandoned, while the rest are abandoned by this very [path].

Even those [defilements] which are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) become thoroughly abandoned only by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*), because the minds that give rise to them have not yet been abandoned. However, some maintain that here there is abandonment by the first path as well.
They explain it, yet that does not cohere with what precedes and follows. Some say there is also abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*); that is merely their own wishful thinking. 73.
Regarding the phrase "But when, monks," the word *yataḥ* means "at which time. "Is abandoned" is said specifically with reference to the moment of the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*).
74. "He [is endowed] with verified confidence in the Buddha"—this refers back to: "But when, monks, covetousness and improper greed are abandoned..."
“He exists; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha. Thus it should be applied to each individual phrase.

For when supramundane confidence has arisen for this bhikkhu by means of the path of non-returning, then at a later time, as he recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the qualities of the Dhamma, and the qualities of the Saṅgha, mundane [confidence] arises in him; all of that is his.
Demonstrating the faith that is a mixture of mundane and supramundane, the Blessed One said, “With verified faith in the Buddha,” and so forth.
Therein, “with verified faith” means with an unshakable and unswerving faith arising from knowing the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha as they truly are.
Now, the method by which that verified faith arose for that bhikkhu as he was recollecting—[that method is as follows:]...
He displayed the three bases of recollection in detail by way of the formula beginning, "Such indeed is the Blessed One," and so forth.
A detailed commentary on their meaning has been set forth in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga* within the discourse on recollection (*anussati-kathā*).
75. Having thus shown his mundane and supramundane confidence mixed together, he now [shows] the abandoning of defilements and his possession of verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
Showing the benefits, such as joy, that arise for one who reflects [on his attainment], he said, "But according to his extent," and so forth.

For when a non-returner reflects on his own abandonment of defilements— just like a king living in a great city who, having quelled a rebellion of bandits in the borderlands, reflects, "These and these defilements of mine have been abandoned"— [he experiences joy].
Strong joy arises. Showing this, the Blessed One said, “But according to the extent of his [attainment],” and so forth.

The meaning of this is: for that non-returner bhikkhu who is thus endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha … [and so on] … in the Dhamma … [and so on] … in the Saṅgha … [and so on] … “the unsurpassed field of merit for the world,” according to the extent of his [attainment], what has been abandoned—
It is relinquished; it is simply cast off according to its respective category (*odhi*). That various class of defilements has been vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished.
"According to its respective category" means there are two categories: the category of defilements (*kilesa-odhi*) and the category of paths (*magga-odhi*).
Therein, even with respect to the category of defilements, those defilements which are to be destroyed by a particular path are unmixed with those to be destroyed by other paths.

Having offered them, those defilements are abandoned by means of their respective floods (*ogha*). Likewise, by way of the paths, whatever defilements are to be abandoned by a particular path, they are abandoned by that very path.
Thus, each class of defilement is simply cast off and relinquished by means of its own respective flood.
Having reflected upon this and attained joy, he further [reflects] with "unshakable confidence in the Buddha":
The connection is: "I am possessed [of this]—thus one gains the knowledge of the meaning (*atthaveda*).
There is also the reading *yatodhī kho pi*. According to that, the meaning is as follows: when for that bhikkhu there has been a relinquishing and a renouncing;
therein, *yata* is a word expressing cause, meaning "since" (*yasmā*). *Odhī* means "below."
Three paths are called "odhis. Why? Because they abandon the defilements that are to be abandoned by the higher paths after having delimited them and divided them into portions;
therefore, they are called "odhis. However, the path of arahantship abandons the defilements without leaving anything remaining;
therefore, it is called "anodhi. And for this bhikkhu, [the defilements] have been abandoned by means of the three lower paths.
Therefore it was said: “But from the time that his limit (odhi) has been abandoned. In this context, *kho pana* is merely a particle.

This, however, is the summarized meaning: because his limit has been abandoned and relinquished, therefore, having reflected upon that and attained a state of joy, he further thereafter thinks, “I am endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha.”
"Those who have heard the Dhamma" (*atthavada*) should be understood according to the text.
In this context, "cast out" (*catta*) is said by way of relinquishing one's own being; "vomited up" (*vanta*) is by way of showing the state of not taking it back again;
"freed" (*mutta*) is by way of liberation from continuity; and "abandoned" (*pahina*) is by way of showing that even what has been freed does not remain anywhere.
"Relinquished" (*paṭinissaṭṭha*) means: it is said by way of showing the relinquishing of what was previously taken up; or by way of showing the state of having been relinquished facing [the truth];
or by way of showing the state of having been relinquished after having overcome [defilements] through the power of meditation.
"He gains knowledge of the meaning, he gains knowledge of the Dhamma": here, this refers specifically to unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*) in the Buddha and the others.
It is "meaning" (*attha*) because it is to be sought after; that is to say, it is what should be approached. It is "Dhamma" because it supports;
that is to say, it prevents one from falling into ruin. "Veda" refers to a text, knowledge, or joy. For in such passages as "one who has gone beyond the three Vedas," the text is called "veda.
[As for the verse: "O Brahmin, you should recognize the one who is a master of Veda (*vedagu*), who possesses nothing in the realm of sense-desires..."

In passages such as "unattached," it refers to knowledge (*ñāṇa*). In passages such as "those who, having experienced joy, wander about in the world," it refers to mental joy (*somanassa*). Here, however, both mental joy and the knowledge associated with mental joy are intended;

therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "He gains the experience of the meaning and he gains the experience of the Dhamma" means that he gains the mental joy which has confirmed confidence (*aveccappasāda*) as its object, and the knowledge consisting of mental joy.
Alternatively, "knowledge of the meaning" (*atthaveda*) refers to the aforementioned kind of knowledge that arises in one who reviews verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*).

"Knowledge of the Dhamma" (*dhammaveda*) refers to the aforementioned kind of knowledge that arises in one who reviews the specific abandonment of defilements, which is the cause of verified confidence.
This is how the meaning here should be understood; for it has been said: "Knowledge regarding the cause... (*Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ*).
“Analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā) is the knowledge of cause and fruit; analytical knowledge of the meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) is the knowledge of the result.

“Gladdening connected with the Dhamma” means the gladdening that arises in one who reviews that very meaning and Dhamma as being the benefit of the meaning and the Dhamma, and as being knowledge itself.
For that [gladdening] is connected with the Dhamma, which occurs in the mode of reviewing and has the characteristic of blamelessness.
It is said: "In one who is gladdened, rapture arises. By this means, through that joy (*pāmojja*), a non-material rapture (*nirāmisā pīti*) arises in one who is gladdened.
"With a rapturous mind" means with a mind delighted by that rapture. "The body becomes tranquil" means the body also becomes tranquil, with its agitation subsided.
"One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness" means that for one whose bodily agitation has thus subsided, there is mental happiness (*cetasikaṃ sukhaṃ*).
He experiences [it]. "The mind becomes concentrated" means that the mind is correctly placed; it remains unmoving as if fixed.

76. Having thus shown the benefits such as joy arising for one who reviews his own abandonment of defilements while endowed with verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*), he now [explains] the reviewing of that [confidence] by way of the section beginning, "And according to my limit... (*yathodhi kho pana me*).
Having manifested the mode of occurrence, he spoke the passage beginning with "But he, monks," in order to show the fruit that indicates the power of that very path of non-returning.
Therein, "of such virtue" (evaṃsīlo) shows his aggregate of virtue associated with the path of non-returning. "Of such nature" (evaṃdhammo)...
"One of such wisdom" indicates the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom associated with that [wisdom].

"Of fine rice" refers to various kinds, such as red rice, fragrant rice, and so forth. "Alms-food" means boiled rice. "With the black grains removed" means from which the black grains have been eliminated.
"That does not become an obstacle for him" means that for a bhikkhu of such a kind, that aforementioned type of alms-food consumption [does not hinder his practice].
It does not act as an obstacle to the path or its fruit; for what obstacle could that [attainment] pose to one who has already acquired those qualities?

Furthermore, even for one who has not yet attained the fourth path and its fruit and begins insight (vipassanā) for their sake, that [attainment] does not become an obstacle; it is simply incapable of acting as an obstacle. Why?
Because his mind has been purified by the path comprised of the aforementioned virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
And since this is precisely the reason here, he spoke the words beginning with "just as if" (seyyathāpi) in order to show an appropriate simile.
In that context, *accham* means clear; *parisuddham* means pure due to the removal of impurities; *pariyodātam* means radiant because of its luminosity.
“Ukkāmukha” means the mouth of a crucible belonging to goldsmiths. For here, the crucible of goldsmiths is called an “ukkā,” whereas elsewhere even lamps and such are so called.
Indeed, in the passage where it says “while the *ukkās* are being held,” it is the lamp that is called an “ukkā.
In the passages where it says “one should prepare the *ukkā*,” or “having prepared the *ukkā*, one should heat the mouth of the crucible (*ukkāmukha*),” it refers to a pan of coals.
In the passage, “Just as the forge-fire of smiths glows within but not without,” it refers to the smith’s bellows.
In the passage, “Such will be the ripening of this omen of a falling meteor,” the force of the wind is called a “meteor.
But in this context, and in other similar instances such as, “Having taken gold with tongs, he throws it into the mouth of the furnace,” [it refers to the furnace].
The crucible of goldsmiths should be understood as the "fire.

Herein, this is the application of the simile: just like a soiled cloth or like impure gold, the mind of this bhikkhu during his time as an ordinary person (puthujjana) should be seen as being accompanied by the stains of sensual lust and other defilements. [The water] is clear...

The path of non-returning is like [the purification of] water and like the mouth of a furnace. Just as the purity of the gold in the crucibles comes about through that water and the mouth of the furnace,
so too does the purity of mind of that bhikkhu come about through the path of non-returning,
which comprises the aforementioned virtue, dharma, and wisdom.

77. Thus, the teaching has come down according to the sequence of connection (*yathānusandhi*) by means of the mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*mettāsahagata*). For there are three kinds of connections:

the connection of inquiry (*pucchānusandhi*), the connection of intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*), and the connection of sequence (*yathānusandhi*). In this regard, when this had been said, a certain monk said this to the Blessed One:
“Could it be, Bhante, that there might be external anxiety (*paritassanā*) where there is nothing? “It could be.”
“‘Monks,’ said the Blessed One. In this way, the connection between questions should be understood by means of the suttas that provide answers to those who ask.

Furthermore, the connection based on intention should be understood by means of a sutta spoken after knowing the underlying disposition of others, such as when [the Buddha] spoke thus: “It might occur to you, brahmin, ‘Perhaps even today the ascetic Gotama is not free from lust.’”

However, regarding the connection (*anusandhi*) between sections: one should understand it according to those suttas where the subsequent teaching occurs—either by way of a quality corresponding to the teaching that arose at the beginning, or by way of its opposite.
For example, in the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, the teaching arose below with virtue (*sīla*), while above it are the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
[The discourse] has arrived. In the *Kakacūpama-sutta*, having arisen from below with the theme of intolerance, the teaching on the simile of the saw arrives above.
In the *Alagaddūpama-sutta*, having arisen below by way of illustrating views, the exposition of the threefold turnings of emptiness arrives above.
In the *Cūḷa-assapura-sutta*, having arisen below by way of illustrating the defilements, the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) arrive above. In the *Kosambiya-sutta*, below...
In the *Bhaṇḍanasutta*, it begins with quarreling, and the qualities of endearment (*sāraṇīyadhamma*) follow later.

In this *Vatthasutta* as well, it begins below with the illumination of the defilements (*kilesa*), and the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) follow later. Therefore it is said: "The teaching proceeds according to the sequence of connection.
Furthermore, both the word-by-word commentary and the method of cultivation regarding the divine abodes have been explained in their entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*.

78. Thus, having shown the development of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) for that non-returner— which serves as the antidote to the defilements such as covetousness and which has gained its footing through the complete abandonment of sensual lust and ill-will, thereby destroying all adversaries—
the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with “So atthi idam” in order to show the insight (vipassanā) leading to Arahantship and the attainment of Arahantship itself.
The meaning of this is as follows: that non-returner, having thus developed the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), emerges from these divine abidings from any one of them;

then, by way of name, he defines those very phenomena of the divine abidings—the heart-base as their physical support and the primary elements as the supports for that base—according to the method of defining the phenomena of primary elements and derived matter by way of form, thinking: "This exists."

He understands; to this extent, the definition of the truth of suffering has been accomplished by him. Then, penetrating the origin of that suffering, he understands: "There is the inferior"; to this extent, the definition of the truth of the origin has been accomplished by him.
Then, investigating the means for its abandonment, he understands: "There is the sublime"; to this extent, the definition of the truth of the path [has been accomplished by him].
It has been said. Then, searching for the state to be attained by that path, he understands: "There is an escape beyond this attainment consisting of perception.
The intended meaning is that he understands: "There is Nibbāna, an escape beyond this attainment of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) which I have reached.
Up to this point, there is the definition of the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca).

"It has been said. For one who knows thus and sees thus—meaning for one who knows the four truths in these four ways through the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) and sees thus through the wisdom of the path (magga-paññā)—the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), just as described in the section on fear and terror...
[and so on] ...until "he understands: 'This is the end of being' (itthattāya)."
Having thus brought the teaching down to the stage of arahantship, the Blessed One now perceived that there was a brahmin in that assembly who maintained that purification comes through bathing;
and knowing that upon hearing this praise of purification through bathing he would go forth and attain arahantship, the Blessed One spoke for the purpose of exhorting him:
"Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu is called one who has bathed."
With the phrase “by means of bathing within,” he states this separate connection. Therein, “by means of bathing within” refers to the internal bathing that arises from the removal of defilements.
79. Regarding “Sundarikabhāradvāja”:
that brahmin was named Bhāradvāja after his own clan, and [he was called] Sundarika after...
However, he held the view that for one who bathes in the river, there is the abandonment of evil;
therefore, he was called "Sundarika Bhāradvāja. Having heard those words of the Blessed One, he thought:
"We praise purification by bathing, and the ascetic Gotama praises it in exactly the same way; now he has the same inclination as we do. Then [he approached] the Blessed One at the Bāhuka...
Having gone to the river and washed away that evil there, he spoke as if he had returned, saying:
"Does the venerable Gotama go to the Bāhukā River to bathe? Without saying either "I am going" or "I am not going," the Blessed One, desiring to uproot the brahmin's wrong view, said:
"What, brahmin, is the use of the Bāhukā River?"
"What will the Bāhukā River do? he said. The meaning of this is: "What purpose is served by the Bāhukā? What will she do?
She is incapable of serving anyone's purpose; why then should I go there?

Then the brahmin, praising her, said, "She is esteemed as rough," and so forth. In that context, "esteemed as rough" (*lokhasammatā*) means she is recognized for her state of being coarse (*lūkhabhāva*).
"It bestows a state of dryness, a state of refinement, and a state of purity"—this is what is meant by "thus esteemed.
There is also a reading, *lokasammatā*; its meaning is: "esteemed as one who leads to the supreme world. "Esteemed as merit" means esteemed as merit (*puñña*).
"He causes to flow forth" means he causes to go, he purifies. "He addressed with verses" means he spoke with verses. Verses.
And when these [verses] are spoken, they are spoken either solely for the purpose of illustrating that meaning for those who delight in verses, or for the purpose of illustrating a specific meaning.
Here, however, it should be understood that these are spoken for the purpose of illustrating both meanings.
For the word *bāhuka* itself is the indicator of the primary meaning here, while the remaining words are indicators of the specific meaning. Just as...
Indeed, Bāhuka, it is in this way that people go to the Adhikakka and other such places to wash away their evil through bathing.
Among them, those who live near these sites bathe three times a day;
those who live further away bathe twice, once, once every day, and so on, up to once a year, according to their distance. Furthermore, those who...
They were unable to go there by any means; therefore, they had water brought from there even in jars and bathed.
All of this was useless; thus, in order to illustrate this specific point, he said, "and also the Adhikakka, etc.
Therein, "Adhikakka" refers to a certain bathing place that received its conventional name because of its bathing facilities. It is also called "Gayā."
A bathing place (tittha) is defined as having the shape of a circular pool.
"Payāga" is also a specific bathing place on the Ganges, located at the spot facing the staircase of King Mahāpanāda’s palace that was submerged in the river;
furthermore, there are these four rivers: the Bāhukā, Sundarikā, Sarassatī, and Bāhumatī. "Foolish" means lacking wisdom. "Leaping in" means entering [the water].
"It does not become pure" means it does not attain purification from the defilements (*kilesa*); it merely washes away dust and dirt.
"What will Sundarikā do?"—what will Sundarikā accomplish in the cleansing of the defilements? The intention is that she is not capable of doing anything at all.
This same method applies to the Payāga and Bāhuka rivers. When these three phrases have been stated, the others as well...

The four characteristics are stated precisely by way of nutriment; therefore, it should be understood that just as the Sundarikā, Payāgā, and Bāhukā rivers do nothing [to purify], so too are the Adhikakka and others.

"Pāpakamminam" means one who is joined with evil deeds of enmity and transgression, or one joined with base deeds;

“Of one who is pure” means of one who is free from defilement. “Always Phaggu” means that for him it is always the Phagguṇī constellation.
It is said that this brahmin held the view: “Whoever bathes on the day of Uttaraphagguṇī in the month of Phagguṇa purifies the evil committed during the entire year.
Therefore, the Blessed One, refuting that view, said: “For one who is indeed always pure...”
"Phaggu": For one free from defilements, the Phaggunī constellation is always auspicious; how could another be purified?
"Uposatha is always" means that for one who is pure, even if they do not formally undertake the factors of the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and other such days, it is always Uposatha.
"Of the pure one with clean deeds" means of one who is pure by virtue of being free from defilements and who possesses clean bodily actions and so forth.
For one who is thus endowed, the undertaking of vows associated with the wholesome is always successfully accomplished; that is, for such a person, the observance of vows is constantly fulfilled.
"Bathe right here" means: bathe right here in this very teaching of mine. What is meant?
"If you desire the washing away of the internal stains of the defilements, then right here in my teaching, with the water of the Eightfold Path..."
“Bathe; for elsewhere this does not exist.
