Regarding the passage beginning with "When it was said thus," etc., it is self-evident because it was spoken in the context of fear and terror (*bhayabherava*).

However, in the passages beginning with "Alone and secluded," one is "alone" through physical seclusion; "secluded" through mental seclusion; and "heedful" by not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Ardent" means by means of ardor, which is defined as physical and mental energy. "Resolute" means through lack of regard for both body and life.
"Dwelling" means abiding in one of the various postures. "Before long" refers to the period following his going forth.
"Noble sons" (kulaputta) are of two kinds: noble sons by birth and noble sons by conduct; this one, however, is a noble son in both respects.

"From home" means from a house. "Household life" (*agāriya*) is that which is beneficial to a house; it refers to the work of farming, cattle-tending, and so forth, for the sake of maintaining a family.
"Homeless life" (*anagāriya*) is that in which there is no household life; this is a designation for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).

"They go forth" means they approach or draw near. "That unsurpassed" means that which is unsurpassed. "The consummation of the holy life" (*brahmacariyapariyosāna*) refers to the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).
The "conclusion" refers to the fruit of arhatship; for it is for that purpose that sons of noble family go forth.

"In this very life" means in that very same personal existence. "Having realized by direct knowledge oneself" means having made it manifest through one's own wisdom, that is, having made it independent of others.
"Having attained and dwelt therein" means having reached and fully accomplished it.
"He dwelt" means: while dwelling thus, he realized, "Birth is exhausted... [as before]... he has directly known. By this, he shows the stage of his reviewing.
But what birth was exhausted for him, and how did he directly know it? It is said:

although this was already stated in the section on fear and terror, it is nevertheless repeated here in brief for the purpose of showing the method of application according to the first person (the practitioner).
We say: its past birth has not yet been exhausted, because it was already exhausted previously; its future birth is not [exhausted], because there is no effort directed toward that;

and its present birth is not [exhausted], because it still exists. However, as for the birth that would arise in the various one-, four-, or five-aggregate existences—classified as the various one-, four-, or five-aggregates—that, by virtue of the path having been cultivated, enters the state of non-arising.

"Exhausted": having reviewed through the cultivation of the path those defilements that have been abandoned, he knows—while recognizing that even though karma still exists in the absence of defilements, it will not lead to rebirth in the future.
"Lived" (*vusita*) means lived, fully lived; the meaning is that it has been performed, practiced, and brought to completion. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*)...

"The holy life has been lived. This means that regarding the four truths, the sixteenfold task—consisting of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing by means of the four paths—has been brought to completion.

"There is nothing further of this nature" means that now there is no further development of the path for the sake of such a state of being, nor for the sake of the sixteenfold task, nor for the destruction of the defilements. Alternatively, "of this nature" (*itthattāya*)...
"In this state," he realized, "there is no further continuity of aggregates beyond this present continuity of aggregates of such a kind.
These five aggregates, however, remain as something fully understood, like a tree whose roots have been cut.
"A certain one" means one person. "An arahant" means that among the arahants—the disciples of the Blessed One—he became an arahant within their ranks.
The commentary on the *Vatthasutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*, is completed. 8.
The commentary on the *Sallekhasutta*.
81. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ*: thus was it heard by me; this is the Sallekha Sutta. Therein, Mahācunda is the name of that elder.
At the time of the evening meal (*sāyanhasamayaṃ*) means at the hour of evening. "Emerging from seclusion" (*paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito*):

here, "seclusion" (*paṭisallānaṃ*) refers to withdrawing from those various conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), a lying low, a hiding away; it is said to be solitude, a state of being alone. He who has emerged from that [state]—

Thus he is said to have "emerged from seclusion. However, because he emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), which is the supreme among forms of seclusion, he is therefore described as "having emerged from seclusion.

"Having paid homage to the Blessed One" means having respectfully saluted the Blessed One with his head, adorned by the brilliance of his seven-fold [curling] hair, or having caused him to be saluted, saying, "May you be well, Cunda. Thus...

After causing him to utter words of greeting, it is said that when the Blessed One has been saluted, he raises his neck like a golden drum and, emitting a Brahma-voice that is pleasant to the ear, lovely, and like a sprinkling of the Deathless, says to each person by name, "May you be happy.
This is the custom of the Tathāgatas. Herein is the supporting sutta:
“Venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and retinue, bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One.

“May Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and retinue, be happy, Pañcasikha; for the devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, and whatever other diverse beings there may be, all desire happiness.
And thus did the Tathāgata [respond] to such a person of great influence.
“They address the *yakkhas*”:
he says this as if turning toward those who are about to be discussed immediately hereafter. “Of many kinds” means of various types. “Views” means wrong views.
“Arise in the world” means they become manifest among sentient beings. “Connected with theories of self” [refers to such statements as] “form... [is the self].”
Connected with the doctrine of self (*attavāda*), which proceeds in the manner beginning with "one regards [the aggregates] as self," there are twenty such views.
Connected with the worldly doctrines (*lokavāda*) is that which proceeds in the manner beginning with "the self and the world are eternal";
these are eight: eternal, non-eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, and neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Because it occurs in such ways as "the self and the world are finite," "infinite," "both finite and infinite," or "neither finite nor infinite.

Regarding the phrase "from the very beginning" and so forth, the meaning is this: "Venerable Sir, for a bhikkhu who attends only to the beginning—that is, attending to that very first attention associated with insight even without yet reaching the path of stream-entry—will these [fetters] be abandoned by him through just this much?"
"By means of this skillful method, there comes about the abandoning and relinquishing of these views.

It should be understood that although the Elder himself was free from overestimation (*adhimānika*), he asked as if he were one possessed of overestimation for the sake of causing those with overestimation to abandon it.
Others, however, say: "The Elder’s pupils [asked] because, through their very initial attention (*ādimanasikāra*), the views were already completely severed and abandoned."
“There are those who perceive [the meditative attainments] thus: ‘These are dwellings in attainment,’ and there are also those who perceive them thus: ‘These are dwellings in effacement.
For their sake, he asks the Blessed One.
Then, showing the means for the abandonment of those views, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “Whatever these...”. In that regard:
The passage beginning with "where these views arise" and so forth is stated with reference to the five aggregates, for it is within these that these views arise.
As it has been said: "Bhikkhus, when there is form, by adhering to form, such a view arises:
'That is the self, that is the world; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.'"
The detailed explanation follows. However, speaking in the singular with respect to the object (*ārammaṇa*), he says "wherein" (*yattha ca*); what is meant is: "in whatever object they arise.
And here, the distinction between these terms—“arise” (*uppajjanti*), “underlie” (*anusenti*), and “manifest” (*samudācaranti*)—should be understood as follows:
by way of birth (*jāti*), those that have not yet been born but are in the process of being born are said to “arise. Those that have been cultivated again and again...
"They persist, firmly rooted and not relinquished. This means they have reached the doors of body and speech and are actively engaged;
this is their distinction. Regarding the phrases "This is not mine," and so forth: that object, consisting of the five aggregates, is not mine; I am not this;
this is not my self—thus one should see it as it truly is with right wisdom.
"Passato" (seeing) should first be understood according to the meaning of the words in this way:
for herein, "this is mine" is the grasping of craving; and while grasping that, one grasps the proliferation of craving, which is divided into the eight hundred types of mental wanderings of craving.
"This I am" is the grasping of conceit; and while grasping that, one grasps the proliferation of conceit, which is of nine types.
He grasps it. Grasping it as "This is my self" is the grasping of views; and in so grasping it, he grasps the proliferation of views (diṭṭhipapañca) consisting of the sixty-two types of views.
Therefore, by saying "This is not mine," the Blessed One rejects the aforementioned proliferation of craving (taṇhāpapañca). By "I am not this," he rejects the proliferation of conceit (mānapapañca);
and by "This is not my self," he rejects the proliferation of views (diṭṭhipapañca). And here, these are precisely those things associated with views.
Craving and conceit are to be understood. "In this way" means in the manner beginning with "This is not mine.
"As it really is" means according to its own nature; that is to say, as it exists. For the pentad of aggregates exists precisely in this manner.
However, the intention is that even when grasped through such notions as "mine," it does not exist in that manner. [One should see it] with right wisdom.
"Seeing" means seeing clearly by means of the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) at the conclusion of the wisdom of the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga).
"In this way, of these" means by this method, of these [views]. "Abandoning" and "relinquishing"—both of these are synonyms for abandoning through complete eradication (samuccheda-pahāna).
Thus, the Blessed One [taught] that the abandoning of views occurs precisely through initial attention (ādi-manasikāra), as was asked by the Venerable Mahācunda: "Is it so? or "Is it not so?"

Having been asked a question by way of those who are conceited (*adhimānika*), and having shown the abandoning of views by means of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*), he now, analyzing the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) of those very conceited ones himself, said: "But it is possible...

and so forth. In this context, "conceited ones" refers to those in whom conceit arises through the perception that they have attained what they have not attained; and when this [conceit] arises, it does not occur among those who follow the worldly cycle.
It arises in foolish worldlings, but not in noble disciples. For a stream-enterer does not give rise to the conceit, "I am a once-returner";
a once-returner does not give rise to [the conceit], "I am a non-returner"; and a non-returner does not give rise to [the conceit], "I am an arahant.
Rather, it is only for one who is a practitioner, whose defilements have been suppressed through either serenity or insight, that it occurs constantly.

It arises in one who is properly applied and has initiated insight. For such a person, not perceiving the active manifestation of defilements—whether those suppressed by serenity (samatha) or those suppressed by insight (vipassanā)—there arises overweening pride (*adhimāna*) such as:
"I am a stream-enterer," or "I am a once-returner," "a non-returner," or "an arahant. This was stated by the Elder Dhammadinna, who dwelt at Talaṅgara and Tissa Mountain.
It was like the case of the elders who were being exhorted.
It is said that while the Elder had not long been ordained, many bhikkhus attained distinction by abiding in his exhortation.
Hearing of this occurrence, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus residing at the Tissamahāvihāra thought, "The Elder is not one who appoints people to improper tasks."
“Bring the Elder,” he said, and dispatched many monks. They went and said, “Friend Dhammadinna, the Saṅgha of monks is summoning you.
He asked, “But why, venerable sirs, do you seek yourselves or another? [They replied,] “As true men, we seek ourselves.
He gave them a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and they all attained *arahantship*. The Saṅgha of monks...
Again, he sent other bhikkhus; in this manner, up to three times, all those who were sent remained right there after attaining arahantship.
Then, because those who had gone did not return, the Saṅgha sent a certain elder who had gone forth late in life.
Having arrived, he said, "Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus residing at Tissa Mahāvihāra has [sent me] to you three times..."
He sent word, saying, "Do you not hold the Saṅgha’s command in high regard? You do not come!
The Elder, thinking "What is this?", without even entering the leaf-hut, had his bowl and robes taken up and departed immediately.
On the way, he entered the Haṅkana Monastery. There, a certain great elder who was more than sixty years old, out of overweening pride, [claimed] Arahantship...
He made this claim. The Elder approached him, paid homage, exchanged greetings, and asked about his spiritual attainments.
The Elder said, “Yes, Dhammadinna; whatever ought to be done by one who has gone forth has been long accomplished by me;
I am now sixty years old. “Venerable sir, do you also exercise supernormal powers? “Yes, Dhammadinna. “It is well, venerable sir!”

"Create an elephant coming toward you," he said. "Very well, venerable sir," replied the Elder, and he created a great white elephant with seven-fold limbs, its trunk—divided into three parts—flapping, and its tusks thrusting forward as if wishing to gore [the other] with its two tusks.
It approached facing him, [just as the Elder had] created it himself. That elephant...
Seeing him, he became afraid and began to flee. At that moment, realizing for himself, "I am not an Arahant," he knelt at the feet of Dhammadinna and said, "Be my refuge, friend.
Dhammadinna comforted the Elder, saying, "Do not grieve, venerable sir; do not be distressed. Arrogance arises only in those who have actually performed the deeds [of realization]."
He gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Standing by that elder’s instruction, he attained *arahantship*.
On Mount Cittalapabbata there was likewise an elder living there. Dhammadinna approached him as well and asked the same question.
He also answered in the same way. Then Dhammadinna said to him, "Venerable sir, do you also exercise supernormal power (*iddhi*)?"
"Yes, sir. "Then, venerable sir, please construct a lotus pond. The Elder constructed it. "Venerable sir, please construct a cluster of lotuses here.
He constructed that as well. "Please construct a great lotus in this cluster of lotuses. He constructed that as well.
[He saw] a female form standing in that cluster of lotuses, singing and dancing with a sweet voice.
"Build it," he said. He built it as well. "Venerable sir, contemplate this again and again," he said, and then entered the palace himself.
As the Elder contemplated it, the defilements that had been suppressed for sixty years stirred within him.
Then, recognizing his own state, he approached the Elder Dhammadinna for a meditation subject, just as the previous Elder had done.
Having taken it up, she attained Arahatship.

Dhammadinnā, too, proceeded by stages to the Tissa Mahāvihāra. At that time, the elders had swept the courtyard of the shrine and were sitting there, having generated rapture directed toward the Buddha; for this was their customary practice.
Therefore, not even one among them asked Dhammadinna for permission, saying, "Please set aside your bowl and robe here.
However, knowing that this must be Dhammadinna, they asked him questions.
When he was asked these questions, he severed [the connection] like a cluster of lotus stalks with a sharp sword and struck the great earth with his toe. "Venerable sir, this..."
"Even the insentient great earth knows the virtue of Dhammadinna, yet you do not know it," she said, and spoke this verse:
"This earth is insentient, yet it discerns virtue and vice;
But you, O Venerable One, though possessed of sentience, do not discern virtue and vice."
And at that very moment, having risen up into the air, he went straight to Mount Talaṅgara-Tissa.
In this way, overweening pride arises in one who performs such an act. Therefore, the Blessed One, analyzing meditative absorption (jhāna) with reference to monks of that kind, said:
"But it is possible," and so forth.

The meaning of this is: there is this reason; it is not that there is none. Because here a certain bhikkhu, having secluded himself from sensual pleasures with those who are outside [the Buddhist fold]...
pe... might enter and dwell in the first jhāna, yet he thinks, "I dwell in effacement.
It is because of that method of practice which polishes away the defilements that I say this.
To say "I dwell [in this]" is not appropriate for one who is conceited; for such a monk, there is neither jhāna, nor effacement (*sallekha*), nor the practice of effacement. Why?
Because it does not serve as a basis for insight (*vipassanā*). For he does not, after attaining jhāna and emerging from it, contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
rather, jhāna merely brings about one-pointedness of mind for him, serving as a pleasant dwelling in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
Therefore, showing this meaning, the Blessed One said: "But these, Cunda, are not called 'effacement' (sallekha) in the Noble Discipline;
rather, these are called 'abidings in happiness in this very life' (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra) in the Noble Discipline.
In this context, the plural number (*ete*) should be understood as referring to the states of jhāna; that is, "these are the states of the first jhāna," and so forth.
This has been stated. Either by way of attainment, for even a single first jhāna becomes manifold because it occurs repeatedly through successive attainments;
or by way of object, for even a single first jhāna becomes manifold because it occurs with respect to various objects such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
This same method applies to the second, third, and fourth jhānas. Regarding the formless jhānas:
However, because there is no difference in their objects, the plural number should be understood as being due to the two preceding reasons alone.

Since it is said that these have both factors (*aṅga*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*), and that they are both peaceful (*santa*) and subtle (*sukhuma*), they should be understood as having been described thus: "These peaceful abidings. This, first of all, is for all four of them...
The general explanation has been given. As for the specific explanation, it should be stated in accordance with the phrases beginning with "all perceptions of form" (*sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ*).
That has already been explained in every detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
83. Thus, because the dwelling in jhāna of a monk who is conceited (*adhimānika*) does not serve as a basis for insight (*vipassanā*), it is not a dwelling of effacement (*sallekha*).
It does not exist; for he does not, having entered a jhāna and emerged from it, contemplate formations (saṅkhāra).

Rather, he possesses a dwelling in happiness in this very life, characterized by one-pointedness of mind. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that point, having analyzed both the fine-material jhānas and the immaterial jhānas, [the text now] presents the basis for where effacement (sallekha) is to be practiced through forty-four modes.
And demonstrating that very effacement (*sallekha*), he said here, "But in this case," and so forth.
Why, then, are non-violence and the rest called "effacements" by means of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*)? Because they have the supramundane as their proximate cause (*pādaka*).
For the eight attainments of outsiders serve only as a basis for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); whereas in the Teaching, even the going for refuge has the supramundane as its proximate cause.
And so too with non-violence and the other [perfections]. By this very sutta it should be understood:

"Just as a gift given to an outsider who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) and possesses the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*), a gift given to one who has gone for refuge to the Triple Gem within the Teaching is of even greater fruit.

It is with reference to this that the *Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi Sutta* states: "Having given a gift to an outsider who is free from passion for sensual pleasures, [the merit] is a hundred thousand times ten millionfold..."
It is said: "An incalculable and immeasurable gift is to be expected from one who has given a gift while practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry;
what need then to speak of one who is already a stream-enterer?

For here, starting from the moment of going for refuge, it is the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry who is intended. This, then, is the construction of the text in this context.
In the word-by-word commentary (*anupada-vaṇṇanā*), however, the word "here" (*idha*) is intended to indicate the basis for violence and so forth.
"Kho pana" is a mere particle. "Vā" is a genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental; this, however, is the summarized meaning:
regarding that basis for violence and so forth which we speak of in the manner beginning with "others will be violent," here, Cunda, you must practice effacement (*sallekha*).

Having thus spoken in brief, he now speaks in detail, saying: "‘Others will be harmful; we shall be harmless here’—thus should effacement be practiced,” and so forth. In this context, *pare* (others) refers to anyone who is not devoted to this practice of effacement.
*Vihimsakā bhavissantī* (will be harmful) means they will cause harm to living beings by means of hands, clods of earth, and so on.
*Mayamettha avihiṃsakā bhavissāmā* (we shall be harmless here) means: [We shall be those who do not inflict such injury.]
But we, in whatever matter others will be thus harmful, in that very matter we shall be harmless;
having generated harmlessness, we shall dwell. Thus, "effacement is to be practiced"—in this way effacement should be practiced by you.
And here, "effacement" (sallekha) should be understood as nothing other than harmlessness (avihiṃsā). For harmlessness effaces (sallekhati) harmfulness.
It cuts that [craving], therefore it is called "effacement" (*sallekha*). This same method applies everywhere. However, this is the distinction:

regarding the phrase "others have wrong view," one should understand that "view" is mentioned here by combining the final wrong view among the courses of kamma with the initial wrong view among the factors of wrongness.
Likewise, in the place where it is said "we here have right view," it refers to right view.

And here, the detailed discussion of the courses of kamma will be made clear in the *Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta*. Regarding the wrong states, wrong view and the others are treated in the *Dvedhāvitakka Sutta*.
This, however, is the summary here: "They take life" means they are killers of living beings; that is the meaning. "What is not given" [is explained as follows:]...
They take what is not given, thus they are *adinnādāyī*; the meaning is "those who steal from another. They practice that which is non-brahma, low, and base dhamma, thus they are *abrahmacārī*;
the meaning is "those who engage in sexual intercourse. They practice the brahma, the supreme, way of conduct, thus they are *brahmacārī*;
the meaning is "those who abstain from sexual intercourse. And here, it should be understood that "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) is effacement (*sallekha*).
For the holy life (*brahmacariya*) indeed polishes away what is not the holy life (*abrahmacariya*). "One who speaks falsely" means a speaker of falsehood; the meaning is:
those who utter empty and untrue speech that destroys the welfare of others. "Those whose speech is malicious" are those who possess malicious speech.
"Those whose speech is harsh" are those who possess harsh speech that cuts to the quick of others. "Those who prattle" refers to those who chatter idle and meaningless words (*sampha-palapa*).

One who indulges in idle chatter is a frivolous talker (*samphappalāpī*). "Coveting" means they are envious (*abhijjhālū*); the meaning is that they have a habit of longing for the property of others.
Those whose minds are corrupted and putrefied are "those of corrupt mind" (*byāpannacittā*). Those whose views are wrong, evil, and censured by the wise are "those of wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhī*);

this refers to those whose views are included within the courses of action, having as their basis such things as "there is no giving," and so forth, and which are included within the category of falsity (*micchatta*).
The meaning is: "endowed with views that do not lead to liberation. Those whose views are "right"—meaning beautiful, excellent, and praised by the wise—are "those of right view" (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).

This refers to those endowed with the view of the ownership of action (*kammassakatā*) such as "there is a gift," which is included within the courses of wholesome action, as well as with the view of the Path (*magga-diṭṭhi*) which is included within the state of correctness.
"Wrong intentions" (*micchā-saṅkappa*) refers to intentions that are unreal, non-leading-to-deliverance, and unwholesome. The same method applies to "wrong speech" (*micchā-vācā*) and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: unlike wrong intention and the others, there is no separate, individual dhamma called "wrong mindfulness" (*micchā-sati*).
Rather, it is a designation for the four unwholesome aggregates (*akusala-khandha*) as they occur when one is thinking about the past. As for that which...

The Blessed One said: “There is this recollection, monks; I do not say it does not exist—for one who recollects the acquisition of a son, monks, or for one who recollects the acquisition of wealth, monks, or for one who recollects the acquisition of fame, monks.
This was said with reference to the arising of a semblance of mindfulness in one who is thinking of this or that.
It should be understood that this has been stated. Regarding the term "one of wrong knowledge" (*micchāñāṇī*):

here, "wrong knowledge" should be understood as delusion (*moha*) arising in the manner of a retrospective reflection—thinking "I have done well"—after having committed an evil deed by way of devising a means for such evil actions.
Persons endowed with that are "ones of wrong knowledge. Regarding "one of right knowledge" (*sammāñāṇī*): here, however, it refers to the nineteenfold retrospective knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa*).
It is called "right knowledge" (*sammāñāṇa*); those persons who possess that are "possessors of right knowledge" (*sammāñāṇī*).

"Those with wrong liberation" (*micchāvimuttī*) means those who, while being actually unliberated, have the perception "we are liberated," or who perceive liberation where there is no liberation. Herein, this is the etymological analysis:
they have a wrong, evil, and perverted liberation, thus they are "those with wrong liberation. And the term "wrong liberation" is used in the manner already described.
This is a designation for unwholesome aggregates that have arisen.

However, with the exception of the eight factors beginning with right view associated with the fruit, the remaining phenomena should be understood as right liberation (*sammā-vimutti*). And because it stands having extracted the barb of wrong liberation (*micchā-vimutti*), it should be understood as "the extraction of the barb" (*sallekha*).
Directing [the practitioner] toward that, he said: "In this regard, we shall become those who possess right liberation."
“Simplicity should be practiced.
The following three [passages] are stated by way of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

However, it should be understood that the first two hindrances are not mentioned here because they have already been stated among the courses of action (*kamma-patha*) as “covetousness” and “ill-will. In that context, by means of sloth and torpor...
"Overwhelmed and overcome" means overwhelmed by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). "Possessed of restlessness" means agitated.
"Doubting" means being unable to reach a conclusion because of deliberation; thus, one is a skeptic (*vicikicchī*).
The ten terms beginning with "angry" are stated by way of the mind's defilements (*upakkilesa*). Regarding those, whatever needs to be said about anger and the others, all of that [is as follows]:
This is stated in the *Dhammadāyāda* and *Vatthu-suttas*. Here, however, is the etymological explanation: "The wrathful" (*kodhana*) means those whose nature is to be angry.
"Resentful" (*upanāhī*) means those whose nature is to harbor resentment; or, "resentful" means those in whom resentment exists. Likewise for the "slanderous" (*makkhī*) and the "envious" (*palāsī*).
"Envious" (*issukī*) means those who envy. "Miserly" (*maccharī*) means those who act miserly; or, "miserly" means those in whom miserliness exists.
They deceive, thus they are "deceitful" (*saṭha*); it is meant that they do not speak rightly. This is a designation for those who are engaged in hypocrisy (*kerāṭika*).

They possess illusion, thus they are "illusionists" (*māyāvī*). Because they possess rigidity, they are "obstinate" (*thaddha*). Through association with excessive conceit, they are "conceited" (*atimānī*).
The "bright side" (*sukkapaṅkha*) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
"Difficult to speak with" (*dubbaca*) means they are painful to address; when spoken to, they do not endure it. The opposite of that are "easy to speak with" (*suvaca*).

Those who have evil friends such as Devadatta and others are "evil-friended" (*pāpamitta*). Those who have virtuous friends such as the Buddhas or those like Sāriputta are "virtue-friended" (*kalyāṇamitta*).
"Negligent" (*pamatta*) means they are heedless due to the laxity of their minds regarding bodily misconduct and so forth. The opposite of that are "heedful" (*appamatta*).

These are to be understood. These three [terms] are stated by way of miscellaneous factors (*pakiṇṇaka*). "Lacking faith" (*assaddha*) and so forth are seven [terms] by way of non-Dhamma (*asaddhamma*).

Therein, they are "lacking faith" (*assaddha*) because faith does not exist in them regarding the three objects. On the side of the wholesome, they are "possessing faith" (*saddha*) because they have faith;

or alternatively, they are "possessing faith" (*saddha*) because faith exists in them. They are "shameless" (*ahirika*) because shame (*hirī*) does not exist in them, [referring to] the attainment of the unwholesome.
This is a designation for those who do not feel disgust. They have a sense of shame (*hirī*) in their minds, or they are endowed with shame; thus, they are "shameful" (*hirimanā*).

They do not tremble [at wrongdoing], thus they are "lacking moral dread" (*anottappī*); what is meant is that they do not fear the attainment of unwholesome states. Those who are the opposite of that are "possessing moral dread" (*ottappī*).
Little has been heard by them, thus they are "of little learning" (*appassutā*). And "little" (*appaṃ*) should not be taken as meaning "a small amount"; rather, it means "there is none."

It should be understood thus: for "of little learning" (*appassuta*) refers to those who have not heard much, being devoid of learning. "Of much learning" (*bahussuta*) means those by whom much has been heard;
this is a designation for those who, having understood even a single verse spoken by the Tathāgata according to its true meaning, practice accordingly.
"Laziness" (*kusīta*) means they sink into what is contemptible; this is a designation for those of inferior energy. "Those by whom energy has been exerted" (*āraddhavīriya*)...

"Those who have aroused energy" is a designation for those who are engaged in right effort. "Those with muddled mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassatī*) means those whose mindfulness has been lost; it is said they are "those whose mindfulness has perished.
"Those with established mindfulness" (*upaṭṭhitassatī*) means those whose mindfulness is firmly set; this is a designation for those whose mindfulness constantly proceeds directed toward the object.
"Those with corrupted wisdom" (*duppaññā*) means those whose wisdom is spoiled; it is said they are "those whose wisdom has perished. "Endowed with wisdom" (*paññāsampannā*)...
"Endowed with wisdom": here, "wisdom" (paññā) should be understood as insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). For it is the fulfillment of the equipment for insight that is brought to bear in this context;
therefore, insight-wisdom alone is intended—this is the instruction of the ancients.
Now, demonstrating the single view that is non-liberating and which acts as an obstacle to supramundane qualities in three ways:
He said, "Those who cling to their own views" (*sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*), and so forth. In this context, those who cling to their own views are *sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*.
Those who take up a fixed position are *ādhānaggāhī*; "fixed position" (*ādhāna*) means firmness; thus the meaning is "those who hold firmly.
Those who relinquish their tenets upon seeing a logical reason are *paṭinissaggī*; [even] with great difficulty, hardship, and toil...
"Difficult to relinquish" (*duppaṭinissaggī*) means that it is not possible to effect a relinquishing by showing reasons.

This is a designation for those who firmly grasp whatever view has arisen within themselves, thinking "this alone is the truth," and do not relinquish it even when addressed by the Buddha and others who show them the reasons. For such individuals, whatever dharma...

Or they grasp what is contrary to the Dhamma; all of that they conceal within themselves, like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs into its own shell, saying, "Thus it was spoken by our teachers; thus we have heard it. They take up the position of a crocodile and do not let go.
The bright side [of the practice] is to be understood as the opposite of what has been described.

84. Having thus shown effacement (*sallekha*) in forty-four ways, he now said, "Even the arising of a thought (*cittuppāda*), Cunda... and so forth, in order to show that even the arising of a thought is of great benefit for that effacement.
Its meaning is as follows: "Cunda, I say that even the arising of a thought toward wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) is of great benefit;
moreover, there is this conformity by body and speech, such that those states follow exactly as the initial thought arose."
"By body" means performing [the action] oneself; "by speech" means commanding others to "do it," or engaging in study, inquiry, and so forth.
What is the point of debate here? For he shows that those [practices] which are of absolute great benefit are indeed to be followed.

But why is even the arising of the thought [of following them] of great benefit in this context? Because it brings about absolute welfare and happiness, and because it is the cause for such following.
For the arising of the thought, “I shall give a gift,” brings about one’s own absolute welfare and happiness and is also the cause for those who follow one’s example;
indeed, because such a thought has arisen, on the very next day one closes off the main street, constructs a great pavilion, and gives a gift to a hundred or a thousand bhikkhus, saying:
“Invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, honor them, and serve them.”

He gives instructions to his attendants. Thus, the arising of the thought, "I will give robes, lodgings, and medicine to the Saṅgha," brings about one's own absolute welfare and happiness and is the cause for those who follow one's example; for it is precisely because of the arising of such a thought that one prepares, gives, and causes others to give robes and so forth.
This same principle applies to the going for refuge and other such acts.
For it is only after first generating the thought, “I go for refuge,” that one subsequently takes the refuge through body or speech.
Likewise, having generated the thought, “I shall undertake the fivefold, eightfold, or tenfold precepts,” one undertakes them through body or speech;
and having generated the thought, “Having gone forth, I shall establish myself in the four precepts,” [one acts accordingly].
One fulfills virtue by fulfilling it through both body and speech.
Having first aroused the thought, "I shall master the Buddha’s word," one masters one Nikāya, or two, three, four, or all five Nikāyas by means of speech.

In this way, [one fulfills virtue] regarding the undertaking of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), the mastery of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, the attainment of jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala).
This should be understood by way of individual enlightenment (paccekabodhi) and perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).
For the arising of the thought, "I shall become a Buddha," brings absolute welfare and happiness to oneself and is also the cause for those who follow one’s example;
indeed, precisely because such a thought has arisen, after a further period of four hundred thousand plus one hundred thousand aeons...
Having fulfilled the perfections through body and speech for incalculable eons, he wanders about delivering the world together with its devas.
Thus, while the arising of the thought [of giving] is beneficial in every respect, it should be understood that compliance through body and speech is exceedingly more beneficial.
Having thus shown the great benefit of the arising of the thought even among wholesome states, he now exhorts him to that end, saying: "Therefore, Cunda... and so forth. This is clear in meaning.

85. Having thus demonstrated the great utility of the arising of consciousness even in the effacement shown in forty-four aspects, he now says "Just as if," etc., showing that this very effacement is the path for the attainment of welfare.

Its meaning is as follows: Cunda, just as there might be a rough road due to stumps, thorns, stones, and so forth, and for the sake of circumventing or avoiding it, there might be another level road, like ground that has been well-prepared, for the purpose of bypassing it; [so too is the case with effacement].
And just as there might be a rugged, uneven ford for that river, crowded with trees at its base, rocky precipices, hollows, crocodiles, and so forth,
yet there might be another ford for the purpose of traversing and avoiding it— a level one, gradually deepening like the steps of a staircase—
by which one who has entered it could easily plunge into and bathe in that river or lake; so too is this.

or cross over; even so, Cunda, for a person who is given to violence—which is like a rugged path and a treacherous ford—non-violence serves as a means of circumvention, being like a level path and a level ford.
For just as a level path and a level ford are prepared for the purpose of avoiding a rugged path and a treacherous ford, so too is non-violence [prepared] for the purpose of avoiding violence.
Non-violence is prepared; one who practices it may, with ease, enter into and experience the success of either the human realm or the divine realm, or even transcend the worlds.
In this same manner, all the following phrases should be construed.

Having thus shown that very [non-violence] to be the path for the attainment of welfare, he now spoke the passage beginning with "Just as if," in order to demonstrate its quality of leading to the higher realms.

The meaning of this is as follows: Cunda, whatever unwholesome states there may be—whether they produce rebirth-linking or not, or whether, once rebirth-linking has been given, they produce its result or not—all of them are by their very nature called "leading to the lower realms," because at the time of fruition they yield results that are undesirable and disagreeable.
And likewise, whatever wholesome states there may be...

Whether they produce rebirth-linking or not, and whether they produce resultant [consciousness] after rebirth-linking has been given or not—all of them, by virtue of their birth, are called "destined for the higher realms" simply because at the time of the result they yield desirable and agreeable results. In the same way, Cunda, for one who is harmful... [as before] ...they are destined for the higher realms. Herein, this is the application of the simile: [The text continues with the comparison: Just as those seeds, though some may have fallen on barren soil, others on good soil, and others on soil that is neither, yet all are called "seeds destined for the higher realms" because they will eventually yield desirable and agreeable fruits; so too, Cunda, for one who is harmful... [as before] ...they are destined for the higher realms. In this regard, the connection between the simile and the meaning is as follows: Just as those seeds, even if they do not immediately sprout, are still called "seeds destined for the higher realms" because they possess the potential to eventually yield desirable and agreeable fruits; so too, Cunda, for one who is harmful... [as before] ...they are destined for the higher realms. Just as all unwholesome states lead to the lower realms, so too does even a single act of cruelty on the part of one who is cruel.
And just as all wholesome states lead to the higher realms, so too does even a single act of non-cruelty on the part of one who is non-cruel.
By this same method, the unwholesome should be illustrated by the unwholesome and the wholesome by the wholesome; such, it is said, is the intended meaning here.

87. Having thus shown that this very *sallekha* (effacement) is to be pursued as a higher factor, he now spoke the passage beginning with "So vata, Cunda" in order to show its capacity to bring about final Nibbāna (*parinibbāpana*). Therein, "he" (*so*) is a designation for the person of the kind already mentioned.
Having introduced the demonstrative statement "his" (*tassa*), [the text continues]: "He who, Cunda, is himself mired in the mire... (*yo attanā palipapalipanno so vata, Cunda*).
"One will pull out [another] who is deeply mired in the mire"—thus the connection should be understood for all the following phrases.
"Deeply mired in the mire" (palipapalipanna) refers to one submerged in deep mud; however, this is not how it is used in the discipline (vinaya) of the Noble Ones.

In the discipline of the Noble Ones, "the mire" (palipa) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇā). One who is "mired" (palipanna) therein is the foolish worldling (bālaputhujjana); therefore—
In this way, the application of the meaning here is to be understood.

Cunda, just as if some man were submerged up to his nose in deep mud and another person, having seized him by the hand or the head while he was still submerged right there, were to think, "I will pull him out"—this is impossible; for there is no means by which he could pull him out and establish him on dry land.
In the same way, it is impossible that one who is himself mired in the mire of the five cords of sensual pleasure could lift up another who is likewise mired in that very mire;
such a thing cannot exist.
It might be argued here that this is improper, as [the Buddha] gives teachings on the Dhamma even to worldlings—whether they be monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen.
Having heard it, they indeed become those who have fully realized the Dhamma; therefore, the statement "one who is stuck in the mud pulls out another" should not be understood in that way.
For it is the Blessed One alone who pulls them out there;
the preachers of the Dhamma receive only praise, just like the reader of a letter sent by a king. For example, regarding a letter sent by a king to a frontier province:
In that regard, people who do not know how to read the letter have it read by someone who does;
having heard its meaning, they carry it out with diligence, thinking, "This is the King's command," and it does not occur to them, "This is the command of the letter-reader.
As for the letter-reader, he receives only praise, such as, "He reads with clear and flawless speech."
In the same way, although preachers of the Dhamma such as Sāriputta and others teach the Dhamma, they are like those who merely read from written leaves.
However, that teaching of the Dhamma belongs to the Blessed One alone, just like a king’s command.
And it should be understood that those who, having heard it, realize the Dhamma, are uplifted by the Blessed One himself. But the preachers of the Dhamma—[are] "unrestrained..."
“They teach the Dhamma with speech that is not smooth,” they receive only mere praise. Therefore, this is indeed appropriate.
The bright side (the positive case) should be understood by reversing what has been stated.

Regarding the phrase “undisciplined, untrained, and not fully extinguished”: herein, he is “undisciplined” because of a lack of finality; he is [untrained] because of a lack of training in discipline.
One who is undisciplined should be understood as "not fully extinguished" because his defilements have not been extinguished.
It is impossible that such a person will discipline another, make him free from craving, train him in the three trainings, or lead him to full extinction by extinguishing his defilements.
The bright side of the matter should be understood by reversing what has been stated.
In the same way, Cunda, regarding the person who is harmful... [and so on] ... "for the sake of final Nibbāna"—here the meaning should be understood as follows:

Just as it is possible that one who is himself not mired in the mire will pull out another who is mired in the mire; that one who is tamed will tame another; that one who is disciplined will discipline another;
and that one who has attained final Nibbāna will lead another to final Nibbāna—this is indeed possible. But what is that? [The path.]

The state of being unafflicted, the state of being afflicted, the state of being tamed, the state of being disciplined, and the state of being fully extinguished (*parinibbuta*). In the same way, Cunda, for a person who is harmful, non-harming is for the sake of his full extinction. What is meant by this?
For one who himself is non-harming, that which is his non-harming serves as the full extinction of that harming which belongs to another who is harmful.
It is possible that one who is himself non-violent will extinguish another’s intention to harm;
for what is that [means]? It is simply non-violence itself. For whatever has been attained by oneself, one is able to encourage another toward that same goal.
Or alternatively, just as it is possible for one who is himself unsoiled, tamed, disciplined, and attained to final nibbāna,
to uplift, tame, discipline, and lead to final nibbāna another who is soiled, untamed, undisciplined, and not attained to final nibbāna— so too, for a person who harms others,
while he is cultivating the path for the abandoning of harming, [the defilements] that have arisen...

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) leads to final Nibbāna. For just as one who has attained final Nibbāna [is capable of cooling another], so too the volition of non-harming alone is capable of cooling the volition of harming for one who has not yet attained final Nibbāna.
It is with the intention of showing this meaning that the Blessed One said, “In the same way, Cunda,” and so forth;

such is how the sense should be understood here. And just as it is in this case, so it is in all the following passages. However, because of the fear of excessive prolixity, a word-by-word commentary (*anupada-yojanā*) has not been provided.

88. Having thus demonstrated his capacity to bring about final Nibbāna, he now concludes that teaching and speaks the words beginning with "Thus, Cunda," in order to urge [him] toward the practice of the Dhamma.
In this context, "the method of effacement" (*sallekhapariyāya*) means the cause of effacement.
This same principle applies everywhere; here, non-violence and so forth are the causes of effacement because they efface violence and the like.

By way of these, they should be understood as follows: as the cause for the arising of the mind because the mind must be produced through them; as the cause for the circumambulation because of the reason for the circumambulation, namely violence and so forth;

as the cause for the upper portion because of the production of the upper portion; and as the cause for final nibbāna because of the bringing about of final nibbāna for those who are violent and so forth.
"By one seeking welfare" means by one desiring welfare. "By one who is compassionate" means by one feeling compassion.
"Out of compassion" means having embraced compassion with the mind; it is also said to mean "having taken it upon oneself.
"That has been done for you by me" means that this has been done for you by me through showing these five methods.
For this alone is the duty of a compassionate Teacher, namely, the teaching of the Dhamma without error. Beyond this, however, is practice.
This is the duty of disciples. Therefore he said: "Cunda, these tree roots... [etc] ...are our instruction.
In this context, by the term "tree roots," he indicates the lodging at the foot of a tree. By the term "empty huts," he indicates a place secluded from people.
With both of these, he points out a lodging suitable for yoga and hands over his inheritance. "Meditate" means by means of meditative reflection upon an object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).
"Contemplate the thirty-eight objects, and through the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), contemplate the aggregates, bases, and so forth as impermanent and so on;
develop both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). This is what is meant. "Do not be negligent" means do not be heedless.
"Lest you be remorseful later" refers to those who, previously—in their youth, in the time of health, and in the time of possessing the favorable conditions for beings—[were negligent].

And at the time when the Teacher was present, being devoid of wise attention, they spent their days and nights eating unwholesome food and indulging in the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of sloth;

they were negligent. Later, in the time of old age, the time of sickness, the time of death, the time of misfortune, and at the time of the Teacher’s final passing away, they will remember that former state of negligence and [the fact of] their death with rebirth.
Seeing the heavy consequences, people become full of remorse; however, showing that you should not be like them, he said, "Do not be remorseful later.
"This is our instruction for you" means that this is our instruction and exhortation to you from us: "Meditate, do not be negligent. This is what is meant.
The commentary on the Sallekha Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 9.
The commentary on the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta.
89. Thus have I heard: this is the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta*. Therein, whether it be the question asked by the Elder, “Friend, ‘right view, right view’ is said;
in what way, friend, is one so called? or “But what, friend, is unwholesome?”—all such questions are indeed inquiries arising from a desire to explain.

In this context, since those who know as well as those who do not—both outsiders and members of the Dispensation alike—call it "right view" on the basis of hearsay and so forth, or even through their own direct experience, he therefore spoke, touching upon that which is the word of many, twice:
"Right view, friend, is called 'right view'. This is the intended meaning here: that it is called "right view" by others as well.
It is so called; furthermore, it is also called "right view" by others. When it is thus spoken of, both with respect to its meaning and its characteristic, one might ask:
"To what extent, friend, is a noble disciple one of right view?
In this context, "one of right view" means one who is endowed with a beautiful and praiseworthy view. However, when this term "right view" refers specifically to the Dhamma itself...
When it functions, its view is beautiful and praised; thus, its meaning should be understood as "right view" (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).

And this right view is twofold: mundane (*lokiyā*) and supramundane (*lokuttarā*). Therein, the knowledge of being the owner of one's own actions (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge conforming to the truths (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) are mundane right view;
or, in brief, all wisdom associated with the taints (*sāsavā paññā*) is mundane. That which is associated with the Noble Path and its Fruits is supramundane.
Supramundane wisdom is right view. However, the person is of three kinds: the worldling (*puthujjana*), the trainee (*sekha*), and the one beyond training (*asekha*).

Among these, the worldling is of two kinds: the outsider and the follower of the Teaching. Therein, the outsider possesses right view through the doctrine of kamma and the view of being the owner of one's kamma;
it is not a right view that accords with the Truths, because he clings to the false view of self.

One who belongs to the Dispensation possesses it by means of both. A trainee possesses right view because of his fixed right view; one beyond training possesses it because of his right view of one beyond training.
However, in this context, the term "one of right view" is intended for one who is endowed with the supramundane wholesome right view that is fixed and leads to liberation.
For this very reason, it is said: "His view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has come to this..."

“True Dhamma”: for it is precisely supramundane wholesome right view that is “straight-going” because it proceeds by way of rectitude without falling into either extreme, and because it has gone forth having utterly severed all crookedness such as bodily deceit;
and one who possesses that very view [is endowed] with unwavering confidence through verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*) in the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
Being thus endowed, one who untangles all the thickets of views, abandons all defilements, emerges from the cycle of birth,
and brings the practice to completion by means of the Noble Path— this is called the True Dhamma proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One,
which plunges into the Deathless and is known as Nibbāna.

"Yato kho" (when indeed) is a term denoting a delimitation of time; it means "at whatever time. "And he understands the unwholesome" means that he understands the unwholesome comprised within the ten courses of unwholesome action.

By way of the function of understanding which has cessation as its object, he penetrates [the truth] as "this is suffering," and thus understands the unwholesome. "And he understands the root of the unwholesome" refers to that...
One understands the unwholesome root that serves as the root condition, penetrating it in that very same way as "this is the origin of suffering.
This same method applies here to the phrase "the wholesome and the wholesome root" as well.
And just as it is here, so too in all subsequent sections, the understanding of the object should be understood as occurring by way of its function (*kicca*). By this much—*ettāvatāpi*.
By this very understanding of the unwholesome and so forth, he possesses right view—meaning he is endowed with the supramundane right view of the kind already described.
"His mind is straightened... [and so on]... this true Dhamma": by this much, the brief teaching is concluded.
This teaching itself is indeed brief, but for those bhikkhus, the penetration through right attention should be understood as occurring only by way of a detailed exposition.
However, it should be understood that on the second occasion, both the teaching and the penetration through attention were explained in detail.
Regarding this, at the conclusion of the detailed teaching, the monks said, "By the brief teaching, the two lower paths were spoken of;
by the detailed teaching, the two higher paths were spoken of," as they considered the words beginning with, "Having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust."
The Elder, however, said: "Even in the brief teaching, the four paths were spoken of as a group; so too in the detailed teaching.
And this investigation that has been revealed here regarding the brief and detailed teachings should be understood in the same manner as explained here for all sections.
For from this point forward, we shall provide only a commentary on the words that have not yet been mentioned or explained.
Commentary on the Unwholesome Courses of Action:

Regarding that, first, in the detailed teaching of the first section, in such passages as "Friend, killing living beings is unwholesome," it should be understood as unwholesome because it proceeds from lack of skill (*akosalla*);
or alternatively, it is unwholesome because it is the opposite of the wholesomeness to be described later. That...
By way of its characteristic, it is blameworthy, has a painful result, and is defiled. This, then, is the commentary on the common terms here. Regarding the uncommon terms:
the taking away of a living being’s life is "taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*); it is said to be the killing of a living being, the slaughter of a living being.

Herein, by conventional usage, a "living being" (*pāṇa*) is a sentient being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). Now, regarding that living being, one who perceives it as a living being...
Killing is the volition of a murderer that arises through either the door of body or the door of speech, instigating an action that cuts off the life-faculty.

Regarding such beings, it is less blameworthy when directed toward small animals among those devoid of special qualities—such as animals—and more blameworthy when directed toward large-bodied beings. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort involved; and even when the effort is equal, because of the greatness of the object.
Among humans and others who possess qualities, the offense is slight when the living being has few qualities, and grave when it has many qualities.

However, when there is equality in the qualities of the body, it should be understood that the offense is slight due to the mildness of the defilements and the means employed, and grave due to their intensity.
This [offense] has five constituent factors: a living being, the perception of that being as such, the intention to kill, the employment of a means, and [the resulting death].

Therefore, it is called "killing. There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishment, by stationary means, by means of spells, and by means of psychic power (*iddhi*).
However, if this were to be explained here in detail, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we shall not elaborate upon it, nor on other such matters.
Those who desire [further detail] should consult the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, and learn from it.
Taking what is not given is *adinnādāna*; it is the seizing of another’s property, theft, or robbery—so it is said.

In this context, "what is not given" refers to that which is owned by another, where another, if they were to exercise their will over it, would be neither liable to punishment nor subject to reproach.
Regarding that which is owned by another, for one who perceives it as such, [the offense] arises from the effort of taking it.
The volition of theft is taking what is not given. That [offense] is less blameworthy when the property of another is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior.
Why? Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*). When the object is equal, it is more blameworthy in the case of property belonging to those who possess superior qualities.
Depending on each respective person of superior quality, it is less blameworthy in the case of property belonging to one of inferior quality compared to that person.

For this [offense], there are five constituent factors: another’s possession, the perception that it is another’s possession, the intention to steal, the effort, and the taking away by means of that [effort].
There are six modes of application, namely those beginning with "by one's own hand" (sāhatthika). These, moreover, correspond respectively to the following types of theft:
theft by taking away, theft by force, theft by concealment, theft by stratagem, and theft by trickery.
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding the term "sexual misconduct" (*kāmesumicchācāra*): here, "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) refers to sexual intercourse. "Misconduct" (*micchācāra*) is a reprehensible and base form of conduct.

By way of its characteristic, sexual misconduct is the volition that transgresses against places where one should not go, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*).

In this context, "unapproachable places" refers first to women protected by men: those protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both mother and father, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by their Dhamma, those who have a protector, and those for whom there is legal punishment—these are the ten types beginning with those protected by their mother.
Then there are those purchased with wealth, those living according to their own will, those living on their earnings, and those living in a robe.

The woman who brings her own bowl, the woman whose head-covering has been removed, the female slave who is also a wife, the female servant who is also a wife, the woman captured under a banner, and the momentary wife—these, along with the ten beginning with the woman bought for money, constitute twenty types of women.

Among women, however, other men [are forbidden] from approaching twelve types: the two protected by guardians and subject to punishment, and the ten beginning with the woman bought for money; this is the "unapproachable place" (agamanīyaṭṭhāna).

This is its name. Furthermore, this sexual misconduct is less blameworthy when directed toward a place that should not be approached if it is devoid of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), but it is greatly blameworthy if [the person] is endowed with virtues such as moral discipline.

It has four constituent factors: the object that should not be approached, the intention to engage in it, the actual effort of engagement, and the acceptance of the penetration of the path into what is not the path.
There is only one mode of action, which is that performed by oneself.
*Musā* refers to a verbal or bodily exertion that destroys one's welfare for one whose primary intention is to deceive.
However, *musāvāda* (false speech) is the volition that, with the intent to deceive, originates the bodily or verbal exertions intended to deceive another. According to another method:
*Musā* is an unreal and untrue matter; *vāda* is the making known of that [matter] as real and true. As for its defining characteristic:
False speech is the volition that originates an expression of something as being thus, by one who desires to make another understand a matter that is not thus as being thus.
It is slight in its degree of fault when the matter it destroys is slight, and grave when the matter is great.

Furthermore, for householders, that which proceeds in the manner of "I have nothing" and so forth out of a desire not to give their own property is slight in its degree of fault; [likewise] for a witness...
Having performed [the act], it is called a grave offense when spoken for the purpose of destroying one's welfare.

For those who have gone forth, having obtained even a small amount of oil or ghee, to speak with a motive of jesting in the manner of an old proverb, saying, "Today, as it were, the oil flows like a river in the village," is a minor offense;
however, for those who speak in the manner of saying they have seen what was not actually seen, it is a grave offense.
It has four constituent factors: a non-factual basis, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and another person’s understanding of that meaning.

There is one mode of application, which is indeed by means of oneself; this should be understood as performing an act of deception through the body, or through what is connected to the body, or through speech. If, by that act, the other person understands that meaning, this—
One is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that originates the action.

Regarding "slanderous speech" and so forth: that speech which, when spoken to someone, creates a sense of intimacy for oneself and a sense of emptiness in the other person’s heart is slanderous speech.
Furthermore, that [speech] by which one makes both oneself and another harsh...
That speech which one utters is itself harsh, neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart; this is harsh speech (*pharusā vācā*).

That by which one prattles nonsense is idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). The volition that is the root of these also receives the same names as malicious speech and the rest, and it is precisely that [volition] which is intended here.
In this context, for one with a defiled mind, for the purpose of causing dissension among others—
Slanderous speech is the volition that originates through bodily or vocal application out of a desire for one's own favor.
It is less blameworthy when directed toward someone of little virtue, and more blameworthy when directed toward someone of great virtue. Its four constituent factors are:

another person who is to be divided; the intention to divide, thinking, "In this way these two will become estranged, they will become separated"; [the act of speaking]; and the completion of the division.
Or, it is the desire for affection, thinking, "May I become beloved and trustworthy," or the effort directed toward that, or the discernment of that purpose.
Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that originates from bodily and vocal exertion intended to cut to the quick of another.
To illustrate this, there is this story: it is said that once a certain boy, disregarding his mother's words, went into the forest.
His mother, unable to turn him back, cursed him, saying, "May a fierce female buffalo pursue you!
Then, right there in the forest, a female buffalo rose up. The boy made an act of truth, saying, "May that which my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass;
may that which she thought in her mind come to pass! The female buffalo stood right there as if bound. Thus...
Even a practice that involves cutting the breast does not constitute harsh speech because of the gentleness of the mind.
For parents sometimes say to their children even such things as, "May thieves cut you into pieces," yet they do not wish for even a lotus leaf to fall upon them.
And teachers and preceptors sometimes say to those dependent on them, "What...? [and so forth].
"These shameless and fearless ones wander about; drive them out! Thus they desire the excellence of their study and realization.
And just as harsh speech does not occur because of gentleness of mind, so too gentle speech does not occur because of gentleness of words.
For the words "Lie down comfortably" spoken by one wishing to have someone killed are not gentle speech.
It is speech. However, because it is harshness of mind, it is indeed "harsh speech.
Depending on the person toward whom it is directed, it is slightly blameworthy if that person has few virtues, and greatly blameworthy if they have great virtues. It has three constituent factors:
another who is to be reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling.
Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal efforts indicating what is meaningless.

It is slightly blameworthy when its habitual practice is weak, and greatly blameworthy when its habitual practice is great. It has two constituent factors: a preoccupation with useless talk such as the *Mahābhārata* war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual speaking of such talk.
It is called *abhijjhā* because it covets; the meaning is that it proceeds by being directed toward another's property and inclining toward it.
Its characteristic is the coveting of another's property, thinking, "O, may this be mine! Like taking what is not given, it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy.
It has two constituent factors: another's property and the intention to appropriate it for oneself.
For even when greed arises with respect to another's property, there is as yet no breach of the course of kamma so long as one does not appropriate it for oneself, thinking, "O, may this be mine!
Malice (vyāpāda) is that which intends harm toward the welfare and happiness of others; its characteristic is mental corruption directed toward the destruction of others, or it is harsh speech.
There is that which is slightly blameworthy and that which is greatly blameworthy. It has two constituent factors: another being and the thought of their destruction.
For even when anger arises with another being as its object, there is no breach of the path of action so long as one does not think of their destruction, such as:
"Oh, would that this person were cut off or destroyed!"
It is wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) because one sees wrongly due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are.

It is characterized by a distorted vision, according to the method beginning with "there is no giving" and so forth. Like frivolous chatter (*samphappalāpa*), it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy.

Furthermore, it is slightly blameworthy when indeterminate (*aniyata*), and greatly blameworthy when determinate (*niyata*). It has two constituent factors: the object and the distortion of the mode in which that object is grasped.
And just as one grasps it, so does it appear to him in that very state.

Furthermore, the analysis of these ten unwholesome courses of action should be understood in five ways: by way of their nature (*dhammata*), by way of their components (*koṭṭhāsa*), by way of their objects (*ārammaṇa*), by way of their feeling (*vedanā*), and by way of their roots (*mūla*).

In this regard, "by way of their nature": among these, the first seven are indeed volitional states (*cetanā-dhamma*) themselves; the three beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*) are associated with volition.

Regarding the "parts": in their sequential order, these eight courses of action—consisting of the seven [unwholesome actions] plus wrong view—are only courses of action (*kammapatha*), not roots (*mūla*).
Covetousness and ill will are both courses of action and roots. For when covetousness reaches the state of a root, it becomes the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akusalamūla*);
ill will is the unwholesome root of hatred (*dosa-akusalamūla*).
Regarding the object: killing has the life-faculty as its object, which is a formation (saṅkhāra). Taking what is not given has either a being or a formation as its object.
Sexual misconduct has formations as its object by way of the tangible; some say it also has a being as its object.
False speech has either a being or a formation as its object. The same applies to malicious speech and harsh speech.
They have beings as their object. Idle chatter has either beings or formations as its object, by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized;
likewise for covetousness. Ill will has beings as its object alone. Wrong view has formations as its object by way of the phenomena belonging to the three planes.
"From feeling": killing living beings is painful to feel. For even though kings, upon seeing a thief, may smile...
When they say, “Go, kill him,” their volition of instigation (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*) is associated only with suffering.

Taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) is associated with all three feelings. Sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*) is associated with two feelings by way of pleasure and equanimity; however, in the mind that performs the final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-citta*), it is not associated with equanimity.
False speech (*musāvāda*) is associated with all three feelings, as is malicious speech (*pisuṇā vācā*). Harsh speech (*pharusā vācā*)...
[False speech] is exclusively painful feeling. Frivolous chatter has all three feelings. Covetousness has two feelings, by way of pleasure and equanimity;
likewise for wrong view. Ill will has painful feeling. As for the roots:
killing living beings has two roots, by way of hatred and delusion. Taking what is not given has [two roots], by way of hatred and delusion, or...
Or [they arise] through greed and delusion. Wrong conduct arises through greed and delusion. False speech arises through hatred and delusion, or through greed and delusion;
likewise for malicious speech and frivolous chatter. Harsh speech arises through hatred and delusion.
Covetousness has one root through delusion, as does ill will. Wrong view has two roots through greed and delusion.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Greed is a root of the unwholesome": it is called greed (*lobha*) because one is greedy; hatred (*dosa*) because one hates; and delusion (*moha*) because one is deluded.
Among these, greed itself is unwholesome by virtue of being blameworthy and having a painful result;

furthermore, it is a "root of the unwholesome" (*akusalamūla*) because it acts as the originator of certain unwholesome states such as killing and so forth through its association with them, and as their decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for others.
And this has also been said: "Friends, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, may even take the life of a living being," and so forth.
The same method applies to hatred and delusion as well in their status as unwholesome roots.
The commentary on the unwholesome courses of action is finished.

In the commentary on the wholesome courses of action (*kusalakammapatha*), regarding the phrases "abstinence from taking life is wholesome" and so forth: *pāṇātipātā* and the others have already been explained. *Veramaṇī* means that which avoids (*maṇati*) enmity (*vera*);

the meaning is that it abandons enmity. Alternatively, one refrains (*viramati*) by means of this [abstinence], which functions as the instrument; here, the letter *ve* has been substituted for the letter *vi*.

Abstention (*veramaṇī*). This, first of all, is the explanation here from the perspective of the phrasing (*byañjana*). From the perspective of the meaning (*attha*), however, abstention is the abstinence associated with wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*).

That abstinence associated with wholesome consciousness which is described as "the refraining, the abstention, at the time of one who refrains from taking life"—that, when classified, is threefold: abstinence through possession (*sampattavirati*) and abstinence through undertaking (*samādānavirati*).

"Abstinence by eradication. In this context, abstinence that arises in those who have not formally undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), but who— having reflected upon their own birth, age, learning, and so forth— do not transgress an available opportunity,
thinking "it is improper for us to do such a thing," should be understood as "abstinence by attainment," like that of the lay follower Cakkana in the island of Sri Lanka.
It is said that while he was still very young, his mother fell ill. A physician declared, "Fresh hare-flesh is required.
Thereupon, Cakkana’s brother sent Cakkana, saying, "Go, dear one, and search the fields.
He went there. At that moment, a hare had come to eat the young grain.
Seeing him, he ran with speed and, bound by a creeper, let out a cry of "Kiri kiri!
Cakkana, hearing that sound, went there, seized him, and thought, "I shall prepare medicine for my mother.
Then he thought again, "It is not fitting for me that, for the sake of my mother's life, I should deprive another of life. Then he said to him, "Go..."
"Enjoy grass and water in the forest together with the hares," he said, and released him. When his brother asked, "Father, was a hare caught?
he explained what had happened. Then his brother rebuked him. He went to his mother and made this resolve, speaking the truth:
"Since the day I was born, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life. At that very moment, his mother became free from illness.
However, the abstinence that arises in those who have undertaken the training precepts— both at the time of undertaking them and thereafter—

by not transgressing the basis even at the cost of their own lives, should be understood as "abstinence through undertaking," such as in the case of the lay follower who lived on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna.
It is said that he, having received the training precepts from the Elder Piṅgala-Buddharakkhita, who resided at the Ambariya Monastery...
He was plowing a field. Then his ox went missing; while searching for it, he climbed Uttaravaḍḍhamāna Mountain, where a great serpent seized him.
He thought, "I will cut off its head with this sharp axe.
Then he thought again, "This is not fitting for me, that I should [break] the training rule in the presence of my venerable teacher who is worthy of respect."
"Having taken it, I shall break it. Having thought this up to three times, [he resolved]:

"I renounce my life, not the training rule," and he cast away the sharp wooden axe that had been placed on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, a great wild beast released him and departed.
It should be understood, however, that the abstinence associated with the Noble Path is "abstinence by eradication" (*samuccheda-virati*). From the moment its arising begins...
“The thought ‘I shall kill a living being’ does not even arise in the minds of noble persons (ariyapuggala).

Yet, this very abstinence (virati) is called ‘wholesome’ (kusala) because it proceeds from skillful application. Alternatively, it is wholesome because it mows down (lunāti) that which is designated as ‘bad’ (kusa)—namely, immorality—due to its lying low (sayaṇa).
Furthermore, it was not called ‘wholesome’ in the context of the question, ‘And what, friends, is the wholesome?’, because that [definition] would have been inappropriate for that specific inquiry.”
