Just as it was for the unwholesome courses of action, so too for these wholesome courses of action, the exposition should be understood by way of five aspects: by way of the nature of the phenomena (*dhamma*), by way of their constituent parts (*koṭṭhāsa*), by way of their objects (*ārammaṇa*), by way of feeling (*vedanā*), and by way of their roots (*mūla*). In that regard, "by way of the nature of the phenomena":

among these, in the first seven cases, both volition (*cetanā*) and the abstinences (*virati*) are applicable; at the end, however, only those associated with volition apply. "By way of their constituent parts":
in the first seven cases, there are only courses of action (*kamma-patha*) and not roots; at the end, however, there are both courses of action and roots.
And as for the roots: having reached non-covetousness as its root, non-greed becomes a wholesome root; non-ill-will becomes the wholesome root of non-hatred;
and right view becomes the wholesome root of non-delusion.
As for the object: the very objects of killing living beings and so forth are themselves the objects of these [unwholesome states], precisely because they are to be transgressed.

For this is indeed called abstinence. Just as the Noble Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, having the life-faculty and so forth as their objects, should be understood to abandon unwholesome conduct such as killing living beings.
As for "from feeling," all [the results] are either pleasant feelings or neutral feelings; for once one has reached the wholesome, there is no such thing as a painful feeling.

Regarding "from the root": for one who abstains from the seven courses of action in their proper order with a consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayuttacitta*), they have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayuttacitta*), they have two roots. Non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) has two roots when abstaining with a consciousness associated with knowledge, and one root when abstaining with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge. Non-greed, however, [is the root] of itself alone.
There is no root; the same method applies to non-ill will (*abyāpāda*) as well. Right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) has two roots by way of non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*).
Regarding the passage "non-greed is a wholesome root" (*alobho kusalamūlaṃ*), etc.: non-greed is that which is not greed; it is a designation for the state that is the opposite of greed.

The same method applies to non-hatred and non-delusion (*amoha*) as well. Among these, non-greed is itself wholesome, and [it is also the root] of these [wholesome states], such as abstaining from taking life (*pāṇātipātā veramaṇī*), and so forth.

The wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*) are so called because they are the "roots" (*mūla*) of certain wholesome states in the sense of being the power that activates their associated factors, and of others in the sense of being the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
This same method applies to non-hatred (*adosa*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) as well regarding their status as wholesome roots.
Now, concluding all that has been taught both in brief and in detail, he speaks the section on absorption (*appanāvāra*), beginning with the words: "But from the moment, friends... and so forth.
"Therein, 'he understands the unwholesome thus' means he understands the unwholesome by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action as they have been specified.

The same method applies to the phrases 'the root of the unwholesome' and so forth. Up to this point, the path of deliverance leading up to Arahantship has been explained for one who takes the four noble truths as his meditation subject according to a single method.
How so? For here, setting aside covetousness, there are the ten unwholesome courses of action."

The wholesome courses of action (*kusalakammapatha*) are the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). Covetousness and greed, which are unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*), are these two factors that, in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), are the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).
In the indirect sense (*pariyāya*), however, all courses of action are the truth of suffering, and all wholesome and unwholesome roots are the truth of origination.
The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*). One who fully understands suffering...

"Abandoning the origin and understanding cessation is the Noble Path; thus, two truths are stated by way of their essential nature, while two are to be understood by way of the 'turning' (āvatta) method.
"Having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust in every respect"—thus, one who understands unwholesome states and so forth in this manner abandons the underlying tendency to lust in all its modes.
"Having abandoned. "Having dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)" means it is said that he has removed the underlying tendency to aversion in every respect.
Up to this point, the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*) has been explained.

"Having uprooted the underlying tendencies of the view and conceit that 'I am'" means that, without leaving out any phenomenon among the five aggregates, he has uprooted them by way of the mode of grasping as "I am."
Having eradicated the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhi-mānānusaya*) that has arisen.
In this context, "the underlying tendency of views" means an underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*) similar to a view;

for this underlying tendency of conceit is said to be similar to a view because it functions as the thought "I am," and therefore it is described in this way. And this conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), in detail...
"One who desires to understand should consult the Khemaka Sutta in the Khandhaka-vagga.
"Having abandoned ignorance" means having abandoned ignorance, the root of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

"Having generated true knowledge" means having generated the knowledge of the path of Arhatship, which eradicates that ignorance. Up to this point, the path of Arhatship has been explained. "In this very life..."
"He makes an end of suffering in this very life" means that he brings about the termination of the suffering of the round of existence within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Even by this much, friends," he thus concludes the teaching; it is said that this is done by way of the penetration of attention as described in this teaching on the courses of action (*kammapatha*).
The rest is exactly according to the method already stated. In this way, he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the paths of the Non-Returner and Arahantship.
The commentary on the wholesome courses of action is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Nutriment: 90.
"It is good, friend," and so forth... "you have come to this True Dhamma"—thus, by way of the wholesome and unwholesome, [the Blessed One addressed] the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having heard this discourse on the Four Truths spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta, those bhikkhus rejoiced with the words, "Excellent, friend!

This means they welcomed it with the very same state of mind that had prompted those words, expressing their appreciation through speech and feeling great joy in their hearts. Now, as for the Elder [Sāriputta], in various ways...
He is capable of teaching the exposition of the Four Truths, as it was said: "Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is able to explain and teach the Four Noble Truths in detail.
Or, because he wished to teach even further and thus said, "Even by this much," those bhikkhus desired to hear the teaching on the Truths according to another method as well.
They asked the Venerable Sāriputta further questions. This means that they asked another, additional question by way of the principle:
"Perhaps, friends, there might be another method or another reason" beyond the question he himself had asked and answered;
or it is said that they asked [questions] in the subsequent portion of the previous question.
[The question] exists. Then, when the Elder was about to explain it to them, he said, "Friends," and so forth. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [previously] explained:
*āhāraṃ* means condition (*paccaya*). For a condition brings (*āharati*) its own fruit; therefore, it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*).

In the phrases "of beings that have come to be" (*bhūtānaṃ sattānaṃ*) and so on, "beings that have come to be" (*bhūtā*) means those who have been born, those who have been produced. "Of those seeking existence" (*sambhavesīnaṃ*) refers to those who seek existence...

They seek and search for birth and rebirth. In that regard, among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), egg-born and womb-born beings are called "seeking rebirth" (*sambhavesin*) as long as they have not yet broken the eggshell or the amniotic sac;

once they have broken the eggshell or the amniotic sac and emerged outside, they are called "become" (*bhūta*). Moisture-born and spontaneously born beings are "seeking rebirth" during the first moment of consciousness.

[They are] called "beings" (bhūta). From the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called "beings. Alternatively, by whichever posture they are born, as long as they have not yet reached another [posture], they are called "seeking existence" (sambhavesin); from then on, they are called "beings.
Or else, "beings" means those who are born and produced, who having been born, do not again enter the reckoning of future existence.
This is a designation for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "Seekers of becoming" (*sambhavesina*) refers to those who seek further existence;
this is a designation for trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) who, because they have not abandoned the fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*), seek rebirth even in the future.
Thus, in every respect, all sentient beings are encompassed by these two terms. And here, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of inclusion; therefore—
The meaning should be understood as "of beings" and "of those seeking rebirth.
"For the sake of stability" means for the purpose of stability. "For the sake of assistance" means for the purpose of assistance or for the purpose of benefit.
This is a difference in phrasing, but the meaning of both terms is one and the same. Alternatively, "for the sake of stability" refers to the phenomena that have arisen in each respective being.
"By way of non-continuity" means for the sake of non-interruption. "For the support" means for the arising of those things not yet arisen.

Both of these [terms] are to be understood in two ways: as for the maintenance and the support of those already come to be, and as for the maintenance and the support of those seeking rebirth (*sambhavesī*).
"Edible food" (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is so called because it must be swallowed after being made into morsels.
"Food" is a designation for the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that has rice, boiled grain, and so forth as its basis. Whether "gross" or "subtle":

it is gross by virtue of the grossness of its basis, and subtle by virtue of the subtlety of its basis. However, in its own nature, because it is included among subtle matter, edible food is indeed subtle.
Furthermore, this grossness and subtlety of its basis should be understood in relation to each successive [level of] support.
Compared to the food of crocodiles, the food of peacocks is subtle;
it is said that crocodiles swallow stones, which dissolve as soon as they reach their stomachs. Peacocks eat creatures such as snakes and scorpions.
Compared to the food of peacocks, the food of hyenas is subtle; it is said that they [eat] horns discarded three years ago.
They also eat bones; these become as soft as tuberous roots merely by being moistened with their saliva.
Compared to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is more refined; they eat the branches of various trees.
Compared to the food of elephants, the food of the gavaya, the gokaṇṇa deer, and others is more refined; it is said that they [eat] sapless [branches].
They eat the leaves and so forth of various trees. Compared to their food, the food of cattle is more subtle;
they eat green and dry grass. Compared to their food, the food of hares is more subtle. Compared to the food of hares, the food of birds is more subtle.
Compared to the food of birds, the food of those living in the borderlands is more subtle. Compared to the food of those living in the borderlands, the food of village headmen...
Food is subtle. Compared to the food of village headmen, the food of kings, royal ministers, and great officials is subtle.
Compared to their food, the food of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) is subtle. Compared to the food of a wheel-turning monarch, the food of the earth-dwelling devas is subtle.

Compared to the food of the earth-dwelling devas, the food of the devas of the Four Great Kings is subtle. And so on, up to the devas who wield power over the creations of others (*paranimmitavasavatti*).
Food must be analyzed in detail; its analysis culminates precisely in its subtlety.
In this regard, within a coarse substance, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) is meager and weak, whereas in a subtle substance it is powerful.
For instance, even after drinking a bowl full of rice-gruel, one becomes hungry in a mere moment and desires to eat anything at all.
However, having drunk even a mere drop of clarified butter, one becomes unwilling to eat for the rest of the day.
In that case, the food dispels fatigue but is not able to sustain [the body]; the nutritive essence sustains [the body] but is not able to dispel fatigue.
But when these two are combined, they both dispel fatigue and sustain [the body].
"Contact as the second" refers to the sixfold contact, beginning with eye-contact. Among these four nutriments, it should be understood as the second nutriment.
This is merely a method of teaching; therefore, one need not investigate here whether it is called "the second" or "the third" for such reasons.
"Mental volition" refers simply to volition itself. "Consciousness" refers to any kind of consciousness whatsoever.
Here it is asked: If the meaning of nutriment (*āhāra*) is the meaning of condition (*paccaya*), then why are only these four mentioned, even though other conditions for sentient beings also exist?
It is said in reply: Because they are the specific conditions for the internal continuity (*ajjhattika-santati*).

For among beings who subsist on physical food, edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is the specific condition for the material body (*rūpakāya*); [and contact is the specific condition] for feeling within the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
Contact [is the condition] for consciousness; mental volition for consciousness; and consciousness for name-and-form. As it has been said:

“Just as, monks, this body is sustained by nutriment, persists in dependence on nutriment, and does not persist without nutriment; so too, with contact as condition there is feeling; with formations as condition there is consciousness; and with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form.”

What, then, is the nutriment here, and what does it nourish? Edible food nourishes the eight material qualities consisting of nutritive essence (*ojā*). Contact-nutriment nourishes the three feelings. Mental volition-nutriment nourishes the three realms of existence. Consciousness-nutriment nourishes the name-and-form at rebirth-linking. How so?
First, edible food, by the mere fact of being placed in the mouth, arouses the eight material qualities.

Furthermore, when it is chewed by the teeth and swallowed, each single morsel likewise arouses eight material qualities. In this way, it nourishes the eight material qualities consisting of nutritive essence.
As for the nutriment of contact: when a contact to be experienced as pleasant arises, it brings about pleasant feeling;
likewise, one to be experienced as painful brings about pain, and one to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant brings about neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Thus, in every way, the nutriment of contact brings about the three kinds of feeling. As for the nutriment of mental volition: volitional action leading to rebirth in the sense-sphere existence brings about sense-sphere existence; those leading to rebirth in the fine-material and immaterial existences bring about their respective existences. Thus, in every way, the nutriment of mental volition brings about the three realms of existence.
As for the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*), it is said that it "brings" those three aggregates associated with it at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*),

as well as the thirty material phenomena that arise by way of the three time-periods, through the method of conditions such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*). Thus, the nutriment of consciousness brings about the mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*) of rebirth-linking.
And here, mental volition is said to "bring about" (āharati) the three realms of existence; thus, it refers specifically to wholesome and unwholesome volitions accompanied by taints (*sāsrava*).
Consciousness is said to "bring about" rebirth-linking mentality-materiality; thus, it refers specifically to rebirth-linking consciousness.
However, these too should be understood as nutriments because they bring about, in a general sense, the states associated with them and the phenomena originated by them.

Among these four nutriments, edible food fulfills its function as nutriment by supporting [the body]. Contact does so by merely touching; mental volition by merely exerting itself; and consciousness by merely cognizing. How so?
Edible food indeed supports the body by maintaining it, thereby serving for the persistence of beings.
For even this body, though produced by kamma, is supported by edible food for ten years, or even for a hundred years.

It remains for as long as the measure of its lifespan. How so? Just as a child, though born of a mother, remains for a long time while being nourished by a nurse who feeds him milk and other sustenance; and just as a house supported by a prop remains [standing]. And this has been said:
"Great King, just as when a house is falling, they support it with another beam, and that which is supported by another beam..."
Just as that house, being thus maintained, does not fall into ruin, even so, Great King, this body is sustained by nutriment;
it persists in dependence upon nutriment.
In this way, edible food fulfills its function as a sustainer. And while performing this function, edible food—
Nutriment is a condition for two continuities of form: that which is produced by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*) and that which is clung-to (*upādinnaka*).
It is a condition by acting as a sustainer for those born of kamma; it is a condition by acting as a generator for those produced by nutriment.
Contact, however, by touching the object that serves as the basis for pleasure and so forth, [functions] through the occurrence of pleasant and other feelings in sentient beings.

It serves for the persistence [of beings]. Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*), by way of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, serves for the persistence of beings because it brings about the root of existence while itself being projected.
Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) serves for the persistence of beings precisely through its cognizing, by means of the continued occurrence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Furthermore, regarding these [nutriments] which accomplish the function of nutriment by way of support and so forth, four dangers are to be seen.
That is to say: in edible food there is fear in attachment itself; in contact there is fear in the act of approaching; in mental volition there is fear in the act of accumulation;
and in consciousness there is fear in the act of impingement. For what reason?

Because by forming an attachment to edible food, beings who prioritize cold and other such conditions perform various tasks such as counting coins for the sake of food, thereby [incurring] no small [amount of suffering].

They undergo suffering. Furthermore, some who have gone forth in this Teaching, by seeking food through improper means such as the practice of medicine and so forth, become objects of reproach even in this very life.

In the future life as well, they become "recluse-ghosts" (*samaṇa-peta*) according to the method described in the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*, beginning with the words, "Even his outer robe is burning and aflame. For this very reason:
It should be understood that it is precisely their craving for edible food that leads them to fear.
Even when they approach through contact, being addicted to the pleasure of touch, they commit offenses against the wives and other possessions guarded and protected by others.
Then, together with those possessions, the owners seize them, cut them into pieces, and [throw them] onto heaps of refuse.
They cast them out or hand them over to the king. Then the king causes various punishments to be inflicted upon them.
And with the breakup of the body, an unhappy destination is to be expected for them.
Thus, all fear—both pertaining to the present life and to future lives—is rooted in the gratification derived from contact. For this reason, one should simply avoid contact as nutriment.
It should be understood that "fear" refers to this.

However, it is precisely through the accumulation (*āyūhana*) of wholesome and unwholesome kamma that all fear rooted therein within the three realms of existence (*bhava*) comes to be. For this reason, it should be understood that in the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*), it is the act of accumulation itself that constitutes fear.
And as for the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), in whichever place it descends, in that very place the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of rebirth-linking arises.
Having been grasped, it is reborn; and when that is reborn, all fears are likewise reborn because they have that as their root.
For this reason, it should be understood that the very "falling upon" (abhinipāta) the nutriment of consciousness is itself fear.
Thus, regarding these nutriments accompanied by fear, the Perfectly Enlightened One [prohibited] the nutriment of physical food for the purpose of exhausting attachment to it.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, as a husband and wife,” and so forth, he taught by way of the simile of the son’s flesh.
For the purpose of exhausting attachment to the nutriment of contact, he taught by way of the simile of the flayed cow, beginning with: “In the same way, bhikkhus, as a flayed cow,” and so forth.

For the purpose of exhausting attachment to the nutriment of mental volition, [he taught] by way of the simile of the charcoal pit, beginning with: “In the same way, bhikkhus, as a charcoal pit,” and so forth.

By way of this method, he taught the simile of the pit of glowing embers. For the purpose of exhausting attachment to the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*), he taught the simile of being struck by a hundred spears, beginning with the words: "Bhikkhus, it is just as if a thief, a wrongdoer...
Herein, having established the actual fact, this is the brief application of the meaning: it is said that two husband and wife, taking their son...
With only a small amount of provisions for the journey, they set out upon a wilderness road five hundred yojanas long.
After they had traveled fifty yojanas, their provisions were exhausted. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they sat down in the scant shade.
Then a man said to his wife, "My dear, for fifty yojanas in every direction from here, there is neither village nor town. Therefore..."
“Whatever much work there is for a man to do, such as plowing or tending cattle, I am no longer able to do that.
Come, kill me, eat half my flesh, and making the other half into provisions, cross the desert together with your son.
She also said, “Husband, whatever much work there is for a woman to do, such as spinning thread and so forth, now I can no longer do that.”
"It is not possible for me to do that. Come, kill me, eat half the meat, and make the other half your provisions;
then cross the wilderness together with your son. Then he said to her: "Lady, by the death of a woman, the death of two is brought about.
For the dull-witted boy cannot live without his mother. If..."
"But we are still alive; perhaps we may obtain another child. Come now, let us kill our son, take his flesh, and cross the wilderness.
Then the mother said to her son, "Dear one, go to your father. He went there. Then his father said, "By me..."
“I have experienced no small amount of suffering through plowing, guarding cattle, and so forth, thinking ‘I shall raise this little son. I cannot kill my own son;
you yourself must kill your own son,” he said. Then, saying, “Dear boy, go right to your mother,” he departed.
Upon his arrival, his mother also said, “While I was longing for a son, I performed the cow-vow and the dog-vow, and made supplications to the deities.”
“Such insignificant suffering as this has been experienced by me; what need is there to speak of when I carried him in my womb?
I cannot kill my son,” she said, and added, “Dear one, go back to your father’s presence. Thus, he died while still on the way between the two places.
Seeing him, they lamented and, in the same manner previously described, took his flesh.
They departed while eating it. For those people, that diet of their own son’s flesh—being repulsive for nine reasons—was neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for finery, nor for adornment;

it was solely for the purpose of crossing the wilderness. If one asks, "By what nine reasons is it repulsive? [they are]: because it is the flesh of one born of the same womb, because it is the flesh of a kinsman, and because it is the flesh of one's own son.
Because it is the flesh of a beloved son, because it is fresh meat, because it is raw meat, because it is not cured with ghee, because it is unsalted, and because it is unsmoked.
Therefore, the bhikkhu who views edible food in this way—as being like the flesh of his own son—exhausts his attachment to it.
This, first of all, is the application of the meaning in the Simile of the Son’s Flesh.
In the simile of the flayed cow, however, just as that cow, having been stripped of its hide from the neck down to the hooves,
becomes a source of suffering while being devoured by worms wherever it stands supported by this or that [object],
so too, contact (phassa), wherever it stands supported by this or that basis (vatthu) or object (ārammaṇa), is a source of suffering arising from that respective basis and object.

It is precisely the basis for the suffering of feeling. Therefore, the bhikkhu who sees the nutriment of contact as being like a flayed cow exhausts his attachment to it; this is the application of the meaning in the simile of the flayed cow.
In the simile of the pit of embers, however, just as that pit of embers is, so too are the three realms of existence in the sense of great burning. Just as...
Two men who drag [something] along by seizing it with various arms represent mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) in the sense of dragging one along through the realms of existence (*bhava*).
Therefore, the monk who sees the nutriment of mental volition as being like those men dragging one along in a pit of glowing embers exhausts his attachment to it;
this is the application of the meaning in the simile of the pit of glowing embers.
In the simile of the three hundred spears, however, when that man is struck by the first hundred spears in the morning, those spears do not remain within his body;
having made a hundred wound-entrances, they pass straight through and fall only on the other side.
The same applies to the other two hundred spears. Thus, by the spears that have passed through without stopping at the places where they fell, [his body becomes covered].
The entire body becomes completely perforated with openings; there is no measure for the pain arising even from a single wound, let alone from three hundred wounds.
In this context, the moment of the descent of the sword is like the moment of the production of rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*).
The formation of the wounds is like the production of the aggregates (*khandha*). The arising of painful feeling within the wounds is like [the suffering] in the produced aggregates.
The arising of various kinds of suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Another method: rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) is like a man who commits a violent crime;
the mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by that consciousness is like the wound-openings produced by his sword-strikes;

and the arising of harsh suffering for that man due to the wound-openings is like the thirty-two types of tortures and the ninety-eight diseases, etc., [that arise] for consciousness conditioned by mind-and-body.

The arising of suffering in its various forms is to be seen. Therefore, the bhikkhu who views the nutriment of consciousness as being like one struck by a hundred spears exhausts his attachment to it; this is the application of the meaning in the simile of being struck by a hundred spears.

Thus, exhausting his attachment to these nutriments, he fully understands all four nutriments, and when these are fully understood, every object that is to be fully understood becomes fully understood. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, when edible food is fully understood, lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood.
When lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter by which a noble disciple might return again to this world.
Bhikkhus, when contact as nutriment is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood.”
[They] come to be. When the three feelings have been fully understood, I say that for the noble disciple there is nothing further to be done.
When the nutriment of mental volition has been fully understood, bhikkhus, the three cravings have been fully understood.
When the three cravings have been fully understood, I say that for the noble disciple there is nothing further to be done. Regarding consciousness, bhikkhus...
“When nutriment is fully understood, name-and-form is fully understood. When name-and-form is fully understood, I say that for the noble disciple there is nothing further to be done.
Thus, with the arising of craving comes the arising of nutriment; from the arising of prior craving comes the arising of the nutriments associated with rebirth-linking.

The meaning is: "it has been produced. How so? At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), there exists nutritive essence (*ojā*) born within the thirty-two types of material phenomena that arise by way of the threefold continuity.
This is the "clung-to" (*upādinnaka*) edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) produced with craving as its condition.

Furthermore, contact (*phassa*) and volition (*cetanā*) associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness, as well as the consciousness itself, are the "clung-to" contact and mental volition produced with craving as their condition.
"Consciousness as nutriment. Thus, first of all, the origin of the nutriments pertaining to rebirth-linking should be understood as arising from prior craving.

Since, however, the nutriments here have been spoken of by mixing together both those that are clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and those that are not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), therefore the origin of the nutriments that are not clung-to should also be understood as arising from craving in this same way.
For among those things originated by the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed...
There is nutritive essence (*ojā*) in material forms; this is the non-clung-to edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) produced with craving as its condition.

Furthermore, contact and volition associated with greed-accompanied consciousness, as well as the consciousness itself, are the non-clung-to contact, mental volition, and consciousness foods produced with craving as their condition.

"With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of nutriment": by the cessation of craving—which is the condition for both types of nutriment, the acquired (*upādinnaka*) and the unacquired (*anupādinnaka*)—the cessation of nutriment is made known. The rest is exactly as previously stated. However, this is the distinction:
here all four truths are stated in their own specific forms. And just as they are here, so too in all subsequent sections.
Therefore, one who is not confused in any respect should extract the truths.
And in all instances, this presentation of the teaching—“Even by this much, friend”—should be applied according to the specific doctrine taught in each respective place.
Herein, first of all, the application is as follows: “Even by this much” means even by way of the attention and penetration described in this teaching on nutriment.
This has been stated. This same method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the section on nutriment is finished.
The commentary on the section on the truths begins.

91. Now, having rejoiced in and expressed appreciation for the Elder’s speech in the same manner as before, saying, "Excellent, friend," those bhikkhus asked further questions. And the Elder answered them by means of another method.
This same procedure applies to all subsequent sections. Therefore, from here on, I shall not repeat such phrases.
In whatever manner he explains it, we shall describe the meaning of each of those.
However, regarding the brief teaching of this section, "he understands suffering," here "suffering" refers to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
As for everything that ought to be said in the detailed teaching, all of that has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the "Exposition of the Truths" (*Saccaniddesa*).
The commentary on the section on the Truths is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on Aging and Death (Jarāmaraṇa-vāra): 92.
From here onwards, the teaching proceeds by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). In that regard, first, concerning the section on aging and death: their...
"Tesam" (of them) should be understood as a collective designation for many beings in brief.
For even if one were to speak for an entire day, saying "the aging of Devadatta," "the aging of Somadatta," and so on, beings would never be exhausted;
yet by these two words, no being remains unaccounted for. Therefore it was said:
“This is, in brief, a general description common to many beings.
In the phrase “in this or that,” this is a general description common to many classes [of beings] according to their destiny and birth.
“In a class of beings” is a specific illustration of what was described by means of that general description. Furthermore, in the passage beginning “aging is decrepitude,” *jarā* refers to...

The description of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-niddesa*). "Decaying" (*jīraṇatā*) is a description of its mode (*ākāra-niddesa*). "Fragmentation" (*khaṇḍicca*) and the others are descriptions of functions (*kicca-niddesa*) that occur when time has passed.
The final two are descriptions of its natural state (*pakati-niddesa*). For by this term "this aging," it is illuminated according to its intrinsic nature;
therefore, this is its description of intrinsic nature. By the term "decaying," it is [described] according to its mode; therefore, this is its description of mode. By the term "fragmentation"...
Because of its function of causing the teeth and nails to become broken when time has passed; by the term *pālicca*, because of its function of causing the hair of the head and body to turn grey;

and by the term *valittacatā*, because of its function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to wrinkle—these three, beginning with *khaṇḍicca*, are descriptions of its functions at the passing of time. By means of these, [the nature] of these...
Manifest aging is demonstrated by way of the observation of its transformations.

For just as the path traversed by water, fire, or wind becomes manifest through the breaking, crushing, burning, or charring of grasses, trees, and so forth, yet that traversed path is not identical to those very elements such as water;
even so, [aging is manifest] in the teeth and other parts by way of their brokenness and so on.
A path already traversed is evident and can be perceived even with eyes open. However, decrepitude and so forth are not themselves aging, for aging is not something cognizable by the eye.
Rather, it is through these terms—"the dwindling of the life-span" and "the ripening of the faculties"—that [aging] becomes manifest specifically upon the passing of time.

It is illustrated by the natural process known as the exhaustion of the life-span and the maturation of the faculties, such as the eye. Therefore, these latter two should be understood as descriptions of the nature [of aging].

In this context, because the life-span of one who has reached old age diminishes, aging is described as "the dwindling of the life-span" by way of a metaphorical designation for its result (*phalūpacāra*).

It is said [thus]. And because the faculties such as the eye, which were very clear in childhood and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects of their own domain, become fully ripened, agitated, and dull when one has reached old age, such that they are incapable of grasping even coarse objects of their own domain;
therefore, it is called "the ripening of the faculties" by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
It has been stated. Furthermore, this aging, as thus described, is of two kinds: manifest and concealed.
Among these, aging regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) is called "manifest aging" because the state of being broken, etc., is seen in the teeth and so forth.
However, it is called "concealed aging" regarding immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) because no such transformation is seen there. In that regard, this state of being broken, etc.,...
That which is seen—because such things as teeth and so forth are easily discernible—is indeed their color;

having seen that with the eye and reflected upon it by means of the mind-door, one knows aging through the thought, "These teeth have been struck by old age," just as one knows the presence of water below by observing the heads of oxen tied up in a watering place.
Furthermore, it is also twofold: without interval (*avīci*) and with interval (*savīci*).

Therein, because the specific differences in color and so forth among gems, gold, silver, coral, the sun, and so on—whether animate beings such as humans or inanimate things such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts—are difficult to discern due to their occurrence at intervals, this aging is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīcijarā*); the meaning is "continuous aging.
However, in other cases among those mentioned above, [aging occurs] with intervals between the specific differences in color and so forth.
Because it is easily understood, aging should be known as "aging with intervals" (*savīcijarā*).

From this point onward, the passage beginning with "of those respective... should be understood according to the method already stated. Regarding the terms "falling away" (*cuti*) and "the state of falling away" (*cavanatā*), "falling away" (*cuti*) is spoken of in the sense of the act of falling away;
this is a collective term for one, four, or five aggregates. "The state of falling away" (*cavanatā*) is expressed by means of an abstract noun (*bhāva-vacana*).
The demonstration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇanidassana*). "Dissolution" (*bhedo*) is the indication of the arising of the breakup of the aggregates at death (*cutikkhandhānaṃ*).
"Disappearance" (*antaradhānaṃ*) is the indication of the non-existence of the broken aggregates at death in any manner whatsoever, just like a broken jar.
"Death" (*maccu maraṇaṃ*) is death known as *maccu*; by this, he excludes the death of annihilation (*samucchedamaraṇa*) and so forth. "Time" (*kālo*)...
“Antaka” means the ender; its activity is “kālakiriyā” (the act of passing away). By this, he illustrates death according to worldly convention (*lokasammuti*).
Now, in order to illustrate it according to ultimate truth (*paramattha*), he says: “The dissolution of the aggregates,” and so forth.

For in ultimate truth, only the aggregates dissolve; no so-called “being” dies at all. However, when the aggregates are dissolving, there is the conventional expression “the being dies,” and when they have dissolved, there is the expression “he has died.”
And here, the dissolution of the aggregates is by way of the four-aggregate [existence], and the casting off of the physical body is by way of the one-aggregate [existence].

Alternatively, it should be understood that the dissolution of the aggregates is by way of the four-aggregate [existence], and the casting off of the physical body is by way of the remaining two. Why?
Because the physical body, which is reckoned as the "form-body" (rūpakāya), occurs in both states of existence. Or else, because—
In the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth, the aggregates simply disintegrate and nothing is deposited;
therefore, in their case, there is the "disintegration of the aggregates. In the human realm and so forth, there is the "deposition of the carcass.
Here, it should be understood that death is called the "deposition of the carcass" because it is the cause for the deposition of the carcass.
"Thus, this aging and this death—this, friends, is called 'aging-and-death'. Having combined both of these together, they are spoken of as "aging-and-death. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on aging-and-death is finished.
The commentary on the section on birth begins.
93. Regarding the section on birth (*jāti*): in such terms as "birth" (*jāti*) and "arising" (*sañjāti*), it is "birth" in the sense of being born;

this is applicable by way of incomplete sense bases (*aparipuṇṇāyatana*). It is "arising" in the sense of fully arising; this is applicable by way of complete sense bases (*paripuṇṇāyatana*). It is "descent" (*okkanti*) in the sense of descending; this is applicable by way of egg-born and womb-born beings (*aṇḍaja-jalābuja*).
For these, while descending—that is, entering—the egg-shell and the amniotic sac respectively.
They take rebirth-linking as if they were visible beings. In the sense of being produced, it is "production" (*abhinibbatti*);
this is appropriate for moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, for they are produced having already become manifest. This, first of all, is the teaching by way of conventional usage.
Now follows the teaching by way of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). For it is only the aggregates (*khandhā*) that appear in the ultimate sense, not a "being" (*satta*).

In that context, "of the aggregates" (khandhānaṃ) should be understood as referring to one [aggregate] in a single-mode existence (ekavokāra-bhava), four [aggregates] in a four-mode existence (catuvokāra-bhava), and five [aggregates] in a five-mode existence (pañcavokāra-bhava).
"Manifestation" (pātubhāvo) means arising. Regarding "of the bases" (āyatanānaṃ), the inclusion here should be understood by way of the bases that arise in their respective locations.
"Acquisition" (paṭilābho) is simply the manifestation within the continuity (santati).

For those [aggregates] become "attained" precisely as they are appearing. With the phrase, "This, friends, is called birth," he provides the conclusion for birth as taught both conventionally and in the ultimate sense.

Furthermore, in the expression "from the origin of existence" (*bhava-samudaya*), it should be understood that "existence" refers to kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*) which serves as the condition for birth. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the section on birth is finished.
Commentary on the section on existence (bhava-vāra). 94.
In the section on existence, "existence in the sense-sphere" (kāmabhava) refers to both kamma-existence (kammabhava) and rebirth-existence (upapattibhava). Therein, what is called kamma-existence...
It is precisely karma that leads to existence in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*).

Because it is the cause for rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), it is called "existence" (*bhava*) by way of a metaphorical designation for its fruit—just as in such expressions as, "The arising of Buddhas is blissful; the accumulation of evil is suffering.
Rebirth-existence refers to the pentad of appropriated aggregates (*upādinnakhandha*) produced by that karma. For it is called "existence" (*bhava*) because one comes to be (*bhavati*) therein.
Thus it has been stated. In this way, both this karma and its resultant rebirth are here called "sense-sphere existence" (*kāmabhava*) in every respect.

This same method applies to fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpabhava* and *arūpabhava*). Regarding the phrase "from the arising of clinging" (*upādānasamudayā*), here clinging is a condition for wholesome karmic existence solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*); however, for unwholesome karmic existence, it is a condition both by way of decisive support and by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), and so forth.
But for all rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), it is solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on existence (*bhavavāra*) is finished.
Commentary on the section on clinging (*upādānavāra*).

95. In the section on clinging (*upādāna*), regarding the terms "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*) and so forth: it is called *kāmupādāna* because one clings to sense-objects by means of this [craving], or because it itself clings to them;
or alternatively, it is *kāmupādāna* because it is both sense-pleasure (*kāma*) and clinging (*upādāna*). "Clinging" (*upādāna*) is said to mean firm grasping.

For here the prefix *upa-* has the sense of firmness, as in such examples as "extreme distress" (*upāyāsa*) or "imminent" (*upakaṭṭha*); it refers to the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

This is a synonym. This is the summary here. In detail, however, this should be understood according to the method stated thus: "In this context, what is clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*)? It is the lustful desire for sense-pleasures.
Likewise, it is "clinging to views" (*diṭṭhupādāna*) because it is both a view and a clinging; or else, it is so called because one clings to a view, or they cling [to it].
Or, by this term "view" (diṭṭhi), "clinging to views" (diṭṭhupādāna) is meant. For a later view clings to a prior view, and they cling to that view as well.
As it is said: "The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is vain," and so forth.

This is a designation for every form of speculative view, with the exception of clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna) and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). This is the meaning here.
This is the summary. In detail, however, this should be understood according to the method stated in the passage: "Therein, what is clinging to views? [The view that] 'there is no giving'...
Likewise, it is *sīlabbatupādāna* because one clings by means of it, or because it itself clings, or because it is both virtue-and-observance (*sīlabbata*) and clinging (*upādāna*).
For the cow-virtue, ox-virtue, and so forth, are themselves clingings due to the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) that purity comes through them.

This is the summary here. For the detailed explanation, however, this should be understood according to the method stated [in the Paṭisambhidāmagga]: "In that regard, what is clinging to rules and observances? It is the purification through the virtue of recluses and brahmins outside of this [Dhamma].
Now, they speak by means of this, thus it is "discourse" (vāda). They cling by means of this, thus it is "clinging" (upādāna). What do they speak, what do they cling to?

Or what? The self. Or, the clinging to the doctrine of self is "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*attavādupādāna*). Alternatively, it is called "clinging to the doctrine of self" because by means of it one clings to the mere doctrine of self as being the self;
this is a designation for the twenty-based view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
This is the summary here. But in detail: "In that regard, what is clinging to the doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling... [and so forth].
This is to be understood according to the method stated as: “one who does not see the Noble Ones. Regarding the phrase “from the arising of craving”:

here, craving is a condition for the clinging to sense-pleasures by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), or by way of immediate, contiguous, absence, disappearance, and repetition; however, for the remaining [types of clinging], it is also by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on clinging is finished.

Commentary on the Section on Craving (Taṇhāvāra) 96. In the section on craving, from "craving for forms" (*rūpataṇhā*) up to "craving for mental phenomena" (*dhammataṇhā*), craving— which occurs in the impulsion process within the eye-door and so forth—
is designated according to its object, which resembles its father, just as one is named after one's father in such expressions as "the merchant’s son" or "the brahmin’s son."
This is the name. And here, craving with visible form as its object is "craving for form" (*rūpatanha*).
When that [craving] proceeds by relishing form through the state of sensual lust, it is "craving for sense-pleasures" (*kāmatanha*).

When it proceeds by relishing form as permanent, stable, and eternal through the state of lust accompanied by the view of eternalism, it is "craving for existence" (*bhavatanha*). Through the state of lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism...
"Form is cut off, destroyed, and will not exist after death"—finding gratification in this way as it occurs is craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
Thus, it is threefold. And just as there is craving for form, so too are there cravings for sounds and the rest; thus these constitute eighteen modes of craving-conduct (*taṇhāvicarita*).
These are eighteen with respect to internal form and so forth, and eighteen with respect to external form and so forth, making thirty-six. Thus...
There are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present, making one hundred and eight.
Based on internal [objects], there are eighteen such as “I am” and “I am thus,” which depend on internal form and so forth;
based on external [objects], there are [eighteen] such as “I am by means of this” and “I am thus by means of this,” which depend on external form and so forth.
"Eighteen" means thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present;

in this way, there are one hundred and eight modes of craving's wandering. When these are further condensed, among the objects such as visible forms and so forth, there are only six groups of craving, which are the three types beginning with sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*). Thus—
Through the meaning of exposition, through the detailed exposition, and again through the summary of that detail, craving is to be understood by the discerning one.
Herein, regarding "the origin of feeling," "feeling" refers to resultant feeling. How does it [arise] at the six doors?
If it is asked, "Is it a condition for craving?"—it is so because of its being gratifying. For, through the gratification of pleasant feeling, beings come to identify with that feeling;
having generated craving for feeling and becoming stained by passion for feeling, they long only for desirable forms at the eye-door.
Having obtained them, they relish them, and they show honor to the painters and others who provided those objects.
Likewise, through the doors of the ear and so forth, they crave desirable sounds and the like; having obtained them, they relish them;
and they show honor to those who provide the objects, such as lute-players, perfumers, cooks, weavers, and various craftsmen. How is this so?
Just as those who cherish their children out of parental affection and claim them as their own show honor to the nurse, providing her only with wholesome ghee, oil, milk, and the like.
They give him drink and feed him. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on craving is finished.
The commentary on the section on feeling.
97. In the section on feeling (*vedanāvāra*), "bodies of feeling" (*vedanākāyā*) means aggregates of feeling. Regarding the passage, "feeling born of eye-contact... pe...

feeling born of mind-contact," because this is taught in the *Vibhaṅga* as follows—"There is feeling born of eye-contact that is wholesome, there is unwholesome, and there is indeterminate"—it refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate feelings occurring in the eye-door and so forth. [Thus it was said: "Sāriputta..."
In such passages as “Mantāṇiputta,” there is a name based on a factor similar to the mother, just as there are names derived from the mother herself. As for the meaning of the words here:
feeling born with eye-contact as its cause is "feeling born of eye-contact. This same method applies everywhere.
This, then, is the comprehensive explanation. However, by way of kamma-result (vipāka), there are two types of eye-consciousness at the eye-door.
Feeling should be understood by way of association with these: the two mind-elements and the three mind-consciousness elements.
This same method applies to the ear-door and so forth. In the mind-door, [feeling] is associated only with the mind-consciousness element.

Regarding the phrase "from the arising of contact": here, in the case of the five doors, it refers to the arising of the eye-contact and so forth that are co-nascent with the feelings based on the five physical bases.
There is an origination. For the remaining [feelings], such as those born of eye-contact and so forth, the conditions exist by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) and other modes.

In the mind-door (*manodvāra*), it should be understood that for the feelings of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), as well as for the feelings of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and death (*cuti*)—which are not door-born—their origination occurs through the origination of the mind-contact (*manosamphassa*) that arises simultaneously with them.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on feeling is finished.
Commentary on the section on contact (Phassavāra): 98.
Regarding the phrase "eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*) in the section on contact, it is contact occurring in the eye. This same method applies everywhere. Eye-contact... [and so forth].
"Body-contact": by this much, ten contacts consisting of the fivefold bases that are the resultants of wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] have been stated.
"Mind-contact": by this term, the remaining twenty-two worldly resultant contacts associated with the mind are included.
"From the arising of the six sense-bases": through the arising of the six bases, beginning with the eye, there is the arising of these six kinds of contact as well.
It should be understood that [it] "occurs. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on contact (*phassavāra*) is finished.
The commentary on the section on the six sense bases (*saḷāyatanavāra*).

99. Regarding what should be said concerning the "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth in the section on the six bases (*saḷāyatanavāra*), all of that follows the very same method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the Description of the Aggregates (*khandhaniddesa*) and the Description of the Bases (*āyatananiddesa*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the origination of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpasamudaya*):
herein, by way of whichever name, whichever form, and whichever name-and-form serves as the condition for whichever base, [it is explained] according to the method in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The arising of the sixfold base should be understood as resulting from the arising of name-and-form, according to the method stated in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
The remainder is exactly as previously described.
The commentary on the section on the sixfold base is concluded.

Commentary on the Section on Name-and-Form (Nāmarūpavāra) 100. In the section on name-and-form, "name" has the characteristic of bending toward [the object], and "form" has the characteristic of being affected.

In its detailed exposition, "feeling" refers to the aggregate of feeling; "perception" refers to the aggregate of perception; and "volition," "contact," and "attention" refer to the aggregate of mental formations.

This is how it should be understood. While it is true that there are other phenomena included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), these three [mental factors] are present even in the most feeble states of consciousness.
Therefore, it is by way of these alone that the aggregate of mental formations is shown here. Regarding the phrase "the four great elements" (*cattāri mahābhūtāni*):
here, "four" (*cattāri*) is a numerical delimitation; "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) is a designation for earth, water, fire, and air.

This is a designation. Furthermore, the reason why those are called "great elements" (mahābhūta), as well as any other method of analysis regarding this matter, has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha-niddesa).
Regarding the phrase "derived from the four great elements" (catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya): here, the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayogatthe*).
"Four great elements" is what is meant. "Derived from" (*upādāya*) means having taken up, having grasped; such is the meaning. Some also say it means "depending on.
The word "occurring" (*vattamāna*) is a textual supplement here. Or, this genitive case-ending has the sense of a collection.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "matter occurring derived from the collection of the four great elements. Thus it is in all instances.

All those four great elements beginning with earth, as well as the twenty-three kinds of derived matter—such as the eye-base and so forth—which exist dependent upon the four great elements and are stated in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself, should all be understood as "matter.
Regarding the phrase "from the arising of consciousness": here, whatever consciousness belongs to whatever mind (nāma)...

And as for that which is the condition for both form and for name-and-form, by way of that, the arising of name-and-form from the arising of consciousness is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on name-and-form is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Consciousness (Viññāṇavāra) 101.
Regarding the section on consciousness: "eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) means consciousness in the eye, or consciousness born from the eye;
thus it is called eye-consciousness. Ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness are to be understood in the same way. As for the other, however, the mind itself is consciousness.

"Mental consciousness" (manoviññāṇa): this is a designation for the resultant consciousness of the three planes, excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness. Regarding "from the arising of formations" (saṅkhārasamudayā):
here, one should understand the arising of consciousness from the arising of formations according to whichever formation serves as the condition for whichever consciousness.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on consciousness is finished.

Commentary on the section on formations (saṅkhāra): In the section on formations, a formation has the characteristic of forming. In the detailed section, however, it is called "bodily formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra).

"Volitional formation of the body" (*kāya-saṅkhāra*) is a volitional formation that proceeds from the body; it is a designation for the twenty types of bodily volition (*kāya-sañcetanā*), consisting of eight wholesome and twelve unwholesome types of sense-sphere volition that proceed by way of impulsion in the door of the body.

"Volitional formation of speech" (*vacī-saṅkhāra*) is a volitional formation that proceeds from speech; it is a designation for the same twenty types of vocal volition (*vacī-sañcetanā*) that proceed by way of the differentiation of utterances in the door of speech.
This is a designation. "Mental formation" (*cittasaṅkhāra*) refers to a formation that proceeds from the mind;

it is a designation for the twenty-nine types of mental volition (*manosañcetanā*)—both mundane wholesome and unwholesome—that arise when one sits in seclusion and reflects, without yet performing any stirring of body or speech.

Regarding the phrase "from the arising of ignorance," here [ignorance] acts as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the wholesome and as a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta*) and so forth for the unwholesome.
It should be understood that ignorance is the condition. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the section on volitional formations is finished.
The commentary on the section on ignorance begins.
103. Regarding the section on ignorance (*avijjā*), "ignorance concerning suffering" means ignorance regarding the truth of suffering;

this is a designation for delusion (*moha*). The same method applies to the phrases "ignorance concerning the origin," and so forth. Therein, ignorance concerning suffering should be understood by way of four reasons:
by inclusion, by basis, by object, and by concealment. For it is thus: because it is included within the truth of suffering, it is [ignorance] concerning suffering.
Included within it, the foundation (vatthu) serves as the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the truth of suffering, and as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for the object;
furthermore, it conceals this truth of suffering by obstructing the penetration of its characteristics as they truly are,
and by not permitting the arising of knowledge therein.
Ignorance regarding origination (samudaya) is to be understood through three reasons: by way of its basis, by way of its object, and by way of concealment.
Ignorance regarding cessation (nirodha) and the path (paṭipadā) is to be understood by only one reason: by way of concealment.
For ignorance is indeed a concealer of cessation and the path, because it prevents the penetration of their true characteristics and obstructs the arising of knowledge regarding them.
It is not included therein because it is not comprised within those two truths.
Those two truths are not its basis because they do not arise simultaneously with it. Nor are they its object, because [ignorance] does not proceed by taking them as its object.
For the latter two truths are difficult to see due to their profundity, and in this case, ignorance—which is like blindness—does not operate. As for the former...
Furthermore, it is profound because its intrinsic characteristic is difficult to see in the sense that it deceives; therein it proceeds by way of grasping through perversion (*vipallāsa*).

Moreover, by the phrase "in suffering," ignorance is explained in terms of its inclusion, its basis, its object, and its function. By the phrase "in the origin of suffering," it is explained in terms of its basis, its object, and its function.
[And by the phrases] "in the cessation of suffering" and "in the way leading to the cessation of suffering," [it is explained in terms of its basis, its object, and its function].

Thus far, [ignorance has been defined] by way of its function. However, it should be understood that it is indicated by its intrinsic nature through the term "non-knowing" (*aññāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "the origin of the taints" (*āsavasamudaya*):

here, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) serve as conditions for ignorance (*avijjā*) by way of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*), and so forth. The taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*), however, serves as a condition only by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the ignorance which has arisen previously is what is called the "taint of ignorance. That [previous ignorance] serves as a condition for the ignorance that arises subsequently...
Ignorance is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). The remainder is exactly as stated in the method already explained.
The commentary on the section on ignorance is finished. [Now begins] the commentary on the section on the taints (*āsava*).
104. Regarding the section on the taints (*āsava*), concerning the phrase "the origination of ignorance" (*avijjā-samudaya*):

here, ignorance (*avijjā*) is a condition for the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) by way of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*), and so forth; it is a condition for the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

Furthermore, in this context, the ignorance that arises repeatedly is to be understood as the "taint of ignorance. Priorly arisen ignorance serves as the decisive support condition for this subsequently arising taint of ignorance.

...it exists. The remainder is exactly as previously stated. This section is spoken by way of showing the condition even for that ignorance (*avijjā*) which is the eldest among the terms for dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
By means of this section thus stated, the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is established. How so?
For with the arising of the taints (*āsava*), there is the arising of ignorance; and with the arising of ignorance, there is also the arising of the taints.
Thus, since the taints (*āsava*) are conditioned by ignorance (*avijjā*), and ignorance is also a condition for the taints, no prior limit (*pubbakoṭi*) of ignorance is discerned.
Because that [limit] is not discerned, the beginninglessness (*anamatagga*) of *saṃsāra* is established.

Thus, all these—namely, the section on the courses of action (*kammapatha-vāra*), the section on nutriment (*āhāra-vāra*), the section on suffering (*dukkha-vāra*), and [the sections on] aging-and-death, birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form—[are explained] in this sutta.
The section on the taints (āsava) of consciousness, volitional formations, and ignorance consists of sixteen sections.
Within these, each section is divided into two parts—concise and detailed—resulting in thirty-two topics.
Thus, in this sutta, the Four Noble Truths are taught within these thirty-two topics. By way of further elaboration upon these very same [topics]...
Arahatta is spoken of in the sixteen places mentioned; however, according to the opinion of the Elder [Mahāsīva], the four truths and the four paths are spoken of in all thirty-two places.

Thus, throughout the entire Word of the Buddha comprised within the five great Nikāyas, there is no such discourse wherein the four truths are repeated thirty-two times and [the paths] likewise thirty-two times.
"Arahantship has been proclaimed apart from this *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta*.

"This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said"—this means that the Venerable Sāriputta spoke the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta*, having adorned it with sixty-four reasons: thirty-two expositions on the Four Noble Truths and thirty-two expositions on Arahantship; [and the assembly was] elated.
Those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta.
The commentary on the section concerning the taints is finished.
[From] the Papañcasūdani, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta*. In that context, "he dwells among the Kurus" means he dwells among those inhabitants of the countryside known as the Kurus.
O princes, even a single province where they dwell is called "Kuru" by conventional usage; [the Buddha dwelt] in that Kuru country.

However, the masters of the commentaries say: in the time of King Mandhātu, among the three continents, the human world known as Jambudīpa was the supreme continent, the birthplace of sublime persons such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, and Wheel-turning Monarchs.

Having heard that it was exceedingly beautiful, they came along with King Mandhātu, the Wheel-turning Monarch, as he traveled through the four continents preceded by the Wheel-treasure. Then the king asked the General-treasure:
"Is there indeed any place more beautiful than the human world?"
“Why, O King, do you speak thus?
Do you not see the majesty of the moon and the sun?
Is their place not more delightful than this?”
The King, preceded by the Wheel-Treasure, went there.

Upon hearing that "Great King Mandhātu has arrived," the Four Great Kings thought, "This king is of great power and majesty; he cannot be resisted through battle," and they surrendered their own kingdoms to him.
Having taken them, he asked again: "Is there any place more delightful than this?"
Then they described the Tāvatiṃsa realm to him: “Your Majesty, the Tāvatiṃsa realm is more delightful.
There, these four Great Kings stand as attendants at the gate of Sakka, the King of the Gods.
Sakka, the King of the Gods, is of great psychic power and great majesty. Furthermore, these are his places of enjoyment: [the palace] is one thousand yojanas in height.”
The Vejayanta Palace; the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods, five hundred yojanas in height; the Vejayanta chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas long;
likewise the elephant Erāvaṇa; the Nandana Grove adorned with a thousand celestial trees, the Cittalātā Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and the Missaka Grove;
and the Pāricchattaka Koviḷāra tree, one hundred yojanas in height, beneath which—
“The Pandukambala stone is sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas high;
it has the color of the jayasumana flower, and because of its softness, half the body of Sakka sinks into it as he sits.
Having heard this, the king, desiring to go there, urged on the Wheel-treasure. It halted in the sky together with him.

With his fourfold army. Then, from the midst of two divine worlds, the Wheel-Treasure descended and established itself upon the earth together with the fourfold army headed by the Counsellor-Treasure.
The king went alone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Upon hearing that Mandhātā had arrived, Sakka went out to meet him.
“Welcome to you, Great King; it is yours, Great King. Command us, Great King,” he said, and having divided the kingdom into two parts along with his dancers, he gave one portion to him.
As soon as the king was established in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his human nature vanished and his divine nature appeared.
It is said that when he sits with Sakka upon the Paṇḍukambala stone, no difference between them is perceived even for the duration of an eyeblink.
Failing to observe this, the devas are deluded regarding the distinction between Sakka and him.
While experiencing celestial splendor there, he exercises sovereignty until thirty-six Sakkas have arisen and passed away.
Exhausted by sensual pleasures, he fell from that state and, having established himself in his own garden, passed away with his body afflicted by wind and heat.

When the Wheel-Treasure had been established upon the earth, the Counsellor-Treasure had the sandals of Mandhātu engraved upon a golden plate and governed the kingdom, saying, "This is the realm of Mandhātu.
Then the people who had come from the three continents once again—
Being unable to go further, they approached the Jewel of the General and requested: "Your Majesty, we have come through the majesty of the King, but now we are unable to proceed;
please grant us a place to dwell. He gave each of them a province.
Among these, the region inhabited by the people who had come from Pubbavideha was called the kingdom of Videha, according to that very same previous designation.
It received the name [Aparanta]. The region inhabited by people who had come from Aparagoyāna received the name the "Aparanta country.
The region inhabited by people who had come from Uttarakuru received the name the "Kuru kingdom.
However, because it comprises many villages, market towns, and so forth, it is expressed in the plural; hence it is said: "He dwells among the Kurus."
"Kammāsadhamma is the name of a market town of the Kurus. Regarding "Kammāsadhamma," some here explain the meaning by substituting the letter *da* for the letter *dha*.
It is "Kammāsadhamma" because the "Kammāsa" was tamed (*damita*) there. "Kammāsa" refers to Kammāsapāda, also called Porisāda.
It is said that where his foot had been pierced by a splinter, as the wound healed, it became like heartwood.
He grew there; therefore, he became known as Kammāsapāda. And in that place, he was tamed and restrained from his nature as a man-eater by whom?
By the Great Being. In which Jātaka did this occur? Some say it was in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka;
however, these elders say it was in the Jayaddisa Jātaka, for it was at that time that the Great Being tamed Kammāsapāda. As it is said:
“When I was the son of Jayaddisa,
the lord of the kingdom of Pañcāla,
I sacrificed my own life and liberated my father.”
"I also inspired confidence in Kammāsapāda.
However, some explain the meaning using the letter *dha* instead.

It is said that among the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kuru, there was a custom (*kuruvatta-dhamma*) according to which, when that *kammāsa* tree grew there, that place was called "Kammāsadhamma," meaning "the place where the custom [of the *kammāsa*] arose."
Thus it is said. This is also the name of the town situated there. Why was it not expressed using the locative case?
Because it was not a place of residence. It is said that the Blessed One had no monastery at all as a place of residence within that town.
However, having departed from the town, there was a great forest grove on a certain delightful piece of ground well-supplied with water.
The Blessed One dwelt there. Having made that town his alms-resort village, the meaning here should be understood thus:
"He dwells among the Kurus; Kammāsadhamma is the name of a town of the Kurus, and he has made that his alms-resort village.
Commentary on the Section of the Summary.
106. “This, monks, is the one-way path. Why did the Blessed One speak this sutta? Because the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kuru were capable of receiving the profound teaching.

It is said that the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru—due to the excellence of the seasonal conditions and the like in that kingdom, and through their cultivation of favorable seasonal conditions—were well-suited for it.
They are always healthy in body and healthy in mind. Because their strength of wisdom is supported by this health of mind and body, they are capable of grasping profound discourse.

Therefore, perceiving in them this capacity for receiving this profound teaching, the Blessed One, having assigned the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) leading to Arahantship across twenty-one stages, [taught] this profound meaning.

He spoke the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. For just as a man, having obtained a golden casket, might place various flowers within it, or having obtained a golden chest, might place the seven precious gems therein, even so did the Blessed One, having obtained the assembly of those dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru, teach the profound instruction. Therefore, there are other profound meanings here as well.

In the Dīghanikāya he taught the Mahānidāna Sutta and the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta; in this Majjhimanikāya, he taught the Sāropama, Rukkhūpama, Raṭṭhapāla, Māgaṇḍiya, Āneñjasappāya, and other discourses as well.
Moreover, in that district, the four assemblies were already by their very nature devoted to the practice of the development of mindfulness.
They dwell [in this way], even their slaves, laborers, and attendants speak only talk connected with the foundations of mindfulness.
Even at water-crossings, spinning places, and other such locations, no idle chatter whatsoever occurs.
If any woman is asked, "Mother, which foundation of mindfulness do you attend to?"...
She says, "Nothing at all. They reproach her, saying, "Shame on your life! Though you are living, you are like one who is dead.
Then, after admonishing her, "Do not act like this again," they cause her to learn one of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
But as for her who says, "I am attending to such-and-such a foundation of mindfulness," they say to her, "Excellent, excellent!"
Having given their applause, they praise him with words such as, "Your life is well-lived; you have indeed attained human birth;

for your sake, the Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared," and so forth. Not only those of the human race, but even animals dwelling in dependence upon them, are possessed of mindfulness and mental attention.
In this regard, there is this story: it is said that a certain actor [found] a young parrot...

Having taken it, he wandered about teaching it. While living near the nuns' quarters, at the time of his departure, he forgot the young parrot and went away. The female novices took it and cared for it;
they gave it the name Buddhārakkhita. One day, seeing him sitting before her, the Elder Nun said, "Buddhārakkhita?"
"What is it, noble sir?
"Is there anyone who pays attention to you?
"There is no one, noble sir."
"Friend, it is not fitting for one living in the presence of those who have gone forth to be negligent regarding one's own person;
some form of mental attention must be maintained. Since you will not be able to attend to anything else, repeat the recitation: 'Bone, bone.
Following the elder nun’s instruction, he went about repeating: "Bone, bone."
One day, while he was sitting on the top of a gateway early in the morning, basking in the morning sun, a bird seized him with its talons.
He cried out, "Kiri kiri! Hearing this, the female novices said, "Venerable Sir, Buddharakkhita has been caught by a bird;
let us release him! Taking up clods of earth and other objects, they pursued him and freed him. Having brought him back, they stood before him.
The Elder Nun asked, “Buddharakkhita, what were you thinking when you were seized by the bird?

“Venerable Lady, I was thinking of nothing else. I was thinking, ‘A heap of bones is merely taking up another heap of bones; in whichever place it shall scatter,’ thus, Venerable Lady, I was thinking only of a heap of bones.”
“Excellent, excellent, Buddhārakkhita! This shall be a condition for you to reach the destruction of existence in the future.

Thus, even those who were animals there were possessed of attention directed toward the foundations of mindfulness; therefore, the Blessed One, generating in them precisely that wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness, spoke this discourse.
