In that context, "the single way" means the one path.
For regarding the path, it is said: "Path, road, way, track, direct route, course, journey;
boat, ford, bridge, raft, and ferry-crossing."
There are many names [for this path]. Here, it is spoken of by the name "going" (*ayana*).
Therefore, regarding the phrase "This, monks, is the one-way path" (*ekāyano ayaṃ maggo*), the meaning should be understood as: "This, monks, is a single path; it is not a forked road.

Alternatively, it is "one-way" (*ekāyana*) because it is to be traveled by one (*ekena ayitabbo*). "By one" means by one who has abandoned association with groups, who is secluded, and whose mind is withdrawn.
*Ayitabbo* means it is to be practiced. Or, *ayana* is that by which one goes; the meaning is that they go from saṃsāra to Nibbāna.
The way of one is the "single way" (*ekāyana*). "Of one" means of the best. And the Blessed One is the best of all beings;
therefore, it is said [the way] "of the Blessed One. For although others also go by it, even so, [it belongs] only to the Blessed One.
It is a "way" (*ayana*) because it has been brought forth by him. As it is said: "For that Blessed One, brahmin, is the arouser of the path not yet arisen," and so forth.
Or, it is a "way" because one goes by it; the meaning is that one proceeds or moves forward.
It is "the single way" (*ekāyana*) because it is the way in this [Dhamma and Vinaya] alone, and not elsewhere. As it is said: "In this..."
“Subhadda, in this Dhamma and Vinaya the Noble Eightfold Path is found. This is merely a difference in teaching, for the meaning is one and the same.

Furthermore, it is called “the way leading to the one” (*ekāyana*) because it goes to the one. Although it proceeds by way of various methods of cultivation in its earlier stages, in its later stage it goes to nothing other than the single Nibbāna; thus it is said. As Brahmā Sahampati said:
“The one who sees the end of birth knows the single path,
the way that leads to welfare, out of compassion;
by this path, those of old have crossed over.”
"And those who cross over, and those who are crossing over, the flood.
However, some say that according to the method of the verse "they do not go to the further shore twice," because one goes to Nibbāna only once, it is therefore called "the single path" (*ekāyana*);
that is not correct. For this meaning [of "single"] is already expressed by the phrase "going once" (*sakiṃ ayana*).

The phrasing must be explained. However, if it were stated with the meaning construed as "one way for this, one destination, one occurrence," the phrasing would be consistent, but the meaning would not be consistent in either case. Why?

Because here the preliminary path (pubbabhāgamagga) is intended. For it is the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), which occurs with the four objects such as the body and so forth, that is intended here.
It is not supramundane. And it comes back many times; its coming back occurs many times.

Furthermore, regarding this term, there was indeed a discussion among the great elders (mahātheras) in the past. The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said, "It is the path of the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
But his teacher, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷasumma, said, "It is the mixed path. "Venerable sir, it is the preliminary stage," [he replied].
"Which one, venerable sir? When the teacher spoke again and again, he remained silent without offering a rebuttal. They rose from their seats without having resolved the question.
Then, as the Elder Teacher was going toward the bathing shed, he thought: "I have taught the mixed path, yet Cūḷanāga speaks by taking only the 'prior portion' (pubbabhāga);
what indeed is the certainty here? Thus he began the Sutta from the beginning.
While turning back from the beginning, he observed at this point: "Bhikkhus, whoever should develop these four foundations of mindfulness thus for seven years.
There is no such thing as a supramundane path that, having arisen, persists for seven years;
the mixed path spoken of by me is not found here—it is only the preliminary path seen by Cūḷanāga.
Knowing that it was possible [to hear the Dhamma], he went when the proclamation for the hearing of the Dhamma on the eighth day had been made.
It is said that the ancient elders were fond of hearing the Dhamma; as soon as they heard the sound, they would rush forward all at once, each thinking, "I first! I first!
And on that day, it was the turn of the Elder Cūḷanāga. By him—
Having sat upon the Dhamma-seat and taken up the fan, when the preliminary verses had been recited, it occurred to the Elder as he stood behind the seat:
"I will not speak without sitting in private. For the ancient Elders were free from envy;
they did not wander about tossing aside their own views like a load of sugarcane, but rather took up the true reason.
They were answering without reason. Therefore, the Elder said, “Friend Cūḷanāga.
[Cūḷanāga] established the Dhamma with a voice like that of his teacher and asked, “What is it, Bhante? “Friend Cūḷanāga, the mixed path spoken of by me is not found;
the path of the preliminary foundations of mindfulness spoken of by you alone is found.”
The Elder thought: “Our teacher was a master of all the scriptures, a possessor of the Three Piṭakas, and one awakened by learning;
yet even for such a bhikkhu this question causes confusion. In the future, my brothers will also confuse themselves with this question.
Therefore, having taken up a discourse from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, I shall render this question unshakeable. Thus he spoke the passage beginning with “the path traveled by only one.”
The path of the foundations of mindfulness in its prior stage is thus described:
“Of paths, the eightfold is best; of truths, the four are supreme;
Dispassion is best among states, and the Visionary is best among bipeds.”
“This is the only path, there is no other, for the purification of vision;
indeed, you should practice this, which crushes the army of Māra.
For by practicing this, you will bring an end to suffering.”
Having cited the sutta, he established it.
In what sense is it called the "path" (magga)? It is so called in the sense of leading to Nibbāna and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.
"For the purification of beings" refers to those whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust and so forth, and by secondary corruptions such as covetousness and improper greed.
For the sake of the purification of beings. For it was by this very path that, beginning with the Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara,
Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara— who appeared in a single aeon above four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons from now—
there arose many Perfectly Enlightened Ones ending with Sakyamuni, as well as many hundreds of Private Buddhas.
And these noble disciples who have transcended the path of calculation—all these beings, having washed away the defilement of the mind, have attained supreme purity.
However, with respect to the defilement of form (*rūpa*), there is no such designation of corruption or purification. For it is said:
"By means of a corrupted form, young men are corrupted."
When form is pure, they are purified; this was not fully declared by the Great Seer.
When the mind is defiled, young men are defiled;
when the mind is pure, they are purified—thus it was said by the Great Seer.

As it is said: "Bhikkhus, through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified. And that purification of the mind occurs by means of this path of the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, he said: "for the purification of beings.
"For the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation" means for the surmounting—that is, the abandoning—of both sorrow and lamentation.

For this path, when developed, leads to the surmounting of sorrow, as in the case of the Great Minister Santati and others, and [to the surmounting of lamentation], as in the case of Paṭācārā and others.
And it leads to the transcendence of lamentation. Therefore he said: "For the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation.
For even though the minister Santati said:
"Purify that which was before; let there be nothing for you afterwards;"
"If you do not grasp at the middle, you will wander in peace.
Upon hearing this verse, she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Paṭācārā—
“Sons are not a refuge, nor is a father, nor even kinsmen;
for one seized by the End-maker, there is no refuge among relatives.
Having heard this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). However, because [she did not see] anything [permanent] within the body, feelings, mind, or phenomena...
There is no such thing as development (bhāvanā) without grasping the Dhamma; therefore, it should be understood that they too have transcended sorrow and lamentation by means of this very path.
"For the subsiding of suffering and dejection" means for the subsiding—meaning the cessation—of these two: bodily suffering and mental dejection.
For this path, when developed, [leads to the goal] just as it did for the Elder Tissa and others.
It leads to the subsiding of suffering and, like that of Sakkā and others, to the subsiding of mental distress.

Herein, this is the clarification of the meaning: It is said that in Sāvatthī, a son of a householder named Tissa, having renounced forty crores of gold, went forth and dwelt in a forest remote from villages. His younger brother’s wife [said]: "Go..."
"Do not deprive him of life," he said, and dispatched five hundred bandits. They went and sat surrounding the Elder.
The Elder asked, "Why have you come, lay followers? "To deprive him of life.
"Lay followers, take a guarantor for me and grant me life for this one night. "Who will be your guarantor in this place, ascetic?"
The Elder took a large stone, broke his two thigh bones, and said, "Is a surety acceptable, lay follower?
They departed and, having made a fire at the head of the walking path, lay down.
As the Elder suppressed the pain and reflected upon his virtue, rapture and gladness arose in him based on that pure virtue. Then, in due course—
Increasing his insight and practicing the duty of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night, he attained Arahantship at the rising of the dawn and uttered this inspired utterance:
“Having split both my feet, I shall make you conscious.”
"I am ashamed, I am humiliated by my death with lust still within me.
Having reflected thus, I saw things as they truly are;
and when the dawn had arrived, I attained arahantship.

Another thirty bhikkhus, having received a meditation subject from the Blessed One and entered the rains retreat in a forest dwelling, lived there saying, "Friends, the duty of a recluse must be performed throughout the three watches of the night; one must not come into each other's presence.
While they were performing their duty as recluses and nodding off at dawn, a tiger—
Having arrived, he would seize one bhikkhu at a time and depart. Not a single one uttered even the words, "A tiger has seized me!
Thus, when five or ten bhikkhus had been devoured, on the Uposatha day, after asking, "Friends, where are the others?
and having learned the truth, they lived saying, "Now, if one is seized, one should say, 'I am seized!'"
Then, in the same manner as before, a tiger seized another young bhikkhu. He cried out, "A tiger, Venerable Sir!
The bhikkhus, taking up walking sticks and torches, pursued it, thinking, "We shall rescue him.
The tiger climbed onto a place where the bhikkhus could not go—a precipitous cliff—and began [to devour] that bhikkhu, starting from his big toe.
He began to eat him. The others also said, "Now, good sir, there is nothing more for us to do; the distinction of a true bhikkhu is indeed manifested in such a situation.

While lying right there in the tiger's mouth, suppressing that pain and developing insight, he became a stream-enterer at the moment the tiger had eaten him down to his ankles, and [remained so] at the moment it had eaten him down to his knees.
The once-returner, having become a non-returner at the very moment the navel was being eaten,
attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) while the heart-flesh had not yet been consumed, and uttered this inspired utterance:
“Virtuous, endowed with vows, wise, and well-concentrated;”
Having for a moment succumbed to negligence, my mind was uplifted by the tiger.
Having caught me in a cage and placed me upon a rock, [the tiger said:
"Let the tiger eat me as he pleases; this body is food for enemies."
"Once the meditation subject has been acquired, death will be auspicious.

Furthermore, there was another elder named Pītamalla Thera. In his lay life, having taken up the banner in three kingdoms, he came to Tambapaṇṇidīpa and, after meeting the king and receiving the king's favor, one day while passing through the door of a straw-mat shop, he thought:
“Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it. When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Having heard this section on "What is Not Yours," he thought, “It seems then that neither form nor feeling belongs to oneself.
Taking that very teaching as his goad, he went out, proceeded to the Mahāvihāra, requested the going forth, and was ordained.
Having been ordained and having mastered the two Matikas, he took thirty monks and went to the courtyard at Gabalavāliya, where he practiced the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
As his feet were failing him, he walked about on his knees.
During the night, a deer-hunter, thinking him to be a deer, struck him with a spear. The spear passed right through him. He had the spear removed.
Having filled his mouth with blades of grass, he had himself seated upon a stone slab;
then, having requested privacy and developed insight, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Upon coughing, he explained the matter to the monks who had come because of the sound, and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):
“‘This form is not yours, O bhikkhus; abandon it—this which was spoken by the Best of Buddhas, the Teacher Supreme over all the world.
Truly, conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to the nature of arising and passing away.’”
“Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is blissful.
Then the bhikkhus said to him, “Venerable sir, if the Perfectly Enlightened One were free from illness, he would surely stretch out his hand and touch your head.
To this extent, this path [is established], as it was for the Elder Tissa and others.
It leads to the cessation of suffering.
However, when Sakka, the lord of the devas, saw five kinds of omens portending his own death, he was terrified by the fear of death and overcome with dejection;
he approached the Blessed One and asked a question. At the conclusion of the answer to that question on equanimity—
Together with eighty thousand deities, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). His rebirth returned to its former state.
The divine son Subrahmā, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs (accharā), enjoyed the splendors of heaven;
there, five hundred nymphs who were plucking flowers from a tree passed away and were reborn in hell. He [wondered], "Why are these taking so long?"
Investigating, he saw that they were reborn in hell; then, examining himself with the thought, "How long indeed is my own lifespan?
he perceived the exhaustion of his own life-span and saw that he too would be reborn right there in hell.
Terrified and overcome with extreme dejection, he thought, "Only the Teacher will dispel this dejection of mine, and no one else," and [he addressed] the remaining five hundred.
Taking the nymphs with her, she approached the Blessed One and asked this question:
"This mind is constantly terrified, and the mental faculty is constantly agitated;
both when misfortunes have not yet arisen and when they have already occurred."
“If there is anything fearless, tell me that when I ask.
Then the Blessed One said to him:
“There is nothing other than awakening, nothing other than austerity, and nothing other than restraint of the faculties.”
"I see no safety for living beings except through the relinquishing of everything.
At the conclusion of this teaching, together with five hundred celestial nymphs, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry;
having made that attainment stable, he departed for the world of the devas. Thus, when this path is cultivated, it leads to the removal of dejection, as in the case of Sakka and others.
It should be understood that this leads to their subsiding.
"For the attainment of the method" (*ñāyassa adhigamāya*): "method" (*ñāya*) refers to the Noble Eightfold Path; it means for its attainment, for its reaching—this is what is said.
For this mundane path of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), cultivated in the prior stage, [leads] to the supramundane path...
It leads to realization. Therefore, he said, "for the realization of the way.

"For the actualization of Nibbāna" means for the actualization of the Deathless, which has received the name "Nibbāna" because it is devoid of the dwelling of craving; what is meant is that it is made directly manifest by oneself.
For when this path is cultivated, it gradually accomplishes the actualization of Nibbāna. Therefore, he said:
“‘For the realization of Nibbāna’—

herein, although the overcoming of sorrow and so forth are established by implication when it is said ‘for the purification of beings,’ they are not evident to others except to those who are skilled in the application of the Dispensation; nor did the Blessed One [state them] first.”
Having made people proficient in the discipline (*vinaya*) of the teaching, he subsequently teaches the Dhamma;

moreover, he makes known each respective meaning by means of the corresponding Sutta. Therefore, here, demonstrating clearly whatever meaning the "one-way path" (*ekāyana-magga*) accomplishes, he says:
"for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation," and so forth. Or rather, because it is the purification of beings—
It leads by the path that goes alone; that [path] comes about through the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation;
the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation comes about through the subsiding of pain and dejection; the subsiding of pain and dejection comes about through the attainment of the True Way;
the attainment of the True Way comes about through the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, showing this sequence as well, he says: "for the purification of beings."
Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with “for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation.
Moreover, this is a praise of the path that goes in one way alone. For just as the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; with its own meaning and its own phrasing; entirely complete and pure...”
"I shall proclaim the pure holy life, namely, the six sets of six"—with these eight phrases he praised the teaching on the six sets of six.

And just as in the teaching on the Noble Lineages, [he said]: "Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages—ancient, long-standing, traditional, original, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated now, and never to be adulterated."
He praised it with nine terms, saying, “It is not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Likewise, he praised this single-path way for the purification of beings with seven terms, beginning with “for the purification of beings.
Why is this so? It is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those bhikkhus; for having heard that praise, those bhikkhus—
“Indeed, this path destroys the four calamities—sorrow, which consists of heart-burning; lamentation, which consists of verbal prolixity; pain, which consists of bodily unease;

and dejection, which consists of mental unease—and it brings about the three excellences: purification, the method, and Nibbāna. Having thus conceived such zeal, one should learn and master this teaching of the Dhamma.
They will think, "This should be memorized, this should be recited, and this path should be developed.
Thus, he spoke in praise of them to arouse their enthusiasm, just as a wool merchant and others speak in praise of woolen blankets and such.
For example, even when a wool merchant of a yellow blanket worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] proclaims, "Buy this blanket!"...
People did not yet know what "asukakambala" (that kind of woolen cloth) was.
For even hair-cloths, wool-cloths, and the like—which are foul-smelling and rough to the touch—are called "kambalas.
But when it was proclaimed that the Gandhāra red woolen cloth was fine, bright, and pleasant to the touch, then those who could afford it took some; those who could not, [did not].
They too desire to see it; even so, when it is said, "This, monks, is the one-way path," it is not yet evident which specific path is meant.
For various kinds of paths that do not lead to liberation are also called simply "paths. But when it is said, "For the purification of beings," and so forth, [it becomes clear]:
"This path, it seems, destroys the four calamities and leads to the three distinctions..."
Speaking in praise of those who, having conceived such enthusiasm, will think, "This teaching of the Dhamma should be learned, mastered, retained, and recited;
and this path should be developed," he said, "For the purification of beings," and so forth.

And just as the simile of the merchant of the yellow woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], so too should the similes of the merchants of the red Jambu-river gold water-clearing jewel, the extremely pure pearl-jewel, the polished coral, and so on, be brought forward here.
*Yadidam* is a particle; its meaning is "those which are these. *Cattāro* (four) is a numerical delimitation;

by this, it indicates that there are neither fewer nor more than that, thus showing the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). *Satipaṭṭhānā* refers to the three foundations of mindfulness:
the objective sphere of mindfulness, the Teacher’s state of being beyond aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in the three ways, and mindfulness itself.
“Monks, I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness;
listen to that... What, monks, is the arising of the body? With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body.

In such passages as these, the object of mindfulness is called a “foundation of mindfulness. Likewise: “The body is the foundation, but not the mindfulness; mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness.”
...and so on in such passages as these. Its meaning is as follows: that in which something is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) is a foundation (*paṭṭhāna*).
What is it that is established? Mindfulness (*sati*). The foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*. Alternatively, a foundation is a place of exertion (*padhāna-ṭṭhāna*).

The foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*, just like the "elephant-place" (*hatthi-ṭṭhāna*), the "horse-place" (*assa-ṭṭhāna*), and so forth. "There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which... [etc.]

In the passage, “The Teacher is worthy to instruct the assembly,” here too, among the disciples who have practiced in three ways, the Teacher’s state of being beyond aversion and attachment is called “the establishment of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Its meaning is as follows: it is an *ṭhāna* (establishment) because it is to be established;
that is, it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness. The establishment by means of mindfulness is “the establishment of mindfulness. “Four... [etc.]

In such passages as, "The foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānā), when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," it is mindfulness itself that is called "foundation of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna).
Its meaning is as follows: it is established (paṭṭhāti), thus it is a foundation (paṭṭhāna);

the meaning is that it stands near, having entered and plunged into [the object], and proceeds. Mindfulness itself is the foundation; hence, "foundation of mindfulness. Alternatively, in the sense of remembering (saraṇa-):

Mindfulness (*sati*) is a foundation (*paṭṭhāna*) in the sense of being established. Thus, it is mindfulness and it is a foundation; therefore, it is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). This is what is intended here.

If this is so, why is the plural form "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*) used? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. For these mindfullnesses are many due to the diversity of their objects.
Then, why is the singular form "the Path" (*maggo*) used? Because of its unity in the sense of being a path. For all four of these mindfullnesses [constitute a single path].
They attain unity in the sense of being the path. For this has been said: “In what sense is it the ‘path’ (magga)?

In the sense of going to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought after by those who desire Nibbāna. And these four, later on, while accomplishing their function with respect to the objects such as the body, go to Nibbāna; and from the very beginning, they are sought after by those who desire Nibbāna.
Therefore, all four [factors] are called "one path. And this being so, the teaching possesses its proper sequence of discourse, as in such passages as:
"Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the path that crushes Māra’s army; listen to that...
What, bhikkhus, is the path that crushes Māra’s army? It is these seven factors of enlightenment," and so forth.
For just as "the crusher of Māra’s army" and "the seven factors of enlightenment" are one in meaning,
with only the phrasing being different here, so too "the path of the single way" and "the four foundations of mindfulness" are one in meaning,

with only the phrasing being different here. Therefore, the singular number should be understood to refer to their oneness in terms of the path, while the plural number refers to the multiplicity of mindfulness due to the diversity of their objects.
But why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? It is for the benefit of those to be trained (*vineyya*).

For among those to be trained—who fall into two groups each according to whether they are dull or sharp, consisting of those of craving-temperament (*taṇhā-carita*) and view-temperament (*diṭṭhi-carita*), and those who follow the vehicle of serenity (*samatha-yānika*) and those who follow the vehicle of insight (*vipassanā-yānika*)—for the one of dull temperament with a craving-temperament, there is the foundation of mindfulness of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*), which is gross.
For one of sharp faculties, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings that is subtle is the path to purification;

for one of dull faculties who is of speculative temperament, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of mind that has not reached a high degree of differentiation is the path to purification; for one of sharp faculties, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of mental objects that has reached a high degree of differentiation is the path to purification;
and for one who is of dull faculties and takes serenity as their vehicle, the sign that is to be attained without difficulty is the path to purification.
The first foundation of mindfulness is the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*). The second is for one whose faculties are sharp, because it does not require fixing upon a coarse object.

For one who follows insight as their vehicle, the third has an object that is not excessively analyzed, being suitable for those of dull faculties; the fourth has an object that is excessively analyzed, being suitable for those of sharp faculties.
Thus, exactly four have been stated, neither fewer nor more.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of abandoning the perversions regarding the body as beautiful, pleasant, permanent, and self. For the body is indeed impure, yet beings are perverted by the perversion of beauty toward it;
therefore, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught so that they might see its impurity and thereby abandon that perversion.
Furthermore, although feeling and the other aggregates are grasped as pleasant, permanent, and self, feeling is actually suffering.
The mind is impermanent, and phenomena are non-self; yet beings are distorted by the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self regarding these things.

Therefore, it should be understood that the remaining three [foundations of mindfulness] are taught for the purpose of abandoning those perversions by showing the nature of suffering and so forth therein.
Thus, it should be known that exactly four [foundations of mindfulness] are taught—neither fewer nor more—for the purpose of abandoning the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.

It should be understood that these four alone have been taught not only for the purpose of abandoning the perversions, but also for the purpose of abandoning the four floods (*oghā*), yokes (*yogā*), taints (*āsava*), ties (*ganthā*), clingings (*upādānā*), and destinations (*gatī*), as well as for the purpose of fully understanding the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*). This, first of all, is the method according to the treatise (*pakaraṇa-naya*).

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated that there is only one foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) by way of its refuge and its convergence into unity, and that it is fourfold by way of its objects (*ārammaṇa*). For just as in a city with four gates, those coming from the east...
Just as those coming from the east take up their goods acquired in the eastern direction and enter the city through the eastern gate;

and those coming from the south, the west, and the north take up their goods acquired in the northern direction and enter the city through the northern gate—so too should this be understood. For the great city of Nibbāna is like that city.
The supramundane Eightfold Path is like a gate; the body and so forth are like the eastern direction and so forth.

Just as those coming from the east take goods originating in the eastern direction and enter the city through the eastern gate, so too those coming by way of the mindfulness of the body develop the fourteen-fold mindfulness of the body and—
By means of the Noble Path produced through the power of the development of the contemplation of the body, they all converge upon the single Nibbāna.
Just as those coming from the south, taking goods produced in the southern region, enter the city itself by way of the southern gate,
so too do those coming by way of the contemplation of feelings enter by means of the ninefold contemplation of feelings.
Having developed it, they converge upon the single Nibbāna alone by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of the development of the contemplation of feelings.
Just as those coming from the west take goods originating in the western region and enter the city itself by way of the western gate,
so too do those coming by way of the contemplation of mind enter by means of the sixteenfold contemplation of mind.
Having developed it, they converge upon the single Nibbāna alone by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of the development of the contemplation of mind (*cittānupassanā*).
Just as those coming from the north take goods originating in the northern region and enter the city itself by way of the northern gate,
so too those coming by way of the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) develop the fivefold contemplation of phenomena.
By means of the Noble Path produced through the power of the development of the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*), they all converge upon the single Nibbāna alone.

Thus, it should be understood that although there is only one foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) by way of its being a refuge and by way of its convergence into unity, it is spoken of as fourfold by way of its objects. "Which four?
is a question asked with the desire to explain. "Here" means in this Dispensation. "O monks" is an address to the persons who receive the Dhamma.

"Bhikkhus" is a designation for a person who accomplishes the practice. Although other gods and humans also accomplish the practice, he says "bhikkhus" because of the excellence of their practice and because it demonstrates the state of being a bhikkhu through that practice.
For among those who receive the Blessed One’s instruction, the bhikkhu is the most excellent; this is because [he is the recipient] of every kind of instruction.

Because he is a vessel [for the Dhamma] and because he is the most excellent, he is called a "bhikkhu. When he is mentioned, the rest are already included, just as when a king is mentioned in contexts such as a royal procession, the rest of the retinue is implied. Furthermore, he who practices this way of practice is called a "bhikkhu";
thus, he said "bhikkhus" also to show that the state of being a bhikkhu consists in practicing the way. One who is practicing...
For whether one be a god or a human, one who possesses these qualities is indeed reckoned as a "bhikkhu. As it is said:
"Even if he were adorned, if he should live in accordance with the Dhamma—peaceful, tamed, self-controlled, and leading the holy life;"
“He who has laid aside the rod toward all beings—he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a bhikkhu.
Here, “body” (kāya) refers to the material body (rūpakāya). For the material body is used here in the sense of a collection of parts, limbs, and phenomena such as hair and so forth.

"Body" (kāya) is intended here in the sense of a collection, just as one speaks of a "body of elephants" or a "body of chariots. And just as it is used in the sense of a collection, so too it is used in the sense of the origin (āya) of things that are loathsome.

For it is the "origin" (āya) of those things that are loathsome—that is, of the most utterly repulsive things—hence it is called "body" (kāya). "Origin" (āya) means the place of arising. Herein, this is the etymological derivation:
they arise from there, thus it is an "origin" (āya). What arises? Loathsome things such as hair and so forth. Thus, it is the "origin of the loathsome" (kucchitānaṃ āyo).
The body. "Contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) means one whose nature is to contemplate the body, or one who is contemplating the body.

Although the word "in the body" (*kāye*) has already been stated, the second mention of "body" in the phrase "contemplating the body" should be understood as being made for the purpose of demonstrating the defining of [the body] as unmixed, its resolution from what is solid, and its analysis.
Therefore, it is not that one contemplates feelings in the body, nor does one contemplate the mind or mental phenomena; rather, [one contemplates the body itself].
"Contemplating the body itself" means that the definition is shown as being unmixed with anything other than the mode of contemplating the body within the basis known as the "body.

Likewise, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon apart from the limbs and members of the body, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man apart from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth.
Furthermore, even that which is here comprised of the collection of primary elements and derived matter—namely, the hair of the head, body hair, and so on—[is to be seen in this way].
Regarding the body, one does not contemplate it as a single entity separate from the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived matter (upādāya); rather,

one contemplates it as a collection of limbs and members like one observing the parts of a chariot, or as a collection of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth like one observing the components of a city,
or indeed as a collection of primary elements and derived matter like one who separates the layers of a plantain trunk or one who opens an empty fist.
By seeing the physical basis designated as a "body" through its various components and as a mere collection, the dismantling of the solid mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*) is demonstrated.
For herein, no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon whatsoever is perceived apart from the aforementioned collection of phenomena;
rather, beings merely apply false adherence (*micchā-abhinivesa*) in such and such ways to that very collection of phenomena.
They act thus. Therefore the ancients said:
“What one sees, that is not seen; what is seen, that one does not see.
Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, he is not released.”
It is said that this is for the purpose of demonstrating the resolution of the compact and so forth. Here, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), this further meaning should also be understood:
namely, that in this one body he is a contemplator of the body alone, and not a contemplator of other phenomena. What is meant?
Just as people might contemplate water even in a mirage where no water exists, it is not so here; [he contemplates] only that which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.

One does not contemplate this body as being permanent, pleasant, self, or beautiful; rather, one contemplates the body precisely as a collection of modes that are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.
Alternatively, there is the body described further on in the sequence beginning with, "Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest...
he breathes in mindfully," and ending with the minute particles and the bones; and also the "earth-body" mentioned here: ...some person [contemplates] the earth-body...

In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the body is described as follows: "One contemplates the water-element, the fire-element, the air-element, the hair-of-the-head element, the hair-of-the-body element, the skin element, the hide element, the flesh element, the blood element, the sinew element, the bone element, and the marrow element as impermanent.
Since one contemplates all of these within this very body, the meaning should also be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*).

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows: because one does not contemplate anything whatsoever in the body that could be grasped as "I" or "mine," but rather contemplates each respective collection of various phenomena such as head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth, one is called "one who contemplates the body as a collection of phenomena consisting of head-hairs, etc.
Furthermore, it is said: "In this body, one contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent," and so on.

Furthermore, according to the method found in the *Paṭisambhidā*, the meaning of "contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*) should also be understood as the contemplation of this entire aggregate of aspects— consisting of the characteristic of impermanence and so forth— by way of the method [of the four foundations of mindfulness].
For in this way, the bhikkhu who has entered upon the practice of contemplating the body in the body contemplates this body through the contemplations of impermanence and the rest.
By means of the seven contemplations, he contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent; he contemplates as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates as non-self, not as self. He becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not passionate;
he causes cessation, not origination; he relinquishes, not grasps. Thus, contemplating that as impermanent...
It should be understood that one abandons the perception of permanence; observing [things] as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure;
observing [them] as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust;
bringing about cessation, one abandons origination; and relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
"Viharati" means he conducts himself. "Ātāpī": one who scorches (ātāpeti) the defilements within the three realms of existence (*bhava*) is called *ātāpa*;
this is a name for energy (*vīriya*). One who possesses such *ātāpa* is an *ātāpī*. "Sampajāno": endowed with the knowledge designated as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
"Satimā": endowed with mindfulness (*sati*) that encompasses the body. Furthermore, because by means of mindfulness one has grasped the object (*ārammaṇa*), [one dwells].
One contemplates with wisdom; for there is no such thing as contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness.

Therefore it was said: "And mindfulness, monks, I call all-beneficial. Thus, by the words "he dwells contemplating the body in the body," the meditation subject of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in body-contemplation has been explained. Alternatively, because one who lacks ardor...
Lack of contentment creates obstacles; one who lacks clear comprehension is confused regarding the adoption of skillful means and the avoidance of unskillful means;
one who is muddled in mindfulness is incapable of relinquishing unskillful means and adopting skillful means. Consequently, his meditation subject does not succeed.
Therefore, in order to show those qualities by whose power it does succeed:
It should be understood that this is what was meant by the words "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.

Thus, having shown the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body and its associated factor, he now says "having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world" in order to show its factor of abandoning.
In this context, "having removed" means either by removal through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by removal by suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).
Or having disciplined [the mind]. "In the world" (*loke*) means in that very body. For here, the body is intended as "the world" in the sense of breaking up and falling apart (*lujjanapalujjana*).
However, since covetousness and dejection are not abandoned merely in the body but are also abandoned in feeling and so forth, it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"The five aggregates of clinging are the world. This is because they are reckoned as the world.
Or rather, this was stated by way of extracting the meaning of those terms. As for what was said, "In that context, what is the world?
This very body is the world," this is precisely the meaning here; the connection should be understood as: "having removed covetousness and dejection regarding that world.
For in this context, by the mention of "covetousness" (abhijjhā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is implied, and by the mention of "dejection" (domanassa), ill will (byāpāda) is implied.
It is included therein; therefore, it should be understood that the abandoning of the hindrances is stated by means of seeing these two powerful states comprised within the hindrances.
And herein, specifically, by the removal of covetousness, there is the removal of attachment rooted in physical excellence, and by the removal of ill-will...

Furthermore, regarding the conflict rooted in bodily failure: through the removal of covetousness there is delight in the body, and through the removal of displeasure there is non-delight in the cultivation of the body;

through the removal of covetousness there is the superimposition of unreal qualities such as beauty and pleasure upon the body, and through the removal of displeasure there is the removal of real qualities such as foulness and suffering from the body.
And its abandoning has been stated. By this, the power of yoga and the capability for yoga of the practitioner are illuminated.

For this is the power of yoga: namely, that one is free from attraction and repulsion, endures both the unpleasant and the pleasant, and is devoid of the rejection of what is real and the imposition of what is unreal.
Being thus free from attraction and repulsion, enduring the unpleasant and the pleasant, he does not reject what is real, nor does he impose what is unreal...
"By not breathing in, one becomes capable of yoga.

Another method: in the phrase "contemplating the body in the body," the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is stated by way of contemplation (*anupassanā*). In the phrase "he dwells," the preservation of the body for one who possesses the meditation subject is stated by way of the dwelling (*vihāra*) mentioned there.
In the passage beginning with "ardent" (*ātāpī*), right effort (*sammappadhāna*) is indicated by "ardor" (*ātāpa*).

It should be understood that mindfulness and clear comprehension are the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) beneficial in all circumstances, or else they are the means for maintaining the meditation subject;
or alternatively, serenity is obtained through mindfulness by way of contemplation of the body, while insight is obtained through clear comprehension;
and it should be understood that the fruit of development is stated as the removal of covetousness and displeasure.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, regarding the term "contemplating" (*anupassī*): What therein is contemplation? It is that wisdom, understanding... [as far as] right view.

This is called contemplation. One who is endowed with this contemplation—fully endowed, arrived at it, fully arrived at it, possessed of it, perfected in it, and equipped with it—is therefore called "one who contemplates."
"Viharati" means he moves about, proceeds, protects, maintains, sustains, conducts himself, and dwells.

Therefore it is said, "he dwells. Regarding "ardent" (*ātāpī*): what therein is ardor? It is the arousal of mental energy... [as above] ...right effort. This is called ardor. One is endowed with this ardor... [as above] ...possessed of it. Therefore it is said, "ardent."

"Clearly comprehending": therein, what is clear comprehension (*sampajañña*)? It is that which is wisdom (*paññā*), understanding (*pajānanā*)... [as far as] right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). This is called clear comprehension. One is endowed with this clear comprehension... [as far as] possessed of it. Therefore, one is said to be "clearly comprehending. "Mindful": therein, what is mindfulness (*sati*)?

It is that which is mindfulness, recollection (*anussati*)... [as far as] right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*). This is called mindfulness. One is endowed with this mindfulness... [as far as] possessed of it. Therefore, one is said to be "mindful."
"Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. In this context, what is the world? This very body is the world; the five aggregates of clinging are also the world.

This is called the world. In this context, what is covetousness? Whatever lust, infatuation, inclination, compliance, delight, delight-lust, and infatuation of the mind—this is called covetousness. In this context, what is dejection?
That mental state which is unpleasant, mental pain, the unpleasant born of mind-contact...
[as above] ...painful feeling—this is called grief (*domanassa*).
Thus, this covetousness and this grief are, in this world, disciplined, thoroughly disciplined, calmed, stilled, pacified, fully pacified, subsided, completely subsided, and dissolved.
"Expelled, dried up, withered away, brought to an end"—thus it is said: "having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This is how the meaning of these words has been stated. This should be understood according to how this method of the Commentary accords with that [explanation].
This, then, is the commentary on the meaning of the summary of the Foundation of Mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body.
“He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena... ...pe... “having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

Herein, the purpose for the repeated mention of feelings and so forth in such passages as “contemplating feelings in feelings” should be understood in the same manner as stated in the section on contemplation of the body.
That is: “contemplating feelings in feelings,” “contemplating the mind in the mind,” and “contemplating phenomena in phenomena.”
Here, however, "feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the three kinds of feeling, and these are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*). Mind (*citta*) is also mundane, as are mental objects (*dhammā*).
Their classification will become clear in the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*).

One who contemplates in such a way that feeling is to be contemplated should be understood as "one who contemplates feelings in feelings. This same method applies to mind and mental objects as well. And how?

"Should feelings be contemplated? First, pleasant feeling is to be contemplated as suffering, painful feeling as an arrow, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it has been said:
"He who saw the pleasant as suffering, saw the painful as an arrow, and saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant as impermanent..."
“That bhikkhu who sees rightly will live in peace.
Furthermore, all these [feelings] should be contemplated as suffering. For it has been said:
“Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering; so I say. And they should also be contemplated in terms of pleasure and pain. As it was said: “Pleasant feeling...”

"The pleasure of stability is the suffering of change"—all this should be expanded in detail. Furthermore, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence (*anicca*).

The rest will become clear in the section on the exposition (*niddesa*) itself. Regarding mental states (*cittadhamma*), first, as for consciousness (*citta*), it should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, through its various distinctions such as object, predominance, co-nascence, plane, kamma, result, and functional.
It should be contemplated by way of the classifications such as "with lust" (*sarāga*) and so forth, which appear in the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*).

Phenomena (*dhammā*) should be contemplated by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), the phenomenon of emptiness (*suññatadhamma*), the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence (*aniccādi*), and the classifications such as "peaceful" (*santa*) and "unpeaceful" (*asantādi*), which appear in the section on the exposition.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. Now, in this context, for one who [possesses] covetousness and dejection regarding the world known as the body—

What has been abandoned in one case is indeed abandoned in the world of feeling and so forth as well. However, it is stated everywhere both with reference to various individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness at each moment of consciousness.
Or rather, what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the others as well;
therefore, it should be understood that this was said in order to demonstrate its abandonment in those other cases too.
The commentary on the section on the summary is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on Mindfulness of Breathing within the Section on Contemplation of the Body (107).
Now, just as a skilled mat-maker [produces] coarse mats, fine mats, small baskets, large baskets, bags, and so forth—
Just as one desiring to make various utensils might obtain a single large bamboo, split it into four parts, and then,
taking each individual section of bamboo and splitting it further, fashion those various utensils; even so, the Blessed One,

desiring to bring about for sentient beings the attainment of manifold distinctions through the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, [taught] the single right mindfulness as "the four foundations of mindfulness."
"Which four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as body," and so forth.

Having thus divided [the subject] into four ways according to the objects of meditation, and having taken each individual foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) from that, he began to explain the section of the exposition by analyzing them, starting with the words, "And how, monks? and so forth.
In this context, the phrase beginning with “And how” (*kathañca*) is a question posed out of a desire to explain in detail. However, the summarized meaning here is as follows:
“In what manner, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? This same method applies to all the sections of questions.
“Here, monks, a monk” (*idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu*) means: “in this dispensation, monks, a monk. For the word *idha* (here) has this sense in this context.

This [phrase] illustrates the Teaching as the support for the person who has produced the contemplation of the body in all its aspects, and it negates the existence of such [contemplation] in other teachings. For it has been said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic...
[and so on] ...other sects are empty of ascetics. Therefore it was said: “In this Teaching, monks.”
“Having gone to the forest... or having gone to an empty hut”—this explains his selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
For this bhikkhu’s mind, which for a long time has been dissipated among objects such as forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject;
it runs only along the wrong road, like a chariot yoked to wild oxen. Therefore, just as...
Suppose there were a cowherd who, having raised a fraudulent calf by drinking all the milk from a deceptive cow, wished to tame it.
He would remove it from the cow, drive a large stake into the ground in a secluded spot, and bind it there with a rope.
Then that calf, after struggling here and there, being unable to escape, would sit down right next to that very stake.

Or might fall upon it; even so, this bhikkhu, desiring to tame the corrupted mind that has long been nourished by drinking the flavors of sense objects such as forms, should withdraw it from those objects like forms and lead it into the forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty hut, where he should bind it to the pillar of the object of mindfulness with the rope of mindfulness. Thus for him—
Although that mind flutters here and there, being unable to escape by severing the tether of mindfulness because it cannot find its former habitual object,
it settles down and lies down upon that very same object by way of access and absorption.
Thus said the ancients:
"Just as a man here would tie up a calf to be tamed by binding it to a post, so too should he bind his own mind firmly to the object of mindfulness.

In this way, that lodging becomes suitable for his development. Therefore it was said: "This is an illustration of his selection of a lodging suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness."

Furthermore, because this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati kammaṭṭhāna*)—which is the pinnacle of body-contemplation and the proximate cause for the distinguished attainments and the pleasant dwellings in the present life of all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—is not easy to accomplish without abandoning a village settlement crowded with the sounds of men, women, elephants, horses, and so forth;
for since meditative absorption (*jhāna*) has sound as its thorn, it must be practiced in a place free from villages. However, in a non-village...

In the forest, it is easy for a practitioner of yoga to grasp this meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), to produce the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), and then, taking that very jhāna as a basis, to comprehend conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and reach the highest fruit, which is Arahantship.
Therefore, showing him a suitable dwelling, the Blessed One said: "Having gone to the forest," and so forth.
For the Blessed One is like a teacher of site-selection (*vatthuvijjācariya*).

Just as a teacher of site-selection, having inspected a plot of land for a city and examined it thoroughly, points out, "Build the city here," and when the city has been completed in safety, receives great honor from the royal court;
even so, [the Blessed One] examines a suitable lodging for a practitioner (*yogāvacara*).
“Here one should apply oneself to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna),” he instructs.
Then, when the yogi applies himself to that meditation subject there and gradually attains arahantship, he receives great honor, thinking, “Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.
This bhikkhu, moreover, is said to be like a leopard. For just as a great king of leopards [enters] the thicket of grass in the forest...
Just as a hunter, having hidden himself by relying on a forest thicket, a jungle, or a mountain cleft, captures wild animals such as buffaloes, oxen, antelopes, and boars;
even so, this bhikkhu who devotes himself to the meditation subject in the forest and other such places captures, in due order, both the four paths and the four noble fruits. Thus said the ancients:
“Just as a leopard, having hidden itself, seizes a deer,
even so this son of the Buddha, devoted to practice and practicing insight,
having entered the forest, seizes the supreme fruit.”

Showing him a forest lodging as a place suitable for the speed of his exertion, the Blessed One said, "Having gone to the forest," and so forth. Hereafter, whatever needs to be said regarding this section on mindfulness of breathing has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

However, for one training by means of these inhalations and exhalations as they have been described thus: "Breathing in long, he understands: 'I breathe in long'... [and so on] ...he trains himself: 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation,'" [the following applies].
The four jhānas arise with the sign of in-breathing and out-breathing as their object.
Having emerged from jhāna, he either examines the in-breaths and out-breaths or the factors of the jhāna. Therein, one who works with the in-breaths and out-breaths reflects:

"On what are these in-breaths and out-breaths dependent? They are dependent on the physical basis (vatthu). The 'physical basis' is the body composed of the primary elements (karajakāya). The 'body composed of the primary elements' consists of the four great elements."
Having thus grasped form as "derived form," he then grasps name as "the pentad of contact and so forth which has that [form] as its object.
Having thus grasped name-and-form, and while seeking its condition, he sees dependent origination beginning with ignorance;
seeing this, he understands: "This is merely a collection of phenomena consisting of conditions and things arisen from conditions; there is no other being or person."
Having dispelled his doubts and applied the three characteristics to name-and-form together with its conditions, he develops insight and gradually attains Arahantship.
This is the way of deliverance for a certain bhikkhu leading up to Arahantship. One who practices meditation (*jhānakammika*) also reflects:
"On what are these jhāna factors dependent? They are dependent on the physical basis (*vatthu*). The physical basis, it is said, is the body composed of the four great elements."

Having defined name-and-form by determining that "the factors of jhāna are name" and "the body born of kamma is form," and while seeking its condition, he sees the mode of conditions beginning with ignorance.
Seeing that "this is merely a mass of conditioned phenomena and their conditionally arisen states;
there is no other being or person," his doubts are dispelled. Having applied the three characteristics to name-and-form together with its conditions, he practices insight.
Increasing it step by step, he eventually attains Arahantship; this is the gateway to liberation for a single bhikkhu leading up to Arahantship.
Thus, "internally" means he dwells contemplating the body in the body with respect to his own inhalations and exhalations;
"externally" means with respect to another’s inhalations and exhalations; and "both internally and externally" means at one time with respect to his own and at another time with respect to another’s.
"Regarding the body of in-breaths and out-breaths": by this, the time when one has set aside the familiar meditation subject and moves back and forth [between them] is described.
However, at one time, both of these are not obtained.
"Contemplating the phenomenon of arising" (*samudayadhammānupassī*): just as, for example, a blacksmith’s bellows, the bellows-tube, and the corresponding effort...

Just as the wind moves back and forth in dependence [on a fan], so too, in dependence on the body born of karma (*karajakāya*), the nostrils, and the mind, the body of inhalation and exhalation moves back and forth for the bhikkhu.

Since the phenomena of the body and so forth are subject to arising, one who contemplates them is said to "dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body. [Likewise,] one who contemplates the nature of passing away...
Just as when a bellows is removed, its pipe is broken, and the corresponding effort is absent, that wind does not flow;
even so, when the body is broken, the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased, that which is called the body of inhalation and exhalation no longer functions.
Thus, seeing that "with the cessation of the body and so forth, there is the cessation of inhalation and exhalation," he is one who contemplates the nature of vanishing.
Or he dwells with regard to the body; thus it is said. "Contemplating the nature of arising and passing away" means contemplating, at one time, arising and, at another time, passing away.

"Or else, 'there is the body'" means that there is only the body—neither a being, nor a person, nor a woman, nor a man, nor a self, nor anything belonging to a self, nor "I," nor "mine," nor anyone, nor anything belonging to anyone.
Thus his mindfulness is established.
The phrase "just enough" (*yāvadeva*) is a definition that delimits the purpose. This is what is meant: the mindfulness that is established is not for any other purpose;
rather, it is just enough for the sake of mere knowledge—for the sake of the measure of knowledge that proceeds higher and higher from one stage to the next.
The meaning is: for the sake of the measure of mindfulness and for the sake of the increase of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
"He dwells independent" means he dwells independent by way of the dependence on craving and the dependence on views.
"And he does not cling to anything in the world" means that in the world he does not grasp at anything—whether form... or consciousness—as "this is my self" or "this belongs to my self."

"Even so" (*evampi*) is the particle *pi* used in the sense of inclusion, referring to what follows. By this phrase, the Blessed One shows that he has handed over the instruction on the section concerning mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānapabba*).
In that context, the mindfulness that grasps inhalation and exhalation is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*);
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin [are the truths of the path].
The Noble Path, which has cessation as its object, is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by striving through the Four Truths, one attains Nibbāna;
this is the door to deliverance for a bhikkhu intent upon inhalation and exhalation, leading all the way to Arahantship.
The commentary on the Chapter on Breathing is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Postures (Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā) 108.
Having thus analyzed body-contemplation by way of inhalation and exhalation, he now says, "And furthermore," etc., in order to analyze it by way of the postures.
In this context, it is true that even dogs, jackals, and the like, when walking, know "we are going."
But this was not said with reference to such a kind of knowing as that.
For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not eradicate the notion of self, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
However, the knowing of this bhikkhu abandons the perception of a being, eradicates the notion of self, and is indeed a meditation subject...

And there is the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). For this was said with reference to such clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) as: "Who goes? Whose is the going? For what reason does one go?
The same method applies to standing and so forth.
In that regard, as for "who goes," no being (*satta*) or person (*puggala*) goes. As for "whose is the going," it belongs to no one.
It is the going of a being or a person. For what reason does one go? One goes by means of the expansion of the air-element of mental activity.
Therefore, when the thought "I am going" arises, it generates that air;
the air generates the intimation (viññatti); and through the expansion of the air-element of mental activity, there is the forward projection of the entire body.
"Going" is what is said. The same method applies to standing and the others as well.
For there too, the thought "I stand" arises; that [thought] generates wind; the wind generates intimation (viññatti);
and the state of the entire body being raised from its base through the expansion of the wind element produced by the mental activity is "standing."
It is said: “I am sitting”—thus a thought arises; that [thought] generates wind; the wind generates intimation (*viññatti*).
Through the expansion of the wind-element of mental activity, the contraction of the lower body and the raised position of the upper body is called "sitting.
“I am lying down”—thus a thought arises; that [thought] generates wind; the wind [generates] intimation...
It is called "stretching out" or "lying down" because of the expansion of the bodily wind-element produced by mental activity, which causes the entire body to extend horizontally.
For one who understands in this way, it occurs to them: "A being goes; a being stands.
Yet, there is no such thing as a being that goes or stands. It is just as when one says, "The cart goes; the cart stands."
It is said that there is no such thing as a "cart" that actually moves or stands;
rather, when four oxen are yoked and driven by a skillful charioteer, the mere conventional expression "the cart moves" or "the cart stands" arises.
In the same way, in the sense of being unknowing, the body is like the cart; the winds of mental consciousness are like the oxen; and the [mental] factor is like the charioteer.
It is the mind. When the thought "I go" or "I stand" arises, the air element, generating intimation, comes into being;
through the expansion of the air element produced by mental activity, going and so forth occur.
Thereafter, there is merely a conventional expression, such as "the being goes," "the being stands," "I go," or "I stand. Therefore he said:
Just as a boat goes by the force of the wind, or an arrow by the force of the bowstring,
so does this body go, driven by the wind. Just as [a cart] moves by means of a rope,
so does this [body] move by means of the rope of the mind.
"Even when the body and the senses are engaged, they go, stand, or sit.
What being indeed could there be here who, without causes and conditions,
might stand or move by his own power?"

Therefore, it should be understood that when he observes walking and so forth as they occur solely by way of cause and condition, he understands: "As I am walking, I am walking"; or, "As I am standing, sitting, or lying down, I am lying down.
Alternatively, the statement "in whatever way his body is disposed, in that very way he understands it" is a comprehensive expression.
This means: in whatever manner his body is situated, in that very manner he understands it.
"He understands: 'That which exists in the mode of going, he goes'; he understands: 'That which exists in the modes of standing, sitting, and lying down, he lies down.
Thus, 'internally' means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by way of comprehending his own four postures.
'Externally' means by way of comprehending another's four postures. 'Internally and externally' means at times..."
He dwells contemplating the body in the body by grasping his own four postures at the appropriate time, and likewise those of another.

Regarding the phrases "contemplating the phenomenon of arising" (*samudayadhammānupassī*) and so forth, the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) should be set forth in five ways according to the method beginning with:
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form. It is with reference to this that it is said here: "contemplating the phenomenon of arising," and so on.
It has been stated. The passage beginning with "Or, 'there is a body' for him," and so forth, is exactly like what was previously said.
Here, however, mindfulness that encompasses the four postures is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that originates it is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*);
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin [are the truths of the path].
The Noble Path, which has cessation as its object, is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by striving through the four truths, one attains Nibbāna.
This is the door to deliverance for a single bhikkhu who maintains the four postures, leading all the way to Arahantship.
The commentary on the section on the postures is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension (Catusampajañña-pabbavaṇṇanā) 109.

Having thus analyzed body-contemplation by way of the postures, he now speaks the passage beginning with “And furthermore” (*puna caparaṃ*) in order to analyze it by way of the fourfold clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*).
Regarding that, first, in the phrase “in going forward and in returning” (*abhikkante paṭikkante*), “going forward” (*abhikkanta*) is said.
Going is *abhikkanta*; returning is *paṭikkanta*. Both of these are found within the four postures (*iriyāpatha*). First, regarding going:
one who moves the body forward is said to "go forth" (*abhikkamati*); one who turns back is said to "return" (*paṭikkamati*).
Even while standing, one who inclines the body forward remains standing yet is said to "go forth"; one who inclines it backward remains standing yet is said to "return."
...so called. Even when sitting, while still seated, as he moves forward facing the front part of the seat, it is called "approaching" (*abhikkamati*);
as he moves back toward the rear part of the seat, it is called "receding" (*paṭikkamati*). The same principle applies to lying down.

"One who acts with clear comprehension" (*sampajānakārī*) means one who performs all duties with clear comprehension, or one whose very activity is clear comprehension. For in such cases as approaching and so forth—
He indeed practices clear comprehension; he is never devoid of clear comprehension in any situation.
In this regard, clear comprehension is fourfold: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion.
Among these, when the intention to go forward arises, instead of going by the power of that thought alone, [he reflects]: "What purpose, indeed, will there be for me in going there?"

"Having discerned what is beneficial and what is not beneficial by considering 'there is' and 'there is not,' the discernment of the beneficial is *sātthaka-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the purposeful).

In this context, "the beneficial" (*attha*) refers to spiritual progress (*vaḍḍhi*) in accordance with the Dhamma, achieved by means of visiting a shrine (*cetiyadassana*), visiting the Bodhi tree (*bodhidassana*), visiting the Saṅgha (*saṅghadassana*), visiting senior elders (*theradassana*), or visiting objects of foulness (*asubhadassana*).
For even upon seeing a shrine or the Bodhi tree, one gains an object of meditation focused on the Buddha; and through visiting the Saṅgha, one gains an object of meditation focused on the Saṅgha.
Having generated rapture, he reaches Arahantship by contemplating that very [rapture] in terms of its exhaustion and passing away.

Having seen those [beings], and having established himself in their instruction, he sees the foul (asubha) and, having generated the first jhāna therein, reaches Arahantship by contemplating that very [jhāna] in terms of its exhaustion and passing away.
Therefore, seeing these [beings] is purposeful. However, some say: "Even for the sake of material goods..."
They say: "Prosperity is indeed the goal, for one has set out to practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*) based upon that.
Furthermore, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable regarding that journey, the discernment of the suitable is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).
For example, visiting a shrine (*cetiya*) is purposeful. However, if there is a great festival (*mahāpūjā*) at the shrine within a radius of ten or twelve *yojanas*—
The assembly gathers. Men and women, adorned and prepared according to their respective means, move about like figures in a painting.
Therein, greed arises toward a desirable object, aversion toward an undesirable one, and delusion toward that which is neither;
or he incurs an offense through physical contact, [endangering] both his life and his holy life.
Or if there is an obstacle, such a place is unsuitable. In the absence of the aforementioned obstacles, it is suitable.
This same principle applies to seeing the Bodhi tree. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful.
However, if people have constructed a great pavilion within a village and are holding an all-night Dhamma discourse, a gathering of people occurs in the manner already described.
When there is an obstacle, such a place is unsuitable; when there is no obstacle, it is suitable. The same principle applies even to seeing elders who are surrounded by large retinues.
Seeing the foul (asubha) is also purposeful. To illustrate this point, there is this story: it is said that a certain young bhikkhu...
Having taken the novice, he went for the purpose of obtaining a tooth-stick. The novice, having stepped off the path and walking ahead, saw a foul object and attained the first jhāna.

Taking that very state as his basis, he contemplated conditioned phenomena, realized the three fruits, and stood there having grasped the meditation subject for the sake of the higher paths. The youth—
Not seeing him, he called out, "Novice! He replied, "Venerable sir, from the day I went forth, I have never before engaged in two conversations at once with a bhikkhu.
On another day as well, I shall produce a superior distinction," and thinking thus, he gave the answer, "What is it, venerable sir? And when told, "Come," he came using only the singular form.
“Venerable sir, please go by this path and, standing for a moment where I am standing, look toward the east,” he said.
Having done so, he attained exactly the same distinction that the other had reached. Thus, one instance of foulness (asubha) arises for the benefit of two people.
Nevertheless, even though it is beneficial in this way, a woman’s foulness is unsuitable for a man.
And for a woman, the unattractiveness of a man is likewise suitable; thus, the discernment of what is suitable (*sappāya-sampajañña*) consists in grasping what is suitable.

Furthermore, for one who has thus grasped what is purposeful and suitable, "discernment of resort" (*gocara-sampajañña*) is the act of taking up—after having learned—the resort known as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of one’s own choice from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, and then proceeding on the alms-round while maintaining that [subject]. To explain this in detail:
This tetrad should be understood. Here, some bhikkhu carries [the burden] but does not bring it back;
another does not carry it but brings it back; another neither carries it nor brings it back; and another both carries it and brings it back.
In this regard, that bhikkhu who, during the day, purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting meditation...
Likewise, having spent the first watch of the night and the middle watch sleeping, and having passed the last watch in sitting and walking meditation,
he should early in the morning perform the duties for the shrine terrace and the Bodhi-tree terrace;
having sprinkled water upon the Bodhi-tree and provided drinking water and water for washing, he should perform all the Khandhaka duties, such as those toward teachers and preceptors.

He conducts himself according to the precepts. Having attended to his bodily needs and entered his lodging, he devotes himself to his meditation subject while sitting cross-legged two or three times, generating internal heat.

Rising at the time for the alms-round, with his meditation subject foremost, he takes his bowl and robe, leaves his lodging, and proceeds toward the shrine terrace while keeping his meditation subject in mind.
Having gone there, if his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), he enters the shrine courtyard without letting go of it.

If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the steps, sets it aside like a commodity held in the hand, and taking up joy with the Buddha as its object, he ascends the shrine courtyard; if it is a great shrine, three times—

Having performed the circumambulation, one should pay homage at four places. If it is a small shrine (*khuddaka-cetiya*), having likewise performed the circumambulation, one should pay homage at eight places.

Having paid homage to the shrine, when one reaches the Bodhi-terrace, one should pay homage to the Bodhi tree by displaying the highest reverence as if in the very presence of the Blessed Buddha. Thus, regarding the shrine and—
Having paid homage to the Bodhi tree and gone to the place where he had deposited his requisites, as if taking up those items with his own hand,
he takes up the meditation subject he had set aside; then, near the village, having put on his robe with the meditation subject foremost in mind,
he enters the village for alms.
Then, when people see him, they think, "Our venerable one has arrived," and go out to meet him.
Taking his bowl, they seat him in a rest-house or in their own home. After giving him rice-gruel, they wash his feet and anoint them with oil until the meal is finished.
Then, sitting before him, they either ask questions or desire to hear the Dhamma. Even if...
The commentators say that one should not fail to give a discourse on the Dhamma, for a Dhamma talk must indeed be given for the purpose of gathering people together.
Indeed, there is no such thing as a Dhamma talk that is divorced from a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Therefore, even when returning after giving a Dhamma talk with a meditation subject as its primary focus, eating food with a meditation subject as its primary focus, and performing the expression of thanks (*anumodanā*), [one should remain mindful].
