Having departed from the village followed by people, he turns back right there and sets out on the road.
Then, novice monks and young bhikkhus who had already left earlier and finished their meal outside the village see him;
they go out to meet him and take his bowl and robe.
It is said that the ancient bhikkhus did not perform their duties by looking up at the faces [of others], thinking, "This one is not our preceptor or teacher.
They performed them according to the limits of their actual relationship. People would ask them, "Venerable sir, what are these people to you?
Are they relatives on your mother's side or on your father's side? [The bhikkhu would reply,] "Having seen what do you ask? [The people would say,] "They are related to you..."
"Affection" means great respect. Friend, they do for us that which is difficult even for parents to do; our very bowl and robe belong to them alone.
By their power, we know neither fear in times of danger nor hunger in times of famine.
Thinking, "There are none such as these who are so helpful to us," he goes along praising their virtues; this is called [affection].
"He takes but does not bring back.
However, for one who performs the aforementioned duties and observances from the very beginning, the fire born of karma blazes up;
releasing the non-clung-to [heat], it seizes the clung-to, sweat breaks out from the body, and [the mind enters] the path of the meditation subject.
He does not climb [the tree]; rather, having taken his bowl and robes, he quickly pays homage at the cetiya and, at the very moment the cattle are leaving, enters the village for alms of rice-gruel.
Having received the gruel, he goes to the sitting-hall and drinks it.
Then, with only two or three mouthfuls, the fire of karma (kammaja-tejo) releases the clung-to (upādinnaka) matter and takes up the unclung-to (anupādinnaka) matter. With a hundred jars—
Having bathed as it were, attained the cooling of the fever of the fire-element, and consumed his rice-gruel under the heading of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*),
he washed his bowl and face; then, attending to the meditation subject during the midday rest, he wandered for alms in the remaining areas,
consumed his food under the heading of the meditation subject, and from that time on, [the object] appeared to him in continuous succession.
Having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he returns; this is called "not carrying it away, but bringing it back.
Monks such as these—having drunk the rice-gruel, begun insight (*vipassanā*), and attained *arahantship* within the Buddha’s dispensation—are beyond counting.
Even in the island of Sri Lanka alone, in various villages, there is no sitting hall where that seat does not exist [where such monks have sat].
"There are no bhikkhus who have attained Arahantship after drinking rice-gruel.

However, one who dwells in negligence, having cast aside his burden, broken all the observances, and lives with a mind bound by the five kinds of mental obstructions, does not even form the perception that "there is such a thing as a meditation subject";
instead, having entered a village for alms, he behaves in an unbecoming manner.
Having lived in close association with householders and having eaten, he goes out empty-handed;
this is called "neither taking nor bringing back.
As for the one described as "both taking and bringing back," he should be understood by way of the practice of going and returning.

For indeed, sons of good family who have gone forth in the Dispensation out of their own desire [for liberation] dwell together—ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred—having made a formal agreement on the duties to be observed. "Friends, you have not gone forth because of debt, nor because of fear, nor because of being driven by a livelihood;
rather, you have gone forth here because you desired to be freed from suffering. Therefore, regarding the defilement that arises while walking..."
"Restrain the defilement that arises while walking right there; restrain it while standing, while sitting, and while lying down—restrain it right where it arises.
Having made this agreement on their conduct, as they went on alms-round, there were rocks at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gavuta, and one gavuta.
They proceeded while attending to the meditation subject with that perception. If, for anyone, while walking...
A defilement arises, and he suppresses it right there. Failing to do so, he remains standing.
Then, even one coming from behind him stands still. He reproaches himself, thinking, "This bhikkhu knows the thought that has arisen in you;
this is not suitable for you," and by increasing his insight, he enters the plane of the Noble Ones right there.
Being unable to do so, he sits down. Then, even one coming from behind him sits down; this is the same method.
Even if he is unable to enter the noble plane (*ariyabhūmi*), he goes along suppressing that defilement and attending only to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
He does not lift his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject. If he should lift it, he turns back.
He returns to the very same spot, just like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, who dwelt at Āḷindaka.
It is said that for nineteen years he lived fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning;
indeed, people along the way—whether plowing, sowing, threshing, or performing other labors—would see the Elder coming in that manner.
Seeing him, they conversed among themselves, saying, "This elder turns back again and again as he goes. Is he perhaps lost on the way, or has he forgotten something?
Ignoring them, he practiced the duties of a recluse with a mind intent solely on his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), and within twenty years, he attained Arahantship.
On the very day he attained Arahantship, at the end of his walking path (caṅkamana),...
The deity residing there stood illuminating the lamp with her fingers. The four Great Kings, Sakka the lord of the gods, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to wait upon him.
Seeing that radiance, on the following day, the Elder Mahātissa the Forest-Dweller asked: "Venerable sir, there was a radiance near you during the night; what was that radiance?"
The Elder, creating a diversion, said, "What is called 'radiance' includes the radiance of a lamp as well as the radiance of a gem," and so forth.
Then, being pressed with the words, "You must conceal it," he admitted, "Yes," and confessed,
just like the Elder Mahānāga who lived in the Kālavalli Pavilion.

He, it is said, while fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning, first resolved to spend seven years standing or walking in order to honor the Great Struggle (*mahāpadhāna*) of the Blessed One.
Then, after fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning for sixteen years, he attained *arahantship*.
He raised his foot with a mind still engaged in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and not with one that was disengaged.

Turning back from his high spirits and approaching the vicinity of the village, he stands in a place that might arouse suspicion—wondering, "Is it a cow or a renunciant?"—and having put on his robe, he washes his bowl with water from within his armpit and makes a mouthful of water. For what reason?
So that when people come to give him alms or pay him homage, even by the mere words, "May you live long! [the merit of their act is increased].
"Distraction regarding the meditation subject occurred. When asked, "Today, venerable sir, what is the date?
or "How many monks are there? or "What is the question?", he would swallow his saliva and reply.

If there were no one to ask about the date and so forth, he would go out at the time of departure, spitting at the village gate, like the fifty monks who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery.
On the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, they made a formal agreement, saying, "Until we have attained arahantship, we shall not speak to one another.
When entering a village for alms, they would rinse their mouths with water before entering.
When questioned regarding the day or other matters, they acted according to the method already described. There, people, seeing the spittle, realized, "Today one has come; today two."
And they thought: "Why is it that these do not speak with us alone, or perhaps even with one another?
If they do not speak with each other, they must certainly have fallen into a dispute; come, let us go and ask them for forgiveness.
Having all gone to the monastery, they did not see even two monks in a single place among the fifty monks. Then he who...
Among them was a man with keen vision who said, "Sirs, such an opportunity does not belong to those who engage in quarreling;
the terrace of the shrine and the terrace of the Bodhi tree have been well-swept, the brooms have been properly set down, and the drinking water and washing water have been well-arranged.
They turned back right there, and those monks, having attained Arahantship within that very month, performed the invitation for purity during the Great Invitation ceremony.
Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kālavalli bower, and like the bhikkhus who had entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery,
lifting his foot with a mind intent solely on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he reached the vicinity of the village. Having rinsed his mouth with water and observed the streets,
he [avoided] places where drunkards, gamblers, and other quarrelsome persons were located, as well as places where fierce elephants, horses, and so forth were present.
Or, if there is none, he enters that street. And while walking for alms there, he does not go with excessive haste as if in a great hurry;
for there is no such thing as a "speedy" alms-food ascetic practice (piṇḍapātika-dhutanga).
Rather, he proceeds remaining motionless, like a water-cart that has reached uneven ground. And having entered each house, [he waits for] one who wishes to give...
Or, if he perceives that the donor is unwilling to give, he should wait for a suitable time, take his almsfood,
and having returned to the monastery— whether inside or outside the village— sit in a comfortable and appropriate place. Attending to his meditation subject,
he should establish the perception of repulsiveness in food by way of the similes of the axle-oil, the wound-ointment, and the son’s flesh.
Reflecting thus, he partakes of food endowed with the eight factors, neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment.
Having eaten and performed his duties regarding water, and having for a moment allayed the fatigue of the meal,
[he practices] after the meal just as before the meal, and in the latter watch of the night just as in the first watch.
And during the last watch of the night, he attends to the meditation subject alone; this is called "carrying away and bringing back.

Now, if one who fulfills this practice of going and returning—known as carrying away and bringing back—is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), they attain Arahantship in the first stage of life itself.
If they do not attain it in the first stage, then they attain it in the middle stage.
If he does not attain it in middle age, then in his final age. If he does not attain it in his final age, then at the time of death.
If he does not attain it at the time of death, then having become a son of the gods.
If he does not attain it by becoming a son of the gods, then when a Buddha has not appeared, he is reborn and realizes pratyekabodhi. If he does not realize pratyekabodhi...
He realizes [the goal]; then, in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of quick higher knowledge, just like the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya;
or one of great wisdom, just like the elder Sāriputta; or one of great psychic power, just like the elder Mahāmoggallāna;
or a bearer of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), just like the elder Mahākassapa; or one possessed of the divine eye.
Or like the elder Anuruddha; or like the elder Upāli, a master of the Vinaya;
or like the elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, a preacher of the Dhamma; or like the elder Revata, a forest-dweller;
or like the elder Ānanda, one of great learning; or like the elder Rāhula, the Son of the Buddha, who is desirous of training.
Thus, in this tetrad, for one who both goes out and returns, clear comprehension of the domain (*gocara-sampajañña*) reaches its culmination.
However, non-delusion regarding going forward and so forth is clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*). This should be understood as follows:
here, when a bhikkhu is going forward or returning, unlike blind worldlings who, in going forward and so forth, [think], "It is a self that goes forward..."
They are deluded, thinking either, "Advancing has been produced by me," or "I am advancing; advancing has been produced by me.

One who is not thus deluded understands that when the thought "I am advancing" arises, simultaneously with that very thought, the mind-originated air-element arises producing intimation (viññatti). Thus, it is by way of the expansion of the air-element of mental activity (*cittakiriyavāyodhātu*)...
This body, esteemed as such, a mere collection of bones, moves forward.

As it moves forward in this way, with each lifting of a foot, two elements—the earth element and the water element—become deficient, weak, and faint, while the other two become predominant and powerful;
the same applies to the setting down and the shifting of the foot. At the moment of releasing the foot, the fire element and the air element become deficient.
The former is weak, while the other two are excessive and powerful. The same applies to the acts of placing down and pressing down.

In that regard, the material and immaterial phenomena occurring during the act of lifting do not reach the stage of shifting forward. Likewise, those occurring during shifting forward do not reach shifting backward;
those occurring during shifting backward do not reach releasing; and those occurring during releasing do not reach placing down.
Proceeding in their respective positions, they do not reach a state of suppression.
Right there, joint by joint, articulation by articulation, and mass by mass, they break apart with a crackling sound like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan.
In this regard, what single entity advances? Or whose is this advancing? For, in the ultimate sense, it is only the elements (dhātu) themselves.
The walking of the elements, the standing of the elements, the sitting of the elements, and the lying down of the elements—
in each respective instance, together with form—
a different consciousness arises, and a different consciousness ceases.
"There is no interruption from the Avīci hell; it flows on like the current of a river.
Thus, non-confusion regarding advancing and so forth is called "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*).
The meaning of the phrase "he acts with clear comprehension when advancing and when retreating" is hereby concluded.

Regarding the terms "looking forward" (*ālokita*) and "looking around" (*vilokita*): here, "looking forward" means gazing straight ahead; "looking around" means looking toward the intermediate directions.

There are also other ways of looking—namely, looking down, looking up, and looking behind—which are termed "looking downward," "looking upward," and "looking backward," but these are not included here.
Only these two are taken because they are appropriate [for a monk], or rather, by way of this [specific] context.
"All these [factors] are indeed included.
In this context, when the thought "I shall look" has arisen, grasping the purpose without looking by means of the mind alone is *sātthaka-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the purposeful).
This should be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as a personal witness (*kāyasakkhin*). For this was said by the Blessed One: "If..."
“Monks, Nanda must look toward the eastern direction. Having applied his whole mind, Nanda looks toward the eastern direction, being fully aware therein:
‘May no covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states flow into me as I look toward the eastern direction. Monks, if...”
“The western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, above, below, and the intermediate directions must be looked at by Nanda.
Having brought everything to mind, Nanda looks toward the intermediate directions. As I look toward the intermediate directions in this way... [he remains] clearly comprehending.
Furthermore, here too, the purposefulness and suitability should be understood in the same manner as was previously stated regarding the visiting of shrines and so forth.

Full awareness of the range of movement (*gocara-sampajañña*), however, is simply the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, those whose meditation subjects are the aggregates, elements, or sense bases should look forward and around precisely by way of their own meditation subject; or else, those whose meditation subjects are the kasiṇas and so forth should do so with the meditation subject as their primary focus.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that looks forward or looks around; rather, [one acts] with the thought, "I shall look. In this mental state...
As it arises, the mind-originated air element arises together with that very consciousness, producing intimation.
Thus, by the mere expansion of the air element produced by mental activity, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper one leaps upward;
there is no one at all opening them with a mechanical device, and from that, eye-consciousness [arises].
"It arises accomplishing the function of seeing. Such clear comprehension here is called "clear comprehension through non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

Furthermore, clear comprehension through non-delusion should be understood here by way of thorough knowledge of the root (*mūla-pariññā*), adventitiousness, and temporariness. First, by way of thorough knowledge of the root:
"The life-continuum, adverting, seeing, receiving,"
Investigation, determining, and the impulsion that is seventh;
therein, the life-continuum proceeds accomplishing the function of a factor for the rebirth-existence.
Having turned it back, the functional mind-element accomplishes the function of adverting. With its cessation, eye-consciousness accomplishes the function of seeing.
While that [sense-consciousness] is performing its function, the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*) performs its function of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*);

following its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element (*vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu*) performs its function of investigating (*santīraṇa*); following its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element (*kriyāmanoviññāṇadhātu*) performs its function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*);
and following its cessation, the impulsion (*javana*) proceeds for seven times. In this regard:
Even in the first impulsion (javana), there is no looking forward or looking around by way of lust, hatred, or delusion, thinking, "This is a woman," or "This is a man.

This is also the case in the second impulsion... and so on up to... the seventh impulsion. However, among these [impulsions], just as among warriors on a battlefield who have fallen down after breaking ranks from top to bottom, there occurs [looking] by way of lust and so forth, thinking, "This is a woman," or "This is a man."
There is looking ahead and looking around. Thus, first of all, non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood here by way of fundamental full understanding.

However, when a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door, after the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and after the adverting consciousness and the others have arisen and ceased in order to accomplish their respective functions, at the end, the impulsion (*javana*) arises. That [impulsion] [arises] after those that arose previously...
In the eye-door, which is like a house belonging to the adverting consciousness and the others, he is like a guest.
Just as it is not fitting for a guest who has entered another's house to request something or issue commands while the owners of the house remain silent,

so too, in the eye-door— which is the house of the adverting consciousness and the others— it is not fitting for him to do so while the adverting consciousness and the others are neither attached nor averse.
And since it is improper for lust, hatred, and delusion to arise in those who are not deluded, thus should clear comprehension through non-delusion be understood by way of its adventitious nature.
Furthermore, those consciousnesses that arise at the eye-door, ending with the stage of determining (voṭṭhabbana), perish right there along with their associated mental states;
they do not see one another and are therefore short-lived and temporary.

They exist. In this regard, just as when all the human inhabitants of a single house have died, it is not fitting for the one survivor—who is himself subject to death at that very moment—to take delight in dancing, singing, and the like;

even so, when among the mental states associated with a single door, such as adverting and so forth, each has perished right where it arose, it is likewise not fitting for the remaining impulsion (javana), which is itself subject to death at that very moment, [to engage in such activity].
"Delight" is not appropriate by way of lust, hatred, and delusion; thus should non-delusive clear comprehension be understood by way of its temporary nature.
Furthermore, this should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions. For herein, both the eye and visible forms belong to the aggregate of form;
seeing belongs to the aggregate of consciousness; and the feeling associated with that [seeing] belongs to the aggregate of feeling.
Perception is the aggregate of perception; contact and the rest are the aggregate of mental formations.
Thus, within the combination of these five aggregates, looking forward and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it that looks forward alone, and who looks around?
Likewise, the eye is the eye-base, visible form is the visible-form-base, seeing is the mind-base, and feeling and the other associated states are the remaining factors.
the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*). Thus, in the coming together of these four bases, looking forward and looking around are discerned.

In that regard, who is it that looks forward? Who is it that looks around? Likewise, there is the eye (*cakkhu*) as the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*), visible form (*rūpa*) as the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), seeing as the eye-consciousness-element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*), and the feeling and other states associated with that as the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*). Thus, in the case of these four elements...
In the combination [of these conditions], looking forward and looking around become manifest. In that regard, who is it that alone looks forward? Who looks around?

Thus, the eye is the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); visible form is the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*); adverting consciousness is the proximity, contiguity, decisive-support, presence, and absence-conditions (*anantara-samanantara-upanissaya-atthi-vigata-paccaya*);

light is the decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*); and feeling and the other mental factors are the co-nascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). It is in this way that, through the combination of these conditions—

Looking forward and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it that looks forward, and who is it that looks around? Thus, in this context, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.
Regarding "in bending and in stretching," this refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs; therein, the bending and stretching occurs solely through the power of the mind.

Having discerned what is beneficial and what is not beneficial regarding the conditions for bending and stretching the hands and feet, the discernment of what is beneficial is "clear comprehension of purposefulness" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
In this regard, if one stands having bent and stretched the hands and feet for too long,
or remains in that state, painful sensations arise moment by moment, the mind fails to attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) falls away.
One does not attain distinction. However, when one bends at the proper time and extends at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise;

the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject reaches full development, and one attains distinction. In this way, the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful should be understood.
Furthermore, even when there is something beneficial, having examined what is suitable and what is unsuitable, the discernment of suitability consists in grasping what is suitable.
In this regard, the following is the method: It is said that in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, young bhikkhus were engaged in recitation.

Behind them, young bhikkhunīs were listening to the Dhamma. There, one young man, extending his hand, came into physical contact [with a bhikkhunī], and for that very reason he was reborn as a householder.
Another bhikkhu, extending his foot, extended it into a fire.
One monk sat in meditation with his foot pressed against a bone; another stretched out his foot on an anthill and was bitten by a venomous snake;

another stretched it out on the crossbar of his robe-shed and was bitten by a jewel-serpent. Therefore, one should not stretch out the foot in such unsuitable places, but should stretch it out in a suitable place.
This is what is meant here by "clear comprehension of suitability."
Clear comprehension of the range of activity (*gocara-sampajañña*), however, should be illustrated by the story of the Great Elder (*mahāthera*).

It is said that while the Great Elder was sitting in his daytime resting place conversing with his pupils, he suddenly flexed his hand, then placed it back in its original position, and finally flexed it slowly.
The pupils asked him, "Why, venerable sir, did you flex your hand so suddenly?"

“Then, having placed it back in its proper position, I slowly bent my arm. “Friend, ever since I began to attend to my meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), my hand has never been bent while leaving the meditation subject aside;
however, just now, while conversing with you, I bent it while leaving the meditation subject aside. Therefore, [I have placed it] back again in its proper position.”
"Excluding the bending. "It is well, Bhante; a bhikkhu indeed ought to be like this.
Thus, even here, it should be understood that *gocara-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the range) is precisely the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Internally, there is no such thing as a self that bends or stretches. [This occurs] through the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) consisting of the mental activity of the aforementioned kind.
Furthermore, just as the movement of hands and feet occurs in a wooden puppet by means of pulling strings, so too does the bending and stretching [of the limbs] take place;
such thorough understanding in this regard should be known as "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*).
Regarding "wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe": here, it refers to the wearing of the outer robe and the inner robe by way of wrapping and draping, and of the bowl...
“Wearing” means using [the robes] by way of receiving alms-food and so forth. In that regard, first, concerning the wearing of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi-cīvara*):

while walking for alms after having dressed and put on [the robes], the acquisition of material food and the purpose described by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with “for the warding off of cold” is what is called the “purpose. By means of that, one should understand “clear comprehension of purposefulness” (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
For one who is accustomed to heat and is weak, a fine robe is suitable; for one who is sensitive to cold, a thick double-layered robe is suitable.
The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is simply unsuitable, for it acts as an impediment when used for closing the door and so forth.
Likewise, robes made of wool, silk, or other such desirable materials are unsuitable; for such things—
In the forest, that which creates an obstacle to one's dwelling alone, or even an obstacle to one's life, is unsuitable.

In the direct sense, however, whatever arises by way of wrong livelihood such as fortune-telling and so forth, and whatever causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline when practiced, that is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. Of that—
Herein, clear comprehension of suitability should be understood by way of wearing [the robe], and clear comprehension of the domain by way of not abandoning the meditation subject.

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that puts on the robe; rather, the putting on of the robe occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element in the form of mental activity of the kind already described.
In this process, the robe is insentient and the body is also insentient. The robe does not...
One knows: "My body is covered. Yet the body does not know: "I am covered by a robe.
It is simply the elements that conceal the collection of elements, just as a cloth or a rag conceals a form made of rags.
Therefore, one should feel no joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe, nor any dejection upon obtaining one that is not beautiful.
For instance, when people offer honor with garlands, perfumes, incense, clothing, and so forth to the Nāgavammika tree,
the cetiya, and other such objects, while others offer dishonor by striking them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, or weapons,
those Nāgavammika trees and the like do not experience either joy or dejection. In the same way, one should not feel joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe.

"Having encountered what is unattractive, there is no mental distress"—it is by means of such reflective analysis (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) that non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*) should be understood here.

Even when holding the bowl, one should not grasp it hastily; rather, with the thought, "By taking this bowl and wandering for alms, I shall obtain food," one should understand purposeful clear comprehension (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) in terms of the benefit to be gained from the act of taking the bowl.
However, for one whose body is emaciated and weak, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For anyone [whose bowl] has been struck by four or five lumps of clay...
It is indeed unsuitable because it is difficult to clean. For a bowl that is hard to wash is not permissible; moreover, it becomes a hindrance for one who is washing it.
A bowl with the color of a gem is alluring and, in the same manner as described regarding the robe, is unsuitable.
However, as for a bowl obtained through making signs and so forth, if one uses it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.

This is exclusively unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. Through that [distinction], one should understand here "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*); and through the mere non-abandonment of the meditation subject, one should understand "clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocara-sampajañña*).

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that takes up the bowl; it is solely by the expansion of the air-element in the form of mental activity, as previously described, [that the action occurs].
However, there is such a thing as taking up a bowl. In that case, the bowl is insentient and the hands are also insentient.
The bowl does not know, "I am being held by the hands," nor do the hands know, "The bowl is being held by us.
It is merely elements grasping a collection of elements, like the grasping of a glowing-hot bowl with tongs. It is by way of reflection occurring in this manner [that one understands].
The clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood.

Furthermore, just as when compassionate persons, seeing destitute people lying in a shelter for the destitute— whose hands and feet are severed, whose wounds are oozing with pus and blood, swarming with maggots, and surrounded by blue flies— provide them with bandages and cloths for their wounds;...
And they bring medicinal ointments in skull-cups and other vessels. In that regard, some receive cloths that are soft, while others receive those that are coarse.
Some receive medicinal bowls that are well-shaped, while others receive those that are ill-shaped;
yet they are neither pleased nor displeased by this, for [the bowl] serves merely as a covering for the wound.
Just as a ragged cloth is sufficient for receiving medicine and a skull-bowl is sufficient for their purpose, even so, that bhikkhu who regards his robe like a ragged cloth for a wound,
his bowl like a skull-bowl for medicine, and the alms-food obtained in the bowl like medicine in the bowl—
this is clear comprehension through non-delusion regarding the wearing of the outer cloak, the bowl, and the robes.
He should be understood as one who acts with supreme clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).

Regarding "eating" and so forth: "eating" refers to the consumption of alms-food; "drinking" to the drinking of rice-gruel and the like; "chewing" to the chewing of flour-based snacks and the like; and "tasting" to the tasting of honey, molasses, and the like.
Therein, even the eightfold [method] described by way of the formula beginning with "not for sport" and so forth—
"Meaning" (attha) means purpose. By way of that, "clear comprehension of what is beneficial" (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.
Furthermore, among coarse or refined, bitter or sweet foods and so forth, whatever food causes discomfort for someone is unsuitable for them.
Moreover, that which is obtained through divination and the like, or when one eats it unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline—[that too is unsuitable].
That which is exclusively unsuitable is "the unwholesome" (viparīta). The opposite is "the suitable.

Herein, "clear comprehension of the suitable" should be understood by way of that [suitability], and "clear comprehension of the domain" (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood by way of not abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" who is an eater; it occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element (vāyodhātu) and the activity of consciousness (cittakiriyā) of the aforementioned kind.
However, there is what is called "the receiving of the bowl. There is what is called "the lowering of the hand into the bowl" by means of the diffusion of the air-element produced by a mental act.
By means of the diffusion of the air-element produced by a mental act alone, there is the making of mouthfuls, the lifting of the mouthfuls, and the opening of the mouth.
No one opens the jawbones with a key or a mechanical device; it is solely by means of the diffusion of the air-element produced by a mental act.
The morsel is placed in the mouth; the upper teeth perform the function of a pestle, the lower teeth perform the function of a mortar, and the tongue performs the function of a hand.
Thus, thin saliva from the tip of the tongue and thick saliva from the root of the tongue smear that morsel there. That [morsel] upon the mortar of the lower teeth...
There is no one who, having turned it over with the tongue and hand, moistened it with saliva, and crushed it between the pestle-like teeth, puts it inside with a spoon or a ladle;
rather, it enters by means of the air element (*vāyodhātu*).
Once entered, there is no one who supports it by making a bed of straw; rather, it remains by means of the air element alone. Thus it stays.
There is no one who, having built a hearth and kindled a fire, stands there cooking; rather, it is cooked by the fire element itself.
There is no one who, as each portion is cooked, removes it outside with a ladle or a stick;
rather, the air element itself carries it out. Thus, the air element brings it in and carries it out, supports it and turns it over, and crushes and dries it up.
And it expels [waste]. The earth element supports, transforms, crushes, and dries up. The water element moistens and maintains its state of moisture.
The fire element matures what has entered within. The space element provides a clear passage.
The consciousness element, through appropriate application in each respective case, exerts itself; it is by way of such reflective contemplation as thus proceeds herein that [this is understood].
Non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood.
Furthermore, herein it should also be understood through the contemplation of the tenfold repulsiveness:
by way of going, seeking, enjoyment, abode, storage, the unripened, the ripened, the fruit, the outflow, and smearing.

Non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood. A detailed exposition on this point, however, should be taken from the "Description of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Nutriment" in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Regarding "the act of defecation and urination": this refers to the performing of defecation and urination.
In that regard, for one who does not evacuate at the proper time, sweat breaks out from the entire body, the eyes roll, and the mind does not become one-pointed.
Furthermore, other diseases arise; however, for one who acts [properly], none of that occurs—this is the meaning here.

By means of this, clear comprehension of purposefulness (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) should be understood. For one who voids excrement or urine in an improper place, there is an offense, infamy increases, and there is a danger to life.
But for one who voids them in a suitable place, none of that occurs.

"It occurs"—this is what is appropriate here. By virtue of that, there is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*); and by virtue of not abandoning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), "clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocara-sampajañña*) should be understood.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that performs the excretion of feces and urine; it occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) arising from mental activity.
However, there is the function of defecation and urination.

Just as when a boil has ripened, the pus and blood issue forth involuntarily through the bursting of the boil, and just as water issues involuntarily from an overfilled water vessel, so too the feces and urine accumulated in the receptacle for digested food and the bladder issue forth involuntarily, being compressed by the force of the wind. And this [process] occurs thus...
When he goes out, the excrement and urine belong neither to that bhikkhu himself nor to another; they are merely the discharge of the body.
How so? Just as when one discards old water from a water-pot, it belongs neither to oneself nor to others;
it is merely the act of clearing away. It is by means of such reflective consideration (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) that this [occurs].
Clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood.
Regarding "going" and so forth: "going" means in the act of walking; "standing" means in the act of standing; "sitting" means in the act of sitting; "lying down" means in the act of sleeping;
"waking" means in the act of being awake; "speaking" means in the act of talking; "silence" means in the act of not talking. "When going, one understands: 'I am going'..."

“Standing, he understands: ‘I am standing’; sitting, he understands: ‘I am sitting’; lying down, he understands: ‘I am lying down’”—in this passage, the long-term postures (addhāna-iriyāpatha) are spoken of.
“In advancing and retreating, in looking forward and looking aside, in bending and stretching”—in this [passage], the intermediate ones are spoken of.
“In going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking”—[in this passage, the short-term ones are spoken of].

But here, the minor modes of conduct (*khuddakacuṇṇikairiyāpathā*) are mentioned. Therefore, in these cases as well, acting with full awareness (*sampajānakāritā*) should be understood in the same manner as described above.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva, who was a master of the Three Piṭakas, said: "When someone, after walking or pacing back and forth for a long time, later stands still and reflects thus:
‘The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of walking have ceased right here,’ this [is full awareness]."

"One who acts with clear comprehension while walking" is so called. When one who is reciting, answering questions, or attending to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) stands for a long time and later, while sitting, reflects thus:

"The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of standing have ceased right here," this is called "one who acts with clear comprehension while standing. [Likewise,] by means of performing recitation and so forth...
Having sat for a long time, later on, when he has lain down, he reflects thus:
"The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred while sitting have ceased right here. This is one who acts with clear comprehension while sitting.
But as for one who, while lying down, either recites his lessons or attends to his meditation subject, falls asleep, and then, having arisen later, [reflects] thus...
He reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of lying down have ceased right here.

This is what is meant by one who acts with clear comprehension both while asleep and while awake. For the non-occurrence of functional consciousnesses is called "sleep," while their occurrence is called "waking.
Furthermore, when speaking, he reflects: "This sound depends upon the lips, the teeth, and the tongue..."
“Dependent on the palate and dependent on an appropriate mental application, it arises. Being mindful and clearly comprehending, he speaks;

or else, after a long time of reciting, expounding the Dhamma, reviewing a meditation subject, or answering a question, later on, having become silent, he reflects thus: “At the time of speaking, [the speech] arose...”
"Only here have material and immaterial phenomena ceased"—one who acts with clear comprehension when speaking is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in speech.
But he who, having remained silent for a long time while attending to the Dhamma or a meditation subject, later reflects thus:

"Material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time I was silent have ceased right here; when there is the occurrence of derived materiality, one is said to 'speak,' but when it is absent..."
"He is called one who is silent"—thus he is called "one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence.
This burden of non-delusion (*asammohadhura*) is what is intended in this Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta*).
However, in the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta*, all four kinds of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) are found. Therefore, specifically here—
The state of acting with clear comprehension (*sampajānakāritā*) should be understood by way of non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*) alone.

Furthermore, in all instances where the phrase "acting with clear comprehension" occurs, the meaning should be understood by way of clear comprehension associated specifically with mindfulness (*sati*).
In the *Vibhaṅga* treatise, however, these terms are analyzed as follows: "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he moves forward; mindful and clearly comprehending, he moves backward."

"Thus internally" means that by way of embracing the four kinds of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), he dwells contemplating the body in the body either in his own body or in another's body, or at one time in his own body and at another time in another's body.

Herein, regarding the phrases "contemplating the nature of arising and passing away," etc., it is the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) alone that should be extracted. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Herein, mindfulness that encompasses the four kinds of clear comprehension is the truth of suffering; the prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin;
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; and the Noble Path of the kind already described is the truth of the path.
Thus, by striving through the four truths, one attains Nibbāna. This refers to one who possesses the four kinds of clear comprehension.
By means of the bhikkhu, this is the door to deliverance leading up to arahantship.
The commentary on the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension is finished.
The commentary on the section on attention to repulsiveness begins.

110. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the fourfold clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*), he now speaks the words beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by way of attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikūlamanasikāra*).

Regarding that, whatever needs to be said concerning the passage beginning with "this very body," all of it has been stated in detail in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga* within the section on the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*). [The word] "both-ways-mouthed" (*ubhatomukhā*)...
“Below and above” means it is provided with two openings. “Of various kinds” means of diverse sorts.
Herein, this is the correlation of the simile: the body composed of the four great elements is like the bag open at both ends;
the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs are like the various kinds of grain mixed and poured into it; and the man with good eyesight is...
Just as for a farmer when he has released that sheaf and is reflecting upon it, the various kinds of grain become manifest;
so too, the manifestation of the thirty-two aspects should be understood as becoming clear for the practitioner of yoga when they reflect upon them.
Thus, "internally" means: in this way, by means of discerning the hair and so forth, either in one's own body or in the body of another, at the appropriate time...
Or he dwells contemplating the body as a body, either his own or that of another, at the appropriate time; from here on, the method is exactly as previously stated.
For in this instance, mindfulness that grasps the thirty-two aspects should be understood as the door to liberation by applying the formula "the truth of suffering" (*dukkhasacca*).
The rest is just as before.
The commentary on the section on contemplation of repulsiveness is finished.
Commentary on the section on contemplation of the elements (111):
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the contemplation of repulsiveness, [the Buddha] now [analyzes it] by way of the contemplation of the elements.
He spoke again, beginning with the words "Furthermore," in order to analyze [the matter]. Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning together with the application of the simile:

Just as some butcher, or a pupil supported by that same butcher’s food and wages, having slaughtered a cow and carved it up, [stands] at the crossroads—known as the central point where four great highways leading to the four directions meet.

Just as one might sit having divided [the body] into various portions, even so a bhikkhu—because the body is situated in whatever way among the four postures, and because it is thus situated, he contemplates the body as it is directed:
"In this body there is the earth element... pe ... the air element."

What is meant? Just as for a cow-slaughterer, even while he is rearing a cow, or bringing it to the slaughterhouse, or having brought it there and tying it up, or while he is killing it, or even while he is looking at the dead carcass—so long as he has not cut it open and divided it into pieces, his perception that "this is a cow" does not disappear. Only after he has divided it...
But when he is seated, the perception of "cow" disappears and the perception of "meat" arises;
it does not occur to him, "I am selling a cow," or "These people are taking a cow. Rather, it occurs to him only, "I am selling meat," or "These people are taking meat.
In the same way, for this bhikkhu also, previously during his time as a foolish worldling...
Whether he has become a householder or one who has gone forth, the perception of "a being" or "an individual" does not disappear so long as he does not analyze this very body,
however it is positioned or disposed, by breaking it down into its solid components and reviewing it according to the elements.
However, for one who reviews it according to the elements, the perception of a "being" disappears, and his mind becomes settled through the mode of the elements alone.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “He contemplates this very body, however it is placed, however it is disposed, as consisting of elements:
‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Just as if, monks, a skilled butcher or his apprentice... [up to] ...the air element.”
The meditator is like the cow-killer; the perception of a "cow" is like the perception of a "being"; the four-way crossroads is like the four postures;
and the act of sitting after having dissected [the body] limb by limb is like the contemplation according to elements. This is the explanation of the text here;
the discussion of the meditation subject, however, is set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Thus internally" means that by means of this discernment of the four elements, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in another's body, or at times in one's own body and at times in another's body. From here on, the method is exactly as stated before.
For here, mindfulness which discerns the four elements is the Truth of Suffering; having made this connection, it is a gateway to liberation.
This is to be understood. The remainder is exactly as before.
The commentary on the section on the contemplation of elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) is finished.
The commentary on the section on the nine charnel-ground contemplations (*navasivathika*).

112. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the attention to the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by means of the nine cemetery sections (*sivathikapabbā*).
Therein, *seyyathāpi passeyya* means "just as one might see.
*Sarīraṃ* means a dead body. *Sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ* means discarded in a charnel ground (*susāna*). *Ekāhaṃ matassa assa* means "it would be one day dead" (*ekāhamataṃ*).
"Dead for two days" means one who has been dead for two days. "Dead for three days" means one who has been dead for three days.
It is called "the bloated" because, like a bellows filled with air, it has become bloated by the successive emergence of a swollen state following the exhaustion of life.
"Vinīla" refers to a discolored state; that which is simply dissolved (vilīna) is "vinīlaka. Alternatively, it is "kucchita" (loathsome) because of its repulsiveness.

*Vinīla* means the livid-blue. This is a designation for the physical carcass when it is mostly blue in color—reddish in the places where flesh has protruded, white in the places where pus has accumulated, and blue in the majority of its blue areas—like a body wrapped in a blue cloth.
*Vipubba* refers to the pus trickling out from nine openings or from fissured parts; it is simply "putrid. *Vipubbameva* means "just putrid."

"Putrid" (*vipubbaka*) means that which is putrefied because it is loathsome; or, it is "putrid" because it is vile and putrefies. "Become putrid" (*vipubbakajāta*) means having become such, having reached that state.
"He applies this very body" means that the bhikkhu applies his own body, together with that [corpse], by means of knowledge.
He brings it near. How? "This body, too, is of such a nature, such a character, and has not transcended this [condition]. This is what is meant:
through the presence of these three factors—vitality (*āyu*), heat (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—this body is capable of standing, walking, and so forth;
but with their departure, this body is also of such a nature, having precisely such a putrid essence, being of such a character, and subject to such states as bloating and the rest.
"It will become" means that it has not transcended such states as bloatedness and so forth;

thus, "internally" means that by discerning such states as bloatedness, one dwells contemplating the body in the body, either in one's own body or in another's body, or at times in one's own body and at times in another's body.
"Being devoured" means sitting within the belly and so forth, repeatedly tearing away the flesh of the belly, the flesh of the lips, the flesh of the eyeballs, and so on.
"Being eaten": "with flesh and blood remaining" means joined with the remaining flesh and blood. "Smeared with fleshless blood":
even when the flesh has been consumed, the blood does not dry up; it is with reference to this that it is said, "smeared with fleshless blood.
"By another [side]" means by another direction or part. "A hand-bone": even though there are sixty-four types of bones in the hand, the hand-bone is treated as a single distinct unit.
"Scattered. The same method applies to foot-bones and so forth. "More than a year old" means having passed a full year.
"Putrid" means that those left in the open air become putrid after more than a year due to contact with wind, heat, and rain;
however, those buried underground remain for a longer time. "Reduced to powder" means scattered as individual grains of dust.
In all instances, the application should be made according to the method already stated, by way of being devoured and so forth.

Thus, "internally" means that by thus discerning [the body] as being devoured and so on, up until its state of being reduced to powder, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in another's body, or at one time in his own body and at another time in another's body.
Standing here, however, the nine cemetery contemplations (*navasivathikā*) should be combined, as they are set forth in the manner beginning with "one day dead," and so on.
All [these] are one; “being devoured by crows,” and so forth, is one; “a skeleton with flesh and blood, bound together by sinews” is one;
“smeared with flesh and blood, bound together by sinews” is one; “devoid of flesh and blood, bound together by sinews” is one;
“bones from which the binding has departed,” and so forth, is one; and “white bones” is one.
“One [sees them] as resembling the color of a conch shell,” one; “heaped up for over three years,” one; “putrid and reduced to powder,” one.
“In this way, monks,” he said, concluding the contemplation of the body after showing these nine cemetery meditations (*śivathika*).
Therein, mindfulness that grasps the nine cemetery meditations is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that gives rise to it is its origin.
The truth of the origin is craving; the non-occurrence of both [suffering and its origin] is the truth of cessation;

and the noble path—which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object—is the truth of the path. Thus, by striving through the four truths alone, one attains extinction (*nibbāna*).
This is the gateway to deliverance for monks who practice the nine cemetery contemplations, leading all the way to Arahantship.
The commentary on the section on the nine charnel-ground contemplations is finished.

At this point, the mindfulness of the body consisting of fourteen sections—the section on breathing, the section on postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, the section on attention to repulsiveness, the section on attention to elements, and the nine sections on the charnel ground—is completed.

Among these, only two—namely, the section on breathing and the section on attention to repulsiveness—are subjects for meditation leading to absorption (*appanā*). However, because the remaining twelve are taught by way of contemplating the dangers (*ādīnava*) in the charnel grounds, they are all subjects for meditation leading only to access concentration (*upacāra*).
The contemplation of the body is finished.
113. Commentary on the Contemplation of Feelings:
Having thus explained the foundation of mindfulness of the contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, the Blessed One now [explains it] in nine ways.
He spoke the passage beginning with “And how, bhikkhus,” in order to explain the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*).
Therein, “a pleasant feeling” means that when one is experiencing a pleasant feeling—whether bodily or mental—one understands: “I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
In this regard, it may be granted that even infants lying on their backs, while experiencing pleasure at the time of drinking milk and so forth, [understand] “pleasure…”
They understand [it] as "he makes known," but this was not said with reference to such a kind of knowing.

For such a kind of knowing does not abandon the apprehension of a being, does not eliminate the perception of a being, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
However, the knowing of this bhikkhu abandons the apprehension of a being and eliminates the perception of a being.
This is both a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and the development of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā*).
For this was said with reference to such clearly comprehending experience as: "Who feels? Whose is the feeling?
For what reason is there feeling? In that context, "who feels?"—no being (*satta*) or person (*puggala*) feels at all. "Whose is the feeling?"—it belongs to no one.
It is the feeling of a being or a person. For what reason? Because feeling has the physical basis and the object as its very substance.
Therefore, he understands thus: "Feeling itself experiences by making this or that basis for pleasure and so forth its object.
However, based on the occurrence of that feeling, there is the mere conventional expression, 'I feel. Thus, it is feeling alone...
One should understand that by taking the physical basis as the object and perceiving that "feeling itself feels," he knows: "I feel a pleasant feeling.
This was like a certain elder at Cittalapabbata.
It is said that when the elder was unwell, he groaned from intense pain and rolled back and forth. A young monk asked him: "Which [feeling] is it for you?"
“Venerable sir, it is the location that breaks. “Friend, there is no such thing as a separate location that breaks;
rather, it is feeling itself that feels by taking the physical basis as its object. “From the moment one knows this, is it appropriate, venerable sir, to endure [the pain]?
“Yes, friend, I endure it. “Endurance, venerable sir, is better. The Elder endured it.
Then the wind tore [his flesh] down to his heart; his internal organs became heaped together upon the bed.
The Elder showed them to the young monk, saying, "Friend, is such endurance sufficient? The young monk remained silent.
The Elder, having balanced his energy and attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), passed away into Parinibbāna as one who has reached the summit of equanimity.

And as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling... pe ...when experiencing a non-sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: "I am experiencing a non-sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Thus the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject of form, while teaching the meditation subject of the formless, spoke by way of feeling. For the meditation subject is twofold: the meditation subject of form and [the meditation subject of the formless].
And there is the immaterial meditation subject. This very thing is also called the discernment of the material and the discernment of the immaterial.
Therein, when the Blessed One was teaching the meditation subject of the material, he taught the analysis of the four elements either by way of concise attention or by way of detailed attention.
Both of these have been shown in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*.

But when explaining the immaterial meditation subject (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), he generally explains it by way of feeling (vedanā). For there are three ways of focusing (abhinivesa) on the immaterial meditation subject:
by way of contact (phassa), by way of feeling, and by way of consciousness (citta). How so?
For some, when the material meditation subject has been grasped either in brief or in detail, there occurs the first impact of the mind and mental factors upon that object.
When contact arises touching that object, it becomes manifest to some; when feeling arises experiencing that object, it becomes manifest to others;
and when consciousness arises cognizing that object after having grasped it, it becomes manifest to still others.
In this regard, for one to whom contact is manifest, he [thinks]: "It is not contact alone..."
“Feeling arises experiencing that very same object along with contact; perception arises perceiving it;
volition arises intending it; and consciousness arises cognizing it. Thus, one discerns precisely the pentad beginning with contact.
For one to whom feeling is clear, [it becomes evident that] “not only does feeling arise, but along with it—”
“While touching that very object, contact (phassa) also arises; perceiving, perception (saññā) also arises; intending, volition (cetanā) also arises;
and cognizing, consciousness (viññāṇa) also arises. Thus he discerns precisely the pentad beginning with contact.
For one to whom consciousness is clear, [he discerns]: “It is not merely consciousness alone that arises; together with it, while touching that very object...”
“Contact also arises; feeling, which experiences, also arises; perception, which perceives, also arises; volition, which intends, also arises.
Thus he discerns only the pentad beginning with contact.
Then, investigating, “On what are these phenomena supported, this pentad of contact? he understands: “They are supported by the physical basis (vatthu).”
The "basis" (vatthu) is the body born of karma; with reference to this it was said: "And this consciousness of mine is supported here, bound here.
In its actual meaning, it consists of both the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived matter (upādārūpa).

Thus, in this context, one sees only name-and-form (nāmarūpa), namely: "the basis is form, and the five beginning with contact are name. Here, "form" refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), and "name" [refers to the other four aggregates].

The four immaterial aggregates—thus there are merely the five aggregates. For there are no five aggregates apart from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), nor is there any name-and-form apart from the five aggregates.
Examining them with the thought, "What are the causes of these five aggregates? he sees that they have ignorance and so forth as their cause. Then...
This is both condition and conditionally arisen; there is no other being or person, but only a mere heap of pure formations.

Thus, having applied the three characteristics by way of name-and-form together with their conditions, he proceeds, contemplating them as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self" according to the sequence of insight.
Thus, one who desires the realization [of the goal] by thinking, "Today, O Noble Ones," having obtained such a day that is favorable in terms of the season,
favorable for the person, favorable for food, and favorable for hearing the Dhamma, sits cross-legged and, bringing insight to its culmination,
establishes himself in Arahantship. In this way, the meditation subject has been explained for these three persons up to the attainment of Arahantship.
Now, here the Blessed One, while explaining the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*), explained it by way of feeling (*vedanā*).
For if it were explained by way of contact (*phassa*) or by way of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), it would not be clear; it would appear as if in darkness.
But by way of feeling, it becomes clear. Why? Because the arising of feelings is manifest. Indeed, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings—
It is manifest. When happiness arises, it shakes and massages the entire body, pervading and overflowing it;

it is as if one were being made to eat hundred-purified ghee, or as if being anointed with hundred-fold refined oil, or as if the fever of the body were being extinguished by a thousand jars of water, while one involuntarily utters the words, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!"
It arises. When suffering arises, it agitates, crushes, pervades, and floods the entire body;
it is as if a red-hot plowshare were being thrust in, as if molten copper were being poured over one, or as if a cluster of wood-torches were being thrown into a forest of dry grass and trees.
One merely cries out in distress, "Alas, what suffering! Alas, what suffering!"
Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings becomes evident.
However, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is difficult to illustrate; it remains obscure and unmanifest, like darkness.

But for one who grasps the method—that when pleasure and pain have departed, there is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling consisting of a neutral mode by way of the negation of the agreeable and the disagreeable—it becomes evident. Just as...

What is it? Just as a deer-hunter, following the tracks of a deer that has fled after climbing onto a rock in the middle of a forest, sees the footprints on both the near and far sides of the rock but does not see them in the middle;
nevertheless, by inference he knows: "It climbed up from this side, descended from that side, and must have gone through this particular spot in the middle of the rock."
Thus, the arising of pleasant feeling is manifest like a footprint at the place where one has ascended;

the arising of painful feeling is manifest like a footprint at the place where one has descended. Just as one grasps the path by way of the method—"having ascended from here, having descended from there, he went thus in the middle"—so too, when pleasure and pain have passed away, there is the state of neutrality consisting in the negation of the agreeable and the disagreeable.
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" becomes clear to one who grasps it by way of its method.
Thus the Blessed One, having first taught the meditation subject of form, subsequently demonstrated the immaterial meditation subject by means of feeling.
And he did not demonstrate it in this way only here; he did so likewise in the *Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya*, the *Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya*, and the *Cūḷavedalla* suttas.
In the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga, the Āneñjasappāya, in the Mahānidāna of the Dīghanikāya,
the Sakkapañha, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, in the Cūḷanidāna Sutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Rukkhopama, the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta,
and throughout the entire Vedanāsaṃyutta— in these and many other suttas, the first meditation subject is the body (rūpa).
Having first explained it, he subsequently demonstrated the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling. And just as in those cases,
so too in this *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, having first explained the material meditation subject, he subsequently demonstrated the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling.
In this regard, concerning the passage beginning with "pleasant feeling," there is this further method of understanding: "He understands:
'I feel a pleasant feeling. Because of the absence of painful feeling at the moment of a pleasant feeling, one who is feeling a pleasant feeling understands:
"I feel a pleasant feeling. By this, [he recognizes] that painful feeling which was previously experienced.
Because that [previous feeling] has now ceased and because this pleasant feeling was non-existent prior to it, one understands:
"Feeling is indeed impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. Thus, one is fully aware of that.
And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time, one experiences only a pleasant feeling.
Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a painful feeling... [or] a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience...”
At that time, one experiences a pleasant feeling; one does not experience a painful feeling; at that time, one experiences only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

But even a pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Even a painful feeling... [and] even a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling... [is likewise].

“Feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent... [and so on] ...it is subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, with painful feeling, and with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived...”
“He understands: ‘The holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Regarding the phrases “sensual pleasure,” and so forth: sensual pleasure refers to the six types of worldly pleasant feelings based on the bait of the five strands of sense pleasure.
Spiritual pleasure refers to the six types of pleasant feelings based on renunciation. Sensual pain refers to the six types of worldly unpleasant feelings based on household life.
The "unworldly painful" refers to the six feelings of mental distress based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*).

The "worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the six feelings of equanimity based on household life (*geha*). The "unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the six feelings of equanimity based on renunciation.
Their detailed classification is found precisely in the text of the *Upari-Paṇṇāsaka*.

"Thus internally" means that by thus discerning pleasant feeling and so forth, he dwells contemplating feelings in his own feelings, or in another's feelings, or at times in his own feelings and at times in another's feelings.

Regarding the phrase "contemplating the nature of arising and passing away," here [the meaning] is through five sets of five aspects concerning feelings, such as: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling," and so on.

One who sees both arising and passing away should be understood as follows: he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings, or at times he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings and at times he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings.
Beyond this, the method is exactly as stated in the section on contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā).

For here, mindfulness that grasps feeling as the truth of suffering—having made this connection—one should understand it as the door to deliverance for the bhikkhu who grasps feeling. The rest is exactly the same.
Thus ends the contemplation of feelings.
Explanation of the Contemplation of Mind.

114. Having thus explained the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of feelings in nine ways, he now spoke the passage beginning with “And how, bhikkhus,” in order to explain contemplation of mind in sixteen ways.
Therein, “with lust” refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed;

“free from lust” refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. This, however, is not a synthesis of phenomena (*dhamma-samodhāna*), because it is a process of comprehension (*sammasana*).

Therefore, in this context, even a single term does not apply to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses (*akusalacitta*) belong neither to the former category nor to the latter.
"With hatred" (*sadosa*) is twofold: that accompanied by hatred (*dosasahagata*). "Free from hatred" (*vītadosa*) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate states.
The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the former category nor to the latter. "With delusion" (*samoha*)...
It is twofold: that accompanied by doubt and that accompanied by restlessness. However, since delusion (*moha*) arises in all unwholesome states, those [two types] are also included here.
Indeed, within this very dyad, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are fully encompassed.
"Free from delusion" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. "Contracted" means fallen under the influence of sloth and torpor.
For this is called "contracted mind. "Distracted" means accompanied by restlessness; for this is called "scattered mind.
"Exalted" refers to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. "Unexalted" refers to the sense-sphere. "Surpassable" refers to the sense-sphere.
"Incomparable" refers to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. Even therein, the fine-material sphere is surpassable, while the immaterial sphere is incomparable.

It belongs exclusively to the formless realm (*ārūpāvacara*). "Concentrated" (*samāhita*) refers to that which possesses either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).

"Unconcentrated" (*asamāhita*) is devoid of both types of concentration. "Liberated" (*vimutta*) means liberated by way of liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vimutti*) and suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*). "Unliberated" (*avimutta*) is devoid of both these liberations;
however, there is no occasion here for liberation by cutting off (*samuccheda*), pacification (*paṭippassaddhi*), or escape (*nissaraṇa*).

"Thus internally" (*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*) means: by thus grasping [the mind] as being with lust and so forth, at whatever moment whatever state of consciousness arises, he dwells contemplating the mind in his own mind or in another's mind;
sometimes in his own mind and sometimes in another's mind. Regarding the phrase "contemplating the phenomenon of arising and passing away" (*samudayavayadhammānupassī*): here...
Furthermore, the arising and passing away of consciousness should be extracted in five ways each, as follows: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of consciousness.
From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated.

For here, mindfulness that grasps the mind is the Truth of Suffering; having made this application, the gateway to liberation for the bhikkhu who grasps the mind should be understood. The rest is just the same.
The commentary on the contemplation of mind is finished.

Now, having thus explained the foundation of mindfulness as the contemplation of mind in sixteen ways, the commentary on the section on the hindrances in the contemplation of phenomena follows. 115. Thus, after explaining the foundation of mindfulness as the contemplation of mind in sixteen ways, [he now explains] the fivefold contemplation of phenomena.
And so he said, beginning with, “And how, bhikkhus,” and so forth. Furthermore, by means of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), the Blessed One taught the discernment of pure form;

by means of the contemplations of feeling and mind, he taught the discernment of pure non-form. Now, in order to teach the discernment of the mixed form-and-non-form, he said, “And how, bhikkhus,” and so forth.
Or else, through the contemplation of the body, there is only the discernment of the aggregate of form.

It has been stated that the discernment of the aggregate of feeling occurs through the contemplation of feelings, and the discernment of the aggregate of consciousness occurs through the contemplation of the mind.
Now, in order to explain the discernment of the aggregates of perception and mental formations as well, he said, "And how, monks," and so forth.
In this context, "present" means existing by way of frequent manifestation; "absent" means [existing] by way of non-manifestation.
Or it is non-existent because it has been abandoned. "And how" means: he understands by what cause the arising of sensual desire occurs;
he understands that cause. The meaning in all instances should be understood according to this method.
In this regard, the arising of sensual desire occurs through unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward a beautiful object (*subha-nimitta*). That beautiful object—
The "sign of the beautiful" (subhanimitta) refers both to that which is called beautiful and to the object of perception that is beautiful.

"Improper attention" (ayoniso-manasikāra) means attention that is unskillful, attention that follows a wrong path—namely, attending to what is impermanent as permanent, to suffering as happiness, to what is non-self as self, or to what is foul as beautiful. For one who frequently engages in such attention, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises.
It arises. Therefore the Blessed One said: “There is, bhikkhus, the sign of the beautiful;
there, the frequent practice of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the increase and expansion of sensual desire that has already arisen.
However, its abandonment occurs through proper attention to the sign of the foul. The “sign of the foul” refers to the foul itself.

The object of meditation is also the foul (aśubha). What is called "appropriate attention" (yonisomanasikāra) is skillful attention, systematic attention—namely, attention directed toward the impermanent as "impermanent," the suffering as "suffering," the non-self as "non-self," or the foul as "foul.
For one who frequently engages in that [attention] therein, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the foul..."
In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the non-nutriments for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: the apprehension of the sign of the unattractive, and the practice of the meditation on the unattractive.
Guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends, and appropriate talk.
For sensual desire is abandoned both by one who learns the tenfold sign of foulness and by one who develops it;

likewise by one who guards the doors of the senses, and by one who is moderate in eating—having the habit of drinking water and sustaining life when there is space for four or five mouthfuls. Therefore this was said:
“Having eaten only four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
Even for one who serves virtuous friends like the Elder Tissa the Meditator on the Foul, who delights in the cultivation of foulness, sensual desire may still arise.
