It is abandoned; it is also abandoned by talk that is suitable and based on the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it is said:

“Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire. Furthermore, he understands that for sensual desire abandoned by these six things, there is no further arising in the future through the path of Arahantship.
But through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward the sign of resistance (*paṭigha-nimitta*), ill will (*byāpāda*) arises.
In this context, both resistance itself and the object of resistance are the "sign of resistance. Improper attention has the same characteristic in all cases.
When one frequently directs [the mind] toward that sign, ill will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "There is..."

“Monks, the sign of repulsion and the frequent practice of improper attention toward it—this is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will.

However, through proper attention to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā cetovimutti*), there is the abandoning of that [ill will]. In each of those instances, it is called “loving-kindness.”

When this is said, both absorption (*appanā*) and access (*upacāra*) concentration are appropriate. "Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers specifically to absorption. "Careful attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*) has the characteristics already described.

For one who frequently practices that [attention] toward that [object], ill-will (*byāpāda*) is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā cetovimutti*);
frequent practice of careful attention toward it is the non-nutriments for ill-will that has not yet arisen..."
“for the non-arising of ill will, or for the abandoning of arisen ill will.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill will:

the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on one’s own karma as one’s own property, frequent analytical reflection, having virtuous friends, and talk that is conducive [to such states]. For, regarding the methods of pervading [the world] by groups, without groups, and by directions—

Ill will is abandoned even by one who learns loving-kindness through a particular individual, and also by one who develops loving-kindness by way of directional pervasion—both specifically and generally.
[One should reflect: "What will you do by being angry with this person? Can you destroy his virtue and so forth?
Surely you have come by your own karma and will go away by your own karma alone; as for another..."
What is called "anger" is like the desire to strike another with things such as glowing charcoal, red-hot iron rods, or excrement.
[One should reflect: "Even though he is angry with you, what will he do? Will he be able to destroy your virtue (sīla) and the other perfections?
He has come here by his own karma and will depart by his own karma; he is like an unwanted gift or like [smoke] blowing against the wind."
“Furthermore, his anger will fall upon his own head like a handful of dust thrown at a wall. Thus, even for one who reflects upon the ownership of kamma by oneself and by another,
or who stands in reflective discernment after having reflected upon the ownership of kamma by both,
or who serves a virtuous friend such as the Elder Assagutta who delights in the cultivation of loving-kindness— such ill-will [does not arise].
It is abandoned. It is also abandoned by talk based on loving-kindness and conducive to it while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it is said:

“Six things lead to the abandoning of ill will. Furthermore, he understands that for ill will abandoned by these six things, there is no further arising in the future through the path of non-returning.
Through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward boredom (*arati*) and the rest, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise.

"Boredom" means dissatisfaction. "Languor" (*tandī*) means physical laziness. "Stretching" (*vijambhitā*) means the bending or stretching of the body. "Gorging after a meal" (*bhattasammada*) means drowsiness following a meal or a feverish state caused by food.
"Mental sluggishness" (*cetaso līnattaṃ*) means a state of sinking in the mind. [One should understand] improper attention toward these factors, beginning with boredom.
For one who frequently indulges in them, sloth and torpor arise. Therefore he said:
"Bhikkhus, there is discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after eating, and mental sluggishness; therein lies the frequent application of improper attention.
This is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the increase and expansion of sloth and torpor that have already arisen."

However, the abandonment of this [laziness] occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward the element of initiative (*ārambhadhātu*) and the others. The "element of initiative" is the initial exertion of energy.
The "element of renunciation" (*nikkamadhātu*) is stronger than that, because it has emerged from indolence.
The "element of perseverance" (*parakkamadhātu*) is even stronger than that, because it advances further and further. Toward this threefold energy, one should apply wise attention.

For one who frequently applies [this energy], sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of perseverance;
the frequent application of wise attention thereto is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: taking note of overeating, changing one’s posture, attending to the perception of light, living in the open air, having virtuous friends, and engaging in appropriate conversation.

For when one who has eaten food that is like a hand-brought meal, a meal from a bowl, a meal with plenty of sauce, a crow-pecked meal, or a meal that leaves one stuffed, sits in a night-vigil or a day-vigil place to practice the duty of a recluse, sloth and torpor [overcome him].
It approaches like a great elephant trampling down [the ground].

However, for a bhikkhu who drinks water after setting aside space for four or five mouthfuls and whose nature is to subsist on that much, such [excessive eating] does not occur; thus, even for one who takes the sign in this way regarding over-eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned.
Furthermore, they are abandoned by one who changes from whichever posture sloth and torpor have descended upon him to another.

Thinness and drowsiness are abandoned by one who attends to the light of the moon, the light of a lamp, and the light of a torch at night, or to the light of the sun during the day; by one who dwells in the open air;
and by one who serves spiritual friends like the Elder Mahākassapa, who have abandoned thinness and drowsiness.
They are also abandoned by talk concerning the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that are appropriate for standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it was said:

“Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor. Furthermore, he understands that for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, there is no further arising in the future through the path of Arahantship.
Through unwise attention regarding the lack of tranquility of the mind, restlessness and remorse arise. Lack of tranquility means...
It is the state of non-quiescence. In meaning, this is simply restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*).
In this regard, restlessness and remorse arise for one who frequently engages in improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). Therefore he said: "Bhikkhus, there is non-quiescence of the mind;
therein, the frequent practice of improper attention is the nutriment for unarisen restlessness and remorse..."
“...for the increase and expansion of restlessness and remorse that have already arisen.
However, the abandoning of this occurs through wise attention toward the tranquility of mind known as concentration. Therefore he said:
“Bhikkhus, there is tranquility of mind; frequent application of wise attention to it is its nutriment.”
“...for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the abandoning of arisen restlessness and remorse.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse:

being learned, being one who asks questions, knowing the Vinaya, associating with elders, having virtuous friends, and appropriate conversation. For by means of great learning alone, one [abandons it]— *Note: The sentence fragment ends mid-thought; the full context would typically continue to explain how these factors contribute to overcoming restlessness and remorse.*

Restlessness and remorse are abandoned even by one who learns two, three, four, or five Nikāyas according to the text and according to the meaning; even by one who frequently inquires into what is allowable and what is not;
even by one who already knows the matter through mastery gained from long-standing practice in the Vinaya regulations; and even by one who approaches elder and senior Theras such as the Elder Upāli.

For one who serves a virtuous friend who is a master of the Vinaya, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. They are also abandoned through appropriate talk concerning what is allowable and what is not allowable, whether standing, sitting, or otherwise.
Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse. When restlessness and remorse have been abandoned by means of these six things, as for restlessness—
He understands: "By means of the path of arahantship, remorse is abandoned; by means of the non-returning path, there is its non-arising in the future.
Regarding states that are occasions for doubt, doubt arises through unwise attention.
Those states which are occasions for doubt are themselves called "doubt" because they are the cause of repeated doubting. In this regard, unwise attention—
In one who frequently engages [in such things], doubt arises. Therefore he said: "Bhikkhus, there are states that are a basis for doubt;
frequent improper attention toward them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt and for the increase, expansion, and abundance of arisen doubt."
However, its abandonment occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward wholesome and other such phenomena. Therefore he said:

"Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, blameworthy and blameless phenomena, phenomena to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and superior phenomena, dark and bright phenomena with their counterparts;
therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the non-arising of [unarisen] [defilements]."
“...or for the non-arising of doubt, or for the abandoning of doubt that has already arisen.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt:

being well-versed in the teachings, being inquisitive, knowing the Vinaya thoroughly, having much resolute confidence, having virtuous friends, and engaging in appropriate discourse. For even by means of great learning, one [abandons it]...
...or, for one who learns the five Nikāyas according to the text and according to the meaning, doubt is abandoned;
likewise for one who frequently engages in inquiry concerning the Three Jewels; for one who has attained mastery in the Vinaya;
for one who possesses abundant resolve known as unwavering confidence in the Three Jewels; and for those devoted to faith such as the Elder Vakkali.

Doubt is abandoned by serving a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta). It is also abandoned by talk concerning the qualities of the Three Jewels that is appropriate to one’s standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt.
And when doubt has been abandoned by these six things, [it is further abandoned] by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga).
He understands: "There will be no further arising in the future.

Thus, with regard to himself or thus, by means of the discernment of the five hindrances, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—either in his own phenomena or in the phenomena of another, or at one time in his own phenomena and at another time in the phenomena of another. [He contemplates] their origin and their passing away.

Herein, among the signs of the beautiful, the signs of the foul, and so forth, [the factors] should be extracted by way of improper attention and proper attention, according to the method stated for the five hindrances.
From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated.

For here, one should understand the door of deliverance for the bhikkhu who discerns the hindrances by making the following application: "The mindfulness that discerns the hindrances is the truth of suffering. The rest is just the same.
The commentary on the section on the hindrances is finished.
Commentary on the section on the aggregates (116):
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five hindrances, [the author] now [proceeds] by way of the five aggregates.
He said, "Furthermore, in order to analyze," and so forth. Therein, "in the five aggregates of clinging" (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*):

the aggregates of clinging are the aggregates that are the basis for clinging; the meaning is "collections of phenomena" (*dhammapuñjā*) or "masses of phenomena" (*dhammarāsayo*) that have become conditions for clinging.
This is the summary here. For a detailed exposition of the aggregates, however, the discussion on the aggregates is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. Thus, "form" means "this is form."
“Form is only this much; there is no form beyond this”—in this way one understands form by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. This is the summary here. In detail, however, form and the other aggregates have been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* within the discussion on the aggregates (*khandha-kathā*).
Thus, “the arising of form” refers to form by way of these five modes, beginning with the arising of ignorance.
The origin. Thus, "the subsiding of form" refers to the subsiding of form by way of five aspects, beginning with the cessation of ignorance;

the same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. This is the summary here. The detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the discussion on the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).
"Thus internally" means that by way of comprehending the five aggregates,
he dwells contemplating phenomena among his own phenomena, or among another's phenomena, or at one time among his own phenomena and at another time among another's phenomena.

Furthermore, "arising and passing away" here refers to the fifty [instances] stated regarding the five aggregates in such passages as, "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form," and so forth.
It should be extracted by way of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). From here on, it is exactly according to the method already stated.

For here, one should understand the door of deliverance for the monk who discerns the aggregates (*khandha*) by making this application: "The mindfulness that discerns the aggregates is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). The rest is just like that.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Aggregates is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Bases (Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā) 117.
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five aggregates, he now speaks the passage beginning with "And further" in order to analyze it by way of the bases.
Therein, "in the six internal and external bases" refers to the eye, the ear, the nose, [the tongue, the body, and the mind].
Regarding these six internal bases— the tongue, the body, and the mind— and these six external bases— visible form, sound, odor, flavor, tangible object, and mental phenomena—
he understands the eye as it really is by way of its essential characteristic;
he understands visible forms externally, which consist of the fourfold origination of matter, as they really are by way of their essential characteristic.

He understands. And as for the fetter that arises dependent upon both— that tenfold fetter consisting of the fetter of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust for existence, envy, stinginess, and ignorance, which arises dependent upon both that eye and those forms—
he understands that too by way of its specific characteristic and essential nature.
But how does this arise? First, in the case of the eye-door:

when one relishes and delights in a desirable object that has come into the range of vision by way of sensual gratification, the fetter of sensual lust arises. When one feels aversion toward an undesirable object, the fetter of resistance arises.
[One thinks: "There is no one else besides me who is capable of discerning this object."
From conceiving, the fetter of conceit arises. For one who grasps at the thought, “This objective form is permanent and stable,” the fetter of views arises.
For one who doubts, thinking, “Is this objective form a being, or is it not a being? the fetter of doubt arises.
For one who longs for existence, thinking, “Alas, this has become easily obtainable for us in a state of prosperity,” the fetter of lust for existence arises.

The fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa-saṃyojana*) arises in one who adopts such rules and observances, thinking, "In the future as well, it will be possible to obtain such [results] by undertaking these rules and observances.
The fetter of envy (*issā-saṃyojana*) arises in one who is envious, thinking, "Oh, that others might not obtain this object of form! [This occurs regarding] the object of form obtained by oneself.
The fetter of stinginess arises in one who is stingy toward another. The fetter of ignorance arises through the power of co-nascent unknowing regarding all things.
And as for the phrase "of that which has not arisen": by whatever cause it has not arisen—namely, by way of its non-manifestation—that tenfold [fetter]...

There is the arising of a fetter, and he understands that cause. And as to how it arises for one who has arisen—meaning, for that tenfold fetter which has arisen either by way of non-abandonment or by way of active manifestation—he understands the cause by which the abandonment of that fetter occurs.
And as to how it is abandoned—for one who has abandoned it—by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) or suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
He also understands the reason why those ten kinds of fetters, once abandoned, do not arise again in the future. By what cause, then, do they not arise again in the future?

First, the fivefold fetters consisting of views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, envy, and avarice do not arise again in the future through the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). As for the two fetters of sensual lust and ill will...

The non-arising in the future of the gross [defilements] occurs through the path of once-returning; of those accompanied by subtle [defilements], through the path of non-returning; and of the three fetters—conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance—through the path of arahantship.

This same method applies to such passages as "he understands the ear and sounds," and so forth. Furthermore, the detailed discussion on the sense bases (āyatana) here should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition of the sense bases.

"Thus internally" means: by way of comprehending the internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*), he dwells contemplating phenomena in his own states; or by way of comprehending the external sense bases (*bāhirāyatana*), he dwells contemplating phenomena in the states of another;
or at one time in his own states and at another time in the states of another.

Furthermore, regarding arising and passing away here, [it is said]: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the eye"—this refers to the sense base of form within the aggregate of form.

In the immaterial bases (*arūpāyatana*), the mind base (*manāyatana*) is to be extracted from the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*), and the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) from the remaining aggregates, according to the method already stated.
Supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) are not to be included here. From this point onward, the method is exactly as previously described.

For here, mindfulness that discerns the bases is itself the truth of suffering; having made this connection, the gateway to deliverance for the bhikkhu discerning the bases should be understood. The rest is just as before.
The commentary on the section on the sense bases is finished.
Commentary on the section on the factors of enlightenment (118):
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the six internal and external sense bases, [the author] now [proceeds] by way of the factors of enlightenment.
He says "furthermore" (*puna caparaṃ*) in order to analyze [the matter]. Therein, "among the factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgesu*) means among the factors of a being who awakens.
"Present" (*santaṃ*) means existing by way of attainment. "The mindfulness factor of enlightenment" (*satisambojjhaṅgaṃ*) means the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness.
For here, the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is "enlightenment" (*sambodhi*) because he awakens starting from the time he has begun insight; or else, it is that by which he [awakens].
One awakens through the harmony of the seven factors beginning with mindfulness; one rises from the sleep of the defilements or penetrates the Truths.
That harmony of factors is *sambodhi*. A factor of that awakening (*sambodhi*), or belonging to that awakening, is a *sambojjhaṅga*.
Therefore it is said: "the awakening-factor known as mindfulness. The same method applies to the remaining awakening-factors as well.
The meaning of the words should be understood.
"Non-existent" means not present by way of non-attainment. And as for the phrases beginning with "for one in whom it has not arisen," regarding the enlightenment factor of mindfulness first:
"Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; therein, there is frequent and wise attention."

“This nutriment leads to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor that has not yet arisen, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the mindfulness enlightenment factor that has already arisen”—thus there is its arising.
In this context, mindfulness itself is the states conducive to the mindfulness enlightenment factor. Proper attention has the very characteristic already described; that—
In one who frequently practices therein, the mindfulness enlightenment factor arises.

Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and being intent upon that [mindfulness].
For, in the seven instances beginning with "the beautiful" (abhikkanta),...

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension by avoiding persons who are forgetful—like crows dropped upon food—and by associating with persons whose mindfulness is established—like the Elder Tissa Datta and the Elder Abhaya;
furthermore, it arises through the inclination, tendency, and leaning of the mind toward the arousal of mindfulness during standing, sitting, and so forth.
And when this has thus arisen by means of these four causes, it is [abandoned] by the path of Arahantship.
He understands: "There is fulfillment of development.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*), however: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena... [and so on] ...dark and bright phenomena that are counterparts to one another;
frequent and thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the unarisen enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena..."
"it leads to the arising, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen factor of investigation of phenomena"—thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the factor of investigation of phenomena: being one who asks questions thoroughly...

These are: making the basis pure, bringing the faculties to evenness, avoiding persons of weak wisdom, associating with persons of wisdom, reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge, and being intent upon that.

In this context, "being a frequent questioner" means having much inquiry based on the meaning of the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path-factors, jhāna-factors, serenity, and insight.
“Making the basis clean” means making the internal and external bases clean.

For when one’s hair, nails, and body hair are too long, or when the body is afflicted by an excess of humors and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclean and impure. But when the robe is worn out and soiled...
When there is a foul odor or the lodging is filthy, then the external object is unrefined and impure.
Therefore, by having the hair and so forth cut, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives and the like,
and by means of anointing and bathing, the internal object must be made refined.
One should make external objects clean by means of sewing, washing, dyeing, ironing, and so forth.
For when these internal and external objects are not clean, the knowledge regarding the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen is also impure,
like the radiance of a lamp-flame produced in dependence on an impure lamp-stand, wick, and oil.

Furthermore, when the internal and external bases are purified, the knowledge regarding the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen therein also becomes clear, like the radiance of a lamp flame arising from a clean lamp-stand, a pure wick, and refined oil.
Therefore it is said: "The act of purifying the basis conduces to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment."
The "balancing of the faculties" means making the faculties, beginning with faith, equal in strength.
For if his faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion,
the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing.

He is unable [to do so]. Therefore, that [restlessness] should be diminished by means of non-attention, either through reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) or by not attending to them in whatever way attention has become strong.
The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration in this regard.
However, if the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is strong, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution (*adhimokkha*).
It is capable [of its own function], but not the others of their respective functions. Therefore, that [hindrance] must be abandoned by the cultivation of serenity and the rest.

In this regard, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited as an illustration. Likewise, in the case of the remaining [hindrances], when one is predominant, it should be understood that the others are incapable of performing their own functions.
In particular, however, they praise here the balance of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy.

For one who has strong faith but weak wisdom has blind faith; he places his trust in what is not a proper basis. One who has strong wisdom but weak faith sides with the faction of the skeptics (kerāṭika);
like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable. Merely by the arising of the thought, it is wholesome...
"One who 'goes too far' (*atidhāvati*)—meaning one who fails to practice giving and so forth—arises in hell.

Through the balancing of both, one gains confidence in the object itself. However, when strong concentration is coupled with weak energy, because concentration belongs to the side of sloth, sloth overcomes it.
When strong energy is coupled with weak concentration, because energy belongs to the side of restlessness, restlessness overcomes it. Samādhi.
But when conjoined with energy, it does not allow one to fall into indolence. Energy, when conjoined with concentration, does not allow one to fall into agitation.
Therefore, these two must be made equal. For through the balancing of both, absorption (*appanā*) occurs.
Furthermore, for one whose work is concentration, even strong faith is appropriate. One who thus has faith and resolves attains absorption.
[The mind] will attain [absorption]. Regarding concentration and wisdom, however, for one whose practice is centered on concentration, strong one-pointedness is required;

for in this way, he attains absorption (appanā). For one whose practice is centered on insight (vipassanā), strong wisdom is required; for in this way, he attains penetration of the characteristics [of phenomena].
Yet, absorption certainly occurs even when both are in equilibrium. Mindfulness, moreover, is strong in all cases.

It is appropriate. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation through faith, energy, and wisdom—which belong to the side of agitation—and from falling into indolence through concentration—which belongs to the side of indolence.
Therefore, it should be desired everywhere, like salt seasoning for all curries, or like a minister with general jurisdiction over all royal affairs.
Therefore he said: “And mindfulness has been called ‘all-beneficial’ by the Blessed One. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection;
moreover, without mindfulness, there is neither the exertion nor the restraint of the mind.
Avoiding persons of poor wisdom means avoiding those dull-witted individuals whose wisdom does not penetrate the analysis of the aggregates and so forth.

Avoidance from afar. "Associating with wise persons" means associating with a person endowed with the wisdom of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-paññā*), which apprehends the fifty characteristics [of formations].

"Reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge" means reflecting on the distinctions of the profound wisdom that operates regarding the profound aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. "Devotion thereto."
It is the state of the mind being inclined, leaning, and tending toward the arousal of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor during activities such as standing and sitting.
Furthermore, he understands that for this [factor] thus arisen, there is fulfillment of development through the path of arahantship.
Regarding the energy enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of perseverance."
In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy,
or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy;
thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reflecting on the fear of the states of misery,
seeing the benefits, reflecting on the path of travel, honoring the alms-food received, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance,
reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of one’s birth, and reflecting on the greatness of one’s fellow celibates.
Avoiding lazy persons, associating with those who have initiated energy, and being intent upon that [energy]. In this regard,
even at the time of experiencing great suffering in the hells— starting from the fivefold torture and imprisonment—
and even when caught in the animal realm by means of nets, fish-traps, and so forth, or when pierced by the blows of whips, thorns, and the like;
Furthermore, it is not possible to arouse the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga) even at times such as when pulling a cart;
nor during the period of hunger and thirst lasting many thousands of years in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya); nor even during the interval between Buddhas (buddhantara);

nor while experiencing the suffering of wind, heat, and so forth with a physical body (attabhāva) consisting of mere skin and bone, measuring sixty or eighty cubits in height among the Kālakañjika asuras.

“This very moment is the time for you, bhikkhu, to exert energy”—thus, even for one who reflects on the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*) arises. It also arises for one who sees the benefit thus:
“It is not possible for a lazy person to attain the nine supramundane states; it is only for one who has initiated energy that this is possible—this is the benefit of energy.
[And it arises] through [the reflection]: “By all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples...”
"This path has been traveled by them and must be traveled; yet it cannot be traveled by one who is indolent"—thus it arises even for one reflecting on the route of travel.

"Those people who attend upon me with alms-food and other requisites are neither my relatives, nor my slaves or laborers, nor do they give these choice alms-foods and such things thinking, 'We shall live depending on him'; rather, it is for the sake of their own merit..."
They give while hoping for great fruit; nor did the Teacher allow you these requisites with the thought,
"Having used these conditions, he will dwell in comfort, possessed of bodily strength," but rather he allowed those requisites with the thought,
"While using these, he will practice the duty of a recluse and be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra."
"Now, if you dwell indolently, you will not honor that almsfood; for it is only for one who has aroused energy that there is what is called 'honoring the almsfood.
Thus, reflection on the honoring of almsfood arises even for one such as the Elder Mahā Mitta.
It is said that the elder resided at a place called Kassaka-leṇa (the Farmer’s Cave). In his alms-resort village, there was a certain great female lay devotee who [honored] the elder...
Having made her a son, she looked after her. One day, while going to the forest, she said to her daughter:
"My dear, in such-and-such a place there are old rice grains; in such-and-such a place there is milk; in such-and-such a place there is ghee; in such-and-such a place there is molasses.
When your brother, Master Mitta, arrives, cook a meal and give it to him along with the milk, ghee, and molasses."
“You may eat, but yesterday I ate leftover rice cooked with sour gruel.
“Mother, what will you eat during the day? “Put some leafy vegetables in it and cook a sour gruel with broken rice; set it aside, mother.
The Elder, having put on his robe and while taking out his bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself: “Great laywoman...”
It is said that she ate her *pārivāsika* meal with rice-gruel; even during the day she will eat only sour gruel made from broken leaves.
Yet, she points out old rice and other provisions for your sake;
relying on this, she does not expect a field, a building site, food, or clothing, but rather aspires to the three types of excellence.
[He thought,] "Can you give her those attainments, or can you not?

Then, thinking, "This almsfood cannot be accepted by you while you are possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion," he placed the bowl into its bag, unfastened the cord, turned back, and went straight to the Kassapa Cave; there he placed the bowl under his bed and the robe on the robe-stand.
"Without attaining Arhatship, I shall not depart," he resolved with such diligence and sat down.
Having lived for a long time with heedfulness, that monk, increasing his insight (vipassanā), attained Arhatship before the morning meal;
like a blossoming lotus, the one whose taints were exhausted smiled and went forth. A deity dwelling in a tree at the entrance of the cave—
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
You whose taints are exhausted—you are worthy of offerings, O venerable one!
Having uttered this inspired utterance, she said, “Venerable sir, by giving almsfood to Arahants such as yourself who have entered for alms, elderly women will be freed from suffering.”
The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking for the time, realized it was already dawn; he took his bowl and robe and entered the village.
The girl, having prepared the meal, sat waiting at the door, thinking, "Now my brother will arrive; now he will arrive.
When the Elder reached the house door, she took the bowl and [filled it] with rice mixed with ghee and molasses.
Having filled the milk alms-bowl, she placed it in his hands. The Elder, having offered words of thanksgiving, saying, "May there be happiness," departed.

She remained standing, gazing intently at him. For at that time, the Elder’s complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were serene, and his face shone with great brilliance, like a palmyra fruit released from its bond.
The Great Laywoman (Mahāupāsikā), having come from the forest, asked, "What is it, mother? Has your brother returned? She related the entire account of what had occurred.
That laywoman, realizing, "Today my son’s task of going forth has reached its conclusion," said, "Mother, is your brother finding delight in the Buddha’s teaching? Is he not weary of it?"
“Indeed, this inheritance of the Teacher is great, namely, what is called the sevenfold noble wealth;

it cannot be acquired by one who is indolent. For just as parents exclude a son who has gone astray, saying, ‘He is no son of ours,’ and he does not receive their inheritance after their passing, even so is it with the indolent person regarding this inheritance of the noble wealth.”
"One does not obtain it; only one who has aroused energy obtains it"—this arises even for one reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance. "Moreover, your Teacher is great;

for at the time of his conception in the mother’s womb, at his Great Departure, at his full enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the Twin Miracle, at his descent from the deva-world, and also at his relinquishing of the life-force..."
Even at the time of his final *parinibbāna*, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled; therefore, even when reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, one thinks:
"Is it fitting for you to become lazy after having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Teacher? Furthermore, regarding birth:
"At present you are not of low birth; you have come from the unbroken lineage of the Great Elect (*Mahāsammata*), in the royal dynasty of Ukkāka."
"You are born as the grandson of the Great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of the auspicious Rāhula.
It is not fitting for one such as you, a son of the Conqueror, to dwell in indolence. Thus it arises even for one who reflects upon the greatness of his birth.
"Both Sāriputta and Moggallāna, as well as the eighty great disciples, through energy alone..."

It also arises for one who reflects on the greatness of their fellow celibates thus: "They have penetrated the supramundane Dhamma; will you follow the path of these fellow celibates, or will you not?
It also arises for one who avoids lazy persons whose physical and mental energy have been abandoned, resembling pythons that remain coiled with their bellies full.

It arises for one who associates with persons of aroused energy and resolute application, and even for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and directed toward the generation of energy while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Furthermore, he understands that when it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.
Regarding the joy enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the joy enlightenment factor; therein..."

"Frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen joy factor of enlightenment, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen joy factor of enlightenment.
In this way, there is its arising. Therein, "joy" itself refers to the states that are the basis for the joy factor of enlightenment; the attention that produces it is [wise attention].
This is called appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*):

recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, recollection of peace, avoidance of coarse persons, cultivation of pleasant persons, reflection on inspiring discourses, and devotion thereto.

For when one recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) arises, pervading the entire body up to the stage of access concentration (*upacāra*). This is also the case for one who recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha,
or for one who reviews the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) that has been guarded unbroken for a long time,
or for a layperson who reviews the ten precepts or the five precepts.
Even for one who, during times of famine, fear, and so forth, gives excellent food to fellow practitioners of the holy life and reflects on that generosity, saying, "Thus indeed have we given";
or even for a householder who, at such a time, reflects on the gift given to those possessed of virtue;
or [one who reflects] on the presence within oneself of those very qualities endowed with which deities attained their divine state.
Also for one who reviews [the attainment], reviewing thus: "The defilements suppressed by this attainment do not manifest even for sixty or seventy years";

and also for one who, due to the lack of respect shown during visits to shrines, visits to the Bodhi tree, or visits to elders—indicating a harsh nature through the absence of serene confidence and affection toward the Buddha and others—is like the back of a donkey.
It arises even for one who avoids coarse persons such as those characterized by passion (rāga), even for one who serves gentle-minded persons full of confidence in the Buddha and so forth,
even for one who reflects upon inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem,
and even for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the arising of joy during standing, sitting, and other postures. For one in whom it has thus arisen:
He understands: "The fulfillment of its development occurs through the path of arahantship.
Regarding the tranquility enlightenment factor: "Monks, there is bodily tranquility and mental tranquility;

frequent and thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen tranquility enlightenment factor, or for the further development of that which has already arisen."
“Or, it leads to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen factor of tranquility.
Thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the factor of tranquility: the practice of refined food; [and so forth].

These are: the practice of pleasant seasons, the practice of pleasant postures, the application of equanimity, avoiding persons with agitated bodies, associating with persons with tranquil bodies, and being intent upon that [tranquility].
For even one who eats choice, succulent, and suitable food, and remains in cool or warm seasons and various postures such as standing;
Tranquility also arises for one who resorts to a suitable climate and mode of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).
However, this was not said with reference to one who is of the nature of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) and is capable of enduring all climates and modes of conduct.

Rather, it arises for one who has both similar and dissimilar [conditions], and who resorts to similar ones while avoiding dissimilar climates and modes of conduct. This is the application of equanimity (*majjhattapayoga*).
It is called the reflection on one’s own and another’s ownership of kamma; it arises through this practice of equanimity.

Even for one who avoids a person whose body is agitated—such as one who wanders about harassing others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth—and who instead associates with a person whose feet and hands are restrained and whose body is tranquil, [this state arises] during standing, sitting, and other postures.
It also arises in one whose mind is inclined, bent, and leaning toward the production of tranquility.
Furthermore, he understands that for that which has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of its development through the path of arahantship.
Regarding the concentration enlightenment factor: "Monks, there is the sign of serenity, the sign of non-distraction; therein..."

“Frequent practice of appropriate attention—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.
Thus there is its arising. In this context, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, in the sense of non-distraction.
And [the phrase] "the sign of non-distraction.
Furthermore, eleven factors lead to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*):
making the basis pure, bringing about the evenness of the faculties, skillfulness regarding the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, and calming the mind at the proper time...
Reproof at the proper time, encouragement at the proper time, equanimity at the proper time, avoidance of persons who are not concentrated,
association with persons who are concentrated, reviewing of the jhānas and liberations, and devotion thereto. Therein,
the making of the basis pure and the balancing of the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated.
Skillfulness regarding the sign (*nimittakusalatā*) means skillfulness in grasping the kasiṇa-sign.

"Exerting the mind at the proper time" means that at whatever time the mind becomes sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, at that time one exerts it by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena and energy.
"Restraining the mind at the proper time" means [at whatever time] due to excessive exertion of energy and so forth...
When the mind is agitated, its suppression at that time is achieved by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

"Encouragement at the proper time" means: when the mind becomes dispirited due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom or because it has not attained the bliss of peace, then at that time [it should be encouraged] by reflecting upon the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
He inspires a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). The eight bases for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four;

the suffering of the lower realms as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past; the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for food in the present.
Furthermore, he generates confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem. This is called "encouragement at the proper time."
Equanimity at the proper time means that when, by means of right practice, the mind has become neither sluggish nor agitated, neither dissatisfied nor over-exerted,
but proceeds evenly toward the object and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), it does not then engage in the functions of exertion, restraint, or encouragement,
just as a charioteer does not intervene when the horses are proceeding evenly. This is called "equanimity at the proper time."
Avoidance of persons unconcentrated means keeping far away from those whose minds are distracted and who have not attained either access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*).
Cultivation of persons concentrated means attending upon, associating with, and revering those whose minds are concentrated by way of either access or absorption.
Devotion to that means [devotion] in standing, sitting, and so forth...
It is the state of the mind being inclined, leaning, and tending toward the very production of concentration. For one who practices in this way, this [concentration] arises.
And he understands that for one in whom it has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of its development through the path of Arahatship.
Regarding the equanimity enlightenment factor: "Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the equanimity enlightenment factor; therein..."

"Frequent practice of appropriate attention—this is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has not yet arisen, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has already arisen.
Thus there is its arising. In this context, "equanimity" itself refers to those phenomena that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Furthermore, five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*):

neutrality toward beings, neutrality toward formations, avoiding persons who cherish beings and formations, associating with persons who are neutral toward beings and formations, and being intent upon that [equanimity].
In this context, one arouses neutrality toward beings in two ways: "You have come here by means of your own karma..."
"You shall go by your own karma; this person too, having come by his own karma, will go by his own karma.
Whom do you cherish?"—thus by reflecting on the ownership of one's own karma; and "In the ultimate sense, there is no self at all;
whom do you cherish?"—thus by reflecting on the absence of a sentient being. In these two ways, [one contemplates] the neutrality of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-majjhattatā*).

He arouses it by reflecting on its ownerlessness thus: "This robe-cloth, having gradually undergone changes in color and reached a state of decay, will become a foot-wiping rag and must eventually be discarded at the end of a staff;
if it had an owner, he would not allow it to perish like this. He reflects: "It is not long-lasting..."
“This is for temporary use”—thus it is by reflecting on its temporary nature. And just as this is applied to the robe, so too should the application be made regarding the bowl and other requisites.
Regarding “avoiding persons who cherish the seven types of conditioned things”:

here, a person—whether a householder who cherishes his own sons, daughters, and so forth, or one gone forth who cherishes his own pupils, co-residents, preceptors, and so forth—performs for them with his own hands such tasks as cutting hair, sewing, washing robes, dyeing, boiling rice in bowls, and so on.
Even when he has not seen him for a moment, he looks here and there like a bewildered deer, wondering, "Where is that novice? Where is that young man?

Even when requested by others for the sake of tasks such as cutting hair, saying, "Please send so-and-so for a moment," he replies, "We ourselves do not even perform our own work; you will only weary yourselves by taking him."
He does not give it. This is called *sattakelāyana*. But he who treats his bowl, robes, stand, walking stick, and so forth as his own property, and does not even allow another’s hand to touch them;
when asked for them temporarily, he says, "We ourselves do not even use these because we regard them as our own—what shall we give to you? This is called *saṅkhārakelāyana*. But he who...
In both of these two types of persons, one who is neutral is "indifferent. This is what is called being neutral toward beings and formations.

Thus, this factor of enlightenment of equanimity arises for one who avoids from afar a person who dotes on beings and formations, for one who associates with a person who is neutral toward beings and formations, and also for one whose mind—in standing, sitting, and so forth—is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of that [equanimity].
It arises. Furthermore, he understands that for what has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of its development through the path of Arahatship.

Thus, "internally" means: having grasped the seven factors of enlightenment within himself, or [grasping them] in another, or at one time grasping the factors of enlightenment within himself and at another time grasping them in another, he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena among all phenomena.

Here, however, the arising and passing away of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) should be understood by way of their production and cessation. From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated.

For here, one should understand the door to deliverance for the bhikkhu who discerns the enlightenment factors by making this application: "The mindfulness that discerns the enlightenment factors is itself the truth of suffering. The rest is just as before.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Enlightenment Factors is finished.
Commentary on the Origin of the Four Truths (Catusaccappabhavaṇṇanā) 119.

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the seven factors of enlightenment, he now speaks the passage beginning with "And furthermore" in order to analyze it by way of the four truths.
Therein, "he understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'" means that, setting aside craving, he understands all phenomena belonging to the three planes as "this is suffering."
He understands suffering according to its true nature; he understands the prior craving that gives rise to and originates that very suffering as "this is the origin of suffering";
he understands the non-occurrence of both as "this is the cessation of suffering";
and he understands the Noble Path—the full comprehension of suffering, the abandoning of the origin, and the realization of cessation—as "this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
The meaning is that he understands [the path] according to its true nature. The remaining discussion on the Noble Truths has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, "internally" means: having comprehended the four truths for oneself, or for another, or having comprehended the four truths for oneself at one time and for another at another time, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
He dwells [thus]. Here, however, the arising and passing away of the four truths should be understood by way of their occurrence and cessation according to how they apply.
From this point on, it is exactly according to the method already stated.

For here, mindfulness that encompasses the four truths is the truth of suffering; having made this application, the door to deliverance for the bhikkhu who encompasses the truths should be understood. The rest is just as before.
The commentary on the origin of the Four Noble Truths is finished.
Up to this point, there have been: mindfulness of breathing; the four postures; the four kinds of clear comprehension; the thirty-two aspects; the analysis of the four elements;

the nine cemetery meditations; the contemplation of feelings; the contemplation of the mind; the discernment of the hindrances; the discernment of the aggregates; and the discernment of the sense bases.
The twenty-one meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) have been stated as the apprehension of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and the apprehension of the truths (sacca).

Among them, mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra), and the nine cemetery meditations (navasivathika) constitute eleven subjects for attainment (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna).

However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, said: "The nine cemetery meditations are mentioned by way of contemplation of disadvantage (ādīnavānupassanā). Therefore, according to his opinion, there are only two [such subjects].
The subjects for meditation leading to absorption (*appanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) are [the first four], while the rest are subjects for access concentration (*upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna*).

But does obsession (*abhinivesa*) arise toward all of these? It does not. For obsession does not arise toward the clear comprehension of postures (*iriyāpatha-sampajañña*) or the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*); it arises toward the others. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "Obsession does indeed arise toward these as well, for this [obsession] exists..."
"Does my fourfold posture exist, or does it not? Does my fourfold clear comprehension exist, or does it not?
Do the five hindrances exist in me, or do they not? Do the seven factors of enlightenment exist in me, or do they not?"—in this way he scrutinizes, and therefore obsession arises everywhere."

137. "Whoever, monks"—that is, whoever it may be, whether a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a layman, or a laywoman—"should thus develop" means they should develop according to the sequence of development described from the beginning.

"To be expected" (pāṭikaṅkha) means it is to be anticipated; the meaning is that it will inevitably come to pass. "The other" (añña) refers to arahantship. "Or with a residue remaining" (sati vā upādisese) refers to a residue of clinging.
Or while it remains unexhausted. "Anāgāmitā" means the state of being a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Having thus shown the liberating nature of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) by way of seven years, he spoke the words beginning with "Let alone, monks," in order to show that it is possible even in a shorter period of time than that.
And all of this refers to a person of medium capacity who is to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
This was said with reference to [a person of] dull wisdom. However, with reference to one of sharp wisdom, it was said: "One instructed in the morning will attain distinction by evening;
one instructed in the evening will attain distinction by morning.
Thus the Blessed One, having shown that "in this way, monks, my teaching leads to liberation," [spoke] regarding all twenty-one points.
Concluding the teaching taught from the standpoint of Arahantship, he said: "Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path...
[as it has been said]... it was with reference to this that this was said. The rest is of plain meaning.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Chapter on the Lion’s Roar.
1. Commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta (The Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar) 139.
“Thus have I heard” introduces the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta.

Since its presentation is based on the arising of a specific purpose, we shall first demonstrate that purpose and then provide a word-by-word commentary on the text in due order. But by what occasion for the arising of this purpose was it spoken?

"Set aside"? Regarding the lamentation of the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthika) on account of gain and honor. It is said that great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One in the manner described in the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta*.
For this worldly existence consists of four measures: those who take form as their measure and have faith in form;
those who take sound as their measure and have faith in sound; those who take coarseness as their measure and have faith in coarseness; and those who take the Dhamma as their measure...
"Confidence in the Dhamma" is established in four ways according to these types of persons.
This is their distinction: What kind of person is one who has form as his measure and confidence in form?
Here, a certain person, having seen the height, or having seen the circumference, or having seen the shape, or having seen the fullness [of a form],...
In this case, having taken that as a measure, he generates confidence; such a person is called one who takes form as the measure and is confident in form.

And what kind of person is one who takes sound as the measure and is confident in sound? Here, a certain person, by means of another’s praise, another’s exaltation, another’s commendation, or another’s eulogy, takes that as a measure and generates confidence; such a person is called...
A person who takes sound as the measure and has faith in sound.
And what is the person who takes coarseness as the measure and has faith in coarseness?
Here, a certain person, upon seeing the coarseness of a robe, or seeing the coarseness of an alms-bowl, or seeing the coarseness of a lodging, or seeing some kind of various ascetic practice...
In that case, having taken [the qualities] as a measure, he generates confidence; this person is called one who takes the coarse as his measure and is confident in the coarse.

And what kind of person is one who takes the Dhamma as his measure and is confident in the Dhamma? Here, a certain person, having seen virtue, or having seen concentration, or having seen wisdom, takes them as a measure therein and generates confidence; this—
It is said that such a person is "one who takes the Dhamma as the measure and has confidence in the Dhamma.
Among these four types of persons, even one who takes the physical form as the measure [perceives] the Blessed One’s excellence of stature,

girth, and shape, his fullness of color and beauty, and— because he is adorned with the eighty minor marks— his appearance like a great golden cloth variegated with various jewels, and because he is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man...
Seeing him— resplendent like the vault of heaven with its host of stars, like a *pāricchattaka* tree in full bloom reaching a hundred *yojanas* in height,
eighteen *ratana*s in stature, encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, and possessing a beautiful, peerless body— he gains confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone.
Even the measure of his fame [is such that] for four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand aeons, the Blessed One fulfilled the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Having heard the report circulating in such a manner as, "The ten intermediate perfections and the ten ultimate perfections have been fulfilled; the sacrifice of limbs,
the sacrifice of wife and children, the sacrifice of kingdom, the sacrifice of self, and the sacrifice of eyes have been performed," he gains confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone.
Seeing even the coarse measure of the Blessed One’s robe, he thought: "If the Blessed One had lived as a householder, he would have worn garments of Kāsī cloth.
But having gone forth, he has made it difficult for himself by being content with this hempen rag-robe. Thus he placed his faith in the Fully Enlightened One alone.
Seeing also the coarseness of his bowl, he thought: "While living as a householder, this man [would have used] vessels of choice gold and silver..."

“Having enjoyed fragrant *śāli* rice fit for the food of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), he has now gone forth, yet taking a stone bowl and wandering for alms from door to door among high and low families, he makes his life burdensome by being content with whatever morsel of alms he receives”—thus he gains confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone.
Even upon seeing the austerity of his lodging, [he thinks]: “This one, having left the household life...”
"Having formerly dwelt in three palaces suitable for the three seasons, surrounded by a threefold troupe of dancers,
and enjoyed the glory of sovereignty as if it were divine prosperity, he has now gone forth into homelessness; dwelling at the foot of trees and in other lodgings,

content with wooden planks, stone slabs, benches, and couches, he performs a difficult task"— thus he gains confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone, even upon seeing his performance of austerities.
—“For six years he will subsist on mere handfuls of bean soup, pea soup, lentil soup, horsetail-grass soup, and so forth;
he will practice breathless meditation, and he will dwell without regard for either his body or his life;
oh, how the Blessed One performs difficult deeds! Thus he gains confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone.
Dhammappamāṇa, too, having seen the Blessed One’s qualities of virtue, qualities of concentration, and qualities of wisdom;
his perfection in the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; his mastery of the higher knowledges; his twin miracles; his descent from the heavens;
and his taming of Pāṭikaputta and other numerous wonders, gained confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone. Those who were thus confident [placed] a great [reliance] upon the Blessed One.
They brought him gain and honor. But for the members of other sects, however, gain and honor declined like that of the crow in the Bāveru Jātaka.
As it is said: “Because of the failure to see the peacock, the sweet-voiced Śikhin;”
There they honored the crow with meat and fruit.
But when the peacock Sarasampanna arrived at Bāveru,
then the gain and honor of the crow diminished.
As long as the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, the bringer of light, had not arisen,
so long did people worship various other ascetics and brahmins.
But when the Buddha, endowed with wisdom, taught the Dhamma;
"Then gain and honor departed from the sectarians.
Having thus abandoned gain and honor, although they had shone with a light the thickness of a single finger-breadth during the night, at the rising of the sun they became lusterless like fireflies.
For just as fireflies [fade] on a dark night;
They manifest radiance, for that is indeed their domain.
And when the light-maker, endowed with rays, rises up,
then the radiance of the fireflies vanishes.
Thus, many heretics here who resemble those who eat filth display their own virtues in this world, which is like the dark fortnight.
But when the Buddha, of immeasurable radiance, arises in the world;
"The heterodox teachers become lusterless, like moths before the sun. Having thus become lusterless,
their bodies covered with scabs, boils, and other ailments, having reached the ultimate state of decay, they go here and there— wherever the Buddha is,
wherever the Dhamma is, wherever the Saṅgha is, and wherever the great assembly of people has gathered— even through the middle of the streets.
Standing at crossroads, at four-way junctions, and even in public assembly halls, they lamented:
"How is it that only the ascetic Gotama is an ascetic, while we are not ascetics? Only the disciples of the ascetic Gotama are ascetics, while our disciples are not ascetics?
Only what is given to the disciples of the ascetic Gotama bears great fruit?"
"Is what is given to us and to our disciples not of great fruit? Is the ascetic Gotama not an ascetic, and are we not also ascetics?
Are the disciples of the ascetic Gotama not ascetics, and are our disciples not also ascetics?
Is what is given to the disciples of the ascetic Gotama of great fruit, and is what is given to us and to our disciples also of great fruit?"
“Give and perform services for the ascetic Gotama and his disciples; give and honor us and our disciples as well!
Did not the ascetic Gotama arise only in recent days, whereas we have arisen in this world from the very beginning?
Thus they clamored in various ways. Then the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—[listened].
Having heard their words, the assembly informed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the sectarians are saying this and that.

Upon hearing this, the Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, do not let yourselves be convinced by the words of the sectarians that 'there is no ascetic other than [the Buddha],' " and thus, while negating the status of an ascetic among those of other sects, he authorized it only here [in his own teaching].
On account of this incident, monks, he spoke this sutta: "Only here, monks, is there a true ascetic.
In this context, "only here" means in this very dispensation (*sāsana*). This restriction, however, should be understood to apply to the subsequent terms as well;
for even the second and other types of ascetics exist only here, not elsewhere. An "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). Therefore, he said: "And who, monks, is the ascetic?"

“The first ascetic: Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the total destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This, monks, is the first ascetic.
The second is the once-returner. Therefore he said: “And who, monks, is the second ascetic? Here, monks,” [he continued].
“Monks, through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, a monk becomes a once-returner;
having returned to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering. This, monks, is the second ascetic.
Regarding the third: he is the non-returner (anāgāmī). Therefore it was said: “And who, monks, is the third ascetic? Here, monks,” [it continues].

“With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu becomes one of spontaneous birth (*opapātiko*), attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is the third ascetic.
The fourth is the arahant. Therefore he said: “And who, bhikkhus, is the fourth ascetic? Here, bhikkhus,” [he continued].

“With the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth ascetic.
Thus, in this context, only the four ascetics who have attained the fruits are intended.

"Empty" means void and hollow. "The doctrines of others" refers to: the four eternalist views, the four partial-eternalist views, the four views on the finite and infinite, the four eel-wrigglers, the two fortuitous-originationists, the sixteen views of those who maintain the existence of consciousness after death, the eight views of those who maintain the non-existence of consciousness after death, the eight views of those who maintain neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness after death, the seven annihilationist views, and the five views of Nibbāna in this very life.
All these sixty-two views are included in the *Brahmajāla*. The doctrines of others outside of this are called "the doctrines of others" (*parappavāda*).
All of them are empty of these four types of fruit-abiding recluses (*phalaṭṭhaka-samaṇa*), for they do not exist here.
Furthermore, it is not only empty of these; it is also empty of the four types of path-abiding recluses (*maggaṭṭhaka-samaṇa*) for the sake of the four paths.
It was empty even of those twelve ascetics who had initiated insight meditation. It was with reference to this very meaning that the Blessed One said during the Mahāparinibbāna:
"Subhadda, in my twenty-ninth year..."
Since I went forth, Subhadda, seeking what is wholesome for more than fifty years;
“There is no ascetic outside of this [teaching] who practices even a portion of the way of the Dhamma.
‘There is no second ascetic, there is no third ascetic, there is no fourth ascetic. The doctrines of others are empty of other ascetics.’”

For here, "one who dwells in a portion" refers to one who has begun insight (āraddhavipassaka). Therefore, having grouped together those on the path of stream-entry—namely, the one who has begun insight, the one established on the path, and the one established in the fruit—he said, "there is not even a first ascetic.

Having grouped together those on the path of once-returning—namely, the one who has begun insight, the one established on the path, and the one established in the fruit—he said, "there is not even a second ascetic."
He said: "The same principle applies to the other two [realms] as well.
But why are these not found elsewhere? Because they are not suitable fields (*akhettatā*).

For just as a mustard seed does not remain on the point of an awl, fire does not burn on the surface of water, and seeds do not sprout on a flat stone, even so it is with the external systems of tenets."
"These ascetics do not arise elsewhere; they arise only within this very teaching.

Why? Because of its quality as a field. Their lack of being a field and their being a field should be understood by the absence and presence, respectively, of the Noble Eightfold Path. Therefore the Blessed One said:
'Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, there also the ascetic...'"
In that [other] place, no ascetic is found; there, a second ascetic is not found; there, a third ascetic is not found;
there, even a fourth ascetic is not found. But in whatever Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found, there an ascetic is found, and a second one as well.
"Therein... [as before] ...there is found even a fourth ascetic. In this Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found;
here alone, Subhadda, is there an ascetic, here a second ascetic, here a third ascetic, here a fourth ascetic; the doctrines of others are empty of true ascetics."
Thus, because the sectarian abodes are not a field while the Dispensation is a field,
just as the lion, the king of beasts— with his well-tanned paws and mane— does not dwell in a charnel ground or a heap of refuse,
but rather plunges into the Himalayas, which extend for three thousand leagues, and dwells only in a jewel cave; and just as the elephant king Chaddanta...
He is not reborn among the nine classes of nāgas, such as the Gocariya or the Hatthikula; he is reborn only in the Chaddanta lineage.
And just as Valāhaka, the king of horses, is not reborn in the lineage of donkeys or the lineage of common mares, but is reborn only in the Sindha lineage on the banks of the Indus;
and just as the heart-stealing jewel-treasure that grants all desires—
It does not arise in a heap of refuse or among sand dunes and the like; it arises only within Mount Vepulla.
And just as the king of fish, Timirapiṅgala, does not arise in small ponds, but arises only in the great ocean which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep;
and just as the king of the Supaṇṇas, measuring one hundred and fifty yojanas, does not [arise] at a village gate...
He dwells in places such as the Eraṇḍa forest, but having plunged into the great ocean, he dwells specifically in the Simbali grove.
And just as Dhataraṭṭha, the golden swan, does not dwell in pits and the like at the village gate, but—surrounded by a retinue of ninety thousand swans—dwells specifically on Mount Cittakūṭa;
and just as the Wheel-turning Monarch, lord of the four continents, does not...
One is born into a low family, yet one is born only into an unadulterated noble kṣatriya family.
In the same way, among these ascetics, not even a single ascetic arises in the domain of other sects; rather, they arise only within the Buddha’s teaching, which is fortified by the Noble Path.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, here alone is there an ascetic... [omitted] ...the teachings of others are empty of ascetics.”
“...by other ascetics.

Regarding the phrase “roar the true lion’s roar”: here, “truly” (*sammā*) means by way of cause, method, and reason. “Lion’s roar” (*sīhanāda*) means the best roar, the fearless roar, the roar that cannot be countered.
Indeed, because these four types of ascetics exist right here, this roar is the best roar.

It is called the "supreme shout" (*uttamanāda*). Because one who says, "These ascetics exist right here," has no fear or apprehension from any other quarter, it is called the "fearless shout" (*abhītanāda*).

Since not even one among Pūraṇa and the others was able to rise up and speak in response to the thought, "These ascetics exist within our own teaching as well," this shout is called the "unanswered shout" (*appaṭināda*). Thus it was said.
“A lion’s roar” means the best roar, the roar of one who is fearless, the roar that cannot be countered.
“Indeed, this possibility exists”: this is the reason that exists. “Those of other sects” (*aññatitthiyā*):

it is for this reason they are called “those of other sects. In this context, the “ford” (*tittha*) must be understood, as must the “founder of the ford” (*titthakara*), and the “sectarians” (*titthiya*).
They should be known; the followers of the sectarians (titthiya) should be known. "Sect" (tittha) refers to the sixty-two views.
For herein, beings cross over, emerge, and perform the act of rising and diving; therefore, they are called "sectarians. One who originates those views is called a "founder of a sect" (titthakara).
Those who have gone forth having adopted his doctrine are called "sectarians" (titthiyā). Those who provide them with requisites—
They should be understood as disciples of other sectarians (*titthiya*). "Wanderers" (*paribbājaka*) refers to those who have gone forth, having abandoned the bonds of household life.
"Support" (*assāsa*) means refuge, a foundation, and a pillar of strength. "Strength" (*bala*) means power. "By which you [say]" means by whichever support or strength you speak thus.
Regarding the phrase, "Friends, there is indeed that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One": here—
This is the summary of the meaning: That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, attained supreme perfect enlightenment;

by that Blessed One, who knows the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions of various beings and perceives the entirety of all knowable phenomena as clearly as an amala fruit placed in the palm of the hand—furthermore, through the recollection of past lives and so forth.

Knowing by means of the divine eye; seeing with the all-encompassing eye that is unimpeded in every respect. Knowing through the three types of clear knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) or the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*);

seeing with the extremely purified physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) those forms of all beings that are beyond the range of the visual faculty, even those situated behind walls and the like. Knowing with the wisdom capable of cognizing all phenomena.
Seeing with the physical eye those forms of all sentient beings that are beyond the reach of the visual field or located behind walls and so forth, by means of the exceedingly purified physical eye.
By one who sees; by one who knows through the wisdom of penetration, which has concentration as its proximate cause and accomplishes one’s own welfare;

and by one who sees through the wisdom of teaching, which has compassion as its proximate cause and accomplishes the welfare of others. By one who is an *arahant* because of having slain the enemies and because of being worthy of the requisites and so forth;
and by one who is a *Sammāsambuddha* because of having awakened to the truths rightly and by himself. Or, by one who knows the obstructive states.
