"By one who sees the Dhamma that leads to liberation; by an Arahant because the enemies of the defilements have been slain;

by a Sammasambuddha because of having perfectly and independently awakened to all phenomena"—thus, by way of the four grounds of self-confidence, he has praised [the Teacher] in four aspects and proclaimed four qualities, which we, seeing them within ourselves, speak of in this way, and not of kings, royal ministers, and so forth.
“Support” refers to bodily strength.
“Confidence in the Teacher” is the confidence that arises in those who recollect the qualities of the Buddha according to the method beginning with, “Such indeed is the Blessed One.
“Confidence in the Dhamma” is [the confidence] of those who recollect the qualities of the Dhamma according to the method beginning with, “The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.”
"Having arisen confidence": "fulfilling the precepts" means fulfilling the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones (*ariyakanta-sīla*).

The "precepts beloved by the Noble Ones" refers to the five precepts; for even when a noble disciple has passed into another existence—even if he does not recognize himself as a noble disciple—he does not transgress them.
For even if someone were to say to him: "Accept this entire sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch..."
“Kill a small fly,” it would be impossible for him to do as he was told.
In this way, the virtues of the Noble Ones are lovely, dear, and pleasing. It is with reference to these that it is said: “fulfilling the precepts.

Furthermore, those who share the same Dhamma are: a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), a male lay follower (upāsaka), and a female lay follower (upāsikā).
These seven are fellow practitioners of the Dhamma (*sahadhammacārino*). For among them, a monk practices the Dhamma together with monks because they share the same training.
Likewise, a bhikkhunī [practices] with bhikkhunīs... and so on... a female lay follower with female lay followers; a stream-enterer with stream-enterers, a once-returner... and so on...
with non-returners, he practices the Dhamma together with them. Therefore, all these are called "fellow practitioners of the Dhamma."
Moreover, here it is specifically the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) who are intended. For even in another existence, there is no dispute among them regarding the vision of the Path;
therefore, they are "those of like Dhamma" (sahadhammika) due to their absolute conformity to the same Dhamma.
By this, the faith that arises in those recollecting the Saṅgha according to the method beginning with, "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well," is described. Up to this point—
The four factors of one who has entered the stream have been declared.
"Friends, these are those four things which have been proclaimed by that Blessed One as both our consolation and our strength, seeing which within ourselves we speak thus.
(141) By the phrase "he who is our Teacher," the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa are pointed out. Just as...
But now, within the Dispensation, there arises a worldly affection toward teachers, preceptors, and others, such as "our teacher" or "our preceptor.
It is with reference to this kind of affection that they speak of "confidence in the Teacher. However, the Elder said:
"Because what is called a 'Teacher' does not belong to one person or two; the Teacher of the world together with its devas is one alone—therefore, the heretics..."
“By the single phrase ‘Our Teacher,’ they have set the Teacher apart and, by that very phrase, have been contradicted and defeated.

As for the phrase “confidence in the Dhamma,” this refers to the worldly affection one feels toward one’s own particular scriptural teachings (pariyatti-dhamma), just as people nowadays claim ownership over the scriptures, saying, “The Dīgha Nikāya is ours,” or “The Majjhima Nikāya is ours. Regarding the phrase “in the virtues” (sīlesu):

[This refers] to the virtue of goats, the virtue of cows, the virtue of rams, the virtue of dogs, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "not here, friends," here the word "here" is said with reference to confidence (*pasāda*).
What is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*)? It means: what is the superior application (*adhikappayoga*)?
When you say, "Let us state the distinction between yourselves and ourselves," what indeed is that? For you have confidence in four points, and we too have it.
"Was it not the case that in this hall you and we stood together, sweet in speech, as if identical, like gold split in two?
Then the Blessed One, breaking through that harmony of theirs, spoke these words beginning with 'Thus they say'. In that context, "one conclusion" means:
He says: "Ask thus: 'Is that final goal, which is the culmination of that confidence, one, or is it many?
For there is no one who does not designate a final goal at some particular time;
for the Brahmā-world is the final goal for the brahmins, the Ābhassara realm for the great ascetics, the Subhakiṇha realm for the wanderers, and [the realm of] the Ājīvakas...
“Of infinite mind”: this refers to the state of non-perception (asaññībhava) thus conceived. In this teaching, however, Arahantship is the final goal.
All these [teachers] indeed declare that Arahantship alone is the final goal; yet, by way of their own views, they designate the Brahma-world and so forth as such.
Therefore, each proclaims a single final goal according to his own particular tenet. To demonstrate this, the Blessed One said:
He said, "Answering correctly," and so forth.

Now, since both the monks and the non-Buddhist teachers (titthiyas) stood as if engaged in a legal dispute, each maintaining their own single conclusion, the Blessed One, demonstrating the proper procedure for inquiry, said:
"But, friends, is that conclusion for one who is still possessed of lust, or for one who is free from lust? and so on.

In this context, since there is no such thing as a "final goal" for those stained by passion and the like—lest it should also apply to jackals, dogs, and so forth—the Tathāgata, seeing this flaw in the views of the heretics, gave his answer in the manner beginning with, "Friends, that final goal belongs to one who is free from passion.

Therein, "of the wise one" (*viddasuno*) means of the learned one. "Of one who has overcome and is opposed to" (*anuruddha-paṭiviruddhassa*) means of one who has overcome passion and is opposed to anger.
"Of one who is opposed. Regarding the phrase "one who delights in proliferation (papañca) and finds pleasure in proliferation": here, *ārāma* means that which they delight in (*āramanti ettha*).

One for whom proliferation is a delight is "one who delights in proliferation" (*papañcārāma*). One for whom there is pleasure in proliferation is "one who finds pleasure in proliferation" (*papañcarati*).
And "proliferation" (*papañca*) is a designation for craving, views, and conceit that proceed by way of being intoxicated and heedless. However, in this context, only craving and views are intended.
In the five instances beginning with "of one who has lust" (*sarāgassa*), only a single defilement is mentioned; however, its diversity should be understood according to its specific modes.

For in the passage where "of one who has lust" is stated, it is taken in the sense of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "Of one who has craving" (*sataṇhassa*) is by way of craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*). "Of one who has clinging" (*saupādānassa*) is by way of grasping.
"Of one who is favorably disposed or unfavorably disposed" (*anuruddha-paṭiviruddhassa*) is by way of pairs. "Of one who delights in proliferation" (*papañcārāmassa*)...
By way of showing the arising of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*). Or, in the phrase "of one possessed of lust" (*sarāgassa*), it is taken here by way of the unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*).
In the phrase "of one possessed of craving" (*sataṇhassa*), it is by way of showing that clinging (*upādāna*) has craving as its condition. The rest is exactly as before. But the Elder said:
"Why should it be thus destroyed? For this is simply a single greed; it is called 'lust' (*rāga*) by way of coloring, and [it is called] 'craving' (*taṇhā*) by way of causing thirst."

“Craving (*taṇhā*). In the sense of grasping, it is clinging (*upādāna*). In the sense of a pair, it is approval and repugnance. In the sense of showing the arising of proliferation (*papañca*), it is proliferation.
Now, in order to show the doctrine of views (*diṭṭhivāda*) which is the root of these defilements, he said: “Bhikkhus, there are these two views,” and so forth.

Therein, the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). The view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*) is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). “Clings to the view of existence” means...

They are attached to the eternalist view by way of craving and views. They have approached it by way of craving and views alone. They have clung to it by way of craving and views alone, having entered into it.
They are opposed to the annihilationist view; thus, they are all in conflict with the proponents of annihilationism, who say:
"You blind fools do not know that this world is eternal; this world is not subject to annihilation."
They live constantly at odds, intent on quarreling and brawling. The same method applies to the second section as well.
Regarding the phrases "the origin" and so forth: there are two origins of views—the momentary origin and the conditional origin.
The momentary origin is the actual arising of views. The conditional origin consists of eight bases. Namely: the aggregates are also a basis for views;...
Ignorance, contact, perception, applied thought, improper attention, evil friends, and the voice of another are bases for views.
"The aggregates are the cause, the aggregates are the condition for views in the sense of their arising based upon them.
Thus the aggregates are also bases for views; so too are ignorance, contact, perception, applied thought, and improper attention."
“An evil friend... the voice of another is the cause, the voice of another is the condition for views in the sense of their origination.
Thus, the voice of another is also a basis for views. Regarding the "passing away" (atthaṅgama), there are only two kinds:

passing away in the sense of momentariness and passing away in the sense of conditionality. Passing away in the sense of momentariness means destruction, vanishing, breaking up, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance. Passing away in the sense of conditionality...
This is called the path of stream-entry. For the path of stream-entry is said to be the uprooting of the basis for views.
They relish the benefit rooted in views; with reference to this it was said:
“Whatever view the teacher holds, such views do his disciples hold. Whatever view the disciples hold, they honor and revere that view in the teacher.”
They honor them, they revere them, and because of that, they receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, monks, is the worldly benefit of right view. “Dangers” refers to the calamities rooted in the adoption of wrong views.
These include the practice of the *vagguli* (bat-like) asceticism, the exertion of squatting, lying on a bed of thorns, the mortification by the five fires, and leaping from heights.
[This] should be understood by way of such things as "the plucking out of hair and beard" and "the meditation on the small pit.
"Escape" refers to Nibbāna, which is called the escape from views. "Not understanding it as it really is" means those who do not know all this according to its true nature.
"They are not fully released from suffering" means they are not released from the entire suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). By this—
This shows that for these [beings], there is no so-called "finality" (niṭṭhā).
"They are liberated from suffering" means they are liberated from the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).
By this, as if settling a legal dispute between two litigants, he establishes the existence of finality within the Teaching itself, showing that for them there *is* indeed such a finality.

143. Now, demonstrating the cutting off of views, he said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clinging," and so forth. The detailed explanation of these has already been given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Those who claim to teach the full understanding of all clinging" means those who profess: "We teach the full understanding—that is, the transcendence—of all forms of clinging.
"Not rightly the full understanding of all clinging" refers to the non-transcendence of all forms of clinging.

They do not explain it correctly. Some explain the full understanding (*pariññā*) of mere clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*); some explain that of mere clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), and some even of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
However, there is no one who explains the full understanding of clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
Showing their distinctions, [the Blessed One] said: "Those who explain the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures," and so forth.
In this regard, all [schools] indeed prescribe the full understanding (*pariññā*) of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).

For even the ninety-six heretical sects do not prescribe that the enjoyment of objects—which constitutes sensual pleasure—is permissible for one who has gone forth, saying, "Sensual pleasures must not be indulged in by one who has gone forth";
rather, they prescribe it as being entirely impermissible. Those, however, who do indulge in them, do so through theft. Therefore it was said:
“‘They prescribe the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures’—because they live having grasped such views as ‘there is no gift,’ and so forth;
because they hold that ‘purification comes through virtue, purification comes through vows, purification comes through spiritual development,’ and do not abandon the acquisition of a self;
therefore, [this does not refer] to clinging to views, nor to clinging to rules and observances.”
They do not prescribe full understanding of the clinging to a self-theory. Why is that? For what reason is there no such prescription?
"Because these venerable ones [do not know]," means: because those venerable ones do not know these three reasons according to their true nature.
As for the reason for prescribing the two kinds of full understanding in this context...
They know views and rules-and-observances as they really are, thinking, "This is to be abandoned.

It is with reference to them that the two subsequent sections are stated. In this regard, those who accept such things as "there is giving" and so forth, they describe the full understanding of the clinging to views.

But those who hold that "there is no purification by virtue, no purification by observance, no purification by cultivation," [they describe the full understanding of the clinging to rules-and-observances].

They grasp [at views], and they prescribe the full understanding of the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*). Yet, not even a single one is able to prescribe the full understanding of the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*).

For even the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*), who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) and can touch the sun and moon with their hands as they walk about, prescribe only three kinds of full understanding; they are unable to relinquish the theory of a self.
Therefore, they fall again and again into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) itself. For these beings are like a rabbit [trapped] on the earth.
In this regard, there is this illustrative parable involving a dialogue on the meaning: it is said that the Earth spoke to a rabbit, "O rabbit!
The rabbit asked, "Who is this? [The Earth replied: "Why is it that you, while I am performing all my postures upon you, defecate and urinate [on me]?"
"Do you not know me? "I have seen you very well; even the place trodden by me feels as if touched by the tips of my fingers.
The water I discharged was but a trifle, and the dung was no larger than a *kataka* fruit.
But the places trodden by elephants, horses, and the like are vast; their urine amounts to a jar, and their excrement to a bushel."
"Enough of you for me! Having said this, he sprang up and fell in another place. Then the earth said to him, "Hey!
Even though you have gone far, have you not indeed fallen right upon me? Disgusted with her once more, he sprang up and fell elsewhere;
in this way, even after leaping and falling for a thousand years, the hare was unable to escape the earth.

He is unable [to do so]. In the same way, although the non-Buddhist teachers (titthiyā) proclaim the full understanding of all clinging (sabbūpādānapariññā), they proclaim the transcendence of only three types of clinging—namely, clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna) and the others.
Yet, they are unable to relinquish their doctrine of self (attavāda); being unable to do so, they fall again and again into the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) alone.

Thus, having stated the doctrine of the severance of views by way of that which the sectarians (tīrthikas) are unable to transcend, he now spoke the words beginning with "In such a Dhamma and Vinaya, monks," in order to show the doctrine of the severance of confidence.
Therein, "Dhamma and Vinaya" refers to both the Dhamma and the Vinaya; by means of both, he demonstrates a teaching that does not lead to liberation.

“The confidence one has in the Teacher does not lead to the right path”—for in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, once the Teacher has passed away, he becomes a lion, a tiger, a leopard, a bear, or a hyena; while his disciples become deer, pigs, or antelopes.
[The Teacher] might then feel either forbearance or loving-kindness toward them, thinking, "These were formerly my attendants and providers of requisites."
Or, failing to show compassion toward them, he falls upon them and drinks their blood, even devouring their large pieces of flesh.
Or else, the Teacher is a cat, while the disciples are chickens or mice; then, as before, he devours them without showing any mercy.
Or again, the Teacher is a hell-guardian and the disciples are beings in hell; [he thinks], "These are mine..."
Without showing compassion, saying, "These were formerly my attendants and providers of requisites," he subjects them to various forms of torture:
he yokes them to burning chariots, makes them climb mountains of glowing coals, casts them into iron cauldrons, and subjects them to many painful conditions.
Or else, when his disciples pass away, they become lions and the like, while the Teacher himself becomes one among deer and other such creatures.
Thinking, "Previously we supported him with these four requisites;
he is our teacher," they fail to develop patience, loving-kindness, or compassion toward him, and instead bring about his ruin and disaster in the manner already described.
Thus, any confidence in the Teacher within a dispensation that does not lead to liberation is not rightly directed; even after persisting for some time, it eventually perishes.

"Faith in the Dhamma": for in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, what is called "faith in the Dhamma" is merely faith in the textual doctrine—consisting of what has been learned, mastered, retained, and recited—but there is no escape from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) therein.
Therefore, whatever faith one has in this [teaching] only makes the round of existence ever more profound; thus, one has not entered the path rightly within the Dispensation.
It is declared to be non-substantial.

As for "fulfilling the practice of the precepts": even that fulfillment of the practice of the precepts—such as the "unborn" precepts (*ajasīla*) and so forth—found within a teaching that does not lead to liberation, because it does not bring about release from existence or escape from the cycle of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*), when perfected, leads instead to birth in the animal realm.
When it ripens, it leads to hell; therefore, it is not said to be well-directed. Regarding the phrase "among those of the same Dhamma":

for in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, among those who are fellow-practitioners (*sahadhammika*), some—having passed away—become lions and the like, while others become deer and the like.
Therein, those who have become lions and so forth [think] toward those who have become deer and the like, "These were our fellow-practitioners."
Without practicing patience and the other virtues, they produce great suffering for one another in the manner previously described.
Therefore, even among those who share the same Dhamma, there is seen here a lack of affection and endearment, as well as a lack of harmony.
Now, showing all these various causes together, the Blessed One asks: "For what reason is this so? "Because it is thus."
“Monks, it is thus,” he said, beginning with those words. Herein, this is the summary meaning:
“It is indeed so, monks, that what was stated by me—‘The confidence one has in the Teacher is not declared to be well-directed,’ and so forth—is exactly so.
Why? Because those qualities such as confidence [exist] in a Dhamma and Vinaya that are poorly proclaimed … [and] not made known by a Perfectly Enlightened One.”
For here, *yathā* is a particle used in the sense of "cause" (*kāraṇatthe*). Therein, *durakkhāte* means "badly spoken";

it is "badly proclaimed" precisely because it was badly established. Furthermore, since this does not lead out toward the goal of the path and its fruits, it is "not conducive to liberation" (*aniyyāniko*).

Because it does not conduce to the subsiding of lust and the other defilements, it is "not conducive to peace" (*anupasamasaṃvattaniko*). It has not been proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One, the Omniscient One.

It is not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. In that which is not leading out, which does not conduce to peace, and which is not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One—by this much the Blessed One shows that confidence in the sectarians is as useless as the confidence of a drunken jackal.
It is said that a certain black jackal entered the city at night, ate some liquor-sediment, and lay down in a *punnāga* grove.
Waking at sunrise while still drowsy, he thought, "It is not possible to go at this time;

we have many enemies, so it would be best to deceive one of them. Seeing a certain brahmin passing by, thinking, "I will deceive this man," he said, "Noble sir, brahmin! "Who is calling the brahmin? "I am, master. "From where?"
"Come here for a moment. "What is it, sir? "Take me outside the village; I will give you two hundred kahāpaṇas.
He [the brahmin] said, "I will take you," and seized him by the feet. "Hey, foolish brahmin! Kahāpaṇas are not something to be thrown away by me;
kahāpaṇas are difficult to obtain. Grasp me firmly! "How, sir, shall I grasp you? [The Buddha replied: "With your upper robe."
“Tie it with a knot, hang it over your shoulder, and take it,” he said.
The brahmin did as instructed and went to a spot near the south gate, asking, “Shall I unload it here? “What place is this? [the king asked.
“This is the great gate,” he replied. “You fool, brahmin! Why would your kinsmen leave a kahāpaṇa coin at the inner gate? Take me further!”
Thus, having gone little by little again and again, he asked, "Shall I land here? Shall I land here?
Being urged on by him, he went to a safe place; when told, "Land there," he landed and took the garment.
The black jackal said, "I told you that I would give you two hundred kahāpaṇas. But I have many kahāpaṇas; it is not just two."
"Take these hundred kahāpaṇas; until I return with more kahāpaṇas, you must remain standing, watching the sun," he said.
Having walked a short distance and then turned back, he spoke again to the brahmin: "Noble brahmin, do not look this way;
remain standing, watching only the sun. Having spoken thus, he entered a ketaka grove and did as he pleased.
He had departed. Even as the brahmin gazed at the sun, sweat broke out from his forehead and his armpits.
Then a tree deity said to him:
"O brahmin, you have believed the jackal who has drunk wine!"
“There are not even a hundred crafts, so how could there be two hundred of bronze?
Just as confidence in a black jackal is useless, so too is it toward the followers of other sects (titthiyas).
Having thus shown the pointlessness of confidence in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, [the text now] shows its great purposefulness in a teaching that does lead to liberation.

To demonstrate this, the Tathāgata said, "Bhikkhus, [it is] thus," and so forth. Therein, "he proclaims the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures" means that by means of the path of Arahantship, he proclaims the full understanding of the abandonment and transcendence of clinging to sensual pleasures;
for the other three types of clinging, he proclaims the full understanding by means of the path of stream-entry. "In such a Dhamma and Discipline, bhikkhus... [and so on].
“Monks, such is the Dhamma and such is the Vinaya. By both of these, he shows the Dispensation as leading to liberation. “Confidence in the Teacher”:
whatever confidence one has in the Teacher regarding such a Dispensation is declared to be rightly directed; it conduces to the escape from the suffering of existence.
In this regard, there are these instances: It is said that the Blessed One was dwelling in the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka. Then, one—
An owl-bird would follow half the way when the Blessed One entered the village for alms,

and would go out half the way to meet him when he was departing. On one occasion, having descended from the mountain at evening time while the Perfectly Enlightened One sat surrounded by the community of monks,
the bird paid homage, spread out its wings, raised its joined palms, and bowed its head down.
He stood there paying homage to the One Possessing the Ten Powers. The Blessed One, looking at him, manifested a smile.
The Elder Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting a smile? "Ānanda, behold this owl-bird;
having developed a serene mind toward me and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it will dwell among the devas for a hundred thousand kappas."
"And after wandering among humans, you will become a Paccekabuddha named Somanassa," he said:
"O Ulūkamaṇḍalakkhika, long-dweller on Vediyaka mountain!
You are happy, noble Kosiya, for you behold the Supreme Buddha who has arisen at the right time."
Having gained confidence in my heart toward the unsurpassed Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
one does not go to the states of misery for a hundred thousand eons.
Having passed away from the world of the devas, impelled by the root of merit, one returns.
"He shall become one of infinite knowledge, renowned as Somanassa.

Furthermore, other stories from the city of Rājagaha—such as the story of the garland-maker Sumanā, the story of the great drum-beater, the story of the peacock-feather fletcher, the story of the lute-player, and the story of the conch-blower—should be expanded upon here. Thus, in the dispensation that leads to liberation...
Faith in the Teacher is rightly directed.
Regarding "faith in the Dhamma": faith in the Dhamma of the liberating teaching is rightly directed.
It bestows prosperity even upon animals who hear it by catching a mere sound; what then need be said regarding those who understand the ultimate truth?
This meaning is to be understood by way of the stories of the divine son Maṇḍūka and others. Regarding "fulfilling the precepts":

in the dispensation that leads to liberation, fulfilling the precepts is also a state of having gone rightly; it brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation. In this regard, the story of the young brahmin Chatta, the story of the novice monk, and others should be illustrated.

Regarding "toward fellow practitioners of the Dhamma": in the dispensation that leads to liberation, being dear and pleasing toward fellow practitioners of the Dhamma is also a state of having gone rightly; it brings about great success. This meaning is to be illustrated by the Vimānavatthu and the Petavatthu. For this has been said:
“I gave milk-rice to a bhikkhu wandering for alms... [and so on] ...molasses...
a piece of sugarcane... a *timbarusaka* fruit... a *kakkārika* cake...
an *eḷāluka* fruit... a vine-fruit... a *phārusaka* fruit... a hand-banner.”
A handful of salt... a handful of flowers... a radish... a handful of neem... sour gruel...
a winnowing-basket scrubber... a waist-belt... a shoulder-strap... a girdle-band... a fan... a palm-leaf fan.
“I gave a peacock-feather fan… an umbrella… sandals… a cake… a sweetmeat… a piece of sugar-cane to a bhikkhu wandering for alms… Behold my celestial mansion;
I am a nymph of beautiful form.”
The passage beginning with "For what reason? (taṃ kissa hetū) and so forth should be understood by applying it according to the method already stated. 145.

Now, in order to show the condition for those forms of clinging (*upādāna*) which the followers of other sects do not correctly describe as fully understood (*pariññā*), but which the Tathāgata does describe, he said:
"And these, monks," and so forth. In that context, regarding the terms "what is their source" (*kiṃnidāna*) and so on, [the meaning of] "source" (*nidāna*) and the others is as follows:
All these are synonyms for "cause" (*kāraṇa*). For a cause is called a "source" (*nidāna*) because it, as it were, instigates the fruit, saying, "Come, take this!
Since [the fruit] is born from that, arises from that, and originates from that, it is called "origination" (*samudaya*), "birth" (*jāti*), and "source" (*pabhava*).
Here, however, is the meaning of the words: "What is the source of these? means *kiṃnidānā*.
"What is their origin? means "what is their source" (*kiṃsamudayā*). "What is their birth? means "what is their origin" (*kiṃjātikā*).

"What is their provenance? means "what is their source" (*kiṃpabhavā*). Since craving (*taṇhā*) is, in the sense already stated, their root-cause (*nidāna*), their origin (*samudaya*), their birth (*jāti*), and their provenance (*pabhava*), he therefore said, "rooted in craving" (*taṇhānidānā*), and so forth. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. Since...

However, the Blessed One knows not only the condition for clinging (*upādāna*), but also the condition for craving (*taṇhā*) which serves as that condition for clinging, and indeed the conditions for feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, which serve as conditions for craving and the rest; therefore, he said, "And this craving, monks," and so on.

"And from which time" (*yato ca kho*) means at whatever time. "Ignorance has been abandoned" (*avijjā pahīnā hoti*) means that ignorance rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) has ceased through non-arising.
"It has been abandoned. "Clear knowledge has arisen" means that the clear knowledge of the path of Arahantship has arisen. "With the fading away of ignorance and the arising of clear knowledge":
that bhikkhu, because ignorance has been abandoned and clear knowledge has arisen, does not take up the clinging to sensual pleasures;
he neither grasps nor approaches it, nor does he grasp the other forms of clinging. Not taking them up, he does not tremble.
Thus, not grasping at any kind of clinging, he does not tremble through the agitation of craving.
Not trembling, and not giving rise to craving, he attains final Nibbāna by himself alone—that is, he attains final Nibbāna through the extinguishing of the defilements (kilesaparinibbāna).
Having thus shown the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), [the text] now shows the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa) of the bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted.
He said, "Birth is exhausted," and so forth. That has the same meaning as what was already stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
2. Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta:
Description of the City of Vesālī 146.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. In this context, "at Vesālī" means in the city of that name. That...
It is said that it came to be known as "Vesālī" because it gradually expanded and became vast. Regarding this, the following is the traditional account:
It is said that a fetus was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Having learned of this, she informed the king.
The king provided her with the necessary care for the pregnancy. While being properly cared for, when the time for the fetus to mature arrived, she went to the birth-chamber.
She entered. For those possessed of merit, the delivery from the womb occurs at dawn;
she was one of them, and therefore at dawn she gave birth to a piece of flesh resembling a layer of lac or a bandhujīvaka flower.
Then [the queen thought]: "Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden images, yet the chief consort gives birth to a piece of flesh"—thus [she spoke] before the king.
Thinking, "Ill repute might arise," and out of fear of such ill repute, he placed that piece of flesh in a vessel, sealed it, affixed the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges.
As soon as it was discarded by the men, deities established a protective guard over it. And there, upon a golden plate, with vermilion, [he wrote]: "Of the King of Bārāṇasī..."
Having written, “The offspring of the chief queen,” they tied it [to the vessel]. Then that vessel, unassailed by dangers such as waves, was carried along by the current of the Ganges.
At that time, a certain ascetic was dwelling on the bank of the Ganges, supported by a family of cowherds.
Having entered the Ganges early in the morning, he saw that vessel coming toward him and, perceiving it to be a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), he seized it. Then, therein—
Having seen that tablet of letters and the royal seal, he released it and beheld that piece of flesh.
Upon seeing it, this thought occurred to him: "There may be an embryo, for there is no foul stench or putridity in it.
He led it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot. Then, after the lapse of half a month, there were two pieces of flesh. The ascetic—
Having seen this, he established it as even more excellent. Then, after another half-month had passed, five boils each arose for the sake of the flesh-mass required for the hands, feet, and head.
Then, after another half-month had passed from that, one flesh-mass became a boy resembling a golden image, and the other became a girl.
Among them, maternal affection for his children arose in the ascetic, and milk flowed from his thumb.
From that time forth, he received milk-rice; having eaten his meal, he would pour the milk into the mouths of the children.
Whatever entered their stomachs appeared as if it were contained within a crystal vessel. Thus...
They were skinless. Others said, "Their skin was so closely adhered to one another that it was as if sewn together.
Thus, because they were either skinless (*nicchavi*) or had closely adhered skin (*līnacchavi*), they became known as Licchavis.
While the ascetic was raising the children, he would enter the village for instruction after sunrise and return before midday. To him—
Knowing of that activity, the cowherds said, “Venerable sir, raising children is an obstacle for those who have gone forth.
Give us the children; we will nourish them, while you attend to your own duties. The ascetic consented, saying, “Very well.
On the following day, the cowherds leveled the path, strewed it with flowers, and raised banners and flags.
Having carried them away while musical instruments were being played, they arrived at the hermitage. The ascetic said, "These children of great merit, you must raise them with diligence;

once they have grown, arrange their marriages among one another. Having satisfied the king with the five products of the cow and obtained a plot of land, build a city there and consecrate the prince as its ruler. Having spoken thus to the children, the ascetic—
She gave them away. Having agreed, saying "Very well," they took the children and raised them.
As the children grew up and were playing, they would strike other cowherd boys with their hands and feet at points of contention.
Those boys would weep. When asked by their parents, "Why are you crying? they would reply, "These [other boys] have no parents; they are being raised by ascetics."
"We are striking them too hard," they said. Then their parents said, "These children are destroying and causing suffering to other children; they should not be kept, they must be avoided.
From that time on, it is said, that region was called Vajjī, measuring one hundred leagues in extent. Then the cowherds [reported] that region to the king.
Having satisfied him, they took him [there]. Having established a city there and consecrated the prince, who was sixteen years of age, they made him king.
They then held a marriage ceremony for him with that maiden and made an agreement:
"No girl from outside shall be brought in, and no girl from here shall be given to anyone else. Through their first cohabitation, two children were born.
A daughter and a son were born. In this way, two children were born sixteen times.

Then, as those children grew up in succession, the city was enclosed three times with a gap of one *gāvuta* between each enclosure, because the original space was insufficient to accommodate their prosperity in terms of gardens, groves, dwelling places, and retinues.
Because it was expanded again and again, it came to be known as Vesālī.
The name [of the city] was Vesālī. Therefore it is said: “In the city named Vesālī.
“Outside the city” means outside the city, not within the city like the Ambapālī grove. This, however, was a forest thicket outside the city, like Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.
Therefore it is said: “Outside the city. “In another part of the city” refers to the city...
"Others" means in the western direction. Regarding "the forest grove": it is said that this forest grove was located about a *gāvuta* from the western side of the city.

There, people constructed a fragrant cell (*gandhakuṭi*) for the Blessed One and, surrounding it, established dwellings for the monks, including night-quarters, day-quarters, walking-paths, caves, huts, and pavilions; the Blessed One resided there.
Therefore it was said: “In a forest grove not far from the city. *Sunakkhatta* is his name; however, because he was the son of the Licchavis, he is called “the son of the Licchavis.
*Acirapakkanta* means that he had recently departed, having left the order and returned to the state of a householder.

*Parisati* means in the midst of the assembly. Regarding the phrase *uttarimanussadhammā*: here, the “human states” (*manussadhammā*) refer to the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapathā*).

He was unable to refute them. Why? Out of fear of being censured. For in Vesālī there were many people who had faith in the Triple Gem, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha.
If one were to say to them, "There is not even the mere tenfold path of wholesome action in the ascetic Gotama," they would ask: "Where did you see the Blessed One killing a living being? Where..."
Having spoken such things as "taking what is not given," do you not know your own measure? Do you chew stones and pebbles thinking, "I have teeth"?
Do you strive to grasp a snake by its tail? Do you wish to play at hide-and-seek with saw-toothed monsters?
They would say, "We shall knock out your teeth from your mouth! Out of fear of their reproach, he is unable to speak thus.
The description of the city of Vesālī is concluded.
Regarding the description of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) and so forth:

thereafter, in order to preclude any further attainment of distinction, he said, "superhuman states, a distinction consisting of noble knowledge and vision" (*uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso*).
In this context, "alamariya" means one who is capable of the noble state; that is to say, one who is competent for the state of an Ariya.
"Ñāṇadassana-visesa" means the excellence of knowledge and vision itself. "Alamariya-ñāṇadassana-visesa" refers to that excellence of knowledge and vision which is capable of the noble state.
As for "ñāṇadassana," it includes the divine eye, insight (vipassanā), the path, the fruit, the reviewing knowledge, and even omniscient knowledge.
It is said: “Being diligent, one attains knowledge and vision. Here, “knowledge and vision” refers to the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
“He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision” refers here to insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
“They are incapable of attaining knowledge and vision, of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment” refers here to the Path (*magga*). “This other [state] beyond human conditions…” [refers to the Fruit].
In the passage, "The distinguished noble knowledge and vision has been attained; a state of ease has been reached," this refers to the fruit (*phala*).

In the passage, "Knowledge and vision arose in me: my deliverance of mind is unshakable; this is the last birth; now there is no further becoming," this refers to the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
And in the passage, "Knowledge and vision arose in me: Āḷāra died seven days ago... [this refers to the knowledge of the passing away of others].
In the phrase “Kālāma,” this refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). However, here the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*) is intended; for it is that which he (the Buddha) rejects.
By the term “hammered out by reasoning” (*takkapariyāhata*), he refutes [the claim of] a teacher. For it occurred to him thus:
“It is not the case that the ascetic Gotama has approached a teacher and acquired some subtle, extraordinary doctrine; rather, it is merely hammered out by reasoning.”
"But having conjectured, 'It will be thus, it will be thus,' he teaches a doctrine hammered out by mere conjecture.
By the phrase "followed by inquiry" (*vīmaṃsānucarita*), he acknowledges his worldly wisdom (*lokiya-paññā*). "The ascetic Gotama is wise;
he possesses that wisdom—which is like Indra’s thunderbolt—and through such inquiry as 'It will turn out thus, it will turn out thus,' from this..."
And having had them follow him, he teaches the Dhamma that has been investigated through such investigation.

By the phrase "from his own inspired eloquence," he conceals his lack of direct personal experience regarding those teachings. For he thought thus: "The ascetic Gotama possesses no subtle internal Dhamma—neither insight, nor the path, nor the fruit, nor reflective knowledge; yet he has acquired a following."
The four castes attend upon him as they do a universal monarch (cakravartin).
His lip-enclosure is well-knit, his tongue is soft, his voice is sweet, and his speech is free from stammering;
whatever occurs to him, he takes that and speaks with spontaneous eloquence, thereby delighting the great multitude.
"And for whatever purpose the Dhamma has been taught to him":

that is to say, for the purpose of overcoming lust, the meditation subject of foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*) was taught; for the purpose of overcoming hatred, the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*);
for the purpose of overcoming delusion, the five factors (*pañca dhammā*); and for the purpose of cutting off discursive thought, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).

"It leads the practitioner rightly to the destruction of suffering": this explains that the Dhamma, when practiced exactly as it has been taught, leads—that is, goes toward—the destruction of the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*) for that practitioner by way of the right cause, method, and reason;
it accomplishes that goal. However, he does not say this out of his own personal inclination. For [this is] the Buddhas'...
If one were to proclaim, "The Dhamma is not leading to liberation," one would not be able to say so. Why? Out of fear of censure.
For in Vesālī there are many lay followers who are stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. They would say:
"Sunakkhatta, you say that the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One does not lead to liberation; if this Dhamma does not lead to liberation, then in this..."

"Otherwise, they might raise an objection according to the method previously stated: 'Why is it that so many stream-enterers, so many once-returners, and so many non-returners have been born in this city?

Being unable to say that his teaching was not conducive to liberation due to this fear of being challenged, his Dhamma leads to deliverance fruitfully, like an arrow released by Arjuna; yet within himself—
He says, "There is nothing.

He heard it, indeed—having heard that speech as it was being spoken here and there in the midst of assemblies among the brahmin and merchant families in Vesālī—but he did not refute it. Why? Out of compassion. For thus it was said to him:
"This man is angry; under the influence of his anger, he will crackle like a fire-hearth into which salt has been thrown while the Veḷuvana grove is being burned.

But if I were to ward him off, he would harbor resentment toward me as well. Thus, there would be excessive resentment toward two people—the Tathāgata and myself. Thinking thus, out of compassion, he did not prevent him.
It occurred to him: "Speaking in dispraise of the Buddhas is like attributing faults to the full moon;
who would take such talk seriously? When his own saliva has dried up and his mouth is parched, he will desist of his own accord.
For this reason, he did not stop him. "Having returned from the alms-round" means having departed from the seeking of alms-food.
147. "Angry" means fierce and harsh. "Foolish person" means an empty person.
For those who lack the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits within that particular existence, the Buddhas call them "foolish persons.
Even when such support exists, if at that moment there is no path or fruit, they still call them "foolish persons. But in this case, regarding that...
The supporting condition for the paths and fruits within his own person had indeed been severed; therefore, he called him a "foolish man.
Furthermore, these words were spoken out of anger; that is to say, this speech of his was uttered through anger.
But why was he angry with the Blessed One? For previously, having approached the Blessed One, he had requested the practice for the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
He asked. Then the Blessed One explained it to him. Having developed the divine eye and increased his vision, he surveyed the world of the gods.
Seeing the sons and daughters of the gods enjoying celestial splendor in the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and the Missakavana Grove, he thought:
"For those established in such perfection of physical form, how sweet..."
Thinking, "Will there indeed be a sound? and desiring to hear it, he approached the One of Ten Powers and asked about the preparatory exercise for the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*).
However, the Blessed One, knowing that he lacked the necessary predisposition (*upanissaya*) for the divine ear-element, did not explain the preparatory exercise.
For Buddhas do not explain the preparatory exercise to one who is devoid of the necessary predisposition. Thus, toward the Blessed One...
Having harbored resentment, he thought: "I first asked the ascetic Gotama about the preliminary practice for the divine eye, and he said, 'Whether that succeeds for me or not, it does not matter.
But when I, through my own personal effort, had accomplished that and asked about the preliminary practice for the divine ear-element, he did not tell me. Surely this is because [he thinks]:"
"He thinks, 'This renunciant king, having produced the knowledge of the divine eye, having produced the knowledge of the divine ear-element,
having produced the knowledge of penetration of minds, and having produced the knowledge of the destruction of the taints,
will become my equal,' and out of envy and stinginess he does not speak to me. Having harbored even greater resentment, he cast off his saffron robes.
Even after entering the state of a householder, he does not wander about in silence; rather, he wanders about slandering the One of Ten Powers with what is untrue and empty.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "And this speech was uttered by him out of anger.
"For this is his character, Sāriputta"—Sāriputta, for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, by the Tathāgata...
While fulfilling the perfections, he exerted effort for this very purpose: "May my teaching of the Dhamma be leading to liberation.
Therefore, whoever should speak thus speaks only praise of the Tathāgata. For this, Sāriputta, is the praise of the Tathāgata;
it shows that this is a quality of the Tathāgata, not a lack of quality.

What does this passage beginning with “This one, indeed, is Sāriputta” show? It shows that the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), which had been denied by Sunakkhatta, exists within himself. The Blessed One [said]: “Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta says, ‘There is no superhuman state in the Tathāgata.
Yet I possess what is called omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa).”

There is the knowledge of the various kinds of psychic power; there is the knowledge of the divine ear-element; there is the knowledge of penetration of minds; there is the knowledge of the ten powers;
there is the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence; there is the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies;
there is the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth; and there is the knowledge that delimits the five destinations.
There is indeed such a thing; all these are indeed superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

To show the meaning that even for this foolish man there will not be even a mere trace of conformity to the Dhamma (*dhammanvaya*) capable of discerning even one such superhuman state, he began this teaching by way of the phrase, "Even this Sāriputta," and so forth. In that regard:
*Anvaya* means "following"; the sense is that one knows or realizes. *Dhammānvaya* is the following of the Dhamma;
this is a designation for the wisdom that knows each and every quality such as omniscience (*sabbaññutā-ñāṇa*).
By such phrases as "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," [he shows] that even such a superhuman quality (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) as my own omniscience exists.
He shows that for that foolish person, there will be no inference of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) even to know that "it exists.

This same application should be understood for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividhañāṇa) and so forth. The commentary on the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), etc., is finished.
Commentary on the Knowledge of the Ten Powers (Dasabalañāṇavaṇṇanā) 148.
And here, although the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā) ought to have been mentioned immediately after the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa),
since the knowledge of the ten powers (dasabalañāṇa) would not be complete if they were mentioned [there], he omits them and instead describes the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the ten powers.
Having fulfilled [the explanation], he spoke the passage beginning with "Sāriputta, there are these ten," in order to demonstrate them.

Therein, "powers of a Tathāgata" (*tathāgatabalāni*) refers to powers belonging exclusively to the Tathāgata, not shared by others. Alternatively, just as the powers of previous Buddhas were acquired through the perfection of their accumulated merit, they are also called "powers attained in that manner.
In this context, the power of a Tathāgata is twofold: physical power (*kāyabala*) and...
And the power of knowledge. Among these, the bodily strength is to be understood according to the breeds of elephants. For this was said by the ancients:
“The Kālāvaka, the Gaṅgeyya, the Paṇḍara, the Tambapiṅgala, the Gandha, the Maṅgala, the Hema, the Uposatha, and the Chaddanta—these are the ten.”
For these are the ten breeds of elephants. Among them, the *kālāvaka* should be understood as the ordinary breed of elephant.
The bodily strength of ten men is equal to that of one *kālāvaka* elephant; the strength of ten *kālāvakas* is equal to that of one *gaṅgeyya*;
the strength of ten *gaṅgeyyas* is equal to that of one *paṇḍara*. The [strength] of...
The value of ten white elephants is equal to that of one tawny elephant. The value of ten tawny elephants is equal to that of one reddish-brown elephant.
The value of ten reddish-brown elephants is equal to that of one scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*). The value of ten scent-elephants is equal to that of one auspicious elephant (*maṅgala*).
The value of ten auspicious elephants is equal to that of one Hemavata elephant. The value of ten [Hemavata elephants]...
That which belongs to ten Hemavatas is equal to one Uposatha elephant. That which belongs to ten Uposathas is equal to one Chaddanta elephant.
That which belongs to ten Chaddantas is equal to one Tathāgata. This very thing is also called the "Nārāyaṇa-compound strength.
By the calculation of ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand million elephants; by the calculation of men, it is the strength of ten... [million men].
The strength of a thousand million men constitutes the physical power of the Tathāgata. As for his power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), it is already set forth in the Canon:

the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*catuvesārajja-ñāṇa*), the unshakable knowledge regarding the eight assemblies, the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth (*catuyoni-paricchedaka-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge that delimits the five destinations (*pañcagati-paricchedaka-ñāṇa*). [In the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*...]
The seventy-three knowledges have arrived; there are seventy-seven knowledges—and thus many thousands of other knowledges as well.

This is what is called the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). Here too, it is specifically the power of knowledge that is intended. For knowledge is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.
"Endowed with which powers" means possessed of, fully endowed with, which ten powers of knowledge. "The place of the bull" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*)...
The "place of the bull" (*āsabhā*) means the best place, the supreme place; or it refers to the "bulls," namely the previous Buddhas, meaning the place belonging to them.

Furthermore, an *usabha* is the leader of a hundred cattle, while a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand cattle. Alternatively, an *usabha* is the leader of a hundred bulls, while a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand bulls.
He is the most excellent of all cattle, capable of enduring all hardships, white, beautiful, and able to carry great burdens—even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps.
The Unshakable Leader (nisabha) is what is intended here by "bull" (usabha); for this too is a synonym for him.
"Belonging to the bull" (āsabha) means "of the bull. "Place" (ṭhāna) refers to the immovable position attained by pressing down upon the earth with all four feet.
Furthermore, it is called "bull-like" (āsabha) because it is like that of a bull; for just as the bull known as the Leader (nisabha), by means of his bull-strength...
Just as an elephant endowed with four feet stands immovably after pressing down upon the earth, so too the Tathāgata,
endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, presses down upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four grounds of self-confidence;
he stands immovably, unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world including the devas.
Standing thus, he claims that bull-like state; he approaches it, does not reject it, and attributes it to himself.
Therefore it is said: "He claims the bull-like state.
"In assemblies" means in the eight kinds of assemblies. "He roars the lion’s roar" means he roars the best roar, the fearless roar, which is like the roar of a lion.
Or he roars a roar. This meaning should be illustrated by the Sīhanāda Sutta.

Just as a lion is called a "lion" (sīha) because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hana*), so too the Tathāgata is called a "lion" because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and his slaying of the doctrines of others.
The roar of such a lion is the "lion's roar" (*sīhanāda*). In that regard, just as a lion [roars] with lion-strength...
Being thus endowed, confident in all respects and free from horripilation, he roars his lion’s roar;

so too the Lion of the Tathāgatas, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, being confident and free from horripilation among the eight assemblies, roars his lion’s roar—endowed with the various graces of teaching in the manner beginning with "form," and so forth. Therefore it was said: "In the assemblies, the lion’s roar..."
"...roars. Regarding the phrase "he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel" (*brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti*): here, "Brahma" (*brahma*) means supreme, most excellent, and distinguished.
As for this word "wheel" (*cakkā*), it is seen to apply to prosperity, characteristics, parts of a chariot, modes of conduct, giving, and to the jewel, the Dhamma, the sun, and so forth.
The Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) is understood here; that [term] should be analyzed in two ways.
For in such passages as, “Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels possessed by which gods and humans,” it is seen in the sense of excellence (*sampatti*).
In the passage, “Wheels were born on the soles of his feet,” it refers to a mark (*lakkhaṇa*). In the phrase, “Like a wheel of a rolling chariot,”...
In the phrase "pada," it refers to the parts of a chariot. In the phrase "four-wheeled, nine-gated," it refers to the modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*).

In the verse, "Give, enjoy, and do not be negligent; set in motion the wheel for all living beings," it refers to giving. In the phrase, "The divine wheel-treasure appeared," it refers to the treasure-wheel (*ratana-cakka*).
In the phrase, "The wheel set in motion by me," it refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhamma-cakka*). [And] for a person struck by desire...
In the phrase "the wheel turns upon the head," it refers to the breast-wheel (*uracakka*). In the phrase "even with a wheel whose edge is like a razor," it refers to a weapon-wheel (*paharaṇacakka*).
In the phrase "a thunderbolt-wheel (*asanivicakka*)," it refers to a circle of lightning (*asanimaṇḍala*).

Here, however, it is intended in the sense of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). That Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*). Of these, that which is developed through wisdom...

The knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) brings about the noble powers for oneself; the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*), impelled by compassion, brings about the noble powers for disciples.
In this regard, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen.

For it is "arising" from the Great Renunciation until the path of Arahatship, and it is called "arisen" at the moment of the fruition (*phala*). Or [alternatively], from the Tusita heaven until the seat of Great Enlightenment...
That which is arising at the moment of the path of Arahatship is called "arisen" at the moment of the fruit.
Alternatively, from the time of the Great Being Dīpaṅkara until the arising of the path of Arahatship, it is called "arisen" at the moment of the fruit.

The knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is also twofold as it occurs: that which occurs until the moment of the stream-entry path of Aññā Koṇḍañña, and [that which occurs] at the moment of the fruit.
This is called "occurrence. Among these, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*), while the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*) is mundane (*lokiya*).
Yet both of these are not shared by others; they are the very own-knowledge (*orasa-ñāṇa*) of the Buddhas alone.
Now, regarding those powers endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his pre-eminent place (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*): starting from the beginning, there are ten... [the text continues].
“Moreover, Sāriputta, these are the powers of a Tathāgata,” thus they were set forth.
To show them in detail, what are the ten? Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata says, “the possible as possible,” and so forth.
In that context, “the possible as possible” means the cause as cause. For it is because the fruit stands upon the cause that its existence is dependent on it.

It both arises and occurs; therefore it is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*). The Blessed One, understanding that "whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, those are the ground;
whatever states are not the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, those are not the ground," [understood] the ground as a ground and the non-ground as a non-ground.

He understands, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. This, moreover, has been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma by way of such passages as: "In this context, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible?
And by the phrase "by which knowledge," it means: "Sāriputta, this too is the Tathāgata’s"—that is, this knowledge of the possible and the impossible belongs to the Tathāgata.
The meaning is that it is called "the power of the Tathāgata. In this way, the application [of the commentary] should be understood for all the terms.
Regarding "of the undertaking of kamma": this refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed after having undertaken it; or alternatively, "kamma" itself is the "undertaking of kamma.

"According to the occasion and the cause" means by way of both conditions (*paccaya*) and causes (*hetu*). In that regard, destiny, the basis, time, and effort [are the factors] for the ripening [of the fruit].

The occasion (*ṭhāna*). Karma is the cause (*hetu*). Furthermore, the detailed exposition of this knowledge has already been set forth in the Abhidhamma in such passages as: "There are certain undertakings of evil kamma that, being obstructed by the attainment of a fortunate rebirth (*gatisampatti*), do not ripen.

"Leading everywhere" (*sabbatthagāminī*) means leading to all destinations (*sabbagati*) and leading to bad destinations (*agati*). "Way" (*paṭipadā*) means the path (*magga*). "As it really is" (*yathābhūtaṃ*).

"He understands" means that even when many people are killing a single living being, he knows the true nature, without error, of the practices comprised by wholesome and unwholesome volition (cetanā) according to this principle:
"The volition of this one will lead to hell; the volition of this one will lead to the animal realm.
And the detailed exposition of this knowledge is [found] therein: *...tattha...* [the text continues].
What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, as it really is, of the way leading everywhere? It is as follows: "Here, the Tathāgata understands:
'This is the path, this is the practice that leads to hell,'" and so on according to the method found in the Abhidhamma.
"Many elements" (*anekadhātu*) means having many elements, such as the eye-element and so forth, or the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth. "Diverse elements" (*nānādhātu*) means...
By way of the distinct characteristics of those very elements, he understands the world as consisting of various kinds of elements. "The world" refers to the world of aggregates, bases, and elements.
"Understands it as it really is" means he penetrates the specific nature of each respective element without error.
This knowledge is called: "In this context, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the world as it really is, with its many and diverse elements? Here...
The Tathāgata understands the diversity of the aggregates,” and so forth; this has been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma.
“Diversity of inclinations” (nānādhimuttikatā) means the state of having diverse inclinations by way of inferior and other types of inclinations. This knowledge is also [described as follows]:
“In that regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the diversity of inclinations of beings as it really is? Here, the Tathāgata...”

"He understands: 'There are beings of inferior disposition,'" and so forth; this has already been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma. "Of other beings" (parasattānaṃ) means of those beings who are preeminent.

"Of other persons" (parapuggalānaṃ) refers to those other beings who are inferior. Alternatively, these two terms have the same meaning; they are stated as two because of the diversity of those to be trained (veneyya). "The penetration of the faculties of others" (indriyaparopariyattaṃ) refers to [the knowledge of] faith and the other faculties.
The meaning is: the higher and lower state of the faculties, as well as their increase and decrease. The detailed exposition of this knowledge is given by the passage beginning:
"In that regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the higher and lower state of the faculties of other beings and other persons as they really are?
Here, the Tathāgata understands the inclinations of beings; he understands their underlying tendencies," and so forth.
[This] is indeed according to the method found in the Abhidhamma.
Regarding "the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments": this refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with "one possessing form sees forms";
the three concentrations beginning with "accompanied by applied and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra); and the attainments of the first jhāna and so forth.
Of the nine successive attainments (*anupubbasamāpatti*). "Defilement" (*saṃkilesa*) refers to states conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya-dhamma*).
"Purification" (*vodāna*) refers to states conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiya-dhamma*). "Emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*)—as it is said: "Purification is also emergence;

emergence from each respective concentration is also emergence"—refers both to the familiar jhānas and to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and fruition attainments (*phalasamāpatti*). For each lower familiar jhāna...
Each preceding one is the proximate cause for each succeeding one. Therefore, it is said: "Purification is also emergence.
However, emergence from all jhānas occurs by means of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs by means of the attainment of fruition.
With reference to this, it is said: "Emergence from each respective concentration is also emergence. This too...

Regarding knowledge, it is explained in detail in the Abhidhamma by way of such passages as: "In this context, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of things as they truly are concerning the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments? There are four types of meditators;
there is a certain meditator who, while experiencing success, perceives it as failure," and so forth. [This concludes the section] on the seven knowledges.

The detailed explanation and analysis has been stated in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* (the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*) within the *Sammohavinodanī*. The discourse on the knowledge of recollecting past lives and the divine eye is elaborated upon in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The discourse on the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) is in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*.
"149. These, Sāriputta... refers to those which were previously stated: "Now, Sāriputta, these ten [powers] of the Tathāgata..."
"I have spoken of the powers of a Tathāgata; these are they," he says, thereby effecting absorption (*appanā*). Herein, there arises the argument of an opponent:

"The so-called knowledge of the ten powers does not exist as something separate; it is merely a classification of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). That should not be viewed in that way.
For the knowledge of the ten powers is indeed one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another. Indeed, the knowledge of the ten powers...
It knows only its own specific function. As for the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), it understands both that [function] and everything remaining beyond it.
For among the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabalañāṇa*): the first knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause; the second, only the variety of kamma and the variety of its results;
the third, only the delimitation of kamma; the fourth, only the causes for the diversity of elements (*dhātu*); the fifth, only the underlying intentions and inclinations of beings; the sixth...
The seventh [knowledge] is precisely the sharpness and dullness of the faculties. The eighth is precisely their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other states.

The ninth is precisely the continuity of the aggregates in previous existences. The tenth is precisely the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings. The eleventh is precisely the analysis of the truths.
But omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) understands both what is to be known by these [ten knowledges] and that which is beyond them.
Furthermore, it does not perform all their functions. For that [knowledge] cannot enter as jhāna; it cannot exercise transformations as psychic power (iddhi);
and it cannot eradicate defilements as the Path (magga). Moreover, the opponent himself should be asked:
"Is this so-called 'knowledge of the Ten Powers' with applied thought and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra), or without applied thought and with only sustained thought (avitakka-vicāramatta)?"
"Without applied thought and without sustained thought, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere; mundane and supramundane"?
Knowing [the answer], he will state that the seven knowledges in succession are "with applied thought and with sustained thought.

He will then state that the two following [knowledges] are "without applied thought and without sustained thought. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints may be with applied thought and with sustained thought, may be without applied thought and with sustained thought only, or may be...
He will say that it is "without applied thought and without sustained thought. Likewise, he will state them in sequence:

seven belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), followed by two belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and finally one supramundane (lokuttara). However, he will state that the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is indeed with applied thought and with sustained thought, belongs only to the sense-sphere, and is mundane (lokiya) alone.
Having thus provided a word-by-word commentary on this section, we shall now explain that the Tathāgata, by means of his knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa*),

first perceives the absence of the veil of defilements— which constitutes the possibility and impossibility for beings to be trained regarding both the attainment and non-attainment of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).
This is because he perceives the presence of the basis for mundane right view and perceives the absence of the basis for fixed wrong view.
Then, by means of the knowledge of the ripening of kamma, he sees their absence of obstruction due to kamma-result, because he perceives a rebirth-linking with three roots.
By means of the knowledge of the way leading everywhere, he sees their absence of obstruction due to kamma, because he perceives the absence of any kamma entailing immediate retribution.

Thus, for those who are unobstructed, by means of the knowledge of the many elements and the diversity of elements, [he discerns] their specific temperament for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma suitable to them.
He sees [them] by seeing the diversity of their elements (*dhātu*).

Then, by means of the knowledge of their diverse inclinations (*adhimutti*), he perceives their inclination for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma according to that inclination, even without employing external effort.

Having thus perceived their inclinations, he perceives the degree of their faculties (*indriya*) by means of the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*), in order to teach the Dhamma according to their capacity and strength.
He sees them, because he perceives the sharpness and flexibility of their faculties such as faith.

Having thus fully understood the higher and lower degrees of others' faculties, if they are far away, he quickly approaches them by means of a specific supernormal power (*iddhi*) due to his mastery over the first jhāna and the others.

And having approached, through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), he [perceives] their cultivation of previous births, and by the power of the divine eye knowledge (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*).
Perceiving the specific state of the mind at present by means of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds— which is to be attained—

and being free from delusion regarding the practice leading to the destruction of the taints through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. Therefore,
it should be understood that these ten powers are stated in this sequence.
In the passages beginning with "Having abandoned that speech, Sāriputta," one is said to abandon that speech when saying, "I shall not speak such speech again.
One is said to abandon the mind when thinking, "I shall not give rise to such a mind again.
One is said to relinquish the view when abandoning it by thinking, "I shall not hold such a view again."
Acting in such a way, he neither abandons nor relinquishes [his evil deeds].
"As he was brought, so he is placed in hell" means that just as he was brought by the guardians of hell and placed in hell, so too should he be understood as being placed in hell.
Now, showing a simile that illustrates this point, he said, "Just as if," and so forth. In that context, regarding the phrases beginning with "endowed with virtue" (sīlasampanno):
The mundane and supramundane virtues, concentration, and wisdom should be understood. It is also appropriate to exclude [the mundane] by way of the supramundane alone.
For this bhikkhu is perfected in virtue through right speech, right action, and right livelihood; he is perfected in concentration through right effort, mindfulness, and concentration;
and he is perfected in wisdom through right view and right intention. Thus, being perfected in virtue and the other factors, such a bhikkhu, in this very life—
"In this very life, one attains final knowledge and reaches Arahantship within this same personal existence;
it is just so, Sāriputta, I say. This case is exactly like this:
just as the fruit arises immediately after the path without any interval, even so, for this person, immediately after death, without any interval, [he falls] into hell."
This shows that there is rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Indeed, throughout the entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*), there is no simile stated more firmly than this one.
Regarding the term *vesārajjāni*:
here, *vesārajja* (intrepidity) is the opposite of *sārajja* (timidity); it refers to the absence of timidity in four specific instances.
This is the name for the knowledge consisting of arisen joy in one who is reflecting. "Of you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One" means:

of you who claim, "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all phenomena have been fully awakened to by me. "These phenomena have not been fully awakened to by you" means these specific phenomena have not been fully realized by you.
"In that regard indeed" means: regarding those very things which have not been fully awakened to.
Regarding the teachings that have been shown: "With the Dhamma" means with a statement accompanied by reason and cause; like Sunakkhatta, one who prattles on is not a measure.
"This is the sign": here, both the person and the teaching are intended by the term "sign.
"I do not see that person who would challenge me back, nor do I see that teaching which, having been shown, [would allow one to say] 'this is [the case]...'"
"He will reproach me, saying, 'This Dhamma has not been fully realized by you'"—this is the meaning here.

"Attained to security" means he has reached security; the remaining two phrases are synonyms for this very term. All of this is stated with reference specifically to the knowledge of fearlessness (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*).
For regarding the Ten-Powered One, [the thought occurs]: "This is the name of a Dhamma that has not been fully realized by you," [addressing] either an accuser person...

For one who reflects, "I say 'I am a Buddha' because I have not seen any dhamma that could serve as a ground for such a challenge, or because I am a Buddha by my very nature," an exceedingly powerful joy arises.

The knowledge associated with that is called "intrepidity" (vesārajja). It is with reference to this that he said, "He has attained security," and so forth. In this same way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
Regarding the phrase "obstructive states" (*antarāyikā dhammā*): here, they are called "obstructive" because they create an obstruction.

In terms of their actual meaning, these refer to the seven classes of offenses when intentionally transgressed. For even a mere *dukkaṭa* or *dubbhāsita* offense, if committed intentionally, creates an obstruction to the paths and fruits.
However, in this context, sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*) is intended. For one who indulges in sexual intercourse...
For indeed, for anyone, there is certainly an obstacle to the path and its fruits.

"But for whom it is for their benefit" means for whom it is for the sake of the destruction of lust and so forth. "The Dhamma was taught" means the Dhamma such as the meditation on foulness was explained.
"In that, alas, [I thought] 'for me'" refers to that Dhamma which does not lead to liberation. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the knowledge of the ten powers is finished. 151.

As for the commentary on the eight assemblies, why was this begun with the words, "Sāriputta, there are these eight"? It is for the purpose of demonstrating the power of the knowledge of intrepidity (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*).

Just as the skill of a preacher of the Dhamma is made manifest when he plunges into an assembly of experts and is capable of delivering a discourse that satisfies the minds of the wise, so too, having encountered these eight assemblies, the state of fearlessness of the knowledge of self-confidence can be known.
Thus, in order to demonstrate the power of the knowledge of self-confidence, he said: "Sāriputta, there are these eight... and so forth.
In this context, "an assembly of khattiyas" refers to the place where khattiyas have gathered and are seated; this same method applies everywhere.
Furthermore, an "assembly of Māra" should be understood as the place where the hosts of Māra’s followers have gathered and are seated, not Māra himself.
