All these assemblies are included here by way of showing the location where they stand. For people say, "The king is seated here."
They were unable even to speak their own dialects, and sweat poured from their armpits. Such was the assembly of high-born kṣatriyas.
The brahmins were skilled in the three Vedas; the householders were skilled in various trades as well as in the analysis of phonemes;
and the ascetics were skilled in the doctrines of their own school and those of others. To deliver a discourse on the Dhamma in their midst was truly extraordinary.
It is a burden. Non-human beings (*amanussa*) are also formidable. For when the mere word "non-human" is uttered, the entire bodies of humans tremble;
or upon seeing their forms or hearing their sounds, sentient beings lose consciousness. Thus, an assembly of non-humans is formidable.
Even for them, delivering a discourse on the Dhamma is an exceedingly great burden. Thus, by way of showing the state of being formidable...
They should be understood as "taken.
"Enters" means he penetrates [into them]. An assembly of many hundreds of kṣatriyas is like the gathering at Bimbisāra’s [court], the gathering of kinsmen, or the gathering of the Licchavis.
It is indeed found in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) as well. But what of the Blessed One? Does he [enter] others...?
"Does he go even to the world-systems? "Yes, he goes. "In what form does he do so? "In whatever form they have, in that very same form he appears. Therefore it was said:
"I recall, Ānanda, having approached an assembly of many hundreds of kṣatriyas;
there, whatever their complexion was, such was my complexion. Whatever their voice was..."
I possess such a voice. I instruct, exhort, inspire, and gladden them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
While I am speaking, they do not know, "Who is this that speaks? Is it a god or a human?
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma, I vanish. And once vanished...
They do not recognize me, thinking, "Who is this who has vanished—is he a deva or a human?
The kṣatriyas are adorned with armlets, bracelets, garlands, perfumes, and the like; they wear garments of various colors and have put on jeweled earrings and diadems.
Does the Blessed One also adorn himself in such a way? And they appear white, black, or even of an unattractive complexion.
"Is the Teacher also like this? [They ask. The Teacher goes by way of his own renunciation alone, but he appears to them having assumed such a form;
having gone there, he shows himself seated upon the royal throne, and they think, "Today our king shines exceedingly. Yet they themselves have broken voices, hoarse voices, and voices like crows.
The Teacher preached the Dhamma with a voice like that of Brahmā.
When it was said, "My voice is just like that," this was spoken with reference to another language; for when humans heard him, they thought, "Today the king speaks with a sweet voice.
And when the Blessed One had finished speaking and departed, the king saw him returning and the inquiry arose, "Who might this be?"

This is what is meant: "Who indeed was this person who, having just now spoken in this place in the Magadhi language and the Sinhalese language with a sweet voice, has vanished? Was it a deva or a human?

And for what purpose did he teach the Dhamma to those who were thus unaware? [The answer is: "For the sake of creating a latent impression (vāsanā). For even the Dhamma heard in such a way becomes a condition in the future."
"He has indeed been" means he teaches in dependence upon the future.
"Having previously sat together" means having previously gathered and sat down. "Having previously conversed" means having previously engaged in talk and discussion.
"Discussion" refers to having also previously entered into a discussion on the Dhamma. "A multitude of several hundred brahmins," and so forth.
Its origin should be understood by way of the meeting with Soṇadaṇḍa and so forth, as well as by way of other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
The commentary on the eight assemblies is finished.
The commentary on the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
152. “Sāriputta, there are these four ‘wombs’ (yonī). Here, “womb” is a term for a category of aggregates, a cause, and the urinary passage.
For in the phrase, “There are four wombs of nāgas, four wombs of supaṇṇas,” it is a category of aggregates that is called a womb.
In the phrase, “For this is a womb for the attainment of the fruit born of the soil,” it is a cause. [And: “Nor do I, O brahmin...”
"I speak of one born from a womb, produced from a mother"—here, "womb" refers to the urinary passage. But here, in this context, "womb" (yoni) is intended to mean a category (khandhakoṭṭhāsa).
Among these, those born from an egg are "egg-born" (aṇḍaja); those born from a moisture-cask are "moisture-born" (jalābuja); those born from dampness are "dampness-born" (saṃsedaja);
and those who, without these causes, are produced as if having descended from above are "spontaneously born" (opapātika). Having burst forth...
“They are born” means that they are born by way of emerging after breaking [the womb].
By the phrases “in putrid filth,” etc., only undesirable places are shown; yet beings are indeed born even in desirable things such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses.

Among the “gods” and so forth, from the Cātumahārājika realm upward, the higher gods are exclusively of apparitional birth (*opapātika*). However, terrestrial gods (*bhūmadeva*) belong to all four modes of birth (*yoni*). And some humans...
Among humans, some are of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), just like the gods. However, for the most part, they are born from a womb (*jalābuja*).

There are also those born from an egg (*aṇḍaja*), such as the two elders, Koṇḍañña and Dvebhātika; and those born from moisture (*saṃsedaja*), such as the brahmin Pokkharasāti who was conceived within a lotus bud, and Queen Padumāvatī, and others.
Likewise, among the beings in the states of deprivation (*vinipātikesu*), the *nijjhāmataṇhika* pretas and the denizens of hell are exclusively of spontaneous birth; as for the rest...

They are also of four modes of origin (*catuyonika*). Just as they are, so too are the *yakkhas*, all quadrupeds, winged creatures, long-bodied beings, and so forth—all of them are indeed of four modes of origin.
The commentary on the four modes of origin is concluded.
Commentary on the Five Destinations (Pañcagativannanā) 153.
"Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Herein, they are called "destinations" (gatiyo) because one must go to them by means of well-done or ill-done kamma.

Furthermore, they are manifold, being classified as: the destination of movement, the destination of rebirth, the destination of inclination, the destination of non-existence, and the destination of accomplishment.

“Gati” means destination. In this context, the phrases “having passed away, I shall go to that destination” and “Whose destination neither gods, nor gandhabbas, nor humans know” refer to what is called the *gatigati* (the movement toward a destination).

The statement, “O monks, regarding these virtuous bhikkhus, I do not know their destination or non-destination,” refers to what is called *nibbattigati* (the destination of rebirth). [And] “Even so, O Brahmā, I—”
“I understand the destination and I understand the speed”—this is called the destination of inclination (*ajjhāsayagati*). “Cessation is the destination of phenomena;

Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant”—this is called the destination of dissolution (*vibhavagati*). “There are only two destinations, and no other”—this is called the destination of result (*nipphattigati*).
Among these, it is the destination of destination (*gatigati*) that is intended here.

In the passage beginning with “Niraya,” *niraya* (hell) is so called in the sense of non-delight (*nirati*) and in the sense of being sapless (*nirassāda*). They are called *tiracchānā* because they move horizontally (*tiriyaṃ añchitā*); their womb is the *tiracchānayoni*.

It is the realm (*visaya*) of those who have reached the state of the departed (*pecca*), thus it is the *pettivisaya*. They are called *manussā* (human beings) because of the abundance of mind (*manaso ussannattā*).
They are called *devā* (gods) because they shine (*dibbanti*) by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure and their own respective splendors. And as for hell...
In the passages beginning with "Sāriputta," the term "hell" refers to the aggregates together with their physical location. The same method applies to the phrases beginning with "the animal realm.
By both the terms "path" and "way," he demonstrates precisely the karma that leads to those aforementioned destinies.
And as for the phrase "and how he has practiced," he explains by combining both—namely, the path and the way—into one, indicating the manner in which he has practiced.
In the case of *apāya* and so forth: it is called *apāya* because it is devoid (*apeta*) of that which is called prosperity (*vaḍḍhi*) or happiness (*sukha*).

It is called *duggati* because it is the destination (*gati*) or resort (*paṭisaraṇa*) of suffering. It is called *vinipāta* because those who have committed evil deeds fall down (*vinipatanti*) into it.
As for the phrase "and I know Nibbāna," this was said to show that he knows not only the various destinations and paths, but also Nibbāna, which is the escape from those destinations.
Here, both "the path" and "the way of practice" refer to the Noble Path itself.
The commentary on the five destinations is finished.
Commentary on the modes of the arising of knowledge.
154. Now, demonstrating the manner in which his own knowledge proceeded regarding the seven and eight points as previously described, he said:

"In this case, Sāriputta," and so forth. Therein, "exclusively painful" means constantly painful and incessantly painful. "Intense" means thick or abundant. "Bitter" means harsh. The phrases beginning with "just as if" are spoken for the purpose of providing a simile.
In that context, *kāsū* refers both to a pit and to a heap. "Why, O charioteer, do you dig a pit in such haste?"
“Tell me, friend, when you are asked:
what will you do with a pit?”—for here, a pit is called a *kāsu*.
“Other men fill a pit of glowing embers, weeping as their limbs are scorched.”
In that context, it refers to a heap; here, however, a pit is intended. For this reason he said, "exceeding a man's height" (*sādhikaporisā*).
In that regard, it is called *sādhikaporisā* because its measure exceeds a man's height; the meaning is "more than five cubits.
The phrase "of those with extinguished embers and extinguished smoke" is stated for the purpose of indicating the intensity of the heat; or rather, even when there are embers or smoke, the wind...
Because it arises [within him], his fever does not become intense. "Overcome by heat" means pursued by heat. "Thirsty" means one in whom craving has arisen.

"Parched with thirst" means desiring water. "By a path that goes in a single way" means by a path that is a single track, where on both sides there is a dense thicket of thorny trees that must be traversed in succession.
"Having directed [his mind]" means having formed an aspiration toward a pit of glowing coals.
There is no such name [for this], but it is stated thus because the posture was assumed with reference to a pit of embers.
"In just the same way" (*evameva kho*): here is the application of the simile—the hell is to be regarded as like the pit of embers;
the karma leading to hell is like the path to the pit of embers; the person endowed with that karma is like one who has set out on the path; and the one with vision...
The Blessed One is like a man with the divine eye. Just as that man, seeing someone set out on a path, recognizes:

"Having gone by this path, this person will fall into a pit of glowing embers," even so the Blessed One knows, regarding any action such as the taking of life being performed: "Having committed this deed, this person will be reborn in hell."
Just as that man later saw [the ember] fallen into the pit of glowing coals, even so the Blessed One, at a later time, thinking,
"Where has that man been reborn after performing that deed?", increased his light and, surveying with the divine eye, saw him reborn in hell,
experiencing the fivefold bondages and other great sufferings. Therein, although...
At the time of accumulating that karma, his appearance was one thing; once reborn in hell, it was another.

Nevertheless, when one looks to see where that being has been reborn after performing that karma, even if he stands in the midst of many thousands of beings, that very same being alone comes into the range of vision as "this is he. They say, "Such is the power of the divine eye."
In the second simile, because there is no burning heat (pariḷāha) in a cesspool as there is in a pit of glowing embers, he did not say "exclusively painful" but rather said "painful," and so forth.
Here too, the application of the simile should be understood in the same manner as before.

For the Blessed One describes this person as being born anywhere among the animal wombs, such as those of elephants, and [suffering] from killing, binding, dragging away, pulling to and fro, and so on.
He sees [the being] experiencing great suffering.
In the third simile, "thin leaves and foliage" does not mean having thin leaves like a layer of clouds;
rather, this was said with reference to its sparse leafiness. "Scanty shade" means sparse shade. "Abounding in suffering" is because, in the realm of the *petas* (hungry ghosts)...
Suffering alone is abundant, while happiness is limited and is to be experienced only occasionally; therefore, he spoke thus.
Here too, the correlation with the simile should be understood in the same manner as before.
In the fourth simile, "dense with leaves and foliage" means having continuous leaves and covered with foliage. "Possessing cool shade" means...
It has a dense shade like a stone parasol. "Abundant pleasant feelings" means that in the human world, among such as the kshatriya clans, abundant pleasant feelings are to be experienced;
this shows: "I see one who, while experiencing those [feelings], is either lying down or sitting.
Here too, the application of the simile should be understood in the same manner as before.
In the fifth simile, "palace" refers to a long palace. "Smeared inside and plastered outside" means it is smeared within and plastered without.

"With bolts fastened" means the door-panel is well-secured together with the door-posts. "Spread with woolen blankets" means spread with black woolen cloth (*kāḷakojava*) having hair more than four finger-breadths in length.
"Spread with fine woolen coverlets" means spread with white woolen rugs made of carded wool. "Spread with cotton-padded quilts" means...

It was spread with a woolen coverlet (*uṇṇāmaya-attharaṇa*) that had thick flowers woven into it. "With a choice spread of antelope skin" means it was spread with an excellent coverlet made from the skin of a *kadalī-miga* (a type of spotted antelope).

It is said that they make that coverlet by spreading an antelope skin over a white cloth and then sewing it together. "With an upper canopy" means together with an upper covering (*uttaracchada*), that is, with an overhead awning (*uttaribaddha*).
The meaning is "together with a red canopy. "With red pillows on both sides" means having red pillows placed on both sides of the couch, namely a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet.
Here too, the application of the simile should be understood in the same manner as before.
However, here is the further connection of the parts: just as that man knows even one who has merely set out on the road, thinking, "This person [is going] by this..."

Just as that man, having gone by way of the road, ascended the palace, entered the gabled chamber, and would either sit or lie down upon the couch—so too, the Blessed One, seeing a person who is accumulating any kind of wholesome kamma among the bases for making merit such as giving and the like, knows:
"Having performed this, this person will be reborn in the world of the devas. Just as that man...
Just as one might, at a later time, ascend that palace, enter the gabled chamber, and see [the person] sitting or reclining on a couch,
experiencing a feeling of absolute and uninterrupted happiness; even so, at a later time, the Blessed One— thinking,
"Where has he been reborn after performing that wholesome deed?"— increased his light and surveyed with the divine eye.
He sees [the person] reborn in the world of the gods, surrounded by throngs of celestial nymphs in the Nandana Grove and other such places, experiencing divine splendor.
The commentary on the manner in which knowledge arises is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on the Destruction of the Taints.
In the section on the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), it is stated, "I see him with this," rather than saying, "with the divine eye" (*dibbena cakkhunā*). Why is that?

Because there is no restriction. For one may see this person even with the divine eye, know them even through the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), and indeed know them even through omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
As for the phrase "exclusively pleasant feeling" (*ekantasukhā vedanā*), although this [is compared] to the happiness of the deva-world...
In terms of their phrasing they are one, but in terms of their meaning they are different.

For the bliss of the deva-worlds is not exclusively blissful because of the presence of the fever of passion and so forth; the bliss of *nibbāna*, however, is exclusively blissful in every respect because it is the subsiding of all fevers.
Even in the simile, it is said: "Just as in a palace there is exclusive bliss. That [bliss] is [the cessation] of the fever of the path...
Because of the lack of tranquility, the state of being emaciated and distressed, and being overcome by thirst, there is not absolute happiness. However,
having descended into a lotus pond in a forest grove, because the dust and grime have been washed away and the fatigue of the journey has been stilled,
and because hunger and thirst have been dispelled by eating the roots of lotus stalks and drinking sweet water, [he put on] a bathing cloth.

Having changed his clothes, put on a smooth silk garment, placed a bag of rice at the head of the bed, wrung out a bathing cloth and placed it over his heart, and lying down while being fanned by a very gentle breeze, he experiences absolute happiness in every respect.
"In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile: the Noble Path is to be understood as being like the lotus pond.
The preliminary practice is like the path to a lotus pond; the person endowed with that practice is like one who has set out on the path;
the Blessed One with his divine eye is like a man with sight; and Nibbāna is like a grove of trees.
Just as that man, upon seeing someone who has set out on the path, knows: "This person, having gone by this path, will bathe in the lotus pond and enjoy himself in the delightful [grove]."
“...will sit or lie down at the foot of a tree in the forest grove,” even so the Blessed One knows one who is fulfilling the practice,
who is delimiting name-and-form, who is performing the investigation of conditions,
and who is practicing the work of insight with the characteristics as its object: “Having fulfilled this practice and exhausted all taints, this person...”
"Having attained and dwelling in the fruit-attainment (phalasamāpatti) described as 'the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,' he will experience exclusively pleasant feeling.
Just as that man, at a later time, having bathed in that lotus pond and entered the forest thicket,
sees [the person] sitting or lying down experiencing exclusively pleasant feeling, even so the Blessed One, at a later time—
He sees that person, having fulfilled the practice, developed the path, and realized the fruit,
having entered the supreme bed of cessation and attained the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object, experiencing exclusively pleasant feeling.
The commentary on the section on the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-vāra) is finished.
155. Regarding the commentary on the purity [attained] through the performance of difficult austerities (*dukkarakārikā*) and so forth:
Why was it begun with the words, “Moreover, Sāriputta, I recall being endowed with the four factors”?
It was begun by way of a separate connection (*pāṭiyekka-anusandhi*). For it is said that Sunakkhatta [held the view] that purity comes through the performance of difficult austerities.
"He is one who has attained such [a state]"—thus he was so named. Then the Blessed One began this teaching to show him:
"I have performed difficult deeds endowed with the four factors while remaining in a single existence; there is no one like me in being a performer of difficult deeds.
If purity were to come through the performance of difficult deeds, then I alone would be pure. Furthermore, this Sunakkhatta [was intent] on the performance of difficult deeds...

He was confident, and this was his state of confidence: "Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son saw the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya, who used four bowls and ate food scattered on the ground, eating with his mouth and consuming with his mouth.
Having seen him, it occurred to him: 'Ah, how handsome indeed is this ascetic who uses four bowls!'"
"He eats food scattered on the ground with his mouth alone; he consumes it with his mouth alone"—this is to be understood according to the method set forth in the Pāṭika Sutta.
Then the Blessed One thought: "This man has faith in the practice of austerities, and by me, while remaining in this very state of existence, [the Dhamma] endowed with four factors..."
"Difficult deeds have been done"—thinking, "Even one who has confidence in those who perform difficult deeds ought to have confidence in me," yet he does not have such confidence in me;
showing this, he began this teaching.
In that context, "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to giving, service, the training precepts, the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), and the teaching of the Dhamma.
Abstention from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, the Uposatha day, the Noble Path, the entire Dispensation, the underlying intention, and energy are all called "vow" (*vata*).
"What is your vow? What indeed is your holy life (*brahmacariya*)?
Of what well-practiced thing is this the result?"
Supernormal power, radiance, strength, heroism,
and rebirth— these, O Naga, are your great celestial mansion.
And I and my wife [are those who dwell] in the world of humans.
We both were masters of generosity endowed with faith;
at that time, my home was like a public well,
and the recluses and brahmins were fully satisfied.
That was my vow, and that was my holy life;
this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct:
psychic power, radiance, strength, vigor, and rebirth.
"And this great celestial mansion of mine, O Wise One.
For in this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, it is stated that "giving is the holy life" (*brahmacariya*). [And the verse:
"With which hand does one give desires? With which hand is there a festival of honey?"
“By what holy life does merit succeed in the hand?
By that holy life, the hand becomes a giver of desires;
by that holy life, the hand becomes a festival of honey. By that holy life of mine, merit succeeds in the hand.”

In this *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu*, it is stated that "service is the holy life" (*brahmacariya*). In this *Tittira-jātaka*, it is stated that "the five training rules (*pañcasikkhāpada*) are the holy life," as in: "Thus indeed, monks, that holy life called 'Tittiriya' came to be.
Furthermore, Pañcasikha, that holy life of mine was not for the sake of disenchantment, nor for dispassion, nor for cessation...
In this *Mahāgovinda Sutta*, it is stated that the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are the holy life (*brahmacariya*): "Just for the sake of rebirth in the Brahma-world.
In the passage, "In one holy life, a thousand [who have] escaped death," it is stated that the teaching of the Dhamma is the holy life.
And in the *Sallekha Sutta*: "Others will be practitioners of the unholy life; we here shall be practitioners of the holy life."
Abstinence from sexual intercourse is called the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"We do not transgress against our wives,
nor do our wives transgress against us."
"Except for those [wives], we lead the holy life;
therefore, indeed, among us the young do not die."—
In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife is called the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
“By a lowly holy life one is reborn as a khattiya;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; and by the highest, one is purified.
Thus, in the Nimi Jātaka, the eightfold Uposatha undertaken for the sake of self-taming is called *brahmacariya*.
“Moreover, Pañcasikha, this holy life of mine is for the sake of utter disenchantment, for the sake of dispassion...
[and so on] ...it is this very Noble Eightfold Path. Thus, in the Mahāgovinda Sutta itself, the Noble Path is called the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
“And this holy life was successful, prosperous, widespread, popular, and far-reaching...”
In the *Pāsādika Sutta*, it is stated that the teaching, which comprises the three trainings, is the holy life (*brahmacariya*) "well-proclaimed by gods and humans.
Furthermore: "Even for those who are not in a hurry, the hope for fruit is fulfilled;
'I have matured the holy life,' know this, O village headman."
In that context, "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to aspiration; here, however, it is intended as energy (*vīriya*).

For this very sutta is the [authoritative] source for the holy life of energy. And because it accomplishes four kinds of difficult tasks within a single lifetime, it is said to be "endowed with four factors."
"I am indeed an ascetic" (*tapassī sudaṃ homī*): *sudaṃ* is merely a particle; the meaning is "I am one who relies on austerity. "A supreme ascetic" (*paramatapassī*):
a supreme ascetic, the best among those who rely on austerity. "I am indeed austere" (*lūkho sudaṃ homī*): I am austere. "Repulsive" (*jegucchī*): repulsed by evil.
"I am indeed secluded" (*pavivitto sudaṃ homī*): I am secluded. "In this regard, Sāriputta, this occurred to me... (*tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputtā*): ...in this matter, Sāriputta, this was my thought.

In this context, regarding the fourfold holy life (*brahmacariya*), he shows: "This is my asceticism (*tapas*)," meaning that in the state of being dependent on asceticism, this practice of mine—such as being a naked ascetic (*acelaka*) and so forth—is my asceticism.

Therein, "naked" (*acelaka*) means one who is without clothes, one who is bare. "One of loose conduct" (*muttācāra*) means one whose conduct is unrestrained; [this refers to] not following the conduct of worldly sons of good family regarding such things as the performance of defecation and other bodily functions.
Being secluded, even while standing, I void excrement, urinate, and eat and consume food.
"Wiping the hands" means that while the alms-food remains in the hand, one wipes the hand with the tongue;
or, having voided excrement, perceiving it as a stick right in the hand, one wipes it with the hand—this is what is shown. They, it seems, designate the stick as a living being.
Therefore, fulfilling their practice, he acted in this way. When addressed with "Come, venerable sir" for the sake of receiving alms, he did not come;
thus he was "not one who comes when called 'Ehi bhaddante'. Likewise, even when addressed with "Stay, venerable sir," he did not stay; thus he was "not one who stays when called 'Tiṭṭha bhaddante'.
For the followers of other sects do not perform either of these two things, thinking, "In this way his word will have been carried out. I too [acted] in this way.
This shows that he intended [to eat]. "Brought" (*abhihaṭa*) refers to almsfood taken and brought earlier.
"Made specifically for [him]" (*uddissakata*) refers to almsfood announced as, "This was made for you. "An invitation" (*nimantana*):
even almsfood invited by saying, "Please enter such-and-such a family, street, or village," I do not accept or take.
"Not from the mouth of a jar" means: I do not accept alms-food being given after it has been drawn out from a jar.
"Not from the mouth of a basket" means: a *kaḷopī* is either a cooking pot or a wicker basket; I do not accept [food] from that either. Why?

Because the jars and baskets would receive a blow from the ladle because of me. "Not with a sheep between" means: [food] being given while making a threshold-block (*ummāra*) serve as an intermediary.
"I do not accept it. Why? Because by depending on me, he obtains an interval for eating. The same principle applies to the staff and the pestle as well.
"Not from two" means that when two people are eating, if one gets up and gives [food] while the other remains, I do not accept it. Why? Because it causes an interruption in the mouthful.
Regarding "not from a pregnant woman," and so forth: in the case of a pregnant woman, the child in her womb suffers; in the case of a nursing woman...
"I do not accept [food] because there is an obstacle to the child's milk, or because there is an obstacle to the pleasure of a woman who has gone to a man.

"Not from those where food is collected" means from meals prepared by collecting [ingredients) together. It is said that during times of famine, disciples of the naked ascetics (acelaka), having solicited rice and other provisions here and there for the sake of the naked ascetics, cook the meal. Even from such [places], the strict naked ascetic does not accept it.
Wherever a dog stands waiting, thinking, "I will get a morsel of food here," I do not take what has been brought there without first giving to it.
Why? Because that would be an obstacle to its obtaining food. "Moving in groups" means moving in large crowds;
for if people see a naked ascetic and enter a house of food, thinking, "We shall give alms to him," [the dog is excluded].
And as they were entering, flies hidden in the openings of the baskets and other containers flew up and swarmed in dense clusters.
Therefore, I did not accept the alms-food brought from there. Why? Because, owing to me, an obstacle to the flies' foraging had arisen;
thus I acted accordingly. "Not *thusodaka*" refers to salted sour gruel (*loṇasovīraka*) made from all the various ingredients of grain. Herein—
And drinking liquor is indeed blameworthy; however, this person perceives it as blameworthy even among all [other things].
An "one-house seeker" (*ekāgārika*) is one who returns after receiving alms at only a single house. An "one-morsel eater" (*ekālopika*) is one who sustains himself with only a single morsel.
The same principle applies to the "two-house seeker" (*dvāgārika*) and so forth. "Of even a single *datti*" means by a single *datti*. A *datti*...
There is a certain small bowl in which they place the first alms-food and set it aside. "One-day interval" means with a single day's interval.
"Half-monthly" means with a half-month's interval. "Eating food by turns" means eating food according to a rotation;
that is, food brought on a one-day turn, a two-day turn, a seven-day turn, or a half-monthly turn—food brought according to such a daily rotation.
"One who eats greens" (*sākabhakkha*) means one who eats fresh greens. "One who eats millet" (*sāmākabhakkha*) means one who eats the grains of millet. Regarding *nīvāra* and the others:
first, *nīvāra* refers to a species of wild rice that grows spontaneously in the forest. "Daddula" is the husk discarded by leather-workers after they have scraped the hide.
"Haṭa" refers to slime, algae, or the resin of trees such as the *kaṇikāra*. "Kaṇa" refers to broken rice. "Ācāma" is...

He eats the burnt rice that clings to the bottom of the cooking pot; they also call this "rice-gruel. Flour and so forth are well known. "One who eats fallen fruit" means one who eats fruit that has dropped.
"Sāṇa" refers to garments made of hemp or bark-fiber. "Masāṇa" refers to garments made of mixed fibers. "Chavadussa" refers to rags discarded from a dead body.
"Cloth made by weaving eraka-grass and so forth" refers to robes woven from such materials. "Rags from a dust heap" (*paṃsukūla*) means discarded scraps thrown upon the earth.
"Bark-cloth" (*tiritāni*) refers to garments made from tree bark. "Antelope skin" (*ajina*) is the hide of the antelope. "Split antelope skin" (*ajinakkhipa*) is that same hide split down the middle;
some also say it refers to one with the hooves attached. "Kusa-grass robe" (*kusacīra*) is a robe made by weaving *kusa* grass. This also applies to robes made of *vāka* grass or wooden boards.
The same method applies here. "Hair-cloth" (*kesakambala*) means a blanket made from human hair. With reference to this, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, whatever garments there are that are woven from threads, the hair-cloth is declared to be the most despised among them.
Bhikkhus, the hair-cloth is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch."
*Vālakambalaṃ*: a blanket made from horse-hair and the like. *Ulūkapakkhaṃ*: a lower garment made by sewing together owl-wings.
*Ubbhaṭṭhaka*: one who stands upright. *Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutta*: devoted to the exertion of squatting;
even when walking, he does so by repeatedly springing up while remaining in a squatting position. *Kaṇṭakāpassayika*: one who uses a bed of thorns.
This shows that having pounded [it] on the ground against either a thorn from a tree or a natural thorn, and having spread a hide there, one performs standing, walking, and so forth.
"Lying down" means that even while lying, one makes one's bed right there.
"Sāyatatiyakaṃ" means three times a day; thinking, "I shall wash away evil three times during the day—at dawn, at noon, and at evening"—[one does so].
He shows that he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water.
"Born of many years' accumulation" means produced over the course of many years. "Dust and dirt" refers to the impurity of dust;

he says this with reference to the time when he undertook the ascetic observance (*vata*) of wearing dust and dirt. "In the state of loathing evil" means in the condition of feeling disgust toward wickedness.
"Even toward a single drop of water, and even toward a mere puddle of water, compassion is established in me;
what need is there to mention others such as pebbles, gravel, sticks, sand, and so forth? For they indeed designate a drop of water and these pebbles, gravel, and so on as "small living beings.
Therefore he said: "Even toward a single drop of water, compassion is established in me."
"I do not kill or harm even a drop of water; for what reason? Lest I bring about the destruction—that is, death—of small living beings that have entered upon uneven ground.

This means: "Lest I bring about the destruction—that is, killing—of small living beings known as drops of water that have gone to uneven places such as low-lying areas, on level ground, or among the tips of grass and branches of trees.
It is with reference to this meaning that he says, "Mindful indeed I advance."
It is said that among the naked ascetics (Acelakas), from the very moment they step upon the ground, there is no such thing as one who is virtuous.
Even when going out for alms, they go only while being immoral; even when eating in the houses of their supporters, they eat only while being immoral;
and even when returning, they return only while being immoral. However, when they have swept the floor with a peacock feather...
When they sit having resolved upon virtue, then they are called "virtuous ones.
"Forest-worker" means one who wanders in the forest for the sake of roots, tubers, fruits, and so forth. "From forest to forest" means from one forest to another;
this same method applies everywhere. "I go" means I proceed. "A forest-dweller" means one born and raised in the forest; this is [the meaning].

He speaks with reference to his own time as an Ājīvaka. It is said that the Bodhisatta went forth into that renunciation for the purpose of investigating the various sects; however, even after realizing its pointlessness, he did not disrobe.
For Bodhisattas are by nature such that they do not turn back from whatever state they enter; yet, having gone forth, he thought, "Let no one see me."
Then he entered the forest. For this reason he said: "May they not see me, and may I not see them.
*Goṭṭhā* means a herd of cattle. *Paṭṭhitagāvo* means cattle that have gone out.

In that context, "standing at the four corners" refers to one who, while standing right at the edge of the forest, sees that the cattle have departed from the cowherds, and [then] both hands and both knees—
The meaning is: having placed [the dung] on the ground, he approached in this manner, walking on all fours.
"I eat those indeed" means that the dung of old calves is coarse, sapless, and lacking in nourishment;
therefore, avoiding those, he eats his fill of the nutritious dung of young calves who are still growing by drinking milk, and then enters the forest grove once more.
Referring to that, he said: "I indeed ate those. "And as long as mine" means for as long a time as my own urine and excrement remained unexhausted.
The meaning is: "As long as the door-sill continued to function for me, so long did I eat only that.
But as time passed and passed, with his flesh and blood exhausted, the door-sill was cut off.
"I eat the dung of calves. "In the great repulsive food" (*mahāvikaṭabhojana*) means in a large repulsive food; the meaning is "in unnatural food. 157.
"Therein, Sāriputta, there was a terrifying quality in that terrifying forest thicket.
*Tatra* (therein) refers back to the preceding statement. *Sudam* is a particle used merely to fill out the meter. *Sāriputta* is a form of address.
This, however, is the construction of the meaning here: “Therein” refers to what was stated as “a certain terrifying forest thicket.
Regarding that which was called a terrifying forest thicket, it occurs in the state of being terrifying of that terrifying forest thicket;
the meaning is that it occurs in the act of being terrifying. What occurs? This occurs: whoever has not yet abandoned lust... [and so on] ...the hairs of his body stand on end.

Alternatively, *tatra* here is the locative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmi-atthe*). *Su* is a particle, as in such expressions as "What indeed, O venerable recluses and brahmins? (*kiṃ su nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā*).

*Idaṃ* is a term of demonstration that presents the intended meaning as if it were directly perceived before one's eyes. *Sudaṃ* means "this indeed" (*su idaṃ*); the elision of the letter *i* should be understood as occurring due to euphonic combination (*sandhi-vasena*). [The faculties are:
the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*), the female-faculty (*itthindriya*), and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).
It is as in the case of expressions such as *kiṃ sūdhavittaṃ*. Here, however, the construction of the meaning (*atthayojanā*) is as follows:
"In regard to the terrifying nature of that terrifying forest grove, Sāriputta, this occurred. In *bhiṃsanakatasmim*, the meaning is "in the state of being terrifying" (*bhiṃsanakabhāve*).
One should understand that there is the elision of one *t*-sound. Alternatively, the reading is simply *bhiṃsanakattasmiṃ*, meaning "by way of the state of being terrifying" (*bhiṃsanakatāya*).
Although it should have been stated as "iti vā," a change of gender has been made; furthermore, this locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
Therefore, the connection should be understood as follows: "In the state of being terrifying (*bhiṃsanakabhāve*), this occurs in those [places];

on account of the state of being terrifying, by reason of the state of being terrifying, due to the state of being terrifying, this occurs in those [places]. Whosoever, not being free from lust, enters that forest grove—for the most part—
The body hairs quiver; the body hairs quiver exceedingly. Having become like needles and like thorns, they stand with their tips pointing upward.
They do not quiver slightly; rather, they quiver in most beings, but they do not quiver in a few individuals who are exceedingly brave.
"Between the two eighths" means four nights at the end of the month of Māgha and four at the beginning of the month of Phagguṇa;

thus, there are eight nights between the two. "In the open air": during the time of snowfall, the Great Being dwelt in the open air at night, and drops of snow remained upon his pores like pearls strung together; his body appeared as if clothed in white silk.
It is as if it were so. "By day in the forest grove" means that by day, when the contact of the sun's heat has caused the drops of frost to vanish, there might even be breath;
yet this person enters the forest grove just as the sun is rising, and there too the frost melting from the sun's heat falls upon his very body.
"By day I dwell in the open air, by night in the forest grove."
It is said that during the summer season he spent his days in the open air; consequently, streams of sweat poured from his armpits.
While it might have been possible for him to find relief at night, he would enter the forest grove just as the sun was setting.
Then, his body—having absorbed the heat of the day within the forest grove—was scorched like a piece of charcoal thrown into an ash-heap. This is not surprising.
"Extraordinary. "Appeared" means it manifested.
"Heated by the sun" means heated by the heat of the day and by the forest's own heat at night. "Well-cooled" means thoroughly cooled by frost at night and by cold water during the day.
"Terrifying" means causing fear. "Naked" means without clothes; for if there were an undergarment or an upper robe...
He shows that he does not even have "cold or heat that would be too oppressive. "And he did not resort to fire" means he did not even approach a fire.
"Dedicated to seeking" means intent upon, or engaged in, the pursuit of purity. "The sage" (muni): at that time, having identified himself as a sage, he speaks thus.

“Bone fragments” (*chavaṭṭhikāni*) refers to half-burnt bones. “Having spread them out” (*upadhāya*) means having arranged them so that they appear like a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet;
he shows that he makes his bed there in this manner. “Village boys” (*gāmaṇḍalā*) refers to cowherd children.
It is said that they went to the Bodhisatta and asked, “Sumedha, why are you sitting in this place?”
"Tell us! they said. The Bodhisatta sat with his face turned downward and did not speak.
Then, thinking "We will not let him go until he speaks," they surrounded him and spat upon him, letting their saliva fall on his body.
Even so, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Then, saying "You do not speak," they urinated over him, discharging urine upon him. The Bodhisatta—
Even so, he would not speak at all. Then they covered him with dust, saying, "Speak! Speak! But the Bodhisatta still would not speak even thus.
Then, thinking that he was not speaking, they took sticks and thrust them into his ear-cavities.
The Bodhisatta, enduring intense, sharp, and bitter sensations of pain, remained as if dead, thinking, "I shall do nothing to anyone."
It remains as it is. Therefore he said: “Indeed, Sāriputta, I do not recall ever having given rise to an evil thought toward them.
The meaning is: “I have not even given rise to an evil thought toward them. Regarding the phrase “there is dwelling in equanimity” (*upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hotī*):

there is dwelling in equanimity. For “dwelling” itself is expressed here by the word “in dwelling” (*vihārasmim*). And for that very reason, in the passage “this indeed was mine,” [the same logic applies]. “This indeed was mine” (*idaṃsu me*)... “this indeed was mine” (*ayaṃsu me*).
The meaning should be understood in this way. By this method, other similar phrases are also to be understood.
By this, he shows the dwelling in equanimity fulfilled during this ninety-first aeon. With reference to this, he said:
"Attaining happiness, I do not lust; in suffering, I am not dejected."
“I am weighed equally in all circumstances; this is my perfection of equanimity.
The commentary on the purity of performing difficult deeds and so forth is finished.
The commentary on the purity of food.
158. “Purity comes through food”: they hold such a view, thinking that it is possible to become pure by means of certain limited foods such as *kola* (jujube) and the like.
“They say thus” means they speak in this way. “With *kola*” means with jujubes. “*Kola*-water” (*kolodaka*) is a drink made by crushing jujubes.
“*Kola*-preparation” (*kolavikati*) refers to various products derived from jujubes, such as jujube syrup, jujube cakes, and jujube sugar. “This is the limit” (*etaparamo*) means this...
"Etapparamo" means that which has this as its ultimate measure. At that time, near the end of ninety-one aeons, the kola-fruit was not the size of a bilva-fruit or a tāla-fruit;
rather, it was only the size of what is the current measure of a kola-fruit—this is the meaning.
(159) "Adhimattakasimānaṃ" means an extreme state of emaciation. "Āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā" means [joints] like those of an eighty-year-old man, or black joints.

He shows that his limbs and members were like those of an *āsītika* creeper or a black creeper, which wither at the joints while becoming raised and swollen in the middle. "Like the footprint of a lip" means that just as the footprint of a lip is deep in the middle,
so too was it for the Bodhisatta, because when his flesh and blood had withered, he had entered into the interior of the anus.
The lower part is deep in the middle. Then, the place where he sits on the ground becomes elevated in the middle, as if pressed by the point of an arrow.

Regarding "like a string of beads": just as a string of beads made by threading them on a cord has depressions between the beads and elevations at the places where the beads sit, so too the backbone is elevated and depressed.

"In the old hall, the rafters" means the rafters of the dilapidated hall; having detached from the bamboo beams, they fall onto the circular rafters, and having detached from the circular rafters, they fall to the ground.
Thus, one is above and one is below, becoming decayed and broken apart.
But for the Bodhisatta, the rafters were not like this; for when his blood was shed and his flesh withered, [the rafters] fell through the gaps between the rafters.
The hides had sunk down; it was with reference to this that it was said.

"Okkhāyikā" means they have entered down below. It is said that when his blood was cut off and his flesh had withered, the sockets of his eyes remained pressed against the brain, and thus his eyeballs became like that. "Āmakacchinno" means...
If it had been cut while very young, it would indeed wither and shrivel when touched by wind and sun.
"As long as, Sāriputta"— meaning, Sāriputta, as long as my skin on the abdomen was still adhering to my backbone— or, Sāriputta,
as long as I engaged in extremely severe and difficult ascetic practices, [my skin on the abdomen remained adhered] to my backbone.
The connection here should be understood as follows: "I have become stuck.
"I am grasping the very backbone" means I am grasping it together with the skin of the belly. "I am grasping the very skin of the belly" means I am grasping it together with the backbone.
"I fall head-first" means that while he is sitting to relieve himself of excrement and urine, the urine does not come out at all, but the feces—just one [piece]...
Two bones of the collarbone protrude. It produces intense pain;
sweat breaks out from the body, and one falls right there on the ground face down. Therefore he said, "I am falling face down.
"That very body" refers to the body at the end of ninety-one eons. However, in the *Mahāsaccaka Sutta*, it refers to the body of one in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*).
He said, "this very body. "With rotten roots" means that they remain as long as there is flesh or blood;
but in the absence of those, they stick to the hands themselves, like hairs on a piece of hide. Referring to this, he said: "Hairs with rotten roots fall from the body.
"The distinction of noble knowledge and vision" refers to the supramundane path capable of bringing about the state of an Ariya. Of this very...
"By means of noble wisdom" means by not having attained insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*). "This which is noble" refers to that path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) which has been attained.

This is what is meant: just as at present path-wisdom has been attained because insight-wisdom has been attained, so too, because insight-wisdom had not been attained ninety-one aeons ago, I did not attain supramundane path-wisdom.
The Theras who are reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, however, say: "Both the wisdom described as 'this very [wisdom]' and the wisdom described as 'noble' are indeed path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*).
Then those bhikkhus said: "If that is so, venerable sir, since the path has not yet been attained, what is meant by the statement, 'I have not attained the path'?
[The Thera replied: "Friends, although I am unable to explain it, both..."
"But it is indeed path-wisdom," and this alone is appropriate here. For otherwise, the description "those which go" would be inconsistent.
The commentary on the purity of nutriment is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the purity of the cycle of existence, etc.

160. "Purification through saṃsāra": they say that one is purified after wandering through many cycles of existence. "Purification through rebirth": they say that one is purified after being reborn many times.
"Purification through residence": they say that one is purified after dwelling in many places.
In all three cases, "saṃsāra" refers to the process of wandering, while "rebirth" refers to the process of taking birth.

"Rebirth" (*upapatti*). "Abode" (*āvāsa*) refers to the aggregates themselves, so called by way of their habitual dwelling. "By sacrifice" (*yaññena*): they say that people are purified by performing many sacrifices.
"By one anointed on the head" (*muddhāvasittena*): by one who has been consecrated on the head with the threefold kṣatriya coronation.
"By the service of fire" (*aggipāricariyāya*): they say that people are purified by attending to many fires.
161. *Daharo* means young. *Yuvā* means endowed with youth. *Susukāḷakeso* means having very black hair.
By the phrase "endowed with auspicious youth," he shows that the very youth by which one is a youth is indeed auspicious and well-attained.
*Paṭhamena vayasā* (by the first stage of life): the first stage of life consists of thirty-three years.

"Endowed with that" is the meaning; "by means of the lucidity of wisdom" (*paññāveyyattiyena*) means by way of the state of lucidity of wisdom. "Aged" (*jiṇṇo*) means worn out by old age. "Advanced in years" (*vuddho*) means one whose limbs and members have become firm through growth.
"Elderly" (*mahallako*) means advanced in birth. "One who has reached a long journey" (*addhagato*) means one who has traversed much of the path and passed a long period of time.
"One who has arrived at the final stage" (*vayo anuppatto*) refers to the third division of a hundred-year lifespan, the final stage of life.
He has arrived. "My age has reached eighty"—it is said that the Blessed One spoke this sutta in the year of his Parinibbāna;

therefore, he spoke thus. "Supreme" (*paramāya*) means the highest. Regarding the terms beginning with "mindfulness" (*sati*), mindfulness is the capacity to grasp even a hundred words or a thousand words while they are being spoken.
That very same capacity for retention and binding [the material] is called "understanding" (*gati*).
"Name. Thus, the energy capable of reciting what has been grasped and retained is called *dhiti* (fortitude).
The capacity to discern its meaning and cause is called *paññā-veyyattiyaṃ* (clarity of wisdom).
"A firm-bowed archer" refers to a marksman standing having taken up a strong bow; a "strong bow" is one with a strength of two thousand [units].

It is said that "the strength of two thousand" refers to that which, when loaded and suspended by a bowstring, releases its weight—such as iron balls and so forth—from the ground once it has been raised to the height of a knee while holding the handle.
"Trained" means one who has mastered a craft after ten or twelve years in a teacher’s household.
"Skilled in hand" means one who merely learns the craft; [whereas] "skilled in hand" [in the other sense] means...
This one, however, is one who has already performed the task and attained mastery. "One who has practiced" means one who has demonstrated his skill in royal households and similar places.
"With a light arrow" means with a bow that has been made very light by hollowing out the interior, filling it with cotton and the like, and undergoing the treatment of lacquering.
For such a bow, while one capable of reaching a single ox [distance] reaches two ox-lengths, one capable of reaching eight ox-lengths reaches sixteen ox-lengths.
He goes. "Without difficulty" means without suffering. "He would pass over" means he would transcend.
Thus, one who possesses preeminent mindfulness is like that archer who quickly passes over the shadow of a span and four finger-breadths;
in the same way, such a person is able to learn, master, recite, and investigate the meanings of even a hundred or a thousand words.
"Capable" is the meaning. "Except for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting": for eating, drinking, and so forth must be done by the Blessed One as well as by the bhikkhus;
therefore, he indicates that these should be excluded only for the duration of their performance.
"Unexhausted indeed" means precisely unspent. For if one bhikkhu asks about the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), [the others remain capable].
One was contemplating feelings, another was contemplating the mind, and another was contemplating mental phenomena.
Thinking, "I will ask him who has been asked," no one looked toward another. Even so, their turn became apparent.
But in the case of the Buddhas, no such turn is apparent; even before the shadow has passed the length of a span and four finger-breadths, the Blessed One [already knows].
He teaches body-contemplation in fourteen ways, feeling-contemplation in nine ways, mind-contemplation in sixteen ways, and phenomena-contemplation in five ways. Let these four stand aside for now;
for there are others regarding the four right efforts, others regarding the bases of psychic power, others regarding the five faculties, and others regarding the five powers.
If others were to ask questions concerning the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eight factors of the path, the Blessed One would explain them as well.
Let alone these eight; if thirty-seven other people were to ask questions concerning the requisites of enlightenment, the Blessed One would explain those as well at that very moment.
Why? Because for as long as worldly people speak even a single word.
The Elder Ānanda spoke eight phrases; yet while the Elder Ānanda was speaking only one phrase, the Blessed One spoke sixteen.
Why? Because the Blessed One’s tongue is soft, his lips are well-kissed, his speech is unslurred, and his mastery over the life-continuum is light.
Therefore he said: “Sāriputta, it is not even exhausted for him...”
“Such is the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma.
In this context, “the teaching of the Dhamma” refers to the establishment of the lineage (the scriptures). “The phrasing of the words of the Dhamma” refers to the phrasing of the words in the Pāḷi;
it is the syllable that makes manifest the meaning of each respective passage. “The response to a question” is the answering of a question. By means of this, what [is attained]?
Does he demonstrate this? When the Tathāgata was formerly in his youth, he was able to speak a word by combining syllables;

he was able to speak a verse by combining words; and he was able to explain the meaning of a verse composed of four, eight, or sixteen syllables per line. But now, in his old age, [he cannot even speak] syllables...
There is no such thing as being unable to speak by combining words into a phrase, or phrases into a verse, or the meaning of a verse;
this shows that all of this remains entirely unexhausted for the Tathāgata, both in his youth and in his old age.
As for the phrase "even on a couch," this was said as a mere supposition for the purpose of illustrating the power of the Buddha.
However, there is no such thing as carrying the One Possessing the Ten Powers (Dasabala) on a couch through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.

For Tathāgatas pass away into final Nibbāna only during the fifth portion of their lifespan, while they are not yet overcome by infirmity and the like, before the golden-hued body has reached discoloration, and while they are still beloved and pleasing to gods and humans.
162. *Nāgasamāla* was the name of that elder. Indeed, within twenty years of the First Enlightenment, just like the elders Upavāna, Nāgita, and Meghiya, he too became an attendant to the Blessed One.

"Fanning" means causing the Blessed One’s physical comfort to arise by means of the very gentle breeze from a palm-leaf fan. "He said this" refers to [the elder] having heard the entire sutta from the Blessed One.
Having become inspired by his encounter with the one who had previously practiced austerities, he spoke these words beginning with, "It is wonderful, venerable sir.

In this context, *acchariya* means that which is worthy of snapping the fingers (in wonder). *Abbhuta* means that which has become what was never before. By both terms, he expresses his own amazement.
"What is the name of this, venerable sir?"—this implies: "Truly, this discourse on the Dhamma is excellent."
He spoke with the intention of having the Blessed One take his name after requesting it from him. Then the Blessed One, while taking his name, said:
"Therefore, indeed, you... and so forth. The meaning of this is:

because your body hairs stood on end upon hearing this discourse, therefore, Nāgasamāla, you should remember this Dhamma exposition as "The Discourse that Causes Body Hairs to Stand on End" (Lomahaṃsana Pariyāya).
The commentary on the "Purification of Saṃsāra," etc., is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
3. Commentary on the Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta 163.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta. In that regard, according to the method of the Vinaya, three persons are called “a number,” and beyond that, it is the Saṅgha.
According to the method of the Suttanta, only three [persons] constitute a group; beyond that, it is the Saṅgha.
"Many" (sambahula) is what is said here. In this context, according to the method of the Suttas, they should be understood as "many.

"They entered for alms" means they had entered; however, they had not yet actually entered at that moment. Nevertheless, because they had set out with the intention, "We shall enter," they are said to have "entered.
This is just as a man who has set out with the thought, "I will go to the village," is asked, "Where is so-and-so? even though he has not yet reached that village.
When it is said, "he has gone to the village," it is spoken thus. "The park of the wanderers" refers to a park belonging to wanderers of other sects located not far from Jetavana;
it was with reference to that that they spoke thus. "The ascetic, friends," means:
"Friends, your teacher, the ascetic Gotama. "The full understanding of sensual pleasures" means he proclaims their abandoning and transcendence.
The same method applies to form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
In that regard, the non-Buddhist teachers, knowing their own doctrines, would describe the full understanding (*pariññā*) of sensual desires while speaking of the first *jhāna*;
they would describe the full understanding of forms while speaking of the formless existence (*arūpabhava*); and they would describe the full understanding of feelings.
They speak of non-percipient existence; yet they do not even know, "This is the first jhāna, this is fine-material existence, this is immaterial existence.
Being unable to define these things, they merely say, "We define, we define.
The Tathāgata defines the full understanding of sensual desires by means of the non-returner path, and the full understanding of form and feeling by means of the arahant path. Thus they...
"Even though there are great distinctions [between us], friends, what distinction is there for us here?"—this is what they said.

In that context, "here" (*idha*) means in this presentation; or, regarding the teaching of the Dhamma, it refers to "the teaching of the Dhamma," namely, our teaching of the Dhamma compared with the teaching of the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama, or our teaching of the Dhamma compared with his.
They say: "Let a distinction be stated regarding the Dhamma-teaching of the ascetic Gotama; what indeed is its name?

This same method applies to the second phrase as well. Thus, like gold broken in the middle, they placed their own mere assertions of tenets on an equal footing with the Teaching. "They did not rejoice" means: "It is even so."
They did not accept it; they did not reject it means they did not refuse it by saying, "This is not so. Why?

It is said that those known as *tīrthikas* are like the blind; they neither rejoiced in [the teaching], thinking, "They might speak whether knowing it or not," nor did they reject it, because by the word "thorough knowledge" (*pariññā*), there was a slight scent of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Or else, those inhabitants of the countryside were [concerned] with their own and others' doctrines...
They did not even consider both [possibilities], thinking, "Are they not well-skilled?
(165). "They will not be able to master it" means they will not be able to speak after having mastered it.
"And further distress" means that because they do not master it, they will fall into even greater suffering. For those who are unable to speak after having mastered it...
For thus suffering arises. Regarding the phrase "just as that, monks, in what is not one's domain": here, *yathā* is a word expressing reason, and *taṃ* is merely a particle.
The meaning is: because the question was asked concerning what is not one's domain. "Together with the devas" means *sadevake*, together with the devas.
The same method applies to [the phrases] "together with Māras," and so forth. Thus, having included three bases in the world, [he says] "two classes of beings."

By "even with these five," he demonstrates that within this world consisting of the realms of beings, including the worlds of devas and so forth, one does not see such a person—whether a deva or a human.

"Or having heard from here" means: having heard from my teaching, even one who is not a Tathāgata and not a disciple of a Tathāgata might please or satisfy [the Tathāgata]. He shows that there is no other way to please him.
166. Now, demonstrating how he gratified their minds by answering those questions, he said, "And who, monks...
and so forth. "Strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇā*): they are called *kāmā* in the sense of being objects of desire; they are called *guṇā* in the sense of being fetters.

For in the passage, "Monks, I allow a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) made of unwashed cloth," the word *guṇa* has the sense of a layer (*paṭala*). [As it is said: "Times pass away, they carry one along..."
In the passage, “The nights, the qualities of youth, pass away in succession,” the meaning of *guṇa* is that of a heap (*rāsa*).
In the passage, “A hundredfold merit is to be expected from a gift,” the meaning of *guṇa* is that of benefit (*ānisaṃsa*). In the passage, “One should make an end with the end-string;
there are many flower-strings,” the meaning of *guṇa* is that of binding (*bandhana*). Here too, this very same sense is intended; therefore it was said: “in the sense of binding.”
“Qualities. “Cognizable by the eye” means they are to be seen by visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).

By this same method, the meaning should be understood for those cognizable by the ear and so forth. “Desirable” means whether they have been sought after or not, they are objects that are desirable; this is the meaning. “Pleasant” means lovely. “Agreeable” means increasing the mind’s satisfaction.
“Of a dear nature” means born of what is dear. “Connected with sensual desire” refers to the object.
It is associated with desire that arises having performed [the action]. "Rajanīyā" means "objects of passion"; the meaning is: things that serve as the cause for the arising of lust. 167.
Regarding the passage beginning "If by finger-calculation," etc.: "muddā" refers to hand-gestures (hand-seals) formed by placing signs upon the finger joints.
"Gaṇanā" refers to counting without gaps. "Saṅkhānaṃ" refers to calculating by summing up. By means of this, one observes the field and thinks, "In this place there will be this much rice."
Having looked at a tree, they know, "There will be this many fruits here"; having looked at the sky, they know, "There will be this many birds in the sky.
*Kasī* means agricultural work. *Vaṇijjā* means trade, such as trading on foot or by land. *Gorakkha* means [the tending of] one's own...
Or, having guarded the cattle of others, one makes a living by the trade of the five products of the cow.
"Archery" refers to the service of attending [the king] while taking up weapons. "Royal service" means attending [the king] after performing royal duties with weapons.
"Any other craft" refers to the remaining crafts such as elephant-riding, horsemanship, and so forth. "Placing cold before him" is like [placing] a target.
"In front of cold water" means being afflicted by the cold. The same method applies to heat as well.
Regarding "gadflies and so forth": *daṃsa* refers to tawny flies; *makasa* refers to all kinds of flies; *sarīsapa* refers to whatever creatures move by crawling.
"Being distressed" means being troubled, being struck. "Dying" means passing away. "This, monks," [means] O monks.

This refers to the affliction of cold and other such conditions that arises from making one’s livelihood through manual labor and the like. "The danger in sensual pleasures" means the calamity within sensual pleasures;
the sense is that it is an affliction (*upassagga*). "Visible here and now" means directly perceptible, to be seen by oneself.

"Mass of suffering" means a heap of suffering. Regarding the phrase "with sensual pleasures as cause," and so forth: in the sense of being a condition, sensual pleasures are its cause, thus it is "sensual-pleasure-cause" (*kāmahetu*). In the sense of being a root, sensual pleasures...
"Of which desire is this the source? means it has desire as its source (*kāmanidāna*). It is stated as "source of desire" (*kāmanidāna*) by means of a change in grammatical gender.

"Of which desires is this the basis? means it has desires as its basis (*kāmādhikaraṇa*) in the sense of being the cause; it is stated as "basis of desire" (*kāmādhikaraṇa*) by means of that same change in gender.
"Precisely because of desires" is a restrictive statement; the meaning is that it arises only with desire as its condition (*kāmapaccayā*).
"Exerting himself" means exerting oneself with the energy that initiates one's livelihood. "Striving" means joining that energy together from before to after.
"Making an effort" means applying exertion, endeavor, and practice. "They do not succeed" means they do not come to fruition;
they do not reach the hand. "He grieves" means he grieves with the powerful sorrow arisen in his mind.
"Is distressed" means he is distressed by the suffering arisen in the body. "Laments" means he laments with speech.
"Beating his breast" means having struck his chest. "Wails" means he weeps. "Falls into delusion" means he becomes utterly bewildered, as if unconscious.
"In vain" means empty. "Fruitless" means without result. "On account of protection" means for the sake of guarding. "What indeed? means "by what means?"
By means of a skillful method (*upāya*). "Whatever wealth was mine" refers to whatever wealth I had produced by performing labor such as plowing and so forth.
"That too is not ours" means that even that is now no longer ours.
Furthermore, monks, by showing the cause through the passage beginning with "for the sake of sensual pleasures," he illuminates the danger (*ādīnava*).
In this context, "on account of sensual pleasures" (*kāmahetu*) means that even kings dispute with other kings because of sensual pleasures.
"With sensual pleasures as the cause" (*kāmanidāna*) is a neuter abstract noun; the meaning is that they dispute having made sensual pleasures the cause.

"On account of sensual pleasures as the legal issue" (*kāmādhikaraṇa*) is likewise a neuter abstract noun; the meaning is that they dispute having made sensual pleasures the legal issue. "Precisely on account of sensual pleasures" (*kāmānameva hetu*) refers to [disputes over] villages, market towns, cities, positions of army commander, chaplain, and other such offices.
The meaning is that they dispute for the very sake of sensual pleasures. "They attack" means they strike. "Sword and shield" refers to both swords and shields, such as those made of wood or leather.
"Having equipped themselves with bows and quivers" means having taken up their bows and fastened their quivers of arrows.
"Arrayed on both sides" means formed into two opposing masses. "They charge" means they enter. "Into arrows" means into shafts. "Flashing like lightning" means...
While they were turning over. "Therein" means in that battle.
And here, "addāvalepanā upakāriyo" refers to the people who, having built the foundations of the rampart with bricks in the shape of a horse's hoof, plastered them above with lime.
Foundations of ramparts constructed in this manner are called *upakāriyo*. With those [foundations] being moistened...

Being drenched with *kalala* (mud), they are called "smeared with mire. "They leap forward" means that even though they are being pierced from below by sharp iron spikes and the like, and even though they are unable to climb due to the slippery nature of the rampart, they nevertheless run right up toward it.
"With dung" means with boiled cow-dung. "With a hundred-fold edge" means with a hundred teeth; having fashioned it in the shape of eight teeth, [it serves as] the city gate.
Thinking, “We shall break [the wall] and enter,” they arrive and, standing at the upper door, cut his binding cords and crush him with that very mass [of earth]. 169.
“They also break into a breach” means they break into the breach of a house. “A plundering” means having struck the village, a great looting.
They do so. "Living as a single householder" means that even fifty or sixty people surround them, seize them by their lives, and force them to bring [the goods].
"Standing on the path" means they perform the work of highway robbery.
"With half-staves" means with clubs used for striking, or staves made by cutting a four-cubit staff in two. "The Bilangathālī" means...
The "sour-gruel skull" torture: while performing this, they split open the skull, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and cast it therein;
by this, the brain matter boils and overflows upward. The "conch-shell-headed" torture:
while performing this conch-shell-headed mutilation, they [cut] along the boundaries of the upper lip, both ears, the crown of the head, and the throat.
Having cut the skin and gathered all the hair together into a single knot, they wrap it with a stick and pull;
the skin comes out along with the hair. Then, having rubbed the skull with coarse gravel while washing it, they make it the color of a conch shell.
"Rāhu’s mouth" refers to the torture of Rāhu’s mouth; those performing it force open the mouth with a spike and [insert it] inside the mouth.
They light lamps. Or, starting from the ears and the crown of the head, they bore out the mouth with a chisel. Blood flows out and fills the mouth.
"A garland of fire" means they wrap the entire body in oil-soaked rags and set it on fire.
"Hand-lamp" means they wrap the hands in oil-soaked rags and light them like a lamp. "Eraka-vatti" refers to the punishment of being whirled around on an eraka plant.
While performing that [punishment], they carve it from the neck down along the leather straps and fix it upon the ankles.
Then, having bound him with ropes, they drag him. He falls down, repeatedly stepping upon his own leather straps.
"The bark-garment punishment" (*cīrakavāsika*) refers to the penal labor of wearing bark garments; while performing that, they likewise carve it along the leather straps and fix it upon the waist.
Starting from the waist, they cut [the skin] and place it upon the ankles.
Thus, the lower part of the body appears as if covered by a garment of strips of cloth. "The Eneyyaka" refers to the Eneyyaka torture.
While performing this, they fix iron rings on both elbows and knees and hammer iron spikes into them. He stands upon the ground supported by those four iron spikes.
Then, surrounding him, they set fire to him. This very same account is also stated in the passage that begins, "Just as the deer-hunter Jotipariggaḥ.
From time to time, they remove the stakes and leave him standing on his four bone-tips alone.
There is no torture like this.
*Baḷisamaṃsika*: Having struck them with fish-hooks from both sides, they tear away the skin, flesh, and sinews. *Kahāpaṇika*:
They pound their entire bodies with sharp axes, starting from the head, shaving them down piece by piece the size of a kahāpaṇa coin.
*Khārāpatacchika*: Having struck the body here and there with weapons, they rub it with lye using brushes.
They rub them together. The skin and flesh fall away and flow off, leaving only a skeleton standing there. "The revolving bar":
having made the person lie on one side, they drive an iron spike through the ear-holes until it is fixed into the earth;
then, seizing him by the feet, they spin him around. "The straw mat": a skilled executioner strips away the outer skin and flesh.
Jackals break the bones with their teeth, seize them by the hair, and toss them up;
there remains only a heap of flesh, which they then take away, wrapping it entirely in the hair. Or, having made it like a bundle of straw, they coil it around.
"By dogs" means that for several days they provide no food, and then have the hungry dogs devour it; in a mere moment, they turn it into nothing but a skeleton of bones.
They perform [it]. "Belonging to the future life" (*samparāyika*) means that its result (*vipāka*) occurs in the future, that is, in the second existence.
170. "The removal of desire and lust" (*chandārāgavinaya*) and "the abandoning of desire and lust" (*chandārāgappahāna*) refer to *nibbāna*.

For it is by coming to *nibbāna* that desire and lust for sense-pleasures are both removed and abandoned; therefore, *nibbāna* is called the removal of desire and lust and the abandoning of desire and lust.

It has been said: "They will fully understand sensual pleasures by themselves" means that they themselves will fully understand those sensual pleasures through the three types of full understanding (*pariññā*).

"For the sake of suchness" (*tathattāya*) means for the state of being thus. "One who has practiced accordingly" (*yathāpaṭipanno*) refers to one who has practiced by means of a particular way of practice (*paṭipadā*).
171. "A daughter of a Kṣatriya," and so forth, refers to one who has taken rebirth through extensive and abundant wholesome karma, [possessing] garments, ornaments, and the like.
This was said to show that she was reborn in a place where she would find a husband. "About fifteen years of age" means she was at the stage of fifteen years.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Why does he include the mention of her age?

It is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of her physical beauty; for even in the case of a woman born into a destitute family, at this time her sense-base of color (vaṇṇāyatana) gradually becomes more radiant. [As for] men...
However, it becomes clear at the age of twenty or twenty-five. By the words "not too tall" and so forth, he illustrates the perfection of the body as being free from the six defects.
"Color-appearance" (*vaṇṇanibhā*) means simply color.
"Worn out" (*jiṇṇa*) means worn out by old age. "Crooked like a rafter" (*gopānasivaṅka*) means crooked like a rafter. "Bent" (*bhogga*) means broken; by this, his...
This illuminates the very state of crookedness. "Devoted to punishment" means having punishment as one's resort, having punishment as one's companion.
"Trembling" means shaking. "Afflicted" means afflicted by old age. "With broken teeth" means having teeth broken by the state of being aged.
"With grey hair" means having white hair. "Shorn" means bald, like one whose hair has been plucked out. "Bald-headed" means having a large bald head.

*Valīmantam*: one whose skin has become wrinkled. *Tilakāhatagattam*: one whose body is covered with white and black moles. *Ābādhikam*: one who is afflicted by disease. *Dukkhitan*: one who has fallen into suffering.
*Bāḷhagilānam*: one who is severely ill. *Sivathikāya chaḍḍitam*:

one cast away in a charnel ground, that is, thrown into a fresh cemetery. The rest here is exactly as stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*. Here too, it is Nibbāna alone that is the removal of desire and lust.
173. “At that time, neither for one’s own affliction”: at that time, one does not intend even for the sake of suffering for oneself.

“Only non-affliction”: only that which is free from suffering. 174. “Monks, because feeling is impermanent”: monks, since feeling is impermanent, therefore this very aspect of impermanence and so forth is the danger (ādīnava) of feeling; the escape (nissaraṇa) is exactly as previously stated.
[From] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Mahā-dukkhakkhandha-sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Cūḷa-dukkhakkhandha-sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷa-dukkhakkhandha-sutta. Therein, "among the Sakyans" means in the country named after them.
For that district came to be known as "Sakya" precisely because it was the dwelling place of the Sakyan princes.
The origin of the Sakyans, however, is recounted in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. "In Kapilavatthu" refers to the city of that name;
for it is called Kapilavatthu because it was built on the site where the seer Kapila resided, and [the Buddha] made that his alms-resort village. "In the Nigrodha Monastery."

The Sakyan named Nigrodha, when the Blessed One arrived at Kapilavatthu on the occasion of a family gathering, had a dwelling constructed in his own park and offered it to the Blessed One; the meaning is that [the Blessed One] dwelt there.
Mahānāma was the brother of the Elder Anuruddha and the son of the Blessed One’s younger paternal uncle—namely, Suddhodana, Sukkodana, Sakkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana.
These five persons were brothers. The lady named Amitā was their sister. Elder Tissa was her son.
