The Tathāgata and Elder Nanda were the sons of Suddhodana; Mahānāma and Elder Anuruddha were the sons of Sukkodana.

Elder Ānanda was the son of Amitodana; he was the younger brother of the Blessed One. Mahānāma was the elder [of the two] and was a noble disciple who had attained the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmī).
"Long night" means: he shows that he has known this for a long time, starting from the moment the fruit of the once-returner arose within him.
"States of greed" means states characterized by greed; he speaks specifically with reference to greed in its various forms. The same method applies to the other two as well.
"They remain having exhausted [them]" means they remain after having been consumed. For this is what is called "exhaustion."

In the passage, “Having exhausted the entire elephant force, the entire cavalry, the entire chariot force, and the entire infantry force, he might release him while still alive,” it occurs in the sense of grasping (*gahaṇa*).

In the passage, “Bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures,” it occurs in the sense of wearing away (*khepana*). Here too, it is in the sense of wearing away.
This is the intended meaning. Therefore it was said: “‘Having exhausted’ means having consumed.
When he asks, “By what have even states of greed at times overwhelmed my mind?,” he is asking by what, at certain times, even states of greed remain having seized his mind.
It is said that this king [thought], “By the path of once-returning, greed, hatred, and delusion are eliminated without remainder...”

He perceives: "It is being abandoned. He also knows: "I have that which has not been abandoned. Based on what has not been abandoned, he even perceives that what has been abandoned has turned back again.
Does such doubt arise in a noble disciple? Yes, it does. Why? Because of a lack of skill regarding designations (*paṇṇatti*).
[This refers to] the designation: "This defilement is to be abandoned by this specific path."...
For even a noble disciple who is unskilled in the designations [of the path] thinks thus: "Does he have no reviewing knowledge? He does have it;
however, it is not complete for everyone. For one reviews only the defilements abandoned; another, only the remaining defilements;
another, only the Path; another, only the Fruit; and another, only Nibbāna. Now, among these—
It is not permissible for one to fail to obtain at least one or two of the five types of reflection.
Thus, for one whose reflection is incomplete, this occurs precisely because of a lack of proficiency in the designation of those defilements that are to be abandoned by the Path. 176.
"That very same thing is yours" means that greed, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned within your continuum, yet you perceive them as abandoned.
"Ahosī" indicates that it has been. "So ca hi te" means "that very nature of greed, hatred, and delusion belonging to you. "Kāme" refers to the two kinds of sensual pleasures.
"Na paribhuñjeyyāsī" shows that you should not enjoy them, but rather should go forth into homelessness just as we have.
(177) "Appassādā" means having little gratification. "Bahudukkhā" means that there is only suffering here, both pertaining to the present life and to future lives.
"Much. "Many afflictions": here, the defilement of affliction (*upāyāsa-kilesa*) pertaining both to the present life and to future lives is indeed much.

"Disadvantage" (*ādīnava*): this refers to the calamity (*upaddava*) pertaining both to the present life and to future lives. "In this regard, moreover": among these sensual pleasures, this disadvantage alone is abundant.
But the gratification (*assāda*), by comparison to the Himalayas, is as small as a mustard seed—slight and trifling. "Even so, Mahānāma..."
"Mahānāma, it is even so for the noble disciple. "Yathābhūtaṃ" means according to its true nature.

This shows that it is well-seen by means of right method, reason, and wisdom (*paññā*). In this context, "by wisdom" means by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), which is to say, by the knowledge of the two lower paths.
"So ca" refers to that very noble disciple who has seen the danger in sensual desires by means of those two paths. By the term "pītisukhaṃ" (joy and happiness)...

He shows two jhānas accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*). "Or something else more peaceful than that" means another state more peaceful than those two jhānas, namely the two higher jhānas and the two paths.

"He does not yet turn back toward sense pleasures" means that although that noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) has stood having penetrated the two paths, he still does not turn away from sense pleasures because he has not yet attained the higher jhānas or the paths.
One does not yet become free from preoccupation with sensual desires; for one who is preoccupied, there is no lack of mental engagement. One remains preoccupied and indeed full of mental effort. Why?
Because of the absence of abandonment by suppression through the four jhānas and the absence of abandonment by eradication through the two paths.
"Even for me" means not only for you, but also for me. "Prior to enlightenment" means prior to the enlightenment of the Path.
"Even earlier. "It was well-seen by wisdom": here, the wisdom of abandoning (*pajahana-paññā*) is intended.
"They did not attain rapture and bliss": they did not obtain the two jhānas accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*). "Or anything more peaceful than that":
here, the two higher jhānas and the four paths (*magga*) are intended. "I recognized": I understood.
179. "Mahānāma, for what reason was this discourse begun with the words 'On one occasion'? This is a separate connection (*pāṭiyekko anusandhi*).

Below, the gratification (*assāda*) and the danger (*ādīnava*) of sensual pleasures were explained, but the escape (*nissaraṇa*) was not explained; it is to explain that which this teaching has been begun.
For the pursuit of sensual pleasure is one extreme, and the pursuit of self-mortification is the other; [this teaching is begun] because of these two extremes.
This teaching was also commenced in order to show the entire dispensation under the heading of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), which is my own instruction.
Regarding "on Mount Vulture Peak" (Gijjhakūṭa): that mountain has a peak resembling a vulture, and for that reason it is called Gijjhakūṭa;
or else, because vultures dwell upon its peaks, it is called Gijjhakūṭa. Regarding "at the side of Isigili":
On the slope of Mount Isigili. "On the Black Rock" means on a rock slab of black color.
"They are standers-up" means they remain standing upright, not sitting. "Self-inflicted" means produced by their own exertion through such practices as standing upright.
"The Nigaṇṭha, friends," [they said], and being unable to state another reason, they threw it upon the Nigaṇṭha.
"Omniscient and all-seeing": this shows that our Teacher knows and sees everything—past, future, and present.

"He claims complete knowledge and vision": our Teacher, knowing the Dhamma without exception, claims a knowledge and vision that is called "complete"; and in making this claim, he claims it in this way:
“Whether walking or standing... [as above] ...is established before me. In this context, *satataṃ* means constantly; *samitaṃ* is a synonym for the same.

“What do you know, friends Nigaṇṭhas, as to how much suffering has been exhausted?”—this was said by the Blessed One because a person knows what they have done. For example, having taken a loan of twenty kahāpaṇas and having paid ten...
He knows, "Ten have been given to me; ten remain. Having given those as well, he knows, "All has been given.
Having harvested a third part of the field, he knows, "One part has been harvested; two remain.
Then, having harvested one more, he knows, "Two have been harvested; one remains. When that too has been harvested, he knows, "It is all finished."
Thus, he shows that one should know what has been done and what remains to be done in all matters, and that you too should understand it in the same way.

By the phrase "the abandoning of unwholesome states," he asks whether there exists in your teaching a Nigaṇṭha— one who, having abandoned the unwholesome and developed the wholesome, has reached the state of purity.
"‘Evaṃ sante’ means when there is such a state of yours as not knowing this. ‘Luddā’ means those of cruel conduct.

‘Lohitapāṇī’ means those whose hands are smeared with blood while depriving living beings of their lives; for even one who kills a living being but whose hand is not smeared with blood is still called ‘lohitapāṇī.
‘Kurūrakammantā’ means those of harsh deeds. Regarding ‘mātari’..."
[They are] those who have committed offenses against their father, or against righteous recluses, brahmins, and so forth; or those such as hunters who perform cruel deeds.
"Indeed, friend Gotama," [they said]—the Nigaṇṭhas began this thinking, "This man points out a fault in our doctrine;
let us also bring a charge against him. Its meaning is: "Friend Gotama, just as you [wear] fine robes..."
"Carrying fine rice and meat, eating them, and dwelling in a fragrant chamber as beautiful as a celestial mansion, you attain happiness through happiness;

but happiness is not to be attained in such a way. Rather, just as we experience various kinds of suffering through such practices as the 'crouching exertion' (ukkuṭikappadhāna), so too must happiness be attained through suffering. [Sukhena]
"And they were both" (*ca hāvu so*)—this means that if happiness were to be attained through happiness, [the Buddha] would have said, "The King would attain it.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that [it is not so]. In that context, *Māgadha* means the lord of the kingdom of Magadha;

*Seniya* is his personal name; *Bimbī* is the name of his physical form (*attabhāva*). He was the very essence of that [form], beautiful to behold, pleasing, and perfected in the excellence of his physical presence.

"Bimbisāra" is what he is called. Regarding the phrase "one who dwells in happiness," these Nigaṇṭhas say this with reference to the King’s enjoyment of prosperity together with three kinds of theatrical performances in his three palaces. "Addhā" means "certainly.

"Sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā" means having acted impulsively, without reflection—just as one who is lustful acts through the power of lust, or one who is corrupt through the power of hatred, or one who is deluded.
He speaks under the influence of delusion; thus he shows that such speech was uttered.
In this context, "I will question you" means I will ask about that matter. "In such a way as may be acceptable to you" means in a manner that would be pleasing to you.
"It is possible" means it can be done. "Without moving" means without wavering. "Experiencing absolute happiness" means experiencing uninterrupted happiness. "I..."
“Friend, I am able... [as before] ...experiencing absolute happiness”—this he said, demonstrating the bliss of his own attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
And here, for the purpose of establishing the discussion, the questions were posed starting from seven days during the King’s turn;
for if it had been stated that he was not able for seven days and nights, it would have been possible to ask about six, five, or four days of happiness.
However, when "seven" is stated for the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāra), it is not surprising that "six," "five," and "four" are subsequently mentioned;
therefore, the teaching was given starting from one. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
[End of] the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Anumāna Sutta: 181.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Anumāna Sutta. Therein, "among the Bhaggas" means in the country named after them; this is the literal meaning of the word.
In this context, it should be understood according to what has been stated. "At Susumāragira" means in the city of that name.
It is said that on the day the site for that city was being demarcated, a crocodile (*suṃsumāra*) made a sound and let out a cry in a nearby lake;
thus, when the city was completed, they gave it the name "Crocodile's Cry" (*Suṃsumāragira*). "At Bhesakaḷāvana" [is explained as follows].
In the forest named Bhesakaḷā (some read the text as "Bhesagaḷāvana"). It was called Migadāya because that forest arose in a place where safety had been granted to deer and birds;
therefore, it is called Migadāya. "He invites" means he asks for their wishes.
"Let them speak" means let them speak by way of advice and instruction; the sense is, "let them instruct."
"I am to be spoken to" means I am to be addressed by you, instructed, and exhorted. "And he is difficult to speak to" means he must be addressed with difficulty;

once addressed, he does not endure it. "By means of the qualities that make one difficult to speak to" refers to the sixteen qualities mentioned below that cause one to be difficult to address. "One who does not receive instruction respectfully" refers to one who, when being spoken to by you...
"Why do you speak to me? I know for myself what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and what is beneficial and what is harmful," he says.
He does not accept this instruction favorably; he accepts it perversely. Therefore, he is called "one who takes [instruction] unfavorably" (*appadakkhiṇaggāhī*).
"Of evil desires" means of base, non-existent, and unrighteous aspirations. "He opposes" means he is antagonistic.
"To stand in opposition" means to disparage, thinking: "What indeed is the use of what you, a fool and an incompetent person, have to say?
Do you really think that even you should be the one to speak? In this way, he provokes. "To counter-charge" means to charge back, saying:
"You too have fallen into the offense named so-and-so; first, then, go and make amends for that. Thus he charges him in return.
“He evades one thing with another” means that by means of another reason or statement, he conceals another reason or statement.
When told, “You have committed an offense,” he says, “Who has committed it? What has been committed? In what has one committed? Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying?
Or, when told, “Have you seen anything of this kind? he closes his ear, saying, “I did not hear it.”

Or he brings it near. How does he divert the matter externally? When asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense?", he says, "I have gone to Pāṭaliputta. When told again, "We do not ask about your going to Pāṭaliputta;
we ask about the offense," he says, "From there I went to the royal palace," or "I went to the royal palace or to the house of a brahmin; I have fallen into an offense."
How does one who says things such as, "I have obtained pork there," distract externally?
Regarding the "apadāna" (precedent): it is his own conduct. It is "not consistent" when someone asks, "Friend, where do you live?
On whose authority do you live? or regarding what he says, "I saw this person committing an offense. At that time, you...

When questioned about his conduct in such a manner as, "What are you doing?", "What is this person doing?", "Where are you staying?", or "Where is that person going?", he is unable to provide a coherent account after having reflected. 183.

Regarding the phrase "In this regard, friend": "friend," refers to those sixteen qualities. "One should thus infer oneself by means of oneself" means that one should thus infer, weigh, and examine oneself by means of oneself.

184. *Paccavekkhitabbaṃ* means it should be reviewed. *Ahorattānusikkhinā* means by one training day and night; the meaning is that by one training in wholesome states both by night and by day, only joy and gladness should be produced.
*Acche vā udakapatte* means in a clear water-vessel. *Mukhanimittaṃ* means the reflection of the face.
*Rajo* means adventitious dust. *Aṅgaṇaṃ* means a mole or a pimple born thereon. All these are evil and unwholesome.

"Having abandoned unwholesome states": by this, he speaks of the abandoning of everything. How so? For when one generates the reflection, "So many unwholesome states are not suitable for one who has gone forth," the abandoning through reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānapahāna*) is spoken of.
When one, having made virtue the foundation and having begun the preliminary work on the *kasiṇas*, produces the eight attainments, there is the abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).

It has been explained thus: for one who increases insight by making meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) its proximate cause, "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*) is explained;

for one who, having increased insight, develops the path (*magga*), "abandonment by eradication" (*samucchedappahāna*) is explained; when the fruit (*phala*) is reached, "abandonment by subsiding" (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*) [is explained];
and when Nibbāna is reached, "abandonment as escape" (*nissaraṇappahāna*) is explained. In this way, all forms of abandonment are indeed explained in this sutta.
The ancients say that this discourse is indeed called the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*. This should be reviewed three times a day.
Having entered one's dwelling place early in the morning and sat down, one should review: "Do these so many defilements exist in me, or do they not?
If one sees that they do exist, [one should strive] for their abandonment.
One should strive [to see them]. If one does not see them, one should be satisfied, thinking, "I have gone forth well.
After finishing the meal, one should reflect while sitting in the night-quarters or the day-quarters. One should also reflect while sitting in the dwelling place in the evening.
If one is unable to do so three times, one should reflect twice.
If one is unable to do so twice, however, one must certainly reflect at least once;
they say it is not permissible not to reflect. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Anumāna-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Cetokhila-sutta*. 185.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the *Cetokhila-sutta*. Therein, "stiffness of mind" (*cetokhila*) refers to states of rigidity and refuse-like impurity within the mind.
"Stumps": they are called "fetters of the mind" (*cetaso vinibandhā*) because they bind the mind and seize it, as if grasping it within a fist.
Regarding "growth" (*vuddhi*) and so forth: through virtue (*sīla*) there is growth; through the Path (*magga*) there is development (*viruḷhi*); and through Nibbāna there is abundance (*vepulla*).

Alternatively, through virtue and concentration (*samādhi*) there is growth; through insight (*vipassanā*) and the Path there is development; and through the Fruits (*phala*) and Nibbāna there is abundance. Regarding the Teacher (*satthari*)...
"He doubts" means he doubts regarding either the Teacher’s body or his qualities. Doubting regarding the body, he doubts:
"Does there exist, or does there not exist, a body adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks? Doubting regarding the qualities, he doubts:
"Does there exist, or does there not exist, the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the past, future, and present? "He is perplexed" means that while investigating, he is distressed.
He falls into distress and is unable to resolve it. "He does not resolve" means he does not obtain the conviction that "it is so.
"He does not become serene" means he is unable to become clear and free from doubt by descending into the [Buddha's] qualities.
"For the sake of ardor" means for the purpose of exerting energy that burns away the defilements. "For the sake of application" means again and again...
"For the sake of yoga. "For the sake of persistence" means for constant practice; "for the sake of striving" means for the purpose of exertion.
"This is the first mental barrenness" means this first state of rigidity of mind, consisting of doubt regarding the Teacher, remains unabandoned by this bhikkhu.
"Regarding the Dhamma" refers both to the Dhamma as the teaching (*pariyatti*) and the Dhamma as realization (*paṭivedha*). One who is wavering regarding the Dhamma as the teaching...
They say that the word of the Buddha consists of the Three Baskets and eighty-four thousand divisions of Dhamma;
yet he doubts whether this indeed exists or not. Doubting regarding the Dhamma of realization, they say: "The path is the outflow of insight;
the fruit is the outflow of the path; and Nibbāna is the relinquishment of all conditioned formations. This...
He doubts whether it exists or does not exist. "He doubts the Saṅgha" means:

by way of such phrases as "well-practised," he doubts whether the Saṅgha—defined as the assembly of the eight types of persons consisting of those established in the four paths and those established in the four fruits—exists or does not exist. One who doubts the training [doubts] the training in higher virtue...
They say, "There is indeed the training in higher mind, there is the training in higher wisdom. He doubts whether that exists or does not exist.
This is the fifth: this is the fifth state of rigidity, rubbish-like state, and stump-like state of the mind, consisting of anger toward one's fellow practitioners of the holy life.
186. *Vinibandhesu*: in the bonds, that is, both in sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) and in defilements (*kilesakāma*). *Kāye*: in one's own body. *Rūpe*: in external forms. *Yāvadatthaṃ*:
as much as one desires, that much. *Udarāvadehakaṃ*: that which fills the belly.
For it is called *udarāvadehaka* because it pervades (*avadehana*) the belly. *Seyyasukhaṃ*: the pleasure of beds and seats, the pleasure of the seasons.

"Or: 'The pleasure of the side' is the pleasure that arises for one lying on his right or left side as he turns over, just as it is when one lies on one's side. 'The pleasure of torpor' is the pleasure of sleep.
'Devoted to' means he dwells intent upon and engaged in [those things]. 'Having made an aspiration' means having formed a wish. Regarding the terms beginning with 'by virtue of':
'virtue' (*sīla*) is the fourfold purification of virtue; 'observance' (*vata*) is the undertaking of a vow."
Austerity is the practice of asceticism. The holy life (*brahmacariya*) is the abstention from sexual intercourse.
"I shall become a god" means I shall become a powerful god; or "another god," meaning one among the gods of little power. 189.
Concentration that proceeds based on desire among the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) is "concentration of desire. The volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) that constitute the exertion are...
The *padhāna-saṅkhārā* (exertion-activities). "Endowed with" means possessed of those qualities.

A "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*) is either a basis for success or that which has become success itself. The same method applies to the remaining [bases]. This is the summary here. The detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*.
Its meaning is also elucidated in the *Visuddhimagga*. Thus, by means of these four bases of success, there is the abandoning through suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).
It has been explained. Regarding the phrase "the fifth is indeed exertion" (*ussoḷhīyeva pañcamī*): here, "exertion" (*ussoḷhī*) indicates the energy that must be applied in every instance.

"Endowed with the fifteen factors of exertion" means being endowed with fifteen factors together with exertion, namely: the abandonment of the five mental barrennesses (*cetokhila*), the abandonment of the five bondages (*vinibandha*), and the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). Thus, he is possessed of these fifteen factors along with exertion.
*Bhabbo* means capable, suitable, or fit. *Abhinibbidāya* means for the breaking of the defilements by means of knowledge.
*Sambodhāya* means for the enlightenment of the four paths. *Anuttarassa* means of the supreme. *Yogakkhemassa* means of the state of arahantship, which is secure from the four bonds (*yoga*).
*Adhigamāya* means for the attainment or acquisition. *Seyyathā* is a particle used in the sense of comparison. *Pīti* is used in the sense of esteem or respect.
By both [passages], the Blessed One shows, "Bhikkhus, it is just as if...

In the case of "eight, ten, or twelve eggs of a hen," although the number of eggs may actually be more or less than what was stated for the hen, it is expressed in this way for the sake of linguistic elegance; for in the world, such an expression is considered elegant.

The word *tānassa* means "they might be," that is, "they would be. "Properly incubated by a hen" means they were properly incubated by their mother-hen as she lay upon them with her wings spread out over them.
"Properly brooded" means they were thoroughly and completely warmed and made warm by her as she caused them to take up the temperature from time to time.
"Thoroughly cultivated" means they have been well developed in every way from time to time; the meaning is that they have been made to take on the scent of a cock.

"Even though this mother hen"—that is, even though she might not have such a desire arise in her despite having practiced diligence through these three types of activity—"nevertheless, those chicks are indeed capable. Thus it is said.
They are indeed capable of emerging safely in the manner described. For, because those eggs are incubated by that hen in these three ways, they do not rot.
Furthermore, their internal moisture is exhausted;
the shell becomes thin, while the claws of their feet and the tip of their beaks become hard. Then, of their own accord—
It reaches full maturity; as the skull becomes thin, light appears outside and is perceived within.
Therefore, thinking, "Alas, for a long time we have lain in confinement with our hands and feet cramped, yet now this external light is seen;
here indeed there will be a pleasant dwelling," they become desirous of exiting and strike the skull with their foot, [stretching] the neck—
They stretch it out, and then that skull splits in two. Then, flapping their wings and crying out in a manner suited to that moment, they indeed emerge;
having emerged, they wander about, beautifying the vicinity of the village.
"In exactly this same way" is the application of the simile. This should be understood by correlating it with its meaning as follows:

Just as the hen’s performance of the threefold action upon her eggs, so too is this bhikkhu’s possession of the fifteen factors of exertion. Just as the eggs do not rot because the hen accomplishes the threefold action, so too,
for a bhikkhu endowed with these fifteen factors, insight-knowledge arises through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation.

Non-decline. Just as the moisture of the eggs is exhausted by performing the three kinds of actions, so too is the moisture of craving that accompanies the three states of existence exhausted for that bhikkhu by accomplishing the three kinds of contemplation.
Just as the shells of the egg-clusters become thin, so too does the shell of the egg of ignorance become thin for the bhikkhu. [Regarding] the claws, beaks, and talons of the chicks...
Just as there is a state of hardness and coarseness [in the egg], so too for a bhikkhu there is a state of sharpness, coarseness, clarity, and courage in his insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
Just as it is the time of maturation for the chicks of a hen, so too for a bhikkhu it is the time of maturation and growth—the time of conception—for his insight-knowledge.
[The hen breaks] the shell of the egg with either the tip of her claw or her beak... for the chicks of a hen.
Just as when one has burst open [the eggshell], spread out one's wings, and safely emerged, so too for that bhikkhu who,
having conceived the embryo of insight-knowledge and wandering about, obtains a favorable season, favorable food, a favorable person,
or a favorable opportunity for hearing the Dhamma, he increases his insight while sitting in a single seat.

The time when one has reached Arahantship in safety— having split the eggshell of ignorance by means of the path to Arahantship attained through gradual progress and having shattered the side of the higher knowledges (abhiññā)— should be understood. Just as a mother hen,
knowing that her chicks have reached maturity, breaks the eggshell, so too the Teacher, knowing the ripening of such a bhikkhu’s knowledge, [acts likewise].
“Cut off your own affection, as one plucks an autumnal lily with the hand;

cultivate only the path to peace, Nibbāna, as taught by the Sugata.”—In this manner, having pervaded [the world] with radiance, he struck the eggshell of ignorance with this verse; at the conclusion of the verse, he...
Having broken the eggshell of ignorance, he attains Arahantship. From that time forth, just as those chicks roam here and there,

beautifying the village fields, so too does this one whose great taints are destroyed enter the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object and wanders about, beautifying the monastery of the Saṅgha.
Thus, in this sutta, four kinds of abandoning are explained. How so?

By means of the abandoning of the mental wastes (*cetokhila*) and the mental shackles (*cetovinibandha*), the abandoning through reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānappahāna*) is explained; by means of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) is explained;
when the path has arrived, the abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*) is explained; and when the fruit has arrived, the abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*) is explained.
The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Cetokhila Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
7. Commentary on the *Vanapatthapariyāya Sutta* 190.

"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Vanapatthapariyāya*. Therein, "*Vanapatthapariyāya*" means either the discourse on the forest-thicket (*vanapattha*) or the teaching concerning the forest-thicket. 191.
"He dwells dependent upon a forest-thicket" means he dwells in a forest grove as a lodging that lies beyond the reach of human habitation.
He dwells performing the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) by relying upon it. Regarding the phrases "not established" and so forth:
mindfulness that was previously unestablished does not become established even while dwelling in reliance upon it; the mind that was previously unconcentrated does not become concentrated;

the taints (āsava) that were previously unabandoned do not go to their destruction; and the unsurpassed security from bondage (anuttara yogakkhema), which had not been attained previously—[is not attained].
The meaning is that one does not attain arahantship. "Requisites for life" means the provisions for life. "To be acquired" means to be gathered together.

"They are acquired with difficulty" means they arise with hardship. "Whether during the portion of the night or the portion of the day" means either in a section of the night or in a section of the day. And here, by one reflecting during the portion of the night:
Having understood this, if it is night, one should set out that very night; however, if there is an obstruction from fierce wild animals or the like during the night, one should wait until sunrise.
If it is known to be daytime, one should set out during the day; however, if there is an obstruction during the day, one should wait until sunset. 192. *Saṅkhāpi*:

thus, having understood the state of non-attainment of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*). In the subsequent section, however, *saṅkhāpi* refers to having understood the state of attainment of the ascetic’s duty.
194. “As long as life” means for as long as life continues; it must be observed for that duration. 195.

This is connected with the phrase “that person” by the words “is not to be followed. “Without asking leave” means, however, that one should depart from this place without asking that person for permission.

197. “Even by calculation”: having thus understood the state of the non-fulfillment of the ascetic’s duty (*śramaṇadharma*), that person is not to be followed; rather, one should depart after asking his leave.

198. “Even when being expelled” means even when being driven out. For such a person, even if he causes a hundred bundles of wood, a hundred water-pots, or a hundred baskets of sand to be brought as a fine, or causes himself to be driven out with the words “Do not live here,” one must ask his forgiveness and reside there for as long as life lasts.
The commentary on the Vanapattha-pariyāya Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 8.
The commentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta.

199. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta. Therein, "the Great Forest" is a natural grove of trees growing together as one with the Himalayas, not like the mixed planted and unplanted groves at Vesālī. "For the day’s abiding" means for the purpose of seclusion during the day.
"By the Beluva staff-tree" means by a young Beluva tree. "Staff-in-hand" does not refer to being weakened by old age.
"With staff in hand. For this man was young, standing in the prime of life;
however, because his mind was set on a staff, he wandered about carrying a golden staff, and for that reason he is called "staff-in-hand" (*daṇḍapāṇī*).

"Walking for the sake of exercise" means walking for the purpose of dispelling fatigue in the legs. "Pacing back and forth" and "wandering about" mean [walking] for the purpose of seeing the monastery, seeing the forest, seeing the mountain, and so forth.
Wandering here and there, it is said that he would sometimes go out unexpectedly and wander about in this manner.

"Leaning on his staff" means having leaned upon a staff; like a cowherd's boy, he stood to one side, placing the staff before him, resting both hands upon the top of the staff, and pressing his chin against his backhand.
200. "Kiṃvādī" means "what is his view? "Kimakkhāyī" means "what does he proclaim? This king, without bowing to the Blessed One, merely exchanged courtesies and then asked a question.
He did not ask out of a desire to understand, but asked without due respect.
Why? It is said that he belongs to the faction of Devadatta. When Devadatta was coming into his presence...
He slanders the Tathāgata. It is said that he speaks thus: "The ascetic Gotama is an enemy to our family;
he does not wish for the prosperity of our clan. Even my sister, having abandoned the enjoyments of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), went forth and became a wanderer, thinking, 'She will perish.
And my nephew, knowing himself to be the seed of a universal monarch, [has gone forth] for the sake of the increase of our family."
Not being satisfied [with me], thinking, "He will perish," he ordained him as well while still a mere child.
But I, unable to live without him, followed him into the homeless life. Even though I had thus gone forth, from the very day of my ordination he did not look at me with straightforward eyes.
Even when speaking in the midst of the assembly, he said things such as, "Devadatta is bound for the states of misery," as if striking me with a great axe.
"He speaks thus. In this way, this king too was divided by Devadatta, and therefore he acted in such a manner.

Then the Blessed One, thinking, "I shall speak to him in such a way that he cannot say, 'This king does not answer when questioned by me,' and so that he understands the meaning of what has been spoken," spoke words appropriate for him.
He said, "One who speaks as he acts," and so forth.
In that context, "he does not stand quarreling with anyone in the world" means that he does not engage in contentious speech or dispute with anyone in the world.
For the Tathāgata does not dispute with the world; rather, it is the world that disputes with the Tathāgata.
When it is said that something is impermanent, he disputes by saying it is permanent; when it is said that something is suffering, non-self, or unattractive, he disputes by saying it is attractive.
Therefore it was said: "Monks, I do not dispute with the world; rather, it is the world that disputes with me.
Likewise, monks, one who speaks according to the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world; only one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma [disputes]."
“He quarrels, monks,” [it is said]. “In what way” (*yathā*) means by which cause. “By sensual pleasures” (*kāmehi*) means both by sensual objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and by defilements (*kilesa-kāma*).
“That brahmin” (*taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ*) refers to that brahmin who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*). “Free from doubt” (*akathaṃkathi*) means one who is without uncertainty.

“With remorse cut off” (*chinnakukkucca*) means one whose remorse of regret (*vippaṭisāra-kukkucca*) and whose remorse of physical agitation (*hatthapāda-kukkucca*) have been severed; thus he is one with remorse cut off. “Regarding existence and non-existence” (*bhavābhava*)...
In repeated existence, whether in a low or a high state—indeed, a high state that has reached its full development is called "non-existence" (abhava).
"Perception" (saññā) here refers to the perception of defilements (kilesa); or rather, it is the defilements themselves that are spoken of by the name "perception.

Therefore, for whatever reason, the perceptions of defilement do not pursue that brahmin whose taints are destroyed, who dwells detached from sensual pleasures, and who does not speak of being "low" in this world.
"And I declare that to be the cause"—this is the meaning here. Thus the Blessed One illuminates his own state of having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*).

"Having brandished" means having drawn out and made to play. "Three-forked" means having three branches. "Forehead-mark" (*nalāṭika*) means showing the three lines on the forehead; the sense is that he caused the wrinkling of the skin to appear. "Leaning on a staff" means [leaning] on a staff.
"Having squeezed it out. There is also a reading, "daṇḍamālubbhā," meaning that he departed after taking [the staff].
201. "A certain one": a certain monk whose name was not well-known. It is said that he was skilled in connecting the sequence of the discourse;
when the Blessed One said, "I have spoken in such a way that Daṇḍapāṇi does not understand," [the monk wondered], "What indeed could the Blessed One have said that is unintelligible?"
Having understood the connection that the question had been stated, and having requested the One of Ten Powers, [he thought], "I shall make this question clear to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus.
Rising from his seat, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his hands in salutation with the ten fingers bright with light, he said:
"But what, venerable Blessed One, is your teaching? and so forth.
"Yatonidānaṃ" is a neuter form used adverbially; the meaning is "by which cause" or "when which cause exists. Regarding "papañcasaññāsaṅkhā," here *saṅkhā* means a portion or section.
*Papañcasaññā* refers to perceptions associated with the proliferations (*papañca*) of craving, conceit, and views; or rather, the proliferations themselves are expressed by the term "perception.
Therefore, the meaning here is "the portions of proliferation. *Samudācaranti* means they occur or proceed.

"Herein, there is nothing to be delighted in": the meaning is that in whatever cause—namely, the twelve sense bases (*dvādasāyatana*)—the conceptualization of proliferation (*papañcasaññā*) operates, herein not even a single sense base is to be delighted in, to be welcomed, or to be adhered to.
In that context, "to be delighted in" means to be delighted in as "I" and "mine. "To be welcomed" means...
"It should be said: 'I' and 'mine. "To be clung to" means that which is fit to be grasped by clinging, swallowing, and finalizing.

By this, he speaks here of the non-occurrence of craving and the other [defilements] themselves. "This very interior" means that the mere absence of delighting and so forth is the interior (*anto*) of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) such as lust.
This same method applies everywhere.
Regarding "taking up a staff" and so forth: the volition by which one takes up a staff is "taking up a staff. The volition by which one takes up or seizes a weapon is "taking up a weapon.
A quarrel that has reached its peak is *kalaha*. A mere dispute over various houses is *viggaha*. A mere dispute over various opinions is *vivāda*. That which proceeds as "you, you" is *tuvaṃ-tuvaṃ*.
Sowing discord where there was harmony is *pesuñña*. That which is not according to the true nature [of things]...
When one utters false speech, that should be understood as "false speech. Regarding the phrase "herein these":
herein, among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), these are the defilements (*kilesa*). For when defilements arise, they arise dependent upon the twelve bases;
and when they cease, they cease within those very twelve bases. Thus, wherever they have arisen, right there they are ceased.
This same point should be illustrated by the question on the truth of the origin:
"Where does this craving arise when it arises? Where does it settle when it settles?
Having said this, [it continues]: "In whatever is lovely and agreeable in the world, there this craving arises when it arises; there it settles."
"Settling down, it settles. And what in the world is of a lovely nature, of a pleasant nature? The eye, in the world, is of a lovely nature, of a pleasant nature," and so on;
in this manner, its arising and its cessation are stated specifically with regard to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
And just as craving, having arisen within the twelve bases and being extinguished upon reaching Nibbāna, does not again manifest within those bases—

Because of their non-existence, they are said to have ceased within the sense-bases (*āyatana*) themselves; in the same way, it should be understood that these evil unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) also cease within the sense-bases.
Alternatively, this very absence of delight and so forth is called the "end" of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) such as lust.
It is in *nibbāna*, which is conventionally designated here as the "end" of these underlying tendencies such as lust, that the evil unwholesome states...
Phenomena cease without remainder. For whatever is not present in a certain place is said to have ceased there;

this point should be illustrated by the question on cessation. Indeed, it has been said: "For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied thought and sustained thought—the formations of speech—become tranquilized," and so forth.

202. "Commended by the Teacher" (*satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito*) means praised by the Teacher. Regarding the word "by the wise" (*viññūnaṃ*), this is also a genitive used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "esteemed by wise fellow-practitioners. "Is able" (*pahoti*) means "is capable. 203.
"Having passed even the root, having passed the trunk": the so-called "pith" (*sāra*) may be located either in the root or in the trunk; the meaning is that one has passed even beyond that.
"Endowed with such" (*evaṃsampadaṃ*) means "possessing such attainment," i.e., of such a kind. "Having surpassed" (*atisitvā*).
Having transcended [all things]. "Knowing he knows" means he knows only that which is to be known; "seeing he sees" means he sees only that which is to be seen.
Or, whereas someone who grasps erroneously does not know even though he thinks he knows, and does not see even though he thinks he sees, the Blessed One is not like that.
The Blessed One, however, knowing, truly knows; seeing, truly sees. And this [Buddha] is, in the sense of being a guide for vision...
He has become vision (*cakkhubhūta*). He has become knowledge (*ñāṇabhūta*) in the sense of making things known.

Or, because he sets forth the Dhamma of the scriptures in the sense of its unerring nature, or because he is composed of the Dhamma uttered by speech after being reflected upon with the heart, he has become the Dhamma (*dhammabhūta*). He has become the Brahma (*brahmabhūta*) in the sense of being supreme.
Alternatively, "he has become vision" means he has become like the eye; thus should the meaning in these passages be understood. This [Buddha]...
He is a "turner" (*vattā*) because he turns the Wheel of Dhamma; a "setter-in-motion" (*pavattā*) because he causes it to proceed.

He is a "guide to the goal" (*atthassa ninnetā*) because of his capacity to extract and demonstrate the meaning. He is a "giver of the Deathless" (*amatassa dātā*) because he bestows the practice for the attainment of the Deathless.

"Holding him in high esteem" means that even when one is being entreated again and again, one still holds him in high esteem; for [the Buddha], standing upon his own perfection of wisdom as a disciple (*sāvakapāramīñāṇe*), from the base of Mount Sineru...
Even if one speaks by making [the matter] difficult to understand—as if one were removing grains of sand—one is indeed showing respect.
What is meant is: "Do not do this; without making us beg again and again, please speak by making it easy for us to understand.
204. Regarding the phrase "Yaṃ kho no āvuso" (Whatever, friends, for us), although it would have been appropriate to say "Yaṃ kho vo" (Whatever, for you), those monks...
Including himself among them, he said, "What [the Blessed One] has taught us. Or, because the summary had indeed been taught to them;
and since it was the Blessed One who taught both the Elder and them, he spoke thus with reference to the word "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), meaning:
"That which our Blessed One, having given you a summary in brief..."

In such passages as "Eye and, friends," this is the meaning: friends, dependent upon the sensitivity of the eye by way of its status as a support, and dependent upon forms produced from the four [elements] by way of their status as objects, that which is called eye-consciousness arises. "The meeting of the three is contact":
through the meeting of those three, that which is called contact arises. Dependent upon that contact, [feeling arises] by way of being co-nascent and so forth.
With contact as condition, feeling arises. Whatever object that feeling feels, that very same object perception perceives;
whatever object perception perceives, that very same object thought thinks about. Whatever object thought thinks about, that very same object conceptual proliferation proliferates.
"With that as the source" means by these causes, such as the eye and visible forms. [It leads to] a person.

"When the conceptual proliferations of perception (*papañca-saññā-saṅkhā*) operate," this means that for a person who has not fully understood the cause [of suffering], the various categories of proliferation (*papañca-koṭṭhāsa*) overwhelm him;
they continue to function within him. In this context, contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saññā*) are co-nascent with visual consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*).

Applied thought (*vitakka*) is to be seen in those states of mind accompanied by applied thought (*savitakka-citta*) that follow immediately after visual consciousness and so forth. These are the "conceptual proliferations" (*papañca-saṅkhā*).
They arise simultaneously with the javana. If this is so, why is there a mention of the past and the future?

It is because they arise in that same manner. For just as the proliferation (*papañca*) pertaining to the eye-door arises now in dependence upon the eye, visible forms, contact, feeling, perception, and applied thought, even so, showing its arising in regard to past and future visible forms cognizable by the eye, he spoke thus.
The same method applies to the passages beginning with "And the ear, friends," and so forth. However, in the sixth door, "mind" (*mano*) refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
"Phenomena" (*dhamma*) refers to the objects of the three planes of existence. "Mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) refers either to adverting (*āvajjana*) or to impulsion (*javana*).
When adverting is taken, contact, feeling, perception, and applied thought are co-nascent with that adverting. Proliferation (*papañca*) is co-nascent with impulsion. When impulsion is taken...
The life-continuum mind that performs the adverting function is called "the mind"; from that point on, all factors beginning with contact are indeed co-nascent with the impulsion.
However, because in the mind-door every object—whether past and so forth—is possible, it is entirely appropriate [to say] "in the past, future, and present.
Now, demonstrating the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he began the teaching with the words, "So, friends... He will explain the designation of contact.
"He will designate the designation of contact thus: 'A single phenomenon called contact arises'—the meaning is that he will demonstrate it.

This method applies everywhere. Having thus demonstrated the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of the twelve sense bases (*dvādasāyatana*) through the principle 'when this exists, this comes to be,' he now demonstrates the cessation of the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) by way of the negation of the twelve sense bases, saying: 'But that, friend...'"
He began the teaching with the words, "When the eye does not exist. The meaning therein should be understood in the manner already stated.
Having thus answered the question, he now said, "Do not have any doubt that this was spoken by a disciple;
this Blessed One sits having taken up the balance of omniscient knowledge. If you so desire, approach him and be free from doubt."
"Both," he said, while urging [him on]; and "but those who desire," and so forth.

"By these modes" means by these reasons—both the specific causes for the arising of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) and the causes for the turning away from and the turning toward the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"By these phrases" means by these combinations of syllables. "By phonemes" means by individual syllables. "The wise one" means...
He is endowed with wisdom. Or, for four reasons, he is wise: skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in the modes of conditions, and skilled in what is possible and impossible.

"Possessed of great wisdom" means he is endowed with a great wisdom capable of comprehending great meanings, great phenomena, great linguistic expressions, and great inspired insights—just as was the case with Mahākaccāna.
The tradition was spoken with reference to what was explained by Mahākaccāna; the meaning is: "Just as it was explained by Mahākaccāna, I too would explain it in exactly that same way.
*Madhupiṇḍika* means a large honey-cake, or a cake bound with a lump of sugar. *Asecanaka* means that which cannot be satiated.
Regarding clarified butter, molasses, honey, sugar, and so forth, one cannot say of them, "this here is weak" or "this there is abundant," because their flavor is blended together.
"Cetaso" means one whose nature is to reflect. "Dabbajātika" means one whose character is wise.

"What is the name of this?"—the Elder, thinking, "This discourse on the Dhamma is exceedingly auspicious; I shall have its name determined by the All-Knowing Wisdom of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers," reflected thus.
He said: "Therefore, because it is as sweet as a lump of honey, you should remember this discourse simply as the 'Madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya' (The Honey-lump Discourse).
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta. Therein, "having made twofold, having made twofold" means into two pairs.
Having made [this distinction]: "Sensual thought" (*kāmavitakka*) is a thought associated with sensual desire.
"Ill-will thought" (*byāpādavitakka*) is a thought associated with ill-will. "Harmful thought" (*vihiṃsāvitakka*) is a thought associated with harmfulness. One portion:
all this thought—whether internal or external, gross or subtle—is entirely on the side of the unwholesome; thus, these three [are so classified].
I made sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty into one section.
Thought associated with renunciation, which is free from sensual desires, is called "thought of renunciation"; it extends as far as the first jhāna.
Thought associated with non-ill will is "thought of non-ill will"; it extends from the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā) up to the first jhāna.
Thought associated with non-harming is "non-harming thought" (*avihiṃsā-vitakka*); it extends from the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*) up to the first *jhāna*.
As for the second portion, since every means belongs exclusively to the side of the wholesome, I have made this the second section.
By this, the time for the Bodhisatta’s restraint of thought is described.
For while the Bodhisatta was exerting himself in striving for six years, thoughts of renunciation and the like occurred in vast multitudes, like floods in a great river.
However, through a lapse of mindfulness, thoughts of sensual desire and the like suddenly arose;
having cut off the flow of wholesome states, they themselves remained as unwholesome javana-moments. Then the Bodhisatta...
He thought: "These thoughts of sensual desire and the like stand cutting off my course of wholesome states; come now, let me dwell having divided these thoughts into two parts.

Thus, he made one part consisting of the unwholesome side—the thoughts of sensual desire and so forth—and the other part consisting of the wholesome side—the thoughts of renunciation and so forth. Then he thought again: "From the unwholesome side..."
“I shall suppress the thought that has arisen, just as one who seizes a black snake by squeezing it with a mantra, or just as one who steps on an enemy by the neck;

I will not allow it to grow. But the thought that has arisen from the side of the wholesome, I shall cause to grow quickly, like a rain cloud in the rainy season, or like a young *sāla* tree in a fertile field. Having done so, he—
He suppressed unwholesome thoughts and increased wholesome thoughts. Thus it should be understood that by this it is stated to be the time for the Bodhisatta’s suppression of thoughts.
Now, showing how those thoughts arose in him and how he suppressed them, [the text says] of him...
He said, “Bhikkhus, for me,” and so forth. Therein, “of one who is heedful” means of one who abides in the non-forgetting of mindfulness (*sati*).
“Ardent” means possessed of the energy of ardor (*ātāpa-vīriya*). “Of one with a resolute mind” means of one whose consciousness is directed [toward the goal].

“The thought of sensual desire arises” refers to when the Bodhisatta, while exerting himself in striving for six years, gave rise to a thought of sensual desire concerning either the pleasure of kingship, or palaces, or theatrical performances, or the harem.
Nor had any sensual thought ever arisen in him regarding any kind of worldly success.
However, when he had reached the extreme limit of emaciation through the cutting off of food due to his ascetic practices, it occurred to him:
"It is not possible to achieve distinction by the cutting off of food; what if I were to take substantial food? He then went to Uruvelā for alms.
He entered. People thought, "In the past, the Great Man would not accept even food brought and offered to him;
surely now his wish has reached its fulfillment, which is why he has come of his own accord," and they served him the most exquisite foods.
Before long, the Bodhisatta’s physical form returned to its natural state. For even one whose body is worn out by old age, having obtained suitable nourishment, [returns to its former condition].
It was not his natural state. However, the Bodhisatta was still young; therefore, as he consumed suitable food, his physical form soon returned to its natural state:
his faculties became serene, his complexion grew pure, and his body—adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—became like the sky filled with a multitude of stars. He...
Having observed this and thinking, "How is it that a body so exhausted has become restored to such normalcy?", he— due to the greatness of his own wisdom—
took even this slight reflection and categorized it as a sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*).
Sitting in front of the leaf-hut, he saw herds of animals such as yaks, spotted deer, gavayas, and red deer making pleasant sounds in the forest.
He sees flocks of birds such as peacocks and wild cocks; ponds covered with blue lotuses, water lilies, and white lotuses; forest groves with branches thickly covered with various flowers;
and the river Nerañjarā with its flow of water as pure as a crystal column.
It occurs to him: "How beautiful indeed are these herds of deer, these flocks of birds, these ponds, these forest groves, and this river Nerañjarā!"
Thus, having taken up even such a limited thought, he made it a sensual thought; therefore it is said: "A sensual thought arises.
"Even for self-affliction" means even for one's own suffering. This same method applies everywhere. But does a Great Being ever have a thought that leads to both kinds of suffering?
No, there is not. However, for one who remains in non-penetration (of the truth), thought persists until—
Because it leads to harm for both, it receives these three names; therefore, he spoke thus.
"Obstructive to wisdom" means that it does not allow mundane or supramundane wisdom that has not yet arisen to arise;

furthermore, even if mundane wisdom has arisen by way of the eight attainments and five higher knowledges, it cuts it off and casts it away, thus it is "obstructive to wisdom. "Belonging to the side of affliction" means belonging to the category of suffering.
That which is called the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) Nibbāna does not allow one to realize it directly; thus, it is "not conducive to Nibbāna.
"It goes to destruction" means it goes to exhaustion, to non-existence. It ceases like a bubble on water. "I shall surely abandon" means I shall indeed abandon.
"I shall surely dispel" means I shall indeed remove. "I have made it to its end" means I have made it devoid of limits, leaving nothing remaining.
I made it completely enclosed and well-defined.
(208) As for "thoughts of ill will": no thought associated with harming others arises in the mind of a Bodhisatta;
rather, there occurs a transformation of the mind due to excessive rain, excessive heat, excessive cold, and so forth.
Referring to that, he said, "thought of ill-will" (*vyāpādavitakka*). As for "thought of cruelty" (*vihiṃsāvitakka*):

no thought associated with causing suffering to others arises in the Great Being; rather, there is a state of agitation and a state of lack of one-pointedness in his mind. Taking that [state] as the basis, he spoke of a "thought of cruelty.
For while sitting at the door of the leaf-hut, he saw predatory beasts such as lions and tigers harming small animals like pigs and other minor creatures.
He sees this. Then, even in this forest that is fearless from every quarter, the Bodhisatta arouses compassion, thinking:
"Enemies of these animals have arisen; the strong devour the weak, and those who have been devoured by the strong continue on.
He also sees cats and other predators devouring chickens, mice, and the like. Having entered the village for alms...

When people are oppressed by royal officials and undergo execution, imprisonment, and so forth, he arouses compassion, thinking that they are unable to live by performing their own work such as farming or trade; it is with reference to this that he said, "thought of cruelty arises.
"In such and such a way" means by this or that mode. This is what is meant: among the thought of sensual desire and the others, whichever...
He applies thought; whatever thought he brings forth, by that very mode of thinking, his mind does not possess the state of sensual thought and so forth.
"He has abandoned thoughts of renunciation" means he abandons thoughts of renunciation.
"He practiced them frequently" means he makes them frequent. "His mind is for the sake of sensual thoughts" means that his mind is directed toward the state of sensual thoughts.
The meaning is that it inclines in exactly the same way as it is associated with sensual thought. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
Now, in order to show a simile that illustrates the meaning, he said "seyyathāpi" (just as if), and so forth. In that context, "kiṭṭhasambādhe" means in a crowded field of grain.
"Ākoṭeyya" means he would strike it straight on the back. "Paṭikoṭeyya" means he would strike it crosswise on the sides.
"He should guard. "He should restrain" means he should stand blocking [the way]. "He should ward off" means he should not allow them to go here and there.

"On that account" means for that reason; the meaning is: because of the other people's eating of the crops by those cattle that have not been guarded in this manner. For the foolish cowherd, failing to guard the cattle in this way, thinks: "This [eating] consumes our food and wages."

"Even if he is unable to protect the cattle straightway, he causes enmity to be incurred with the families," meaning that the owners of the cattle suffer death and other calamities at their hands, as do the owners of the fodder.
However, the wise man, perceiving these four dangers, protects the cattle with great care; it is with reference to him that this was said. "Disadvantage" (ādīnava) means misfortune.
"Okāra" means something base, or an entry-point into the aggregates. "Saṅkileśa" means the state of being defiled.

"Nekkhamme" means in renunciation. "Ānisaṃsa" means the side of purification. "Vodānapakkha" is a synonym for that very same thing; the meaning is: they saw the side of purification of wholesome states within renunciation.
209. "Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) refers to all wholesome states that have escaped from sensual desires; when summarized under a single principle, it is *nibbāna* alone.
Herein is the application of the simile: the object of perception such as forms and so forth is like the cramped field;
the deceitful mind is like the rogue bull; the Bodhisatta is like the wise cowherd; and the fourfold fear is like the danger to oneself, to others, and to both.
The thought of development is like the wise cowherd who, seeing four kinds of danger, guards his cattle with diligence in the crowded fields; likewise,
it is the guarding of the mind by the Bodhisatta while exerting himself in striving for six years,
seeing the dangers such as self-harm, so that thoughts of sensual desire and the like do not arise toward objects such as forms.

In the phrases beginning with "increasing wisdom" (*paññāvuddhika*), it is called "increasing wisdom" because it leads to the arising of mundane and supramundane wisdom that has not yet arisen, and to the growth of that which has already arisen.

It is called "on the side of non-affliction" (*avighātapakkhika*) because it does not lead to a portion of suffering. It is called "conducive to Nibbāna" (*nibbānasaṃvattanika*) because it leads to the realization of the element of Nibbāna.
"Monks, even if one were to reflect upon it throughout the entire night... (*rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ*...).
"Even if that thought were to arise, it would cause me distress; 'on that account' means rooted in that.

'It would weigh upon me' means it would be agitated, which is to say it would lead to restlessness. 'Far' means distant. 'From concentration' means from both access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
'Then, monks, I directed my mind inwardly'—that is, monks, [I thought]: 'May my mind not [stray] from concentration.'"
"Let it be far away"—this means I settle the mind within itself; "I place it in its own range.
"I quiet it"—I cause it to settle right there. "I make it one-pointed"—I make it unified.
"I concentrate it"—I properly apply it; the meaning is that I fix it well. "May my mind not be agitated"—may my mind not be disturbed.
The meaning is: "May it not lead to agitation.
210. Regarding the passage, "There arises a thought of non-ill-will... [and] a thought of non-cruelty":

here, that very thought which arose together with the aforementioned nascent insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) and was called a "thought of renunciation" (nekkhamma-vitakka) in the sense of being the opposite of sensual desire, is now [called a thought of non-ill-will] in the sense of being the opposite of ill-will (byāpāda).
It is called "thought of non-ill will" (*abyāpādavitakka*) and also "thought of non-cruelty" (*avihiṃsāvitakka*) in the sense of being the opposite of cruelty.
Up to this point, the time for the Bodhisatta’s establishment of insight (*vipassanā*) by relying on meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) has been described.
For one whose concentration (*samādhi*) is still tender and whose insight is also [tender], if he sits for too long after establishing insight—
The body becomes exhausted; an inner fire as it were arises; sweat breaks out from the armpits;
a column of steam as it were rises from the head; and the mind is struck, distressed, and agitated.
Having again entered that attainment, he tames it, makes it supple, and composes it, and then establishes insight once more. For him, again—
For one who has been sitting for too long, it remains exactly as it was. He enters the attainment once more and does the same.
Indeed, attainment is of great service to insight (vipassanā).
Just as a shield-wall is of great service to a warrior, who relies upon it when entering battle, [so too is attainment].
Therein, having performed his duty together with the elephants, horses, and warriors,
when his weapons are exhausted or when he feels a desire to eat and so forth, he turns back, enters the palisade of shields,
takes up more weapons, rests, eats, drinks water, and puts on his armor; having done each of these things, he enters the battle once again.
Having performed his duty there, he enters the barracks again when oppressed by the need for excretion and so forth, or for some other business.
Having steadied himself there, he enters the battle once more;
thus, for a warrior, the barracks are as very helpful to insight as meditative attainment is.
However, for a warrior who has crossed the battlefield through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), insight (*vipassanā*) is even more helpful than a shield or a palisade.
For although one establishes insight by depending on meditative attainment, it is insight that, once it has gained strength,
protects the attainment and makes it firm.
For just as on dry land, even a ship becomes a burden for a boat, and even a cartload of goods becomes a burden for a cart;

but once they reach water, even a cart, even a cartload of goods, and even the yoked oxen become a burden for a ship—whereby the ship cuts across the current and reaches a good port in safety—even so, although one establishes insight (vipassanā) by depending upon meditative attainment (samāpatti), [the attainment]... [is a burden for insight].
Furthermore, having attained firmness, he protects even the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and makes it firm.

For meditative attainment is like a cart that has reached dry land, while insight (*vipassanā*) is like a ship that has reached water. Thus, it should be understood that up to this point, the time for the Bodhisatta to establish insight by relying upon meditative attainment has been described.
The passage beginning with "Whatever [it may be]" (yaññadeva) should be understood according to what was stated regarding the dark side (kaṇhapakkha).

Here too, in order to show a simile that illustrates the meaning, he said "Just as if" (seyyathāpi), and so forth. In that context, "collected from the vicinity of the village" (gāmantasambhatesu) means brought from the vicinity of the village.

"It is merely a matter for mindfulness" (satikaraṇīyameva hoti) means that one need only exercise the mere production of mindfulness, thinking, "These are cows. One does not need to go here and there to perform tasks such as beating them.
There is none. Regarding the phrase "these phenomena," one need only give rise to the thought that "these are the phenomena of serenity and insight.
By this, the time when the Bodhisatta’s serenity and insight reached full maturity is described.
It is said that at that time, as he sat for the purpose of attaining absorption, the eight attainments appeared before his mind through a single act of adverting.
Having established insight (vipassanā) while sitting, one ascends all seven contemplations simultaneously. 215.
What does "just as if" (seyyathāpi) show here? This is a separate connection (anusandhi).
For the Blessed One began this teaching showing his service for the welfare of beings and the perfection of his status as a Teacher. In that context, "in the forest" (araññe)...
*In the forest* (*aṭaviyaṃ*). *In the woods* (*pavane*) means in a grove of trees. In meaning, these two are one and the same; however, the second is a synonym for the first.
*Desiring what is not free from the yokes* (*ayogakkhemakāmo*) means not desiring the security and fearless state that is free from the four yokes, but rather desiring fear itself.

*Bringing well-being* (*sovatthiko*) means bringing about a state of well-being. *Leading to joy* (*pītigamanīyo*) means leading to satisfaction. [The variant] "leading to rapture" (*pītagamanīyo*)...
Or this is another reading. "He should cover" means he should block it with branches and the like. "He should open" means he should make the opening wide and clear.
"A wrong path" means a non-path obstructed by water, forests, mountains, and so forth.
"He should set down a decoy deer" means he should station a single island-deer in one place, as if it were wandering among their own herd. "A decoy female deer" [is caught] with a long rope.
Just as a deer-catcher, having gone to the forest—the dwelling place of deer—and having observed, "They live here; they exit by this path;
they roam there; they drink there; they enter by this path," [binds a deer].
Having blocked the path and opened up a byway, and having stationed the male and female deer-trapper, he himself stood in a concealed place holding a spear.

Then, in the evening, the deer, having wandered in the forest where there was no fear from any quarter and having drunk water, came near their dwelling place while playing with their fawns; and the male and female deer-trapper—
Seeing [the deer], they enter without fear, thinking, "Our companions must have arrived.
But seeing the path blocked, they think, "This is not the way; this must be the way," and take to a bypath.
The deer-hunter does nothing for a while, but once they have all entered, he strikes the very last one slowly. That one becomes terrified, and then—
All of them, terrified and thinking "danger has arisen," look ahead;

seeing the path blocked by water, forest, or mountain, and unable to enter the dense forest on either side because it is like a chain of fingers, they begin to try to exit by the very path they entered.
The hunter [observes] their state of turning back.
Having understood this, he begins from the start and slaughters thirty or forty deer.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "In this way, monks, after some time, that great herd of deer would meet with ruin and disaster.
Regarding the statement, "This is a designation for delight-and-lust; this is a designation for ignorance," because these beings [are bound] by ignorance...
Having become ignorant and being bound by the passion of delight (*nandīrāga*), they are led toward objects such as forms (*rūpa*) and suffer slaughter by the weapon of the suffering of saṃsāra.
Therefore, the Blessed One, having identified "delight" (*nandīrāga*) as the dwelling place and "ignorance" (*avijjā*) as that which frequents the dwelling place, demonstrated this.
For a deer-hunter, at times, wipes their bodies with a branch-breaking cloth and removes the scent of humans.

Having left the male deer in one place and released the female deer together with the tether, she conceals herself, takes up a spear, and stands near the male deer; meanwhile, the female deer goes toward the place where the herd of deer is grazing.
Seeing her, the deer stand with their heads held high, and she too stands with her head held high.
Thinking, "This one is of the same species as us," they take her as their mate. She too approaches slowly, as if grazing on grass.
Having caught her scent, the forest leader of the herd releases his own mate and turns toward her;
for to living beings, the new and the novel are always dear. [Seeing] that the female deer had come very close to the forest deer—
Without giving it up, as if facing it, she retreats backward and goes into the presence of the mate;
wherever her rope becomes snagged, she strikes that spot with her hoof to free herself.
When a forest deer sees the mate, he becomes infatuated with the female, and out of jealousy toward the mate, he arches his back and shakes his head.
He stands still; at that moment, even if someone were to lick his tongue with a spear, he would not know "what is this?
If it is easy for him to strike the deer from above as he moves along, he bends his back.
If it is easy for him to strike from below, he raises his chest. Then the hunter strikes the wild deer with a spear.
Having killed it right there, he takes the meat and departs. In the same way, just as that deer, being infatuated with the bait,
becomes envious of his own companions and knows nothing even while licking the spear with his tongue, so too these beings, infatuated by ignorance, blinded and knowing nothing,
fall into delight and lust for forms and other sense-objects, [pierced] by the spear of the suffering of saṃsāra.
The Blessed One showed that they "suffer slaughter" by identifying "dwelling in a home" as delight and lust (*nandī-rāga*), and "home-dwelling" as ignorance (*avijjā*).
Thus, monks, I have opened up the secure path;
for, monks, having attained full enlightenment through acting for the welfare of these beings, I did not remain silent after declaring "I am a Buddha," but rather set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
By teaching the Dhamma starting from that point, he showed his own conduct for the welfare of others: he revealed the secure, noble Eightfold Path; he closed off the wrong path;
he uprooted and cast down the craving for pleasure—the "home-life"—which was previously unknown to those capable individuals such as Koṇḍañña and others, having cut it through in two;
and he expelled and utterly eradicated the ignorance that wanders as a "home-dweller."
The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Dvedhāvitakka-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
10. Commentary on the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta 216.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta. In this context, “one devoted to higher consciousness” (*adhicittamanuyutto*):

the mind that has arisen by way of the ten courses of wholesome action is simply “mind”; the mind of the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) which serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*) is “higher than that mind.”
“Citta” means higher mind (*adhicitta*). “Devoted to” means devoted to that higher mind; the sense is that he is applied and intent upon it.

In this regard, after the meal, having returned from his alms round, this bhikkhu takes his sitting mat and, at the foot of a certain tree, or in a forest thicket, or at the base of a mountain, or in a mountain cave, practices the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

Even when departing with the thought, "I shall do it," he is devoted to higher consciousness; even when having gone there and removing blades of grass and leaves from his sitting or standing place with his hands or feet, he is still devoted to higher consciousness.
But once seated, having washed his hands and feet, having folded his legs crosswise, and having taken up his primary meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he dwells devoted to higher consciousness.
“Signs” (*nimittāni*) means causes (*kāraṇāni*). “From time to time” (*kālena kālaṃ*) means at every occasion.
But surely a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) should be kept in mind continuously, without abandoning it for even a moment; why then did the Blessed One say “from time to time”?
For in the Canon, thirty-eight meditation subjects are analyzed; among these, a bhikkhu should take up that meditation subject which is pleasing to his own mind.
While one is sitting having grasped [these signs], there is no need for attention to these signs as long as no defilement arises at all.
But when it does arise, he spoke thus to show that one should grasp these [signs] and extract the tumor (abbuda) arisen in the mind.
"Associated with desire" means accompanied by desire, conjoined with lust. And the field for these three types of thought is—
And the object must also be known. In this regard, for those [states] associated with desire, the field consists of the eight greed-accompanied unwholesome consciousnesses;
for those associated with hatred, the two accompanied by displeasure; and for those associated with delusion, all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.
However, the two consciousnesses associated with doubt and restlessness are their individual fields. This applies to all of them.
Beings and formations are the object, for those [states] arise with respect to beings and formations that are regarded as desirable, undesirable, or neutral.
Another sign associated with the wholesome should also be brought to mind;
that is, one should bring to mind another sign based on the wholesome, other than that [previous] sign. In this context, "another sign" refers to that which is associated with zeal (*chanda*).

When thoughts directed toward beings arise, the meditation on the foul (*asubhabhāvanā*) is another sign (*nimitta*). When thoughts directed toward formations (*saṅkhāra*) arise, the attention to impermanence (*anicca-manasikāra*) is another sign.
When thoughts directed toward beings who are full of hatred arise, the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) is another sign.
When thoughts directed toward formations arise, the attention to elements (*dhātu-manasikāra*) is another sign. In whatever case thoughts directed toward delusion (*moha*) arise—
When greed has arisen toward beings, there is another method called "the support of five things" (*pañcadhammūpanissaya*).

For instance, when greed arises toward beings by way of such thoughts as "His hands are beautiful" or "His feet are beautiful," one should apply the perception of foulness (*asubha*) [to counteract it].
One should ask: "In what are you infatuated? You are infatuated with the hair of the head. With the body hair... [and so on] ...you are infatuated with the urine."

This so-called personal existence is erected by three hundred bones, bound together by nine hundred sinews, plastered over with nine hundred pieces of flesh, enveloped in moist skin, and concealed by the color of the outer integument;
from its nine openings and ninety thousand pores of the body, impurity flows forth; it is filled with putrid matter and is foul-smelling.
When one contemplates the foul by reflecting: "It is loathsome, repulsive, a collection of thirty-two types of filth;
