there is no essence or excellence here," the greed that has arisen toward sentient beings is abandoned. Thus, for such a person, this contemplation of the foul becomes what is called "another sign.
When greed arises toward conditioned things such as the bowl and robes, he establishes equanimity toward those formations in two ways.

By attending to it according to the method described in the commentary on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*)—that is, by way of its ownerlessness and its being merely temporary—that [aversion] is abandoned.
Thus, for him, the act of attending to it as impermanent becomes what is called "another sign" (*nimitta*).

However, when faults arise toward beings, loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be developed by means of such teachings as the removal of resentment and the parable of the saw; for one who develops that, hatred [is abandoned].
It is abandoned; therefore, for him, the development of loving-kindness becomes known as another sign.

But when a fault arises regarding stumps, thorns, grass, leaves, and so forth, one should apply mindfulness to the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) by way of such questions as: "At whom are you angry? Is it at the earth element or the water element? Or who is this that is said to be 'angry'? Is it the earth element or the water element? and so on.
As he does so, his fault is abandoned. Therefore, for him, the attention to elements becomes what is called another sign.
But when delusion arises anywhere—“Living with teachers, recitation, questioning about what has been recited;”
“Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time, discerning what is possible and impossible—by depending on these five qualities, the element of delusion is abandoned.
These are the five qualities upon which one should depend. For a bhikkhu living in dependence upon a teacher: “The teacher...”

When he is thus prepared, his delusion is abandoned. Even when receiving instruction, [he thinks]: “The teacher imposes a disciplinary task on one who does not receive the instruction at the time of instruction, or who recites it poorly.”
In whatever way he is prepared, in that way his delusion is abandoned. By approaching monks who are worthy of respect and training, and inquiring, "Venerable sir, how is this?
What is the meaning of this?", he dispels doubt; in this way, too, his delusion is abandoned.
By going at the proper time to a place for hearing the Dhamma and listening to the Dhamma attentively, even regarding those [teachings]...
In those instances, the meaning becomes clear; thus his delusion is abandoned.

He becomes skilled in determining what is a valid reason and what is not a valid reason through the discernment of the possible and the impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna-vinicchaya*); thus his delusion is abandoned. Therefore, this fivefold proximate cause of the Dhamma (*pañcadhammūpanissaya*) constitutes for him what is called a "sign" (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, these applied thoughts (*vitakka*) are abandoned even by one who develops any one among the thirty-eight meditation objects.
However, these signs (*nimitta*) are direct opposites and function as antidotes. When lust and the other defilements are abandoned by means of these, they are thoroughly abandoned.
For just as one extinguishes a fire by striking it with wet wood, with sand, or with branches and so forth, [so too are the defilements abandoned].
Water, however, is the direct opposite of fire; by means of it, one who is extinguished is well-extinguished.
Likewise, by these signs, lust and the other defilements that have been abandoned are well-abandoned. Therefore, it should be understood that these [signs] are mentioned.
"Connected with the wholesome" means dependent on the wholesome and serving as a condition for the wholesome. "Internally only" means precisely within the internal range of the object.
"Palagaṇḍo" means a carpenter. "With a fine peg" means with a peg made of heartwood that is finer than the peg which he intends to remove.
"A coarse peg" refers to an uneven peg driven into a plank of sandalwood or a plank of heartwood.
"He would strike it down" means he would strike it with a mallet. "He would drive it out" means while striking it in this manner, [he would extract it] from the plank.
He would remove it. "He would pull it out" means that, realizing "now many have gone out," he would shake it with his hand and drag it out.
In this analogy, the mind is like the board; unwholesome thoughts are like the coarse fibers;

another wholesome sign, such as the meditation on foulness, is like the fine fibers; and the removal of the coarse fibers by means of the fine fibers is like the removal [of unwholesome thoughts] by means of the meditation on foulness and so forth.
The removal of those thoughts by means of wholesome signs. 217.
The passage beginning with “by a snake’s carcass,” etc., is stated for the purpose of demonstrating a corpse that is exceedingly loathsome and repulsive.
“Hanging from the neck” means brought and tied around the neck by some enemy facing him. “Would be repelled” (*aṭṭiyeyya*) means he would be distressed (*aṭṭo*) and pained.
One would feel shame; one would feel abhorrence—that is, one would become disgusted.

They are abandoned: thus, by examining with the power of one's own wisdom that these unwholesome states are blameworthy and result in suffering, they are abandoned by one who feels disgust toward them as if toward a snake’s carcass and the like. But for one who...
If one is unable to investigate by means of the power of wisdom, one should approach a teacher, a preceptor,
or some other venerable fellow-celibate, or the senior of the Saṅgha, and having struck the gong or convened the community of monks themselves,
announce the matter; for when many have assembled, there will surely be at least one wise person.
He will explain that this very danger must be seen in these [thoughts], or he will suppress those thoughts by means of talk on the repulsiveness of the body and so forth.
(218) One should apply oneself to non-attention and non-mindfulness; that thought should neither be remembered nor attended to, but rather by one who is occupied with something else.

It must be so. For just as a man who does not wish to see a form would close his eyes, even so, when thoughts arise in the mind of a bhikkhu sitting after taking up the fundamental meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he should become occupied with something else.
In this way, that thought is abandoned; once it is abandoned, he should again sit taking up the meditation subject.
If it is not abandoned, then a discourse on the Dhamma has been committed to memory; that should be recited aloud.

Even if it is not abandoned while one is otherwise occupied, there is a small book inside a bag in which praises of the Buddha and praises of the Dhamma have been written; having taken that out, one should recite it while being otherwise occupied.
It must be so. Even if it is not abandoned in this way, one should take the fire-drills out of the bag and, while attending to them by thinking, "This is the upper drill-wood;
this is the lower drill-wood," one should occupy oneself with something else.
Even if it is not abandoned in this way, one should take out the small box and [attend to its contents] by thinking, "This is the needle-case; this is the pair of tweezers; this is the nail-cutter."
Thinking, "This is called a needle," one who is providing such requisites must be occupied with something else.
Even if it is not abandoned in this way, when taking up a needle to sew a worn spot in his robe, he must be occupied with something else.
Thus, as long as it is not abandoned, he must remain occupied with something else while performing various wholesome deeds.
Having abandoned it, one should sit down again taking up the original meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), but one should not undertake new work. Why?
Because when discursive thought (*vitakka*) has ceased, there is no opportunity for attention to the meditation subject.
However, the ancient wise ones cut off discursive thought even while performing new work. Here is an account of that:
It is said that the preceptor of the novice Tissa was living at the Tissamahāvihāra. The novice Tissa said, "Venerable sir, I am weary.
Then the Elder said to him, "Bathing water is difficult to obtain in this monastery; take me and go to Cittalapabbata.
He did so. There, the Elder said to him, "This monastery belongs entirely to the Saṅgha."
“Make one place for personal use. Saying, “Very well, venerable sir,” he began from the beginning and,
undertaking all three together— the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the clearing of the mountain cave, and the preliminary work for the fire-element kasiṇa— he brought the meditation subject to absorption,
completed the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, finished the construction of the cave, and having done everything, [he reported].
He gave notice to his preceptor. The preceptor said, "Sāmaṇera, you have endured suffering; stay here for today.

Spending that night in the cave, he obtained favorable conditions for the climate, developed insight (vipassanā), attained Arahatship, and passed away into Parinibbāna right there. They took his relics and erected a stupa. Even today...
It is known as the Tissattheracetiya. This section is called the "Section on Mindfulness. 219.
Being unable to suppress discursive thoughts while standing there, [the Buddha] spoke the passage beginning with "But if, monks...

in order to show the section on the breaking of the root of thought, saying, "Standing here, one will suppress them. Therein, the "stilling of the formative activity of thought" (vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhāna) is...
"Should be brought to mind" (*manasikātabba*): it is called a "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it constructs; the meaning is that it is a condition, a cause, or a root.

It is called a "basis" (*saṇṭhāna*) because one stands firm upon it. Thus, "the basis for the volitional formation of applied thought" (*vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhāna*) means the basis for the volitional formation of applied thought;
that should be brought to mind. This is what is meant: "By what cause, by what condition, by what reason has this applied thought arisen?"—thus [one should attend] to the applied thoughts.
"The root and the root-of-roots should be brought to mind. [He thinks: "Why indeed am I going quickly?
For what reason am I going quickly? What if I were to go slowly? [He reflects: "What use have I for this rapid pace? I shall go slowly.
Having thought thus, he would go slowly. This method applies everywhere.
In this context, the time when that man travels swiftly is like the time when this bhikkhu mounts upon his applied thought (*vitakka*).
The time when he travels slowly is like the time when this bhikkhu cuts off the movement of applied thought.

The time when he stands still is like the time when, the movement of applied thought having been cut off, the mind enters the original meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). The time when he sits down...
The time when he has increased his insight and attained Arahantship is like this [person’s] lying down.
The time when he passes the day in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as its object is like this [person’s] sleeping.
In that state, for one who goes to the very root of these thoughts, asking, "What is the cause of these thoughts? What is their condition?", the movement of thought becomes slackened.
When that [concentration] has become slack and is reaching its limit, applied thoughts (*vitakka*) cease entirely. This meaning should also be illustrated by the *Duddubha Jātaka*:
It is said that while a hare was sleeping at the foot of a *beluva* tree, a ripe *beluva* fruit fell from its stalk and landed near his ear.
At the sound of it, he woke up with the perception that "the earth is splitting apart" and fled in haste.
Seeing him, the other four-footed animals fled from his presence as well. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a lion. He thought:
"This earth is said to break apart at the destruction of an eon; there is no breaking of the earth in the interim.
What if I were to go right down to the very root and investigate? Starting from the elephant-king and going down to the hare, he asked: "By you..."
“Father, have you seen the earth splitting open? The hare replied, “Yes, my lord. The lion said, “Come, sir, show me.
The hare said, “I cannot, master. “Come here, you, do not be afraid! he said, and taking him by the hand with a gentle and soft touch, they went. Standing not far from a tree, the hare said:
“O Blessed One, it thunders in the place where I dwell;”
“I too do not know this; what is it that makes this sound like a drum?”—thus he spoke the verse.

The Bodhisatta said, “Stay right here,” and having gone to the foot of the tree, he saw the place where the hare was lying, he saw the *beluva* fruit, and looking up, he saw the stalk. Having seen it, [he thought], “This hare is here...”

Having understood that while he was lying down and asleep, the hare had fled upon hearing the sound of this [fruit] falling at his ear, thinking, "The earth is splitting apart," the Bodhisatta asked the hare about the reason for this. The hare replied, "Yes, Your Majesty. Then the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:
"Upon hearing the fallen *beluva* fruit, the hare ran away, thinking it was a *duddubha* [thunder]."
“Having heard Sasa’s words, the herd of deer was filled with dread.
Then the Bodhisatta comforted the herd of deer, saying, “Do not be afraid. Thus, for one who goes to the very root of the roots of thoughts, thoughts are abandoned. 220.

Standing on this section concerning the breaking of the roots of thoughts, the Buddha spoke the passage beginning with “But if, monks, to him... in order to show another method for one who is unable to suppress thoughts in this way, stating that they should be suppressed in the following manner.

"Pressing tooth against tooth" means placing the upper tooth upon the lower tooth. "With the mind [one should] restrain the mind" means that with a wholesome mind one should suppress an unwholesome mind.
"A strong man" means just as a powerful man endowed with great strength might seize a weak man by the head, the neck, or the shoulder, and restrain or crush him.

Just as one might cause intense heat, making another scorched, exhausted, and as if overcome by fainting, even so the bhikkhu, becoming a rival to his thoughts and overcoming them by asking, "Who are you?
And who am I?", exerts great energy, thinking: "Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood in this body dry up."
Showing that thoughts are to be suppressed, he brought forward this simile which illustrates the meaning.
"When, monks," etc.—this is called the "Analysis of Exhaustion" (*pariyādānabhājaniya*), and its meaning is quite plain.
Just as a teacher, having had a prince who has come from another kingdom learn the craft of the five weapons, says: "Go, [my son]," etc.
"Take the sovereignty over your own kingdom. If bandits rise up against you on the way, proceed by using your bow.
If your bow is lost or broken, [use] a spear or a sword. Having thus shown what must be done with even these five weapons, he dismissed him.
He did accordingly, went to his own kingdom, seized the sovereignty, and [enjoyed] the glory of kingship.
He experiences it. In the same way, the Blessed One, while exhorting a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness toward the attainment of Arahatship, said:

"If unwholesome thoughts arise within him, he will stand on the side of the 'sign of others' (*aññanimitta*), suppress them, increase his insight (*vipassanā*), and reach Arahatship. If he is unable to do so there, he will stand on the side of 'disadvantage' (*ādīnava*)."
"If he is unable even there, let him stand at the section on non-existence; if he is unable even there, let him stand at the section on the breaking of the roots of thought;
if he is unable even there, let him stand at the section on suppression, suppress his thoughts, increase his insight, and thereby attain Arahatship. Thus he taught these five sections.
"Mastered in the paths of the movement of thought" means that he is said to have practiced mastery and attained proficiency in the pathways of the movement of thought.
"Whatever thought he may wish to think"—this is stated for the purpose of showing the manner of his mastery.
For previously, whatever thought he desired to think, he would not think it; and whatever thought he did not desire to think, he would [think it].
He applies thought. Now, however, because he has attained mastery, whatever thought he wishes to apply, that very thought he applies;
whatever thought he does not wish to apply, that thought he does not apply. Therefore it is said:
"Whatever thought he desires, that thought he will apply; whatever thought he does not desire, that thought he will not apply."
"He has cut off craving," and so forth— all this has already been stated in the *Sabbāsava Sutta*.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
The first part of the Commentary on the First Fifty [Discourses] is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the First Fifty Discourses of the Majjhima Nikāya (Second Part)
3. The Chapter on Similes (Opamma-vagga) 1. Commentary on the Sutta of the Simile of the Saw (Kakacūpama-sutta) 222.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Sutta of the Simile of the Saw. In this context, “Moḷiyaphagguna”: *moḷī* is called a crest (*cūḷā*). As it has been said: [text continues]
Having severed his topknot, which was scented with the finest perfumes,
the Bull of the Sakyas cast it into the air;
like Vāsava with his excellent jeweled casket, he offered it as a gift.
“The thousand-eyed one received [it] with his head.
In his time as a householder, she was very large; therefore, the designation “Moḷiyaphagguna” arose for him.

Even after he had gone forth, they knew him by that same name. “Ativelan” means having exceeded the proper limit (*vela*). In this context, there is the limit of time (*kālavelā*) and the limit of the boundary (*sīmavelā*).
“Sīlavelā” refers to three kinds of *velā*. “At that time (*velāyaṃ*) he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*)” (Dhp Vagga-uddāna; Gāthā-uddāna;
Mahāvagga 1–3)—this is called the *kālavelā* (time-boundary). “The established Dhamma does not overstep its boundary (*velaṃ nātivattatī*)”—this is called the *sīmavelā* (limit-boundary).
And [in the passage] “the non-transgression of the *velā* is the destruction of the bridge,” and “this *velā* is in the sense of non-transgression.”
And this is what is called the "boundary of virtue" (*sīlavelā*). He transgressed all three of these. For there is a specific time for exhorting the bhikkhunīs;
even though he exhorted them after the sun had set, he transgressed that boundary of time as well. There is also a limit and a demarcation regarding the measure for exhorting the bhikkhunīs;
by exhorting them with more than six or five statements, he transgressed that boundary of the limit as well.

He transgressed. Furthermore, by speaking while accompanied by frivolity (*dava*), he speaks to the extent that it constitutes a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*); in this way, he also transgressed the boundary of virtue (*sīlavela*).

"In association" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) means having become mixed together, sharing the same pleasure and pain. "In the presence of" (*sammukhā*) means before [the person]. "He speaks dispraise" (*avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati*) means...
But seeing them performing such tasks as cooking and pounding, he speaks of their faults, saying: "There is no such thing as an offense for these women;
these bhikkhunīs are ill-behaved, difficult to speak with, and shameless. He also creates a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), saying:
"From the moment these bhikkhunīs were seen by these bhikkhus, their eyes have been burning; in this monastery there is an offering of flowers..."
Or [the duties] such as washing the seats and cleaning the surroundings proceed by means of these [nuns]. These daughters of good family are modest;
yet they drag out a legal dispute, saying: "You say this and that to them, but this is the offense you have committed; come before those who hold the Vinaya and give me a formal decision."
"He speaks dispraise of Moḷiyaphagguna" means that for this bhikkhu there is no such thing as an offense-free state.
He speaks of his lack of virtue, saying, "The door of his dwelling cell is never empty of bhikkhunīs.
And they create legal disputes, meaning that from the time these bhikkhus saw the elder Moḷiyaphagguna, their eyes burned with resentment.
In this monastery, it is not even possible for others to look about for a place to stay.
When bhikkhunīs come to the monastery, they receive exhortation, hospitality, or the assignment of study-texts only by depending on the Elder.
This young man is modest and scrupulous; how can you say such things as "this" and "that"? Come, [go] into the presence of those who are experts in the Vinaya.
They drag the legal case forward, saying, "Give a judgment!
That bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One neither out of a desire for affection nor with the intention of causing a schism, but out of a desire for his welfare.
It seems he had a single thought: "As this bhikkhu lives in such close association, disrepute will arise for him."
Thus, it would indeed bring disrepute to the Dispensation (*sāsana*). However, [thinking], "If spoken by another, this man will not desist;

but having been taught the Dhamma and exhorted by the Blessed One, he will desist," out of a desire for his welfare, he addressed the Blessed One with these words, beginning with, "Venerable Sir, may the Venerable One...
(223). *Āmantehi* means "make known. *Āmanteti* means "calls out."
224. "Saddhā" means through faith. "Therefore" (tasmā) means because you are both a son of good family and one who has gone forth out of faith;

or else, because while you are living in association with them, mental distress would arise toward those who might abuse or strike you, but when such association is abandoned, it will not arise—therefore. "Therein" (tattha) means in that [matter].

Regarding "speaking dispraise": "worldly" (*gehasita*) means dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Desires" (*chanda*) refers both to the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*) and the desire of aversion (*paṭigha-chanda*).
"Distorted" (*vipariṇata*): even a mind that is lustful is distorted; a mind that is hateful or deluded is also distorted.
However, in this context, it is permissible [to speak of] a lustful mind by way of the desire of craving, and a hateful mind by way of the desire of aversion.
"Compassionate for their welfare" means feeling compassion for them through their welfare, pervading them with welfare. "Not with a mind of ill-will" means I shall not have a mind of hatred.

225. Now, why did the Blessed One begin [this instruction]? It is said that even after hearing this much advice, Phagguna did not even give rise to the thought, "I will desist from, I will abstain from contact with bhikkhunīs. However, together with the Blessed One, he was like a target...

He stood there, having turned away [from them]. Then, just as a longing arises for food in one who is hungry, for drink in one who is thirsty, or for warmth in one touched by cold or for comfort in one who is suffering—just so, upon seeing this difficult-to-speak-to bhikkhu, bhikkhus who were easy to speak with came into his range of vision during the First Enlightenment. Then, of those...
Desiring to speak in praise [of the Blessed One], he began this teaching.
In this context, "they attained" means they grasped or fulfilled [the purpose]. "At one time" means at a certain occasion.
"Eating at a single sitting" refers to a single meal before midday; for even if one has eaten seven times from sunrise until noon, it is still considered a single meal.
Here, eating at a single sitting is precisely what is intended. "Freedom from illness" means being free from disease.
"Freedom from affliction" means being free from suffering. "Lightness of body" means the body’s rising up with ease. "Strength" means physical strength.
"Comfortable dwelling" means the body’s dwelling in happiness. What is stated by this? The time for abandoning untimely eating during the day is stated.
In the Bhaddāli Sutta, however, the time for abandoning untimely eating at night is mentioned.

For these two types of eating, the Blessed One did not cause [people] to abandon all at once. Why? Because these very two types of eating have been habitual for beings within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
There are sons of good family who are delicate; they would become exhausted if they were to abandon both types of eating simultaneously.
Therefore, having caused them to abandon [the two] together, he had them abandon them separately: daytime eating at the wrong time at one time, and nighttime eating at the wrong time at another.
Among those, the time when daytime eating at the wrong time was caused to be abandoned is told here.
In that regard, since the Buddhas do not cause people to abandon things by showing fear or by threatening them, but rather cause them to abandon things by showing the benefits,
For it is in this way that beings abandon [defilements] with ease. Therefore, showing the benefit, he pointed out these five qualities.
As for the phrase "instruction should be given," there was nothing further to be done regarding the Teaching;
it was merely a matter of arousing mindfulness by saying, "Do this, do not do that. By doing just that much, they performed what was to be done and abandoned what was to be abandoned.
“Bhikkhus, at the time of the first enlightenment, the bhikkhus were easy to speak to, obedient, and responsive to instruction.
Now, in order to bring forward a simile illustrating their quality of being easy to speak to, he said, “Just as if,” and so forth. In that context, *subhūmiyam* means on level ground.
As for the phrase, “One should plant seeds in a good field on level ground where stumps have been cleared away,” it refers here to—
"Maṇḍabhūmi" means "good ground. "At the crossroads of the four great highways" refers to the place where two great roads intersect.
"A chariot with well-trained horses" is a chariot drawn by horses that have been properly broken in.
"With the goad lowered" means the goad is placed horizontally so that it can be grasped by one standing on the chariot. "A trainer of draft animals" is a horse-trainer.
"He drives the steeds to be tamed" means he is a trainer of steeds to be tamed (*assadammasārathi*). "Wherever he wishes" means by whichever path he desires.
"To wherever he wishes" means to whichever destination he desires. "He would drive them" means he would send them straight forward. "He would drive them back" means he would turn them back.
"In just this way" means just as that charioteer desires to go by whichever path, so too—
The horses are already mounted; whichever destination he desires, that very destination is already reached.
Having sent forth the chariot, the horses need neither be restrained nor prodded with a goad.
One need only observe their movement as they leave marks upon the level ground with their hooves. In the same way, for me too, among those bhikkhus again and again—
There was no need for anything to be said. It was enough merely to arouse mindfulness by saying, "Do this;

do not do that. By that alone, they performed what was to be done and abandoned what was not to be done. Therefore, because they were easy to speak with and possessed the capacity for application, they abandoned [faults] through the mere arousal of mindfulness; therefore, you too should abandon them.
The meaning is as follows. "With *elaṇḍa* plants": it is said that *elaṇḍa* plants are destroyers of the *sāla* trees; therefore, he spoke thus. "One should cleanse":
one should cleanse by cutting down both the *elaṇḍa* plants and other creepers and removing them outside. "Well-established": well-situated. "One should maintain properly":
by establishing a boundary and watering it, and also by digging at the roots from time to time.

He would raise and nourish [the child] properly even by cutting down creepers, shrubs, and the like, by taking away the *kipilla* and *pūṭaka* insects, and by taking away the spiderwebs and dried sticks.
"Growth" and so forth have already been explained in their proper places. 226.

Now, in order to show the fault of impatience (*akkhanti*), he spoke the passage beginning with "In the past... (*bhūtapubbaṃ*). Therein, "Vedehikā" refers to [the daughter] of one who lived in the kingdom of Videha.
"Daughter. Alternatively, "knowledge" (*veda*) refers to wisdom; one who strives or conducts herself by means of that knowledge is a "knower" (*vedehikā*), meaning a wise woman.
"Housewife" (*gahapatānī*) means the mistress of the household. "Fame" (*kittisadda*) means the sound of renown. "Gentle" (*soratā*) means endowed with gentleness (*soracca*).

"Humble" (*nivātā*) means modest in conduct. "Tranquil" (*upasantā*) means extinguished [of defilements]. "Skilled" (*dakkhā*) [refers to being adept] in tasks such as cooking food, spreading out beds, and lighting lamps.
*Chekā*: "Analasā" means industrious; "susaṃvihitakammantā" means having one's work well-organized.
He shows that while one [wife] is industrious, the other is not like her, for whatever vessel she takes up, she either breaks it or makes a hole in it.
"Rising by day" means she rose after sunrise, having failed to perform the duties that ought to be done early in the morning, such as milking the cows.
"Hey, you black one! means "O black woman. "Why have you risen by day? means "Is there something unwell with you?
Why have you risen by day? "Indeed, nothing at all, you wretch! means "If there is nothing unwell with you—if your head does not ache, nor..."
Her back [was aching], yet why did that wicked slave-girl rise so early in the day? Becoming angry and displeased, she made a frown.
"She rose even earlier in the day" means that on the following day she rose even sooner.
Speaking words of displeasure means saying such things as, "O wicked slave-girl, you do not know your own measure; do you think fire is cold? Now I shall discipline you! and so forth.
She uttered angry words.

"To those who live in the neighboring houses" means to those residing in the immediate vicinity. "She caused them to revile" means she caused them to treat her with contempt. "Fierce" means unchaste and wicked.
Thus, twice as many faults arose as there were virtues. For virtues, indeed, arrive only very gradually.
Defilements spread throughout a single day. "Extremely gentle" (*soratasorata*) means exceedingly gentle;
he reaches the point where it must be said whether he is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arahant. "Touching" means they come into range by touching or striking.
"Then the bhikkhu should be known as gentle" means that the bhikkhu who stands firm in the patience of endurance is to be known as gentle.

It is to be understood as follows: "For the sake of robes... [and so on]... for the sake of requisites" refers to one who, when receiving these very excellent robes and so forth, performs services such as massaging the feet or rubbing the back with a single word [of gratitude]. "Not obtaining them" means not obtaining them in the same manner as one previously did.
"Honoring the Dhamma alone" means performing honor and well-done service toward the Dhamma alone.
"Treating as heavy" means making it a heavy burden. "Honoring" means making it dear through the mind.
"Worshiping" means worshiping with the offering of requisites. "Reverencing" means reverencing the Dhamma itself, showing respect and humble conduct. 227.
Having thus shown the fault in intolerance, [the text now states] that those who endure [insults] endure them in this way; thus, the five...
Showing this in the course of his speech, he said: "These five, monks," and so forth. Therein, "at the right time" means at a fitting and appropriate time.
"True" means real and existing. "Gentle" means well-spoken. "Endowed with meaning" means based on purpose and based on reason.
"At the wrong time" and so forth are to be understood as the opposites of those very qualities. "With a mind of loving-kindness."
"Having become one whose mind possesses loving-kindness" (*uppannamettacittā*); "possessing hatred within" (*dosantarā*) means having a corrupted mind, with hatred arisen within.
"Therein" (*tatra*) refers to those paths of speech. "Pervading" (*pharitvā*) means resolving upon it. And as for "having that as its object" (*tadārammaṇaṃ*):
how does one make the entire world have that as its object? Having taken up the person who has come along the five paths of speech, [one directs] the mind of loving-kindness...
Having made that very mind of loving-kindness the object, one then makes all beings the object; thus it is said that one "makes the entire world its object.
Herein, this is the meaning of the words: *tadārammaṇañca* means having made that very mind of loving-kindness the object.
*Sabbāvantaṃ* means possessing all beings. *Lokaṃ* means the world of beings. *Vipulena* means by way of many beings as the object.
"Exalted" means belonging to the exalted plane. "Immeasurable" means well-developed. "Harmless" means free from malice. "Unafflicted" means free from suffering.
"Pervading, we shall dwell"—this means that we shall dwell having resolved upon such a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, making both that person and the entire world the object of that mind.
228. Now, bringing forth a simile that illustrates this meaning, he said, "Just as if," and so forth.
Therein, "I shall make it non-earth" means "I shall turn it into what is not earth. "In this and that place" means in various locations.
"Should scatter" means that having taken up soil from a basket, one should scatter it like seeds. "Should spit" means one should drop saliva. "Non-earth"—[the rest follows].
"Could he do so? means: even by applying effort through both body and speech, would he be able to make the earth not-earth?
"Deep" means: it is deep by virtue of its thickness, being two hundred thousand and forty million leagues deep.
"Immeasurable" means: it is, moreover, unlimited across its breadth. "In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile: like the earth...

For loving-kindness (mettā-citta) must be regarded as such. Just as a person who has come carrying a spade and a basket is unable to turn the great earth into non-earth with that spade and basket, even so,
a person who has come employing the five modes of speech will not be able to alter the state of one’s mind of loving-kindness.
229. In this second simile, "yellow" refers to anything of yellow color, such as turmeric. "Blue" refers to either bronze-blue or the blue of the *palāsa* flower.

"Formless" (*arūpī*) means without form. But surely, the space between two pieces of wood, or two trees, or two beds, or two rocks is described as having a delimited form; why, then, is it said here that it is "formless"?

Because it is the negation of the state of being visible. For this very reason, it is said to be "non-demonstrable" (*anidassana*). Indeed, in that [space], it is impossible to write down form or to show the manifestation of form;
therefore, it is called "formless" (*arūpī*). "Non-demonstrable" means it is not within the range of the visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
In the application of the simile here, loving-kindness (*mettācitta*) is like space. The four [elements] with the *tulika* as the fifth—
The five paths of speech are like the five colors; the person who has come taking those five paths of speech is like the man who has come taking the five colors with a brush.

Just as that man cannot produce the manifestation of a form in the sky by means of the five colors and a brush, so too a person who has come taking the five paths of speech cannot effect a transformation in a mind of loving-kindness.
...having done so, he will not be able to demonstrate the arising of hatred.

230. In the third simile, "blazing" means set on fire. Regarding the words "deep and immeasurable": in this Ganges River, there are deep places measuring a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, or even a full *yojana*.
Its breadth is likewise of such a measure; as for its length—
But [it is] five hundred yojanas [deep]. How is it that it is deep and immeasurable?

Because by this method, even if one were to turn it over, it could not be heated like water on a stove. However, standing water could be heated by some means even to the extent of a finger’s breadth or half a finger’s breadth;
but this [ocean] cannot be so. Therefore, thus...

Thus it was said. In the application of the simile here, loving-kindness (*mettacitta*) is like the Ganges River, and the person who has come taking a torch is like the individual who has come taking up the five modes of speech.
Just as he cannot heat the Ganges with a burning torch, so too the person who has come taking up the five modes of speech cannot cause any alteration in the state of loving-kindness.
"He will not be able to do it.
In the fourth simile, "a cat's skin-sack" refers to a bag made of cat hide. "Well-beaten" means thoroughly beaten.
"Well-rubbed down" means rubbed down well on the inside, the outside, and all around. "Fuzzy" means like the cotton of the *simbali* tree or the fibers of the *latātūla* plant.
"Chinnasassarā" means those whose sound of laughter has been cut off. "Chinnabhabbharā" means those whose sound of lamentation has been cut off. Regarding the application of the simile here:
loving-kindness (*mettā-citta*) is like the cat’s skin-bag;
the person who comes taking sticks and pebbles is like the individual who comes having seized the five paths of speech. Just as he [strikes] the cat’s skin-bag with a stick or a pebble...

Just as one cannot produce a sound that is "sarasara" or "bharabhara," so too, a person who comes having grasped the five pathways of speech will not be able to cause a change in your mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) or to bring about a state of being overcome by hatred. 232.
*Ocarakā* means those who move about, those who go below; the meaning is "those who perform low deeds. *Yo mano padūseyya* means...
If a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī should corrupt their mind, they should not endure being cut with a saw. By that non-endurance, such a person does not carry out my instruction;
by that non-endurance, they do not follow my advice. However, there is no offense in this case. 233.
"Whether slight or gross" means whether of minor censure or of great censure. "That which you should not endure."
The meaning is: "that which should not be accepted by you. "Certainly not, Bhante," [they replied].

The intention is: "Venerable Sir, we do not see any course of speech that should not be accepted. Thus the Blessed One, reaching the peak with the attainment of Arahatship, concluded the teaching according to the sequence of the discourse for the long-term welfare and happiness [of beings].
The commentary on the Kakacūpama Sutta in the Papañcasūdani, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 2.
The commentary on the Alagaddūpama Sutta.
234. “Thus have I heard” introduces the *Alagaddūpama-sutta* (The Simile of the Snake). In that context, *gaddhabādhino* means those who harassed vultures (*gaddha*).
One whose ancestors were such harassers of vultures is a *gaddhabādhipubbo*; the meaning is: of one born into a family of vulture-killers.

They are called *antarāyikā* because they create obstacles to heaven and liberation. They do so by way of [unwholesome] actions, defilements, karmic results, slanders, and transgressions of the rules.
It is fivefold. Among these, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya*) are called "obstructions to karma.

Likewise, the act of violating a bhikkhunī is an obstruction only to liberation, not to heaven. The states of fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi*) are called "obstructions to defilements" (*kilesa*).
The states of rebirth-linking for eunuchs, animals, and those with both sexual organs are called "obstructions to fruition" (*vipāka*).

The offenses consisting of slandering the Noble Ones are called "obstructions caused by slander"; they remain such only as long as one does not ask the Noble One for forgiveness, and no longer after that.
The seven classes of offenses committed intentionally are called "obstructions caused by transgression of the command";
they remain such only as long as one continues to claim the status of a monk, or does not undergo rehabilitation, or does not confess them, and no longer after that.
In this case, there was a monk who was learned and a preacher of the Dhamma;

he knew of those obstacles that are external, but because he was unskilled in the Vinaya, he did not know of those obstacles consisting of the transgression of formal rules (paṇṇatti). Therefore, having gone into seclusion, he thought thus:
"These householders, while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, are even stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. So too are the monks [who enjoy] pleasing things..."
They see forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on] ...they touch tangibles cognizable by the body; they enjoy soft coverlets, robes, and so forth—all this is permissible.
Why then are only the forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles belonging to women not permissible?
These too are permissible. Thus, having compared taste with taste, and having considered both enjoyment with desire and lust, and...

Treating the enjoyment of that which is devoid of desire and lust as one and the same, it was as if he were attempting to bring an extremely fine thread together with coarse hemp, or as if he were trying to join Mount Sineru with a mustard seed; having thus given rise to an evil view, he thought:
"Why has the Blessed One, with such great effort—as if binding the great ocean—laid down the first *pārājika* offense?"
"There is no fault here"—by speaking thus, he contradicted the knowledge of omniscience, obstructed the knowledge of fearlessness, and cast stumps and thorns into the Noble Path;
he dealt a blow to the Wheel of the Conqueror’s command by asserting that there is no fault in sexual intercourse.
Therefore he said: "In this way, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One," and so forth.
"Evaṃ byā kho" means "it is indeed thus. Regarding such terms as "samanuyuñjanti" (interrogate), they interrogate when asking, "What is your tenet?
State your tenet. They cross-examine when establishing a view. They reprove when asking for the reason, "For what reason do you say this?
Regarding "aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā" (like a skeleton) and so forth, [the phrase] "aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā" means like a skeleton.

In the sense of providing little gratification; like a piece of meat, in the sense of being common to many; like a grass torch, in the sense of burning up; like a pit of embers, in the sense of great torment;
like a dream, in the sense of appearing for only a short time; like a borrowed object, in the sense of being temporary;
like the fruit of a tree, in the sense of crushing all the limbs and members; like a butcher’s block and knife...
In the sense of cutting down further. Like a spear or a stake in the sense of piercing through. Like the head of a snake in the sense of being dangerous and fearful.
"By the power of strength" means by the power of views. "Adhering" means by the adherence to views. "He speaks having adhered" means he speaks having resolved upon it, or he proclaims it.
"Since, monks, those bhikkhus... means when those bhikkhus... "Thus indeed, Bhante, have I been instructed by the Blessed One."
Although he wished to say, "I do not have this myself," out of his own inclination, he accepted it through the power of the Blessed One;
for indeed, it is said that there is no one capable of engaging in two kinds of conversation in the presence of the Buddhas.
"Of whom, O foolish man, are you [the disciple]?"—O foolish man, of which kshatriya or brahmin?
“Whether it be a farmer, a merchant, an artisan, a laborer, a householder, one gone forth, a deva, or a human—do you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way?
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus; this is the separate connection (*pāṭiyekko anusandhi*).
It is said that Ariṭṭha thought: “The Blessed One calls me a ‘foolish person,’ yet he does not...”
By the mere utterance of the words "foolish man" (moghapurisa), there is no removal of the decisive support (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits.
For even the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta was admonished by the Blessed One with the address "foolish man," saying: "Foolish man, you have indeed turned too quickly toward abundance.
Yet later, that elder, striving and exerting himself, realized the six direct knowledges (abhiññā). I too [must apply] such energy.

“Having taken it up, I shall produce the paths and fruits. Then the Blessed One, demonstrating that for him who had been released from his bonds there was no further growth—just like a withered leaf—began this teaching:

“Bhikkhus, what do you think of this? This Ariṭṭha, possessing such a view, [was examined] by the knowledge of omniscience... [and so forth]. "Even though he has been made warm... means, "Bhikkhus, what do you think of this? regarding this Ariṭṭha who held such a conviction, by means of the knowledge of omniscience...

Having opposed [the truth], having obstructed the knowledge of fearlessness, and striking a blow at the wheel of the Tathāgata’s command—even so, could there be even a "warmth" in this Dhamma and Vinaya?
Just as even when a great mass of fire has been extinguished, there remains at least a tiny spark of fire, depending on which another great mass of fire might arise; is it not so? What then?
"Does he possess even a slight spark of knowledge (*ñāṇusmā*) by means of which, through striving, he might realize the paths and fruits?"—
"Certainly not, venerable sir."— "Venerable sir, how could one who holds such a view possess such a spark of knowledge?"—
They say this while rejecting the state of being "heated" (*usmīkata*) by a spark of knowledge capable of serving as a condition for the paths and fruits. "Maṅkubhūto" means having become lusterless.
"Pattakkhandho" means one whose shoulder (of the body) has fallen. "Appaṭibhāno" means seeing no resource at all;

with his resource shattered, reflecting upon his own incapacity—thinking, "Even though I have obtained such a teaching that leads to liberation, I am indeed one whose nature is not to grow, and I have become one for whom the conditions [for progress] have been destroyed"—he sat down scratching the ground with his big toe.
“You will indeed be known” is also a separate connection [in the narrative]. It is said that Ariṭṭha thought:
“The Blessed One says that my support for the paths and fruits has been cut off;
yet Buddhas do not teach the Dhamma only to those who possess such a support, they teach it even to those who lack it. Having received the ‘Well-spoken Admonition’ from the Teacher, I—”
“I shall perform wholesome deeds that will lead to my own success. Then the Blessed One, putting an end to his exhortation, said, “You shall be known,” and so forth.
The meaning of this is: “O foolish man, you alone shall be known in the hells and other realms because of this evil speculative view;
there is no such thing as ‘the Sugata’s instruction’ for you from my presence, and I have no concern with you.”
"Here, monks, I shall question you.
Now, "Then the Blessed One... is also a separate connection.
For at this point, the Blessed One clears the assembly and expels Ariṭṭha from the group. For if it were to occur to anyone present in the assembly:
“Will this Ariṭṭha be able to speak what has not been spoken by the Blessed One?
Perhaps he spoke impulsively when the discourse was begun by the Blessed One in the midst of the assembly? However, it is not only Ariṭṭha who hears what is thus spoken;
others will have heard it as well. Then it might also occur to him: “The Teacher is rebuking Ariṭṭha...”
"Even upon hearing, 'I too should thus restrain myself,' he would fall into silence. "They will not do all that," [the Buddha thought].
Since it had not been spoken by me, nor heard by anyone else, he cleared the assembly's misconception with the words, "You too, monks," and so forth.
By clearing the assembly's misconception, Ariṭṭha was indeed expelled from the community.
Now, in order to clarify Ariṭṭha’s tenet, the Buddha said: "That monk, O bhikkhus," and so forth. Therein, regarding the phrases "apart from sensual pleasures" and so on:

that monk, O bhikkhus, who holds the tenet that "these are not sufficient to cause an obstacle for one who indulges in them"—he, indeed, [must indulge] apart from both the sensual pleasures of defilement (*kilesakāma*) and from the perceptions and thoughts associated with those sensual pleasures of defilement; these are the phenomena [he must avoid].
"It is impossible, it cannot happen, that he, having abandoned these things and being without these qualities, would indulge in worldly pleasures or engage in sexual intercourse;
there is no such cause for this, it is an impossibility, it is out of the question.
(238) Thus the Blessed One spoke, as if saying: "This Ariṭṭha is like a washerman who [uses] both fragrant and foul-smelling [dyes], and even those that are worn out..."
Just as one might make a single bundle of cloths, both new and pure as well as old and impure,
even so there is the enjoyment of choice robes and other requisites by monks who lack desire and lust, which causes an obstacle for householders whose morality is unbound,
and the enjoyment of [such things] with desire and lust by monks whose morality is bound, which acts as a hindrance.
Having thus set forth the view of Ariṭṭha—that one makes everything identical—[the Blessed One] now spoke the passage beginning with "In this case, monks, some...
in order to show the fault of wrongly grasping the scriptures (*pariyatti*). In that context, "they master" means they learn.

Regarding the terms *sutta* and so forth: [the *sutta* category includes] the two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra; and within the *Suttanipāta*, the Maṅgala-sutta, Ratana-sutta, Nālaka-sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka-sutta.
Furthermore, other words of the Tathāgata called *sutta* should be understood as *sutta*.
All *sutta* that contains verses should be understood as *geyya*, especially the entire Sagāthāvagga in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, *sutta* that is devoid of verses, and whatever other word of the Buddha is not included within the eight *aṅgas*, that is *veyyākaraṇa*.
It should be understood as follows: the *Dhammapada*, the *Theragāthā*, the *Therīgāthā*, and the pure verses not titled as specific suttas within the *Suttanipāta* are to be known as *gāthā*.
The eighty-two discourses (*suttanta*) associated with verses consisting of joy and knowledge are to be known as *udāna*.
The one hundred and ten discourses occurring in the manner beginning with “This was said by the Blessed One” (*vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā*) are to be known as *itivuttaka*.
They are to be understood as follows: the more than five hundred Jātakas, beginning with the *Apaṇṇaka-jātaka*, are to be understood as the *Jātaka*.

All discourses (*suttanta*) proceeding in the manner of "Bhikkhus, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in Ānanda," and so forth, which are connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, are to be understood as the *Abbhutadhamma*.
These include the *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sammādiṭṭhi*, *Sakkapañha*, *Saṅkhārabhājaniya*, *Mahāpuṇṇama-sutta*, and others.
All those discourses that have been requested, having repeatedly received both knowledge and satisfaction, are to be understood as *vedalla*.
"They do not examine the meaning" means they do not see or grasp the meaning of the meaning, the meaning of the cause. "Of those who do not examine" refers to those who are not examining.
"They do not endure contemplation" means they do not become established [in the mind] and do not come into the range of perception.
The meaning is that it is impossible to know: "In this place, virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, the round of existence, and the cessation of the round were taught.
"And they [study] for the sake of finding fault" means that they master [the texts] with the aim of attributing faults to the doctrines of others.
"And for the sake of escaping such arguments" means for the sake of escaping arguments in that manner.
The meaning is that they master the teachings for this very reason: thinking, "When others attribute faults to our own doctrine, we shall thus clear away those faults.

And they do not experience its purpose: those who grasp things wrongly do not experience the purpose of that Dhamma for the sake of which sons of noble family master the Dhamma—namely, the goal of either the path or the fruit.
Furthermore, even those who are unable to level a censure against the opponent’s doctrine or to defend their own doctrine do not actually attain that goal either. 239. “One who desires a *alagadda*”:
one who desires a venomous snake. For *gada* is a name for poison; because it possesses (*atthi*) that [poison] fully (*alaṃ*) and completely, it is called an *alagadda*.
“Wealth” (*bhoga*) refers here to the body. But in this context, monks, some sons of good family [seek] the Dhamma...
"They master" means they learn by way of mastery for the purpose of crossing over. For there are three kinds of mastery:
the mastery of the water-snake, the mastery for crossing over, and the mastery of the storekeeper.
Among these, one who has learned the word of the Buddha [thinks], "In this way I shall obtain robes and so forth," or "In the midst of the fourfold assembly..."
If one masters [the teachings] for the sake of gain and honor, thinking, "They will know me," that mastery is called "mastery of a poisonous snake.
For one who masters in such a way, it would be better not to master the Buddha’s word at all than to fall asleep after having mastered it.
However, he who, having learned the Buddha’s word, fulfills virtue in the places where virtue is taught, and [fulfills concentration] in the places where concentration is taught...
Having caused [the student] to grasp the womb of concentration, he masters it with the thought: "I shall establish insight wherever insight is required;
I shall develop the path and realize the fruit wherever the path and fruit are required. For such a person, that mastery of the scriptures is called the "mastery for crossing over."
But for one whose taints are destroyed, the mastery of the scriptures is called the "treasurer's mastery.

For him, there is nothing that is not fully understood, abandoned, cultivated, or realized. He has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, cultivated the path, and realized the fruit;
therefore, when he masters the word of the Buddha, he is a bearer of the lineage, a protector of the tradition, and a guardian of the heritage.
Having sacrificed [his own comfort], he learns it. Thus, his mastery of the scriptures is called "the treasury-master’s mastery.
But as for the worldling who, when those who bear the texts are unable to stay in one place due to hunger, fear, and so forth, does not himself grow weary through wandering for alms, thinking:
"May the exceedingly sweet word of the Buddha not be lost; I shall uphold the tradition (tantra)," [he too masters it].
If one masters [the teachings] thinking, "I shall establish the lineage; I shall preserve the tradition," that mastery is a mastery of a storekeeper;
does it not exist? It does not exist. Why? Because it was mastered without standing in its own place.
For a worldling, what is called mastery is either like seizing a water-snake or like crossing over; for the seven types of trainees, it is only the crossing over.
For one whose taints are destroyed, this is merely the mastery of a storehouse-keeper; however, in this context, what is intended is the mastery of deliverance.

Regarding the phrase "they endure contemplation": in the passages concerning virtue and so forth, here virtue is mentioned, here concentration, here insight, here the path, here the fruit, here the round of existence, and here the cessation of the round—these come into the range of vision.
"And they experience its meaning" means that for the sake of those paths and fruits for which they have mastered the teachings,
they experience the meaning of that Dhamma by realizing the fruit after developing the path based on well-mastered scripture.
Even though they are able to level criticisms against the doctrines of others, they [do not] attribute the faults raised against their own doctrine to whatever point they desire.

Even those who are able to take [the defilements] and release them still experience [their results]. "They lead to welfare and happiness for a long time" means that even for those fulfilling virtue (sīla) and the other perfections in the contexts where virtue and so forth are taught;
or for those raising objections against the doctrines of others through reasoning consistent with the Dhamma;
or for those removing faults from their own position; or for those who, having attained Arahatship, preach the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly—[all these lead to welfare and happiness].
Even for those who enjoy the four requisites offered by those inspired by his teaching of the Dhamma, these lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
Having thus shown the benefit of properly grasping the Buddha’s word, he now exhorts them to apply themselves to it: "Therefore, in this regard..."
He said, "O bhikkhus," and so forth. Therein, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means:

because a poorly grasped scripture leads to harm and suffering for a long time—just like a snake caught by the wrong end—whereas a well-grasped scripture leads to welfare and happiness for a long time—just like a snake caught by the right end;
that is the meaning. Likewise, "you should bear it in mind thus" means: in exactly that way.

You should hold it; you should accept it for that very reason. Or else, those who are experienced bhikkhus—meaning other experienced and wise bhikkhus such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāna, and so forth—should be consulted.
However, like Ariṭṭha, one must not throw mud or refuse into my teaching.
240. “Like a raft” (*kullūpama*) means similar to a raft. “For the purpose of crossing over” means for the purpose of crossing over the four floods.
Regarding “the ocean” (*aṇṇava*): water that is deep but not broad, or broad but not deep, is not called an ocean.
However, that which is both deep and broad is called an ocean. Therefore, it is great.
"Abounding in water" means there is great, wide, and deep water; this is the meaning here.
"Perilous" means where the dwelling places of thieves are seen—where their standing places, sitting places, or lying-down places are seen.
"Dangerous" means where people are seen to have been killed by thieves, robbed, or beaten.
They are seen. "Uttarasetu" means a bridge built across the surface of a body of water. "Having bound a raft" (*kulla*):

a raft (*kulla*) is that which is constructed and tied together as a bundle for the purpose of crossing. However, mats, baskets, and the like, which are bound by being spread out, are called "floats" (*uḷumpa*).

"Having left behind" (*uccāretvā*) means having set aside. "One who performs what is to be done" (*kiccakārī*) means one who acts appropriately, one who acts suitably; the meaning is "one who acts in a fitting manner."

"Even mental phenomena (*dhammā*) are to be abandoned by you. Here, "mental phenomena" refers to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). For the Blessed One caused the abandoning of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) for both serenity and insight. Where did he cause the abandoning of desire and lust for serenity?
"Thus, Udāyi, I say there is even the abandoning of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; do you see, Udāyi, that fetter (*saṃyojana*)? [he asked].
In the passage, “Whether subtle or gross, that which I do not say should be abandoned,” he caused the abandonment of desire and lust for serenity (*samatha*).

In the passage, “If you, monks, would not adhere to, cherish, or treasure this view, though it be so pure and so bright,” he caused the abandonment of desire and lust for insight (*vipassanā*). But here, however—
Causing them to abandon both, he said: "Even phenomena (dhammā) must be abandoned, how much more so non-phenomena (adhammā).
Herein, this is the intended meaning: "Monks, I speak of the abandoning of desire and lust even for such things as these which are truly desirable;
how much more so for this base practice, this village custom, this practice of the outcastes, this vile thing, this mere water-side affair?"
"Where this foolish man Ariṭṭha, perceiving them as faultless, says that desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure are not capable of being an obstacle—
just as with Ariṭṭha, you too must not throw mud or refuse into my teaching.
In this way, by means of this exhortation as well, the Blessed One rebukes Ariṭṭha himself.

241. Now, in order to show that whoever grasps at the five aggregates by way of the threefold grasping—thinking "I" and "mine"—casts filth and rubbish into my teaching, just as Ariṭṭha did, he said: "Bhikkhus, these six," and so forth.
In this context, "bases for views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni*) means both the view itself is a basis for views, and the object of a view is also a basis for views.

There is also a condition for views. In such expressions as "This form is mine," "this is mine" (*etaṃ mama*) refers to the grasping of craving (*taṇhāggāha*). "I am this" (*eso hamasmi*) refers to the grasping of conceit (*mānaggāha*).
"This is my self" (*eso me attā*) refers to the grasping of views (*diṭṭhiggāha*). Thus, craving, conceit, and views are explained as having form as their object.

However, it should not be said that "form is the self. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. What is seen is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*); what is heard is the sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*).
The sensed consists of the sense-sphere of odors, the sense-sphere of tastes, and the sense-sphere of tangibles; for it is called "sensed" because it is to be grasped upon being reached.
The remaining seven sense-spheres are called "cognized. "Attained" means attained either by seeking or without seeking.
"Sought" means that which is sought, whether already attained or not yet attained. "Mentally explored" refers to the mind.
It has been pursued by the mind. For in this world, there is that which is obtained after searching and that which is not obtained after searching;
there is also that which is obtained without searching and that which is not obtained without searching. In this context, what is obtained after searching is called "obtained";
what is not obtained after searching is called "searched for. What is obtained without searching... [and so on].
And that which is not obtained is called "mentally traversed.
Alternatively, whether it has been obtained after searching or obtained without searching, it is called "obtained" in the sense of being acquired.
That which was not obtained despite searching is called "searched for. That which was not obtained without searching is called "mentally traversed. Or else, all [of these]...
Because it is investigated by the mind, it is called "investigated by the mind. By this, craving, conceit, and views having consciousness as their object are described;
through the elegance of the teaching, consciousness was previously shown by way of objects such as what has been seen and so forth.
"That which is a basis for views" refers to that basis for views which occurs in the manner beginning with "that which is this world," and so on.

“The world is the self”: this refers to the view that occurs in the manner described by the passage beginning, “one regards form as the self,” which grasps both the world and the self as being one and the same; it was said with reference to that. “Having passed away, I shall exist”:
“I, having gone to the other world, shall be eternal, permanent, everlasting, and subject to no change,” [as distinct] from Sineru, the great earth, the great ocean, and so forth.
"I shall remain exactly the same as those who hold to eternalism. He regards even that [view] as "mine," thinking: "This view is mine;
this am I; this is my self. By this, craving, conceit, and views having the [wrong] view as their object are explained.
This occurs at the time when the preceding view is grasped by the subsequent view, just as during the stage of counter-insight (*paṭivipassanā*) in the course of insight (*vipassanā*).
In the bright fortnight (the path of purification), by the thought "form is not mine," the grasping of craving, conceit, and views regarding form is rejected.
The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. Regarding the term *samanupassati* ("regards"), its meaning consists of four kinds of regard:
the regard of craving, the regard of conceit, the regard of views, and the regard of knowledge. These [four] belong to the dark fortnight (the side of defilement).
This should be understood by way of the contemplation of knowledge on the bright side among the three types of contemplation.
"He does not tremble when there is nothing" means that he does not tremble with fear or with the trembling of craving toward what is non-existent.
By this, the Blessed One brought the teaching to its culmination, demonstrating the one whose taints are destroyed who does not tremble at the destruction of the internal aggregates.
242. When this was said, a certain monk—meaning a certain monk skilled in the sequence of the teaching—[reflected]:
"The Blessed One has concluded his teaching by showing the one whose taints are destroyed as being undistressed at the destruction of the internal aggregates.
Now, while there is one who is undistressed internally, [he considers] one who is distressed internally regarding the internal [to be] external..."
"Whether one is distressed or undistressed by the loss of requisites, one must remain undistressed. Thus, for these four reasons, this question should be asked.
Having reflected thus, he arranged his robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in salutation, and said this to the Blessed One:
"‘Non-existence externally’ means the loss of external requisites. ‘Alas, it has come to me!’..."
"Ah, what a fine carriage, vehicle, bullion, or gold I once had! is the meaning.

"That indeed is no longer mine" means that it is now no longer mine; it has been taken away by kings or thieves, burnt by fire, swept away by water, or worn out through use. "May it indeed be mine" means: may a carriage or vehicle be mine.
"Gold, silver, rice, paddy, barley, and wheat—'Alas, I do not obtain that!
Because he sits without performing the appropriate work for it when he does not obtain it, thinking, 'Now I do not obtain it,' he sorrows; this is the sorrow of the householder.
For one who has gone forth, it should be understood by way of the bowl, robes, and so forth."
In the section on non-terror, "it does not occur thus" means that because those defilements by which it might occur thus have been abandoned, it does not occur thus.

"Views, bases for views, adherence to views, obsession by views, misapprehension, and underlying tendencies" refers to views, bases for views, adherence to views, obsession by views, misapprehension, and underlying tendencies. "For the stilling of all formations" means...

For the sake of Nibbāna. For it is by coming to Nibbāna that all stirrings of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), all tremblings of conditioned phenomena, and all quiverings of conditioned phenomena are stilled and completely pacified;
therefore, it is called "the stilling of all conditioned phenomena.

And it is by coming to that very state that these acquisitions—namely, the acquisition of the aggregates (*khandha*), the acquisition of defilements (*kilesa*), the acquisition of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the acquisition of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*)—are relinquished.
Craving is exhausted, fades away, and ceases; therefore, it is said: "The relinquishing of all acquisitions is the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation.
"For the sake of Nibbāna" is the description of its essential nature.
Thus, by all these words, the meaning is illuminated: that he teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna.
"It occurs to him thus" means that it occurs to that theorist: "I shall be annihilated," "I shall perish," "I shall no longer exist.

For fear arises in one who hears the Dhamma being taught after the three characteristics have been applied to it and made connected with emptiness. Indeed, this has been said: "For this, monks, is fear..."
“May I not be for the uninstructed worldling, and may it not be for me.
(243) Thus far, emptiness has been explained by way of these four alternatives (*catukka*):
the destruction of external requisites—whether they perish or do not perish—and the destruction of internal aggregates—whether they perish or do not perish. Now, [the following is said]:
Having designated external requisites as "possessions" (*pariggaha*), having designated the twenty-based view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) as "clinging to a self" (*attavādupādāna*),
and having designated the sixty-two views headed by the view of individuality as "the basis for views" (*diṭṭhinissaya*), [the Buddha] spoke the passage beginning with "That, monks,
is possession" in order to demonstrate the threefold emptiness (*suññatā*). Therein, "possession" refers to that which is external.
"Appurtenances. "You might take possession of them" means as a wise person would take possession. "And I too, monks," means:
"Monks, you do not see it, and I too do not see it"; thus he shows that such a possession does not exist.
In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.

244. Having thus shown emptiness through the threefold method, he now speaks the passage beginning with "Bhikkhus, when there is a self" in order to show the twofold method by treating the internal aggregates as "self" and external requisites as "belonging to the self.
Therein, this is the summary meaning: Bhikkhus, when there is a self, [one regards] this collection of requisites as "belonging to the self."
Or, while the requisites exist within oneself, one might think, "This is my self; this self is the owner of these requisites"—thus one would say "I am.

It would be logical to say "I am" when there is a sense of "mine," and "mine" when there is a sense of "I am. "Truly" means from the perspective of what has come to be (*bhūta*); "really" means from the perspective of suchness (*tathatā*) or stability.
Now, one who does not grasp these five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self by way of the three turnings:
Showing that this Ariṭṭha, like [the others], was throwing mud and refuse into my teaching, he said: "What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent?
and so forth. Therein, "impermanent, venerable sir" means: venerable sir, because having come to be, it does not remain, therefore it is impermanent.
It is so called in the sense of being subject to arising and passing away, and in the sense of opposing permanence through its state of change and temporality.
It is impermanent for four reasons. "Suffering, venerable sir," means that it is suffering in the sense of being oppressed;
it is suffering for four reasons in the sense of the suffering of burning, the suffering of being the basis for suffering, and the negation of pleasure.
"Subject to change" means having the nature of undergoing transition through the passage of existence, and having the nature of abandoning its original state. It is fit...
"Is it now appropriate to regard that as 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'?
"Is it right, venerable sir, to grasp those three—craving, conceit, and views—in such a way as 'I' and 'mine'? "Certainly not, venerable sir.
By this, those bhikkhus acknowledge that form is non-self because it is beyond one's control. This is in the sense of its being empty, ownerless, without a master, and a negation of a self.
It is selfless for four reasons.
For the Blessed One demonstrates selflessness in some instances by way of impermanence, in some by way of suffering, and in some by way of both.
"If one were to say that the eye is the self, that is not tenable; for the eye has both arising and passing away."
It is discerned. Furthermore, for one in whom both arising and passing away are discerned, it occurs to him: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say, "The eye is my self"; thus, the eye is non-self.
For in this *Chachakka Sutta*, he demonstrates non-selfhood by way of impermanence: "And here, this form..."
"Bhikkhus, if form were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain regarding form:

'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. But because, bhikkhus, form is not-self, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot obtain regarding form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.'"
In this *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*, the absence of self is demonstrated by way of suffering: “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self;
what is non-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
In this Arahant Sutta, he demonstrates selflessness by way of both [impermanence and suffering]. Why? Because impermanence and suffering are manifest, whereas selflessness is not.
For when things such as vessels used for consumption are broken, people say, "Oh, how impermanent! but there is no one who says, "Oh, how selfless!"
When boils, pustules, and the like arise on the body, or when one is pierced by a thorn, people say, "Oh, what suffering!
But there is no one who says, "Oh, what non-self! Why is that? Because this so-called characteristic of non-self is unmanifest, difficult to see, and hard to establish.
Therefore, the Blessed One demonstrates it either by way of impermanence, or by way of suffering, or by way of both.
This was demonstrated even in this threefold cycle by way of impermanence and suffering alone.

The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. Therefore, "Bhikkhus, since... means: Bhikkhus, because form is now, and at other times as well, impermanent, suffering, and non-self; that is the meaning. "Whatever form," and so forth, have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the Exposition of the Aggregates.
245. "He becomes disenchanted" means he becomes weary. And here, "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) is intended as insight leading to emergence.
Indeed, there are many names for insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*). For it is called "the culmination of perception" (*saññagga*) in some places;

"knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) in some places; "the factor of striving for purification" (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*) in some places; "purification by knowledge and vision of the way" (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) in some places;
"the exhaustion of absorption in that" (*tammayatāpariyādāna*) in some places; in some places it is given by three names; and in some places by two.
In that regard, first, in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*, it is stated as the "pinnacle of perception" (*saññagga*) thus: "Perception, Poṭṭhapāda, arises first; knowledge arises later.
In the *Susīma Sutta*, it is stated as "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) thus: "First, Susīma, comes knowledge of the stability of phenomena;
later comes knowledge of Nibbāna. In the *Dasuttara Sutta*, it is called "the factor of exertion for the purification of knowledge and vision of the way" (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*).

Thus, the terms for purification have been explained. In the *Rathavinīta Sutta*, it is stated: "Friend, for the sake of what is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the purpose of purification by knowledge and vision of the way? Thus, purification by knowledge and vision of the way has been explained. In the *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga*:
"Bhikkhus, depending on non-identification, relying on non-identification, there is that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity..."
“Having avoided that [state], by relying upon and depending on that equanimity which is unified and based on unity, there comes to be the abandoning of this [equanimity] in this way;
there comes to be the surmounting of it in this way. Thus, the exhaustion of being-made-of-that (tammayatā) is stated.
In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: “The desire for deliverance, the contemplation of reflection, and equanimity regarding formations—these states...”
It is stated in three ways as "identical in meaning, differing only in phrasing.
In the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated in two ways as "adaptation is a condition for change-of-lineage by way of proximity-condition; adaptation is a condition for cleansing by way of proximity-condition.
However, in this *Alagaddūpama Sutta*, it is presented under the name "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) as "one becomes disenchanted."

"Through disenchantment one becomes dispassionate": here "dispassion" refers to the Path. "Through dispassion one is liberated": here it is the Fruit that is described as being liberated by means of the Path. "When there is liberation, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated'"—here "reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇā) is described.
Having thus shown the one whose mind is liberated and who has destroyed the great taints, [the Buddha] now speaks the passage beginning with "This, monks...
while assigning names to him according to his five actual qualities. "Ignorance" (avijjā) refers to ignorance rooted in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). For this...
It is called a "cross-bar" (*paligha*) in the sense of being difficult to remove. Because it has been removed by him, he is called "one who has removed the cross-bar.
"Made like a palm stump" means made like a palm tree with its head cut off, or like the base of a palm tree after the tree has been uprooted with its roots;
just as that palm tree is no longer perceived again at that site, so too [the offense] is rendered non-existent for future prescription.
This is the meaning. "Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobbhavika*) means that which brings about renewed existence. Regarding the terms "the round of births" (*jātisaṃsāra*) and so forth:
the formative volition of karma (*kammābhisaṅkhāra*) is the condition for those aggregates of renewed existence which have thus received their name by way of both being born and wandering on.
For it is called "encompassing" (*parikkhā*) because it stands having encompassed [them] by way of causing repeated arising; therefore, this...
Because it is cluttered and scattered, it is called "cluttered and surrounded. "Craving" refers to craving rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
