For this [craving] is called a "pillar" in the sense that it has gone deep down. Therefore, because that pillar has been pulled out—uprooted and cast away—he is called "one who has pulled out the pillar.
"Lower-fettering" means those things which lead downward, serving as conditions for rebirth in the realm of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*).

For these are called "bolts" (aggala) because they stand having closed off the mind, like a door-panel closing a city gate. Therefore, because he has rejected and broken them, he is called "boltless" (niraggaḷa).
"Noble" (ariya) means free from defilements and utterly pure. "With banner lowered" (pannaddhaja) means one whose banner of conceit (māna) has fallen.

"With burden laid down" (pannabhāra) refers to the burden of the aggregates (khandha), the burden of defilements (kilesa), the burden of volitional formations (abhisankhāra), and the burden of the five strands of sensual pleasure (pañca-kāmaguṇa).

"One whose burden has been laid down" (*pannabhāra*) means one who has laid down wisdom (*paññā*). Furthermore, it is intended here as "one whose burden has been laid down" because the burden of conceit (*māna*) alone has been set aside.

"Dissociated" (*visaṃyutta*) means dissociated from the four yokes (*yoga*) and from all defilements (*kilesa*). However, it is intended here as "dissociated" because of being dissociated specifically from the yoke of conceit (*asmimāna-yoga*).
"Conceit of 'I am'" (*asmimāna*) is the conceit "I am" with respect to form (*rūpa*), [and likewise] with respect to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), ... [and so forth].
Regarding volitional formations... regarding consciousness, there is the conceit "I am.

To this extent, the Blessed One has shown the time of the one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), who—having destroyed the defilements by means of the Path and having entered the supreme bed of cessation—abides having attained the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object. For it is just as with two cities:
There was one city of thieves and one city of safety. Then, it might occur to a certain great warrior:
"As long as this city of thieves stands, so long will the city of safety not be freed from fear;
I shall make the city of thieves a non-city. Having thus put on his armor and taken up his sword, he approached the city of thieves and stood at the city gate.
Having cut down the raised pillar with his sword, broken the door-panels and the door-bolts,
lifted up the cross-bar, breached the wall, and cleared away the moat; having cast down the flags raised for the sake of the city’s beauty and set the city ablaze with fire,
he entered the city of Khema, ascended the palace, and sat surrounded by his circle of kinsmen.

One might eat food mixed with poison; in this way, *sakkāya* (the basis for personal existence) is like a city of thieves, *nibbāna* is like a city of safety, and the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is like a great warrior.
It occurs to him: "As long as the cycle of *sakkāya* continues, there is no liberation from the thirty-two tortures, the ninety-eight diseases, and the twenty-five great fears.
Like that great warrior, he puts on the armor of virtue (*sīlasannāha*) and takes up the sword of wisdom (*paññākhagga*).
Having seized it with his sword, he plucked out the stake of craving by means of the path of arahantship—just as a soldier [plucks out] a wooden stake;
having thrown open the bolt of the five lower fetters like the city gate-bar of a fortress;
having cast aside the crossbar of ignorance like a soldier [removing] a crossbar; and having broken down the wall like a soldier [breaking] a rampart.
Breaking the formative volitional formations (*kammābhisaṅkhāra*) and having exhausted the cycle of birth and wandering,
that warrior— having felled the banner of conceit like a flag raised for the beautification of a city, and having set ablaze the city of *sakkāya*—

enters the city of the extinction of defilements (*kilesanibbāna*), which is like delicious food in the upper palace of the city of security, taking as his object the cessation of the deathless (*amatanirodha*).
Experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he passes his time.
Now, showing that the consciousness of one whose mind is thus liberated and whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted cannot be attained by others, [the Blessed One] said:
"But when the mind is thus liberated," and so forth. Therein, "they seek" means searching and investigating. "This is dependent upon... [and so on].

This is dependent on a name. Regarding the phrase "of the Tathāgata": here, both the sentient being (*satta*)—the Tathāgata as the supreme person who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*)—is intended.
"Incomprehensible" (*ananuvijjo*) means either not found (*asaṃvijjamāno*) or unfindable (*avindeyyo*).
For if "Tathāgata" refers to the sentient being, the meaning "not found" is appropriate; if it refers to one who has destroyed the taints, the meaning "unfindable" is appropriate.
In this regard, the intention of the former method is as follows: "Bhikkhus, even while still living in this very life, I do not designate one whose taints are destroyed as a 'being' or a 'person.
But when he has attained final Nibbāna without rebirth, how could I designate that one whose taints are destroyed as a 'being' or a 'person'? The Tathāgata is unfathomable; for indeed—"
In the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "being" (satta). Even if they were to search for this consciousness that is dependent upon that which does not exist, what would they find?
The meaning is: how could they obtain it? In the second method, the intention is this:
"O monks, even while I am living in this very life, one whose taints are exhausted [I describe] by way of consciousness to Indra and the others."

I say it is unknowable. For even the gods, including the Saindas, the Brahmas, and the Pajāpatis, though they search for it, are not able to know the insight-consciousness, the path-consciousness, or the fruition-consciousness of one whose taints are destroyed, such that they could know: "This consciousness is occurring in dependence upon this specific object.
If they cannot know this of one who has attained final Nibbāna without rebirth, what will they know?
"By the non-existent" means by that which does not exist. "By the empty" means by that which is hollow. "By the false" means by lying speech.

"By the untruthful" means by that which is not there. "They misrepresent" means they speak over and above; they speak having exceeded [the facts]. "Disciplinarian" (*venayika*): it is called *vinaya* because it disciplines (*vinayati*) or destroys (*vināseti*);
that very thing is the *venayika*. The intended meaning is "one who destroys beings. And as it is said: "In such a way as I am not, O monks..."
"Monks, by whatever manner I am not a destroyer of beings, and by whatever reason I do not speak thus, that is to say, by whatever cause I do not prescribe the destruction of beings—
this is what is meant: 'Inasmuch as I am not a destroyer of beings and do not prescribe the destruction of beings,
so those worthy recluses and brahmins call me a "destroyer," a recluse...'"

By saying "Gotama," they falsely, vainly, falsely, and untruthfully misrepresent him by saying, "The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings," and by saying, "He proclaims the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being," they misrepresent him by saying, "He proclaims the destruction of beings.
"In the past" means previously, at the very seat of Great Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa). "And now" means at this present time during his teaching of the Dhamma.

"I proclaim suffering and the cessation of suffering"—the meaning is that even while dwelling on the seat of enlightenment before setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, and even while teaching the Dhamma from the time the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion onwards, I proclaim only the Four Truths.
For here, by the mention of "suffering," its root, which is the origin (samudaya), is implied; and by the mention of "cessation," that which brings it about...
It should be understood that the path has indeed been taken. "Therein" means in that exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
"Others" refers to persons who are incapable of understanding or penetrating the truths. "Abuse" means they abuse them by means of the ten grounds for abuse.
"Revile" means they revile them with their speech. "Hurt and harass" means with the intention: "We shall hurt them; we shall harass them."
They strike and cause suffering. "Therein" means among those insults and so forth, or toward those other persons.
"Ill-will" (āghāta) is anger. "Resentment" (appaccaya) is mental distress. "Discontent" (anabhiraddhi) is dissatisfaction.
"And therein" refers specifically to the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths. "Others" refers to those who seek to understand and penetrate the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths.

"Competent persons. "Ānanda" refers to the joy of bliss (*ānanda-pīti*). "Exultation" (*uppilāvitatta*) refers to the joy of exhilaration (*uppilāpana-pīti*). "Therein" (*tatra*) means precisely in the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths.
"In that" (*tatra*) refers to honors and so forth. "This which was previously fully understood" (*yaṃ kho idaṃ pubbe pariññātaṃ*):

this pentad of aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*) was previously fully understood by means of the three types of full understanding at the Seat of Enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that pentad of aggregates.
"These. What is meant by this? Even in that regard, it does not occur to the Tathāgata, "These honors are being performed for me," or "I am experiencing these.
It occurs to him only this much: "The very pentad of aggregates previously fully understood is what experiences these honors.
Therefore, because they are incapable of penetrating the Truths, they revile even the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the remainder should be understood in the manner already stated.

247. "Therefore, monks, that which is not yours"—since the abandonment of desire and lust even for what belongs to oneself leads to welfare and happiness for a long time, therefore the meaning is: "That which is not yours, abandon it."
"Or one may act according to conditions" means that one may act in whatever way one desires.
"For this, venerable sir, is not our self," they say; "venerable sir, this grass, wood, branches, and foliage is neither our self nor our form, nor is it our consciousness.
"Nor is it ours" means that even our requisites such as robes and so forth do not belong to us.

The meaning is as follows. "In the same way, monks, whatever is not yours, abandon that," said the Blessed One. By showing that the pentad of aggregates alone is "not yours," he causes it to be abandoned;
yet this is not done by tearing it out or pulling it out. Rather, he causes it to be abandoned through the removal of desire and lust (*chandarāga-vinaya*). 248.
Regarding the phrase "thus well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*), it is appropriate to cite this point starting from the threefold revolution (*tiparivaṭṭa*) onwards.
It is even appropriate to bring this matter forward, starting from the point that through mere affection one is destined for heaven, and proceeding in reverse order down to this present state.
"Well-expounded" means well-spoken. Precisely because it is well-spoken, it is clear, revealed, and made manifest.
"With its tatters cut away": here "tatters" refers to a worn-out cloth that is torn, broken, sewn together in various places, knotted, and decayed.
He who does not possess that [robe], but wears an unwashed cloth eight or nine cubits in length, is called a "wearer of rags" (*chinnapilotika*).
This Dhamma is likewise; for herein there is no state of being cut, torn, sewn, or knotted by way of hypocrisy and the like.
Moreover, "rags" (*pilotika*) refers to refuse. And in this Dispensation, it is impossible for the refuse of a recluse to find a footing.
He does not obtain it. Therefore he said:
"Sweep away the kāraṇḍava reeds, and pull out the rubbish;
then winnow away the chaff, those who are not ascetics but pride themselves on being ascetics."
"Having expelled those of evil desires, those of evil conduct and resort,
dwell in purity together with the pure, being mindful. Then,
being harmonious and prudent, you shall make an end of suffering."
Thus, because the refuse of the ascetic life has been cut away, this Dhamma is called "one whose shreds are severed.
"The round does not exist for them to be described" means that for them the round has reached the state of being unmanifested; it has become devoid of manifestation.
A Great One with such taints destroyed arises only within the well-proclaimed Dispensation. And as it is with one whose taints are destroyed, so it is with Non-returners and the others as well.
In this context, the Dhammānusārī (follower by Dhamma) and the Saddhānusārī (follower by faith)—these two are those established on the path of stream-entry. As it is said:

"And what kind of person is a Dhammānusārī? It is the person who, while practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, possesses a predominant faculty of wisdom; one whose noble path is carried by wisdom and preceded by wisdom."
He develops [it]. This person is called a follower of the Dhamma (dhammānusārī). A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is a follower of the Dhamma;
one established in the fruit is one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto). And what is a person who is a follower by faith (saddhānusārī)?
It is that person who, while practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, possesses a preponderance of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya).
"One develops the Noble Path with faith as its vehicle and faith as its precursor. This person is called a 'follower by faith' (saddhānusārī).
A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is a follower by faith; one established in the fruit is 'liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta).

By the phrase "those who have even a mere measure of faith and a mere measure of affection toward me," it refers to those who possess no other noble quality (ariyadhamma) besides that, [and who place their trust] in the Tathāgata.
However, there is merely faith and merely affection. These are the individuals intended as "insight-observers.
For when bhikkhus who are insight-observers sit having thus established insight, a single faith and a single affection arise toward the One of Ten Powers.
By that faith and by that affection, they are as if held by the hand and placed in heaven; it is said that their destination is certain.
The ancient elders, however, call such a bhikkhu a "minor stream-enterer" (*cūḷasotāpanna*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Alagaddūpama-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
3. Commentary on the Vammika Sutta (The Ant-hill Discourse).
249. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Vammika Sutta. In this context, "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment.
"Kumārakassapa" is his name; however, because he went forth while still a youth, the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa here; this is the fruit..."
When it was said, "Give either solid food or soft food to Kassapa," [the question arose] "To which Kassapa?
Because he had taken the name "Kumārakassapa" (Young Kassapa), from that time on, even in his old age, he was called only "Kumārakassapa.
Furthermore, they knew him as "Kumārakassapa" because he was the king's foster son. This, however, was due to his previous practice...
The Discourse on Manifestation from the Beginning—
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there was a son of a merchant. Then one day,
seeing the Blessed One appointing a certain disciple as his successor in the position of chief preacher, he gave alms to the Blessed One for seven days.
Having given [the gift], he made this aspiration: "May I too, O Blessed One, in the future become a disciple of a Buddha, eloquent in varied discourse just like this elder.
While performing meritorious deeds, he went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, yet he was unable to achieve any distinction.

At that time, it is said, while the teaching of the Blessed One who had attained final Nibbāna was declining, five bhikkhus constructed a ladder, climbed a mountain, and practiced the ascetic life (samaṇadhamma).
On the third day, the senior elder of the group attained Arahantship.
On the fourth day, the junior elder became a Non-returner (anāgāmī). The other three, being unable to achieve any further distinction, [remained] in the world of the gods.

They were reborn. While they were enjoying prosperity among gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, one of them was reborn into a royal family at Takkasilā and became a king named Pukkusāti.

Having gone forth under the Blessed One, while traveling toward Rājagaha, he heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma in a potter’s workshop and attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
One [monk] was born into a noble family on a certain seaport town; having boarded a ship, his vessel was wrecked, and he attained prosperity by wearing garments of bark.
Having given rise to the thought, "I am an Arahant," he was exhorted by a benevolent deity who said, "You are not an Arahant;
go and ask the Teacher a question. Having done so, he attained the fruit of Arahantship.
He was born in Rājagaha from the womb of a certain girl of good family.

Having first requested permission from her parents but not obtaining it for her own going forth, she went to her husband’s home; there, unaware that she was pregnant, she gratified her husband, and with his consent, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs.
When the bhikkhunīs saw the signs of her pregnancy, they [reported it] to Devadatta.
They asked him, and he said, "She is no longer a female ascetic. They asked the Ten-Powered One, and the Teacher entrusted the matter to the Elder Upāli.
The Elder, having summoned the families residing in the city of Sāvatthī as well as the laywoman Visākhā, investigated the case and declared:
"The pregnancy was conceived previously; her ordination is valid. The Teacher remarked, "The legal question has been well adjudicated," and [praised] the Elder.
She gave her approval. That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image;
taking him, King Pasenadi of Kosala raised him. Having given him the name Kassapa, the king later adorned him, led him into the presence of the Teacher, and had him ordained.
Thus, because he was the king’s foster-son, they knew him as “Kumārakassapa.”
"In the forest named Andhavana. It is said that this forest, having retained its name throughout the time of two Buddhas, was known simply as Andhavana.
Herein is the explanation of the rule: for the bodily relics of Buddhas of short lifespan do not remain as a single solid mass;
by the power of their resolve, they are scattered. For this very reason, even in our own case, the Blessed One—
At the time of his Parinibbāna, [the Buddha] resolved: "I shall not remain for long; I have been seen by few beings, while those who have not seen me are far more numerous.
May they take my relics and, worshipping them here and there, become destined for heaven.
Thus he willed that his own body be dispersed. However, for Buddhas of long life, such as Suvaṇṇakkhandha...
The relic-body remained as a single solid mass.
It remained exactly so for the Blessed One Kassapa as well. Then the great multitude gathered together and deliberated, saying, "The relics cannot be separated because they are a single solid mass;
what shall we do? Having thus reflected, they decided, "We shall construct a stūpa that is likewise a single solid mass."
"But how large should it be? they asked. Some said, "Seven yojanas. "That is too large; it will not be possible to maintain it in the future," they said.
"Let it be six yojanas," "five yojanas"... "four yojanas"... "three yojanas"... "two yojanas"... "one yojana," they decided.
Then, determining what kind of bricks should be used, they made the outermost bricks out of red gold.
"Let them be worth one hundred thousand [pieces] each; let those on the inner edge be worth fifty thousand.
Having decided that the function of clay should be performed with yellow orpiment and red arsenic, and the function of water with oil, they divided the four faces into four parts.
The king took one face, Prince Pathavindara took one, and the ministers...
One became a general as the eldest [of his kin], and one became a merchant (*seṭṭhi*) as the eldest of the districts.
There, because of their great wealth, even the king had gold brought out and began work with it taken into his own mouth;
so too did the viceroy and the general. But when the merchant took his portion into his mouth, the work lagged behind. Then, [there was] the one named Yasorata...
There was a certain lay follower, a master of the Three Piṭakas, a reciter, a non-returner, and a noble disciple.
Knowing that his work would be delayed, he harnessed five hundred carts, went to the countryside, and said:

"The Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, having remained for twenty thousand years, has attained final Nibbāna. A jeweled stupa one league in size is being constructed for him; whoever is able to give, let them give."
"Let him give gold, or bullion, or the seven precious gems, or yellow orpiment, or red arsenic," he thus encouraged them.
People gave gold, silver, and other such things according to their own means; those who were unable to afford these gave even oil, rice, and the like.
The lay follower sent oil, rice, and other provisions for the wages and food of the laborers, while the remainder [was used by] the others.
Having caused gold to be purchased, he sent it; in this manner, he traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
When the work at the cetiya was finished, they sent a letter from the site of the cetiya, saying:
"The work is finished; let the teacher come and worship the cetiya. He too sent a letter, saying: "I have exhorted the whole of Jambudīpa."
"Take whatever materials are available and complete the work. The two letters met on the way;
however, from the teacher's letter, the letter from the site of the cetiya reached the teacher’s hand first.
Having read the letter, he set out alone, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the cetiya. On the way, in a forest wilderness, five...
Sixty thousand robbers rose up. Among them, some who saw him said, "This man has gathered all the gold and bullion from the whole of Jambudīpa;
surely the jars of treasure have come rolling out for us," and having informed the rest, they seized him.
"Why, dear ones, do you seize me? [They replied: "By you, all the gold and bullion from the whole of Jambudīpa has been gathered."
"Give us a little bit as well. "Do you not know? The Blessed One Kassapa has attained final Nibbāna, and a jeweled stupa one *yojana* in height is being constructed for him;
it was for that purpose that I was exhorted by others, not for my own sake.
Whatever I have received from various places has been sent right there [to the stupa], but I have kept nothing except for this single lower garment (*nivāsana*) I am wearing."
“There is not even a single kākani coin of other wealth.
Some said, “Teacher, release him in this way. Others said, “This man is honored by the king and honored by the ministers;
if they see him anywhere in our city streets, they will report it to the king, the royal ministers, and so forth, and he will meet with ruin and disaster.”
“...should cause him to attain [death],” they said. The lay follower replied, “Sirs, I shall not do this.
This was out of compassion for them, and not from a lack of attachment to his own life.
Then, while they were disputing over whether he should be seized or released, those who held the view that he should be seized became the majority and took his life.
Due to their offense against those noble disciples of powerful virtue, their eyes vanished like the flame of an extinguished lamp.
Lamenting, "O where is our sight? O where is our sight?", some were led home by their relatives;
others who were not their kin, being without protectors, remained right there in the forest at the foot of trees or in leaf-huts. [The forest...]
People who arrived out of compassion would give them rice, cooked food from their own provisions, or travel expenses.
When people who had gone for the sake of wood, leaves, and so forth returned, they were asked, "Where did you go? and they would reply, "We went to the Andhavana.
Thus, during the time of both Buddhas, that forest was known simply as the Andhavana. During the time of Buddha Kassapa...

This was once a wilderness in a desolate region. In the time of our Blessed One, it was a forest retreat (padhānaghara) situated behind Jetavana, not far from Sāvatthī, where noble sons seeking solitude resided;
there, at that time, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa dwelt, fulfilling the practice of a trainee (sekha). Therefore, it was said:
“Dwelling in the Andhavana forest.
“A certain deity”: the meaning is a certain deity who was not well-known by name or clan.
“Does the Blessed One, venerable sir, recall having spoken in brief to a certain person of great influence regarding liberation through the destruction of craving?”
In this context, however, even Sakka, the king of the gods, is referred to as "a certain one. Furthermore, the term *devatā* is a common designation for both gods and goddesses;

yet in this specific sense, a god (*devo*) is intended. Regarding the phrase "when the night had advanced" (*abhikkantāya rattiyā*), the word *abhikkanta* is seen used in the senses of excellence, beauty, loveliness, and appreciation, among others. Among these—“excellent... [text fragment]” —
In such passages as, "Venerable sir, it is night; the first watch has passed; the community of monks has been sitting for a long time;
let the Blessed One, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha to the monks," it is seen in the sense of *destruction*.
In such passages as, "This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," it is seen in the sense of *beautiful*.
“Who is it that worships my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory, illuminating all directions with most excellent beauty?”—in such passages as these, it means “handsome.
In such passages as “Excellent, Master Gotama,” it means “rejoicing. But here, however—
"At the end": by this, "when the night has passed away" is what is meant.
In this context, it should be understood that this son of the gods arrived immediately following the middle watch of the night. Regarding the phrase "of surpassing beauty" (*abhikkantavaṇṇa*):

here, the word *abhikkanta* means "excellent" or "beautiful. The word *vaṇṇa*, however, [is used] in reference to skin, praise, lineage, the cause of a group, shape, measure, the sense-base of form, and so forth.
It is seen. In this context: in such passages as “The Blessed One is golden-hued,” it refers to the skin;

in such passages as “But when, householder, were the praises of the ascetic Gotama uttered? it refers to praise; in such passages as “There are these four castes, Master Gotama,” it refers to the social class;
and in such passages as “Now by what quality is one called a ‘scent-thief’? it refers to [a specific characteristic].

In the sense of cause: in such passages as “having manifested the form of a great king of elephants,” it refers to shape. In such passages as “there are three qualities of the bowl,” it refers to measure.
In such passages as “color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence,” it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
Here, however, it should be understood as the skin. Thus, “of surpassing beauty” means having the beauty of beautiful skin, or having the beauty of a pleasing color.

This has been said. For when deities come to the human world, they abandon their natural form and natural psychic power (*iddhi*), assume a gross physical body, and manifest an extraordinary appearance and extraordinary psychic power;
they come with a deliberately fashioned body, just like people going to theatrical performances and the like. This son of the gods also came in that very same way. Therefore...
It is said, “of surpassing beauty.
Regarding the term *kevalakappa*: here, the word *kevala* has many meanings, such as "without remainder," "majority," "unmixed," "excessive," "firmness," and "disjunction.
For instance, in such passages as “the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is complete, perfect, and pure,” its meaning is "without remainder."
In such passages as, “The whole of Aṅga and Magadha will approach, bringing abundant food, both hard and soft,” it means *abundance*.
In such passages as, “There is the origin of the entire mass of suffering,” it means *unmixedness*.
In such passages as, “Surely this venerable one has only mere faith,” it means *non-excess*. [Regarding] “Of the venerable Anuruddha...”
In such passages as, "The co-resident named Bāhiya has stood for the entire duration [of his life] intent upon schism in the Saṅgha," the word *kappa* has the sense of firmness (*daḷhattha*).

In such passages as, "The Perfect One (*kevalī*), having lived [the holy life], is called the Supreme Person," it signifies dissociation (*visaṃyoga*). However, here its intended meaning is "without remainder" (*anavasesatta*).

Furthermore, this word *kappa* has many meanings, such as: conviction (*abhisaddahana*), conventional usage (*vohāra*), time (*kāla*), designation (*paññatti*), cutting (*chedana*), alternative (*vikappa*), a small portion (*leśa*), and totality (*samantabhāva*).
For instance, in such passages as, "This is indeed credible for Master Gotama, as it is for an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha," the meaning is "firm conviction.
In such passages as, "Monks, I allow you to consume fruit according to the five rules for monks," the meaning is "convention.
And in such passages as, "By means of which I indeed dwell constantly throughout my life," the meaning is "habitual practice."
*Kāla*: In such passages as “Thus spoke the venerable Kappa,” it means a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as “adorned, with hair and beard trimmed,” it means cutting (*chedana*).

In such passages as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted (*kappati dvaṅgulakappo*),” it means an arrangement (*vikappa*). In such passages as “there is the opportunity (*atthi kappo*) to lie down,” it means a slight amount (*leso*).
In such passages as “having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove (*kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ*),” it means all-aroundness (*samantabhāvo*). Here [in this context]...

The meaning intended here is its state of being all-encompassing. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the entire blind forest," the sense should be understood as "the blind forest completely and without exception.
"Having illuminated" means having pervaded [it] with the radiance arising from his robes, ornaments, and body, like the moon or the sun.
"And as if making a single radiance and a single light" means he made them appear as one. "He stood to one side" means he stood in one corner, in one place.
"He said this" means he spoke these words beginning with "Bhikkhu, bhikkhu.

But why did he speak thus without bowing, using the very designation "ascetic"? It was because of his habitual perception and mode of address toward ascetics. For it is said that such was his [perception].
He thought: "This one was formerly a master in the sense-sphere realm. But I, from that time onwards, have been a celibate practitioner.
Thus, the perception of him as a recluse arose in him; therefore, not having paid homage, he addressed him using the conventional term "recluse.
It is said that this son of the gods was formerly a companion of the Elder. From what time? From the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa.
This is that very person who, among the five companions mentioned in the *Pubbayoga*, was called the junior elder (*anuthera*) and became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) on the fourth day.
It is said that at that time, supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) arrived for them along with the Elder of the Sangha’s attainment of Arahantship.
Thinking, "My task has reached its culmination," he rose into the air, washed his face at Lake Anotatta, and—
Having brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and returned, he said, "Friends, eat this almsfood and practice the duty of a recluse with diligence.
The others replied, "Friend, we have no such agreement as this:
'He who first attains a distinction and brings back almsfood shall eat what he has brought, and the rest [shall eat what they have brought]'."
“The duty of a recluse must be performed. “By means of your own supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), you have brought your task to completion.
We too, if we possess such supporting conditions, shall bring our task to completion. This is a distraction for us; you may go.
Having departed as he pleased, he attained final nibbāna at the end of his life.
On the following day, the junior elder realized the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) came to him as well.
He too, having brought almsfood in the same manner, was refused by them; he went wherever it was convenient for him and, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*).
While remaining in the Pure Abodes and looking back upon those two companions, he saw that one had already attained final Nibbāna at that time, while the other had only recently done so.

Seeing that another person, having attained the noble plane in the presence of the Blessed One, was now living in the port city of Suppāraka due to gain and honor, having conceived the thought, "I am an Arahant," [the Elder] approached him and exhorted him, saying: "You are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahantship;
go, approach the Blessed One, and listen to the Dhamma. He, too, while walking through the village...

Having requested instruction from the Blessed One, Bāhiya was exhorted by the Blessed One in brief, saying: "Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: 'In the seen, there shall be only the seen.
Having received this exhortation, he attained the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*).
Then, another person, looking for him here and there, saw that he was dwelling in the Andhavana forest, fulfilling the practice of one in training (*sekkhapaṭipada*).
Having seen this, he thought: "I shall go into the presence of my friend;
however, it is not fitting for one who goes to go with empty hands, so I ought to take some gift along. Now, my friend lives on a mountain peak free from worldly desires;
even when I stood in the air and offered him alms-food, he did not consume it, but instead practiced the duty of a recluse."
"Now, what material gift will he take? I shall go taking the gift of the Dhamma.
While still standing in the Brahma-world, as if stringing together a garland of jewels, he analyzed fifteen questions;
then, taking that gift of the Dhamma, he returned and stood not far from his companion. Because of his habitual practice of the perception of a recluse, he did not even salute him.
Having addressed him as "Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu," he spoke these words beginning with "This is an anthill.
In this context, the repetition "Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu" should be understood as an emphatic address due to the urgency of the situation.
Or, just as a forehead does not shine with a single mole, but shines like a blossoming ornament when others are added around it, so too speech [shines] with more than a single word.
"It does not shine; it shines like something blooming and adorned together with its surrounding parts.
Thus he spoke even while making that statement bloom and adorn it by means of those surrounding words.
"This anthill"—there is no such thing as an anthill standing before one in reality; rather, it is [referred to] as standing before one by way of the teaching.
He said this as if showing [the way]. "A spade" (*laṅgi*): taking up a tool, he dug and saw a crossbar.
"Lift up the spade, O wise one, dig away!"—my dear, O wise one, that which is called a "spade" smokes at night and blazes by day.
"Lift it up"—it digs further on from what is beyond. In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. "A swelling" (*uddhumāyika*)...
A frog. A *caṅkavāra* is a sieve for straining alkaline water. A tortoise is a turtle.
A butcher’s block is both a knife for cutting meat and a chopping block. A piece of meat is a lump of raw flesh about the size of a *nisada* leaf.
He saw a great serpent with a hood like a cluster of jasmine flowers, encircled by three folds of skin.
"Do not disturb the nāga" means: do not disturb the nāga by throwing sticks, vines, or even dust and sand at him with the tip of a staff or the tip of a creeper.
"Pay homage to the nāga" means: stepping aside from the windward side, put on clean clothes and pay homage to the nāga.
Wealth "rested upon by a nāga" lasts for as long as seven generations of one's family.
"While you eat, it will not be exhausted; the Nāga will give you even more wealth than what you have consumed. Therefore, pay homage to the Nāga. Regarding the phrase "or having heard from here":
in the *Dukkhakkhandha Sutta*, the word "from" (*ito*) refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*);
it is not so here. Here, however, it refers to the son of the gods (*devaputta*). Therefore, the meaning here is: "or else, having heard from me."

251. "Of that which consists of the four great elements" (*cātummahābhūtikassa*) means made of the four great elements. "This is a designation for the body" (*kāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ*) is a name for the physical frame.

For just as an external anthill is called an "anthill" for four reasons—namely, because it "vomits" (*vamati*), thus it is a "vomit-maker" (*vantaka*), a "support for vomit" (*vantussaya*), and a "connection with the moisture of vomit" (*vanta-sineha-sambandha*)—so too this [body] contains various kinds of things such as snakes, mongooses, rats, owls, and crickets.
It is called a *vammika* because it vomits out small creatures; it is called a *vammika* because it is vomited up by termites.
It is called a *vammika* because it has been heaped up by the dust and powder raised from the mouths and beaks of termites until it reaches the height of a hip or even the height of a man.

Due to being bound together by the moisture of the saliva vomited by the termites, it does not crumble even when it rains for seven days and seven nights, nor does it collapse even in the heat of summer.
Then, having taken a handful of soil, when it is pressed with the fist, moisture comes out; thus, because it is bound together by vomited moisture, it is called a "termite-mound" (*vammika*).
In this same way, this body is also a "termite-mound," for in the manner described by the phrase "from the eye, the eye-excrement," and so forth, it vomits various kinds of impure filth.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed [are like this] through the exhaustion of attachment to this personal existence.
Because they have gone away after casting off their own personal existence (*attabhāva*), this anthill is called "vomited by the Noble Ones" (*vantakoti*).

Furthermore, because all that by which this [body]—propped up by three hundred bones, bound together by sinews, smeared with flesh, covered with raw skin, and colored by the outer integument—deceives living beings, is itself vomited by the Noble Ones;
thus the anthill is also called "the bed of what has been vomited" (*vantussaya*). "Craving gives birth to a person; its mind..."
"runs about. Thus, because it is produced by craving (*taṇhā*), it is bound by the very "moisture of craving" (*taṇhāsineha*) which has been vomited up by the Noble Ones (*ariya*);
hence it is called "bound by vomited moisture" (*vanta-sineha*).
And just as within an anthill (*vammika*) various kinds of creatures are born right there, void excrement and urine are deposited, the sick lie down, and the dead fall; thus, it belongs to them.
It becomes a maternity home, a latrine, a sickroom, and a charnel ground.
Thus, even the bodies of wealthy kṣatriyas and others—though protected by guards, adorned, and beautified—are the bodies of those possessed of great power;

yet, disregarding this, there are creatures dwelling in the skin, creatures dwelling in the hide, creatures dwelling in the flesh, creatures dwelling in the sinews, and creatures dwelling in the bones and bone-marrow.
Thus, by counting families, about eighty thousand families of worms are born right within the body;
they discharge excrement and urine, lie down afflicted by disease, and fall dead.
Therefore, this [body] is the birth-chamber, the latrine, the infirmary, and the cemetery for those living beings, and it is designated as a "mound" (*vammiko*).
He has gone. Therefore the Blessed One said: “‘An anthill,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements.
“Born of mother and father” means produced from what originates from the mother and the father, having come into being through the semen and blood of the mother and father.
“Built up by boiled rice and sour gruel” means accumulated and increased by means of both boiled rice and sour gruel.
"Subject to being rubbed, massaged, broken, and destroyed": herein, this body is "subject to impermanence" in the sense of its non-existence after having come to be.

It is "subject to rubbing" by means of the application of unguents for the purpose of counteracting foul odors. It is "subject to massaging" by means of light rubbing for the purpose of dispelling afflictions in the limbs and members.
Or, as in childhood, when it is laid upon the thighs due to dwelling in the womb...
It is subject to being rubbed down by means of pulling, pressing, and so forth, for the purpose of restoring the proper shape of those various ill-formed limbs.
And even while being thus cared for, it is subject to breaking up and disintegration; it both breaks and scatters—this is the meaning of its having such a nature.
In this context, the "origin" is indicated by the terms: produced from mother and father, accumulated through boiled rice and sour gruel, and maintained by clothing and rubbing down.

By means of the phrases concerning impermanence, breaking up, and destruction, passing away has been explained. Thus, it should be understood that by these seven phrases, the rise and fall, the increase and decrease, and the arising and passing away of the body composed of the four great elements have been described.
"In the daytime work" refers to the tasks to be performed during the day. Regarding the word "smoking" (*dhūmāyana*): here, this term *dhūma* [is used] for anger and for craving.
In the context of "thought" (*vitakka*) and the "five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañca kāmaguṇā*), the term *dhamma* refers to the teaching of the Dhamma; it applies to these meanings.
However, in the phrase "Anger is the smoke, shame is the ash," it applies to anger.
In the phrase "Beings are smoking with desire," it applies to craving (*taṇhā*). Furthermore, at that time, a certain monk was sitting not far from the Blessed One, smoking.
In this context, it refers to applied thought (*vitakka*).
"Sensual pleasures are a mire, sensual pleasures are a quagmire;
this fear has been proclaimed as having three roots."
“Dust and smoke have been proclaimed by me;
having abandoned these, O Brahmadatta, go forth!”—here [the dust] refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
“One becomes a maker of smoke”—here it refers to the teaching of the Dhamma. “The banner of the chariot... [is as follows:]...
In the passage, “Smoke is the sign of fire,” it refers to natural smoke; here, however, this term is intended to mean *vitakka* (applied thought).
Therefore he said, “This is the smoking at night.
“This is a designation for the Tathāgata”: for the Tathāgata is a *brāhmaṇa* because of having banished (*bāhitattā*) seven things.
...by name. As it is said: “Bhikkhu, one is a brahmin because of having banished seven things.
Which seven? Lust has been banished, hatred... delusion... conceit... the view of a self-identity... doubt... and adherence to rules and observances have been banished.
Bhikkhu, because of having banished these seven things, one is a brahmin. [He was named] Sumedha.
“Of beautiful wisdom. Regarding the term *sekkhassa*: here, one who trains is a *sekkha*. As it is said:
“One trains, monk, therefore one is called a *sekkha*. And what does he train in? He trains in higher virtue, he trains in higher mind, and he trains in higher wisdom.”
“Designation for wisdom” means that this is a designation for mundane and supramundane wisdom, not for a weapon or a tool.
“Of the arousal of energy” refers to bodily and mental energy; that [energy] follows the course of wisdom alone.
For mundane wisdom it is mundane, and for supramundane wisdom it is supramundane. Here, however, is the clarification of the meaning:

It is said that a certain brahmin from the countryside would leave his village early in the morning with his young students, spend the day teaching the mantras in the forest, and return to the village in the evening.
On the way, there was an anthill that smoked by night and blazed by day.
The brahmin said to his pupil, the young student Sumedha: "Dear son, this..."
“The anthill smokes at night and blazes by day; we shall see its transformation. Break it open, divide it into four parts, and throw them away.
“Very well,” he replied, took a spade, stood with feet level on the ground, and did exactly so.
In this context, the Blessed One is like the teacher-brahmin, and the novice monk is like the young brahmin Sumedha.
The body is like an anthill. It was like the time when the Brahmin said, “Son, this anthill smokes at night and blazes by day;

we shall observe its transformation; break it open, divide it into four parts, and throw them away,” so too did the Blessed One say, “Monk, analyze the body composed of the four great elements by dividing it into four parts.”
It is the time for speaking. Just as one who says "very well" takes up a spade and acts accordingly, so too for a bhikkhu in training:
"That which is the state of rigidity among the twenty parts is the earth element; that which is the state of cohesion among the twelve parts is the water element;
that which is the state of maturation among the four parts is the fire element; that which is [the state of distension] among the six parts..."
"The state of distension is the air element"—in this way, the discernment of the body by way of the analysis of the four elements is to be understood.
As for the statement, "Monks, it is like a crutch," why did the Blessed One show ignorance as being like a crutch?
For just as when a city gate is closed and the bolt is set, the passage of the great multitude is cut off, those who are inside the city...

Those that are inside remain inside; those that are outside remain outside. In the same way, for one upon whom the snare of ignorance falls at the entrance to knowledge, the progress of knowledge leading to the attainment of Nibbāna is cut off. Therefore, he showed it by making ignorance the "snare.
In the phrase "abandon ignorance," the abandoning of ignorance is explained here by way of grasping the meditation subject and thorough inquiry.
“‘A bloated one,’ monks—here, what is called a ‘bloated frog’ is not large; it is the size of a fingernail’s back.
It dwells among old leaves, or between grass blades, or among creepers.
When touched by the tip of a stick, or the tip of a creeper, or by a handful of dust, it expands until it becomes large and round, the size of a beluva fruit.”
Having offered [the sacrifice] and placed its four legs in the air, once it has lost its way, it falls into the power of its enemies and becomes mere food for crows, hawks, and the like.
In the same way, this anger, when first arising, is merely a turbidity of the mind.
At that moment, if not restrained, it increases and leads to the distortion of the face. If still unrestrained at that point, it leads to the clashing of the jaws.
If it is not restrained then, it leads to the utterance of harsh speech. If it is not restrained then, it leads to looking about in all directions.
If it is not restrained then, it leads to dragging and pulling. If it is not restrained then, it leads to the seizing of hands, clods, sticks, and weapons.
If it is not restrained then, it leads to the striking down with sticks and weapons. If it is not restrained then, it even leads to killing others.

It even leads to one’s own destruction. For it has been said: “When this anger, having caused another to be slain, causes oneself to be slain as well, to that extent this anger has reached its highest peak and attained its greatest expansion.

In this context, just as when a bloated corpse has its four feet raised into the air, its movement ceases, and the bloated corpse falls under the power of its enemies and becomes food for crows and other scavengers; so too...
In the same way, a person possessed of anger, having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), is unable to develop it;
he falls under the power of his enemies and becomes subject to all Māras to do with as they please. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“‘Bloating,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the agitation of anger. In this context, the agitation of anger is anger itself when it has reached a state of intensity.
In the phrase "Abandon anger and distress," the abandonment through reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhānappahāna*) is spoken of.

Regarding the term "a forked path": just as a man traveling along a road through a wilderness, possessing wealth and possessions, might reach a forked path and—unable to decide, thinking, "Should I go by this way or should I go by that?"—stands right there;

Just as robbers, having risen up against someone, bring about their ruin and disaster, even so, when a bhikkhu has taken up his fundamental meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and sits down, if doubt regarding the Buddha and the other [Three Jewels] arises, he is unable to progress in that meditation subject;
then all the Māras, beginning with the defilement-māra (kilesamāra), bring about his ruin and disaster. Thus, doubt is like a forked path.
It exists. Therefore the Blessed One said: “‘A forked path,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for doubt.
Regarding the phrase “abandon doubt,” the abandonment of doubt here is explained by way of grasping the meditation subject and thorough inquiry.
Regarding the phrase “a state of confusion,” it is like when washermen throw alkaline water into a straining cloth; then, even if one jar of water—
Even two, ten, or twenty [drops], or even a hundred pots, continue to leak; not even a mere splash of water remains.
In the same way, no wholesome state remains within a person who possesses the hindrances.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “‘The leaking roof,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for these five hindrances. Abandon them.

Regarding the phrase "the five hindrances" (*pañcanīvaraṇa*), here the abandoning of the hindrances is explained by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and by way of their specific factors (*tadaṅga*). Regarding the term "tortoise" (*kumma*):

just as a tortoise has five limbs—namely, four feet and a head—in the same way, when all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) are taken up, they consist of exactly five aggregates (*khandha*). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The tortoise..."

“Monk, this is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging. In the phrase “abandon the five aggregates of clinging,” the abandonment of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) regarding the five aggregates is taught.
Regarding the phrase “with the sword and the butcher’s block”: just as meat is placed upon a butcher’s block and chopped with a sword, so too are these beings...

Being slaughtered by the defilements of sensual desire for the sake of the objects of sensual desire, they are cut and hacked by those very defilements while placed upon the objects of sensual desire.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "The 'swords and carving-boards,' bhikkhu, is a designation for these five strands of sensual pleasure.
In the phrase "abandon the five strands of sensual pleasure," the abandoning of desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is taught.
“‘A piece of meat,’ monks—here, this so-called ‘piece of meat’ is desired by many people;
even humans such as kṣatriyas and others long for it, and even animals such as crows and others do so.

For these beings, being intoxicated by ignorance and having fallen into delight and lust, increase the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Or, just as a piece of meat sticks wherever it is placed, so too do these [beings].”
Beings bound by delight-and-lust (nandirāga) cling to the cycle of existence; even when encountering suffering, they do not grow weary of it. Thus, delight-and-lust is like a piece of meat.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “‘A piece of meat,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for delight-and-lust.
In the phrase “abandon delight-and-lust,” the abandonment of delight-and-lust through the fourth path is spoken of.

"Bhikkhu, 'nāga' is a designation for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed. Herein, the sense in which one whose taints are destroyed is called a "nāga" has already been explained in the *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta*.
"Pay homage to the nāga" means to the Buddha-nāga whose taints are destroyed:
"That Blessed One is a Buddha; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of awakening. That Blessed One is self-controlled; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of self-control."
"He teaches the Dhamma; that Blessed One is peaceful and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of peace; that Blessed One has crossed over and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of crossing over;
that Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of final Nibbāna"—thus you should pay homage to him.
This is the meaning here. Thus this Sutta became the meditation subject for the Elder. And the Elder [took] this very...
Having taken the discourse as his meditation subject and having developed insight, he attained Arahantship.

"This is its meaning" means this is the meaning of this question. Thus the Blessed One, like one taking a peak of jewels from a heap of gems, brought the teaching to its conclusion according to the sequence of the connection.
The commentary on the Vammikasutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 4.
The commentary on the Rathavinītasutta.
252. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Rathavinīta Sutta. Therein, "at Rājagaha" means in the city of that name;
for it is called Rājagaha because it was presided over by Mandhātu, Mahāgovinda, and others. Others explain its derivation in different ways, but what is the use of them?
This is simply the name of that city. Furthermore, this [name] applies both during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti).
It was a city that remained empty at other times, possessed by *yakkhas*, and stood as a forest retreat for them.
Regarding "Veḷuvana, the Kalandaka-nivāpa": *Veḷuvana* is the name of that park;
it is said to have been surrounded by bamboos and an eighteen-cubit wall, provided with gate-towers and watchtowers, blue-lustrous, and delightful. By that...
It is called Veḷuvana. And because they gave fodder for the squirrels there, it is called Kalandakanivāpa.
It is said that formerly a certain king, having come there for the sake of a pleasure excursion in the park, fell asleep after being intoxicated by wine while reclining during the day.
His attendants, thinking "the king is asleep," wandered here and there, tempted by flowers, fruits, and other such things.
He set out, and then, drawn by the scent of the liquor, a black snake emerged from a certain hollow tree and came toward the king.
Seeing it, the tree deity, thinking, "I shall give life to the king," approached in the guise of a crow and made a sound at the root of his ear.
The king woke up; the black snake turned back. Seeing this, he thought, "By her, my life was saved."
Thinking, “It has been given,” he established a supply of fodder there for the black birds and had the proclamation of safety (abhayaghosana) made.
Therefore, from that time forward, it became known as “Kalandakanivāpa. *Kalandaka* is a name for black birds.
*Jātibhūmika* means inhabitants of the native land. In this context, *jātibhūmi* refers to the place of birth. Furthermore, that [place] was neither...
The birthplace of the great kings of Kosala and others, nor that of the brahmin Caṅkī and others, nor that of Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, and others,
nor that of the eighty great disciples and other beings, is called a "birthplace" (*jātibhūmi*). However, on the day he was born,
the ten-thousandfold world system was fragrant with scattered flowers, perfumes, powders, and scents, like a single banner, like the Nandana Grove in full bloom.
Shining brightly, he remained unshaken like a drop of water on a lotus leaf;
and many miracles occurred, such as those born blind seeing forms and so forth. The birthplace of that omniscient Bodhisatta was the Sākiya country, with Kapilavatthu as its capital;
this is called his "birthplace" (*jātibhūmi*).
The Commentary on the Reverence for the Dhamma:
"Having spent the rains" means having completed the three-month rains residence and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.

"The Blessed One said this" refers to his performing a hospitable welcome for the newcomers with such words as, "Bhikkhus, I hope you have been well," and so forth; and then [he asked], "Who indeed..."
He spoke these words beginning with, "O bhikkhus... It is said that those bhikkhus were asked by way of greeting: "I hope, bhikkhus, that you are faring well; I hope you are getting along;
I hope you have come this long journey without much fatigue; I hope you have not been troubled for alms;
and from where, bhikkhus, have you come? To which they replied: "The Blessed One [was staying] in the Sākiya country..."
“We have come from Kapilavatthu, from our native land,” they said.

Then the Blessed One did not inquire after the health of Great King Suddhodana, nor of Sakkodana, nor Sukkodana, nor Dhotodana, nor Amitodana, nor of Queen Amittā, nor of Mahāpajāpatī, nor of the entire Śākya circle; rather, he himself [inquired].
And asking about a bhikkhu who had attained the ten bases of discourse and who, being endowed with practice, encouraged others therein,
he spoke these words beginning with, "Who, bhikkhus, is it? But why did the Blessed One,
instead of inquiring after the health of Suddhodana and the others, inquire specifically about such a bhikkhu?
Because of being beloved. For the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who have entered the practice are dear and pleasing to the Buddhas. Why is that?

Because of their reverence for the Dhamma. The Tathāgatas are indeed reverent toward the Dhamma, and this quality of theirs—reverence for the Dhamma—arose from the inclination they formed at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, [expressed in the thought]:
"One who dwells without respect and without deference lives in suffering."
This is to be understood. Indeed, out of reverence for the Dhamma alone, on the day of the Elder Mahākassapa’s Great Departure, the Blessed One traveled three *gāvutas* along the road to meet him.

Having traveled more than one hundred and thirty *yojanas*, he taught the Dhamma on the banks of the Ganges and established Mahākappina, together with his assembly, in Arahatship. During one afternoon meal...

Having traveled a road of forty-five yojanas, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma for three watches of the night at the residence of a potter and established the noble youth Pukkusāti in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Having traveled one hundred and twenty yojanas, he bestowed favor upon the novice Vanavāsī. Having traveled a road of sixty yojanas, he taught the Dhamma to the Elder Khadiravaniya.
Knowing that the Elder Anuruddha was seated in the Pācīnavaṃsa Grove reflecting upon the thoughts of a Great Man (*mahāpurisavitakka*),

he traveled there through the air, descended before the Elder, and offered his approval (*sādhukāra*). Having had a dwelling prepared for the Elder Koṭikaṇṇa-Soṇa within the same Perfumed Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*),
and having requested him to give a Dharma teaching at dawn, [the Buddha listened] until the conclusion of the formal recitation (*sarabhañña*).
He gave his approval. Having traveled three *gāvutas* along the road, he spoke on the benefits of the flavor of concord at the Gośīrṣa Sāla Grove, the dwelling place of the three noble sons.

The Blessed One Kassapa, having gained confidence that "this is a noble disciple established in the fruit of non-returning," went to the residence of Ghaṭīkāra the potter, took the food with his own hand, and partook of it.
When the time for the commencement of the rains retreat had approached, our Blessed One set out on a journey from Jetavana, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
King Pasenadi of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and the others were unable to turn him back.
Having returned home, Anāthapiṇḍika sat down overcome with dejection. Then a female slave named Puṇṇā said to him, "You are overcome with dejection."
“My lord,” she replied, “indeed, I was unable to turn back the Teacher. Then the thought arose in me:
‘For these three months, I shall not be able to hear the Dhamma, nor shall I be able to give gifts according to my intention.
My lord, I too will turn back the Teacher. “If you are able to turn him back, you shall indeed be a free woman. She went and—
Lying down at the feet of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, he said, "May the Blessed One turn back. [The Blessed One replied: "Puṇṇa, you live a life dependent on others;
what will you do for me? [Puṇṇa said: "You yourselves know that I have no gift to give to the Blessed One;
however, because of your turning back, I shall establish myself in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. The Blessed One—
"Excellent, excellent, Puṇṇā! Having uttered this word of praise, he turned back and entered the Jeta Grove itself.
This story became well known. When the merchant heard that the Blessed One had indeed turned back because of Puṇṇā, he set her free from slavery and established her in the position of his daughter.
She requested the going-forth and was ordained; having gone forth, she applied herself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*). Then the Teacher—
Knowing that he had begun the practice of insight, [the Buddha] uttered this verse of illumination:
“Fill the True Dhamma to fullness, Like the moon on the fifteenth day;
With wisdom made complete, You shall bring an end to suffering.”
At the conclusion of the verses, having attained *arahantship*, she became a renowned female disciple. Thus, the Tathāgatas are reverent toward the Dhamma.

Even while the Elder Nanda was teaching the Dhamma in the assembly hall, the Blessed One went there while still unwashed and, standing for the entire three watches of the night, listened to the discourse on the Dhamma;
at the conclusion of the teaching, he gave his approval. The Elder, having returned and paid homage, said:
“Venerable sir, at what time did you arrive? he asked. “Just as you had begun the discourse,” [the Buddha replied].

“You have performed a difficult task, venerable sir, for you are delicate like a Buddha. “Nanda, if you were able to teach for an aeon, I would remain standing and listen for even that length of time,” the Blessed One said. Such is the reverence for the Dhamma of the Tathāgatas.

Because they value the Dhamma, those who have entered upon the practice are dear to them; therefore, he questioned one who has entered upon the practice. Now, "one who has entered upon the practice" is fourfold:
one who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others; one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit;
one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others; and one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others.

In this regard, one who himself possesses mastery over the ten bases of discourse but does not exhort or instruct others therein—like the Venerable Bākula—is said to be practicing for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others;
the Blessed One does not question such a bhikkhu. Why? Because he does not stand on the side of the growth of my teaching.

But he who, not having attained the ten bases of discourse, instructs others for the sake of receiving the duties performed by them—like Upananda the Sakyan-son—is one practicing for the benefit of others and not for his own benefit;
such a person he does not question. Why? Because his craving has not been abandoned, like a large basket.

One who has not himself attained the ten bases of discourse and does not advise others on them, like Lāḷudāyī, is practicing neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others; such a person one should not ask. Why?
Because within him the defilements are as great as if they were to be cut by an axe.

But he who himself is a recipient of the ten bases of discourse and also instructs others in them is said to be practicing for his own welfare and for the welfare of others, like the eighty great elders such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and so forth;
it is such a bhikkhu that [the Blessed One] questions. Why? Because he stands on the side of the growth of my teaching. Here too—
Questioning in this very manner, he said, "Who then, monks," and so forth.

When those monks had been thus questioned by the Blessed One, the Blessed One asked them about a monk who, in his own native land, was practicing for the welfare of both [self and others], had attained the ten bases of discourse, and was of such a character there—asking, "Who then is such as this? and not [anything else].
There was mutual reflection or deliberation. Why? Because the Venerable Mantāṇiputta was well-known and renowned in that country like the moon or the sun stationed in the midst of the sky.

Therefore, having heard the sound of the rain-clouds, those bhikkhus—assembled together like a dense mass of clouds—began to recite their studies with great intensity, like bhikkhus who have commenced [the rains retreat].
And as they reported their teacher, the Elder Puṇṇa, to the Blessed One, their mouths—unable to fully express the Elder’s virtues—spoke all at once:
“Venerable Sir, there is an elder named Puṇṇa,” and so forth. Therein, “Puṇṇa” is the name of that elder.
However, because he was the son of Mantāṇī, he is called “Mantāṇiputta. He was highly esteemed.
He was honored for the sake of honoring his virtues. Regarding the commentary on "fewness of wishes" (*appicchatā*):
"Few-wished" (*appiccha*) means one who is devoid of wishing, wishless, and free from craving. Here, indeed, the phrasing is as if it were incomplete, yet the meaning is—
But it is without remainder; for there is not even a minute particle of evil desire within him. He is one whose taints are destroyed, having abandoned craving in every respect.

Furthermore, in this context, the following distinction should be understood: lack of fewness of wishes (*atricchātā*), evil desire (*pāpicchātā*), great desire (*mahicchātā*), and fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*).
Therein, "lack of fewness of wishes" is the longing for the gains of others when one is unsatisfied with one's own entire acquisitions. For one who is possessed of that—
Even a cooked cake from a single portion appears as if it were not well-baked and small when it falls into one’s own bowl;
yet that very same thing, when placed in another’s bowl, appears as if well-baked and large.

However, the estimation of non-existent virtues, lack of moderation in receiving, and evil desire are what is called *pāpicchatā*. Regarding this, it is said: "In this case, someone who is actually faithless claims to be faithful..."
This is indeed taught in the Abhidhamma in such passages as, "May people know me [to be thus]," and so forth. A person endowed with that [conceit] becomes established in hypocrisy (*kohañña*).
Furthermore, the lack of moderation in receiving gifts and the desire for much is called great longing (*mahicchatā*).
That too is described as: "In this case, someone being faithful desires, 'May people know me to be faithful'; being virtuous..."
"May people know me as one who is virtuous"—it is by this very method that [the person] has come to be so designated. A person endowed with such [craving] is difficult to satisfy;
even his own mother, once she has given birth, is unable to capture his heart. Therefore, it is said:
"The mass of fire, the ocean, and the person of great craving..."
“Let him provide requisites by means of a cart; let these three satisfy you.
Furthermore, the concealment of one’s existing virtues, moderation in receiving gifts, and fewness of desires is what is called *appicchatā* (fewness of wishes).
A person endowed with this, out of a desire to hide even the virtues present within themselves, [thinks], “Being faithful, I am faithful,” and so forth.

He does not wish for people to know him. Being virtuous, secluded, learned, energetic, endowed with concentration, wise, and having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*), he does not wish for people to know him as "one who has exhausted the taints," just like the Elder Majjhantika.
It is said that while the Elder was one of great exhaustion of taints, his bowl and robe were worth only a mere penny; thus, to King Asoka...
On the day of the great festival for the monastery of the Dhamma-king, he was the senior elder of the Saṅgha.

Seeing his extreme asceticism, people said to him, "Venerable sir, please stay outside for a little while. The Elder thought, "If no one shows hospitality toward a king like me, who has destroyed the taints, who else will?
Thereupon, he sank into the earth and, while still taking up the alms-food offered to the senior elder of the Saṅgha, [emerged again].
He plunges in. Being thus one whose taints are exhausted, he does not desire that people know him as "one whose taints are exhausted.
But a bhikkhu who is thus of few desires generates unarisen gain, stabilizes arisen gain, and wins over the hearts of donors;
for in whatever way he takes little because of his own fewness of desires, in that same way...
Likewise, people who have confidence in his conduct give much to him.

There is another fourfold kind of fewness of wishes: fewness of wishes regarding requisites (*paccaya-appiccha*), fewness of wishes regarding ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga-appiccha*), fewness of wishes regarding learning (*pariyatti-appiccha*), and fewness of wishes regarding attainment (*adhigama-appiccha*).
Among these, one who has few wishes regarding the four requisites is called "few in wishes regarding requisites"; he [is content with whatever] the donor provides.
He knows the measure of the gift, he knows the measure of the object to be given, and he knows his own strength.
For if the object to be given is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, he takes little according to the donor’s wish.

If the object to be given is small but the donor wishes to give much, he takes little according to the measure of the object to be given. If both the object to be given and the donor [are abundant]...
One who wishes to give much, knowing his own strength, takes only according to measure.

One who does not wish to make known the presence within himself of the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) is called "one who has few desires regarding the ascetic practices" (dhutaṅga-appiccha).
To illustrate this, there are these examples: it is said that the Elder Mahāsumana, a dweller in charnel grounds (sosānika), spent sixty years in a charnel ground.
He was so absorbed that not even another single bhikkhu knew him; for this very reason he said:
"For sixty years in the charnel ground I have dwelt without interruption;
no companion would know me—oh, what a supreme dweller in the charnel ground!"
Two brothers, the elders Dvebhātiya, lived on Cetiyapabbata. Of them, the younger brother took some pieces of sugarcane sent by his attendant and went to the elder.
"Venerable sir, please partake," he said. It was the time for the elder to finish his meal and rinse his mouth;
he replied, "Enough, friend. "Venerable sir, are you one who eats from a single sitting? he asked.
"Friend, bring me a piece of sugarcane. Although he had been a one-meal-eater for fifty years, he consumed it while concealing his ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*);
having rinsed his mouth, he then returned, having reaffirmed his commitment to the practice.
However, one who does not wish to make known his great learning, like the Elder Tissa of Sāketa, is one who has few desires regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti-appiccha*).
It is said that the Elder, thinking there was no time for formal recitation and interrogation, did not grant an opportunity for them;
instead, being urged with the words, "Venerable sir, you will obtain the exhaustion of death," he dismissed his following and went to the Kaṇikāravālikasamudda Monastery.
There, during the rainy season, acting as a benefactor to the elders, novices, and middle-ranking monks, on the Uposatha day of the Great Pavāraṇā—
Having stirred the populace with a discourse on the Dhamma, he departed.

However, one who has become a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) or any other stage of attainment, yet does not wish to make known that status as a stream-enterer and so forth, is called "one who has few desires regarding attainment" (*adhigama-appiccha*), such as the three clansmen and Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
But the Venerable Puṇṇa, having abandoned excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire, [possessed] that which is entirely the opposite of desire...
Because he was endowed with the purity of fewness of wishes known as non-greed (*alobha*), he was named Appiccha (“Few-wishes”).

To the bhikkhus as well, he spoke on the discourse of fewness of wishes, showing them the danger in these states—“Friends, excessive wishing, evil wishing, and great wishing are qualities that must be abandoned”—and [instructing] that they should conduct themselves by undertaking such fewness of wishes. By that...
It is said: "He himself is of few desires and is one who speaks to the bhikkhus on the subject of fewness of desires.
Now, we shall illuminate the specific meaning of the phrases beginning with "he himself is content," and so forth. As for the grammatical construction, it is according to the method already stated.
It should be understood. "Contented" means being endowed with contentment regarding various requisites. Furthermore, this contentment is of twelve kinds.
That is to say, there are three kinds regarding robes: contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment with whatever is suitable, and contentment with what is appropriate;
likewise for almsfood and the other requisites. This is the detailed explanation of its divisions.
Here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether it be beautiful or ugly. He maintains himself with that alone and does not long for another;
even if he receives one, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever robe is obtained.
Now, if someone is naturally weak, or is overcome by illness or old age, and finds it exhausting to wear a heavy robe, he [should share it] with a bhikkhu of similar standing.
Even when he exchanges that [robe] for a light one and makes do with it, he remains content; this is his contentment regarding robes according to his strength.
Another person obtains excellent requisites; having received any one of fine robes such as those made of silk, or many robes, [he thinks]:
"This is suitable for the elders who have long been ordained; this is suitable for those of great learning."
Having given [robes] with the thought, "May this be for those who are ill,
may this be for those who have little gain," even if one wears a robe made from their old robes or from rags scavenged from rubbish heaps, one is indeed content;
this is his contentment with robes as they truly are.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined;
he sustains himself with that alone and does not long for anything else, nor does he accept more even when it is offered—this is his contentment with whatever almsfood is obtained.
However, if he receives almsfood that is contrary to his own natural constitution or contrary to his illness, such that by consuming it...

He becomes uncomfortable; yet, having given that [food] to a bhikkhu of similar standing and having eaten suitable food from that person's hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength.
Another obtains a great deal of excellent almsfood; he [should give] that, like a robe, to those who have long been ordained, to the learned, to those of little gain, and to the sick.
Having given them [the choice portion] or having wandered for alms with what remains, even when eating mixed food, he remains content;
this is his contentment with what is appropriate regarding almsfood.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives a lodging that is either pleasing or unpleasing; he feels neither elation nor...
He does not give rise to aversion; he is content with whatever dwelling place he obtains, even if it is merely a bed of grass.

This is his contentment with whatever dwelling is obtained. However, if he receives a dwelling that is contrary to his natural disposition or contrary to his illness, such that he finds it uncomfortable while living there, he gives it to a fellow monk of similar character.
Even while dwelling in a suitable lodging belonging to him, he remains content; this is his contentment with a lodging according to his strength.
Another person of great merit receives many excellent lodgings, such as caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and so forth;
having given these away like robes and other requisites to those who have long been ordained, to the learned, to those of little gain, and to the sick, he dwells wherever he may be.
He is indeed content; this is his contentment with a dwelling-place as is appropriate for him. Furthermore, having reflected thus:

"A superior dwelling-place is a ground for negligence; sloth and torpor descend upon one sitting there, and when one overcome by sleep wakes up again, evil thoughts manifest," he does not accept even such a dwelling-place when it is offered.
Having rejected that [luxury], even while dwelling in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or elsewhere, he remains content;
this too is his contentment with a lodging as it happens to be suitable.
Furthermore, in this case, a bhikkhu receives medicinal requisites, whether coarse or refined; whatever he receives, by that alone—
He is contented; he does not long for anything else, and even when he receives something, he does not take it.

This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine. Furthermore, one who needs oil and receives molasses gives that to a fellow monk, takes oil from his hand, or seeks out something else entirely, and even while preparing medicine with those things, he remains truly contented.
