This is his contentment with medicinal requisites according to his strength. Another person of great merit receives abundant high-quality medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses;

yet, like [one who is content with] robes, he gives these to those who have been long ordained, to the learned, to those of little gain, and to the sick, and even while subsisting on whatever is brought by others, he remains truly contented. Furthermore, there is one who [uses] *muttaharītaka* (urine-soaked myrobalan) in a single vessel...

Setting aside the four sweets for one occasion, when told, "Venerable sir, take whatever you wish," if his illness is relieved even by one of those [other medicines], then—thinking that the so-called *muttaharītaka* (urine-harītakī) was praised by the Buddha and others—he rejects the four sweets and prepares his medicine with *muttaharītaka* alone; he is thus supremely content. This is his [practice].
Contentment with whatever is suitable regarding the requisite of medicine for the sick.
Among these three types of contentment for each of the requisites, however, contentment with what is suitable is the foremost.
The Venerable Puṇṇa was content in each of the requisites by means of these three forms of contentment. And this is the discourse on contentment.
And he spoke this discourse on contentment to the bhikkhus as well.
Regarding the praise of the threefold seclusion:
one who is "secluded" is endowed with these three kinds of seclusion—seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions.

In this regard, one goes alone, one stands alone, one sits alone, one lies down alone, one enters the village for alms alone, one returns alone, one applies oneself to walking meditation alone, one wanders alone, and one dwells alone—this is called physical seclusion (*kāyapaviveka*).
The eight attainments (*samāpatti*), however, are called mental seclusion (*cittapaviveka*). Nibbāna is the seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhipaviveka*).
Indeed, it has been said: "Physical seclusion belongs to those who dwell secluded from the body and delight in renunciation;

mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity; and seclusion from the substrates of existence belongs to persons who are substrate-free and have reached the unconditioned.
Thus, he is one who delivers this discourse on seclusion even to the bhikkhus.
The Explanation of the Five Kinds of Association: "Unassociated" means being devoid of the five kinds of association. The five kinds of association are:
association by hearing, association by seeing, association by conversing, association by sharing enjoyments, and physical association. Among these, here a bhikkhu hears: "In such-and-such a place..."
“In a village or a town, there is a woman or a maiden who is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.

Having heard this, he becomes despondent and disheartened; he is unable to maintain the holy life and, without disclosing his weakness in the training, he reverts to the lower life. Thus is the excellence of form and so forth described by others.
Lust arising by way of the cognitive process of ear-consciousness in one hearing the sounds of one's own laughing, talking, singing, or music is called "contact through hearing.
This is to be understood by way of the example of the Paccekabodhisatta Anitthigandha and the young man Tiṣya who dwelt in the cave with five door-bars.
It is said that while the young man was traveling through the air, he [beheld] the daughter of a blacksmith living in a mountain village together with five maidens.
Having gone to the lotus pond, bathed, and adorned herself with lotuses, she was heard singing with a sweet voice;
pierced by sensual lust, [the king] fell away from his excellence and met with ruin and disaster.
Here, however, a monk does not merely hear of it, but rather sees for himself a woman or a girl who is beautiful and lovely to behold.
He is inspiring and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion. Upon seeing him, one becomes despondent and discouraged;
unable to maintain the holy life, and without declaring one's weakness in training, one falls back to the lower state.
Thus, for one who gazes upon a form of a dissimilar class, the lust that arises by way of the cognitive process of eye-consciousness is "contact through seeing."
This is the story. He should be understood thus:
It is said that a certain young man went to the Kāladīghavāpi Monastery for the purpose of receiving a recitation.
Seeing an obstacle to his progress, the teacher did not grant him leave. The youth followed him again and again. The teacher said, "If you do not go wandering within the village..."

"I shall give you the recitation," he said. Having accepted with "Very well," and once the recitation was finished, he paid homage to his teacher and, while departing, thought, "My teacher does not allow me to wander in this village; what could be the reason?
Putting on his robe, he entered the village. A certain young woman, dressed in yellow garments, stood in her house; seeing the youth, she conceived a sense of passion.
Having brought rice-gruel with a ladle and poured it into his bowl, she turned back and lay down on her bed.
Then her parents asked her, "What is it, daughter? She replied, "If I find a young man who has gone out through the gate, I shall live; if I do not find one, I shall die.
Her parents went in haste, reached the young man at the village gate, and having paid homage to him, said, "Please turn back."
“Venerable sir, please accept almsfood,” they said. The youth replied, “Enough, I am going.
They then made their request, saying, “Venerable sir, this is the reason: ‘In our house, venerable sir, there is such-and-such wealth;
we have only one daughter. You will stand in the place of our eldest son; it will be possible for us to live in comfort. The youth—
Thinking, "I have no need for this obstacle," she departed without taking it.
Her parents went to her and said, "Daughter, we were unable to turn our young man back; you shall obtain whatever other husband you desire.
Get up, eat, and drink! But she, being unwilling, remained without food for seven days.
Having offered the fire, she passed away. Her parents performed the funeral rites for her body and gave that yellow robe to the community of monks at the Dhura Monastery.
The monks tore the robe into pieces and distributed them. An elderly monk, having taken his own portion, arrived at the Kalyāṇī Monastery.
He too, thinking, "I shall worship the cetiya," remained right there as a young novice.
Having gone there, he sat down in the daytime resting place. The elder took that piece of cloth and said to the junior monk, "Use this to clean my water-strainer.
The junior monk asked the great elder, "Where was this obtained? He then related the entire account.
Upon hearing it, [the elder] thought, "He did not obtain a life together with one such as her," and [was consumed] by the fire of passion.
Being consumed by passion right there, he died on the spot.
However, "mutual conversation" refers to the arising of lust through mutual talk and chatter,
or the act of taking and using the belongings of a bhikkhu from a bhikkhunī, or the belongings of a bhikkhunī from a bhikkhu.
The arising of lust is what is called "contact through sexual enjoyment. It should be understood as follows:
it is said that at the festival for the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery, there were one hundred thousand bhikkhus and ninety thousand bhikkhunīs.
A certain novice monk, while going along carrying hot gruel, once placed it on the hem of his robe and once on the ground. A certain novice nun, seeing him, [said: "Here..."
Saying, "Set down your bowl and go," she gave him a shallow dish. Later on, when a certain danger arose, they went to the other side of the ocean. Among them, the bhikkhunī arrived first.

Hearing that "a Sinhalese bhikkhu has reportedly arrived," she went to the Elder, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down. She said, "Venerable sir, at the time of the festival for Maricavaṭṭi Vihāra..."
“How many years have you been ordained? he asked. At that time, I was a novice monk of seven years’ standing.

“And how many years have you been ordained? [she asked]. “I am also a novice nun of seven years’ standing; I gave a bowl to a certain novice who was going along carrying hot gruel, in order for him to set it down,” she replied.
The Elder said, “I am that very person,” and taking out the bowl, he showed it to them. By this much alone—
Being unable to maintain the holy life due to association, even two [monks] who were sixty years of age fell away from it.
However, bodily contact that arises through the grasping of hands and so forth is what is called "bodily contact. In this regard, there is this story:
it is said that young bhikkhus were reciting their lessons on the courtyard of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya). Behind them, young bhikkhunīs [were listening to] the Dhamma...
They heard this. Thereupon, one young man, reaching out his hand, touched the body of a certain young nun.
She took that hand and placed it upon her own breast; through such contact, both of them became dissatisfied with the religious life and returned to the state of householders.
[The commentary on the section concerning those who seize and so forth.]
Regarding these five types of social contact (*saṃsagga*), for a bhikkhu, hearing, seeing, conversing, sharing enjoyments, and physical contact with other bhikkhus occur constantly.
With bhikkhunīs, all except physical contact occur from time to time.
Likewise, with male and female lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*), all occur from time to time. For among these, [the latter] arise from the emergence of defilements (*kilesa*).
The mind must be guarded. For one bhikkhu is a "grasper-grasper," another is a "grasper-releaser," another is a "releaser-grasper," and another is a "releaser-releaser.

In this regard, the bhikkhu whom people approach with the intent to grasp after first enticing him with material gifts, and who also approaches people with the intent to grasp after enticing them with flowers, fruits, and so forth—this one is called a "grasper-grasper. But as for the one...
When people approach in the manner described, and the bhikkhu approaches by virtue of being a worthy recipient (*dakkhiṇeyya*), this is called "one who takes by way of a grasp" (*gāhamuttaka*).

When people give the four requisites to someone by virtue of their being a worthy recipient, but the bhikkhu approaches with the intention of taking them after having won them over with flowers, fruits, and so forth, this is called "one who grasps what has been released" (*muttagāhaka*). [This applies] when people also [give to him] by virtue of his being a worthy recipient...

When the four requisites are given, and the bhikkhu, like the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa, consumes them by virtue of being a worthy recipient of offerings, this is called "the one who has already received his share" (*muttamuttaka*).
It is said that a certain female lay devotee attended upon an elder for twelve years. One day, a fire broke out in that village.
He set the houses on fire. Other monks who were his family-visiting associates came and offered greetings, saying, “What is it, lay sister?
Were you unable to save any of your belongings? The people said, “The elder who is our mother’s family-visiting associate will surely arrive at the very time for the meal.
On the following day, the elder, having observed the proper time for the alms-round, [set out].
He arrived. The female lay devotee had him sit in the shade of a wall, prepared almsfood, and gave it to him.
When the elders had finished their meal and departed, people said, "The elder who attends upon our mother has come right at the time for eating.
The female lay devotee replied, "Those who attend upon you are suitable for you; the elder is suitable for me alone."

He said: "But the Venerable Mantāṇiputta, being unattached through these five kinds of social contact even with the four assemblies, was one who had cast off the world and was completely free from it.
And just as he himself was unattached, so too did he speak to the bhikkhus regarding that lack of attachment."
"Exerted in energy" means one who has applied energy; the meaning is that his physical and mental energy is complete.

For a bhikkhu who does not allow a defilement arisen while walking to reach the standing position, nor a defilement arisen while standing to reach the sitting position, nor a defilement arisen while sitting to reach the lying-down position—he is like one who seizes a black snake after having subdued it with a spell.
He moves about as if trampling an enemy under his neck; such a person is called "one who has aroused energy. The Elder was just like that.
He also gave discourses on the arousal of energy to the bhikkhus in exactly the same way. Regarding the phrases "endowed with virtue" and so forth:
"virtue" (sīla) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue. "Concentration" (samādhi) refers to the eight [attainments] that serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā).
The attainments (*samāpattiyo*). Wisdom (*paññā*) is mundane and supramundane knowledge. Liberation (*vimutti*) is the noble fruit (*ariyaphala*).

The knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is the nineteenfold reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). The Elder himself was endowed with virtue and the other factors, and he was one who spoke to the monks on virtue and the rest.
Since he exhorted them by means of the ten bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*), he is called an "exhorter" (*ovādaka*). Just as, for instance, one...
He merely advises; he is unable to make [the meaning] known by turning over a subtle point. The Elder is not like that.
Rather, the Elder makes those ten bases of discourse understood, thus he is "one who makes understood" (*viññāpaka*). One person is able to make [it] understood, but is unable to show the reason.
The Elder shows the reason as well, thus he is "one who points out" (*sandassaka*). Another [is able to show] the existing reason...
He shows [the way], but he is not able to cause others to grasp it. An elder who is also able to cause them to grasp it is an "exhorter" (*samādapaka*).
Having thus exhorted them, he further inspires the bhikkhus by generating enthusiasm for those topics of discussion; thus he is an "inspirer" (*samuttejaka*).
Once enthusiasm has arisen, he gladdens them by speaking in praise; thus he is a "gladdener" (*sampahaṃsaka*).
Commentary on the Five Gains (Pañcalābhavaṇṇanā):

253. “Well-gained are these gains!”—while there are indeed gains consisting of qualities such as human existence and the going-forth into homelessness for others as well, for the Venerable Puṇṇa, however, these are truly well-gained gains;
the meaning is that such praise has been proclaimed in the very presence of the Teacher.
Furthermore, praise spoken by the unwise does not bring such gain; rather, praise spoken by the wise brings gain.
Likewise, praise from householders does not bring such gain as praise from those who say, "We shall speak in praise":
"Our noble sir is gentle, amiable, and pleasant to converse with; he provides for those who come to the monastery with rice gruel, alms-food, molasses, and so forth."

When one speaks thus, one is actually speaking dispraise. When one intends to speak dispraise, saying, "This elder is dull-witted, weak, frowning, and there is no trust between him and me," one is actually speaking praise.
Even among fellow practitioners, speaking praise of the Teacher in his absence does not yield as much gain [as when he is present].
But because it is a great gain in the presence of the Teacher, he said, "A well-gained gain," for this reason as well.
"Piece by piece" means having entered into each of the ten bases of discourse one after another.
"And the Teacher rejoices in that" means he approves of it, saying, "It is so; that bhikkhu is of few desires, and that bhikkhu is content."
Thus, there are five gains: praise by the wise is one; [praise] by fellow practitioners of the holy life is another; [praise] in the presence of the Teacher is another;
[praise] for each and every small portion is another; and the Teacher’s exultant approval is another. With reference to these five gains, he said, "It is a gain well-gained.
"Kadāci" means at some time or other. "Karahaci" is a synonym for that same word. "Appeva nāma siyā" means perhaps it might be so.
"Conversation" (*kathāsallāpa*) means that perhaps there might even be some exchange of talk.

It is said that the Elder had never before seen the Venerable Puṇṇa, nor had he ever heard his discourse on the Dhamma. Thus, longing for both the sight of him and a discourse on the Dhamma, he spoke in this way.
Commentary on the Wandering, etc. (254).

"As long as he so desired" means having dwelt according to his inclination. For when Buddhas dwell in a single location, it may happen that due to a deficiency in shade, water, and so forth, or an uncomfortable lodging, or because of the lack of faith and other such qualities in people, [they depart].
There is no such thing as lack of delight. Because they take pleasure in their prosperity, thinking, "We dwell here in comfort," there is no long-term residence for them.
However, wherever the Tathāgata dwells, beings either establish themselves in the refuges, undertake the precepts, or go forth into homelessness;
it is from that place that they gain the necessary support (upanissaya) for the path of stream-entry and the others.
In that regard, the Buddhas dwell with the intention of establishing beings in those attainments;
when they are absent, they depart. Therefore it is said: "having dwelt according to his inclination.
"Wandering on tour" means traveling along a journey. And this wandering of the Blessed One is of two kinds: hurried wandering and unhurried wandering.
In this context, "hurried journey" (*turitacārikā*) refers to going immediately upon seeing a person capable of being enlightened, even if they are far away, for the purpose of awakening them.
This is to be seen in such instances as the Buddha’s meeting Mahākassapa halfway.
For the Blessed One, while going out to meet Mahākassapa, traveled three *gāvutas* in a single moment; he likewise traveled thirty *yojanas* for the sake of Āḷavaka, and similarly for Aṅgulimāla.
For Pukkusāti, however, he went forty-five yojanas; for Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas;
for the sake of Khadiravaniya, seven hundred yojanas; and for the novice Vanavāsī Tissa, the student of the General of the Dhamma, one hundred and ninety-three yojanas.
One day, it is said, the Elder said, "Venerable sir, I shall go to the presence of the novice Tissa.
The Blessed One replied, "I too will go," and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, announce to the twenty thousand monks who possess the six supernormal powers: 'The Blessed One will go to the presence of the forest-dwelling novice Tissa.'"

Then, on the second day, surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were exhausted, he rose into the air and descended at the gate of his alms-village, located two hundred yojanas away, and put on his robe.
Seeing him, the people going to their work said, "The Teacher has come, sirs; do not go to work! and having prepared seats and given him rice-gruel, they [waited].
While they were performing their drinking ceremony, they asked the young bhikkhus, "Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One going?
[The bhikkhus replied: "Lay followers, the Blessed One is not going elsewhere; he has come right here for the purpose of seeing the novice Tissa.
They thought, "It seems the Teacher has come to see our own family preceptor, the Elder! Indeed, our Elder is no ordinary man!"
They were filled with joy.
Then, at the conclusion of the Blessed One’s meal, the novice, having wandered for alms in the village, asked, "Lay followers, has the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus arrived?
They replied to him, "Venerable sir, the Teacher has arrived," and he [went] to the Blessed One.
Having approached, he requested almsfood. The Teacher took his bowl in his hand and said, "Enough, Tissa;
the meal is finished. Then, having asked permission from his preceptor, he sat down on his own seat and performed the meal-rite.
At the conclusion of his meal-rite, the Teacher uttered a blessing and departed.
Standing at the gate of the village, he asked, "Tissa, which is the path leading to your dwelling? "This one, Blessed One," he replied.

"Go ahead, Tissa, and show me the way," said the Blessed One. It is said that although the Blessed One is the guide to the entire world including the devas, thinking, "I shall have the opportunity to see the novice on the entire three-league journey," he had him act as his guide along the way.
Thus, having gone to his own dwelling place, he performed the duties of service for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One asked him, "Tissa, which is your walking path?
Having gone there and sat down on the stone seat where the novice sat, he asked, "Tissa, do you dwell happily in this place?
He replied, "Yes, venerable sir; for one dwelling in this place..."
As he heard the sounds of lions, tigers, elephants, deer, leopards, and other wild animals, the perception of the forest arose within him, and he thought, "By means of this, I dwell in happiness.
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Tissa, assemble the community of monks; I shall give you the inheritance of a Buddha.
When the community of monks had assembled, the Blessed One conferred full ordination upon him and returned to his own dwelling place.
This is called a hurried journey (*turitacārikā*).

However, the traveling of one who supports the world through alms-gathering and other means, day by day, by way of visiting villages and market towns at a pace of half a *yojana* or a *yojana*, is called an unhurried journey (*aturitacārikā*). While wandering on this [latter] journey...
The Blessed One wanders about in one of these three circles—the great circle, the middle circle, or the final circle.
Among them, the great circle is eight hundred yojanas; the middle circle is six hundred yojanas; and the final circle is three hundred yojanas.
When he desires to wander in the great circle, [he does so] at the Great Invitation (mahāpavāraṇā).

Having performed the *pavāraṇā*, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*), he sets out surrounded by a great community of monks. For a hundred leagues around, there was a single roar of acclaim;
those who arrived first were able to offer invitations, while the hospitality intended for the other two circles converged upon the Great Circle.
There, the Blessed One stayed for one or two days in various villages and market towns.
Favoring the great multitude with material gifts and increasing their wholesome merit conducive to the turning away from suffering through the gift of the Dhamma,
he concludes his wandering tour after nine months.
However, if during the rains retreat the monks' serenity and insight are still immature, he does not conclude the *Pavāraṇā* at the Great *Pavāraṇā*.

Having granted the invitation for the *pavāraṇā* ceremony and having performed the *pavāraṇā* on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, he sets out surrounded by a great community of monks and proceeds to the Middle Region on the first day of the month of Migasira.
For other reasons as well, when desiring to wander through the Middle Region, he likewise departs only after staying there for four months.
In the same manner as described, there is honor and hospitality in the other two regions, but [the greatest] in the Middle Region.
He returns. The Blessed One, favoring the world in the same manner as before, concludes his wandering tour within eight months.

However, if even after the Blessed One has spent four months in the rains retreat, the beings to be converted (*veneyya-sattā*) have faculties that are not yet mature, he waits for the maturation of their faculties and remains right there for another month, or two, three, or four months.
Having stayed there, surrounded by a great community of bhikkhus, he sets out. In the same manner as previously described, the honor paid in the other two circles descends into the inner circle.
The Blessed One, favoring the world in the same way as before, completes his wandering tour in seven, six, five, or four months. Thus, in these three circles—
While wandering on his journey anywhere at all, he does not travel for the sake of robes or other requisites. Rather, [he thinks]:
"When will those who are unfortunate, foolish, aged, and sick come to see the Tathāgata?
While I am wandering on my journey, the great multitude will obtain the sight of the Tathāgata; therein, some will clarify their minds, and some will [offer] garlands and so forth."
Some will honor him, some will give alms with their ladles, some will abandon wrong view and become possessed of right view;
that will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time—thus he wanders on tour out of compassion for the world.
Furthermore, the Blessed Buddhas wander on tour for four reasons: for the sake of physical well-being through walking about, and...
For the purpose of desiring an occasion for the arising of a matter; for the purpose of laying down a training rule for the monks;
and for the purpose of awakening those beings capable of being awakened whose faculties have reached maturity here and there.
Furthermore, the Blessed Buddhas go on tour for four other reasons: thinking, "They will go for refuge to the Buddha," or "They will go for refuge to the Dhamma."
"Thinking, 'They will go,' or 'They will go for refuge to the Saṅgha,' or 'I shall satisfy the four assemblies with a great rain of Dhamma.
Furthermore, Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on tour for five other reasons:

thinking, 'They will abstain from the destruction of life,' or 'from taking what is not given,' or 'from sexual misconduct,' or 'from false speech,' or 'from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.'"
Or they will cease. For eight other reasons the Blessed Buddhas go on tour:
thinking, "They will attain the first jhāna," or "the second" ... pe ... or "they will attain the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For these eight other reasons the Blessed Buddhas go on tour.
—“They will attain the path of stream-entry,” or “They will realize the fruit of stream-entry”… [and so on] …“They will realize the fruit of arahantship.
This is the unhurried journey; it is this that is intended here. Furthermore, it is twofold:
the regular journey and the irregular journey. Of these, that which goes for the sake of a single being who is to be awakened is the [regular journey].
"Fixed wandering" means [wandering] according to a fixed route. However, that which one wanders by following the sequence of villages, market towns, and cities is called "unfixed wandering.
This is what is intended here.

"Having put away the lodgings" means having stored away the lodgings. While the Elder was putting them away, he did not [put away] his small bowl and large bowl, his small ladle and large ladle, his cotton cloth robe, his dukūla cloth robe, and so forth.
Having made a bundle, or having filled jars with ghee, oil, and so forth, she hid them in the inner chamber, closed the door, and had the key, seal, and other such items secured.

She thought: "If there is no bhikkhu, novice, monastery attendant, or lay devotee [to see to it], then having placed bed upon bed on four stones, and chair upon chair, [she would place the goods] on a clothes-stand or a clothes-line."

However, because of the statement, "Or, having made a heap [of bedding] above and having closed the door and window, one should depart," he sent away the resident monk by means of a mere request for leave.
He set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī, desiring to see the Teacher; that is, toward whichever direction Sāvatthī lay.
He departed. As he was departing, he did not have King Suddhodana informed, nor did he have clarified butter, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth brought along;
rather, having left the herd like a rutting elephant, and being without the duty of companionship like a lion, he took only his bowl and robe and departed all alone.
But why did he depart with five hundred of his own resident pupils?
"Did he not go to Rājagaha with [the Buddha], but has now departed?"—this is no reason for his departure. Rājagaha is sixty yojanas from Kapilavatthu, while Sāvatthī is fifteen.
Having come from Rājagaha, forty-five yojanas away, the Teacher was dwelling in Sāvatthī;
hearing that he had now become near, he departed. As one going into the presence of the Buddhas...
For even if one were to travel a thousand *yojanas*, bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) could not be obtained at that time.
When traveling with many people, while one says "I am going," another says "I am staying right here"; and while one says "I am staying," another says "I am going.
Therefore, having entered meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) whenever one so desires, [one should practice].
If one is unable to sit down in a comfortable lodging or to obtain physical seclusion, all of that is easily obtained by one who is alone;
therefore, not going at that time, he departed now. Regarding the phrase "while wandering on a journey":
although this so-called "journey" (cārikā) belongs only to Buddhas for the purpose of gathering the great multitude, [it is undertaken here for other reasons].

It is possible; however, by way of a conventional term derived from "Buddha," it is said that even disciples are so called, just as a fan made of reeds and the like is called a "palmyra-fan" (*tālavaṇṭa*).

"By whom [the Blessed One]" refers to [the Elder Sāriputta or the Elder Mahāmoggallāna], who, having walked for alms in a certain village not far from Sāvatthī and finished his meal, entered the Jeta Grove [to visit] the Elder Sāriputta or the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
Or, having gone to his dwelling place, washed his feet, anointed them, and drunk water or a beverage, he rested for a short while;
yet, without even forming the thought, "I shall see the Teacher," he went straight to the Gandhakuṭi courtyard.
For one who wishes to see the Teacher, there is no other business for the Elder than that. Therefore—
He did not even conceive the thought, "I will see the Teacher after taking either Rāhula or Ānanda and asking for leave.
For the Elder was himself a favorite in the Buddha’s dispensation, like a great warrior who has won victory in battle for a king.
Just as such a warrior, when desiring to see the king, has no other way to perform the act of seeing him than by serving [the king] directly; so it was with him.
One sees for oneself what is dear. Likewise, the Elder was also dear to the Buddha’s teaching;
thinking that he had no need to see the Teacher after having served another, he washed his feet, wiped them on a foot-wiping cloth, and approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, moreover, saw that "Mantāṇiputta will arrive even at this very pre-dawn hour. Therefore—
Having entered the Fragrant Chamber, he sat down after rising once his agitation had subsided, even without having fastened the bolt.
The Elder pushed aside the door-leaf, entered the Fragrant Chamber, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.
"With a discourse on the Dhamma": while the Blessed One was delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, [he spoke] in the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta concerning three clansmen.

He spoke on the benefit of harmony; in the *Sekha-sutta*, on the benefit of a guest-house; in the *Ghaṭīkāra-sutta*, on the discourse concerning past lives connected with the attainment of mindfulness;
in the *Raṭṭhapāla-sutta*, on the four summaries of the Dhamma; in the *Sela-sutta*, on the discourse regarding the benefits of the drink;
and while speaking the Dhamma talk to the elder Bhagu in the *Upakkilesa-sutta*, he spoke on the benefit of solitude.
While preaching this *Rathavinīta Sutta* to the Venerable Puṇṇa, he demonstrated the teaching known as the "Infinite Method" (*anantanaya*), which is based upon ten topics of discourse.
[He showed that] this too is simply a discourse on fewness of desires and a discourse on contentment.
It was like a disciple who has attained analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*) standing on the shore and reaching out his hand toward the great ocean.
Regarding the phrase "where the Blind Men’s Grove is": it is said that at that time, after the midday meal, Jetavana was crowded;
many kṣatriyas, brahmins, and others would gather there, making it like the encampment of a universal monarch’s army, so that seclusion could not be found.
The Blind Men’s Grove, however, was secluded like a meditation hall; therefore, he approached the Blind Men’s Grove.
But why did he not see the Great Elders? It was because it occurred to him:
"Having come in the evening and seen the Great Elders, I shall then see the One of Ten Powers; thus there will be one visit for the Great Elders and two for the Teacher.
Then, having paid homage to the Teacher, I shall go back to my own dwelling place."
Commentary on the Questions on the Seven Purifications: 256.
"He was constantly praising him" means that he lived praising his virtues again and again.
It is said that from then on, day after day in the midst of the Saṅgha, the Elder would say: "Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī, is indeed praised by the four assemblies..."
“Not associating with anyone, he will come for the purpose of seeing the One of Ten Powers; I wonder if he will depart without even seeing me?
Thus he spoke of the virtues of the Venerable Puṇṇa for the sake of arousing mindfulness in the elders, novices, and those of middle standing.
For it occurred to him: “Elder monks do not remain within the monastery at all times; [they go out] through talk of their virtues.”
"When this has been told, whichever monk sees him will come and report it.
Then the Elder's own pupil saw the Venerable Mantāṇiputta entering the Perfumed Chamber, carrying his bowl and robe.
But how did he recognize him? [It was] while [the Elder] was speaking, saying, "Puṇṇa, Puṇṇa!"—thus he knew.
Through the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, he recognized: "This is that elder, whom my preceptor used to praise so often.
Thus, having returned, he informed the elder. "Taking his sitting mat" (*nisīdana*): a "sitting mat" is said to be a seat with a fringe, not woven.
But the elder went taking a piece of hide. "Behind, behind" means from behind.
"From behind. "Looking at the head": one who walks looking at his back when on high ground and looking at his head when on low ground is also called "one who looks at the head.
Being such, he followed. For although the Elder walked very close due to the sound of his restrained footsteps, he did not disturb him with that sound;
rather, knowing, "This is not the time for social greetings," [he remained silent].
But he was not too close; for the Blind Men’s Grove is large, and thinking, "Friend Puṇṇa, if you do not see him hidden in one place, you must call out 'Puṇṇa!
Puṇṇa! in a way that is not distressing," he went along looking up at his head, neither too far away, in order to know where he was sitting.
"He sat down for the midday rest" means he sat down for the purpose of the midday rest.
In that regard, the Venerable Puṇṇa was of noble brahmin birth, as was the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder Puṇṇa was golden-hued, as was the Elder Sāriputta.
The Elder Puṇṇa had attained the meditative absorption of the fruit of Arahantship, as had the Elder Sāriputta.
The Elder Puṇṇa had fulfilled his aspiration for one hundred thousand eons, as had the Elder Sāriputta for more than one hundred thousand eons.
One incalculable aeon [ago]. Puṇṇa Thera was one who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and was a great one whose taints were destroyed; so too was Sāriputta Thera.

Thus, like two lions entering a single golden cave, like two tigers descending upon a single stretch of ground for a spring, like two six-tusked royal elephants entering a single grove of blossoming *sāla* trees, [they entered] a single forest of *simbali* trees.
Like two king-suparṇas who have entered [the sky], like two Vessavaṇas mounted upon a single man-borne vehicle,
like two Sakkas seated upon a single pale-white woolen stone, and like two Hārita Great Brahmās within a single celestial mansion—
those two were both of brahmin birth, both golden-hued, both attainers of meditative attainments, and both perfected in their noble resolve.
Two who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and were great ones with taints destroyed entered a single forest grove and graced that woodland place.
"Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One," [said one]. "Friend, why should the venerable one live the holy life under the Blessed One?
This was the venerable Sāriputta’s account of his living the holy life under that Blessed One.
Although he already knew, he asked in order to initiate the discourse;
for if a preceding discussion is not established, a subsequent one does not arise, and therefore he asked in this way. The Elder, granting his consent, said, "So it is, friend.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, desiring to hear the answer to the question, asked: "Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of purification of virtue?"
“...one lives the holy life,” he asked, enumerating the seven purifications in succession. The detailed explanation of these is set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.

However, because even for one established in the fourfold purification of virtue and so forth, the dwelling in the holy life does not reach its ultimate consummation, the Venerable Puṇṇa rejected everything, saying, “Certainly not, friend.”
"For what purpose, friends, do you lead the holy life?"—if the holy life is not lived for the sake of purification of virtue and so forth, then he asked:
"For what purpose, then, is it lived? "It is, friends, for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
Here, "final Nibbāna through non-clinging" means final Nibbāna without conditions. Clinging is twofold: clinging as grasping and clinging as condition. Clinging as grasping...

"Name" refers to the fourfold [clinging], beginning with clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). "Conditioned clinging" refers to the conditions stated thus: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.

In this regard, the teachers who maintain the doctrine of grasping hold that "Nibbāna without clinging" is the fruit of Arahantship occurring when one does not grasp at any phenomenon whatsoever through any of the four types of clinging.
They speak thus. For that [Nibbāna], while not being associated with clinging (*upādāna*), does not cling to any phenomenon;

and because it is born at the moment of the final extinction of the defilements (*kilesa*), it is called "Parinibbāna. However, for those who maintain the doctrine of "clinging as a condition" (*paccayūpādānavādin*), "non-clinging Parinibbāna" (*anupādāparinibbāna*) means "conditionless Parinibbāna" (*appaccayaparinibbāna*).
It is precisely the unconditioned, deathless element (*asaṅkhata-amatadhātu*), which has not arisen by way of conditions, that is "non-clinging Parinibbāna."

They speak thus: "This is the end, this is the limit, this is the final goal. For one who has attained parinibbāna through non-clinging, the living of the holy life (brahmacariya) is said to have reached its pinnacle.
Therefore, the Elder said, "for the sake of parinibbāna through non-clinging.
Then, questioning him, the Venerable Sāriputta asked: "Friend, is purification of virtue itself parinibbāna through non-clinging?"
He began the question again.
The Elder, likewise rejecting it in all the subsequent turns, pointed out the flaw at the conclusion by saying, "If, friend, there were purification of virtue," and so forth.
In that context, *paññapeyya* means "if he were to point out. Being still possessed of clinging (*saupādāna*), [he could not attain] final nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*).

"He would describe" means: he would describe that which is of the nature of inclusion as being of the nature of exclusion; that which is of the nature of having conditions as being of the nature of being without conditions; and that which is of the nature of the conditioned as being of the nature of the unconditioned.

However, in the *Ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*, it says: "He would describe that which is of the nature of having conditions as being of the nature of being without conditions, and that which is of the nature of the conditioned as being of the nature of the unconditioned."

"Should describe" (paññapeyya) is to be understood in this very sense. Regarding the phrase "the worldling, friend," here the worldly, foolish worldling who follows the cycle of existence (vaṭṭānugata) is to be seen.
For he is entirely devoid of even the mere fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), being altogether apart from these qualities.
"For by that reason" (tena hi): for the reason that some wise ones understand the meaning through a simile, for that reason [he gives] a simile.
The meaning is: "I shall do those. 259.
Regarding the description of the seven chariots tamed:
"seven chariots tamed" means seven chariots yoked with well-trained noble horses. "Merely for the sake of purification of the mind": this refers to the purpose of mental purity.
"Friends, this so-called purification of virtue is for the sake of purification of mind. 'For the sake of purification of mind' is an ablative expression.

However, the meaning here is this: as long as there is the goal known as purification of mind, so long must this purification of virtue be desired. And this purification of mind is the goal of purification of virtue; it is its limit."
This is the conclusion: for one established in the purification of mind, the task of the purification of virtue is indeed accomplished.
This same method applies to all the passages.
Here, however, is the correlation with the simile: just as King Pasenadi of Kosala was afraid of old age and death, so too is the practitioner.
The practitioner of yoga is to be seen as follows: the city of Sāvatthī is like the city of *sakkāya* (personality-belief); the city of Sāketa is like the city of Nibbāna;

and the time when an urgent task arises for a king in Sāketa—one that must be reached by traveling swiftly—is like the time when the duty of the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four Noble Truths arises for the practitioner.
The seven purifications are like seven chariots. The time of mounting the first chariot is like the time of abiding in purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).

The time of mounting the second and subsequent chariots by means of the first chariot and so forth is like the time of abiding in purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*) and the others by means of purification of virtue and the others.
Having descended at the gate of the inner palace in Sāketa by means of the seventh chariot—
The time for the practitioner to experience supramundane bliss should be seen as being like the time when one, surrounded by a circle of kinsmen and friends on an upper palace, enjoys delicious food;
it is like having exhausted all defilements through the purification of knowledge and vision, ascending the sublime palace of the Dhamma, and—
accompanied by more than fifty wholesome states— entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as its object while seated upon the couch of cessation (nirodhasayana).
Thus, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, questioned the Venerable Puṇṇa—who had attained the ten bases of discourse—concerning the seven purifications.
The Venerable Puṇṇa answered the ten bases of discourse. Now, did the General of the Dhamma ask these questions knowing [the answers], or did he ask them without knowing?
Or was it because he was skilled in the "grounds" (*tittha*) that he asked about the subject matter?
Or did he answer outside his domain while being unskilled in the sects? And as for the Elder Puṇṇa, did he answer having known [the answer], or without knowing it?

Or did he answer within his domain while being skilled in the sects, or outside his domain while being unskilled in the sects? For one who says that the General of the Dharma (Sāriputta) asked the question within his domain after knowing [the answer] and being skilled in the sects—[that person is speaking of] the General of the Dharma himself.

One might say this. If one were to say that, having understood [the matter], he became skilled in establishing [his position] and answered the question regarding the subject-matter, one would be referring specifically to the Elder Puṇṇa.

For what is condensed in the *Visuddhimagga* is expanded in the *Kathāvatthu*, and what is condensed in the *Kathāvatthu* is expanded in the *Visuddhimagga*. This should be understood by way of this method.

For among the purifications, one—purification of virtue—has come down as four topics of discourse: the talk on fewness of wishes, the talk on contentment, the talk on non-association, and the talk on virtue.
One—purification of mind—has come down as three topics of discourse: the talk on seclusion, the talk on the arousal of energy, and the talk on concentration.
Thus, that which was summarized under the purifications has been presented here under the topics of discourse.
It is expanded. In the *Kathāvatthu*, however, one discourse on wisdom appears as the five purifications:

purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision.
Thus, that which is concise in the *Kathāvatthu* is expanded in the [treatise on] purifications.
Therefore, when the Elder Sāriputta questioned the seven purifications, he did not ask anything else; he asked only about the ten bases of discourse.
And when the Elder Puṇṇa answered the seven purifications, he did not answer anything else; he answered only about the ten bases of discourse.
Thus, both of them, having understood this and being skilled in the [proper] domain, asked questions only within that very domain.
"And they replied" is how it should be understood. 260.
"What is the name of the venerable one?"—the Elder did not not know his name; however, knowing it well, he asked [this] thinking, "I shall obtain the opportunity to exchange greetings.
"And how is the venerable one?"—this, moreover, the Elder said while exchanging greetings. "The son of Mantāṇī."
The son of the brahmin Mantāṇī. Regarding the word *yathā*: here *tanti* is a mere particle;
the concise meaning here is that it was explained exactly as it ought to be explained by a learned disciple.
*Anumassa anumassa* means having entered into and penetrated each of the ten bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*). Regarding *celaṇḍupakena*: here *cela* refers to cloth.
"A *aṇḍupaka* is a head-wrap. By placing a cloth wrap upon his head and carrying the Venerable One while having him sit there, even fellow celibates would be able to see him;
thus, even such a sight as obtained would be a gain for them. By this hypothetical scenario (*aṭṭhāna-parikappa*), he showed a means for frequent seeing.
For if one does not carry him in this way, one who wishes to ask a question—
Or, for one who wishes to hear the Dhamma, it may be necessary to wander about searching [for a teacher], asking, "Where is the elder standing?

Where is he sitting? However, for those who carry him about in this way, they are able to ask questions or listen to the Dhamma at any desired moment, having lowered him from their heads and seated him upon a magnificent throne. Thus, by means of imagining such an impossible situation...
He showed him the means for frequent seeing.
"Sāriputta"—thinking thus, "I am the son of the brahmin woman Sārī," so do my fellow celibates know me.
"Satthukappena" means "one who resembles the Teacher. Thus, with a single phrase, the Venerable Puṇṇa [addressed] the Elder Sāriputta.
He lifted it up as if he were placing it against the orb of the moon. For at this point, the Elder’s status as an exclusive preacher of the Dhamma became manifest.

Indeed, one who says that a minister or a chaplain is "great" might as well say that a king is like a commoner, an ox is the size of an elephant, a reservoir is the size of the ocean, or light is the size of the light of the sun and moon; beyond this—
There is no talk whatsoever regarding their greatness. One who says even a disciple is "great" would be saying he is a counterpart to the Teacher;
beyond that, there is no talk of his greatness. Thus, with a single word, the Venerable Puṇṇa lifted the Elder up as if striking him against the orb of the moon.
"There would not even be so much as this for us to express" means that for one who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), there is no such thing as a lack of eloquence.

As for this simile that was brought forward, we would not bring it forth; we would speak only of the meaning. For a simile is brought forward for those who do not understand—this is the intended meaning here.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), having rejected even this [point], it says: "As for what is called a simile..."
It is brought forward even in the presence of the Buddhas; however, out of reverence for the Elder, he spoke thus.
"Questioned bit by bit" means questioned after having repeatedly delved into the ten bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*). Now, which is more difficult:
the asking of the question or the answering of it? It is not difficult to ask a question once one has mastered the material.
But the answering is difficult. Both the question, when made with its underlying cause or reason, and the answer itself are indeed difficult.
"They rejoiced" means they rejoiced with minds of equanimity. Thus the teaching is concluded according to the sequence of the narrative.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Rathavinīta-sutta* is finished.
5. The commentary on the *Nivāpa-sutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Nivāpa-sutta*. In that context, "a deer-trapper" is one who, for the purpose of catching deer, [goes] into the forest...
He sows grass seeds [thinking]: "When the deer come to eat this grass, I will easily capture them.
*Nivāpa* means sowing; *nivutta* means what has been sown. *Migajāta* means a herd of deer. *Anupakhajja* means having entered among them.
*Mucchitā* means intoxicated by the intoxication of craving; the meaning is that their hearts have been entered by craving and they have been brought to a state of infatuation.
"They will fall into intoxication" means they will fall into the intoxication of pride (*māna-mada*). "Negligence" means the state of having abandoned mindfulness.
"They will become subject to being done with as we wish" means they will be made to act exactly as we desire.
"In this [place] he scatters" means in this place for scattering fodder. It is said there is a certain grass called *nivāpa-tiṇa*, which is excellent in the heat of summer; it is such that...
When the heat becomes intense, it becomes as dense and solid as a grove of wild rice or a mass of clouds;
hunters then cultivate and sow it in a place free from water, erect a fence, set up a gate, and guard it.
Then, when a great heat comes and all the grasses have withered, even water sufficient for a mere lick of the tongue becomes difficult to find.
At that time, the deer, while eating dry grass and old leaves, wander about as if trembling;
yet, upon smelling the scent of the baited trap, they disregard the risk of slaughter and captivity and enter, completely covering the enclosure.
For those deer find the baited grass exceedingly dear and pleasing. Seeing them, the trapper—two... [text continues]
For three days he acts as if negligent; he stands with the door open.
In the fodder-pasture there are water-troughs here and there; deer enter through the open door, and having merely grazed and drunk, they depart.
On the following day, thinking "they did nothing at all," he shakes his ears and, having eaten and drunk, [proceeds].
They go about without haste; on the following day, thinking there is nothing for anyone to do, they eat and drink as much as they desire and enter the circular enclosure to lie down.
When the hunters perceive their state of negligence, they close the door, surround them, and after beating them starting from one end, they depart;
thus, those [deer] fall into the power of the hunter at that baited spot.
They become subject to being done with according to one's will. 262.
"Therein, monks"—that is, monks, among those species of deer. "The first species of deer": there is no second species of deer;
however, the Blessed One, having established them according to the order of their arrival, designated them as "the first" and "the second."
He showed them by assigning the names "Third" and "Fourth. Regarding "by the power of supernormal success" (*iddhānubhāva*):
it is so called because of the state of being able to act according to one's will; for here, both "success" (*iddhi*) and "power" (*ānubhāva*) are intended to mean mastery (*vasībhāva*).
263. "By fear and enjoyment": due to fear and enjoyment. "Strength and energy": this refers to the wind-element that moves back and forth; the meaning is that it has declined.
264. "We shall make our lair depending on this," they thought; for there was fear even for those eating while lying inside, and fear even for those coming from outside to eat.
"But we shall make our lair in a secluded spot, depending on that place where the bait is set.
Thus they made their lair depending on it. As for the phrase "they made their lair depending on it": hunters do not [set out] at all times.
They became heedful. Thinking, "We shall lie down here and there among the circles of trees and at the foot of the fences;

then, when they have departed for the sake of rinsing their mouths or for the purpose of eating, we will enter the fodder field, eat our fill, and return to our dwelling place," they took up their position near the fodder field.
They made their lairs in dense thickets, groves, at the foot of trees, and so forth.

"They ate" means that, having recognized the time when the hunters were negligent according to the manner already described, they entered very quickly and ate. "Trained hunters" means those skilled in the art of hunting.
"Possessing psychic power" means as if they possessed psychic power (*iddhi*). "Other beings" refers to the *yakkhas*. [Thinking], "These are not deer," [they perceived] their coming or going.
"We do not know by which path they come or where they go. "With snares for catching deer" means with nets for catching deer.
"They surrounded it on every side, including the surrounding area," meaning: "These are great deceivers;
they will not go far away, but will remain right here, lying down"—thus [they surrounded] the area around the field of bait.
They surrounded a large space. "They saw" means that, having thus surrounded it and shaken the net of snares all around, they looked and saw.
"Where those [beings] had gone" means they saw that place where those beings had entered the grasp. 265.
"What if we were to go where there is no going?"—it is said that they thought thus: "Having lain down inside, [we shall go] inside..."

“There is fear even for those who are eating; there is fear even for those who come from outside to eat, and fear even for those who eat while staying nearby, for they too have been caught by being enclosed within the net of snares. Therefore, it occurred to them:
“What if we were to go to a place that is neither accessible nor within the range of the snarer or his followers?”
"Let us make our bed there. "Others will disturb them": those living further away from here and there will disturb them.
"Disturbed by them, they will disturb others": being disturbed by them, they too will disturb others living even further away.
"In this way, all the deer of this breed will be completely freed from this bait that has been laid down": thus, from this bait laid down by us...
"All herds and troops of deer will release and abandon them. "We shall look on with indifference" means we shall not be occupied with their capture.
For while it is possible to catch one as they come along—whether it be a youngling, an old animal, a weak one, or one separated from the herd—there is nothing to be gained when they do not come.
"O monks, they looked on with indifference," thinking thus, they remained uninvolved. 267.

Regarding the phrase "that bait laid out for Māra and these worldly baits": here, "bait" (nivāpa) or "worldly baits" (lokāmisa) is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure which constitute the bait of the round of existence (vaṭṭāmisa). Māra did not [scatter them] like seeds...
Sowing the strands of sensual pleasure, one wanders about; however, for those greedy for the strands of sensual pleasure, he holds sway over them from above.
Therefore, the strands of sensual pleasure are called "Māra’s bait. Thus it was said: "That bait laid down by Māra. They were not released from Māra’s supernatural power;
they fell under Māra’s control, becoming subject to his doing as he pleased. This is the simile that comes from the renunciation of [the Buddha] together with his sons and wife.

268. Regarding the phrase "he fell away from the liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti parihāyi*): here, "liberation of mind" refers to the aspiration that arose [in him], thinking, "I shall dwell in the forest.
"He fell away" is the meaning. "In this same way, I consider these two" is the simile for the renunciation of the *brāhmaṇadhammika*.
For the brahmins, having practiced the celibate life of a youth (*komārabrahmacariya*) for forty-eight years, out of fear of the interruption of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭupaccheda*),...
Thinking, "We shall continue our lineage," they seek wealth, take a wife, and live in the midst of the household.

When a son is born, thinking, "A son has been born to us; the cycle is not cut off, the lineage is joined," they either go forth again into homelessness or remain in that very same life with their family.
269. "In this way, monks, even those third recluses and brahmins were not liberated.
Like the previous ones, they too were not released from Māra’s power of psychic influence; they remained subject to his doing with them as he pleased.
But what did they do? Having descended into villages, market towns, and royal capitals, they established hermitages in various groves and parks and lived there.
They had the noble youths trained in various crafts, such as the skills of elephant-riding, horsemanship, and charioteering.
Thus, having surrounded them with the net of views of Māra the Evil One—just as the third group of deer was surrounded by the net of snares—they became subject to his doing with them as he pleased.
"In this same way, I [regard] these fourth [group]," with this he brought forth a simile for this teaching.
271. “He made Māra blind” does not mean that he pierced Māra’s eyes.
Rather, when a bhikkhu has attained jhāna as the basis for insight (vipassanā), Māra is unable to see him, thinking, “My mind is operating by depending on such-and-such an object.
Therefore it is said: “He made Māra blind. By that same method, “he struck down Māra’s eyeless one.”
Just as Māra’s eye becomes trackless, footless, baseless, and objectless—this is the meaning of "having struck him down.
"The Evil One has gone beyond sight" means that by that very method, he has gone beyond the sight of Māra the Evil One;
for he cannot see with his own fleshly eye that bhikkhu who has attained the jhāna based on insight (vipassanā).

One is able to see the body of knowledge (*ñāṇasarīra*). "And having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed" means that by means of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), having seen the four noble truths, the four taints are utterly destroyed. "He has crossed over attachment to the world":
it is called "attachment" (*visattikā*) because it exists in the state of being attached and clinging to the world. Alternatively, in what sense is it "attachment"?

*Visattikā*: It is called *visattikā* because it is spread out (*visata*); it is called *visattikā* because it is diffused (*visaṭa*); it is called *visattikā* because it is extensive (*vipula*); it is called *visattikā* because it is vast (*visāla*); it is called *visattikā* because it is uneven (*visama*);
it is called *visattikā* because it clings (*visakkati*); it is called *visattikā* because it carries poison (*visaṃ harati*);

it is called *visattikā* because it is deceptive (*visamvādikā*); it is called *visattikā* because its root is poison (*visamūla*); it is called *visattikā* because its fruit is poison (*visaphala*); it is called *visattikā* because its enjoyment is poison (*visaparibhoga*).
"Or rather, that craving is vast, being attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Thus he has crossed over, has gone beyond, and has emerged from that craving which is designated as "attachment" (*visattikā*). Therefore it is said: "He has crossed over attachment to the world.
(From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya)
The commentary on the Nivāpa Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Pāsarāsi Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Pāsarāsi Sutta. In that context, those who are entreating say, "It would be well for us, friends."
It is said that these five hundred monks, residents of the countryside, arrived at Sāvatthī thinking, "We shall see the One of Ten Powers.
They had indeed obtained the sight of the Teacher, but they had not yet heard his Dhamma discourse.
Out of reverence for the Teacher, they were unable to say, "Venerable Sir, please speak a Dhamma discourse to us. For Buddhas are indeed venerable.
Like a solitary-roaming lion, king of beasts; like an elephant in rut; like a hooded venomous snake;
and like a great mass of fire, he is difficult to approach. And this has also been said:
"Just as a terrible venomous snake, or a maned king of beasts..."
“Like a tusker elephant with its tusks, so are the Buddhas difficult to approach.
Since those bhikkhus were unable to request [the teaching] from the Teacher themselves—who was thus difficult to approach—they requested the Venerable Ānanda, saying, “It would be well, friend.
[Ānanda said,] “Perhaps you might obtain it. But why did the Elder say to those bhikkhus, “Of the brahmin Rammaka...”?
"Why did he say, 'You should go to the hermitage'? It was because of the visibility of the Ten-Powered One's actions. For the Elder perceives the actions of the One of Ten Powers:
"Today the Teacher, having stayed at Jetavana, will spend the day's rest at the Eastern Park;
today, having stayed at the Eastern Park, will spend the day's rest at Jetavana; today he will enter for alms all alone."
“Today, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he will set out on a journey through the countryside at this time.

But does he possess the knowledge of others’ minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) for the purpose of knowing this? No, he does not. Rather, he knows it through the faculty of inference (*anumānabuddhi*), by grasping the method based on actions already performed.
For on whatever day the Blessed One, having stayed at Jetavana, spends the midday rest in the Eastern Monastery...
When he wishes to enter [the village] for alms, he then displays the manner of putting away the requisites for lodgings; the Elder puts away the broom, the refuse, and so forth.
This same procedure applies when, having stayed at the Eastern Monastery, he comes to the Jeta Grove for his midday rest.
But when he wishes to enter alone for alms, he performs his bodily grooming early in the morning and enters the Fragrant Chamber.
Having entered and closed the door, he sat down after attaining the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*).

The Elder, knowing through that sign that "today the Blessed One is sitting having seen a kinsman who is to be awakened," gave notice to the monks, saying: "Friends, today the Blessed One wishes to enter alone;
you should prepare yourselves for almsround. But when [the Buddha was] surrounded by the community of monks...
When he wishes to enter [the Gandhakuti], he then leaves the door of the Fragrant Chamber half-open, enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), and sits down.
The Elder, having perceived this through that sign, gives the signal to the monks to take their bowls and robes.
When he wishes to set out on a journey through the countryside, he then eats one or two mouthfuls in excess.
At all times he would mount his walking-path and pace back and forth; the Elder, perceiving this through that sign, gave notice to the bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Blessed One wishes to go on a journey through the countryside; perform what needs to be done for him.
For twenty years after his first enlightenment, the Blessed One lived without a fixed residence, and afterwards for twenty-five years.
While living in dependence on Sāvatthī itself, he would occupy two places on alternate days.
Having stayed in the Jeta Grove during the night, on the following day he would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the southern gate surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
then, having departed through the eastern gate, he would spend the day’s rest in the Eastern Park (Pubbārāma). During the night, he remained in the Eastern Park.

Having stayed there, on the following day he entered Sāvatthī for alms through the eastern gate, and having departed through the southern gate, he took his midday rest in Jeta’s Grove. Why? Out of compassion for two families:
for one standing in a human body, such as Anāthapiṇḍika; and for one standing in a female body, such as Visākhā.
There is no woman known to have made such a sacrifice of wealth for the sake of the Tathāgata;
therefore, out of compassion for them, the Blessed One partakes of these two meals on that one day. On that particular day, however, he stayed at Jetavana;
therefore the Elder said: "Today the Blessed One, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, in the evening time [washed] his limbs..."
"He will go to the eastern bathing pool to bathe; then, after I have bathed my limbs and requested the Blessed One to stay, I will take him to the hermitage of the brahmin Ramaka and depart.
In this way, these bhikkhus will receive a discourse on the Dhamma from the presence of the Blessed One. Having thought thus, he spoke to those bhikkhus as follows.
"The Mansion of Migāra’s Mother" refers to the mansion of Visākhā. For she was called "Migāra’s Mother" because she was placed by the merchant Migāra in the position of a mother.
"Emerging from seclusion": it is said that in that mansion, between the private chambers of two great disciples, there was a private chamber for the Blessed One.
The Elder opened the door and [entered] the inner chamber.
Having swept the floor and removed the floral refuse, he arranged the couches and seats and signaled to the Teacher.
The Teacher entered the inner chamber and, mindful and clearly comprehending, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture.
Having allayed his fatigue, he arose, entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), and remained seated. In the evening, he emerged from that state.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "having emerged from seclusion.
To "bathe" means: for one who bathes by rubbing his limbs with powder, clay, and so forth, or by scrubbing them with a wash-basin, a handful of earth, or similar things, he is said to "bathe.
One who, without doing so, simply bathes in the natural way, "bathes by pouring water over himself" (*parisiñcati*).
It is said. Even on the Blessed One’s body, dust and dirt do not adhere;
however, for the purpose of adjusting to the weather, the Blessed One enters the water alone. Therefore he said: “to bathe his limbs. “Pubbakoṭṭhaka” means the eastern gatehouse.
It is said that the monastery at Sāvatthī was sometimes large and sometimes small; for instance, during the time of Vipassī [Buddha]...
In the time of the Blessed One [Kakusandha], it was one *yojana* in extent; in the time of Sikhī, three *gāvutas*; in the time of Vessabhū, half a *yojana*;
in the time of Kakusandha, the measure of one *gāvuta*; in the time of Koṇāgamana, the measure of half a *gāvuta*; in the time of Kassapa, the measure of twenty *usabhas*;
and in the time of our Blessed One, it arose with the measure of eight *karīsas*. That city was sometimes near his monastery.
Sometimes it is to the east, sometimes to the south, sometimes to the west, and sometimes to the north.
However, the spot where the four legs of the couch are fixed in the Gandhakuṭī at Jetavana remains immovable.

For there are four places known as the immovable shrines (*acalacetiyatthāna*): the place of the Great Enlightenment Seat (*mahābodhipallaṅka*) at Bodh-Gayā, and the place of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana.
The place where the staircase was established at the gate of Saṅkassanagara at the time of the descent from heaven is called Mañcapādaṭṭhāna.
This Pubba-koṭṭhaka, however, was a gate-tower at the eastern gate during the time when the Dasabala Kassapa resided there for twenty usabhas;
even now it is known as Pubba-koṭṭhaka. During the time of Kassapa Dasabala, [the river] Aciravatī...
Flowing around the city and reaching the eastern gate, it broke through with its waters and created a great lake that was level at the surface yet gradually deepened.
Therein were separate bathing places: one for the king, one for the citizens, one for the Saṅgha of monks, and one for the Buddhas; thus they were delightful and distinct from one another.

[The sands were] like scattered strips of silver. Thus the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, approached that eastern gatehouse of such a kind in order to bathe his limbs. Then the Venerable Ānanda brought forward a bathing robe.
The Blessed One, having removed his red double-layered upper garment (*dupaṭṭa*), put on the bathing robe. The Elder [Ānanda], together with the *dupaṭṭa*...
He placed the great robe in his own hands. The Blessed One entered the water.

At the very moment he stepped into the water, all the fish and turtles became golden-colored. It was as if streams of liquid gold were being poured from mechanical tubes, or as if a sheet of gold cloth were being spread out.
Then, having shown the Blessed One the proper manner of bathing, he bathed.

When he had stepped out [of the water], the Elder offered him a red double-layered cloth (*rattadupaṭṭa*). The Blessed One, having dressed himself in it, fastened his girdle which resembled a flash of lightning, gathered his great outer robe (*mahācīvara*) by its edges, and having made it resemble the interior of a lotus, stood holding the two corners that were offered to him.
Thus it is said: "Having bathed his limbs at Pubbakoṭṭhaka..."
Having stepped out, he stood there clad in a single robe.

As the Blessed One stood thus, his body shone as if mocking with its splendor the fully blossomed lake of lotuses and water-lilies, the Pāricchattaka tree in full bloom, and the vault of heaven radiant with the shimmering rays of the stars. He was resplendent, graced by the circle of his fathom-wide aura.

A garland of his thirty-two excellent marks was arranged there like a garland of thirty-two moons, like a garland of thirty-two suns, and like thirty-two wheel-turning monarchs, thirty-two kings of the gods, and thirty-two great Brahmās set in succession;
it shone most brilliantly—this is what is called the "ground of complexion" (*vaṇṇabhūmi*). In such places as these, the bodily color of the Buddhas [is displayed].
Or, when a capable Dhamma-preacher fills out the discourse by bringing forth the praise of virtues, or by means of prose passages, verses, meanings, similes, and reasons—it is fitting [to listen];
in such instances, the strength of the Dhamma-preacher should be understood.
273. “Making his limbs shrivel” means making them return to their natural state, making them waterless, drying them up.
The meaning is as follows: for one who puts on a robe with limbs wet with water, the folds of the robe rise up and the requisites become soiled.
However, dust and dirt do not adhere to the bodies of the Buddhas;

like a drop of water placed upon a lotus leaf, the water rolls off and passes away. Even though this was the case, out of reverence for the training, the Blessed One [said], "The duty of one gone forth..."
Saying, "It is called 'name,'" he took hold of both corners of the great robe (*mahācīvara*) and stood there, covering his body from the front.
At that moment, the Elder thought: "From the time the Blessed One put on the great robe and set out toward the Migāramātupāsāda, he will be difficult to turn back;
for indeed, it is impossible to thwart the intention of the Buddhas."
It is as perilous as reaching out one's hand to catch a solitary roaming lion,
as touching the trunk of a rutting noble elephant, or as grasping the neck of a venomous snake of fierce power.
It was for this very reason that [the Blessed One], having described the excellence of the brahmin Rammaka’s hermitage, [urged] the Blessed One to go there.
"I shall request it. He did accordingly. Therefore it is said: "Then the Venerable Ānanda... out of compassion.

In this context, "out of compassion" means: out of regard for the five hundred bhikkhus who had gone to that hermitage to hear a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One; that is to say, having felt pity for them.
"By means of a discourse on the Dhamma": they were seated together, praising one or another of the ten perfections as well as the Great Renunciation. "Waiting" means looking on.
The meaning is that he did not enter abruptly, thinking "I am the Buddha," but remained there until that discourse was concluded. "He struck the bolt" means...
He gave a signal on the door-panel with his fingernail. "They opened [the door]" means that because they were sitting with their ears pricked, they came at that very moment and opened it.
"On seats prepared" means that, it is said, during the time of the Buddha, wherever even a single bhikkhu dwelt, a seat for the Buddha was always prepared there.
Why? It is said that the Blessed One would take his meditation subject from those very places.
While dwelling in a comfortable location, he reflects: "So-and-so has gone away after receiving a meditation subject from me;
will he be able to produce a distinction or not? Then he sees him having abandoned the meditation subject and engaging in unwholesome thoughts.
Thereupon, [he thinks]: "How can this be so, in the presence of a Teacher such as I..."
“Thinking, ‘If this son of good family dwells having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*),
unwholesome thoughts will overcome him and cause him to wander in the beginningless round of suffering (*vaṭṭadukkha*),’ [the deity], for the sake of favoring him, manifested himself right there,
exhorted that son of good family, and then, soaring into the air, returned once more to his own dwelling place. Thus being exhorted,”
Those bhikkhus thought: “The Teacher, knowing our thoughts, has come and shows himself standing right near us;
at such a moment, the effort of searching for a seat, thinking, ‘Venerable sir, sit here, sit here,’ would be a burden.
Thus, they remained there having already prepared their seats. Whoever had a stool, he prepared it.
One who has nothing prepares either a couch, a plank, a piece of wood, a stone, or a heap of sand.
Failing to find these, they even gather old leaves, spread a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) upon them, and place it there.
But in this case, the seat was already naturally prepared; it is with reference to that that it is said: "He sat down on the prepared seat."
*Kāya nu* means: "By what discourse are you seated? is the meaning. There is also a textual reading, *kāya netthā*, which means: "By what [discourse] is there here? is the meaning.
There is also a textual reading, *kāya notthā*, the meaning of which is the same as the former.
*Antarā kathā* means another discourse occurring in between [the usual topics], such as between the attention to meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), recitations, or inquiries.
"Discourse": "Incomplete" means it was left unfinished due to my arrival, not having reached its conclusion.
"Then the Blessed One arrived": at that time, the Blessed One came. "Or a discourse on the Dhamma":
a discourse on the Dhamma based on the ten topics of discourse. "Or noble silence": here, even the second jhāna is considered noble silence.

And also the original meditation subject (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, a bhikkhu who is seated having entered that jhāna, as well as one who is seated having taken up the original meditation subject, should be understood as being seated in noble silence. 274.
"Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of search"—what is the connection [to this]? Those bhikkhus [were listening] face-to-face to a discourse on the Dhamma...
Thinking, "We shall listen," they made the Elder their burden; the Elder went to their hermitage.
Having sat down there, they engaged in worldly talk for a long time and then sat listening to a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One began this teaching to show them: "This quest of yours is called the Noble Quest. In that regard, what is it?
"Monks, the ignoble search": here, just as a man skilled in the path, first pointing out the path to ruin that must be avoided, says,
"Abandon the left and take the right," so too the Blessed One, through his skill in teaching,
first explained the ignoble search which must be abandoned, thinking, "I shall later explain the other," thus following the sequence of the summary.
Having broken [the seal], he spoke thus: "Subject to birth" means having the nature of being born. "Subject to aging" means having the nature of growing old.

"Subject to illness" means having the nature of being ill. "Subject to death" means having the nature of dying. "Subject to sorrow" means having the nature of grieving. "Subject to defilement" means having the nature of becoming defiled.
"Son and wife" means both son and wife. This method applies everywhere. Regarding "gold and silver":
here, "gold" (*jātarūpa*) means gold; "silver" (*rajata*) means whatever is used for trade, such as iron coins and the like.
"These acquisitions, monks, are subject to birth" means that these so-called acquisitions of the five strands of sensual pleasure are all subject to birth.
[The text] shows this. In the section on the nature of disease (*byādhidhammavāra*) and others, gold and silver are not included;
for these do not have diseases such as headaches, nor do they undergo death in the form of passing away (*cuti*) like sentient beings, nor does sorrow arise [in them].

However, because they become defiled by impurities such as iron and other metals, they are included in the section on the nature of defilement (*saṃkilesadhammavāra*). Likewise, because they are produced by temperature (*utusamuṭṭhāna*),...
In the section on the nature of birth (*jātidhamma*), [the search] is included because it leads to decay;
