and in the section on the nature of aging (*jarādhamma*), it is included because it takes up impurity. 275. “This, monks, is the noble search”: this should be understood as the ‘noble search’ both because it is faultless and because it is to be sought after by the noble ones (*ariya*).
276. Why did he begin with the words, “I too, monks, at one time”? It was in order to show the Great Renunciation starting from its very root.
Thus it occurred to him: "Monks, in the past I too pursued the ignoble quest.
Having abandoned that and pursued the noble quest, I attained omniscience. The group-of-five monks also pursued the ignoble quest;
having abandoned that and pursued the noble quest, they have reached the stage where the taints are exhausted. You too..."
“Both I and the group of five have ascended the path; the Noble Search is your search.
Thus he began this teaching in order to show his own Great Renunciation from its very beginning.
277. In that context, “being still young” means being still in one’s youth. “With hair still quite black” means having hair that is perfectly black, indeed hair the color of collyrium.
"Hutvā" means "having offered. "Bhadrena" means "by the auspicious one. "Paṭhamena vayasā" means "by the first of the three stages of life.
"Akāmakānaṃ" means "of those who do not desire it"; here the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. "Assumukhānaṃ" means "those whose faces have tears [upon them]";
the meaning is "of those with tear-stained faces. "Rudantānaṃ" means "of those weeping," that is, crying out and lamenting.
"Seeking what that is wholesome? means seeking "what is wholesome. "The unsurpassed, supreme state of peace" means the supreme state known as peace;
the meaning is, while searching for Nibbāna. "Where Āḷāra Kālāma [dwells]"—here, *Āḷāra* is his name;
it is said that he was long and tawny, and thus his name became Āḷāra. *Kālāma* is his clan name. "While the venerable one was dwelling... [and so forth].
"Let the venerable one dwell. "Wherein a wise man"—that is, wherein a person of wisdom [dwells]. "His own teacher’s doctrine"—that is, his own teacher’s system.
"Having attained, let him dwell"—that is, having acquired it, let him dwell.
To this extent, he has made an opening. "That doctrine"—that is, that system and tradition of theirs. "I mastered"—that is, having heard it, I learned it by heart.
“By the mere movement of the lips” means by the mere striking of the lips for the purpose of receiving what was spoken by him;

the meaning is: by the mere movement of the lips back and forth. “By the mere response to what was spoken” means by the mere replying to what was spoken by him. “The claim of knowledge” means the claim that “I know.
“The claim of seniority” means the claim of being established [in the teaching]; it is the claim that “I am an elder (thera) here.”

The statement: "I and others as well" means that it is not only I, but many others also speak thus. "Merely by way of faith" means without having realized it through wisdom, but solely by means of pure faith alone.
It is said that even while learning the Dhamma by word of mouth, the Bodhisatta thought:
"Kālāma does not possess merely the mastery of the scriptures regarding this Dhamma; surely he has attained the seven meditative absorptions (samāpatti)."
He understood, “I am an attainer,” and this thought occurred to him:
“You have proclaimed the base of nothingness” means you have made me know the seven meditative attainments (samāpatti) culminating in the base of nothingness.
“Faith” refers to the faith for the purpose of producing these seven attainments. The same applies to energy and the other [faculties].

"May I strive": may I apply myself to practice. "Before long, having realized that Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, having attained it, may I dwell therein"—it is said that the Bodhisatta, exerting his energy, produced the seven meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in just a few days, as if stretching out seven golden ladders; therefore he spoke thus.
“Gains for us, friends!”—it is said that this Kālāma was free from envy. Therefore, without harboring envy by thinking, “This man has only recently arrived;
what has he done to produce this Dhamma? he spoke thus, manifesting his faith as one who was inspired with confidence:
“Both of us together shall lead this group. Having said, “This group is large; let both of us lead it,” he gave notice to the group.
He gave [the gift], saying: “I too am an attainer of the seven meditative attainments (samāpatti), and the Great Man is likewise an attainer of only the seven;
so many people learn the preliminary service (parikamma) from the Great Man, and so many from me. Thus, having divided [the disciples] in the middle, he gave them away.
“Exalted” (uḷārāya) means supreme. Regarding “worship” (pūjāya): it is said that both the women and men who were attendants of Kālāmāsa offered perfumes, garlands, and other such items.
They come bringing [offerings]. Kālāma says, “Go, pay honor to the Great Man.
Having honored him, they honor Kālāma with whatever remains. They bring costly beds and chairs;
having had those given to the Great Man, if anything remains, he takes it for himself. In every place they go, there is excellent lodging.
Having had the Bodhisatta look after [the food], he took the remainder for himself. Thus he honored him with sublime worship.

Regarding the phrases "this Dhamma is not for disenchantment," and so forth: this Dhamma of the seven attainments is neither for the purpose of disenchantment with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), nor for the purpose of dispassion, nor for the purpose of the cessation of lust and the like, nor for the purpose of peace, nor for the purpose of directly knowing the Dhamma that is to be directly known.
The meaning is that it does not lead to the enlightenment of the four paths, nor to the realization of Nibbāna.

"Only as far as rebirth in the base of nothingness" means that it leads only as far as rebirth in the existence of the base of nothingness, where the lifespan is measured at sixty thousand kappas, but not beyond that.
Thus, this is indeed subject to the nature of returning once more.
And whatever state he attains, that is indeed not liberated from birth, aging, and death; it is merely surrounded by the snare of Māra.
From that point on, however, the Great Being was like a man with an empty stomach who, having obtained delicious food, eats it with delight, yet afterwards discards it due to bile, phlegm, or flies.
Just as one does not give rise to the thought, "I shall eat even a single morsel again," so too,
although these seven attainments have been produced with great effort, having seen the danger in them— namely, this distinction of returning again and so forth—
one does not think: "I shall advert to this state again, or attain it, or resolve upon it, or emerge from it."
Or "I shall review it"—he did not even give rise to such a thought. "Having adorned" means having adorned again and again, thinking, "Enough with this," "Enough with this.
"Becoming disillusioned" means having become weary of it. "I departed" means I went away. 278.
"Rāma indeed did not know this Dhamma"—here too, the Bodhisatta knew it even while he was still learning that Dhamma.
“This teaching of the eight attainments is not something merely learned by word of mouth from the water; surely he is one who has actually attained the eight attainments.
Then it occurred to him: “Rāma did not dwell knowing and seeing [as he claimed],” and so forth. The rest here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous section.
279. Regarding the phrase "where [is] Uruvelā, the village of Senā": here, *uruvelā* means a great bank (*mahāvelā*), that is to say, a great heap of sand.
Alternatively, *uru* refers to sand, and *velā* means a boundary (*mariyādā*). Because it was brought [to that place] by the force of overstepping a boundary, it is called *uruvelā*;
this is how the meaning should be understood here. It is said that in the past, before the Buddhas had appeared, ten thousand sons of noble family went forth as ascetics.
Having gone forth and dwelling in that region, they gathered together one day and established a formal agreement:
"Bodily and verbal actions are indeed evident to others, but mental action is not.
Therefore, whoever entertains a thought of sensual desire, ill will, or cruelty, another shall be their reprover."
"There is no other punishment for him; let him, having reproached himself by his own self, bring sand in a leaf-bag and scatter it in this place—this shall be his disciplinary task.
From that time forth, whoever conceived such a thought would scatter sand there in a leaf-bag, and thus gradually a great heap of sand was formed there. Then...
Later generations surrounded that spot and made it a shrine site; it was with reference to this that it was said: "Uruvelā means a great bank (mahāvelā), which signifies a great heap of sand.
It was also said with reference to that very same place: "Alternatively, 'uru' refers to sand, and 'velā' refers to a boundary.
Because it was brought [to that place] by the cause of overstepping the boundary, it is called Uruvelā; thus the meaning should be understood here."
“Senānigama” means the market town of the army. It is said that in that place there was a military encampment for the people of the first eon;
therefore, that locality is called Senānigama. There is also a reading “Senāni-gāma. The meaning is:

the village of Senāni, who was the father of Sujātā. “Tadavasarim” means I entered there. “Ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ” means a delightful region of land, variegated with various kinds of water and land flowers in full bloom.
I saw a delightful region of land; and I saw a charming grove of trees, like a cluster of peacock feathers, inspiring serene confidence.
And I saw the flowing river—the River Nerañjarā—with its clear, cool, blue water resembling a mass of jewels, flowing on.
It was white, meaning pure and free from mud; it had beautiful landing-stairs, meaning with [banks] gradually deepening.
It was endowed with beautiful bathing places. "Delightful" means it was like a sheet of silver, strewn with sand, abounding in fish and turtles, and lovely to behold.

"And on all sides, a village for alms" means that not far from that spot, on all sides, he saw a village for alms that was well-suited for coming and going and where alms-food was easily obtained for those who had successfully gone forth. "Alaṃ vata" means "it is indeed sufficient."
"He sat down right there" refers to his sitting upon the Bodhi throne.
For in the preceding sutta, "right there" intended the place where he performed austerities; here, however, it refers to the Bodhi throne. Therefore he said, "he sat down right there.
"This is sufficient for striving" means that having thought, "this place is capable for the purpose of striving," he sat down.
280. *Ajjhagamam* means I attained, I acquired. "And knowledge and vision arose for me" means that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), capable of seeing all phenomena, arose for me.
"My deliverance is unshakable" means that my deliverance, which is the fruit of Arhatship, is unshakable both by virtue of its own unshakeability and by virtue of its unshakeable object;
for it is called "unshakable" because it is not disturbed by lust and the other defilements. Thus, it is unshakable by way of its unshakeability as well.
"Unshakable Nibbāna has this as its object" means it is unshakable (*akuppa*). "This is the final birth" means this is the very last birth.
"Now there is no further becoming" shows that the knowledge of reviewing has arisen in him, [thinking]: "Now, for me, there is no further rebirth-linking."
281. *Adhigato* means penetrated. *Dhammo* refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
*Gambhīro* is a term that excludes superficiality. Because it is profound, it is *duddaso*—difficult to see; it must be seen with difficulty and cannot be seen easily.
Precisely because it is difficult to see, it is *duranubodho*—difficult to realize; it must be understood with difficulty and cannot be understood easily. *Santo* means extinguished (*nibbuto*).
"Exalted" (*paṇīta*) means unsurpassable. These two terms are stated with reference exclusively to the supramundane (*lokuttara*).
"Beyond the sphere of reasoning" (*atakkāvacara*) means it is not to be traversed or fathomed by reasoning; it is to be traversed by wisdom alone. "Subtle" (*nipuṇa*) means delicate.

"To be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīya*) means to be known by the wise who have entered upon the right practice. "Delighting in attachment" (*ālayarāma*) refers to beings [who delight] in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
They adhere; therefore they are called "attachments" (*ālaya*). The eight hundred modes of craving's wandering adhere; therefore they are called "attachments.

They delight in those attachments, thus they are "delighting in attachments" (*ālayarāmā*). They take pleasure in attachments, thus they are "pleased with attachments" (*ālayaratā*). They rejoice thoroughly in attachments, thus they are "thoroughly rejoicing in attachments" (*ālayasammuditā*).
For just as [people delight] in a well-prepared place endowed with trees laden with flowers and fruit...
Having entered the garden, the king delights in each of those excellences; enraptured, joyful, and exceedingly glad, he does not grow weary and does not wish to depart even at the end of the day.
In the same way, through these abodes of sensual desire and abodes of craving, beings delight;
enraptured and unwearying, they dwell within the cycle of saṃsāra. Therefore, for their sake, the Blessed One [teaches] both kinds...
Showing the *ālaya* (the underlying substrate) to be like a pleasure garden, he said, "delighting in the *ālaya*," and so forth.

*Yadidaṃ* is an indeclinable particle; its meaning should be understood as "that which here" when referring to a location, and "this which" when referring to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Regarding the phrase "dependent origination by way of specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppāda*): the conditions for these [factors] are "specific conditions" (*idappaccayā*).

"Specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*) is simply the state of being a specific condition (*idappaccaya*); and since that specific conditionality is itself dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), it is called "specific conditionality-dependent origination.
This is a designation for the conditions such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). "The stilling of all formations," and so forth—all this refers exclusively to Nibbāna.
For it is by resorting to that [Nibbāna] that all the stirrings of formations (*saṅkhāra-vipphandita*) are stilled and completely pacified; therefore, it is called "the stilling of all formations."

It is so called because by depending upon it, all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all craving (taṇhā) is exhausted, all defilements and lusts (kilesa-rāga) fade away, and all suffering (dukkha) ceases. Therefore, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, and cessation are so called.
Furthermore, this craving leads from existence to existence, or from fruit to fruit.
It is called "woven" (*vāna*) because it weaves together, joins, and stitches together;
that which has emerged from this is "unwoven" (*nibbāna*). "That would be weariness for me" means that the teaching given to those who do not understand would be weariness for me;
the meaning is that it would be an affliction for me. What is stated is that it would be both bodily weariness and bodily affliction.
But in the minds of the Buddhas, neither of these two occurs. The particle *api ssu* is used in the sense of emphasis (*anubrūhana*);
it indicates that "not only did this thought arise, but these verses also occurred to me. *Mam* means "to me. *Anacchariyā* means "not wonderful" (*anu-acchariyā*).
*Paṭibhaṃsu* means they became the objective range of knowledge known as intuition (*paṭibhāna*); they reached the state of being fit for thorough reflection.
"By means of difficulty" means by means of suffering, not by a painful path of practice. For the four paths of the Buddhas are indeed paths of pleasant practice.

However, at the time of fulfilling the perfections, while he was still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion, he would cut off his head—though it was adorned and prepared—for the beggars who came to him one after another;
he would draw out the blood from his neck and pluck out his well-anointed eyes.

This was said with reference to the practice leading to the future state (āgamaniya-paṭipadā) for one who gives such things as "a son who is the lamp of his family lineage" or "a wife who is pleasing in conduct," and for one who undergoes cutting, breaking, and so forth in other bodily existences similar to those of Khantivādi and others.
Here, the syllable *ha* in *halan* is merely a particle; the meaning is *alan*. *Pakāsituṃ* means "to teach"; thus, [it was taught] with difficulty.
"It is sufficient to teach the Dhamma that has been realized; it is enough to teach it—what is the purpose of teaching it? This is what is meant.
"By those overcome by lust and hatred" means by those who are touched by lust and hatred, or followed by lust and hatred.

"Going against the stream" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which goes against the stream of [views such as] permanence and so forth, by way of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.
"Intoxicated by passion" means they are stained by passion for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*), passion for existence (*bhavarāga*), and passion for views (*diṭṭhirāga*).
"They shall not see" means they will not perceive things according to their true nature—that they are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul;
since they do not see this, who could possibly cause them to grasp it? "Enveloped by a mass of darkness" means they are overwhelmed by the heap of ignorance (*avijjā*).

282. "By way of indifference" means by way of a state of being free from exertion; the meaning is: by way of having no desire to teach. But why did his mind incline in this way? Was it not said: "I am liberated, I shall liberate others; I have crossed over, I shall help others cross? What need have I for living in disguise? Having realized the Dhamma here, and having attained omniscience, I shall lead across the world together with its devas"?—[It was because of the following: "If I were to teach the Dhamma, others would not understand me; that would be wearying for me, and it would be a weariness. And: "The Dhamma is subtle and difficult to see, difficult to comprehend; those who are attached to their own views will not accept it. And: "Even when the Buddhas appear in the world, beings are still hard to instruct. And: "The world is blinded by ignorance; it does not see the Truth. And: "The world is shrouded in darkness; how can I make it see? And: "The world is sunk in the great flood; how can I rescue it? And: "The world is on fire; how can I extinguish it? And: "The world is entangled in the net of craving; how can I release it? And: "The world is bound by the bonds of Māra; how can I free it? And: "The world is oppressed by suffering; how can I relieve it? And: "The world is afflicted by old age, disease, and death; how can I bring about its peace? And: "The world is subject to birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; how can I bring about its liberation? And: "The world is subject to the round of rebirths; how can I bring about its cessation? And: "The world is subject to the three realms of existence; how can I bring about its transcendence? And: "The world is subject to the four floods; how can I bring about its crossing? And: "The world is subject to the five aggregates of clinging; how can I bring about its relinquishment? And: "The world is subject to the six sense bases; how can I bring about its mastery? And: "The world is subject to the seven stations of consciousness; how can I bring about its transcendence? And: "The world is subject to the eight worldly conditions; how can I bring about its equanimity? And: "The world is subject to the nine abodes of beings; how can I bring about its deliverance? And: "The world is subject to the ten bases of fear; how can I bring about its safety? And: "The world is subject to the eleven modes of conduct; how can I bring about its purification? And: "The world is subject to the twelve links of dependent origination; how can I bring about its cessation? And: "The world is subject to the thirteen types of craving; how can I bring about its abandonment? And: "The world is subject to the fourteen kinds of conceit; how can I bring about its uprooting? And: "The world is subject to the fifteen kinds of delusion; how can I bring about its dispelling? And: "The world is subject to the sixteen kinds of heedlessness; how can I bring about its restraint? And: "The world is subject to the seventeen kinds of negligence; how can I bring about its vigilance? And: "The world is subject to the eighteen kinds of mental distraction; how can I bring about its concentration? And: "The world is subject to the nineteen kinds of defilement; how can I bring about its purification? And: "The world is subject to the twenty kinds of wrong view; how can I bring about its eradication? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-one kinds of attachment; how can I bring about its relinquishment? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-two faculties; how can I bring about their mastery? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-three kinds of obstruction; how can I bring about its removal? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-four kinds of fetter; how can I bring about its loosening? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-five kinds of bondage; how can I bring about its release? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-six kinds of confinement; how can I bring about its opening? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-seven kinds of entanglement; how can I bring about its disentangling? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-eight kinds of obscuration; how can I bring about its illumination? And: "The world is subject to the twenty-nine kinds of concealment; how can I bring about its revelation? And: "The world is subject to the thirty kinds of deception; how can I bring about its truth? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-one kinds of illusion; how can I bring about its reality? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-two kinds of error; how can I bring about its correction? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-three kinds of perversion; how can I bring about its rectification? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-four kinds of inversion; how can I bring about its restoration? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-five kinds of distortion; how can I bring about its normalization? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-six kinds of deviation; how can I bring about its alignment? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-seven kinds of misdirection; how can I bring about its guidance? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-eight kinds of wandering; how can I bring about its stabilization? And: "The world is subject to the thirty-nine kinds of drifting; how can I bring about its anchoring? And: "The world is subject to the forty kinds of turbulence; how can I bring about its calm? And: "The world is subject to the forty-one kinds of agitation; how can I bring about its tranquility? And: "The world is subject to the forty-two kinds of unrest; how can I bring about its peace? And: "The world is subject to the forty-three kinds of disturbance; how can I bring about its composure? And: "The world is subject to the forty-four kinds of conflict; how can I bring about its harmony? And: "The world is subject to the forty-five kinds of strife; how can I bring about its reconciliation? And: "The world is subject to the forty-six kinds of discord; how can I bring about its unity? And: "The world is subject to the forty-seven kinds of dissension; how can I bring about its concord? And: "The world is subject to the forty-eight kinds of division; how can I bring about its integration? And: "The world is subject to the forty-nine kinds of separation; how can I bring about its union? And: "The world is subject to the fifty kinds of alienation; how can I bring about its togetherness? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-one kinds of estrangement; how can I bring about its intimacy? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-two kinds of isolation; how can I bring about its communion? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-three kinds of solitude; how can I bring about its fellowship? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-four kinds of loneliness; how can I bring about its companionship? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-five kinds of desolation; how can I bring about its prosperity? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-six kinds of ruin; how can I bring about its well-being? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-seven kinds of decay; how can I bring about its renewal? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-eight kinds of decline; how can I bring about its growth? And: "The world is subject to the fifty-nine kinds of loss; how can I bring about its gain? And: "The world is subject to the sixty kinds of failure; how can I bring about its success? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-one kinds of defeat; how can I bring about its victory? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-two kinds of subjugation; how can I bring about its sovereignty? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-three kinds of servitude; how can I bring about its freedom? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-four kinds of bondage; how can I bring about its liberation? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-five kinds of captivity; how can I bring about its release? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-six kinds of imprisonment; how can I bring about its emancipation? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-seven kinds of confinement; how can I bring about its deliverance? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-eight kinds of restriction; how can I bring about its expansion? And: "The world is subject to the sixty-nine kinds of limitation; how can I bring about its breadth? And: "The world is subject to the seventy kinds of narrowness; how can I bring about its vastness? And: "The world is subject to the seventy-one kinds of contraction; how can I bring about its extension? And: "The world is subject to the seventy-two kinds of compression; how can I bring about its relaxation? And: "
"Having made the aspiration and fulfilled the perfections, he attained omniscience. This is true;

however, it was through the power of such reflection that his mind thus inclined. For when he had attained omniscience and was reflecting upon the density of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma, the density of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma appeared to him in every aspect.

They became visible. Then, as he reflected, "These beings are like gourds filled with sour gruel, like bowls filled with buttermilk, like rags soaked in fat and oil, and like hands smeared with collyrium;
they are filled with defilements, excessively defiled, dyed by lust, corrupted by hatred, and bewildered by delusion—what indeed will they penetrate?
his mind inclined in this way through the power of reflecting upon the thicket of defilements.
“And this Dhamma is profound like the mass of water that sustains the earth;
it is difficult to see, like a mustard seed placed on a mountain and hidden from view; it is difficult to realize, like joining the tip of a hair split a hundredfold to the tip of another hair.
For was it not by striving to penetrate this Dhamma that I [realized] what is called ‘the giving of the ungiven’?”
Is there no such thing as unguarded virtue? Is there no such thing as any perfections not yet fulfilled?
Even as I was dispersing the host of Māra as if it were effortless, the earth did not tremble; even as I was recollecting my past lives during the first watch of the night, it did not tremble;
even as I was purifying the divine eye during the middle watch, it did not tremble.

Furthermore, it should be understood that his mind was inclined in this way through the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, thinking: "While I was penetrating dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) during the last watch of the night, even as I did so, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled.
Thus, even by one such as myself with sharp wisdom, this Dhamma was penetrated only with great difficulty; how then will the common people of the world penetrate it?"
Furthermore, when requested by Brahmā, his mind inclined toward the desire to teach because the Blessed One knew:
"When my mind inclines toward indolence, Mahābrahmā will request a teaching of the Dhamma from me;
and these beings hold Brahmā in high esteem, so they will think: 'The Teacher indeed was unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but then Mahābrahmā requested him.'"
"...will listen with eager intent, thinking: 'Truly, this Dhamma is peaceful; truly, this Dhamma is sublime!
It should be understood that for this reason also, his mind inclined toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma. Regarding Sahampati:
it is said that in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was an elder named Sahaka who had attained the first jhāna.
Having been reborn, he was born as a Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon in the plane of the first jhāna.
There, they recognize him as Sahampati Brahmā; it is with reference to him that the Buddha said, "of the Brahmā Sahampati.
"Alas, sir, he perishes!"—it is said that he uttered this sound in such a way that all the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world system heard it.
They assembled. "Yatra hi nāma" means "in which world indeed. "Appeared before them" means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmās.
"Of little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātiko*): they are of such a nature that in their eye of wisdom there is little—that is, limited—dust of passion, hatred, and delusion;
thus they are "of little dust in their eyes. "Because of not having heard" means due to the lack of hearing [the Dhamma]. "Will become" means...

He shows that there will not be just one or two, but many hundreds of thousands who have performed their duties under previous Buddhas by means of the ten meritorious deeds; who, like lotuses that have reached maturity upon contact with the rays of the sun,
long for the teaching of the Dhamma itself and are ready to enter the plane of the Noble Ones at the conclusion of even a four-line stanza— those who will become knowers of the Dhamma.
"Pāturahosi" means he appeared. "Cintito samalehi" means thought out by the six teachers who were possessed of impurity.
For they, having arisen earlier, taught a doctrine of impure wrong views that was like scattering thorns throughout the whole of Jambudīpa and like sprinkling poison.
"Apāpura etaṃ" means open this; [the door] of the Deathless.
"The door" refers to the Noble Path, which serves as the gateway to the deathless Nibbāna. "Let them hear the Dhamma realized by the Stainless One" means:

"O Blessed One, let these beings first hear the Dhamma of the Four Truths realized by the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is stainless due to the absence of the stains of passion and so forth"—thus he entreats.
"Just as one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain": this means just as one who stands upon the peak of a solid rock mountain.
For one standing there, there is no need for such actions as turning the neck or stretching out the arms in order to see.
"Like that" (*tathūpama*) means comparable to that, resembling a rocky mountain. Here, however, is the summary of the meaning: just as on the summit of a rocky mountain...

Just as a man with keen vision, standing on a mountain peak, might look all around at the multitude of people, so too, O wise one of beautiful wisdom, you—having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, possessing the all-seeing eye of the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge—should yourself, free from sorrow, look upon, observe, and examine the multitude of people who are immersed in sorrow and overcome by birth and aging.
This is the intended meaning here: just as, for instance, at the foot of a mountain...
Having made a large field on all sides, they would build small huts there along the embankments of the furrows and kindle fires at night.
And suppose there were a darkness endowed with four factors;

then, for a man with clear vision standing upon the summit of that mountain and looking down at the ground, neither the field, nor the embankments, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping therein would be visible.
Only the mere glow of a fire in their huts would be visible.

Thus, for the Tathāgata who has ascended the Palace of Dhamma and surveys the world of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of the Buddha-eye even when sitting in a solitary dwelling on the right knee; they are like arrows shot in the night. Those...
But those individuals who are to be converted and have performed wholesome deeds come into his range even if they are standing far away, just as fire and the Himavanta mountain do.
And this has been said: "The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himavanta mountain."
"Those who are not present here are not seen, like arrows shot in the night.
Thus he spoke, requesting the Blessed One to undertake a journey for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Regarding the terms "Hero" (*vīra*) and so forth:
the Blessed One is a "Hero" because of his possession of vigor; he is a "Victor in Battle" because he has conquered the Māras of the sons of gods, death, and the defilements.
He is a caravan leader (*satthavāha*) because he is capable of acting as a guide for those to be trained (*veneyya*) in order to cross over the wilderness of birth and so forth.

He should be understood as "debtless" (*anaṇa*) because he is free from the debt of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). 283. "Entreaty" (*ajjhesanā*) means a request. "With the Buddha-eye" refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*) and the knowledge of their underlying tendencies and dispositions (*āsayānusayañāṇa*).
Now, these two types of knowledge are called the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakkhu*); omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is the "Universal Eye" (*samantacakkhu*);
and the three knowledges of the path are the "Dharma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*). Regarding the terms "with little dust" (*apparajakkha*) and so forth:

those whose passion and other defilements (*rāgādiraja*) are few in their eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), according to the method already stated, are "those with little dust"; those for whom it is great are "those with much dust. Those whose faith and other [faculties]...
Those whose faculties are sharp are "those with sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriya*). Those whose [faculties] are dull are "those with dull faculties" (*mudindriya*).
Those whose very modes—faith and so forth—are beautiful are "those of good disposition" (*svākāra*).
Those who perceive the reasons explained and can be made to understand easily are "those easy to instruct" (*suviññāpayā*). Those who view both the next world and wrongdoing as fearsome are...
Those who see the fear of blame and the next world. Here is the Pāḷi on this point:
"A person endowed with faith has little dust [on their eyes]; a person lacking faith has much dust. One who is energetic... one who is lazy...
one who is established in mindfulness... one who is muddled in mindfulness... one who is concentrated... one who is unconcentrated... one who is wise..."
A person of weak wisdom has great defilement. Likewise, a person of faith has sharp faculties...
[and so on] ...a person of wisdom sees the fear of blame regarding the next world, whereas a person of weak wisdom does not see the fear of blame regarding the next world.

"World" refers to the world of aggregates, the world of sense-bases, the world of elements, the world of fortunate existence, the world of the origin of fortunate existence, and the world of unfortunate existence.
The world as the source of misfortune; the one world: all beings subsist by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds:
the three feelings. Four worlds: the four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging.
Six worlds: the six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight...
Worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: the ten bases.
Twelve worlds: the twelve bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements.
"Faults" (vajja) refers to all defilements as faults, all misconduct as faults, all volitional formations as faults, and all kamma leading to existence as faults.
"Thus, in this world and in this realm of Mara, an intense perception of danger is established, just as toward an executioner with a raised sword.
In these fifty ways, he knows, sees, understands, and penetrates these five faculties.
This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the degrees of the faculties of others."
"Uppaliniyaṃ" means in a grove of blue lotuses. The same method applies to the others as well.
"Antonimuggaposīni" refers to those that are nourished while remaining submerged within [the water]. "Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni" means standing having risen above the water.
Among these, those that stand having risen above [the water] remain awaiting contact with the rays of the sun; they are destined to flower today. Those...
Those standing level with the water will flower on the following day. Those that have not emerged from the water but remain submerged within it will flower on the third day.
Furthermore, there are other types of lotuses, such as the *saroga-uppala* and so forth, which do not emerge from the water and will not flower at all;
they will simply become food for fish and turtles. These [are what] the text...
They have not yet been mounted. But having brought them forth, they are to be illustrated;

thus they are illustrated. For just as there are those four kinds of flowers, even so there are four types of persons: the one who gains knowledge through a brief summary (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū), the one who is led to understanding (neyyo), and the one for whom the words are the limit (padaparamo).
Among these, "the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs at the very moment it is uttered..."

This person is called one who understands through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*). That person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail, this person is called one who understands through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*).
That person for whom [realization occurs] by means of recitation, by means of inquiry, by means of wise attention, and by serving and associating with virtuous friends...
For one who attends upon [the teaching], there comes about the gradual realization of the Dhamma; this person is called "one to be guided" (*neyya*).

That person for whom, despite hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, there is no realization of the Dhamma in that very lifetime—this person is called "one for whom the words are the limit" (*padaparama*).
In this regard, the Blessed One [compared them] to the *uppala* grove and so forth.

Surveying the ten-thousandfold world system, he saw: "Those who blossom today are those who understand through a condensed teaching; those who blossom tomorrow are those who understand through an expanded teaching;
those who blossom on the third day are those who must be guided; and those whose flowers are to be eaten by fish and turtles are those for whom the word alone is supreme.
And as he looked, he saw: "So many have little dust in their eyes; so many have great dust in their eyes."
There too, he saw in every way that "this many are those who understand through a condensed statement.
In this regard, for three types of persons, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma achieves its purpose within this very lifetime.
For those who are "word-perfect" (padaparama), it serves as a latent impression (vāsanā) for the future. Then the Blessed One [considered] these four types of persons...

Having understood that the teaching of the Dhamma brings about welfare, and having conceived the desire to teach it, he further divided all beings within the three realms of existence into two classes according to their capacity and incapacity. With reference to these, it was said:

"Which are those beings who are incapable? Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of karma, possessed of the obstruction of defilements, and possessed of the obstruction of kamma-result..."

“Those who are possessed of lack of faith, lack of desire [for the good], and lack of wisdom are incapable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states; these beings are incapable.

Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not hindered by kamma-obstruction... [and so on]... these beings are capable. In this context, having set aside all incapable persons, one should consider only the capable persons with wisdom.

Having examined them, he divided them into six groups, thinking: "So many are of a lustful temperament, so many are of a hateful or deluded temperament, and so many are of a discursive, faithful, or intellectual temperament.
Having done this, he thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma. "Paccabhāsiṃ" means I replied.
"Apārutā" means opened. "The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path, for it is indeed the door to that which is called the Deathless.
He shows that he has opened and left standing the door to Nibbāna. "Let them release their faith" means:
let everyone release, that is, relinquish, their own faith. Regarding the last two lines, the meaning is this:
for although I myself am well-versed in and have thoroughly mastered this sublime and supreme Dhamma, I have nevertheless perceived it as a weariness of body and speech.
"I did not speak. But now, let all people bring vessels of faith; I shall fill their intentions.

(284) "Bhikkhus, this occurred to me" means that this thought connected with the teaching of the Dhamma arose: "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?"—this is the meaning. But when did this [thought arise]?
Did it arise? It arose on the eighth day after he had become a Buddha.

Herein is the sequential account: it is said that on the day of the Great Renunciation, the Bodhisatta, his heart filled with agitation upon seeing the harem left open, addressed Channa, saying, "Bring Kaṇḍaka," and accompanied by Channa, he mounted the back of the king of horses.
Having departed from the city, he showed the site of the Kaṇḍaka-turning-back monument;
then, having crossed three kingdoms and gone forth on the bank of the Anomā River, he wandered by stages on his journey until, after walking for alms in Rājagaha, he sat upon Paṇḍava Mountain.
There, when asked his name and clan by King Magadhisara, [the king] said, "Accept this kingdom."

He said, “Enough, Great King; I have no need for kingship. Having renounced the kingdom, I have gone forth with the thought, ‘I shall become one who has lifted the veil from the world by devoting myself to the exertion for the welfare of the world.
Then, having been given the promise, “In that case, once you have become a Buddha, you should first enter my realm,” he [dismissed] Kālāma and Udaka.
Having approached them, finding no essence in their teaching of the Dhamma, he departed from there.
Although he practiced austerities for six years at Uruvelā, being unable to penetrate the Deathless (amata), he nourished his body by partaking of substantial food.
At that time, in the village of Uruvelā, a daughter of a householder named Sujātā made an aspiration under a banyan tree.
“If I go to a family home of equal birth and obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I shall perform an offering ceremony (*balikamma*),” she thought.

Her aspiration was fulfilled. On the full moon day of the month of Visākha, thinking, “I will perform the offering ceremony early in the morning,” she prepared rice porridge (*pāyasa*) at the very time of dawn during the night. While that rice porridge was cooking—
Vast, magnificent flowers rose up and moved about, turning to the right; not even a single drop fell outside.
Mahābrahmā held a parasol. The four World-Protectors took up their positions for protection with swords in hand.
Sakka kindled the fire by rubbing together fire-sticks. The deities gathered vital essence from the four continents.
They threw it there. The Bodhisatta, awaiting the time for his alms-round, went early in the morning and sat down at the foot of a tree.
The nurse, who had gone to clear the area around the tree, returned and informed Sujātā: "A deity is sitting at the foot of the tree.
Sujātā, having adorned herself with all her finery, [prepared] a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces].
Having increased the milk-rice and covered it with another golden bowl, she lifted it up and departed. Seeing the Great Man,
she placed the bowl in his hands along with the food, paid homage, and said, "Just as my own wish has been fulfilled,
may yours also be fulfilled," and then she left.

The Bodhisatta went to the bank of the Nerañjarā River, set down the golden bowl on the shore, bathed, and having emerged from the water, he ate the milk-rice while dividing it into forty-nine mouthfuls.
Then he threw the bowl away, saying, "If I shall become a Buddha this day, let the bowl go against the current!
The bowl went against the current, stopped for a short distance, and [remained] before Kāla, the King of Nagas.
Having entered the hall, he stood there holding aloft the alms-bowls of the three Buddhas.

The Great Being, having spent the day in meditation within the forest grove, took the eight handfuls of grass given by the Sottiya at evening time, ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and stood on the southern side. That spot was like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf.
It shook as if it were being moved. The Great Being thought, "This cannot sustain my virtue," and went toward the western quarter;
it shook in the same way. He went toward the northern quarter; it shook in the same way. He went toward the eastern quarter;
there, a space the size of a cross-legged seat remained as firm as a well-planted post driven into the ground.

It became immovable. The Great Being thought, "This spot is the place where all Buddhas break and shatter the defilements," and grasping those blades of grass at their tips, he shook them. They became as if cut by the edge of a painter's brush.
The Bodhisatta resolved with fourfold energy: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained enlightenment."
Having resolved upon his purpose, he sat down cross-legged. At that very moment,
Māra manifested a thousand arms, mounted the elephant named Girimekhala— who was one hundred and fifty yojanas high—
and taking along an army of Māra ninety yojanas in extent, he approached like a mountain, looking on with a sidelong glance as if about to overwhelm him.
He approached. The Great Being thought: "While I was fulfilling the ten perfections, there was no other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who could serve as my witness.
However, during my seven previous existences as Vessantara, this great earth was my witness;
and now too, it is this very same insentient great earth, appearing like a wooden log, that is my witness."

“Witness! he cried, stretching out his hand. At that very moment, the great earth, emitting hundreds and thousands of roars like a bronze bowl struck by an iron rod, thundered and rolled, casting Māra’s army against the rim of the world-system.
Having dispersed Māra’s forces while the sun was still shining, the Great Being, during the first watch of the night, attained the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*).

Having purified the divine eye during the middle watch of the night, and having applied his knowledge to dependent origination during the last watch, he contemplated the cycle of existence and its cessation;

then, upon the rising of the dawn, having become a Buddha, he sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, thinking: "For many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, I have exerted effort for the sake of this very seat."
Then, a doubt arose in some of the deities: "Are there indeed other qualities that lead to Buddhahood?
Thereupon, on the eighth day, the Blessed One emerged from his meditative attainment;

perceiving the deities' doubt, and for the purpose of dispelling it, he rose into the air, displayed the Twin Miracle, and having dispelled their doubt, [slightly shifted] from his cross-legged posture...

Standing on the northern side of the eastern base, he spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at both the throne and the Bodhi tree— the place where he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kappas;
that spot became known as the Animisa Cetiya (the Unblinking Shrine).

Then, walking back and forth on a jeweled walkway that extended from east to west between the place where he sat cross-legged and the spot where he stood, he passed seven days; that place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya (Jeweled Walkway Shrine).
Then, in the western direction, the deities constructed a jeweled house, and there, sitting cross-legged, [he recited] the Abhidhammapitaka.
In particular, he spent seven days there investigating the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations) with its infinite methods;

that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya. Having thus spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, on the fifth week he departed from the foot of the Bodhi tree and approached the Ajapāla banyan tree. There, too, he [contemplated] the Dhamma...
Investigating [the Dhamma] and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he sat down; and while investigating the Dhamma, he hereupon discerned the path of method in the Abhidhamma as follows:
first the treatise called the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, then the *Vibhaṅga* treatise, the *Dhātukathā* treatise, the *Puggalapaññatti* treatise, the treatise called the *Kathāvatthu*, and the *Yamaka*.
...the manual named *Nāma-pakaraṇa*, and after that, the Great Manual named *Paṭṭhāna*.
There, as his mind entered into the subtle and delicate *paṭṭhāna*, joy arose;

when joy arose, the blood became clear, and when the blood was clear, the skin became clear. When the skin was clear, from the front part of his body [there appeared] things the size of gabled houses and so forth.
The rays, having arisen, leapt into the sky like a herd of six-tusked nāga elephants and surged into infinite world-systems in the eastern direction;
having arisen from his back, they surged into the western direction; having arisen from the right shoulder, they surged into the southern direction;
and having arisen from the left shoulder, they surged into the northern direction into infinite world-systems.
From the soles of his feet, rays of light the color of coral sprouts issued forth;
piercing through the great earth and splitting the waters in two, they burst through the mass of air and entered the cloudless sky.
From his head, a circle of blue-colored rays arose like a revolving jeweled garland; piercing through the six celestial worlds, they reached the nine Brahma worlds.
Having pierced through the Vehapphala realm and the five Suddhāvāsa heavens, and having transcended the four formless realms, they entered the unblemished space.
On that day, in immeasurable world-systems, immeasurable beings all became golden-colored.
And from the Blessed One’s body on that day, those rays have continued to emerge even until this very day.
Infinite world-systems indeed pass by.
Thus the Blessed One, having spent seven days at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, sat for the next seven days under the Mucalinda tree;
and as soon as he had sat down, a great unseasonable cloud arose, filling the entire interior of the world-system.
It is said that such a great cloud rains only at two times: when a Wheel-turning Monarch has appeared, or when a Buddha has appeared.
In this case, it arose during the time of a Buddha. When he had appeared, Mucalinda the Naga King thought:
"This cloud has arisen just as the Teacher has entered my abode; it is fitting that I provide him with a dwelling."
Although he was capable of constructing a palace made of the seven precious gems, thinking, "If it were built in this way, it would not be of great fruit for me;

rather, I shall perform bodily service for the One Possessing the Ten Powers," he assumed a massive body, surrounded the Teacher seven times with his coils, and held his hood over him. Within that enclosure, there was space—
At its base, it was the size of the Lohapāsāda palace. The Nāga king’s intention was that the Teacher should dwell there in whatever posture he desired; therefore, he enclosed such a vast space.
In the center, a jeweled couch was prepared, above which was a canopy of cloth variegated with golden stars and draped with hanging garlands of perfumes and flowers.
It was so. Lamps lit with fragrant oil were burning in the four corners, and sandalwood caskets were set out opened in the four directions.
Thus the Blessed One spent that week there, and for the following week he sat at the Rājāyatana tree.
On the eighth week, having eaten a tooth-stick and medicinal myrobalan brought by Sakka, Lord of the Devas, [he emerged from jhāna].
Having washed his face and partaken of the alms-food offered by Tapussa and Bhallika from four exquisite stone bowls presented by the Four World-Protectors,
he returned once more and sat down at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree; there, this reflection,
which is the habitual practice of all Buddhas, arose in him.

In this context, "wise" means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*). "Clever" means endowed with dexterity (*veyyattiya*). "Intelligent" means endowed with the wisdom that arises from the situation (*ṭhānuppattikā paññā*).

"Of a nature with little dust in one's eyes" means one whose nature is free from defilements and who is a purified being, due to the suppression [of defilements] by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
"He will understand" means he will observe and penetrate. And "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*)...

"But knowledge and vision arose in me" means: the Blessed One, not reaching a conclusion based solely on what was said by the deity, himself looked with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and saw that [the person] would pass away seven days from now and be reborn in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). Referring to this, he said: "And knowledge and vision arose in me."
"Mahājāniyo" means one who has a great loss (*mahatī jāni*); he is so called because he has fallen away from the fruits of the path that ought to have been attained within seven days.
Because he was reborn at an inopportune time (*akkhaṇe*), he lacks the clarity of hearing even to listen to the Dhamma being taught as it is being delivered;
nor does he possess the feet to come here to the place of Dhamma teaching. Thus, it is shown that he has become "one of great loss."
“Passed away at midnight” means he passed away at the middle of the night. And as for my knowledge: my own omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) also arose.
Here too, it seems, the Blessed One did not reach a conclusion based on the word of a deity, but rather, surveying with his omniscient knowledge, [he knew]:
“Having passed away yesterday at midnight, Udaka Rāmaputta has been reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).”
He saw [them]. Therefore he spoke thus. The rest is exactly as in the previous method. "Of great benefit" means very helpful.

"They waited upon him who was intent on striving" means they waited upon him whose personal existence had been dispatched for the sake of striving by sweeping the dwelling place and the courtyard, by following him while carrying his bowl and robes, and by providing water for rinsing the mouth, tooth-sticks, and so forth. But who were those known as the group of five? They are these—
Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, Jotimantī,
Yañña, Subhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta—
these were the eight brahmins at that time.
"Those possessing the six marks interpreted the prophecy.
At the time of the Bodhisatta’s birth, there were eight brahmins who received the dream-interpretations and those who received the analysis of the physical marks.
Among them, three gave two-fold interpretations: "Endowed with these marks, if he dwells in the household life..."
“He becomes a wheel-turning monarch, or if he goes forth, he becomes a Buddha. Thus the five brahmins gave categorical answers:
“One endowed with these marks does not remain in the household life; he becomes a Buddha indeed.
Of them, the first three followed the words of their own mantras, but these five had transcended the words of the mantras. They [reported] what they themselves had received...
Having offered the full bowl to their kinsmen, they thought, "This Great Man will not dwell in the household;
he will certainly become a Buddha," and with their doubts dispelled, they went forth as ascetics under the Bodhisatta.
Some say these were his sons, but that is rejected in the Aṭṭhakathā.
It is said that these men mastered many mantras even during their childhood; therefore, the brahmins established them in the position of teachers.

Later, thinking, "It will not be possible for us to go forth into homelessness after we have abandoned our wives and children and our topknots," they went forth while still young and wandered about enjoying delightful dwellings. From time to time, however, [they would ask], "What..."
"O, the Great Being has gone forth on the Great Renunciation! they asked. People replied, "Where will you see the Great Being?
He enjoys celestial splendor like a god amidst three palaces and three kinds of theatrical performances.
Hearing this, [the king thought], "The Great Being's knowledge has not yet reached maturity," and he remained unconcerned.
They indeed dwelt there. But why did the Blessed One say here, "These five companions from the group were very helpful"?
Does he teach the Dhamma only to those who have been helpful, and not to those who have not been helpful? No, he does not fail to teach them.
For it was by way of prior intimacy that he looked back toward Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta. However, in this Buddha-field, setting aside—
There was no one capable of realizing the Dhamma before Aññā Koṇḍañña. Why? Because of his specific *upanissaya* (decisive support).
It is said that formerly, in a time when they were performing meritorious deeds, there were two brothers. They cultivated their crops together.
There, the elder brother thought, "I must give the gift of the first-fruits nine times during a single harvest. At the time of sowing, he [prepared] the seed-grain...
Having given it a name, at the time when the crop was ready to ripen, he consulted with his younger brother, saying, "At the time of ripening, we shall cut open the crop and take [the essence].
The younger brother said, "Do you wish to destroy the young grain? When the elder brother realized that the younger brother would not comply, he divided the field;
then, from his own portion, he cut open the crop, extracted the milk, and [mixed it] with ghee and molasses.
Having joined [the grain], he gave it; at the time of the *puthuka* (threshed grain), having had the *puthuka* prepared, he gave it;

at the time of winnowing, the best of the winnowed; at the time of binding into bundles, the best of the bundles; at the time of sheaves and so forth, the best of the sheaves, the best of the threshing-floor, the best of the granary, and the best of the storehouse—thus he gave the first-fruits offering nine times during a single harvest.
His younger brother, however, gave after setting aside [the very best]. Among them, the elder became the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña.
The youngest was the wanderer Subhadda. Thus, because nine of the foremost gifts had been given for a single harvest, there was no one else besides the Elder capable of realizing the Dhamma first.
As for the statement, "These group-of-five monks have been very helpful," that was said merely as a recollection of their assistance.

"At Isipatana, in the Deer Park": it is said that in that place, before the Buddhas had appeared, the Paccekabuddhas would spend seven days in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) on Mount Gandhamādana;
then, emerging from cessation, they would chew a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* vine, wash their faces in Lake Anotatta, take their bowls and robes, and descend by way of the air. There—
Having put on their robes and wandered for alms in the city, they would rise up from that very spot at the time of departure even after finishing their meal.
Thus, because seers (ṛṣis) alight here and take flight from here, that place became known as Isipatana (“The Seers’ Landing”).
Furthermore, because it was given as a sanctuary for deer, it is called Migadāya (“Deer Park”). Therefore it is said: “At Isipatana, in the Deer Park.”
285. “Between Gayā and the Bodhi” means at a place three *gāvutas* apart from both Gayā and the Bodhi tree.
For Gayā is three *gāvutas* from the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and Benares is eighteen *yojanas*.
Upaka saw the Blessed One between the seat of enlightenment and Gayā. Because it is joined with the word *antarā*, the accusative case is used.
It is said. In such instances, grammarians employ the word *antara* only once, as in the expression "he goes between the village and the river.

That [word] must also be construed with the second member [of the compound]. If it were not so construed, the accusative case would not be attained. However, in this case, it is stated precisely after having been so construed. Regarding the phrase "one who has set out on a journey," it refers to one who has entered upon what is designated as a journey (*addhāna*).
"One who has set out on a journey" means one who has entered upon a long road. For in the *Vibhaṅga* [of the *Khandhakas*], regarding the time of traveling on a journey, there is the statement:
"One may eat [the meal] thinking, 'I shall go two yojanas,'" and thus even two yojanas constitute a journey.
From the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) to Gayā, however, is three gavutas.
"Sabbābhibhū" means he stands having overcome all phenomena of the three planes.
"Sabbavidū" means he has known and understood all phenomena of the four planes. "Anupalitto sabbadhammesu" means he is unstained by the defilement of attachment to all phenomena of the three planes.
"Sabbaṃ jahā" means he stands having abandoned all phenomena of the three planes. "Taṇhākkhaye vimutto" means liberated in the destruction of craving.
It is liberated from the object by means of the extinction of craving, which is Nibbāna. "Having known it all for myself" means having understood all phenomena of the four planes by oneself.
"Whom should I point to? means whom else should I point to, thinking, "This one is my teacher"?
"I have no teacher" means that regarding supramundane phenomena, I have no one who can be called my teacher. "There is no person equal to me."
There is no person who is my equal. He is called the *Sammāsambuddha* because he has awakened to the Four Truths by himself through reasoned methods.
He is "cooled" (*sītibhūta*) because he has extinguished the fire of all defilements (*kilesa*). He is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*) because of the very cessation of those defilements.
"Kāsīnāṃ puraṃ" means the city in the kingdom of Kāsī. "I shall beat the drum of the Deathless" (*āhañchaṃ amatadundubhiṃ*) refers to the attainment of the Wheel of Dhamma.
"I shall go, thinking, 'I will beat the drum of the Deathless. You ought to become an Anantajina, an Anantajina"—it is fitting for you to be so called.
"It might be, friend, that it would indeed be so. He departed; he went to the country named Vaṅkahāra.
There, he took up residence near a certain village of deer-hunters. The chief hunter attended upon him.
In that country, there were fierce flies. So they had him live in a single jar.
A deer-hunter, who was going far away on a hunt, said, "Do not neglect our Arahant," and having given instructions to his daughter named Chāva, he departed along with his sons and brothers.
That daughter of his was beautiful and possessed of perfect physical proportions. On the second day—
When Upaka arrived home and saw that girl approaching to serve him after having performed all the customary attentions, he was so overcome by passion that he was unable even to eat.
Taking his food in the bowl, he went to his dwelling place;
setting the food aside in a corner, he lay down without food, thinking: "If I obtain Chāva, I shall live; if not, I shall die."
On the seventh day, the hunter arrived and asked Upaka about his daughter’s welfare.
She replied, “He came for only a single day and has not returned since.

Thinking, “I will approach him in the guise of a visitor and ask,” the hunter went there at that very moment and, while touching his feet, asked, “Venerable sir, are you unwell? Upaka, however, was groaning.
It was indeed turning back. He said, "Venerable sir, speak; I will do everything that is possible for me to do.
Upaka said, "If I obtain food, I shall live; if not, death right here is better.
"But do you know, venerable sir, any craft? "I do not know," he replied. "Venerable sir, it is not possible for one who does not know any craft..."
"To establish a household.
He said, "I do not know any craft; however, I shall be your meat-provisioner and I will sell the meat.
The hunter, thinking, "This is exactly what we also desire," gave him an upper garment and [sent him] home.
Having brought her back, he gave her to him. Following their cohabitation, a son was born. They gave him the name Subhadda.
When he was crying, his mother, speaking disparagingly, mocked Upaka with songs of praise for her son, saying such things as, "Son of a meat-seller!
Son of a deer-hunter! Do not cry! She said, "Bhadde, you think I am without a protector. There is..."
“I have a friend named Anantajina; I shall go into his presence,” he said.
The charnel-ground scavenger, knowing that the man was thus distressed, spoke to him again and again. One day, however, without telling anyone, he set out toward the Middle Country.
At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Great Monastery in Jeta’s Grove. Then the Blessed One—
He had previously instructed the monks: "Monks, whoever comes asking for 'Anantajina,' you should show him to me.
Then Upaka, asking, "Where does Anantajina dwell? arrived in due course at Sāvatthī.
Standing in the middle of the monastery, he asked, "Where is Anantajina? The monks [reported this] to the Blessed One.
They led him into the presence [of the Blessed One]. Upon seeing the Blessed One, he said, "Does the Blessed One recognize me?
"Yes, Upaka, I recognize you; but where have you been living? "In the country of Vaṅkahāra, venerable sir.
"Upaka, you have grown old; will you be able to go forth? "I shall go forth, venerable sir. Having granted him the going-forth, the Blessed One gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
He gave it away. While practicing his meditation subject, he established himself in the fruit of non-returning and passed away, being reborn in the Aviha heaven.
At the very moment of his rebirth, he attained Arahantship. For seven beings who were merely reborn in the Aviha heaven attained Arahantship; he was one among them.
For this has been said:
“The seven bhikkhus reborn in the Aviha realm have attained liberation;
with lust and hatred utterly destroyed, they have crossed over the world’s attachment.”
Upaka, Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti—these three;
Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bahuraggi, and Saṅgiya:
having abandoned their human bodies, they have attained union with the divine.
286. *Saṇṭhapesuṃ* means they made an agreement. *Bāhulliko* refers to one who practices for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth.
*Padhānavibbhanto* means fallen away from, departed from, or lost the exertion. *Āvatto bāhullāya* means turned back toward an abundance of robes and so forth.
Furthermore, *āsanaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ* means that, moreover, a seat should be set aside for him in a noble family.
They said, "A seat should be prepared for one who has been born [into this world].
"They were unable" means that, being overwhelmed by the majesty and power of the Buddha, they were unable to abide by their own agreement.
"Addressing him by name and with the term 'friend'" means they called out, "Gotama," and "Friend. "Friend Gotama, at the time we were striving in Uruvelā, [we gave] your bowl and robe..."
The meaning is: "They were talking in this manner, saying, 'We took [the requisites] and wandered about; we gave him water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks;
we swept the dwelling-cell where he had stayed. Afterward, who performed his duties? We wonder whether he did not feel anxious when we had departed.
*Iriyāya* means by way of difficult conduct. *Paṭipadāya* means by way of difficult practice. *Dukkarakārikāya* means...
By means of the performance of austerities, such as consuming food like watered-down mung-bean soup until it makes a *pasatapasata* sound. "Do you know of me? (*abhijānātha me no*) means:
do you indeed know of me? The meaning of "this kind of manifestation" (*evarūpaṃ pabhāvitaṃ etan-ti*) is: this kind of division of speech.
"Did I, while striving at Uruvelā, come by night or by day for the sake of gathering you together and for the sake of not causing you distress?"
The intention [of the Blessed One] was: “Friends, do not engage in discursive thought; neither a radiance nor a sign appears to me.

Having regained mindfulness at that very moment, and having conceived a sense of reverence, they said, “Come now, surely this one has become a Buddha,” and out of faith they replied, “Indeed it is so, venerable sir. I was indeed able...
"Monks, in order to convince the group-of-five monks, I was able, monks, to make them know that 'I am the Buddha.
Then, on the very day of the Uposatha, the Blessed One arrived.
Having made his own state of Buddhahood known, and having made the Elder Koṇḍañña a bodily witness, he [preached] the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta."
He preached. At the conclusion of the discourse, the Elder, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The teaching was finished while the sun was still shining. The Blessed One entered the rains retreat right there.
"Monks, I am indeed instructing two monks," and so forth—this began from the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada) even for the sake of alms-food.

This was said for the purpose of illustrating not entering the village. For the Blessed One remained right within the monastery in order to purify the defilements that had arisen in those bhikkhus regarding their meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Whenever a defilement regarding a meditation subject arose, those bhikkhus would go into the presence of the Blessed One and inquire about it.
The Blessed One, too, would go to the place where they were sitting and remove the defilement.
Then, while they were being exhorted by the Blessed One after he had thus served them their meal, the Elder Vappa became a stream-enterer on the first day of the fortnight;
the Elder Bhaddiya on the second; the Elder Mahānāma on the third; and the Elder Assaji on the fourth.
But on the fifth day of the fortnight, having assembled them all together, [the Blessed One preached] the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta.
He preached, and at the conclusion of the discourse, they all were established in the fruit of arahantship. Therefore he said:
"Then, monks, while being thus exhorted by me... [the Pañcavaggiya bhikkhus] attained Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage...
there is now no further becoming. This much of the path of discourse the Blessed One [had previously]...
He spoke thus, bringing forward this single connection: "You too have ascended the very same path as I and the group-of-five; the Noble Search is your search. 287.
Now, since the pursuit of the five strands of sensual pleasure belongs not only to householders, but also to those who have gone forth—four [types of such seekers]...
For those who consume things without reflecting on the conditions [for their use], there is the ignoble search characterized by the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate this, the Blessed One said: "Monks, these five strands of sensual pleasure," and so forth.

In that context, among new robes, alms bowls, and so on, four strands of sensual pleasure are obtained: forms cognizable by the eye, and so on. However, the flavor here is the flavor of enjoyment (*paribhoga-rasa*).
...there is. In the case of agreeable almsfood and medicine, all five [qualities] are obtained. In the case of lodgings, as with robes, there are four.
As for flavor (*rasa*), here too it is only the flavor of enjoyment. Why did he begin with the words, "Whatever, monks"?
Having thus shown the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), he now intends to show those who might say: "From the time of going forth, this has been a search unworthy of the noble ones."

"How could there be such a thing for those who have gone forth on the Noble Search?"—in order to refute this, he began this teaching to show that "even for those who have gone forth, the enjoyment of the four requisites without reflection is indeed an ignoble search.
In this context, *gadhitā* means "addicted" through the greed of craving (*taṇhāgedha*). *Mucchitā* means "infatuated" by the infatuation of craving (*taṇhāmucchā*).
*Ajjhōpannā* means immersed by craving (*taṇhā*). *Anādīnavadassāvino* means not seeing the danger (*ādīnava*).
*Anissaraṇapaññā*—here "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) refers to the knowledge of reflection; they are devoid of that.
Now, in order to provide an illustration that establishes this meaning, he said, "Just as if, monks," and so forth. In this regard:
The correlation of the similes should be understood as follows: the forest deer is like the ascetics and brahmins;

the snare set by the hunter in the forest is like the four requisites; and the time when the deer lies down after covering himself with the hunter’s heap of snares is like the time when those [ascetics] consume the four requisites without reflecting upon them. When the hunter approaches the deer...

The time when ascetics and brahmins could do as they pleased was like a time when a deer had no choice but to go where it wished; the meaning is that it was a time when they had fallen under the power of Māra.
However, the ascetics’ and brahmins’ reflective enjoyment of the four requisites was like a deer lying down upon a heap of snares while still unbound;
their going wherever they pleased was like a deer’s going wherever it wishes when hunters are approaching.
In this way, it should be understood that ascetics and brahmins do not fall under the power of Māra. "Confident" means fearless and free from apprehension.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Pāsarāsi Sutta is finished.
"The Noble Search" (Ariyapariyesanā) is also a name for this very same discourse.
7. Commentary on the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta.
288. Thus have I heard: this is the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta (The Short Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint).

Therein, regarding the phrase "with a chariot drawn by entirely white mares": "Indeed, the horses were yoked, being white with white ornaments. The chariot was white, with white ornaments and white trappings;
the reins were white, the whip was white, the parasol was white, the turban was white, the garments were white, and the sandals were white."
“...he was being fanned with a white yak-tail fan,” thus it was said. With these words, [he was seated] upon a chariot yoked to four white mares.
Now, this kind of chariot is of two types: the war-chariot and the ornamental chariot.
Of these, the war-chariot is square in shape, not very large, and capable of carrying two or three persons. The ornamental chariot is large.

It was long in length and broad in width. Therein, eight or ten people—such as the umbrella-bearer, the chowrie-waver, and the palm-leaf-fan bearer—could easily stand, sit, or lie down. This too was indeed a decorated chariot.
It was complete with wheels, a fender, and a pole, and it was encased in silver. The mares...
By its very nature, it was white in color. Its trappings were likewise made of silver. Its reins were well-adorned with silver tubes.
Even the whip-handle was encrusted with silver. The brahmin, too, having dressed himself in white garments, wore a white upper robe;
he anointed himself with white unguent, put on a white garland, and [adorned] his ten fingers...
His finger-rings, earrings for the ears, and other such ornaments were likewise made of silver.
His retinue of brahmins, numbering about ten thousand, was similarly adorned with white garments, ointments, garlands, and ornaments. Therefore it is said:
"In a chariot drawn by all-white mares."
"He departs from Sāvatthī" means that, it is said, he performs a circumambulation of the city once every six months.
Even before the time arrives, an announcement is made: "In this many days from now, he will perform the circumambulation of the city.
Having heard this, those who had not departed from the city do not depart; and even those who had already departed, [return].
They came, thinking, "We shall behold the glory and prosperity of the meritorious one. On whatever day the brahmin wandered through the city,
they would rise early in the morning, sweep the city streets, scatter sand, strew flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient,
set out full water-jars, raise plantain trees and banners, and perfume the entire city with incense.
The brahmin, having bathed his head early in the morning and eaten before the midday meal, adorned himself with white garments and other ornaments in the manner previously described.

Descending from the palace, he mounted his chariot. Then those brahmins, all dressed in white garments, anointed with perfumes, and adorned with garlands and ornaments, surrounded him holding white parasols. Thereafter, for the purpose of assembling the great multitude, [he spoke] first of all...
Having scattered various fruits for the young children, he immediately thereafter scattered silver coins; after that, he scattered *kahāpaṇa* coins.
A great multitude of people gathered together. Shouts of joy and the tossing of garments went forth.
Then, while the Brahmins were performing auspicious rites and blessings such as the *maṅgalika* and *sovatthika*, [the King] was endowed with great prosperity.
He wanders through the city. Meritorious people, having ascended palaces of one story and so forth, open the window shutters—which resemble parrot feathers—and look out.
