The Brahmin also, as if overwhelming the city with the excellence of his own glory and splendor, faces toward the southern gate. Therefore it is said: “He goes out from Sāvatthī.”
"During the day" means during the daytime; the meaning is "at midday.
"The mendicant Pilotika" refers to a mendicant who had received the name "Pilotika" by way of being designated with a feminine gender term.
It is said that this mendicant was young, in the prime of his life, golden-hued, and an attendant of the Buddha; from early morning, he [attended] both the Tathāgata and the great elders.
Having paid his respects and taken his requisites, such as the triple staff and water-pot, he departed from Jetavana and set out toward the city. From afar, the other saw him approaching;
recognizing that he had gradually come into his presence, he spoke these words, addressing him by his clan name: "Well now, from where has the venerable Vacchāyana come?"
He said: "The venerable Vacchāyana thinks the ascetic Gotama is wise; does he think so, or not?
This is the meaning here.
And who am I, sir, in knowing the ascetic Gotama’s proficiency in wisdom? Who indeed am I?"

"I shall know the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama"—how indeed shall I know the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama, and for what reason shall I know it? In this way, he demonstrates his own state of ignorance in every respect.
"He too must surely be like him" refers to one who would know the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama.
He too, having surely fulfilled the ten perfections, must have attained omniscience and would be a Buddha just like him.
Just as one who wishes to measure Mount Sineru, the Himalayas, the earth, or the sky must obtain a measuring rod or a rope of the same size,
so too, even by one who knows the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama, his knowledge of omniscience must be understood as being identical to his own.
It indicates that it is appropriate to obtain [this]. However, the reduplication (*āmeḍita*) here is used by way of emphasis.
"Exalted" (*uḷārāya*) means superior or best. "And who am I, sir?"—sir, who indeed am I in the praising of the ascetic Gotama?
And "who shall praise the ascetic Gotama"—for what reason shall I praise him? "Praised by the praised" refers to [him who is praised] for all his virtues.
He is praised solely by his own qualities, which are superior and extolled by the whole world; there is no need for him to be praised by others.
For just as a *campaka* flower, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or red sandalwood is both beautiful and fragrant through their own color, scent, and splendor, and not by any adventitious colors or scents—
There is no need for him to perform the function of praising himself.

Just as a precious gem or the lunar disc shines by its own radiance and has no need for another to illuminate it, so too the ascetic Gotama is praised and lauded by his own virtues—which are extolled by the whole world—and has been raised to the state of supremacy over all the world; he has no need for another to praise him.
He exists. Or, he is "praised by those who are praised," thus "praised by the praised.
Who indeed are called "the praised"? King Pasenadi of Kosala is praised by the inhabitants of Kāsi and Kosala; Bimbisāra is praised by the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha.
The Licchavis of Vesālī are praised by the inhabitants of the Vajji kingdom. The Mallas of Pāvā and the Mallas of Kusinārā—
There were also those various kṣatriyas praised by their respective localities; the brahmins headed by Caṅkī and others [praised] by groups of brahmins;
the laymen headed by Anāthapiṇḍika and others by many hundreds of groups of laymen; the laywomen headed by Visākhā and others by many hundreds of laywomen;
the wanderers headed by Sakuludāyin and others by many hundreds of wanderers; and the nuns headed by the elder Uppalavaṇṇā and others.
The Great Female Disciples were praised by many hundreds of bhikkhunīs; the Great Disciples, such as the Elder Sāriputta and others, were praised by many hundreds of bhikkhus;
the gods, such as Sakka and others, were praised by many thousands of gods; and the Brahmās, such as Mahābrahmā and others, were praised by many thousands of Brahmās.
Since they all extol, describe, and praise the One Possessing the Ten Powers, the Blessed One is called "Praised by the Praised" (*pasatthapasattha*).
"Advantages" means benefits. Then the wanderer, explaining the reason for his own faith, said:

"Just as if, sir, a skilled elephant-forest trainer," and so forth. In this context, an "elephant-forest trainer" (*nāgavanika*) is a person who dwells in the elephant forest and has not yet mastered the craft.
However, further on, the term "elephant-forest trainer" refers to a person who has mastered the craft. "Four footprints" means four...
"Footprints of knowledge" (*ñāṇapadāni*) means the marks of knowledge; the meaning is "places trodden upon by knowledge.

Regarding the passage beginning with "a wise khattiya," etc.: "wise" (*paṇḍita*) means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*). "Clever" (*nipuṇa*) means subtle, possessing refined intelligence, and capable of penetrating subtle distinctions in meaning.
"One who has refuted the doctrines of others" (*kataparappavāda*) means one who has understood the doctrines of others.
And in their cultivation of conversation with others.

"Like hair-splitting archers" means like archers who split hairs. "They move as if piercing them" means they move as if piercing even the subtle views of others with the range of their own wisdom, just as a hair-splitter pierces a hair;
this is the meaning. "They formulate questions" means [questions] consisting of two or three lines.
They even pose questions consisting of four lines. They think, "We shall bring forward a dispute," meaning they will bring forward a fault.

And they do not ask the ascetic Gotama a question; why do they not ask? It is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly, he surveyed the inclinations of the assembly, and then he saw: "These wise khattiyas [possess] hidden secrets..."

"Having made the questions the very core of their inquiry, they have come. Even though he had not been asked by them, [the Blessed One] thought: "If one were to ask such questions, there would be so many faults;
in answering, so many [qualities]; regarding the meaning, the phrases, and the syllables, it would be thus when asking these questions, and thus when answering.
Thus, having made those questions brought forward the very core of the inquiry, [he spoke] in a discourse on the Dhamma.
Having inserted [the questions] within [the discourse], he destroys them. The wise khattiyas become glad-minded, thinking: "It is better indeed for us that we did not ask these questions;
for had we asked them, the ascetic Gotama would have cast us out, leaving us without a foothold.
Moreover, when the Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they pervade the assembly with loving-kindness (*mettā*); through this pervasion of loving-kindness by the One of Ten Powers...
The minds of the great multitude become serene. For the Buddhas have indeed attained the perfection of form;
they are endowed with vision, possess sweet voices, soft tongues, and well-polished lips and teeth. They preach the Dhamma as if sprinkling the heart with the Deathless.
Therein, through their pervasion of loving-kindness, those whose minds are thus serene think: "Such is their discourse, free from duplicity and never in vain."

Thinking, “We shall not be able to hold a contrary position in debate with the Blessed One who speaks discourse leading to liberation,” they do not ask [further questions] simply out of their own faith.
*Aññadatthu* means “absolutely. *Sāvakā sampajjanti* means that they become disciples by way of going for refuge. *Tadanuttaraṃ*...
That unsurpassed goal. "The consummation of the holy life" (*brahmacariyapariyosāna*) refers to the fruit of arhatship, which constitutes the culmination of the holy life of the path;

for it is for that purpose that they go forth. "Alas, sir, we would have been lost! means: "Sir, if we had not approached him—if by this mere non-approaching, by this mere lack of paying homage, we had indeed been lost. [But] by the mere act of approaching...
The meaning is: "He has not fallen away from us. The second phrase is a synonym for the first. Regarding the expressions "being merely non-recluses" and so forth:
they are "merely non-recluses" because they have not stilled (asamita) evil deeds; and they are "merely non-Brahmins" because they have not removed (abāhita) [defilements].
The meaning is that they are "merely non-Arahants" because they have not slain (ahata) the enemies that are the defilements.
290. "He uttered an *udāna*" means he uttered an utterance.

For just as that oil which cannot be contained within a measure and flows over is called a "sprinkling" (*avaseka*), and that water which cannot be contained within a pond and overflows it is called a "flood" (*ogha*), even so, that speech consisting of rapture which [overflows] the heart...
If it cannot be grasped, and being excessive, does not remain within but issues forth, that is called an *udāna*.
The meaning is that he uttered such a word consisting of rapture (*pīti*). "The Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint" means that the elephant’s footprint is the simile for this teaching;
thus it is the "Elephant’s Footprint Simile. It is not complete in detail merely by this much.

[The text] shows this. A "forest-keeper of elephants" (nāgavanika) is one who has mastered the art of elephant-training and wanders through elephant forests. Now, why is it not stated here that he is "skilled" (kusala)? Because later on, in the analysis, it says, "he who is skilled.
For anyone who enters [the forest] does so, but he who is skilled does not reach his goal immediately. Therefore, instead of saying "skilled" here, it is stated later.
291. *Vāmanikā* means short; they are not long even in height, though they are elephants with large bellies.
*Uccā ca nisevitaṃ* refers to the place where [the elephant] rubs against the trunk of a banyan tree or similar tree, which is seven or eight cubits high.
*Uccā kāḷārikā* means that they are tall, having legs like staffs, and are "black-toothed" (*kāḷārikā*) because of the blackness of their tusks. It is said that one of their tusks...
One is elevated, one is depressed; both are sparse and not close together.

"High and scarred by the teeth" means that in the trunk-region of trees such as the *vaṭa* tree, which are seven or eight *ratana*s in height, the place cut by the tusks is like the spot struck by an axe.
"The ones called *kaṇeruka* are high" means that they have long legs resembling staffs and are tall.
And as for the *kaṇeruka* elephants, they are called *kaṇeruka* because of their tusks; it is said that those tusks are like flower buds (*makuḷa-dāṭhā*), and therefore they are called *kaṇeruka*.
"He reaches the conclusion" means that the elephant-keeper reached the certainty: "The elephant whose tracks I have been following is indeed this one, and no other.
For when I first saw the footprints, I thought, 'These must be the footprints of a dwarf.'"
He does not reach a conclusion; even when he sees something further along the way, he does not reach a conclusion, thinking, "This will be for the ox-carts" or "This will be for the young elephants.
All of that is merely the track of this very great elephant; it is only upon seeing the great elephant itself that he reaches a conclusion.
"In the same way," here is the application of the simile: from the beginning up to [the point where] the elephant-grove...
The teaching of the Dhamma should be understood as the abandoning of the hindrances. The practitioner is like a skilled elephant-trapper;
the Perfectly Enlightened One is like a great elephant; and the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges are like the great footprint of the elephant.
Even though the elephant-trapper sees the elephant’s footprint here and there, he might think it is the footprint of a dwarf, a black ox, or a young elephant.
The thought "this will be the footprint" involves a lack of final certainty for the yogin, just as when one has not yet reached a conclusion;
likewise, the thought "these so-called jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā) exist even among outside wanderers" involves a lack of final certainty.

For a noble disciple, however, it is like reaching a state of final certainty upon seeing a great elephant: "The footprint seen here and there by me belongs to this very same great elephant, and to no other. This is the nature of Arahantship.
Having reached the final conclusion. Furthermore, this correlation of the simile may be made even by standing at the very end;
it is certainly appropriate here as well. However, taking the textual passage (*pāḷipada*) that has arrived in its proper sequence, it is treated right here.
In that context, *idha* is a particle used to indicate location. This [particle] is sometimes spoken with reference to the world, as it is said: "Here..."
“The Tathāgata appears in the world. In some cases, it refers to the teaching, as it is said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic;
right here is the second ascetic. In some cases, it refers to a location, as it is said:
“While standing right here, even though I have become a deva...”
“Furthermore, O dear sir, I have obtained life again; know this thus.
In some instances, [the particle] is used merely for the sake of completing the metrical line, as it is said: “In this case, monks, I would have been one who has finished eating and has been invited.
However, in this instance, it should be understood as being spoken with reference to the world. This is what is meant: “O Brahmin, in this world...”
“A Tathāgata arises, an Arahant... [as above] ...a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Regarding this, the term *tathāgata* is explained in the *Mūlapariyāya*, while the terms beginning with *arahant* are detailed in the *Visuddhimagga*.
As for the phrase “arises in the world,” here “world” (*loka*) is threefold: the world as space, the world of sentient beings, and the world of formations. However, in this context...
The world of beings is intended here. Furthermore, when a Tathāgata arises, he does not arise in the world of the gods, nor in the Brahma-world, but arises only in the human world.
Even within the human world, he does not arise in another world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), but in this very world-system.
Even there, he does not arise in all places; [for it is said]: "In the eastern direction, there is a market town named Gajaṅgala. Beyond that..."
The Mahāsāla [village], beyond which lie the border regions and within which lies the middle country.
To the southeast is the river named Sallavatī; beyond it lie the border regions, and within it lies the middle country.
To the south is the market town named Setakaṇṇikā; beyond it lie the border regions, and within it lies the middle country. To the west...
"To the north is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the bordering provinces, and on this side is the middle country.
To the north is the mountain named Usiraddhaja; beyond that are the bordering provinces, and on this side is the middle country. Thus it was demarcated:
three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference.

It arises in the Middle Country. Not only does the Tathāgata arise there, but Paccekabuddhas, the Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Elders, the Mother of the Buddha, the Father of the Buddha, Wheel-turning Monarchs, and other Brahmins and householders who have attained the essence [of the Dhamma] also arise in this very place.
Therein, from the time the Tathāgata partook of the meal of honeyed milk-rice given by Sujātā, [he remained in that state].
Up until the path of arahantship, it is said to be "arising"; at the fruit of arahantship, it is said to be "arisen.
Alternatively, from the Great Renunciation up until the path of arahantship; or from the Tusita heaven up until the path of arahantship;
or from the presence of Dīpaṅkara Buddha up until the path of arahantship—up until that point, it is said to be "arising"; at the fruit of arahantship, it is said to be "arisen. Here, first of all:
The statement "he arises" is said with reference to the state of having already arisen; thus, the meaning here is: "the Tathāgata has arisen in the world.
"This world" means this world, which the Blessed One [perceives]; he now points out what is to be described.

"Together with the devas" (sadevaka) means together with the devas. Likewise, "together with Māra" (samāraka). "Together with Brahmā" (sabrahmaka). "Together with recluses and brahmins" (sasamaṇabrāhmaṇī).
"Together with recluses and brahmins" (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi*). It is called "the people" (*pajā*) because they have been born; that is the people. "Together with gods and humans" (*sadevamanussaṃ*).
Therein, by the term "together with gods," the inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere gods (*pañcakāmāvacaradeva*) should be understood.

By the term "together with Māra," the inclusion of the sixth class of sense-sphere gods is meant. By the term "together with Brahmā," the inclusion of the Brahmā-world deities such as those belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm is meant. By the term "together with recluses and brahmins,"...
The inclusion of "ascetics and brahmins who are enemies and adversaries of the Dispensation" refers to those ascetics and brahmins who have suppressed evil and cast out evil;
the inclusion of "beings" (pajā) refers to the world of sentient beings; and the inclusion of "together with devas and humans" refers to conventional devas and the remainder of the human race.

Thus, it should be understood that here, by means of three terms, the world of sentient beings is taken together with the physical world (okāsaloka), whereas by means of two terms, only the world of sentient beings is taken.
Another method: by the inclusion of "together with devas," the world of the immaterial-sphere devas is included; by the inclusion of "together with Māras," the world of the six sense-sphere devas;

by the inclusion of "together with Brahmās," the world of the form-sphere Brahmās; and by the inclusion of "together with recluses and brahmins, etc.," either the human world along with the conventional devas according to the four assemblies, or the entire world of all remaining beings.
Furthermore, by the expression "together with the devas" (sadevaka), he states that the entire world has been realized from the highest limit.
Then, for those who might have thought, "Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere heavens, and one who wields mastery;
has even he been realized by him?"—in order to dispel their doubt, he said "together with Māra" (samāraka). For those, however, who thought, "Brahmā..."
"Possessing great power, he radiates light with a single finger over one thousand world-systems; with two...
[and so on] ...with ten fingers, he radiates light over ten thousand world-systems, and he experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti).
Has he too realized this? Dispelling their doubt, he said: "Together with Brahmā."
Then, for those who thought, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the Teaching;
have they too been realized?"—dispelling their doubt, he said, "With its recluses and brahmins, with its generation...
Having thus declared that even the most eminent [beings] had been realized, he then spoke by way of defining the limit of eminence, starting from the conventional deities and the rest of humanity.
Declaring that he has realized this state for the rest of the world of beings, he said, "together with its gods and humans. This is the sequence of the meanings here. However, the Ancients have said:
"Together with its gods" means the remainder of the world along with the deities; "together with Māra" means the remainder of the world along with Māra;
"together with Brahmā" means the remainder of the world along with the Brahmās. Thus, all those who have entered the three realms of existence...

Having included all beings within three aspects and three locations, and then encompassing them again with two phrases, he said: "the generation together with its recluses and brahmins, with its devas and humans.
Thus, by these five phrases and in those respective ways, the entire triple world (*tedhātuka*) alone is encompassed.

"Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and made it known" means: *sayam* = having realized it himself, being independent of others; *abhiññā* = by means of direct knowledge (*abhiññāya*).
"Having known by superior knowledge" means having understood. "Having realized" means having made it directly manifest; by this, inference and other such means are excluded.
"He proclaims" means he awakens, makes known, and reveals. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [as above] ...good in the end;
that Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, even having abandoned the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion...
He teaches the Dhamma. And whether he teaches it little or much, he teaches it as being good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
This means that he teaches it having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the beginning; likewise in the middle;
and likewise having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the end.
In this regard, there is the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching, and there is that of the Dispensation. First, concerning the teaching:
even in a four-line stanza, the first line is called the beginning; the next two are called the middle; and the final one is called the end.

In a sutta consisting of a single sequence of meaning, the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning, the words "Thus he spoke" (idam avoca) are the end, and everything between the two is the middle. In a sutta consisting of multiple sequences of meaning...
The first connection of a sutta is its beginning; the final connection is its conclusion; and in the middle there may be one, two, or many, which together constitute the middle itself.
Furthermore, for the Teaching (Sāsana), virtue, concentration, and insight are called the beginning.
And this has been said: "What is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight. "There is, bhikkhus..."
“The Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Thus, the Noble Path so described is called the “middle,” while the fruit and Nibbāna are called the “culmination.
For it is said here: “It is for this purpose, Brahmin, that the holy life is lived; this is its core, this is its culmination. And: “For Nibbāna is the immersion...”
"Friend Visākha, the holy life is lived with Nibbāna as its goal and Nibbāna as its consummation.
In this context, it is said that "Nibbāna is the consummation. Here, however, what is intended is the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching.
For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, he shows virtue at the beginning, the path in the middle, and Nibbāna at the end.
Therefore it was said: "He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Consequently, when another preacher of the Dhamma speaks the Dhamma, he should show virtue in the beginning, clarify the path in the middle;
“Nirvana at the conclusion—this is the established method of the speaker.
Regarding the phrase “with meaning and with phrasing”: one whose teaching is based on descriptions of rice-gruel, meals, women, men, and so forth, does not teach with meaning.
The Blessed One, however, having abandoned such teaching, relies instead upon the four foundations of mindfulness and the like.
He teaches the teaching. Therefore, it is said that "he teaches with meaning.

However, for one whose teaching is joined with only a single consonant, or consists entirely of labial consonants, or consists entirely of unaspirated or nasalized consonants, his teaching is called "without phonetic excellence" (*abyañjanā*) because of the lack of full phonetic completeness, like the languages of the Damilas, Kirātas, Savaras, and other Mlecchas. But the Blessed One—
“Lax and forceful, long and short, heavy and light, nasalized (niggahīta);
connected, distinct, and released—thus is the tenfold classification according to the intelligence regarding phonemes.

Having thus taught the Dhamma without omitting any of these ten kinds of phonemes and having ensured that the phonemes are complete, he teaches the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said: “He teaches the Dhamma with its phonemes.”
“Kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ”: here, *kevala* is a term for the whole; *paripuṇṇa* is a term for that which is neither deficient nor excessive.
This is what is meant: “He teaches only what is entirely complete; there is no teaching even in part that is incomplete.
*Parisuddhaṃ*: free from defilement. For [he teaches] that which, by depending on this Dhamma-teaching, leads to gain or honor...
If one teaches with the thought, "I shall obtain [gain]," his teaching is impure.

But the Blessed One, being indifferent to worldly gain, teaches with a heart softened by the cultivation of loving-kindness that pervades for the welfare of others, and with a mind established in a nature of uplifting compassion.
Therefore, he is said to "teach the Dhamma in its purity. Regarding the phrase "he reveals the holy life" (*brahmacariya*): here, "holy life" refers to...
The entire teaching is comprised within the three trainings. Therefore, "he reveals the holy life" means that he teaches the Dhamma which is good in the beginning...
[and so on] ... and completely pure. And while teaching thus, he reveals the holy life—the entire teaching comprised within the three trainings.
This is how the meaning should be understood here. "Holy life" (*brahmacariya*) is used in the sense of being supreme.
The "conduct of one who has become sublime" (brahmabhūta-cariya) means, it is said, the conduct of those who have become sublime, such as the Buddhas and others.
"That Dhamma" refers to that Dhamma endowed with the aforementioned excellence. Why is the householder specified first in the phrase "a householder hears"?
It is because [the householder] has subdued pride and because [the teaching] is intended for those in whom it is prevalent; for, as a general rule, [those from] the kṣatriya clan...
Those who have gone forth take pride based on their birth; those who have gone forth from brahmin families take pride based on their mantras;
those who have gone forth from low-born families are unable to establish themselves because of their low birth.
But householders’ sons, having ploughed the earth with sweat dripping from their armpits and salt blooming upon their backs, have subdued their pride and arrogance.

They did so. Having gone forth, they abandoned pride and arrogance, mastered the word of the Buddha according to their ability, and by applying themselves to the work of insight (vipassanā), they were able to establish themselves in Arahatship.
Those who went forth after leaving other families were not many; rather, householders were numerous. Thus, because their pride was humbled and [the number of such] was abundant, first—
"He points out the householder" means:
"in one of the other families" means in one of the other clans. "Reborn" means born again.
"He gains faith in the Tathāgata" means that, having heard the perfectly pure Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata, the Lord of the Dhamma, thinking: "He is a Perfectly Enlightened One."
"Indeed, Blessed One," he gains faith. "Thus he reflects" means he contemplates in this way:

"Household life is confinement. Even if a husband and wife live in a house sixty cubits square or even a hundred leagues apart, their household life is still indeed a confinement in the sense that it involves possessions and hindrances. "A path of dust" refers to the dust of passion and so forth.
“Place of arising” (*uṭṭhānaṭṭhāna*) is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. It is also appropriate [to understand it] as the path of arrival.

Because it is like an open space (*abbhokāsa*) in the sense of being unattached, it is called “open space. For one who has gone forth, even while dwelling in gabled houses, jeweled palaces, celestial mansions, and so forth—places that are concealed with closed doors and windows—he is neither attached, nor clinging, nor bound. Therefore it is said: “Open space.”

“...the going forth. Furthermore, the household life is cramped because there is no opportunity for the performance of wholesome deeds. It is a path of dust, like an uncleaned rubbish heap, because it is a place where dust—that is, the dust of the defilements—accumulates. The going forth is open space, because there is ample opportunity for the performance of wholesome deeds according to one’s pleasure. Regarding the passage, “It is not easy... one should go forth,” this is the brief explanation: as for this holy life of the three trainings, [The text continues: ...it is not easy to lead the holy life of the three trainings in its entirety, in all its purity, and in all its perfection, while living in a household. It must be practiced as entirely fulfilled, by maintaining it unbroken for even a single day so that it may reach the final moment of consciousness;
and it must be practiced as entirely purified, by keeping it unstained by the impurities of the defilements for even a single day so that it may reach the final moment of consciousness.
It must be practiced like a polished conch—smooth as a carved shell and resembling a cleansed conch. This is not easy to do while living at home.
"While living as a householder, dwelling in the midst of a home, it is impossible for me to practice the holy life that is entirely perfect, pure, and polished...

What if I were now to shave off my hair and beard, don yellow robes dyed with the juice of kasāya—robes suitable for those practicing the holy life—and having clothed myself in them, go forth from the home into the homeless state? In this regard:
And because the work of farming, trade, and so forth, which is beneficial for a householder, is called "household life" (*agāriya*), and that does not exist for one who has gone forth;
therefore, it should be known that going forth is "the homeless state" (*anagāriya*). That is the homeless state. "I would go forth" means I would practice [it].
"Little" refers to a mass of wealth below a thousand [pieces of gold]; from a thousand onwards, it is "great."
In the sense of binding, "relatives" (*ñāti*) themselves are the "circle of relatives" (*ñātiparivaṭṭo*). That [circle] is small when it is below twenty [in number], and large from twenty onwards.

292. "Having entered upon the training and way of life of the bhikkhus": that which is the training of the bhikkhus known as higher morality (*adhisīla*), and that wherein they live together—sharing a single livelihood and living in common—that is the training consisting of the rules of conduct (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One.
"He has entered upon the training and the way of life therein" means he has entered upon the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus.
"Entered upon" means fulfilling the training and, by not transgressing the way of life, having approached both of them; this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrases "having abandoned the destruction of life," and so forth, the discussion of the destruction of life and the other offenses has already been explained in detail below. "Having abandoned" refers to this volition known as the destruction of life.
"Having abandoned immorality": "He is abstinent" means that from the moment it is abandoned, he remains indeed abstinent from that immorality.
"One who has laid aside the rod, laid aside the weapon":
the meaning is that he has set aside both the rod and the weapon because he no longer takes up a rod or a weapon for the purpose of harming others. And here, setting aside...
Every staff and all remaining implements should be understood as a "weapon" (*sattha*) because of their nature of harming living beings.
However, when monks go about carrying a walking stick, a tooth-stick scraper, or a needle case, they do not do so for the purpose of injuring others;
therefore, one who has laid aside the staff is reckoned as one who has laid aside the weapon. [The term] *lajjī* means...

He is endowed with a sense of shame (*lajjā*) characterized by a loathing for evil. "Endowed with compassion" (*dayāpanno*) means he has attained a state of compassion, that is, a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings" (*sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī*) means one who feels sympathy through their welfare toward all living beings;
the meaning is that, by virtue of being thus endowed with compassion, his heart is intent on the welfare of all living beings. "Dwells" (*viharati*) means he conducts himself or protects [himself].
One who takes only what is given is a "giver-taker" (*dinnādāyī*). One who expects only what is given even with the mind is one who "expects only what is given" (*dinnapāṭikaṅkhī*).

It is called *thena* because it is stolen; *athena* means not stolen. Precisely because of this state of being un-stolen, it is "become pure. By "self" (*attanā*) is meant by way of the personal existence (*attabhāvena*);
thus, it is said that he dwells having made his personal existence un-stolen and become pure.
*Abrahmacariya* means a non-noble practice. One who practices the noble (*brahma*) or supreme conduct is a *brahmacārī*. An *ārācārī* is one who lives far removed from unchaste conduct.

*Methuna* refers to those unwholesome states known by the conventional designation "sexual intercourse" because they are practiced by those possessed by lust due to their similarity [to it], and thus they have come to be reckoned as "sexual intercourse. *Gāmadhammā* means the practices of village-dwellers.
One who speaks truth is a "truth-speaker" (*saccavādī*). One who joins and unites truth with truth is a "truth-uniter" (*saccasandho*);

the meaning is that he does not speak falsehood from time to time. For in the case of a person who sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes truth, because his speech is interrupted by falsehood, truth is not joined with truth.
Therefore, such a person is not a truth-uniter; but this one is not like that.
Because one does not speak falsehood even for the sake of one's life, but rather adheres to truth with truth, one is called "one who adheres to truth" (*saccasaṃdha*).
"Firm" (*theta*) means stable; the meaning is that one whose speech is stable.
For one person is not of stable speech—like turmeric dye, like a wooden stake driven into a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on the back of a horse. Another is like a line carved in stone.
He is firm in speech like a city gatepost (*indakhīla*); even if his head were being cut off with a sword, he would not speak two different accounts.
This is called "trustworthy" (*theto*). "Reliable" (*paccayiko*) means one who is to be trusted, that is, one who inspires faith.
For a certain person is not reliable; when it is said, "Who said this? It was so-and-so," [others might say], "Do not believe his word."
He becomes subject to being spoken to. One person is "trustworthy" (*paccayika*): when it is said, "By whom was this said?
By so-and-so," he becomes subject to being told, "If it was said by him, that alone is the authority; there is nothing further to be examined;
it is exactly thus. This is called "trustworthy. He is "non-deceptive toward the world" because of his truthfulness toward the world.
The meaning is "he does not deceive.
"For the sake of dividing these" means for the purpose of creating a rift between those from whose presence he has heard [the words], as mentioned in the phrase "having heard from them.
Or, "for the reconciliation of those who are divided" refers to two friends, or two people such as co-residents under the same preceptor (*upajjhāya*), who have become estranged due to some cause.
A reconciler (*sandhānakārako*) is one who, having approached each of those who are divided, says such things as, "For those born into such a family and so learned as yourselves,
this is not fitting," and so forth, thereby effecting reconciliation. A restorer (*anuppādātā*) is one who, seeing two people in harmony, says such things as,
"This is worthy of you who are born into such a family and endowed with such qualities," and so forth.
The meaning is: having spoken thus, he should perform an act of strengthening. "One whose monastery is harmonious" (*samaggārāma*) means:
where there is no harmony, he does not even wish to dwell there; this is the meaning. There is also a textual reading of *samaggarāmo*, which has the same meaning here.
"One who delights in harmony" (*samaggarata*) means: one who delights in those who are harmonious, and does not wish to go elsewhere abandoning them; this is the meaning.
One who rejoices even upon seeing or hearing those who are in harmony is called "one who delights in harmony" (*samagganandī*).
"He speaks words that create harmony" means he speaks only those words that bring beings into harmony and which illuminate the virtue of concord, and not others.
"Faultless" (*nelā*): *ela* is said to mean fault; that which has no *ela* is *nelā*, meaning faultless. As in the phrase, "The white-canopied chariot with faultless wheels."
It is like the salt mentioned here. "Pleasant to the ear" means it is pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of its phrasing (*byañjana*);

it does not produce ear-ache like the piercing of a needle. It is "endearing" (*pemanīyā*) because, through the sweetness of its meaning (*attha*), it generates affection rather than irritation throughout the entire body.
It is "heart-reaching" (*hadayaṅgamā*) because it goes to the heart, entering the mind easily without being obstructed.
"Porī" means "of the city" because it is full of virtues; it also means "refined" like a woman raised in the city, or "belonging to the city.
The meaning is "the speech of the city-dwellers. For the inhabitants of the city speak appropriately:
they call one who is merely a father "father," one who is merely a mother "mother," and one who is merely a brother "brother. Such speech belongs to the multitude of people.
"Beloved by many" means she is dear to many people. Because of that very quality of being beloved, she is pleasing to many people and increases their mental well-being;
thus, she is "pleasing to many. One who speaks at the proper time is a "speaker at the right time"; the meaning is that one speaks having observed the appropriate moment for what ought to be said.

One who speaks what is real, true, and in accordance with the actual nature of things is a "speaker of truth. [One who speaks] only that which is based on benefits pertaining to the present life and the future life...

One who speaks having established [the meaning] is an "expositor of the meaning" (atthavādī). One who speaks having established [the teaching] based on the nine supramundane states is an "expositor of the Dhamma" (dhammavādī).

One who speaks having established [the discipline] based on the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment is an "expositor of the Vinaya" (vinayavādī). A "repository" (nidhāna) is said to be a place of deposit;
one who possesses such a repository is "possessing a repository" (nidhānavatī), meaning she has spoken words that are fit to be deposited in the heart.

Meaning: "At the proper time" means that even while speaking such words, one does not speak at an improper time with the thought, "I shall speak words containing hidden treasure," but rather speaks having considered the appropriate occasion; this is the meaning.
"With a foundation" means with a simile, or with a reason; this is the meaning. "With a conclusion" means showing a limit so that its limit becomes evident.
The meaning is: "He speaks thus. "Beneficial" (*atthasaṃhita*) means that it is endowed with meaning because it cannot be exhausted even by one who analyzes it through many methods;

or, he speaks speech that is "beneficial" because it is connected with the meaning that the speaker of meaning (*atthavādī*) speaks, meaning that he does not set aside one thing and speak another. This is what is intended.
"293. Regarding 'the destruction of the seed-planting and the crop-planting':

this means abstaining from the disturbance—by way of cutting, splitting, cooking, and so forth—of both the fivefold group of seeds (namely, root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and seed-seeds) and any group of living beings such as green grasses, trees, and the like. "One who eats but one meal [a day]"...
There are two meals: the morning meal (*pātarāsabhatta*) and the evening meal (*sāyamāsabhatta*).
Of these, the morning meal is delimited by the end of midday, while the other is from after midday until before dawn.
Therefore, even one who eats ten times within midday remains a "one-meal-eater" (*ekabhattika*); it is with reference to this that he is called "a one-meal-eater. Eating at night...
One who has desisted from that [eating] at night is "desisting from eating at night" (*rattūparato*). Food taken after midday until the setting of the sun is called "untimely food" (*vikālabhojana*).
One who abstains from that is "abstaining from untimely food. Because it is not in conformity with the Teaching (*sāsana*), viewing spectacles is a hindrance;
thus, it is called "viewing spectacles" (*visūkadassana*). Dancing is dancing performed by oneself or by causing others to dance, and so forth.

And "song" (*gītā*) and "instrumental music" (*vāditā*), as well as the "viewing of performances" (*visūkadassanā*) consisting of dances and so forth—even those occurring merely for the sake of watching peacock dances and the like—constitute "dancing, singing, instrumental music, and viewing performances.

Indeed, neither for monks nor for nuns is it permissible to perform dances and such themselves, to cause others to perform them, or even to watch them when performed by others. Regarding garlands and so forth...
“Flower” (*mālā*) refers to any kind of flower. “Fragrance” (*gandha*) refers to any kind of fragrant substance. “Ointment” (*vilepana*) refers to that which colors the skin.
In this context, one who wears it is said to “wear” (*dhāreti*); one who fills out deficient parts is said to “adorn” (*maṇḍeti*);
and one who relishes it by way of its fragrance and its coloring of the skin is said to “decorate” (*vibhūseti*). “Place” (*ṭhāna*) means a cause. Therefore, by whatever unvirtuous volition...
The meaning is that he abstains from those things such as wearing garlands, which the great multitude of people practices.
"High bed" refers to one exceeding the prescribed measure; "luxurious bed" refers to an unworthy covering. The meaning is that he abstains from these.
"Jātarūpa" means gold; "rajata" means a coin, a copper māsaka, a lacquer māsaka, or a wooden māsaka.
Regarding those things that enter into common usage, he abstains from accepting both;

the meaning is that he neither accepts them himself, nor causes them to be accepted, nor consents to their being deposited for him. "Accepting raw grain" refers to the acceptance of the seven kinds of raw grain, namely:
rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and kudrūsa grass. And it is not only the acceptance of these that is prohibited...

Even touching raw meat is not permitted for monks. Regarding "the acceptance of raw meat": here, except where specifically authorized, the acceptance of raw meat, raw fish, and so forth is indeed not permitted for monks, but touching them is not [prohibited].
Regarding "the acceptance of women and girls": here, a "woman" is one who has gone to another man; the other is called a "girl. Of these two—
Both receiving and touching [such things] are indeed improper. Regarding "the receiving of female and male slaves": here, their receiving specifically as female and male slaves is not permitted;
however, it is permitted if one says, "I give [them] as a *kappiyakāraka* (one who prepares what is allowable)," or "I give [him] as a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*).
As for the items beginning with goats and sheep and ending with fields and land, the method for determining what is allowable and what is unallowable is according to the Vinaya.
It is to be examined. In this context, "field" (*khetta*) refers to that in which the primary grain (*pubbaṇṇa*) grows.
"Site" (*vatthu*) refers to that in which the secondary grain (*aparaṇṇa*) grows; or else, that in which both grow is a field, while ground prepared for that purpose is a site.
Furthermore, by way of the terms "field" and "site," cultivated ponds and so forth are also included here. "Messengership" (*dūteyya*) is what is called...
The work of a messenger (*dūtakamma*) consists of traveling here and there after taking a letter or a message from householders.
"Going on an errand" (*pahiṇagamana*) refers to short trips sent from one house to another. "Devotion" (*anuyoga*) means the performance of both of those;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "devotion to the work of a messenger and to going on errands."
"Buying and selling" means both buying and selling. Regarding "false weights and so forth," *kūṭa* means deception.
Therein, false weighing first is fourfold: false in form, false in the parts, false in the grasping, and false by concealment.
Among these, "false in form" (*rūpakūṭa*) means making two scales that look identical, using the larger one when taking [goods] and the smaller one when giving.
He gives. Regarding "cheating by the corner" (*aṅgakūṭa*): when taking, he steps on the scale with his hand at the rear;
when giving, he does so at the front. Regarding "cheating by the grasp" (*gahaṇakūṭa*): when taking, he grasps the rope at the base; when giving, he grasps it at the top.
Regarding "cheating by concealment" (*paṭicchannakūṭa*): having made a hollow in the scale and filled it inside with iron filings, when taking, he places it at the rear; when giving...
"At the top portion. *Kaṃsa* refers to a golden bowl; cheating with that is *kaṃsakūṭa*.
How so? Having made one golden bowl, he makes two or three other bowls of iron colored like gold.
Then, having gone to a country and entered some respectable family, saying, "Buy golden vessels," when asked the price, [he offers] one of lesser value.
They desired to give [the bowls]. Then, when they asked, "How is it to be known whether these are made of gold?
he said, "Take them after testing them," and having struck the golden bowl against a stone, he gave away all the bowls and departed.
There are three kinds of deception by measure (*mānakūṭa*): that which breaks the heart, that which breaks the tip, and that which breaks the cord. Among these, the breaking of the heart—
The "measuring by drops" (*sappitelādiminanakāla*) occurs when measuring ghee, oil, and the like.
For one who takes them, having said "pour slowly," they take it after causing much to flow into the vessel through a hole at the bottom;

one who gives them closes the hole and gives it quickly, filling [the vessel] rapidly. The "breaking of the crest" (*sikhābhedo*) occurs when measuring sesame, rice, and the like. For one who takes them...
He takes [the land] after slowly raising the measuring cord; the giver gives by filling it quickly while cutting the cord.
"Breaking the rope" occurs at the time of measuring fields and lands. For those who do not receive a bribe measure even a small field as large.
Regarding "undoing" (*ukkoṭana*) and so forth: "undoing" is the taking of a bribe to make an owner non-owner. "Deception" is by various...
Deceiving others by means of stratagems. Here is one such instance: it is said that a certain hunter was coming along, having caught both a deer and a fawn.
A certain rogue asked him, "Sir, what is the price of the deer? What is the price of the fawn?
When he replied, "The deer is two kahāpaṇas, and the fawn is one," the rogue gave a kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and departed.
Having gone a short distance, he turned back and said, "Sir, I have no need for the fawn; give me a deer.
The other replied, "In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas. He said, "But sir, did you not already give me one kahāpaṇa?
"Yes, it was given. "Take this fawn as well; thus, both that kahāpaṇa and this fawn, which is worth a kahāpaṇa,"
"A fawn will be worth two kahāpaṇas. Perceiving that he was speaking with a motive, he took the fawn and gave it to the deer.
"A rogue" means one who, through trickery or deceit, calls a non-girdle a girdle, a non-jewel a jewel, or what is not gold...

"Gold" refers to deception by means of a counterfeit. "Crooked practice" (*sāciyoga*) means crooked application; this is a name for those very acts such as "bargaining back" (*ukkoṭana*) and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "crooked practice of bargaining back," "crooked practice of deception," and "crooked practice of guile.
Some say that "crooked practice" is the exchange of one thing while showing another. However, that too is simply a form of deception.
It is included. Among "cutting" and the others: "cutting" refers to the cutting off of hands and so forth. "Slaying" means killing. "Binding" is binding with ropes and the like.
"Robbery" (*viparāmoso*) is twofold: robbery by snow and robbery by thickets.
That which occurs when people, being hidden by falling snow during the winter season, plunder those traveling on the road—that is robbery by snow. That which... [is robbery by thickets].

They steal by concealing themselves in bushes and such; this is "stealing from a thicket" (*gumbaviparāmoso*). "Looting" (*ālopa*) refers to the act of plundering villages, market towns, and so forth.
"Violence" (*sahasākāra*) is a rash or forceful act; it is the seizing of desired goods after entering a house and placing a weapon upon people's chests.
Thus, he abstains from this cutting... [and so on] ...up to violence.

294. "Thus he is content" means that this bhikkhu is endowed with the twelvefold contentment regarding requisites (*itara-itara-paccaya-santosā*) as described below in relation to the four requisites.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu endowed with these twelve kinds of contentment regarding requisites, eight articles are permissible: the three robes, the alms-bowl, and the tooth-stick cutter.
One needle, a waistband, and a water-strainer. And this has also been said:
“The three robes and the bowl, The razor, the needle, and the waistband— Together with the water-strainer, these eight Are for the bhikkhu who is devoted to yoga.”

All of these serve both to sustain the body and to sustain the belly. How so? First, when one goes about having put on and wrapped oneself in the three robes, they sustain and nourish the body; thus, they are "sustainers of the body.
Furthermore, when one strains water with the hem of the robe and drinks it, or when one gathers fruits and other foodstuffs to eat, they sustain the belly.

"Poses" means it serves for the maintenance of the belly. Even the bowl, having been used by him to draw water, serves for the maintenance of the body at the time of bathing and at the time of preparing the surroundings of the hut;
and when used to take up food and eat, it serves for the maintenance of the belly.
Even the axe, when used for cutting tooth-sticks, and for assembling the parts and legs of beds and stools, or the poles of the robe-hut, [serves for the maintenance of the body].
It serves the body when sugarcane, coconut, and other such items are being peeled; it serves the stomach when they are used to fill the belly.
Even a needle serves the body when sewing robes, and serves the stomach when used to pierce cakes or fruit for eating.
A waistband serves the body when one goes about wearing it, and serves the stomach when sugarcane and other items are tied up for carrying.
The water-strainer is for the maintenance of the stomach. Having strained water with it at the time of bathing and at the time of cleaning the lodgings, it serves for the maintenance of the body;
and at the time of straining drinking water, or when taking sesame, rice, parched grain, and so forth with that same [strainer] at the time of eating, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach.
This, then, is the measure of requisites for one who possesses eight requisites.
For one who has nine requisites, when entering a dwelling, either a mat already present there or a key is permitted.
For one who has ten requisites, either a sitting mat or a piece of leather is permitted.
For one who has eleven requisites, either a walking stick or an oil tube is permitted. For one who has twelve requisites, either a sunshade or sandals [is permitted].
Or it is permissible. Among these, only the one who possesses eight requisites is contented; the others are not contented and should not be called "of great desire" or "a heavy burden.
For even they are indeed few in desire, contented, easy to support, and live a simple life.
However, the Blessed One did not speak this sutta with reference to them; he spoke it with reference to the one who possesses eight requisites. He...

Indeed, having placed the small needle-case and the needle inside a water-strainer and set them within his bowl, and having hung the bowl from the shoulder-strap and fastened the triple robe to his body, he departs at ease wherever he wishes.
There is nothing for him to take back with him; thus the Blessed One, demonstrating this bhikkhu’s mode of living with great lightness, said:
"He is content with robes for the sake of bodily protection," and so forth, he said.
Therein, "for the sake of bodily protection" means merely for the purpose of maintaining the body. "For the sake of stomach protection" means merely for the purpose of maintaining the stomach.
"Having taken up [only] that, he departs" means having taken all those eight requisites and keeping them fastened to his body.
Having done so, he goes forth; he has no attachment or bond of thought such as, "This is my monastery, this my cell, this my attendant.

Like an arrow released from its string, like a rutting elephant that has strayed from the herd, he dwells alone, standing alone and sitting alone, enjoying whatever lodging he desires—whether a forest thicket, the foot of a tree, or a mountain cave.
In all modes of conduct, he is alone and without a second.
He is impartial toward the four quarters and free from aversion,
content with whatever comes his way.
“Enduring hardships with composure and fearlessness,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus one attains the state described as being “like the rhinoceros horn.”
Now, in order to establish that meaning by means of a simile, he said, "Just as," and so forth. Therein, "a winged bird" (*pakkhī sakuṇo*) means a bird possessed of wings.
"Flies" (*ḍeti*) means it flies up. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here:
having learned that "in such-and-such a place there is a tree with ripe fruit," birds come from various directions and, with their claws, wings, beaks, and so on, [take] its fruits.
They eat, piercing and shaking [the fruit]. They have no thought such as, "This is for today; this will be for tomorrow.
But when the fruit is exhausted, they do not establish a guard over the tree, nor do they station a foot, a claw, or a beak there;
rather, having become indifferent toward that tree, each goes whichever direction he desires.
Just as one who has laid down his burden rises and goes, even so this bhikkhu sets out free from attachment and without longing.
Therefore it is said: "Having taken it up, he sets out. "By the noble" means by that which is faultless.
"Internally" means within one's own person. "Bliss free from blame" means faultless bliss.
295. "Thus, having seen a form with the eye" means that this bhikkhu, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having perceived a form by means of visual consciousness.
Whatever else needs to be said regarding the remaining phrases has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Unstained happiness" (*abyāsekasukha*) means happiness not drenched by defilements; it also means undiluted happiness.
It has been said. For the happiness of restraint of the sense faculties is undistracted because it proceeds by way of merely seeing what is seen and so forth among the seen and the rest.

"In going forward and in returning": that bhikkhu, endowed with restraint of the six sense faculties including the mind, acts with clear comprehension by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension in these seven instances beginning with going forward and returning.
This is so. Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta].
296. What does he show by the passage beginning with "And by this"? He shows the fulfillment of the requisites for dwelling in the forest.
For one who lacks these four requisites, dwelling in the forest does not succeed; [he would be] like those among the animals or the forest-dwellers.
Or he incurs censure from others; deities dwelling in the forest let out terrifying cries, saying, "What is the use of such an evil bhikkhu living in the forest?
and they strike their heads with their hands, making gestures as if fleeing.
They spread his ill repute, saying, "Such-and-such a bhikkhu, having entered the forest, committed this and that evil deed."
But for one who possesses these four conditions, dwelling in the forest succeeds.

For he, reflecting upon his own virtue and seeing no blemish or mole whatsoever, generates rapture; then, contemplating that very rapture as subject to destruction and vanishing, he enters the plane of the Noble Ones.
The deities dwelling in the forest become delighted and praise him.
They proclaim [his fame], and thus his reputation spreads like a drop of oil cast upon water.
In this context, "secluded" (*vivitta*) means empty, quiet, and silent; such is the meaning. It is with reference to this very point that the *Vibhaṅga* states:
"Secluded means that even if the lodging is nearby, it is not crowded with householders or renunciants."
Therefore it is said, "it is secluded. It is called *senāsana* because one lies down (*seti*) and sits (*āsati*) therein; this is a designation for beds, chairs, and so forth.

Thus he said: "‘Recluse’s seat’ (*senāsana*) means a bed is a recluse’s seat, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery (*vihāra*), a gabled house (*aḍḍhayoga*), a palace (*pāsāda*), a tower (*hammiya*), a cave (*guhā*), a watchtower (*aṭṭa*), a storied building (*māḷa*), a rock shelter (*leṇa*), or a bamboo thicket (*veḷugumba*)."
“The foot of a tree, a pavilion, or wherever monks return—that is all ‘lodging.
Furthermore, “a vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, and a cave”—this is called a vihāra lodging.
“A bed, a chair, a mattress, and a pillow”—this is called a bed-and-chair lodging. “A rug,”...
“A patchwork of leather, a grass mat, a leaf mat”—this is called a *santhata* (spread) lodging.
“Or where monks return”—this is called an *okāsa* (open space) lodging. Thus there are four kinds of lodgings, and all of them are indeed included by the term “lodging.
Now, for this [monk] who is like a bird and wanders in the four directions...
Showing what is appropriate for a bhikkhu, he said: "In the forest, at the foot of a tree," and so forth.
Therein, regarding "the forest" (*arañña*): "Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is forest"—this is the definition of "forest" as it appears in the context of the bhikkhunīs.
"A forest dwelling (*āraññaka*) is a resting place that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant"—this is [the definition].
However, what is appropriate for this bhikkhu and its characteristics are explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
"At the foot of a tree" means any secluded place at the foot of a tree that provides shade. "A mountain" means a rock formation.
For there, having performed one's water-related duties by the waterfalls, as one sits in the cool shade of the trees while the various directions are becoming visible, [the mind becomes clear].
When fanned by a cool breeze, the mind becomes one-pointed. "Kandara" means that which is split (*kaṃ*);
it refers to a mountain region fissured by water, which they call a river-basin (*nadītumba*) or a river-glen (*nadīkuñja*).
For there, the sand is like silver plates, and at its head, the dense forest is like a canopy of jewels.

Water flows like a mass of jewels. Having descended into such a cave, having drunk the water, having cooled one's limbs, and having spread out a rag-robe upon the sand, the mind becomes one-pointed for one who sits and practices the duty of a recluse.
"A mountain cave" (*giriguhā*) refers to the space between two mountains, or within a single mountain.
A great chasm resembling a mountain cleft. The characteristics of a charnel ground (*susāna*) are described in the *Visuddhimagga*.
A forest retreat (*vanapattha*) is a place beyond the human habitations where people neither plough nor sow.

For this very reason it is said: "‘Forest retreat’ is a designation for remote lodgings," and so forth. An open space (*abbhokāsa*) is that which is uncovered; however, one who so desires may [use] this [open space].
Having made a robe-shed, he dwells there. "A heap of straw" means a pile of straw.
For they make a dwelling resembling a mountain cave by taking straw out from a large heap of straw;
or, having thrown straw over bushes, thickets, and the like, they practice the duty of a recluse sitting beneath it—it is with reference to this that this was said.
"After the meal" means after the meal. "Having returned from the alms-round" means having returned from the search for almsfood.
"Cross-legged" means a seat with the thighs bound all around. "Having folded" means having bound [the legs].
"Having set the body erect" means having placed the upper part of the body straight, setting the tip of one against the tip of the eighteen vertebrae.
For one sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not sag.
Then, those pains that would arise moment by moment due to their sagging do not arise.
When they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not slip away, and it attains growth and expansion. "Having established mindfulness directed to the mouth" means:
The meaning is: having established mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject, or having placed it near the mouth. For this very reason, it is said in the Vibhaṅga:
"This mindfulness is established, well-established, either on the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth;
therefore it is said, 'having established mindfulness facing the mouth. Alternatively, "pari" has the sense of embracing, and "mukha" means...
"‘Leading out’ (niyyāna) is the sense of escape; ‘mindfulness’ (sati) is the sense of establishing; therefore it is called ‘mindfulness directed to the face’ (parimukhaṃ satiṃ).
Thus the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*. In this regard, the summary is: “having established mindfulness that has discerned the escape.

Regarding the phrase “covetousness for the world” (*abhijjhaṃ loke*): here, the world (*loka*) is the five aggregates of clinging in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. Therefore, in the five [aggregates]...
The meaning here is: having abandoned lust for the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) and suppressed sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
"Free from covetousness" means free from covetousness by way of suppression, not in the manner of visual consciousness; this is the meaning.
"He purifies the mind of covetousness" means he completely liberates the mind from covetousness, so that it releases him and, having released him, [remains].
And "he does not take it up again" means he acts in this way. The same method applies to the phrases "having abandoned ill will and hatred," and so forth.
Ill will (*byāpāda*) is so called because by means of it the mind becomes corrupted, abandoning its former natural state, like meat that has turned putrid.
Hatred (*padosa*) is so called because through the occurrence of a change one becomes corrupt, or because one corrupts or destroys another. Both of these are synonyms for anger (*kodha*).
Sloth (*thīna*) is a sickness of the mind; torpor (*middha*) is a sickness of the mental factors (*cetasika*). Sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) refers to both of these together.
"Perceiving light" (*ālokasaññī*) means being endowed with a perception that is purified and free from hindrances, due to the capacity to recognize the light seen during the day even at night.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" (*sato sampajāno*) means being endowed with both mindfulness (*sati*) and knowledge (*ñāṇa*). This is the pair.
It is said because of its helpfulness to the perception of light (*ālokasaññā*). Restlessness and worry together are *uddhaccakukkucca*.
"One who has crossed beyond doubt" means one who stands having crossed over and transcended doubt. "One who is without perplexity" means that [doubt] does not proceed in the form, "How is this?
How is this? "In wholesome states" means in blameless states. "Are these indeed wholesome? How are these... [and so forth].
The meaning is that one does not doubt or hesitate thus: “Are they wholesome? This is the summary here.
However, whatever needs to be said regarding these hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in terms of their etymological derivation, characteristics, and so forth, has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
297. Regarding “weakening wisdom”: when these five hindrances arise, they weaken both unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom.
They do not allow wisdom to arise, and even when the eight attainments or the five direct knowledges have arisen, they cut them off and cause them to fall;

therefore, they are called "those that weaken wisdom. "The footprint of the Tathāgata" (tathāgatapada) means this too is called the footprint of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, the track of his knowledge, the place traversed by his knowledge. "Resorted to by the Tathāgata" (tathāgatanisevita)...
It is the place rubbed by the smooth surface of the Tathāgata’s knowledge. "Stained by the Tathāgata" means the place stained by the fangs of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
"He understands it as it really is" means he understands it according to its true nature.

"But the noble disciple has not yet reached the final goal" means that because these meditative absorptions and direct knowledges are shared even with outsiders, he has not yet reached the final goal. This applies also at the moment of the Path.
Because his task is not yet finished, he has not yet reached the final conclusion. Nevertheless, he "reaches the conclusion" (niṭṭhaṃ gacchati);

that is to say, just as a forest-keeper beholding a great elephant at the moment of the Path realizes, "This is the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," he reaches the conclusion regarding the Three Jewels in this manner.
He "has reached the conclusion" (niṭṭhaṃ gato hoti) in this way at the moment of the Path.
Reaching the conclusion, at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship, because all duties have been completed, he has reached the conclusion regarding the Three Jewels in every respect.
The remainder is of plain meaning. Thus ends [the section] from the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Cūḷahatthipadopama-sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta. In that context, "of those that roam the jungle" means those that move upon the surface of the earth.

"Living beings" (*pāṇā*) means four-footed living beings. "Classes of feet" (*padajātāni*) means feet. "They go to a collection" (*samodhānaṃ gacchanti*) means they go to a heap or a massing together.
"It is declared the foremost" (*aggamakkhāyati*) means it is declared the best.

"By way of greatness" (*mahantattena*) means it is declared the foremost by virtue of its magnitude, not by virtue of its qualities; this is the meaning. "Whatever wholesome states" (*ye keci kusalā dhammā*) means whatever mundane or...
Or, supramundane wholesome states. Regarding the phrase "they come under inclusion," there are four kinds of inclusion here:

inclusion by genus (*sajātisaṅgaha*), inclusion by kinship (*sañjātisaṅgaha*), inclusion by action (*kiriyasaṅgaha*), and inclusion by enumeration (*gaṇanasaṅgaha*). Among these, inclusion by genus refers to an inclusion based on a common birth, such as: "Let all the khattiyas come; let all the brahmins come. "All those from Kosala... [and so forth].
“‘All those from Māgadha’—this kind of grouping by way of birthplace is called ‘grouping by birthplace.
‘All charioteers, all archers’—this kind of grouping by way of activity is called ‘grouping by activity.
‘To which aggregate-count does the eye-base belong? The eye-base belongs to the count of the form aggregate. If indeed...’”

"The eye-base goes into the enumeration of the aggregate of form; therefore, indeed, it should be said that the eye-base is included within the aggregate of form"—this is what is called inclusion by enumeration.
In this instance as well, this very [type of inclusion] is intended.
But is it not the case that, regarding the question: "Of the four noble truths, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?"...

Because it is stated in the *Vissajjana* (Exposition) that "in the [scheme of] answering, the truth of origination is unwholesome (*akusala*), the truth of the path is wholesome (*kusala*), the truth of cessation is indeterminate (*abyākata*), and the truth of suffering may be wholesome, may be unwholesome,

or may be indeterminate," even wholesome states belonging to all four planes (*catubhūmaka*) pertain to only one and a half truths. Now, for what reason did the Great Elder [include them] within the enumeration of the four noble truths?
Is it said that "it goes"? Because it is included within the truths (*sacca*). For instance, as it is said:

"Monks, these one hundred and fifty-two training rules (*sikkhāpada*) come up for recitation every half-month, wherein clansmen who desire their own welfare train themselves. Monks, there are these three trainings:

the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*), and the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*). In this context, "these one hundred and fifty-two... [is used].

The one hundred and fifty training rules constitute only the single training in higher virtue; yet it is shown that one who trains in that [training] also trains in the three trainings, because they are included within those trainings.

And just as, among the four parts of a single elephant’s footprint, there are footprints of jackals, hares, deer, and so forth that have entered into one part, and others that have entered into two, three, or all four parts.
The footprints are indeed subsumed within the footprint of the elephant, for they are not released from the elephant's footprint because they are included within it.
In the same way, even when phenomena are counted among one, two, three, or four truths, they are still counted among the four truths, because they are included within the truths.
Thus, even when wholesome phenomena are counted as one and a half truths...
“All these are included within the four noble truths,” he said.

Regarding what should be said concerning the summary sections such as “the noble truth of suffering” and so forth, as well as the detailed expositions such as “birth is suffering” and so forth, that has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Only the sequence of the teaching itself should be understood here.
301. Just as a skilled basket-maker, having obtained a well-grown bamboo, cuts it into four parts;
then, setting aside three portions, he takes one and divides it into five; then, setting aside four of those, he takes one and splits it, making five sections;
then, setting aside four of those, he takes one and [distinguishes] the belly portion and the back portion.
Having split it in two and set aside the back portion, one might take the belly portion and from it fashion various bamboo products such as caskets, fans, or winnowing-fans;
yet it cannot be said that he will not employ the back portion, the other four sections, the other four parts, or the other three parts for work. However, he cannot employ them all at once.

"It is not possible; he will lead [the listener] there by degrees. In the same way, this Great Elder, having obtained a well-grown bamboo cane like a reed-weaver, and having begun this great sutta as if dividing it into four sections, established the table of contents (mātikā) according to the Four Noble Truths.
Just as the reed-weaver sets aside three sections and takes one, he divided that into five parts.
Just as the potter, having set aside three of the Noble Truths and taken up the single Truth of Suffering,
divided it fivefold according to the aggregates; and just as that maker of earthenware, having set aside four portions and taken one part,
split it into five, so too did the Elder, having set aside the four immaterial aggregates, [take] the aggregate of form...
Analyzing them, he divided [matter] into five parts: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the matter derived from the four great elements (*upādāyarūpa*).

Then, just as that mold-maker, having set aside four lumps, took one and split it into two parts—the belly portion and the back portion—so too did the Elder, having set aside the matter derived from the elements and the three [other] elements.
While analyzing the single earth element, he showed it to be twofold by way of the internal and the external.
Just as that bowl-maker, setting aside the back portion and taking the belly portion, fashioned various kinds of bowl-work, even so the Elder,
setting aside the external earth element, analyzed the internal earth element in twenty ways.
To demonstrate this, he said, "And what, friends, is the internal earth element? and so forth.

Just as a mold-maker will gradually bring the back part, the other four sections, the other four parts, and the other three parts to the work, for it is not possible to bring them all at once; so too [the elements must be analyzed step by step].

In this way, the Elder too will demonstrate the external earth element, the other three elements, derived matter, the other four immaterial aggregates, and the other three Noble Truths by analyzing them in successive order;
for it is not possible to demonstrate them all at once. Furthermore, this sequence should be clarified by means of the simile of the prince.
It is said, O Great King, that there was a certain monarch who had more than a thousand sons.
He placed their ornaments and requisites into four caskets and gave them to his eldest son, saying:
"My dear son, when such a festival occurs, you should give these ornaments to your brothers when they come to ask for them. He replied, "Very well."

"O gods," he thought, and he placed it away in the inner chamber. On such a festive day, the princes went into the presence of the king and said, "Father, give us our ornaments; we shall play at the festival. [The king replied:
"Sons, the ornaments have been placed by me in the hand of your eldest brother. Have them brought and put them on. Having agreed, saying "Very well," they—
Having gone into his presence, they said, "It is said that the jewelry belonging to us is in your hands; give it back.

He replied, "I shall do so," and opening the chest, he took out four boxes; setting three aside, he opened one, from which he took out five caskets; setting four aside, he opened one, and from those five...
When the caskets had been brought out, he set aside four of them, opened one, and placed its lid on the side;
then, having taken out various kinds of ornaments such as those for the hands and feet, he gave them away.
Although he had not yet finished distributing the contents of the other four caskets, the other four boxes, and the other three chests, he continued to give them away.
However, he will give it gradually, for it is not possible to give it all at once.
In this regard, the Blessed One is to be seen as like a great king. And this has been said:
"I am a king, O Sela," said the Blessed One, "the unsurpassed King of Dhamma. The Elder Sāriputta is like the eldest son; and this too has been said: "That which..."
“Monks, speaking rightly, one should say of him: ‘The Blessed One’s own son, born from his mouth, born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma, not an heir to material things.
Speaking rightly, one should say of Sāriputta alone: ‘The Blessed One’s own son... not an heir to material things.
The Saṅgha of monks should be regarded as being like more than a thousand princes. And this has also been said:”
“More than a thousand bhikkhus attend upon the Sugata as he teaches the stainless Dhamma, Nibbāna, which is free from fear from any quarter.
Having placed the king’s ornaments for his sons into four caskets, [he placed them] in the hand of the eldest son.
It was as if the time had come for the Blessed One to place the exposition of the Four Noble Truths into the hands of the General of the Dhamma;

for this very reason he said: "Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is capable of explaining, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and making plain the Four Noble Truths in detail. At such a moment—

Just as it would be the time for those princes to approach the king and ask for his ornaments, so it was the time for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to come at the commencement of the rainy season retreat and request a teaching on the Dhamma. Indeed, this Sutta was taught when the commencement of the rainy season was drawing near. [The Buddha said:
"O King, 'Sons, I have placed an ornament in the hand of your eldest brother.'"
Just as at the time when it was said, "Having had that brought, put it on," so too did the Fully Enlightened One send the monks to the presence of the General of the Dhamma, saying:
"Monks, serve Sāriputta and Moggallāna; associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna. These monks are wise and helpful to their fellow celibates."
Just as the princes, having heard the king’s words, went to their eldest brother and asked for his ornaments as if they were begging,
so too did the monks, having heard the Teacher’s discourse, approach the Dhamma-Senāpati and request a teaching on the Dhamma.
And just as the eldest brother opened the chest, brought out four boxes, and set them down, so it was with the Dhamma-Senāpati.
Having begun this sutta, there is the establishment of the matrix (mātikā) by way of the Four Noble Truths.

Just as one might set out three caskets, open one, and then take out five boxes from it, so too, having established the other three Noble Truths, there is the demonstration of the five aggregates while analyzing the Noble Truth of Suffering. Having set out four boxes...

Just as one might open a single casket and then take out five smaller caskets, so too, for one who sets aside the four immaterial aggregates and analyzes the single material aggregate, there is the demonstration of its fivefold division by way of the four great elements and derived matter. 302.
Just as one might set aside four caskets, open one, and place its lid on the side, then give away hand-gear, foot-gear, and ornaments; likewise...
