Just as one who analyzes the earth element alone—setting aside the three great primary elements and derived matter—sets aside the external covering as it were, so too, for the purpose of showing the internal earth element through its various characteristics in twenty ways, there is the statement beginning with:
"And what, friends, is the internal earth element? and so forth.

Then, just as that prince was gradually led out from those four caskets, four bags, and three boxes and presented with the gift of ornaments, so too for the Elder— and for the other three great elements,
the derived matter, the four immaterial aggregates, and the three noble truths— there followed a gradual [explanation].
The vision should be understood by way of division. As for what was said, beginning with, "And what, friends, is the internal earth element?":
therein, both *ajjhattaṃ* (internal) and *paccattaṃ* (personal) are synonyms for one's own [body]. *Kakkhaḷaṃ* means hard. *Kharigataṃ* means coarse.
*Upādinnaṃ* (clung-to) does not refer exclusively to that which is originated by kamma; rather, it refers to it without distinction.

This is a designation for the "body-as-a-basis. For whether the body-as-a-basis is clung-to (*upādinna*) or not-clung-to (*anupādinna*), everything is called "clung-to" by way of being grasped, seized, and misapprehended.
That is to say: head-hairs, body-hairs... [and so on] ...stomach-intestines, excrement;
thus has the meditation subject been analyzed first according to the internal earth element for a clansman who takes the elements as his meditation subject. Now, herein:
Everything that must be done by one who desires to attain Arahantship by developing insight after beginning with mental attention has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, the brain has not yet been included here in the canonical text.
Having brought that in as well and defined it according to its color, shape, and so forth, in the same manner described in the *Visuddhimagga*, [one should contemplate]: "This too..."
"One should attend to it thus: 'The earth element is indeed insentient, indeterminate, empty, and rigid.
As for the phrase "or whatever else," this is stated for the purpose of including the earth element that is present within the other three components.
"And whatever internal earth element there is" refers to this internal earth element of the kind already described.
"And that which is external" refers to the external earth element as it appears in the *Vibhaṅga* by way of the method beginning with "iron, copper, tin, lead," and so forth.
To this extent, the Elder has shown the internal earth element in detail through twenty aspects according to its various characteristics, but the external one only in brief.
Why? Because it is in the place where beings have attachment, craving, and longing.
When obsession, grasping, and misapprehension are powerful, the Buddhas or their disciples give an extensive discourse for the purpose of uprooting those attachments and so forth.
But where they are not powerful, they speak in brief because there is no need for further action. For just as a farmer, while plowing a field, [wherever...]
The plough gets stuck because of the strength of the roots and creepers;
having set aside the oxen there, one must exert great effort while repeatedly cutting away the roots and creepers and clearing the soil.
But where those are absent, one simply ploughs by applying strong effort and striking the oxen on their backs. This should be understood as being exactly like that.
"It is simply the earth element"—this shows that although it is twofold, in terms of its stiffness, hardness, and roughness, it has the single characteristic of the earth element alone, friend;

thus he demonstrates by joining the internal with the external. Since the insentient nature of the external earth element is manifest, but not that of the internal, therefore it is similar to the external.
For one who grasps [the internal] as being indeed insentient, there is an easy mastery over pleasure. How so?
Just as a wild ox, when yoked together with a tamed ox, may for a few days act restlessly and struggle, but then before long comes under control;
even so, for one who grasps the internal [elements] as being exactly the same as the external, the state of insentience [of the internal] lasts for only a few days.
It does not appear; then, before long, its insentient nature becomes manifest.
Regarding that, one should see both of them with right wisdom as they truly are, thinking: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self.
"As it truly is" means according to its actual nature; for its nature is impermanence and so forth, and therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
The meaning is: "It should be viewed thus.

Why was it begun with the words, "There is indeed that, friends"? It was for the purpose of showing the destruction of the external earth element by way of the external water element, and then, even more specifically, to show the destruction of the appropriated earth element that constitutes the physical body.
"It churns" means that it becomes agitated as it increases by way of the water-dissolution.

"At that time, the external earth element has disappeared" means that at that time, the entire earth element—consisting of mountains and so forth—that had existed throughout the hundred thousand million world-systems, having been dissolved by the salt-water and followed by the water, disappears. Having dissolved...
It becomes nothing but water. "So vast" means so great.
"Two hundred thousand and forty nahutas—this much, by its thickness, is reckoned as this Earth."
Thus, it is great by its very thickness; but in terms of breadth, it is equal in measure to a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Impermanence" (*aniccatā*) is the state of non-existence after having existed. "The nature of destruction" (*khayadhammatā*) is the inherent tendency to go toward destruction.

"The nature of decay" (*vayadhammatā*) is the inherent tendency to go toward decline. "The nature of change" (*vipariṇāmadhammatā*) is the inherent tendency to abandon one's original state. Thus, by all these [terms]...
By these words, the characteristic of impermanence alone is stated. But whatever is impermanent is suffering;
and whatever is suffering is non-self—thus all three characteristics are indeed included. "Of one for whom the measure has been reached" means of one whose duration is limited;
therein, the limited duration of this body should be understood in two ways: by the limitation of its persistence and by the limitation of its inherent nature.
Indeed, in the past mental moment he lived, he does not live, and he will not live. In the future mental moment he will live, he does not live, and he did not live.
In the present mental moment he lives, he did not live, and he will not live—thus it is said.
“Life and the personal existence, and all pleasure and pain, are joined together in a single mind; that moment passes swiftly.
This was said for the purpose of showing the limited duration of this very [mind]. Thus, by way of the limitation of its duration, its state of being limited should be understood.
Furthermore, its nature as a "personal protective charm" (sarasaparitta) should be understood by way of its being bound up with inhalation and exhalation,

and so forth. For it is explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* that the life of beings is bound up with inhalation, the life of beings is bound up with exhalation, the life of beings is bound up with inhalation and exhalation,
the life of beings is bound up with the primary elements, the life of beings is bound up with physical nutriment, and the life of beings is bound up with consciousness.
"Of one seized by craving" means: of one who has grasped, taken up, and clung to [the notion] "I," or "mine," or "I am.

"Then indeed, there is no more of this for him" means: then, for that bhikkhu who sees having thus applied the three characteristics, there is no more of this threefold seizing by craving, conceit, and views regarding the internal earth element, such as "I am," and so forth.

The meaning is: "it does not exist, nor does it certainly exist. And just as there is the disappearance of the external earth element by way of the water element, so too is there the disappearance of the external earth element by way of the fire element and the air element; however, here only one has been mentioned. The others should also be understood according to their meaning.
"If, friend," [he says], referring here to that bhikkhu who practices the meditation subject of the elements, as he establishes his comprehension at the door of the ear.
He displays his strength. "They revile" means they revile him by means of the ten grounds for reviling.

"They abuse" means they abuse him with words, saying, "This and that was done by you; we shall do such and such to you. "They irritate" means they provoke him. "They harass" means they cause him pain; all this is said to be merely provocation by speech.
"He, in this way" refers to that practitioner of the meditation subject on the elements (dhātukammaṭṭhānika) in this manner.
He is clearly comprehending. "This has arisen for me": it has arisen by way of its state of having already arisen and its state of arising through manifestation.
Ear-contact-born [feeling] is born from ear-contact by way of being its decisive support;

it is the javana-feeling of the ear-door. "Contact is impermanent": he sees that, having been ear-contact, it is impermanent in the sense of non-existence. Feeling and the other factors are likewise associated with ear-contact.
It should be understood thus: "Only the element as object" means only that object which is reckoned as an element.
"Enters into" means he descends into it. "Is confident" means he is confident in that object; or rather, this is a locative expression.

Due to the euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*) of the phonemes, it is stated as "only the element as object" (*dhātārammaṇameva*); the meaning here is "only in the element as object" (*dhātārammaṇeyeva*). "Resolves" means by way of the elements.

Thus he attains resolve; he neither lusts nor hates. For when an object enters the range of the ear-door, he performs a comprehensive examination by way of its fundamental full understanding (*mūla-pariññā*), its adventitious nature (*āgantuka-tā*), and its temporary nature (*tāvakālika*).

The detailed exposition of this has been stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* under the section on mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*). However, that was stated there with reference to the eye-door; here—
It should be understood by way of the ear door.
For when one who has thus performed the preliminary investigation, being a practitioner of the meditation subject of the elements and possessing powerful insight,
even if improper attention arises toward an object that has entered the range of the eye door and so forth, after reaching the stage of determining (voṭṭhabbana), for one or two moments—
Having obtained such repeated practice, the mind enters back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and does not arise again through the influence of lust and so forth;

this is one who possesses sharp insight that has reached its ultimate limit. For another person, however, the impulsion (javana) occurs once by way of lust and so forth, but at the conclusion of the impulsion, as he reflects, "Thus did my impulsion impel," the object becomes clearly discerned precisely through that very influence of lust and so forth.
Again, it does not occur in that way. When another person adverts in this manner only once, the impulsion still occurs by way of lust and so forth on the second occasion;

however, when he adverts at the conclusion of the second occasion, thinking, "In this way my impulsion has occurred," the object becomes clearly discerned, and on the third occasion it does not arise in that same way. Herein, the first person is very quick-witted.
The third [type of person] is "excessively dull. However, by way of the second [type], this meaning should be understood in this sutta, in the *Laṭukikopama*, and in the *Indriyabhāvanā*.
Having thus shown the power of one who takes the elements as his meditation subject (*dhātukammaṭṭhānika*) by way of discerning [the elements] at the ear-door, now, at the body-door—
He said, "If, friend," and so forth, illustrating this. For when encountering an undesirable object, one fatigues at two points:

the ear-door and the body-door. Therefore, it is just as if a field-owner, taking a spade and walking through his field, were to break up the earth with the spade only in the weak spots, without placing a lump of clay here or there.

He gives a lump of grass and clay. In the same way, the Great Elder, thinking that in the future clansmen who desire training and are intent on striving will establish restraint at these two doors and quickly bring an end to birth, aging, and death,
began this teaching while bestowing a firm restraint upon these very two doors.
In that context, "they assail" means they attack. "By contact with the hand" means by the striking of the hand; the same method applies to the others as well.
"Of such a nature" means having such an intrinsic character (*sabhāva*). "In what is thus" means in what has such an intrinsic character. "They move" means they proceed.
Thus, in passages such as "recalling the Buddha," even one who recalls [him] according to the method beginning with "Thus indeed was the Blessed One," [is said to be "recalling the Buddha"].
One recollects by thinking, "This was indeed said by the Blessed One," and thus one truly recollects.

Recollecting according to the method beginning with, "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One," one recollects the Dhamma; recollecting the teaching on the simile of the saw, one also truly recollects.
Recollecting according to the method beginning with, "The Saṅgha has practiced well," one recollects the Saṅgha.
Even one who recollects the virtues of a bhikkhu enduring the sawing of his body continues to recollect them.

Regarding the statement "equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established," it is insight-equanimity (*vipassanūpekkhā*) that is intended here. Regarding the statement "equanimity supported by the wholesome becomes established," it is the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) that is intended;
and although this [sixfold equanimity] exists for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) toward desirable and undesirable objects, [the former does not].

It proceeds by way of non-attachment and so forth; however, because this bhikkhu, through the power of energy and the accomplishment of development, establishes his own insight in the state of the six-factored equanimity of one whose taints are destroyed, it is thus that insight itself comes to be known as "the six-factored equanimity.

(303) In the description of the water element (*āpodhātu*), "that which has gone into the waters" (*āpogata*) refers to the characteristic of the moist, liquid state found in all water. Regarding "bile, phlegm," and so forth...
However, everything that ought to be said regarding this, together with the method of its cultivation, has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"It becomes agitated" (*pakuppati*) means it increases by way of a flood, or water rises up from the ocean; this is its ordinary agitation.

But at the time of the universal dissolution by water (*āposaṃvaṭṭakāla*), the hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) become entirely filled with water. "They subside" (*ogacchanti*) means they go downwards.
Like water placed on a heated pan, they reach exhaustion and destruction. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before. 304.

In the description of the fire element (*tejodhātu*), "gone into the state of fire" (*tejogata*) means that which has entered into all fires and possesses the characteristic of heat. Or, it is "fire itself" that has attained the state of being fire; thus it is "gone into the state of fire.
This same method applies to the preceding "gone into the state of water" (*āpogata*) and the subsequent "gone into the state of air" (*vāyogata*). By which...
And by that which consists of fire: when that is disturbed, this body becomes feverish; it becomes heated through the state of one-day-old fever and so forth.
And by that through which one ages: by which this body grows old, reaching a deficiency of the sense faculties, the exhaustion of strength, and the state of wrinkles, grey hair, and so on.
And by that through which one is consumed: by which, when disturbed, this body is consumed.

And that person, crying out "I am burning! I am burning!", longs for an ointment of sandalwood from Sātaka, Sappi, Gosīsa, and so forth, washed a hundred times, as well as the breeze from a palm-leaf fan.
And by means of that [fire], whatever has been eaten, drunk, chewed, or tasted undergoes proper digestion—namely, what was eaten such as boiled rice and the like;
what was drunk such as beverages and the like; what was chewed such as flour-based snacks and the like; or what was tasted such as mangoes, honey, molasses, and so forth.
It reaches full ripening; the meaning is that it undergoes separation by way of its essence as juice and so forth. This is the summary here.
As for what should be said in detail, all of that—including the method of meditation—has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Grass-blade" (*haritanta*) means simply grass. The meaning is that it is extinguished by resorting to green grass and the like. "Path-end" (*panthanta*) means simply a great road.
"Selantaṃ" means a mountain. "Udakantaṃ" means water. "A delightful region of land" refers to a secluded, open area of ground free from grass, thickets, and the like.
"Without food" means without sustenance or without fuel; this too is stated as a natural transformation of fire (*tejo*).
However, at the time of the conflagration of the world, after burning a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), not even so much as a residue of ash remains.
It does not remain. "With a hide-scraping tool" means with a scraper for leather.
"Seeking fire" means that, having taken such a subtle fuel, they search for fire—that which, upon finding even a slight warmth, bursts into flames.
The rest here should also be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
305. In the description of the air element (*vāyodhātu*): "Upward-moving winds" refers to the upward-ascending winds that cause the occurrence of eructations, hiccups, and so forth.
"Downward-moving winds" refers to the downward-descending winds that expel feces, urine, and so forth. "Winds residing in the belly" refers to the winds outside the intestines.
"Winds residing in the bowels" refers to the winds inside the intestines. "Those following the limbs and members" refers to [the winds] following along the network of vessels (*dhamanījāla*).

Throughout the entire body, there are winds that pervade every limb and member, which produce such actions as contracting and extending. "In-breath" (*assāsa*) is the air entering through the nostrils;
"out-breath" (*passāsa*) is the air exiting through the nostrils. This is the summary here.
As for what should be said in detail, all of it—along with the method of meditation—is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"It carries even a village" means that it goes along taking even an entire village, reducing it to dust and fragments;

the same principle applies to market towns and so forth. Here, the transformation of the wind element is shown by way of its destruction of a hundred thousand million world-systems at the time of the wind-samvatta.
"By fanning" means by means of a fire-fan. "In the eaves" means on the roof-peak; for it is there that the water flows off.
Therefore, it is called "outflow" (*ossavana*). The remainder here should also be construed in the same manner as before.
306. In the phrase "Just as, friends," what is being shown here? It shows the insentient nature of the great elements mentioned above.
"Wood" refers to a collection of materials. "Creeper" refers to a binding creeper. "Grass" refers to thatching grass. "Clay" refers to...
An anulepa-mattika (a plaster of clay). "The space is enclosed" means that these pieces of wood and so forth have been arranged around it both inside and out, such that a space remains;
thus, it comes to be designated as a "house. It is merely a conventional designation (*paññatti*) that it is a "house.
However, when the wood and other materials are piled up separately, they are simply called a "pile of wood" or a "pile of creepers. In the same way...

The word *ko* means: just so, the space that stands surrounding the bones and other parts both inside and outside is designated as "form" (*rūpa*) in dependence upon those very bones and other parts, and it comes to be conventionally expressed as "the body.
Just as a house, which is designated as such in dependence upon timber and other materials, is called a "house of a kshatriya" or a "house of a brahmin," so too is this [the case here].
The body of a kṣatriya is called the body of a brāhmaṇa; herein no being or soul whatsoever is found.

Friend, why was this internal eye introduced? Because previously derived matter, the four formless aggregates, and the three noble truths had not been explained; now, this teaching is undertaken in order to explain them.

"Exerted. In this context, "the eye is unimpaired" means that even when the clarity of the eye has ceased, or when it is damaged, or when it is obstructed by bile, phlegm, or blood, the eye is unable to serve as a condition for eye-consciousness; it is then indeed impaired.
However, that which is capable of serving as a condition for eye-consciousness is called "unimpaired. As for the external...

And "external forms" refers to external forms arising from the four [types of] origination. "The corresponding adverting" means the attention that arises by turning back the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in dependence upon that eye and those forms;
the meaning is the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) at the eye-door capable of turning back the life-continuum.
That [adverting] does not occur even when the forms have not come within range, nor for one who is otherwise occupied.
*Tajjassa* means "of that which corresponds to it. *Viññāṇabhāgassa* means "of the portion consisting of consciousness.
In the passage beginning with *yaṃ tathābhūtassa*, he shows the Four Truths by way of the sense doors.

Therein, *tathābhūtassa* means "of one who has become such," that is, of one accompanied by eye-consciousness; the meaning is "of one possessing eye-consciousness. *Rūpaṃ* refers to the object of eye-consciousness.

Because it does not produce matter, the triad-originated materiality is not found at the moment of eye-consciousness; however, in the immediately succeeding mental moment, even the tetrad-originated materiality is obtained.
"Is included" means it is counted. Feeling and the other [mental factors] are associated exclusively with eye-consciousness.
Consciousness, too, is specifically eye-consciousness. And here, "volitional formations" refers specifically to volition (*cetanā*). "Inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) means being together as one.
*Saṅgaha* means gathering. *Sannipāta* means meeting. *Samavāya* means a collection.
"He who sees dependent origination" means he who sees conditions. "He sees the Dhamma" means he sees the phenomena that have arisen dependently.

"Desire" (*chanda*) and all the other terms are merely synonyms for craving (*taṇhā*); for craving is called "desire" (*chanda*) because it acts as a desire, and it is called "attachment" (*ālaya*) because it acts as a clinging.
*Anunaya* (attachment) is so called by way of causing inclination. *Ajjhosāna* (clinging) is said to be by way of plunging into and swallowing [the object].
"The removal of desire-and-lust" (*chandārāga-vinaya*) and "the abandoning of desire-and-lust" (*chandārāga-pahāna*) are synonyms for Nibbāna itself.

Thus, while three of the truths have already appeared in the Canon, the Truth of the Path must be brought in and understood; whatever view or intention exists regarding these three points [is the Truth of the Path].
Speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and penetration through development—this is the path.

"Much has been done" means that even to this extent, much of the Blessed One’s teaching has been accomplished. This same method applies to the sections beginning with, "Friend, the internal ear... and so forth.

However, in the case of the mind-door, what is called the "internal mind" is the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*). Even though that has ceased, it [serves as the basis] for the adverting consciousness...
That which is incapable of serving as a condition, even while occurring in a state of dullness or weakness, is said to be "broken.
However, that which is capable of serving as a condition for adverting is said to be "unbroken. And "external phenomena" refers to the object consisting of mental phenomena (*dhammārammaṇa*).
The phrase "not yet [capable] of that" is stated specifically with reference to the moment of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). This is the second section.

This was said with reference to something else, such as by means of reviewing well-mastered jhāna, or by attention directed toward a well-mastered meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), or by the recitation and so forth of well-mastered Buddha-words.
In this context, "matter" (rūpa) includes that which arises from all four origins;
for mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) originates matter, feeling and the other [mental factors] are associated with mind-consciousness, and consciousness itself is simply mind-consciousness.

In this context, however, formations (*saṅkhārā*) are taken specifically by way of contact (*phassa*) and volition (*cetanā*). The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.

Thus, the Great Elder, having come back after contemplating only a single portion below, stood at this point and, dividing everything that had been taught below according to its respective doors, brought the discourse to its conclusion following the proper sequence of connection.
The commentary on the Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 9.
The commentary on the Mahāsāropama-sutta.

307. Thus have I heard: this is the Mahāsāropama Sutta. Therein, "not long after he had departed" means that not long after he had departed—having split the Saṅgha and committed the offense of shedding blood—he was born separately while still wearing his monastic robes.

Here, although it is not specified which son of good family it is, it should be understood that this was said with reference specifically to Devadatta. For he [was born] in the lineage of Okkāka, within the unbroken succession of the Great Elect (Mahāsammata).
Because he is born, he is a son of noble birth (*jātikulaputta*). "Immersed" (*otīṇṇa*) means that for whom birth has entered within;
he is called "immersed in birth. The same method applies to old age and the rest. Regarding "gain, honor, and so forth": "gain" refers to the four requisites;
"honor" is the state of being well-treated by those very [requisites]; "fame" is the speaking of praise. "Produces" means brings about. "Unrecognized" refers to two...
They are not seen in places where people gather; they do not even receive enough food and clothing. "Of little influence" means having few attendants;
they do not obtain anyone to walk before them or behind them.
"That which is to be made of heartwood by heartwood" refers to anything that must be fashioned from the heartwood of a tree, such as axles, wheels, yokes, ploughs, and so forth.

"He took hold of the branches and foliage of the holy life" means that the four requisites of the holy life of the Dispensation—which has the essence of the path and its fruits—are called "branches and foliage," and he took hold of them.
And "he reached a stopping point by means of that" means that by means of those very [requisites], he fell into a state of complacency, thinking, "This is enough;
I have attained the essence."
310. "He attains knowledge and vision": Devadatta possessed the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*). Among these five higher knowledges, the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*) stands at the pinnacle;
it is this that is referred to as "knowledge and vision" in this sutta. "They dwell without knowing and without seeing":
they dwell without knowing any subtle form, not even seeing something as small as a dust-demon (*piśāca*).
“He attains the ‘liberation not dependent on time’ (asamayavimokkha). When it is asked, “What is the liberation not dependent on time?

The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is the liberation not dependent on time,” he thus attains, accomplishes, and acquires these nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma).
For the mundane attainments (lokiya-samāpatti) [are abandoned] by their opposing states at the very moment they are entered.

They are liberated; therefore, it is called "temporary liberation" (*samaya-vimokkha*) in this way: "What is temporary liberation? The four jhānas and the four formless-sphere attainments—this is temporary liberation.
However, supramundane states are liberated from time to time, for once the paths and fruits have been liberated, they remain liberated forever. Nibbāna [is liberated] from all defilements...
"Utterly liberated indeed"—these nine factors are called "liberation not contingent on time" (*asamayavimokkha*).
"Unshakable liberation of mind" refers to the liberation consisting of the fruit of arahantship. "This is the purpose of this" means for the sake of that;
this holy life (*brahmacariya*) is for the sake of the fruit of arahantship. What is meant is: "this is its purpose. "This is the essence" means this fruit of arahantship.
"The essence of the holy life. "This is the consummation" means that this fruit of arahantship is the consummation of the holy life;
this is its limit, for there is nothing further to be attained beyond this. Thus he concluded the teaching by following the natural sequence of the discourse.
From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Mahāsāropama-sutta is finished.
10. The commentary on the Cūḷasāropama-sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷasāropama-sutta. Therein, Piṅgalakoccha means that the brahmin was of a tawny (piṅgala) complexion.
His name was Koccha; therefore, he is called Piṅgalakoccha. Regarding the terms *saṅghinaḥ* and so forth:

they are called *saṅghinaḥ* because this community (*saṅgha*), which is defined as a group of those who have gone forth, belongs to them. They are called *gaṇinaḥ* because this very group (*gaṇa*) belongs to them.

They are called *gaṇācariyā* because they are the teachers of that group by way of instructing them in proper conduct. They are known, renowned, and famous. "Having few desires and being content, through their state of having few desires..."

They are called "famous" (*yasassino*) because they possess a reputation that has arisen in such a manner as: "They do not even wear a lower garment," and so forth. "Founders of sects" (*titthakarā*) means those who establish doctrines.
"Regarded as good" (*sādhusammatā*) means they are thus esteemed [with the thought]: "These people are good, beautiful, and true men.
"Of the many folk" (*bahujanassa*) refers to the unlearned, blind, foolish worldling (*puthujjana*). Now, in order to show who they are, he said: "Namely, Pūraṇa," and so forth.
In this context, "Pūraṇa" is the name of that one who claimed the status of a teacher; "Kassapa" is his clan name.
It is said that he was born completing the number of ninety-nine servants for a certain family, and therefore they gave him the name "Pūraṇa.
Because he was a servant of good omen (*maṅgaladāsa*), there was no one to tell him, "This is ill-done," or "This has not been done. [Thinking,] "Why should I live here?"...
He fled. Then the thieves stripped him of his clothes.
Not knowing how to cover himself even with leaves or grass, he entered a village wearing only his golden skin. When people saw him, they thought, "This ascetic is an Arahant;
he is free from desire, and there is no one like him," and they approached him bringing cakes, rice, and other offerings. He [thought], "Because I have no cloth to wear..."
Thinking, "This has arisen," from that point on he did not wear even a garment after receiving one; he took up the very same renunciation.
Five hundred other men also went forth in his presence; with reference to him, it is said, "Pūraṇa Kassapa. "Makkhali" is his name.
Because he was born in Gosālā, "Gosāla" is his second name. It is said that on a muddy road...
As he was walking along carrying an oil jar on the ground, his master said, "Dear boy, do not stumble!
He stumbled through negligence and fell; out of fear of his master, he began to run away.
The master ran after him and seized him by the corner of his garment. He too cast off the garment and fled naked; the rest is exactly like the story of Pūraṇa.
“Ajita” is his name. He wears a blanket of hair, thus he is “Kesakambala.
Combining these two names, he is called “Ajita Kesakambala. In this context, a “kesakambala” is a blanket made from human hair;
there is no garment more loathsome than that. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, just as, for example...”
“Some are made of woven cloth; among these, the hair-blanket is declared the most wretched.
Monks, the hair-blanket is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch.
Thus, combining his name and clan, he is called “Pakudha Kaccāyana.”

He is called one who rejects cold water; even after defecating, he does not perform his ablutions with it, but only after obtaining hot water or sour gruel, or by crossing a river or the water from a road.
Or, thinking "my virtue (sīla) would be broken," he builds a mound of sand, resolves upon his virtue, and then proceeds. Such a person possesses the attainment of being devoid of grace.
Sañjaya was his name; "son of Belaṭṭha" means Belaṭṭhaputta.

Because he spoke thus—"We have no fetter of defilement, no entanglement of defilement; we are free from the fetters of defilement"—he acquired the name Nigaṇṭha (the Fetterless) based on that reputation.
"Son of Nāṭa" means Nāṭaputta. "They fully understood" means they knew exactly as they had claimed.
This is what is meant: if their declaration were leading to liberation, they would all have directly known [the truth]. If it were not, they would not have directly known it.
Therefore, the meaning of this question is: "Is their declaration leading to liberation or not?
Then the Blessed One, having rejected [the question] with the words "No" because there was no point in explaining its lack of leading-to-liberation quality, [proceeded] by means of a simile.
Intending to proclaim the goal, he said, "I shall teach you the Dhamma, O Brahmin," in order to teach the Dhamma itself.
Therein, "for the sake of realization" means for the purpose of making it manifest. "He does not generate desire" means he does not generate the desire consisting of the wish to act.
"He does not exert effort" means he does not apply energy or striving. "And he is one whose conduct is sluggish" means his disposition is characterized by dullness.
...it exists. "Lax" means one who holds loosely; having made the teaching lax, he grasps it, rather than grasping it firmly. 323.
Here, Brahmin, regarding the statement "a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures," how is it that these states beginning with the first jhāna become superior through knowledge and vision?
Because they serve as the foundation for cessation. For the states below—the first jhāna and so forth—...

"Those that lead to insight are here [in this teaching] those that lead to cessation; therefore, they should be understood as being more excellent. Thus the Blessed One concluded this sutta according to its own internal sequence.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin was established in the refuges.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Cūḷasāropama Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Mahāyamaka Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta. 325.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta. Therein, "dwelling at Nātika":

Nātika is the name of two villages belonging to the sons of two paternal uncles and a maternal uncle, situated near a certain pond; [the Buddha was] in one of those villages. "In the Brick Hall": [this refers to] the Giñjakāvasatha.
In a dwelling made of bricks. It is said that on one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour through the Vajji country gathering a great multitude of people, he arrived at Nādikā.

The people residing in Nādikā, having given a great alms-offering to the Blessed One and heard his discourse on the Dhamma, with hearts full of faith, deliberated, “We shall build a residence for the Teacher,” and [prepared] bricks alone.
Having constructed a palace displaying figures of wild beasts and other forms upon its walls, stairs, and pillars; having plastered it with lime;
having completed the floral and vine-work carvings; and having prepared floor coverings, couches, seats, and so forth, they offered it to the Teacher.
Furthermore, people there successively built night-stations, day-stations, pavilions, and walkways for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Thus that monastery became great. It was with reference to this that it was said, "in the Brick Hall.
Regarding the phrase "at the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove": there, from the trunk of one principal tree, a branch grew out in the shape of a cow's horn;
because of that tree, the entire grove came to be known as the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove.
"Reached the Saṅkha [lake]. "Dāya" is a general term for forest; therefore, "Gosiṅgasālavanadāya" means the forest of the Gosiṅga Sāl-tree grove.

"They dwell" means they dwell experiencing the flavor of harmony. For while the period when these sons of good family were ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) was described in the *Upari-panṇāsaka*, here it is the period when their taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
At that time, they had attained satisfaction and had gained a firm footing.
Having attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and become those whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), they dwelt there experiencing the flavor of harmony.
It was with reference to this that it was said:
"He approached the Gosiṅga Sāl forest grove," [meaning] either to the Dhamma General and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
Without taking leave of any of his eighty great disciples— even including the Elder Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma—
the Blessed One took his own bowl and robe and approached all alone, like an elephant that has left the herd,
like a black lion that has left its pride, or like a cloud dispersed by the wind. But why did the Blessed One go there himself?
Three sons of good family dwell experiencing the flavor of concord, because of their encouragement, out of compassion for future generations, and out of reverence for the Dhamma.

For it occurred to him thus: "Having encouraged and uplifted these sons of good family, and having established a bond of hospitality with them, I shall teach them the Dhamma. Thus, first of all, it is by way of encouragement.
He arrived. Furthermore, this thought occurred to him: "In the future, sons of good family, thinking 'Who indeed would not live in harmony?

One must live in harmony,' will themselves go into the presence of those living in concord, and after making friendly greetings and teaching the Dhamma, they will take up the three sons of good family as their own;
thus, quickly bringing an end to suffering, they will dwell in harmony."
“They will do so. Thus he went out of compassion for future generations.

Buddhas are indeed those who hold the Dhamma dear, and this quality of theirs—this reverence for the Dhamma—is revealed in the *Rathavinīta Sutta*. Therefore, out of this reverence for the Dhamma, he went out thinking, “I shall uphold the Dhamma.”
A "guardian of the forest" (*dāyapāla*) is a forest protector. Just as people might enter that forest at any desired spot and carry away flowers, fruits, resin, or forest materials,
he sits at the gate set for that walled-off forest and guards and protects it so that they do not take anything.
Therefore, he is called a "guardian of the inheritance. "Those who desire their own welfare" means they dwell with a disposition that seeks their own benefit.

For one who, even after going forth in this Dispensation, maintains his livelihood through the twenty-one kinds of improper search—such as by practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, or traveling on errands—is not said to be "one who desires his own welfare.
However, one who has gone forth in this Dispensation [and avoids] the twenty-one kinds of improper search...

Having abandoned [worldly life], established himself in the fourfold purification of virtue, mastered the word of the Buddha, and undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) suitable for him, he takes up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) according to his own preference among the thirty-eight objects;

then, having left the village and entered the forest, he dwells performing the work of insight (vipassanā) after having attained the meditative absorptions (samāpatti). This one is "one who desires his own welfare."
...by name. Those three sons of good family were also such as this. Therefore it is said: “They lived desiring their own welfare.
“Do not cause them discomfort”—he thus restrained the Blessed One, saying, “Do not cause them unease.
For he thought: “These sons of good family live in harmony; and in the place where one of them has gone, there may arise quarrels, strife, and disputes.”
They are quarreling; he wanders about like a fierce bull with sharp horns, goring them. Thus, there can be no traveling by a single path for two [of them].
Perhaps he too, acting in this way, might break the harmonious dwelling of these sons of noble family.
Furthermore, he is handsome, golden-hued, and—so it seems—greedy for delicious flavors; from the moment he departs, for those who provide choice food...
By praising his own attendants and so forth, he would cause these sons of good family to break their state of heedfulness.
Furthermore, the dwelling places of these sons of good family were fixed and delimited:
three leaf-huts, three walking-places, three daytime-resting spots, and three beds and seats. Yet this ascetic is large-bodied and older.
"I think this will happen. He will expel these sons of good family from their lodgings at an improper time.
In every way, they will find it uncomfortable. Not wishing for them to suffer such discomfort, he restrained the Blessed One, saying, "Do not cause them distress.
But did he restrain him knowing this, or unknowing? Unknowing. For although [the danger] was known to the Tathāgata since the moment of his conception...
From that time forth, miracles such as the shaking of ten thousand world-systems occurred;

however, those weak human beings dwelling in the forest, being preoccupied with their own work, were unable to perceive them. And when the Perfectly Enlightened One, surrounded by many thousands of bhikkhus, [shone] with fathom-wide radiance, the glory of the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—
When he wanders about displaying the majesty of a Buddha, he is to be recognized even without being asked, "Who is this?
On that occasion, however, the Blessed One concealed all that majesty of a Buddha within the folds of his robe;
like the full moon shrouded by a mass of clouds, he himself took up his bowl and robes and went forth in the guise of a stranger. Thus...
Not knowing him, the park keeper stopped him.
As for the phrase "he said this": it is said that the Elder, having heard the park keeper’s words, thought, "We three people are living here;
there are no other renunciants at all, yet this park keeper speaks as if to a renunciant."
Thinking, “Who might this be with whom I shall converse? he rose from his daytime resting place, stood at the gate, and while looking down the road, he saw the Blessed One.
At the mere sight of the elder, the Blessed One emitted a radiance from his body;
adorned with the eighty minor marks, his fathom-wide aura shone like an outspread cloth of refined gold. The elder—
“[This] park-keeper does not realize that he is speaking with the foremost person in the world, like one who extends his hand to seize a venomous snake by the neck;
rather, he is speaking as if with some ordinary bhikkhu. Thinking thus, [the Buddha] spoke these words of restraint:
“Do not, friend park-keeper,” and so forth.
"He approached him" (tenupasaṅkami): why did he approach without going out to meet the Blessed One? It is said that this thought occurred to him:
"We three live together in harmony; if I were to go out to meet him alone, our so-called 'living in harmony' would cease to exist.
Therefore, I shall go out to meet him taking my dear friends with me. Just as...
The Blessed One thought, "Just as I am dear to them, so too are my companions dear to me. Desiring to go out to meet them together with them, he approached without doing so himself.
Some, however, say that the path by which the Blessed One was coming led to the end of the walking-path at the door of the leaf-hut where those elders were;
therefore, the Elder went there as if giving notice to them. "Come forth! [he said].

"Come this way. He washed his feet: having taken water the color of jewels with his webbed hands, which resembled blooming lotuses, he sprinkled the water upon his gold-colored heels and washed them, rubbing foot against foot.
One might ask: "Since dust and dirt do not adhere to the bodies of Buddhas, why did he wash them? [It was] for the sake of the body...
It was for the purpose of taking water and for the purpose of gladdening their hearts. The Blessed One washed his feet with the water brought by us and made use of it;
thus, through the power of intense joy, the hearts of those bhikkhus were delighted, and therefore he washed them.
The Blessed One said this to the Venerable Anuruddha; it is said that he was the eldest among them.
326. When he had gathered them together, since this act was effectively accomplished for the rest as well, the Elder alone spoke these words beginning with, “I hope it is well with you, Anuruddha.
In this context, *kacci* is a particle used in the sense of inquiry. *Vo* is the genitive case ending. This is what is meant:
“I hope, Anuruddhas, that it is bearable for you; does your mode of conduct suit you? I hope it is sustainable; I hope your life is maintained?”
"Does he maintain himself? Is he sustained? He asks this regarding the proper conduct for alms-gathering: "I hope you do not suffer from lack of alms; I hope alms are easily obtained by you;
and upon seeing you arrive, I hope people consider it their duty to give even a ladle of gruel or a spoonful of food. Why?
Because it is possible to practice the Dhamma of a recluse only when one does not suffer for the sake of the requisites, or [to fulfill] the proper conduct itself.
"This is for renunciants. Then, when he had given his reply, [the Blessed One said]: "Anuruddhas, you are royal renunciants of great merit;
while people are dwelling in the forest, whom else do they think they should give to?
Yet, having eaten this, why do you dwell rubbing against one another like young deer?"
By asking, "Or do you possess the state of harmony? he inquired about the flavor of concord; thus he said, "But are you, Anuruddhas, living in harmony?

and so forth. In this context, "become like milk and water" means: just as milk and water blend together, do not remain separate, and reach a state as if they were one, does he ask, "Do you likewise dwell with mental states that have attained unity through harmony?"
"By loving eyes" means that the eyes with which one looks after having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) are called "loving eyes.
He asks: "Do you dwell looking at one another with such eyes? "Certainly," is an indeclinable particle used in the sense of certainty;
it means, "Indeed we do, venerable sir. As for the phrase "But how so?": here, "yathā" is a mere particle.
"How" is a question regarding the cause. What is meant is: "In what way do you dwell thus? For what reason do you dwell? Tell me that reason.
"Loving bodily action" is bodily action that proceeds by way of a mind of loving-kindness.
"Both openly and in private" means both in the presence of others and behind their backs. The same method applies to the other [types of action] as well.
In this regard, bodily and verbal actions are found when living together; the others are found when living apart. Mental action is found everywhere.

For when, among those living together, a bed, a stool, a wooden vessel, or an earthenware vessel has been left outside by one person, seeing it, one should not show contempt by asking, "Who used this?", but rather [take it up] oneself.
Bodily loving-kindness performed in the presence of another occurs when one picks up what has been poorly placed and puts it away, or when one tidies a place that requires maintenance.
Bodily loving-kindness performed in the absence of another occurs when, after someone has departed,
one puts back in its original place bedding or requisites that were poorly laid out, or tidies a place that requires maintenance.

This is called loving bodily action. Furthermore, when living together with them, engaging in sweet, friendly, welcoming, consoling, and Dhamma-based conversation, reciting, discussing, asking questions, and answering questions—such acts performed in their presence are called loving verbal action. Regarding the elders, however...

When my dear companions, the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila, have departed, speaking of their virtues—such as "the Venerable Nandiya is thus endowed with virtue" and "the Venerable Kimila is thus endowed with proper conduct"—is called verbal action of loving-kindness in their absence. However, for one who directs their attention thus:
"May my dear friend, the Venerable Nandiya, be free from enmity; may the Venerable Kimila be free from affliction and happy," this applies both in their presence and in their absence.
There is indeed mental action of loving-kindness.
For our bodies, venerable sir, are indeed diverse; for it is not possible to crush our bodies together like flour and clay to make them one.
But our minds, I think, are one—in the sense of being beneficial and in the sense of being uninterrupted.

It shows that, in the sense of being without dispute and in the sense of being in harmony, they are one and the same. But how is it that, having set aside their own views, they conducted themselves according to the views of others?
For instance, in one person’s bowl dirt appeared; in another’s robe there was a stain;
in another’s case, there was work to be done on the border. Thereupon, the one whose bowl had become dirty said: "Friends, mine..."
When it was said that "it is permissible to cook the dirt that has arisen on the bowl," the others did not say, "My robe must be washed" or "My border-work must be done";
instead, they entered the forest, brought firewood, and having cut it,
they performed the border-work on the bowl-rim, and only after that did they wash their robes or perform the border-work.
"Friends, it is fitting for me to wash my soiled robe; it is fitting for me to clear up and repair my leaf-hut," even if this were reported first, the principle remains the same.
"Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha! said the Blessed One. [He then repeated: "And we, venerable sir, did not suffer from lack of almsfood."

When this was said, he did not give his approval. Why? Because this so-called "edible food" is something practiced and constantly practiced by these beings both in the world of misery and in the world of gods and humans.
Furthermore, this dwelling in the world is for the most part prone to dispute;
in both the world of misery and the world of gods and humans, these beings are indeed mutually opposed, and for them, a time of harmony is difficult to find.
Because living together in harmony is difficult to find—occurring only occasionally—the Blessed One here gave his approval.
Now, asking about their characteristic of heedfulness, he said, "But do you, Anuruddha," and so forth.
In that context, *vo* is merely a particle, or it is the second-person plural pronoun; the meaning is "do you. *Amhākam* means "among us three persons."
"He returns from alms-round" means that having wandered for alms in the village, he returns.
"A bowl for refuse" refers to a small box-like bowl which, after being washed, is set aside for the purpose of putting away leftover alms-food.
"He who comes later"—it is said that those elder monks do not enter the alms-round together, for they delight in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Having attended to their bodies early in the morning, fulfilled their duties, entered their lodgings, and set a time limit, they sit having attained the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Among them, he who sat down first rises first according to his own predetermined time limit;
having returned from his alms round and arrived at the place for his meal, he knows [that the time has come].
—“Two monks will come later; I have arrived first.
Then, having covered the bowl and performed the arrangement of the seats and other duties, if there is only a small amount left in the bowl, he sits down and eats.
If there is a surplus, he places it in the refuse-bowl, covers the bowl, and eats. Having finished his meal and washed the bowl, he...
Having rinsed his mouth with water and placed it in his bag, he takes up his bowl and robes and enters his own dwelling place.
The second monk also arrives and realizes, "One has come first; one has come later. If there is just enough food in the bowl, he eats it.
If it is insufficient, he takes some from the discarded scraps and eats it. If there is an excess...
[The third monk] puts [the food] into his alms-bowl, eats only the proper measure, and enters his dwelling place just as the first elder did.
The third one also arrives and realizes: "Two arrived first; I am later.
He too, like the second elder, finishes eating, washes his bowl, rinses it clean, and places it in its bag.
Having dismissed [the guests], he removes and puts away the seats;

having discarded the remaining water from the drinking jars or the rinsing jars, he turns them upside down; if there is leftover food in the alms-bowl, he disposes of it according to the prescribed method, washes the bowl, and puts it away;
he sweeps the dining hall, and then discards the refuse.
Having thrown out the broom and placed it where it was free from termites, he takes his bowl and robe and enters his dwelling place.
This is the duty regarding the dining hall where the elders perform their meal duties in the forest outside the monastery.
It is with reference to this that the passage beginning with "he who comes later" was spoken.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "He who sees," etc., should be understood as referring to the conduct within their monastery.
In that context, *vaccaghaṭa* means a water-pot for rinsing. *Ritta* means empty; *tuccha* is a synonym for the same. *Avisaya* means impossible to lift, i.e., too heavy.
*Hatthavikārena* means by a gesture of the hand. It is said that they [would signal] whatever was empty among the water-jars and so forth.
Having taken it and gone to the lotus pond, they washed it inside and out, strained the water, and set it on the bank;
then they signaled to another monk with a gesture of the hand, making no sound either specifically or generally.
Why did they not make a specific sound? Lest that sound should disturb the monk. Why did they not make a general sound? [Lest it disturb others.]
Do they not do so? When the word "indiscriminately" is given, both might come out, each thinking, "I first! I first!

and thus, when a task must be performed by two, there would be an interruption of the work for the third. However, being one who uses controlled steps, he goes near another monk's daytime resting place; having ascertained that he has been seen by him, he makes a hand signal.

As for the phrase "every five days," the mention of the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day refers, first of all, to the regular hearing of the Dhamma.

There the three of them would sit down and, regarding one of the three Piṭakas, they would ask each other questions and provide answers to one another; while they were doing this, the dawn would break.

It was with reference to this that it was said. Up to this point, although the Elder was asked about the characteristic of heedfulness by the Blessed One, he has answered by means of the very grounds for heedlessness.

For other bhikkhus, there is the time of entering for alms-round, the time of departing, the changing of undergarments, the donning of robes, wandering for alms within the village, and giving Dhamma talks.

Therefore, the Elder, showing that there is no time for negligence once he has left these many places behind, applied the characteristic of diligence precisely to those very points where negligence might occur.

The Elder also answered in accordance with that very question. In this regard, because the bliss of non-experiencing is more peaceful and more sublime than the bliss of experiencing, [it is so described].

“It is indeed a gain, venerable sir! It is truly a great gain for those inhabitants of the Vajji country who are able to see the Blessed One and these three sons of noble family, able to pay homage to them, able to give gifts, and able to hear the Dhamma.”
“They obtain them; ‘of them,’ Bhante, means ‘of the Vajjis. Regarding “having heard the sound”:
it is said that he, by means of his own *yakkha*-power, produced a great sound that overwhelmed the entire Vajji kingdom and uttered those words.

In this way, the Blessed One concluded his teaching according to the sequence of the narrative.

The commentary on the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta is finished.
2. The commentary on the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta: 332.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta. Therein, the phrase "at the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Grove" is stated for the purpose of indicating the location where [the Buddha] was staying.

It has been stated. For in other suttas, after first indicating the village of resort with the words, “He dwells at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park,” he subsequently indicates the place of residence.
But in this Mahāgoṣiṅga Sutta, the Blessed One’s village of resort is not fixed; it will be some village or other as his resort. Therefore, [the text] indicates only the place of residence.

It has been fully elucidated. This sutta is known as "The Forest Origin. "With a large number" means with many. "With those well-known, well-known" means with those who are renowned and famous everywhere.

"Together with elders and disciples": they are called "elders" (*thera*) because they are endowed with qualities that make one firm, such as restraint according to the *Pātimokkha*; they are called "disciples" (*sāvaka*) because they were born at the end of hearing [the Dhamma].
"On one side. Now, in order to show those elders by their specific identities, he said, "By the Venerable Sāriputta," and so forth.
Therein, the Venerable Sāriputta was well-known in the Buddha’s dispensation for his own qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest.
He was as manifest and renowned as the sun standing in the midst of the sky to those with eyes, or like the moon, or like the ocean to those standing on the seashore.
Furthermore, his greatness should not be understood merely by way of the qualities mentioned in this sutta;
for there are other suttas besides this, such as the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta*, the *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta*, the *Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta*, the *Sīhanāda Sutta*, the *Rathavinīta*,
the *Mahāhatthipadopama*, the *Mahāvedalla*, the *Cātuma Sutta*, the *Dīghanakha*, the *Anupada Sutta*, the *Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta*, and the *Saccavibhaṅga Sutta*.

The greatness of the Elder should also be understood by way of these discourses: the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta, the Sampasādanīya Sutta, the Saṅgīti Sutta, the Dasuttara Sutta, the Pavāraṇā Sutta, the Susīma Sutta, the Therapañha Sutta, the Mahāniddesa, the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the Therīsīhanāda Sutta, the Abhinikkhamana Sutta, and the Etadagga Sutta. For in the Etadagga [Sutta]...
“It is this, monks, who is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus of great wisdom, namely Sāriputta,” it was said.
Mahāmoggallāna, too, is great and renowned—just like the Elder [Sāriputta]—both by virtue of his qualities such as moral discipline and by virtue of the qualities mentioned in this sutta.
Furthermore, there are the *Anumānasutta*, the *Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasutta*, and the *Māratajjaniyasutta* [attributed to him].

The greatness [of the Elder] should also be understood by way of these: the shaking of the palace, the entire discourse on the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the subduing of Nanda and Upananda, the Twin Miracle at the time of the wonders, the journey to the world of the gods, the *Vimānavatthu* and *Petavatthu*, and the Elder’s Great Departure.
For in the *Etadagga* (Discourse on the Foremost), it is said: "This, monks, is the foremost among my disciples..."
"It is among the bhikkhus possessing psychic power that Mahāmoggallāna is foremost," so it was said.

Moreover, Mahākassapa is likewise great, renowned, and well-known—both for his virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and others, and for the qualities mentioned in this sutta, just like the Elder [Mahāmoggallāna].
Furthermore, there are his *Cīvaraparivattana-sutta*, *Jiṇṇacīvara-sutta*, and the entire *Candopama-sutta*.
The greatness [of this sutta] should also be understood by way of the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*, the *Mahāariyavaṃsa-sutta*, and the Elder’s “Going Forth as Foremost.

The Elder Anuruddha, too, was renowned, famous, and great, both through his virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and others, and through the qualities mentioned in this very sutta.
Furthermore, there are also the *Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta*, the *Naḷakapāna Sutta*, the *Anuttariya Sutta*, the *Upakkilesa Sutta*, the *Anuruddha Saṃyutta*, the *Mahāpurisa-vitakka Sutta*,

Mahākassapa himself was a proponent of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); the Venerable Anuruddha himself possessed the divine eye; the Venerable Revata himself delighted in meditative absorption (jhāna);
and the Venerable Ānanda himself was learned, having surrounded the One of Ten Powers at that time with many other learned bhikkhus.
Thus, at that time, these and other renowned great elders numbered about thirty thousand.
It should be understood that the monks lived surrounding the One of Ten Powers.
"Emerging from seclusion" means emerging from the solitude of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

"He approached the venerable Mahākassapa" means that, it is said, when the Elder had emerged from seclusion and was surveying the western region, he saw a intoxicated nobleman playing at the edge of a forest.
He saw the solar disc, fifty yojanas in full extent, passing away like an earring falling from an ear,
like a red woolen cloth being gathered up and placed in a casket, and like a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand pieces falling from a jeweled ivory peg.
Immediately thereafter, he looked toward the eastern world-system.
Like a silver wheel being turned by one who has grasped its rim; like a stream of milk-cream emerging from a silver peak;

and like a white swan with outspread wings soaring into the sky—it rose from the depths of the ocean with the hue of a cloud, adorned with the marks of a Great Man upon the summit of the Eastern Cakkavāḷa mountain.
He saw the moon’s disk, which was forty-nine yojanas in extent. Then he looked at the Sāla grove.
At that time, the Sāla trees, from their roots up to their tips, were in full bloom; they shone like those draped in fine *dukūla* cloth or like those strung with clusters of pearls.
The surface of the earth appeared adorned as if by an offering of strewn flowers here and there.
As the pollen of the flowers fell, it was as if the forest were being drenched with liquid lac.
Swarms of bees and honey-bees, intoxicated by the pride of the flower-pollen, wandered through the depths of the woods as if singing.
And at that time, it was indeed the Uposatha day. Then the Elder thought, "How shall I spend this night? For noble disciples (ariyasāvakas) [do not neglect such occasions].
And indeed, they were fond of hearing the Dhamma. Then it occurred to him:
"Today, having gone into the presence of my elder brother, the Elder Dhammasenāpati, I shall spend the time delighting in the Dhamma.
But as he was going, he did not go alone; rather, thinking, "I will go taking with me my dear friend, the Elder Mahākassapa," he set out.
Rising from his seat and shaking out his leather mat, he approached the Venerable Mahākassapa.

"Very well, friend," replied the Venerable Mahākassapa; for since a noble disciple is one who truly delights in hearing the Dhamma, having heard those words, he said: "Go, friend; my head or back aches somewhat."
Without making a formal request for instruction, with a heart full of joy, he said, "So be it, friend," and so forth.
Having assented, he rose from his seat, shook out his leather mat, and followed after Mahāmoggallāna.
At that time, the two great elders appeared like two moon-disks or two sun-disks standing in succession, or like two Chaddanta elephant-kings.
They shone like two elephants in rut, like two lions, and like two tigers.
At that time, the Elder Anuruddha, sitting in his daytime resting place, saw the two great elders approaching the presence of the Elder Sāriputta;
looking toward the western world-system, he saw the sun entering the forest edge, and looking toward the eastern world-system, he saw the moon [emerging] from the forest edge.
Looking at the sāla grove as if it were rising up, and seeing that the entire sāla forest was in full bloom, he thought: "Today is the Uposatha day;
these elder brothers of mine are going to the presence of the Dhammasenāpati, so there must be a great hearing of the Dhamma.
I too shall partake in the hearing of the Dhamma. Having said this, from his sitting place...
Having risen and shaken out his leather mat, he went forth following step by step behind the great elders.
Thus it is said: “Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, and the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Sāriputta.
They approached means that the three moons stood in succession.
Shining like moons, like suns, and like lions, they approached.
As those great elders were approaching in this manner, the Venerable Ānanda, while sitting in his own daytime resting place, saw them and thought:
"Today there will be a great hearing of the Dhamma; I too ought to partake in it."
"But I shall not go alone; I will take my dear companion, the Elder Revata, with me.
All this should be understood in detail according to the same method already described regarding the visits of Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, and Anuruddha.
Thus those two men stood one after the other like two moons, like two suns, like two lions.
And they approached, shining brightly. Therefore it is said: “The Venerable Sāriputta saw them,” and so forth.

Having seen [them], he spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda; that is, having seen them from afar, as the preliminary conversation gradually unfolded, he spoke these words beginning with, “Let the Venerable One come.
Regarding the phrase, “It is delightful, friend,” there are two kinds of delightfulness (*rāmaṇeyyaka*).
The beauty of forests and the beauty of individuals. Therein, "forest" refers to that which is covered with *nāga*, *salaḷa*, *sāla*, *campaka*, and other such trees;
it possesses dense shade, is laden with flowers and fruit, consists of various kinds of trees, is well-supplied with water, and is secluded from the village.
This is called the beauty of forests. With reference to this, it was said:
“Delightful are the forests, where people find no pleasure;
those free from passion will delight there, not those who seek sensual desires.

Furthermore, even if a forest is arid, waterless, scantily shaded, and overgrown with thorns, if noble ones such as Buddhas dwell therein, this is called “delightfulness by way of the person. It is with reference to this that it was said:
“Whether in a village or in the forest, whether in a valley or on a plateau—wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful.
Here, however, both of these [conditions] are found. For at that time, the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove was in full bloom with all its blossoms.

Fragrant with the scent of flowers, there dwells in this world—including its devas—the Supreme Person, the Perfectly Enlightened One, together with thirty thousand bhikkhus renowned for their direct knowledge.
It was with reference to him that it was said: "Friend Ānanda, the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove is delightful."
"It scatters away faults" means it is free from these five defilements: mist, haze, smoke, dust, and Rāhu.
"In full bloom on all sides" means it is blossomed everywhere; from the roots up to the tips, there is not a single spot that has not flowered.
"Divine fragrances, as it were, waft forth" refers to the divine scents of mandārava flowers, koviḷāra flowers, pāricchattaka trees, sandalwood, and aromatic powders.
They blow forth on all sides; what is meant is that they blow as if from the place where Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Nimmānarati, and Mahābrahmā have descended.
"In what manner, friend Ānanda?"—the Elder Ānanda was the youngest member of the Saṅgha among those five elders.
Why did the Elder ask him that very question first? Because of mutual affection (*mamāyittā*). For those two Elders were mutually affectionate toward one another.
The Elder Sāriputta was affectionate toward the Elder Ānanda, thinking, "He performs the service of attending upon the Teacher that ought to be performed by me.
The Elder Ānanda was affectionate toward the Elder Sāriputta, thinking, "He is the foremost among the Blessed One’s disciples," as he was toward a young member of a noble family.
Having granted them the going-forth, he caused them to take ordination under the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder Sāriputta did exactly the same.
In this way, there were five hundred bhikkhus who, having each given their own bowl and robe, were granted the going-forth and caused to take ordination.
Even when the Venerable Ānanda obtained fine robes and other requisites, he gave them to the Elder alone.
It is said that a certain brahmin thought: "Worship of the Jewel of the Buddha and the Jewel of the Saṅgha is well known;
how, then, is the Jewel of the Dhamma worshipped? He approached the Blessed One and asked about this matter.
The Blessed One said: "If you, brahmin, desire to worship the Jewel of the Dhamma, [you should honor] one who is learned..."
"Who should I honor? he asked. "Venerable sir, please tell me who is very learned," he said, inquiring of the community of monks.
He approached the community of monks and said, "Venerable sirs, please tell me who is very learned. "The Elder Ānanda, O Brahmin," they replied.
The Brahmin honored the Elder with a robe worth a thousand pieces of gold. The Elder took it and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One asked, "Ānanda, from where did you obtain this? "Venerable sir, it was given by a certain brahmin;
however, I wish to give it to the Venerable Sāriputta. "Give it, Ānanda. "He has set out on his alms-round, venerable sir.
"Give it when he returns. "A training rule has been laid down, venerable sir. "But when will Sāriputta return? "In about ten days."
"Venerable sir," [he said]. [The Buddha] laid down the training rule: "I allow, Ānanda, an extra robe to be kept for a maximum of ten days.
The Elder Sāriputta likewise gave whatever pleasing thing he obtained to the Elder Ānanda.
Thus those two elders treated each other as their own; because they were thus treating each other as their own, [the Buddha] first asked about it.
Furthermore, this inquiry for consent must be asked starting from the junior monks. Therefore, the Elder thought:
"I will ask Ānanda first; Ānanda will answer according to his own inspiration.
Then I will ask Revata, Anuruddha, Mahākassapa, and Mahāmoggallāna. Mahāmoggallāna will [answer] according to his own..."
“He will answer with inspired eloquence. Then the five elders will question me, and I too shall answer with my own inspired eloquence.
Even at this point, this teaching of the Dhamma will not have reached its peak or its full expansion;
therefore, let us all approach the One of Ten Powers and ask him, for the Teacher, with his knowledge of omniscience—
He will explain it. To this extent, this teaching of the Dhamma will reach its peak and attain full maturity.
For just as a legal case arising in a district reaches the village headman; when he is unable to decide it, it reaches the provincial governor;
when he is unable, the chief justice minister; and when he is unable, the commander-in-chief... [the rest of the sentence continues].
If the viceroy is unable [to decide], and if he is unable to decide it, the matter reaches the king;
from the time the king has decided it, the dispute no longer circulates back and forth, for it is settled by the king’s word alone.
In the same way, Ānanda, I shall first question Ānanda... [and so on] ... then we all, having approached the One of Ten Powers, shall ask him—the Teacher.
He will answer with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). To this extent, this teaching of the Dhamma will reach its pinnacle and attain full expansion.
Thus, asking for consent, the Elder first questioned the Elder Ānanda.

"He is one who has heard much" means that much has been heard by him—the ninefold teaching of the Master (*satthusāsana*), according to the sequence of the Canon (*pāḷi*), the connections (*anusandhi*), and the preceding and following passages.
"Uggahitaṃ hoti" means "it has been grasped. "Sutadhara" means one who is a receptacle for what has been heard.
For he from whom what was learned here and there slips away—like water in a cracked jar and not remaining—is unable to explain or recite even a single sutta or Jātaka in the midst of an assembly;
such a person is not called a "sutadhara. But as for him whose learning...

The word of the Buddha remains exactly as it was at the time of its acquisition; even if one does not recite it for ten or twenty years, it is not lost—one such as this is called a "retainer of what has been heard" (*sutadhara*).

"Accumulation of what has been heard" (*sutasannicaya*) means being a repository of what has been heard. For just as what has been heard is accumulated in the casket of the heart like an inscription on stone, or like lion’s fat placed in a golden jar.
And that which remains through attachment, like [something held] in the hand, is called "accumulation of what has been heard" (*sutasannicaya*).
"Retained" (*dhāta*) means it is mastered and stable. For some, the Buddha-word they have learned is not retained, mastered, or stabilized;
when told, "Recite such-and-such a sutta or Jātaka," they say, "I shall know it after I have rehearsed it, compared it, and investigated it. For others...
"Mastered" means it has become proficient, like the flow of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-sota);
when told, "Recite such-and-such a Sutta or Jātaka," one extracts it and recites that very same one. It is with reference to this that it is said, "mastered.
"Familiarized by speech" means rehearsed orally by way of the ten Suttas, the ten Vaggas, and the ten Paññāsas.
“Examined with the mind” means examined by the consciousness; for one who recites the Buddha’s word verbally and then reflects upon it with the mind, it becomes clear in various respects.
It appears as clearly as a form to one standing by a lit great lamp.
Referring to this, it is said: “Mentally cultivated and examined with the mind. “Thoroughly penetrated by view” means...
It has been well-penetrated through wisdom both in terms of its meaning and its cause.

Regarding the phrase "with complete words and phrases" (*parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi*): here, a word itself is called a "phrase" (*padabyañjana*) because it expresses the meaning. That [word] is said to be "complete" (*parimaṇḍala*) when it fulfills the phonemes (*akkhara*) and does not omit any of the ten types of phonetic intelligence. Such is the meaning of "with words and phrases that are complete. Furthermore—

When a bhikkhu, while teaching the Dhamma in an assembly, sets aside a discourse (*sutta*) or a birth story (*jātaka*) and brings forward another discourse intended for refutation, he tells a simile for it, explains its meaning, and thus, having grasped this [new material], casts away that [former one], carrying it along on one side;
then, knowing the right time, he emerges from his meditation. But the discourse that was set aside remains merely as something set aside.
...is present; his discourse is called "well-rounded" (*aparimaṇḍala*).

But he who, having set aside a *sutta* or a *jātaka*, does not go even a single word outside [of it], and without obscuring the connection and the sequence of the text, stands by the method given by the teachers and—like one delimiting with a measuring cord, or like one sending water into a deep matrix—[explains] the word...
He proceeds like a well-bred Sindha horse while galloping; his discourse is called "well-rounded" (*parimaṇḍala*).
It is with reference to such a discourse that it is said: "with well-rounded words and phrases.
Regarding the term "connected in succession" (*anuppabandha*): here, when a bhikkhu, while preaching the Dhamma, begins either a Sutta or a Jātaka...
From the time he began, as if hurriedly and urgently rubbing a fire-drill, or as if eating hot food, he—
treating every point already grasped in the sequence of the text’s connections as already grasped, and every point not yet grasped as not yet grasped—
drove it forward like a monitor lizard moving among old leaves, striking here and there and driving it on.
He departs. Furthermore, one who preaches the Dhamma sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly, sometimes with a loud voice, and sometimes with a low voice.

Just as a "ghost-fire" (petaggi) sometimes blazes up and sometimes goes out, even so here there is one called a "ghost-fire Dhamma-preacher," who repeatedly begins his discourse when the assembly wishes to rise.
Furthermore, when someone speaking falters here and there, speaking as if gasping or weeping,
the discourse of all such persons is called "unconnected" (appabandha). However, one who, having undertaken a Sutta and adhering to the method provided by the teachers,
causes it to flow like the current of a river with an uninterrupted stream— like water gushing from the celestial Gaṅgā— [is one whose discourse is well-connected].
How does he cause [the discourse] to proceed without interruption? His discourse becomes continuous. It is with reference to this that it is said:
