"by means of a continuous connection. "For the uprooting of the underlying tendencies" means for the purpose of uprooting the seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
"By such a one" means by a monk who is thus very learned, together with a hundred such monks or a thousand such monks.
Or, by pressing corner of his outer robe against corner of his outer robe, or by sitting cross-legged against a cross-legged position, he would cause the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove to shine.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood for all instances.
334. One for whom seclusion is a pleasure is "one who delights in seclusion" (*paṭisallānārāma*). One who rejoices in seclusion is "one who delights in seclusion" (*paṭisallānarata*).
"335. A thousand worlds": this refers to a thousand world-systems (*lokadhātu*). For the Elder’s constant range of attention is bound to this much;
however, if he so desires, the Elder can indeed survey many thousands of world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Having gone to the excellent upper palace": having gone to the top of an excellent seven- or nine-storeyed palace. "A thousand wheel-rims" (*nemimaṇḍala*).

Suppose a man were to stand on the hub of a chariot wheel that had been set down in the courtyard of a palace, with its rim touching the rim of the wheel, and having opened a thousand windows, were to look out;
for him, the hub would be visible, as well as the spokes, the spaces between the spokes, and the rim. In the same way, friend, such a person is one who possesses the divine eye.
With the divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, a bhikkhu surveys a thousand worlds.
To him, as if he were a man standing on a palace, the thousand Sinerus in the thousand world-systems become manifest like the hubs of wheels;
the islands become manifest like spokes; the people dwelling on those islands become manifest like the spaces between the spokes; and the surrounding rims become manifest like the wheel-rims.
The mountains of the world-system (cakkavāḷapabbatā) become manifest. 336.
"A forest-dweller" (āraññiko) is one who has undertaken the forest-dwelling ascetic practice (araññadhutaṅga). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. 337.
"And they do not cause confusion" means they do not obscure [the meaning]. For it is by making a question causal—that is, providing a reason—that one asks it.
"Even being unable to answer, he delays"—this means he does not do so.
"It flows on" means it proceeds like the water of a river's current.
"By whichever abiding-attainment" means by whichever mundane abiding-attainment or by whichever supramundane abiding-attainment.
"Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!"—this expression of approval was given to the Elder Ānanda.
However, the Blessed One was conversing with the Elder Sāriputta; this same method applies everywhere.

"Just as Ānanda would" means that just as Ānanda himself, in giving a correct explanation, would explain it, so too was it explained by Ānanda in a manner entirely appropriate to himself and in accordance with his own inclination.
The meaning is "expounded. For the Elder Ānanda was himself learned, and his own inclination was thus:

"Oh, may my fellow-celibates in the Dispensation be learned! Why? Because for one who is learned, what is permissible and what is impermissible, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is grave and what is light, and what is curable and what is incurable, becomes evident. A learned person [should] the Buddha-word that has been mastered...
Having reflected thus: "In this place virtue was taught; in this, concentration; in this, insight;

in this, the path, fruit, and Nibbāna," one fulfills virtue at the point where virtue occurs, fulfills concentration at the point where concentration occurs, causes the embryo of insight to be conceived at the point where insight occurs, develops the path, and [attains] the fruit.
He realizes it. Therefore, the elder’s aspiration is this:

"Oh, may my fellow celibates, having mastered one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas and reflecting upon them, fulfill virtue and the other qualities wherever they are mentioned therein, and thus gradually realize the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna. The same method applies to the remaining sections as well.
340. For the Venerable Revata was inclined toward meditation and delighted in meditation; therefore, it occurred to him:

"Oh, that my fellow-celibates might sit alone, perform the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, attain the eight meditative absorptions, and, increasing insight based on those states of jhāna, realize the supramundane Dhamma! It was for this reason that he spoke thus.
341. The Venerable Anuruddha possessed the divine eye, and this thought occurred to him:
"Oh, if only my fellow celibates would increase their light and, with the divine eye, see beings passing away and being reborn across many thousands of world-systems;
and having stirred their hearts with fear of the round of existence, increase their insight and [realize] the supramundane Dhamma."
“May they realize [it]!”—it was for this reason that he spoke thus.
Venerable Mahākassapa was an advocate of the ascetic practices (*dhutavāda*); it occurred to him:

“Oh, may my fellow-celibates, having become advocates of the ascetic practices, cause the craving for requisites to wither away through the power of the ascetic practices, and having shaken off other various defilements as well...”
"Having increased their insight, they shall realize the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma). It was for this reason that he spoke thus.
343. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī).

However, [the Buddha] knew the subtle distinctions between moments of consciousness, the aggregates (khandha), the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), the entry into the jhānas, the entry into the objects of meditation (ārammaṇa), and the defining of the factors (aṅga-vavatthāna).

The determination of the object, the shifting of factors, the shifting of objects, the expansion on one side, and the expansion on both sides are evident only to an Abhidhamma teacher of the Dhamma. For a non-Abhidhamma teacher, when preaching the Dhamma, does not know: "This is our own position (sakavāda);
this is the opponent's position (paravāda). Thinking, "I shall explain our own position," he explains the opponent's position; [and] thinking, "I shall explain the opponent's position..."

"One who proclaims their own doctrine [merely] proclaims their own doctrine; they contradict another doctrine. An Abhidhamma master proclaims his own doctrine according to the principles of his own doctrine, and proclaims the opponent's doctrine according to the principles of that opponent's doctrine; he does not contradict another doctrine. Therefore, it occurred to the Elder:
'Oh, if only my fellow celibates were to become Abhidhamma masters and apply their knowledge to subtle points...'"
“Having increased their insight (vipassanā), they shall realize the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma). It was for this reason that he answered thus.
344. The Venerable Sāriputta had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī);
it is only one who possesses wisdom who is able to bring the mind under his own control, not one who lacks wisdom. For one lacking wisdom, having allowed the arisen mind to be controlled by itself—
Even after struggling to and fro for some days, he falls into ruin by returning to the state of a householder.

Therefore, the Elder thinks: "Oh, that my fellow-celibates would become masters of their own minds, bringing the mind under their own control, shattering all its various pursuits and agitations, and not allowing it to go even slightly outside!"
“By developing insight without delay, they would realize the supramundane Dhamma. It was for this reason that he spoke thus. 345.

“Sāriputta, all of you have spoken well in your own way. Sāriputta, it is because there is a reason for the Saṅghārāma to be beautiful not only through bhikkhus who are learned, but also through those who delight in meditation and those who possess the divine eye.
"There is a ground for excellence even in those who speak of ascetic practices (dhuta), even in those who are experts in the Abhidhamma, and even in those who have mastery over the mind.
Therefore, the well-spoken words of all of you are excellent by way of their respective methods; for each reason, they are indeed well-spoken and not ill-spoken.
Furthermore, listen also to me—listen also to my words. I shall not break this cross-legged posture until [my purpose is fulfilled]."
The meaning is: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture nor release it until I have resolved upon this fourfold energy.

It is said that when his knowledge had reached full maturity, the Blessed One, having renounced royal splendor and gone forth, eventually ascended the seat of enlightenment, resolved upon the fourfold energy, and sat down with legs crossed in the invincible posture.

"Having sat down with firm resolve, he shattered the crowns of the three Māras and, at the time of dawn, having made the ten-thousandfold world-system resound, he penetrated omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
He spoke thus with reference to his own Great Enlightenment Seat (*mahābodhipallaṅka*).
Furthermore, out of compassion for future generations, he showed the excellence of the practice even to those who are merely virtuous ordinary persons (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*).
He spoke thus. For the Blessed One saw: "In the future, sons of good family with such inclinations will reflect thus:
'When the Blessed One was speaking the Mahā-Gosiṅga Sutta, he said here, "Sāriputta, after his meal...
[as above] ...Sāriputta, it is by such a bhikkhu as this that the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove would be illumined. We [should consider] the Blessed One’s inclination. "

‘We shall take it up,’ they will think; and having returned from their almsround after the meal, they will resolve upon the fourfold energy, being firm in their undertaking, thinking, ‘We shall not break this cross-legged posture until we have attained arahantship,’ and they will consider that the duty of a recluse must be performed.
Practicing in this way, in just a few days they will make an end of birth, aging, and death.”
Out of compassion for future generations, and showing the standard of practice for a "good ordinary person" (puthujjana-kalyāṇaka), he spoke thus:
"Sāriputta, such a bhikkhu would indeed illuminate the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove.
Sāriputta, by such a bhikkhu—without any further qualification—the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove would truly shine, according to the very sequence of the discourse.
"He brought the teaching to a conclusion.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
3. Commentary on the Mahāgopālaka Sutta 346.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the Mahāgopālaka Sutta. Regarding this, there are three methods of exposition:

the single-stalk method (*ekanāḷika*), the four-cornered method (*caturassa*), and the sitting-in-a-circle method (*nisinnavattika*). Among these, the "single-stalk method" refers to reciting the text and then explaining the meaning of each individual word. [The passage continues: "The unwise..."

The exposition consisting of fourfold groupings— showing the cowherd, showing the unwise monk, showing the wise cowherd, and showing the wise monk— is called "the square" (*caturassa*). Reaching the conclusion by showing the unwise cowherd,
reaching the conclusion by showing the unwise monk, [and reaching the conclusion by showing] the wise...

"Reaching the conclusion by showing the cowherd, and reaching the conclusion by showing the wise monk"—this is called the "sitting-in-a-circle" method (*nisinnavattikā*). This is the practice of all the teachers here.
"Monks, with eleven factors" means with eleven divisions of non-virtue. "A herd of cattle" means a group of cows. "To tend" means...
To wander about after having taken possession [of them]. To make them prosper means to cause them to increase. "In this world" means in this world.
"He does not know form" means he does not know form either by way of number or by way of color.
"He does not know by way of number" means he does not know the count, such as "I have a hundred or a thousand cows. When his cows have been seized or have fled...
Having counted his herd of cattle, if he thinks, "So many are not to be seen today," he does not search for them while wandering through two or three villages or through the forest.

Even when other people's cows have entered his own herd, he counts his herd and, thinking, "These so many cows do not belong to us," he beats them with a stick and does not drive them out; thus, his lost cows remain lost.

When the owners of the cows see him wandering about having seized their cows, they say, "This man has been taking our milch-cows for all this time," and after reprimanding him, they take back their own cows and depart.
Consequently, his herd of cattle diminishes, and he is excluded from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow.
He does not know them by color—that is, "so many cows are white, so many are red, so many..."
He does not know, "So many are black, so many are brindled, so many are blue. When the cows have been seized... [as before] ...he is excluded even from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow.
"He is not skilled in marks" means he does not know the marks—such as the varieties of scars from bows, spears, or spikes—made upon the bodies of the cows;
thus, when the cows have been seized or have fled, he does not know, "Today, such-and-such a mark was on this cow, and such-and-such a mark was on that cow."
“They are not seen” … [and so on] … he is excluded even from the use of the five products of the cow.
“He does not remove flies”: when cows are struck by stumps, thorns, and the like, sores develop;
blue flies lay eggs there, and these are called *āsāṭikā*. Having removed them with a stick, one should apply medicine.
[The cow] becomes [ill]. A foolish cowherd does not do so; therefore it is said: "He is not one who removes flies.

His cows' wounds increase and become deep; parasites enter their bellies, and the cows, overcome by sickness, are unable either to eat grass to their heart's content or to drink water. In that state, the milk of the cows—
The wound festers, the speed of the oxen declines, and there is a danger to the lives of both. Thus his herd of cattle diminishes, and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.
"He does not dress the wound" means that, in the same manner as described for the oxen, a wound that has arisen is not treated with medicine and bandaged with cloth.
It must be bound with a cloth or a rag and covered. A foolish cowherd does not do so;
consequently, pus oozes from the cows' wounds, and as these rub against one another, other wounds are produced in others as well.
Thus, the cattle overcome by illness are unable to eat grass to their fill... [and so on] ...and he becomes an outcast.
"He does not make smoke" means that during the rainy season, when gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like are abundant and the herd of cattle has entered the forest, smoke ought to be made here and there;

an unwise cowherd does not do this. The herd of cattle, harassed all night by gadflies and the like, fails to obtain sleep, and on the following day, [they remain] here and there in the forest at the roots of trees and so forth.
Having lain down, he sleeps; he does not even get to eat grass as much as he desires... [and so on] ...he is excluded even from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow.
"He does not know the ford" means he does not know whether the ford is level or uneven, or whether it has a current or is stagnant;
he drives the cows across by a non-ford. As they step onto stones and such at an uneven ford, their feet—
They break apart; when they have entered a deep, treacherous ford, crocodiles and other predators seize them.
One comes to say, "Today so many cows are lost," or "Today so many [are lost]. In this way, his herd diminishes, and he is excluded from even the five products of the cow.
"He does not know whether it has been drunk" means that he knows neither what has been drunk nor what has not been drunk. For by the cowherd [it is known]: "This cow has drunk..."
"One has drunk from this one; this one found a place at the watering-place, while this one did not"—in this way, what has been drunk and what has not must be known.

Furthermore, having guarded the herd of cattle in the forest for part of the day, thinking, "I will give them water to drink," he goes toward a river or a pond. There, the great bulls, the young bulls, and the strong cows—
The weak and aged cattle, having struck one another with their horns or flanks to make room for themselves, enter water reaching up to their thighs and drink as much as they desire.
The remainder, finding no space, stand on the bank and drink muddy water mixed with silt, or do not drink at all. Then the cowherd [drives] them onto his back...
Having struck them, he drives them back into the forest;

there, the cows, being yellowish and withering from thirst, are unable to eat as much grass as they require, and consequently the cows' milk dries up and their speed diminishes... [and so on] ...until they become outsiders.
"He does not know the path" means he does not know: "This road is level and safe; this one is uneven, dangerous, and fearful."
He knows this. Avoiding the level and secure path, he leads the herd onto another path;

there, the cattle, overwhelmed by the scent of lions, tigers, and the like, or by the threat of robbers, stand with their necks held up like startled deer, neither eating grass to their heart's content nor drinking water.
In that regard, the cows' milk dries up... [and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He is not skilled in pastures" means: a cowherd ought indeed to be skilled in pastures;
he must know the five-day rotation or the seven-day rotation. Having grazed the herd of cows in one direction, he should not graze them there again on the following day.
For a place frequented by a large herd of cattle becomes as bare and stripped as the surface of a drum; even the water is stirred up.

Therefore, it is appropriate to let them graze there again on the fifth or seventh day, for by that much time the grass has grown back and the water has settled. This, however, refers to this five-day or seven-day rotation.
Or, if he does not know [the way], he guards only those places that have been guarded day after day.
Then his herd of cattle does not obtain green grass; eating dry grass and drinking muddy water mixed with silt, the milk of the cows there ceases...
[and so on] ...until they become outsiders.

"And she is one who milks without leaving a remainder": this means that a wise cowherd, until the calf's flesh and blood are restored, should milk her with some remainder left by setting aside one or two udders. This [cowherd] milks without leaving anything for the calf;
the milk-drinking calf dries up from thirst for milk, and being unable to sustain itself, it trembles before its mother.
Falling down in front [of him], it dies. Seeing her calf, the mother thinks, "My little one does not even get to drink its own mother's milk.
Out of grief for her son, she is unable to eat grass or drink water to her heart's content;
the milk in her udders dries up. Thus, even her herd of cattle declines, and she is excluded from the five products of the cow.
They are "cow-fathers" (gopitaro) because they take the place of fathers for the cows. They are "cow-guides" (gopariṇāyakā) because they lead the cows away, taking them as they please.
"Not with excessive honor": for a wise cowherd honors such a bull with excessive honor;
he gives him choice cow-food, adorns him with perfumes and five-finger marks, puts garlands upon him, and [treats his] horns...
He keeps [the bulls] in caskets of gold and silver, and having lit a lamp at night, he has them lie beneath a canopy of cloth.
But this man does not offer even a single honor to them;
the bulls, receiving no extra veneration, do not protect the herd nor ward off dangers. Thus his herd declines, and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

347. *Idha* means in this teaching. *Na rūpaññū hoti* means he does not know, in two ways—either by way of enumeration or by way of origination—the form described as “the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
He is said not to know it by way of enumeration [as follows]: “The eye-base, the ear, nose, tongue, and body-bases; the visible-object, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible-object bases...”

The twenty-five categories of form as they appear in the Canon— namely, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, the space element, the water element,
the lightness of form, its malleability, its wieldiness, integration, continuity, decay, the impermanence of form,
and physical nutriment— one does not know them. It is just as if...
Just as that cowherd does not know the form of the cows by way of counting, so too is this bhikkhu.

Not knowing form by way of counting, he is unable to bring his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to its culmination, even though he has discerned form, defined the formless, discerned both form and the formless, observed the conditions, and applied the characteristics. Just as...
The herd of that cowherd does not increase; likewise, in this teaching, there is no growth through virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruits, and Nibbāna.

And just as that cowherd is excluded from the five products of the cow, so too [is one who lacks these qualities] excluded from the aggregate of the virtue of the Asekhas, the aggregate of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He stands outside the five aggregates of Dhamma.
Regarding origination, he does not know it by name, thinking: "This much form has a single origination; this much has a double origination; this much has a triple origination;
this much has a quadruple origination; this much does not originate from anything."
He knows [only this]. Just as that cowherd does not know the form of the cows by way of their color, so too is this bhikkhu.
Not knowing form by way of its origination, having grasped form and defined the formless... he remains an outsider. He is "not skilled in characteristics" means:
"the fool is characterized by his actions; the wise man is characterized by his actions"—thus it is said.
He does not know that wholesome and unwholesome kamma is the characteristic of the wise and the foolish. Not knowing this, he does not avoid fools and attend upon the wise.

By not avoiding fools and attending upon the wise, he does not know what is allowable and what is not allowable, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is heavy and what is light, what is curable and what is incurable, and what is a proper cause and what is not.
Not knowing these things, [he fails to apply himself to] the meditation subject...

Having taken them up, he is unable to increase them. Just as that cowherd’s herd does not increase, so too in this teaching one does not increase through the aforementioned virtues and other qualities;
and like the cowherd, one remains excluded from the five products of the cow, which correspond to the five aggregates of Dhamma.
"He does not remove the fly" means that when a thought of sensual desire has arisen, he does not dispel it;

failing to remove this unwholesome thought—the "fly"—he wanders under the sway of his thoughts and is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Just as for that cowherd... [and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He does not cover his wounds" means that by way of the passage beginning "seeing a form with the eye, he grasps at its signs," he grasps at the signs in all objects;
thus, like that cowherd who does not cover his wounds, he does not accomplish restraint.
Wandering about with his doors wide open, he is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject... [and so on] ...he remains an outsider.
"He does not produce smoke" means that this cowherd does not produce the "smoke" of the teaching of the Dhamma;

he does not deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, nor a recitation (*sara-bhañña*), nor a seated talk (*upanisinnakathā*), nor an expression of thanks (*anumodanā*). Consequently, people do not recognize him as being learned or virtuous;
and failing to recognize his virtues or lack thereof, they do not provide him with the four requisites.

Thus, being exhausted by these conditions, he is unable to recite the Buddha’s word, fulfill his duties and observances, or take up and develop a meditation subject... [and so on] ...he becomes an outsider.
"He does not know the ford" means that he does not approach learned bhikkhus who have become fords; even if he does approach them, [he does not ask].
“Venerable sir, how is this phrasing to be applied? What is the meaning of this statement?

What does the canonical text say in this place? What does the meaning illuminate in this place?”—if one does not inquire thus, does not question thus, it means that one does not make [the meaning] known.
To such a person who does not inquire in this way, they do not reveal what has not been revealed, nor do they explain it by analyzing it.
They do not show [what should be shown]; they do not clarify what has not been clarified; they do not make manifest what is not manifest.
And regarding "various states that are grounds for doubt": among the many kinds of doubts, they do not dispel even a single doubt.
For it is doubt itself that is called "states that are grounds for doubt. In this context, the meaning is that they do not remove even a single doubt.
Thus, having failed to approach such a ford of great learning, this bhikkhu—possessing doubts—is unable to take up and develop his meditation subject.
Just as that cowherd did not know the ford, so too this bhikkhu does not know the ford of the Dhamma;
not knowing it, he asks questions outside his domain, approaching an Abhidhammika to inquire about what is allowable and what is not.
He asks; having approached a master of the Vinaya, he asks about the delimitation of the material and the immaterial.
Being questioned on matters outside their own domain, they are unable to explain. Thus, being himself full of doubt, he is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject...

[and so on] ...he becomes an outsider. "He does not know what has been drunk" means: just as that cowherd does not know which cows have been watered and which have not, so too he does not know the joy associated with the Dhamma.
He does not know, he does not obtain; relying on the basis of meritorious action consisting in hearing, he finds no benefit.
Having gone to the head of the assembly for hearing the Dhamma, he does not listen attentively; sitting there, he falls asleep, talks, or becomes distracted by other things.
Not listening to the Dhamma attentively, he is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject.
He is able... [as before] ...he becomes an outsider.

"He does not know the path" means that this cowherd, like one who does not distinguish between the right and wrong paths, does not understand the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is—thinking, "This is mundane; this is supramundane. Not understanding it, he adheres to the mundane path.
He is unable to produce the supramundane... [and so on] ...he remains an outsider.

"He is not skilled in his pasture" means that, like a cowherd who attends to his cattle only every five days or seven days, he does not understand the four foundations of mindfulness as they truly are, distinguishing:
"These are mundane; these are supramundane. Not knowing this, regarding subtle matters, he himself...
Having exercised his knowledge and become intent upon the mundane foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), he is unable to produce the supramundane; ... [omission] ... he remains an outsider.
"And he is one who milks dry" means that, not knowing the proper measure in receiving, he milks it completely.

In the section on the exposition (*niddesa*), regarding the phrase "inviting [the cow] to be brought," they invite her after having brought her forward. Here, there are two kinds of bringing: bringing by speech and...
And there is the offering of requisites. "Offering by speech" means that people go into the presence of a bhikkhu and invite him, saying, "Venerable sir, please say what you need.
"Offering of requisites" means that they take such things as robes or oil and molasses, go into the presence of a bhikkhu, and say, "Venerable sir, please accept whatever you require."
In this context, "the bhikkhu does not know moderation" means that the bhikkhu does not know the proper measure regarding those requisites.

The meaning is that, instead of taking what is appropriate in measure according to the method taught in the *Rathavinīta Sutta*—namely, "The donor’s capacity must be understood; the nature of the gift must be understood; one’s own strength must be understood"—he takes everything that is brought to him. People...
Being remorseful, they did not bring more food and offer it again. Exhausted by those requisites, he was unable to take up and develop his meditation subject... [and so on] ...he became an outsider.
Because he did not honor them with extra offerings, that cowherd—just as one would treat great bulls—treated those elder monks in this way...
Neither openly nor in private did they honor them with loving-kindness through bodily actions and so forth, nor with exceptional worship. Consequently, thinking,
"These do not show us respect," the elders did not win over the junior monks by means of the two kinds of gathering—
neither by the gathering of material goods, such as robes, alms-bowls, bowl-appurtenances, or dwelling places.
Even when they become exhausted and withered, they do not tend to them. They do not teach them the Pāḷi, nor the Aṭṭhakathā, nor the compositions on Dhamma, nor the secret texts.
The novices, failing to receive these two kinds of support from the elders in every respect, are unable to establish themselves in this Dispensation. Just as that cowherd’s herd...
It does not increase; in this way, virtue and the other qualities do not increase.

And just as that cowherd is excluded from the five products of the cow, so too they are excluded from the five aggregates of the Dhamma. The bright side (the positive sequence) should be understood by applying the reversal of what was stated for the dark side.
The commentary on the Mahāgopālaka Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 4.
The commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta.
350. Thus have I heard: this is the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta. Therein, "at Ukkacelā" refers to a city of that name.
It is said that while that city was being built, at night a fish came ashore from the current of the Ganges.
People soaked their cloths (*cela*) in oil-pans, made torches, and caught the fish. When the city was finished and they were giving it a name, [they said], "By us, for the site of the city..."
On the day he was caught, because the fish had been caught with a net (*cela*), they gave him the name Ukkacelā. He addressed the bhikkhus:

at a certain place on the sandy bank of the Ganges where the entire river was clearly visible, having sat down in the evening surrounded by a great community of bhikkhus, [he saw] the great Ganges flowing full.
Looking out, he reflected: "Has anyone here, in the past, attained prosperity or decline by depending on this Ganges?

Having thus applied his mind, he saw that in the past, many hundreds of thousands of herds of cattle, under the guidance of a foolish cowherd, fell into the whirlpools of this Ganges and entered the ocean;
whereas another herd of many hundreds of thousands of cattle, under the guidance of a wise cowherd—

He saw that safety had arisen, prosperity had arisen, and health had arisen. Having seen this, he thought, "Based on this reason, I shall teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus," and addressed the bhikkhus:
"Māgadhaka" means one who dwells in the kingdom of Magadha. "Duppaññajātiko" means one whose nature is devoid of wisdom, slow-witted, and dull-witted.
"Without having observed" means without having looked closely or reflected. "He began to ferry across" means he started to cross over.
Regarding the phrase "to the further shore, to the beautiful Videhas": on this side of the Ganges is the kingdom of Magadha, and on the far side is the kingdom of Videha.
Thinking, "I will take the cattle from the kingdom of Magadha to the kingdom of Videha and protect them," he began to ferry them across to the further shore. That...
It was said with intentional meaning: “the further shore of the Suvidēhas. “Having made a circle” means having formed a ring.
“They fell into misfortune and ruin” means they met with decline and destruction; they entered the great ocean itself.
Therefore, while that cowherd was driving the cattle down to the near bank of the Ganges, [he saw] both the level fords and the uneven fords...
He should observe that in the middle of the Ganges, two or three sandbanks should be marked for the cattle to rest upon.
Likewise, on the opposite bank, three or four landing places should be noted: "From this landing place they will depart to take that one;
from that one they will depart to take this one. But this foolish cowherd, on the near bank—
Without even looking to see whether the ford for the cattle’s descent was level or uneven,
and without noticing two or three sandbanks in the middle of the Ganges for the cattle to rest upon, and without examining the four or five landing places on the opposite bank,
he drove the cows down at a place that was no ford at all. Then, because of his great speed, the great bull—
And because of his great strength, having cut across the current of the Ganges and reached the opposite bank, he saw a broken embankment and a thicket of thorny bushes;
realizing, "This is a difficult place to settle," and finding no place even for the tip of his yoke to rest upon, he turned back.
The cows, thinking, "The Great Bull has turned back, we too shall turn back," turned back. From that great...
At the place where the herd of oxen was turning back, the water parted and a whirlpool arose in the middle of the Gaṅgā.
The herd of oxen entered the whirlpool and reached the ocean itself; not even a single ox remained unharmed. Therefore it is said:
"Right there they met with ruin and disaster."
"Unwholesome in this world" means that here in this world, within the aggregates, elements, and bases, they are unwholesome and unskillful; the same principle applies to the next world as well.
"The realm of Māra" refers to the phenomena of the three planes of existence. "Beyond the realm of Māra" refers to the nine supramundane phenomena.
"The realm of Death" likewise refers only to the phenomena of the three planes of existence. "Beyond the realm of Death" refers to the nine supramundane phenomena. Therein, the unwholesome...
"Unshakable. As for the meaning of the word: *māradheyya* is Māra’s domain (*dheyya*). "Domain" (*dheyya*) means a place, a site, a residence, or a range of activity.
The same principle applies to *maccudheyya* (the domain of Death). "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to such ascetics and brahmins;
by this, it should be understood that the six teachers are indicated.
351. Having thus concluded the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*), he spoke the passage beginning with "Once upon a time, monks" in order to show the bright side (*sukkapa-kkha*).
Therein, "powerful oxen" refers to both tamed bulls and milch cows. "Oxen to be trained" refers to both oxen that must be broken in and unweaned calves.
"Calf-crossers" refers to powerful calves who have passed beyond the state of being a calf. "Calves" refers to young calves still dependent on their mothers.

*Kisābalaka* means having little flesh and blood, and being weak in physical strength. *Tāvadeva jātako* means one born on that very day. *Mātugoravakena vuyhamāno* means being carried along by the mother’s sense of reverence;
she goes while making a sign of respect by repeatedly calling out "Hum" from the front, cutting through the water with her chest.
The calf, following the cow as she goes with the water cut through her chest due to that sense of reverence, [follows] her.
“It is said: ‘being carried away by respect for women.
(352) “Having cut off Māra’s stream” means having cut off Māra’s stream of craving by means of the path of arahantship.

“They have gone to the further shore” means that, like great bulls reaching the far bank of a river, they have gone to Nibbāna, the further shore of saṃsāra. “They went to the further shore” [refers to] the great bulls.
At the moment they reached the further shore, having crossed three sections of the Ganges' current, they saw the great bulls who had already reached the other side;

following the path taken by them, they went to the further shore. "They will go to the further shore" means that those who have exhausted three sections of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths, and who now stand with the remainder of the stream of craving [to be abandoned] by the path of Arahantship.
"Having cut [the bonds], they will go to Nibbāna, the further shore of saṃsāra, just as powerful oxen go to the other side of a river.
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. "Followers of Dhamma" and "followers by faith"—these two are those who possess the first path.
"By the Knower" means by the Buddha, who knows all phenomena. "Well-expounded" means well-proclaimed. "Opened" means revealed.
“The door to the Deathless” means the Noble Path. “For the attainment of Nibbāna” means it is opened for that purpose.

“Made free from the reed of conceit” means made devoid of the reed of pride (*māna*). “Strive for security” means strive for Arahantship with the desire to act; the meaning is: “be those who wish to act, who wish to bring it about.
There is also a reading, “you have already attained. Having obtained such a Teacher, you have indeed attained.
"Name" is the meaning. The rest is clear throughout. The Blessed One, however, brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely following the sequence of the connection.
Thus ends the commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
5. Commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta 353.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta. Therein, “in the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Forest”:
the so-called Great Forest is a large, naturally grown, uncultivated, and well-defined forest. Furthermore, the Great Forest is located in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu.
Being joined as one with the Himālaya mountains and extending without interruption until it reaches the great ocean—this [palace] is not like that.
A vast forest that has its own boundaries is called a "great forest" (*mahāvana*). However, this gabled hall (*kūṭāgārasālā*) was built within a monastery established in dependence on a great forest;
it was constructed with a gabled roof, covered with a *haṃsavaṭṭaka* (swan-patterned) thatch, and endowed with every excellence for the Buddha.
The Blessed One’s Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi) should be understood.

Regarding Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta: it is said that formerly a certain Nigaṇṭha and a Nigaṇṭhī, having each mastered five hundred points of debate, traveled throughout Jambudīpa thinking, "We shall engage in debate," and eventually met in Vesālī. The Licchavi kings...
Having seen them, they asked, "Who are you? Who are you? The Nigaṇṭha replied, "I wander throughout Jambudīpa thinking, 'I shall establish my doctrine.
The female Nigaṇṭha said the same. The Licchavis said, "Establish your doctrines with one another right here.
The female Nigaṇṭha questioned him on the five hundred points of doctrine she had mastered, and the Nigaṇṭha explained them. By the Nigaṇṭha...
Even when questioned, the Nigaṇṭhī spoke [only of her own views]. There was neither victory nor defeat for either;
both were exactly equal. The Licchavis said, “What will you two do wandering about as equals?
Live right here,” and having given them a house, they established offerings for them. Through their cohabitation, four daughters were born: one was Saccā.
One was named Lolā, one Paṭācārā, and one Ācāravatī. They too were wise;
they mastered five hundred points of debate each as taught by their parents. When they reached maturity, their parents said to them:
"In our family, daughters have previously been sent off to a husband's home after being given gold, silver, and other such wealth."
“There is no one who can defeat their doctrine. However, for any householder who is able to defeat their doctrine, they become his foot-servants;
for any renunciant who is able to defeat them, they go forth in his presence. What will you do?
“We too shall act in exactly this way. Then all four took the guise of female wanderers and [said], “This Jambudīpa...”
“...it is known by the name of the Jambu tree. Having taken a branch of the Jambu tree, they set out on their journey.

Reaching whichever village they arrived at, they would place the Jambu banner upon a heap of dust or a heap of sand at its gate, saying, “Whoever is able to enter into debate with us, let him crush this [banner],” and then they would enter the village.
In this manner, they wandered from village to village.
Having reached Sāvatthī, she placed the Jambudhvaja banner at the village gate just as before, announced her arrival to the people who had gathered there, and entered the city.
At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Jetavana, dependent on Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Sāriputta [inquired after] those who were ill...
While asking about places that had not been watched over and himself keeping watch, because of the great importance of his own duty, he entered the village for alms earlier than the other bhikkhus.
Seeing the Jambudhvaja tree at the village gate, he asked the boys, "What is this?
They reported the matter to him. He said, "Then crush it! They replied, "We cannot, venerable sir; we are afraid. "Boys," [he said].
"Do not be afraid," he said. "When it is asked, 'By whom was our Jambudhvaja crushed?', you should say:
'It was crushed by the Elder Sāriputta, a disciple of the Buddha. Those who wish to challenge him to a debate should go to the Elder at Jetavana.
Having heard the Elder's words, they crushed the Jambudhvaja and discarded it. The Elder, having gone for alms, [continued on his way].
He went to the monastery. The female wanderers, having departed from the village, asked, "By whom was our banner crushed?

The children reported the matter to them. The female wanderers entered the village again, taking each street in turn, and said, "It is said that the Buddha’s disciple named Sāriputta will debate with us; those who wish to hear it..."
"Come forth! they announced. The great multitude came out, and along with them, the female wanderers went to Jetavana.
The Elder thought, "The arrival of women in our dwelling place is not conducive to comfort," and so he sat down in the middle of the monastery.
The female wanderers approached and asked the Elder, "Have you caused our banner to be trampled?"
"Yes, it was ground by me," she replied. "Then we shall have a debate with you," they said. "Very well, let us do so;
who shall ask the questions and who shall provide the answers? She said, "The right to ask the questions has fallen to us;
however, you are women, so you must ask first. Then all four of them stood in the four directions and [recited] what they had learned in the presence of their parents.
They asked a thousand questions. The Elder, like one cutting a lotus stalk with a knife, explained each question as it was asked, making it free from roots and free from knots;
having explained, he said, "Ask again. "We know only this much, venerable sir," they replied.
The Elder said, "A thousand questions were asked by you and answered by me; however—"
“I shall ask but one question; you must answer it. Seeing that they were within the Elder’s domain, they were unable to say, “Ask, venerable sir, we shall answer.
They spoke again, saying, “Speak, venerable sir; knowing [the answer], we shall explain it.
The Elder said, “This is the first question to be taught after ordaining sons of good family,” and then—“One...
"What was its name? he asked. They did not see either its end or its limit. The Elder said, "Tell me. "We do not see it, Bhante," they replied.
"A thousand questions were asked by you and answered by me; yet you are not able to answer even a single question for me.
This being the case, who has won and who has lost? "The victory is yours, Bhante."

“We have been defeated; what will you do now? Having reported the words spoken by their parents, they said, “We shall go forth in your presence. [The teachers replied: “It is not fitting for women to go forth in our presence.
However, having received our instruction, go to the nuns’ quarters and go forth there.”
Saying "Very well," they accepted the Elder's instruction, went into the presence of the community of bhikkhunīs, and received the going-forth.
Having gone forth, being diligent and ardent, they attained arahantship before long.
This Saccaka was the youngest brother of those four; he possessed even more superior wisdom than all four of them, and even than their mother and father.
Having mastered a thousand doctrines from the Sāṃkhyas and even more from non-Buddhist systems, he remained right there in Vesālī without going anywhere else, teaching crafts to the king’s sons.

Because his wisdom was so overflowing, fearing that his belly might burst, he wandered about with an iron band wrapped around his stomach; it was with reference to him that it was said, “Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas.”
"An expounder of talk": *bhassa* is said to mean the path of speech; he expounds—that is, speaks—that, thus he is an "expounder of talk.
"One who claims to be wise": such is the claim, "I am wise. "Esteemed as good by the many":

whatever he predicts regarding the movement of the constellations, for the most part comes to pass exactly so; therefore, he is one who has gained the reputation of being good and auspicious—thus [he is regarded].
"Appointed by the great multitude" means he was authorized by the public. "Engaged in debate with debate" means he had been charged with fault through a course of argumentation.
"The Venerable Assaji" refers to the Elder Assaji, who was the teacher of the Elder Sāriputta.
"Wandering on foot for exercise" means wandering from one Licchavi royal residence to another in order to go from house to house. [He went] where the Venerable...
"He approached Assaji"—for what purpose did he approach him? For the sake of knowing the [proper] occasion.
It seems this was his thought: "I have been wandering about thinking, 'I shall refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama,' yet because I did not know his [proper] occasion, I did not refute it.
For a doctrine refuted after one has understood another's position is truly refuted."
There is one named Assaji. This disciple of the ascetic Gotama is known as the Elder Assaji;
he is skilled in the system of his own Teacher. Having questioned him and established [the matter] for myself, I shall refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.
Therefore, he approached him. He asks: “How does he guide? How does he instruct? means: in what manner does he lead, and in what manner does he train?
However, since there would be occasion for objection if one were to say "suffering," and because the paths and fruits are also figuratively described as suffering,
and since if one were to say "suffering" the Elder might be asked, "Venerable Assaji, for what purpose did you go forth?"— and if he were then to say,
"For the sake of the path and the fruit"— [the other] would say, "This is not [the case], Venerable Assaji."
If one were to level the charge: "This so-called 'dispensation' (sāsana) is actually a great slaughter-ground;

this is a mere echo of hell; there is no hope for you of happiness; you wander about, rising again and again, only to exhaust yourselves in suffering," then it would not be proper to employ figurative speech (*pariyāyakathā*) against the opponent.
Rather, one should speak to him in non-figurative terms (*nippariyāyakathā*) such that he becomes without a foothold.
Thinking, "I shall speak," he spoke this discourse—“Form, monks, is impermanent”—precisely by way of its impermanence and non-self.
"Dussuta" means unfit to hear. 354.
"In the assembly hall" (santhāgāre) refers to the hall used as an assembly hall for giving counsel on affairs for royal families. "He approached where those Licchavis were."
It occurred to him: "Previously, because I did not know the proper time, I was unable to refute the argument of the ascetic Gotama.
But now I know the time spoken of by his great disciple, and these five hundred Licchavis, my own pupils, have assembled here.
I shall go with them and refute the argument of the ascetic Gotama."
Therefore he approached him. "By one among those well-known" means by one among the five bhikkhu elders who were well-known.

"As it was established" means as it had been established by him. [The Buddha] spoke while turning his back right then, thinking: "If he establishes himself in this way, then he will say something else entirely; what can I do about that? "He might pull [him] toward him."
He would drag it toward himself. "He drags around" means he leads it forward.
"He drags around thoroughly" means he drags it at one time and leads it around at another. "The malt-house mat" refers to the straw mat in a tavern.
"A gambler at the malt-house" is a gambler at a tavern. "Having seized the tail by the ear" means, wishing to wash the bag used for straining liquor.
Having grasped it by both ears for the purpose of shaking off the chaff, one should "shake it out" (odhuneyya) by turning it face downwards;
one should "shake it up" (niddhuneyya) by turning it face upwards; one should "thump it" (nipphoṭeyya) by striking it repeatedly. Regarding the term "sāṇa-cloth":
here, people take hemp fibers for the purpose of making a hempen garment and form them into a handful.
Having formed a fist, they throw it into the water. On the third day, these become thoroughly soaked.
Then people, taking sour gruel, liquor, and so forth, go there and take a handful of hemp;
they place it once on the southern plank, once on the left plank, and once on the front plank—thus upon the three planks from right, left, and facing forward.
Striking one another, they ate and drank sour gruel, liquor, and other drinks, chewing and rinsing their mouths. It was a great sport.

When the king’s elephant saw that sport, he entered deep water, took up water with his trunk, and played by pouring it once into his frontal globes, once upon his back, once on both sides, and once between his tusks.
Taking that up, that kind of game is called "the hemp-washer"; it is with reference to this that it was said: "He plays a game called the hemp-washer.
Is he who will refute the Blessed One's doctrine the venerable Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta?
That Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta who will refute the Blessed One's doctrine—who is he, as a being?
"Is it you who are a *yakkha*, or perhaps Indra, or perhaps Brahmā, who will refute the Blessed One’s doctrine?
For it is not possible for an ordinary human being to refute the Blessed One’s doctrine"—this is the intended meaning here.
"At that time" means at the very moment when Saccaka entered the monastery; at what [time]? At that [time].
"But at what time did he enter? At the time of the great midday. "But why was he walking at that time?
For the purpose of dispelling the lethargy and drowsiness caused by the consumption of fine food; or perhaps they were practitioners of daytime meditation.
For when such people walk after the meal, bathe, allow their bodies to take on the natural temperature, and then sit down to practice the duties of a recluse, [they find it conducive].
His mind became one-pointed. Regarding the phrase "where those bhikkhus were": it is said that he went from cell to cell asking, "Where is the ascetic Gotama?
and thinking, "I shall enter after searching," he saw those bhikkhus clad in rag-robes walking up and down on the *caṅkama* like elephants in the forest.
With reference to them, the words "where those bhikkhus were" and so forth were spoken. Where?
"Where, sir, is he now? In which dwelling or pavilion? is the meaning. "He is there, Aggivessana," [said the monk].
At that time, it is said, the Blessed One had entered the meditative attainment of great compassion at dawn;
having spread the net of omniscient knowledge over the ten thousand world-systems and surveying those beings capable of being awakened, he saw: "Tomorrow, Saccaka..."
“The son of the Nigaṇṭhas, having gathered a great assembly of Licchavis, will come wishing to challenge me to a debate. Therefore,
having attended to his personal needs early in the morning and being surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he thought, “After walking for alms in Vesālī and returning from the almsround,
I shall sit in the Fragrant Cottage in a place that is comfortable for the great assembly to sit,” and so he entered the Fragrant Cottage.
Without entering the great forest, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.

Those monks, having performed their duties toward the Blessed One, returned; when questioned by Saccaka, they pointed out the Blessed One sitting at a distance, saying, "This, Aggivessana, is the Blessed One."
"Accompanied by a great assembly of Licchavis" means that, as stated below, he was surrounded by about five hundred Licchavis.

These were indeed his own pupils; however, Saccaka, who lived within Vesālī, having heard that the Blessed One was being approached by one seeking debate, took about five hundred Licchavi princes and [joined] the conversation between the two wise men.
"Let us listen"—thus most of the people departed, and so that assembly became vast and beyond counting.
It was with reference to this that it was said. Having paid homage with palms joined, those belonging to both sides thought thus:
"If those of wrong view should challenge us, saying, 'Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?'"
To them we shall say: “Is it not considered that one has paid homage even by merely joining the palms?
If those of right view should challenge us, saying, “Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?”, we shall reply: “Is it only by striking the ground with the head that one has paid homage?
Is not the act of joining the palms also indeed homage? [Thus spoke] the one named Gotama, sir.
“Gotama, those who say, ‘I am the son of so-and-so, named Datta, or named Mitta; I have come here,’ are announcing their names.
Those who say, ‘Venerable Gotama, I am a Vāsiṭṭha, I am a Kaccāna; I have come here,’ are announcing their clan.
It is said that these impoverished sons of noble families think, ‘In the midst of this assembly, we shall become well-known by way of our names and clans.’”
They did so. But those who sat in silence were both hypocrites and blind fools.

Among them, the hypocrites sat in silence thinking, "By engaging in one or two conversations and exchanges of talk, one becomes trustworthy; once trust has been established, it is not proper not to give one or two alms.
Thus they sat silent to extricate themselves from that situation. The blind fools, however, [sat silent] out of sheer ignorance.
They sat there in silence like lumps of clay cast aside anywhere.
Then, teaching them something, providing some scope, and giving some reason, the Blessed One spoke—arousing their enthusiasm to ask questions—saying:
"Ask, Aggivessana, whatever you desire. The meaning of this is: "Ask, if..."
“If you wish, there is no burden for me in answering your questions. Or else, he extended an invitation of omniscience, saying, “Ask whatever you wish;
I shall answer it all,” an invitation not shared even by the Paccekabuddhas or the foremost disciples of the Buddha.
For they do not say, “Ask whatever you wish,” but rather, “Having heard it, we shall know. But the Buddhas say, “Ask, friend...”
Or "Ask whenever you wish," or "Ask, Great King,
whenever you wish," or "Ask me, Vāsava, whatever question you desire;
I shall bring each and every question of yours to its conclusion."
“Then, bhikkhu, sit down on your own seat and ask whatever you wish,” or alternatively:
“Whether it be Bāvari’s or yours, let all your doubts be cleared;
having been granted leave, ask whatever you desire.”
“Ask me, Sabhiya, whatever question you desire;
I shall bring you to the end of each and every question. Thus they invited all those yakkhas, lords of men, devas, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers to put questions to the Omniscient One.

It is not surprising that the Blessed One, having attained the stage of a Buddha, should perform this invitation for criticism (*pavāraṇā*). For even while he was on the stage of a Bodhisattva and still abiding in partial knowledge, he said:
"Koṇḍañña, answer the questions!
These sages of noble character are making a request."
"Koṇḍañña, this is the law among men:
that one who has grown old must bear this burden.
Thus was he requested by the seers for the sake of Sakka and the others.
“Let the worthy ones ask, having been granted the opportunity,
whatever question they desire in their minds;
for I shall answer each one of them for you.”
"Having known for myself this world and the next.
Thus, during the time of Sarabhaṅga and in the Sambhava Jātaka, having wandered three times throughout the whole of Jambudīpa and not seeing anyone who could provide an end to his questions,
when he was asked a question by the very aged brahmin and granted the opportunity, [the boy] was seven years old by birth.
While playing with sand on the street, sitting cross-legged right there in the middle of the road, he said:
"Truly, I shall tell you, just as one who is skilled would;
but the king himself must know whether you will do it or not."
He invited [the Buddha] to the proclamation of omniscience.
When the Blessed One had thus been invited to the proclamation of omniscience, he, being delighted, spoke the words beginning with “But how, Master Gotama,” in order to ask a question.
Then the Blessed One said to him: “See, sir, how one thing is spoken by the disciple and another thing is spoken by the Teacher; is it not so?”
"I said beforehand: 'If he establishes himself in the manner established by his own disciple, then I shall bring forward this challenge.
But he speaks something entirely different; what can I do about that?
Thinking thus, so as not to give the Nigaṇṭha an opportunity to speak, he spoke according to the same method previously explained by the Elder Assaji.

"Thus indeed, Aggivessana," [the Blessed One] said, beginning with those words. "A simile occurs to me, Master Gotama"—this means, "Master Gotama, a certain simile presents itself to me; I shall bring it forth.
"Let it occur to you, Aggivessana"—that is, "Let it present itself to you, Aggivessana; bring forth that simile with confidence," the Blessed One said. "Exerting strength" means...
"By means of physical strength" refers to occupations such as agriculture, trade, and so forth. "One who has form as self" (*rūpattā*) means one for whom form is the self;
this indicates a person who stands having grasped form as the self. "Established in form" means being established in that form which has been grasped as the self.
"Produces merit or demerit" means wholesome or unwholesome [kamma].
Or he acquires it. This same method applies to the aggregates of feeling and so forth as well. What does this illustrate?
These five aggregates are the foundation for these beings, just like the earth; established upon these five aggregates, they accumulate what is called wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
You, by denying such a self that actually exists, [assert that] "the five aggregates are non-self."
"Let it shine" means he brought forth a simile by making it exceedingly well-reasoned. And this simile brought forth by this Nigaṇṭha is indeed definitive;
for there is no one other than an omniscient Buddha capable of cutting through his argument and pointing out its flaw.
For there are two kinds of persons: those to be guided by a Buddha and those to be guided by a disciple. Regarding those to be guided by a disciple...
Disciples also discipline those who are to be disciplined; Buddhas also do so. However, disciples are unable to discipline those who are to be disciplined by a Buddha;

only Buddhas can discipline them. This Nigaṇṭha, too, is one who is to be disciplined by a Buddha; therefore, there is no one capable of refuting his doctrine or pointing out its flaws other than a Buddha.
For this reason, the Blessed One himself spoke the words beginning with "Is it not you, Aggivessana? in order to demonstrate the defects in his doctrine.
Then the Nigaṇṭha thought: “The ascetic Gotama is establishing his doctrine far too strongly against me;
if there is any further flaw, he will refute me alone. Come now, I shall place this doctrine upon the heads of the great multitude as well.
Therefore, he spoke thus: “I too, Master Gotama, say this: form is mine...”
“‘The self... [and so on] ...consciousness is my self,’ and this great multitude [of people] [holds the same view].
But the Blessed One is a far superior debater to the Nigaṇṭha—by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, even a hundred-thousandfold. Therefore he thought:
‘This Nigaṇṭha, having freed himself, is casting his challenge upon the heads of the great multitude; I shall not allow him to escape with his life.’”
“Having turned back the great multitude, I shall refute him alone. Then he said to him, “What is it to you, Aggivessana? and so forth. The meaning of this is:
This multitude has not come to bring charges against my doctrine; rather, you yourself have come, having gathered the whole of Vesālī together, to bring charges against my doctrine.
Therefore, you yourself must resolve your own position; do not [burden] the heads of the great multitude.
"‘You admit it,’ [the Buddha said]. Admitting this, he replied, ‘Indeed, Master Gotama, I do,’ and so forth.
(357) Thus, having established the Nigaṇṭha’s position, the Blessed One began the inquiry with the words, ‘In that case, Aggivessana.
In this context, ‘in that case’ (*tena hi*) is a particle used in the sense of a reason. Since you admit the five aggregates to be the self..."

Therefore, this is the meaning. "In his own conquered realm" means in his own kingdom. "Let him have executed" or "let him have executed" means to cause to be executed one who is deserving of execution, one fit to be put to death.
"Let him have fined" or "let him have fined" means to cause to be fined one who is deserving of a fine, one fit to be fined—to deprive him of his wealth.
"Let him have banished" or "let him have banished" means one who is deserving of banishment from his own kingdom.
"To ordain" means to lead [one] out. "He is fit to behave" (*vattati*) means he both behaves (*vattati*) and is worthy to behave;

it indicates that he is suitable to behave. Thus, the Nigaṇṭha, for the sake of shattering his own doctrine, clarifies by way of distinction—as if a fool were sharpening a weapon for his own destruction—the very reason brought forward. "Let my form be thus."

"May my form be such as this: pleasing, handsome, adorned and prepared, like a golden archway or a well-decorated canvas painting—delightful to behold. "May my form not be thus" means: may my form not be such as this;
may it not be ugly, ill-proportioned, wrinkled and grey-haired, and covered with moles and freckles.
The Nigaṇṭha remained silent because he realized his failure in this point, thinking: “The ascetic Gotama has brought forward a reason to shatter my doctrine;
out of foolishness, I attempted to explain it by making distinctions. Now I am ruined.
If I say ‘It is so,’ these kings will rise up and say, ‘Aggivessana, you have no mastery over your own form.’”

"You say it 'turns out well. If it turns out well for you in regard to your physical form, why is it that you do not shine as these Licchavi kings do—with their bodies resembling those of the gods of the Thirty-three, handsome and pleasing?
But if I say it does not turn out well, the ascetic Gotama will rise up and say, 'Aggivessana, formerly it used to turn out well for you...'"
"Having said, 'I dwell in form,' he will now raise the objection that you are denying it.
"Whether one says 'it is so' there is one fault; whether one says 'it is not so' there is another fault," he remained silent.
A second time the Blessed One questioned him, and a second time he remained silent. For if one does not answer when questioned by the Blessed One up to three times, [the penalty is] sevenfold...

The head bursts open; and Buddhas, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons solely for the sake of sentient beings, possess intense compassion for all beings.
Therefore, without asking a third time, the Blessed One then said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta: "Now answer this," and so forth.
In this context, *sahadhammikaṃ* means "with reason" or "with cause. *Vajirapāṇi* means one who has a thunderbolt (*vajira*) in his hand.
*Yakkho* does not refer to just any being called a *yakkha*, but should be understood as Sakka, the king of the gods.
*Ādittaṃ* means having the color of fire. *Sampajjalitaṃ* means thoroughly ablaze. *Sajotibhūtaṃ* means become luminous on all sides; the meaning is that it has become a single mass of flames.
"He stands" means that he stood having assumed various hideous forms, such as a large head, fangs resembling the buds of a *kandala* lily, and terrifying eyes, nose, and so forth.
But why did he come? For the purpose of eliciting a view [from the Nāga].
Furthermore, it was because of his thought regarding the teaching of the Dhamma: "If I were to teach the Dhamma, others might not understand me."
When the Blessed One had become indifferent [to teaching], Sakka came together with Mahābrahmā and made this promise: “Blessed One, please teach the Dhamma;
if we do not comply with your command, we shall compel others to do so. Let the Wheel of Dhamma belong to you, and the Wheel of Commandment to us.
Therefore, he has come thinking, “Today, having terrified Saccaka, I will cause him to answer my questions.”
If both the Blessed One and Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta were to see it, and others too were to see it, that would be no small matter;

they would say, "The ascetic Gotama, knowing that Saccaka was not entering into his own doctrine, summoned a spirit and showed him to him, and then Saccaka spoke out of fear. Therefore, the Blessed One alone saw it.
And Saccaka saw him. Upon seeing him, sweat broke out from his entire body, and as it churned within his belly, he let out a great cry.
Looking around, wondering, "Are others seeing this too?", he did not see even a single hair standing on end in anyone else. Then he thought:
"This fear has arisen for me alone. If I say, 'I am a *yakkha*, what will they say?'"
"‘There are eyes; you alone see the spirit. It is as if, without having first seen the spirit, you see the spirit only because it has been thrown into the lap of the ascetic Gotama,’ they would say.
Having thought this, and considering, “Now I have no other refuge here except for the ascetic Gotama,” Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-son... [and so on].
He said this to the Blessed One: “Seeking refuge” means seeking that which is called refuge. “Seeking shelter” means seeking that which is called shelter.
“Seeking a resort” means seeking that which is called a resort. And herein, it is called *tāṇa* because it protects and guards;
it is called *leṇa* because one hides within it; it is called *saraṇa* because one goes toward it—the meaning being that it destroys and dispels fear.
"Having brought to mind" means having placed in the mind, having reflected upon, and having scrutinized it.

"May my feeling be thus" means may it be wholesome indeed, may it be pleasant indeed. "May my perception be thus" means may it be wholesome indeed, may it be pleasant indeed, may it be associated with joy indeed.
The same method applies to mental formations (*saṅkhāra*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). As for "may it not be," the meaning here is the opposite of what was stated above.
It should be understood. "Kallaṃ nu" means "is it proper? "Samanupassituṃ" means to view [it] by way of craving, conceit, and views, thinking: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
"No hidaṃ, bho Gotama" means "Certainly not, Master Gotama; this is not proper, Master Gotama.
Thus the Blessed One was like a skilled snake-charmer who, having had a person bitten by a snake, makes that very same snake bite again.
He would have him defeated; thus, in that very assembly, he made Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, speak by that same mouth:
"The five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. "Clinging to suffering" means clinging to this suffering of the five aggregates by means of craving and views.
It should be understood as "approached" and "clung to" by way of craving and views alone. This is also the case in such passages as, "This suffering is mine," and so forth.
The meaning is that one contemplates the suffering of the five aggregates by way of craving, conceit, and views.

"One should fully understand" means one should thoroughly know [them] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self through the full understanding of scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*). "Having encompassed" means having brought them to destruction, decline, and non-arising.
359. "New" means young. "Not yet curled" means at the time of taking the flower, there is a single [bud] inside the size of a thumb.
"A solid block" (*ghanadaṇḍaka*) arises; the meaning is that he is devoid of it. "Empty" (*rittō*) means void, lacking internal essence.
Because of being empty, he is "hollow" (*tuccho*). "Defeated" (*aparaddho*) means vanquished. "But you have spoken thus," said the Blessed One, speaking this while rebuking him for his talkativeness.
It is said that in the past, he had approached the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa and others.
He asked a question. They were unable to answer it. Then, having caused a great commotion in their midst, he rose and departed proclaiming his victory.
Thinking, "I shall treat even the Perfectly Enlightened One in the same way," he approached him—
“O, what indeed is this tree, with its withered leaves and thorns,
where my head has been shattered by a single blow? Thus,
like a soft-beaked bird accustomed to sapless trees that strikes against a *khadira* (acacia) tree, he [realized] the essence of omniscient wisdom.
Having struck with the beak of his knowledge and attained the firmness of omniscient wisdom, he understood it. Proclaiming this in the midst of the assembly, he said:

"But what was spoken by you," and so forth. "There is none now" means that one should not say there is no such thing as sweat in the body subject to grasping (*upādinnaka*); rather, he says there is none *now*. He revealed his golden-hued body.
He did not uncover his entire body. For Buddhas, having fastened their neck-ties, teach the Dhamma in the assembly with their bodies covered.
Then the Blessed One took hold of his robe at the place directly in front of the throat and let it down by a measure of four finger-breadths.
As soon as it was let down, golden rays issued forth in dense clusters from that spot, like [the light] from a golden jar.

Like streams of liquid red gold, and like flashes of lightning emerging from a red-colored cloud, they issued forth and leaped into the air, circling their great trunk—which resembled a golden drum—and their supreme head, before ascending into the sky. But why did the Blessed One act in this way?
It was for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of the great multitude. For the great multitude had thought: "The ascetic Gotama has perspired..."
When he said, "It does not exist," beads of sweat poured from Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son as if he were mounted upon a machine.
But the ascetic Gotama sat there draped in his thick double-layered robe;
how could it be known whether sweat existed within him or not? To dispel that doubt, he acted in this way.
“Maṅkubhūto” means one who has become dispirited. “Pattakkhandho” means one whose shoulders have drooped. “Appaṭibhāno” means seeing nothing further [to say].
“Nisīdi” means he sat down while scratching the ground with his big toe.
360. “Dummukho” does not mean one with an ugly face; for he was handsome and pleasing. This, however, was his name. He was incapable...
He shows that because all the embankments have collapsed, one who has cut off his path is unable to descend into that lotus pond again;
there, it becomes food for crows, hawks, and the like. "Quibbles" (*visūkāyikāni*) refers to quibbles regarding views.
"Perversions" (*visevitāni*) refers to the practice of views. "Flickerings" (*vipphanditāni*) refers to the flickerings of views. "That is to say, the intent to debate."
Here, *yadidaṃ* is a mere particle. It shows that one who intends to debate, thinking "I shall launch a challenge," is incapable of approaching with such an aspiration;
rather, it indicates that he might approach for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. Why did he say this to Dummukha, the son of the Licchavis?
It is said that at the time when the simile was being presented to Dummukha, the other Licchavi youths also thought: [text continues]
“This Nigaṇṭha has long held us in contempt at our place of learning; now is the time to turn our backs on this enemy.

We too shall each bring forth a simile and deal with him in such a way—as if striking down a fallen mallet with the blow of a hand—that he will never again be able to lift his head in the midst of an assembly.”
Having made these similes, they sat waiting for the conclusion of Dummukha’s speech. Saccaka, understanding their intention, thought:
"All of these are standing with their necks craned and their lips quivering;
if they are permitted to bring forward individual similes, I shall not be able to lift my head again in the midst of this assembly."

"Come now, having rebuked Dummukha and cut off the opportunity for speech so that no other may have a chance, I shall ask the ascetic Gotama a question"—thinking thus, he spoke these words. In this context, "wait" (āgamehi) means "stay;
do not speak further."
361. “Let this stand, Master Gotama,” [he said]. “Master Gotama, let this speech of ours and that of other various recluses and brahmins stand.
‘It is but a lamentation, it is considered a wail’—for this statement is like a lamentation;

the meaning is that it is merely a state of uttering confused cries. Alternatively, in the phrase ‘let this stand,’ one should supply the word ‘speech’ (*kathā*) and say: ‘[Let] the lamentation of speech stand as a wail.’”
Regarding the word *maññeti*, the meaning here is that this utterance of speech is merely a lamentation, as it were.
Now, asking the question, he said, "To what extent," and so forth. In that context, "one who has attained intrepidity" means one who has attained knowledge.
"Not dependent on others" means not subject to others. Then the Blessed One, answering his question, said, "In this case, Aggivessana," and so forth; that—
The meaning is indeed clear. However, because the word "sees" (*passati*) is used here, the stage of one in training (*sekkhabhūmi*) is indicated.
Therefore, asking about the higher stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhūmi*), he asked the second question, and the Blessed One answered that as well.

In that context, regarding the phrases beginning with "supreme vision" (*dassanānuttariya*), "supreme vision" refers to mundane and supramundane wisdom (*paññā*). "Supreme practice" (*paṭipadānuttariya*) refers to mundane and supramundane practice.
"Supreme liberation" refers to mundane and supramundane liberation; or, taking only the purely supramundane, "supreme vision" refers to the right view of the path to Arahantship.
"Supreme practice" refers to the remaining factors of the path. "Supreme liberation" refers to the liberation of the highest fruit (Arahantship);
or, for one whose taints are exhausted, the vision of Nibbāna is called supreme vision. [The rest are] the factors of the path.
The unsurpassedness of the practice (*paṭipadānuttariya*). It should be understood that the unsurpassedness of liberation (*vimuttānuttariya*) is the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*).

"He is the Buddha, the Blessed One": that Blessed One has himself awakened to the four truths. "For the sake of awakening" means he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of others' awakening to the four truths.
Regarding "tamed" (*danta*) and so forth: "tamed" means free from turbulence; "for the sake of taming" means for the sake of freedom from turbulence; "peaceful" (*santa*)...

"Peaceful" means through the subsiding of all defilements (*sabbakilesa*). "For the sake of tranquility" means for the subsiding of defilements. "Crossed over" means crossed over the four floods (*oghā*). "For the sake of crossing over" means for the crossing over of the four floods.
"Parinibbuted" means parinibbuted by the parinibbāna of defilements. "For the sake of parinibbāna" means for the purpose of the parinibbāna of defilements.
362. "Dhaṃsī" means those who destroy virtues. "Pagabbā" means those possessed of verbal impudence. "Āsādetabbaṃ" means to be struck or assailed.
"Āsajja" means having struck. "Natveva bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ" indicates that there is no power in anyone to depart with their own doctrine intact after having assailed the venerable Gotama.
For the Blessed One does not cause the interruption of anyone’s life, like an elephant or other such creatures.
However, this Nigaṇṭha did not bring these three similes for the purpose of exalting the Blessed One; he brought them solely for the purpose of exalting himself.
For just as a king, having had some enemy executed, might say, "Such indeed was a hero, such a man endowed with strength," [so too has this Nigaṇṭha spoken].

Even one who praises an adversary merely praises himself. In the same way, sir Gotama, even while extolling the Blessed One with such words as "He is like a rutting elephant," etc., those who seek debate would think: "We alone are heroes, we alone are wise, we alone are learned;
we are just like that rutting elephant, like a blazing mass of fire, and like a hooded venomous snake."
“‘We approached the Perfectly Enlightened One’—thus he exalts himself. Having thus exalted himself, while inviting the Blessed One, he said, ‘May [the Blessed One] consent,’ and so forth.
In this context, ‘may he consent’ means may he accept.
‘For tomorrow’ means for the sake of that merit, joy, and gladness which will arise for me tomorrow from performing service toward you. The Blessed One consented.

"By silence," [the Blessed One said], meaning that the Blessed One, without moving either a limb of the body or a member of speech, but maintaining patience within himself, consented by means of silence.
It is said that he accepted it mentally for the sake of favoring Saccaka.
