"Whatever you might consider appropriate for him"—it is said that those Licchavis had five hundred pots of *pañcathālipāka* (fivefold rice-milk porridge) prepared for him.
They bring regular meals. It is with reference to this that he says: "Tomorrow, you should bring whatever you consider suitable and allowable for the ascetic Gotama;
for you are attendants upon the ascetic Gotama and know what is allowable and what is not, what is proper and what is improper.
Regarding the phrase "they brought the offering of food," it refers to that which was to be brought.
They brought the meal. "Exquisite" means the most excellent. "With his own hand" means with his own hand.
"Having satisfied" means having fully satisfied, having made him completely content and satiated according to his need.

"Having invited to eat" means having properly invited, having had him decline further by making hand gestures such as "enough, enough. "One who has eaten" means one who has finished eating. "One who has removed the bowl from his hand" means...
“With hand withdrawn from the bowl” means with the hand removed. There is also a reading, “onittapattapāṇiṃ,” the meaning of which is:
one whose bowl has been set aside (onitta) from the hand is “onittapattapāṇī.
He, having washed both his hands and the bowl, and having placed the bowl to one side, sat down; this is the meaning. “He sat down to one side” means...
The meaning is that, having recognized the Blessed One to be such as this, he sat down in one place.
"And merit" means the merit found in this gift; the meaning is that it will become the aggregates of result in the future. "A field of merit" refers to the very retinue of those aggregates of result.
"May it be for the happiness of the givers" means: may it be for the sake of the happiness of these Licchavis. This, it is said, was what he [said].
"I am one who has gone forth; it is not fitting for one who has gone forth to hand over his own gift," thinking thus, he spoke as he was handing it over to them.

Then the Blessed One, because what had been given by the Licchavis was given to Saccaka and not to the Blessed One, whereas what had been given by Saccaka was given to the Blessed One, spoke the words beginning with "Aggivessana, that which... in order to illuminate that matter. Thus.
The Blessed One returned the offering given to him by the Nigaṇṭha even before the latter’s death, thinking,
"This shall serve as a latent predisposition for him in the future.
From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta is finished.
6. The commentary on the Mahāsaccaka Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāsaccaka Sutta. Therein, "at one time" means "and at that time."
And by the three phrases beginning with "at the time of the morning," only one single occasion is stated.

For after the bhikkhus have performed their duties, washed their faces, taken up their bowls and robes, and paid homage at the shrine, there comes a time when they stand in the thought-hall, wondering, "Which village shall we enter?
It was at such a time as this that the Blessed One, having put on his upper robe, the *ratta-dupaṭṭa*, [proceeded].

Having fastened his waist-band and arranged his rag-robe over one shoulder, he emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and stood at its entrance, surrounded by the community of monks. With reference to this, it is said:
"At one time" (*ekam samayam*), "at that time" (*tena kho pana samayena*), and "in the forenoon" (*pubbaṇhasamaye*). "Desiring to enter" means for the sake of alms.
"‘I shall enter’—thus he had made his resolve. ‘He approached him’—why did he approach? With the intention of launching a debate.

For it occurred to him: ‘Previously, through my own lack of wisdom, I went to the presence of the ascetic Gotama taking the entire assembly of Vesālī with me, and I became humiliated in the midst of that assembly. Now, instead of doing so, I will go alone.’"
“I shall initiate a debate. If I am able to defeat the ascetic Gotama, I will establish my own doctrine and achieve victory.
But if the ascetic Gotama should be victorious, no one will know of it, like a dance performed in the dark.
Having taken up what is called the “Sleeping Man” question, he approached with this intention for debate.
"Out of compassion" means out of consideration for Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta. It is said that the Elder thought thus:
"If he sits with the Blessed One for a moment, he will obtain the sight of the Buddha and the hearing of the Dhamma;
that will lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, having requested the Blessed One, [he offered] a rag-robe.

“Having prepared a seat with fourfold folds, may the Blessed One sit,” he said. Perceiving that Ānanda was speaking for a specific reason, the Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. As for the statement, “He said this to the Blessed One”:

setting aside the question which he had brought having made it the core of his inquiry, and merely carrying it along by the side for the time being, he spoke these words beginning with, “Are you well, Master Gotama? and so forth.
365. "They touch it, sir Gotama"—this means that those ascetics and brahmins touch, obtain, and experience the bodily painful feeling arisen in the body.
"Stiffness of the thighs" (*ūrukkhambho*) refers to the state of the thighs being paralyzed;
the meaning is the rigidity of the thighs. However, here the future tense has been used in the sense of expressing astonishment.
"It follows the body" means it is concomitant with the body and subject to the body's control. "Development of the body," however, refers to insight (vipassanā);
by means of that, there is no such thing as reaching mental distraction. Thus, the Nigaṇṭha speaks of that which is non-existent, unreal, and does not exist.
"Development of the mind," moreover, refers to serenity (samatha); and for a person endowed with concentration—
"There are no such things as thigh-pillars and so forth," thus the Nigaṇṭha spoke this which is entirely non-existent. However, it is said in the Commentary:
"Just as when one says 'formerly there was' and then asserts that even a thigh-pillar will exist, the future form does not correspond;
likewise, the meaning does not correspond either, for he speaks of what is non-existent, unreal, and absent."
"No cultivation of the body" is said with reference to the practice of self-mortification, such as the fivefold heat-exertion;
for that indeed is what they call "cultivation of the body. But having seen what did he say this? It is said that he would come to the monastery every day at midday;
at that time, however, the monks, having put away their bowls and robes, were each in their own night-quarters or day-quarters.
They enter into seclusion. Seeing them thus secluded, he spoke thus, thinking: "These people devote themselves merely to the cultivation of the mind; they possess no cultivation of the body.
Then the Blessed One questioned him: "But how, Aggivessana, have you heard about the cultivation of the body?"
He said: Expounding upon that, he spoke as follows, beginning with "Nanda Vaccha," and so forth.
Therein, "Nanda" is his name; "Vaccha" is his clan (*gotra*). "Kisa" is his name; "Saṅkicca" is his clan.
"Makkhali Gosāla" has already been mentioned above. "These"—that is, these three persons; it is said they had reached the pinnacle of defiled asceticism. "Exalted, exalted" means...
"Exquisite, exquisite" means they cause strength to be taken up. "They increase" means they make it grow. "They fatten" means they produce an increase in bodily fat.
"Having abandoned the former" means having abandoned the former practice of asceticism.
"Accumulating later" means they subsequently satisfy and nourish [the body] with choice foods and the like. "There is accumulation and depletion" means there is both growth and decline.
And [he said]: "Thus, for this body, at one time there is growth and at another time decline;

only growth and decline are perceived, but the cultivation of the body (*kāyabhāvanā*) is not perceived. Having thus demonstrated this, he asked about the cultivation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*), saying:
"But how, Aggivessana, have you heard of the cultivation of the mind? [The other] replied: "I am unable to explain it," meaning that he was unable to speak after having mastered it.
He was unable to do so, just like an ordinary foolish person.

(367) "But how could you? means: since you do not know such coarse and weak development of the body, how will you know the subtle and refined development of the mind? At this point, however, the Elder Codanālaya—
Thinking, “This phrase is not the word of the Buddha,” he set down his seedling and began to depart.
Then the Elder Mahāsīva said to him: “Bhikkhus, the accumulation, the diminution, the acquisition, and the relinquishment of this body composed of the four great elements are seen.
Having heard that, he reflected: “The insight that has arisen belongs to one who is comprehending the gross body.”
"It is appropriate to say they are gross. 368.

"One who craves pleasure" means one endowed with craving for pleasure. As for the statement, "Upon the cessation of a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises," it does not arise immediately [afterward];
for in the *Paṭṭhāna*, the relation of immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) between pleasure and pain is not established.
It is prohibited. However, because suffering does not arise while pleasure has not yet ceased, it is stated here in this way.
"It remains having exhausted" means it remains after having consumed [the fuel] and grasped [it].
"On both sides" means having become on both sides, with pleasure as one side and suffering as the other side.
"Even when a pleasant feeling has arisen, it does not persist by taking possession of the mind, because the body has been developed.
Even when a painful feeling has arisen, it does not persist by taking possession of the mind, because the mind has been developed.
Here, the development of the body is insight (vipassanā), and the development of the mind is concentration (samādhi). Furthermore, insight is the opposite of pleasure and is proximate to pain.
Concentration is the opposite of suffering and is close to happiness. How so?
For one who sits having established insight, as time passes by, it is as if sparks are flying up here and there;
sweat breaks out from the armpits, and it is as if a whirlpool of heat arises from the crown of the head—thus the mind is struck, afflicted, and agitated.
Thus, first of all, insight is opposed to pleasure and is close to pain.

But when bodily or mental pain has arisen, for one who has entered upon an attainment by suppressing that pain, at the moment of attainment the pain has receded far away and no small measure of pleasure descends upon them. Thus, concentration is opposed to pain.
It is close to pleasure. Just as insight (vipassanā) is opposed to pleasure and is close to pain, so it is not with concentration (samādhi).
And just as concentration is opposed to pain and is close to pleasure, so it is not with insight. Therefore it was said:
"Even when a pleasant feeling has arisen, it does not persist by taking possession of the mind, because of the development of the body."
“Even arisen painful feeling does not persist by seizing the mind, because the mind has been developed.
“Having assailed and brought near” means having struck at the virtues and having drawn [the mind] near. “That indeed would be mine” means that indeed would be my mind.
“What could it be for us, Aggivessana? means, Aggivessana, what would it not become? It will certainly come to be.
"Do not perceive it thus: 'Pleasant and painful feelings indeed arise in me, but once they have arisen, I do not allow them to take possession of my mind.
Now, wishing to explain this matter and to deliver a teaching of the Dhamma that inspires confidence, he began from the very beginning with the Great Renunciation. Therein: 'Here, for me...'"

"Aggivessana, before my enlightenment... [as before] ...I sat down right there, thinking, 'This is sufficient for striving'—all this should be understood according to the method already stated below in the Pāsarāsi Sutta. This, however, is the distinction:
in that case it was sitting at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), whereas here it was the practice of austerities."
374. *Allakaṭṭhaṃ* means fresh udumbara wood. *Sasnehaṃ* means with sap. *Kāmehi* means by way of sensual objects (*vatthukāma*). *Avūpakaṭṭhā* means not withdrawn.
In the passage beginning with *kāmacchanda*, it is precisely the defilement of sensuality (*kilesakāma*) that is called "desire" (*chanda*) because it acts as a desire;

"affection" (*sneha*) because it acts as an affection; "infatuation" (*mucchā*) because it acts as an infatuation; "thirst" (*pipāsā*) because it acts as a thirst; and "consuming" (*anudahanavasena*)...

It should be understood as "fever" (*pariḷāha*). "Produced by self-inflicted means" (*opakkamikā*) means produced by [one's own] exertion. "For knowledge, for vision, for supreme enlightenment"—all this is indeed a synonym for the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*).
Here, however, is the application of the simile: for just as a moist, sap-filled fig-wood log [is consumed by fire], so too is the defilement of passion (*kilesa-kāma*).
Persons who have not escaped from desire for the basis (*vatthukāma*) are soaked by the defilement of desire (*kilesakāma*), like an object placed in water.

Just as fire is not produced even by churning, those who have not escaped from desire for the basis through the defilement of desire do not attain the supramundane path because of their afflictions (*opakkamikā vedanā*). Just as fire is not produced even without churning...
Even without afflictive pains, those individuals do not attain the supramundane path. The second simile should also be understood according to this same method.

However, this is the distinction: the former is a simile for the going forth of one who has a wife and children, while the latter is a simile for the going forth of a brahmin in accordance with the Dhamma.
376. Regarding the third simile, "a withered thicket": it is devoid of moisture and waterless. "Cast upon dry land" means cast either upon a mountain plateau or upon the surface of the earth.
Here too, this is the application of the simile: persons who have emerged from both defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*) and object-desire (*vatthukāma*) are like a dried-up thicket;
their state of being cast upon dry land far away from water [is like their distance from the two kinds of desire].

Just as fire is produced by friction, so too is the attainment of the supramundane path through the experience of pain— whether by way of being an open-air dweller (*abbhokāsika*) or a bed-washer (*nesajjika*), and so forth— even for those who have escaped from objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*) because they are not satiated by the desire of the defilements (*kilesakāma*).
Just as fire is produced merely by rubbing together the dry branch of one tree with another, [so too is the path attained].

"Just as [one might attain the supramundane path] by a pleasant practice even without the pains resulting from self-inflicted exertion"—this simile was brought forward by the Blessed One for his own sake.
Now, demonstrating his own practice of austerities, he said, "Then for me," and so forth. But why did the Blessed One [say this]?
Is it not possible to become a Buddha without performing difficult deeds? Indeed, one is capable whether one performs them or not.
But why did he perform them? [He thought: "I shall demonstrate my own prowess to the world including the devas; otherwise, that quality of the friction of energy would cause me to decline.
For even a noble king, though having obtained a kingdom inherited through his lineage, is not so delighted while merely sitting in his palace.
It is just as when one has taken an army, given two or three battles in combat, crushed the enemy, and attained sovereignty.
For one who thus enjoys the glory of sovereignty, having looked upon his assembly and recalled his own prowess, [he thinks]:
"In such-and-such a place, having performed such-and-such a deed, I destroyed such-and-such and such-and-such an enemy..."
As he thought, "By piercing thus and striking thus, I have attained this royal glory," a powerful joy arose within him.
In the very same way, the Blessed One performed a difficult feat, thinking: "I shall demonstrate my prowess to the world with its devas;
for that prowess will cause me exceeding delight and will produce joy."
Moreover, out of compassion for future generations, he indeed performed it;

for future generations might think, "Even though the Perfectly Enlightened One attained omniscient knowledge after fulfilling the perfections for four incalculable aeons plus a hundred thousand aeons and exerting himself in striving, how much more, then, must we ourselves apply the energy of striving!
Thus they would conceive the need to practice such vigor.
This being so, out of compassion for future generations, he indeed acted [in this way], thinking, "In this manner, one will quickly make an end to birth, aging, and death.
"Having set his teeth against his teeth" means having placed the upper teeth upon the lower teeth. "With his mind [upon] the mind" means with a wholesome mind [upon] an unwholesome mind.
"I would restrain" means I would restrain it. "I would press down" means I would press it down. "I would torment" means...

Having heated it, I would perform the crushing of the vital energy (*vīriya*). "Agitated" (*sāraddha*) means "eagerly striving" (*sadaratha*). "Of one pierced by exertion" (*padhānābhitunna*) means pierced or struck by exertion;
this is the meaning. 378. "Breathless" (*appāṇaka*) means without inhalation.
"From the smith's bellows" (*kammāragaggariyā*) means from the smith’s pipe. "Pain in the head" (*sīsavedanā*).
"They exist" means that powerful headaches arise, provoked by winds that are unable to escape from anywhere.

"One should give a head-wrap" means one should provide a bandage for the head. "Deities" refers to the deities dwelling at the edge of the Bodhisatta’s walking path and in the vicinity of the leaf-hut compound.
At that time, it is said, when an excessive bodily fever arose in the Bodhisatta, he fell into a swoon. While sitting on the walking path itself, he collapsed.
Seeing this, the deities spoke thus: "This is surely the dwelling of an Arahant," speaking according to their conviction that "Arahants are like the dead.
Among them, those deities who thought, "He has passed away," [spoke accordingly].
They said, "Having gone, they reported to the Great King Suddhodana: 'Your son has passed away. [The King asked:
'Has my son passed away after becoming a Buddha, or without having become one? [They replied: 'He was unable to become a Buddha;
he fell down right on the ground of his striving and passed away. [The King said: 'I do not believe it; for my son, there is no such thing as passing away without attaining enlightenment.'"

Later on, after the Fully Enlightened One had set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion and had gradually traveled to Rājagaha and reached Kapilavatthu, King Suddhodana took his bowl, led him up to the palace, and provided him with rice gruel and solid food.
Then, at the interval between meals, he related this matter [to the Buddha]: "When you were engaged in your striving, O Blessed One..."
“Deities came and said, ‘Great King, your son has passed away. Do you believe this, Great King?
“I do not believe it, Blessed One. “Now, Great King, having witnessed such wonders since receiving the dream, how will you not believe?
“I too have become a Buddha, and you too have become the father of a Buddha; however, previously...”

While my wisdom was still immature and I was practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, even during the time I was a youth named Dhammapāla who had gone away to learn a craft, they brought me a sheep’s bone and showed it to me, saying, "Your son, the youth Dhammapāla, has died; here are his bones.
At that time as well, you [said], "There is no such thing as premature death for my son; I..."
"‘I believe,’ you said, O Great King. On account of this occasion, the Blessed One related the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka.
“Do not, dear sir,” they said, out of affection. This term “dear sir” (mārisa) is indeed a term of endearment used by devas.
“Ajajjita” means fasting. “I say ‘halan’” means I say “alan”; it means “enough with this.”
"Do not do this; we shall endure," such was the meaning of his refusal. 380–1.
*Maṅguracchavī* means having the skin of the *maṅgura* fish. *Etāva paramam*: even among those feelings, this alone is the limit, the supreme measure.
In the workplace of his father Sakka... [omission] ...having attained the first *jhāna*.
"Viharitā" means that there is, it is said, a day for the King known as the "Auspicious Day of Sowing" (vappamaṅgaladivasa). On that occasion, they prepare many kinds of hard and soft foods.

Having had the city streets cleaned, full water-jars placed, and banners, flags, and so forth hoisted, they decorate the entire city like a celestial mansion of the gods. All the slaves, laborers, and others are dressed in new, unwashed garments.
Adorned with perfumes, garlands, and other ornaments, they gather at the royal court.
For the king’s agricultural work, one hundred thousand ploughs are normally yoked; however, on that day, they yoke only seven hundred and ninety-nine.
All the ploughs, together with their oxen, reins, and traces, are encrusted with silver like the chariot of Jānussoni. The king’s own supporting plough—
It was adorned with red gold. Even the horns of the oxen, as well as the reins and goads, were adorned with gold.
As the king went forth with a great retinue, he took his son with him.
At the place of labor, there was a rose-apple tree with thick foliage and leaves, providing dense shade. Beneath it—

Having prepared a bed for the prince, having had a canopy inlaid with golden stars fastened above it, having had it enclosed by a curtain-wall, and having established a guard, the king adorned himself with all his ornaments and, surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the place where the ploughing was to be performed.
There, the king took hold of a golden plough; the ministers took seventy-nine silver ploughs less one.
Having taken hold of them, they ploughed here and there. But the king went from this side to the other, or from the other side back to this one.
At that spot there was great prosperity; the nurses sitting around the Bodhisatta, thinking, "We shall see the king's prosperity," emerged from within the enclosure.
The Bodhisatta, looking here and there, saw no one at all.
Rising with speed, he sat cross-legged, took hold of his mindfulness of breathing, and attained the first jhāna.
The nurses, wandering among the food and snacks, were delayed for a short while;

the shadows of the other trees had turned back, but the shadow of that tree remained standing, forming a perfect circle around him. Seeing that the noble son was all alone, the nurses hurried [to him].
Having lifted the curtain and entering within, they saw the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged on the couch and that miracle;
having gone [to the king], they reported it to the king: "Your Majesty, the prince is sitting thus;
while the shadows of other trees have turned back, the shadow of the rose-apple tree remains circular. The king came with haste and, seeing the miracle—
“This is your second salutation, dear son,” he said, and paid homage to his son. It was with reference to this that it was said:
“In his father Sakka’s workplace... having attained and dwelt in the first jhāna. One might wonder:
“Could this be the path to enlightenment?”—that is, could this first jhāna of mindfulness of breathing be the path for the sake of awakening?
"Consciousness following mindfulness" (*satānusāriviññāṇa*) means: "This will not be the path to enlightenment;

rather, it will be the first jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*). Thus, the consciousness that arises immediately after mindfulness has arisen once or twice is called "consciousness following mindfulness.
"That which is bliss" refers to the bliss of the first jhāna of mindfulness of breathing.
382. "They were present" means they were present by performing duties such as sweeping the precincts of the leaf-hut.

"One who is luxurious" means one who is addicted to the abundance of requisites. "He reverted to luxury" means that, having become greedy for flavors, he turned toward the sake of choice alms-food and so forth.
"They departed in disillusionment" means that, having become weary, they departed according to the very law of the Dhamma from the Bodhisatta.
At the time he attained full enlightenment, they departed as was their natural custom in order to provide him with physical seclusion.

As they went, they did not go to any other place, but proceeded directly to Bārāṇasī. While they were gone, the Bodhisatta, having obtained physical seclusion for half a month, sat upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment and penetrated the knowledge of omniscience.
383. "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," and so forth, is to be understood in the same manner as explained under the section on fear and terror.
387. "But I do recall," etc., is a separate transition. It is said that the Nigaṇṭha thought:
"I asked the ascetic Gotama one question. The ascetic Gotama said to me: 'Furthermore, Aggivessana, furthermore... [The text continues with the repetition.]
"Is he speaking while failing to show the conclusion, saying 'Me, Aggivessana'? "Or is he angry?
Then, Aggivessana, when the Tathāgata was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, there was not even one person who could say, "The ascetic Gotama is angry.
It is solely for the purpose of awakening others and for their penetration of the truth that the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma.
"He teaches" means that he began this teaching of the Dhamma while demonstrating [this]. In that context, "with reference to" (*ārabbha*) refers to the intended object.
"Only so far as" (*yāvadeva*) is the delimitation of the purpose and the scope. This is what is meant:
the sole purpose of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is to make others understand; therefore, he does not teach to only one person, but to all who are capable of understanding.
"He teaches. What does this phrase "in that very same former [discourse]" show? It is said that Saccaka thought: "The ascetic Gotama is handsome and pleasing;
his lip-enclosure is well-formed, his tongue is soft, and his mode of speech is sweet;
he wanders about, as it were, delighting the assembly, yet within him there is no one-pointedness of mind. Then the Blessed One—
Aggivessana, the Tathāgata does not wander about seeking to please an assembly;

even before an assembly as vast as the limits of the world-system, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma. He spoke thus to show that he dwells alone to this extent—unflagging, unsullied, devoted to the attainment of the fruit of emptiness.
"Internally indeed" means internally with respect to the range [of his senses]. "I cause them to settle down" means I cause them to sit down;

for at the very moment the assembly gives its applause, the Tathāgata, having delimited that moment by his prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*), enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Even while the sound of the applause has not yet ceased, he emerges from that attainment and stands up from the place where he was sitting.

He teaches the Dhamma starting from that point; for the latent tendencies of the Buddhas are light, and thus they enter into attainment during both the inhalation and the exhalation. By the words "whereby indeed for all time," he shows:
"In that sign of concentration by which fruit-concentration (phala-samādhi) I dwell at all times, I steady my mind and concentrate it."

"Okappaniyametan" means "this is to be believed. Having thus accepted the Blessed One’s state of one-pointed mind, he now, making his own thigh the wager, asks the question he had brought with him, saying:
"But does Master Gotama recall sleeping during the day? For just as a dog [might lick] unbroken milk-rice porridge mixed with ghee...
Even after being fed his fill, one who sees excrement cannot go on without eating it;
even if he does not eat it, he goes only after smelling it, for it is said that if he goes without having smelled it, his head will ache.

In the same way, this Teacher also delivers a pleasing Dhamma teaching—like milk and thickened milk that have not been mixed—which begins from his Great Renunciation and continues until the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*). For him...
However, having heard such a teaching on the Dhamma, not even a mere spark of confidence in the Teacher arose in him;
therefore, making it his core concern, and being unable to go away without asking about the question he had brought, he spoke thus.

In that regard, since dullness and drowsiness (*thina-middha*) are abandoned by all those whose taints are destroyed through the path of Arhatship alone, whereas bodily distress (*kāya-daratha*) exists even for those who still possess clinging (*upādinnaka*).
It applies also to what is not clung-to (*anupādinna*). For instance, lotuses and water-lilies bloom at one time and remain as buds at another;
likewise, the leaves of certain trees close in the evening and spread open at dawn.
Thus, it is precisely the distress of the body that is clung-to which, by way of its own distressing nature, is intended here as the stream of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-sota*).
That [state] exists even for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). It is with reference to this that he said, "I recall," and so forth.
"They speak of dwelling in delusion" means they say it is a dwelling in delusion.
389. "Repeatedly assailing" means having struck, having struck. "With imputations" means with statements made by way of attribution. "By means of paths of speech" means...

"By means of words. "Having rejoiced and having expressed appreciation" means: having rejoiced by accepting [the teaching] with the mind, saying "Very well," and having expressed appreciation by praising it with speech.
Two discourses were spoken by the Blessed One to this Nigaṇṭha.
The first discourse is one *bhāṇavāra*; this one is one and a half; thus, even after hearing these two and a half *bhāṇavāras*, this Nigaṇṭha did not [attain realization].
He had attained realization, yet he had not gone forth as a monk, nor was he established in the refuges. Why did the Blessed One teach him the Dhamma?
It was for the sake of creating a latent impression (*vāsana*) for the future. For the Blessed One saw:
"At present this man lacks the necessary support (*upanissaya*), but after more than two hundred years have passed since my final *parinibbāna*, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi..."

“The Dispensation shall be established. Therein, having been reborn in that noble family, when the time arrives, he will go forth, master the Three Piṭakas, develop insight, and attaining Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he will become a great one whose taints are destroyed, known as Kāḷabuddharakkhita.
Having seen this, he taught the Dhamma for the sake of creating a latent impression (vāsanā) for the future.
He too, when the Teaching was firmly established on that very island of Tambapaṇṇi,

passed away from the world of the gods and was reborn in a family of ministers in a village where the monks of Dakkhiṇagiri Monastery went for alms. When he reached an age capable of undertaking the going-forth, he did so,
mastered the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas, and while leading a community of disciples, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, he set out to see his preceptor.

He arrived. Then his preceptor, thinking, "I shall reprove my co-resident," had studied the entire word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tipiṭaka*) and, upon his arrival, did not even engage in a mere exchange of words with him.
Rising at dawn, he went into the presence of the Elder and said: "Venerable sir, while you were occupied with the work of study, I [remained] in your presence..."
“When he arrived, you did not even speak a single word to him; what fault is it of mine? he asked.
The Elder said, “Friend Buddhārakkhita, by this much alone, do you imagine that the task of going forth has reached its conclusion for you?
“What shall I do, venerable sir? [The Elder replied: “Having dispelled the crowd and cut through your proliferation, [go] to the Cetiyapabbata monastery.”
"Go and practice the duty of a recluse. Abiding by his preceptor’s instruction, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Having become a man of merit honored by kings, he lived at the Cetiyapabbata Monastery surrounded by a great community of bhikkhus.
At that time, King Tissa, while performing the Uposatha observance, was staying in the Royal Cave on Cetiyapabbata.
He gave instructions to the monk who was his attendant, saying: "When my noble master answers a question or delivers a discourse on the Dhamma, you should give me a signal.

On one day for hearing the Dhamma, the Elder, surrounded by the community of monks, ascended the terrace of the Kaṇṭaka Cetiya, paid homage to the shrine, and stood at the foot of the Kāḷatimbaru tree.
He stood there. Then a certain elder who lived on almsfood asked him a question regarding the Kāḷakārāma Sutta.
The elder said, "Friend, is it not today the day for hearing the Dhamma? "Yes, venerable sir, it is the day for hearing the Dhamma.
"In that case, bring a seat; let us sit right here and listen to the Dhamma. Then he [prepared] a seat at the foot of a tree.
Having prepared it, they gave it to him. The Elder, having recited the preliminary verses, began the Kāḷakārāma Sutta.
His young attendant signaled to the king. The king arrived even before the preliminary verses were finished.

Upon arriving, he stood at the edge of the assembly in an unrecognized guise and listened to the Dhamma standing there throughout the three watches of the night. Then he said to the Elder, "This is what the Blessed One said."
At the time of his speaking, he gave a cry of approval. The Elder, knowing this, asked: "When did you arrive, Great King?
"At the very moment the previous verses were recited for the purpose of restoration, Bhante. "This was difficult for you to do, Great King.
"This was not difficult, Bhante, provided that from the moment my noble master began his discourse on the Dhamma, I remained focused on not even a single word of it."
He made a vow, saying: "May I never have ownership over even a space as small as the tip of a needle or a hair on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
In that sutta, however, the qualities of the Buddha were fully illustrated; therefore, the king asked: "Venerable sir, are the qualities of the Buddha only this many, or are there others?
[The Elder replied: "Great King, what has been told by me is but a small portion; what remains untold is immeasurable. [The king asked: "What is the simile for it?"

"Venerable sir, please do so. "Great king, just as in a rice field measuring a thousand cartloads, the remaining rice after taking a single rice stalk is vast, even so, the qualities I have described are few, while the remainder are many. "Venerable sir, give me another simile.
"Great king, it is as if one were to hold a needle-point directly in front of the flood-filled waters of the great Ganges."
"Water that has been drawn up by the tip of a needle is small, while what remains is vast; even so, the virtues described by me are few, while those remaining are many.
"Furthermore, venerable sir, please provide another simile. "In this case, great king, there are birds called *cātaka* that wander about sporting in the sky.
That is a small species of bird; what indeed is the space for the spreading of its wings in the sky?"
"Much, Venerable Sir, is the remaining space; little is that space for stretching out one's wings. What do you say, Bhante?
Is the space for stretching out one's wings small, while the remainder is great? "In the same way, Great King, the qualities of a Buddha that have been spoken of by me are few;
the remainder are many, infinite, and immeasurable. "Well spoken, Bhante! The infinite qualities of a Buddha have been compared to infinite space itself."
“We have faith in you, noble sir, but we are unable to do what is appropriate for you.
This poor gift of mine—this kingdom of three hundred yojanas on this island of Tambapaṇṇi—we give it to you, noble sir. “You have shown your faith, Great King;
however, we give back to you alone the kingdom that was given to us, in accordance with the Dhamma.”
"O Great King, rule the kingdom with impartiality.
The commentary on the Mahāsaccaka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is hereby concluded.
7. Commentary on the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta 390.

"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta. Therein, "in the Eastern Park, at Migāra’s Mother’s Mansion" means in the monastery known as the Eastern Park, at the mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Regarding this, the sequential account is as follows: in the past, at the limit of one hundred thousand aeons ago...
A certain female lay follower invited the Blessed One Padumuttara and, having given alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and made this aspiration:
“In the future, may I be the foremost attendant of a Buddha such as you. For one hundred thousand aeons, she [dwelt] among gods and humans.

Having wandered through the cycle of existence, she took rebirth at the time of our Blessed One in the city of Bhaddiya, in the womb of Queen Sumanā, the wife of the merchant Dhanañjaya, the son of the merchant Meṇḍaka.
At the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā. When the Blessed One arrived at the city of Bhaddiya, she [accompanied him] with five hundred maidens.
Having gone out to meet the Blessed One, she became a stream-enterer at their very first meeting.
Later, when she went to the house of Puṇṇavaḍḍhana Kumāra, the son of the Migāra seṭṭhi in Sāvatthī, the seṭṭhi established her in the position of mother;
therefore, she is called Migāramātā.
And for her as she was going to Pāṭikula, her father had a great garland-ornament named Mahālatāpiḷandhana made.
For that ornament, four *nāḷi*s of diamonds were used, eleven *nāḷi*s of pearls, twenty-two *nāḷi*s of coral, and thirty-three *nāḷi*s of gems;
thus it was completed with these and other seven-colored jewels.
She arrived. That ornament, fastened upon her head, brushed against her as far down as the backs of her feet; yet that woman was able to bear it, possessing the strength of five elephants.

Later on, having become the foremost attendant of the One Possessing Ten Powers, she gave away that ornament and, while having a monastery built for the Blessed One at a cost of nine hundred million, [she dug] to a depth of a hand’s span...
He had a palace built on a plot of ground. On its upper floor there were five hundred chambers, and on the lower floor another five;

thus it was adorned with a thousand chambers. Thinking, "The bare palace does not look beautiful," she had it surrounded by five hundred two-peaked houses, five hundred small palaces, and five hundred long halls.
The festival for the monastery reached completion in four months.
Just as there was no one else in the female form comparable to Visākhā in her relinquishment of wealth for the Buddha’s teaching,
so too there was no one else in the male form comparable to Anāthapiṇḍika in his relinquishment of wealth for the Buddha’s teaching.
There was no [other] name for it. For he, having spent fifty-four crores, built the Great Monastery named Jetavana in a place to the south of Sāvatthī, similar to the Mahāvihāra at Anurādhapura.
Visākhā built the Eastern Monastery (Pubbārāma) in a place to the east of Sāvatthī, similar to the Uttamadevī-vihāra.
The Blessed One [bestowed his favor] upon these two families.
Out of compassion, while residing in dependence on Sāvatthī, he lived a fixed residence in these two monasteries:
he stayed one rainy season in Jeta’s Grove and one in the Eastern Park. At this particular time, however, the Blessed One was staying in the Eastern Park.
Therefore it is said: “In the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.”
"To what extent, venerable sir? means "By how much, venerable sir? "In brief, he is liberated through the destruction of craving" means:
by making Nibbāna—the destruction of craving—the object [of his mind], he is liberated because his consciousness is freed;
to what extent, in brief, is he called "liberated through the destruction of craving"? It is by way of that practice through which he becomes liberated through the destruction of craving.

He asks: "Please teach in brief the preliminary practice for a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted. "Accantaniṭṭho": one who has gone beyond the "end," which is defined as destruction and vanishing, is *accantā*.
One who possesses such an absolute end (*accantā niṭṭhā*) is *accantaniṭṭho*; the meaning is that he is one whose end is absolute, whose end is exclusive, and whose end is perpetual.
"Accantaṃ yogakkhemī": one who is absolutely secure from bondage (*yogakkhemī*); that is, one who is eternally secure from bondage.
The meaning is as follows. "One who practices the holy life to the ultimate" (*accantabrahmacārī*) means one who practices the holy life constantly; this is the meaning.
"One whose ultimate is the end" (*accantapariyosāno*) refers to one for whom the ultimate is the final goal, according to the same method as before.

"The best among gods and humans" (*seṭṭho devamanussānaṃ*) means the most excellent and supreme among both gods and humans. To what extent does such a bhikkhu become [this], and how quickly can he be described in brief?
He requests the Blessed One, saying, "Please speak on the practice. But why does he make such a request so urgently? It is because he desires to experience the sport [of the gods].

It is said that, having ordered a pleasure excursion in the park and having had the Four Great Kings take up guard in the four directions, surrounded by the hosts of devas in the two deva-worlds, together with two hundred and fifty million celestial dancers, he mounted Erāvaṇa.

Having ascended and standing at the park gate, he reflected on this question: "To what extent is the preliminary practice leading to the goal for one who is liberated through the destruction of craving and whose taints are exhausted? Then it occurred to him:
"This question is exceedingly magnificent; if I enter the park without first resolving this question,"
“Crushed by the objects of the six sense-doors, I shall not be able to attend to this question again; let the pleasure-garden excursion be for now.
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and asked this question, I shall play in the garden once I have mastered the answer.
Saying this, he vanished from the back of the elephant and appeared in the presence of the Blessed One. Those four Great Kings also provided protection.
Having taken it, she stood right where she had been; the host of attendant devas, the dancers, and even Erāvaṇa, the king of the nāgas, all stood right there at the gate of the pleasure grove.
Thus, rushing with great speed out of a desire to enjoy the sport, he spoke these words:
"All phenomena are not fit for adherence. Here, "all phenomena" refers to the five aggregates and the twelve sense bases.
The eighteen elements—all of these are incapable, insufficient, incompetent, and unfit for adherence by way of craving and views. Why?
Because they do not persist in the manner in which they are grasped. For even when grasped as permanent, they turn out to be impermanent;
even when grasped as pleasant, they turn out to be painful; and even when grasped as self, they turn out to be non-self.
Therefore, it is not sufficient for adherence. "He directly knows" means he directly knows [it] through the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
"He fully understands" means he fully understands it through the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇa-pariññā*) in that very same way.

"Whatever feeling whatsoever" means he experiences any feeling at all, even the slightest feeling associated with the fivefold sense-consciousness. By this, the Blessed One [addressed] Sakka, the lord of the devas.
Having produced [the meditation subject] by way of feeling, he shows the discernment of the formless.
However, if the meditation subject of feeling had not been explained previously, it would have to be explained at this point;

but since it was explained previously, it should be understood according to the method stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta]. Regarding the phrase "contemplating impermanence," here impermanence is to be understood.
Contemplation of impermanence is to be understood, and one who contemplates impermanence is to be understood.

In this context, "impermanent" refers to the five aggregates, for they are impermanent in the sense of arising and passing away. "Contemplation of impermanence" is the knowledge that sees the five aggregates as subject to destruction and dissolution.
"One who contemplates impermanence" is the person endowed with that knowledge. Therefore, "one who contemplates impermanence..."
"Abides" means he abides contemplating [them] as impermanent; this is the meaning here.
Regarding "contemplating fading away" (*virāgānupassī*): there are two kinds of fading away here—fading away as destruction (*khayavirāga*) and absolute fading away (*accantavirāga*).

In that regard, contemplation of the destruction and fall of formations is one kind of contemplation of fading away, while the knowledge of the path of seeing, which views Nibbāna—the absolute fading away—as fading away, is also contemplation of fading away.
A person who possesses both [of these] factors is called "one who contemplates fading away" (*virāgānupassī*); it is with reference to such a person that it is said, "contemplating fading away.
The meaning is: contemplating from the perspective of fading away. The same method applies to "one who contemplates cessation" (*nirodhānupassī*); for cessation is indeed twofold:

cessation as destruction (*khayanirodha*) and absolute cessation (*accantanirōdha*). Regarding "one who contemplates relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassī*), here "relinquishment" (*paṭinissagga*) is so called...
Relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāga-vossagga*) and relinquishment as leaping forward (*pakkhandana-vossagga*).
Therein, relinquishment as giving up is insight (*vipassanā*); for by way of its specific factor (*tadaṅga*), it relinquishes both defilements and the aggregates.
Relinquishment as leaping forward is the path (*magga*); for it leaps forward toward Nibbāna from the perspective of the object. Or rather, it is simply relinquishment for two reasons.

Because of the relinquishing of the aggregates and the defilements by way of their total eradication, and because of the "launching forth" (pakkhandana) of the mind into Nibbāna, it is called "relinquishment as abandonment" (*pariccāga-vossagga*) since one abandons both defilements and aggregates, and "relinquishment as launching forth" (*pakkhandana-vossagga*) since the mind launches forth into cessation, the element of Nibbāna.
Both of these apply to the Path. A person who possesses both of these [qualities]...
Because he is endowed with this contemplation of relinquishment, he is called "one who contemplates relinquishment. It is with reference to this that it is said, "contemplating relinquishment.
"He does not cling to anything in the world" means that he does not, by way of craving, cling to, grasp, or misapprehend even a single conditioned thing (*saṅkhāra*).
"Not clinging, he does not tremble" means that, not grasping [anything], he does not become agitated.

"He does not tremble through the agitation of craving. "He attains final nibbāna within himself" means that he personally attains final nibbāna through the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*).
Furthermore, by the words "Birth is exhausted," etc., his very act of reviewing [the attainment] is shown.
Thus, having been asked by Sakka, Lord of the Devas, for a brief account of the preliminary practice of one whose taints were destroyed, the Blessed One spoke concisely.
Having done so, he spoke quickly and in brief.
"He was sitting not far away" means he was sitting in the adjacent gabled chamber. "Having fully realized" (abhisamecca) means having approached through knowledge;
the meaning is "having known. This is what is meant: "What indeed has he known, that he has rejoiced?"

Or did he say it without knowing? But why did it occur to him in this way? It is said that the Elder did not hear the sound of the Blessed One’s answer to the question, but he did hear the sound of King Sakka, the lord of the devas, saying, “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
It is said that King Sakka, the lord of the devas, offered his approval with a great voice. Therefore, why did he not hear the sound of the Blessed One?
"Did he hear it? Because [the Buddha] makes his audience understood according to their capacity.

For when Buddhas preach the Dhamma, the sound is heard by an assembly that extends as far as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), yet without exceeding those limits, not even so much as a finger's breadth escapes outward.
Why? So that such sweet speech may not go to waste. At that time, the Blessed One was at the Migāramātupāsāda.
He was seated in the inner chamber of the gabled hall made of the seven precious gems;
on his right side was the gabled hall where the Elder Sāriputta resided, and on his left side that of Mahāmoggallāna, with no intervening gap or opening between them.
Therefore, the Elder did not hear the Blessed One’s voice, but heard only that of Sakka.
"With five hundred musical instruments" means with five hundred sets of fivefold musical instruments. A "fivefold musical instrument" is one endowed with these five components:
the stretched (*ātata*), the loose-stretched (*vitata*), the both-stretched-and-loose-stretched (*ātatavitata*), the hollow (*susira*), and the solid (*ghana*).
Among these, the "stretched" refers to single-sided instruments such as drums covered with leather; the "loose-stretched" refers to those with two sides.

"Ātatavitata" refers to stringed instruments such as the *paṇava* drum. "Susira" refers to wind instruments such as the flute (*vaṃsa*). "Ghana" refers to percussion instruments such as the *sammatāla*.
"Upagato" means approached. "Samaṅgībhūto" is a synonym for that same state. "Paricāreti" means that while experiencing that prosperity, he directs his sense-faculties here and there.
This is what is meant: [he does so] by means of the five hundred musical instruments being played in a surrounding circle.
Having become thus endowed, he experiences divine success. "Having removed" means having taken away;
the meaning is "having caused them to be made silent. For just as nowadays, when kings who have faith see a monk worthy of respect, they say to the actors, "A certain noble sir is coming;
dear ones, do not sing, do not play instruments, do not dance."
They offered him hospitality; Sakka, too, upon seeing the Elder, acted in this same way.
"It has been a long time, dear Moggallāna, since you have employed such a means"—this is a form of customary polite address in the world.
For when worldly people see someone of a pleasing nature who has arrived after a long absence, even if they have never met before, they say: "Whence have you come? It has been a long time..."
They say things such as, "Sir, you have arrived; how did you know the path for coming here? You are lost!
But he spoke thus precisely because he had come here before. For the Elder goes on visits to the deva-world from time to time.
Therein, "he made an occasion" means he made a turn; that is to say, "for the purpose of coming here," which refers to the turn for coming here.
"Venerable sir, it has been a long time since you last came"—this is what is meant. "This seat is prepared" means that having had a jeweled couch a *yojana* in length prepared, he spoke thus.
Regarding the phrase "busy with many duties, with much to do": here, those who have many duties are "busy with many duties"; "with much to do" refers to those who have many tasks to perform.

This is a synonym for that very thing. "Perhaps [there may be] some small matter of one's own" means that one's own business (*sakaraṇīya*) is indeed small and slight, not much; however, the business of the gods is great.

For, beginning from the earth, the eight posts are cut down in the presence of Sakka for the sake of the wish-fulfilling tree, the women, and so forth. Therefore, specifying it, he said: "Furthermore, [it concerns] only the Tāvatiṃsa gods."
Regarding "that which is to be done": for the daughters and sons of the gods are born upon their laps;
female attendants are born upon the bed; the goddesses who provide ornaments and decorations are born surrounding the bed;
and those who perform services are born within the celestial mansion (*vimāna*). For these beings, there is no need for legal proceedings or courts of law. However, as for those...
They are born in the space between the boundary lines; being unable to determine whether they belong to "my domain" or "your domain," they dispute and question Sakka, the King of Devas.
He says that they belong to whichever one’s celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is closer.
If both are at an equal distance, he says they belong to whichever one stands looking toward the mansion.
He speaks thus. If he does not look at even one of them, he makes that [object] his own for the purpose of ending the quarrel between the two.
With reference to this, he said, "on account of the business of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Furthermore, even such a playful activity as this is indeed a "business" for him.
“That which vanishes from us so quickly” means that which does not appear to us immediately, like a form in darkness.
By this, he indicates: “Venerable sir, I do not perceive that answer to the question.
The Elder thought: “Why does this yakkha indicate his state of non-perception? Is he avoiding it out of fear?”

Reflecting thus—"The devas are indeed greatly deluded; being overwhelmed by the objects of the six doors, they do not even know whether they have eaten or not, or whether they have drunk or not—how then could they forget this here? he understood.
Some, however, say: "The Elder was his teacher and one to be revered; therefore, [he thought], 'Right now, in the presence of the Supreme Person in the world...'"
"He has come having mastered the question, yet he has just now entered among the actors"—thinking, "The Elder might thus rebuke me," he spoke thus out of fear.
But what is this called deception? Such deception does not belong to a noble disciple;
therefore, it should be understood that he did not perceive [the truth] due to his state of delusion. Why, then, did he perceive it later on?
The Elder, having generated in him joy and a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), removed his darkness; therefore, he perceived [the truth].
Now, in order to inform the Elder of the reason for what had happened to himself in the past, Sakka said, "In the past," and so forth.
Therein, *samupabyūḷho* means gathered together, assembled into a mass. *Asurā parājiniṃsu* means the asuras were defeated.
They attained [this state]. But when were they defeated? At the time of Sakka’s rebirth.

It is said that in his immediately preceding existence, Sakka was a young brahmin named Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha; he was wise and competent, and his conduct was like that of a Bodhisatta.
Having taken thirty-three men with him, he performed meritorious deeds. One day, of his own...
Having investigated with wisdom, he cleared away the refuse from both sides in the center of the village where the great multitude had gathered, making that place exceedingly beautiful;
then he had a pavilion constructed there, and later, as time passed, he had a hall built.
Furthermore, extending a quarter-league, a half-yojana, three-quarters of a league, or even a full yojana beyond the village...
Having deliberated, he made the uneven ground level together with those companions.

All of them, being of one mind, performed much merit by constructing bridges at places where bridges were needed, and by building pavilions, halls, lotus ponds, and planting groves of trees in places suitable for such works.
Having fulfilled the seven precepts, Magha, upon the dissolution of the body...
Together with his companions, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
At that time, the hosts of asuras were dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world. All those asuras were equal in lifespan and equal in appearance to the devas;
seeing Sakka and his retinue, they thought, "These are newly born young devas who have just arrived."
They prepared a great drink. Sakka gave a sign to the sons of the gods, saying: "While we were performing wholesome deeds, we did not share them with others;
therefore, you must not drink the 'swollen' drink (gaṇḍapāna), but merely take a sip.
They did accordingly. Having drunk the 'swollen' drink, the foolish asuras became intoxicated and fell asleep. Sakka [then acted] for the sake of the gods...
Having given them a sign, he made them grasp his feet and hurled them down to the base of Sineru.
At the foot of Sineru there is a place called the Abode of the Asuras, equal in size to the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world. There the asuras dwell.
They too have a tree called Cittapāṭali; they know when it flowers: "This is not Tāvatiṃsa; we have been deceived by Sakka."
"Let us go! they said. "Seize them! Having said this, they ascended [Mount Sineru] like ants from the foot of an anthill when it rains, circling around Sineru.
There, at times the devas were victorious, and at times the asuras.
When the devas were victorious, they pursued the asuras as far as the surface of the ocean. When the asuras were victorious, [they pursued the devas].
The gods pursued them as far as the foot of the altar. In that battle, victory belonged to the gods;
they pursued the asuras as far as the back of the ocean. Having driven the asuras to flight, Sakka established guards at five locations.
Having thus provided for their protection, he placed statues of Indra with thunderbolts in hand at the feet of the altar. From time to time, the asuras...
Having risen and seen those images, they turn back from that very spot, thinking, "Sakka remains vigilant.
"Turning back from there" means turning back from the place of victory. "Attendants" refers to those who perform tasks such as preparing garlands and perfumes. 393.
"And Vessavaṇa the Great King"—it is said that he is Sakka’s favorite and a trusted confidant; therefore, by Sakka...
He went along with him. "Having placed [him] in front" means having made him precede.
"They entered" means that having entered, they stood looking about after the doors had been half-closed.
"Behold this, Mārisa Moggallāna, the loveliness of the Vejayanta Palace," [he said]; "Mārisa Moggallāna, behold this too, the loveliness of the Vejayanta Palace."
"Behold, behold the golden pillars, behold the silver pillars, the gem pillars, the coral pillars,
the ruby pillars, the emerald pillars, the pearl pillars, and the pillars made of the seven precious gems; behold also the animal figures in those very vessels made of gold and the other materials"—
thus he spoke, showing the beauty of the place beginning with the rows of pillars.
"Like one who has performed merit in the past": the meaning is that he shines just as one who has performed merit in the past ought to shine by means of a place for enjoyment.
"This yakkha indeed dwells exceedingly intoxicated": he is excessively intoxicated by his own splendor, consisting of his palace and his retinue of dancers.
"He performed a feat of supernormal power (iddhābhisaṅkhāra)" means he exercised his psychic power.

Having entered the water-kasina attainment, he resolved upon a feat of supernormal power, thinking, "Let the area where the palace stands become water," and struck the corner pillar of the palace with his big toe.
That palace shook back and forth, just like a bowl placed on the surface of water when its rim is tapped with a finger.
It moved and did not remain still. In the same way, it shook, trembled, and quaked;

the pillars, rafters, joints, lintels, and cross-beams began to emit a rattling sound as if they were about to fall. Therefore it is said: "it made them shake, it made them tremble, it made them quake.
"A state of wonder and amazement arose" means: "Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how marvelous!"—thus a sense of wonder and amazement was born.
And they became filled with joy and possessed of intense gladness. "Aroused" (*saṃviggā*) means agitated.

"With hair standing on end" (*lomahaṭṭhajātā*) means having the hair of the body bristling; the meaning is that their bodies were covered with upright hairs, like jeweled ivory pegs set into a golden wall.
Now, this "bristling of the hair" occurs both through joy and through grief; but in this instance, it is due to joy.

He was born. For the Elder performed that miracle in order to stir Sakka with a surge of joy; therefore, the meaning is: "having perceived the bristling of his hair due to being stirred by a surge of joy.
(394) "In this matter, dear sir," he said, because the Elder had now dispelled his darkness by generating a surge of joyful inspiration.
Therefore, having observed this, he spoke thus: "Is that Blessed One your teacher, dear sir?
To which place have you gone? When he replied, "I am in the presence of my Teacher," they asked, "In this world of the devas, you stand as if on one leg;
why do you speak thus? and they questioned him, "Is that Blessed One your teacher, dear sir?"

Regarding the phrase "He is my fellow-celibate (*sabrahmacārī*)," although the Elder was a homeless one endowed with resolute intention and a chief disciple, while Sakka was a householder, they were nevertheless fellow-celibates by virtue of the holy life of the Path; therefore, he spoke thus:
"Oh, surely that Blessed One is your Teacher!"—for if even your fellow-celibate possesses such great power, how much more so must that Blessed One of yours!
Thinking, "Oh, how great indeed is his psychic power! and having developed a longing to witness the Teacher’s miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), they spoke thus.

(395) "Of one who is well-known" (*ñātaññatarassa*) means of one who is renowned; for Sakka is one among those who are renowned. The rest is clear everywhere. However, the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely according to the sequence of the discourse.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.
The commentary on the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta: 396.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta. Therein, "a resort of views" refers to [the passage] in the Alagaddūpama Sutta.
It was said that "mere attainment" refers to a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*), whereas here it refers to the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

That monk was one of great learning, while this one was of little learning; as a reciter of the Jātakas, he would recount a Jātaka of the Blessed One and say, "Monks, at that time I was Vessantara, Mahosadha, Vidhurapaṇḍita, Senakapaṇḍita, or King Mahājanaka."
He hears [this] while correlating [the teachings]. Then this thought occurred to him: "These aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations cease right there and then;
but consciousness runs on and wanders about from this world to the other world, and from the other world back to this world.
Thus the view of eternalism arose. Therefore he said: "This very same consciousness runs on and wanders about, and it is not another."
But the Fully Enlightened One has said: "Consciousness arises through the occurrence of conditions; when a condition exists, it arises; without a condition, there is no arising of consciousness.

Therefore, this monk speaks what was not spoken by the Buddha, strikes at the Wheel of the Conqueror, obstructs the knowledge of fearlessness, deceives people who desire to hear, [and deviates] from the path of the Noble Ones.
Having fallen away from the upright path, he has set out for the harm and suffering of the great multitude.

Just as a great thief arising within a king’s realm arises for the harm and suffering of the great multitude, so too should it be understood that he has arisen as a thief within the Conqueror’s Dispensation for the harm and suffering of the great multitude. "A number of bhikkhus" refers to those dwelling in the countryside.
"Alms-collecting bhikkhus. "They approached him" means: thinking, "If he were to gain this assembly, he might even cause the Dispensation to disappear;
therefore, before he gains a following, we must separate him from his speculative views," they approached him without remaining or sitting in the very places where they had heard [of him].
398. “What is that consciousness, Sāti? “Which consciousness, venerable sir, do you have in mind when you say, ‘What is that consciousness?
“That which speaks and feels, venerable sir, and which experiences here and there the result of good and evil deeds;
that which, venerable sir, speaks and feels, and which [experiences] here and there the results of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.”
“He experiences the result [of karma]. This, venerable sir, is consciousness; it is with reference to this that I speak.
“Of whom indeed?”—of which one among the khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, or humans?
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus. Why did he address them? It is said that Sāti thought thus: [“I am the one who speaks of this”].
“The Teacher calls me a ‘foolish man’ (*moghapurisa*), yet being called a foolish man does not, by that mere fact, mean one lacks the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits.

For even the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta was admonished by the Blessed One with the words, ‘Foolish man, you have indeed turned too quickly toward abundance,’ using the term ‘foolish man. Later on, that elder, striving and exerting himself...”
“He realized the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). I too, by exerting such energy, shall bring forth the paths and fruits.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks, showing that this man, having his conditions severed, was one whose Dhamma would not grow within the Dispensation.
“He has been made warm,” etc., has the same intended meaning as what was stated above. “Then the Blessed One”—this also constitutes a separate connection (*anusandhi*).
It occurred to Sātissa: “The Blessed One says that I lack the necessary support for the paths and fruits;
what can be done when such support is absent? For the Tathāgatas do not teach the Dhamma only to those who possess support;
they teach it to anyone at all. Having received the Sugata’s exhortation from the presence of the Buddha, I shall attain the excellence of heaven.”

“I shall do what is wholesome. Then the Blessed One, quelling the Sugata’s exhortation by saying, “I give you no counsel or instruction, you foolish man,” began this teaching. Its meaning should be understood in the manner already stated above.
Now, purifying the assembly’s conviction, he said, “In this matter, monks, I will question you,” and so forth.
All of that should be understood according to the method already stated below.
Now, in order to show that consciousness possesses conditions, the Buddha said: “Whatever, monks...,” and so forth.
Therein, “dependent on mind and mental objects” means dependent on the life-continuum mind together with the adverting consciousness and on mental objects belonging to the three planes of existence.
The phrase "dependent on wood," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of illustrating the simile. What does it demonstrate?

It demonstrates the absence of transition between doors. For just as a fire burning dependent on wood burns only when the condition of fuel is present, and in its absence—due to the deficiency of conditions—it is extinguished right there, rather than transitioning to splinters and so forth to be designated as "splinter-fire" and so on; [so too is the case with consciousness].

Just as that [light] does not go elsewhere, so too, the consciousness arisen in dependence upon the eye and visible forms arises only when its conditions—namely, the eye, visible forms, light, and attention—are present at that door;
when they are absent, it ceases right there due to the deficiency of conditions.
It does not migrate to the ear and other doors to receive the designation of "ear-consciousness" and so forth. This same principle applies to all instances.
Thus the Blessed One rebuked Sāti, saying: "I do not say that there is even a mere transference of the door in the occurrence of consciousness;
yet this misguided man Sāti speaks of a transference of existence.
Having thus shown the conditioned nature of consciousness, he now [addresses] the five aggregates as well.
Demonstrating its state of being conditioned (*sappaccaya*), he said, "This has come to be" (*bhūtam idam*), and so forth.

Therein, "this has come to be" means that this pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) is born, become, and produced. "And you, monks, see that this has come to be" means that you yourselves perceive it as such.
"Its origination is from nutriment" (*tadāhārasambhavam*) means that this pentad of aggregates originates from nutriment—that is, it originates from conditions; when there is a condition, it arises.
"See it thus," he asks. "With the cessation of its nutriment": with the cessation of its condition. "'Has this come to be, or has it not? means:
"Has this indeed come to be, or has it not come to be? "'Does it originate from the arising of that nutriment, or does it not? means:
"Does this aggregate-pentad that has come to be originate from the arising of its conditions, or does it not? "'With the cessation of that nutriment'": with the cessation of that condition...
"Subject to cessation": "Is it not subject to cessation? means: "Is this phenomenon indeed subject to cessation, or is it not? "Seeing with right wisdom":

this refers to one who sees correctly with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) the pentad of aggregates as they have arisen, come to be, and been produced, according to their actual nature and characteristics.
"Well seen with wisdom": it is well seen by the wisdom of insight in the manner already described.
Thus, by taking the acknowledgment from each of those who examined that question, he demonstrates the conditionality of the five aggregates.
Now, regarding the wisdom by which they have clearly seen that pentad of aggregates as conditioned and subject to cessation— therein:
Inquiring about the state of being free from craving, he said: "If this, O you... and so forth. Therein, "view" (*diṭṭhi*) refers to the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammā-diṭṭhi*).
It is purified by the seeing of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and cleansed by the seeing of conditions (*paccaya*).

"You might adhere" (*allīyetha*) means that you might dwell having adhered through craving and views. "You might cherish" (*kelāyetha*) means that you might dwell playing with craving and views. "You might treasure" (*dhanāyetha*)...
"Desiring wealth, you might fall into greed. 'You would make it yours' means you would produce a sense of ownership through craving and views.

'For the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping' means that this Dhamma, which I have taught as being like a raft for the purpose of crossing over the four floods, is not for the purpose of grasping out of attachment. Would you understand that? [He replied: "By way of contrast."
The bright side (sukkapaṅkha) is to be understood.
Now, in order to show the condition for those aggregates, he said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments," and so forth;
that too has the same meaning as what was already stated. Just as when one person is told, "Know this," [he might reply], "Not only this, but his mother as well..."
"I know even the mother of my mother"—knowing in this way by way of lineage is indeed what is meant by "knowing well.
In the same way, the Blessed One does not merely know the aggregates alone;
he knows the conditions for the aggregates, and the conditions for those conditions as well—thus he knows the entire succession of conditions. Now, demonstrating that power of a Buddha, [he says]:
In order to show the succession of conditions, he said, "And these, monks, are the four nutriments," and so forth. That has already been explained.

Thus, monks, "with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations... [and so on] ...there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering"—herein, however, the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) might be expanded upon; that has indeed been expanded upon in the *Visuddhimagga*.
404. "When this exists, that comes to be": when this condition, beginning with ignorance, exists, this result, beginning with volitional formations, comes to be.
"With the arising of this, that arises": with the arising of this condition, beginning with ignorance, this result, beginning with volitional formations, arises.
Therefore it was said: "That is to say, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]... and so forth."

“...there is an arising. Having thus shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he now spoke the passage beginning with “But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance,” in order to show the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).
In this context, “but with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance” means: “of ignorance alone indeed.

“With the remainderless cessation” means with the cessation through non-arising by means of the path known as fading away (*virāga*). “Cessation of volitional formations” means the cessation through non-arising of volitional formations.

Furthermore, in order to show that with the cessation of formations (*saṅkhāra*) thus ceased, there is the cessation of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and with the cessation of consciousness and the subsequent factors, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the rest are indeed ceased, it was said:

"With the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness," and so forth, concluding with, "Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In that context, the word "entire" (*kevala*) means:
The meaning is: of the whole, or of the pure, [that is], devoid of sentient beings (*sattavirahita*). "Of the mass of suffering" means of the heap of suffering.
"Cessation occurs" means non-arising occurs.
406. "When this is absent," etc., is to be understood by way of the opposite of what was previously stated.

407. Having thus explained the cycle of the world’s turning and its unturning, he now asks about the absence of that "running back and forth" which is abandoned by one who understands this twelvefold wheel of conditions together with insight and the path, saying:
"But do you, monks," and so forth. Therein, "knowing thus" means knowing thus together with insight and the path. Thus...
"Passantā" is a synonym for that very term. "Pubbaṇtaṃ" means the prior portion; the meaning is the past aggregates, elements, and bases.
"Paṭidhāveyyātha" means you would run back toward them by way of craving and views. The rest has already been explained in detail in the *Sabbāsava-sutta*.
Now, asking about their immovability therein: "Bhikkhus, knowing thus, would you..."
"Seeing it thus, you should say: 'The Teacher is our heavy burden,' and so forth. In this context, "heavy" (*garu*) means weighty;
one must follow him even against one's will. "Ascetic" (*samaṇa*) refers to the Buddha-ascetic. "You might point to another teacher" means:
"This Teacher is unable to accomplish our purpose"—would you, having such a perception, point to another external teacher?
"You should point them out. Regarding "many recluses and brahmins": having formed this perception, [point them out] as many sectarian recluses and brahmins.
Regarding "vows, superstitious practices, and auspicious rites": these are the undertaking of vows, superstitious views, and the auspicious rites based on what has been seen, heard, or thought.
"You should regard them as essential" means you should perceive these very things as being essential.
"Having offered it, you should return. The meaning is: "In this way, you should take back what was relinquished.
"Known by oneself" means known by one's own knowledge. "Seen by oneself" means seen by one's own eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
"Realized by oneself" means personally clarified, made manifest. "I have brought you [to this], monks"—by this, I have brought you, monks... [to this].
The meaning is that they have been led to, or brought to, Nibbāna by means of a Dhamma whose intrinsic nature is "visible here and now" (sanditthika) and so forth.

The meaning of "visible here and now" and the other terms has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "This was said with reference to this" means that this statement was spoken with reference to the fact that you yourselves have directly known it, and so on.

408. But why, monks, does he begin with "Of three"? One might ask: "Has not the teaching already been brought to its conclusion above by way of the round [of existence] and the unraveling of the round?
Yes, it has been brought to its conclusion. However, this is a separate connection [in the discourse]: "For this world-dwelling is deluded regarding rebirth-linking;
having destroyed that point of delusion, I shall make it clear"—it is for this reason that he gave this teaching.
He began [the discourse]. Furthermore, ignorance is the root of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and the arising of a Buddha is the root of the cessation of the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).

Having thus shown ignorance as the root of the cycle and the arising of a Buddha as the root of its cessation, he began this teaching with the thought: "Once more, I shall bring the teaching to its conclusion by way of both the cycle and its cessation.
In that context, "assemblies" (*sannipātā*) means by way of their being gathered together into a collective mass.
"Of the womb" means of the being who is to be born in the womb. "There is an entry" means there is a birth.
For in some instances, "womb" refers to the mother's belly, as it is said:
"The night in which the youth first dwells in the womb..."
“He goes as if already risen; having gone, he does not return.

In some contexts, this refers to a being born from a womb. As it is said: “But just as, Ānanda, other women give birth after carrying a fetus in their womb for nine or ten months,” here it is the [womb-born] being that is intended.
Referring to this, it was said: "There is the descent into the womb.
"Here" means in this world of sentient beings. "And the mother is in her season"—this was said with reference to the time of the fertile period.
