It is said that in whatever part of a woman's body a child is to be conceived, a large blood-blisters forms there, which then bursts.
It flows out; the physical basis (vatthu) becomes pure. When the physical basis is pure and the mother and father have come together once, for up to seven days it remains as a field (khetta).
At that time, a child is indeed produced even by the touching of the limbs, such as by grasping the hands or pulling the hair.
"Gandhabba" refers to the being who has arrived there. "Is present" means [not] for the mother and father...
One who stands nearby, observing the conjunction [of the elements], is said to be "present.
However, the intended meaning here is that, according to the *Kammayantayanīti*, a single being is destined to be reborn in that place.
"With great uncertainty" means with a profound doubt regarding life, such as: "Shall I remain free from illness, or shall it be my son? For this is blood.
"Monks," he said; for at that time, it is said, the blood of the maternal uncle, having reached that place, became pale due to affection for his son.
Therefore he spoke thus. "Vaṅkaka" refers to a small plough used as a toy by village children.
"Ghaṭikā" is called a game played with a short stick struck by a long stick. "Mokkhacika" is a game of tumbling in the air.
Or, taking a stick and placing it on the ground, one plays by turning it over from bottom to top;
this is what is meant. A *ciṅgulaka* is called a wheel made of palm leaves or similar materials that revolves when struck by the wind.
A *pattāḷhaka* is called a leaf-tube, with which people play by measuring sand and other substances. A *rathaka* is a small chariot.
A *dhanukampi* is simply a small bow. 409. *Sārajjati* means he arouses lust (*rāga*). *Byāpajjati* means he arouses ill will (*byāpāda*).

*Anupaṭṭhitakāyasatī* means body-mindfulness (*kāyasati*) regarding the body; the meaning is that he has not established it. *Parittaceto* means one whose mind is unwholesome (*akusalacitta*). Wherein for him...
"They are evil" means that he does not know or attain that attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) in which these [defilements] cease.
"Favoring and opposing" refers to both lust (*rāga*) and hatred (*dosa*). "He delights" means he delights by way of craving (*taṇhā*);
by way of craving alone, saying "Oh, what happiness! and so forth, he approves. "He remains clinging" means by means of the grasping of craving-clinging (*taṇhā-ajjhosāna*).
Having swallowed it and digested it, he grasps it. Whether it be pleasure or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, let him rejoice;
but how can one rejoice in pain? One who grasps it thinking, "I am suffering, this is my suffering," is said to rejoice.
"Delight arises" means craving arises. "That is clinging" means that very craving is called clinging in the sense of grasping. Of that...

“With clinging as condition, existence arises... [etc. ...thus there is an origin. This, indeed, was shown by the Blessed One once more as the wheel of conditions in its two connections and three summaries.
Now, in order to show the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), he said: “In this world, monks, a Tathāgata arises,” and so forth.
In this context, "one whose mind is immeasurable" means one who possesses an immeasurable, supramundane mind;

the meaning is: one who is endowed with the path-consciousness. "Bhikkhus, remember this teaching of mine in brief regarding liberation through the destruction of craving" means, bhikkhus, you should always [retain] this brief teaching of mine concerning liberation through the destruction of craving.
You should bear this in mind and not neglect it. For herein, the teaching is called "liberation" because it is the cause for the attainment of liberation.

Regarding the phrase "entangled in the great net of craving and the snare of craving": craving itself, in the sense of being interwoven, is called the "great net of craving," and in the sense of being joined together, it is called a "snare.
Thus, in this great net of craving and this snare of craving, [he bound] this monk Sāti.
"Maintain [him] as one who has put on the son of the fisherman. The meaning is: "Maintain him as one who has entered within and is included therein.
The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
[End of the] *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Mahāassapura Sutta: 415.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahāassapura Sutta. Therein, “among the Aṅgas” means the princes of the country named Aṅga.
The dwelling place of those people, even though it was but a single district, is called "Aṅga" by conventional usage;

thus, [the phrase] "in Aṅga" means in that district of Aṅga. Assapura is a market town (nigama) of the Aṅgas; it is a market town of the Aṅga district that has acquired the common designation of a city by the name Assapura.
The meaning is that [the Blessed One] dwelt there, having made that [town] his alms-residence village. "The Blessed One said this": this refers to [the words] "recluses..."
“Monks, people perceive you as ‘ascetics,’” he said, beginning with these words.
But why did he speak thus? It is said that in that town, the people were faithful and confident, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha;
they would praise even a newly ordained novice as if he were a senior elder of a hundred years’ standing.
Seeing the community of monks entering for alms in the morning, even those going to the fields with seed, ploughs, and so forth,
or entering the forest with axes and such tools, would set aside those implements and sweep the place where the community of monks was to sit—
whether it be a sitting hall, a pavilion, or the foot of a tree.
Having prepared seats, set out water for drinking free from dust, and seated the community of monks, they give them rice gruel, hard food, and other provisions;
then, having dismissed the community of monks once their meal is finished, they take those utensils and go to a field or a forest to perform their own work.
Even at the place of labor, there is no other talk for them but this.
There are none. The eight persons—the four who stand upon the paths and the four who abide in the fruits—are called the Noble Saṅgha.

They speak in praise of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha alone, saying: "They are endowed with such virtue, such conduct, and such practice; they are modest, amiable, and possessed of sublime qualities. Having returned from their places of work and finished their evening meal...
Whether sitting at their own doorways or having entered their bedchambers,
they spoke only in praise of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Seeing the profound devotion of those people, the Blessed One directed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to accept almsfood from them and said this:

"Those qualities that make one a recluse and those that make one a brahmin" means those qualities which, when undertaken and fulfilled, make one a *samaṇa* who has stilled evil and a *brāhmaṇa* who has banished evil.
"Bhikkhus, there are these three things for a recluse that are conducive to recluseship, the duties of a recluse.
Which three? The undertaking of the training in higher virtue, the undertaking of the training in higher mind, [and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom]."
In the phrase “the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom,” the duties to be performed by a recluse (*samaṇa*) are stated; these too indeed constitute the qualities that make one a recluse.
However, here the teaching is expanded upon by way of moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), and so forth.

In the expression “thus this is ours,” the word “not” (*no*) is a mere particle; the meaning is “thus this is ours. Both [the terms] “of great fruit” (*mahapphalā*) and “of great benefit” (*mahānisaṃsā*) [are used].
In meaning, they are one and the same. "Not barren" means not fruitless; "fruitful" is a synonym for that very same meaning.
For that which has no fruit is called barren. "With increase" means with growth; this is a synonym for being fruitful.
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves"—thus the Blessed One said.
By this much, he spoke in praise of such qualities as moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*). Why? For the purpose of cutting off the path of speech.
For if some foolish bhikkhu who had recently gone forth were to say, "The Blessed One says that one should live having undertaken the qualities of moral shame and dread of blame;
what, then, is the benefit in undertaking and living by them?"—it was for the purpose of cutting off his speech.
And this is the benefit: for when these qualities are undertaken and fulfilled, they make one a "recluse (samaṇa) who has stilled evil" and a "brahmin (brāhmaṇa) who has banished evil.

They produce the acquisition of the four requisites, bring about great fruitfulness for those who provide those requisites, and make the going-forth fruitful, productive, and glorious—thus he spoke in praise. This is the summary here.
In detail, however, the description of its qualities should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta].

416. By "conscience and shame" (*hirī-ottappa*): this refers to both conscience (*hirī*) and shame (*ottappa*), as detailed thus: "that which one feels shame for when there is a reason to feel shame, and that which one feels dread of when there is a reason to feel dread.
Furthermore, in this context, conscience originates from within oneself, while shame originates from without.

Moral dread (*ottappa*). Moral shame (*hirī*) has oneself as its governing principle; moral dread has the world as its governing principle. Moral shame is established on the nature of modesty; moral dread is established on the nature of fear.
Furthermore, a detailed exposition of these two in all their aspects is given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Moreover, these two states are called "states that protect the world" (*lokapāla-dhamma*) because they protect the world. As it is said:
“Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world. Which two? A sense of shame (*hirī*) and a sense of dread (*ottappa*).
These, monks, are the two bright qualities that protect the world.
If these two bright qualities did not protect the world, the designation ‘mother,’ ‘maternal aunt,’ or ‘uncle’s wife’ would not be known here.”

Or, [if one were to think], "She is the wife of a teacher" or "She is the spouse of venerable ones," the world would fall into confusion, just as it is with goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, dogs and jackals.
These very things are called "divine qualities" (*devadhamma*) in these Jātaka stories. As it is said:
"Endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, established in bright qualities..."
“Worthy and true men in the world are called ‘those who possess the divine nature.
This was shown by the Elder Mahācunda with reference to the practice of the effacement of defilements. As it is said:
“‘Others will be shameless, but we shall here be possessed of shame’—thus effacement should be practiced. Others will be lacking in moral dread...”
“Thinking, ‘There will be others here; we too shall be conscientious in this matter,’ one should practice effacement.
This is shown by taking it as the full acceptance of the Elder Mahākassapa’s exhortation. For it was said: “Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
‘Strong shame and fear of wrongdoing shall be established in me toward elders, novices, and those of middle standing. Thus indeed...”
“Kassapa, you should train in these. Here, however, these are shown as what are called the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Since, at this point, the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattha*) has reached its culmination, he spoke the passage beginning with “But it may be, monks, that for you...
in order to show other qualities that make one a recluse. In that context, the “goal of recluseship” is [explained] in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
To this extent, [the Blessed One said]: “And what, bhikkhus, is the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*)? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path. That is to say: right view … right concentration.
This, bhikkhus, is called the state of a recluse. And what, bhikkhus, is the goal of the state of a recluse (*sāmaññattha*)?
The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the goal of the state of a recluse.”
“The goal of recluseship”: the path is called “recluseship,” while the fruits and Nibbāna are called “the goal of recluseship.
However, it should be understood that in this context, the goal of recluseship is explained by taking both the path and the fruit together.
“I announce” means I speak; “I make known” means I cause [others] to understand.
417. Regarding the phrase "Our bodily conduct is purified": here, bodily conduct is twofold—purified and unpurified.
For a monk who kills living beings, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, his bodily conduct is called unpurified;
this is prohibited by way of the courses of kamma (*karmapatha*) alone. However, [that which is prohibited] by means of the hand or a clod of earth...
Or if one strikes or harms another with a staff or a weapon, that person’s bodily conduct is called impure;
this too is prohibited by the very bond of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

In this sutta, however, without mentioning either of these two, that which is called supreme effacement (*paramasallekha*) is taught. For when a monk [is present] while others are drinking water from a water-pot or from bowls...
Or, when crows are eating food, if one raises a hand, a staff, or a clod of earth to drive them away, his bodily conduct is impure.
The opposite is called pure. "Exposed" (*uttāno*) means elevated and manifest.
"Open" (*vivaṭo*) means uncovered and unshielded. By both terms, he illuminates purity itself. And "without cracks" (*na ca chiddavā*)—
"Always the same" means being without gaps at intervals. "Restrained" means having closed the doors to the defilements by closing them off, not for the purpose of concealing faults.
418. Regarding verbal conduct as well:
a bhikkhu who speaks falsely, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, or engages in idle chatter...
He prattles; his verbal conduct is called "impure. This, however, is prohibited by way of the courses of kamma (*kammappatha*).
But he who speaks disparagingly using such terms as "householder," "slave," or "servant," his verbal conduct is called "impure.
This, however, is forbidden specifically by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). In this sutta, both of these [types of speech] are addressed.
Without speaking, that which is called "the supreme scraping away" (paramasallekha) was described.
For instance, when a young bhikkhu or a novice says, "Venerable sir, have you seen our preceptor?", [if one replies], "Friends, many bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs were wandering in one place;
your preceptor must have gone away after picking up a bundle of vegetables for sale," and so forth.
Even one who intends it as a joke speaks such words according to this method; his verbal conduct is thus impure. The opposite is called pure. 419. Regarding mental conduct:
if a bhikkhu is covetous, ill-willed, or holds wrong view, his mental conduct is called impure.
This, however, is prohibited specifically by way of the courses of action (*kammappatha*). But as for that which is placed nearby...
If one accepts gold and silver, one’s mental conduct is called impure. This too is prohibited by the very bond of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
In this sutta, however, without mentioning either of these two, that which is called "the supreme effacement" (*paramasallekha*) is taught.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu who thinks thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of cruelty—his...
The mental conduct is impure. The opposite is called pure.

420. Regarding livelihood: that monk who, for the sake of livelihood, practices medical treatment, acts as a messenger, performs incisions on boils, applies ointments to wounds, or prepares medicinal oils—thus maintains his life by means of the twenty-one kinds of wrong search. Or again, whoever...
If one eats after having requested [these things], one's livelihood is called impure.

This, however, is prohibited specifically by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). In this sutta, without mentioning either of these two, that which is called "supreme effacement" (*paramasallekha*) is taught.
For when a bhikkhu has obtained ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, thinking, "I shall eat them tomorrow or the day after," [he does not consume them].

He consumes what has been stored up; or else, having seen neem sprouts and the like, he says to the novices, "Eat the sprouts," and the novices, thinking, "The elder wishes to eat," prepare them as *kappiya* (permissible) and give them to him;
or he says to the young novices, "Drink water, friends," and they, thinking, "The elder wishes to drink water," wash the water-jar...
If one uses even such things [as teeth], one's livelihood is called impure; the opposite is called pure.
422. "One who knows moderation": one who knows moderation, what is appropriate, and the proper measure in seeking, receiving, and using. 423. "Devoted to wakefulness":
having divided the night and day into six parts, [one who does not sleep] in even one of those parts.
Having granted the opportunity, they were devoted and intent upon the five portions of wakefulness.
Regarding the "lion’s posture": here there are four postures—the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, the posture of the hungry ghosts, the lion’s posture, and the posture of the Tathāgata.

Among these, “for the most part, bhikkhus, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side”—this is the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures; for among them, for the most part, there is no one who lies on the right side.

“Monks, for the most part, the hungry ghosts (petas) lie on their backs”—this is the posture of the hungry ghosts; for because they have little flesh and blood, being bound together by a mass of bones, they are unable to lie on one side and thus lie only on their backs.
“Monks, for the most part, Sīha, the king of beasts, lies on his right side with his tail tucked between his thighs”—this is the lion’s posture (sīhaseyyā).
For because of his preponderance of fiery energy (tejo), Sīha, the king of beasts, [places] his two forefeet upon one [thigh].

Having placed one hind foot in its proper position and inserted the tail into the space between the thighs, he lies down after noting the positions where the toes of both the front and hind feet rest, placing his head upon the tops of his two front feet.
Even when waking after having slept for a whole day, he does not wake with alarm; rather, he raises his head and [looks at] his front feet.

He observes the space where he stands. If he finds that he has left some spot, he becomes displeased, thinking, "This is not worthy of your birth nor of your courageous nature," and lies down right there instead of setting out for his almsround.
But if he finds that he has not left it, he is joyful and elated, thinking, "This is worthy of your birth and your courageous nature."
Having risen and stretched like a lion, shaken its mane, and roared the lion’s roar three times, it sets out for its prey.
However, the posture of the fourth jhāna is called the "Tathāgata-posture.
Of these, the lion-posture is the one mentioned here. For this is indeed called the supreme posture because of its fiery (majestic) physical bearing. "Foot upon foot... [etc.]
"Placing the left foot upon the right foot": *accādhāya* means having placed it over, having set it down slightly beyond [the other].
For when the ankle touches the ankle, or the knee the knee, pain arises frequently;
the mind does not become one-pointed, and the bed becomes uncomfortable. However, when it is placed so as not to touch [the other], in that way...
Feeling does not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the bed becomes comfortable; therefore, he spoke thus. 425.
"He looks upon the world with covetousness," and so forth, is explained in detail in the *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta*. 426.
As for this simile that was spoken, beginning with "Just as if, monks": therein, "having taken a loan" means [for the sake of] interest.
"Having taken the wealth": "Byantīkareyya" means he should make it free from its end (*vigatanta*).
He should act in such a way that not even a mere *kākaṇika* coin remains as their limit; the meaning is that he should completely discharge it.
"On that account" (*tatonidānaṃ*) means on account of freedom from debt. For when he reflects, "I am debt-free," he obtains powerful gladness (*pāmojja*) and attains powerful joy (*somanassa*).
Therefore it was said: “He would find gladness; he would attain joy.
Because he afflicts the four postures as if cutting them with a saw by the arising of discordant feelings, it is called *ābādha* (affliction);
one who has this is *ābādhika* (afflicted). He is pained by the suffering originating from that. “Severely ill” means gravely ill.
“Would not delight him” means it would not be pleasing to him because he is overwhelmed by a severe illness. “Strength” means simply strength;
the meaning is that there would be no strength in his body. “On that account” refers to the cause of health, for when one reflects, “I am healthy,” both of those things [delight and joy] arise.
Therefore it was said: “He might find delight, he might attain gladness. Not...
“*Cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo*” means that there would not be even a single *kākaṇika*-worth of loss of wealth.
“*Tatonidānan*” means on account of imprisonment; the rest should be applied to all the terms in the manner already explained.
“*Anattādhīno*” means not dependent upon oneself; one does not obtain the freedom to do whatever one pleases. “*Parādhīno*” means dependent upon others.
He proceeds solely according to another’s will. "Not going where he desires" means that in whichever direction his desire arises for travel, he does not obtain the opportunity to go there.
"From slavery" means from the state of being a slave. "A free man" means one who is his own master.
"On that account" means on account of being a free man. "A desert road" means a wilderness path.
"Waterless long road" means a long journey without water. "On that account" means on account of the ground of safety (*khemantabhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase "when these five hindrances are not abandoned," here the Blessed One shows that the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) when unabandoned is like a debt, while the remaining ones are like diseases and so forth.
In this regard, the similarity is as follows: for one who has taken a loan from others...

He destroys it. Even when told by those people, "Pay the debt," even when spoken to harshly, even when being bound, and even when being struck, he is unable to resist anything at all; he endures it all, for that debt is the cause of his endurance.
In the same way, whoever is lustful toward something through sensual desire and grasps that object with a mass of craving, he—by means of that—[is destroyed].
Even when being spoken to harshly, being bound, or being struck, he endures it all.
For his reason for enduring is sensual desire, just as in the case of women who are being killed by their husbands. Thus, sensual desire should be regarded as being like a debt.
Just as a person afflicted with a bile disease does not perceive the taste of honey, sugar, and the like even when they are given to him,

but instead vomits them out, thinking, "They are bitter, they are bitter," so too, one whose mind is corrupted does not accept even a slight instruction when being exhorted by preceptors and teachers who desire his welfare; rather, he says things such as, "You are harassing me excessively."

Having said this, he departs. Just as that man, due to being afflicted by a bile disease, does not experience the flavor of honey, sugar, and other such things, so too one who is afflicted by anger does not experience the flavor of the Dispensation, consisting of the various forms of meditative bliss and so forth. Thus, ill will (byāpāda) should be regarded as a disease.
Furthermore, just as a man bound in a prison on a festival day [does not enjoy] even the beginning of the festival...
He does not see the middle, nor the end. On the second day, having been released, even when he hears such things as, "Oh, what a delightful constellation last night!
Oh, what dancing! Oh, what singing! he gives no reply. For what reason? Because he did not experience the constellation.
In the same way, a bhikkhu overcome by sloth and torpor [gives no response] even while a discourse on the Dhamma is being delivered in various ways.
He knows neither its beginning, nor its middle, nor its end.
Even when he hears those who, after the teaching has been concluded, speak in praise of the Dhamma-savana, saying, "Oh, what a Dhamma-savana! Oh, what a reason!
Oh, what a simile!", he does not give them a reply. Why is that? Because, due to sloth and torpor, he did not experience the discourse on the Dhamma.
In this way, sloth and torpor should be regarded as a prison house.
Just as a slave, even while playing at a festival, might be told: "There is an urgent task that must be done;
go there quickly! If you do not go, I shall cut off your hands and feet, or your ears and nose."
It passes away so quickly that one has no opportunity to experience the beginning, middle, or end of the constellation.

Why? Because of dependence on others. In the same way, even for one who has entered the forest for the sake of seclusion but lacks gratitude toward the Vinaya, if the perception of "unallowable meat" arises regarding some kind of meat—even if it is allowable meat—they abandon seclusion and [return] for the sake of purifying their virtue.
One must go into the presence of a master of the Vinaya; one does not obtain the experience of the bliss of seclusion. Why?
Because of being overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*). Thus, restlessness and remorse should be regarded as a form of slavery.
Furthermore, it is like a man traveling on a long desert road who encounters robbers who have plundered people and created an opportunity for violence.
Seeing even the sound of a staff or the cry of a bird, he becomes suspicious and apprehensive, thinking, "Thieves have arrived.
He goes forward, he stops, and he turns back; the place where he has come from is more often the place where he has gone.
With great difficulty and hardship, he may reach a land of safety, or he may not reach it at all. In the same way, for one who [is thus] in the eight situations...
Doubt arises in him. Doubting in such a manner as, "Is he a Buddha or is he not a Buddha?", he is unable to resolve his mind and grasp [the truth] through faith.

Being unable to do so, he does not attain either the path or the fruit—just as one who, on a long journey through a wilderness, repeatedly looks back and forth, wondering "Are there robbers or not?", fails to penetrate [the way].

Just as the state of being startled (*chambhitatta*) arising in the mind creates an obstacle to reaching a place of safety, so too does doubt—arousing a state of being startled in the mind through repeated shifting and wavering and a lack of penetration in the manner of "Is he a Buddha or not a Buddha?
and so forth—create an obstacle to attaining the plane of the Noble Ones; thus it should be regarded as like a road through a wilderness.

Now, monks, just as with the phrase "freedom from debt," here the Blessed One shows that the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), when abandoned, is like freedom from debt, while the remaining [hindrances] are like health and so forth.
In this regard, the similarity is as follows: suppose a man, having taken a loan and applied it to his work, finds his enterprise successful;
he then reflects, "This debt is indeed a root of bondage," and [repays] it together with the interest.
Having paid off the debt, he would have the document torn up. From that time on, no one would send him a messenger nor a letter;
even when seeing his creditors, if he wished, he would rise from his seat, but if he did not wish, he would not rise.
Why? Because of his lack of attachment and non-clinging toward them. In the same way, a bhikkhu [reflects]: "This is what is called sensual desire..."
Regarding the "root of obstacles": by developing the six factors in the manner taught in the *Satipaṭṭhāna*, one abandons the hindrance of sensual desire.

For one who has thus abandoned sensual desire, just as a man freed from debt feels neither fear nor trepidation upon seeing his creditors, so too he feels neither attachment nor bondage toward the property of others.
Even when one sees divine forms, defilement does not arise. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of sensual desire as being like freedom from debt.
Just as that man afflicted with a bile disease, having pacified that illness through medical treatment, experiences the taste of honey, sugar, and other such things from then on;
even so, the bhikkhu [reflects]: "This ill will is indeed a bringer of harm."
By developing six qualities, one abandons the hindrance of ill will.

Having thus abandoned ill will, just as a person freed from a bile disease partakes with relish of sweet things such as honey and sugar, even so, when being trained in the rules of conduct and other precepts, he accepts them with his head bowed and trains with relish. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of ill will as being like health.
Just as that man who was imprisoned on a festival day, thinking on another festival day,
"Previously I was bound through the fault of negligence and did not enjoy that festival;
now I shall be heedful," ensures that his enemies find no opportunity— so too, having become heedful and enjoyed the festival, [he does not fall back].

—“Oh, what a festival! Oh, what a festival! he exclaimed with a cry of joy. In the same way, bhikkhu, by developing six qualities and thinking, “This sloth and torpor is indeed a great cause of harm,” one abandons the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
Having thus abandoned sloth and torpor, just as a man released from bondage might, for seven days, [observe] the beginning, middle, and end of a festival, so too...
He experiences it. In the same way, a bhikkhu who experiences the beginning, middle, and end of the "Dhamma-constellation" attains arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of sloth and torpor as being like liberation from bondage.
Just as a slave, by relying on some friend and giving wealth to his masters, makes himself free;

Having done so, from that time forth he may do whatever he wishes. In the same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, "This restlessness and remorse are indeed productive of great harm," develops six qualities and abandons restlessness and remorse.
Having thus abandoned restlessness and remorse, he does whatever he wishes, just as a person who is his own master does whatever he wishes; no one [can stop him].
Just as one turns back from something by force, even so, when a bhikkhu practices the way of renunciation according to his pleasure,
restlessness and remorse do not turn him back from it by force. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of restlessness and remorse as being like that of a free man.
Just as a strong man, taking hold of the essentials of his hand, equipped with weapons, and accompanied by a retinue, might set out upon a wilderness;

and seeing him from afar, the bandits would flee; and having safely crossed that wilderness, he would reach a place of safety and be glad and joyful—just so, a bhikkhu [should reflect]: "This thing called doubt is a bringer of harm."
Having developed six qualities, one abandons doubt. Having thus abandoned doubt,
just as a strong man equipped with weapons and accompanied by a retinue emerges safely and reaches a land of security, disregarding bandits as if they were mere grass,
even so, having crossed the wilderness of misconduct, one reaches the supreme land of security, the deathless Nibbāna.
One attains [suffering]. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of doubt as being like reaching a land of safety (*khemantabhūmi*).
427. "This very body" refers to this body born of karma. "It moistens" means it drenches or lubricates; it produces the joy and happiness that occur everywhere.
"It permeates" means it flows all around. "It fills" means it fills it like a bellows with air.
"Parippharati" means it pervades all around. "Of the entire body" means of that bhikkhu’s body, including all its parts.

There is not even a minute spot in any location where the continuity of the acquired [body] proceeds—such as where the skin, flesh, and blood are found—that is not touched by the happiness of the first jhāna.
"Dakkho" means clever, capable, or skilled in [preparing] bath-powders.
To prepare, to mix, and to knead. "In a bronze bowl" means in a vessel made of any metal whatsoever. A clay vessel, however, is not durable;
it would break while one is kneading, and therefore that is not mentioned. "Sprinkling repeatedly" means sprinkling again and again.
"One should knead" means taking the bronze bowl with the left hand and [kneading] with the right hand.
Having sprinkled water in the proper measure again and again, one should knead it while rubbing it together.
"Followed by moisture" means followed by the moisture of water. "Pervaded by moisture" means completely permeated by the moisture of water.
"Internally and externally" means together with both the internal part and the external part; the meaning is that it is entirely suffused with the moisture of water on every side. Not...
"And dripping" means that water drips drop by drop; it can be caught with one hand, or with two, or with three fingers, and even rubbed [into the skin]—this is the meaning. 428.
In the simile for the happiness of the second jhāna, "with water welling up" means with water that has welled up; it does not mean having welled up from below.
"Water rising up" means water that breaks forth from within. "The mouth of the stream" means the path by which it comes.
"A god" means a cloud. "From time to time" means at various times; the meaning is either every half-month or every ten days. "Showers" means rain.
"Should not pour down" means should not enter [the lake], should not rain; this is the meaning. "Cold showers of water breaking forth."
The cool water, filling that lake, breaks forth by welling up. For the water rising from below, as it rises higher and higher, agitates the water;
the water entering from the four directions agitates the water with old leaves, grass, sticks, poles, and so forth;
the rainwater agitates the water with the falling of its streams and bubbles. It remains just as it is.
But having become [the water], as it arises like a manifestation of psychic power (iddhi-nimmita), there is no such thing as saying "this area is pervaded by the water" or "this area is not pervaded.
Therefore, there is no such thing as an unpervaded space. In this context, the physical body (karaja-kāya) is like the lake, and the bliss of the second jhāna is like the water.
The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
429. In this simile for the bliss of the third jhāna: it is called *uppalinī* because there are water lilies (*uppala*) here.
The same method applies to the other two terms as well. And herein, among the white, red, and blue varieties, any kind of water lily is simply an *uppala*;

a hundred-petaled white one is a *puṇḍarīka*, while a hundred-petaled [red] one is a *paduma*. Or, even without restricting the number of petals, a white one is a *paduma* and a red one is a *puṇḍarīka*.

This is the analysis here. "Not emerged from the water" means they have not risen out of the water. "Growing submerged within the water" means they grow while remaining submerged within the surface of the water;
the meaning is that they increase. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before. 430.
In the simile for the bliss of the fourth jhāna, regarding the phrase "with a mind that is purified and cleansed," it is in the sense of being free from defilements (*nirupakkilesa*).
It is pure. It should be understood as "brightly radiant" in the sense of luminosity. "With a white cloth"—this is said for the purpose of providing warmth.
For with a soiled cloth there is no provision of warmth; however, with one that is washed clean and pure at that moment, the provision of warmth is powerful.
In this simile, the cloth is like the physical body composed of the four great elements (*karaja-kāya*). The provision of warmth is like the bliss of the fourth jhāna.

Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: just as when a well-washed man sits with a pure cloth draped over his head, the bodily heat pervades the entire cloth so that there is no part of it not touched by it;
even so, no part of the bhikkhu’s material body remains untouched by the bliss of the fourth jhāna. It is the mind of the fourth jhāna itself [that pervades it].
Or it is like a cloth and the temperature that originates from it, which permeates it.
For just as, even when a white cloth does not actually touch the body in some places, the body is nevertheless touched everywhere by the temperature originating from that cloth;
so too, the bhikkhu’s physical body is touched everywhere by the subtle matter originated by the fourth jhāna.
"Occurs"—thus should the meaning be understood here.

431. In the simile for the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), the actions performed on that very day are manifest; therefore, only the three villages visited on that day are taken as the example.
Therein, the person who has gone to the three villages is to be seen as one who has attained the knowledge of past lives. The three villages are...

The three states of existence (bhava) should be understood as being like those [three villages]. Just as the deeds performed by that man during that day in the three villages become manifest, so too should the deeds performed in the three states of existence be understood to become manifest for the monk who sits having directed his mind toward past lives (pubbenivāsa).
In the simile of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), "two houses" means two dwellings. "With six doors" means with front doors. "While walking back and forth" means...

“They wander from one to another. “Wandering about” means wandering here and there; furthermore, it should be understood as entering this house after departing from that house, or departing from this house after entering that house.
In this context, the two houses with their doors are like death and rebirth-linking; the man with eyes is like one who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye. For one with eyes...

Just as it is clear to a man standing between two houses while he watches the people entering and leaving those two dwellings, so too is it clear to one who possesses the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) when he gazes with increased light upon beings passing away and being reborn.
But are they clear to the knowledge (ñāṇa) or to the person (puggala)? They are clear to the knowledge. And because they are clear to that [knowledge],...
[This] is indeed manifest to the person. 433.
In the simile for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*), "summit of the mountain" (*pabbatamatthake*) means on the peak of a mountain.

"Unstirred" (*anāvila*) means free from mud. "Oysters and shells" (*sippisambuka*) is a compound of oysters and shells. "Gravel and pebbles" (*sakkharakathala*) is a compound of gravel and pebbles. [And] of fish...
A shoal of fish is like a mass of fish. Regarding the phrase "whether standing or moving": here, gravel and pebbles remain stationary;

the others, however, both move and remain stationary. Just as when cows are found standing or sitting at intervals, yet because those that are moving are taken as the reference, the others are also said to be "moving," so too [it is with] that which is merely standing.
It is said that, taking the pebble and the stone as a basis, the other two also remain; and taking the other two as moving, the pebble and the stone are also said to move.
In this context, it is like the time when a man with sight, standing on the bank and looking, clearly perceives the shells, snails, and so forth;
likewise for one who has directed the mind toward the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) and is sitting [in meditation].
The time when a bhikkhu has made the four truths manifest should be understood.
Now, taking up the name of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) according to its characteristics and qualities through seven aspects, [the Blessed One] said:
"This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is a recluse (*samaṇa*)," and so forth. Therein, "In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a recluse."
Regarding the passage beginning with "he is," monks: a bhikkhu is a *samaṇa* because he has stilled evil; he is a *brāhmaṇa* because he has banished evil;
he is a *nhātaka* because he has washed away the defilements—the meaning being that he has cleansed the defilements.

He is a *vedagu* because he has gone to the end of unwholesome states by means of the knowledges consisting of the four paths—the meaning being that they have been fully understood. By that very [knowledge], they have been understood by him...
He says, "They are," and so forth. One is a *sottiya* because of having heard (*sutatta*) the defilements; the meaning is that they have been heard [of] and thus destroyed (*apahata*).

One is a *ariya* because of being far from (*ārakatta*) the defilements; the meaning is that they have been slain. One is an *arahant* because of being far from (*ārakatta*) them; the meaning is that one has become distant from them. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Mahāassapura Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, within the Papañcasūdanī, is completed. 10.
The commentary on the Cūḷaassapura Sutta.

435. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ*... thus begins the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta. The reason for its teaching is the same as before. *Samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadā* means the practice appropriate for recluses, the practice in conformity with recluses.
436. Regarding the phrases *samaṇamala* (stains of the recluse) and so forth: when these states arise, they make the recluse stained and defiled; therefore, they are called "stains of the recluse.
By means of these, recluses become corrupted and fall into wrongdoing; therefore, they are called "faults of the recluse."
They are so called because, having arisen, they make ascetics bitter, devoid of essence, and wither them; therefore, they are called "ascetic-dregs" (*samaṇakasaṭa*).
"Bases for those bound for states of loss" means the causes that produce rebirth in the miserable realms (*apāya*).

"Conditions for experiencing a bad destination" means the conditions for the ripening-feeling (*vipākavedanā*) in a state of misery. "That which is born of death" means that humans [use] sharp iron...
Having finely ground that iron powder, they mix it with meat and feed it to herons.
Unable to pass excrement, they die. If they do not die, they kill them by beating them.
Then, having slit open their bellies, they wash them with water, take the powder, mix it again with meat, and feed it to them once more—in this manner...
Having had it eaten seven times, they fashion a weapon from the iron filings thus obtained. Well-trained smiths, having received a large fee for their manual labor, manufacture it.
Because it is produced from the flesh of a dead bird, it is called "dead-bird iron" (*mataja*); it is exceedingly sharp.
"Yellow-sharpened" (*pītanisita*) means both soaked in water and well-polished on a whetstone. "With the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭiyā*)—
*Kosiyā*: "Sampārutaṃ" means covered; "sampaliveṭhitaṃ" means wrapped all around. 437. *Rajojallikassa*:
one who wears dust and dirt. *Udakorohakassa*: one who descends into water three times a day.
*Rukkhamūlikassa*: one who dwells at the foot of a tree. *Abbhokāsikassa*: one who dwells in the open air.
"Of one who stands up" means of one who remains standing. "Of one who eats by turns" means of one who eats according to a monthly or half-monthly rotation.
All of this is spoken according to the external tradition (the forest-dwelling sect).
For in this teaching (the Theravāda), a monk wearing a robe is not called a *saṅghāṭika* (one who wears the outer robe). Practices such as bearing dust and dirt do not exist at all in this teaching.
The word of the Buddha is called only "the word of the Buddha" (buddhavacana), not "a mantra. However, one may only be designated as a "tree-root dweller" or a "dweller in the open air.
Even that [designation] is spoken according to the external tradition (bāhirasamaya).
"As soon as born" means on the very day he was born. "One should make him wear a saṅghāṭī" means having dressed him in and covered him with a saṅghāṭī robe.
They would do so. This method applies everywhere.
"He regards himself as purified" means he sees himself being purified; however, he cannot yet be called "purified.
"Gladness arises" means a state of satisfaction arises. "In one who is glad, rapture [arises]" means in one who is satisfied...
Rapture arises, shaking the entire body. "The body of one whose mind is rapturous" refers to the mental body (nāmakāya) of a person associated with rapture.
"It becomes tranquil" means it becomes free from distress. "He experiences pleasure" means he experiences both bodily and mental pleasure.
"The mind becomes concentrated" means that the mind of one who is gratified by this pleasure of renunciation becomes concentrated.

It becomes as if it has reached absorption (*appanā*). With the thought "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena cetasā*), the teaching initiated below concerning the defilements descends, like rain falling on a mountain, into the development of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) according to its proper sequence.
Whatever needs to be said regarding that has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Just as if, monks, there were a lotus pond... (*Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pokkharaṇī*...).
In the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the path was compared to a lotus pond; here, it should be understood that the Dispensation (sāsana) is compared [to it].
"One becomes a recluse through the destruction of the taints" means that because all defilements have been stilled, one becomes a recluse in the ultimate sense.
The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is completed.
5. The Shorter Twin Section (Cūḷayamakavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Sāleyyaka Sutta (Sāleyyakasuttavaṇṇanā) 439.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Sāleyyaka Sutta. Regarding the phrase "among the Kosalans": the Kosalans were the princes of the realm.
The country where they dwell is called “Kosala” by way of conventional usage, even though it is but a single district; [the Buddha spoke] in that Kosala country.

However, the ancients say: because in the past, having heard that Prince Mahāpanāda did not even so much as smile after seeing various theatrical performances, the king said, “Whoever makes my son laugh, him I shall adorn with every ornament.”

Then, when the great multitude had gathered even after the ploughs had been abandoned, the people were unable to make him laugh by performing various entertainments for more than seven years. Thereupon, Sakka dispatched a celestial dancer;
he made them laugh by displaying a divine performance. Then those people turned toward their respective places of residence.
They departed. On their way back, seeing friends, relatives, and others on the opposite path, they exchanged greetings and said, "Is it well with you, sir?
Is it well with you, sir? Therefore, because of that expression "well, well" (*kusala*, *kusala*), that region is called Kosala.

"Wandering on a journey" means wandering on a journey without haste. "Together with a great community of bhikkhus" means together with a great community of bhikkhus that is not limited [in number], such as one hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand.
"A brahmin village" is called a "brahmin village" whether it is a village where brahmins have gathered or a village belonging to brahmins.
Here, a village of assembly is intended. "He arrived there" means he reached it; the sense is that he had arrived. However, the monastery here is unspecified;
therefore, it should be understood that not far from it there will be a certain grove suitable for the Buddhas, and the Teacher went to that grove.
"They heard" means they listened or perceived, following the sound of the speech that had reached the door of their ears.
They knew. *Kho* is a particle used for emphasis or as a mere filler to complete the meter.
In this context, it should be understood that through its sense of emphasis, the meaning is: "They indeed heard; there was no obstacle whatsoever to their hearing.
Through its function as a filler, it serves merely to provide elegance of expression (*byañjana-siliṭṭhatā*).
Now, in order to reveal the matter they had heard, it was said: "The ascetic, indeed, sirs, Gotama... and so forth.
Therein, he should be understood as an "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) because of his having stilled evil. "Indeed" (*khalu*) is a particle used in the sense of tradition or hearsay.
"Sirs" (*bho*) is merely a form of mutual address among them. "Gotama" is a designation of the Blessed One by way of his clan. Therefore: "The ascetic, indeed, sirs..."
Regarding the term "Gotama," the meaning here should be understood as: "O sir, this ascetic is of the Gotama clan.

"Son of the Sakyas" (Sakyaputta) is an indication of the Blessed One’s high birth. "One who has gone forth from the Sakya clan" (Sakyakulā pabbajito) is an illustration of his having gone forth out of faith.
It shows that he went forth out of faith, abandoning that very clan while it was still undiminished and not overcome by any loss.
This has been said. What follows merely explains the meaning already stated. "Taṃ kho pana" (but as for that) is used in the sense of specifying a particular state;
the meaning is: "of that venerable Gotama. "Kalyāṇa" means endowed with excellent qualities; "supreme" is what is meant.
"Kittisadda" refers to fame itself, or the sound of praise. "Abbhuggata" means having spread throughout the world including the devas.

Having overwhelmed [all other qualities], he has risen up. How so? “Such indeed is that Blessed One... [as before] ...the Buddha, the Blessed One. Herein, this is the connection of the words: “That Blessed One is such-and-such an Arahant, such-and-such a Fully Enlightened One...

[as before] ...such-and-such a Blessed One. This means: “For this and that reason. In that context, because of being far removed (*ārakatta*), because of the enemies (*arīnaṃ*) and because of the spokes (*arānaṃ*)... [etc.]

Having established the outline by way of such reasons as "because he has struck down [the defilements]," "because he is worthy of the requisites and so forth," and "because he is devoid of (rahābhāva) the performance of evil," all these terms have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha;
therefore, their detailed exposition should be taken from there.
“Sādhu kho panā” means “it is indeed excellent”; it is said to be conducive to welfare and conducive to happiness.

“Of such Arahants” refers to those like the venerable Gotama—such persons whose sight is difficult to obtain even in hundreds of thousands of millions of aeons, who are encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, and who are adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two supreme marks of a Great Man.

Of the Arahants—whose bodies are beautiful and well-proportioned, whose appearance is never tiring to behold, whose voices are exceedingly sweet as they proclaim the Dhamma, and who have acquired the title "Arahant" in the world through the realization of qualities exactly as they are—to see them is good; for even a mere glance, having opened eyes that are serene with faith, is beneficial.
Moreover, if one hears the Dhamma with a Brahma-voice endowed with the eight factors...

Having formed the aspiration, "If we can hear even a single word as he descends, it will be even better," they approached the Blessed One with joyful minds, having abandoned all their duties. They said this to him:
for there are two kinds of questions—questions of householders and questions of those who have gone forth. In that regard: "What, venerable sir, is wholesome?"... [and so on].

By the method of the question, "What is unwholesome? the inquiry of the householder is introduced. By the method of the statement, "Venerable sir, these are the five aggregates of clinging," the inquiry of the homeless one is introduced.
However, asking a question as a householder suited to their own status, they spoke these words:
"What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason... To them, the Blessed One [spoke] as follows:
They were unable to discern [the meaning]. Thus, answering the question in brief for the time being, he said: "Householders, it is because of unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct," and so forth.
But why did the Blessed One answer in such a way that they could not discern it? For they imagined themselves to be wise;
had the meaning been explained in detail from the very beginning without establishing the matrix (*mātikā*), they would have discerned it accordingly.
Thinking that the teaching was superficial, they despised it; they became speakers who said, "We too, when speaking, would speak in exactly this way.
Therefore, so that they would not be able to discern [the depth], the Blessed One answered the question very briefly for the time being.
Then, when those who could not discern it requested an exposition in detail, he [taught] in detail.
In order to teach [this], he said, "Therefore, householders," and so forth. Therein, "therefore" (*tena hi*) is a particle used in the sense of a reason;
the meaning is: "because you entreat me. 440.
"Threefold" means by way of three parts. "By body" means by way of the bodily door. "Unrighteous conduct and immoral conduct" (*adhammacariyā-visamacariyā*).

"Unrighteous conduct" (*adhammacariyā*) refers to uneven conduct (*visamacariyā*). Herein, the meaning of the words is as follows: "conduct that is unrighteous" (*adhammassa cariyā*) is "unrighteous conduct";
the meaning is "the performance of what is unrighteous. It is "uneven conduct," or "the conduct of an uneven action," thus it is "uneven conduct.
Since it is both unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, it is called "unrighteous and uneven conduct. By this same method, [the term is applied] to all [the following].
The meaning should be understood according to the black and white categories. "Cruel" means harsh. "Fierce" means violent.
"Blood-stained hands" means that when one deprives another of life, their hands become smeared with blood;
even if they do not actually become smeared, such a person is still called "one with blood-stained hands. "Devoted to killing and striking" means devoted to killing others and dealing blows.
"And intent on killing another" means being engaged in the act of taking another's life. "Having become devoid of compassion" means having fallen into a state of mercilessness.

"That which belongs to another" means that which is the property of another. "The wealth and requisites of another" means the wealth and personal belongings belonging to that very other person—those articles of equipment that produce satisfaction.
"Whether it has gone to a village" means whether it has been placed within a village.
"Or what has gone into the forest" means placed in the forest, on the tops of trees, on mountain peaks, and so forth.
"Not given" means not given by those others either by body or by speech. "Characterized as theft": here, *theno* means a thief.
The state of being a thief is *theyya*; this is a designation for the mind of one who intends to take away. *Saṅkhā* and *saṅkhāta* are identical in meaning.
This is a designation for a "constituent" (*koṭṭhāsa*), as in such passages as, "For conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) and reckoning (*saṅkhā*) have their source in perception" (*saññānidānā*).
It is called "reckoned as theft" (*theyyasaṅkhāta*) because it is both theft and reckoned; the meaning is that it is a single constituent of consciousness reckoned as a mind of theft.
And this nominative case ending is used in the sense of the instrumental; therefore, it should be understood in meaning as "by what is reckoned as theft."

Regarding the terms beginning with *māturakkhitā* (protected by her mother): she who, when her father is lost or dead, is looked after by her mother with food, clothing, and so forth, [with the thought] "I shall give her to a family home once she has reached marriageable age"—she is called *māturakkhitā*.

By this same method, those protected by their fathers (*piturakkhitā*) and others should also be understood. Furthermore, among families of similar status, an agreement is made even regarding pregnancies in the womb.
They say: “If I have a son, she shall be your daughter; she may not go elsewhere, let her belong to my son alone.

Thus, even while pregnant, she is called one who has a husband (*sassāmikā*). Furthermore, there are those for whom a penalty has been established with reference to a specific village, house, or street, such as: “Whoever approaches a woman named so-and-so, his punishment shall be this much.”

But those who are "with a protective guard" (saparidaṇḍā) means: even if she is merely encircled by a string of garlands—meaning, at the very least, that she is encircled by even just a single string of garlands thrown over her by someone with the perception, "She shall be my wife.
And one who engages in conduct toward such women refers to such women as mentioned in the *Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta*.
One becomes a transgressor by way of the characteristic of sexual misconduct as it has been described.
"In an assembly" means standing in an assembly. "In a gathering" means standing in a gathering. "In the midst of kinsmen" means standing in the midst of heirs.
"In the midst of a guild" means standing in the midst of a company. "In the midst of the royal court" means [standing] in the midst of the royal family.

He stands in the midst of a great legal dispute. "Brought forward" means brought for the purpose of questioning. "Questioned by way of witnesses" means questioned having made witnesses [part of the process].

"Come here, O man!"—this is a form of address. "For one's own sake or for another's sake" means either for the sake of oneself or for the sake of another, such as for the sake of hands, feet, and so forth, or for the sake of wealth.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of some small material thing," here "material thing" (āmisa) refers to...
"Gain" is intended [here]. "Something" means whatever trifling thing; the meaning is: for the sake of even a bribe as small as a partridge bone, a piece of ghee, or a lump of butter.
"He speaks a conscious lie" means he is one who utters a falsehood while fully aware of it.

"For the purpose of dividing these" means for the purpose of creating a rift between those from whom he heard what was said. "For the purpose of dividing those" [means for the purpose of creating a rift between those to whom he reports it].
"It is for the sake of the division of those whose proximity has been mentioned as 'among whom [it is heard] there'.
Thus, "one who causes the division of those who are united" refers to one who creates a rift between two friends who are in harmony. Or, "one who provides for those who are divided":
[the thought is], "What you have done is excellent; by abandoning that [thought], you will cause great harm in just a few days"—thus, toward those who are already divided.
Furthermore, the meaning is: one who does not reconcile, one who does not provide support, and one who shows a cause [for division].

One whose delight is in factions (*vagga*) is a "faction-delighter" (*vaggārāma*). One who delights in factions is a "faction-pleaser" (*vaggārata*). One who rejoices upon seeing or hearing of factions is a "faction-rejoicer" (*vagganandī*).
"Speech that creates factions" refers to that speech which causes even harmonious beings to become divided or split.
He speaks that speech which is the cause of quarreling.

"Blisters" (*aṇḍakā*): just as blisters arise on a tree that has a disease, so too, due to its state of being corrupted by defilement, blisters are produced through words such as reviling and insulting.
"Harsh" (*kakkasā*): they are putrid. Just as a rotten tree is harsh and exudes powder, [so too are these words].
Thus it is harsh; it enters as if grinding the ear. Therefore it is called "harsh.

"Pungent to others" means it is bitter, unpleasant, and provocative of hatred for others. "Provocative of resentment in others" means that like a crooked thorny branch, having pierced the vital spots, it provokes resentment in others and acts as an obstacle, preventing even those who wish to go from going. "Adjacent to anger."
They are proximate to anger. "Conducive to non-concentration" means they do not lead to either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).
Thus, all of these are synonyms for speech that is tainted by defilement.

"One who speaks at the wrong time" is one who speaks at an improper occasion. "One who speaks what is untrue" is one who speaks of that which does not exist. "One who speaks what is unbeneficial" is one who speaks that which is based on no valid reason.
A speaker. One who speaks what is not the Dhamma is one who speaks what is unreal. One who speaks what is not the Vinaya is one who speaks what is unrelated to restraint and discipline.
One who speaks words that are "unfit for deposit" is one who utters speech that is unsuitable to be placed within the casket of the heart.
"At the wrong time" means he is a speaker at a time before or after the proper time for speaking, which is an inappropriate time. "Without a basis" means...
It is devoid of the wording of the discourses (*sutta*). "Having no limit" (*apariyantavati*) means it is without boundary;
having set aside a discourse or a birth story (*jātaka*), one brings forward its attainment, a simile, or a narrative basis, and speaks only of external talk.
Whatever has been set aside remains set aside. One thinks: "Is he speaking a discourse, or is he speaking a birth story? There is no end or limit to this!"

one comes to say, "We see it. Just as on every branch of a banyan tree that has grown, new shoots descend, and wherever they have descended, they continue to grow further after spreading out, so too [the creeper] goes for half a league or even a full league.
But as it goes on and on, the original root-tree perishes, and only those born from the lineage remain standing. In the same way, this [creeper] also—
There is one called a "Nigrodha-dhammakathika" (a speaker of the Dhamma like a banyan tree); having merely set down each point as it is set down, he goes along carrying it about as if on his side.

However, for one who, even when speaking much, is able to bring forward and make known that "this was said for this purpose," it is proper for him to speak. "Inconducive to the goal" means not dependent upon the goal.
“He covets” means he looks with covetousness. “Aho vata” is a particle used in the sense of aspiration.
Here, the breach of the course of kamma does not occur merely by looking with covetousness. However, when one appropriates it for oneself, thinking, “O, may this be mine!
May I exercise control over this!”—then the breach of the course of kamma occurs; this is what is intended here.

"Malicious-minded" (*byāpannacitta*) means one whose mind is ruined or whose mind has become putrid. "With corrupt intention" (*paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappa*) means one whose mental intention is defiled by hatred.

"Let them be slain" (*haññantu*) means let them be killed. "Let them be destroyed" (*vajjhantu*) means let them meet their death. "Or let them not even exist" (*mā vā ahesuṃ*) means let them not exist at all.
Here too, the completion of the course of kamma does not occur through mere anger alone; it occurs only through the actual thought, "Let them be slain," and so forth. Therefore, it is stated thus.
"One of wrong view" means one who possesses unwholesome vision. "One of perverted vision" means one whose vision is distorted.

"There is no gift" is said with reference to the absence of fruit for what has been given. "Sacrifice" (yiṭṭha) refers to a great offering. "Offering" (huta) is intended to mean hospitality consisting of food parcels;
he rejects both of these with reference precisely to the absence of fruit. "Of well-done and ill-done deeds..."
"Of good and bad deeds" means of wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. "There is no fruit, no ripening" means he says that whatever is called "fruit" or "ripening" does not exist.
"There is no this world" means for one standing in the next world, this world does not exist.
"There is no other world" means even for one standing in this world, the next world does not exist; everyone is simply annihilated right there and then.
He shows [this]. "There is no mother, there is no father"—he says this by way of the absence of fruit for right conduct and wrong conduct toward them.
"There are no beings of spontaneous birth"—he says that there are no beings who, having passed away, are reborn [by spontaneous generation].
"Having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, they make it known"—those who, having directly known this world and the other world, [proclaim it] with superior wisdom...
Having made it personally evident through wisdom, they proclaim it; this indicates the non-existence of omniscient Buddhas.
To this extent, the ten-based wrong view has been explained.
(441) "Having abandoned the destruction of life," and so forth—the seven courses of kamma have been detailed in the *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta*. Non-covetousness and the others are of plain meaning.
442. “May I arise in companionship” means: may I attain a state of being together. “Of the gods of the Brahma-body” refers to the gods of the plane of the first jhāna.
Regarding “the Ābhā gods,” there is no separate class named Ābhā; this is a designation for the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara gods.

The mention of “the Parittābhā gods” and so forth, however, is not taken as a single group, but rather as a classification of those very same beings. This also applies to the cases of “the Parittasubhā gods” and so on.
The same method applies here. Thus, having shown the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*), the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
Standing at this point, however, the worlds of the gods (*devaloka*) must be included. First, by way of the three planes of jhāna, there are nine Brahma-worlds;
the five Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) together with the four formless realms (*ārūpa*) make nine, which, together with the Vehapphala realm, makes nineteen.
Including the non-percipient beings, there are twenty Brahmā worlds; thus, together with the six sense-sphere realms, they are called the twenty-six divine worlds.
For all of these, the Blessed One has shown that their arising is produced by the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).
Among them, first, the arising of the six sense-sphere realms occurs solely through the ripening of the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*). As for the higher divine worlds...
However, these courses of action are spoken of by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). For the ten wholesome courses of action are virtue (*sīla*);

and for one possessed of virtue, the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the kasiṇas succeeds. Having established oneself in virtue, having performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, and having produced the first jhāna, one is reborn in the plane of the first jhāna;
and by developing the second and subsequent jhānas, one is reborn in the planes of the second jhāna and so forth.
He is reborn; having made fine-material-sphere jhāna the basis and having developed insight, he becomes established in the fruit of non-returning and is reborn in the five Pure Abodes;

having made fine-material-sphere jhāna the basis and having produced an immaterial-sphere attainment, he is reborn in the four immaterial realms; having made fine-material and immaterial jhāna the basis and having developed insight...
One attains arahantship. However, the state of non-perception (asaññabhava) is the habitual practice of external ascetics and wanderers, and thus it is not explained here.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
[End of] the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Sāleyyaka Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verañjaka Sutta: 444.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Verañjaka Sutta. In that context, "Verañjakā" means the inhabitants of Verañja. By some...
"By some duty" means by some unspecified task. Everything else is to be understood according to the method already stated in the previous sutta.

For the only difference here is that this teaching is given with reference to the person, stating "one who acts contrary to the Dhamma, one who acts unjustly," whereas in the previous sutta it was given with reference to the phenomena (dhamma). The rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the Verañjaka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 3.
The commentary on the Mahāvedalla Sutta.
449. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāvedalla Sutta. In that context, *āyasmā* is a term of respect and deference.
*Mahākoṭṭhika* is the name of that elder. *Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito* means he has emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Regarding the phrase *duppañño duppañño*, there is no such thing as "corrupt wisdom" here; the meaning is "one of little wisdom" or "one devoid of wisdom."
"To what extent" (*kittāvatā*) is a question regarding the delimitation of a cause; the meaning is: "By how much is it so called? Now, this type of question is fivefold:

the question for the illumination of the unseen, the question for the correlation of the seen, the question for the cutting off of doubt, the question for assent, and the question out of a desire to speak. This is their distinction: * **The question for the illumination of the unseen** (*adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*) is that which asks about something not yet understood, such as: "Is there a path leading to Nibbāna? * **The question for the correlation of the seen** (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā*) is that which asks for the connection between two things already known, such as: "Are all conditioned phenomena impermanent? Is all that is impermanent suffering? * **The question for the cutting off of doubt** (*vimaticchedanā-pucchā*) is that which asks to resolve uncertainty, such as: "Is it the case that the Blessed One is omniscient and all-seeing? * **The question for assent** (*anumati-pucchā*) is that which asks for permission or agreement, such as: "May I go to the village? or "May I enter the monastery?

* **The question out of a desire to speak** (*kathetukamyatā-pucchā*) is that which asks with the intention of eliciting an explanation, such as: "What is the Dhamma? or "How is one a disciple of the Blessed One? This is the distinction between them.
What is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen? There is a characteristic that is by nature unknown, unseen, unmeasured, unexamined, unmanifested, and unclarified;
one asks a question for the sake of knowing it, seeing it, measuring it, examining it, manifesting it, and clarifying it. This is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen.

What is the question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen? One’s own natural characteristic is known—seen, weighed, judged, made clear, and fully discerned—and one asks a question in order to correlate it with other wise persons.
This is the question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt? One who is by nature prone to uncertainty, prone to perplexity, and full of hesitation—thinking, "Is it thus?
Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?"—asks a question for the sake of cutting off that doubt.
This is a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt.
“Bhikkhus, what do you think: is form permanent or impermanent?”—having obtained such consent, a question asked at the time of teaching the Dhamma is called a “question for obtaining consent.

“Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness; which four?”—such a question, asked by [the Buddha] himself to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus when he wishes to answer it himself, is called a “question out of a desire to speak. Among those, here...
The inquiry concerning the correlation with what has been seen is intended here.

For the Elder, having sat in his own daytime resting place, raised the question himself and, resolving it himself, brought this discourse from the beginning to its conclusion. For some are indeed able only to raise a question.
One person is unable to determine [the meaning]; another is able to determine it but not to formulate [the teaching];
another is unable to do either; and another is able to do both. Among them, the Elder is indeed able to do both.
Why? Because of his great wisdom. For, by relying on great wisdom, in this Dispensation there are the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahākaccāna, the Elder Puṇṇa, and others.
The Elder Kumāra Kassapa, the Elder Ānanda, and this very Venerable One—these many elders have attained distinguished states.
For it is not possible for a bhikkhu endowed with merely some small measure of wisdom to reach the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*);
however, it is possible for one of great wisdom. Thus, because of his great wisdom, the Elder Sāriputta [is preeminent].
He has attained that state. Indeed, there is no one equal to the Elder in wisdom. For this very reason, the Blessed One placed him at the head of the foremost disciples:
"Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who possess great wisdom, the foremost is Sāriputta.
Likewise, it is not possible for a bhikkhu endowed with merely some small measure of wisdom to [equal] the Blessed One.
In order to analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by correlating and harmonizing it with the knowledge of omniscience, only one of great wisdom would be capable;
thus, through his great wisdom, the Elder Mahākaccāna became competent in that regard.
For this very reason, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my [disciples]..."
"Among the disciples who are monks, it is Mahākaccāna who, when something has been spoken in brief by the Teacher, analyzes its meaning in detail. Likewise,
it is not possible for a monk endowed with only a small measure of wisdom, while delivering a discourse on the Dhamma,
to bring forward the ten bases of discourse and analyze the seven purifications while delivering that discourse on the Dhamma.

"But it is possible for one of great wisdom to speak," [the Buddha thought]. Thus, by virtue of his great wisdom, the Elder Puṇṇa sat in the midst of the fourfold assembly upon a decorated Dharma-seat;
grasping a painted fan, he spoke the Dhamma with playful grace like the full moon.
For this very reason, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are preachers of the Dhamma, this is the foremost."
"Namely, Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.
Likewise, a bhikkhu endowed with even a small measure of wisdom, when preaching the Dhamma,
like a blind man who has missed his way here and there and must grasp the tip of a staff, [proceeds] along a narrow footpath or a bridge of sticks.

And he proceeded as if he were actually ascending. But the Elder of Great Wisdom, having set forth even a four-line stanza, brought forward similes and reasons, and having taken up the entire word of the Buddha from the Three Baskets, explained it by arranging it from bottom to top.
And because of his great wisdom, the Elder Kumāra Kassapa, having set forth a four-line stanza, [brought forward] similes and reasons...

Having brought them back and harmonizing them with those [already existing texts], as if causing five-colored flowers to bloom in a lake, or as if lighting a thousand oil-lamps on the summit of Mount Sineru, he recited the Buddha-word contained in the Three Piṭakas, arranging it from beginning to end.
For that very reason, the Blessed One placed him in this foremost position: "Bhikkhus, among my [disciples]..."
“Among the disciples, the monks who are expounders of the minds [of others], this one is Kumārakassapa.
Likewise, a monk endowed with only a small amount of wisdom is unable to grasp even a four-line stanza in four months;
however, one of great wisdom, standing upon a single word, can grasp a hundred words or even a thousand words.

He grasps it. However, because of his great wisdom, the Elder Ānanda, standing upon the extraction of a single word, grasps it all at once as soon as he hears it, without asking again—just as one who gathers flowers from a creeper takes sixty thousand words and fifteen thousand verses in a single stroke.
Whatever he has grasped remains like an inscription carved on stone or within a golden vessel.
And like lion’s fat that has been poured [into a vessel], it remains exactly in the form in which it was taken. For this very reason, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position:

“Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are possessed of speed, Ānanda is foremost; among those possessed of mindfulness, those possessed of steadfastness, those of great learning, and those who are attendants, Ānanda is foremost.”

Indeed, it is not possible for a bhikkhu endowed with only a small measure of wisdom to reach the pinnacle of the various analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). However, one who possesses great wisdom is able to do so;

thus, through his great wisdom, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita attained the manifold analytical knowledges, which abound in infinite methods by virtue of his prior application to realization, inquiry, and hearing.
For this very reason, the Blessed One placed him at the head of that class.
—“This is the foremost, monks, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), namely Mahākoṭṭhita.
Thus, by virtue of his great wisdom, the Elder was capable both of formulating questions and of resolving them.
Sitting in his daytime resting place, he himself formulated all the questions and resolved them himself; it was while doing so that he [recited] this discourse.
From beginning to end, having brought it to its conclusion: "Truly beautiful is this teaching of the Dhamma;
I shall compare it with that of my elder brother, the General of the Dhamma.
Then, established by both of us with one mind and one intention, it will become exceedingly weighty, like a stone parasol for those seeking to cross over the four floods."
