“Like a ship stationed at a port, or like a chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbred horses for those wishing to travel the road, it will be of great benefit.
Thus he asked the question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen. Therefore it was said: “Among these, here the question intended is that which correlates what has been seen.
Regarding the phrase “he does not understand”: because he does not understand, therefore he is called one of “weak wisdom” (duppañña); this is the meaning. This...

The method is the same everywhere. “He does not understand ‘this is suffering’” means that he does not understand the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) according to its true essential characteristic—that this is suffering, that this is the extent of suffering, and that there is nothing beyond this.

“This is the origin of suffering” means that craving (*taṇhā*), which brings about the suffering of the process of existence (*pavatti*), is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*)—according to its true essential characteristic.

He does not understand. He does not understand, according to their true essential characteristics, that "this is the cessation of suffering" means that having reached this particular state, both [suffering and its origin] cease;
and that Nibbāna, the non-occurrence of both, is the Truth of Cessation.
He does not understand that "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" means that this practice goes toward the cessation of suffering.
"He does not understand the truth of the path according to its specific characteristic as it actually is. In the subsequent section as well, the meaning should be understood by this same method.
In brief, however, it should be understood that the person here described is one who takes the four truths as his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
For he learns the four truths from hearing them in the presence of a teacher; setting aside craving, [the remaining] things belonging to the three planes...

Phenomena are the truth of suffering, craving is the truth of the origin, the non-occurrence of both is Nibbāna, the truth of cessation, and the path that fully understands the truth of suffering, abandons the truth of the origin, and leads to cessation is the truth of the path.
Having grasped it thus, one adheres to it. In this context, the first two truths are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), while the latter two are the unrolling of the round (*vivaṭṭa*).
There is attachment to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), not to its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*); therefore, one who is thus attached attaches himself to the truth of suffering.
Having defined the truth of suffering as the five aggregates beginning with form, and having entered the practice by way of the meditation subject on the elements, he defines it thus:
"The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements are 'form.'"
"Feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness that have that as their object are 'name'"—thus, like splitting a twin palm tree trunk, he defines them, determining:
"These two things are name-and-form. Furthermore, this is not without cause;
it has causes and conditions. And what is its condition? It is the factors such as ignorance. Thus, [he discerns] both the conditions and the phenomena arisen from those conditions.
And having thus determined them, he applies the characteristic of impermanence by way of the non-existence after having been;

then, having applied the three characteristics— namely, that they are suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, and non-self in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery—
he reaches the supramundane path while comprehending through the sequence of insight.
At the moment of the path, one penetrates the four truths by a single penetration and realizes them by a single realization.

One penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding; one penetrates the origin through the penetration of abandoning; one penetrates cessation through the penetration of realization;
and one penetrates the path through the penetration of cultivation. One realizes suffering through the realization of full understanding; one [realizes] the origin...
He realizes suffering through the realization of abandoning, cessation through the realization of verification, and the path through the realization of cultivation.
He penetrates three truths by way of their function, and cessation by way of its object.

At that moment, there occurs for him an application of mind, an attention, and a reflection consisting of: "I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, and I cultivate the path."
There is none. However, for one who is grasping this [cessation], the path—while accomplishing the tasks such as full understanding regarding the three truths—penetrates cessation as its object.
Therefore, it is said that "he is possessed of wisdom. Herein, at the lower limit, he is a stream-enterer; at the upper limit, he is one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

"He is wise" is the definition provided. But as for one who, having mastered the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas—both in terms of the text, the meaning, the connections, and the sequence from beginning to end—and who wanders about arranging them from bottom to top, yet possesses not even a mere grasp of them by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self:
is such a person called "wise," or is he called "of dull wisdom"? He is indeed one whose temperament is dominated by consciousness (*viññāṇacarita*).

"One should not say [he] is wise. Now, as for one who, having applied the three characteristics and contemplating according to the sequence of insight, practices for Arahantship day after day—is such a person called "wise" or "of dull wisdom"?
When associated with what is dear, he belongs to the side of the wise; however, in the Sutta, only penetration (*paṭivedha*) is spoken of.

Regarding "consciousness, consciousness": what is he asking here? He asks, thinking: "I ask about that consciousness which, having comprehended the formations (*saṅkhāra*), has made this person known as 'wise'—that is, the consciousness of arrival-insight (*āgamana-vipassanā*), the mind that performs the action.
"He cognizes even pleasure" means he cognizes even the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). The same method applies to the following two phrases as well. By this...

The Elder taught the formless meditation subject by way of the feelings as they appear in the passage beginning, “When feeling a pleasant feeling, one understands: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling,’” and so forth.
Its meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta].
He asks: “Are they conjoined (*saṃsaṭṭhā*)—conjoined in the sense of conjunction through such characteristics as simultaneous arising—or are they unconjoined?”
And here, it should not be understood that the Elder asks as if he were ignorant of the distinction between planes, having mixed together these two mundane and supramundane states—

namely, path-wisdom and insight-consciousness. Rather, he asks regarding the state of their being conjoined with path-wisdom and path-consciousness, and with insight-wisdom and insight-consciousness respectively.
"He asks" is how it should be understood. The Elder, answering that very point for him, said: "These states are conjoined," and so forth.
Therein, "and it is not possible [to separate] these states" refers to these two states which arise together, both at the moment of the mundane path and at the moment of the supramundane path.
"Having separated them again and again" means having made them distinct from one another.
The meaning is that, having turned back [from that], it is not possible to show a distinction by way of object, basis, arising, or cessation.
However, each of those respective phenomena has its own specific domain;
for when reaching mundane phenomena, the mind is the chief and the precursor, but when reaching supramundane phenomena, wisdom is.
For even when the Fully Enlightened One asks about worldly phenomena, he does not ask, "Bhikkhu, what wisdom have you attained?
Is it the wisdom of the first path, or the wisdom of the second, third, or fourth path? Nor does he ask, "Bhikkhu, what is your contact (phassa)?
What is your feeling (vedanā)? What is your perception (saññā)? What is your volition (cetanā)?"—it is according to the nature of the mind [that he asks].
However, he asks, "Bhikkhu, what is your state of mind? Even when defining wholesome and unwholesome states, he defines them solely by way of the mind, saying:
"States are preceded by mind, led by mind, and made of mind," and "Which states are wholesome?
At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen... When asking about the supramundane, [he does so]...
But why does he not ask, "Bhikkhu, what is contact? What is feeling? What is perception? What is volition? Instead, he asks in terms of wisdom alone:
"Bhikkhu, what wisdom have you attained? Is it the wisdom of the first path, or rather the wisdom of the second, third, or fourth path?
Thus he asks specifically by way of wisdom.
In the *Indriyasaṃyutta* it is also said: “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. And where, bhikkhus, is the faculty of faith to be seen?
It is to be seen in the four factors of stream-entry. And where, bhikkhus, [is the faculty of energy to be seen?]”
Wherein is the faculty of energy to be seen? Herein, in the four right endeavors, the faculty of energy is to be seen.
And wherein, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness to be seen? Herein, in the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness is to be seen.
And wherein, monks, is the faculty of concentration to be seen? Herein, in the four jhānas...
“The faculty of concentration is to be seen. And where, monks, is the faculty of wisdom to be seen?
It is in the Four Noble Truths that the faculty of wisdom is to be seen. Thus, mundane and supramundane phenomena were explained precisely within their own respective domains.
For it is just as when four sons of a merchant, with a king as the fifth among their companions, say, “We shall play at the festival of the constellations.”
When they had entered the street and reached the house of one merchant’s son, the other four sat in silence;
the master of that house alone managed the affairs within the home, saying, "Give them hard food and soft food; give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth.
When they reached the house of the second, the third, and the fourth, the other four likewise remained silent.
They sit down, and the master of the house himself directs affairs in the home, saying, "Give these people hard food and soft food;

give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth. Then, at the very last, when they have gone to the king's palace—even though the king is the sovereign everywhere—on this occasion, it is in his own palace that he says, "Give these people hard food and soft food..."
"Give us perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth," he deliberates. In exactly the same way, when the five faculties—
with faith as the fifth— arise upon a single object as if those friends were entering the street together,
just as in the first house the other four sit in silence while only the master of the house deliberates, so too do the factors of stream-entry.
Having reached the state characterized by resolve, the faculty of faith alone becomes the chief and the forerunner,
while the others follow in its wake. Just as in the house of the second [son], the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates,
so too, having reached the right efforts, the faculty of energy— characterized by exertion— becomes the chief and the forerunner.

The remaining [faculties] follow along with it. Just as in the third house the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates, so too, having reached the foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness alone—characterized by establishing—is the chief and the forerunner, while the remaining ones follow along with it.
Just as in the fourth house the other four [sit in silence...]

They sit down, while the master of the house alone deliberates; even so, having attained the jhānas and liberations, the faculty of concentration—characterized by non-distraction—is the foremost and the leader, while the others follow in its wake.
But when they have all finally entered the king’s house, just as the other four sit in silence while the king alone deliberates in the house, so too it is with the Noble Truths.

Having attained [the analytical knowledges], the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), characterized by discernment, alone becomes the chief and the forerunner, while the remaining [faculties] follow in its wake.

Thus, when the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita was ranked foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he asked about mundane phenomena (lokīyadhamma) making the mind the chief and the mind the forerunner; but when asking about supramundane phenomena (lokuttaradhamma), he asked about wisdom.
Having made wisdom his leader and his forerunner, the Elder asked. The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, answered in exactly the same way.
"That which one understands" means that path-wisdom understands this Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths according to the method beginning with "This is suffering.
"That which one cognizes" means that path-consciousness likewise cognizes that very same thing. "That which one cognizes" means... [and so on].
Insight-consciousness cognizes [the object] by way of the method beginning with "formations are impermanent. "One understands that" means that insight-wisdom likewise understands it in that same way.
Therefore, "these states"—for that reason, these states. "Conjoined" means conjoined by virtue of having a single arising, a single cessation, a single basis, and a single object.
"Wisdom should be developed"—this is said with reference to path-wisdom; however, the consciousness associated with it...
It must indeed be developed together with that [wisdom]. "Consciousness is to be fully understood"—this was said with reference to insight-consciousness (*vipassanā-viññāṇa*).
However, the wisdom associated with it must be thoroughly known together with it.
450. Why does he ask, "Feeling, feeling"? He asks because he intends to inquire about the characteristic of feeling (*vedanā-lakkhaṇa*).

Even so, it should be noted that what is intended here is specifically the feeling belonging to the sphere of the three planes (*tebhūmika*) that arises during the course of contemplation (*sammasana*).
"He feels pleasure" means he feels—that is, experiences—the pleasant object. The same method applies to the following two phrases as well.
"For if this form, Mahāli, were exclusively suffering—overwhelmed by suffering, fallen into suffering, and not free from it..."
If form were pleasant, Mahāli, beings would not become infatuated with form.
But because form is pleasant, beset by pleasure, overwhelmed by pleasure, and is not overwhelmed by suffering, therefore beings become infatuated with form; through infatuation they become fettered;
through being fettered they become defiled. Feeling here... perception... volitional formations... and consciousness here too, Mahāli, [is likewise].
For by this method of the Mahāli Sutta—“If it were exclusively suffering... [and so on]...
they would become defiled”—it is here stated that the object (ārammaṇa) is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Furthermore, having made a previous pleasant feeling the object, one experiences another pleasant feeling; having made a previous painful feeling the object...
Another painful feeling feels [it]; having made the previous neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling its object, another neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling feels [it].
This is how the meaning should be understood here. For it has been said that "feeling itself feels," and there is no other so-called "feeler" whatsoever.

"Perception, perception"—what does he ask here? He asks for the characteristic of all perception. "Of all-perceiving perception"? Whether it be "the characteristic of all perception" or "the characteristic of all-perceiving perception," it is one and the same thing.

Nevertheless, it should be noted that what is intended here is specifically the perception involved in the contemplation of the three planes (*tebhūmika-sammasanacāra*). "One perceives blue" refers to a blue flower.
Or, having performed the preliminary work on a cloth, one perceives while inducing access concentration or absorption.

In this context, both the perception of the preliminary work, the perception of access, and the perception of absorption are appropriate. The perception that arises as "blue, blue" regarding a blue object is also indeed appropriate;
the same method applies to yellow and the other colors as well.
Regarding the phrase, "And what, friends, is feeling": why is wisdom (*paññā*) not included here when these three—feeling, perception, and consciousness—are taken?

Because it does not include everything. For if wisdom were included, only those things associated with wisdom (*sampayutta*), such as feeling and the rest, would be obtained, and not those dissociated from it (*vippayutta*). But by not including that [wisdom], when these [three] are taken, both those associated with wisdom and...
And even as few as two fivefold-sensory consciousness states (pañcaviññāṇa-dhamma) may be found as dissociated [from the mind].

For example, suppose three men were to say, "It is thread, it is thread," while a fourth says, "It is a thread strung with jewels. Of these, the first three obtain any kind of thread in abundance—whether it be spun by reasoning, or made from cloth, bark, and so forth—even down to a spider's web.
But one who is searching for a thread strung with jewels...

It acquires [the object] slowly; it should be understood as being of such a nature. Or rather, they say that wisdom (*paññā*) is not included here because it has been omitted due to its association with consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
"Whatever, friends, one feels" means whatever object the feeling (*vedanā*) feels, perception (*saññā*) likewise perceives that very same thing. "Whatever one perceives" means whatever object...
“Perception perceives” means that consciousness also cognizes that very same thing.
Now, the distinction between “perceives,” “cognizes,” and “understands” should be understood here. In this context, the distinction lies merely in the prefixes;
the word *jānāti* (he knows), however, is without distinction. Within its own sense of knowing, too, a distinction should be understood. For perception—
Perception merely perceives the object by way of blue and so forth; it is not able to bring about the penetration of the characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Consciousness both perceives the object by way of blue and so forth and brings about the penetration of the characteristics such as impermanence;
yet, even though it strives, it is not able to bring about the manifestation of the Path. Wisdom, however, [perceives] the object by way of blue and so forth...
It perceives; it brings about the penetration of the characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth; and it is also capable of bringing about the manifestation of the path through exertion.

For example, when a pile of kahāpaṇa coins has been made upon a money-changer’s board, and three people—a child who has not yet developed intelligence, a villager, and a great money-changer—stand looking at them, the child who has not yet developed intelligence [perceives] only the state of the kahāpaṇas as variegated, multicolored, square, and circular.
He knows this, but he does not know that "this is the enjoyment and utility for human beings, esteemed as a treasure.
A village dweller knows both its nature as a gem and its status as an object of enjoyment and utility for humans;
however, he does not know, "This one is counterfeit, this one is clever, this one is worn out, this one is smooth. Likewise, a great money-changer [knows] even the nature of the gem and so forth...
It knows both the state of being considered a "gem" and the state of being counterfeit and so forth; and knowing it, one recognizes it even upon seeing the form,
or by hearing the sound when it is struck, or by smelling its fragrance, or by tasting its flavor,

or by feeling its weight with the hand— knowing, for instance, that it was made in such-and-such a village, or in such-and-such a market town, or in such-and-such a city, or in the shade of such-and-such a mountain.
One knows, "It was built on the bank of such-and-such a river," or "It was built by such-and-such a teacher.
In the same way, perception—like a child who has not yet developed intelligence seeing a coin—perceives only the mere object by way of its blue color and so forth.

Consciousness, however—like an adult villager seeing a coin—not only perceives the object by way of its blue color and so forth, but also penetrates its characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth.

It brings about [realization]. Wisdom, like a great money-changer’s examination of a coin, perceives the object by way of its blue color and so forth, brings about the penetration of the characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth, and brings about the manifestation of the path through striving.
Yet, the distinction between these two is difficult to discern.
Therefore the Venerable Nāgasena said: "A difficult thing, Great King, was accomplished by the Blessed One.
What, Bhante Nāgasena, was accomplished as a difficult task by the Blessed One? A difficult thing, Great King, was accomplished by the Blessed One:
the defining of these immaterial mental states—the mind and its concomitants—as they proceed upon a single object, [stating]: 'This is contact...'"
“This is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.
For just as if these five oils— sesame oil, mustard oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil— were placed together in a single vessel and stirred all day with two churning sticks,
one could not then distinguish each one, saying, “This is sesame oil,” or “This is mustard oil.”
To extract [these factors] individually is difficult; this is even more difficult than that.

However, because he had thoroughly penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, the Blessed One—the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma—declared the differentiation of these formless states as they occur upon a single object.
Just as at the place where the five great rivers enter the ocean, one can say, "This is the Ganges..."
"Water; this is from the Yamunā"—thus this meaning should also be understood by means of drawing out water separately. 451.

"By that which has escaped" (*nissaṭṭhena*) means either by that which has escaped or by that which has been relinquished. In that context, if the sense is "by that which has escaped," it is an ablative expression (*nissakkavacana*);
if the sense is "by that which has been relinquished," it should be understood as an instrumental expression (*karaṇavacana*).

This is what is meant: [it is] "renounced" because it has emerged from the five faculties and functions at the mind-door, or because the five faculties have not attained the status of its physical basis (*vatthu*).
"Purified" means free from defilements (*nirupakkilesa*). "By mental consciousness" means by a fourth-jhāna consciousness belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
"What is to be known? means whatever is to be cognized. "Whatever... [etc.]
In such passages as “there is a state that is ‘to-be-understood’ (neyya),” it is said that what is to be known is the “to-be-understood.

How is it that the base of infinite space is called “to-be-understood,” given that the attainment of the formless realm is reached by means of the fourth jhāna consciousness of the fine-material sphere?

It is because one who is established in the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere is able to produce the attainment of the formless realm; for it is while standing upon this [jhāna] that it succeeds.
Therefore, he said, "The base of infinite space is to be understood," and so forth. Now, why was the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception not mentioned?
Because there is no separate fixation upon it. For in that state, comprehension is obtained by way of groups and by way of method;
even in a monk who resembles the General of the Dhamma, no separate fixation arises. Therefore, the Elder also said:
“Thus indeed these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they pass away”—having thus comprehended them by way of clusters and by way of method, he let go.

But the Blessed One, because the knowledge of omniscience was within his grasp, even regarding the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, extracted more than fifty phenomena individually by way of their distinct factors, [saying]: “To whatever extent there are attainments of perception...”
"By that much, there is penetration of final knowledge," he said.
"He understands with the eye of wisdom" means he understands by means of wisdom that has become like an eye in the sense of being the guide for vision.

In this context, there are two kinds of wisdom: the wisdom of concentration (*samādhi-paññā*) and the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). By way of its function and its non-delusion, it is through the wisdom of concentration...
And he understands. By means of the penetration of the characteristics through insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), knowing by way of the object has been explained.

"What is its purpose?"—what is its aim? Regarding the phrases "for the purpose of direct knowledge" (*abhiññattha*) and so forth: it is "for the purpose of direct knowledge" because it directly knows the states that are to be directly known;

it is "for the purpose of full understanding" (*pariññattha*) because it fully understands the states that are to be fully understood; it is "for the purpose of abandoning" (*pahānattha*) because it abandons the states that are to be abandoned. Furthermore, this...

The mundane [knowledges] have the purpose of direct knowledge and the purpose of full understanding; they have the purpose of abandoning by way of suppression. The supramundane [knowledges] also have the purpose of direct knowledge and the purpose of full understanding;

they have the purpose of abandoning by way of eradication. Therein, the mundane [knowledges] understand by way of function and by way of non-delusion, while the supramundane [knowledges] understand by way of non-delusion alone.
"452. For the arising of right view": this refers to both insight-right-view and path-right-view.
"And the voice of another" is the hearing of the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress]. "And wise attention" is one's own skillful attention.
In this regard, even among disciples, two conditions must be obtained for the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). For the Elder [had practiced] for more than a hundred thousand aeons...
Even after fulfilling the perfections for one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), he was unable, by his own nature, to abandon even a minute defilement (*kilesa*).
His realization arose upon hearing this verse from the Elder Assaji: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause...
However, for Paccekabuddhas and Omniscient Buddhas, there is no dependence on the voice of another; [realization occurs] through right attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) alone.
Having stood [in that state], they give rise to both private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) and omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
"Supported" means having received assistance. "Right view" refers to the right view of the path to arahantship.

That which has the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) produced at the moment of fruition is "having liberation of mind as its fruit. That very fruit, termed liberation of mind, is the benefit (ānisaṃsa).
"Of the mind" means having the fruit of liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) as its benefit. The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
Here, it should be understood that the wisdom of the fourth fruit is called "liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*), while the remaining factors are "liberation of mind.

Regarding the phrases "supported by virtue" and so forth: "virtue" refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*); "learning" refers to hearing the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress]; and "discussion" refers to discourse that cuts through stumbling and faltering regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Samatha" refers to the eight attainments that lead to insight (*vipassanā*). "Vipassanā" refers to the sevenfold contemplation.

Indeed, for one who fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue, listens to the teachings conducive [to practice], cuts off stumbling and faltering regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), applies effort toward the eight attainments that lead to insight, and develops the sevenfold contemplation—
The path to arahantship, having arisen, bestows its fruit.
For example, one who wishes to enjoy a sweet, ripe mango first makes a sturdy water-reservoir around the mango sapling and secures it;
then, taking a jar, he pours water into it from time to time, so that the water does not escape.
He makes the boundary firm. He removes whatever is nearby—whether it be a creeper, a dry stick, an anthill, or a spider’s web.
Taking a spade, he digs around the roots from time to time.
Thus, for one who is diligent and performs these five actions, that mango tree grows and yields fruit.
This should be understood as follows: Morality (sīla) is to be seen like the construction of a fence around a tree;
listening to the Dhamma (dhammassavana) is like the occasional sprinkling of water; serenity (samatha) is like making the boundary firm;
and cutting away stumbling and slipping in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is like clearing away creepers and the like from nearby.
The cultivation of the seven contemplations is like the digging for roots from time to time with a spade.
Just as the mango tree, when assisted by those five causes, reaches the time of yielding sweet fruit,
so too should it be understood that this bhikkhu’s right view— assisted by these five qualities— reaches the time of yielding the fruit of arahantship.
453. "But, friend, when it is asked 'How many kinds of existence (bhava) are there?', what is being asked here? The connection follows back to the very root.

He asks this thinking, "I shall ask about those kinds of existence from which one who is of poor wisdom does not emerge. In that context, "existence in the sense-sphere" (kāmabhava) refers to both the karma leading to existence in the sense-sphere and the appropriated aggregates produced by that karma; having combined these two together, he calls them "existence in the sense-sphere."

The same method applies to the realms of form and formlessness as well. "In the future" means in what is yet to come. "The production of renewed existence" means the manifestation of renewed existence (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*).
Here, he asks because he intends to inquire about the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"Delighting here and there" refers to delighting in forms, delighting in sounds, and so forth—delighting in this or that place; and here the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. By means of such delighting here and there...
The meaning is that there is the production of renewed existence (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*). For up to this point, there is going, there is coming, there is going and coming;
thus, having brought the cycle (*vaṭṭa*) to its conclusion, he has demonstrated how it turns. Now, asking about the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), he said, "But how, friends," and so forth.
In the reply to that, "through the fading away of ignorance" (*avijjāvirāga*) means through the destruction and cessation of ignorance.
"By the arising of true knowledge" means by the arising of the knowledge of the path of arahantship. Is it that ignorance has ceased previously, or that true knowledge has arisen previously?
Neither of these two should be said. Just as darkness is dispelled by the lighting of a lamp, ignorance is indeed ceased by the arising of true knowledge.
"By the cessation of craving" means by the destruction and cessation of craving. [The result is] the non-manifestation of renewed existence.
"It does not exist": thus he showed that there is no further arising of renewed existence in the future; that going and coming, the cycle of going and coming, is cut off;
and that the round of existence does not turn—having brought this to its ultimate conclusion, he demonstrated it as "the turning away" (*vivaṭṭa*).
"But which one, friends?"—what is he asking here? He asks about a monk who is liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), who from time to time...
He enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). [The questioner] asks, thinking, "I shall ask about his first jhāna, which serves as the basis for that cessation.
What does he ask here by saying "the first jhāna"? The monk who enters the attainment of cessation must know the definition of the factors and the delimitation of the components;
namely, that this jhāna is five-factored, four-factored, or three-factored.
"Consisting of five factors": he asks this intending to inquire about the definition of the factors and the delimitation of their components.

Regarding "applied thought" (vitakka) and the others: applied thought has the characteristic of directing onto; sustained thought (vicāra) has the characteristic of examining; rapture (pīti) has the characteristic of pervading; pleasure (sukha) has the characteristic of gratification;
and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) has the characteristic of non-distraction—these five states occur.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned the factors": what is being asked here? One who enters the attainment of cessation must know which factors are helpful and which are unhelpful; thinking, "I shall ask about those," he asks this question. The answer, however, is quite evident here.
Thus, below, the first jhāna serving as the basis for cessation was taken up; above, its immediate condition, the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, [is discussed].

He will ask [the following]. However, it should be understood that the six attainments (*samāpatti*) were omitted in between, either because their method was already shown or because they were left out.
455. Now, asking about the five sensitive organs (*pasāda*) which have consciousness as their support, he says: "These five, friends," and so forth.
Therein, *gocaravisayaṃ* means an object (*visaya*) that has become a range (*gocara*). *Aññamaññassa* means that the eye [is the range] of the ear, or the ear of the eye.
In this way, he does not experience the objective domain of each individual sense-faculty.
For if one were to bring together various forms as objects—such as blue and so forth—and present them to the ear-faculty, saying, "Come now, define and analyze this: what exactly is this object?
then visual consciousness itself, even without speaking, would by its own inherent nature say: "Hey, you blind fool!..."
"Even if you were to run for a hundred years or a thousand years, where else could you find anyone who knows this except me?
Bring it here and place it before my eyes; I shall know whether this object is blue or yellow.
For this is not within the domain of another; this is my domain alone. The same method applies to the other doors as well.
"In this way, these do not experience one another's range or domain. To the question "What is their resort?
he asks: what is their resort? What do they resort to? "The mind is their resort" means the impulsion-mind (*javana-manas*) is their resort.
"And the mind of these... refers either to the mind-door impulsion-mind or to the five-door impulsion-mind of these [consciousnesses].
It experiences its objective field by way of attachment and so forth. For visual consciousness is merely the seeing of form;
herein there is no attachment, aversion, or delusion. However, it is the impulsion (javana) at this door that becomes attached, averse, or deluded.
The same principle applies to auditory consciousness and the others as well.

In this regard, there is this simile: it is said that five weak tax-collectors, having served the king, obtained a meager income with great difficulty and hardship in a village consisting of only five families.
There, their share was either a portion of fish, a portion of meat, or a *yuttika* coin, or a *bandha* coin, or a *māpahāra* coin, or an eight-coin piece, or a sixteen-coin piece.
The fine amounts to only this much: either thirty-two kahāpaṇas or sixty-four kahāpaṇas.
Only the king takes the great tribute consisting of a hundred items, five hundred items, or a thousand items.
In this context, the five kinds of confidence are to be seen as like a village of five families; the five consciousnesses are like five weak bailiffs; and the king is like [the king].
The impulsion (javana) is like the limited attainment of income by weak tax-collectors; it consists merely in the seeing of forms and so forth by the eye-consciousness and the rest.

However, lust and the other [mental factors] do not exist in these [five sense-consciousnesses]. Lust and the others in those doors should be understood as being like the king’s great seizure of power.
456. "Friend, these five"—in this context, what is being asked? It refers to the five sensitive organs within cessation.
For when the occurrence consisting of kamma-result is taking place, the immaterial phenomena serve as powerful conditions for the sensitive organs.
But for one who, having suppressed that occurrence, has entered the attainment of cessation—what do the five sensitive organs depend upon to persist within that cessation?
Thinking, "I shall ask this," he asks. "Dependent on vitality" means they persist dependent on the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
"Dependent on heat" means the life-faculty persists dependent on the heat born of karma (*kammaja-teja*).
However, since the heat born of karma also does not persist without the life-faculty, he said, "Heat persists dependent on vitality. "From burning" means from blazing. "The flame..."
"Dependent on": dependent on the crest of the flame. "A radiance is perceived": a light is perceived.
"Dependent on the radiance, a flame": dependent on that light, the crest of the flame is perceived.
In the same way, friend, when it is said, "vitality persists dependent on heat," here the fire born of karma is like the crest of the flame.
The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is like light. For when a flame of a net arises, it arises having taken up light;
by means of that very light produced by itself, it too becomes manifest as minute, gross, long, or short.

In this context, just as the manifestation of that very movement of the net occurs through the light produced by the movement of the net, so too [is the manifestation] through the production of the primary elements born of karma (*kammaja-mahābhūta*), which has arisen in dependence upon heat.
The maintenance of heat by the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). For the life-faculty maintains the activity of the kamma-born fire for ten years... [and so on] ...even for a hundred years.

Thus, since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as conditions for the derived matter (*upādārūpa*) by way of being its support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and so forth, vitality (*āyu*) persists in dependence upon heat.
Since the life-faculty maintains the primary elements, heat [persists] in dependence upon vitality.
It should be understood that it "persists dependent [on something].
457. "Life-formations" (*āyu-saṅkhārā*) means life itself. "Phenomena to be felt" (*vedanīyā dhammā*) means feeling-phenomena themselves.
"Emergence is discerned" means emergence from meditative attainment is discerned. For when a bhikkhu, having become weary of the occurrence of the formless, [perceives] perception and...

Having ceased feeling and entered the attainment of cessation, mental states arise for him by way of the material life-faculty as a condition, according to the time previously determined. In this manner, the occurrence of the material and immaterial proceeds. How so?
Just as a man, distressed by the movement of a firebrand, strikes it with water, thereby causing the firebrand to cease its movement and [covering it] with ashes...

Having covered the embers, he sits in silence. But when he has need of the flame again, he removes the ashes, turns the embers over, provides fuel, and applies the breath of his mouth or the wind from a fan.

Then the occurrence of the flame proceeds once more. In the same way, the immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) are like the occurrence of the flame. When the man becomes weary of the occurrence of the flame—

Just as one who has extinguished a fire by pouring water over it, covered the embers with ashes, and sat in silence, so too does a bhikkhu, becoming weary of the occurrence of the formless (*arūpa*), arrest perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), and enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The life-faculty of form (*rūpajīvitindriya*) is like the embers covered by ashes. When that person again requires the fire, he removes the ashes and so forth.

The departure of the bhikkhu at the predetermined time is like that [extinguishing]. When immaterial phenomena arise again, the occurrence of both material and immaterial phenomena should be understood as being like the movement of a flame.
These three factors—the life-span, heat, and consciousness—constitute the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*), which consists of the karma-born fire-element and consciousness.
When they abandon this physical body, then it lies cast upon the earth like an insentient log;
such is the meaning. And this has been said:
"When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body..."
"Then he lies cast away, unconscious, feeding on another's food.

Here, "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) are inhalation and exhalation. "Verbal formations" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) are applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*). "Mental formations" (*cittasaṅkhāra*) are perception and feeling (*saññā-vedanā*).
"Vitality" (*āyu*) is the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*). "Decayed" (*paribhinna*) means impaired; the sense is that they have perished. In this regard, some...
Because of the statement, “For one who has attained the attainment of cessation, only the mental formations have ceased,” they claim that the mind is not ceased;
therefore, they say this attainment is accompanied by consciousness. They should be asked:
“Because of the statement, ‘His verbal formations also have ceased,’ would speech then be unceased? Consequently, could one who has attained cessation speak Dhamma or even recite [the scriptures]?”

One might have to sit while performing [the rite]. Furthermore, because of the statement, "In the case of one who is dead and has passed away, even his mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*) have ceased," it would follow that the mind [of the deceased] has not ceased;
therefore, for one who burns parents or Arahants who have passed away, an immediate offense (*ānantariyakamma*) would be committed.
Thus, without adhering to the literal expression, according to the method of the teachers—
Having stood [firmly], the meaning must be examined; for the meaning is the refuge, not the letter.

Regarding the phrase "the faculties are serene": when the occurrence consisting of kamma-formations is proceeding and the sense-faculties are being struck by external objects, the faculties become weary, impaired, and as if defiled by wind and other such disturbances.
It is like a slave set free by a king at a crossroads.

Furthermore, just as a mirror placed inside a casket or a chest after being wrapped in a cloth shines all the more within, so too do the five translucent organs shine intensely within the cessation of a bhikkhu who has attained cessation.
Therefore it is said: "The faculties are serene."
458. "Friend, as for 'how many conditions,' what is he asking here? He asks thinking, 'I shall ask about the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the proximity condition for cessation.
In its answer, however, four conditions of departure are stated: 'with the abandoning of pleasure,' and so forth.
As for 'for the signless,' what is he asking here? He asks thinking, 'I shall ask about the attainment of fruition emerging from cessation.'"

He asks this because emergence from the remaining attainments occurs by means of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), whereas emergence from cessation occurs through the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) which is the natural outflow of insight (*vipassanā*);
therefore, he asks specifically about that. "Of all signs" refers to all objects such as form and so forth.
"Attention to the signless element" refers to attention directed toward the element of Nibbāna, which is free from all signs.

This was said with reference to the attention (manasikāra) that arises simultaneously with the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Thus, below, the first jhāna serving as the basis for cessation (nirodhapādaka) was taken;
the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), which is the immediate condition (anantarapaccaya) for cessation, was taken;
and here, the attainment of fruition emerging from cessation is taken.
At this point, a discussion on cessation (*nirodha*) ought to be told. This is presented in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* as follows:
"The knowledge of the attainment of cessation is the wisdom consisting in mastery through two powers, the subsiding of three formations, sixteen modes of knowledge, and nine modes of concentration.
However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, it is treated in its entirety.
The discussion on the exposition has been told.
Now, asking about the attainment of functional consciousness, he said: "But, friend, how many conditions are there?
and so forth. For indeed, there is no such thing as a "maintenance" for the attainment of fruition emerging from cessation; having proceeded for only one or two mental moments, it ceases.

It descends into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). For this bhikkhu, having sat for seven days suppressing the occurrence of the formless, does not remain long in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) that emerges from cessation.
However, in the case of the functional attainment (*valañjanasamāpatti*), the limit of duration is the only measure;
therefore, that is called "stability. Hence he said: "for the stability of the signless liberation of mind. For the sake of its long-term stability—
The meaning is "how many conditions. In the response, however, the delimitation of time was stated as "prior volitional formation" (*pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro*).
With the phrase "for emergence" (*vuṭṭhānāya*), he here asks about the emergence from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
In its response as well, "attention to all signs" (*sabbanimittānañca manasikāro*) refers to the attention co-arising with the life-continuum by way of signs such as visible forms.
459. "And as for this, 'friend,' what does he ask here? There is nothing new here. He asks, thinking:
'I am asking by bringing together into one those very same phenomena already explained below. But where were they explained? In this passage:
'One perceives blue, one perceives yellow, one perceives red, and one perceives white. Thus it is said at that place.
The immeasurable liberation of mind has been explained. In the passage, “‘There is nothing’ is to be understood as the base of nothingness,” it is *ākiñcañña* (nothingness).

In the passage, “One understands with the eye of wisdom,” it is *suññatā* (emptiness). In the passage, “But, friends, how many conditions are there for the maintenance and emergence from the signless liberation of mind? it is *animittā* (the signless). Thus, these have already been explained below in this [work].

He asks by bringing [these] together from their respective places. However, having rejected that [objection] and stated that these have been pointed out in their respective places, the *Aṭṭhakathā* reaches its conclusion:
"He asks here in order to have it explained by making manifest that there are four other things (*dhamma*) with a single name, and one thing (*dhamma*) with four names. Of that...
Regarding the answer: "Friends, this is called the immeasurable liberation of mind"—it is called "immeasurable" because of its immeasurable pervasiveness.
For it either pervades immeasurable beings, or it pervades even a single being without exception. Regarding the answer:
"Friends, this is called 'nothingness'"—it is "nothingness" because of the absence of any "something" (kiñcana) as an object. Or, by way of self...
It is empty of a self (atta) designated as "being," "sustainer," "person," and so forth. Or, it is empty of what belongs to a self (attaniya), that is, empty of requisites such as robes and the like.
It is signless (animittā) precisely because of the absence of signs of lust and so on; this is said with reference to the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.
"Both different in meaning and different in phrasing": their phrasing (byañjana) is different and their meaning (attha) is also different. In that regard:

The diversity of the phrasing is indeed evident. As for the meaning: the immeasurable liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) is "exalted" (*mahaggata*) in terms of its plane, being of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*);

in terms of its object, it has the seven conceptual objects (*paññatti-ārammaṇa*). The base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) is "exalted" in terms of its plane, being of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*);
in terms of its object, it has an object that cannot be specified. The base of emptiness (*suññatāyatana*) in terms of its plane is of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); in terms of its object—
They have formations as their object. For here, "emptiness" (suññatā) is intended in the sense of insight (vipassanā). They are signless (animittā) by way of plane, being supramundane (lokuttara);
they have Nibbāna as their object by way of object.
As it is said in such passages as, "Lust, friend, is a maker of measure," there is what is called rotten-leaf water at the foot of a mountain.
It is black in color; to those looking at it, it appears as if it were a hundred fathoms deep.
Even for one who takes a staff or a rope to measure it, it does not even reach as far as the covering of his own heels.
In the same way, as long as lust and the other defilements have not arisen, it is impossible to perceive the person as a "stream-enterer," a "once-returner," or a "non-returner."
And it appears as such. But when lust and the other defilements arise in him, then he is known as "lustful," "hateful," or "deluded.
Thus, these [defilements] are called "measure-makers" because they arise as if showing the measure of the person, as in "this one is of such an extent.
"As far, friend, as there are immeasurable deliverances of mind" means however many immeasurable deliverances of mind there are.
But how many are they? There are twelve: the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), the four paths, and the four fruits.
Among these, the divine abodes are "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) because of their pervasive and boundless nature. The remaining ones are immeasurable due to the absence of defilements that act as limits.
Nibbāna is indeed immeasurable as well, but it is not included here because it is not a liberation of mind (cetovimutti).
"Unshakable" refers to the liberation of mind that is the fruit of arahantship; for it is the eldest of all those [liberations], and therefore it is said to be "declared the foremost.
"Lust, friend, is a burden" means that lust, having arisen, burdens, crushes, and fetters the person;
therefore it is called a "burden. It is said that people, while having oxen trample a threshing floor, say: "Trample, Kapila! Trample!"

They call them "black. Thus, the meaning of *maddana* (crushing) should be understood as the meaning of *kiñcana* (burden/possessiveness). The same method applies to hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*).

The so-called "deliverances of mind through nothingness" (*ākiñcaññā cetovimuttiyo*) consist of nine things: the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), the paths (*magga*), and the fruits (*phala*).

In that context, the base of nothingness is called "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*) because it has no *kiñcana* (burden/object) as its objective support (*ārammaṇa*). As for the paths and fruits, they are [the absence of] *kiñcanas*.

They are "nothingnesses" (ākiñcaññāni) because of the absence of the defilements that act as fetters for those who seek to overcome them. Nibbāna is also nothingness, but it is not the liberation of mind (cetovimutti);
therefore, it is not included here.
In passages such as "Lust, friend, is the making of signs," it is just as when two calves belonging to two different families are similar to one another.
They exist. As long as no mark has been made upon them, it is impossible to know, "This calf belongs to such-and-such a family;
this one belongs to such-and-such a family. But when a mark—such as a spear-point or the like—is made upon them, then it becomes possible to know.
In the same way, as long as lust does not arise in a person, [it is impossible to know him].
It is not possible to know whether this person is noble or a worldling.
However, when lust arises within him, it arises as if creating a sign for the recognition that "this person is one possessed of lust"; therefore, he is called "one who makes a sign.
The same principle applies to hatred and delusion as well.
The signless liberation of mind consists of thirteen states: insight, the four formless attainments, the four paths, and the four fruits.
Among these, insight is called "signless" because it eliminates the signs of permanence, pleasure, and self.
The four formless attainments are called "signless" due to the absence of the sign of form. The paths and fruits [are likewise signless].
They are "signless" (animitta) due to the absence of the defilements that produce signs.
Nibbāna is also signless, but it is not the liberation of mind (cetovimutti); therefore, it was not included. Now, why was the emptiness liberation (suññatā cetovimutti) not included separately?
Because, according to such statements as "empty of lust," it is already permeated throughout all [the other liberations], and thus it was not taken separately. They have the same meaning (ekattha).
They are identical in meaning by way of their object. For "the immeasurable," "nothingness," "emptiness," and "the signless"—all these are indeed names for Nibbāna itself.
Thus, in this manner, they are identical in meaning. However, in another sense, they are different in phrasing:
they are "immeasurable" in one place, "nothingness" in another, "emptiness" in another, and "the signless" in another; it is in this manner that they differ in expression.
Thus the Elder brought his teaching to its conclusion by following the very sequence [of the discourse].
The commentary on the Mahāvedalla Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
4. Commentary on the Cūḷavedalla Sutta 460.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷavedalla Sutta. In this context, "the lay follower Visākha" means a lay follower named Visākha.
"Where Dhammadinnā was" means he approached the place where the bhikkhunī named Dhammadinnā was. But who is she?
Who was Visākha? Who was Dhammadinnā? Why did he approach her? Visākha was the husband of Dhammadinnā during her time as a householder.

When the Blessed One, having awakened to perfect self-enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, had trained such noble sons as Yasa and others, and having reached Uruvelā, there trained the thousand matted-hair ascetics along with the former matted-hair ascetics...

Having gone to Rājagaha together with bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted, he taught the Dhamma to King Bimbisāra, who had arrived with a retinue of twelve hundred thousand for the purpose of seeing the Buddha. At that time, among the twelve hundred thousand who had come with the king,
one hundred thousand declared themselves lay followers (upāsaka), while eleven hundred thousand attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
They established themselves together with King Bimbisāra. This lay follower was one of them;

having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry at their very first meeting, he later heard the Dhamma on another day and attained the fruit of once-returning, and subsequently, on yet another day, he heard the Dhamma and established himself in the fruit of non-returning. He was a non-returner.

Having made the offering, as he was returning home, instead of coming as he usually did—looking here and there, smiling, and chatting—he did not come in that manner; rather, with his faculties and mind composed, he approached.
Dhammadinnā, having opened the lion-window and looking out at the street, observed the manner of his arrival.
Thinking, "What could this be? she went out to meet him and, standing at the top of the stairs, extended her hand for him to take hold of.
The lay devotee withdrew his hand. She thought, "I shall find out at the time of the morning meal.
Previously, the lay devotee used to eat together with her; however, on that day, he did not seek her permission.
He ate all alone, like a bhikkhu practicing yoga. She thought, "I shall find out at evening time.
That day, the lay follower did not enter the bedchamber; instead, having had another chamber prepared and a proper couch arranged, he lay down there.
The laywoman wondered, "Does he have some desire for someone outside, or has he been alienated by someone?"
Thinking, "Has he departed, or is there some fault on my part? she was overcome with intense dejection.
Concluding, "I shall be able to find out after staying for one or two days," she went to his attendance hall, paid homage, and stood there.
The lay follower asked, "Dhammadinnā, why have you come at an improper time? She replied, "Yes, noble son, I have come; it is not you—"
“As before, Dhammadinna, do you have any longing for what is external? “There is none, sir. “Is there anyone else who causes dissension?
“There is no such person either, sir. “If that is so, then some fault must lie with me alone.
“There is no fault in you either. “Then why is it that even a mere exchange of ordinary conversation with me does not take place as it did before?”
"Do you not do it? He thought: "This so-called supramundane Dhamma is weighty and profound; it should not be disclosed.
However, if I do not speak of it, she will tear her heart asunder and die right here. Out of compassion for her, he spoke:
"Dhammadinnā, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, I have attained what is called the supramundane Dhamma."
For one who has attained such a state, worldly activities of this kind are not appropriate.
If you so desire, there is a wealth of eighty crores—forty crores for you and forty crores for me;
being the master of this, dwell here in the position of a mother or a sister to me. I shall subsist on the mere morsel of food provided by you.
“If you do not do so, take these riches and go to your family home;
even if you have no desire for the outside world, I shall support you, placing you in the position of a sister or a daughter.
She thought: “There is no ordinary man who would speak thus. Surely he has attained the supreme supramundane Dhamma.”
“...has been penetrated. But must that Dhamma be realized by men alone, or can women also penetrate it?
He said this to Visākhā: “Is this Dhamma to be obtained by men alone, or can it also be obtained by women?
“What do you say, Dhammadinnā? Those who have practiced the way are the heirs of this Dhamma. Regarding that which...
"Whoever possesses the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya) attains this. This being so, please grant me permission to go forth.
"Very well, Bhaddā; I too wish to engage you on this very path, but I did not speak because I was unaware of your intention.
Having said this, she immediately went into the presence of King Bimbisāra, paid homage, and stood there.
The king asked, "Householder, why have you come at this unseasonable hour? Dhammadinnā replied, "Great King, she says she wishes to go forth.
"What else does she require? "Nothing else, Your Majesty;
she requires a golden palanquin and that the city be cleaned. The king gave her a golden palanquin and had the city cleaned.
Visākha had Dhammadinnā bathed with scented water, adorned her with all kinds of ornaments, seated her in a golden palanquin, and surrounded her with a circle of kinsmen.

Honoring her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings as if performing a city procession, he went to the nuns’ residence and said, “Venerable ladies, please grant Dhammadinnā the going-forth. The nuns [said], “One...
“Householder, it is permissible to endure two or three faults,” they said. “There is no fault at all, noble lady; one goes forth out of faith.
Then a certain competent elder nun, having explained the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*), shaved his hair and gave him the going-forth.
Visākha, saying, “Delightful, noble lady! Well-proclaimed is the Dhamma,” paid homage and departed.
From the day she went forth, gain and honor arose for her. Being hindered by that very thing, she found no opportunity to practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Then, taking her preceptor and teacher, the elder nuns (*therī*), they went to the countryside;

having had her instructed in a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from among the thirty-eight objects of focus according to her own preference, she began to practice the duty of a recluse. Because she was endowed with a resolute aspiration (*abhinīhāra*), [she attained success].
However, she did not suffer for very long.
For from this point forward, at the end of one hundred thousand eons, a teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
At that time, she was a female slave in a certain family; having sold her own hair, [she gave it] to the chief disciple named Sujāta Thera.
Having given the gift, she made a resolution. By virtue of the perfection of that resolution and its dedication, she did not suffer for long;
in just a few days, having attained Arahantship, she thought: "The purpose for which I went forth in the Dispensation has reached its culmination.
What need have I for living in the countryside? My kinsmen will perform meritorious deeds, and the community of bhikkhunīs as well."
“Without being exhausted by the conditions, I shall go to Rājagaha,” he said, and taking the community of bhikkhunīs with him, he went to Rājagaha itself.

When Visākha heard, “It is said that Dhammadinnā has arrived,” he thought, “Not long after going forth she went to the countryside, and not long after returning from there she has come back; what could this be? I will go and find out.”
By his second journey, he went to the nuns’ quarters. Therefore it was said: “Then the lay follower Visākha approached the nun Dhammadinnā. He said this:
he spoke these words beginning with “This is identity” (sakkāyo). Why did he say this? It is said that this thought occurred to him: “Are you enjoying yourself?”
“‘You do not find delight, noble lady’—such a question is not the work of a wise person. I shall ask the question by way of the five aggregates of clinging;
through the answer to that question, I will know whether she finds delight or does not find delight.
That is why he spoke thus. Upon hearing this, Dhammadinnā said: “Friend Visākha, it has not been long since I went forth from my own [home].”
Without saying, "How shall I know another's body? or "I will go to other elder nuns and ask," she stood upon the domain of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*),
as if accepting what was placed before her, as if untying a knot on a single side,
as if clearing a path for elephants through a thicket, and as if opening a casket with the tip of a sword.
While answering the question, he said: "Friend Visākha, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging," and so forth.
In this context, "five" is a numerical delimitation. "Aggregates subject to clinging" means aggregates that have become conditions for clinging;
in this manner, the exposition of the aggregates subject to clinging should be explained here in detail. That exposition, moreover, has been set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, this should be understood there according to the method already explained. Whatever is to be said regarding the origin of identity (*sakkāya-samudaya*) and so forth has already been stated below in those respective places.
However, having heard this exposition of the Four Noble Truths, Visākha understood the elder nun’s state of delight. For whoever...
He becomes weary of and dissatisfied with the Buddha’s teaching;

thus, when questioned again and again on these matters, he is unable to answer, like one trying to grasp individual strands of hair with a pair of tongs, or like one attempting to lift up sand from the foot of Mount Sineru.
For these Four Truths are as manifest in the Buddha’s teaching as the sun and moon are in the world.
For even the Blessed One and the great elders teach the truths themselves when they have gone into the midst of the assembly;
and the community of monks, from the very day of their going forth, causes sons of good family to learn the question: "What are the four? They are the four noble truths.
And this Dhammadinnā, established in skillful means, wise, competent, and having grasped the method, was capable of speaking even based on what she had heard.
Therefore, thinking, "It is not possible to know the extent to which she has penetrated the Truths by this much;

it can only be known by answering questions that analyze the Truths," he withdrew the two Truths mentioned above, concealed them, and intending to ask a knotty question (*gaṇṭhipañha*), he spoke as follows, beginning with, "Is it that very [Truth], Noble Lady? and so forth.

Regarding the answer to that: "Friend Visākha, it is not the case that clinging itself is those [aggregates]. This is because clinging is only one part of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);
therefore, those five aggregates of clinging are not themselves clinging, nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates of clinging.
For if it were the same as them, then the intrinsic nature of form and the other aggregates would also be clinging; and if it were something apart from them, [clinging would exist independently].

In the systems of other teachers, [the self] might be something dissociated from the aggregates—like a latent tendency (*anusaya*), like a mere designation (*paññatti*), or like *nibbāna*—or else a sixth aggregate would have to be postulated;

therefore, he answered in this way. Having heard that answer, Visākha reached the conclusion: "This one has found a firm footing," for it is not possible for one whose taints (*āsava*) are not yet exhausted [to do so].

It was impossible to answer such a profound question—one that is subtle, concealed, struck by the three characteristics, and difficult to fathom—without becoming entangled or digressing, as if one were trying to light a thousand lamps at once. But having reached a definitive conclusion, [the Buddha thought]:

"This Dhammadinnā has gained a firm footing in the Teaching; she has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and reached fearlessness (vesārajjappatta); she stands at the pinnacle of existence, a great one whose taints are exhausted (mahākhīṇāsavā)."

Thinking, “He is capable of answering the question I have asked; now, however, I shall ask him a question that goes to the very core,” he spoke the words beginning with “But how, venerable sir? while posing that question. 461.
Regarding the answer to that, the passage beginning with “the uninstructed person” has already been explained in detail in the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*. As for “regarding form as self”:
“Here, someone regards form as self: ‘What is form, that am I; what I am, that is form. Thus he regards form and self as non-dual.
Just as, for example, when an oil lamp is burning, one regards the flame and the color as non-dual—‘What is the flame, that is the color;
what is the color, that is the flame’—even so, here someone [regards form as self].”
“He regards form as self... [and so on] ...he regards it as non-dual”—thus he sees form as self by means of the vision of wrong view (*diṭṭhipassanā*).
Or, “one who possesses form is the self”: having grasped the formless as the self, he regards that self as possessing form, like a tree possessing shade.
Or, “form is in the self”: having grasped the formless alone as the self, [he regards it as being] in the flower...

One regards form as being in oneself, like a fragrance; or one regards oneself as being in form, like a gem in a casket—having grasped the formless itself as the self, one regards the self as being within form. The same method applies to such passages as "feeling as self.
In that context, "regards form as self" means that pure form alone is stated to be the self; or [it means] "possessing form."
"One regards self as form, or form as in self, or self as in form; one regards feeling as self... perception... volitional formations...
consciousness as self"—in these seven instances, the formless is stated to be "self.
Or, "one regards self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling"—thus, in the case of the four aggregates, there are three [modes].
By way of these three, a self consisting of a mixture of form and formless is described in twelve places. Among those, the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is described in these five places:
"one regards form as self... feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self";
in the remaining [seven] places, it is the view of eternalism (*sassatadṛṣṭi*). Thus, there are fifteen views of existence (*bhavadṛṣṭi*) here.
There are five views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*). Regarding "form is not the self," one does not regard form as the self;
rather, one regards it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. One does not regard the self as possessing form...
[and so on] ...nor does one regard the self as being within consciousness. In every way, one does not regard these five aggregates as the self by any means whatsoever.
Furthermore, one regards them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. To this extent,
for the Elder Nun who was thus answering the previous question— “In this way, friend Visākha, personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) comes to be”—
there is going, there is coming, there is going and coming, and the round of existence (vaṭṭa) proceeds.

Having brought the cycle (vaṭṭa) to its conclusion, it was thus demonstrated. In this way, friend Visākha, when answering the final question— "How is it that personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) does not exist?"—

it was demonstrated by reaching the pinnacle of the turning away from the cycle (vivaṭṭa), showing that there is no going, no coming, no going-and-coming, and that what is called a "cycle" no longer revolves.
462. "But what, noble lady, is the Noble Eightfold Path?"—this question should have been answered by the Elder Nun after asking him in return:
"Lay follower, you asked about the Path previously; why do you ask about the Path again here?
However, through her own proficiency and wisdom, she discerned his intention: "By this lay follower..."

"Below, the Path was asked by way of practice; here, however, he will wish to ask about it by way of its inclusion within or exclusion from the conditioned and the unconditioned, the mundane and the supramundane.
Therefore, without asking a counter-question, he answered each and every thing that was asked.
In this context, "conditioned" means that which is willed, fashioned, planned, exerted, made, and produced by one who attains [meditative absorption].
It should be attained. Furthermore, friend Visākha, regarding the statement "the Noble Eightfold Path is comprised within three aggregates":

since the Path has specific instances (sappadesa) while the three aggregates are without specific instances (nippadesa), it is therefore—due to its having specific instances—comprised by the three aggregates which are without specific instances, just as a city is comprised by a kingdom.
In that context, the three beginning with right speech are simply virtue (sīla).
Therefore, they are included within the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) by way of their common origin.
For although in the text the designation "aggregate of virtue" is made as if it were a locative case, its meaning should rather be understood in the sense of the instrumental.

However, among the three beginning with right effort, concentration is unable, by its own nature, to settle upon the object with one-pointedness; it is through the function of exertion in energy, however, that—
And it is able to provide assistance to one who is accomplishing the function of non-forgetfulness while practicing mindfulness.
In this regard, there is this simile: Suppose three friends have entered a park intending to enjoy a festival;
one of them, upon seeing a *campaka* tree in full bloom, might not be able to grasp it even by raising his hand.
Then a second person might bend down and offer his back; though standing upon that man’s back, he would still be unable to grasp [the flowers] because of trembling.

Then the other might offer him his shoulder; standing upon one man’s back and leaning against the shoulder of another, he could pluck flowers as he pleased, adorn himself with them, and enjoy the festival. This is exactly how it is.
It should be seen thus: for the three qualities beginning with right effort, which arise together, are like three friends who have entered a garden together;

the object is like a fully blossomed *campaka* flower; concentration is like one who, despite raising his hand, is unable to grasp it, or like one who, by his own nature, is unable to settle in one-pointedness upon the object. The back...
Viriya is like a companion who has given his back, while sati is like a companion who stands supporting one's shoulder. Just as,
when standing on the back of one and leaning upon the shoulder of another,
a person is able to gather flowers according to their desire, so too, while viriya performs the function of exertion and sati performs the function of non-forgetfulness, [the practitioner succeeds].
Concentration that has received assistance is able to settle upon the object with one-pointedness.

Therefore, it is concentration itself that is here included in the aggregate of concentration by way of its intrinsic nature (*sajātito*). Effort and mindfulness, however, are included by way of their function (*kiriyato*).
As for right view and right intention, wisdom—by its own essential nature—takes as its object [the aggregates] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
He is unable to determine it, but he is able to do so by repeatedly striking at the thoughts.

How? Just as a money-changer, wishing to examine all sides of a coin while holding it in his hand, cannot turn it over merely by the power of his eyes, but is able to turn it over with his fingers and examine it from this side and that.
In the same way, wisdom (paññā) is not able by its own nature to determine an object in terms of impermanence and so forth;

rather, it is only when it is given [the object] by applied thought (vitakka)—which has the characteristic of directing and the function of striking and rubbing, as if hammering and turning it over—that it is able to determine it.
Therefore, here too, it is right view itself that, by way of its own kind, constitutes the aggregate of wisdom.
It is included. Right intention, however, is included by way of activity. Thus, the Path is comprised within these three aggregates.
Therefore it was said: “Friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is indeed comprised within three aggregates.
Now, asking about the Path-concentration belonging to a single moment of consciousness, together with its object and its requisites: which...

He said, "Panāyya," and so forth. In its explanation: the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are mindfulness that has arisen at the moment of the Path by way of accomplishing the four functions;

that is the sign (*nimitta*) in the sense of being a condition for concentration. The four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are energy that has arisen precisely by way of accomplishing the four functions;
that is the equipment (*parikkhāra*) in the sense of being an attendant. "Of those very same states" refers to those...

Regarding the states associated with the path: among the terms beginning with "cultivation" (*āsevanā*), it is stated that cultivation and the others occur within a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).
However, the caviller (*vitaṇḍavādī*) argues: "There is no such thing as a path occurring in a single moment of consciousness;

for since there is the statement, 'One should thus develop [it] for seven years,' the development of the path lasts for seven years as well. But the defilements are severed quickly—in seven [moments]."
He says, "They are cut off by knowledges. He should be told: "Produce a sutta.

Certainly, seeing nothing else, he will bring forward this very sutta—"The cultivation, development, and frequent practice of those same states"—and then say, "One cultivates with one mind, develops with another, and practices frequently with yet another. Then he should be told:
"But is this sutta of interpretable meaning (neyyattha) or of definitive meaning (nītattha)? To that he will say: "It is of definitive meaning;

the meaning is exactly as the sutta states. This is the reply to him: If that were so, then while one person is practicing one state of mind, another might practice a different one, and yet another a further different one;
in this way, even throughout the day there would be only practice [of various things], so how [could there be a single, unified development]?

If one who is developing one [meditation subject] gives rise to another while still developing it, and yet another while developing that one—thus, there would be only development even for a whole day;
where then is the repetition, where is the frequent practice?
Or if one who is frequently practicing one gives rise to another while still frequently practicing it, and yet another while frequently practicing that one...
In this way, even during the day there would be only the act of repetition; where, then, would there be cultivation (*āsevanā*), and where development (*bhāvanā*)?
Or alternatively, one might say: "With one moment of consciousness one repeats, with two one develops, and with three one repeats frequently.
Or with two one repeats, with three one develops, and with one one repeats frequently. Or with three one repeats, and with one one develops."
