“He develops [the mind] by means of two [factors]. He should be told: “Do not say whatever you like just so that I may obtain a sutta.
One who answers a question must speak after having lived in the presence of a teacher, mastered the word of the Buddha, and understood the flavor of its meaning.
This repetition is indeed momentary, occurring within a single moment of consciousness; this cultivation is momentary.”
“Cultivation consists of a single moment of consciousness. There is no supramundane path leading to destruction that is said to consist of multiple moments of consciousness;
it should be made known as being ‘of only a single moment of consciousness. If he perceives this, let him perceive it. If he does not perceive it, send him away, saying:
‘Enter the monastery early in the morning and drink some rice-gruel. Thus should he be dismissed.

463. “But, Noble Lady, how many formations (saṅkhāra) are there?”—what is he asking here? He asks thinking, “I shall ask about those formations by ceasing which one enters the attainment of cessation.

Knowing his intention, the Elder Nun, although many formations such as the formation of merit exist, explained only the bodily formations and so forth, saying: “There are these three, friend,” and so on.
In this context, it is called a bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) because it is formed, made, and produced by the body due to its connection with the body.

It is called a verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) because it forms, makes, and produces speech. It is called a mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) because it is formed, made, and produced by the mind due to its connection with the mind.
But what is he asking here, "Which, venerable sir"? He is asking about these formations.
When mixed together, they are confused, indistinct, and difficult to clarify.

For instance, when the eight wholesome volitions and the twelve unwholesome volitions of the sense sphere arise at the body door by bringing about seizing, grasping, releasing, and pressing, these twenty wholesome and unwholesome volitions as well as the in-breaths and out-breaths are called simply "bodily formations. At the speech door, there is the movement of the jaws.
The twenty types of volition (cetanā) that have arisen after reaching vocal expression— of the kind already described— as well as applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra),
are called the verbal formation (vacī-saṅkhāra). Furthermore, the twenty-nine types of wholesome and unwholesome volition that have arisen while one is sitting in private thinking,
before they have reached the doors of body and speech, as well as these two factors— perception (saññā) and feeling (vedanā)— are called the mental formation (citta-saṅkhāra).
"In this way, these formations are mutually mixed, agitated, indistinct, and difficult to illuminate. Thinking, 'I shall explain them after making them clear and distinct,' he asks.
But why does he ask, 'What, venerable sir'?
Here he asks for the word-meaning (*padattha*) of the names "bodily formation" and so forth. In the answer to that, [the phrase] "bound up with the body" is used.

"Dependent on the body": they exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not. "Bound up with the mind": dependent on the mind, they exist when the mind exists and do not exist when it does not.
464. Now, does this person master the cessation of perception and feeling, or does he not? One who has attained mastery...
Or, asking in order to know whether they have mastered that [state] there, he said: "But how, Noble Lady, does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling come about?
and so forth. In his answer, the two phrases "they will enter" or "I am entering" describe the time of entering the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
By the phrase "having entered," internal cessation is described. Likewise, by the first two phrases, the time when one possesses consciousness is indicated.

The period without consciousness has been explained by means of the latter [simile]. "The mind was previously developed in such a way" means that even before the attainment of cessation—at the very time of delimiting the duration—one develops the thought that delimits the duration, thinking, "I shall remain without consciousness for this long.
"That which leads one to suchness" refers to the person whose mind has been developed in this manner.
It leads toward suchness, which is the state of being without mind.
First, verbal formation ceases; that is, it ceases first among the remaining formations, right within the second jhāna.
After that, bodily formation ceases; that is, subsequently, bodily formation ceases in the fourth jhāna. After that, mental formation ceases.
Beyond that, the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) ceases within the cessation [of consciousness].
By the two phrases "I shall emerge" or "I am emerging," the time of internal cessation is described. By the phrase "emerged," the time of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is indicated.
Likewise, by the first two phrases the period of being without consciousness is described, and by the last one, the period of having consciousness. As before, so it is here.
"The mind is cultivated" means that at the very time of delimiting the duration prior to the attainment of cessation,
the mind that delimits the duration— "I shall remain without consciousness for this much time and thereafter become conscious again"—
is cultivated. "That which leads one to suchness" means that the mind thus cultivated leads the person to suchness.
He brings [the mind] to a state possessing consciousness. Thus, the time of entering the attainment of cessation was taken up below; here, it is the time of emerging from cessation.
Now is the occasion to discuss the discourse on cessation, so the discourse on cessation should be told. That discourse, moreover, begins:
"Because of being endowed with two powers, because of the subsiding of three formations, and by means of sixteen modes of knowledge..."

Having established the outline: “The wisdom consisting in mastery through the nine modes of conduct in concentration is knowledge of the attainment of cessation,” this has been explained in every detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.
But what is this so-called “cessation”? It is the non-occurrence of the four aggregates following their analytical reflection. Now, for what purpose do they attain this?
They enter this attainment for the purpose of thinking: "We shall dwell happily for seven days without consciousness, weary of the occurrence of mental formations;
this indeed is Nibbāna in the present life, namely cessation.
First, the mental formation arises; for when one emerges from cessation, the fruit-attainment consciousness [arises].
It arises first. Referring to the perception and feeling associated with it, he said, "The mental formation arises first.
After that, the bodily formation: following that, at the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the bodily formation arises.
But does the attainment of fruition not arouse inhalation and exhalation? It does arouse them.
However, for this [person], the attainment of fruition belonging to the fourth jhāna does not originate [the breaths]. Or rather, what is the use of this?

Whether the attainment of fruition belongs to the first jhāna, or to the second, third, or fourth jhāna, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from a peaceful attainment, the inhalations and exhalations are beyond reckoning.
The fact that they are beyond reckoning is illustrated by the case of the Elder Sañjīva.

This is to be understood. For when the Elder Sañjīva emerged from attainment and walked while treading upon glowing embers resembling kiṃsuka flowers, not even a thread of his robe was burned, nor was there even the slightest appearance of heat;
they say this is indeed the fruit of attainment. In the same way, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from such an attainment, the inhalations and exhalations [do not occur].
"It is called 'abstraction' (abbōhārikā)" should be understood as being said in reference to the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) itself.
"Then there is the verbal formation" means that after that, at the time of the movement of articulation consisting of functional activity, the verbal formation arises.

Does the life-continuum not arouse applied thought and sustained thought? It does arouse them. However, the applied thought and sustained thought that arise from it [are those belonging to the functional consciousness].
"It is not possible to formulate speech"—this was said with reference to the very time of the functioning of the vocal intimation (*vācaṃ-abhisaṅkhātuṃ*).
"Contact as emptiness" (*suññato phasso*) and so forth should be explained both by way of their quality (*saguṇena*) and by way of their object (*ārammaṇena*). First, by way of their quality:

"emptiness" (*suññatā*) is the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); referring to the contact that is co-nascent with that attainment, it is called "contact as emptiness. The same applies to "the signless" (*animitta*) and "the desireless" (*appaṇihita*).
This is the method. As for the object, however, Nibbāna is called "void" (suñña) because it is void of lust and the other defilements;
it is "signless" (animitta) because of the absence of the signs of lust and so forth; and it is "wishless" (appaṇihita) because of the absence of the yearnings of lust, hatred, and delusion.
Contact that arises in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) by taking the void Nibbāna as its object is called "void contact. The same method applies to the signless and the wishless as well.
There is another discourse on what is to be arrived at, namely, emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animittā*), and desirelessness (*appaṇihitā*); for this is also called insight (*vipassanā*).

In that regard, when a bhikkhu, having discerned formations as impermanent and having seen them as impermanent, emerges from them as impermanent, his insight leading to emergence is called "signless" (*animittā*). When [he] has discerned them as suffering and [has seen them] as suffering...

Having seen [the formations] as suffering, one emerges from them; for such a person, it is called "the signless" (*appaṇihita*). Having comprehended them as non-self and having seen them as non-self, one emerges from them as non-self; for such a person, it is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*).

In this context, the path associated with signless insight is called "signless," and the fruit of the signless path is called "signless. Regarding the contact that arises simultaneously with the attainment of the signless fruit:
When touching, it is said that "signless contact touches. The same method applies to wishless and empty [contacts] as well.
However, if this were explained by means of what is to be arrived at, one would fall into the alternative [view] that "contact is either empty, or signless, or wishless";
therefore, it must be explained by means of both its quality and its object. For in this way, the three contacts "touch"—this is consistent.

In such passages as "inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekaninna*), Nibbāna is called "seclusion" (*viveka*). That which is inclined toward, or bent down toward, that seclusion is "inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekaninna*).
That which stands as if it were curved toward seclusion after having come from elsewhere is "sloping toward seclusion" (*vivekapoṇa*).
That which stands as if falling toward seclusion is "leaning toward seclusion" (*vivekapabbhāra*).
465. Now, thinking, "I shall ask about those feelings by ceasing which one enters the attainment of cessation," he asks:

"But how many, noble lady, are the feelings? Regarding the phrases "bodily" (*kāyika*) and so forth, it should be understood that pleasure associated with the five sense doors is called "bodily," while that associated with the mind door is called "mental" (*cetasika*).
Therein, "pleasure" (*sukha*) is a description of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Delightful" (*sāta*)...
This is a synonym illustrating its sweet nature. "Vedayita" (the felt) illustrates the state of being felt;
it is a common term for all feelings (*vedanā*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

In such expressions as "the pleasure of stability and the pain of change," the presence of a pleasant feeling is "pleasure" (*sukha*), while its absence is "pain" (*dukkha*). The presence of a painful feeling is "pain."
The state of non-existence is happiness. The meaning is that the state of knowing the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is happiness, while the state of not knowing it is suffering.

"What underlying tendency lies latent? asks which underlying tendency lies latent. He asks this question regarding the underlying tendencies because they are, in the sense of being unabandoned, as if "lying down" (anusaya).
"Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust does not lie latent in all pleasant feelings"—it is not so.
The underlying tendency to lust underlies every pleasant feeling.

This means that it is not the case that this [tendency] has been abandoned in relation to every pleasant feeling, nor does it arise by taking every pleasant feeling as its object. This same method applies everywhere.
"What is to be abandoned?"—this is what is called the question regarding abandonment.
"By that, he abandons lust"—here, with a single explanation, he answered two questions.
In this case, a bhikkhu, having suppressed the underlying tendency to lust, enters the first jhāna;
then, having ensured that the underlying tendency to lust suppressed by the jhāna remains suppressed, he develops insight and eradicates it by means of the path of non-returning. He...
Although [the defilements] have been abandoned by the path of non-returning, they are said not to underlie the first jhāna precisely because they have been suppressed. Therefore it is said:
"Therein the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie. "That sphere" (tadāyatana) means that sphere;
the meaning is that it is Arahantship, which serves as a foundation by way of being the supreme consolation. Thus, "in the unsurpassed" refers to those liberations so named.

"Generating longing for arahantship" means one who establishes an aspiration (*patthana*). "Depression arises with longing as its condition" means that depression arises rooted in the establishment of an aspiration.

However, this does not arise rooted in the mere establishment of an aspiration; rather, it arises rooted in non-attainment for one who, having aspired, fails to obtain [the goal]. Thus it is said: "Depression arises with longing as its condition."

It has been said. In that regard, although what is called mental grief (*domanassa*) is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*), they say that this particular kind of mental grief is fit to be cultivated.
For practitioners (*yogī*) undertake a practice for three months, six months, or nine months.
Among them, one who has undertaken such a practice thinks: "I shall attain Arhatship within the very limit of this time."
Though he applied himself and strove, he was unable to reach his goal within the time limit he had set for himself;
consequently, a powerful dejection arose in him, and streams of tears flowed from his eyes, just like those of the Elder Mahāphussadeva, who lived at Āḷindika.
It is said that for nineteen years the elder fulfilled the practice of going forth and returning. Then, thinking, "In this very round, I shall attain Arahatship,"...
Thinking, "In this present year, I shall perform the *visuddhi-pavāraṇā*," he bound his mind [to this resolve] and spent nineteen years practicing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
On the day the *pavāraṇā* arrived, there was no day for the Elder to shed even a single tear.
However, in his twentieth year, he attained *arahatta*.
"By means of that, he abandons aversion": here, one abandons aversion by means of mental distress (*domanassa*) alone.
For there is no such thing as abandoning aversion by means of aversion itself, nor abandoning mental distress by means of mental distress.
However, this bhikkhu, having undertaken one of the practices lasting three months or more, reflects thus: "Behold, bhikkhu, what is the use of your virtue?"
“Is there a deficiency in my virtue, or in my energy, or in my wisdom? Is it not the case that my virtue is perfectly pure, my energy well-sustained, and my wisdom carries me forward with courage?
Having reflected thus, thinking, “I shall not allow this dejection to arise again,” he makes his energy firm for the remainder of the month or the remainder of the half-month.
Or, in the ninth month, he eradicates it by means of the path of non-returning.
In this manner, one truly abandons resentment through resentment itself, and dejection through dejection itself.
"The underlying tendency to resentment does not lie latent there" means that in such dejection, the underlying tendency to resentment does not remain latent.
It does not arise with reference to that; the meaning is that the underlying tendency to aversion has been abandoned therein. "He abandons ignorance by means of that" means:
here a bhikkhu, having suppressed the underlying tendency to ignorance, enters the fourth jhāna;
having ensured that the underlying tendency to ignorance suppressed by the jhāna remains suppressed, he develops insight and eradicates it by means of the path of Arahantship.
Thus, although ignorance has been abandoned by the path of arahantship, it is said not to underlie [the mind] in the fourth jhāna precisely because it has been suppressed.
Therefore he said: "Therein the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie.
Now, asking a question by way of a simile, he said: "But for one who is happy, O Venerable Sir," and so forth. In the answer to that:
Since suffering is the opposite of pleasure and pleasure is the opposite of suffering, the simile of "dissimilar" has been stated in reference to those two feelings.
However, since equanimity is dark, indistinct, and difficult to illuminate, and ignorance is likewise, the simile of "similar" has been stated here in that regard.
For in whatever places ignorance creates darkness, in those very same places knowledge [creates light].

"Dispels darkness" refers to a dissimilar counterpart. "But ignorance, friends," here both these phenomena are described as a similar counterpart because they are taintless (*anāsava*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).
"But liberation, friends," here it is described as a similar counterpart in the sense of being taintless, supramundane, and indeterminate (*abyākata*). "You have transgressed."

The meaning is: "In this matter, you have gone beyond the question. "He was unable to grasp the limit of the questions" means he was unable to grasp the measure or boundary of the questions; he asked about something that has no counterpart.
This so-called *nibbāna* has no counterpart; it cannot be compared with any other phenomenon such as blue or yellow.
This was said in order to show that you ask this with such an intention; such is the meaning.
At this point, this lay follower is like a monk who, having received a ticket-meal at the seventh house, passes by seven houses and stands at the door of the eighth, having missed all seven houses.

He did not understand; in this way, it should be understood that by asking about a counterpart for that which has no counterpart, he has failed in all seven questions concerning counterparts. "Plunged into Nibbāna" means having entered within Nibbāna.
"Having Nibbāna as its ultimate goal" means that Nibbāna is its supreme destination (*parāyaṇa*), its final resort; it does not go beyond that.
The meaning is as follows: *nibbānapariyosānaṃ* means that which has Nibbāna as its consummation (*pariyosāna*) or its end (*avasāna*).

"Those who are wise" (*paṇḍitā*) means those endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*); the meaning is those skilled in the elements (*dhātu*), skilled in the sense-bases (*āyatana*), skilled in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and skilled in what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*).
"Of great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*) means [those who possess] great wisdom regarding great meanings, great phenomena, and great linguistic expressions (*nirutti*).
They were endowed with wisdom capable of grasping great insights.
"Just as it was declared by Dhammadinnā"—meaning, "I too would declare it in exactly the same way as the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has declared.
To this extent, moreover, this discourse is known as spoken by the Victor (the Buddha), and not spoken by a disciple. For just as [it is when] royal ministers...
A written document does not attain the designation of a "royal edict" as long as it has not been sealed with the royal seal;

however, once merely sealed, it is called a royal edict. Likewise, because this discourse has been sealed with the seal of the Victor’s word—namely, the thought, "I too would explain it in exactly this way"—this sutta is said to have been spoken by the Victor through his direct utterance.
He was born. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Cūḷavedalla Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
5. Commentary on the Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta 468.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta. In this context, "undertakings of dhamma" (*dhammasamādānāni*) means that "dhamma" refers to things undertaken.
"Pleasure in the present" (*paccuppannasukha*) means pleasure in the present; it is pleasant and easy to perform at the moment of its execution.
It is possible to fulfill [them] with ease. "Resulting in suffering in the future" means that at the time of ripening in the future, there is a result of suffering.
The meaning in all these instances should be understood by this method.

469. "There is no fault in sensual pleasures" means there is no fault either in objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāmā*) or in defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāmā*). "They reach a state of being drunk" means...

The meaning is that they fall into a state of being drunk, of being consumed, of being enjoyed according to their desire by the defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*) within the object-desires (*vatthukāma*).
"By those with bound top-knots" means by those whose hair is tied in a top-knot (*moḷi*). "By female wanderers" means by female ascetic wanderers (*tāpasaparibbājikā*).
"They speak thus" means they say this. "They proclaim full understanding" means they proclaim abandonment and transcendence.
“Māluvā-sipāṭikā” means a ripened māluvā creeper that has grown long. “It might burst open” means it might split after drying up in the heat.
“At the foot of a sāla tree” means in the vicinity of a sāla tree. “It would fall into a state of terror”—why does it fall into such a state? Out of fear for the destruction of its dwelling.
For from a māluvā seed fallen at the root of a tree, a creeper arises and climbs the tree. When it has large leaves...
It has many leaves and is endowed with leaves resembling those of the *koviḷāra* tree.
Then, clinging to that tree from its very roots, it covers all the branches and remains there, producing a great burden.
When the wind blows or when the rain falls, it creates a torrent [of foliage] over all the primary and secondary branches of that tree.
It breaks and casts it down to the ground. Consequently, the celestial mansion (vimāna) established upon that tree is shattered and destroyed.
Thus, out of fear for the destruction of her dwelling, she falls into a state of terror.
An "ārāma-devatā" is a deity residing here and there in flower gardens and fruit orchards. A "vana-devatā" is...
Deities dwelling in forests such as Andhavana and Subhagavana;
tree deities are deities dwelling in specifically distinguished trees such as the *naḷeru* and *pucimanda*;

and deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants—namely, in medicinal herbs such as *harītakī* and *āmalakī*, in grasses such as the palm and coconut, and in forest-giant trees (*vanappati*).
"Forest-workers" refers to those people wandering about for some kind of work in the forest, such as clearing land, weeding, fetching timber, or tending cattle.
"They might uproot it" means they might eat it. "Hanging down" means hanging down as if playing in the places repeatedly struck by the wind.
"It is pleasant for her" means that even the touch of such a māluvā creeper is pleasant, and seeing it is also pleasant.
"This will be a drinking circle for my children, it will be a playground;
I have obtained a second celestial mansion"—thus she spoke, having conceived joy even at the sight and touch of the creeper.
"It would form a canopy" means it would stand over the branches like a parasol. "It would produce a mass" means below...
It would produce a dense mass. Having climbed up and wound itself all around the tree, it would then descend again and take hold of the ground;

this is the meaning. "It would split it open" means that having formed such a mass, it would then climb back up from there as far as the root with its descending branches, winding around all the branches, and reaching the top, by that very same process...

Then, having descended and ascended again, and having entwined the entire tree so as to completely envelop it, placing all the branches below and standing herself above, she would shatter it—meaning she would break it—even while the wind was blowing or the rain was falling.
Only the mere stump would remain; therein, whatever mansion made of interlaced branches exists, that [would be destroyed] along with the branches.
As they broke here and there, breaking right where they were shattered, and as all the branches were broken, everything was destroyed.
However, the tree-based celestial mansion (*vimāna*) does not perish as long as even the mere root of the tree remains. But this mansion was branch-based;
therefore, it was destroyed when all the branches were completely shattered. The deity stood upon a stump, holding her children.
They began to lament.

"One of intense lustful nature" means one whose character is thick with passion. "Experiences suffering and mental distress born of lust" means that, due to having an intense lustful nature, he grasps at the signs (*nimitta*) in every object seen. Then his teachers and preceptors...
They order him to perform penance. While constantly performing penance, he experiences pain and mental distress, yet he does not commit any transgression.
Being "naturally prone to intense hatred," he becomes angry even over a trivial matter;
he speaks while engaging in such acts as grasping the hands with young novices. He too [experiences] pain and mental distress on account of that penance.
He experiences [the result]. One whose nature is deluded, however, does not perceive what has been done here as "done" nor what has not been done as "not done";
he fails in those various duties. He too experiences pain and mental distress as a consequence of his punishment. 472.
"Not of a nature characterized by intense lust," and so forth, should be understood according to the method of the opposites of what was stated above. But why is this [stated] here?
Is there anyone whose nature is characterized by intense lust and so forth, and anyone whose nature is not characterized by intense lust and so forth? It is according to the law of karma.

For when, at the moment of accumulating karma, greed is strong and non-greed is weak, while non-hatred and non-delusion are strong and hatred and delusion are weak, then that weak non-greed is unable to overcome the greed;
however, the strong non-hatred and non-delusion are able to overcome hatred and delusion.
They are able [to do so]. Therefore, by way of the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) bestowed by that karma, he is born fierce;
yet he is of a pleasant disposition, free from anger, wise, and possesses knowledge like a thunderbolt.
However, for one at the moment of accumulating karma (*kammāyūhana*) when greed and hatred are powerful, while non-greed and non-hatred are weak, and non-delusion is strong—
Delusion is dull; by the same principle as before, such a person is both greedy and corrupt, yet he possesses wisdom, with knowledge like a thunderbolt, like the Elder Dattābhaya.

However, for one at the moment of accumulating karma whose greed, hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are dull, he is likewise—by the same principle as before—both greedy and dull-witted, yet he is of a pleasant disposition and free from anger.

Likewise, at the moment of accumulating karma, for one in whom greed, hatred, and delusion are powerful while non-greed and the others are weak, that person is—as before—both greedy, hateful, and deluded.

However, for one in whom non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are powerful while the others are weak, that person has few defilements as before; even upon seeing a divine object, they remain unshaken, yet they may be hateful and of dull wisdom.

Furthermore, when at the moment of accumulating kamma non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, that person—by the same method as before—is both non-greedy and of pleasant character, yet he is deluded.

Likewise, when at the moment of accumulating kamma non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, that person—by the same method as before—is both non-greedy and wise, yet he is hateful and prone to anger.

But for one at the moment of accumulating karma in whom the three qualities beginning with non-greed are powerful, while greed and the others are weak, he is non-greedy, non-hating, and wise, like the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta: 473.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta. In that context, “thus-desiring” means having such a wish; “thus-intending” means...
"Thus inclined" means thus disposed; "thus intent" means thus possessing such a view. "Therein" refers to that increase of the undesirable and the decrease of the desirable.
"Rooted in the Blessed One" means those for whom the Blessed One is the root. This is what is meant:
"Venerable sir, these teachings of ours were previously originated by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa; in him..."
"For one entire interval between Buddhas after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, there was no other ascetic or brahmin capable of producing these teachings;
yet it was by the Blessed One that these teachings were produced. For it is by depending upon the Blessed One that we understand and penetrate these teachings.
Thus, "Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One; the Blessed One is their guide."

For the Blessed One is the leader, the trainer, and the guide of phenomena. Those phenomena which are shown by being individually named according to their true nature are said to have the Blessed One as their leader (*bhagavaṃnettika*). They have the Blessed One as their refuge (*bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇa*):
when the phenomena of the four planes come within the range of the knowledge of omniscience, they are said to "return" to the Blessed One; thus, they have the Blessed One as their refuge.

“They return” means they come back, they gather together. Furthermore, when the Blessed One was seated at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa), contact (phassa) approached him by way of his realization, asking:
“Blessed One, what is my name? “In the sense of touching, you are called ‘contact.
Feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), formations (saṅkhārā), and consciousness (viññāṇa) approached him, asking: “Blessed One, what is my name? “In the sense of cognizing...”
"Consciousness is called 'name'"—thus, by grasping the individual names of the phenomena belonging to the four planes according to their true nature, the Blessed One "takes refuge in the Dhamma";
this is why he is "one who has the Dhamma as his refuge. "Let it occur to the Blessed One alone" means:
let the meaning of this speech be established for the Blessed One alone; the sense is, "You yourself must explain and give it to us."

474. “To be cultivated” means to be relied upon. “To be frequented” means to be approached. “As one who is ignorant” means as one who is ignorant, a fool, an ordinary person blind with ignorance. “As one who is wise” means as one who is wise, intelligent, a learned person. 475. “There is, monks, an undertaking of things,” etc.
In the previous sutta, the summary (mātikā) was established by way of a reversed order;

here, however, the Teacher established the summary according to the very nature of the things themselves. Therein, “undertaking of things” refers to the grasping of things such as the destruction of life and so forth.
476. *Avijjāgato* means possessed of ignorance.
477. *Vijjāgato* means possessed of true knowledge (*vijjā*), that is, one who possesses wisdom (*paññavā*).
478. Regarding the phrase *sahāpi dukkhena*: here, first of all, wrong conduct, covetousness, and wrong view—these three [arise] from prior volition.
Furthermore, suffering feelings arise by way of two types of volition: the volition that performs the act and the volition that approves it.
However, the volition that resolves upon the act is associated either with pleasure or with equanimity.

As for the remaining seven courses of action, such as killing living beings and so forth, they result in suffering feelings by way of all three types of volition. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Even together with suffering... and so forth.
“...by grief. Here, it should be understood that grief itself is suffering (*dukkha*).
Or, for one who engages in seeking, bodily suffering is also included both in the prior stage and the subsequent stage. 479.
Regarding the phrase “even with pleasure,” first, these three—killing living beings, harsh speech, and ill-will—are [accompanied] by a prior volition.
And through two types of volition—the volition of application (*payoga-cetanā*) and the volition of determination (*niṭṭhāpana-cetanā*)—there are pleasant feelings (*sukha-vedanā*).

However, the volition of determination is associated only with painful feeling (*dukkha-sampayutta*). The remaining seven [types of consciousness] have pleasant feeling by way of all three types of volition.

Furthermore, in the phrase "together with joy" (*saha somanassena*), it should be understood that "joy" (*somanassa*) itself is what is meant here by "pleasure. This applies to one who possesses a desirable tactile object (*iṭṭha-phoṭṭhabba*).
Or even bodily pleasure in the prior or subsequent stages is indeed permissible. 480.
Regarding the third undertaking of dhamma: here, a certain person is a fisherman or a deer-hunter;
he makes his living depending solely on the injury of living beings. To him, a venerable bhikkhu [teaches] the danger in the destruction of life, even against his will.
Having explained the benefits of abstaining from taking life, he gives the training precept. Even when receiving it, he does so while being distressed and dejected.
Later, after a few days have passed, even though he is unable to maintain the restraint, he remains distressed;
thus, his prior and subsequent volitions are accompanied by suffering. This is the volition that brings about the final determination.
However, in all instances, the meaning should be understood as "accompanied by pleasure" or "accompanied by equanimity.

Thus, this was said—"even with pain, even with mental grief"—referring specifically to the volition of the preceding and succeeding stages. And here, it should be understood that "mental grief" itself is what constitutes "pain."

481. In the fourth undertaking of a wholesome dhamma (*dhammasamādāna*), in all ten instances, the three types of volition—the preliminary, the subsequent, and the consummating—necessarily associate with pleasure (*sukha*).
With reference to this, it is said: "Together with pleasure, together with joy (*somanassa*).
And here, it should be understood that "pleasure" refers specifically to joy.
482. "A bitter gourd" means a gourd with a bitter taste. "Mixed with poison" means combined, blended, and stirred together with *halāhala* poison.
"It will not please" means it will not be liked; it will not bring satisfaction.
"You will go" means you will depart. "One might drink it without reflection" means one might drink it without having examined it.
483. *Āpānīyakaṃso*: a bronze vessel filled with *āpānīya*, that is, a sweet drink. *Vaṇṇasampanno*: endowed with a beautiful color, such as the color of the drink;
it is also called a "drink-bronze" (*pānakakaṃso*) by virtue of the drink placed within the bronze vessel. *Chādessati*:
for wherever that *halāhala* poison is placed, it imparts its own flavor to that very thing. By means of that—
It is said, “it will conceal. 484.

*Pūtimutta* means simply urine. For just as a human being, though possessing a golden complexion, is called nothing but a “rotten body,” and even a young *galocilatā* creeper that has grown on that very day is called a “rotten creeper,” so too urine, even when freshly voided at that moment, is indeed *pūtimutta*.
“With various medicines” means with various herbs such as *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and so forth. “May he be well” means that he may become healthy, free from disease, and of golden complexion.
“Curd and honey” means very pure curd and very sweet honey.
“Mixed together in one place” means having been made into one, blended, and stirred together. “Of him” refers to him who is drinking that medicine of the four sweets (*catumadhura*).
It would be appropriate. And as for this blood that flows mixed with hemorrhoids, this is not a medicine for it;
rather, by solidifying the food, it creates a barrier in the passage. However, as for the blood mixed with bile, this [medicine] is sufficient for producing a cooling effect upon it.
486. *Viddha* means pierced through. The meaning is that it has become distant due to the departure of the clouds.
*Vigatavalāhaka* means free from clouds; *deva* means in the sky. *Ākāsagataṃ tamagataṃ* means darkness situated in the sky.
*Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇaparappavāda* means the doctrines of others known as the many recluses and brahmins. *Abhivihacca* means having struck down. It shines forth.
And it heats and shines exceedingly at the time of midday in the autumn season, just as the sun emits radiance, heats, and glows.
This sutta, moreover, was extremely dear and pleasing to the deities. Herein is the story:
it is said that in the southern direction, in the province of Hatthibhoga, there was a monastery named Saṅgara-vihāra. At the door of its dining hall stood a saṅgara tree.
The deity inhabiting the tree, having heard this Sutta being recited by a young monk according to the *sara-bhañña* method during the night, gave her approval, saying, "Excellent!
The young monk asked, "Who is this? She replied, "Venerable sir, I am the deity inhabiting this tree.
"In what, O deity, are you pleased—was it the sound or the Sutta? "Venerable sir, as for sound..."

"Whoever it may be, they certainly have it; I am confident in the Sutta. On the day the Teacher spoke while seated in Jeta’s Grove, and today as well, there is no difference even in a single syllable. "Did you hear this, O deity, on the day the Teacher spoke?
"Yes, venerable sir. "Where were you standing when you heard it? "I had gone to Jeta’s Grove, venerable sir, but among those of great influence—"
"When the deities were arriving there, not finding space, they stood right here and heard [the sound].
"Is it possible for one standing here to hear the sound clearly? "But, venerable sir, do you hear my voice? "Yes, deity.
"It is as if, venerable sir, we were sitting at the side of your right ear while you spoke. "But what about the Teacher, deity?"
"Do you see form? "I cannot remain still, Bhante, thinking that the Teacher is looking at me alone.
"Were you able to produce a distinction [in your meditation], O deity? At that very moment, the deity vanished.
It is said that on that day, this son of the gods was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, this discourse is dear and pleasing to the deities.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
7. Commentary on the Vīmaṃsaka Sutta 487.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the Vīmaṃsaka Sutta. Regarding the phrase "by one who investigates," there are three types of investigators:
the investigator of meaning, the investigator of conditioned phenomena, and the investigator of the Teacher. Among these, it is said: "Friends, people are wise when they are investigators."
Herein, the investigator of meaning has arrived. "When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements,
skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible— by this much, Ānanda,
it is sufficient to call a wise bhikkhu an 'investigator,'"— herein, the investigator of formations has arrived.
In this sutta, however, one who tests the Teacher is intended. *Cetopariyāya* means the range of the mind, the delimitation of the mind.
*Samannesanā* means seeking, searching, and investigation. *Iti viññāṇāya* means for the purpose of understanding in this way.
(488) “The Tathāgata is to be examined in two respects”: here, he shows the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) of relying upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*).
For this support known as a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta) is indeed great. Its greatness should be understood in this way:
on one occasion, the Venerable Ānanda reflected that half of his own power was due to his own majesty and half was due to the power of his good friends;
unable to determine it by his own nature alone, he approached the Blessed One and asked him.
—“Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life, namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
The Blessed One said: “Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda!
This is the whole of the holy life, Ānanda, namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.”

For a monk who has a good friend, Ānanda, who has a good companion, who has a good associate, it is to be expected that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path. And how, Ānanda, does a monk who has a good friend...
[develop] the Noble Eightfold Path? He develops the Noble Eightfold Path... [and so on].
He cultivates the Eightfold Path. Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view... [and so on] ...he develops right concentration, which is based on seclusion.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu has good friends... [and so on] ...and he cultivates it.
By this method, Ānanda, it should be understood: "The entire holy life consists in this, namely, having good friends."
“Having virtuous companionship and virtuous fellowship, Ānanda—by relying on me as a virtuous friend, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth;
beings subject to aging... [and so on] ...beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
Even when speaking of the external excellence of the bhikkhus, he said:
"Bhikkhus, considering an external factor, I do not see any other single factor that leads to such great benefit as this, bhikkhus:
having virtuous friends. Having virtuous friends, bhikkhus, leads to great benefit."—[Thus spoke] Mahācunda.

Even when teaching the practice for the wearing away of the defilements, he said: “One should practice wearing away [the defilements] with the thought: ‘Others will have evil friends; we, however, shall have virtuous friends here.
And even when teaching the qualities that ripen liberation to the Elder Meghiya, he said: “Meghiya, for one whose mental liberation is not yet matured, five things lead to its maturation.”
“What five? Here, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has good friends. Thus [the Buddha] specifically emphasized the support of having good friends.
Even when giving his frequent exhortation to the Venerable Rāhula, his beloved son, he said:
“Associate with good friends, and dwell in a remote lodging.”
“Secluded and free from noise, be moderate in eating.
Regarding robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings—
do not create craving for these, lest you return again to this world.”
He spoke first of all regarding the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*).
Such is the great importance of this necessary condition of a spiritual friend. Here too, the Blessed One, demonstrating that, began his teaching with the words:
"In two qualities, the Tathāgata is to be sought. The meaning is: "A wise bhikkhu should seek and search for the Tathāgata in these two qualities. By this, the Blessed One—

Thinking, "This man is of noble birth," or "He is endowed with the marks," or "He is handsome and beautiful to behold," or "He is well-known and distinguished," or "Relying on him, I shall obtain requisites such as robes"—having thought thus, there is no need for one to dwell relying on me.
But he who perceives thus: "This person is capable of being my teacher and performing the duties of a teacher..."
"Let him accomplish it," he roars this lion’s roar, thinking, "Let him attend upon me. Indeed, this sutta is called the "Buddha’s Lion’s Roar.
Now, in order to show those two qualities, he said, "among those cognizable by the eye and the ear.
Therein, the Teacher’s bodily conduct is the quality cognizable by the eye for one who investigates; his verbal conduct is the quality cognizable by the ear.
Now, showing the manner in which they are to be examined among those [qualities], he said: "Those that are defiled," and so forth.
Therein, "defiled" means associated with the defilements (*kilesa*). Furthermore, these are not cognizable by the eye or the ear.

However, just as it is understood that there is a fish inside when the water is moving or when bubbles are emerging, so too [is it known] of one who is committing killing and so forth, or false speech and so forth.
Or, having seen and heard the bodily and verbal conduct of one who speaks thus, it is understood that the mind which gives rise to them is defiled.
Therefore he spoke in this way. For the bodily and verbal conduct of one whose mind is defiled is indeed called "defiled.
"They do not exist for the Tathāgata" means they are not present in the Tathāgata; they are not found.
The meaning is that he knows it thus. For they are not perceived because of their very non-existence, not because of being concealed.
Thus, one day, while inviting the Saṅgha of bhikkhus regarding these matters, the Blessed One said: "Come now, bhikkhus, let me invite you;
do not find fault with me for anything, whether bodily or verbal. Thus...

When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, he said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, we do not reproach the Blessed One for anything, whether bodily or verbal.
For the Blessed One, venerable sir, is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path..."
“The discoverer of the path, the proclaimer of the unproclaimed path, the knower of the path, the perceiver of the path, the one skilled in the path;
and now, Bhante, the disciples dwell following that path, having attained it afterwards.
Thus pure were the Tathāgata’s bodily and verbal conduct. Furthermore, the young brahmin Uttara found nothing in the Tathāgata’s doors of body and speech that was not to be approved.
Thinking, "I shall see something [wrong]," he followed him for seven months, yet he did not see even so much as a hair's breadth [of fault].
What indeed could this man, while still a human being, have found unappealing in the bodily and verbal doors of one who had become a Buddha?
Even the divine son Māra, searching for six years from the time of the Bodhisatta’s Great Renunciation, did not find anything unappealing [in him].
He did not see even so much as a mere thought arising in his mind. It is said that Māra thought:
“If I perceive even a single unwholesome thought in him, I shall strike him right there on the head and depart.
Having failed to see anything for six years, and having followed him for another year after he had become a Buddha, and finding no fault whatsoever, he paid homage at the time of his departure—
“O Great Hero of great merit, blazing with supernatural power and glory,
who has transcended all enmity and fear— I pay homage at the feet of Gotama.
Having spoken this verse, he departed.
"Mixed" means that at one time they are dark and at another time they are bright; thus they are variegated. "Pure" means completely purified and free from defilements.
"Are found" means that pure qualities exist and are apprehended. For the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct and so forth are indeed pure. Therefore he said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four things for a Tathāgata that need no protection. Which four? Pure bodily conduct..."
“Monks, the Tathāgata has no misconduct of body such that the Tathāgata would need to guard it, thinking:
‘Lest another should know this of me. He is pure in verbal conduct... pure in mental conduct... and pure in livelihood, monks;
the Tathāgata has no wrong livelihood such that the Tathāgata would need to guard it, thinking: ‘Lest...”
“Another has known this of me.
This wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*) refers to this blameless virtue consisting of the eight factors of right livelihood. [He thinks:
“Has this venerable one long since attained this—having been endowed with it for a very long time—or has he only recently attained it?”
The meaning is: "Let him investigate thus: 'Was it committed yesterday, or the day before, or on the very next day?
For when someone living in a certain place commits much wrong livelihood, that becomes apparent and manifest upon the lapse of time.
He might go to some frontier village or to the seashore, build a leaf-hut, and...
He dwelt as if he were a forest-dweller. People, having conceived high regard for him, provided him with excellent requisites.
When the monks living in the countryside saw his preferential treatment, they thought, "This venerable one is indeed excessively arrogant;
who could this be? Investigating further, they discovered, "He is a monk who fled from such-and-such a place after committing such-and-such wrong livelihood."

Realizing that it was impossible to perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremony with him, they assembled and carried out one of the formal acts (kamma), such as a suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), according to the Dhamma and in accordance with justice.
He spoke thus in order to investigate whether or not such a concealed practice existed.
"He knows thus" means he knows: "I have attained this for a long time; I have not attained it only recently.

And this is no wonder, that the Tathāgata’s virtue of the eightfold livelihood should have been pure for a long time now that he has attained omniscience, when it was already so even during his time as a Bodhisatta.
It is said that in the past, the King of Gandhāra and the King of Videha were both companions.

Having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, they handed over their kingdoms to their sons and went forth as forest-dwelling seers (*isi-pabbajjā*). They wandered for alms in a certain village in the wilderness.
Now, it is said that in border regions salt is difficult to obtain. There, having received saltless rice-gruel in a certain hall—
Having sat down, they drink. From time to time, people bring salt and give it to them.
One day, a certain man belonging to the Vedehi clan put some salt into a leaf and gave it to them.
The Vedehi took it and, having set half near Gandhāri and half near himself, saw that there was a small amount remaining after they had consumed it. [Thinking], "Do not..."
“Lest this be lost,” he wrapped it in a leaf and placed it in a thicket of grass.
Then, one day at the time of drinking rice-gruel, being mindful and looking about, he saw it; having approached the sage Gandhārī, he said, “Teacher, take a little from here.
“From where did you get that, Vedehi? [She replied,] “On that day, thinking ‘Lest it be lost,’ I [took what remained after eating].”
"Set aside. The sage of Gandhāra did not wish to accept it; having drunk only unsalted gruel, he said to the seer Vedeha:
"Having abandoned sixteen full thousand villages and flourishing storehouses, why do you now make a hoard?"

Vedehī said: “You have gone forth having abandoned kingship; why now, because of storing a mere measure of salt, do you act in a way that is unbecoming of one who has gone forth? “What have I done, Vedehī? he asked. Then she said to him:
“Having left the realm of Gandhāra, which abounds in wealth and grain, you went forth from the position of a ruler; now here you rule once more.”
Gandhāra said:
"I speak the Dhamma, O Videhan; unrighteousness does not please me.
As I speak the Dhamma, no evil defiles me."
Vedeha said:
“In whatever way another person might experience vexation,
a wise person should not utter such speech, even if it were for a great purpose.”
Gandhāra said:
"Whether it be crushed or not, whether it be scattered in abundance;
as I speak the Dhamma, no evil shall cling to me."
Then, thinking, "O Videhan, he who lacks even his own intelligence and does not train in the Vinaya under a teacher wanders like a blind elephant in the forest," he said:
"If one has neither personal intelligence nor is well-trained in the Vinaya,
many people would wander like a blind elephant in the forest."
"And because some here have been well-trained under a teacher, therefore, disciplined in the discipline, they walk with minds well-composed.
Having spoken thus, and realizing that the Vedehi had not known [the truth], he asked forgiveness from the sage Gandhāri. Both of them...
Having practiced austerity, they went to the Brahma-world. Thus, even during the time of the Tathāgata’s existence as a bodhisatta, his virtue of the eightfold livelihood was pure for a long time.
"This venerable one, this monk, is possessed of fame"—this venerable one, our Teacher, is a monk of renown.
"Has he attained a state of being well-known and prominent, and has he himself attained excellence in his retinue?

By this, it is shown that they should investigate thus: "Do any dangers appear in him because of his state of being well-known and prominent, and because of his reliance on fame, or not? [The Buddha said: "Not yet, monks."

Monks, as long as a bhikkhu has not attained recognition among kings, royal ministers, and others, or has not acquired a circle of followers, certain defects such as conceit and arrogance do not manifest;
he dwells as if perfectly tranquil, like a stream-enterer or a once-returner. Is he then a noble one (ariya) or an ordinary person (puthujjana)?
It is not possible to know [his intent].
But when, monks— meaning, when a certain monk here becomes well-known or endowed with a large retinue—
he is like a rogue bull piercing a herd of cattle with his sharp horns, or like one trampling a herd of deer.
Like a wild beast, he prods other bhikkhus here and there; lacking respect and behaving improperly, he walks as if his feet were brushing against the ground with their very tips.

On the other hand, a certain son of good family bows down even more deeply—like a rice plant heavy with the weight of its fruit—the more he becomes well-known and famous among kings, royal ministers, and others.

When people approach him, he reflects upon his state of nothingness (*akiñcanabhāva*), establishes the perception of being a recluse (*samaṇasaññā*), and—like a bull with its horns sawn off, or like a low-caste child—becomes gentle, humble, and lowly-minded.

He thus practices for the welfare and happiness of both the Saṅgha of monks and the world with its devas. It is with reference to such a practice that it was said: "In this regard, there are no dangers for him."
The Tathāgata, however, is "neutral" (tādī) toward the eight worldly conditions;
for he is neutral in gain and neutral in loss, neutral in fame and neutral in disrepute, neutral in praise and neutral in blame, and neutral in pleasure and neutral in pain.
Therefore, in every respect, no such disadvantages are found in him here. "Having ceased through fearlessness" means having become fearless.
"Resting" (*uparato*) means completely resting or constantly resting. Or else, one who rests not out of fear is "rested through fearlessness" (*abhayūparato*). For there are four fears:

the fear of defilements (*kilesa-bhaya*), the fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-bhaya*), the fear of an evil rebirth (*duggati-bhaya*), and the fear of reproach (*upavāda-bhaya*). An ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) fears all four.
Those in training (*sekkhā*) [fear] three, for they have abandoned the fear of an evil rebirth; thus, there are seven types of those in training.
One who has ceased from fear is called "one who has ceased from fear because his taints are destroyed," for he possesses not even a single fear. Is it that he has no fear of opponents' doctrines?
No, he does not. Rather, out of compassion for others, thinking, "May beings not come to ruin on account of one such as me whose taints are destroyed," he guards against reproach.
This was like the Elder Yasa, who dwelt at the Mūluppalavāpi Monastery.
It is said that the Elder entered the village of Mūluppalavāpi for alms.
When he reached the door of his supporter’s family, they took his bowl and prepared a seat leaning against a wooden bench on the bare ground.
A daughter of the ministers also sat down, having prepared a lower seat on the opposite side of that same bench. A resident monk—
Later, having entered for alms and standing at the gate, the elder observed that [the monk] was sitting on the same bed with the minister’s daughter.

Perceiving this, he thought, "This paṃsukūlika dwells as if perfectly tranquil even within the monastery, yet here in the village he sits on the same bed with his female attendants. Then he wondered, "What indeed should I do?"
Having looked again and again, thinking "it was badly seen," he departed while maintaining that very perception.
The Elder, too, having finished his meal and gone to the monastery, entered his dwelling place, closed the door, and sat down.

The resident monk, having also finished his meal and gone to the monastery, with an unrestrained intention, thinking, "I will reprimand that refuse-rag wearer and drive him out of the monastery," [approached].
Having gone to the elder’s dwelling, he took water from the vessel used for consumption with his cupped hands and washed the elder’s feet while making a great noise.
The elder, reflecting, "Who is this one who behaves so lack of restraint?

and knowing everything through his supernormal knowledge, thought, "May this man not go to a state of misery by harboring malice toward me. Thereupon, he rose into the air and stood near the circular canopy.
He sat down cross-legged. The resident monk, acting with ill-intent, lifted the bolt, opened the door, and entered;
not seeing the Elder, he thought, "He must have gone below the bed," and looking there, not seeing him even there, he began to leave.
The Elder coughed. The other, looking upward and seeing him, [prepared] to wait upon him.
Unable to do otherwise, he said: "Friend, it is not fitting for you, who are endowed with such great power and are a wearer of rag-robes, to sit on the same couch with a female attendant.
"Venerable sir, those who have gone forth do not sit on the same couch with women; this was a misjudgment on your part.
In this way, those whose taints are destroyed protect themselves from reproach out of compassion for others.

"By the destruction of lust" means precisely by the destruction of lust. Because he is free from lust, he does not indulge in sensual pleasures; nor does he refrain from them through deliberate reflection.

"And that"—having thus understood the Tathāgata’s abandonment of the defilements, whether he is standing or sitting in various places, or even when seated upon the adorned Dharma-throne in the midst of the fourfold assembly—it is thus said:
"The Teacher is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion."

The meaning is that others might ask that investigating bhikkhu—who was thus speaking in praise of the Tathāgata’s abandonment of defilements, who was as utterly pure as the moon released from clouds, with taints exhausted and stains discarded—the following: "In what ways...?
*Ākāra* means reasons; *anvaya* means subsequent understandings. "Or dwelling in the Saṅgha" refers to those times when he dwelt among a group of indeterminate number.
"Living in the midst of the community of monks, or living alone—I desire, O bhikkhus, to retreat in seclusion for half a month, to retreat in seclusion for three months.
Thus he lived alone both during his retreat and in the Pālileyyaka forest grove.
"Sugata" means those who have gone well, who have practiced rightly, who are doers, and who are appropriately engaged. Such as these...

Indeed, there are some bhikkhus who are "ill-faring"—that is, those who have gone astray, who have practiced wrongly, who are full of physical rigidity, and who have abandoned their meditation subjects;

such ones also exist. There are some who "instruct a group"—that is, those bound by the ties of a group, who delight in the group, who are devoted to the group, and who maintain the group; such ones also exist. Those who are the opposites of these are "withdrawn from the group."
There are also those who dwell detached and liberated.

There are also bhikkhus who appear amidst material things—greedy for material things, with eyes fixed on material things—who wander about solely for the sake of the four requisites of material sustenance;
yet there are also those who are unsullied by material things, having turned away from the four requisites.
There are those who dwell like the moon released from clouds. "This venerable one does not despise him for that reason":
the Teacher does not despise this person for such-and-such a practice; he thinks, "This one is a practitioner," "This one has withdrawn from the group and is detached.
"This one is unsullied by material things, his mind turned away from the requisites."
"Like the moon released from clouds"—thus, for him, there is no exalting based on worldly attachments.

The meaning is that there is also no disparaging based on worldly attachments, such as thinking: "This one is practicing wrongly," "He is a non-doer," "He is full of physical lethargy," "He has abandoned his meditation subject," "He is bound by ties to a group," "He is greedy for material things," "He is fickle," or "His eyes are fixed on material gain. What is the purpose of this?
What has been taught? The Tathāgata’s state of equanimity toward all beings has been taught. For it is said:
“The Sage is equal toward Devadatta, the murderer; toward Aṅgulimāla, the thief;
and toward Dhanapāla and Rāhula—he is the same toward them all.”

489. "In that regard, monks"—that is, among those two types of investigators. There is the investigator of the "knot" (*gaṇṭhivīmaṃsaka*), who is referred to in the question, "But what are the venerable one's modes of conduct?";
and there is the investigator of the "root" (*mūlavīmaṃsaka*), who is referred to in the statement, "This venerable one has abstained out of fearlessness.
Among these, it is the investigator of the root alone who should further question the Tathāgata. For he [the investigator of the root] previously [inquired] regarding the very speech of another.
"Reached the conclusion": another person might speak both having known [the matter] and without having known it; thus their speech may be either true or false.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should not reach a conclusion based solely on another's speech, but rather inquire further from the Tathāgata himself. Regarding the phrase "while explaining":
since there is no such thing as a false explanation for the Tathāgata, he therefore explains correctly.
It is said: "Rather than saying 'wrongly,' let him declare [it as it is].
"This is my path, this is my range" means: "This is my path, this is my range. There is also the reading "etāpātho"; its meaning is:
"My eightfold livelihood-virtue (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) is pure; therefore, because of that purity, I am 'etāpātho' in the gateway of knowledge for the inquiring bhikkhu."
Thus, it is said: "I go within range. "But I am not made of that" means: "Even by virtue of that perfectly pure morality, I am not made of it;
I am not possessed of craving for it. By this he demonstrates: "Because my morality is perfectly pure, I am free from craving. "Higher and higher, more and more sublime" means:
he teaches having made it progressively higher and increasingly more sublime. "With its dark and bright counterparts" means: [he teaches] with their respective opposites.

Both the dark and the bright; and indeed, having made them mutually opposed and possessed of counterparts—having set aside the dark as the counterpart to the bright, and having set aside the bright as the counterpart to the dark—he teaches the dark and the bright by thus making them mutually opposed.
When teaching the dark, he teaches it with its aspiration and its result; when teaching the bright, he likewise teaches it with its aspiration and its result.

He teaches. Having directly known a certain aspect of the Dhamma among the teachings, he reaches a conclusion regarding that Dhamma; thus, having taught the Dhamma, he reaches a conclusion regarding the Dhamma of the teaching by means of a certain aspect of the Dhamma of penetration.
He gains confidence in the Teacher: having thus reached a conclusion regarding the Dhamma, he [recognizes] him all the more as a Perfectly Enlightened One.
One has confidence in the Blessed One as the Teacher. Furthermore, the Dhamma proclaimed by that Blessed One is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One because it leads to liberation.

And the Saṅgha that practices that Dhamma is well-practiced because it has entered upon a practice free from crookedness and other such defects; thus one has confidence in the Dhamma and in the Saṅgha as well. And that...
To that bhikkhu who was thus confident and who was speaking here and there in praise of the Three Jewels:
"By these modes" means by these reasons for testing the Teacher. "By these phrases" means by these phrases consisting of a collection of syllables.
"By these phonemes" means by these syllables spoken here. "Faith is established" means that conviction is firmly settled.
"Rooted" means having its root produced by way of the stream-entry path; for the stream-entry path is indeed called the "root" of faith.
"Possessing form" means having a cause, because it is grasped after investigating the reason. "Based on seeing" means based on the stream-entry path;
for that [path] is called "seeing. "Firm" means stable. "Irremovable" means impossible to take away by a recluse.
It is by a śramaṇa who has extinguished evil, or by a brāhmaṇa who has banished evil; or by a deva, whether as a deva by birth or as Māra,
the wielder of power— for the faith of one who has entered the stream cannot be shaken even by Māra the wielder of power, just like that of Sūrambaṭṭha.
It is said that after hearing the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he became a stream-enterer and returned home.
Then Māra, having conjured up the form of a Buddha adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks, stood at his house door and sent word: "The Teacher has arrived.
Sūra thought, "I have just now returned from being in the presence of the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma; what could this possibly mean?"
Having approached and paid homage with the recognition that he was the Teacher, he stood there. Māra said:
"Sūrambaṭṭha, that which I told you—that form is impermanent... [and so on] ...that consciousness is impermanent—was spoken by me hastily, without due reflection.
Therefore, you should grasp that form is permanent... [and so on] ...that consciousness is permanent. Sūra thought:
"It is impossible that the Buddhas would say anything without having reflected upon it or without direct knowledge;
surely this Māra has come here for the purpose of disturbing me. Then you said to him, "Māra!
He was unable to utter a falsehood and confessed, "Yes, I am Māra. When asked, "For what purpose have you come? he replied, "For the purpose of shaking your faith."
He said: "Kanha the Evil One, you stand there all alone; even a hundred or a thousand Māras like you would be unable to shake my faith.
Faith that has come through the Path is unshakable, like Mount Sineru standing firm upon the rocky earth. Why are you here?
With these words, he snapped his fingers. Unable to remain, the Evil One vanished right then and there.
"By Brahmā" means by one of the various Brahmās, such as those belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm, or by someone else in the world;
apart from these recluses and others, it cannot be carried away by anyone else in the world. "Investigation of the Dhamma" means investigation of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"Well-investigated according to the nature of things" means well-investigated by way of the nature of things (*dhammatā*), that is, thoroughly investigated by way of its very intrinsic nature.
The meaning is "it happens. The remainder is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the *Vīmaṃsaka-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kosambiya Sutta 491.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Kosambiya Sutta. Therein, “at Kosambī” means in the city of that name.
It is said that in various places within that city—such as its parks, lotus ponds, and so forth—only *kosamba* trees were found in abundance.
Therefore, it came to be known as Kosambī. Some say it was so called because it was built not far from the hermitage of the seer named Kusamba.
"Ghosita’s Monastery" refers to the monastery constructed by the merchant Ghosita.
It is said that in former times there was a kingdom called Addilaraṭṭha. From there, a poor man named Kotūhalaka, out of fear of famine—
Traveling through a land of abundant harvests that was bounded by fields, he and his wife were unable to carry their son;
so, leaving him behind, they departed. The mother turned back, took the child, and went on.
They entered a village of cowherds, where at that time milk-rice had been prepared for the herdsmen; having obtained some from there, they ate it.
Then that man, having eaten a great quantity of milk-rice, being unable to digest it, died during the night and took rebirth right there in the womb of a female dog, becoming a dog.
He became dear and pleasing to the cowherd, and the cowherd attended upon a paccekabuddha. At the conclusion of his meal, the paccekabuddha—
He gave a morsel of food to a dog. Having conceived affection for the Paccekabuddha, the dog went with the cowherd even to the leaf-hut.
When the cowherd was not present, at the time for the meal, the dog went there by himself to announce the time at the door of the leaf-hut.
He bellowed; even on the road, upon seeing fierce wild animals, he would bellow and drive them away.
Having died with a gentle mind toward the Paccekabuddhas, he was reborn in the world of the devas. There, his name became Ghosaka-devaputta.
Falling from that heavenly realm, he was reborn in a certain family home in Kosambī. A childless merchant [adopted him].
Having given wealth to his parents and making him his son, he took him [into his household]. Then, when his own sons were born, he attempted to have them killed seven times.
By virtue of his merit, however, he did not meet death in any of those seven places;
finally, having obtained his livelihood through the ingenuity of a merchant’s daughter, he later attained the position of a merchant chief upon the passing away of his father.
He was born as the merchant named Ghosita. Furthermore, there were two other merchants in Kosambī, namely the merchant Kukkuṭa and the merchant Pāvārika;
with these, there were three in total.
At that time, at the foot of a mountain, there were five hundred seers who were the spiritual preceptors for those friends, the merchants.
They lived there. From time to time, they would come to human habitations for the sake of obtaining salt and sour gruel.
Then, on one occasion during the summer season, while traveling along the road to a human settlement, they passed through a great waterless wilderness.
At the edge of the wilderness, seeing a large banyan tree, they thought: "As magnificent as this tree is, there must surely be someone of great power here."
"A deity must be present here; it would be excellent indeed if she were to give us water or food.

Having understood the intention of the seers, the deity thought, "I shall provide for them," and by her own supernatural power, she caused a stream of water as thick as a plow-shaft to flow from between the branches.
The company of seers [beheld] that column of water resembling a mass of silver.
Having seen this, he took water from his own vessels, used it for his needs, and thought: "The deity has given us water for our use;
however, this is a great wilderness devoid of villages. It would be well indeed if she were to give us food as well.
By virtue of her intention toward the seers, the deity provided divine rice gruel, hard food, and other provisions, and satisfied them.
The seers thought: “The deity has given us even the water for our use and our food—all of it.
It would be well indeed if she were to show herself to us.
The deity, understanding their intention, revealed half her body. They said: “Deity, you are great!”
“Sir, having performed what deed did you attain this prosperity? “Venerable sir, it was by performing a very small and insignificant deed.
“For that deity attained this prosperity by relying on the practice of even half an Uposatha day.
It is said that this young god was once a laborer in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika. Indeed, in the house of the merchant, on the Uposatha days...”
Including even the slaves and laborers, everyone observed the Uposatha. One day, this laborer rose alone early in the morning and went to his work.
The great merchant, observing the men who were receiving their rations, realized that he alone had gone into the forest and gave him a portion of fodder for his evening meal. The cook—
A female slave, having cooked food for only one person, increased the portion of food when he returned from the forest and gave it to him.
The laborer said: "On other days at this time the house was filled with a single sound; today it is exceedingly quiet.
What could this be? She explained it to him: "Today all the people in this house are observing the Uposatha."
“The great merchant gave you alone the sacrificial offering. “Is that so, mother? “Yes, master.
“Mother, ask the great merchant whether, at this time, for one who has undertaken the Uposatha, the Uposatha rite is valid or not.
Having gone there, she asked him, and the great merchant said: “The entire Uposatha rite is not valid; however, half of the rite is valid.”
"Let him observe the Uposatha. The laborer, having refrained from eating his meal and rinsed his mouth, observed the Uposatha and went to his dwelling place where he lay down.
Because his body was depleted of food, his wind-humor became agitated during the night.
Having passed away at dawn, by the result of that partial observance of the Uposatha ceremony, he [was reborn] in the Mahāvaṭṭanī forest under a *nigrodha* tree.
He was reborn as a son of the gods. He reported that occurrence to the seers. The seers asked:
"Have you ever heard before of 'the Buddha,' 'the Dhamma,' and 'the Saṅgha'? Has a Buddha perhaps arisen in the world?
"Yes, venerable sirs, one has arisen. "Where does he dwell now? "In dependence on Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove."
"Venerable sirs," they said. "Wait here for a moment while we go to see the Teacher.

Delighted and joyful, they departed and eventually arrived at the city of Kosambī. Hearing that "the seers have arrived," the great merchant went out to meet them, invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept our alms tomorrow," and on the following day, he [prepared for] the community of seers...
They gave a great gift. Having eaten, the seers asked, "We shall depart. [The people said:
"Venerable sirs, at other times you would stay for one month, two, three, or even four months before departing.
But on this occasion, you have come yesterday and say you will depart this very day; what is the reason for this? [The seers replied: "Yes, householders, a Buddha has arisen in the world."
"Furthermore, it is not possible to know if there will be an obstacle to life; therefore, we are going in haste.
"In that case, venerable sirs, let us also go; please go together with us. "You are householders indeed, with your great entanglements;
you stay behind, we shall go on ahead. Having departed, they stayed for two days at a certain place.
Arriving at Sāvatthī as if by swift travel, they went directly into the presence of the Teacher in the Jetavana monastery.
Having heard the Teacher’s sweet discourse on the Dhamma, they all went forth and attained arahantship.
Those three merchants also, with five hundred carts each, brought ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, as well as fine linen and silk garments.
Taking [the relics], they departed from Kosambī and, traveling by stages, reached Sāvatthī.
Having pitched camp on the outskirts of the Jeta Grove, they went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side.
The Teacher delivered a sweet discourse on the Dhamma to all three friends. They were filled with intense joy toward the Teacher.
Having invited them, they gave a great almsgiving on the following day. Having invited them again, they did so on the next day as well;
thus, after giving alms for half a month, they lay down at the Blessed One’s feet, saying, “Please give us your promise to come to our country.
The Blessed One said, “Householders, Tathāgatas indeed delight in empty dwellings. At that point, the promise was granted.
"Is she indeed given away? the householders observed, and thinking, "She has been promised by the Blessed One," they paid homage to the One of Ten Powers and departed.

Along the way, at intervals of one *yojana* each, they had monasteries constructed, and eventually reaching Kosambī, they announced, "A Buddha has appeared in the world! Then those three men, in their respective monasteries, made great [preparations]...
Having made a gift of wealth, they had monasteries built for the Blessed One’s residence.
Among them, the one built by the merchant Kukkuṭa was called the Kukkuṭārāma; the one built by the merchant Pāvārika in the mango grove was called the Pāvārikambavana;
and the one built by Ghosita was called the Ghositārāma. It is with reference to this that it is said: “in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita.”
Regarding the passage beginning with *bhaṇḍanajātā*: "quarrel" (*bhaṇḍana*) refers to the preliminary stage of a dispute; those in whom this has arisen are "those who have given rise to quarrels.
