Those in whom a dispute has reached its climax through such means as seizing by the hands are "those who have given rise to strife.

A "contention" (*vivāda*) is a contradictory assertion; those who have fallen into that are "those involved in contention. "With the weapons of the mouth" means with the weapons of speech. "Piercing" means...

"Confusing": they neither cause one another to understand nor do they submit to being made understood; that is to say, even after showing both the meaning and the reason, they do not make themselves known to each other.
Even if they begin to try to make themselves understood, they still do not submit to being made understood;
the meaning is that they do not wish to be known. The same method applies to "discontent. In this regard—
And *nijjhatti* is simply a synonym for *saññatti*. But why did these two become engaged in a quarrel? It was on account of a trivial matter.
It is said that two monks were living together in one residence: one was a master of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) and the other a master of the Suttantas (*suttantika*).
One day, the monk who was a master of the Suttantas entered the restroom, and having placed the remainder of the water used for rinsing in a vessel, he went out.
The Vinayadhara entered later; seeing that water, he went out and asked that bhikkhu, "Friend, was this water set aside by you?
"Yes, friend. "Do you not know that there is an offense here? "Yes, I do not know. "There is an offense here, friend. "If there is one, I shall confess it. "But if, friend..."
"Since it was done unintentionally and through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense for you. Thus, he held the view that there was no offense regarding that transgression.
The Vinayadhara informed his own dependents, "This Suttantika does not even know when he incurs an offense.
When they saw his dependents, [they said], "Your preceptor, even after incurring an offense, [does not recognize] the state of being an offense..."
"He does not know," they said. They went and reported this to their own preceptor. He spoke thus:
"This master of the Vinaya previously said 'it is no offense,' but now he says 'it is an offense'; he is a liar.
They went and, saying "Your preceptor is a liar," thus increased their mutual quarreling; it was with reference to this that it was said.
“He said this to the Blessed One” means he spoke these words beginning with, “Venerable sir, here in Kosambī the bhikkhus have come to quarreling.
And he did not say this out of a desire for affection nor with the intention of causing a schism; rather, it was out of a desire for their welfare and benefit.
It is said that this bhikkhu was a promoter of concord; therefore, he thought: “Since these bhikkhus have begun a dispute...”

“I am not able to bring about reconciliation, nor can any other bhikkhu; perhaps the Blessed One, who is peerless in the world with its devas, might go himself, or summon them to his presence, and by delivering a discourse on the Dhamma connected with patience, loving-kindness, and conciliation, bring about their harmony.
Out of a desire for their welfare and benefit, he went and spoke thus.
492. "Bhikkhus, there are these six things that are to be remembered. Thus the teaching was commenced below concerning strife and quarreling.
At this point, the six things to be remembered are presented; in this way, this *Kosambiya-sutta* proceeds according to its proper sequence.
Therein, "to be remembered" (*sāraṇīya*) means they are worthy of being recollected and should not be forgotten even when a long period of time has passed.

Those qualities which one fulfills make one dear to one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life; thus they are called "endearing. They are called "reverential" because they cause one to be held in high esteem.

"For the sake of gathering" means for the purpose of bringing together. "For the sake of non-dispute" means for the purpose of avoiding contention. "For the sake of concord" means for the purpose of a state of harmony.
"For the sake of unity" means for the purpose of oneness, for the purpose of not creating division. "They conduce to" means they result in.
"Bodily action of loving-kindness" (*mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ*) means bodily action to be performed with a mind of loving-kindness. The same principle applies to verbal and mental actions as well.

These are presented from the perspective of monks, yet they are certainly found among laypeople too. For monks, the fulfillment of the duties of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika-dhamma*) with a mind of loving-kindness is what is called "bodily action of loving-kindness. For laypeople, [it includes] going for the purpose of worshipping a *cetiya* or worshipping the Bodhi tree...
Physical acts of loving-kindness consist of such things as going to invite the Saṅgha, meeting monks when they have entered the village for alms,
receiving their bowls, preparing seats for them, and following them [as they depart].

Loving-kindness of mind consists of establishing the training rules regarding proper conduct for monks with a heart of loving-kindness, as well as speaking on meditation subjects and teaching the Dhamma.
Even the word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka is called loving verbal action.

And for laypeople, it includes: "We shall go for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya; we shall go for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi tree; we shall listen to the Dhamma; we shall perform offerings of lamps, garlands, and flowers;
we shall conduct ourselves by undertaking the three types of good conduct; we shall give alms-food by ticket and so forth; we shall provide the rains-retreat gift."
When he says, "We shall give; today we shall give the four requisites to the Saṅgha;

having invited the Saṅgha, prepare the various kinds of food, arrange the seats, set out drinking water, go out to meet the Saṅgha and lead them in, and having seated them on the prepared seats, perform the service with hearts full of devotion and zeal."
Loving verbal action (mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ) is as follows:

having risen early in the morning, monks attend to their physical needs, perform duties such as the circumambulation of the shrine terrace (cetiyangaṇavatta), and sit in a secluded place, thinking, "May the monks in this monastery be happy, free from enmity and free from affliction. This is loving-kindness.
This is called mental action (*manokamma*). For laypeople, the thought, "May the noble ones be happy, free from enmity and free from affliction," is called loving-kindness as mental action.

"Both openly and in secret" means both in their presence and in their absence. In that regard, joining as a companion for novices in tasks such as making robes is called loving-kindness as bodily action in their presence. Furthermore, [offering] services to elders, such as washing their feet, prostrating, and fanning them, is likewise [loving-kindness].
All forms of respectful service performed in person are called "loving bodily action in the presence.

When both parties have placed wooden articles and the like down poorly, to put them away again without showing contempt for them—as if one had oneself placed them down poorly—is called "loving bodily action behind one's back.
Addressing someone by name, such as "Venerable Deva" or "Venerable Tissa," is called "loving verbal action in the presence."
Furthermore, when someone who is not present in the monastery asks, "Where is our venerable elder?
When will our Elder Tissa come?"—such words of endearment are called verbal action of loving-kindness in the absence of the person.
However, opening one's eyes, which are moistened and lubricated by the oil of loving-kindness, and looking with a very serene face, is [loving-kindness] in the presence of the person.

Loving mental action (*mettā-manokamma*) is as follows: the elder Deva and the elder Tissa [thinking], "May he be well and free from illness," such mental attention directed toward one who is absent is called loving mental action.
"Gains" (*lābhā*) refers to requisites obtained, such as robes and so forth. "Righteous" (*dhammikā*) means having avoided wrong livelihood, including its various forms such as hypocrisy (*kuhana*).
It has arisen through a righteous and equitable practice of wandering for alms.
"Even as much as what is contained in his bowl" means, at the very least, even that which is contained within the bowl, down to the measure of two or three spoonfuls of alms-food.
"One who enjoys without partiality": here, there are two kinds of partiality—partiality regarding material goods and partiality regarding individuals.
In this context, the mental differentiation, thinking, "I will give this much, I will not give that much," is called *āmisapaṭivibhatta* (differentiation regarding material things).

Furthermore, the mental differentiation, thinking, "I will give to such-and-such a person, I will not give to such-and-such a person," is called *puggalapaṭivibhatta* (differentiation regarding persons).
One who eats without performing either of these two is called an *appaṭivibhattabhogī* (one who consumes without differentiation).
"Sharing enjoyments with virtuous fellow-practitioners": herein, this is the characteristic of one who shares enjoyments.
Whatever excellent thing is obtained, he does not give it to householders under the pretext of seeking gain through gain, nor does he consume it himself;
rather, while receiving it, he takes it thinking, "May it be shared in common with the Saṅgha," and strikes the gong.
Having struck it, one should enjoy it as if it were the property of the Saṅgha. Now, who fulfills this duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) and who does not?
First of all, one who is immoral does not fulfill it; for the virtuous do not accept what belongs to him.
However, one who is pure in virtue and does not break the rules of conduct fulfills it.

In this regard, the following is the proper conduct: if one gives specifically for the sake of one’s mother, father, teacher, preceptor, or others, one is giving what ought to be given, yet it does not constitute the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (the duty of kindliness);

rather, it is called "tending to an impediment. For the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* is appropriate only for one whose impediments have been relinquished; however, by that person giving specifically [for others], [it applies] to the sick, the attendants of the sick, newcomers, and those departing.
The taking of the outer robe and bowl must be given to one who has newly gone forth and does not know how to do so.
Having given these to them, the remainder should not be distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder in small portions; rather, whatever each person takes, that much should be given to him.
If nothing remains, one should go out again for alms and, starting from the seat of the senior elder, give whatever is excellent.
Having given [the portion], the remainder should be consumed; however, because of the statement "by those who are virtuous," it is even permissible not to give to one who is immoral.
Furthermore, this *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (obligatory duty of hospitality) is fulfilled by a well-trained assembly, not by an untrained assembly.
For in a well-trained assembly, one who receives [food] from elsewhere does not take it [from the host], and even one who does not receive it from elsewhere takes only a moderate amount.

He accepts [only] what is sufficient, not more. Furthermore, this quality of courtesy (*sāraṇīyadhamma*) is fulfilled in twelve years even for one who gives whatever is obtained after wandering for alms again and again, but not before that.
For if, even in the twelfth year, one who has fulfilled the quality of courtesy places his bowl full of almsfood in the refectory (*āsanasālā*) and goes to bathe—

As he was departing, the senior elder of the Saṅgha asked, "Whose bowl is this? When it was said, "It belongs to one who fulfills the qualities of endearment (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*)," [the elder] said, "Bring it here!
Having distributed all the alms-food and eaten, he set down the empty bowl.
Then that monk, seeing the empty bowl, felt dejection, thinking, "They have consumed everything without leaving anything for me. This is the quality of endearment.
It is broken; furthermore, it must be fulfilled for another twelve years, for this is similar to the probation (*parivāsa*) imposed on those belonging to other sects (*titthiya*).

Once a breach has occurred, it must indeed be fulfilled again. However, for one who generates joy, thinking, "It is truly a gain for me, it is truly well-acquired by me, that my fellow celibates enjoy what is in my bowl without even asking for permission," for him there is that which is called "full" (*puṇṇa*).
Furthermore, for one who has thus fulfilled the qualities conducive to being endearing, there is neither envy nor avarice;
he is beloved by people and finds requisites easily. Even when what is placed in his bowl is given to him, it is never exhausted;
he receives the finest goods in the place where divisible items are distributed; and when danger or famine arises, the deities exert themselves on his behalf.
In this regard, there are these instances: It is said that the Elder Tissa, a resident of Leṇagiri, lived near Mahāgāma.
Fifty great elders, while traveling to Nāgadīpa to pay homage to the cetiya, went for alms in Girigāma and departed without having received anything.
As the elder was entering [the village], he saw them and asked, "Venerable sirs, have you received anything?"
“We reflected on it, friend,” they replied. Knowing that it could not be obtained, he said, “Venerable sirs, please remain right here until I return.
“Friend, we fifty people did not receive even enough to moisten a bowl,” they said.
“Venerable sir, those who are permanent residents (nevāsika) are capable; even when they do not receive anything, they know the nature of the path for alms-round. Thus spoke the elders.
They arrived. The Elder entered the village. At the main house, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and stood watching for the Elder;
as soon as the Elder reached her door, she filled his bowl and gave it to him.
Taking it, he went to the presence of the Elders and said to the senior of the Saṅgha, "Take this, venerable sir. The Elder [replied], "By so many of us..."
“Nothing has been obtained; this one has returned so quickly, having taken it—what could it be? he thought, and looked toward the faces of the others.
The Elder, knowing the matter by the mere look of his face, said, “The alms-food has been obtained righteously and justly;
take it without scruple, venerable sirs,” and starting from the beginning, he gave as much as they required to all of them, and he himself also ate as much as he required.
Then, at the conclusion of his meal, the elders asked him: "Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma?
"Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma. "Friend, have you attained the jhānas? "Venerable sirs, I have not attained even those. "Friend, do you not possess the miracle?
"Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the qualities that are conducive to harmony; it is through that Dhamma..."
"From the moment it was filled, even if there were a hundred thousand bhikkhus, what was in the bowl would not be exhausted.
"Excellent, excellent, worthy man! This is truly worthy of you. This, first of all, is the story regarding how "what was in the bowl did not diminish.
Furthermore, when this very elder went to the place of almsgiving for the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering at Cetiyapabbata, he said: "In this..."
“What excellent goods are there in this place? he asked. “Two robes, venerable sir,” they replied.
“These shall come to me. Hearing that, the minister informed the king: “A young man spoke thus.
“The mind of a youth is such, but for the great elders, fine robes are appropriate,” the king said, and thinking, “I shall give them to the great elders,” he set them aside.
As he was giving to the Saṅgha of monks standing in order, even though those robes were placed upon his head, they would not reach his hand;
instead, others would reach it. But at the time of giving to the youth, they did reach his hand.
Having placed them in the youth’s hand, he looked at the face of his minister, had the youth sit down, gave the gift, and dismissed the Saṅgha.
Sitting down near the young man, he asked, "Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?
Without speaking even indirectly about what was not true, he replied, "Great King, I possess no supramundane Dhamma.
"But, venerable sir, did you not say so previously? "Yes, Great King; I am one who fulfills the qualities of endearment (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*). Regarding that...
"From the time I fulfilled the Dhamma, the best goods have come to me in the place where the goods for distribution are kept.
"Excellent, excellent, venerable sir! This is worthy of you," he said, and having paid homage, he departed.
This is the story regarding the phrase: "The best goods have come to me in the place where the goods for distribution are kept."
But during the time of the danger from Brāhmaṇatissa, the inhabitants of Bhātaragāma fled without even informing the Elder Nun Nāgā.
At dawn, the Elder Nun said to the young nuns, “The village is exceedingly quiet; wait and observe.
They went and, having learned that everyone had departed, returned and informed the Elder Nun. Upon hearing this, she said, “Do not you... [fear].”
“Reflect upon their state of having departed; apply yourselves solely to your own recitation, questioning, and systematic attention,” she said.
Then, at the time for alms-round, she dressed herself and stood at the village gate at the foot of a banyan tree, with herself as the twelfth in the group.
The deity dwelling in that tree gave alms-food to all twelve bhikkhunīs and said, “Noble ladies,…”
"Do not go elsewhere; come here always," she said. Now, the Elder’s younger brother was a monk named Nāgatthera.
Thinking, "There is great danger here; it is not possible to subsist here, we shall go to the other shore," he set out from his own residence with eleven others, including himself as the twelfth.
Seeing the Elder nun, he thought, "I will go [to her]," and arrived at Bhātaragāma. The Elder nun—
Hearing that the elders had arrived, she went to them and asked, "What is it, noble sirs? He explained the situation to her.
She said, "Stay in the monastery for just one day today; you may depart tomorrow. The elders went to the monastery.
On the following day, the elder nun, having walked for alms at the foot of a tree, approached the elder and [offered] this alms-food.
“Eat it,” he said. The Elder, saying, “It will suffice, Elder,” remained silent. [The other] said, “Venerable sir, this alms-food is lawful;
eat it without scruple. “It will suffice, Elder,” he replied. She took the bowl and threw it into the air;
the bowl remained suspended in the air. The Elder thought, “Even though it remains at the height of seven palm trees, it is still the meal of a bhikkhunī.”
Having said, "Elder," [he thought: "Fear does not exist at all times;

when fear has subsided, while I am speaking of the Noble Lineage, I shall not be able to maintain my composure if I am mentally reproached, saying, 'O alms-collecting monk, you spent the day eating the meal of the nuns!
Therefore, be heedful, Elders! Having said this, he ascended the path.
The tree deity, standing there thinking, "If the Elder eats the almsfood from the hand of the Elder Nun, I will not turn him back;

but if he does not eat it, I shall turn him back," saw the Elder's departure, descended from the tree, and said, "Venerable Sir, give me the bowl. Having taken the bowl, she led the Elder to the very foot of the tree.

Having brought [the Elder] and prepared a seat, she gave him almsfood; when he had finished his meal, she made a formal promise and attended upon twelve bhikkhunīs and twelve bhikkhus for seven years.
This is the story regarding the phrase "the deity applied herself with zeal," for in that case, the Elder Nun fulfilled the qualities conducive to conciliation (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*).

Regarding the terms "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*) and so forth: for one who has violated a training rule either at the beginning or at the end among the seven classes of offenses, their virtue is called "broken," like a garment torn at the edge.
For one, however, who has violated it in the middle, it is called "perforated," like a garment with a hole in the middle. For one, moreover, who [violates] two or three in succession...
When there are distinct [scars], it is called "spotted" (*sabala*), like a cow that has a color different from its own—such as black, red, or other hues—appearing on its back or belly.
However, when there are distinct [scars] here and there, it is called "speckled" (*kammāsa*), like a cow variegated with different-colored spots here and there. But when [the scars] are entirely...
All these are unbroken; thus, those virtues of his are called "unbroken, flawless, unblemished, and untarnished.
Furthermore, they are "liberating" because they release one from the slavery of craving and establish one in the state of freedom.

They are "praised by the wise" because they are commended by the Buddhas and other wise ones. They are "unadhered-to" because they are not clung to by craving or views. [As for the phrase] "this indeed you..."

They are "unassailable" because they cannot be assailed by anyone. They are called "conducive to concentration" because they lead to either access-concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) or absorption-concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
"He dwells having attained the commonality of virtue" means that his virtue has reached a state of equality with those monks dwelling in various directions and regions.

He dwells. For the virtue (*sīla*) of those who have entered the stream (*sotāpanna*) and so forth remains exactly the same as the virtue of other stream-enterers and so forth, even when they dwell in the midst of the ocean or in the world of the gods;
there is no difference in the virtue of the Path (*maggasīla*). It is with reference to this that it was said.

"This view" (*yāyaṃ diṭṭhī*) refers to right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) associated with the Path. "Noble" (*ariyā*) means faultless. "Leads out" (*niyyātī*) means it is conducive to deliverance (*niyyānika*).
"Of one who acts thus" means of one who acts accordingly. "For the destruction of suffering" means for the sake of the destruction of all suffering.
"Having attained the commonality of view" means having entered into a state of shared view, he dwells [therein].

"The foremost" means the eldest. "It encompasses all the rafters" means it is inclusive. "It brings together the assembly of all the rafters" means it is a unifier; the meaning is "that which unifies."
"That which is called the pinnacle" refers to what is known as the pinnacle of a gabled house (*kūṭāgāra*), namely the peak.
For palaces with five stories and so forth stand supported by a pinnacle; when that falls, everything from the clay foundation upward collapses.
Therefore he spoke thus. "In the same way" means: just as the pinnacle is to the gabled house, so too [is this] among these qualities conducive to socializing (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*).
This noble view should be understood as being foremost, inclusive, and comprehensive. 493.

And how, monks, is it that this view—regarding the statement, "Monks, this view which is the view of the path of stream-entry is noble, leading out, and leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering"—is so? By what means and for what reason?
The meaning is "it has been relinquished. "He is one whose mind is obsessed" means that even by this much he is indeed called one whose mind is obsessed;
this same method applies everywhere. "My mind is well-directed" means my consciousness is properly established.
"For the awakening to the truths" means for the sake of awakening to the four truths. Regarding "noble," and so forth, that is knowledge.
Because it belongs to the noble ones (*ariya*) and not to worldlings (*puthujjana*), it is called "noble.
Because it belongs only to those who possess supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) and not to others, it is called "supramundane.
Because it is absent in worldlings, it is said to be "unshared with worldlings. This same method applies to all sections.

494. “I obtain tranquility within myself” (*paccattaṃ samathaṃ*) means that one obtains tranquility in one’s own mind. The same applies to “extinction” (*nibbuti*). Here, “tranquility” (*samatha*) is one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), and “extinction” (*nibbuti*) is the subsiding of the defilements.

495. “By such a view” (*tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā*) means by such a view of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). 496. “By way of the nature of things” (*dhammatāya*) means by its inherent nature (*sabhāva*).

“This is the nature of things” (*dhammatā esā*) means this is its inherent nature. “Emergence is manifested” (*vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati*) refers to [the emergence from the meditative attainment] by means of a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*).
Or rather, an emergence [from the offense] is seen through confession or instruction.

For when a noble disciple incurs an offense, among the grave offenses he incurs only those like the "building of a hut," and among the light offenses, only those like "sleeping together," which are unintentional;
and even that, having incurred it unintentionally and not intentionally, he does not conceal. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "But then, he quickly... and so forth.
“Dahara” means young. “Kumāra” means not old. “Manda” means dull due to the dullness of the eyes, ears, and so forth.
“Uttānaseyyaka” means lying on one’s back because of extreme youth; the meaning is that he is unable to lie on either his right or left side.
“Having stepped on a coal” means with a hand or foot extended here and there.
Or having touched it. For people who touch it in this way, their hand does not burn quickly;
indeed, some, having taken a coal with their hand, even go a long distance while turning it over. But the hands and feet of a youth are delicate;
as soon as he is touched by it, being burned, he lets out a cry of "Ouch! and quickly withdraws his hand.
Therefore, he is shown here as being young. Even an elder, when burning with fever, endures it; but this person is unable to endure it. For that reason also, he is shown as being young.

"He confesses" means that when there is a fellow monk present who can receive the offense, one does not wait for a day or a night, but confesses during the night before even the fourth watch of the night has passed.
Having gone to the place of residence, he indeed teaches [the Dhamma].
"High and low" means high and low [tasks]. "What is to be done" means tasks that ought to be performed after having said, "What shall I do?
Among these, "high work" refers to the making of robes, dyeing them, plastering work on a cetiya, and [work] in the uposatha hall, the cetiya house, or the bodhi house.
"Work that ought to be done," and so forth. "Low work" (avacakamma) refers to minor tasks such as washing and anointing the feet;

alternatively, high work (uccakamma) refers to tasks such as plastering at a cetiya. In that same context, low work includes cooking astringent decoctions, fetching water, scrubbing the stomach, binding resin, and so on.
"He has become diligent" (ussukkaṃ āpanno hoti) means he has undertaken the state of diligence—that which is to be done.
"He practices accordingly. "He has intense longing" means he has a deep aspiration.
"She licks up the calf" means she eats while licking the grass. "She gazes at the calf" means she looks toward the calf.
For a cow with a young calf does not go far away in the forest, leaving behind her calf who has come to her side and is lying in one place.
Just as a cow, while grazing in a place near her calf, plucks the grass and, lifting up her neck,
gazes exclusively toward her calf; even so, a stream-enterer, while performing various high and low duties,
inclines toward that [goal], acting with unremitting persistence, intense desire, and profound aspiration.

In this regard, there is this story: While the plastering work at the Mahācetiya was being carried out, it is said that a certain noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), taking a plaster vessel with one hand and a trowel with the other, climbed onto the courtyard of the shrine thinking, "I shall perform the plastering work.
A certain monk, possessed of great physical strength, went and stood near the elder. When the elder saw someone else...
"He became distracted" means that he went from that place to another place. That monk also returned to that very same spot. The Elder went to yet another place;
thus, after they had come to several places, [the Elder] said: "Good man, why does this great shrine courtyard not find space in another location? The other did not depart.
498. "Endowed with strength" means possessed of strength. "Making it a bone" means making it an object of necessity;
the sense is, having become one who has need of it. "Attending to it" means placing it in the mind.
"Applying the whole heart" means applying oneself with the entire mind without allowing even the slightest distraction. "With the ear pricked up" means with the ear fixed intently.

For noble disciples are lovers of hearing the Dhamma; having gone to a place for hearing the Dhamma, they do not sit down while nodding off to sleep, nor conversing with anyone, nor with distracted minds.
Rather, as if partaking of the Deathless, they remain insatiable in hearing the Dhamma until the dawn breaks. Therefore, he spoke thus.
"500. 'The nature of things is well-investigated' means that the intrinsic nature has been thoroughly examined.
'For the realization of the fruit of stream-entry' is an instrumental expression; the meaning is 'by means of the knowledge that realizes the fruit of stream-entry.
'Thus endowed with the seven factors' means thus endowed with these seven kinds of knowledge of great reviewing. This, first of all, is the common explanation of the teachers."
Indeed, there is no such thing as a supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) that consists of many thought-moments (cittakkhaṇa).
However, the caviller (vitaṇḍavādī) claims that there is no path consisting of even a single thought-moment;

for according to the statement, "One should thus develop it for seven years," the development of the path (maggabhāvanā) occurs over seven years. But the defilements (kilesa), being easily severed, [are cut off] by seven...
He says, "They are cut off by knowledges. He should be told, "Bring a sutta. Certainly, seeing no other sutta, he will bring and show this very one:
"This first knowledge is attained by him; this second knowledge...
[and so on] ...this seventh knowledge is attained by him. Then he should be asked: "But what is this sutta?"
“Of interpretable meaning or of definitive meaning? To this he will say: “It is of definitive meaning; its meaning is exactly as it is in the sutta. He should be asked:
“What is the meaning of the statement, ‘The nature of things is well-established for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry’?
Certainly he will say, “Its meaning is for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. Then he should be asked: “One who possesses the path...”
“He realizes the fruit; he is one who possesses the fruit. If [the opponent] knows this, he will say, “One who possesses the fruit realizes it.
Then he should be told: “In this way, monks, a noble disciple endowed with the seven factors is one who possesses the fruit of stream-entry.
[If you think otherwise,] here, without having developed the path, the noble disciple would—like a frog leaping up—seize only the fruit.

"Do not say just anything, thinking 'I have received the Sutta from him. When answering a question, one must indeed have lived in the presence of a teacher, mastered the word of the Buddha, and understood the flavor of its meaning.
"These seven knowledges are precisely the reviewing knowledges of a noble disciple; the supramundane path is said to consist of many mind-moments."
"It does not exist; it lasts for only a single moment of consciousness"—thus he should be made to understand. If he understands, let him understand.
If he does not understand, he should be dismissed with the words: "Go, enter the monastery early in the morning and drink some conjey. The rest is clear in all respects.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Kosambiya Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Brahmanimantanika Sutta: 501.
“Thus have I heard” introduces the Brahmanimantanika Sutta. Therein, “a pernicious view” means a base [view].
The eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). This [view] says that what is impermanent—the state of Brahmā together with his body—is "permanent.
"Stable" (*dhuva*) and so forth are synonyms for that very same thing. In this context, "stable" means firm. "Eternal" (*sassata*) means existing at all times.
"Absolute" (*kevala*) means unbroken and complete. "Of an indestructible nature" (*acavanadhamma*) means having an indestructible essence. For in such passages as "this is not born," and so on...
He speaks with the intention that in this place there is no one who is being born, living, dying, passing away, or reappearing.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and other than this," he thinks that there is no other escape higher than this Brahma-abode together with its body;
thus, a firmly established eternalist view has arisen in him. Such is his doctrine.
But he rejects everything above that—the three higher stages of meditation (*jhāna*), the four paths, the four fruits, and *nibbāna*.
"Enveloped in ignorance" (*avijjāgato*) means one who has entered into, is possessed of, ignorance; one who is ignorant and blinded. "Yatra hi nāma" means "he who indeed. 502.
Now, monks, as for "Māra the Evil One," how did Māra see the Blessed One? It is said that he [saw] himself...
Sitting in his dwelling, from time to time he would direct his attention toward the Teacher, thinking, "In which village or town does the ascetic Gotama dwell today?
On this occasion, directing his attention and learning that the Teacher was staying in the Subhaga Grove near Ukkatthā,
he looked to see where he had gone and saw him departing for the Brahma-world.

“The ascetic Gotama goes to the Brahma-world; as soon as he has finished preaching the Dhamma there and his assembly of Brahmās does not pass beyond my domain, I shall go and create a lack of desire for his teaching of the Dhamma.
Having followed on the Teacher’s footsteps, he stood within the assembly of Brahmās, his body invisible. He [thought]: “By the Teacher...”
Knowing that the Brahmā Baka had been refuted, he stood there as a support for the Brahmā. Therefore it was said:
"Then, monks, Māra the Evil One...
Having entered the retinue of Brahmā means having entered the body of one member of Brahmā’s retinue. [He approached] the Great Brahmā.
But he is not able to enter into the retinue of the Brahmapurohita devas. "Do not insult him" means: do not disparage him.

"The Conqueror" (*abhibhū*) means one who stands having overcome [all things] as the eldest. "Unconquered" (*anabhibhūta*) means not overcome by others. "Aññadatthu" is a particle used for an exclusive statement.
"The Seer" (*dasa*) refers to seeing; it indicates that he sees everything. "The Lord of Power" (*vasavattī*) refers to all people.
He causes the world to revolve. He is the Lord in the world; he is the Lord. He is the maker and the fashioner of the world;
he demonstrates that the earth, the Himavat, Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa, the great oceans, the moon, and the sun were fashioned by him.
He is the best and the ordainer of the world. "You shall be a khattiya," [he says]. You...

He shows that beings proceed as directed thus: "one called a brahmin, one called a vaiśya, one called a śūdra, one called a householder, one called a renunciant—even down to becoming a camel or an ox.
Regarding the phrase "the Master, the Father of those born and yet to be born": he is called the "Master" because of his mastery (*vasitā*) attained through practice;
he is called the "Father" of both those who have been born and those who are yet to be born. In this context, [the reference is] to those born from eggs and those born from a womb.
Beings within the eggshell and within the womb are called "potential" (*bhavya*); from the moment they have emerged outside, they are "actualized" (*bhūta*).
Moisture-born beings are "potential" during the first moment of consciousness and "actualized" from the second moment onward.

Beings of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) should be understood as "potential" during the first posture and "actualized" from the second posture onward. All of them, with the recognition that "these are my sons," [the father...]
"Of those who were and will be," he said.

"Censurers of earth": this indicates that just as you now censure and loathe the earth, thinking, "It is impermanent, suffering, and non-self," so too did they of old censure the earth; it was not only you who did so. The same applies to the phrases "censurers of water," and so forth.
The same method applies here. "Established in a lowly body" means they were reborn in the four states of misery (*apāya*).

"Praising the earth" means that instead of criticizing the earth as you do, they praised it, saying, "It is permanent, stable, eternal, indestructible, indivisible, and imperishable"—thus they were speakers in praise of the earth. "Delighting in the earth" means...
Those who delight in the earth by way of craving and views—this same method applies to the rest as well.

“Established in a sublime body” means reborn in the Brahma-world. “Taṃ tāham” means “therefore, for that reason, I [say this]. “Iṅgha” is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. “Upātivattittha” means they have transcended.
There is also a reading “upātivattito,” which has the same meaning. “Paṭippaṇāmeyya” means he would drive away with a staff.
Having struck it with a four-handled mallet, he would crush it. "Into the precipice of hell" means into a great abyss a hundred fathoms deep.
"He would fail" means that he would be unable to grasp it in a place suitable for grasping with the hand, or to stand upon it in a place suitable for standing with the foot.
"Do you not see, monk? means, "Monk, do you not see this assembly of Brahmās?"
"Do you see this assembly gathered together, shining, radiant, and illuminating?"—this shows the power of psychic majesty (*iddhānubhāva*) of those who abide by the Brahmā’s instruction.
"Thus, monks, Māra the Evil One led me to the assembly of Brahmā"—monks, did not Māra the Evil One [say]:
"Do you not, monk, see the assembly of Brahmā in its glory and splendor"?

"Shining, radiant, and illuminating—if you too, without transgressing the word of Mahābrahmā, were to do exactly what Brahmā tells you, then you too would shine in this very way with glory and splendor.
Speaking thus, he led me toward the assembly of Brahmā; he brought me there. "Do not think so"—do not entertain such a thought.
"You are Māra, the Evil One. "Evil One, I am called 'Māra' because I bring death to the great multitude;
I am called 'the Evil One' (Pāpimā) because I create evil, wretched, and disgraceful things for the great multitude—thus I know myself.
503. "The whole span of life" means the entire lifespan. "They would thus come to know" means they would [know] by means of such great ascetic practice.
"You are possessed of such qualities; but you were born only yesterday—what do you know? Even now the scent of milk wafts from your mouth," he said, poking him as he spoke.
"You will cleave to the earth" means that having cleaved to the earth, having swallowed it and made it your own, you will seize it through craving, conceit, and views.
"You will be one who dwells near me" means you will be one who lies close to me.
The meaning is: "You shall follow me when I go, stand by me when I stand, sit near me when I am seated, and lie down near me when I am lying down.
"One who sleeps on my body" means one who sleeps upon my person.
"To be dealt with according to my wish and to be cast out" means that whatever I desire for myself must be done, and furthermore, even after being cast out from the *jajjharikā* thicket...
"You shall become lower than a lowly person, even lower than a *lakuṇḍaka*"; this is the meaning.
By this, he either flatters or disparages the Blessed One. "Flatters" means:
"If you, monk, will cling to the earth through craving and so forth, you will be one who stays close to me; when I go, you will go."
"If you stand, I shall stand; if you sit, I shall sit; if you lie down, I shall lie down.
Having excluded all other people, I shall make you my trusted confidant"—in this way, first, he flatters him. But with the remaining words, he disparages him.
This is the intended meaning here: "If you are to be attached to the earth, you will be a mere dweller upon its surface."
"You shall be mine; you will come after waiting for my departure and so forth, or you will stand, sit, or lie down [with me];

regarding my person, you will provide me with protection, but as for you, I shall do with you as I please, even casting you out from the *jajjharikā* thicket or the *lakuṇḍaka* reed-bed"—in this way, one indeed insults [the other]. But this Brahmā...
Because he is dependent on honor, it is precisely disparagement that is intended here. The same principle applies to the cases beginning with "Āpa.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "He said to me, 'I am Brahmā,'" the Blessed One now [thinks]: "This Brahmā is dependent on honor;
he conceives the thought 'I know,' and being intoxicated by his own glory, he does not see anything capable of even touching his body. To restrain him slightly—"
Having thought, “It is fitting,” he began this teaching. Therein, “I understand their destiny” means I understand their accomplishment.
“And their radiance” means I understand their power. “Thus of great influence” means thus of great fame and great retinue.
“As far as the moon and sun revolve” means in as much space as the moon and sun move about. “The quarters shine.”
"Virocanā" means shining and illuminating the directions, or the directions being made to shine and illuminate by them.

"A thousandfold world-system" (*sahassadhā loka*) means a world divided into a thousand parts by that same measure; the meaning is a thousand world-systems together with this [central] world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Your power prevails there" (*ettha te vattate vaso*) means that within this thousandfold world-system, your authority prevails. And "one after another" (*paroparañca*)...
"You know" means that you know the beings—high and low, inferior and superior—within thousands of world-systems, one after another.

"Furthermore, you know those with passion and those free from passion" means that not only do you know them one after another as "this one is a possessor of psychic power (iddhi) and this one is an ordinary person," but you also know people according to their possession or absence of passion, such as "this one has passion and this one is free from passion. "The state of being thus and the state of being otherwise" [is explained as follows].
"Suchness" (*itthaṃbhāvo*) refers to this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "Otherness" (*aññathābhāvo*) refers to the remaining nine hundred [world-systems] other than this.

"The coming and going of beings" (*sattānaṃ āgatiṃ gatiṃ*): herein, you know the coming of beings by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and their going by way of death (*cuti*) within these thousand world-systems.
Yet, you have the perception, "I am too great," for you are indeed known as Sahassibrahmā, distinct from others.
"But as for you, there is no limit to the number of Brahmās— two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, five thousand, ten thousand,
or even a hundred thousand; yet you imagine yourself to be great, like one who strives to measure the extent of a cloth with a four-cubit rag," thus he rebukes him.
"Reborn here" means reborn here in the plane of the first jhāna.
"Therefore you do not know that" means for that reason you do not know that body. "Not even equal to you" means that even having reached the state of what is to be known, I am not your equal.
"Having understood" means having known. "How could there be inferiority? means how could there be a state of being lower than you on my part?

It is said that this Brahmā was one who had been reborn in a lower realm; during a time when no Buddha had appeared, he went forth as a seer, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).

Having passed away without falling away from his jhāna, he was reborn in the Vehapphala Brahma-world of the fourth jhāna plane, taking up a lifespan of five hundred aeons. There, he remained for the full duration of his life.
Having remained there, having performed the lower rebirth, and having developed the sublime third jhāna, he was reborn in the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world, where he lived for sixty-four kappas.
There, having developed the second jhāna, he was reborn among the Ābhassara devas, where he lived for eight kappas.
There, having developed the first jhāna, [he was reborn] in the plane of the first jhāna.
Having been reborn with a lifespan of an eon, he knew both the karma he had performed and the place where he was reborn during the initial period;
however, as time passed, he forgot both and gave rise to the view of eternalism (*sassataditthi*). Therefore, the Blessed One said to him:
"Because of that, you do not know this... [etc. ...whence could there be any passing away?"
Then Brahmā thought: "The ascetic Gotama knows my lifespan, my place of rebirth, and my past deeds;
come now, I shall ask him about my past deeds. He questioned the Teacher regarding his own past deeds. The Teacher explained it to him.
It seems that in the past, after being born into a noble family and seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he [thought]: "Of birth, old age, sickness, and death..."

Thinking, “I shall bring [this suffering] to an end,” he went forth, took up the ascetic life of a seer (*isi-pabbajjā*), and having attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and become a master of the jhānas that serve as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), he had a leaf-hut built on the bank of the Ganges and spent his time delighting in the joy of meditation (*jhāna-rati*).
At that time, from time to time, caravan leaders set out across the desert wilderness with five hundred carts. However, it was not possible to travel through the desert wilderness during the day.
They set out during the night. Then, as the oxen yoked to the front yoke of the first cart were traveling, they turned back and faced the path from which they had come.
The other carts likewise turned back, and when dawn broke, they realized they had returned.
That was the day they were to cross the wilderness, but all their wood and water had been completely exhausted.
Therefore, thinking, "There is no life for us now," the men tied their oxen to the wheels,
entered the shade of the carts, and lay down. The ascetic, having emerged from his leaf-hut early in the morning and sitting at the door of the hut,
was looking toward the Ganges when he saw the river being swept away by a great flood of water, carrying along a mass of rolling jewels.
Seeing her approaching as if she were [the water itself], he thought: "Are there indeed beings in this world who are suffering from the lack of such sweet water?

While reflecting thus, he saw that army in the desert wilderness and, thinking, "May these beings not perish," [he willed that] "from here, a great mass of water shall break off and flow toward the army in the desert wilderness."

"Let it go," he resolved with a mind of supernormal power (*abhiññā*). Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, the water flowed there as if it had been set down in a table of contents (*mātikā*).
The people, awakened by the sound of the water, saw the water and were filled with joy;
having bathed and drunk, they also gave water to their oxen and went safely to their desired destination. The Teacher, showing that former deed of the Brahmā, said:
“That which you caused many people to drink when they were thirsty and overcome by the heat—
that was your former practice of vows and virtuous conduct.”
"I remember it as if I had just woken from sleep"—
with these words he spoke this verse.
On another occasion, the ascetic built a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges and lived there, depending upon a forest village.
At that time, robbers had raided that village; having seized the valuables, they were departing with cows and young calves.
The cows, the dogs, and the people all raised a great outcry. Hearing that sound, the ascetic reflected, "What could this be? and perceiving that "fear has arisen among the people," he [acted].

Thinking, "While I am watching, may these beings not perish," he entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and upon emerging, by means of a mind of direct knowledge, he conjured up a fourfold army on the path ahead of the thieves, ready for action as they approached.
When the thieves saw it, thinking, "It is the king," they abandoned their plunder and fled. The ascetic [said], "Whatever belongs to whom..."
“Let this property belong to him alone,” he resolved, and it became exactly so. The great multitude attained safety.
The Teacher, showing this too as his former deed, said:
“The people who were seized on the banks of the Eṇī River...”
“I liberated the one being led away as a captive;
I recall that former practice of my vows and virtuous conduct,
just like one awakened from sleep.”
He spoke this verse. Here, "on the bank of the Eṇī" means on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, on one occasion, a family living upstream on the Gaṅgā established a friendly relationship with a family living downstream;
they fastened together a pair of boats, loaded them with much solid and soft food as well as perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and [set out].
He came along with the current of the Ganges. As the people ate, feasted, danced, and sang, they were filled with intense joy as if traveling in a celestial chariot (*devavimāna*).
Seeing this, the Naga of the Ganges became angry and thought, "These people pay me no heed at all;
now I shall cast them into the very ocean! Having manifested a massive physical form, he [stirred] the water.
Splitting himself in two, he rose up, spread out his hood, and stood there making a hissing sound. When the great multitude saw this, they were terrified and raised a cry.
The ascetic, sitting in his leaf-hut, heard it and thought, "These people are coming along singing and dancing, filled with joy;
but now they have raised a cry of fear—what could this be? As he reflected, he saw the king of the nāgas.

“May these beings not perish while I am looking on,” he thought; and having entered the jhāna that serves as a basis for direct knowledge, he cast off his human form, assumed the shape of a garuḷa, and showed himself to the nāga king. Terrified, the nāga king withdrew his hood and plunged into the water.
The great multitude attained safety. The Teacher, pointing out this past deed of his, said:
“Having seized a boat upon the current of the Ganges,
a human-like Nāga was captured by a fierce serpent;
you released him by force, having overcome him.”
“I remember that ancient practice of yours, your conduct and virtue,
just as one who has awakened from sleep remembers a dream”—
with these words he spoke this verse.
At another time, having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he became an ascetic named Kesava.
At that time, our Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Kappa, who served as Kesava’s attendant and pupil;
he was one who promised obedience, acted agreeably, was endowed with wisdom, and sought his teacher’s welfare. Kesava could not live without him.
He was unable [to live independently] and thus made his livelihood by depending on him alone. The Teacher, showing this as well as his past karma, said:
“Kappa was your attendant; you thought yourself equal to one who possesses the wisdom of a Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“I recall that ancient practice of yours, your conduct and virtue,
just as one who has awakened from sleep recalls a dream.
Thus he spoke this verse.
Thus the Teacher revealed the karma performed by Brahmā in his various states of existence. Even as the Teacher was speaking, Brahmā perceived it all;
like forms appearing when a thousand lamps are lit, all his karmas became manifest to him.
With a mind full of faith, he spoke this verse:
“Truly you understand this lifespan of mine;
you know other things as well, for you are a Buddha.
For such is the blazing majesty of that [knowledge].”
"Shining, he stands in the Brahma-world.
Then, the Blessed One, revealing to him a state of peerless equality, spoke the verse beginning with "The earth indeed, I am the Brahmā.
In that context, "not experienced by the earth in its earth-ness" means not experienced by the earth in its specific nature as earth.
"Unattained. But what is that? It is *nibbāna*. For because it has escaped from everything conditioned (*saṅkhata*), it is called "unattained" by way of the nature of earth.
"Having directly known that" means having known and realized that *nibbāna*. "I did not take up earth" means I did not grasp at earth through craving, views, or conceit.
The same method applies to water and the other elements. The detailed explanation, however, is in the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*.
It should be understood in the manner already stated.

"If, dear sir, you say 'everything by way of everything,'" Brahmā spoke thus because he was taking offense at the word "everything" (sabba), having pointed to it as the very word for his own doctrine.
But the Teacher, referring to *sakkāya* (personality-existence), said "everything."
Brahmā speaks with reference to the "all-in-all. You say, "It is all," yet you also say, "There is nothing that has not been experienced as all.
If there is nothing that has not been experienced as all, then there is something that has not been experienced [as such].
Let your words not be empty, let them not be hollow; may your speech not be void.
Thinking, "Let it not be empty," he rebukes the Teacher with a falsehood.
But the Teacher is a superior debater a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold compared to this Brahmā;
therefore, in order to crush his argument, [the Teacher says], "I shall speak of everything, and I shall speak of that which has never been experienced before; listen to me."
Bringing forward the reason, he said, "consciousness," and so forth. Therein, "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) means that which is to be cognized. "Invisible" (*anidassana*):
it is called invisible because it does not come within the range of visual consciousness; by these two terms, Nibbāna alone is expressed. "Endless" (*ananta*):
this is called endless because it is devoid of the extremes of arising and passing away. For this has also been said:
“Beings have ends, while that which has not come to be is endless;
the ends of beings are seen, and the ends of beings are made manifest.
“Radiant on all sides” means endowed with light in every respect. For there is no other phenomenon more radiant or more luminous than Nibbāna.
There is nothing more pure or more brilliant than it. Or, because it is so abundant everywhere and is not lacking anywhere, it is called *sabbatopabha*.
For one cannot say that Nibbāna does not exist in such-and-such a direction among the eastern directions and so forth.
Alternatively, *pabha* is a name for a ford; since it has a ford on every side, it is *sabbatopabha*.
It is said that for Nibbāna, just as there is no place that is not a ford in the great ocean— wherever one wishes to descend, that very spot is a ford— likewise,

among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), whatever means by which one wishes to descend into Nibbāna, that very means is a ford. There is no meditation subject that is not a ford for reaching Nibbāna.
Therefore it was said: "shining on all sides. Regarding the phrase "by way of the earth-nature of the earth":
that Nibbāna is not experienced by way of the earth-nature of the earth, nor by way of the water-nature (*āpādi-sabhāva*) of the other elements such as water and so forth.
Thus, by way of the totality of all classes of phenomena belonging to the three planes which constitute the objective domain for those like you, that consciousness is non-manifest (*anidassana*).
He established the doctrine that "the infinite is not experienced from any side.
Then Brahmā, having been made to answer by the Teacher point after point, seeing nothing at all to grasp, and wishing to perform a playful display, said:
"Well then, dear sir, let me vanish from you. In this context, "vanish" refers to the miracle of invisibility.
"I shall do so," he said. "If you are able," means: "If you can vanish from my sight, then vanish and perform a miracle. "He was not able to vanish from my sight" means:
he was not able to vanish from me. But what did he wish to do? He wished to go to the root-rebirth (the Brahma-world). For among the Brahmas—
The fundamental rebirth-body (*mūlapaṭisandhika-attabhāva*) is subtle; it is beyond the reach of others, and they remain only with a constructed body (*abhisaṅkhata-kāya*).
The Teacher did not allow him to go to that fundamental rebirth.

Or, even without going to the fundamental rebirth, he might have made himself vanish by means of that very darkness and become invisible; the Teacher dispelled that darkness, and therefore [he was unable] to vanish.
He was unable [to do so]. Being unable, he hid in a celestial mansion (*vimāna*), he hid in a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*), and he sat down squatting.
The host of Brahmas played a joke: "This is indeed the crane-Brahmā;

he hides in a celestial mansion, he hides in a wish-fulfilling tree, and he sits down squatting. You, O Brahmā, have become invisible! Thus they conceived this perception. He, by the host of Brahmas...
He was ridiculed and became dejected.
When this was said, O monks— "O monks, when that Brahmā said to me, 'Come now, dear sir,
let us disappear,' and seeing that he was unable to disappear, I said this to him."
Regarding the statement "He spoke this verse," why did the Blessed One speak this verse?

He spoke the verse while remaining invisible so that there would be no opportunity for the host of Brahmās to say, "How can it be known whether the ascetic Gotama exists or does not exist in this place?
Thus he spoke the verse while vanishing from sight.
"In that regard, 'having seen fear in existence' means: having indeed seen fear in existence. And 'seeing this one who seeks non-existence' means:

having repeatedly seen even this sevenfold existence of beings—consisting of the three types beginning with sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*)—as one who seeks non-existence, who is searching for non-existence.
'They do not welcome existence' means: they do not welcome any form of existence by way of craving or views."
"They did not seek after it" means they did not pursue it. "And they did not cling to delight" means they did not take hold of the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).
Thus, the Teacher taught the Dhamma, proclaiming the Four Noble Truths.
At the conclusion of the teaching, ten thousand Brahmās, having conceived the embryo of insight (*vipassanā*) by following the course of the teaching, drank the nectar of the path and its fruit.
"Acchariyabbhutacittajātā" means they became filled with wonder, filled with amazement, and filled with joy.

"Samūlaṃ bhavaṃ udabbahī" means that at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), through his various teachings, he uprooted existence—including its very roots—for himself and for many other gods and humans;
the meaning is that he pulled it out and eradicated it.
505. At that time, however, Māra the Evil One, overcome by anger, thought:
"While I was wandering about, this ascetic Gotama has delivered a discourse on the Dhamma and brought ten thousand Brahmās under his sway.
Because he was thus overcome by anger, he fixed his attention upon the body of a certain member of the Brahma assembly; to demonstrate this, [the text says] "Then..."
He said, "Bhikkhus, if you... and so forth. In that context, "If you have thus awakened" means if you yourself have awakened to the Four Truths.
"Do not lead disciples" means do not lead householders or those who have gone forth to that Dhamma.
"Established in inferior bodies" means established in the four states of misery (apāya). "In superior bodies" [means established in the higher realms].
"Established" means established in the Brahma-world. With reference to whom does he say this? It refers to those ascetics and wanderers who have gone forth in the external renunciate life.
For when no Buddha has appeared in the world, sons of noble family go forth into the ascetic life;
without investigating anything for anyone, they live as solitary wanderers, produce meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and are reborn in the Brahma-world.
Referring to this, he spoke thus: "It is indeed wholesome not to instruct others, dear sir.

This means that it is wholesome, better even, to refrain from instructing others, to refrain from admonishing them, and to refrain from delivering a discourse on the Dhamma. "Do not advise others" means:

do not wander about at times traveling through the human world, at times through the world of the devas, at times through the world of Brahmā, and at times through the world of the nāgas; [rather, remain] in one place.
"Sitting in his place, he should pass the time with the bliss of the jhānas, the paths, and the fruits.

"By way of not addressing" means by way of not speaking to him. "And by way of Brahmā’s invitation" refers to the invitation spoken by Baka Brahmā using the Brahmā-standards (brahmaṭṭhāna), beginning with the words, "Sir, this world is eternal," and so forth. "Therefore" means for that reason. Of this exposition...
The designation *brahmanimantanika* (invited by Brahmā) has arisen as a conventional term, a common usage, a designation, and a description. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Brahmanimantanika-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
10. Commentary on the Māratajjanīya Sutta 506.

"Thus have I heard" refers to the Māratajjanīya Sutta. Therein, "entered into the belly" means having entered the stomach, he has gone inside the intestines, sitting in the place of the lower abdomen (*pakkāsaya*). "As if very heavy" means as if exceedingly heavy.

"Stiff" means like a heap of stones. "He thinks it is filled with meat" means that, for one who has eaten a meal of meat, it is as if his belly were filled with meat, as if he were carrying a bag full of meat, or as if he were a piece of raw meat; such is the meaning. "Having entered the vihāra":

if this heaviness is due to a fault in the food, and walking in the open air is not suitable, then having descended from the walkway (caṅkama) and entered the leaf-hut (paṇṇasālā), [he sits] in the place naturally prepared.
He sat down on his seat. "He reflected thoroughly within himself" means that, while considering, "What indeed is this?", he applied his mind by means of his own skillful method.
However, if the Elder had reflected upon his own virtue, [he would have thought]:
"May whatever has been consumed yesterday, the day before, or the day after tomorrow that remains undigested, or any other discordant fault, all be digested."
“May it be comfortable,” he thought, and would have touched his belly with his hand; but Māra the Evil One would have vanished and departed.
However, the Elder did not do so, but applied his mind thoroughly. [He reflected: “Let him not harass the Tathāgata.
For just as parents are indeed harassed when their children are harassed, so too are teachers and preceptors harassed when their co-residents and pupils are harassed.
When the countryside is harassed, the king is harassed; likewise, when a disciple of the Tathāgata is harassed, the Tathāgata is harassed.
Therefore he said: "Do not harass the Tathāgata.

"He stood pressed against the door-sill" means he stood right up against the door-sill. "Door-sill" (aggaḷa) refers to a door-panel (kavāṭa). The meaning is that, having risen up with his mouth [from inside] and gone out from the leaf-hut, he stood leaning against the door-panel of the outer leaf-hut.
507. Why did he begin this teaching with the words, "In the past, O Evil One"? It is said that the Elder thought:
"The scent of humans causes distress even to deities dwelling in the sky when they are a hundred *yojanas* away. For it has been said:
'O Prince, the scent of humans troubles the gods for a hundred *yojanas*. Yet this Māra is a native of the city, well-acquainted [with us], and of great power."
Being endowed with such majesty as the king of the gods, having entered my womb and sat within the intestines in the region of the stomach, he must have become exceedingly defiled.
For one who is able to enter and sit in such a loathsome and repulsive place, what else could there be that he would not do? What else would he feel shame for? You—
Thinking, "When it is said, 'He is my kinsman,' there is no one who does not become softened;
well then, having penetrated his kinship, I shall release him by a gentle means," he began this teaching:
"You were my nephew"—that you at that time were my nephew. This is according to the lineage.
It has been said. However, in the world of the gods, there is no such thing as Māra ruling by way of a lineage of father or grandfather;
rather, through the power of merit, he was reborn as a king of the gods in the celestial realm, and having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away.
Another person, by virtue of their own karma, was reborn in that very place as the sovereign. Thus, this Māra also—
Then, having passed away from there and performed wholesome deeds once more, he should be understood to have been reborn at this time in that preeminent position.
*Vidhura* means one whose burden has departed; the meaning is that he is peerless among others. *Appakasirena* means without hardship. *Pasupālaka* means goat and sheep herders.
*Pathāvino* means those who have set out upon the road. *Kāye upacinitvā* means having gathered around the body.
"Having built a funeral pyre and set fire to it, they departed"—by this much they meant that the body would reach its final end;
thus, having observed the dimensions of the pyre and set fire to it from the four directions, they departed.
The pyre blazed like the flame of a lamp, and for the Elder it was as if he had entered and sat within a water-cave. "Having shaken out his robes."
Having emerged from meditative absorption, he shook out his robes while treading upon embers that were smokeless and the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers.
Yet there was not even a trace of heat in his body, nor did even a single thread of his robes catch fire; such is the fruit of meditative attainment.
"Abuse us" means abuse us with the ten grounds for abuse. "Revile us" means revile us with speech.
"Harass" means strike. "Torment" means cause suffering. All of this is a synonym for verbal harassment.
"As Dūsi Māra did to them" means as Dūsi Māra did to these [monks]. "He would find an opportunity" means he would find a flaw;
the meaning is that he would find an object and a condition for the arising of defilements. Regarding "shavelings," etc., [the word] "shaveling" refers to those who are shaven-headed.
It would have been appropriate to call them "ascetics" (samaṇa), yet these people, treating them with contempt, called them "shaveling ascetics" (muṇḍaka-samaṇaka).
"Ibbhā" refers to householders (gahapatika). "Kiṇhā" means dark-skinned; the meaning is "black. Regarding the term "bandhupādāpaccā": here, "bandhu" is intended to mean Brahmā.
For Brahmins refer to him as "grandfather" (pitāmaha). Those who are descendants of his feet are "pādāpaccā"—descendants from the feet of Brahmā.
The intention is that they were born from the back of the feet. It is said that this is their doctrine: "Brahmins issued from the mouth of Brahmā; Kṣatriyas from his chest;
Vaiśyas from his navel; Śūdras from his thighs; and ascetics (śramaṇas) from the back of his feet.
"We are meditators, we are meditators" means "we are meditators, we are meditators. "Born of sweetness" means born of indolence.
"Jhāyanti" means they think. "Pajjhāyanti" and the following terms are augmented by means of prefixes.
"Mūsikaṃ maggayamāno" means seeking a mouse that has emerged from a hollow tree in the evening for the sake of its feeding ground, searching for it upon a branch of the tree.
It is said that he stands perfectly still, as if utterly tranquil; when the right moment arrives, he suddenly seizes the mouse.
*Kotthu* means a jackal; some also call it *soṇa*. *Sandhisamalasaṅkaṭire* means at a junction (*sandhi*), in filth (*samala*), and in a rubbish heap (*saṅkaṭira*).
Therein, a "junction" (*sandhi*) refers to a house junction. "Filth" (*samala*) refers to a sewer for excrement.
A "rubbish heap" (*saṅkaṭira*) refers to a place for refuse. *Vahacchinno* means one who has emerged from the wilderness with his provisions cut off. *Sandhisamalasaṅkaṭire*... [repeated].
Whether at a joint, in a sore, or in a narrow space—he too meditates motionless, as if his limbs were bound.
Regarding the phrase "they are reborn in hell": if Māra were to act by taking possession of human bodies in this way, it would not be unwholesome for humans;
it would belong to Māra alone. However, without taking possession of the body, [he acts] upon a dissimilar object.
It shows the object of remorse; at that time, indeed, it is like monks quickly seizing [the net] as they cover over the fish,
like those holding a net as they catch fish, like those setting a snare on a perch as they bind birds,
like those hunting deer in the forest with dogs, or like those taking a woman and sitting in a drinking hall.
He showed it as if dancing, as if singing, and as if non-human beings were sitting and standing in the night-quarters and day-quarters of the bhikkhunīs.
Even those who had gone to the forest, to the woods, or to the monastery, seeing this object of remorse, returned and told others: "The recluses are doing such un-recluse-like things!"
“They act inappropriately; what virtue can come from giving to these people? Do not give anything to them!
Thus, those people, reviling virtuous ones wherever they saw them, generated demerit and became fillers of the states of misery (apāya).
Therefore it is said: “They are reborn in hell.”
509. *Anvāviṭṭhā* means pervaded. *Pharitvā vihariṃsu* does not mean they merely dwelt having pervaded;

rather, standing upon the exhortation of the Blessed One Kakusandha, these [monks] developed these four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), increased insight (*vipassanā*) based on the foundation of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and were established in Arahantship.
510. "I do not know either coming or going" means I do not know the place of arrival by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), nor the place of departure by way of death (*cuti*).
"There might be a change of mind" means there might be a change of state due to joy (*somanassa*).
"They are reborn in the heavenly world"—here too, the meaning should be understood in the same manner as before. For just as previously [it was said that] it causes remorse...
It shows the object; likewise here too, it inspires confidence.

It is said that at that time, in the place where people were looking, he saw monks as if walking in the air, as if standing, as if sitting cross-legged, as if performing embroidery in the air, as if reading books, and as if spreading out robes in the air to let their bodies take on the temperature [of the air].
He made it appear as if they were newly ordained monks walking through the air, or like young novices standing in the sky plucking flowers.
People who had gone to the forest, to the woods, or to the monastery, seeing this conduct of the renunciants, returned and told others:
"Among the bhikkhus, even the novices possess such great supernormal power."
“O you of great power, what is given to these is called ‘of great fruit’; give to them and honor them!
Then those people, honoring the Saṅgha of monks with the four requisites and performing much merit, became fillers of the path to heaven.
Therefore it is said: “They are reborn in the heavenly world.”
"Come, monks, dwell contemplating foulness in the body," said the Blessed One, as he wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, even going to the dwelling places of two or three monks:

"Monks, when a monk dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness, his mind recoils, shrinks away, turns back, and does not extend toward sexual intercourse; instead, equanimity or revulsion becomes established."

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated in the perception of repulsiveness in food, his mind shrinks away from craving for flavors, recoils, turns back, and does not extend toward it; either equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated in the perception of non-delight in the entire world...”
The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away from worldly spectacles; it does not extend toward them, but settles into equanimity or revulsion.
For a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of impermanence, gain, honor, and fame [do not captivate his heart].
"The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away; it does not extend forward, but rather settles into equanimity or aversion.
Having thus shown the benefit, he said:
"Come, monks, dwell contemplating the foulness in the body, perceiving the repulsiveness in food, and in the entire world..."
"Perceiving dissatisfaction in all conditioned phenomena and contemplating their impermanence"—these four meditation subjects he taught.

Those monks, practicing these four meditation subjects, developed insight, exhausted all taints, and established themselves in Arahatship; these four meditation subjects are indeed pacifiers of passion.
"Those possessed by hatred and delusion, those struck by lust and aversion, and those struck by hatred and delusion.
(512) "Having taken a pebble" means having taken a stone the size of what fits inside a closed fist.
For this [king], even after having the brahmins and householders revile the bhikkhus, [continued to provide] gain and honor for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus on account of the brahmins and householders.

Even after causing [the rock] to rise, finding no opening, and now desiring to strike with his own hand, he fixed his intent upon the body of a certain boy and seized such a stone. With reference to this, it is said: "having taken a pebble.
"I shall split your head" means he split the head; the thick skin was torn apart and the flesh became divided. The pebble—
Without breaking his skull, he turned back, striking right against the bone.
"He looked with the 'elephant’s backward glance'" means that just as a noble elephant, wishing to look this way or that,
turns his entire body back instead of merely twisting his neck to look, so too did he turn his entire body back and look.
For while the bones of ordinary people stand touching end to end, and those of Paccekabuddhas touch at their tips, it is not so with the Buddhas.
Rather, the bones of the Buddhas stand joined together like a chain;
therefore, when looking back, they are unable to turn their necks. Just as an elephant-king [looks] toward the rear...

Desiring to look back, he turned around with his entire body; such is how one must turn. Therefore, the Blessed One, having turned around with his entire body like a golden statue turned by a machine, looked back.
Having looked back and standing there, he said, "This Māra Dūsī does not know his measure. The meaning of this is: this wicked Māra Dūsī...
"While making it, he did not know the measure;
he made it exceed the measure. "Simultaneously with the looking back" means: together with the very moment of the Blessed One Kakusandha’s looking back.
"And fell from that place" means: having passed away from that divine state, he was reborn in the Great Hell. While passing away...
For one does not pass away from wherever one happens to be standing; therefore, it should be understood that he passed away after having come to the world of the Vasavatti devas.
Furthermore, because of the statement, "after looking back at the world," it should be understood that he did not pass away simply because the Blessed One had looked upon him;
this was merely a demonstration of the time of his passing. However, because he had failed the eminent Great Disciples, his life-span was severed right there, as if struck by an axe.
It should be understood that [the word] "gone" (*gata*) is used. "There are three names" means there are three designations.
"Consisting of the six bases of contact" (*cha-phassāyatanika*) means it is the condition for individual feeling within the six bases of contact.
"Pierced by stakes" (*saṅku-samāhata*) means pierced by iron spikes. "To be experienced individually" (*paccatta-vedanīya*) means that which produces feeling for oneself alone. By the stake...
“May a spike meet in his heart” means that one iron spike should meet another iron spike in the middle of his heart.
It is said that for those reborn in that hell, their physical form is three gavutas in height; the Elder’s body was likewise of such a size.
Then the hell-wardens took iron spikes the size of palm trunks, blazing, flaming, and glowing with fire.
Taking hold of him themselves and turning back again and again,
they beat his heart’s core as if pounding bread in a bread-basket, saying, “It was by thinking of this very spot that you committed evil. Thus,
fifty people beating him toward his feet and fifty people beating him toward his head, they go on for five hundred years.
Having reached both extremes and returning again, they arrive at the center of the heart after five hundred years.
It is with reference to this that it was said thus.
"The emergence" refers to the feeling that emerges as kamma-result (vipāka). It is said that this is more painful than the feeling in the Great Hell.

For just as the seven days of nursing care following the drinking of oil are more painful than the seven days of convalescence, so too they say that the resultant feelings arising from the egress [of consciousness] in the *ussada* hells are more painful than the suffering of the great hells (*mahāniraya*). "Just as in the case of a fish":
for the head of a human being is rounded; when struck with a spear, the blow finds no firm resistance and slips away, whereas the head of a fish—
It is long and broad; it receives a blow; because one does not miss [the mark], the performance of the task is easy; therefore, such is the head. 513.
*Vidhuraṃ sāvakamāsajja* means having struck a disciple who is off-target. *Paccattavedanā* means by oneself.
They produce individual sensations. Regarding the phrase "such was the hell," in this context the hell should be illustrated by means of the *Devadūta Sutta*.
"You shall undergo black suffering" means, O Māra Kāḷaka, you will experience suffering. "In the midst of the river":
in the midst of the great ocean, celestial mansions (*vimāna*) produced with water as their foundation endure for an eon (*kappa*); of those [mansions made of] beryl...
Their color is like [that of gold], and their flames shine like a mass of burning reed-fire on a mountain peak;
they are radiant and possessed of splendor. In those celestial mansions (*vimāna*), apsarases of various colors—such as blue and others—dance.
"He who understands this" means he who knows this account of the celestial mansions (*vimānavatthu*). Thus, in this context, it is by way of the *vimāna-peta-vatthu* alone...
The meaning should be understood. “He shook it with his big toe”—this is to be illustrated by the *Pāsādakampana Sutta*.
“Who [shook] the Vejayanta Palace”—this is to be illustrated by the *Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya-vimutti Sutta*. “He questioned Sakka”—this too is to be illustrated by that same sutta.
“Near the Sudhamma assembly hall”—that is, in the vicinity of the Sudhamma assembly hall; however, this...
In the Brahma-world there is the Sudhammā assembly hall, but not in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Indeed, there is no world of the devas that is devoid of the Sudhammā assembly hall.

"Radiant in the Brahma-world" refers to the effulgence of the Blessed One when he sat in the Brahma-world having entered the fire-element absorption together with disciples such as Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākassapa. For at one time, the Blessed One...
Having assembled in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods in the Brahma-world, as the host of Brahmas was thinking,
"Is there perhaps some ascetic or brahmin of such great psychic power who would be able to come here?", Mahāmoggallāna, perceiving the thought of that host of Brahmas,
went there and sat upon the head of the host of Brahmas; having entered the fire-element attainment, [he appeared before] Mahāmoggallāna and the others.
He thought of their arrival. They too went and paid homage to the Teacher;

then, having attained the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), they each sat down in the various directions, and the entire Brahma-world became a single expanse of light. The Teacher taught the Dhamma that reveals the Four Noble Truths.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many thousands of Brahmas were established in the paths and fruits. That...
These verses were spoken with intentional meaning (*saṇḍhāya*), and this matter should be illustrated by means of the *Aññatara-brahma-sutta*.
"He touched with liberation" means he contacted it through the liberation of meditative absorption (*jhāna-vimokkha*). "The forest" refers to Jambudīpa.
"Of Pūrvavideha" refers to the continent of Pūrvavideha. And "those men who dwell on the earth"—the "men who dwell on the earth" are those of Aparagoyāna.
And [the beings] of Uttarakuru—thus it is said that he touched them all as well. This matter, however, should be illustrated by the taming of Nanda and Upananda;
the story is explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on supernormal powers (*iddhi*). "He produced demerit" means he acquired demerit.
"Do not set your hope on the monks" means do not harbor the hope, "I shall harass the monks. The rest...
"Everywhere it is indeed clear.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Māratajjanīya-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
The commentary on the First Fifty [Discourses] is finished.
